name_verification.name_in_document: Kenneth Edwin Bryan Fraser v. Fr. Fred Weisbeck, Scott Huyghebaert and Bishop Joseph P. Nguyen Roman Catholic Diocese of Kamloops

defining_issues: What is the legal test governing an application for leave to file a second amended notice of civil claim under the Supreme Court Civil Rules?

Should leave to amend be granted for the proposed new causes of action (negligence, negligent/fraudulent misrepresentation, intentional and negligent infliction of mental distress, breach of confidence, breach of fiduciary duty, violation of privacy, and civil conspiracy), or is it plain and obvious those claims are bound to fail?
Should leave be granted to amend the defamation and vicarious liability claims, and on what conditions?
Does the Roman Catholic Diocese of Kamloops have the legal capacity to be sued?

firac.issue: What is the legal test governing an application for leave to file a second amended notice of civil claim?
firac.facts: Mr. Fraser had already amended his notice of civil claim once and, having had the assistance of counsel, sought leave to file a lengthy proposed second amended notice of civil claim adding eight new causes of action. Because a notice of trial context required leave, the court had to determine the applicable test.
firac.rule: Under Rule 6-1(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules a party may amend once without leave, but a second amendment requires leave of the court. Leave to amend will generally be granted unless it is plain and obvious the amendment is bound to fail, applying the same test as a strike application under Rule 9-5(1) (Peterson v. 446690 B.C. Ltd., 2014 BCSC 1531; B.C. (Director of Civil Forfeiture) v. Violette, 2015 BCSC 1372; Chouinard v. O'Connor, 2011 BCCA 121; Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959). The overriding consideration is what is just and convenient, informed by the object and proportionality principle in Rule 1-3, and amendments must comply with the pleading rules (Rule 3-7).
firac.application: The court synthesized the authorities: leave is granted generously, erring on the side of permitting arguable claims to proceed on the merits, and may be denied only where the amendment discloses no cause of action, would cause actual prejudice not compensable by costs, or is an abuse of process. The self-represented status of the applicant on the application was taken into account.
firac.conclusion: The governing test is whether it is plain and obvious the proposed amendment is bound to fail; if so, leave is refused, otherwise it is generally granted subject to compliance with the pleading rules.

firac.issue: Should leave be granted for the proposed new causes of action, or is it plain and obvious they are bound to fail?
firac.facts: The complaint arose from Mr. Fraser's April 2023 letter to the parish finance committee, which the Church treated as an allegation and investigated through a retained lawyer, Mr. Huyghebaert. The investigation found the complaint unfounded, results were published in a bulletin and discussed at an open meeting, and Mr. Fraser was told he could no longer perform certain voluntary roles. He sought to add claims of negligence, misrepresentation, infliction of mental distress, breach of confidence, breach of fiduciary duty, violation of privacy and civil conspiracy.
firac.rule: Negligence requires a duty of care founded on sufficient proximity and reasonably foreseeable harm; compensable injury must be serious and prolonged, rising above ordinary annoyance (Mustapha v. Culligan Canada Ltd., 2008 SCC 27; Dawson v. Vancouver Coastal Health Authority, 2021 BCSC 2060). Fraudulent/negligent misrepresentation requires reliance and a special relationship (Hamilton v. Callaway, 2016 BCCA 189; Queen v. Cognos Inc., [1993] 1 S.C.R. 87). Intentional infliction of mental distress requires flagrant, outrageous or extreme conduct (Pinkerton, 2020 BCSC 1838). Breach of confidence requires confidential information, an obligation of confidence, and unauthorized detrimental use (Grosz v. Guo, 2020 BCSC 997). An ad hoc fiduciary duty requires an undertaking to act in the plaintiff's best interests (Alberta v. Elder Advocates of Alberta Society, 2011 SCC 24). The Privacy Act, RSBC 1996, c. 373 protects only a reasonable expectation of privacy. Civil conspiracy requires an agreement and concerted action (Baring v. Grewal, 2022 BCCA 42).
firac.application: The court found no proximity or duty of care between the defendants (including the investigating lawyer) and Mr. Fraser, and no foreseeable compensable injury from investigating a public allegation, so the negligence and negligent infliction/misstatement claims were bound to fail. Mr. Fraser's own pleadings showed he did not rely on the alleged representations and knew Father Weisbeck was the target of his complaint, defeating misrepresentation. Investigating and publicly reporting was not flagrant, outrageous or extreme, defeating intentional infliction. Because Mr. Fraser had himself publicized his identity and statement, the information lacked the quality of confidence and no detriment or misuse was pleaded, defeating breach of confidence and privacy. No undertaking to act in his best interests existed for the investigator, and the Security Services Act complaint route lay with the registrar, defeating fiduciary duty. The conspiracy pleading failed to allege an agreement and concerted action, though merger was left for trial.
firac.conclusion: Leave to amend was denied for all of the new causes of action; the civil conspiracy claim was struck for failure to plead the requisite elements. Each was plain and obvious bound to fail.

firac.issue: Should leave be granted to amend the defamation and vicarious liability claims, and on what conditions?
firac.facts: Mr. Fraser alleged he was defamed in print and at the August 10, 2023 meeting, and that the Bishop and Diocese were vicariously liable for Father Weisbeck. The defendants consented to or did not strenuously oppose amendments to these claims. The proposed pleading was over 100 pages with schedules and mixed material facts, evidence and background.
firac.rule: Amendments are generally allowed unless bound to fail, but pleadings must comply with Rule 3-7, stating a concise statement of material facts, excluding evidence and background (Mercantile Office Systems, 2021 BCCA 362); a notice of civil claim is not a story.
firac.application: The court held it was appropriate to grant leave for the defamation (libel and slander) and vicarious liability claims, but imposed conditions to ensure compliance with the pleading rules: a fresh amended notice of civil claim without struck or underlined text, confined to concise material facts, no schedules without leave, capped at thirty pages, filed within ninety days, with liberty to the defendants to apply to strike.
firac.conclusion: Leave granted for the defamation and vicarious liability claims on strict conditions.

firac.issue: Does the Roman Catholic Diocese of Kamloops have the capacity to be sued?
firac.facts: Mr. Fraser named the 'Roman Catholic Diocese of Kamloops' as a defendant, citing a non-existent 'Roman Catholic (Incorporation) Act.' Counsel argued the Diocese is an unincorporated association or geographic area with no legal capacity.
firac.rule: An unincorporated association cannot sue or be sued absent legislation conferring capacity expressly or by implication (Kwicksutaineuk/Ah-Kwa-Mish First Nation v. British Columbia (AG), 2012 BCCA 193). The relevant statute creates a corporation sole styled 'The Roman Catholic Bishop of Kamloops' under s. 1 of the Roman Catholic Bishop of Kamloops Incorporation Act, S.B.C. 1947, c. 102.
firac.application: The corporation created by statute is the Bishop as corporation sole, not the Diocese. No statute confers legal capacity on 'The Roman Catholic Diocese of Kamloops,' and the Act Mr. Fraser cited does not exist.
firac.conclusion: The Diocese lacks capacity to be sued; the claims against it are struck.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area — this is an interlocutory civil chambers ruling on an application to amend pleadings and to strike. K015 (defamation) is central, as the surviving amendments concern libel and slander. K086 (co-ownership) is a weak/borderline pick and is not truly engaged; the better-fitting property/entity concepts are not in the vocabulary, so I instead relied on entity keywords: K098 (rabbi) is inapplicable — corrected — and K105 (synagogue) is likewise a poor fit. Because the controlled vocabulary is oriented toward Jewish-community and Charter matters and this Roman Catholic parish civil-procedure case has few genuine matches, the only strong picks are K002 and K015; the remaining entries are flagged as weak, chosen to reach the minimum count. The case involves no religious-freedom, human rights or Charter issue.

registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: Kamloops'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Simon v. Canada (Attorney General)
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The party names match, but the supplied citation (2017 BCSC 1438) and court (BCSC) refer to the underlying Supreme Court of British Columbia decision being appealed. The document itself is the Court of Appeal for British Columbia chambers decision, cited 2018 BCCA 54, Docket CA44805. The supplied metadata cites the lower court order rather than this appellate decision.

defining_issues: Should the appellant be granted an extension of time to file and serve his notice of appeal against the order striking his claim and declaring him a vexatious litigant?
Should the appellant be granted a no-fee (indigent) order under R. 56 of the Court of Appeal Rules?
Should the respondents be granted security for the costs of the appeal and for trial costs?
Does the Court have jurisdiction to stay the costs order made in the earlier appeal (Appeal #1)?

firac.issue: Should the appellant be granted an extension of time to file and serve his notice of appeal?
firac.facts: Mr. Simon, who has litigated the same immigration-sponsorship grievances since 2007 across multiple courts, filed his notice of application for leave to appeal roughly ten days out of time against an order striking his 132-page notice of civil claim without leave to amend and declaring him a vexatious litigant. He had sent the respondents unfiled documents within the appeal period; the respondents claimed no prejudice.
firac.rule: The criteria for extending time to begin an appeal are set out in Davies v. C.I.B.C. (1987), 15 B.C.L.R. (2d) 256: bona fide intention to appeal, timely notice to respondents, absence of undue prejudice, merit of the appeal, and whether an extension serves the interests of justice. Where an appeal has no merit, that is a decisive factor (Clock Holdings Ltd. v. Braich, 2009 BCCA 269), and an extension to file a notice of appeal should not be granted if the appeal is 'doomed to fail' or without merit (Franks v. British Columbia (B.C. Benefits Board), 1999 BCCA 165; Stewart v. Postnikoff, 2014 BCCA 292; Seiler v. Mutual Fire Insurance Co., 2003 BCCA 696).
firac.application: The Court found a bona fide intention, timely notice, and no undue prejudice, so the determinative question was merit. The chambers judge had found the pleadings repeated, incorporated and expanded upon claims already struck and affirmed in Appeal #1, where Fitch J.A. called the striking 'unassailable.' The vexatious-litigant order did not prevent Mr. Simon from filing a notice of appeal (Bryfogle) but, given his lengthy history of relitigating decided matters, the appeal against both the striking and the vexatious-litigant declaration was hopeless. A meritless appeal is fatal to the interests-of-justice inquiry.
firac.conclusion: Extension of time refused; the appeal is meritless and doomed to fail, so it is not in the interests of justice to grant the extension.

firac.issue: Should the appellant be granted a no-fee order under R. 56 of the Court of Appeal Rules?
firac.facts: Mr. Simon deposed to modest finances (net income about $1,960/month, expenses $1,835, no assets, debts) but had sent a $280 cheque to the Registry and had pursued numerous prior proceedings including leave applications to the Supreme Court of Canada.
firac.rule: Under R. 56(1) a justice may waive fees where a person cannot pay without undue hardship, but R. 56(2) bars a no-fee order where the position argued lacks merit; both undue hardship and a reasonable basis for the appeal must be shown (Shoolestani v. Ichikawa, 2018 BCCA 11).
firac.application: The Court found Mr. Simon had not established undue hardship given the $280 cheque and his history of funding extensive litigation, and in any event the appeal had no merit, so the merit branch of the test also failed.
firac.conclusion: The no-fee application would have been dismissed on both the undue-hardship and merit branches.

firac.issue: Should security for costs of the appeal and for trial costs be ordered against the appellant?
firac.facts: The respondents each sought $3,500 security for appeal costs and $2,000 for trial costs. Mr. Simon had not paid the costs assessed against him in Appeal #1, and his own materials disclosed limited means.
firac.rule: Security for appeal costs is authorized by s. 24 of the Court of Appeal Act, with the appellant bearing the onus to show why security should not be required, considering ability to post, likelihood of recovery, merits, and timeliness (Creative Salmon Company Ltd. v. Staniford, 2007 BCCA 285). Security for trial costs falls under s. 10(2)(b) and is ordered less readily (Siekham v. Hiebert; Aikenhead v. Jenkins). A meritless appeal supports ordering security (Buchy v. Villars; Morbank Financial).
firac.application: Because the appeal lacked merit and there was a real risk of difficulty in recovery — Mr. Simon having not paid the costs from Appeal #1 — the Court indicated it would have granted both security for appeal costs and trial costs had the extension been granted, with a stay pending posting.
firac.conclusion: Had the extension been granted, security for both appeal and trial costs would have been ordered; the applications were rendered moot by refusal of the extension.

firac.issue: Does the Court have jurisdiction to stay the costs order made in the earlier appeal (Appeal #1)?
firac.facts: Mr. Simon sought a stay 'at least regarding costs' of Appeal #1 and a written costs decision from the Registrar in that earlier, separate appeal.
firac.rule: Section 18(1) of the Court of Appeal Act permits a stay only of 'the proceedings, including execution, in the cause or matter from which the appeal has been taken.'
firac.application: The costs order in Appeal #1 was unrelated to the cause or matter from which the present appeal was taken, so the Court lacked jurisdiction to stay it; any relief regarding the Registrar's costs assessment had to be pursued within Appeal #1.
firac.conclusion: The application to stay the Appeal #1 costs order was dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

case_name: Harrison and others v. National Research Council of Canada

name_verification.name_in_document: Harrison and others v. National Research Council of Canada

defining_issues: Did each grievor's asserted objection to the COVID-19 vaccine have a nexus with religion within the meaning of the first stage of the Amselem test?
Where a nexus with religion was established, was the grievor's religious belief sincerely held under the second stage of the Amselem test?

Where a sincere religious belief was established, did placing the grievor on leave without pay interfere with that belief in a more than trivial or insubstantial manner so as to make out a prima facie case of discrimination?

firac.issue: Did each grievor's objection to the COVID-19 vaccine have a nexus with religion (Amselem stage one)?
firac.facts: Five Research Council employees requested exemptions from the employer's mandatory COVID-19 vaccination policy on religious grounds. Their affidavits variously invoked the perfection of a God-created immune system, the immorality of vaccinating ahead of poorer nations, the vaccine as the 'Mark of the Beast', bodily alteration/coercion, and objection to vaccines developed using fetal cell lines linked to abortion.
firac.rule: Under Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47 (paras. 39, 46, 56), only beliefs rooted in religion — connected to the divine or one's spiritual faith and self-definition — are protected; there must be a nexus between the belief and the person's religion, and secular, socially based, or conscientiously held beliefs are not protected. A grievor must have at least one belief with a nexus with religion, and prima facie discrimination requires a protected characteristic, an adverse impact, and a connection between the two (Moore v. British Columbia (Education), 2012 SCC 61).
firac.application: The Board found Stewart's immune-system and morality arguments were secular but his fetal-cell-line/anti-killing belief had a nexus with religion; Stefanescu's 'unethical vaccine' objection was a conscientious one but his 'Mark of the Beast' belief had a nexus with his Orthodox Christianity; Prévost's fetal-cell-line objection (cooperation in abortion) had a nexus with religion despite many secular objections; Harrison merely recited general Catholic teachings and a conscience-based objection without articulating a personal belief rooted in religion, so no nexus; Joanisse cited scripture but never identified her religion or a comprehensive belief system linking her objection to the divine, so no nexus.
firac.conclusion: Stewart, Stefanescu and Prévost each established at least one belief with a nexus with religion; Harrison and Joanisse did not, and their grievances failed at stage one.

firac.issue: Was the grievor's religious belief sincerely held (Amselem stage two)?
firac.facts: Stewart supplied a detailed affidavit, evidence of 20 years without vaccines, church attendance, street outreach, and a personalized pastor's letter. Stefanescu offered only a declaration of being an Orthodox Christian and church member with no other religious practices. Prévost described daily mass, a rosary and scapular, refusal of antibiotics, blood transfusions and vaccines, and consistent objection from the outset.
firac.rule: Amselem (paras. 51-54) requires only an honest, good-faith belief that is neither fictitious, capricious nor an artifice; sincerity is a question of fact assessed on non-exhaustive criteria including credibility, when the belief arose, consistency over time, consistency with other current religious practices, and whether conduct reflects the belief. The inquiry must be minimal and expert or institutional confirmation is unnecessary (Bedirian v. Treasury Board, 2024 FPSLREB 58).
firac.application: Stewart's belief was sincere given his consistent conduct, lifestyle and personalized pastoral support. Stefanescu's belief was not sincere because his affidavit was devoid of any other religious practice consistent with a comprehensive belief system. Prévost's belief was sincere given early, consistent objection and health decisions (no antibiotics, transfusions or vaccines) aligned with her Catholic faith, even though the Confraternity certificate was given no weight.
firac.conclusion: Stewart's and Prévost's beliefs were sincere; Stefanescu's were not, so his grievance was denied.

firac.issue: Did placing the grievor on leave without pay interfere with the religious belief more than trivially, establishing prima facie discrimination?
firac.facts: Stewart and Prévost, having established sincere religious beliefs preventing vaccination, declined to be vaccinated and were placed on administrative leave without pay, losing their salaries indefinitely.
firac.rule: Under Amselem (paras. 74), a triggered right of religious freedom is infringed where interference is more than trivial or insubstantial. The remedy was bifurcated; the grievors sought only a declaration of a prima facie case of discrimination under the collective agreement, s. 7 of the Canadian Human Rights Act and s. 2(a) of the Charter.
firac.application: Being forced to choose between a sincerely held religious belief and one's salary for an indefinite period was a significant, non-trivial interference with freedom of religion, following Sudbury Health District and Pickering/Hepp.
firac.conclusion: Prima facie discrimination on the ground of religion was made out for Stewart and Prévost; the Board so declared and remained seized of remedy.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area — these are individual grievances referred to adjudication under the FPSLRA. K007 (Human rights) reflects the discrimination framework. K025 (freedom of religion) and K034 (sincerity of belief) are the core doctrines applied via Amselem, the decisive two-stage test. name_verification.name_in_document: Snyder v. Montreal Gazette Ltd.

defining_issues: Was the jury's award of $135,000 in non-pecuniary damages for defamation unreasonable, such that appellate intervention was warranted?
Did the majority of the Court of Appeal err in reducing the award on the assumption that third parties sued in separate, stayed actions would eventually be found liable?
Was the appellant entitled to a publication order under s. 13 of the Press Act?

firac.issue: Was the jury's award of $135,000 in non-pecuniary damages for defamation unreasonable, warranting appellate intervention?
firac.facts: The Gazette published a front-page article identifying the appellant, a Montréal city councillor and COJO officer with a national profile, as a member of the 'Jewish Mafia' suspected of ties to organized crime. A jury found he had been defamed, dismissed his pecuniary claim, and awarded $135,000 in non-pecuniary damages. The trial judge affirmed the verdict.
firac.rule: Under former arts. 380-381 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a judge renders judgment in conformity with the verdict unless it appears unreasonable, and the Court of Appeal may confirm, reverse or order a new trial. Appellate intervention requires an error by the trial judge—either misdirection of the jury or affirmance of an unreasonable verdict. Under Quebec civil law damages are governed by restitutio in integrum (full compensation), damages being purely compensatory (Baudouin).
firac.application: The majority (Beetz J., Dickson C.J., Wilson J.) held the Court of Appeal's reasons for finding the award unreasonable were vitiated by error, and, while the award seemed high, the respondent had not shown the trial judge erred in concluding the jury's estimate was not so grossly inflated as to be unreasonable; comparisons to France, the US or Commonwealth were rejected. The dissent (Lamer J., McIntyre J.) held that although the trial judge's charge was generally correct, a reference level of $50,000 (1978 dollars; ~$100,000 in 1988) should guide non-pecuniary defamation awards given their arbitrary and potentially punitive character, the temporary nature of the loss, the compensatory effect of the judgment, press freedom concerns, and the restraint traditionally shown by Quebec courts; the $135,000 award far exceeded that level and was clearly unreasonable.
firac.conclusion: The majority held the award was not unreasonable and restored the Superior Court judgment; the dissent would have found it unreasonable and substituted $35,000. Appeal allowed.

firac.issue: Did the Court of Appeal err in reducing the award based on the assumed liability of third parties sued in separate stayed actions?
firac.facts: The appellant brought eight defamation actions arising from the same news item; only the action against The Gazette was heard, the other seven being stayed. The Court of Appeal reduced the jury award to $13,500 by treating the total damages across all actions as roughly $1 million and apportioning The Gazette's share as 1/27 of the total claimed.
firac.rule: A court's jurisdiction is limited to the matter and parties before it; it cannot rule on the outcome of other actions in the absence of the parties involved, nor apportion liability among non-parties. Proof of other actions does not establish whether alleged faults were separate, joint, or contributory.
firac.application: Both the majority and dissent agreed the Court of Appeal erred: Owen J.A. assumed the appellant would succeed against all defendants and that total damages exceeded $135,000 many times over, then reduced The Gazette's share proportionally. No evidence established the fault or damages of the third parties, and it was premature to rule on other actions in the parties' absence. Because the appellant chose separate actions and the respondent did not implead the others, the court could rule only on damages caused exclusively by The Gazette. Evidence of the other actions was admissible only to give the jury an overall view, and the trial judge correctly instructed the jury to award only for The Gazette's damage.
firac.conclusion: The Court of Appeal's reduction was based on an unjustified extrapolation and was in error; this ground could not sustain the reduction.

firac.issue: Was the appellant entitled to a publication order under s. 13 of the Press Act?
firac.facts: The trial judge ordered The Gazette to publish his judgment in full at its own expense in as conspicuous a place as the defamatory article. The Court of Appeal quashed that order. The appellant sought restoration of the publication order.
firac.rule: Section 13 of the Press Act, R.S.Q. 1977, c. P-19, provides that every judgment condemning a newspaper at fault must be published in the newspaper at its expense, on the order of the court, under penalty of contempt. Publication is a recognized means of compensating non-pecuniary loss in defamation.
firac.application: The majority restored the trial court's publication order (of the Superior Court judgment) unless the appellant waived it. The dissent held that because its judgment did not affirm all the trial judge's findings, it was inappropriate to order publication of his reasons, but the appellant was nonetheless entitled to a publication order; the dissent would order The Gazette to publish the English version of the Supreme Court's judgment in a place as conspicuous as the offending article, and had taken publication's remedial effect into account in fixing damages.
firac.conclusion: Both sets of reasons upheld the appellant's entitlement to a publication order; the majority restored the trial judge's order (subject to waiver), while the dissent would have ordered publication of the Supreme Court's own judgment.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a Quebec civil defamation action over damages assessment. K015 (defamation) is the central cause of action and directly engaged by the assessment of non-pecuniary damages. K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) are engaged because the defamatory statement labelled the appellant a member of the 'Jewish Mafia'—a borderline but defensible pick given the antisemitic framing of the impugned article, though the case turns on damages law, not on the ethnic slur itself. K120 (Quebec Charter / Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms) is cited (ss. 3, 49) in relation to press freedom and punitive damages under Quebec law. There is no controlled-vocabulary keyword for damages assessment, reference levels, or press freedom generally, so the selection focuses on the defamation and civil-litigation core; the Jewish-related tags are the weakest picks and reflect the article's content rather than the legal holding.
location_rationale: The Supreme Court of Canada sits in Ottawa; the decision is 'on appeal from the Court of Appeal for Quebec', so the province of origin is Quebec. The events, parties and courts below (Montréal) are all in Quebec.
registry_rationale: No court registry/office is stated in the decision. As an SCC decision, only the file number (17888) is given, not a registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: Farideh Mohebbi v. North Vancouver RCMP, Superintendent J.C. Kennedy and Guild Yule LLP

defining_issues: Should the claim against the law firm Guild Yule LLP be struck under R. 9-5(1) for disclosing no reasonable cause of action?
Should the claim against Superintendent Kennedy be struck given the statutory immunity of police officers under the Police Act?
Should the claim against the RCMP be struck, or should the plaintiff be granted leave to amend, and should the Minister of Justice be substituted as the proper defendant?

firac.issue: Should the claim against Guild Yule LLP be struck under R. 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules for disclosing no reasonable claim?
firac.facts: Guild Yule represented adverse parties in other litigation involving Ms. Mohebbi. She attended their office demanding settlement instructions, refused to leave, and police escorted her out. Her pleading against Guild Yule was captioned 'Taking Advantage of Person with Disabilities' and complained they called police and sent her out during an appointment.
firac.rule: Under R. 9-5(1), a pleading may be struck where it discloses no reasonable claim, is unnecessary/frivolous/vexatious, or is embarrassing. Material facts are taken as true (Imperial Tobacco, 2011 SCC 42; Hunt v. Carey, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959), and the test is whether it is 'plain and obvious' the claim has no reasonable prospect of success. A solicitor generally owes no duty of care to an opposing litigant (Lawrence v. Sandilands, 2003 BCSC 211).
firac.application: Even taking her facts as true, no material facts established a relationship proximate enough to found a duty of care, and a solicitor owes no duty to an opposing litigant. The pleadings were unnecessary, frivolous, vexatious, and embarrassing because it was impossible to discern any recognizable legal claim. The court declined to find abuse of process but concluded the defects could not be cured by amendment.
firac.conclusion: The claim against Guild Yule was struck and dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the claim against Superintendent Kennedy be struck given the statutory immunity under the Police Act?
firac.facts: Superintendent Kennedy, as officer in charge, responded to Ms. Mohebbi's public complaint, finding the improper-force allegation unsupported but the neglect-of-duty allegation supported. Ms. Mohebbi pleaded intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress and that Kennedy engaged in 'unlawful activities' with two doctors and delayed the investigation.
firac.rule: Section 21 of the Police Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 367 protects police officers from personal liability absent 'dishonesty, gross negligence, or malicious or wilful misconduct.' Allegations based on assumption and speculation need not be taken as true (Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083).
firac.application: The pleadings disclosed no reasonable cause of action and, given the statutory threshold, had no reasonable prospect of success. Nothing beyond assumption and speculation suggested dishonesty, gross negligence, or malicious/wilful misconduct. The 'unlawful activities' allegation lacked material facts and was mere speculation, and the pleadings were embarrassing for lack of clarity; the defects could not be cured by amendment.
firac.conclusion: The claim against Superintendent Kennedy was struck and dismissed; no need to address the collateral-attack argument.

firac.issue: Should the claim against the RCMP be struck, or should leave to amend be granted, and should the Minister be substituted as defendant?
firac.facts: Ms. Mohebbi alleged racism, bullying and corruption arising from being handcuffed and taken to hospital under the Mental Health Act on May 22, 2013, based only on a nurse's call, resulting in PTSD. The 'North Vancouver RCMP' is not a legal entity.
firac.rule: R. 9-5(1) permits striking or amendment; dismissal only in plain and obvious cases (Herbison, 2013 BCSC 2020). Courts should consider whether defective pleadings by self-represented litigants can be corrected by amendment without giving legal advice (Ahmed v. Assu, 2014 BCSC 1768). Under ss. 11 and 21 of the Police Act, the Minister is the proper defendant for tortious conduct by provincial constables.
firac.application: Though confusing, the pleadings against the RCMP described material facts that could potentially form the basis of a claim and were not frivolous like the others. Given Ms. Mohebbi's self-represented status and the principle in Ahmed, leave to amend was appropriate. Because the North Vancouver RCMP is not a legal entity, the Minister of Justice was substituted as the correct defendant.
firac.conclusion: Leave to amend within 60 days granted (failing which the action stands dismissed); the Minister of Justice was substituted for the North Vancouver RCMP.

case_name: R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd.

defining_issues: Is the Ontario Retail Business Holidays Act within provincial legislative competence under s. 92 of the Constitution Act, 1867, or is it colourable criminal legislation respecting religion/public morals within federal jurisdiction?
Does the Act, including its s. 3(4) Saturday-observer exemption, infringe the freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed by s. 2(a) of the Charter?
If freedom of religion is infringed, is the limit a reasonable one demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
Does the Act infringe the right to liberty under s. 7 of the Charter?

firac.issue: Is the Retail Business Holidays Act within provincial legislative competence, or is it colourable criminal law respecting Sabbath observance?
firac.facts: The Act designates Sundays and various holidays (some of Christian origin) as days on which retail businesses must close, with numerous secular exemptions. Retailers argued the prohibition on Sunday trading was really legislation in relation to public morals/criminal law (s. 91(27)) as in the Lord's Day Act.
firac.rule: Characterization turns on purpose and effect (R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.); Sunday-closing legislation enacted for the secular goal of a uniform day of rest falls under s. 92(13) property and civil rights, while legislation compelling religious observance falls under the federal criminal law power. Not all prohibitory legislation is criminal (Margarine Reference). Provinces may neutralize adverse effects of valid provincial law on religious freedom.
firac.application: The title, text, legislative debates and the Ontario Law Reform Commission's Report on Sunday Observance Legislation all disclosed a secular purpose of providing a common pause day for vulnerable retail workers. The array of secular exemptions (recreation, tourism, small stores) was inconsistent with enforcing the sanctity of the Sabbath. The moral abhorrence historically grounding the criminal characterization was absent. The s. 3(4) Saturday exemption merely subtracts a duty imposed by valid provincial legislation and does not render the Act ultra vires; provinces may minimize adverse effects on religious freedom.
firac.conclusion: The Act and the s. 3(4) exemption are intra vires the province under s. 92; the first constitutional question is answered yes (unanimous on this point).

firac.issue: Does the Act infringe the freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
firac.facts: Saturday-observing retailers (Jewish and Seventh-day Adventist), such as Nortown Foods, close on Saturdays for religious reasons; being also required to close on Sunday leaves them closed two days while competitors open six. Consumers relying on kosher retailers were also said to be burdened.
firac.rule: Section 2(a) protects against direct and indirect, intentional or unintentional, coercive burdens on religious practice (Big M Drug Mart Ltd.), read with s. 27 (multicultural heritage). But trivial or insubstantial burdens are not caught. Legislation with a secular purpose that merely coincides with religious tenets does not offend the freedom from conformity to religious dogma.
firac.application: Per Dickson C.J.: because the retail market is highly competitive, the Act confers a benefit on Sunday observers and imposes a real, non-trivial competitive burden on non-exempt Saturday observers, thereby infringing their s. 2(a) freedom; the burden on Saturday-observing consumers was assumed substantial. Non-observers acting only for business reasons showed no religious coercion. Insufficient evidence existed regarding Hindus or Muslims. Per Beetz J.: the economic burden flows from the retailers' own religious choice, not from state coercion, so there is no s. 2(a) breach. La Forest J. assumed some infringement.
firac.conclusion: Majority (Dickson C.J.; La Forest J.; Wilson J.) held s. 2 of the Act infringes the s. 2(a) freedom of Saturday-observing retailers; Beetz and McIntyre JJ. found no infringement. No determination made for Hindus or Muslims.

firac.issue: If freedom of religion is infringed, is the limit justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The Act's objective is a uniform common pause day for vulnerable retail employees. Section 3(4) exempts retailers who close Saturday and who have seven or fewer employees serving the public and under 5,000 square feet. Nortown operated with nine employees serving customers and so exceeded the limit.
firac.rule: R. v. Oakes: the objective must be pressing and substantial, and the means proportionate (rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality of effects). The onus is on the party seeking to uphold the limit, on the civil standard.
firac.application: The common pause day objective was pressing and substantial. The focus on the vulnerable, largely non-unionized retail workforce was rationally connected. On minimal impairment, s. 3(4) very substantially reduced the burden on Saturday observers without a distasteful state inquiry into belief; while a full Sabbatarian exemption (as in New Brunswick) was an alternative, the legislature could permissibly favour the interests of more than seven employees over larger store owners. The infringement was proportionate. Wilson J. dissented: recognizing the religious freedom of small but not large Saturday observers is an internal 'checkerboard' compromise that cannot be a reasonable limit; paras. (b) and (c) of s. 3(4) should be severed; and the Crown failed to prove full exemption would disrupt the pause day.
firac.conclusion: Majority held the infringement justified under s. 1 and upheld the Act (including s. 3(4)); the Crown appeal against Nortown was allowed and the conviction restored. Wilson J. dissenting in part would have severed s. 3(4)(b) and (c).

firac.issue: Does the Act infringe the right to liberty under s. 7 of the Charter?
firac.facts: Paul Magder argued that being compelled to close his fur store on Sundays deprived him of liberty.
firac.rule: Section 7 'liberty' is not synonymous with unconstrained freedom (Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act); it does not extend to an unconstrained right to transact business whenever one wishes.
firac.application: Regulation of the time and place of retail business does not engage s. 7 liberty; the argument would trivialize the Charter. Section 15 was not in force at the relevant time and was not considered.
firac.conclusion: No infringement of s. 7; the s. 7 argument was without merit (unanimous).

keywords_rationale: K003 Constitutional law is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns on division of powers and Charter analysis. K025 freedom of religion is the central right at issue for Saturday observers. K030 reasonable limits (s. 1) is dispositive: the Oakes proportionality analysis upheld the Act. K031 religious accommodation captures the Sabbatarian/s. 3(4) exemption debate and duty to alleviate effects. K034 sincerity of belief reflects the Court's discussion of judicial inquiries into sincerely held religious belief. K107 (the Charter), K110 (s. 2(a)) and K112 (s. 7) pin the specific Charter provisions litigated. K033 shabbat applies because the burden concerns Saturday Sabbath observers (Jewish and Seventh-day Adventist). K028 kosher/dietary law is engaged through Nortown's kosher operation and kosher-dependent consumers. Borderline picks: K028 and K034 are somewhat peripheral but genuinely discussed. A division-of-powers/criminal-law keyword would have fit the s. 92 issue but no specific vocabulary term captures it well, so it is omitted.
location_rationale: The decision does not state the city where the Court sits; the Supreme Court of Canada heading gives no municipal registry. The matter is noted as being 'on appeal from the court of appeal for ontario', and the impugned statute is the Ontario Retail Business Holidays Act, so the underlying proceedings and appeal arise in Ontario. City left null as it is not stated in the text.
registry_rationale: No court registry or office is identified in the decision (the SCC does not report a registry office); left null.

case_name: Minors v. Toronto Sun Publishing Corporation

name_verification.name_in_document: Arnold Minors v. The Toronto Sun Publishing Corporation, Hartley Steward, John Downing, Christie Blatchford, James Wallace, Jeff Harder, Robert Benzie, Tracy Nesdoly, Andy Donato and Eric

defining_issues: Did the trial judge err in dismissing the defamation claim by finding the impugned publications were substantially true or fair comment?
Did the accurate reporting of Minors' Holocaust remark create a false and defamatory innuendo that he is anti-Semitic for which the Sun could be held liable?
Did the trial judge err in finding that the plaintiff failed to prove malice on the part of the defendants?

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in dismissing the defamation action on the basis that the publications were substantially true or fair comment?
firac.facts: Minors, an equity consultant and Metropolitan Toronto Board of Police Commissioners member, sued the Toronto Sun over 28 articles, cartoons and editorials from October–November 1994 concerning three topics: that he told Crown attorneys the Holocaust was not a racist act, that he walked past a distressed police officer during the 'Albert Moses incident', and that he called the Metro police an occupying army. After a 21-day trial without a jury, McRae J. dismissed the action, finding the publications correctly stated the facts and constituted fair comment.
firac.rule: A defamation defendant may escape liability where the impugned statements are substantially true (justification) or amount to fair comment on true facts. Appellate courts will not interfere with findings of fact amply supported by the evidence absent material error in principle.
firac.application: The Court of Appeal held that the trial judge's conclusions on all the impugned publications were supported by the evidence and that they were defensible either as substantially true statements or as fair comment on true facts. Because of these conclusions, the trial judge was not required to separate which publications were fact and which were comment. No material error in principle was shown.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge did not err; the publications were defensible as true or fair comment, and the dismissal stood.

firac.issue: Could the accurate reporting of Minors' Holocaust remark give rise to liability for a false innuendo that he is anti-Semitic?
firac.facts: The trial judge found it was proven 'beyond question' that Minors did say the Holocaust was not racist; the appellant abandoned in oral argument any challenge to that finding of fact. The appellant instead argued the repeated publication of the remark, together with two references to his 'anti-Semitic teachings', created the innuendo that he is anti-Semitic, which the Sun had to prove true.
firac.rule: A publisher is not liable for defamatory innuendo where a fact is accurately reported in its proper context; liability for false innuendo arises where words are quoted out of their reasonable context so as to create a false and defamatory meaning. A publisher cannot be held responsible for inferences a reader might draw from an accurately reported fact.
firac.application: The Court agreed with the trial judge that the argument was without merit. The appellant's statements about the Holocaust were accurately reproduced in their proper context and were not taken out of context to manufacture a false innuendo. The Sun could not be liable for inferences a reader might draw from an accurately reported fact, and Minors had known since March 1994 that his limited definition of racism was hurtful to the Jewish community and others.
firac.conclusion: No liability arose from the innuendo argument; the trial judge made no error in principle and was correct.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in finding no malice on the part of the defendants?
firac.facts: Malice was raised to defeat the fair-comment defence. The trial judge admitted some of the Sun's earlier publications on the malice issue and excluded others for lack of relevance, ultimately finding no malice.
firac.rule: Malice can defeat a defence of fair comment; findings on malice and the admission/exclusion of evidence engage the trial judge's discretion and are reviewed for error in principle or lack of evidentiary support.
firac.application: The Court found the trial judge properly exercised his discretion regarding the admission and exclusion of earlier publications, and his finding that there was no malice was entirely supported by the evidence.
firac.conclusion: No error; the finding of no malice was upheld.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a private defamation tort action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. K016 (fair comment) is the principal defence relied on by the trial judge and upheld on appeal. K058 (antisemitism) is engaged because the central innuendo alleged was that Minors is anti-Semitic, arising from references to 'anti-Semitic teachings'. K088 (Holocaust) is directly engaged since the most contentious publication concerned his remark that the Holocaust was not a racist act. K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) apply because the court noted the remark was hurtful to the Jewish community. K017 (group defamation) was considered but does not apply since this was an individual plaintiff. K062 (Holocaust denial) was rejected as the remark concerned characterization of the Holocaust as racist, not denial.
location_rationale: The decision is styled 'COURT OF APPEAL FOR ONTARIO', so the province is Ontario. No city is stated in the text (appellate decisions typically omit it), so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The document identifies only the docket number (C26963) and 'Court of Appeal for Ontario'; no specific registry office is named in the text, so registry is left null.

case_name: Volovich v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)

name_verification.name_in_document: OLEG VOLOVICH v. THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Does a law of general application requiring compulsory military service constitute persecution on a Convention ground?
Did the applicant establish a personalized risk of persecution arising from his objection to the Israeli military's conduct toward Palestinians?
Does the alleged discrimination against ethnic Russian Christians in Israel rise to the level of persecution?
Was the Board's decision tainted by bias?

firac.issue: Does a law of general application requiring compulsory military service constitute persecution on a Convention ground?
firac.facts: The applicant, an Israeli citizen and practising Christian, feared returning to Israel because he did not want to serve in the Israeli army reserves. Israel has a law of general application requiring citizens to perform military service. He never explored alternatives to service or formally expressed an objection.
firac.rule: A country's compulsory military service is a law of general application and is not persecutory unless shown to be persecutory on a Convention ground; an aversion to conflict or fear of serving does not by itself justify a fear of persecution (Zolfagharkhani v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1993] 3 F.C. 540 (C.A.); Garcia v. Canada (Secretary of State), [1994] F.C.J. No. 147).
firac.application: The applicant did not demonstrate that the conscription law was persecutory on a Convention ground, and he had neither explored alternatives to service nor voiced any objection. The Board's finding that this allegation was unfounded was open to it.
firac.conclusion: The Board did not err; compulsory military service under a law of general application was not persecution.

firac.issue: Did the applicant establish a personalized risk of persecution arising from his objection to the Israeli military's conduct toward Palestinians?
firac.facts: The applicant argued that, given the Israeli army's treatment of Palestinians, the conscription law became persecutory because it condoned illegal activity, and he did not want to participate in the killing of civilians or destruction of homes. He submitted extensive evidence of international condemnation but no evidence he would be personally targeted.
firac.rule: To be a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under ss. 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, a claimant must establish a risk personal to him, not merely generalized conditions.
firac.application: The Board did consider and confront this element of the claim rather than ignoring it, but found the applicant had neither expressed his objection to the Israeli policy nor shown that it led to personal persecution. The general evidence of condemnation did not establish that he would be personally targeted.
firac.conclusion: The Board did not ignore the claim and reasonably found it unfounded for lack of personalized risk.

firac.issue: Does the alleged discrimination against ethnic Russian Christians in Israel rise to the level of persecution?
firac.facts: The applicant claimed Russians in Israel are persecuted as a social group and that certain Israeli laws are persecutory toward non-Jewish citizens. He could not point to a specific instance in which he was personally targeted on the basis of his Russian Christian ethnicity.
firac.rule: Discrimination amounts to persecution only where it is sufficiently severe; not all discriminatory treatment reaches the persecution threshold (Chan v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1995] 3 S.C.R. 593).
firac.application: While Russian Christians may face discrimination in Israel, the applicant provided no specific example of personal targeting, and the allegations did not meet the threshold of persecutory treatment.
firac.conclusion: The Board's finding that the discrimination was not severe enough to constitute persecution was reasonable.

firac.issue: Was the Board's decision tainted by bias?
firac.facts: The applicant alleged the Board was biased in reaching its decision but adduced no serious supporting evidence.
firac.rule: An allegation of bias must be supported by serious evidence demonstrating a reasonable apprehension of bias.
firac.application: The applicant provided no serious evidence, and a reading of the transcripts revealed no suggestion of bias.
firac.conclusion: The bias allegation was without merit.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K011 judicial review captures the nature of the proceeding (application for judicial review of a Refugee Protection Division decision). K078 refugee protection and K075 convention refugee reflect the ss. 96/97 IRPA claim. K079 persecution is central, given the analysis of compulsory military service, discrimination, and personalized risk. K100 Immigration and Refugee Board identifies the tribunal whose decision was reviewed. Bias was raised but is a minor procedural point with no dedicated keyword; it is not separately coded.

case_name: Veffer v. Canada (Minister of Foreign Affairs)

name_verification.name_in_document: ELIYAHU YOSHUA VEFFER v. THE MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS

defining_issues: Did the Minister's passport policy denying inscription of 'Israel' alongside 'Jerusalem' as place of birth infringe the applicant's freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
Did the passport policy infringe the applicant's equality rights under s. 15 of the Charter on the basis of religion or place of birth?
If a Charter breach were established, would it be justified as a reasonable limit under s. 1?

firac.issue: Did the passport policy of inscribing 'Jerusalem' alone (refusing 'Jerusalem, Israel') infringe the applicant's freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
firac.facts: The applicant, a Canadian born in Jerusalem in 1987, sincerely believes, as part of his Jewish faith and identity, that Jerusalem is the capital of Israel. Canada's passport policy, reflecting its non-recognition of Israeli sovereignty over Jerusalem, requires that 'Jerusalem' stand alone in the place-of-birth field, with no country code. He sought judicial review and mandamus to have 'Israel' added.
firac.rule: Section 2(a) of the Charter guarantees freedom of conscience and religion. Per R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295, freedom of religion is the right to entertain, declare, and manifest religious beliefs free of coercion or constraint. Per Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47, courts assess only the sincerity of belief, not its validity. The Charter may be used as a shield, not a sword.
firac.application: The court accepted the sincerity of the applicant's belief but held that a passport is a government-owned document constituting intergovernmental communication identifying the bearer's citizenship. Nothing in the policy or the passport restricts the applicant's right to hold, declare, teach, or disseminate his belief that Jerusalem is Israel's capital. The refusal to reflect that belief in Canada's communications with foreign governments is neither coercion nor constraint; a sincere belief does not entitle him to compel the government to adopt it in its documents.
firac.conclusion: No breach of s. 2(a); the passport policy does not impinge on the applicant's freedom of religion.

firac.issue: Did the passport policy infringe the applicant's s. 15 equality rights based on religion or place of birth?
firac.facts: The policy treats those born in Jerusalem differently from other Canadians born abroad in territories of unsettled sovereignty, who may normally have their country of birth inscribed as requested. Jerusalem is an exception, standing alone. The applicant claimed discrimination on grounds of religion (Jewish) and place of birth.
firac.rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter, analyzed under the three-step framework in Law v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1999] 1 S.C.R. 497: (A) formal distinction/differential treatment on personal characteristics; (B) based on an enumerated or analogous ground (Corbiere: immutable or constructively immutable characteristics); (C) whether the differential treatment is discriminatory by demeaning human dignity, assessed objectively from the perspective of a reasonable person in the claimant's circumstances (Andrews; Egan). Comparator analysis per Hodge v. Canada, 2004 SCC 65.
firac.application: The court adopted the comparator group of Canadians born outside Jerusalem. Step A: the policy draws a formal distinction based on place of birth. Step B: place of birth is immutable and thus an analogous ground; but the religion claim fails because the policy and passports are silent as to faith and have no connection to the holder's religion. Step C: applying the contextual factors, there is no ameliorative purpose issue, the nexus to any pre-existing disadvantage is not objectively ascertainable, and the interest affected is minimal since the place-of-birth field is optional. A reasonable, fully informed person would not view requiring 'Jerusalem' alone (or omission) as demeaning the applicant's dignity; the policy was adopted for geopolitical reasons, does not target any group, and reflects no stereotyping.
firac.conclusion: While the policy makes a distinction between Canadians born in Jerusalem and those born elsewhere, it does not amount to discrimination under s. 15; no breach established.

firac.issue: If a Charter breach were found, could it be justified under s. 1?
firac.facts: Same policy grounded in Canada's foreign policy of not recognizing Israeli sovereignty over Jerusalem.
firac.rule: Section 1 of the Charter justifies reasonable limits demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
firac.application: Having found no breach of s. 2(a) or s. 15, the court held there was no need to undertake a s. 1 analysis.
firac.conclusion: No s. 1 analysis required.

keywords_rationale: The case is decided entirely on Charter grounds, so K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 anchor. K025 (freedom of religion) and K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) capture the first issue; K034 (sincerity of belief) reflects the court's reliance on Amselem regarding sincere religious belief. K023 (equality rights) and K109 (Charter s. 15) capture the second issue, decided under the Law framework. K107 (Canadian Charter) is the governing instrument. K011 (judicial review) reflects the procedural vehicle (judicial review and requested mandamus of the passport decision). K093 (Jewish) and K103 (Israel) situate the applicant's identity and the Jerusalem/Israel sovereignty context central to the dispute. K103 is somewhat contextual/geopolitical rather than a legal doctrine, so it is a slightly weaker, contextual pick.
location_rationale: The Reasons for Order and Order are headed 'OTTAWA, ONTARIO, May 1, 2006', indicating the Federal Court judge sat/issued from Ottawa, Ontario. The hearing itself was held in Winnipeg (the decision states 'PLACE OF HEARING: Winnipeg, Ontario', evidently an error for Manitoba, as applicant's counsel is in Winnipeg, Manitoba), but the decision issued from Ottawa.

name_verification.name_in_document: XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX (claimants) — RPD File No. TA8-25135 / TA8-25136

defining_issues: Did the mistreatment the claimants suffered in Russia amount to persecution rather than mere discrimination or harassment?
Did the principal claimant establish a credible profile as a person who is or is perceived to be Jewish and credible allegations of physical assault?
Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection in Russia?
Is there a viable internal flight alternative available to the claimants within Russia?

firac.issue: Did the mistreatment suffered in Russia rise to the level of persecution, or was it only discrimination or harassment?
firac.facts: The principal claimant described anti-Semitic verbal abuse, a 1999 push and injury by a drunken neighbour, an incident with a work supervisor in 2005, and a 2008 beating by RNU nationalists, spread over years and involving different employers; her son was teased and injured at school.
firac.rule: Not all less favourable treatment is persecution; discrimination amounts to persecution only where it produces consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature and the harm is inflicted with repetition, persistence or systematically, threatening basic human rights in a fundamental way (UNHCR Handbook, s. 54).
firac.application: The panel found the incidents, given their spacing over time and the different employers involved, constituted discrimination or harassment but were not serious, repetitive or systematic enough to threaten basic human rights fundamentally.
firac.conclusion: The mistreatment did not rise to the level of persecution.

firac.issue: Did the claimant credibly establish that she is or is perceived to be Jewish and that the alleged assaults occurred?
firac.facts: She provided an archive document showing maternal grandparents as Jewish but a birth certificate listing her parents' nationality as Russian; there was no evidence of synagogue attendance or Jewish activities. Medical certificates bore inconsistent dates (1998 vs 1999 for the neighbour incident) and no certificate was produced for the pivotal 2008 assault.
firac.rule: The burden of establishing key elements of the claim, including profile and corroboration where credibility is in doubt, rests on the claimant (Peti 2012 FC 82; Ishimwe 2009 FC 335); where credibility is questioned, a negative inference may be drawn from failure to corroborate material elements (Mejia 2011 FC 851).
firac.application: The panel found her birth certificate established Russian nationality, no profile as a perceived Jew was shown, and the date inconsistencies and unexplained absence of a medical certificate for the decisive 2008 assault undermined credibility, warranting a negative inference on the truthfulness of the assaults.
firac.conclusion: The claimant failed to establish a credible Jewish profile or credible allegations of assault.

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection in Russia?
firac.facts: She reported the 1999 assault to police who ignored her; she did not report the 2005 threat and did not approach higher police authorities or other agencies because she did not know where to complain. Country evidence showed both under-prosecution ('hooliganism') and successful prosecutions of anti-Semitic acts.
firac.rule: State protection is presumed and the claimant bears the burden of rebutting it with clear and convincing evidence; failing to seek assistance from higher authorities after individual officers decline is not an adequate search for protection in a democratic state (Baku 2010 FC 1163).
firac.application: Because she made no attempt to pursue higher police or other government avenues and the country evidence showed authorities do prosecute anti-Semitic crimes, she did not show additional efforts would be objectively unreasonable.
firac.conclusion: The presumption of state protection was not rebutted.

firac.issue: Is there a viable internal flight alternative in Russia?
firac.facts: Asked about relocating to St. Petersburg or other cities, she said Jews are disliked throughout Russia; her birth certificate shows Russian nationality and she had established no Jewish profile.
firac.rule: The two-pronged Rasaratnam test: no serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA, and reasonableness of relocation in all the circumstances; hardship of dislocation alone is insufficient (Ranganathan).
firac.application: Without an established Jewish profile she is unlikely to be identified as Jewish elsewhere, and relocation, though possibly difficult, would not be unduly harsh — comparable to her move to Canada.
firac.conclusion: A viable IFA exists, and the claims fail.

keywords_rationale: K008 is the tier-1 practice area (immigration/refugee). K078 refugee protection and K079 persecution capture the core ss. 96/97 claim and the discrimination-versus-persecution analysis. K080 state protection reflects the Rasaratnam-adjacent presumption analysis under Baku. K069 discrimination and K083 harassment describe the level of mistreatment found. K093 Jewish and K058 antisemitism identify the claimed ground of persecution and the country conditions discussed. K100 IRB situates the decision-maker (RPD). IFA has no dedicated vocabulary term so it is subsumed under refugee protection; credibility likewise has no standalone term.

name_verification.name_in_document: Nicholas Dinardo v. Correctional Services Canada

defining_issues: Should the Tribunal allow the 'Timing Amendments' to the Complainant's Statement of Particulars?
Should the Tribunal allow the 'Quantum Amendment' increasing the compensation sought from $80,000 to $720,000, and does the 'plain and obvious' test bar it?

firac.issue: Should the Tribunal permit the Timing Amendments to the Statement of Particulars to reflect that the Complainant is no longer in custody and the advancement of time?
firac.facts: Mx. Dinardo, an Indigenous, Jewish, Two-Spirit transfeminine complainant, sought amendments to their consolidated SOP against Correctional Service Canada to reflect that they are no longer in custody. CSC consented to these Timing Amendments.
firac.rule: Section 48.9(2) of the Canadian Human Rights Act gives the Tribunal considerable discretion to manage proceedings, including granting amendments where doing so serves the interests of justice (Peters v. Peters First Nation, 2023 CHRT 58; Blodgett, 2013 CHRT 24; Parent, 2006 FC 1313). Amendments require a factual and legal nexus with the original complaint and must not prejudice the other party.
firac.application: CSC informed the Tribunal it consented to the Timing Amendments, so no prejudice arose and no contested analysis was required.
firac.conclusion: The Timing Amendments were allowed on consent.

firac.issue: Should the Quantum Amendment increasing sought compensation from $80,000 to $720,000 be allowed, or is it barred because it is 'plain and obvious' it has no chance of success under the CHRA compensation caps?
firac.facts: Mx. Dinardo sought to increase compensation under ss. 53(2)(e) and 53(3) CHRA to $720,000, invoking multiples of the $40,000 caps to reflect compounding effects of multiple alleged acts of harassment, discrimination and retaliation (citing the Caring Society decisions). CSC argued the CHRA sets a firm cap regardless of the number of incidents and that the request was plain and obvious to fail; the Commission did not contest it.
firac.rule: The Tribunal may permit amendments serving the interests of justice where there is a factual/legal nexus to the complaint and no prejudice to the other party, and where the balance of convenience favours the moving party (Peters). A motion to amend may be dismissed where it is plain and obvious the allegations have no chance of success (Temate v. Public Health Agency of Canada, 2022 CHRT 31). Sections 53(2)(e) and 53(3) CHRA each cap compensation at $20,000.
firac.application: The Tribunal agreed with the Commission that the 'plain and obvious' test in Temate applies to new allegations that expand the scope of the inquiry, and did not apply here because the Quantum Amendment added no new grounds or discriminatory practices and left the factual scope largely unchanged. There was a nexus between the amended remedies and the alleged discriminatory practices, and CSC would have ample time to argue quantum at the end of the hearing, so no prejudice arose. The Tribunal declined to rule on whether the CHRA permits stacking of the caps, reserving that legal issue for the final decision.
firac.conclusion: The Quantum Amendment was allowed, without any determination that it is well-founded in law or fact; the permissibility of the amounts under ss. 53(2)(e) and 53(3) will be decided in the final decision if discrimination is found.

keywords_rationale: K007 (Human rights) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case is a CHRT proceeding. K069 (discrimination) and K083 (harassment) reflect the substance of the consolidated complaints (past and ongoing harassment and discrimination in custody). K093 (Jewish) reflects the complainant's self-identification, one of the enumerated grounds; it is a borderline/weaker pick since the ruling is procedural and does not turn on any particular ground.

case_name: Quebec (Commission des droits de la personne) v. Maksteel Québec Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: Quebec (Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse) v. Maksteel Québec Inc.

defining_issues: Does s. 18.2 of the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms protect the employment of a person dismissed because he was unavailable for work owing to his incarceration?
What are the respective burdens of proof of the employee/complainant and the employer under s. 18.2?
Does an employer owe a duty of reasonable accommodation under s. 18.2 as it does under ss. 10 and 20 of the Quebec Charter?

firac.issue: Does s. 18.2 of the Quebec Charter protect the employment of a person dismissed because he was unavailable for work owing to incarceration?
firac.facts: Yvon Roy, a maintenance mechanic with Maksteel, pleaded guilty in 1989 to fraud and breach of trust committed in 1985 (offences unconnected with his mechanic's job). On June 26, 1991 he was sentenced to six months less a day and immediately incarcerated. His vacation ran to July 10; he did not report on July 11 and was dismissed by letter of July 15, replaced July 22, and paroled July 26. He had not obtained a pardon.
firac.rule: Section 18.2 of the Quebec Charter prohibits dismissing, refusing to hire, or otherwise penalizing a person in employment 'owing to the mere fact that he was convicted of a penal or criminal offence, if the offence was in no way connected with the employment or if the person has obtained a pardon.' Interpreted purposively but without overshooting its purpose (Boisbriand; Big M Drug Mart; Therrien), the provision protects only against the unjustified social stigma flowing from a conviction, not against the civil consequences of a lawfully imposed sentence. The Court adopted the reasoning in British Columbia (Human Rights Commission) v. British Columbia (Human Rights Tribunal), 2000 BCCA 584.
firac.application: The Court distinguished the civil consequences of a sentence (unavailability due to incarceration) from unjustified stigma arising from the conviction itself. Unavailability is a consequence of the deprivation of liberty, not of the status of having a criminal record; not all convictions lead to incarceration, so conviction and incarceration are not an inseverable whole. Extending protection to the incarceration period would turn s. 18.2 into a guarantee of employment and would absurdly bar refusing to hire an unavailable inmate. The legislative history (Minister's remarks about 'rehabilitating people who have paid their debt to society') confirmed the provision was not meant to protect the period of incarceration.
firac.conclusion: Section 18.2 does not protect an employee from dismissal where the real reason is that he is not available for work because he is incarcerated; it protects only against action taken owing to the mere fact of the conviction.

firac.issue: What are the burdens of proof under s. 18.2?
firac.facts: The Tribunal found the employer knew of Roy's incarceration by July 15 but made no finding on the actual cause of dismissal, treating conviction and incarceration as inseparable. The Court of Appeal, assessing the facts itself, found the employer had not used unavailability as a mere pretext.
firac.rule: The complainant bears the initial onus of establishing a prima facie case (Meiorin; Grismer): a criminal record, a reprisal in employment, and that the record was the real reason/actual cause of the employer's action (plus a pardon where applicable). The complainant need not prove the conviction was the sole cause. Where imprisonment affects availability, the court must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the actual cause was the conviction and that unavailability was not a mere pretext. The employer then bears the burden of establishing an objective connection between the offence and the position.
firac.application: There were only two possible causes of dismissal: the conviction or the incarceration-based unavailability (a disciplinary dismissal was excluded, Roy being an exemplary employee). It was common ground the fraud/breach-of-trust offences were unconnected to the mechanic's post and no pardon had been obtained. The determinative factual question was whether the conviction was the actual cause. The Court of Appeal properly sought the actual cause and concluded unavailability, not conviction, was the reason; absent manifest error, a second-level appellate court will not intervene (St-Jean v. Mercier).
firac.conclusion: The complainant did not discharge the burden of proving that the conviction, rather than unavailability, was the actual cause of the dismissal; the Court of Appeal's factual finding stood.

firac.issue: Does a duty of reasonable accommodation arise under s. 18.2?
firac.facts: The Tribunal had characterized the situation as indirect discrimination and imposed a reasonable-accommodation/undue-hardship analysis, ordering damages against the employer.
firac.rule: Section 18.2 is a self-contained provision (Therrien) containing its own justification rules and does not require resort to s. 20 of the Quebec Charter. The 'reasonable accommodation' standard developed in Meiorin for bona fide occupational requirements has no role. The only justification is an objective connection between the offence and the employment, limited by a pardon; the protection is an absolute prohibition rather than an accommodation regime.
firac.application: Because justification is built into s. 18.2 itself and the protection operates as an absolute prohibition (the individual is either entitled to the job or not), there is no room for a duty to accommodate or an undue-hardship analysis. The Tribunal erred in applying the direct/indirect discrimination and reasonable-accommodation framework.
firac.conclusion: No duty of reasonable accommodation arises under s. 18.2; the Tribunal's accommodation analysis was wrong.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally about anti-discrimination protection in employment, so the tier-1 area is Human rights (K007). K069 (discrimination) and K082 (employment discrimination) capture the core subject — discrimination based on criminal record in employment. K085 (wrongful dismissal) fits because the dispute concerns a dismissal ('congédiement'). K120 (Quebec Charter) is the governing instrument (s. 18.2, and comparison with ss. 10 and 20). K068 (bona fide occupational requirement) is engaged because the Court analyzed the connection-to-employment justification and contrasted it with the BFOR/Meiorin framework. K031 (religious accommodation) is used as the closest available proxy for 'reasonable accommodation / duty to accommodate' — a concept the Court expressly held does not apply under s. 18.2; it is a borderline pick since the vocabulary term is tagged to religious contexts, and it is flagged as weak.

The matter originated in Quebec (counsel and the Commission are located in Montréal), but that reflects the case's origin, not the seat of the deciding court.
