name_verification.name_in_document: [no public name] — RPD File No. TA9-04094

defining_issues: Was cause shown to proceed with the hearing despite the claimant's earlier illness-related absence?
Was the claimant a credible witness regarding his claimed practice of Christianity in a house church in China and his fear of persecution?

Does the claimant, as a practicing Christian in an unregistered house church, face a serious possibility of persecution if returned to Fujian province, China, so as to qualify under s. 96 or s. 97(1) of the IRPA?

firac.issue: Was cause shown to proceed with the hearing despite the claimant's earlier illness-related absence?
firac.facts: The initial hearing set for September 30, 2009 did not proceed because the claimant was ill; counsel provided a medical note, and a Show Cause hearing was scheduled for November 25, 2009.
firac.rule: A claimant who misses a scheduled hearing must show cause for the failure to attend before the matter proceeds.
firac.application: The panel accepted a medical note from Dr. XXXXX of the XXXXX Medical Centre confirming the claimant had been seen and was unfit to attend the September 30, 2009 hearing.
firac.conclusion: Cause was shown; the hearing proceeded on November 25, 2009.

firac.issue: Was the claimant a credible witness regarding his religious practice and subjective fear?
firac.facts: The claimant claimed to have attended a house church in China, fled a PSB raid, and travelled to Canada by smuggler. He could not name the passport he travelled under or the countries he transited, gave inconsistent accounts of what happened to his passport, and showed only limited knowledge of Christianity at his port-of-entry interview but solid knowledge by the hearing.
firac.rule: Credibility findings may rest on the cumulative effect of concerns (Sheikh v. Canada (MEI), [1990] 3 F.C. 238 (C.A.)); uncontradicted evidence may be rejected if it does not accord with the probabilities of the case (Faryna v. Chorny, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 354 (B.C.C.A.)); evidence must be probably, not merely possibly, credible (Orelien v. Canada (MEI), [1992] 1 F.C. 592 (C.A.)).
firac.application: The panel drew negative inferences from the implausibility that an individual with twelve years of education travelling on commercial airlines would not know the passport name or transit countries, and from contradictory statements about the passport. It found much of the claimant's religious knowledge was acquired after arrival in Canada, though it accepted he attended a house church in China only briefly and now practices Christianity in Canada.
firac.conclusion: On a balance of probabilities the claimant was not a credible witness regarding his profile as a persecuted house-church member, though the panel accepted limited attendance in China and genuine practice in Canada.

firac.issue: Does the claimant face a serious possibility of persecution if returned to Fujian province as a member of an unregistered house church?
firac.facts: The claimant is from Fujian province, a small (fifteen-member) house church, an ordinary member (not a leader). Documentary evidence described Fujian and Guangdong as having among the most liberal religious policies in China, with no reported arrests of lay Christians in Fujian since 2002.
firac.rule: Sections 96 and 97(1) IRPA require the claimant to establish a serious possibility of persecution or a personalized risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or torture.
firac.application: Weighing extensive country documentation, the panel found the likelihood of an ordinary unregistered-church member being harassed in Fujian so small that no serious possibility of persecution existed; arrests documented elsewhere in China occurred in other provinces, and problems typically arose only for larger churches, leaders, or groups with outside links, none of which applied to the claimant.
firac.conclusion: No serious possibility of persecution was established; the claimant could practice his religion in an unregistered church in Fujian without a serious possibility of persecution.

keywords_rationale: K008 is the tier-1 practice area (immigration/refugee). K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the s. 96/97 claim. K079 (persecution) is central to the well-founded-fear analysis. K025 (freedom of religion) and K034 (sincerity of belief) reflect the core question of whether the claimant genuinely practices Christianity — K034 is borderline since it derives from a Charter context but aptly captures the panel's assessment of the sincerity/genuineness of religious practice. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the deciding tribunal (RPD).
location_rationale: The decision states "Place of Hearing: Toronto, Ontario", establishing city and province.
registry_rationale: The Refugee Protection Division is a national tribunal division of the IRB; no distinct court registry office is named, only the place of hearing (Toronto), so registry is left null.

case_name: Jewish National Fund of Canada Inc. v. Canada (National Revenue)

name_verification.name_in_document: JEWISH NATIONAL FUND OF CANADA INC., FONDS NATIONAL JUIF DU CANADA INC. v. MINISTER OF NATIONAL REVENUE

defining_issues: Where a party alleges bias or breach of procedural fairness, what is the scope of a tribunal's disclosure obligation under Rules 317 and 318 of the Federal Courts Rules, and had the Minister met it?
Must the Minister produce further materials said to have been considered by the Charities Directorate that were not before the Appeals Branch?
Should specific documents referred to in, or omitted from, the certified tribunal record be produced?
Is a supplementary search of CRA records and an updated affidavit warranted?
Were the Minister's redactions for privilege and taxpayer information adequately justified?

firac.issue: What is the scope of the Rule 317/318 disclosure obligation where bias and procedural unfairness are alleged, and did the Minister satisfy it?
firac.facts: JNF appeals the Minister's confirmation of intent to revoke its charitable registration, alleging a reasonable apprehension of bias flowing from public and media pressure on CRA, and procedural unfairness. It moved under Rule 318(4) for unredacted certified materials and an affidavit describing CRA's search. The Minister filed a Certified Tribunal Record and the Brant Affidavit and did not object under Rule 318(2).
firac.rule: Rules 317 and 318 of the Federal Courts Rules; a requesting party is entitled to material before the decision-maker unless the decision-maker objects (Lukács v. Canada (Transportation Agency), 2016 FCA 103; Ron W. Cameron Charitable Foundation, 2023 FCA 175). Where bias or breach of procedural fairness is alleged, disclosure is broadened to documents in the tribunal's possession, control or power relevant to those allegations (Humane Society of Canada Foundation, 2018 FCA 66; Air Passenger Rights, 2021 FCA 201), but a party may not embark on a fishing expedition.
firac.application: The Court found JNF's bias allegation to be a tenable ground properly pleaded and particularized in the Amended Notice of Appeal, triggering the broadened disclosure obligation. It was not satisfied the Minister had produced all relevant materials, including communications from and to the public involving either the Charities Directorate or the Appeals Branch.
firac.conclusion: The Court ordered the Minister to disclose any further materials in CRA's possession relevant to the bias allegation, or to file an updated affidavit confirming full compliance.

firac.issue: Must the Minister produce further Charities Directorate materials?
firac.facts: JNF argued the CTR incompletely captured documents considered by the Charities Directorate in issuing the notice of intention to revoke, or that CRA's search was inadequate; the Minister said all such documents in CRA's possession were included, except conceded draft media lines.
firac.rule: Relevance under Rule 317 is defined by the grounds of appeal; only relevant material before the decision-maker must be produced (Ron W. Cameron at para. 10).
firac.application: The Court found JNF's reference to unspecified Access to Information documents did not establish omission of relevant material, but accepted the Minister's concession regarding draft media lines intended for CRA spokespersons.
firac.conclusion: No further Charities Directorate production ordered except the draft media lines, which are to be added to the CTR.

firac.issue: Should specific documents referred to in, or missing from, the CTR be produced?
firac.facts: JNF identified documents and attachments referenced in emails within the CTR, and specific documents received through its Access to Information request that were relevant to bias but absent from the CTR. The Minister did not address these specifics and maintained full disclosure.
firac.rule: Rules 317/318 require production of relevant material before the decision-maker; the Court reconciles meaningful review, procedural fairness and confidentiality (Girouard v. Canadian Judicial Council, 2019 FCA 252).
firac.application: The Court found JNF's arguments persuasively suggested omission of specific relevant materials, which the Minister had not answered.
firac.conclusion: The Court ordered production of the documents identified in paragraphs 63–65 and 70–72 of JNF's written representations.

firac.issue: Is a supplementary search and updated affidavit warranted?
firac.facts: JNF sought a second search and a senior-official affidavit describing its scope. The Minister maintained all relevant materials were produced or did not exist, relying on the Brant Affidavit.
firac.rule: An inadequate evidentiary record may immunize decision-makers from review and undermine accountability; the Court seeks to ensure a sufficient record for meaningful review (Lukács; Girouard).
firac.application: Given the disclosure deficiencies identified, the Court concluded a supplementary search by senior CRA representatives, including the Charities Directorate, was required, with an affidavit detailing who conducted it and confirming completeness.
firac.conclusion: The Court ordered a supplementary search and an updated affidavit and certificate, to be served and filed within 30 days.

firac.issue: Were the redactions for privilege and taxpayer information adequately justified?
firac.facts: JNF challenged redactions as bald assertions, arguing solicitor-client privilege must be supported by affidavit and that redacted personal/third-party information could assist its case. The Minister argued no affidavit is required for privilege and that seeking taxpayer information was a fishing expedition.
firac.rule: The Court must balance meaningful review and procedural fairness against protection of legitimate confidentiality interests (Lukács at para. 15); privacy and taxpayer confidentiality obligations constrain disclosure.
firac.application: The Court found JNF's request for redacted taxpayer/personal information speculative and potentially protected by privacy law, but held the Minister had not sufficiently justified the scope and necessity of the privilege-based redactions.
firac.conclusion: Redactions of taxpayer information upheld; the Court set a timetable for JNF to specify challenged privilege redactions and for the Minister to justify them and provide sealed unredacted copies for the Court's review.

keywords_rationale: The case is a Federal Court of Appeal motion governing production of the tribunal record on an appeal, so Administrative law (K001) is the primary tier-1 area. Judicial review (K011) applies because Rules 317/318 embody the principle that review is premised on the record before the decision-maker, and the appeal is reviewed on that footing. Procedural fairness (K012) is central: the disclosure obligation is broadened precisely because JNF alleges bias and breach of procedural fairness. K104 (Palestine) reflects the specific contested materials relayed from a group in Ramallah, Palestinian Authority via Global Affairs. K093 (Jewish) is a weak/entity pick tied to the appellant Jewish National Fund of Canada; it is included to reach the minimum and is flagged as borderline since the case turns on tax-charity disclosure procedure rather than any Jewish-community substantive issue. The vocabulary lacks tax/charity-registration keywords, which would otherwise be the closest substantive match.

registry_rationale: No court registry office is named; this is a Federal Court of Appeal motion dealt with in writing, so registry is left null.

name_verification.discrepancy_note: The party names match, but the supplied citation (2022 BCSC 2119) and court (BCSC) do not match the decision, which is a British Columbia Court of Appeal judgment cited as 2022 BCCA 359. The BCSC decision under appeal is indexed at 2022 BCSC 1696, not 2022 BCSC 2119.

defining_issues: Should leave to appeal be granted from a chambers judge's discretionary interlocutory order dismissing an application to set aside a Master's adjournment order?

firac.issue: Should the appellant be granted leave to appeal the chambers judge's order dismissing her application to set aside Master Robertson's adjournment order?
firac.facts: Ms. Gong sued Mr. O'Neill, a Residential Tenancy Branch arbitrator, and he applied to strike her claim as frivolous and vexatious. Master Robertson adjourned that dismissal application peremptorily to August 30, 2022, and ordered response materials by August 2, 2022. Ms. Gong sought, by notice of application, to set aside the Master's order; the chambers judge dismissed that application, holding it was in substance an appeal that could not be brought by notice of application, while leaving her filed notice of appeal intact. Subsequently the August 30 hearing was repeatedly adjourned and the dismissal application was set to complete November 15, 2022.
firac.rule: Under the Court of Appeal Rules, B.C. Reg. 120/2022, leave to appeal is required for a limited appeal order, including an order granting an adjournment (s. 11(e)) and a Supreme Court judge's order granting or refusing an appeal from such an order (s. 11(g)); s. 12(a). Leave is assessed on the Goldman, Sachs & Co. v. Sessions, 2000 BCCA 326 factors: significance to the practice, significance to the action, prima facie merit (versus frivolity), and whether the appeal will unduly hinder the action — all under the rubric of the interests of justice (Vancouver (City) v. Zhang, 2007 BCCA 280; Movassaghi v. Aghtai, 2010 BCCA 175).
firac.application: The order was a discretionary interlocutory order and a limited appeal order requiring leave. Applying the Goldman Sachs factors: the appeal raised no issue of general importance to the practice; it had no significance to the action because the chambers judge decided neither the dismissal application nor the merits of the appeal from the Master, and expressly allowed Ms. Gong's notice of appeal to proceed; the appeal was without merit because the chambers judge was correct that a Master's order cannot be appealed by notice of application; and, given the litigation history, the appeal risked only delaying the action. Subsequent events (adjournment of the August 30 hearing to November 15) rendered the appeal effectively moot and devoid of practical utility.
firac.conclusion: Leave to appeal was refused; it would not be in the interests of justice to grant leave for an appeal with no merit, no practical utility, and that could only unduly hinder the progress of the action. Costs to Mr. O'Neill.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area, as the case concerns leave to appeal an interlocutory order in a civil action. K001 (Administrative law) and K011 (judicial review) are included because the underlying dispute arose from decisions of a Residential Tenancy Branch arbitrator, which Ms. Gong also challenged by judicial review — these are background/weak picks not central to the leave decision. K012 (procedural fairness) reflects Ms. Gong's argument that the Master's timeline gave her insufficient time to respond; it is a weak/borderline pick. K014 (standard of review) is a weak pick reflecting the appellate review posture. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated civil-procedure/leave-to-appeal term, so several picks are flagged as approximate.

defining_issues: Did the RPD err in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility?
Does the Appellant's cumulative experience of discrimination, harassment and violence in Ukraine amount to a serious possibility of persecution on the basis of her mixed Ukrainian/Roma ethnicity?
Can the Appellant benefit from adequate state protection or an internal flight alternative in Ukraine?

firac.issue: Did the RPD err in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility?
firac.facts: The RPD rejected the elderly Appellant's claim as not credible, faulting her uncertainty about which ethnicity was on her USSR-issued birth certificate, giving low weight to a Roma community letter, finding she merely recited her BOC narrative, questioning the medical report and her delay in leaving Ukraine, and noting her lack of interest in her home.
firac.rule: The RAD reviews RPD decisions on a correctness standard after an independent assessment (Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93), with deference only where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing oral credibility.
firac.application: The RAD found the RPD's adverse findings unsustainable: expressing uncertainty about her birth certificate was not 'evasive'; the RPD never made a clear finding on her ethnic identity; in an inquisitorial process it could have called the letter's author; testimony consistent with a detailed narrative does not indicate fabrication; the medical, delay, and home-interest findings ignored her reasonable explanations (fear of leaving her home unattended, grief at her husband's grave, ineligibility for medical insurance at her sister's address).
firac.conclusion: The RPD made overriding errors in assessing credibility; those findings were set aside and the RAD conducted its own assessment, accepting the Appellant as of mixed Roma-Ukrainian ethnicity and credible.

firac.issue: Does the cumulative discrimination, harassment and violence amount to a serious possibility of persecution?
firac.facts: The Appellant, a woman in her eighties perceived as Roma, faced lifelong discrimination: forced resignation from her job in 1993, anti-Roma graffiti and swastikas on her home, threats, pressure to sell her land to a nationalist businessman, a neighbour's arson, and an October 2017 assault requiring a week's hospitalization, followed by threatening phone calls.
firac.rule: A well-founded fear of persecution requires 'sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights' (Ward, [1993] 2 SCR 689); discrimination must be serious or systematic (Sagharichi; Rajudeen); cumulative measures may together constitute persecution (UNHCR Handbook paras 54-55; Bayrak, 2013 FC 1056), assessed by their effect on the individual.
firac.application: The RAD conducted an individualized assessment: escalating incidents since the 2014 rise of nationalism, an anti-Roma motivated assault, threats to her life, and vulnerability from advanced age, combined with her high profile as an open supporter of Roma, produced apprehension and insecurity. Objective country evidence showed Roma are the leading target of ethnic bias in Ukraine, with violent attacks, hate crimes, and inadequate police response.
firac.conclusion: The cumulative acts of discrimination, harassment and violence constitute persecution, establishing a serious possibility of persecution based on her Roma ethnicity.

firac.issue: Can the Appellant benefit from adequate state protection or an internal flight alternative?
firac.facts: The Appellant repeatedly sought police assistance but officers were rude, refused to open complaints, closed her file, and told her to relocate. Country evidence documented police failure to protect Roma and an unimplemented protection strategy.
firac.rule: A state is presumed capable of protecting its citizens; the claimant must adduce relevant, reliable and convincing evidence rebutting this on a balance of probabilities (Flores Carrillo, 2008 FCA), assessed contextually (Gonzales Torres) with the Gender Guidelines. For IFA, the claimant must show it is unreasonable to seek refuge elsewhere (Momodu; Abdalghader).
firac.application: The Appellant's lived experience of police inaction, combined with documentary evidence of impunity and failure of Ukrainian authorities to protect Roma, rebutted the presumption of state protection. Discrimination against Roma was found to be the same throughout Ukraine, so no viable IFA existed.
firac.conclusion: The Appellant rebutted the presumption of adequate state protection and had no internal flight alternative.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the core determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. K079 (persecution) is central given the cumulative-discrimination-amounting-to-persecution analysis. K080 (state protection) reflects the express finding rebutting the presumption of state protection and the related IFA analysis. K014 (standard of review) applies because the RAD expressly applied the correctness standard from Huruglica. K065 (racism) captures the anti-Roma ethnic discrimination and hate-motivated violence at the heart of the claim. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) situates the tribunal (RAD). Roma ethnicity has no dedicated keyword, so racism is the closest fit; it is a slightly broad pick but well grounded in the anti-Roma slurs, graffiti and attacks.

Do a bargaining agent's public political statements constitute intimidation or coercion to compel an employee to cease membership under s. 189(1) of the Act?

firac.issue: Does the Board have jurisdiction over a duty-of-fair-representation complaint arising from a bargaining agent's public statements on broader social or political issues?
firac.facts: Tamar Messer, a PSAC member, complained that PSAC's October 14, 2023 public statement about the violence in Palestine and Israel and its joining the 'Ceasefire Now' coalition were discriminatory against Jewish people and perpetuated antisemitism and support for terrorism, in breach of PSAC's duty of fair representation.
firac.rule: Section 187 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act codifies the duty of fair representation, which governs a bargaining agent's 'representation of any employee in the bargaining unit.' The duty applies only where the subject of the representation (1) falls under the Act or applicable collective agreement, and (2) involves a dispute with the employer (Hancock v. PIPSC, 2023 FPSLREB 51; Serediuk, 2023 FPSLREB 71). The Board applied an arguable-case analysis, taking the alleged facts as true.
firac.application: PSAC's public statements about the violence in Palestine and Israel have nothing to do with the Act, the collective agreement, or the complainant's relationship with her employer. The complainant's concern that she could not be fairly represented was hypothetical, as no concrete labour relations dispute with her employer had arisen to trigger the duty. Allegations of systemic racism within PSAC concern its internal affairs and fall outside the Board's jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: The complaint falls outside the Board's jurisdiction under s. 187; even accepting the alleged facts, no arguable case of a breach of the duty of fair representation was made out.

firac.issue: Do a bargaining agent's public political statements amount to intimidation or coercion compelling an employee to cease membership under s. 189(1) of the Act?
firac.facts: The complainant, citing s. 96 of the Canada Labour Code, argued that PSAC's public statements compelled her to cease her membership because she felt uncomfortable being represented by it.
firac.rule: Section 189(1) of the Act provides that no person shall seek by intimidation or coercion to compel an employee to cease membership in an employee organization. The phrase requires 'threats or coercion amounting to constraint or intimidation' viewed in a labour relations context (Desgagnés Marine, 2008 CIRB 429). The Supreme Court has affirmed that unions may lawfully engage in political activity (Lavigne v. OPSEU, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 211; Dunmore, 2001 SCC 94).
firac.application: The Board treated the s. 96 reference as invoking the equivalent s. 189(1). The public statements complained of did not rise to the level of a constraint or intimidation. The Act contains no rules restricting a bargaining agent's political activity, and taking political positions does not deprive PSAC of its status as bargaining agent or otherwise violate the Act.
firac.conclusion: The public statements did not constitute intimidation or coercion under s. 189(1); the complaint could not succeed on this basis either.

case_name: MG v. Minister of Employment and Social Development

name_verification.name_in_document: MG v Minister of Employment and Social Development

defining_issues: Did the Claimant have a severe (and prolonged) disability by his December 31, 2003 qualifying period?
Did the Claimant become severely and prolongedly disabled within the prorated qualifying window between January 1 and April 30, 2014?
Did the Claimant meet the CPP definition of incapacity so as to permit disability payments retroactive beyond the date fixed by the statutory 15-month/four-month rules?

Was the Claimant denied procedural fairness by, among other things, the Minister changing its position at the hearing, the conduct of the Minister's representative, limits on Navigator assistance, and the handling of potential bias allegations?

firac.issue: Did the Claimant have a severe and prolonged disability by his December 31, 2003 qualifying period?
firac.facts: The Claimant, a psychotherapist injured in a 1999 car accident, was diagnosed in 2003 with post-concussion syndrome, mild cognitive disorder, adjustment disorders and fatigue. He continued a part-time psychotherapy practice for years, worked roughly 15 client-service hours weekly, wrote professional articles, built a website, travelled and drove. There was no medical evidence between August 2003 and June 2009.
firac.rule: Under s. 42(2)(a) of the Canada Pension Plan a disability is severe if it renders a person incapable regularly of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation. All conditions must be assessed together (Bungay, 2011 FCA 47); personal characteristics are considered (Villani, 2002 FCA 248); and where residual capacity exists, the claimant must show efforts to obtain/maintain work failed for health reasons (Inclima, 2003 FCA 117). Business loss is not necessarily indicative of incapacity (Kiriakidis, 2011 FCA 316).
firac.application: Relying on the contemporaneous 2003 reports of Dr. Keith and Mr. Sullivan over later retrospective evidence, the member found the Claimant retained residual work capacity of about 15 client-service hours per week and continued that practice for years. His education, age and language were positive factors. His low net self-employment income reflected heavy business expenses (vehicle, meals) rather than lack of capacity, and employed psychotherapy work would likely have been substantially gainful. He did not show his efforts to maintain work failed due to health.
firac.conclusion: The Claimant did not have a severe disability by December 31, 2003.

firac.issue: Did the Claimant become severely and prolongedly disabled between January 1 and April 30, 2014?
firac.facts: After his mother's 2010 accident and sharp decline beginning January 11, 2014 (when her dog was euthanized), the Claimant suffered a major depressive setback with suicidal ideation, emotional lability, memory and concentration deficits, and spent about 12 hours a day in bed. He stopped treating patients, sold his car, condo and life insurance, and could perform only brief, exhausting election work.
firac.rule: Same severe/prolonged definitions under s. 42(2)(a); prolonged means likely long continued and of indefinite duration or likely to result in death. Residual-capacity and Inclima principles apply.
firac.application: Although near-contemporaneous medical evidence for 2014 was scarce, the member accepted the 2016 diagnoses (MDD, adjustment disorder with anxiety) and Dr. Keith's evidence that the impairments existed and persisted. Suicidal ideation precluded therapy; sleep, memory, focus and emotional limitations precluded clerical, teaching, writing or presenting work. Closing five files on his own schedule and minimal election work confirmed rather than negated severity. Dr. Keith's poor prognosis and expectation of no return to competitive work made the disability prolonged. The member declined to adopt the Minister's late position that no 2014 onset could be found.
firac.conclusion: The Claimant became severely disabled as of January 11, 2014, and the disability was also prolonged by the April 30, 2014 qualifying date.

firac.issue: Did the Claimant meet the CPP incapacity test entitling him to additional retroactivity beyond July 2015?
firac.facts: The Claimant applied on June 28, 2016, asserting incapacity variously since 1999, 2011, or January 2014. Dr. Keith's April 2019 Declaration of Incapacity said incapacity ran continuously from September 2011. During 2014-2016 he managed his mother's care and insurance claims, corresponded with Dr. Keith, sold assets, renewed and later dropped professional memberships, worked as an election worker, moved, and discussed applying before applying in June 2016.
firac.rule: Section 60(9)-(10) CPP: incapacity exists where a person is incapable of forming or expressing an intention to make an application, and the incapacity must be continuous. The threshold is low and does not depend on capacity to complete an application (Walls, 2022 FCA 47). Medical declarations are not determinative (Flaig, 2017 FC 531). The Blue framework (2021 FCA 211, para 42) requires considering the applicant's evidence, medical evidence, other activities, and what those activities reveal about capacity to form/express intent. A choice not to apply (e.g., not to be a 'free rider') does not show incapacity (Sedrak, 2008 FCA 86).
firac.application: The member gave little weight to Dr. Keith's inconsistent declarations and her misunderstanding of the legal test, and noted the very act of applying in June 2016 (of which Dr. Keith was aware) contradicted continuous incapacity from 2011. The Claimant's extensive decision-making—caring for his mother, settling insurance claims, selling property, election work, and correspondence—showed capacity to form and express intentions. Unlike the 'most unusual' applicant in Blue, his disability was not rooted in trauma from hospitals, the medical profession or authority; he continued engaging with his psychologist and the system. His delay reflected a conscious desire not to be a 'free rider,' not incapacity.
firac.conclusion: The Claimant did not establish CPP incapacity; payments start July 2015 (deemed disability March 2015, four months later).

firac.issue: Was the Claimant denied procedural fairness?
firac.facts: The Claimant did not attend the second hearing day for medical reasons, filed dozens of late document batches, complained about limited Navigator access, made Charter and anti-Semitism allegations, demanded removal of the Minister's representative and forced settlement, and made statements arguably raising bias against the member. The Minister changed its position at the close of the hearing to no longer concede a 2014 onset.
firac.rule: Procedural fairness under the SST Rules (ss. 6, 8, 42); the reasonable-apprehension-of-bias test from Committee for Justice and Liberty v National Energy Board, [1978] 1 SCR 369. The Tribunal's Charter jurisdiction is limited to CPP legislation, not party conduct.
firac.application: The member admitted all late evidence and submissions in the interests of fairness, provided the hearing recording, posed the Claimant's relevant questions to the Minister's witness, and gave extended time for closing submissions. A party may change position based on the evidence, and the Claimant had ample opportunity to respond. Navigators are neutral, non-legal aides and the Claimant received exceptional assistance; the Tribunal has no obligation to equalize representation. The Charter complaints concerned conduct, outside the Tribunal's jurisdiction. The member found the Claimant did not actually wish to pursue a formal bias allegation, preferring a merits decision to seek relief in the federal courts, and declined to adjudicate anti-Semitism allegations about others' motivations as irrelevant to disability.
firac.conclusion: No breach of procedural fairness occurred; the appeal proceeded on the merits.

defining_issues: What is the claimant's country of former habitual residence for the purposes of a stateless Palestinian's refugee claim?
Did the claimant establish a credible and well-founded subjective fear of persecution, particularly in light of her return to the West Bank (re-availment)?

Does the claimant face a well-founded fear of persecution under s. 96 or a personalized risk under s. 97 by reason of being an elderly Palestinian woman or her past interactions with the Israeli authorities?

firac.issue: What is the claimant's country of former habitual residence for a stateless Palestinian?
firac.facts: The claimant is a stateless Palestinian, formerly holding a Jordanian passport that was confiscated in 2011. She had resided in the West Bank, with her Schedule A indicating residence there from 2005 and her primary address in the West Bank.
firac.rule: For stateless claimants, the country of former habitual residence is assessed under Maarouf v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1994] 1 F.C. 723, considering whether the person was admitted for continuing residence of some duration and whether there was a significant period of de facto residence; the claimant need not be legally able to return.
firac.application: Applying the Maarouf factors, the panel found the claimant had a significant period of de facto residence in the West Bank, accepting it as her primary address.
firac.conclusion: The Palestinian Occupied Territories (West Bank) is the claimant's country of former habitual residence.

firac.issue: Did the claimant establish a credible subjective fear of persecution given her voluntary return to the West Bank?
firac.facts: After travelling to the U.S.A. in January 2015 to join her son, the claimant voluntarily returned to the West Bank in March 2015 for medical treatment and lived there until December 2015, when she left to join her son in Canada. She also filed a post-hearing affidavit adding allegations of settler attacks not mentioned during her testimony.
firac.rule: A well-founded fear of persecution requires both a subjective and an objective component: Canada (Attorney General) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689. Re-availment and self-endangering conduct undermine subjective fear, and unexplained material omissions support a negative credibility inference.
firac.application: The panel found the claimant's return to and six-month residence in the West Bank inconsistent with genuine fear, undermining both subjective and objective fear. The post-hearing affidavit alleging settler assaults was rejected because the material was never raised in her lengthy BOC or oral testimony, and her age did not adequately explain such significant omissions.
firac.conclusion: The claimant did not establish a credible subjective fear; her re-availment and self-endangering conduct rendered her allegations not credible.

firac.issue: Does the claimant face a well-founded fear of persecution or personalized risk as an elderly Palestinian woman or due to past dealings with the Israeli authorities?
firac.facts: The claimant relied on being an elderly, vulnerable Palestinian woman unable to live alone, past interrogations connected to her daughter's 1991 assault and her son-in-law's involvement in the resistance, and generalized violence, checkpoints and settler attacks in the West Bank.
firac.rule: Section 96 requires a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground; s. 97(1)(b) excludes risks faced generally by other individuals in the country. Gender-based claims are assessed under Guideline 4 (female refugee claimants fearing gender-based persecution).
firac.application: The panel found the claimant's ability to leave, return and leave again showed she was not of interest to the IDF; she had lived largely alone with a home and medical coverage. The documentary evidence showed hardships (movement restrictions, economic impacts, settler and IDF violence) affecting the general West Bank population and did not meet the threshold for persecution. Her gender claim was undercut by her own testimony attributing her fear to being Palestinian and her daughter's actions, not gender.
firac.conclusion: The claimant faces only generalized risk shared by the West Bank population, not personalized persecution; the s. 96 and s. 97 claims fail.

case_name: Canadian Society for the Advancement of Science in Public Policy v. British Columbia

name_verification.name_in_document: Canadian Society for the Advancement of Science in Public Policy v. British Columbia

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff's notice of civil claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1) as an abuse of process and as disclosing no reasonable cause of action, given that it is in essence an administrative challenge to government COVID-19 measures cast as a Charter damages claim, overlaps with prior proceedings, and rests on constantly changing pleadings?

Do the pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action for Charter damages, having regard to the statutory immunity of the Provincial Health Officer under s. 92 of the Public Health Act, the appropriateness of Charter damages, and the substantive requirements of ss. 2(c)/(d), 7, 9 and 15 of the Charter?

Does the proposed proceeding satisfy the five certification requirements under s. 4(1) of the Class Proceedings Act (cause of action, identifiable class, common issues, preferable procedure, appropriate representative plaintiff)?
Should the plaintiff's application to amend its notice of civil claim (the June 2023 FANCC) be allowed?

firac.issue: Should the claim be struck as an abuse of process and as disclosing no reasonable cause of action?
firac.facts: The Society challenged some 50-70 COVID-19 orders made under the Emergency Program Act, Public Health Act and COVID-19 Related Measures Act, seeking both declarations that the orders be set aside as unreasonable/ultra vires and s. 24(1) Charter damages. It had already brought two other petitions (the Gatherings Petition, dismissed, and the Health Workers Petition, discontinued) against Dr. Henry over the same orders. The pleadings were amended eight times, including after the certification hearing, and were replete with argument and rhetorical matter (e.g. the Hippocratic Oath).
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim, are vexatious, or are an abuse of process; the test under (a) is whether it is 'plain and obvious' the claim cannot succeed (Hunt v. Carey; Imperial Tobacco). A civil action that in essential character seeks to invalidate administrative decisions is an impermissible collateral attack and must proceed by judicial review (TeleZone; Greengen; Scow; Weisenburger). Multiplicity of proceedings and relitigation can constitute abuse of process (Métis Nation; Toronto (City) v. CUPE).
firac.application: The court found the claim's essential character was an administrative challenge to the government's pandemic measures, dressed as a Charter damages action to bypass the deferential judicial review process; the plaintiff was not content to let the decisions stand. The overlapping prior petitions, the constantly mutating pleadings (following White v. Glaxosmithkline), and the persistently vexatious, unparticularised pleadings each independently amounted to abuse of process. Hoogerbrug and Warner BCCA had already decided key issues (reasonableness of the emergency, s. 7 and s. 2 claims), rendering the claim bound to fail.
firac.conclusion: The claim was struck in its entirety as an abuse of process and as disclosing no reasonable cause of action.

firac.issue: Do the pleadings disclose a viable claim for Charter damages given s. 92 immunity and the Ward/Power framework?
firac.facts: The plaintiff sought s. 24(1) Charter damages from the Province and the Health Officer for alleged breaches of ss. 2(c)/(d), 7, 9 and 15, with a proposed aggregate damages scheme funded by the public payable back to the public (all adult British Columbians).
firac.rule: PHA s. 92 immunises a health officer from damages proceedings absent bad faith (Ernst v. Alberta Energy Regulator). Charter damages require the four-step Ward/Power analysis; countervailing factors such as the availability of judicial review and good-governance concerns can render damages inappropriate. Section 7 protects fundamental personal choices, not economic/lifestyle interests (Malmo-Levine; Godbout; Siemens); vaccination requirements do not engage s. 7 (Hoogerbrug; Maddock); s. 9 requires arbitrary detention (Spencer); s. 15 requires a distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground (Corbiere; Beaudoin).
firac.application: It was plain and obvious s. 92 barred any damages claim against the Health Officer, no bad faith being pleaded. Charter damages failed at the third Ward/Power step: judicial review was a more effective and appropriate remedy, good governance weighed against damages, and awarding damages to a class of all adults would be circular. The individual Charter claims were foreclosed by binding authority and lacked material facts: access to bars/restaurants and choice to remain unvaccinated do not engage s. 7; no arbitrary detention arose; requiring a second dose sooner was not an analogous ground under s. 15; and even proven breaches would be justified under s. 1 per Beaudoin BCCA and Hoogerbrug.
firac.conclusion: No viable Charter damages claim was disclosed against the Health Officer or the Province; the constitutional claims were bound to fail.

firac.issue: Does the proposed proceeding meet the s. 4(1) certification requirements?
firac.facts: The proposed class was all adult British Columbians (~4 million) in three subclasses (medical, vaccination, religious), with 26 proposed common issues, the corporate Society (later three individuals) as representative plaintiff, and a boilerplate litigation plan.
firac.rule: Section 4(1) requires all five conditions: a cause of action, an identifiable class of two or more, common issues, preferable procedure, and an appropriate representative plaintiff who can fairly represent the class and provide a workable litigation plan (Hollick; Dutton; Pro-Sys; AIC Limited). The court is a gatekeeper (Kett; Babstock). Charter claims requiring individualised inquiry are rarely certifiable (Thorburn; Ewert; Monaco; KO; Dang).
firac.application: The claim disclosed no cause of action (s. 4(1)(a)); the class and subclasses were simultaneously vague and overbroad (s. 4(1)(b)); the Charter and damages issues required individualised inquiry into each member's harm, causation and reasons, so no genuine common issues advanced the claim (s. 4(1)(c)); aggregate damages were unworkable; individual issues overwhelmingly predominated, making a class proceeding neither efficient nor preferable and duplicative of other proceedings (s. 4(1)(d)); and the corporate Society could not meet s. 2(4), while the proposed individuals, the boilerplate plan, missed deadlines and inexperienced sole counsel showed inadequacy (s. 4(1)(e)).
firac.conclusion: The plaintiff failed to establish any of the five s. 4(1) requirements; certification would have been refused in any event.

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's application to amend be allowed?
firac.facts: After eight versions of the claim, the plaintiff sought to amend to the June 2023 FANCC delivered six weeks after the certification hearing, on which the defendants had not made submissions.
firac.rule: Amendments are generally allowed unless they fail to disclose a cause of action or cause non-compensable prejudice (Peterson v. 446690 B.C. Ltd.); leave to amend may be refused where the pleading is fundamentally deficient and the plaintiff has had ample opportunity to 'get it right' (WCB v. Sort; Sandhu).
firac.application: Even considering the proposed FANCC, the claim remained deficient on every s. 4(1) requirement and the strike grounds. The late amendments prejudiced the defendants, whose submissions predated them, and the plaintiff had had eight opportunities and years to formulate a proper claim while ignoring court warnings.
firac.conclusion: The application to amend was denied.

case_name: El Khatib v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)

name_verification.name_in_document: HAISAM EL KHATIB v. THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Was the RAD's conclusion that the applicant had no serious possibility of persecution in the proposed internal flight alternative (Zahlé) reasonable?
Did the RAD unreasonably fail to consider country condition and other evidence contradicting its conclusions?
Was the RAD's assessment of the second prong of the IFA test (whether relocation was unreasonable or unduly harsh) reasonable in light of the Israel–Lebanon conflict?

firac.issue: Was the RAD's conclusion that the applicant faced no serious possibility of persecution in the proposed internal flight alternative of Zahlé reasonable?
firac.facts: Mr. El Khatib, a Lebanese Sunni Muslim who converted to Christianity and whose son converted to Judaism, claimed he would face antisemitic and religious persecution anywhere in Lebanon. The RPD and RAD found Zahlé, a majority-Christian city, to be a viable IFA. He argued the true agent of persecution was Lebanese society as a whole, and pointed to an attack by masked men, a 2023 antisemitic attack on his son in Tripoli, and country condition evidence.
firac.rule: Once an IFA is proposed, the claimant bears the onus of showing it is not viable (Thirunavukkarasu v Canada, 1993 CanLII 3011 (FCA)). The two-prong test requires (1) no serious possibility of persecution in the IFA, and (2) that relocation not be unreasonable or unduly harsh (Rasaratnam v Canada, 1991 CanLII 13517 (FCA)). The standard of review is reasonableness (Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65). Claimants are expected to take reasonable steps to reduce risk (Sanchez v Canada, 2007 FCA 99).
firac.application: The RAD considered and rejected both that the Ras Nahash community would pursue him and that Lebanese society as a whole posed a risk. The Court found the asserted risk depended on the inference that people would inevitably discover his son's conversion, which was not inevitable; his son had already deleted public Facebook posts, and expecting the applicant to take similar steps did not equate to living in hiding or concealing a core component of identity. The 2023 Tripoli attack did not necessarily extend to the IFA, and the risk from Hezbollah was speculative absent evidence of direct targeting in Zahlé.
firac.conclusion: The RAD's conclusion that there was no serious possibility of persecution in Zahlé was reasonable.

firac.issue: Did the RAD unreasonably fail to consider country condition and other evidence contradicting its conclusions?
firac.facts: The applicant argued the RAD ignored country condition evidence about antisemitism and persecution of Christian converts in Lebanon, and evidence of risk from Hezbollah and extremist groups.
firac.rule: The RAD is presumed to have considered all evidence, and failure to mention a particular item is not by itself an error (Penez v Canada, 2017 FC 1001; Cepeda-Gutierrez, 1998 CanLII 8667 (FC)). However, failing to address evidence that directly contradicts a material conclusion may show the decision was unresponsive (Pantoja v Canada, 2022 FC 1790; Vavilov at para 126).
firac.application: The Court found the unmentioned evidence did not directly contradict the RAD's findings; indeed, several country condition documents, read in full, undermined the applicant's position and suggested relative inter-sectarian harmony in most urban communities, including an article about a Christian convert fleeing to Lebanon for safety. The applicant's materials contained sweeping generalizations rather than proof of a serious risk throughout Lebanon.
firac.conclusion: The RAD did not err by not specifically referring to this evidence; its treatment of the record was reasonable.

firac.issue: Was the RAD's assessment that relocation to Zahlé was not unreasonable or unduly harsh reasonable, given the Israel–Lebanon conflict?
firac.facts: The applicant submitted evidence of Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon in 2024, including near Zahlé, arguing this made the IFA unduly harsh.
firac.rule: The second prong of the IFA test asks whether relocation would be unreasonable or unduly harsh in all the claimant's circumstances (Rasaratnam). Generalized country danger is distinct from the persecution ground of a refugee claim and may instead be relevant to a subsequent risk or humanitarian assessment.
firac.application: The Court noted the claim rested on religious persecution, not general danger. The evidence showed airstrikes struck Zahlé on one particular day in 2024, and it was open to the RAD, on a forward-looking basis, to find Zahlé remained a reasonable IFA. Ongoing conflict risk might be relevant to a later assessment but did not displace the RAD's conclusions.
firac.conclusion: The RAD's second-prong finding was reasonable; the airstrike evidence did not render the IFA unduly harsh.

defining_issues: Did the incompetence of the applicant's former counsel—particularly leaving him to draft his own deficient PIF narrative without guidance—result in a breach of natural justice sufficient to quash the RPD decision?
Was the RPD's credibility finding that the applicant is not Roma, based on his physical appearance, reasonable?

firac.issue: Did the incompetence of former counsel amount to a breach of procedural fairness/natural justice warranting quashing the RPD decision?
firac.facts: The applicant, a Hungarian Roma claimant, was left by the law office of Mr. Hohots to write his own PIF narrative, a short general paragraph, without being told what a PIF narrative required, without translation of the Question 31 instructions, and without advice to add detail even when he inquired. Counsel Mr. Uppal met him only briefly before the hearing. The RPD refused the claim for lack of credible basis, relying heavily on omissions between the PIF and the oral testimony. The applicant complained to the Law Society; former counsel denied the allegations and blamed the applicant's lack of diligence.
firac.rule: To establish a breach of fairness based on incompetent counsel the applicant must: (a) give notice to former counsel and provide an opportunity to respond; (b) establish that the act or omission constituted incompetence without the wisdom of hindsight; and (c) establish that the outcome would have been different / that the reliability of the result was compromised (R. v G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22; Memari; El Kaissi). The threshold is very high and only 'extraordinary' cases qualify (El Ghazaly). Procedural fairness is reviewed on correctness (Sketchley; Baker; CUPE).
firac.application: The Court held that regardless of the disputed evidence, the inadequacies on the face of the PIF narrative were undisputed and supported the applicant's account that he was left to prepare this critical document alone without guidance on what the RPD expected. Competent counsel would have known the narrative did not comply with RPD expectations and was 'a negative credibility finding waiting to happen.' The RPD's negative credibility findings—addressing each incident of persecution and then noting its omission from the PIF—permeated the whole decision. The applicant showed he could have adduced further evidence had he been properly guided. The Court found this an extraordinary case, akin to El Kaissi and Memari, where incompetent representation was serious enough to compromise the reliability of the decision.
firac.conclusion: There was a breach of natural justice; the incompetence of counsel compromised the RPD decision. Application allowed.

firac.issue: Was the RPD's finding that the applicant is not Roma, based on his skin colour and physical appearance, reasonable?
firac.facts: The RPD found the applicant lacking in credibility and additionally noted he had 'white skin' and dark hair, whereas Roma are stereotypically identified by dark skin pigmentation, concluding on a balance of probabilities he was not Roma. The applicant argued this relied on stereotype and racial profiling (citing Szostak, Pluhar, Vodics, Kotkova).
firac.rule: Credibility findings are reviewed on reasonableness (Aguebor; Dunsmuir). Findings of ethnicity must be based on evidence, not on generalizations, stereotyping or racial profiling; sworn testimony of ethnicity is presumed truthful and cannot be rebutted by stereotypical assumptions (Vodics; Kotkova; Pluhar; Szostak).
firac.application: The Court, having found a determinative breach of procedural fairness on the counsel-incompetence issue, held there was no point in considering the remaining issues further, being convinced the matter had to be sent back for reconsideration.
firac.conclusion: Not decided; the Court declined to address this issue given the disposition on the first issue.

name_verification.name_in_document: GHILAD PAZ v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Did the RAD err in its assessment of and refusal to admit the applicant's new evidence on appeal?
Did the RAD err in declining to hold an oral hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA?
Did the RAD reasonably conclude that adequate state protection was available to the applicant in Israel?

firac.issue: Did the RAD err in its assessment of and refusal to admit the applicant's new evidence on appeal?
firac.facts: Paz, an Israeli BDS activist, submitted numerous new articles to the RAD without following the procedure in Rules 29 and 37 of the RAD Rules or explaining how the evidence met s. 110(4) of the IRPA. The RAD admitted some articles bearing directly on state protection for left-wing activists and rejected or did not admit others.
firac.rule: Under s. 110(4) of the IRPA and Rules 29/37 of the RAD Rules, an appellant must request authorization to file new evidence, support it by affidavit, and explain how it meets the newness/relevance requirements (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Singh, 2016 FCA 96; Galamb v Canada, 2016 FC 1230). A decision-maker need not mention every piece of evidence. Reasonableness applies (Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65).
firac.application: The applicant failed to make the required submissions demonstrating newness and relevance. Following Galamb, the RAD acted within the range of acceptable outcomes; indeed it admitted some evidence despite the procedural default. A decision-maker is not required to reference every document to show it was considered.
firac.conclusion: The RAD's assessment of the new evidence was reasonable.

firac.issue: Did the RAD err in declining to hold an oral hearing?
firac.facts: The applicant initially did not request a hearing but later asked for one regarding the admissibility of new evidence. The RAD found the new evidence raised a credibility issue but was not central to the claim and did not contain sufficient information about Israel's ability to protect its citizens.
firac.rule: Section 110(3) IRPA directs the RAD to proceed on the RPD record; s. 110(6) permits a hearing only where new evidence raises a serious credibility issue, is central to the claim, and would justify allowing or rejecting it — and even then the RAD retains discretion not to hold one. Reasonableness applies.
firac.application: The importance of the underlying free-speech issues is irrelevant to the s. 110(6) analysis. The applicant made no submissions relating his evidence to the s. 110(6) criteria, and the RAD thoroughly assessed the statutory test, finding the evidence not central and insufficient on state protection.
firac.conclusion: The RAD's decision not to hold a hearing was reasonable.

firac.issue: Did the RAD reasonably conclude that adequate state protection was available to the applicant in Israel?
firac.facts: Paz claimed fear of persecution by Israeli officials and citizens due to his BDS activism, pointing to ministerial threats, anti-boycott legislation, attacks on activists, and his father's job loss. He left Israel before any sanction was taken against him and never sought protection from Israeli authorities.
firac.rule: A state is presumed capable of protecting its citizens absent a complete breakdown of state apparatus; the claimant must rebut this with clear and convincing evidence and must exhaust all objectively reasonable avenues of protection, with a higher burden in more democratic states (Canada (AG) v Ward, [1993] 2 SCR 689; Hinzman v Canada, 2007 FCA 171; Komatsia v Canada, 2017 FC 695). Reasonableness applies (Dunsmuir; Vavilov).
firac.application: Israel is a democratic state with civilian control of security forces, independent judges, and administrative/legal remedies available to those whose rights are violated. Despite concerning treatment of dissidents and anti-BDS laws, the applicant never personally sought and was refused state protection, having left pre-emptively before any measures were taken against him. The Court will not re-weigh the evidence; the RAD applied the correct jurisprudence.
firac.conclusion: The RAD reasonably found the applicant failed to rebut the presumption of state protection; the application for judicial review is dismissed and no question is certified.

Anti-Zionism (K056) was considered but boycott/BDS is more precise.

name_verification.name_in_document: XXXX XXXX (RPD File No. TA9-06911)

defining_issues: Did the claimant provide sufficient credible evidence to establish her allegations of anti-Semitic persecution in Ukraine?
Did the claimant rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence?
Is the claimant a Convention refugee under s. 96 or a person in need of protection under s. 97(1) of the IRPA?

firac.issue: Did the claimant provide sufficient credible evidence to establish her allegations of anti-Semitic persecution in Ukraine?
firac.facts: The claimant, a Ukrainian citizen with a Jewish mother, alleged she suffered insults, discrimination, harassment and physical abuse in her small hometown because she was known to be Jewish. Yet she remained in that town for nine years (1999–2008) before moving, waited two years to relocate after a 2006 attack, and submitted a medical certificate and police report that did not correspond to incidents in her narrative and lacked official letterheads (using only rubber stamps).
firac.rule: Assessing evidence and testimony and determining the probative value to be attached to them falls within the Board's purview (Peti v. M.C.I., 2012 FC 82). The RPD need not confront a claimant with every inconsistency or implausibility, particularly where she is represented by counsel (Mahdoon v. M.C.I., 2011 FC 284). Country condition documentation confirmed the widespread availability of fraudulent medical and police reports in Ukraine.
firac.application: The panel found the claim of persecution implausible given the claimant's nine-year continued residence in a town where everyone allegedly knew she was Jewish, and her explanation for the two-year delay in moving contradicted her accounts of ongoing threats and assaults. The police report referred to no incident in her narrative and was given no probative value; the hospital's refusal to provide a report for one incident while issuing one two months later for another was unexplained. The absence of printed letterheads, combined with documented prevalence of fraudulent documents in Ukraine, led the panel to give the medical and police reports no weight and to draw a negative inference over the totality of the evidence.
firac.conclusion: The claimant did not provide sufficient credible evidence to support her allegations; the panel drew a negative credibility inference casting doubt on her entire claim.

firac.issue: Did the claimant rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence?
firac.facts: The claimant complained to local police about anti-Semitic acts but received no assistance. She did not approach higher police authorities or other agencies such as the prosecutor's office, testifying she believed any complaint would simply be referred back to local authorities, based on hearsay within her small town rather than personal knowledge.
firac.rule: There is a presumption that a democratic state can protect its nationals; the burden of proving ineffectiveness lies with the claimant (Villafranca; Baku v. M.C.I., 2010 FC 1163; Gutierrez v. M.C.I., 2009 FC 487). No state guarantees perfect protection (Zalzali; Villafranca), and the mere fact that a state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption where the state effectively controls its territory and makes serious efforts to protect citizens.
firac.application: The claimant's failure to seek assistance from higher authorities did not constitute an adequate search for state protection in a democratic state. Her belief that further complaints would be futile rested on hearsay, not personal knowledge. Country documentation showed Ukrainian officials prosecuting anti-Semitic acts, senior politicians speaking out against extremism, and security services acting to prevent hate crimes, demonstrating serious state efforts.
firac.conclusion: The claimant did not rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.

firac.issue: Is the claimant a Convention refugee under s. 96 or a person in need of protection under s. 97(1) of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The claimant sought protection based on fear of anti-Semitic persecution in Ukraine. Country documentation showed declining numbers of anti-Semitic incidents relative to a substantial Jewish population, ongoing governmental efforts to combat anti-Semitism, and a thriving Jewish community.
firac.rule: Sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA require, respectively, a serious possibility of persecution and, on a balance of probabilities, a personal risk to life, risk of cruel and unusual treatment/punishment, or danger of torture.
firac.application: Given the panel's credibility findings, the failure to rebut state protection, the relatively low number of anti-Semitic incidents against a Jewish population of 103,600 to 370,000, and the government's efforts to prosecute and combat anti-Semitism, the panel found no serious possibility of persecution and no personal risk on a balance of probabilities. No evidence supported a danger of torture under s. 97(1)(a).
firac.conclusion: The claimant is neither a Convention refugee under s. 96 nor a person in need of protection under s. 97(1); the claim was rejected.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) capture the core s. 96 claim of feared anti-Semitic persecution. K080 (state protection) is central to the second issue and the decisive analysis. K025 (freedom of religion) is a borderline pick — the claim relates to Jewish nationality/ethnicity more than religious practice, but it is a reasonable tag given the anti-Semitic religious dimension. Credibility was central but no controlled-vocabulary keyword captures it directly.

name_verification.name_in_document: [no public name] (RPD File No. TB0-14758 / TB0-14759)

defining_issues: Did the claimants provide credible and reliable evidence establishing the alleged persecution based on the male claimant's Jewish background?
Did the mistreatment experienced by the claimants in Russia rise to the level of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA?
Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence?
Are the claimants persons in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA?

firac.issue: Was the claimants' evidence of persecution credible and reliable?
firac.facts: The male claimant, Jewish on his father's side, alleged a lifetime of mistreatment in Russia culminating in assaults in 2010. His hearing testimony diverged from his PIF narrative on key points: whether the 2010 attackers were nationalists issuing a 'last warning', whether he received medical treatment, whether police were called, and whether a 2008 attack was reported to police. He could not describe the content of a radio advertisement he allegedly placed to start a Jewish mixed-marriage group and provided no documentary support for its registration or a police report from a 1995 assault.
firac.rule: A refugee claimant must provide credible and trustworthy evidence to support the allegations underlying the claim; material inconsistencies between the PIF narrative and oral testimony, and unexplained absence of reasonably available corroboration, may support adverse credibility findings.
firac.application: The panel identified multiple material discrepancies between the narrative and oral testimony regarding the most serious and determinative 2010 incident, rejected the claimant's explanations (confusion, trying to forget), found the account of the radio group effort not credible given the absence of documentation and inability to recall the ad, and found the failure to report or corroborate other incidents unreliable. The panel concluded central allegations were fabricated or exaggerated to embellish the claim.
firac.conclusion: Much of the evidence of serious harm was found unreliable; the panel accepted only that the male claimant is part Jewish and suffered insults, vandalism and graffiti.

firac.issue: Did the accepted mistreatment amount to persecution under section 96?
firac.facts: What remained after credibility findings was a history of insults, ostracism, graffiti on the apartment/car, and vandalism of the grandfather's tombstone. The male claimant completed a college education (though not his first-choice university) and held several jobs; his non-Jewish wife worked in human resources without adverse treatment.
firac.rule: Discrimination amounts to persecution only where it is sufficiently serious, cumulatively or otherwise, to deny or seriously undermine fundamental human rights.
firac.application: The panel found the claimant was able to obtain education and employment, the alleged job losses were not shown to be due to his Jewish background (one being linked to refusing extortion, another recorded as a voluntary departure), and no fundamental human right was denied. Even cumulatively, the mistreatment, while difficult, did not reach the threshold of persecution.
firac.conclusion: The mistreatment did not rise to the level of persecution.

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection?
firac.facts: Russia is a functioning democratic state. The claimants reported vandalism of the tombstone and car damage to police and were dissatisfied with the responses; other incidents were not reported, in one case because an attacker's brother was a police officer. Documentary evidence showed Russia making serious efforts against anti-Semitism, prosecutions of offenders, and declining vandalism figures (30 acts in 2007 to 8 in 2010).
firac.rule: A state is presumed capable of protecting its citizens absent complete breakdown (Ward); the claimant must rebut this with clear and convincing evidence that protection is inadequate, and the burden increases with the state's level of democracy (Villafranca, Kadenko, Flores Carillo). Adequacy, not perfection, is the test.
firac.application: The panel found the police responses reflected practical realities (unknown perpetrators) rather than unwillingness to protect; subjective fear was not a valid basis to avoid reporting; and the documentary record showed serious and improving state efforts to combat anti-Semitism, especially in larger centres like Moscow and St. Petersburg. The claimants had not exhausted reasonable avenues.
firac.conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence; state protection was determinative against the section 96 claim.

firac.issue: Are the claimants persons in need of protection under section 97?
firac.facts: The claimants were not denied education, health care, or a means of existence, and no reliable residual evidence supported a personalized risk to life or of cruel treatment or torture.
firac.rule: Section 97(1) IRPA requires a claimant to establish, on a balance of probabilities, a personal risk to life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture on return.
firac.application: The state-protection analysis applied equally, and there was no reliable residual evidence upon which a section 97 claim could rest.
firac.conclusion: The claimants are not persons in need of protection under section 97.

case_name: Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia

name_verification.name_in_document: Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia

defining_issues: Does the Canadian citizenship requirement for admission to the British Columbia bar under s. 42 of the Barristers and Solicitors Act infringe the equality rights guaranteed by s. 15(1) of the Charter?
What is the proper approach to interpreting s. 15(1) and the meaning of 'discrimination', including whether citizenship is a ground analogous to those enumerated?
If s. 15(1) is infringed, is the citizenship requirement a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter?

firac.issue: Does the Canadian citizenship requirement for admission to the British Columbia bar infringe s. 15(1) of the Charter?
firac.facts: Andrews, a British subject permanently resident in Canada, met all requirements for admission to the B.C. bar except Canadian citizenship. Section 42 of the Barristers and Solicitors Act limited call to the bar to Canadian citizens. Co-respondent Kinersly, an American permanent resident articling in B.C., was similarly affected. Permanent residents had to wait at least three years to acquire citizenship.
firac.rule: Section 15(1) guarantees equality before and under the law and equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination. Discrimination is a distinction, intentional or not, based on grounds relating to personal characteristics of an individual or group, which imposes burdens or withholds benefits not imposed on others. A complainant must show unequal treatment or differential impact plus that the distinction is discriminatory on an enumerated or analogous ground.
firac.application: Section 42 draws a distinction between citizens and non-citizens, barring an entire class of otherwise qualified permanent residents from the practice of law solely on the basis of citizenship status, without regard to their merits or qualifications. Non-citizens permanently resident in Canada are a 'discrete and insular minority' lacking political power. Citizenship is a personal characteristic largely beyond the individual's control and analogous to the enumerated grounds. The requirement imposes a real burden of delay and exclusion.
firac.conclusion: The citizenship requirement infringes s. 15(1); the first constitutional question is answered yes.

firac.issue: What is the proper approach to s. 15(1) and the meaning of discrimination, and is citizenship an analogous ground?
firac.facts: The courts below adopted differing tests: the trial judge used an 'irrelevant personal characteristic/irrationality' test; the Court of Appeal (McLachlin J.A.) built reasonableness into s. 15(1) itself via a 'similarly situated' fair-minded analysis. Professor Hogg advocated treating every legal distinction as a breach shunted to s. 1.
firac.rule: The Court rejects the 'similarly situated' test as deficient (it could justify discriminatory laws) and rejects both the 'every distinction' approach and building justification into s. 15(1). It adopts the 'enumerated and analogous grounds' approach: s. 15(1) prohibits distinctions involving prejudice or disadvantage based on enumerated or analogous grounds; justification is reserved for s. 1. The two steps must be kept analytically distinct because of the different burdens of proof (citizen proves infringement; state justifies).
firac.application: Discrimination principles developed under Human Rights Acts (O'Malley, Action Travail des Femmes) apply to s. 15(1), but the enumerated grounds are non-exhaustive and include analogous grounds. Non-citizenship is a personal characteristic sharing the features of the enumerated grounds — typically immutable, politically powerless group, historically subject to discrimination — and thus qualifies as an analogous ground.
firac.conclusion: The enumerated-and-analogous-grounds approach governs s. 15(1); citizenship is an analogous ground, so the exclusion of non-citizens falls within s. 15(1)'s protection.

firac.issue: Is the citizenship requirement a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The Law Society and Attorney General justified the requirement on three grounds: that citizenship ensures familiarity with Canadian institutions and customs; implies commitment to Canadian society; and that lawyers play a role in the governance of the country warranting citizenship.
firac.rule: Section 1 requires the objective to be pressing and substantial and the means to satisfy proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, and effects not outweighing the objective): R. v. Oakes; R. v. Edwards Books. The state bears the onus of justification, an onerous burden where the discrimination targets disadvantaged groups.
firac.application: Per the majority (Wilson, La Forest JJ.), the objectives are not achieved by the citizenship requirement: citizenship does not ensure familiarity with Canadian institutions (natural-born Canadians may live abroad) or commitment (non-citizens may be deeply committed; an oath of allegiance is available), and the practice of law is primarily a private profession not requiring citizenship. Less drastic means (residence, training, examinations, declaration of intent) exist, making the requirement over-inclusive and failing rational connection/minimal impairment. McIntyre and Lamer JJ. dissented, viewing the requirement as reasonable given lawyers' role in the administration of justice and the modest three-year maximum delay.
firac.conclusion: By majority the requirement is not justified under s. 1; the second constitutional question is answered no. Appeal dismissed (McIntyre and Lamer JJ. dissenting).

name_verification.name_in_document: DMITRI ZLOBINSKI and THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Did the PRRA Tribunal breach procedural fairness by relying on extrinsic documentary evidence about changed country conditions that post-dated the applicant's submissions without disclosing it or inviting further submissions?

firac.issue: Did the Tribunal breach procedural fairness by failing to disclose extrinsic documentary evidence on changed country conditions that became available only after the applicant filed his PRRA submissions?
firac.facts: The applicant, a Ukrainian citizen of Jewish ancestry with a history of drug-related convictions, was ordered deported and made a PRRA application claiming risk of persecution and mistreatment in Ukraine. The Tribunal conducted independent internet research and relied on three documents (two US State Department reports and an Overseas Security Advisory Council 2006 Crime and Safety Report). Two of the three documents post-dated the applicant's November 2005 submissions; only one (the International Religious Freedom Report) was available at that time. The Tribunal did not disclose these sources or invite further submissions before rejecting the PRRA.
firac.rule: Where questions of procedural fairness are engaged, no pragmatic and functional analysis is required (Dr. Q v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia, [2003] 1 S.C.R. 226; C.U.P.E. v. Ontario (Minister of Labour), [2003] 1 S.C.R. 539). Under Mancia v. Canada (M.C.I.), [1998] F.C.J. No. 565 (F.C.A.), fairness requires disclosure of documents relied on regarding general country conditions that became available after an applicant's submissions only where they are novel and significant and evidence changes in general country conditions that may affect the decision.
firac.application: The Court found the applicant's argument failed. The second document was available when the applicant made his final submissions. The remaining information relied on was not novel: the anti-Semitism material was public, did not indicate a significant change in country conditions or that anti-Semitism was systematic or widespread, and addressed the 2005 situation—the same year the applicant applied. The narcotics/drug-crime evidence was likewise not novel, reflecting an ongoing and growing problem and a government policy in place since 2003. Because the undisclosed evidence was not determinative and not novel or significant within the meaning of Mancia, disclosure was not required.
firac.conclusion: No breach of procedural fairness occurred; the Tribunal's decision was reasonable with no reviewable error.
