registry_rationale: No specific court registry is stated in the decision; the SCC file number (23188) is given but no registry office.

case_name: Thomson Newspapers Co. v. Canada (Attorney General)

name_verification.name_in_document: Thomson Newspapers Co. v. Canada (Attorney General)

defining_issues: Does s. 322.1 of the Canada Elections Act, which prohibits publication, broadcast or dissemination of opinion survey results during the final three days of a federal election campaign, infringe freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter?
If s. 322.1 infringes s. 2(b), is that infringement a reasonable limit demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society under s. 1 of the Charter?
Does s. 322.1 infringe the right to vote guaranteed by s. 3 of the Charter?

firac.issue: Does the prohibition on publishing opinion survey results in the final three days of a federal election campaign infringe freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter?
firac.facts: Section 322.1 of the Canada Elections Act bars broadcasting, publishing or disseminating opinion survey results respecting how electors will vote or an election issue from midnight the Friday before polling day until the close of all polling stations. Newspaper publishers challenged the provision. The Attorney General conceded the prima facie infringement.
firac.rule: Under the Irwin Toy test, any activity that conveys or attempts to convey meaning falls within s. 2(b), and a law restricting such expression infringes the guarantee (Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (A.G.), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 927; R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697).
firac.application: Publication of opinion survey results is an activity that conveys meaning and therefore falls within the ambit of s. 2(b). By prohibiting broadcast, publication or dissemination of poll results in the final three days, s. 322.1 restricts that expression. The Court interpreted the ban to apply only to 'new' poll results undisclosed as of the Friday midnight, allowing discussion of previously released polls.
firac.conclusion: Section 322.1 infringes s. 2(b) of the Charter; this was conceded and the Court agreed.

firac.issue: Is the infringement of freedom of expression justified as a reasonable limit under s. 1 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The government advanced as its sole objective before the Court the prevention of the distorting effect of opinion polls released late in a campaign when there is insufficient time to respond. Social science evidence (the Lortie Commission, the Lachapelle Study) was inconclusive about the actual influence of polls. Alternatives such as mandatory disclosure of methodological information without a ban (adopted in B.C.) existed.
firac.rule: The Oakes test (R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103) requires a pressing and substantial objective and proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, and balance of salutary and deleterious effects), applied with close attention to context; the civil standard of proof applies (RJR-MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (A.G.), [1995] 3 S.C.R. 199; Dagenais v. CBC, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 835). Deference depends on factors including the vulnerability of the protected group and the nature of the expression.
firac.application: The 'rest period' objective was not pressing and substantial, but guarding against inaccurate late-campaign polls by allowing scrutiny was. The ban was rationally connected only to a limited degree, since s. 322.1 did not require publication of methodological information. It failed minimal impairment: voters are not a vulnerable group; they are rational actors exposed to numerous polls; the ban was both overbroad (banning accurate polls) and underbroad (not disabusing voters of polls lacking methodology). A less intrusive equally effective alternative—mandatory disclosure of methodology without a ban—was unexplained. On final balancing, the profound impact of a complete ban on political information at a crucial time outweighed the speculative, marginal benefits, since the government cannot take the most naive voter as the constitutional standard.
firac.conclusion: The infringement is not justified under s. 1; s. 322.1 is of no force or effect (majority per Bastarache J.). The dissent (Gonthier J., with Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé J.) would have upheld it as a reasonable limit.

firac.issue: Does s. 322.1 infringe the right to vote under s. 3 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The appellants argued the partial poll ban deprived voters of information relevant to exercising their vote, hindering the electoral process. Poll information was said to assist strategic voters.
firac.rule: Section 3 guarantees the right to 'effective representation' (Reference re Provincial Electoral Boundaries (Sask.), [1991] 2 S.C.R. 158). A restriction on information infringes s. 3 only if it undermines the guarantee of effective representation.
firac.application: The majority found it unnecessary to decide the informational content of s. 3 given its conclusion under s. 2(b), and left the issue aside because the evidence linking the banned information and electoral integrity was too sparse. The dissent held the short blackout does not undermine effective representation—indeed it assists it, since a strategic vote cannot be meaningfully cast on information that cannot be scrutinized in time.
firac.conclusion: The majority made no ruling on s. 3; the dissent found no infringement of s. 3. The courts below likewise found no s. 3 violation.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the primary tier-1 area, as the case concerns Charter validity of an elections statute. K024 (freedom of expression) is the core right at issue under s. 2(b), and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) is the specific provision engaged. K030 (reasonable limits (s.1)/Oakes test) captures the decisive proportionality analysis. K107 (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms) applies as the governing instrument. K002 (Civil litigation) is a weaker/borderline pick reflecting the declaratory application procedure but is the closest available civil-procedure tier-1 for the remedy sought. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is a weak/borderline pick — the case involved declaratory relief rather than an injunction, so it is flagged as not strongly applicable; it is included to reach the minimum. Right-to-vote (s. 3) has no dedicated keyword in the vocabulary, so it is captured under the Charter/constitutional keywords.

registry_rationale: No court registry is stated in the decision; the SCC identifies only the file number (25593), not a registry office.

name_verification.name_in_document: XXXX XXXX (a.k.a XXXX XXXX) — RAD File TB8-25520

defining_issues: Did the RPD/RAD err in finding the Appellant not credible, in particular in giving no weight to the PSB summons as a fraudulent document?
Even if the Appellant is a Pentecostal Christian, is there a serious possibility that he would be persecuted for practising Christianity if returned to Guangdong Province, China?

firac.issue: Was the RPD correct to place no weight on the PSB summons and to find the Appellant not credible regarding being wanted by the Chinese authorities?
firac.facts: The Appellant alleged he attended the unregistered Olive Tree Church, was detained in a March 2017 raid, later questioned by the Foshan PSB, and was issued a summons after leaving China. He mailed supporting documents (Hukou, RIC, birth certificate, summons, Administrative Punishment decision) to Canada in one envelope whose postage date predated a birth certificate it allegedly contained.
firac.rule: On appeal the RAD applies the correctness standard per Canada (M.C.I.) v. Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93. Per Jiang v. Canada, 2018 FC 1064, authenticity of a document may be questioned based on small or microscopic differences from an authentic counterpart; per the China NDP (item 9.10), summonses have not varied in format since 2003 and no regional variations exist. Submitting a fraudulent document damages credibility and may undermine related documents (Uddin 2002 FCT 451; Gochez).
firac.application: The RAD found the Appellant's explanation for the envelope/birth-certificate date inconsistency unreasonable, as he was shown that very document when questioned. Comparing the summons to the NDP sample, the RAD identified formatting, spacing and language differences (Chinese vs English date, line placement) showing it was fraudulent. Reliance on a fraudulent summons damaged his credibility and undermined the interrelated Administrative Punishment decision, on which no weight could be placed.
firac.conclusion: The RAD found on a balance of probabilities that the summons was fraudulent, that the Appellant never attended the Olive Tree Church and was not being investigated or wanted by the PSB; it therefore declined to address the RPD's implausibility and subjective-fear findings that depended on him being wanted.

firac.issue: Would the Appellant face a serious possibility of persecution for practising Christianity as a Pentecostal Protestant if returned to Guangdong Province?
firac.facts: The Appellant claimed to be Pentecostal, attended a house church in China, and since arriving in Canada has attended the Living Stone Assembly and been baptized. The RPD had made errors impugning his religious knowledge and finding it implausible he would attend a house church.
firac.rule: Refugee protection under the IRPA requires a serious possibility of persecution. Country condition (NDP) evidence: Pentecostal Christians are not on the list of banned 'evil cults'; upwards of 23 million-plus Protestants worship at unregistered churches, often tolerated by local officials; the UK Home Office assesses risk to ordinary Christians as very low; Guangdong has traditionally been more tolerant.
firac.application: The RAD agreed the RPD erred on religious knowledge (bar is low; the Appellant was new to the faith) and on the house-church implausibility finding, but held these errors were not determinative. Reviewing NDP evidence on Guangdong and the Appellant's home area of Baiyun, Guangzhou, the RAD found the cited incidents were mostly from 2016 or earlier, unrelated to the Appellant, and few relative to the number of Christians worshipping in unregistered churches.
firac.conclusion: The RAD found on a balance of probabilities that the Appellant could practise his religion in the Christian congregation of his choice in Guangdong without a serious possibility of persecution.

case_name: Little Shuswap Lake Indian Band v. August-Sjodin

name_verification.name_in_document: Little Shuswap Lake Indian Band v. August-Sjodin
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The style of cause matches, but the supplied citation (2016 BCSC 1214) is the earlier injunction judgment of Justice Hyslop. This decision is the contempt ruling, correctly cited as 2020 BCSC 607. The supplied citation is therefore wrong for this decision.

defining_issues: Did the Band prove beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of civil contempt for the defendant's entry into the Quaaout Resort and Conference Centre in breach of the July 4, 2016 injunction?
Should special costs be awarded against the defendant for the contempt application?

firac.issue: Did the Band establish, to the criminal standard, that the defendant committed civil contempt by breaching Justice Hyslop's July 4, 2016 injunction on December 20 and 22, 2016?
firac.facts: On July 4, 2016 (2016 BCSC 1214), Justice Hyslop permanently restrained August-Sjodin, an OPCA/'freeman on the land' litigant, from entering the Quaaout Resort and Conference Centre. Written reasons were sent to him. Operations Manager Rhys Laug saw him inside the premises on December 22, 2016, spoke with him as he left (August-Sjodin asserting the court had no jurisdiction 'over these lands'), and confirmed his presence on December 20 and 22 via surveillance footage and signed pool waiver forms bearing one of the unique names he uses.
firac.rule: Civil contempt is quasi-criminal and must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt (Carey v. Laiken, 2015 SCC 17). Its three elements (Carey at paras. 32-35) are: (1) a court order that clearly and unequivocally states what must or must not be done; (2) actual knowledge of the order by the alleged contemnor (Pintea v. Johns, 2017 SCC 23; Rule 22-8(14) permits a finding on actual notice without service); and (3) the intentional doing of a prohibited act. The mens rea is wilful, not accidental, disobedience (North Vancouver (District) v. Sorrenti, 2004 BCCA 316); intention relates to the act, not the disobedience (TG Industries; MacMillan Bloedel). Strictissimi juris applies (Peel Financial; Bassette v. Maggee).
firac.application: Order 1(d) clearly and unequivocally barred entry to the Quaaout Resort and Conference Centre. The defendant had actual knowledge: the reasons were sent to him, and his statements to Laug and to the court confirmed awareness (he simply denied the court's jurisdiction). Laug's credible, reliable evidence—direct observation, surveillance footage, and signed waiver forms—proved that August-Sjodin entered the premises on both dates, remained for extended periods, used the pool, and made no attempt to hide his presence. His breaches were open, brazen and without lawful excuse.
firac.conclusion: All three elements were proven beyond a reasonable doubt; the defendant was found in contempt for both the December 20 and December 22, 2016 breaches.

firac.issue: Should the defendant pay special costs of the contempt application?
firac.facts: The defendant wilfully and flagrantly disobeyed the injunction on two occasions, remained unapologetic and defiant that he was not bound to comply, and forced the Band to bring this application to enforce its order.
firac.rule: A court may award special costs where a party's conduct is reprehensible; a party holding a court order is entitled to have it obeyed without incurring further expense.
firac.application: The defendant's repeated, open and unrepentant defiance, and the resulting damage to the Band and its members, made his conduct reprehensible and justified an elevated costs award.
firac.conclusion: Special costs of the application were awarded against the defendant, to be assessed.

name_verification.name_in_document: FARAJ HASAN ABED ALFATTAH SHARAWI v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Was the RPD's adverse credibility determination, based on inconsistencies between the applicant's Basis of Claim form and oral testimony and on his delay in claiming asylum, reasonable?
Did the RPD reasonably assess the country condition evidence in relation to the applicant's personal circumstances in refusing refugee protection?

firac.issue: Was the RPD's adverse credibility determination reasonable?
firac.facts: The stateless Palestinian applicant claimed fear of persecution in Hebron, West Bank. He had twice overstayed U.S. visas, worked without authorization for about 30 months, failed to make an asylum claim in the U.S., and could not corroborate consulting an immigration attorney. His testimony evolved and was inconsistent with his BOC regarding assaults by settlers, an attack on his son, and why he closed his repair shop. The RPD also found his U.S. marriage was part of a sponsorship scheme.
firac.rule: Credibility findings of the RPD are reviewed on a reasonableness standard with considerable deference (Aguebor; Cambara; Dunsmuir). The RPD may rely on inconsistencies between past statements (BOC) and oral testimony to assess credibility (Liu; Eustace; Rrukaj). Delay in claiming and failure to claim protection at the first opportunity may undermine subjective fear.
firac.application: The Court found the RPD reasonably relied on the inconsistencies between the applicant's evolving testimony and his BOC statements. The applicant did not specifically contest the negative credibility findings related to the Hebron events. The 30-month delay, unauthorized work, and failure to seek asylum in the U.S., together with the inability to corroborate the attorney consultation, reasonably supported an adverse credibility inference. The Court rejected the argument that expecting proof of contacting a lawyer was unreasonable, noting the applicant was put on notice and only some proof was expected.
firac.conclusion: The RPD's credibility determination was reasonable and entitled to deference.

firac.issue: Did the RPD reasonably assess the country condition evidence relative to the applicant's personal situation?
firac.facts: The National Documentation Package for Palestine supported general allegations of discriminatory treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank. The applicant argued this corroborated his testimony. The RPD accepted life can be difficult in the West Bank but found the applicant not credible and unable to link general conditions to his personal circumstances.
firac.rule: A claimant cannot rely solely on country condition evidence to establish a claim (Nagy; Horvath; Tamas) and bears the burden of establishing a link between general documentary evidence and personal circumstances (Balogh). Being a Palestinian in the West Bank is not, in itself, sufficient to establish more than a mere possibility of persecution (Csonka). General human rights problems must be tied to the claimant's profile (Tamas).
firac.application: Because the applicant's personal account of risk was found not credible, he could not use country condition evidence to bridge the gap. He pointed to nothing in the documentary evidence tying his specific profile to persecution. The RPD reasonably concluded that the mere fact of being a Palestinian from the West Bank did not establish a serious possibility of persecution.
firac.conclusion: The RPD's treatment of the country condition evidence was reasonable; the applicant failed to link general conditions to his individual situation.

case_name: 0962118 B.C. Ltd. v. Salty's Fish & Chips Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: 0962118 B.C. Ltd. v. Salty's Fish & Chips Ltd.

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff corporation be ordered to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act given its inability to satisfy a costs award?
Would ordering security for costs unfairly stifle the plaintiff's claim, and does the intertwined nature of the counterclaim and counterclaim-to-counterclaim weigh against ordering security?

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff corporation be ordered to post security for costs where it concedes it has no exigible assets to satisfy a potential costs award?
firac.facts: The plaintiff, a corporation incorporated by Ms. Enslow, operated an unprofitable Salty's Fish & Chips franchise outlet in Langford. It conceded it has no exigible assets and could not pay a costs award. The defendants sought security of $55,000 (later suggesting $25,000), based on their bill of costs estimating trial costs of just over $24,000.
firac.rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 permits the court to require security for costs where it appears a corporate plaintiff will be unable to pay the defendant's costs if the defence succeeds. As a master, the applicant may rely only on the statutory authority (Emperor Oil Ltd. v. Panorama Petroleum Inc., 2015 BCSC 1498). The test (per Integrated Contractors Ltd. v. Leduc Developments Ltd., 2009 BCSC 965) requires the applicant to establish a prima facie case that the corporation could not pay costs; the respondent may resist by showing exigible assets or no arguable defence.
firac.application: The plaintiff conceded the defendants met the first stage and that it had no exigible assets. Its argument that there was no arguable defence failed because the threshold is low and the statement of defence pleaded positive allegations relied on in the counterclaim, unlike a mere denial. The defendants therefore established the statutory precondition for security.
firac.conclusion: The statutory threshold was met, but the court's discretion still had to be exercised in light of the additional factors.

firac.issue: Do the discretionary factors — potential stifling of the claim and the intertwined nature of the counterclaims — militate against ordering security for costs?
firac.facts: Ms. Enslow, the plaintiff's operating mind, had a very modest income, no assets, and acknowledged borrowing from an unidentified source. The defendants brought a counterclaim against the plaintiff and guarantors; Ms. Enslow brought a counterclaim-to-counterclaim alleging intimidation, unlawful interference with economic relations and conversion, seeking return of $230,000 arising from the same business dealings. Ms. Enslow was not asked to post security.
firac.rule: Discretionary factors from ICL: (a) security may be refused where it would unfairly stifle a valid claim (Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golfcourse Ltd.); the respondent must show not only lack of assets but inability to raise funds, supported by affidavit evidence; (b) security may be refused where a counterclaim is sufficiently intertwined with the defence (Gray v. Powerassist Technologies Inc.); (c) security may be refused where the impecuniosity was caused by the applicant's impugned actions. The objective of s. 236 is to protect the community against litigious abuse by artificial persons, not to stifle genuine claims by indigent companies (Pearson v. Naydler; Keary Developments Ltd. v. Tarmac Construction Ltd.).
firac.application: The plaintiff failed to prove stifling because Ms. Enslow did not establish she could not raise funds — she admitted borrowing without stating any limits. Nor was impecuniosity shown to flow from the defendants' actions, given the plaintiff never owned assets and operated in the red. However, the counterclaims were sufficiently intertwined: under Rule 3-4 the defendants' counterclaim could proceed even if the plaintiff's claim were stayed, leaving the plaintiff defending a claim founded on the same business dealings without prosecuting its own action, and unjustly staying Ms. Enslow's counterclaim-to-counterclaim for which no security was sought. This factor weighed heavily against security, and the proceeding did not amount to litigious abuse.
firac.conclusion: The intertwined-counterclaim factor decisively favoured the plaintiff, and the court declined to order security.

name_verification.name_in_document: Render v. ThyssenKrupp Elevator (Canada) Limited

defining_issues: Did the trial judge make palpable and overriding errors in his factual and credibility findings that the buttocks contact was not accidental and that the appellant lacked genuine remorse?
Did the trial judge err in law in finding just cause for dismissal under the McKinley proportionality analysis, and was the employer required to consider alternative disciplinary measures?
Is the appellant entitled to statutory termination pay under the Employment Standards Act, 2000, or is he disentitled as an employee guilty of 'wilful misconduct' under O. Reg. 288/01?
Did the trial judge err in declining to award punitive damages for the respondent's litigation misconduct?
Did the trial judge err in awarding the respondent 50% of its costs despite that litigation misconduct?

firac.issue: Did the trial judge make palpable and overriding errors in finding that the contact was deliberate and that the appellant's remorse was not genuine?
firac.facts: The appellant, a 30-year managerial employee, slapped a female co-worker, Ms. Vieira, on the buttocks during workplace horseplay and said 'good game'. He claimed the contact was accidental (loss of balance) and that he apologized several times. The trial judge rejected the accident claim and found the remorse insincere.
firac.rule: Findings of fact and credibility are reviewed for palpable and overriding error or misapprehension of the evidence: Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, at para. 23.
firac.application: The trial judge gave detailed reasons: the appellant only claimed accident days later when termination arose; 'good game' matched the male employees' buttock-slapping ritual; he could have stopped his arm; and his failure to accept the conduct as sexual harassment, plus the '$10 to shake my hand' comment, undermined his remorse. The appellant's submissions amounted to a request to reweigh evidence, which does not permit appellate intervention.
firac.conclusion: No palpable and overriding error was shown; the factual and credibility findings were entitled to deference and stood.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in law in finding just cause, and did the employer have a standalone duty to consider alternative discipline?
firac.facts: The employer had a zero-tolerance Anti-Harassment Policy communicated eight days before the incident and a progressive discipline policy. The appellant was a supervisor responsible for implementing the policies. Termination was based solely on the non-consensual touching of a private body part.
firac.rule: The governing rule for termination for cause is proportionality: McKinley v. BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38, at paras. 48, 53. The three-step test (nature/extent of misconduct; surrounding circumstances; whether dismissal is proportional) is set out in Dowling and reaffirmed in Hucsko v. A.O. Smith Enterprises, 2021 ONCA 728. There is no free-standing duty to consider alternative measures; the question is whether the sanction ultimately imposed was proportionate (McCallum v. Saputo, 2021 MBCA 62).
firac.application: The trial judge applied the contextual proportionality analysis: he weighed the appellant's supervisory role, the recently implemented zero-tolerance policy, the sexual and demeaning nature of the touching, and the appellant's failure to appreciate its seriousness, against his 30-year unblemished record. The employer did in fact consider alternatives but concluded retention would signal condonation. Treatment of other employees could not overwhelm the fact-specific analysis. The trial judge applied the correct test and his conclusion deserved deference.
firac.conclusion: No legal error; the finding of just cause was upheld and the wrongful dismissal appeal dismissed.

firac.issue: Is the appellant entitled to statutory termination pay, or disentitled for 'wilful misconduct'?
firac.facts: The appellant, employed over eight years, received no termination, severance or vacation pay. The ESA issue was not pleaded but was raised in opening and supported by evidence that he received nothing. The trial judge did not address it.
firac.rule: ESA, 2000, ss. 54, 57(h), 61 provide eight weeks' termination pay for 8+ year employees; ESA s. 5(1) bars contracting out. Disentitlement requires 'wilful misconduct, disobedience or wilful neglect of duty that is not trivial and has not been condoned': O. Reg. 288/01, ss. 2(1)3 and 9(1)6. This standard is higher than common-law just cause and requires deliberate, intentional wrongdoing — 'being bad on purpose': Plester v. Polyone Canada Inc., 2011 ONSC 6068.
firac.application: Because the issue was raised in the opening and the evidence was in the record, the court permitted the claim on appeal. Although the touching was found not accidental, there was no finding it was preplanned; it occurred in the heat of the moment in reaction to a slight and so did not meet the higher 'wilful misconduct' threshold. He proved eight weeks' termination pay, but severance could not be awarded because there was no evidence of the required $2.5 million payroll (s. 64(1)(b)).
firac.conclusion: Appeal allowed on ESA entitlement; the appellant awarded eight weeks' statutory termination pay, but not the 26 weeks' severance.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in declining to award punitive damages for the respondent's litigation misconduct?
firac.facts: The respondent hired a media consultant who issued a sensationalist press release to 40 outlets containing unproven allegations and facilitated a breach of the witness exclusion order.
firac.rule: Litigation misconduct can be an independent actionable wrong supporting punitive damages, but such damages remain 'the exception rather than the norm': McCabe v. Roman Catholic Episcopal Corp., 2019 ONCA 213, at para. 48.
firac.application: The trial judge chose to address the misconduct through the costs award rather than punitive damages. He was entitled to take that approach and his exercise of discretion was owed deference.
firac.conclusion: No error; the refusal to award punitive damages was upheld.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in awarding the respondent 50% of its costs despite the litigation misconduct?
firac.facts: The trial judge reduced the respondent's costs by 50% (awarding $73,696.66 against the appellant) as the sanction for the misconduct, treating the respondent as fully successful.
firac.rule: Costs are discretionary, but appellate intervention is available where there are strong grounds that the judge erred in exercising discretion (Brad-Jay Investments v. Szijjarto). Conduct of the parties during litigation is a most important factor (Andrews v. Andrews); an improper press release intended to pressure the opponent may disentitle a party to costs entirely (Georg v. Hassanali). Leave to appeal costs is unnecessary where the underlying result changed: Courts of Justice Act, s. 133(b).
firac.application: Because the appellant succeeded on the ESA claim, the respondent was no longer fully successful, so no leave was needed. The litigation misconduct — tainting witness evidence and possibly seeking to influence the court — was particularly egregious and undermined the fairness and integrity of the judicial system, warranting complete denial of costs rather than a 50% reduction.
firac.conclusion: Appeal allowed on costs; the costs award set aside and no costs of the trial ordered; no costs of the appeal given divided success.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns dismissal for cause. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the central claim — termination for cause and ESA termination pay. K083 (harassment) captures the sexual harassment/unwanted touching that grounded the dismissal. name_verification.name_in_document: MUKHAILO DUCHKO v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Did the RPD err by failing to consider the totality of the evidence regarding the rise of anti-Semitism in Ukraine?
Was the RPD's preference of one documentary source over another, without explaining the basis, unreasonable for lacking transparency and intelligibility?

firac.issue: Did the RPD err by failing to consider the totality of the evidence regarding the rise of anti-Semitism in Ukraine when assessing the applicant's fear of persecution?
firac.facts: The applicant, a 58-year-old Jewish man from Sambor in western Ukraine, claimed protection under s. 96 of the IRPA based on fear of Ukrainian nationalists. Conflicting documentary evidence existed: counsel's material (Exhibit 3) and reports from Israel's Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and the World Jewish Congress indicated a surge in anti-Semitic violence, while the U.S. State Department Religious Freedom Report (Exhibit 7), relying on local monitoring groups, contradicted this. The RPD preferred the latter and concluded incidents were isolated and did not amount to persecution.
firac.rule: A decision-maker must consider the totality of the evidence, and failing to address evidence squarely contradicting its conclusion may be a reviewable error (Cepeda-Gutierrez v Canada (MCI), 1998 CarswellNat 1981 at para 17). Under s. 96 IRPA the claimant must show more than a mere possibility of persecution.
firac.application: The Court found that the RPD's acceptance of the contested researcher's opinion (that the Israeli Ministry report was 'flawed and amateurish') without careful scrutiny and verification resulted in an unfounded limiting of the body of evidence relevant to the claim. This limiting failed to grapple with the totality of the evidence demonstrating a rise in anti-Semitism.
firac.conclusion: The Court held the RPD's failure to consider the totality of the evidence was a reviewable error rendering the decision unreasonable.

firac.issue: Was the RPD's preference for one documentary source over another unreasonable for lacking transparency and intelligibility?
firac.facts: The RPD preferred evidence from local and regional Jewish minority-rights monitoring groups cited in the U.S. State Department report and dismissed the Israeli Ministry figures based on a single researcher's criticism, without explaining the process by which it determined one source to be more rigorous than the other.
firac.rule: Reasonable administrative decisions must meet the standards of transparency and intelligibility.
firac.application: The Court agreed that the process by which the RPD concluded one source was more rigorous than another was unknown and unexplained, so it did not meet the decision-making standards of transparency and intelligibility, and the RPD accepted a contested opinion without scrutiny.
firac.conclusion: The Court held the decision was unreasonable, set it aside, and remitted the matter for redetermination by a different decision-maker; no question was certified.

name_verification.name_in_document: Besler v. Clausen

defining_issues: Should the malicious prosecution action be dismissed under Rule 9-5(1)(a) as disclosing no reasonable cause of action, given the requirement that a private complainant have 'initiated' the prosecution?
Should the pleadings be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b) as unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious?
Should the action be dismissed under Rule 9-5(1)(d) as an abuse of process?
How should costs be allocated where the application to dismiss failed but the pleadings were nonetheless deficient?

firac.issue: Should the malicious prosecution action be dismissed under Rule 9-5(1)(a) as disclosing no reasonable cause of action?
firac.facts: Brad and Darren Besler sued their neighbours (the operators of a mushroom facility) alleging that the defendants procured their criminal prosecution for mischief and criminal harassment by providing false information to the RCMP and Crown. The Beslers were convicted of mischief at trial, but that conviction was overturned on appeal (2022 BCSC 484). The MP Defendants applied to strike the entire 155-paragraph notice of civil claim.
firac.rule: Under R. 9-5(1)(a), pleadings may be struck only where it is 'plain and obvious' the claim is certain to fail because of a radical defect; facts are assumed true and the approach is generous (Kindylides v. John Does, 2020 BCCA 330). Malicious prosecution requires the four Nelles v. Ontario elements: prosecution initiated by the defendant, terminated in the plaintiff's favour, without reasonable and probable cause, and motivated by malice. A private complainant 'initiates' a prosecution only in exceptional circumstances where the facts were so peculiarly within the complainant's knowledge that the Crown could exercise no independent discretion (Chaudhry v. Khan, 2015 ONSC 1847).
firac.application: The court could not determine on the pleadings alone (even considering the Provincial Court and appeal reasons, admissible under the Hamouth exception) whether the defendants' allegations to the RCMP were so peculiarly within their knowledge that the Crown had no independent discretion. It was not plain and obvious the claim was certain to fail, and there was a chance the plaintiffs might succeed, so they should not be driven from the judgment seat despite the defendants' strong potential defence.
firac.conclusion: Not plain and obvious; the R. 9-5(1)(a) application was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the pleadings be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b) as unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious?
firac.facts: The MP NOCC was prolix, 25 pages with 155 paragraphs of statement of facts, much of it concerning property and bylaw disputes unrelated to the criminal proceeding (e.g. a 2021 kitchen construction two years after charges were laid).
firac.rule: A pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not establish the cause of action, advances no claim known in law, cannot succeed, or wastes court resources (Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083). Subsections of R. 9-5(1) may be read together (Willson v. British Columbia, 2012 BCSC 1256).
firac.application: Although the pleading was prolix and ran afoul of R. 3-1(2)(a), the underlying malicious prosecution claim was recognized in law and arguable, so wholesale dismissal on this basis was not warranted. The court identified extraneous paragraphs but declined to strike the entire claim, leaving the defendants free to bring a further, targeted strike application against an amended pleading.
firac.conclusion: Application to dismiss the whole action under R. 9-5(1)(b) dismissed, with directions to amend.

firac.issue: Should the action be dismissed under Rule 9-5(1)(d) as an abuse of process?
firac.facts: The MP Action shared core facts with a separate malicious prosecution action against the Crown (Besler v. BC Prosecution Service, 2025 BCCA 81), which the Court of Appeal had allowed to proceed.
firac.rule: Abuse of process is a flexible doctrine protecting judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of justice; categories are open and include sham proceedings or those pursued for an ulterior purpose (Sahyoun v. Ho, 2015 BCSC 392; Chernen v. Robertson, 2014 BCSC 1358).
firac.application: Since the Court of Appeal had permitted the related malicious prosecution claim against the Crown to continue, the MP Action was not a mere sham or deception. While the court had 'genuine concerns' the action was being pursued for an ulterior purpose, that concern did not rise to a level warranting complete dismissal at this stage.
firac.conclusion: R. 9-5(1)(d) application dismissed.

firac.issue: How should costs be allocated where the strike application failed but the pleadings were deficient?
firac.facts: The application was one component of a multi-day hearing; the plaintiffs had earlier been cautioned about prolix pleadings (2023 BCSC 2590) yet did not provide a draft amended NOCC.
firac.rule: Costs are discretionary under Rule 14-1, assessed under the Tariff in Appendix B.
firac.application: Despite losing the application, the MP Defendants had good reason to complain about the prolix, defective pleading, and the plaintiffs could have prepared a proper amended claim. The court awarded the MP Defendants their costs of the application in any event of the cause (not payable forthwith), assessed as one full day of ordinary difficulty; no order as to Bartlett, which did not participate.
firac.conclusion: Application dismissed but MP Defendants awarded costs in any event of the cause.

name_verification.name_in_document: [no style of cause — anonymized claimants; RPD File No. TB2-00633]

defining_issues: Did the claimants establish, on a credible basis, that they faced persecution in Ukraine on account of their actual or perceived Jewish identity?
Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection in Ukraine?
Did the claimants qualify as persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA?

firac.issue: Did the claimants establish, on a credible basis, that they faced persecution in Ukraine on account of their actual or perceived Jewish identity?
firac.facts: The principal claimant was raised in a Jewish family by his Jewish grandmother, observed the Sabbath and was perceived as Jewish; his wife, though not Jewish, was perceived as such through marriage. They alleged anti-Semitic abuse, a beating linked to his father's former business partner, and a second assault by the wife's relatives, supported by medical reports and letters from a rabbi.
firac.rule: Under s. 96 IRPA a claimant must establish a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground. Sworn testimony is presumed true absent valid reason to doubt it (Maldonado v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1980] 2 F.C. 302 (C.A.)).
firac.application: The panel accepted the claimants' personal and Jewish identities but found aspects of the principal claimant's account implausible — notably his continuing to approach the business partner he blamed for a beating, and inconsistencies about police complaints. It found any beating connected to the business partner was motivated by a business dispute, with anti-Semitic slurs incidental, and that the medical reports could not establish who the attackers were or their motive. It conceded the later assault by the wife's relatives could plausibly have an anti-Semitic motive.
firac.conclusion: The credibility concerns and the assessment that the principal alleged harm was corporate rather than persecutory undermined the claim; even a plausible anti-Semitic assault was insufficient absent proof of absence of state protection.

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection in Ukraine?
firac.facts: The claimants alleged police were indifferent and refused to take reports because they were Jewish. Both the Board's National Documentation Package and the claimants' package were before the panel, presenting conflicting pictures of the situation of Ukrainian Jews.
firac.rule: A claimant bears the onus of rebutting the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence that the state is unable or unwilling to protect.
firac.application: The panel preferred the Board's documentary evidence, drawn from credible sources (US DOS, Amnesty International, Freedom House, Human Rights Watch, UN Special Rapporteur), which showed anti-Semitic incidents were rare and authorities took steps to address them, over the claimants' largely internet-sourced package. It found little independent evidence, doubted the claim that police would not take a report where two attackers were identifiable, and concluded the claimants failed to establish an absence of state protection.
firac.conclusion: The claimants did not meet their onus to establish that adequate state protection would not be forthcoming; they were found not to be Convention refugees.

firac.issue: Did the claimants qualify as persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The alleged risk arose principally from the female claimant's relatives in a particular locality of Ukraine.
firac.rule: Section 97(1)(b) IRPA requires a personalized risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment faced in every part of the country and not faced generally by others.
firac.application: The panel found Ukraine is a large country and the claimants had not established that they would be at risk from the wife's relatives throughout its territory, so the risk was not faced in every part of the country.
firac.conclusion: The claimants did not meet the definition of persons in need of protection under s. 97.

name_verification.name_in_document: XXXX XXXX (RAD File No. VB6-03789)

defining_issues: Should the appellant's proposed documents be admitted as 'new evidence' under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA?
Did the RPD err in failing to find that the cumulative discrimination and harassment the appellant experienced amounted to persecution?
Did the RPD err in finding that adequate state protection was available to the appellant in Israel?

firac.issue: Should the appellant's proposed documents be admitted as 'new evidence' under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The appellant tendered eight articles (Exhibits A–H) about racism and discrimination against Ethiopian Jews and Christians in Israel, asserting they supported his appeal grounds.
firac.rule: Subsection 110(4) IRPA permits only evidence arising after the RPD rejection, not reasonably available before it, or that could not reasonably have been expected to be presented; the implicit Raza criteria apply per Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Singh, 2016 FCA 96, and the RAD is not a forum to complete a deficient RPD record.
firac.application: Exhibits A, C, F, G and H were already before the RPD and so were not new. Exhibits B, D and E were dated before the RPD hearing, were reasonably available (including a publicly accessible Wikipedia page), and the appellant offered no persuasive explanation why they were not presented earlier; evidence merely contradicting RPD findings does not qualify as new.
firac.conclusion: None of the documents met the subsection 110(4) test and all were rejected as new evidence.

firac.issue: Did the RPD err in failing to find that the cumulative discrimination and harassment the appellant experienced amounted to persecution?
firac.facts: The appellant, an Ethiopian-born Israeli citizen, alleged a 2012 sexual humiliation, a 2013 beating and interrogation by Haifa police, and threats from unknown persons; he had also attended university and been employed in Israel.
firac.rule: Discrimination amounts to persecution only where measures cause substantially prejudicial consequences or deny a core human right (UNHCR Handbook para. 54); cumulative harassment may constitute persecution where it shows a serious and systematic pattern (Oyarzo; Retnem); where state protection is available for the alleged discriminatory events, a cumulative assessment is unnecessary (Gebre-Hiwet, 2010 FC 482).
firac.application: Applying the correctness standard from Huruglica (accepting the RPD's positive credibility finding), the RAD found the incidents were random, non-systematic attacks; there was little evidence Christians could not practise their faith in Israel, and the appellant's education and employment history was inconsistent with persecution-level discrimination.
firac.conclusion: The appellant's experiences amounted at most to discrimination and harassment, not persecution; the RPD did not err.

firac.issue: Did the RPD err in finding that adequate state protection was available to the appellant in Israel?
firac.facts: The appellant reported incidents only to the Machash and received no response, then did not pursue other avenues, saying he needed a documented Machash response first. Israel is a multi-party parliamentary democracy with a functioning police force and oversight bodies.
firac.rule: There is a presumption of state protection rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence on a balance of probabilities (Flores Carrillo, 2008 FCA 94; Nadeem, 2001 FCT 1263); a claimant must take all reasonable steps to seek protection, including through separate oversight and complaint mechanisms (Peralta); no state can guarantee perfect protection (Villafranca; Zalzali).
firac.application: The appellant failed to approach concurrent recourse avenues such as the Police Complaints Unit, the State Comptroller or NGOs, and his explanation for not doing so was unsatisfactory. Country reports showed Israel makes serious efforts to protect Ethiopian Israelis and to hold officials accountable, so the presumption was not rebutted.
firac.conclusion: Adequate state protection was available; the RPD did not err and the appeal fails.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the ss. 96/97 claim. K080 (state protection) was the determinative issue, and K079 (persecution) frames the discrimination-versus-persecution analysis. K069 (discrimination) and K065 (racism) reflect the anti-Ethiopian racial discrimination alleged. K014 (standard of review) covers the Huruglica correctness analysis applied by the RAD. K103 (Israel) is the relevant country. Racism (K065) is somewhat secondary but genuinely engaged given the Ethiopian-Israeli racial discrimination evidence.
