registry_rationale: The RAD file number prefix 'VB' and the notation that the appeal was 'considered at Vancouver, BC' indicate the Vancouver office; national tribunal so registry is inferred from the hearing location.

case_name: AB v. Canada Employment Insurance Commission

name_verification.name_in_document: AB v Canada Employment Insurance Commission

defining_issues: Did the Appellant voluntarily leave his employment?
Did any of the circumstances listed in s. 29(c) of the Employment Insurance Act exist when the Appellant quit?
Did the Appellant have just cause for leaving, i.e. no reasonable alternative to quitting when he did, disqualifying him from EI benefits under s. 30?

firac.issue: Did the Appellant voluntarily leave his employment?
firac.facts: The Appellant, an accounting assistant controller, quit on May 3, 2024 (last day May 10, 2024) and applied for EI sickness benefits, later converting to regular benefits. The Record of Employment confirmed he quit and he agreed he quit.
firac.rule: Under the Employment Insurance Act a claimant who voluntarily leaves employment must establish just cause; the threshold question is whether the leaving was voluntary.
firac.application: The member accepted the leaving was voluntary because the Appellant admitted quitting and the employer's Record of Employment corroborated it, with no contradicting evidence.
firac.conclusion: The Appellant voluntarily left his job.

firac.issue: Did any of the circumstances listed in s. 29(c) of the Employment Insurance Act exist when the Appellant quit?
firac.facts: The Appellant alleged harassment/bullying by his supervisor, a discriminatory remark ('F'ing Jews') made in his presence as he is Jewish, unhealthy working conditions, a 2022 aggressive antagonistic incident with his supervisor, and undue pressure to leave through write-ups, schedule changes, micromanagement, and unethical bonus/tip practices.
firac.rule: Section 29(c) of the Act enumerates circumstances (harassment, discrimination within the meaning of the Canadian Human Rights Act, danger to health or safety, antagonism with a supervisor where the claimant is not primarily responsible, undue pressure to leave, etc.) relevant to just cause; harassment must render the workplace intolerable (CUB 58193) and health-based claims require medical evidence, attempts to resolve with the employer, and efforts to find other work.
firac.application: The member found the described incidents, while unprofessional or annoying, did not amount to harassment and did not render the workplace intolerable; the single antisemitic remark, not directed at the Appellant, did not reach the level of discrimination; the health/safety claim failed for lack of medical documentation and no attempt to raise concerns with the employer; the 2022 antagonism was a one-off two years earlier that did not cause the departure. Only the cumulative 'relatively minor things' constituted undue pressure to leave.
firac.conclusion: The only s. 29(c) circumstance established was undue pressure by the employer to leave.

firac.issue: Did the Appellant have just cause for leaving, i.e. no reasonable alternative to quitting?
firac.facts: The Appellant cited health and mental-health reasons but had no medical note supporting a need to quit (his doctor was away and would have recommended a leave, not quitting), never requested a leave of absence (the employer said it would have granted up to six months), and did not follow up on his bullying complaint despite an HR meeting invitation.
firac.rule: Under s. 30 and s. 29(c) of the Act, and Canada (AG) v White, 2011 FCA 190, just cause exists only where, having regard to all the circumstances, the claimant had no reasonable alternative to leaving when they did; the claimant bears the burden on a balance of probabilities.
firac.application: Even accepting undue pressure, the member found the Appellant had reasonable alternatives: request a leave of absence, wait for his returning doctor or obtain a medical note (including from a walk-in clinic or emergency department), and raise his concerns with the employer before resigning. He pursued none of these.
firac.conclusion: The Appellant had reasonable alternatives, so he did not have just cause and is disqualified from receiving EI benefits.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the primary tier-1 area, as the case turns on voluntary leaving and just cause under the Employment Insurance Act. K083 (harassment) and K069 (discrimination) are directly engaged, being enumerated s. 29(c) circumstances the member analysed. K057 (antisemitic slurs) and K058 (antisemitism) capture the supervisor's 'F'ing Jews' remark central to the discrimination analysis, and K093 (Jewish) reflects the Appellant's identity as the affected group. K007 (Human rights) is included because the discrimination analysis turned on the prohibited grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act, though it is secondary to the labour/EI focus. There is no EI-benefit-specific keyword in the vocabulary, so the labour tier-1 term is the closest fit — a mild limitation flagged here.
location_rationale: The Social Security Tribunal is a national tribunal and the decision states no seat city; the hearing was by videoconference. Province is inferred as Ontario from para 45, which notes the Appellant was a worker 'in Ontario' protected by the Ontario Employment Standards Act and the Ontario Human Rights Code.
registry_rationale: No court registry or office is identified; the matter is a Social Security Tribunal General Division – Employment Insurance Section proceeding heard by videoconference, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: XXXX XXXX (RPD File No. TB6-16896)

defining_issues: Was the claimant credible regarding his central allegation of being a Kurdish political activist known to and persecuted by the Turkish authorities?
Did the claimant's failure to claim asylum in Mexico and to pursue his claim in the United States undermine his subjective fear?
Did the claimant's ability to exit Turkey on a genuine passport undermine the credibility of his persecution allegations?
Absent the discredited activist profile, does the claimant face a serious possibility of persecution or s. 97 risk simply as an Alevi Kurd and HDP supporter?

firac.issue: Was the claimant credible regarding his central allegation of being a Kurdish political activist known to and persecuted by the Turkish authorities?
firac.facts: The claimant, a 23-year-old Alevi Kurd from Turkey, alleged four arrests, detentions and torture between 2013 and 2016 due to his HDP membership and Kurdish activism. His Schedule A stated he had never been detained, his POE interview denied any arrest and did not mention persecution, and his HDP membership date differed between his narrative (2014) and Schedule A (2007). He attributed all discrepancies to a poor POE interpreter and errors in the forms.
firac.rule: A claim under ss. 96 and 97 of the IRPA must be established with credible and trustworthy evidence; material inconsistencies, omissions and implausibilities between a claimant's testimony, BOC and POE statements may support an adverse credibility finding on a balance of probabilities.
firac.application: The panel found the interpretation explanation implausible given that other detailed information (family relationships, circumstances in Turkey) had been accurately recorded, that the claimant confirmed he understood the interpreter and signed a declaration of accuracy, and that the most significant allegations—arrests and torture—were entirely absent from the POE account. The panel concluded the claimant had altered his evidence to align with the US INS narrative likely provided by the smuggler.
firac.conclusion: The panel found the claimant not credible on the material aspect that he is a known Kurdish political activist arrested and tortured by Turkish authorities.

firac.issue: Did the claimant's failure to claim asylum in Mexico and to pursue his claim in the United States undermine his subjective fear?
firac.facts: The claimant travelled through Mexico (10–12 days, no claim) and the United States (started but did not fully prosecute an asylum claim) before entering Canada illegally, explaining he always intended to reach his uncle in Canada, though he lives in Toronto rather than with the uncle in Edmonton.
firac.rule: A genuine subjective fear is ordinarily demonstrated by claiming protection at the earliest opportunity in a safe country; absent a reasonable explanation, a failure to do so supports a negative credibility inference.
firac.application: The panel found Mexico and the US have well-developed asylum systems, and the reliance-on-uncle explanation was undermined because the claimant never lived with the uncle and stayed alone in Toronto. It characterized the conduct as forum shopping inconsistent with genuine fear.
firac.conclusion: The panel drew a negative inference on the claimant's credibility for failing to claim in Mexico and pursue his US claim.

firac.issue: Did the claimant's ability to exit Turkey on a genuine passport undermine the credibility of his persecution allegations?
firac.facts: The claimant left Turkey on his own genuine passport through an airport with stringent exit controls; he explained at the hearing (but not in his narrative or Schedule 12) that an agent bribed officials.
firac.rule: Where documentary evidence establishes stringent exit controls, an unimpeded departure on a genuine passport by a person allegedly wanted by authorities may undermine credibility, and material omissions of facilitators are relevant.
firac.application: Relying on RIRs describing Turkey's stringent airport exit controls, the panel found it implausible that a known Kurdish activist previously detained and tortured could exit without questioning, and treated the bribery explanation as a material omission and inadequate.
firac.conclusion: The panel found the unimpeded departure on a genuine passport further undermined the claimant's credibility.

firac.issue: Absent the discredited activist profile, does the claimant face a serious possibility of persecution or s. 97 risk simply as an Alevi Kurd and HDP supporter?
firac.facts: The panel accepted the claimant is an Alevi Kurd who may attend peaceful demonstrations and support leftist causes, but found he was not a senior HDP member or a Kurdish activist known to authorities.
firac.rule: Under s. 96, a claimant must show a serious possibility of persecution; under s. 97, a risk on a balance of probabilities. Country documentation is assessed to determine whether a claimant's profile attracts persecutory treatment.
firac.application: Relying on UK Home Office and RIR country evidence, the panel found that ordinary HDP members and Alevis face discrimination but not persecution, and only senior HDP members or those suspected of PKK links are at particular risk. The claimant lacked such a profile, and there was insufficient evidence he could not practise his Alevi faith.
firac.conclusion: The panel found no serious possibility of persecution or s. 97 risk based solely on the claimant's identity as an Alevi Kurd and peaceful leftist supporter.

keywords_rationale: K008 is the tier-1 practice area (immigration/refugee). K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the ss. 96/97 IRPA claim. K079 (persecution) is central to the s. 96 analysis of whether an Alevi Kurd/HDP supporter faces persecution. K069 (discrimination) reflects the country evidence on discrimination against Alevis and Kurds falling short of persecution. K087 (protest/demonstration) reflects the claimant's alleged arrests at demonstrations and peaceful activism. K100 (IRB) identifies the deciding institution. Freedom of religion (K025) was considered but is a weaker pick since the religious ground was resolved as discrimination rather than persecution, so it was omitted.
location_rationale: The decision states "Place of Hearing: Toronto, Ontario" and identifies the panel of the Refugee Protection Division; the file bears RPD File No. TB6-16896.
registry_rationale: The RPD hearings were held in Toronto, Ontario, indicating the matter proceeded through the Toronto office of the Immigration and Refugee Board.

case_name: Bonitto v. Halifax Regional School Board

name_verification.name_in_document: Sean Bonitto v. Halifax Regional School Board

defining_issues: Are the Charter s. 2(a) and 2(b) rights of a parent to distribute gospel tracts on a public elementary school's grounds during school hours constitutionally protected given the location?
Did the school board's refusal to permit distribution of the gospel tracts infringe the parent's freedom of religion and/or freedom of expression?
If there was an infringement, was it justified as a proportionate exercise of the principal's statutory discretion under the Doré framework?

firac.issue: Is a public elementary school's grounds, during school hours, a location where a parent's s. 2(a)/(b) rights to distribute religious literature are constitutionally protected?
firac.facts: Mr. Bonitto, a fundamentalist Christian and parent of two Park West School students, distributed gospel tracts to persons on school grounds, including students, during school hours while attending to drop off or retrieve his children. Park West is leased by the Halifax Regional School Board from a private company for weekday hours and operated under the Education Act.
firac.rule: City of Montreal v. 2952-1366 Québec Inc., 2005 SCC 62 sets the test for s. 2(b) protection on government-owned property: whether the place is one where expression is consistent with the values s. 2(b) serves (democratic discourse, truth finding, self-fulfillment), considering (a) the historical or actual function of the place and (b) whether other aspects suggest expression would undermine those values. The Protection of Property Act, R.S.N.S. 1989, c. 363 lets the occupier control access. The Court held the same location analysis applies to a s. 2(a) claim where the alleged infringement is a bar to disseminating religious materials.
firac.application: The Court found the school has a strong private element: parents have only implied permission for legitimate purposes and must report to the office, unlike the public airport areas in Committee for the Commonwealth of Canada. The actual function—delivering the public school program to children aged 4 to 15 with neutrality on religion—is incompatible with open public expression of a message asserting one religion's superiority; such distribution would be disruptive, raise safety and age-appropriateness concerns, and there was no historical use of school grounds for uncontrolled distribution (other religious groups had sought and been denied permission).
firac.conclusion: Park West School is not a location where the parent's s. 2(a) or s. 2(b) rights to distribute gospel tracts are constitutionally protected; the activity is excluded from protection by reason of location.

firac.issue: Did the refusal to permit distribution of the gospel tracts infringe Mr. Bonitto's s. 2(a) and/or s. 2(b) rights?
firac.facts: Mr. Bonitto sincerely believes he is commissioned to preach the gospel to every creature and carries and hands out Bible tracts everywhere, whose core message is that only those who accept Jesus Christ will avoid hell. The principal, using the Distribution and Display of Materials Policy, refused approval and directed him to stop distributing on school grounds during school hours.
firac.rule: Freedom of religion analysis: Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47 and Hutterian Brethren v. Alberta, 2009 SCC 37 require (1) a sincere belief with a nexus to religion and (2) interference that is more than trivial or insubstantial, assessed objectively (S.L. v. Commission scolaire des Chênes, 2012 SCC 7), with competing rights of others considered (Amselem, para. 62). Freedom of religion includes dissemination (Whatcott, 2013 SCC 11; Big M Drug Mart). Section 2(b) analysis follows Irwin Toy / City of Montréal / CBC v. Canada, 2011 SCC 2 (expressive content; location/method exclusion; infringement by purpose or effect).
firac.application: The Court accepted the belief was sincere with a clear religious nexus and that handing out tracts is a core religious practice; the interference, assessed at the location complained of, was more than trivial. However, weighing competing rights, the Court found permitting distribution of materials favouring one religion would violate the non-Christian students' right to a religiously neutral education and amount to indoctrination (Zylberberg; Canadian Civil Liberties Association v. Ontario), affecting a diverse student body (over 50 cultures, roughly one quarter Muslim). The same reasoning applied to the s. 2(b) claim.
firac.conclusion: The refusal did not infringe Mr. Bonitto's freedom of religion or expression, because the impact of the distribution on the rights of other individuals removed the activity from protection.

firac.issue: If there was an infringement, did the HRSB justify it as a proportionate exercise of statutory discretion?
firac.facts: The principal exercised discretion under the HRSB Distribution and Display of Materials Policy, authorized by the Education Act. Mr. Bonitto challenged the decision (not the policy). Several tracts contained graphic imagery (e.g., a cat being sacrificed, a chainsaw-wielding pumpkin figure, detailed crucifixion injuries) and messages condemning homosexuality and other faiths.
firac.rule: Doré v. Barreau du Québec, 2012 SCC 12: an administrative decision engaging Charter values is reviewed for reasonableness by asking whether the decision-maker proportionately balanced the Charter protections against the statutory objectives, giving a margin of appreciation so long as the decision falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes.
firac.application: The Court identified the statutory objectives as religious neutrality, inclusion in the school community, and student safety. The gospel tracts were directly contrary to these objectives, risked violating non-Christian students' rights, excluding students and parents, and exposing young children to age-inappropriate content. Given the paramount importance of the objectives and that all materials shared the same core message, an absolute ban on distribution on school grounds during school hours fell within the range of acceptable outcomes; limiting recipients by age would not have achieved a proportionate balance.
firac.conclusion: Assuming there was an infringement, the HRSB justified it; the principal's decision reflected a proportionate balancing and was reasonable. As no infringement occurred and the decision was valid, no remedy issue arose.

keywords_rationale: The case turns on Charter analysis (K003 Constitutional law as tier-1 practice area) in a public school context, making Education law relevant too but the dominant framing is constitutional; K005 education law is engaged because the dispute concerns a public school's operation and neutrality. K024 freedom of expression and K025 freedom of religion are the core s. 2(b) and s. 2(a) rights litigated, with K110 (s. 2(a)) and K111 (s. 2(b)) as the specific Charter provisions. K034 sincerity of belief captures the Amselem/Hutterian first-stage test the Court applied. K010 Doré/Loyola framework governs the justification analysis, and K011 judicial review reflects the reasonableness review of the principal's discretionary decision. K041 campus/university is a slightly imperfect fit but is the closest 'school setting' keyword available; K107 flags the Canadian Charter as the operative statute. Equality/discrimination keywords were deliberately excluded because the Court expressly held no discrimination claim was advanced.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'SUPREME COURT OF Nova Scotia', 'Heard: November 25, 27 and 28, 2013, in Halifax, Nova Scotia', and 'Registry: Halifax'.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly lists 'Registry: Halifax' and the docket 'Halifax, No. 346361'.

name_verification.name_in_document: YURI SVERDLOV (a.k.a. YOURI SAVARDELOV), MAYA SVERDLOVA (a.k.a. MAYA SVERDLOV) v. THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Did the Board err in finding that the applicants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection in Israel?
Did the Board fail to have regard to the applicants' post-hearing submissions and documentary evidence?

firac.issue: Did the Board err in a reviewable manner in finding that the applicants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection available in Israel?
firac.facts: The applicants, citizens of Israel (a Jehovah's Witness wife and her Jewish husband), claimed refugee protection fearing persecution. The Board found Israel is a democracy providing effective protection to persons similarly situated (former Russian citizens and non-Jews), and that the applicants had not exhausted reasonable remedies—they could not name the senders of hate notes, failed to file a written report on the most serious incident, and speculated about a gas stove malfunction.
firac.rule: An applicant must demonstrate with clear and convincing evidence that the state is unable or unwilling to protect them (Canada (Attorney General) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689). In a democratic state that burden is not easily satisfied, and applicants must show they exhausted all reasonable remedies (Canada (MCI) v. Kadenko (1996), 143 D.L.R. (4th) 532 (F.C.A.)).
firac.application: The Board examined extensive documentary evidence on Israel's democracy and the effectiveness of protection for former Russians and non-Jews. The Court found the Board reasonably concluded the applicants did not give police adequate opportunity to provide protection, since no names, no formal complaint, and pure speculation were involved. The minor error about an address on one complaint was not material given the other evidence, and the Board's in-hearing reference to discrimination against non-Jews was not an admission that protection was unavailable.
firac.conclusion: The Board did not err; the applicants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection, and this determinative finding disposed of the claim.

firac.issue: Did the Board fail to have regard to the applicants' post-hearing submissions and documentary evidence?
firac.facts: The applicants' counsel submitted post-hearing materials, largely website documents in the nature of hate propaganda, not verified by any independent third party.
firac.rule: A failure to have regard to the evidence can ground review, but the Board is presumed to have considered all evidence before it, particularly where it forms part of the Certified Tribunal Record.
firac.application: The post-hearing submissions were in the Certified Tribunal Record, triggering the presumption they were considered. The Court found nothing in the package requiring specific mention: the attached documents were unverified, appeared to be online hate propaganda, and lacked credibility or reliability. The Board acknowledged difficulties faced by Russian émigrés and proselytizing Christians, showing awareness of the evidence.
firac.conclusion: The Board did not make its decision without regard to the evidence; the presumption of consideration was not rebutted.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K080 (state protection) is the determinative issue—rebutting the presumption of state protection under Ward and Kadenko. K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) reflect the ss. 96/97 refugee claim and the alleged fear of persecution. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) reflect the procedural posture and the reviewable-error analysis. K103 (Israel) is the country of nationality central to the state-protection analysis. K093 (Jewish) applies as the husband is Jewish and the claim concerned treatment of non-Jews/mixed marriage. Borderline: K093 is factual context rather than a legal issue, but relevant to the persecution/state-protection framing.
location_rationale: The decision is dated at 'Ottawa, Ontario, June 19, 2007' where the reasons were rendered. The hearing took place in Toronto ('PLACE OF HEARING: Toronto, Ontario').
registry_rationale: The matter was heard in Toronto, Ontario, and counsel/solicitors of record are located in Toronto; the Federal Court sat in Toronto for the hearing.

name_verification.name_in_document: Richard Warman v. Terry Tremaine

defining_issues: Does the Tribunal have jurisdiction to prohibit a person from acting as an agent for a party, and should it exclude Paul Fromm on that basis?
Could the Tribunal admit and consider post-referral internet postings that were not specifically listed in the original complaint?

Did the respondent commit a discriminatory practice under s. 13(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act by repeatedly communicating, via the Internet, messages likely to expose Jews, Blacks and other non-whites to hatred or contempt?
What remedies were available — specifically, was the complainant entitled to special compensation under s. 54(1)(b), and what penalty was warranted under s. 54(1)(c)?

firac.issue: Does the Tribunal have jurisdiction to bar a chosen lay agent, and should it exclude Paul Fromm?
firac.facts: Tremaine sought to have Paul Fromm act as his representative. The Commission moved to bar Fromm, relying on his contemptuous published comments about the Tribunal (calling it a 'Soviet style kangaroo court' and its decisions 'Stalinist lunacy'), an alleged conflict of interest arising from his acrimonious relationship with the complainant, and a claim that his participation would hinder the hearing.
firac.rule: Parties before adjudicative tribunals generally have a common-law right to an agent of their choosing, but tribunals retain a residual discretion to override this where the agent would hinder rather than facilitate the process (Thomas v. Assn. of New Brunswick Registered Nursing Assistants (2003), 230 D.L.R. 337; Filgueira v. Garfield Container Transport Inc.). Section 50(1) CHRA guarantees a right to counsel, and s. 48.9 requires informal and expeditious proceedings consistent with natural justice.
firac.application: The Tribunal held it had jurisdiction to allow or prohibit an agent. On the conflict-of-interest ground, no specific conflict was explained; on the 'hindrance' ground, no supporting evidence was led. Fromm's disrespectful comments, though real, were better addressed in another forum, and so long as he accepted the Tribunal's authority and acted respectfully there was no basis to exclude him. The Commission had also failed to serve Fromm personally, which alone would have justified dismissing the motion.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal had jurisdiction but declined to exercise it; the motion to exclude Fromm was denied, and the three-year general prohibition became moot.

firac.issue: Could post-referral postings not listed in the complaint be admitted?
firac.facts: The Commission introduced internet postings, including ones made after the complaint was filed, that were not specifically listed in the original complaint. No motion to amend was filed. Tremaine objected but admitted authoring all the postings, which had been disclosed to him before the hearing.
firac.rule: The essential question is whether it would be fair to admit post-referral evidence; where there is no surprise and the respondent knows the evidence relates to the same matter as the complaint, admission causes no prejudice (Warman v. Winnicki, 2006 CHRT 20; LeBlanc v. Canada Post Corporation (1992), 18 CHRR D/57).
firac.application: The evidence went to whether Tremaine was engaged in an ongoing s. 13(1) violation; the complaint itself described the two listed postings as 'samples.' There was no surprise, disclosure had occurred, and Tremaine admitted authorship. The additional postings were sufficiently similar to the complaint so as not to constitute a new or separate complaint.
firac.conclusion: The post-referral evidence was properly admitted.

firac.issue: Did Tremaine's internet postings constitute a discriminatory practice under s. 13(1) CHRA?
firac.facts: Under the pseudonym 'mathdoktor99' and his own name, Tremaine posted numerous messages on Stormfront and his NSPC website describing Jews as a 'parasitic race' and 'vermin,' denying the Holocaust ('holohoax'), depicting Blacks as intellectually inferior and criminal, and calling for the expulsion, sterilization or deportation of Jews, Blacks and other non-whites from Canada. He admitted authorship and, at the hearing, repudiated an earlier apology and reaffirmed his views.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) CHRA (as extended by s. 13(2) to internet communications) makes it a discriminatory practice to repeatedly communicate by telecommunication matter likely to expose persons to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground. Intent is not required (O'Malley; Taylor); truth is no defence (Taylor). 'Hatred' means extreme ill-will allowing no redeeming qualities; 'contempt' means looking down upon (Nealy v. Johnson; Canada (HRC) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 SCR 892). Posting on a publicly accessible website satisfies 'repeatedly' (Schnell; Winnicki).
firac.application: Tremaine admitted repeated communication; posting on publicly accessible websites satisfied the 'repeatedly' and telecommunication-undertaking elements, and the 'in-house/private communication' argument was rejected. The messages, assessed by their own language and tone, dehumanized Jews, Blacks and other non-whites as vermin, parasites, criminals and inferiors, and even endorsed violence — placing them well beyond legitimate political debate and clearly likely to expose the targeted groups to hatred or contempt.
firac.conclusion: The s. 13(1) complaint was substantiated; a discriminatory practice was established.

firac.issue: What remedies were warranted, including compensation and penalty?
firac.facts: Warman sought a cease-and-desist order, $10,000 special compensation under s. 54(1)(b), and a $10,000 penalty under s. 54(1)(c). Warman led no evidence that he was personally a victim and had abandoned his retaliation claim. Tremaine had no prior discriminatory practices, briefly ceased posting and once apologized, but reaffirmed his views; he earned about $600 a month.
firac.rule: Section 54(1)(a) permits a cease-and-desist order. Section 54(1)(b) permits up to $20,000 special compensation only where a victim is specifically identified in the communication and the respondent acted wilfully or recklessly; s. 40(5)(b) confirms a s. 13 complaint need not have an identifiable victim. Section 54(1)(c) permits a penalty up to $10,000, with s. 54(1.1) factors (nature and gravity, wilfulness, prior practices, ability to pay).
firac.application: A cease-and-desist order was appropriate given its practical and symbolic value. Compensation under s. 54(1)(b) failed because Warman led no evidence he was a victim and could not resurrect his abandoned retaliation claim. On penalty, the messages were malicious and extreme and Tremaine showed no remorse, but he had no prior record, briefly desisted, and had limited means, so a mid-range penalty was fixed.
firac.conclusion: Cease-and-desist order granted; special compensation refused; penalty of $4,000 imposed, payable within 120 days.

keywords_rationale: K007 (Human rights) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case is a statutory human-rights complaint under the CHRA. K061 (hate speech) and K070 (discriminatory messages) capture the core s. 13(1) finding of matter likely to expose groups to hatred or contempt. K063 (online hate/social media) reflects that all impugned material was posted on Stormfront and the NSPC website. K058 (antisemitism), K062 (Holocaust denial) and K066 (white supremacism) reflect the specific content — 'parasitic race,' the 'holohoax,' and National-Socialist/white-nationalist ideology. K113 (CHRA s. 13) and K108 (Canadian Human Rights Act) are the governing statutory provisions. K072 (human rights tribunal) identifies the adjudicative forum. K093 (Jewish) reflects the primary targeted group. Racism (K065) also fits given anti-Black content but was omitted to stay within the strongest picks; it is a borderline additional candidate.
location_rationale: The decision is signed 'OTTAWA, Ontario' by Member Michel Doucet, and the style of cause lists the place of hearing as 'Ottawa, Ontario' (August 8 to 11, 2006).
registry_rationale: The Canadian Human Rights Tribunal is a national tribunal; the decision identifies only a tribunal file number (T1104/8505) and no separate court registry, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: [no style of cause — anonymized private proceeding], RAD File TB8-08255 et al.

defining_issues: Should the appellant's proposed new evidence (three web articles) be admitted under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA?
Did the appellants rebut the presumption of state protection in Venezuela?
Does the discrimination and racially-tinged mistreatment experienced by the ethnic-Chinese appellants amount to persecution under section 96?
Were the adult appellants properly excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E of the Convention?

firac.issue: Should the appellant's proposed new evidence be admitted under s. 110(4) of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The appellant tendered three news articles from a website said to reprint Venezuelan newspaper reports about attacks on Chinese businesses. Counsel conceded the articles addressed issues Chinese people in Venezuela had faced since before the RPD hearing, and no date of original publication was provided.
firac.rule: Subsection 110(4) IRPA permits new evidence only if it arose after the RPD rejection, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been expected to be presented. Per Singh (2016 FCA 96) and Abdullahi (2016 FC 260), s. 110(4) is not a tune-up procedure to complete a deficient record; an applicant must put their best foot forward before the RPD.
firac.application: The articles were reprints of material published before the web dates, and the content concerned conditions predating the RPD hearing. With no evidence of when the underlying articles were first produced, the panel could not find the content new. The onus was on the appellant to show the statutory requirements were met, and he failed.
firac.conclusion: The new evidence was rejected as inadmissible.

firac.issue: Did the appellants rebut the presumption of state protection in Venezuela?
firac.facts: The appellants complained of racist mistreatment by some police, but police attended and filed a report after looters damaged the principal appellant's shop during a riot. The appellants did not escalate the one unhelpful officer's conduct to a higher authority and left Venezuela about a month after the looting.
firac.rule: A claimant must take all reasonable steps to seek protection (Peralta, 2002 FCT 989). Where the state is a functioning democracy, failure to pursue protection is usually fatal (Camacho, 2007 FC 830), even where the system has gaps (Salazar Santos, 2007 FC 793); local policing failures do not equal lack of state protection unless part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal (Zhuravlvev, [2000] 4 F.C. 3).
firac.application: The police responded to the looting complaint, evidencing accessible protection. One or two racist officers did not rebut the presumption, and the appellants failed to seek redress from higher authorities. The country evidence showed generalized, largely random violence affecting all Venezuelans, not a broader pattern of state refusal to protect Chinese people.
firac.conclusion: The appellants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection.

firac.issue: Does the discrimination experienced by the appellants amount to persecution under s. 96?
firac.facts: The principal appellant described insults ('stinky Chinamen', 'Chinese Pig'), looting of his shop, and being treated as an outsider. The looting occurred in a riot in which some 80% of food stores were looted, and the appellants could not identify perpetrators.
firac.rule: Persecution means a 'sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights demonstrative of a failure of state protection' (Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689). Discrimination may amount to persecution only where serious or systematic enough to be so characterized (Sagharichi, F.C.A.).
firac.application: The looting and destruction, though accompanied by racial slurs, were part of generalized criminal violence not racially motivated; the NDP did not show Chinese being treated worse generally. Being a victim of a racially motivated crime once or twice does not equal persecution, and no sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights was shown. The Chinese Embassy safety notice was given little weight, being comparable to general travel warnings issued by other states.
firac.conclusion: The mistreatment amounted to discrimination and generalized crime, not persecution; the RPD committed no error on this issue.

firac.issue: Were the adult appellants properly excluded under Article 1E of the Convention?
firac.facts: The adult appellants held renewable five-year status in Venezuela substantially similar to that of nationals; renewal had required bribes, and counsel argued the loss of their business meant they could no longer afford the bribes.
firac.rule: Article 1E excludes persons with status substantially similar to nationals of a third country. Under Zeng (2010 FCA 118), if the claimant currently has such status, they are excluded; if not, further questions about loss of or access to status and balancing of factors apply.
firac.application: Applying the first Zeng question, the adult appellants currently had status substantially similar to Venezuelan nationals, so they are excluded. Despite the bribe concern, nothing prevented them from obtaining work and earning the needed funds on return, and they faced no more than a mere possibility of Convention-related risk in Venezuela, so no assessment of the claim against China was required.
firac.conclusion: The exclusion under Article 1E was upheld; the minor appellants' claims, being dependent on the adults', also failed.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) capture the core s. 96 analysis and the Ward definition of persecution. K080 (state protection) is central, as the presumption of state protection was the primary determinative issue alongside IFA. K069 (discrimination) and K065 (racism) reflect the finding that the appellants suffered discrimination/racially tinged crime falling short of persecution. K014 (standard of review) is engaged because the panel applied the correctness standard per Huruglica. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the deciding body. Article 1E exclusion is a significant issue but has no dedicated vocabulary term (K077 inadmissibility is a different concept), so it is left uncoded; K065/K069 are somewhat overlapping but both fit the ethnicity-based facts.
location_rationale: The decision states 'Appeal considered / heard at Toronto, ON', establishing the hearing city as Toronto in Ontario.
registry_rationale: The matter was heard by the Refugee Appeal Division at Toronto, ON; the Toronto office is the applicable registry as indicated by the hearing location.

case_name: Law Society of British Columbia v. Trinity Western University

name_verification.name_in_document: Law Society of British Columbia v. Trinity Western University

defining_issues: Was the Law Society of British Columbia entitled under its enabling statute (the Legal Profession Act) to consider a proposed law school's mandatory admissions covenant, and to hold a binding referendum of its members, in deciding whether to approve the school?
Did the LSBC's decision not to approve TWU's proposed law school limit freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?

If freedom of religion was limited, did the LSBC's decision reflect a proportionate balancing of that Charter protection against the LSBC's statutory objectives under the Doré/Loyola framework, so as to be reasonable?

firac.issue: Was the LSBC entitled under its enabling statute to consider TWU's admissions covenant and to hold a binding referendum of members in deciding whether to approve the proposed law school?
firac.facts: TWU, an evangelical Christian university, proposed a law school requiring all students and faculty to sign a Community Covenant Agreement prohibiting sexual intimacy except within marriage between a man and a woman. Under Law Society Rule 2-27, a Federation-approved faculty is 'approved' unless the Benchers resolve otherwise. After a Special General Meeting and a binding referendum of members, the Benchers passed a resolution declaring TWU's proposed school not approved.
firac.rule: Section 3 of the Legal Profession Act, S.B.C. 1998, c. 9 makes it the LSBC's object and duty to uphold and protect the public interest in the administration of justice, including 'preserving and protecting the rights and freedoms of all persons'; ss. 11, 20(1)(a) and 21(1)(b) confer broad rule-making authority. Law societies self-regulate in the public interest and their interpretation of the 'public interest' is owed deference (Green v. Law Society of Manitoba, 2017 SCC 20; Pearlman; Ryan). Section 13 does not exhaustively limit when Benchers may be bound by a referendum.
firac.application: The majority held the LPA requires the Benchers to consider the overarching public-interest objective in setting admission requirements, including whether to approve a law school. It was reasonable for the LSBC to treat equal access to the profession, diversity in the bar, and prevention of harm to LGBTQ students as valid public-interest concerns. Considering the covenant did not turn the LSBC into a human rights tribunal or into a regulator of law schools; it acted as gatekeeper to the profession. Section 13 did not preclude the Benchers from choosing to be bound by a referendum, even on a Charter-implicating issue.
firac.conclusion: The LSBC was entitled to consider TWU's admissions covenant and to proceed by referendum; the decision fell within its statutory mandate.

firac.issue: Did the LSBC's decision limit freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
firac.facts: Members of the TWU community sincerely believe that studying law in an environment defined by religious beliefs, where all abide by the Covenant, contributes to their spiritual development. Denial of approval prevented TWU from operating an approved law school governed by the mandatory Covenant.
firac.rule: Section 2(a) is limited where a claimant (1) sincerely believes in a practice or belief with a nexus to religion and (2) shows the state conduct interferes more than trivially with the ability to act on it (Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47; Ktunaxa Nation, 2017 SCC 54; Big M Drug Mart). Religious freedom is individual but also profoundly communitarian (Loyola; Hutterian Brethren).
firac.application: The majority found the sincerity of belief clear on the record and held that precluding an approved TWU law school with the mandatory Covenant limited members' ability to enhance their spiritual development by studying in an environment infused with their religious beliefs. It was unnecessary to decide whether TWU as an institution held s. 2(a) rights, or to separately analyse ss. 2(b), 2(d) and 15. (Rowe J. would have found s. 2(a) not engaged because the claim sought to constrain non-believers; the dissent found a profound interference.)
firac.conclusion: The LSBC's decision limited the religious freedom of members of the TWU community, engaging s. 2(a).

firac.issue: Did the LSBC's decision reflect a proportionate balancing of freedom of religion against its statutory objectives, making it reasonable under the Doré/Loyola framework?
firac.facts: The LSBC faced a binary choice: approve or reject the proposed school with its mandatory Covenant. The Covenant would effectively bar most LGBTQ students from 60 law-school seats and require them to deny a core part of their identity for three years. TWU showed no willingness to make the Covenant non-mandatory.
firac.rule: Discretionary administrative decisions engaging the Charter are reviewed under Doré v. Barreau du Québec, 2012 SCC 12 and Loyola High School v. Quebec (A.G.), 2015 SCC 12: the decision is reasonable if it reflects a proportionate balancing of the Charter protection with the statutory objectives, giving effect as fully as possible to the protection given the mandate, with analytical harmony to the minimal-impairment and balancing stages of R. v. Oakes.
firac.application: The majority held the limitation on religious freedom was of minor significance because a mandatory covenant was not absolutely required for the religious practice and students viewed the environment as preferred rather than necessary; the decision did not prevent anyone from practising their faith or from becoming a lawyer. On the other side, refusing approval significantly advanced equal access to and diversity within the profession and prevented significant harm to LGBTQ people, maintaining public confidence in the administration of justice. Given significant statutory benefits, minor Charter impact, and no reasonable less-restrictive alternative, the decision struck a proportionate balance. Formal reasons were not required as the Benchers were elected and alive to the issues.
firac.conclusion: The decision was a proportionate balance and therefore reasonable; the LSBC's resolution was restored.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally an administrative-law judicial review of a law society's Charter-engaging decision, so K001 (Administrative law, the primary area), K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review/reasonableness) are core. K010 (Doré/Loyola framework) is the specific proportionate-balancing test applied. K025 (freedom of religion) is the Charter right at issue, with K034 (sincerity of belief) engaged at the first stage of the s. 2(a) analysis and K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) as the specific provision. K013 (professional discipline/law society regulation) captures the LSBC's self-regulatory public-interest mandate over admission to the profession. K041 (campus/university) and K042 (code of conduct) reflect the university and the Community Covenant. K107 (Canadian Charter) anchors the constitutional statute relied on. Borderline picks: K041 and K042 are somewhat descriptive rather than doctrinal, and equality/LGBTQ concerns (no clean vocabulary match) drove much of the balancing but are only indirectly captured.
location_rationale: The decision is a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, which sits in Ottawa, Ontario. The text notes 'on appeal from the court of appeal for british columbia' but the SCC itself sits in Ottawa; the case originated in British Columbia (Langley/Vancouver).
registry_rationale: The SCC does not use a court registry in the manner of trial courts; the docket/file number is 37318 but no registry office is stated, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Richard Warman v. Canadian Heritage Alliance and Melissa Guille

defining_issues: May the Tribunal make findings on additional examples of alleged hate messages that were disclosed in evidence but never incorporated into the complaint forms, over the respondent's objection?

Was the impugned material posted on the Canadian Heritage Alliance website likely to expose persons or groups to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground, contrary to s. 13(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act?
Can Ms. Guille, as site administrator/webmaster, be held liable under s. 13 for hateful material she did not personally author but allowed to remain on the website?
Is the Canadian Heritage Alliance a 'group of persons acting in concert' for the purposes of s. 13(1) of the Act?
Should a penalty under s. 54(1)(c) be imposed in addition to a cease and desist order?

firac.issue: May the Tribunal make findings on additional examples of alleged hate messages disclosed in evidence but never added to the complaint forms, over the respondent's objection?
firac.facts: Warman's two complaint forms cited eight representative postings from the CHA website. At the hearing the Complainant and the Commission introduced some 37 further postings and articles (Exhibit HR-1, Tab C) that were never incorporated by amendment into the complaints. The Respondents objected, arguing they were entitled to know the case they had to meet.
firac.rule: Natural justice and procedural fairness require that a respondent be fully apprised, from the outset and throughout, of the case to be met. Section 48.9 CHRA requires informal and expeditious proceedings but only as natural justice permits. Because s. 13 complaints carry a potential penalty of up to $10,000 (s. 54(1.1)), the penal element heightens the fairness concern. Prior decisions (Kyburz 2003 CHRT 18; Winnicki 2006 CHRT 20; Kouba 2006 CHRT 50; Leblanc) were distinguished on the basis that in those cases either the complaint was amended or the respondent did not object.
firac.application: The complaint forms were never amended to add the extra material and the Respondents objected. The word 'ongoing' on the forms did not license the parties to add events at will without respecting natural justice. Had Ms. Guille been told earlier which postings were problematic, she could have removed them. The eight original examples were in any event sufficient to make out the case.
firac.conclusion: The objection was well founded; the Tribunal declined to make findings on the additional material listed in Annex I and confined its analysis to the eight examples in the complaint forms.

firac.issue: Was the impugned material likely to expose persons or groups to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground under s. 13(1)?
firac.facts: The eight examples included Holocaust-denial threads, articles advocating the extermination or expulsion of Jews and Blacks, claims that Jews control the media and commit ritual crimes, and material portraying racial mixing as a disease ('Black Plague'), plus a 'Museum of Jewish Crimes' compilation.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) CHRA. The meaning of 'likely,' 'expose,' 'hatred' and 'contempt' follows Nealy v. Johnston (1989): hatred connotes extreme ill will with no redeeming qualities; contempt connotes looking down on the group; it need not be shown anyone actually reacted. Warman v. Kouba (2006 CHRT 50) sets out eleven non-exhaustive hallmarks of hate messages. Freedom of expression (Charter) is not absolute.
firac.application: Applying the Nealy meaning and the Kouba hallmarks, the Tribunal found passages calling for Jews and Blacks to be 'exterminated root and branch,' expelled or 'massacred,' and material dehumanizing them (disease, savages, vermin). These went well beyond promoting European heritage and created conditions for hatred and contempt against identifiable groups.
firac.conclusion: The material was likely to expose Jews and Blacks to hatred or contempt on prohibited grounds and thus contravened s. 13.

firac.issue: Can Ms. Guille as webmaster be liable for material she did not personally author?
firac.facts: Ms. Guille registered and built the CHA website, was its administrator/webmaster with full power to edit, remove and moderate content, appointed moderators, edited some impugned articles to 'conform to Canadian law,' and reminded posters of forum rules.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) applies to a person who communicates or 'causes to be communicated' the impugned matter. A site administrator who exercises full control over content and could remove it is responsible for what appears on the site.
firac.application: The evidence established beyond doubt that Ms. Guille had full control over the website. It was no excuse that she did not author the articles; as administrator she was responsible for putting in place controls to prevent breaches of s. 13.
firac.conclusion: Ms. Guille caused the impugned material to be communicated and is liable under s. 13(1).

firac.issue: Is the Canadian Heritage Alliance a 'group of persons acting in concert' under s. 13(1)?
firac.facts: CHA described itself as 'a collection of dissident writers and concerned Canadians' and 'a Canadian political lobby group, formed in August 2000,' publishing a newsletter and issuing membership cards, though it argued it was merely a website.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) applies to 'a person or a group of persons acting in concert.' Whether a formal membership exists is not conclusive.
firac.application: CHA's own self-description as a collection of writers and a political lobby group was sufficient to show it is a group of persons acting in concert, regardless of the absence of a traditional membership list.
firac.conclusion: CHA is a group of persons acting in concert, a proper respondent, and subject to an order.

firac.issue: Should a penalty be imposed in addition to a cease and desist order?
firac.facts: Only a few of Ms. Guille's own postings were flagged and none called for extermination or expulsion. She removed the impugned material as soon as she received the complaint, maintained forum rules, edited violent content, and disavowed violence. She earned $14/hour, received $325/month child support, paid $750 rent and was raising a teenager alone. No prior discriminatory practices were shown.
firac.rule: Section 54(1)(c) permits a penalty up to $10,000; s. 54(1.1) requires consideration of the nature, circumstances, extent and gravity of the practice, the wilfulness/intent, prior practices and ability to pay. The Act is primarily remedial, not punitive. A range of prior penalties (Tremaine $4,000; Winnicki $6,000; Kulbashian/Richardson/Harrison $1,000; Kouba/Kyburz $7,500; Bahr $5,000; Beaumont $1,500) was reviewed.
firac.application: Given that Ms. Guille's own postings did not call for extermination or expulsion, that she removed and edited material promptly, had no prior practices, limited financial means, and the remedial purpose of the Act, a penalty would impose undue hardship and was not warranted.
firac.conclusion: No penalty imposed. A cease and desist order was issued together with an order that Ms. Guille work with the Commission for one year to redress and prevent the practice; execution suspended 30 days for the constitutional challenge.

keywords_rationale: The case is a statutory human rights determination (K007 practice area) under s. 13 CHRA (K113) of the Canadian Human Rights Act (K108) concerning hate messages (K061) posted on a website/internet forum (K063). The impugned content included Holocaust denial (K062) and antisemitic material (K058), tied to white-supremacist/neo-Nazi views (K066), constituting discriminatory messages (K070) targeting Jews (K093) and Black people. Procedural fairness (K012) was genuinely contested and determined the scope of the findings. Freedom of expression (K024) was expressly weighed against s. 13. K093 (Jewish) is the strongest of the target-group entity tags; a Black/African group tag was unavailable in the vocabulary. Borderline: K024 is engaged only briefly but the Tribunal expressly addressed the free-expression limit, so it is retained.
location_rationale: The reasons are signed "OTTAWA, Ontario" by Member Pierre Deschamps, so the Tribunal issued the decision from Ottawa, Ontario. (The hearings themselves were held in Toronto, Ontario over 2006-2007.)
registry_rationale: The Canadian Human Rights Tribunal is a national tribunal and no specific registry office is stated in the decision, so registry is left null.

case_name: Jewish Community Council of Montreal v. Canada (Attorney General)

name_verification.name_in_document: THE JEWISH COMMUNITY COUNCIL OF MONTREAL, KASHRUTH COUNCIL OF CANADA, RABBI ABRAHAM BANON, 4412532 CANADA INC. (D/B/A KOSHER MEHADRIN), and 1458935 ONTARIO LTD. (D/B/A SHEFA MEATS) v ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA

defining_issues: Was the relief sought a mandatory injunction requiring a 'strong prima facie case', or a prohibitive injunction subject only to the 'serious question' threshold?
Would injunctive relief have practical utility given the Respondent's argument that the Guidelines are non-binding and no declaration could settle a live controversy?
Did the Applicants raise a serious question to be tried regarding infringement of freedom of religion (s. 2(a)), equality (s. 15), and the reasonableness/vires of the Guidelines?
Did the Applicants establish irreparable harm that could not be compensated in damages?
Did the balance of convenience favour granting the injunction in light of the public interest in animal welfare?

firac.issue: Was the relief sought a mandatory injunction requiring a 'strong prima facie case', or a prohibitive injunction subject only to the 'serious question' threshold?
firac.facts: The Applicants sought to prevent the CFIA from enforcing the three indicators of unconsciousness in its Guidelines for ritual (kosher) slaughter, effectively reverting to the practice in place before June 2023. The Respondent argued this required the CFIA to take positive actions (modify and republish the Guidelines, retrain inspectors, notify licence holders), making it a mandatory injunction.
firac.rule: A mandatory injunction requires the respondent to do something and demands a 'strong prima facie case' (R v Canadian Broadcasting Corp, 2018 SCC 5 at paras 13–15). A prohibitive injunction preserving the status quo is assessed on the lower RJR-MacDonald 'serious question' threshold. Injunctions maintaining the status quo, even where continuation of an existing practice is required, are not automatically mandatory (AC and JF v Alberta, 2021 ABCA 24).
firac.application: The Court found the relief precludes the CFIA from strictly applying the Guidelines and reverts to the situation before June 2023, thereby preserving the status quo—i.e. preventing the Respondent from doing something. Because the Guidelines are non-binding and licence holders may use other methods, no republication or retraining is required; the evidence of required 'positive action' was unconvincing. Any 'mandatory aspect' (informing inspectors and licence holders of suspension) was merely incidental and insufficient to require a strong prima facie case.
firac.conclusion: The relief was a prohibitive injunction preserving the status quo; the lower 'serious question' threshold applied.

firac.issue: Would injunctive relief have practical utility given the argument that the Guidelines are non-binding?
firac.facts: The Respondent argued that because the Guidelines are not incorporated by reference into the SFCR, a declaration of unconstitutionality would have no value and there was no 'live controversy', particularly since closed slaughterhouses made no commitment to resume kosher production.
firac.rule: A remedy must settle a live controversy to have practical utility (Little Sisters, 2000 SCC 69; Shot Both Sides v Canada, 2024 SCC 12; Ewert v Canada, 2018 SCC 30; Daniels v Canada, 2016 SCC 12).
firac.application: The Court found that although the Guidelines are not 'binding' in the formal sense, the evidence (including cross-examination of L-P Vaillancourt) showed that inspectors require at least one of the three indicators, and failure to comply could lead to non-conformance and licence suspension—so the Guidelines are binding at an operational/practical level. There was sufficient evidence that licence holders treat them as binding and would resume production if enforcement ceased. Relief therefore had practical utility.
firac.conclusion: The relief had practical utility; the Court could grant an effective remedy addressing the operationally binding nature of the Guidelines.

firac.issue: Did the Applicants raise a serious question to be tried regarding freedom of religion, equality, and the reasonableness/vires of the Guidelines?
firac.facts: Kosher dietary laws (kashrut) and shechita are central to Jewish practice. Enforcement of the Guidelines reduced kosher beef supply by 55% and veal by 90%, closed several plants, and reduced Rabbi Banon's shechita work by over half. The Applicants argued the three indicators effectively require the animal to be brain-dead, exceeding the s. 143 SFCR requirement of unconsciousness.
firac.rule: The first branch of the RJR-MacDonald test requires only a non-frivolous, non-vexatious issue (Metropolitan Stores; RJR). Freedom of religion requires sincere belief with a nexus to religion and non-trivial interference (Amselem, 2004 SCC 47; Ktunaxa, 2017 SCC 54; Loyola, 2015 SCC 12). Equality under s. 15 requires a distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground that reinforces disadvantage (R v Sharma, 2022 SCC 39). Indirect or unintentional burdens fall within s. 2(a) (R v Edwards Books).
firac.application: On the low threshold, the Court found serious questions: the sincere belief in eating kosher meat and the substantial reduction in supply raised more than trivial interference with religious freedom; Rabbi Banon's sincere belief that performing shechita is a religious practice, reduced by half, raised a serious s. 2(a) issue; Rabbi Banon had standing to raise s. 15 and the distinction based on religion was arguable; and whether the Guidelines impose a stricter standard than s. 143 SFCR requires was a serious reasonableness/vires question.
firac.conclusion: The Applicants demonstrated serious questions to be tried on all three grounds—none frivolous or vexatious.

firac.issue: Did the Applicants establish irreparable harm not compensable in damages?
firac.facts: Rabbi Banon's shechita practice was reduced by about two days per week; kosher veal was nearly unobtainable and beef available only at prohibitive cost; many Jews could not access kosher meat with a special role in their tradition. The Respondent argued harm was speculative, self-inflicted (Mehadrin's exports), and compensable.
firac.rule: Irreparable harm must be shown with a convincing level of particularity (Glooscap, 2012 FCA 255) and is harm not quantifiable or not curable by damages (Metropolitan Stores; RJR). In the Charter context even quantifiable loss may be irreparable, and a breach of a Charter right can itself constitute irreparable harm (143471 Canada, 1994 CanLII 89). Risks to a minority community's way of life and traditions may constitute irreparable harm (Namgis, 2018 FC 334).
firac.application: The Court held the limits to Rabbi Banon's and the Jewish community's exercise of religion and equality are not quantifiable and not adequately compensable in damages. It rejected the 'self-inflicted' argument, accepting Mr. Rosenfeld's explanation for exports and finding importation subject to quotas did not offset the reduction. It accepted evidence that beef and veal are hard to find. Purely economic losses (Rabbi Banon's income, Mehadrin/Shefa supply chain) were compensable and not irreparable, but the religious/equality impacts were.
firac.conclusion: Irreparable harm was established through the impact on the practice of the Jewish faith by Rabbi Banon and the community (and MK and COR).

firac.issue: Did the balance of convenience favour granting the injunction given the public interest in animal welfare?
firac.facts: The CFIA's enforcement of the three indicators protects animal welfare (presumed to serve the public interest). Section 143 SFCR (requiring unconsciousness before suspension) predates the 2019 Guidelines, and kosher slaughter was compliant for years before June 2023 enforcement. Dr. Appelt observed an 'expertly conducted slaughter process' at Establishment C in 2018 with no non-compliance, before the Guidelines' indicators were required.
firac.rule: The balance of convenience weighs the greater harm from granting or refusing relief, factoring in the public interest (RJR at 342, 344). A public authority is presumed to represent the public interest, but applicants may show relief will not harm the public interest (Harper, 2000 SCC 57; Roach, Constitutional Remedies). The public interest includes minority communities (Reference re Secession of Québec).
firac.application: The Court found the CFIA could continue enforcing s. 143 and ensure animals are unconscious before suspension using other historically-used indicators, so suspending the Guidelines would have minimal impact on animal welfare and the public interest. The number of kosher licence holders is small and well known to the CFIA. Conversely, refusing relief would significantly impact the Charter rights of Rabbi Banon and the Jewish community. The public interest, which includes minority communities, did not favour enforcing the Guidelines where other measures achieve the same result.
firac.conclusion: The balance of convenience favoured the Applicants; issuing the injunction was just and equitable in all the circumstances.

name_verification.name_in_document: Neha Deol v. Dreyer Davison LLP and Rowan Davison

defining_issues: What is the true nature of the plaintiff's claim — a claim for damages for sexual harassment per se, or a claim in constructive dismissal?
Is it plain and obvious that the claim falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal, ousting the court's jurisdiction?
Is it plain and obvious that the claim falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Workers' Compensation Board?
Does the notice of civil claim disclose any reasonable cause of action against Mr. Davison personally?
Is it plain and obvious that the pleadings disclose no basis for aggravated or punitive damages, and which portions of the pleadings should be struck?

firac.issue: Is the plaintiff's claim properly characterized as one in constructive dismissal rather than a stand-alone claim for damages for sexual harassment?
firac.facts: Ms. Deol, a lawyer formerly employed by Dreyer Davison LLP, pleaded that Mr. Davison subjected her to sexually inappropriate conduct and that the firm's inadequate response created 'an objectively intolerable working environment' amounting to repudiation of her employment contract. Her pleadings were described as scattered and often sounding in sexual harassment per se, but she expressly pleaded repudiation and constructive dismissal.
firac.rule: On a Rule 9-5(1)(a) strike application a claim is struck only if it is plain and obvious, assuming the facts pleaded true, that no reasonable cause of action is disclosed (R. v. Imperial Tobacco, 2011 SCC 42). Constructive dismissal under the second branch of Potter v. New Brunswick Legal Aid, 2015 SCC 10 arises where the employer's cumulative conduct makes continued employment intolerable, assessed objectively; a specific breached term need not be identified.
firac.application: Despite deficiencies, the NOCC expressly pleaded the essential elements of second-branch constructive dismissal — an objectively intolerable working environment amounting to repudiation. The particulars of harassment and the firm's failure to address it were relevant to whether the employer repudiated the contract. Claims for damages in lieu of notice, aggravated ('mental distress'/moral) and punitive damages are recognized heads flowing from constructive dismissal.
firac.conclusion: The NOCC sufficiently pleads an action for constructive dismissal; the claim is not merely a disguised sexual-harassment action.'

firac.issue: Does the BCHRT have exclusive jurisdiction over the claim because the conduct amounts to sexual harassment/discrimination?
firac.facts: Defendants argued that sexual harassment is gender-based discrimination remediable only before the BCHRT, relying on Seneca College v. Bhadauria and Honda v. Keays, and pointed to Hall and Schulz where similar claims were struck.
firac.rule: Bhadauria forecloses a civil action based directly on a breach of human rights legislation, but the courts retain jurisdiction over recognized common law causes of action (e.g., breach of contract/constructive dismissal) even where the same facts engage discrimination: Lewis v. WestJet Airlines Ltd., 2019 BCCA 63. Statutory obligations are not implied contract terms (Macaraeg), but a contractual breach may coincide with a statutory breach.
firac.application: The court found the Honda comments at paras. 63–64 on Bhadauria to be obiter, resting on the reversal of the trial judge's discrimination findings. Following Lewis, discriminatory conduct may also ground a constructive dismissal claim even absent an express anti-harassment contract term; the second branch of Potter requires no specific term. Honda and Bhadauria do not oust the superior court's jurisdiction over a recognized contract claim merely because discriminatory conduct is alleged.
firac.conclusion: The BCHRT does not have exclusive jurisdiction; the constructive dismissal claim may proceed in the court.

firac.issue: Does the Workers' Compensation Board have exclusive jurisdiction over the claim?
firac.facts: Defendants argued that injuries from workplace/sexual harassment fall within the WCB scheme; a WCAT s. 257 certification application was pending. Ms. Deol maintained she sought contract damages, not personal-injury compensation.
firac.rule: The Workers Compensation Act provides a comprehensive scheme: s. 5.1 compensates work-related 'mental disorders,' s. 10(1) bars suing an employer for personal injury arising out of employment, and s. 96(1) grants the WCB exclusive jurisdiction. Compensation is not payable for a mental disorder caused by the decision to terminate. General damages in lieu of notice are distinct from personal-injury damages.
firac.application: Claims genuinely sounding in personal injury arising in the course of employment fall outside the court's first-instance jurisdiction. General damages (in lieu of notice) and aggravated damages arising from the manner of dismissal are contract remedies within the court's jurisdiction and not compensation for a compensable mental disorder. Para. 20 ('grave personal effects...foreseeable at the time of dismissal') properly pleads aggravated damages, but para. 21 ('suffered and will continue to suffer as a result of the foregoing') strayed into a personal-injury/tort claim for ongoing injury from the harassment itself.
firac.conclusion: The claim, as clarified, does not fall within the WCB's exclusive jurisdiction; para. 21 is struck as pleading personal injury.

firac.issue: Does the NOCC disclose a reasonable cause of action against Mr. Davison personally?
firac.facts: Mr. Davison is a partner but not a party to Ms. Deol's employment contract, which was with the firm. She named him because he was primarily responsible for the conduct and to secure collection of any judgment.
firac.rule: A claim in contract must be brought against a party to the contract. Direct claims against an individual for discriminatory or injurious conduct belong before the BCHRT (discrimination) or the WCB (personal/mental injury).
firac.application: Ms. Deol's contract was with the firm, not Mr. Davison, so no contract claim lies against him. Any direct remedy against him for his conduct must be pursued before the BCHRT or WCB. Her collection concern provided no legal basis for naming him personally.
firac.conclusion: The claims against Mr. Davison personally are dismissed; the NOCC must be amended to remove him and direct the breach-of-contract allegations to the firm.

firac.issue: Is it plain and obvious the pleadings disclose no basis for aggravated or punitive damages, and which portions should be struck?
firac.facts: Ms. Deol claimed aggravated and punitive damages and pleaded general statements (paras. 14–19) about the prevalence and non-adjudication of workplace sexual harassment, and sought at para. 22(a) 'further meaningful development of the common law.'
firac.rule: Aggravated (moral) damages require unfair/bad-faith conduct in the manner of dismissal causing mental distress (Honda v. Keays, 2008 SCC 39; Cottrill, 2018 BCCA 383) and need no independent actionable wrong. Punitive damages require an independent actionable wrong, which may be a breach of the contractual duty of good faith (Whiten v. Pilot Insurance, 2002 SCC 18); facts justifying them must be pleaded with particularity.
firac.application: For second-branch constructive dismissal, cumulative past acts may form part of the 'manner of dismissal,' so aggravated damages are arguable. On punitive damages, whether discriminatory conduct is an independent actionable wrong was left open in Honda; in any event Ms. Deol pleaded other alleged good-faith/fair-dealing breaches capable of grounding an actionable wrong, so the claim is not plainly untenable. However, paras. 14–17 and 19 addressed only general (societal) deterrence, were not rationally connected to the defendants' conduct or the contract, and para. 22(a) articulated no known relief.
firac.conclusion: Neither the aggravated nor punitive damages claims are struck, but paras. 14–17, 19, 21 and 22(a) are struck; the balance of the strike application is dismissed, costs in the cause.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area — the case turns on constructive dismissal and employment remedies. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the core cause of action, engaged through the constructive-dismissal analysis under Potter. K083 (harassment) captures the pleaded sexual harassment central to the repudiation allegation. K082 (employment discrimination) and K069 (discrimination) reflect the jurisdictional debate over whether the conduct is discriminatory conduct exclusively for a tribunal. K072 (human rights tribunal) is directly engaged by the argument that the BCHRT has exclusive jurisdiction. K007 (Human rights) is included as a secondary practice-area anchor because the Bhadauria/Honda jurisdictional analysis is grounded in human rights legislation. K002 (Civil litigation) is a borderline pick reflecting the Rule 9-5 strike/pleadings context; it is weaker than the employment-focused keywords but captures the procedural posture. No keyword for WCB/workers' compensation exists in the vocabulary, so that significant strand is covered indirectly.

name_verification.name_in_document: Regina v. Roy Arthur Topham

defining_issues: Was Dr. Jay's expert opinion relevant to the post-trial constitutional challenge to s. 319(2) of the Criminal Code and the Bedford threshold for reconsidering Keegstra?
Does an exclusionary principle bar the accused from adducing expert evidence that amounts to a collateral attack on the jury's verdict?

firac.issue: Was the proposed expert opinion relevant to the constitutional challenge and to the Bedford threshold for reconsidering Keegstra?
firac.facts: After a jury convicted Topham under s. 319(2) for wilfully promoting hatred against Jewish people, he pursued a post-trial constitutional challenge to s. 319(2), arguing the law had developed since Keegstra (citing Whatcott). He sought to enter a report of Dr. Timothy Jay, a cognitive psychologist, opining that a satirical reading of the article 'Israel Must Perish' by an average adult reader would not be considered hate speech.
firac.rule: Expert evidence must satisfy the Mohan/White Burgess threshold, the first requirement being relevance. On a challenge to the constitutionality of legislation, admissible evidence elucidates the legislative framework, factual context, purpose, mischief and effect of the provision (Chamberlain v. Surrey School District No. 36). Under Bedford, a prior binding decision may be revisited only where a new legal issue is raised, the law has significantly developed, or the evidence fundamentally shifts the parameters of the debate.
firac.application: The Court found Dr. Jay's opinion was in substance a critique of the jury's factual conclusion, not evidence about the legislative framework, purpose or effect of s. 319(2). It raised no new legal issue, reflected no development in the law since Keegstra, and did not shift the parameters of the debate. It fell within none of the Chamberlain categories and did not engage the Bedford threshold.
firac.conclusion: The opinion had no relevance to any issue on the application; the necessity and qualification requirements did not need to be decided because relevance failed.

firac.issue: Does an exclusionary principle bar the accused from adducing evidence that collaterally attacks the jury's verdict?
firac.facts: Dr. Jay's report challenged, indirectly, the jury's conclusion by suggesting a satirical reading of the impugned article would not amount to hate speech, after the jury had already convicted.
firac.rule: Once a verdict is rendered, the parties have no further right to call evidence about the facts of the offence; an accused cannot lead evidence attacking the factual root of the conviction, as this would bring the administration of justice into disrepute and offend finality/res judicata (R. v. Gauthier; R. v. Braun; R. v. Ferguson — a judge is bound by the express and implied factual findings essential to the jury's verdict).
firac.application: Although this was not a sentencing hearing, the Court held the same principle applies by analogy: the constitutional challenge did not permit re-examination of the jury's findings. Dr. Jay's opinion amounted to an impermissible collateral attack on the verdict and the issue it touched was res judicata.
firac.conclusion: An exclusionary principle applied; the report was inadmissible on this independent ground as well.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary practice area, as the case arises from a s. 319(2) conviction. K115 pinpoints Criminal Code s. 319(2) and K067/K061 capture the wilful promotion of hatred / hate speech at the heart of the charge.
