name_verification.name_in_document: Y.Z. AND THE CANADIAN ASSOCIATION OF REFUGEE LAWYERS v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION AND THE MINISTER OF PUBLIC SAFETY AND EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS (and G.S. AND C.S. v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION)

defining_issues: Should the constitutionality of the entire Designated Countries of Origin regime (section 109.1 and the Thresholds Order) be assessed, or only paragraph 110(2)(d.1) of the IRPA?
Does the Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers (CARL) have public interest standing?
Does paragraph 110(2)(d.1) of the IRPA, which denies DCO refugee claimants an appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division, infringe subsection 15(1) of the Charter?
Does paragraph 110(2)(d.1) of the IRPA infringe section 7 of the Charter?
If paragraph 110(2)(d.1) infringes the Charter, is it justified under section 1?
What is the appropriate remedy and should questions be certified?

firac.issue: Should the Court assess the constitutionality of the entire DCO regime (s. 109.1 and the Thresholds Order) or only paragraph 110(2)(d.1)?
firac.facts: The applicants challenged the whole DCO regime, including the country-designation mechanism, while the respondents said only paragraph 110(2)(d.1) was properly in issue. The relief sought had expanded over time and the record lacked full evidence of the consequences of designation, such as work-permit delays, abbreviated timelines and the 36-month PRRA bar.
firac.rule: Courts should avoid unnecessary constitutional pronouncements (Phillips v Nova Scotia; Ishaq) and must not decide Charter issues in a factual vacuum (Mackay v Manitoba).
firac.application: A finding that paragraph 110(2)(d.1) is unconstitutional would give the individual applicants the substantive relief they sought (access to the RAD). The evidentiary record was insufficient to assess the work-permit, timeline and PRRA-bar consequences, none of the individual applicants was yet affected by the 36-month PRRA bar, and the abbreviated timelines had not actually prejudiced them.
firac.conclusion: The Court confined its analysis to paragraph 110(2)(d.1); it declined to rule on section 109.1 or the Thresholds Order.

firac.issue: Does CARL have public interest standing?
firac.facts: CARL, an association of experienced refugee lawyers, joined Y.Z.'s application from the outset, had raised DCO concerns before Parliament, secured Legal Aid test-case funding, and helped prepare the record. The respondents argued CARL added nothing distinct and that individual litigants were an effective vehicle.
firac.rule: Public interest standing requires (1) a serious justiciable issue, (2) a real stake or genuine interest, and (3) that the proposed suit be a reasonable and effective way to bring the issue to court (Canada (AG) v Downtown Eastside Sex Workers, 2012 SCC 45). Standing need not be proven by preliminary motion (Finlay; s. 18.1(1) Federal Courts Act).
firac.application: The respondents conceded a serious justiciable issue. CARL was not a mere busybody but an engaged organization with expertise; joining three individual applicants conserved judicial resources and ensured the litigation could continue if the individuals became unable to proceed, particularly given the risk of deportation and lack of means facing other DCO claimants.
firac.conclusion: CARL was granted public interest standing.

firac.issue: Does paragraph 110(2)(d.1) of the IRPA infringe subsection 15(1) of the Charter?
firac.facts: Paragraph 110(2)(d.1) denies an appeal to the RAD to all refugee claimants from designated countries of origin, while non-DCO claimants may appeal unless otherwise precluded. Statistics showed many genuine claims (e.g. Hungary acceptance rates of 44%) are made by DCO nationals.
firac.rule: Section 15(1) protects substantive equality through a two-part test: (1) does the law create a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground, and (2) does the distinction create a disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping (Withler; Taypotat; Andrews). National origin is an enumerated ground and includes discrimination between classes of non-citizens based on country of origin (Canadian Doctors; Hape).
firac.application: The provision draws a clear distinction on the basis of national origin, treating DCO claimants differently regardless of their personal circumstances. It perpetuates the stereotype that DCO claimants are 'bogus' queue-jumpers, even though those denied an appeal are, in effect, the genuine claimants whose claims had a credible basis and were not manifestly unfounded (fraudulent or abandoned claims already lose the appeal under ss. 110(2)(b) and (c)). Access to the RAD is a substantial benefit denied on the basis of national origin.
firac.conclusion: Paragraph 110(2)(d.1) violates subsection 15(1) of the Charter.

firac.issue: Does paragraph 110(2)(d.1) infringe section 7 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The applicants argued that denying an appeal increases the risk of refoulement contrary to the principles of fundamental justice, framing the argument largely around the designation mechanism and gross disproportionality of the whole DCO regime.
firac.rule: There is no constitutional right to an appeal, nor does such a right flow from the rule of law (Charkaoui v Canada, 2007 SCC 9; R v Meltzer; Kourtessis).
firac.application: The section 7 arguments were mainly directed at the country-selection mechanism, which the Court had already declined to assess. In any event, the absence of a RAD appeal does not itself offend the principles of fundamental justice because there is no constitutional right to an appeal.
firac.conclusion: Paragraph 110(2)(d.1) does not infringe section 7 of the Charter.

firac.issue: Is the section 15(1) infringement justified under section 1 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The government's reforms sought to address a slow, backlogged refugee system (roughly 20-month waits, 4.5-year removal times). Denying the RAD appeal to DCO claimants was said to reduce layers of recourse and speed removals; removal times for DCO and non-DCO claimants were nearly identical (116 vs 122 days).
firac.rule: The Oakes test: a pressing and substantial objective, plus proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionate effects); the negative impact on rights must be proportionate to the law's goal (Oakes; Bedford; RJR-MacDonald).
firac.application: While Canada had a pressing and substantial objective and the measure may be rationally connected, it was not minimally impairing. The goal of deterring abusive or unfounded claims could already be achieved through ss. 107(2), 107.1 and paras 110(2)(b) and (c) (no credible basis, manifestly unfounded, withdrawn/abandoned), which bar appeals without distinguishing by national origin. The respondents proved no additional deterrent effect, and DCO claimants also lose the automatic stay of removal, increasing the risk of refoulement and stress. The deleterious effects were disproportionate.
firac.conclusion: The infringement is not justified under section 1; paragraph 110(2)(d.1) cannot be saved.

firac.issue: What is the appropriate remedy and should questions be certified?
firac.facts: The applicants sought declarations of invalidity for the whole DCO regime and orders sending appeals to the RAD; the respondents sought a 12-month suspension of any declaration of invalidity.
firac.rule: Section 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 renders inconsistent laws of no force or effect; suspension of a declaration is appropriate only where an immediate declaration would endanger the public, threaten the rule of law, or deprive deserving persons of benefits (Schachter). Certification under s. 74(d) IRPA requires a dispositive question of general importance (Zhang).
firac.application: The Court declared paragraph 110(2)(d.1) inconsistent with s. 15(1) and of no force and effect, set aside the RAD decisions, and returned G.S. and C.S.'s appeals for redetermination (Y.Z.'s RPD decision having already been set aside). No Schachter criterion justified suspending the declaration; every day the provision remained in force denied DCO claimants equality. Two questions on Charter compliance and s. 1 justification were certified.
firac.conclusion: Applications granted in part; paragraph 110(2)(d.1) declared invalid with immediate effect; RAD decisions set aside and G.S./C.S. appeals remitted; two questions certified.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns the IRPA refugee-determination scheme and the Designated Countries of Origin regime. K003 (Constitutional law) and K023 (equality rights), with K109 (Charter s. 15), capture the core holding that para 110(2)(d.1) violates the s. 15(1) equality guarantee on the basis of national origin. K112 (Charter s. 7) reflects the rejected section 7 argument, which was a defining issue. K030 (reasonable limits s. 1) covers the Oakes/minimal-impairment analysis. K011 (judicial review) reflects the procedural vehicle (judicial review of RAD decisions under s. 72). K078 (refugee protection) situates the subject matter. K081 (stay of removal) is engaged because loss of the automatic stay for DCO claimants was central to the s. 1 reasoning. K069 (discrimination) ties to the substantive-equality analysis. Standing was significant but has no dedicated vocabulary term; K011 is the closest procedural fit.
location_rationale: The reasons are dated and issued at 'Ottawa, Ontario, July 23, 2015'. The style of cause and hearing information confirm Ontario. The matter was heard in Toronto (PLACE OF HEARING: Toronto, Ontario).
registry_rationale: The Federal Court is a national court without a fixed provincial registry, but the hearing took place in Toronto and solicitors of record and the Deputy Attorney General office are listed in Toronto, so Toronto is the operative registry/hearing location.

defining_issues: Did the anti-Semitic harassment the claimant experienced in Russia rise to the level of persecution or otherwise establish a need for protection?
Was there adequate state protection, and was the claimant's fear both subjectively and objectively well-founded given her delay in claiming?
Did the claimant have a viable internal flight alternative within Russia?

firac.issue: Did the general anti-Semitic harassment the claimant experienced amount to persecution under s. 96 or a risk under s. 97 of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The 85-year-old claimant, a non-religious Russian citizen of Jewish nationality, said anti-Semitic social behaviour grew after 1992. She and her late husband were never specifically targeted but were treated like other Jewish families in their building; verbal harassment and harassing phone calls were, in her experience, 'normal' public behaviour. She reported two incidents by telephone to police with no result and never filed a written report.
firac.rule: To qualify as a Convention refugee under s. 96 IRPA the harm feared must rise to the level of persecution; discrimination or harassment that does not reach that intensity is insufficient. Section 97 requires a personalized risk.
firac.application: The panel found the harassment was general rather than targeted at the claimant and, though anti-social, did not reach the intensity of persecution. It was supported by the documentary evidence (Exhibits C-4 and R/A-1) that such conduct is discouraged in Russia.
firac.conclusion: The mistreatment did not constitute persecution or a s. 97 risk.

firac.issue: Was state protection available, and was the claimant's fear genuine and well-founded given her delayed claim?
firac.facts: The claimant made only two phone calls to police and filed no written report; her neighbours experienced the same indifference. She obtained a visitor visa in 2004, claimed refugee status only in March 2005, and admitted the CIC interviewer first suggested the claim. Her anxiety arose after her husband's 2003 death and diminished once she lived with her daughter in Canada.
firac.rule: A claimant must rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence, and must establish a subjectively genuine and objectively well-founded fear; unexplained delay and failure to claim at the first opportunity undermine subjective fear.
firac.application: The panel held that police inability to resolve harassment did not amount to state complicity, that Russia is not a lawless state, and that the claimant's calm in Canada was better explained by family reunification and relief from the loneliness following her husband's death. Her failure to raise any fear before being prompted at the CIC interview belied a genuine fear.
firac.conclusion: State protection was available and the claimant lacked a genuine, well-founded fear.

firac.issue: Did the claimant have a viable internal flight alternative in Russia?
firac.facts: The claimant never considered relocating within Russia, citing limited mobility (she uses a wheelchair) and her wish to reunite with her daughter. Vladivostok was raised as a potential IFA.
firac.rule: A claimant must show that a proposed IFA is not viable, i.e. that there is a serious possibility of persecution there or that relocation would be unreasonable in the circumstances.
firac.application: The panel noted that her limited mobility did not prevent her from travelling thousands of miles to Canada, so it could not reasonably preclude internal relocation; her reluctance was driven by the desire to reunite with her daughter.
firac.conclusion: The claimant did not rebut the viable IFA in Vladivostok.

keywords_rationale: K008 is the tier-1 practice area (immigration/refugee law). K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the s. 96/s. 97 claim. K079 (persecution) is central since the determinative issue was whether harassment reached persecution. K080 (state protection) reflects the finding that Russian police indifference did not amount to state complicity. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) identify the basis of the claim — fear as a member of the Jewish community. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the adjudicating institution. The internal flight alternative and delay issues have no dedicated vocabulary entry, so no keyword was assigned to them.

registry_rationale: The matter was heard by the Refugee Protection Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board with the hearing held in Toronto; the Toronto office/registry is inferred from the place of hearing.

case_name: LaBranche v. Treasury Board (Department of Foreign Affairs and International Trade)

name_verification.name_in_document: LaBranche v. Treasury Board (Department of Foreign Affairs and International Trade)

defining_issues: Is a grievance alleging religious discrimination and failure to accommodate adjudicable under s. 209(1)(a) of the PSLRA where the employer says its harassment policy is not part of the collective agreement?

Did the workplace incidents alleged by the grievor occur and, if so, did they constitute discrimination on the basis of religious affiliation contrary to clause 16.01 of the collective agreement and the CHRA?
Did the grievor communicate a complaint of discrimination and harassment that the employer was obliged to investigate and address, and did it fail to do so?
Did the employer owe and breach a duty to accommodate the grievor's disability caused by the workplace discrimination?
Is the employer liable for discrimination even though the author of the anonymous correspondence could not be identified?
Could the adjudicator consider subsequent-event evidence (the early termination of the secondment) in fashioning a remedy?

firac.issue: Is a grievance alleging religious discrimination and failure to accommodate adjudicable under the PSLRA?
firac.facts: The grievor invoked article 16 (no discrimination) and article 50 (religious observance) of the collective agreement and the CHRA. The employer objected that its harassment policy was not incorporated into the collective agreement, so the grievance fell outside an adjudicator's jurisdiction.
firac.rule: Section 209(1)(a) of the PSLRA permits referral to adjudication of grievances concerning the interpretation or application of a collective agreement; ss. 226(1)(g)-(h) allow an adjudicator to interpret and apply the CHRA and grant CHRA relief. Souaker v. Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, 2009 PSLRB 145 holds that where a change in conditions of employment is alleged to be discriminatory and the collective agreement bars discrimination, the grievance engages the agreement.
firac.application: Clause 16.01 grants employees a substantive right to equal, non-discriminatory treatment, and clause 50 imposes a duty to accommodate religious observance. An allegation that the employer breached these provisions is an allegation about the application of the collective agreement under s. 209(1)(a), independent of any separate harassment policy.
firac.conclusion: The objection was dismissed; the adjudicator had jurisdiction to decide the grievance.

firac.issue: Did the alleged incidents occur and amount to religious discrimination?
firac.facts: After Ms. Lévesque became administrative assistant, the grievor's informal religious-leave arrangement was challenged, she was required to complete leave/overtime forms, her pre-authorized Shabbat-related Paris layover was questioned, comments were made about her modest dress and not participating in dress-down Fridays, and false reports (the Akitt incident) were used against her; anonymous antisemitic and threatening correspondence referencing her religion was also received.
firac.rule: Discrimination is a distinction based on personal characteristics imposing burdens or withholding benefits (Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143). The complainant must establish a prima facie case on the balance of probabilities (O'Malley), after which the employer must give a non-discriminatory explanation; intent is irrelevant (Marinaki). Circumstantial evidence may suffice (Brooks v. Attorney General, 2006 FC 1244).
firac.application: The adjudicator found Ms. Lévesque's denial of knowledge of the grievor's faith not credible and found the interference with religious leave, the unjustified challenge to the CEO-authorized Paris layover, and the dress-related comments by Lévesque, Pezzack and Crone were discriminatory, regardless of intent; the Akitt episode showed a pattern of interference contributing to a hostile environment. Only the unproven 'explain your beliefs to staff' allegation failed for lack of corroboration.
firac.conclusion: Most incidents occurred and constituted discrimination based on religious affiliation, creating a poisoned workplace contrary to clause 16.01 and para. 7(b) of the CHRA.

firac.issue: Did the grievor communicate a complaint the employer failed to investigate and address?
firac.facts: The grievor raised concerns of anti-Semitism verbally (spring 2006, Nov. 21 and Dec. 8, 2006) and in writing, notably a Dec. 27, 2006 email attaching 'A Chronology of Hatred at Passport Canada,' plus notice she was consulting the Canadian Human Rights Commission. The employer's investigation focused only on identifying the author of the anonymous letters and treated the chronology as fact-gathering, not a harassment complaint; managers wrongly believed a formal union-filed complaint was required.
firac.rule: Neither the collective agreement nor the CHRA requires a formal written complaint. Under clause 16.01 the employer has an ongoing, proactive duty to monitor, investigate and remedy discrimination once it is brought to its attention; eliminating workplace discrimination is the employer's responsibility (O'Malley; Hill v. Air Canada, 2003 CHRT 9 on hostile environment).
firac.application: The grievor plainly communicated complaints going well beyond the anonymous letters. The employer limited its inquiry to finding the letter-writer, ignored the other incidents, mistakenly required a formal complaint, and treated a post-hoc staff meeting as sufficient. This did not discharge its diligence obligation.
firac.conclusion: The employer failed to ensure a workplace free of discrimination and failed to promptly investigate the grievor's complaints.

firac.issue: Did the employer breach a duty to accommodate the grievor's disability?
firac.facts: The grievor went on medical leave after the threats, supplying medical certificates the employer never challenged. The employer required a certificate, offered EAP, taxi chits and brief administrative leave, then terminated her secondment effective Feb. 7, 2007, before her Feb. 19 return-to-work date, without exploring alternative work.
firac.rule: An employer must accommodate a disabled employee to the point of undue hardship and bears the onus of proving undue hardship (O'Malley); the duty is ongoing and requires looking beyond the employee's own position for suitable work.
firac.application: The timing and evidence showed the grievor's emotional/physical distress resulted from the discrimination and the employer's inaction. The employer wrongly assumed no duty because the secondment was ending, made no genuine effort to find alternative work (as it had for Ms. Bowman), and led no evidence of undue hardship.
firac.conclusion: The employer breached its duty to accommodate under ss. 7 and 15 of the CHRA.

firac.issue: Is the employer liable despite the unidentified perpetrator of the anonymous correspondence?
firac.facts: IT analysis indicated the antisemitic email likely originated from an insider with detailed personal knowledge; the author was never identified. The employer argued it could not be liable for acts of unknown persons.
firac.rule: Robichaud v. Canada (Treasury Board), [1987] 2 S.C.R. 84 establishes statutory employer liability for job-related acts and places organizational responsibility to take effective remedial action; the CHRA aims to remove discrimination, not punish, so intent and identifying a culprit are not determinative.
firac.application: The discrimination—whether the anonymous correspondence or the acts of Lévesque, Crone and Pezzack—was workplace-related. The employer turned a blind eye to evidence of an internal source and failed to take effective remedial action.
firac.conclusion: The employer is liable for the discrimination regardless of the unidentified author.

firac.issue: Could subsequent-event evidence of the termination of the secondment be considered?
firac.facts: The grievor filed her grievance on Jan. 23, 2007 and was notified of termination of her secondment on Jan. 24, 2007, effective Feb. 7, 2007; she did not grieve the termination but asked it be considered in remedy.
firac.rule: Cie minière Québec Cartier v. Québec, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1095 permits reliance on subsequent-event evidence where relevant to the issue in dispute; PSLRA s. 226(1)(d) allows admission of evidence whether or not admissible in court, and s. 228(2) empowers the adjudicator to make any order considered appropriate.
firac.application: The termination was relevant because it confirmed the ongoing, discriminatory nature of the employer's response and occurred while the grievor was ill from the discrimination and before she could seek accommodation for her return; the two-week-notice justification was 'window dressing' given incomplete projects and unfilled positions.
firac.conclusion: The subsequent-event evidence was admissible and considered; the termination was found to be the culminating discriminatory act.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a public-service grievance referred to adjudication. K084 (labour arbitration/grievance) captures the procedural vehicle and the s. 209 adjudicability ruling. K082 (employment discrimination) and K069 (discrimination) reflect the core finding of adverse differentiation under para. 7(b) CHRA and clause 16.01. K083 (harassment) reflects the poisoned-workplace/hostile-environment analysis. K031 (religious accommodation) covers the duty-to-accommodate findings under clause 50 and ss. 7/15 CHRA. K073 (prima facie discrimination) reflects the O'Malley burden-shifting framework applied. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) are engaged by the antisemitic correspondence and the grievor's observant Jewish identity. K108 (Canadian Human Rights Act) is the governing statute. Freedom of religion (K025) was not chosen because the case turns on statutory human-rights/collective-agreement discrimination rather than Charter s. 2(a); religious dress (K032) is a borderline omission given the dress-related comments but is subsumed within the discrimination keywords.
location_rationale: The decision states it was 'Heard at Ottawa, Ontario' on the listed hearing dates, fixing the city as Ottawa and the province as Ontario.
registry_rationale: No registry office is named; the matter was an individual grievance referred to adjudication before a national labour relations board (PSLRB), so registry is left null.

case_name: Jazairi v. Ontario Human Rights Commission

name_verification.name_in_document: NURI T. JAZAIRI v. ONTARIO HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION, YORK UNIVERSITY, HARRY ARTHURS, SENATE COMMITTEE ON TENURE AND PROMOTION, FACULTY COMMITTEE ON TENURE AND PROMOTION, TOM TRAVES, JOHN C. EVANS, ELIE APPELBAUM and ROGER LATHAM

defining_issues: Does the prohibition against discrimination on the basis of 'creed' in s. 5(1) of the Ontario Human Rights Code include discrimination on the basis of 'political opinion'?
If the Code does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of political opinion, does that omission violate s. 15(1) of the Charter, and if so is it justified under s. 1?
Should the court in any event exercise its discretion to refuse the discretionary remedy of judicial review?

firac.issue: Does 'creed' in s. 5(1) of the Human Rights Code encompass 'political opinion'?
firac.facts: The appellant, a Muslim Arab economics professor at York University, alleged that his promotion to full professor was delayed because two colleagues submitted unsolicited negative letters motivated by disagreement with his political views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. He complained to the Commission on grounds of race, religion and political opinion; the Commission declined to appoint a Board of Inquiry, finding any differential treatment was based on political remarks, not creed.
firac.rule: Section 5(1) of the Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19, prohibits discrimination in employment on enumerated grounds including 'creed'. Following the Divisional Court's reasoning, 'creed' requires a recognizable cohesive belief system or structure, not mere political opinion.
firac.application: The court agreed with the Divisional Court that the appellant's personal opinion on the single issue of the relationship between Palestinians and Israel does not amount to a creed. Whether some other political belief system could constitute a creed was not before the court, and it was a mistake to decide such important issues in the abstract on hypothetical scenarios.
firac.conclusion: Mere political opinion is not within the meaning of 'creed' in the Code; the appellant's views did not amount to a creed.

firac.issue: Does the omission of 'political opinion' as a prohibited ground of discrimination in the Code violate s. 15(1) of the Charter?
firac.facts: The appellant sought a declaration that 'political opinion' is an analogous ground of discrimination that should be read into s. 5(1) of the Code. He argued that a colleague's disagreement with his political views should have disqualified that colleague from criticizing his credentials.
firac.rule: The s. 15(1) analysis from Law v. Canada, [1999] S.C.J. No. 12, and M. v. H., [1999] S.C.J. No. 23, asks whether differential treatment based on an enumerated or analogous ground discriminates by imposing a burden or withholding a benefit in a manner that reflects stereotype or otherwise demeans human dignity, considering the nature and scope of the interest affected. Freedom to express political opinion is already protected by s. 2(b) of the Charter.
firac.application: Analyzing the claim in its specific factual context rather than abstractly, the court found the appellant's human dignity was never engaged, let alone violated. Nothing on the record suggested his political beliefs made him less worthy of advancement or that he belonged to a group deserving protection. The decision-makers were not shown to have known of the letter writers' alleged improper motivation, and the offending letters had been withdrawn at the appellant's own request.
firac.conclusion: There was no violation of s. 15(1); the omission of political opinion from the Code did not offend the equality guarantee on these facts, so no s. 1 justification analysis was required.

firac.issue: Should judicial review be refused as a matter of discretion regardless of the merits?
firac.facts: The Commission had kept the file open for over six years, questioned numerous witnesses, and found only that the Senate committee was aware of the controversy the letters generated. The strongest available finding could not establish that decision-makers were influenced by the appellant's political views.
firac.rule: Judicial review relief is discretionary; the court retains discretion to refuse prerogative relief (Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1, ss. 2(5)-(6); Canadian Pacific Ltd. v. Matsqui Indian Band (1995), 122 D.L.R. (4th) 129). Relief may be refused where it would have no practical effect. A court will only extend legislation where the remedy flows with sufficient precision from constitutional requirements (Schachter v. Canada; Vriend v. Alberta).
firac.application: Even if there had been error below, the court would refuse judicial review because it would have no practical effect: there was no reason to believe the appellant would ultimately succeed even if the Commission had jurisdiction over political opinion, and the record did not provide a sufficient factual basis to read a new ground into the Code with the required precision.
firac.conclusion: The court would in any event decline the discretionary remedy of judicial review.

case_name: Keezio Group, LLC v. The Shrunks' Family Toy Company Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: Keezio Group, LLC v. The Shrunks' Family Toy Company Inc.

defining_issues: Is Keezio entitled to security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act against The Shrunks as plaintiff by counterclaim?
Where the counterclaim substantially overlaps with the main claim, what amount of security should be ordered?

firac.issue: Is the applicant entitled to an order for security for costs under s. 236 of the BCBCA against a corporate plaintiff by counterclaim?
firac.facts: Keezio, a defendant by counterclaim, sought security for costs of $74,354.90 against The Shrunks, a corporate plaintiff by counterclaim in a dispute between competitors in the inflatable-bed market. The Shrunks had not filed its annual return for two years, owned no land, and provided no evidence of ability to pay an adverse costs award. It argued only that Keezio had an arguable defence and that the claims mirrored each other.
firac.rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act permits the court to require security where a corporate plaintiff 'will be unable to pay the costs of the defendant' if the defence succeeds. The discretionary principles are set out in Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Court Ltd. and the four-part test in Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress: (1) inability to pay costs; (2) exigible assets to satisfy costs; (3) an arguable defence; (4) undue hardship stifling the claim. Per Ocean Pastures Corp. v. Old Masset and Fat Mel's Restaurant Ltd., once inability to pay is shown, security is generally ordered unless there is no arguable defence. The threshold for an arguable defence is low—the defence need only be bona fide and arguable, not sure to succeed.
firac.application: The Shrunks provided no evidence it could pay an adverse award, had not filed returns for two years and owned no land, satisfying the first two branches. It did not argue hardship or stifling, so those factors were not weighed. Its argument that Keezio lacked an arguable defence failed given the low threshold, and its claims (truth of the statements, trademark and copyright infringement) plainly left Keezio a bona fide arguable defence. The court found entitlement was not in issue—only quantum.
firac.conclusion: Keezio was entitled to security for costs; the only remaining question was the appropriate amount.

firac.issue: What amount of security should be ordered where the counterclaim substantially overlaps with the plaintiff-by-counterclaim's own claim in the main action?
firac.facts: The Shrunks argued the counterclaim wholly overlapped the main claim so Keezio would incur no additional costs. The copyright allegation was said to be advanced only by Mr. Cirjak (not subject to the application), but the wording arguably also engaged The Shrunks. A draft bill of costs claimed $74,354.90, including a $30,000 expert report and maximum tariff items, much of which would be incurred defending the main action in any event (ten-day trial, document discovery).
firac.rule: Per Gray v. Powerassist Technologies Inc. and Trak Energy Corp. v. Happy Valley Resort, where a counterclaim overlaps a plaintiff's claim the court considers the degree to which costs would be incurred in any event and the greater potential for injustice where claims significantly overlap. Under Kropp the court may order any amount up to the full claim so long as more than nominal.
firac.application: The court accepted there would be additional costs to defend the counterclaim (including the arguably-included copyright allegation), so entitlement stood. However, the $30,000 accounting/infringement expert report and many maximum tariff steps such as the trial and document discovery would be required for the main claim regardless. Rather than the 50% ($37,177.45) proposed, the court set a reduced figure reflecting the true incremental cost of the counterclaim.
firac.conclusion: Security was ordered in the amount of $25,000, payable within 14 days, with the counterclaim stayed until posted; Keezio could apply for further security and was awarded costs of the application.

case_name: Presch v. Alma Mater Society of UBC

name_verification.name_in_document: Presch v. Alma Mater Society of the University of British Columbia

defining_issues: Does the Proposed Referendum Question violate the AMS bylaws and Code by failing to be capable of a 'yes' or 'no' answer, such that the court should intervene under the Societies Act?

Does the Proposed Referendum Question breach the Code because implementing it would break a contract without stating the intent to break it and the penalty, as required by Section IX, Article 4(2)(c)?
Is there any 'irregularity' in the conduct of the AMS's affairs warranting the court's exercise of its remedial or restraining powers under ss. 104 and 105 of the Societies Act?

firac.issue: Does the Proposed Referendum Question violate the AMS bylaws and Code by failing to be capable of a 'yes' or 'no' answer?
firac.facts: The AMS scheduled a referendum asking members whether they support boycotting products and divesting from companies that support 'Israeli war crimes, illegal occupation, and the oppression of Palestinians.' The petitioner argued the question was a loaded, ambiguous one that could not yield a meaningful yes/no answer, as required by Bylaw 4(2) and Section IX, Article 4(2)(a) of the Code.
firac.rule: Bylaw 4(2) requires the referendum text be drafted 'to ensure that the question is capable of being answered "yes" or "no"' and, if Council is of the opinion it does not meet this requirement, Council must refer it to the AMS student court to 'prepare a clear and unambiguous question.' The court cannot alter or impose bylaws or fill gaps (Erickson v. Luggi, 2004 BCCA 52; Bector v. Vedic Hindu Cultural Society, 2014 BCSC 230).
firac.application: The court held Bylaw 4(2) establishes a two-stage process with two distinct standards: a low first-stage bar that the question merely be capable of a 'yes' or 'no' answer, and a higher 'clear and unambiguous' standard applied only by the student court at the second stage if the first is not met. The word 'meaningful' cannot be read into the bylaw. The bylaws and Code impose almost no constraints on the form or content of referendum questions and permit purely political referenda, as illustrated by past AMS referenda on the Vietnam War, abortion and South Africa. Authorities relied on by the petitioner (Burlington, Markus, Whitecourt) involved local-government monetary or zoning plebiscites where clarity was essential, and were far removed from an AMS political referendum. Although the Proposed Question was 'loaded' and leading, nothing in the bylaws or Code prohibits a loaded question or requires that voter intent or consequences be clear.
firac.conclusion: The question was capable of a 'yes' or 'no' answer; the conduct of the AMS Council and president did not violate the bylaws or Code.

firac.issue: Does the Proposed Question breach Section IX, Article 4(2)(c) of the Code because implementing it would break a contract without stating the intent and penalty?
firac.facts: The Code requires that where a proposed question 'would break a contract,' the intent to break it and the penalty must be stated in the question. The SPHR proponent (Mr. Buffie) deposed the question was kept general and he was aware of no contracts that would have to be broken; the AMS president deposed the question did not require breaking any current contracts.
firac.rule: Section IX, Article 4(2)(c) of the Code: where a proposed question would break a contract, the intent to break it must be specifically stated and the penalty must be included in the question. The provision's purpose is to give voters relevant information.
firac.application: The court found it unnecessary to resolve the two possible interpretations of the provision because there was no evidence that implementing the referendum would result in the breach or breaking of any contract. Any effect on future purchasing decisions remained hypothetical.
firac.conclusion: No breach of Section IX, Article 4(2)(c) was established; the argument was rejected.

firac.issue: Is there an irregularity warranting the court's intervention under ss. 104 and 105 of the Societies Act?
firac.facts: The petitioner sought orders under ss. 104 and 105 of the Societies Act, S.B.C. 2015, c. 18, to invalidate the AMS decision to put the question to a vote and/or enjoin the referendum.
firac.rule: Section 105 permits the court to remedy an omission, defect, error or irregularity in the conduct of a society's affairs that results in a breach of the Act or default in compliance with the bylaws; courts take a cautious approach and will not interfere in a society's internal democratic governance absent a proven irregularity connected to the relief sought (Bector; Samra v. Guru Nanak Gurdwara Society, 2008 BCCA 202; Garcha v. Khalsa Diwan Society, 2006 BCCA 140). Section 104 permits compliance or restraining orders where a person contravenes or is about to contravene the bylaws.
firac.application: Having found no breach of the bylaws or Code, the court found no irregularity within s. 105. Section 104 likewise did not apply, so it was unnecessary to decide whether the AMS or its president was a 'person' under s. 104(1)(a). The court emphasized its reluctance to interfere in the internal, free and democratic processes of the society, especially where an order could be seen as taking sides on a political issue, though it would enforce the law if illegality were shown.
firac.conclusion: No irregularity was found; there was no basis to intervene and the petition was dismissed (no order as to costs).

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area, as the case is a petition under the Societies Act concerning a society's internal governance. K041 (campus/university) and K042 (code of conduct) capture the university student-union setting and the AMS Code/bylaws at the heart of the dispute. name_verification.name_in_document: ZSOLT JOZSEF MUDRAK, PATRIK ZOLTAN FEKE, ZSOLT MUDRAK, RENATA FUTO v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Did the Board err by failing to conduct a separate analysis under section 97 of the IRPA?
Did the Board err in finding that Hungary was able to provide adequate state protection to Roma claimants?
Did the Board err in finding that the applicants ought to have sought state protection, including complaining to policing oversight agencies, before claiming refugee status?

firac.issue: Did the Board err by failing to conduct a separate section 97 analysis after finding the applicants were not Convention refugees under section 96?
firac.facts: The Board found the applicants suffered discrimination in employment, health care, housing and social services but that this did not rise to the level of persecution, and that adequate state protection existed. The applicants argued a separate s. 97 analysis was nonetheless required, citing Dunkova.
firac.rule: The risk of harm for persecution under s. 96 (per Rajudeen) is of similar or wider scope, and the legal standard lower, than the risk of death or cruel and unusual treatment required under s. 97 (Li; Peter). A separate s. 97 analysis is not required where the s. 96 personal-circumstances and state-protection findings resolve the same questions (Racz).
firac.application: Because the applicants' personal circumstances did not establish a risk of persecution under the lower s. 96 threshold, they could not reasonably establish a s. 97 risk on the same facts. The Board's state-protection finding equally disposed of any s. 97 claim, and there was no separate evidence on state protection that a s. 97 analysis would have addressed.
firac.conclusion: No separate s. 97 analysis was required; the Board did not err.

firac.issue: Did the Board err in concluding that Hungary was able to provide adequate state protection to Roma citizens?
firac.facts: The applicants, Hungarian Roma, described several violent and discriminatory incidents. The Board catalogued extensive Hungarian legislative measures, oversight bodies (IPCB, ETA, RPOA, Minorities Ombudsman), policing structures and integration programs, while acknowledging widespread anti-Roma violence and discrimination.
firac.rule: A state is presumed capable of protecting its citizens absent complete breakdown; the applicant must rebut this with clear and convincing evidence (Canada (AG) v Ward). The threshold for adequate protection should not be set too high (Smirnov). Assessment of state protection is a question of mixed fact and law reviewed on reasonableness (Hinzman; Dunsmuir), falling within the Board's core expertise (Majlat).
firac.application: The Court held it is not the reviewing court's role to re-weigh voluminous country-condition evidence or to require the Board to demonstrate the 'operational adequacy' of protection measures, which would improperly reverse the presumption of state protection and shift the onus to the Board. Extensive legislation and oversight mechanisms strengthen rather than undermine the presumption of protection in a democracy. The Board correctly stated and applied the law to the totality of the evidence.
firac.conclusion: The Board's finding of adequate state protection was reasonable; no reviewable error.

firac.issue: Did the Board err in finding the applicants were required to seek and exhaust state protection, including complaining to policing oversight agencies, when they had not followed up on alleged police inaction?
firac.facts: Of four incidents, the police investigated two (one closed for lack of evidence, one where police intervened to prevent harm), while for the other two the applicants took no steps to follow up or complain to oversight agencies about alleged police failures to report.
firac.rule: In a developed democracy a claimant bears a heavy burden to prove he exhausted all available protections and is excused only in exceptional circumstances (Hinzman; Ward). The requirement to access protection extends to policing oversight agencies, particularly for random attacks and where no risk of harm arises from complaining.
firac.application: The Court disagreed with jurisprudence excusing Roma claimants from complaining to oversight agencies. Since random attacks require community-level, forward-looking protection, and since complaining to diligent oversight agencies carries no risk of harm and generates corroboration, it was objectively unreasonable for the applicants not to pursue those avenues. The Board reasonably concluded the applicants had not rebutted the presumption of state protection.
firac.conclusion: The Board did not err in requiring the applicants to have sought state protection including oversight agencies; application dismissed.

K080 (state protection) is the central doctrine — adequacy and the 'operational adequacy' debate. K079 (persecution) reflects the discrimination-versus-persecution analysis. defining_issues: Should the interim Alberta orders on guardianship, access, and child support be set aside or varied at this stage?

Does the British Columbia court have jurisdiction to order the husband, a dual Iranian-Canadian citizen residing in Iran, to take steps in Iran to facilitate an Iranian divorce, an Iranian passport, and the lifting of a travel ban for the wife?

firac.issue: Should the interim Alberta orders granting the mother sole guardianship, ordering child support, and prohibiting the father's contact with the child be set aside or varied?
firac.facts: Farshid, now living in Iran, sought to set aside a January 24, 2014 ex parte Alberta order granting Leila sole custody/decision-making (equated to sole guardianship in BC) and requiring child support of $594/month plus $275/month for s. 7 expenses, and to set aside an April 10, 2017 Alberta order directing no contact with the eight-year-old son Ryan. He sought interim joint guardianship, revised support, and parenting time/contact. Ryan, born prematurely and described as delicate and sensitive, had not seen his father since separation (age two or three) and had paid nothing toward support.
firac.rule: The BC court's jurisdiction to address the Alberta orders derives from ss. 6 and 16 of the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), the child now residing in North Vancouver; the Family Law Act, S.B.C. 2011, c. 25, also applies. An interim custody order may be varied without a material change in circumstances (Javid v. Kurytnik, 2006 BCCA 565). The governing consideration is the best interests of the child.
firac.application: The court found it not in Ryan's best interests to reunite him with his father until reunification was better planned, fearing brief contact followed by renewed absence causing confusion and instability. Farshid filed almost no particulars of a contact plan or evidence of financial capacity to travel from Iran and maintain contact. He also filed no evidence justifying converting sole guardianship into joint guardianship, and it was premature to relieve him of retroactive and ongoing support given he had paid nothing.
firac.conclusion: The court declined to make significant changes to the Alberta orders. Farshid remains at liberty under the April 10, 2017 order to apply for access (likely supervised) upon filing a detailed plan and financial evidence; guardianship and support obligations remain unchanged. All further proceedings will be in BC courts.

firac.issue: Can the BC court order the husband, resident in Iran, to take steps in Iran to facilitate an Iranian divorce, obtain an Iranian passport for the wife, and lift the Iranian travel ban against her?
firac.facts: Although divorced in Alberta on July 3, 2014, the parties remained married under Iranian law. Leila sought orders requiring Farshid, a dual Iranian-Canadian citizen residing in Iran, within seven days to do all necessary to allow her to obtain an Iranian divorce and passport and to lift the Iranian travel ban against her. Each party has a lawyer in Iran, and no expert evidence on Iranian law was tendered.
firac.rule: The party relied on Bakhshi v. Hosseinzadeh, 2015 ONSC 7407 and Etemad v. Hasanzadeh, 2014 ONSC 6737; a court requires a jurisdictional basis and, where foreign law is engaged, expert evidence to guide it.
firac.application: The court read neither cited authority as conferring jurisdiction to order a person residing in Iran to take steps there to facilitate an Iranian divorce or travel rights. Absent any expert evidence on Iranian law, the requested relief could not be granted.
firac.conclusion: Leila's applications failed; she will need to proceed in Iran, through Iranian counsel, for that relief.

name_verification.name_in_document: Gunnar S. Paulsson v. Leo Cooper, The Board of Trustees of and for the University of Illinois, The American Association for the Advancement of Slavic Studies, and Slavic Review

defining_issues: Did the motion judge err in concluding that the Ontario court could not assume jurisdiction over the out-of-province defendants in a libel action arising from a book review distributed in Ontario?
Should the Ontario court decline to exercise jurisdiction on the basis of forum non conveniens because a more appropriate forum exists?

firac.issue: Did the motion judge err in concluding that the Ontario court could not assume jurisdiction over the out-of-province defendants in a libel action arising from distribution of an allegedly defamatory book review in Ontario?
firac.facts: The appellant, a long-time Ontario resident and Holocaust scholar, sued in Ontario over a book review of his book published in the U.S. academic journal Slavic Review. Eighty-one paper copies of the June 2004 issue were distributed to university and public libraries in Ontario (out of total circulation of 3,528). None of the defendants (in the U.S. and Australia) resides in Ontario. The motion judge, applying the Muscutt criteria, found the connections weak and no reasonably foreseeable harm in Ontario, and stayed the action.
firac.rule: Under Van Breda v. Village Resorts Ltd., 2010 ONCA 84, where a claim falls within a condition for service ex juris without a court order under rule 17.02 of the Rules of Civil Procedure (here 17.02(g), a tort committed in Ontario), a real and substantial connection is presumed, which the defendant may rebut. In defamation, publication occurs where the material is read/communicated to a third party (Raymond Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada). The connections between the claim and the forum and between the defendant and the forum are the most significant factors; Moran v. Pyle National (Canada) Ltd., [1975] 1 S.C.R. 393 supports jurisdiction where a defendant could reasonably foresee its product entering normal channels causing harm in the forum.
firac.application: The 81 copies distributed and read in Ontario libraries constitute publication of the alleged libel in Ontario, a tort committed in Ontario under rule 17.02(g), raising a presumption of jurisdiction. Reputational damage attaches to the person in his place of residence; the appellant had lived in Ontario for over a year before publication, distinguishing Bangoura v. Washington Post. The respondents, by placing the journal into normal distribution channels aimed at the academic community, could reasonably foresee harm to the appellant in his home province. The motion judge erred by conflating where damage occurred with proof of actual damages, by discounting circumstantial proof of publication, and by treating the limited number of copies as determinative. The respondents did not rebut the presumption.
firac.conclusion: The motion judge erred; there is a real and substantial connection between the claim and Ontario, and the Ontario court may properly assume jurisdiction.

firac.issue: Should the Ontario court decline jurisdiction on the ground that a more appropriate forum exists (forum non conveniens)?
firac.facts: The defendants are located in Australia, New York, Massachusetts and Illinois; the plaintiff and his witnesses are in Ontario. The defamation was committed in Ontario and alleged damages sustained there. The University of Illinois raised the Illinois State Immunity Act but the record was insufficient to decide it.
firac.rule: A stay for forum non conveniens requires 'some other forum more convenient and appropriate for the pursuit of this action and for securing the ends of justice' (Antares Shipping Corp. v. The Ship 'Capricorn'; Amchem Products Inc. v. British Columbia (WCB)). Jurisdiction and forum are assessed separately (Van Breda). Because the tort was committed in Ontario, Ontario defamation law applies (Tolofson v. Jensen; Black v. Breeden).
firac.application: No matter where the action is heard in North America, witnesses would have to travel; on witness availability and convenience alone no other forum is more convenient. Ontario law applies since the defamation was committed and damages sustained here. The State Immunity Act issue could not be resolved on the record and the motion judge's refusal to determine it was not disturbed.
firac.conclusion: There is no other more just or convenient forum; the Ontario court should not decline jurisdiction. Appeal allowed; stay set aside and Ontario Superior Court declared to have jurisdiction.
