defining_issues: Did the claimant establish a well-founded fear of persecution in Ukraine on the basis of her Jewish religion?
Was adequate state protection available to the claimant in Ukraine?
Did credibility concerns undermine the essential elements of the claim?

firac.issue: Did the claimant establish a well-founded fear of persecution in Ukraine on the basis of her Jewish religion?
firac.facts: A 27-year-old Ukrainian woman born in Lviv to a Ukrainian father and Jewish mother described lifelong anti-Semitic abuse: harassment at school, difficulty in education and employment, threatening notes telling her to leave for Israel, anti-Jewish graffiti on her door, and several assaults by Ukrainian nationalists and others that left her hospitalized with concussions and internal bleeding.
firac.rule: A Convention refugee under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, must show a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground (here, religion), requiring both subjective fear and an objective basis; there must be more than a mere possibility of serious harm.
firac.application: The member found the claimant was perceived as Jewish and was a victim of anti-Semitism resulting at times in physical harm, and that her continuing subjective fear was supported by objective country evidence documenting assaults on Jews, vandalism of cemeteries and memorials, anti-Semitic publications, and a rising nationalist trend that could produce new outbursts of anti-Semitism.
firac.conclusion: The claimant established more than a mere possibility of serious harm or death at the hands of Ukrainian anti-Semites because of her Jewish religion.

firac.issue: Was adequate state protection available to the claimant in Ukraine?
firac.facts: When the claimant reported anti-Jewish graffiti to police they merely told her to repaint her door; country reports showed the government took some steps in 2004 but a jailed ultra-nationalist won a legislative seat and anti-Semitic incidents remained unresolved.
firac.rule: A claimant must rebut the presumption of state protection by showing the state is unwilling or unable to protect; protection must be adequate in practice.
firac.application: The member relied on documentary evidence indicating that, despite some governmental measures, the police cannot be said to be able to protect Jews from anti-Semitic persecution in Ukraine, and that the authorities would be unwilling to protect the claimant.
firac.conclusion: State protection was not adequately available, satisfying this element of the claim.

firac.issue: Did credibility concerns undermine the essential elements of the claim?
firac.facts: The member did not believe all of the claimant's evidence and noted that at times her behaviour appeared inconsistent with genuine subjective fear.
firac.rule: A claimant need not have every aspect of the evidence believed; the essential elements of the claim must be established on the evidence as a whole.
firac.application: Although not all evidence was accepted, the member was satisfied that the claimant was perceived as Jewish, suffered anti-Semitic harm, and retained a subjective fear supported by objective evidence.
firac.conclusion: The credibility concerns did not defeat the essential elements of the Convention refugee claim.

keywords_rationale: K008 is the tier-1 practice area (immigration/refugee). K075 (convention refugee) and K078 (refugee protection) capture the disposition. K079 (persecution) and K080 (state protection) are the two determinative doctrinal elements. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) identify the ground of persecution. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the deciding institution. Charter freedom-of-religion keywords were not selected because the claim turns on refugee-law persecution rather than Charter analysis.
location_rationale: The reasons close with "DATED at Toronto this 2nd day of December 2005", placing the hearing and decision in Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The decision was issued by the Refugee Protection Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board and dated at Toronto; the Toronto office is the operative registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: Regina v. Othman Ayed Hamdan

defining_issues: Did the Crown prove the actus reus of counselling mischief to property (Count 3) through the accused's Facebook posts?
Did the Crown prove the actus reus of counselling murder and assault causing bodily harm (Counts 1 and 2)?
Did the Crown prove the mens rea for counselling murder and assault causing bodily harm (Counts 1 and 2)?
Must the accused be acquitted on Count 4 (knowingly instructing a person to carry out terrorist activity) if the counselling counts fail?

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove the actus reus of counselling mischief to property (Count 3) through the accused's Facebook posts?
firac.facts: The Crown relied on Key Posts 1–3, made on the 'Adam Khalifa' profile in September 2014, which noted weak security at a Revelstoke dam and the Nipigon River bridge and the ease of obtaining firearms/explosives licences in Canada, shortly after an ISIS spokesman's speech calling for attacks in Canada.
firac.rule: Under s. 464(a) and s. 22(3) of the Criminal Code, counselling requires the deliberate encouragement or active inducement of a criminal offence (R. v. Hamilton, 2005 SCC 47, para. 29; Mugesera v. Canada, 2005 SCC 40; R. v. Déry, 2006 SCC 53). Courts must not expand counselling to catch cyberspace expression (Hamilton, paras. 30–31), and expression of political/religious belief is not criminalized (R. v. Khawaja, 2010 ONCA 862).
firac.application: The posts merely identified potential targets and legal facts; they did not describe how to commit the offence and did not even 'plant a seed' as in R. v. Sonne, 2012 ONSC 2126. A mere temporal link to the al-Adnani speech, or reading the posts collectively with 85 other posts made over ten months on 14 accounts, could not establish active inducement without impermissibly expanding the offence. Key Post 50 could not assist because it targeted killing, not property.
firac.conclusion: The Crown failed to prove the actus reus of Count 3; the accused was not guilty of counselling mischief.

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove the actus reus of counselling murder and assault causing bodily harm (Counts 1 and 2)?
firac.facts: The Crown relied on numerous posts 'saluting' lone-wolf attackers, blaming Western policy, and Key Post 50 (the 'Lone Wolf Post' giving detailed killing methods) and Key Post 40 ('lone wolves activate all across the #USA'). Some posts were incompletely captured because the RCMP used screenshot software that failed to preserve source code, comments and full timelines.
firac.rule: The statements must be viewed objectively and must actively promote, advocate or encourage the offence (Hamilton; Mugesera). Context, including surrounding posts and missing dialogue, is relevant to meaning (Sonne; R. v. Hunter). Support for or explanation of terrorism, without direct inducement, is protected expression.
firac.application: Most posts expressed offensive but political opinions—explaining or applauding attacks—rather than inducing them, so they did not meet the high threshold. Key Post 50 was, on its face, active inducement by its author, but missing context and the accused's evidence that he posted it for 'definition' purposes and disagreed with the author left a reasonable doubt about its meaning. Only Key Post 40, captured in full with no distancing commentary, objectively amounted to an active inducement to commit lone-wolf murders/assaults.
firac.conclusion: The Crown proved the actus reus only through Key Post 40; the other posts, including Key Post 50, did not satisfy the actus reus.

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove the mens rea for counselling murder and assault causing bodily harm (Counts 1 and 2)?
firac.facts: The accused testified for seven days, gave a lengthy voluntary police statement, used his own name and IP address, and explained that his Facebook activity was intended to highlight injustice, 'speak truth to power' and provoke debate. He conceded Key Post 40 sounded 'really bad' but said he re-posted the ISIS feed to contrast ISIS recruitment with Facebook/CIA suppression of Muslim expression, and that he was against killing innocents.
firac.rule: Mens rea for counselling requires intent that the offence be committed, or knowing counselling while aware of the unjustified risk it would be committed (Hamilton, para. 29). Credibility is assessed under R. v. W.(D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742; exculpatory statements need only raise a reasonable doubt (R. v. Rojas, 2008 SCC 56). Motive, background and conduct are relevant to intent (R. v. Jeffers, 2012 ONCA 1).
firac.application: The court accepted the accused's evidence about his mixed, non-jihadist political and religious views and his general purpose in running the accounts, which was inconsistent with ISIS doctrine. Although the court did not fully accept his explanation of Key Post 40, that evidence, together with his openness with police and lack of a committed ideology, raised a reasonable doubt whether he intended to incite, or was aware of the unjustified risk of, murder or assault.
firac.conclusion: The Crown failed to prove mens rea; the accused was not guilty on Counts 1 and 2 (making it unnecessary to decide the s. 83.2 terrorist-group element).

firac.issue: Must the accused be acquitted on Count 4 (knowingly instructing a person to carry out terrorist activity) if the counselling counts fail?
firac.facts: Count 4 charged the accused under s. 83.22(1) of the Code with knowingly instructing any person to carry out a terrorist activity; the Crown treated it as alternative to Counts 1–3 and conceded he could not be convicted if the counselling counts failed.
firac.rule: Section 83.22(1) requires knowingly instructing a person to carry out terrorist activity; because it engages Part II.1 of the Code, a high mens rea threshold applies (R. v. Khawaja, 2012 SCC 69). Its actus reus and mens rea are at least as onerous as the counselling offences.
firac.application: Since the Crown failed to prove the counselling offences—particularly the required intent—it likewise could not meet the more onerous requirements of s. 83.22.
firac.conclusion: The Crown failed to prove Count 4; the accused was found not guilty.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary practice area—four Criminal Code terrorism/counselling charges. K037 (terrorism) is central: the counts were laid under Part II.1 (ss. 83.2, 83.22) in association with ISIS. K036 (mischief) matches Count 3, counselling mischief to property. K063 (online hate / social media) captures the Facebook-post medium that framed the whole analysis. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) reflect the court's repeated caution against criminalizing protected political/religious expression, with K003 (Constitutional law) as their tier-1 parent. K061 (hate speech) was considered but rejected as a weak fit, since the case concerned counselling offences, not hate propaganda.
location_rationale: The header states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA', 'Registry: Vancouver', and the place of trial and judgment is given as 'Vancouver, B.C.'
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly lists 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: A. B., C. D. AND E. F. v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Was the Member's finding that the applicant was excluded from refugee protection under Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention reasonable?
Did the Member err in his treatment of the evidence bearing on the merits of the refugee claim, including the state-protection and psychiatric evidence?
Did the Member exceed his jurisdiction, breach procedural fairness, or give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias?

firac.issue: Was the Member's finding that the applicant committed a serious non-political crime (child abduction) and was therefore excluded under Article 1F(b) reasonable?
firac.facts: The principal applicant, a Roma woman and former Member of the European Parliament, removed her adopted daughter from Hungary in November 2011 contrary to a custody order and did not return within the two-week window the order permitted; the child was later ordered returned to her father under the Hague Convention by the Ontario Court of Justice. The Minister intervened alleging exclusion under Article 1F(b) on the basis of child abduction (Criminal Code ss. 282/283, each carrying a ten-year maximum). The Member requested submissions on Febles but treated para. 62 as mere obiter and relied on the existence of the Hague Convention as the standard of seriousness.
firac.rule: Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention (incorporated by s. 98 IRPA) excludes persons where there are serious reasons for considering they committed a serious non-political crime abroad before entry. Under Febles v Canada, 2014 SCC 68 (para. 62), the ten-year-maximum guideline is not a rigid presumption; where a Criminal Code offence has a wide sentencing range, a claimant whose crime falls at the low end should not be presumptively excluded, and the rule must not be applied mechanistically. Seriousness is assessed on the Jayasekara v Canada, 2008 FCA 404 factors (elements of the crime, mode of prosecution, penalty prescribed, facts, mitigating/aggravating circumstances), and the failure to consider likely sentencing range is a reviewable error (Jung, 2015 FC 464; Tabagua, 2015 FC 709; Hersy, 2016 FC 190).
firac.application: The Court held the Member failed to conduct a Febles analysis, wrongly dismissing para. 62 as obiter and never considering whether the ten-year presumption was rebutted. Even presumptively serious crimes remain rebuttable. On the Jayasekara factors, the Member's mode-of-prosecution analysis ignored that ss. 282/283 are hybrid offences carrying only up to six months on summary conviction (s. 787), producing a range from six months to ten years that he never weighed; his penalty analysis reduced seriousness to the mere existence of the Hague Convention. Jayasekara para. 37 does not make an international convention the sole 'standard'; Kovacs treats the Hague Convention as only one non-determinative factor and predates Febles. The absence of charges did not excuse the sentencing-range analysis.
firac.conclusion: The exclusion finding was unreasonable; the Member failed to apply Febles and erred in applying the Jayasekara factors. The Court did not need to decide the applicant's further argument that the abduction crime occurred in Canada.

firac.issue: Did the Member err in treating the state-protection and psychiatric evidence on the merits of the claim?
firac.facts: The Member made an alternative merits determination, finding the applicant not credible, that she had not established subjective fear, and that she had not rebutted the presumption of state protection. She relied on an Amnesty International letter and expert affidavits describing risks to Roma-rights activists, and on two psychiatric reports (Thirlwell and Kumar). She had received 24-hour police protection during her MEP term.
firac.rule: Credibility and weighing of evidence attract deference on reasonableness (Aguebor; Huang); a decision-maker is presumed to have considered all evidence and need not mention every item (Cepeda-Gutierrez). A claimant must rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence (Ward v Canada; Flores Carillo, 2008 FCA 94). Credibility findings may extend to documentary evidence based on the claimant's self-reporting (Sitnikova, 2016 FC 464; Lawal).
firac.application: The Member did not ignore the Amnesty and expert evidence but reasonably found the applicant, having received police protection when requested, did not fit the profile of an unprotected activist. The psychiatric reports were reasonably given little weight: the Kumar letter was a brief note about pre-hearing anxiety, and the Thirlwell report rested on the applicant's self-reported (and disbelieved) narrative. Kanthasamy was issued after the decision and did not undermine this assessment; the reviewing court will not re-weigh evidence.
firac.conclusion: No reviewable error; the state-protection finding was reasonable and the applicant failed to rebut the presumption with clear and convincing evidence.

firac.issue: Did the Member exceed his jurisdiction, breach procedural fairness, or display a reasonable apprehension of bias in dealing with related claims and the applicant's conduct?
firac.facts: The Member commented on the credibility of refugee claims of the applicant's sister and mother (pending before another member) and of an alleged former employee (already rejected), finding the applicant a 'willing accomplice' in a 'fraudulent' claim. The applicant argued the Member exceeded his jurisdiction, denied procedural fairness to third parties, and that the litany of negative findings and strong language showed bias.
firac.rule: Procedural-fairness and jurisdictional questions are reviewed on correctness (Dunsmuir). The test for reasonable apprehension of bias is whether an informed person, viewing the matter realistically, would think it more likely than not the decision-maker would not decide fairly (Committee for Justice and Liberty; R v RDS, [1997] 3 SCR 484); allegations require cogent, material evidence and meet a high threshold (Arthur v Canada, 2001 FCA 223; Zhu). Bias arising from written reasons is not waived.
firac.application: The Member expressly stated he was not the decision-maker for the family members' claims and only weighed them for relevance; he gave them little weight rather than 'ruling' on them. He disclosed the former employee's documents and gave the applicant an opportunity to respond by affidavit, so no fairness breach occurred, and he was not adjudicating that already-rejected claim. Although some language was overly editorial and the 'willing accomplice' finding unnecessary, reading the decision and transcripts as a whole, the numerous unchallenged credibility findings had independent evidentiary support and did not meet the high bias threshold.
firac.conclusion: No jurisdictional excess, no breach of procedural fairness, and no reasonable apprehension of bias established.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the s. 96/97 claim and the exclusion determination under Article 1F(b). K079 (persecution) and K080 (state protection) are central to the reasonable alternative merits finding that decided the case. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review — reasonableness/correctness) frame the entire analysis. K012 (procedural fairness) covers the third-issue fairness/jurisdiction/bias arguments reviewed on correctness. K047 (best interests of the child) is a borderline but justified pick because the exclusion turned on Hague Convention child abduction; it is weaker than the others since the case is about seriousness of the crime rather than a custody determination.
location_rationale: The decision header reads 'Ottawa, Ontario, December 16, 2016', identifying where the judgment was rendered. The style of cause block lists 'PLACE OF HEARING: Toronto, Ontario', so the matter was heard in Toronto while the reasons issued from Ottawa.
registry_rationale: This is a Federal Court decision; the 'PLACE OF HEARING: Toronto, Ontario' entry and the applicants' solicitors (Refugee Law Office, Toronto) indicate the Toronto office/registry handled the hearing. Federal Court file no. IMM-919-15.

name_verification.name_in_document: William Fowler v. The Attorney General of Canada

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff's pleadings be struck as disclosing no reasonable claim under Rule 9-5(1)(a)?
Should the pleadings be struck as unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious under Rule 9-5(1)(b)?
Do the pleadings adequately establish causes of action in negligence, defamation, and harassment, and should leave to amend be granted?

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's pleadings be struck as disclosing no reasonable claim under Rule 9-5(1)(a)?
firac.facts: Fowler, an inmate serving a life sentence, filed a brief Notice of Civil Claim against the Attorney General of Canada alleging harassment, false and derogatory reports, file contamination, and discrimination by Correctional Service of Canada, seeking $6,666,666 from some 30 named parties. His 50-plus pages of particulars provided a prolix narrative of interactions with CSC employees rather than clarifying the claim.
firac.rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(a) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules the court may strike a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim. On such a motion the truth of pleaded facts is assumed (Hunt v. Carey Canada, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959), and pleadings must state material facts relating them to the cause of action relied upon (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42; Pellikaan v. Canada, 2002 FCT 221; Kelly Lake Cree Nation).
firac.application: The court found no coherent cause of action could be discerned from the pleadings or particulars. The defamation claim failed to plead the defamatory words, their derogatory sense, reference to the plaintiff, or publication to a third party (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61; Micka). There is no recognized tort of harassment, and even assuming one exists, no material facts supported intentional infliction of mental suffering (Prinzo; Mainland Sawmills). The negligence claim rested on an impenetrable narrative mixing fact, conjecture and opinion.
firac.conclusion: The defamation and harassment claims were struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a) as disclosing no cause of action, without leave to amend.

firac.issue: Should the pleadings be struck as unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious under Rule 9-5(1)(b)?
firac.facts: The Notice of Civil Claim and particulars were prolix, over-broad, and reliant on irrelevant recitations of evidence and narrative, sought a criminal investigation, named parties not properly identified, and made allegations outside the scope of the original claim.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1)(b) permits striking pleadings that are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious. 'Frivolous' means without substance, groundless, trifling with the court (Jerry Rose Jr. v. UBC; McNutt); 'vexatious' where it does not establish a cause of action known to law; 'scandalous' where so irrelevant as to cause useless expense and prejudice (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress). Subsections (a) and (b) are disjunctive.
firac.application: The court held the pleadings and responses were so prolix, over-broad and reliant on irrelevant narrative as to be impossible to respond to meaningfully, drawing the parties into unproductive and expensive litigation, akin to Homalco Indian Band where the pleading was 'prolix and convoluted' and embarrassing.
firac.conclusion: The pleadings fell afoul of Rule 9-5(1)(b); the negligence claim in particular was struck on this basis.

firac.issue: Do the pleadings establish causes of action in negligence, defamation and harassment, and should leave to amend be granted?
firac.facts: The apparent negligence claim rested on allegations of file contamination and insertion of inaccurate information; the defamation and harassment claims lacked pleaded particulars and legal foundation.
firac.rule: A negligence claim requires a duty of care, breach of the standard of care, and resulting damages (Micka v. Oliver & District Community Economic Development Society, 2008 BCSC 1623). A plaintiff should not be driven from the judgment seat if there is a chance of success (Hunt v. Carey Canada). Leave to amend may be granted where an amended pleading could disclose a cause of action.
firac.application: The defamation and harassment claims could not be salvaged and were struck without leave. For negligence, though material facts and damages were currently indiscernible, the court could not say that an amended pleading could not disclose a cause of action assuming the facts true, so amendment was appropriate.
firac.conclusion: Negligence claim struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b) but with leave to amend within 60 days; proceedings stayed pending an adequately amended statement of claim, failing which the defendant may reset its dismissal application.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a civil pleadings/motion-to-strike matter. K015 (defamation) applies because the court analysed and struck the defamation claim under the Grant v. Torstar elements. K083 (harassment) applies to the plaintiff's harassment allegations and the court's discussion of whether a tort of harassment exists. K001 (Administrative law) and K011 (judicial review) are borderline/weak — included because the claim arises from Correctional Service of Canada conduct and the reasons reference parallel judicial review proceedings in Spidel, but the case is fundamentally a civil pleadings matter, not an administrative law review. No keyword for negligence or motion to strike exists in the vocabulary, so the closest civil-litigation terms were chosen.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Registry: Vancouver' and 'Place and Date of Hearing: Vancouver, B.C.' and 'Place and Date of Judgment: Vancouver, B.C.', with the court being the Supreme Court of British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The header explicitly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Willow v. Chong

defining_issues: Should the claims against the Agency defendants (PCTIA and its Registrar) be struck as an impermissible collateral attack on decisions made under the Private Career Training Institutions Act, and do the pleaded torts (misfeasance in public office, abuse of process, interference with contractual/economic relations, conspiracy, Charter breaches) disclose reasonable causes of action?
Should the claims against the Crown defendants be struck for disclosing no reasonable cause of action?

Should the claims against the Ministers be struck as an abuse of process and/or as disclosing no reasonable cause of action, given they duplicate the plaintiffs' defence in the earlier Ministers' Action?
Should the Registrar, Mr. Wright, be personally liable, given the personal-liability protection in s. 21 of the PCTI Act?

firac.issue: Should the claims against the Agency defendants be struck as a collateral attack on administrative decisions and as disclosing no reasonable cause of action?
firac.facts: Shanghai College was registered and accredited under the PCTI Act. After a student complaint, PCTIA refunded tuition to the student, demanded reimbursement from the College, searched its premises, seized documents, and cancelled its registration and accreditation. The plaintiffs never appealed to the PCTIA board or sought judicial review, instead suing for damages alleging misfeasance in public office, abuse of process, intentional interference with contractual/economic relations, conspiracy, and breaches of ss. 6(2)(b) and 8 of the Charter.
firac.rule: Under Rule 9-5(1) a pleading may be struck where it discloses no reasonable claim (Hunt v Carey; R. v Imperial Tobacco — 'plain and obvious' test), is unnecessary/vexatious, or is an abuse of process. A civil damages claim is an impermissible collateral attack where the essential complaint concerns the fairness or correctness of an administrative decision that is appealable or judicially reviewable (Cimaco International Sales Inc. v British Columbia, 2010 BCCA 342; Stephen v HMTQ; Varzeliotis v British Columbia). The unavailability of damages on judicial review does not by itself ground a damages action absent viable independent causes of action. The elements of misfeasance in public office (Odhavji Estate v Woodhouse), abuse of process (Border Enterprises), interference with contractual/economic relations (Potter v Rowe; Reid), and conspiracy (Kuhn) must be pleaded with material facts.
firac.application: The court found the plaintiffs' essential complaint was dissatisfaction with PCTIA's decisions and its alleged breaches of natural justice/due process — matters properly pursued by statutory appeal or judicial review under the Judicial Review Procedure Act. The plaintiffs had not pursued those remedies. Each pleaded tort consisted of bare, speculative allegations without supporting material facts: misfeasance lacked pleaded deliberate unlawful conduct and awareness of harm; abuse of process confused procedural fairness with the tort and pleaded no act in furtherance; interference torts rested only on a bare 'primary purpose other than carrying the law into effect'; conspiracy pleaded no intentional participation in an agreement; the s. 6(2)(b) claim failed under Skapinker (no independent right to work); and the s. 8 claim, whatever its merits regarding economic interests, was in essence a natural-justice complaint for judicial review.
firac.conclusion: The claims against the Agency defendants disclosed no reasonable cause of action and, as damages claims added to an essentially administrative-law complaint, constituted an impermissible collateral attack; they were struck as an abuse of process.

firac.issue: Should the claims against the Crown defendants be struck for disclosing no reasonable cause of action?
firac.facts: Her Majesty the Queen in right of British Columbia and the Attorney General were named as defendants, but the Notice of Civil Claim asserted no specific allegations against them; counsel could only presume they were added on a possible vicarious-liability basis.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1)(a): a pleading disclosing no reasonable claim may be struck.
firac.application: The claim made no allegations against the Crown defendants and disclosed no cause of action against them.
firac.conclusion: The claims against the Crown defendants were struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a).

firac.issue: Should the claims against the Ministers be struck as an abuse of process and/or as disclosing no reasonable claim?
firac.facts: The Ministers had earlier commenced the Ministers' Action seeking injunctions restraining the College from issuing degree certificates; an interlocutory injunction on the same terms as the final relief was granted on February 7, 2011, and no further steps were taken. In this action the plaintiffs made the identical allegations they had raised in their defence to the Ministers' Action, adding a claim for damages. The named Ministers no longer held those positions and were nominal defendants.
firac.rule: Abuse of process (Rule 9-5(1)(b) and (d)) is a flexible doctrine allowing the court to prevent re-litigation that offends judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of justice (Toronto (City) v CUPE, Local 79, 2003 SCC 63). Issue estoppel requires the same issue, a final prior decision, and the same parties. The tort of abuse of process requires wilful misuse of court process for an improper purpose plus resulting damage, pleaded with material facts.
firac.application: Permitting the same allegations to be litigated in two extant proceedings, where a binding interlocutory injunction inconsistent with the claims was in place and where the second action arose from the first, was vexatious and contrary to the interests of justice. The abuse-of-process tort claim consisted of bare allegations without material facts; the res judicata allegation failed because the Ministers were not parties to the Federal Court proceedings; and as nominal defendants who no longer held office, they could not have committed the wilful acts the tort requires. The Charter and vicarious-liability claims failed for the same reasons as against the Agency defendants and as pure speculation.
firac.conclusion: The claims against the Ministers were struck both as an abuse of process under Rule 9-5(1)(b) and (d) and as disclosing no reasonable claim under Rule 9-5(1)(a).

firac.issue: Should the Registrar, Mr. Wright, be personally liable?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs alleged malice and 'malfeasance' by Mr. Wright in authorizing the search and seizure, but pleaded nothing suggesting he acted outside the scope of his employment or with an identity or interest separate from PCTIA. Section 21 of the PCTI Act protects board members, officers and employees from liability except where they act in bad faith.
firac.rule: Officers and employees are protected from personal liability unless their actions are themselves tortious or exhibit a separate identity or interest from the corporation (ScotiaMcLeod Inc. v Peoples Jewellers Ltd.). Section 21 PCTI Act grants statutory immunity except for bad faith.
firac.application: The allegations against Mr. Wright were essentially the same as those against PCTIA, with nothing showing conduct separate from his employment. While bad-faith allegations would fall outside s. 21's protection, given the court's conclusion that all the underlying causes of action were bound to fail, the claims against Mr. Wright personally were also certain to fail.
firac.conclusion: The claims against Mr. Wright personally were struck as certain to fail.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary practice area — the case concerns a civil damages action and applications to strike pleadings/summary judgment. K011 (judicial review) and K001 (Administrative law) are central because the reasoning turns on the collateral-attack doctrine: the plaintiffs should have pursued statutory appeal or judicial review rather than a damages action. K014 (standard of review) is a weaker/borderline pick reflecting the administrative-law framing, though the case is really about collateral attack and pleading sufficiency rather than review standards — flagged as weak. K107 (Canadian Charter) and its specific provisions K111 (s. 2(b)) — note the pleaded Charter claim was s. 6(2)(b) mobility/livelihood, for which no closer vocabulary ID exists, so K111 is an imperfect match — and K112 (s. 7 / life, liberty, security, engaged in the s. 8 unreasonable search and seizure analysis) capture the Charter dimension. The Charter keyword IDs are approximate because the vocabulary lacks entries for s. 6(2)(b) and s. 8 specifically; they are included to flag the constitutional pleadings that were struck.

registry_rationale: The decision expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver' beneath the docket number.

name_verification.name_in_document: DILSHOD ISMAILOV v. THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: What standard of review applies to this Court's review of the RAD, and what standard the RAD was to apply to the RPD?

Did the RAD err by failing to assess the risk of persecution to the applicant if he were perceived in Uzbekistan to be an adherent of the Gulen movement, rather than only whether he was an active practitioner?

firac.issue: What standard of review governs the Court's review of the RAD and the RAD's review of the RPD?
firac.facts: The applicant, a citizen of Uzbekistan claiming religious persecution as a Gulen adherent, sought judicial review of a RAD decision confirming the RPD's rejection of his refugee claim after multiple redeterminations.
firac.rule: On judicial review of the RAD, the standard is reasonableness (Canada (MCI) v. Huruglica, 2016, 396 D.L.R. (4th) 527 (F.C.A.) at para 35; Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 190 at para 47). On appeal from the RPD, the RAD applies correctness to findings of fact and mixed fact and law that do not raise credibility issues of oral evidence (Huruglica at paras 77, 103).
firac.application: The Court applied reasonableness to the RAD's decision, examining whether it was intelligible, transparent, justifiable and within the range of defensible outcomes. The dispositive issue—the RAD's failure to assess perceived-adherence risk—raised no oral-evidence credibility issue, so correctness was the standard the RAD owed the RPD.
firac.conclusion: Reasonableness applies to the Court's review of the RAD; correctness applied to the RAD's review of the relevant RPD findings.

firac.issue: Did the RAD err by failing to consider the risk to the applicant if he were perceived in Uzbekistan to be an adherent of the Gulen movement?
firac.facts: The RAD found the applicant was not an 'active practitioner' of the Gulen movement or Said Nursi teachings and would not face persecution on that basis. It found that in Uzbekistan religious freedom is limited to government-recognized religions and that the Gulen movement is not recognized. The applicant argued the RAD failed to address risk based on perceived religious affiliation.
firac.rule: The failure to consider the risk arising from a perception that a person practises a religion subject to state persecution is a reviewable error; the question is not whether the applicant holds the belief but whether potential persecutors would ascribe that belief to him, assessed from the persecutor's perspective (Chekroun v. Canada (MCI) (2013), 436 F.T.R. 1 at para 55; Ward v. Canada, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689 at para 83; Kandiah v. Canada, [1994] F.C.J. No. 1876).
firac.application: The RAD confined itself to finding the applicant was not an active participant in the movement and did not address whether he would face risk if the Uzbek state perceived him as a Gulen adherent, where such adherents do not enjoy state protection. It never analysed the risk from the viewpoint of the persecutor, the state.
firac.conclusion: The RAD committed a reviewable error; the application for judicial review was allowed, the decision set aside, and the matter remitted to a differently constituted RAD panel for redetermination. No question was certified.

defining_issues: Does the claimant have a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Russia such that she is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection?

firac.issue: Does the claimant have a viable internal flight alternative in Yekaterinburg that defeats her claim under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The claimant, a fair-skinned Orthodox Christian Russian citizen, was harassed and beaten by skinheads in her home city who perceived her as connected to Jews because her daughter had married a Jewish man and moved to Israel. Her son was also attacked. Police told her they could not deal with the skinheads. She fled to Canada and claimed refugee protection. The panel proposed Yekaterinburg as an IFA and raised the issue before and at the hearing.
firac.rule: The two-prong IFA test from Rasaratnam v. Canada (MEI), [1992] 1 F.C. 706 (C.A.): (1) no serious possibility of persecution (or, on a balance of probabilities, risk under s. 97) in the proposed area, and (2) conditions such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, for the claimant to seek refuge there. A high threshold applies to unreasonableness (Thirunavukkarasu; Ranganathan), and mere dislocation hardship or being economically better off in Canada is not undue hardship. Once IFA is raised, the onus is on the claimant to show none exists. The Chairperson's Gender Guidelines were also considered.
firac.application: On the first prong, the panel found the anti-Semitic targeting was localized, arising from rumours in the claimant's home community about her daughter and trips to Israel; there was no evidence such targeting by association would follow her elsewhere, and she lacked the risk factors (being foreign, Asian, Caucasus origin, dark-skinned, non-Orthodox) documented for skinhead violence. Her trouble-free period living in Moscow supported this. On the second prong, the panel found the 'propiska'/registration concerns did not fit her profile; documentary evidence showed freedom to choose residence with 90 days to register, scarce evidence of registration barriers in Yekaterinburg, and that a valid Russian passport holder not fearing state mistreatment can resettle. Economic disadvantage, loss of public-sector pay/pension, and absence of friends were significant but did not meet the high unreasonableness threshold. The Gender Guidelines did not assist since her son faced similar targeting, indicating the harm was not gender-based.
firac.conclusion: A viable IFA exists in Yekaterinburg; the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, and the claim is rejected.

name_verification.name_in_document: VAHID MAJIDIGORUH v. JAZZ AVIATION LP

defining_issues: Was the Canadian Human Rights Commission's investigation into the complaint sufficiently thorough and neutral so as to satisfy the duty of procedural fairness?
Was the Commission's decision to dismiss the complaint on the basis that further inquiry was not warranted reasonable?
Could the applicant raise an allegation of investigator bias on judicial review having failed to raise it before the Commission?

firac.issue: Was the Commission's investigation sufficiently thorough and neutral to meet the duty of procedural fairness?
firac.facts: The applicant complained his employer discriminated against him based on race, national/ethnic origin and age. The investigator declined to review audio recordings the applicant provided (citing inability to authenticate voices/context) and declined to interview two crew chiefs (because the harassment was not in dispute). The applicant received the investigation report and filed a written response.
firac.rule: Commission investigations must be both neutral and thorough (Slattery v. Canada (CHRC), [1994] 2 F.C. 574). Judicial review is warranted only where an investigator fails to investigate 'obviously crucial evidence' (Slattery, para. 56); the test is whether it should have been obvious to a reasonable person that the evidence was crucial (Gosal v. Canada (AG), 2011 FC 570). Investigations need not be perfect (Tahmourpour v. Canada, 2005 FCA 113), and some defects may be cured by the parties' right to make submissions on the report; only flaws 'so fundamental that they cannot be remedied by the parties' further responding submissions' justify intervention (Sketchley v. Canada (AG), 2005 FCA 404).
firac.application: The Court agreed the investigator's stated rationale for refusing to listen to the recordings was unreasonable, but, having listened to them, found they were not 'obviously crucial evidence' and were brief snippets the applicant could—and did—summarize in his responding submissions, so the Commissioners were aware of their content. The failure to interview the two crew chiefs was not fatal since the applicant never explained what their evidence would add. The applicant was able to raise his other concerns (friendly union officials, timeline of harassment, email about the supervisor position) in his response. None amounted to fundamental, unremediable flaws.
firac.conclusion: The investigation, though imperfect, met the requisite standard of fairness; any defects were curable and were in fact addressed through the applicant's responding submissions.

firac.issue: Was the Commission's decision to dismiss the complaint as not warranting further inquiry reasonable?
firac.facts: The investigator found the applicant had been harassed by his supervisor but that the conduct was not linked to a prohibited ground; the employer took timely and appropriate action (training, coaching, and ultimately termination of the supervisor). The reduction of crew chiefs at the Vancouver base was made in consultation with the union under the collective agreement and affected others, without changing the applicant's designation or pay; the applicant had never asked his manager for the shift supervisor role.
firac.rule: The Commission is not an adjudicative body; its role is to assess the sufficiency of the evidence and decide whether an inquiry is warranted (Cooper v. Canada (CHRC), [1996] 3 S.C.R. 854; SEPQA, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 879). It has broad discretion in this screening function (Halifax v. Nova Scotia (HRC), 2012 SCC 10; Bell Canada, [1999] 1 F.C. 113). The reviewing court asks only whether the decision was reasonable, not whether it would have reached the same conclusion.
firac.application: On the evidence, the investigator reasonably concluded that the harassment was not tied to a prohibited ground and that adverse differential treatment (the crew reduction and non-selection as shift supervisor) was not established. The Court's role was limited to reasonableness, not re-deciding the merits.
firac.conclusion: The decision to dismiss the complaint was reasonable and disclosed no basis for the Court to intervene.

firac.issue: Could the applicant raise an allegation of investigator bias for the first time on judicial review?
firac.facts: The applicant alleged the investigator prejudged the case by saying she did not see the complaint proceeding to the Tribunal. There was no evidentiary support in his affidavit, and he had never raised the concern with the investigator or in his submissions to the Commission.
firac.rule: An objection based on a reasonable apprehension of bias must be raised at the earliest practicable opportunity, failing which the right to object is waived (Canada (HRC) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892; Zündel v. Canada (CHRC); In Re Human Rights Tribunal and Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd., [1986] 1 F.C. 103).
firac.application: The allegation lacked any evidentiary foundation, and the applicant failed to raise the bias concern before the investigator or the Commission at the earliest opportunity, so he was deemed to have waived it.
firac.conclusion: The bias argument could not be raised on judicial review and was rejected.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally an administrative law judicial review (K001, K011) of a Canadian Human Rights Commission screening decision, engaging the duty of procedural fairness / thoroughness of investigation (K012) and the reasonableness standard of review (K014). The Commission itself is captured by K072 (human rights commission). case_name: Toronto (City) Board of Education v. O.S.S.T.F., District 15

name_verification.name_in_document: Toronto (City) Board of Education v. O.S.S.T.F., District 15

defining_issues: What is the applicable standard of review for a labour arbitration board's decision on just cause and penalty when the decision is protected by a broad privative clause?
Was the arbitration board's decision to conditionally reinstate the teacher, based on a finding that his misconduct was temporary, patently unreasonable given the evidence on the record?
Can misconduct occurring outside teaching hours ground disciplinary discharge of a teacher, and what standard of professional conduct applies under s. 264(1)(c) of the Education Act?

firac.issue: What standard of review applies to a labour arbitration board's determination of just cause and appropriate penalty where its decision is protected by a strong privative clause?
firac.facts: The grievor's discharge was arbitrated under a collective agreement governed by the School Boards and Teachers Collective Negotiations Act, whose s. 72 contains a broad privative clause insulating arbitration decisions from judicial review. The Board of Arbitration set aside the dismissal and ordered conditional reinstatement.
firac.rule: Curial deference is at its highest where a tribunal protected by a true privative clause decides a matter within its jurisdiction with no statutory right of appeal (Pezim v. British Columbia (Superintendent of Brokers); PSAC No. 2). Whether there is 'just cause' for discipline falls within an arbitration board's jurisdiction and can be set aside only if patently unreasonable (Blanchard v. Control Data). Interpretation of 'outside' legislation is generally reviewable on correctness (Bradco), subject to an exception for statutes intimately connected with the tribunal's mandate (CBC v. Canada (Labour Relations Board)).
firac.application: The Court held that determining whether the failure to meet statutory standards was temporary and whether discharge was appropriate lay within the board's jurisdiction. Since both parties agreed the letters breached s. 264(1)(c), no correctness determination on the statute was needed. The strong privative clause and the sensitive, expert nature of labour relations demanded the patently unreasonable standard, an extremely high threshold from which there must be no retreat. L'Heureux-Dubé J. agreed with the standard applied, though she suggested a pragmatic and functional analysis could support something closer to correctness.
firac.conclusion: The patently unreasonable standard governs; the board's decision could be quashed only if it was clearly irrational or based on no evidence.

firac.issue: Was the arbitration board's conclusion that the teacher's misconduct was temporary, and its resulting order of conditional reinstatement, patently unreasonable?
firac.facts: Bhadauria wrote two abusive and threatening letters comparing Board officials to Hitler, Stalin and mass killers and expressing wishes they had been shot. Psychiatric and psychological assessments found no mental illness and no risk of physical violence, but predicted his verbal attacks would continue. He wrote a third, still bitter, letter after dismissal and showed no remorse. The majority attributed his conduct to the stress of the human rights hearings, found him 'not beyond redemption,' and reinstated him conditionally.
firac.rule: A finding based on 'no evidence' is patently unreasonable; a court intervenes only where the evidence, viewed reasonably, is incapable of supporting the tribunal's findings (Lester; Douglas Aircraft). Insufficiency of evidence alone is not reviewable. A reviewing court may examine the record to assess the basis for challenged inferences (National Corn Growers). Subsequent-event evidence may be considered if it sheds light on the reasonableness of the dismissal (Cie minière Québec Cartier).
firac.application: The majority's reinstatement hinged entirely on the inference that the misconduct was temporary. All the evidence the board relied on contradicted that inference: it accepted the Director's evidence that Bhadauria was unfit to teach, rejected his own testimony, accepted the experts' opinions that his verbal harassment would continue, and had before it a third letter (written after dismissal) confirming persistent bitterness and lack of judgment that the majority failed even to mention. The absence of remorse further confirmed persistence. With no evidence capable of supporting the finding of temporariness, the 'leap of faith' returning him to the classroom lacked any rational basis.
firac.conclusion: The board's decision was patently unreasonable; the arbitration award was quashed and the appeal allowed.

firac.issue: Can off-duty misconduct ground the discharge of a teacher, and what standard of conduct does s. 264(1)(c) of the Education Act impose?
firac.facts: The letters may have been written outside teaching hours. The employer discharged Bhadauria for unprofessional conduct, poor judgment and attitudes rendering him incapable of fulfilling his duties as a teacher under the Education Act.
firac.rule: Section 264(1)(c) of the Education Act sets idealistic, aspirational standards; only significant breaches justify discipline. Teachers occupy positions of trust and must teach by example inside and outside the classroom; their conduct is assessed by reference to their position, not by whether it occurs in or out of the classroom (Ross v. New Brunswick School District No. 15; R. v. Audet). Off-duty conduct can ground discipline or discharge because of the teacher's community position.
firac.application: The Court held the letters constituted very significant, if not extreme, misconduct—threats of violence, not mere workplace complaints—and that their being written off duty could neither excuse nor lessen their seriousness. Arbitrators must recognize the sensitivity of the educational setting, the vulnerability of students and the need for public confidence, and ensure a person clearly incapable of fulfilling teaching duties is not returned to the classroom. L'Heureux-Dubé J. would have held the two letters, per se, so gravely prejudiced the grievor's status as a role model as to constitute just cause for discharge regardless of temporariness.
firac.conclusion: Off-duty misconduct can justify discharge; the letters were a significant breach of the s. 264(1)(c) standard, reinforcing that reinstatement was inappropriate.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns grievance arbitration of a discharge. name_verification.name_in_document: XXXX XXXX (RAD File TC0-01158)

defining_issues: Should the appellant's proposed new evidence be admitted under s. 110(4) of the IRPA (and, for the second tranche, rule 29 of the RAD Rules and the Raza/Singh criteria)?
Was an oral hearing warranted under s. 110(6) of the IRPA?

Did the RPD err in its credibility findings, in particular by allowing an adverse inference drawn from the Instagram exchange to permeate the balance of its assessment and by discounting corroborating evidence?

Is the appellant a Convention refugee under s. 96 or a person in need of protection under s. 97(1) of the IRPA, having regard to persecution of Roma in Hungary and the availability of state protection?

firac.issue: Should the appellant's proposed new evidence be admitted under s. 110(4) of the IRPA and, for the later tranche, rule 29 of the RAD Rules?
firac.facts: The appellant tendered two tranches of new evidence: with his record, two affidavits, a letter from the Roma Community Centre (RCC) and a letter from his current in-laws; and, after the appeal was perfected, a second affidavit and a corrected letter from the Hungarian ethnic-minorities advocacy association (EKE). The affidavits largely re-argued RPD findings and supplemented testimony that had been available at the RPD hearing.
firac.rule: Subsection 110(4) IRPA admits new evidence only if it arose after the RPD rejection, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been expected to be presented; such evidence must also be relevant, credible and new (Raza v. Canada, 2007 FCA 385; Canada v. Singh, 2016 FCA 96). Claimants must put their best foot forward at the RPD, and the RAD is not a forum to cure a deficient record. Evidence filed after perfection must additionally satisfy rule 29(4) of the RAD Rules (relevance, probative value, newness, and whether it could reasonably have been provided earlier).
firac.application: The panel found both of the appellant's affidavits were essentially argument and supplementation of evidence available before the RPD, and refused them (save a portion of the second affidavit explaining delay in obtaining the corrected letter). The in-laws' letter was rejected because its authors were family, non-independent, and aware of the process, so it was reasonably available earlier. The RCC letter post-dated the hearing and, in the interests of natural justice, was admitted. The corrected EKE letter, addressing a deficiency the RPD had noted, was found relevant and probative and admitted under rule 29 with some latitude.
firac.conclusion: The affidavits and the in-laws' letter were excluded; the RCC letter and the corrected EKE letter were admitted, along with the portion of the second affidavit explaining the delay.

firac.issue: Was an oral hearing warranted under s. 110(6) of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The appellant requested an oral hearing under s. 110(6) in connection with his new evidence.
firac.rule: Subsection 110(3) IRPA requires the RAD to proceed without a hearing except where the admissible new evidence raises a serious credibility issue, is central to the decision, and if accepted would justify allowing or rejecting the claim (s. 110(6)).
firac.application: The panel found the admitted new evidence did not meet those conjunctive requirements — it was neither determinative of nor central to the decision — so the statutory precondition for an oral hearing was not satisfied.
firac.conclusion: The request for an oral hearing was denied.

firac.issue: Did the RPD err in its credibility findings by allowing an inference drawn from the Instagram exchange to taint the whole assessment and by discounting corroborating evidence?
firac.facts: At the hearing the appellant denied having an Instagram profile; counsel later reported he had two inactive accounts he could no longer access. The RPD treated this as a willingness to lie and made a global adverse credibility finding, gave no weight to his wife's affidavit and little weight to a pastor's letter.
firac.rule: The RAD reviews the RPD on a correctness standard after an independent examination of the evidence, deferring only where the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in assessing oral testimony (Canada v. Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93; Rozas del Solar v. Canada, 2018 FC 1145). Credibility findings must be grounded in the evidence and not rest on peripheral matters.
firac.application: On independent review the panel found no meaningful RPD advantage. The inactive, inaccessible Instagram accounts had nothing to do with the core of the claim and the incorrect answer did not evidence a deliberate intent to mislead; the resulting adverse inference improperly pervaded the decision. The wife's affidavit — from a person already accepted as a Convention refugee, candid about her pending PR status — was highly corroborative of the appellant's Roma ethnicity and Faith Church membership, and the RPD erred in giving it no weight. The pastor's letter linked the Hungarian and Canadian Faith Church and corroborated the appellant's ethnicity and continued membership.
firac.conclusion: The RPD's credibility analysis was tainted and could not be sustained; the corroborating affidavit and pastor's letter were accepted as credible and sufficient to establish the appellant's Roma ethnicity and Faith Church membership.

firac.issue: Is the appellant a Convention refugee under s. 96 or a person in need of protection under s. 97(1) of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The appellant, a Hungarian Roma and Faith Church adherent, described lifelong systemic discrimination in education and employment, bullying, two assaults by right-wing individuals, death threats and an armed assault by his neo-Nazi-suspected father-in-law, and unsuccessful attempts to obtain police protection.
firac.rule: Section 96 IRPA (Convention refugee — serious possibility of persecution for a Convention ground) and s. 97(1) (person in need of protection); assessment includes cumulative discrimination amounting to persecution and the availability of adequate state protection, informed by the National Documentation Package.
firac.application: Having accepted the appellant's ethnicity and religious membership, the panel found the pervasive discrimination he suffered on both grounds cumulatively amounted to persecution, consistent with NDP evidence on treatment of Roma in Hungary. His past persecution and failed attempts to secure police protection, together with the objective evidence, established a serious possibility of persecution on return and the absence of adequate state protection.
firac.conclusion: The appellant is a Convention refugee and a person in need of protection; the RPD decision was set aside under s. 111(1)(b) and the appeal allowed.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K075 (convention refugee) and K078 (refugee protection) capture the s. 96/97 determination substituted by the RAD. K079 (persecution) and K080 (state protection) reflect the merits analysis — cumulative discrimination amounting to persecution and inadequate state protection for Roma in Hungary. K014 (standard of review) applies because the RAD expressly reviewed the RPD on a correctness standard per Huruglica. K065 (racism) fits the anti-Roma ethnic discrimination central to the claim. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) is the relevant institutional entity (RAD/RPD). defining_issues: Did the RPD err in its credibility findings, in particular in drawing a negative inference from the absence of corroborative documentation of the alleged detention?

Do the country-condition documents support a serious possibility of persecution for Pentecostal/house-church Christians in Fujian Province, both as to past events and on a forward-looking/sur place basis?
Did the RPD apply the correct legal test and standard of proof for refugee protection under section 96?

firac.issue: Did the RPD err in its credibility findings, including drawing a negative inference from the lack of corroborative documentation of the claimed detention?
firac.facts: The Appellants, Pentecostal Christians from Fujian, alleged that PSB officers raided their house church in 2017 and detained and tortured them for about thirty days. They produced a Hukou and marriage certificate but no documentation of the detention, despite the Principal Appellant having told the Port of Entry officer that receipts and detention-related papers could be mailed from China.
firac.rule: On appeal the RAD applies a correctness standard, deferring to the RPD only where it had a meaningful advantage in assessing oral testimony (Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93). A negative inference may be drawn from a lack of corroborative evidence where it is reasonable to expect such evidence.
firac.application: The RAD reviewed the audio recording and found it unreasonable that the Appellants failed to produce detention documents shown to be available in China, given the POE exchange, the BOC instructions, and their representation by experienced counsel and their production of other documents. This concern combined with the female Appellant's contradictory statements about her fears and the objective country evidence.
firac.conclusion: The RAD found the RPD did not err; on a balance of probabilities the Appellants were not detained as alleged and their core allegations were not credible.

firac.issue: Do the country-condition documents establish a serious possibility of persecution for Pentecostal/house-church Christians in Fujian Province?
firac.facts: The Appellants are Pentecostal Christians (a Protestant denomination) from XXXX district, XXXX city, Fujian Province, and now attend a Pentecostal congregation in Canada where they were baptized.
firac.rule: Sur place and forward-looking risk are assessed against the National Documentation Package; the test is whether there is a reasonable or serious possibility of persecution (Adjei v. Canada, [1989] 2 F.C. 680).
firac.application: Conducting its own independent analysis of the NDP, the RAD found Pentecostals are not among the banned 'evil cult' groups, that authorities are generally tolerant of house/small-group worship, that Fujian is one of the more liberal provinces with a low recorded degree of religious persecution, and that the escalated crackdowns were concentrated in Zhejiang. The few Fujian incidents cited involved banned groups or occurred in areas unrelated to the Appellants.
firac.conclusion: The RAD found no serious possibility of persecution; the Appellants could practise their faith in an unregistered church in Fujian without fear of persecution.

firac.issue: Did the RPD apply the correct legal test and standard of proof under section 96?
firac.facts: The Appellants argued the RPD used a 'serious possibility' standard rather than the 'more than a mere possibility' test for Convention refugee status.
firac.rule: Factual findings are made on a balance of probabilities; the test for Convention refugee status requires 'good grounds' / a 'reasonable' or 'serious possibility' of persecution (Adjei).
firac.application: The RAD held that 'more than a mere possibility' and 'serious possibility' describe the same threshold and that the RPD clearly understood and applied the correct legal test and standard.
firac.conclusion: No error; the RPD applied the correct test and standard of proof.

defining_issues: Against which country of reference should the claimant's protection claim be assessed?
Do the discriminatory acts and violence the claimant experienced in Slovakia because of his Roma ethnicity amount to persecution under s. 96 of the IRPA?
Did the claimant's failure to claim refugee protection during earlier trips to Canada and his voluntary return to Slovakia undermine a subjective fear of persecution?
Did the claimant rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in the Slovak Republic under s. 97 of the IRPA?

firac.issue: Against which country of reference should the claimant's protection claim be assessed?
firac.facts: The claimant held a certified Slovak passport. Counsel raised a possible entitlement to Czech citizenship because the claimant's mother was born in territory now part of the Czech Republic. No Czech government documents establishing Czech citizenship or automatic entitlement were in evidence.
firac.rule: A protection claim must be assessed against each country of nationality; the claimant must establish citizenship or automatic entitlement to citizenship on a balance of probabilities. Czech citizenship law generally does not recognize dual nationality except in limited circumstances.
firac.application: The panel found the Slovak passport established Slovak citizenship on a balance of probabilities, and that the Czech citizenship laws did not grant the claimant automatic citizenship. No official Czech documents supported a Czech citizenship entitlement.
firac.conclusion: The claim was assessed only against the Slovak Republic, the claimant's sole country of nationality.

firac.issue: Do the discriminatory acts and violence the claimant experienced in Slovakia because of his Roma ethnicity amount to persecution under s. 96?
firac.facts: The claimant, a Roma man, endured insults, being spat upon, denial of employment, and physical beatings in school and adulthood over roughly 27 years. He resided at the same address for nearly 10 years, completed 11 years of schooling, and survived on social assistance.
firac.rule: Persecution is defined as the systematic, sustained or repeated violation of fundamental human rights (UNHCR guidance). Discrimination becomes persecution only where it prevents access to health care, education, state protection, housing or employment necessary to survive; the test is forward-looking.
firac.application: The panel found the insults, attacks and denial of employment, individually or cumulatively, did not reach the seriousness of persecution. The claimant could access social welfare, complete education, maintain a stable address and approach police. Roma face discrimination but the documentary evidence did not establish they are persecuted.
firac.conclusion: The mistreatment amounted to discrimination and harassment, not persecution; the s. 96 claim failed.

firac.issue: Did the claimant's failure to claim protection on earlier trips to Canada and his voluntary return to Slovakia undermine his subjective fear?
firac.facts: The claimant travelled to Canada in 2005 and 2006 but made no refugee claim on either occasion, and voluntarily returned to Slovakia each time. He only claimed protection on his 2008 arrival. He gave explanations relating to his sister's pending claim, lack of work permit, and his spouse's homesickness.
firac.rule: Conduct inconsistent with a subjective fear of persecution — such as failure to claim at the first available opportunity and voluntary reavailment to the country of alleged persecution — can negate subjective fear.
firac.application: The panel rejected the claimant's explanations, finding that a person genuinely fearing persecution would have claimed at the first opportunity rather than returning to the feared country. His repeated failure to claim and re-availment were inconsistent with subjective fear.
firac.conclusion: The claimant's conduct was inconsistent with a subjective fear of persecution, further undermining the s. 96 claim.

firac.issue: Did the claimant rebut the presumption of adequate state protection under s. 97?
firac.facts: After beatings in 2000 and 2008 the claimant went to police, who disbelieved and dismissed him; on one occasion police nearby ignored an attack. He made no complaint to senior police or other oversight bodies, saying he feared reprisal and did not know where else to turn. The Slovak Republic is a multiparty parliamentary democracy taking documented, if imperfect, steps against anti-Roma discrimination and police misconduct.
firac.rule: A state is presumed capable of protecting its citizens absent complete breakdown (Ward). Rebutting the presumption requires clear and convincing evidence of inability to protect; the test is adequacy, not perfection. In a functioning democracy the burden increases with the level of democracy (Kadenko), and a claimant must take reasonable steps to exhaust available avenues (Camacho, Santos).
firac.application: The panel found Slovakia a functioning democracy making serious efforts to protect Roma, with police-oversight and anti-discrimination mechanisms. The claimant's failure to complain about police misconduct to oversight bodies or other agencies was objectively unreasonable. Country evidence showed no systemic denial of protection or state breakdown. Prior refugee determinations of family members were not binding and lacked evidentiary context.
firac.conclusion: The claimant did not rebut the presumption of adequate state protection with clear and convincing evidence; the s. 97 claim failed.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) capture the core s. 96 analysis of whether ethnic mistreatment rose to persecution. K080 (state protection) is the determinative issue under s. 97, the central Ward/Kadenko analysis. K081 (stay of removal) is borderline/weak — the case is a refugee determination rather than a removal stay, but it is the closest removal-related tag; flagged as weak. K065 (racism) reflects the racially/ethnically motivated discrimination and skinhead violence against the Roma claimant. K069 (discrimination) captures the discrimination-versus-persecution distinction central to the reasoning. No hate-speech or Charter keywords apply as the case turns on refugee eligibility and state protection.

registry_rationale: The RPD proceeding was heard in Toronto, Ontario, as stated under 'Place of Hearing'; the Refugee Protection Division registry is thus Toronto.

name_verification.name_in_document: Kariminia v. Nasser
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied citation (2018 BCSC 695) refers to this Court's First Reasons in the same matter, not to the present decision, which is cited as 2023 BCSC 1954. The party names are consistent; the supplied citation matches an earlier related judgment rather than this decision.

defining_issues: Is the respondent barred by res judicata or abuse of process from having the issue of the Loan addressed further after prior reasons made no findings on it?
Should the claimant be permitted to rely on new affidavit evidence under the Palmer fresh-evidence test?
What amount of the Loan constitutes family property and what amount, if any, was repaid to the claimant?
What costs should be awarded, and is the respondent entitled to special costs?

firac.issue: Is the respondent barred by res judicata (cause of action estoppel) or abuse of process from having the Loan issue determined, where the Court's earlier reasons made no findings on it?
firac.facts: The Loan of 3,600,000,000 Rials was mentioned in the 2018 First Reasons but the Court made no finding on whether it was family property or on repayment amounts, as Mr. Kariminia was absent and evidence was insufficient. Ms. Nasser later obtained further Iranian court documents in November 2020 and sought a declaration that the Loan was family property.
firac.rule: Doctrines of res judicata (cause of action estoppel) and abuse of process may bar re-litigation of previously determined matters, but courts retain discretion to allow determination on the merits where it is in the interest of justice: Wozny v. Gelber, 2021 BCSC 314 at para. 46.
firac.application: The Court found the First Reasons did not extinguish the family law claim regarding the Loan, as no finding was made on whether it was family property, the amount advanced, or repayments. It was not clear the 2018 application was a summary trial. New documents obtained from Iran justified further consideration, and deciding the issue on its merits was the only way to achieve a just outcome.
firac.conclusion: The doctrines do not apply; Ms. Nasser is entitled to have the Loan issue addressed further.

firac.issue: Should the claimant be permitted to rely on the New Affidavits under the fresh-evidence test?
firac.facts: Mr. Kariminia sought to introduce three affidavits (from brother Ramin, brother Amin, and the Uncle) to clarify who funded the Loan and whether repayments were made to him, while the matter was adjourned for further submissions and before judgment.
firac.rule: The test for admitting fresh evidence in Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759: (1) due diligence; (2) relevance to a decisive issue; (3) credibility; (4) potential to affect the result. The test is 'purposive, fact-driven, and driven by an overarching concern for the interests of justice': Barendregt v. Grebliunas, 2022 SCC 22 at para. 31.
firac.application: For Ramin's affidavit, all four branches were met: due diligence was satisfied because Ramin was previously unwilling to participate and additional leeway applies to obtaining evidence from Iran; the evidence was relevant to who funded the Loan and repayments; it was credible on a holistic view; and it could affect the result. For the affidavits of Amin and the Uncle, the due-diligence branch was not met and they added nothing not already before the Court.
firac.conclusion: Affidavit #1 of Ramin Kariminia is admitted; the affidavits of Amin and the Uncle are refused.

firac.issue: What portion of the Loan is family property, and what amount, if any, was repaid to the claimant?
firac.facts: The parties agreed that a loan made from family money during cohabitation is family property and repayments divisible equally. Mr. Kariminia gave inconsistent evidence on his contribution (ranging from $75,000 line of credit to 5-20% to $20,000-$30,000). Ramin's evidence was that $60,000 was transferred, of which ~$29,000 went to buy a home for Ms. Nasser's mother, leaving ~$31,000 to the Loan. Documents relied on by Ms. Nasser contained mistranslations and errors.
firac.rule: Family property division under the Family Law Act; a party alleging hidden assets must provide a 'strong evidentiary basis': Laxton v. Coglon, 2008 BCSC 42 at para. 31. Courts must be mindful not to assess conduct of persons from another culture by Canadian assumptions: Fu v. Zhu, 2018 BCSC 9 at para. 41.
firac.application: Given the parties' financial situation, the Court was not persuaded Mr. Kariminia loaned the full ~$360,000. Accepting Ramin's evidence, the Court found ~$31,000 CAD was contributed by Mr. Kariminia to the Loan. On repayment, Ms. Nasser's translated documents were unreliable (mistranslations, arithmetic errors, a sum tied to the mother's house purchase), and Ramin's evidence established that repayments and sale proceeds went to Ramin, not Mr. Kariminia. Ms. Nasser did not establish the strong evidentiary basis needed to show hidden assets.
firac.conclusion: $31,000 of the Loan is declared family property; no repayment to Mr. Kariminia was established as of separation; any future recovery must be shared equally.

firac.issue: What costs should be awarded, and is Ms. Nasser entitled to special costs?
firac.facts: Ms. Nasser sought special costs, alleging Mr. Kariminia concealed the Loan proceeds. Mr. Kariminia substantially succeeded in opposing the application but had failed to disclose Iranian court documents and gave misleading, confusing affidavit evidence, forcing Ms. Nasser to obtain and translate the records.
firac.rule: Special costs require 'reprehensible' conduct deserving of reproof or rebuke: Yusufi v. Yusufi, 2022 BCSC 900 at para. 60; Hu v. Dickson, 2015 BCSC 218. Under R. 16-1(7) Supreme Court Family Rules costs follow substantial success unless the court orders otherwise, with discretion exercised judicially: D.N. v. M.R., 2020 BCSC 475.
firac.application: Mr. Kariminia's conduct was 'problematic' but not reprehensible, so special costs were refused. Though he achieved substantial success, the Court exercised its discretion to deprive him of costs due to his failure to disclose documents, misleading evidence, and the waste of court time and added expense to Ms. Nasser. Ms. Nasser was entitled to reimbursement of disbursements for obtaining and translating the Iranian court records that Mr. Kariminia should have produced.
firac.conclusion: Special costs dismissed; each party bears its own costs except Ms. Nasser is fully reimbursed for disbursements incurred obtaining and translating the Iranian documents.

K002 (Civil litigation) is included because the outcome turned heavily on general civil doctrines: res judicata/abuse of process, the Palmer fresh-evidence test, and costs. The controlled list does not contain dedicated keywords for family property division, res judicata, fresh evidence, or costs, which limits precision here.
