registry_rationale: The matter proceeded in the Federal Court's Toronto registry — the place of hearing is listed as Toronto, Ontario and counsel (Davis & Grice; Attorney General of Canada) are based in Toronto.

case_name: Payne v. Ontario Human Rights Commission

name_verification.name_in_document: Payne v. Ontario Human Rights Commission

defining_issues: On an application for judicial review of a decision of the Human Rights Commission not to refer a complaint to a board of inquiry, what is the scope of a party's right to examine a witness (the Registrar and staff) under Rule 39.03?
Does s. 30 of the Ontario Human Rights Code shield the Commission and its staff from being examined under Rule 39.03?
How does the doctrine of deliberative secrecy and the required factual threshold affect the right to examine a senior Commission official privy to the decision-making process?
Were the portions of the appellant's affidavit setting out material that was not before the Commission properly struck?

firac.issue: What is the scope of the right to examine the Commission's Registrar and staff under Rule 39.03 on judicial review of a decision not to refer a human rights complaint to a board of inquiry?
firac.facts: Payne complained to the Ontario Human Rights Commission of discrimination and reprisal after her demotion and dismissal from Youth Clinical Services following an on-air anti-Semitic remark. Two Case Analysis Reports recommended referral, but the Commissioners, by majority, declined to refer the complaint and upheld that decision on reconsideration. On judicial review Payne served a sweeping Notice of Examination on the Registrar demanding production of the Commission's entire files and disclosure of all staff communications with Commissioners.
firac.rule: Rule 39.03 permits examination of a witness before the hearing of a pending application; Canada Metal Co. v. Heap (1975), 7 O.R. (2d) 185 establishes a prima facie right to examine on matters relevant to an issue on the application, limited only by relevance and abuse of process. There is no right to examination for discovery on judicial review (Ellis-Don). The record on judicial review is 'the record of the proceedings in which the decision was made' (Judicial Review Procedure Act, s. 10), but the superior court may insist on a full and accurate record of what actually transpired before the tribunal.
firac.application: The majority (Sharpe J.A.) held the proposed examination was far too broad—an impermissible general discovery amounting to a 'fishing expedition'—and that Payne had no right to rummage through the Commission's files. However, a party is entitled to have produced a complete account of the facts, recommendations and considerations actually placed before the Commissioners, since a tribunal cannot immunize its process by filing an incomplete record. Because a fundamental human right was at stake and the only recourse was judicial review, and because the sole legitimate factor for the Commission was the merit of the complaint, a focused examination was warranted. Abella J.A., dissenting, would have barred the examination entirely.
firac.conclusion: Appeal allowed in part: the sweeping examination was refused, but a narrowly focused Rule 39.03 examination was permitted to determine what documents, facts, considerations or recommendations not disclosed in the record were before the Commissioners, whether 'strategic factors' underlay the decision, and whether undisclosed reasons existed.

firac.issue: Does s. 30 of the Ontario Human Rights Code bar examination of Commission members and staff under Rule 39.03?
firac.facts: The Commission argued that s. 30, which protects members and employees from being required to give testimony as to 'information obtained in the course of an investigation,' operated as a complete statutory shield analogous to s. 111 of the Labour Relations Act considered in Ellis-Don.
firac.rule: Ontario Human Rights Code s. 30; contrasted with Ontario Labour Relations Act s. 111 (which broadly protects testimony 'respecting information obtained in the discharge of their duties'). Legislatures may enact codes protecting confidentiality (Glover; Cook v. Ip; Ellis-Don).
firac.application: The majority read s. 30 narrowly: it protects only the product of the Commission's investigative efforts, not a general prohibition on examination. Unlike the far broader s. 111 in Ellis-Don, s. 30's language does not prevent producing before the court a full account of the material actually presented to the Commissioners when they disposed of the complaint; to read it otherwise would circumscribe the complainant's right to fairness. Abella J.A., dissenting, found s. 30 almost identical in effect to s. 111 and thus a complete bar.
firac.conclusion: The majority held s. 30 does not preclude the focused examination; it only supports denying a general production of the entire file.

firac.issue: How do deliberative secrecy and the applicable factual threshold constrain examination of a senior Commission official privy to the decision-making process?
firac.facts: Payne relied on the affidavit of former Commissioner St. Clair Wharton, who described the Commission's practices—staff overriding Case Analysis Reports, reliance on 'strategic' cost considerations, pre-drafted reasons not reflecting actual discussions—and gave his recollection of the September 1996 meeting. The Commission did not cross-examine or contradict the affidavit.
firac.rule: Deliberative secrecy of administrative decision-makers is qualified, not absolute, and must yield where a litigant presents valid reasons to believe natural justice was not observed (Tremblay v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales), [1992] 1 S.C.R. 952; Agnew v. Ontario Association of Architects). Staff participation does not automatically taint a decision (Consolidated-Bathurst). The threshold is not a 'heavy onus' or proof of the case; an applicant must present some basis for a clearly articulated and objectively reasonable concern that a relevant legal right may have been infringed, but examinations based on conjecture or speculation are not allowed.
firac.application: The majority rejected the 'reasonable evidentiary foundation'/'heavy onus' standard as inimical to effective judicial review, holding it would force applicants to prove their case before obtaining evidence. Because the Commission conducted deliberations in the presence of and with input from non-members, its process was more exposed to review. The unchallenged Wharton affidavit raised objectively reasonable concerns (staff control, reliance on legally irrelevant strategic/cost factors, inadequate reasons, and an incomplete record) sufficiently connected to Payne's complaint to rise above speculation. Abella J.A. viewed the affidavit as mere conjecture insufficient to meet any threshold.
firac.conclusion: The majority held the threshold was met, permitting the focused examination touching only on facts, recommendations and considerations actually before the Commissioners and on whether strategic factors or undisclosed reasons played a role.

firac.issue: Were the portions of Payne's affidavit setting out material not before the Commission properly struck?
firac.facts: Payne's judicial review affidavit set out at length her own version of events at YCS and her dealings with the Commission—material that had not been before the Commissioners when they decided.
firac.rule: On judicial review the court reviews the record before the decision-maker; evidence not before the tribunal is generally inadmissible.
firac.application: Both Abella and Sharpe JJ.A. agreed that because the struck paragraphs contained information that was not before the Commission when it decided, they were properly struck.
firac.conclusion: The appeal from the order striking those portions of the affidavit was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally about administrative-law procedure on judicial review, so K001 (Administrative law, tier-1 practice area) and K011 (judicial review) are core, as is K012 (procedural fairness/natural justice), the value the examination sought to vindicate. K072 (human rights commission/tribunal) and K119 (Human Rights Code) identify the decision-maker and governing statute (ss. 30, 34, 36, 37). K069 (discrimination) and K082 (employment discrimination) reflect the underlying complaint of workplace discrimination, demotion, dismissal and reprisal. K058 (antisemitism) is included because the anti-Semitic remark and its fallout are the central factual driver of the whole dispute; it is a factual rather than doctrinal pick and is somewhat borderline. K065 (racism) could equally have been chosen given the systemic-racism allegations but was omitted to keep the list focused.

name_verification.name_in_document: Richard Warman v. Eldon Warman

defining_issues: Did Eldon Warman engage in a discriminatory practice under s. 13 of the Canadian Human Rights Act by repeatedly communicating internet messages likely to expose Jewish people to hatred or contempt?

Should the Tribunal impose the penalty of up to $10,000 sought under s. 54(1)(c) of the Canadian Human Rights Act, given unresolved constitutional and proportionality concerns and the respondent's non-participation?

firac.issue: Did Eldon Warman contravene s. 13 of the Canadian Human Rights Act by repeatedly posting internet messages likely to expose Jewish people to hatred or contempt?
firac.facts: Richard Warman, an anti-hate campaigner unrelated to the respondent, compiled numerous e-mail postings, bulletin-board messages and newsgroup entries authored by Eldon Warman, a leading figure in a 'detax'/sovereign-citizen movement. The messages portrayed Jews as an evil conspiracy of 'banksters', used dehumanizing slurs, referenced concentration-camp 'soap and lampshades', and blamed Jewish people for a range of ills. The respondent's name and e-mail addresses appeared on the postings; he refused service and did not participate.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) CHRA makes it a discriminatory practice to communicate telephonically, repeatedly, matter likely to expose persons to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground; s. 13(2) extends this to internet communications. The provision is a reasonable limit on freedom of expression (Charter s. 2(b)) upheld under s. 1 in Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892. The words 'expose', 'hatred' and 'contempt' bear their ordinary meanings and require a certain gravity; trivial comments are not caught.
firac.application: On a balance of probabilities the Tribunal inferred, from the consistent voice, return addresses and website registration, that Eldon Warman authored the postings. Though some content was political and thus protected, the postings vilified and dehumanized Jewish people, promoting hatred and contempt that strikes at their equality and dignity. The frequency and internet posting satisfied the 'repeatedly' requirement, and the material was well beyond trivial or legitimate debate.
firac.conclusion: The complaint was substantiated. A cease-and-desist order was granted (per Warman v. Kyburz, 2003 CHRT 18); the material was subsequently removed from the internet, meeting the Act's remedial purpose.

firac.issue: Should the Tribunal impose the $10,000 penalty under s. 54(1)(c) of the Canadian Human Rights Act despite unresolved constitutional and proportionality concerns and the respondent's absence?
firac.facts: The Commission sought the maximum $10,000 penalty under s. 54(1)(c). The respondent refused to recognize the Tribunal's authority and did not appear, so no submissions were made on his behalf. Penalty caselaw was sparse (only Kyburz had awarded one, uncontested), and s. 54(1)(c) was added in 1998, after Taylor.
firac.rule: Section 54(1)(c) permits a penalty up to $10,000 for a substantiated s. 13 complaint; s. 54(1.1) lists factors (nature, gravity, wilfulness, prior practices, ability to pay). Taylor upheld s. 13 as remedial, not punitive; the penalty provision is severable and, being inherently punitive, was not addressed in Taylor. The Tribunal must ensure a fair hearing and proper airing of constitutional issues even where the respondent does not appear.
firac.application: The Tribunal found the constitutionality of the punitive penalty unresolved, distinguishing it from the remedial scheme upheld in Taylor and noting the absence of criminal-process safeguards (higher burden, mens rea, strict evidence rules) for what is effectively punishment. Comparison with R. v. Ahenakew (a $1,000 fine on conviction) raised proportionality concerns about a $10,000 civil penalty imposed in absentia. With no submissions from the respondent and no reliable range of precedents, the Tribunal could not fairly fix a penalty.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal reserved jurisdiction for 30 days, requiring the Complainant and Commission to decide whether to make further submissions and to give constitutional notice under Rule 9(7) before any penalty could be considered.

keywords_rationale: K007 (Human rights) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a CHRA complaint. K061 (hate speech) and K070 (discriminatory messages) capture the core s. 13 discriminatory practice; K113 (CHRA s. 13) is the governing statute. K063 (online hate/social media) reflects the internet postings, the express subject of s. 13(2). K058 (antisemitism), K057 (antisemitic slurs) and K093 (Jewish) identify the targeted group and the nature of the messages. K024 (freedom of expression) and K030 (reasonable limits s. 1) capture the Taylor s. 2(b)/s. 1 analysis central to both liability and the penalty discussion. K030 is somewhat secondary (the s. 1 question was left open for the penalty), but the constitutional framing is prominent throughout. I omitted Holocaust denial (the 'soap and lampshades' reference exploits but does not deny the Shoah).
location_rationale: The decision is signed 'OTTAWA, Ontario September 23, 2005' and the style of cause records the hearing as held April 25, 26, 27, 2005 and May 26, 2005 in Ottawa, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The Canadian Human Rights Tribunal is a national tribunal; the hearing and decision were seated at Ottawa, Ontario, which serves as the effective registry/office for this file (T998/11804).

name_verification.name_in_document: MARIAM JOSEPH LATIF, FARHAD YACIN MOHAMOUD v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Was the Tribunal's assessment of the applicants' credibility unreasonable?
Did the Tribunal unreasonably fail to consider the principal applicant's own risk of persecution arising from her opposition to her daughter's female genital mutilation?

firac.issue: Was the Refugee Protection Division's adverse credibility assessment of the principal applicant and her son unreasonable?
firac.facts: The principal applicant and her son (the male applicant), citizens of Djibouti, claimed refugee protection. The Tribunal found numerous contradictions between the Basis of Claim forms, port-of-entry statements, and hearing testimony. The principal applicant gave differing accounts of why she was detained (her husband vs. her Jewish/Christian-sounding name), and the male applicant's passport stamps showed he was outside Djibouti during a period he claimed to have been detained there.
firac.rule: Credibility findings are reviewed on the reasonableness standard (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9; Ramirez v Canada, 2007 FC 721). While a tribunal should not base findings on microscopic examination of peripheral issues or impugn credibility solely because port-of-entry information lacks detail (Lubana v Canada, 2003 FCT 116; Cetinkaya v Canada, 2012 FC 8), it may draw negative inferences from significant contradictions and omissions between port-of-entry statements and later testimony (Singh v Canada, 2008 FC 453; Jean-Baptiste v Canada, 2009 FC 1261).
firac.application: The Court distinguished Cetinkaya, noting that here the applicants had not merely added detail but had changed their stories, and there were significant contradictions and omissions on key elements of the claims, including the passport evidence contradicting the male applicant's alleged detention date. The Tribunal did not doubt credibility merely for lack of detail but for genuine inconsistencies.
firac.conclusion: The credibility findings were reasonable; the Tribunal reasonably disbelieved the applicants' account of political activity and being targeted by Djiboutian authorities, and the decision regarding the male applicant was upheld.

firac.issue: Did the Tribunal unreasonably conclude that the record did not support the principal applicant being at risk because of her opposition to her daughter's FGM?
firac.facts: The Tribunal accepted that the minor daughter faced a serious possibility of FGM in Djibouti and allowed her claim, but rejected the mother's claim on the basis that she had not declared she feared for herself over her opposition to the practice. The record showed the mother could not directly oppose the husband's grandmother, who insisted on the excision, and could act only through her husband because of cultural norms.
firac.rule: The Board must consider all grounds for a refugee claim even if not raised at the hearing (Canada (AG) v Ward, [1993] 2 SCR 689; Viafara v Canada, 2006 FC 1526). UNHCR guidance (Guidance Note on Refugee Claims relating to FGM) and Guideline 4 recognize a parent may have a claim in their own right where forced to witness the child's suffering or where they risk persecution for opposing the practice. Reasonableness applies (Dunsmuir).
firac.application: The Court found the mother's opposition and the constraints of cultural norms were evident in the Tribunal's own paragraph 81, establishing a basis for her subjective fear. Given the accepted risk to the daughter, the Tribunal should have assessed the mother's own risk under the FGM Guidance Note and Guideline 4. The risk was not hypothetical merely because she could avoid it by leaving the daughter behind, since a mother is not free to abandon her child. Rejecting a protection need on the basis that a person could avoid harm by acquiescing in the persecutory conduct is unacceptable.
firac.conclusion: The refusal of the principal applicant's claim was unreasonable; that part of the decision was set aside and referred to a different member for redetermination, while the male applicant's determination stood. No question was certified.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) capture the reasonableness review of an RPD decision under s. 72(1) IRPA. K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) are central, including gender-related persecution via FGM. K047 (best interests of the child) applies because the mother's risk derived from protecting her daughter from FGM and the daughter's claim was allowed. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the RPD as the tribunal reviewed. No dedicated 'credibility' keyword exists in the vocabulary, so credibility is captured indirectly through the refugee/judicial review terms.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Ottawa, Ontario, December 22, 2015' and the style of cause lists the place of hearing as 'ottawa, ontario'.
registry_rationale: As a Federal Court matter, the proceeding was heard and decided at Ottawa, Ontario; no separate registry office is named beyond the Ottawa place of hearing, which serves as the registry reference.

name_verification.name_in_document: [no public name — anonymized: XXXX XXXX et al.]

defining_issues: Did the RPD err in finding no nexus between the Appellants' fear and a Convention ground, i.e. did the discrimination and harassment they faced in Argentina amount to persecution based on race?
Did the RPD err in finding that the Appellants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection in Argentina?
Are the Appellants excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E given their status in Argentina, and did the panel properly assess their claim against Argentina?

firac.issue: Did the discrimination, harassment and criminal incidents experienced by the Appellants in Argentina establish a nexus to a Convention ground (race/Chinese ethnicity) rising to the level of persecution?
firac.facts: The Appellants, ethnic Chinese permanent residents/citizens of Argentina, recounted incidents of racial slurs from customers, a 2009 robbery, a 2015 extortion phone call, and bullying/discrimination of the minor Appellants at school. The panel found them credible but concluded the incidents were random and criminal, experienced by other ethnic minorities as well.
firac.rule: Under s. 96 of the IRPA, a refugee claimant must establish a well-founded fear of persecution linked to a Convention ground. Discrimination does not necessarily amount to persecution. As cited by the Appellants (Hathaway, The Law of Refugee Status), a Convention ground need only be a contributing factor to the risk. The RAD applies a correctness standard per Huruglica (2014 FC 799; 2016 FCA 93), conducting an independent assessment while respecting the RPD's credibility advantages.
firac.application: The RAD independently reviewed the record and country documentation. It accepted that race and foreigner identity generate widespread prejudice in Argentina directed at Chinese and other groups, but found the three harassment incidents over three years, the robbery and the extortion call did not rise to the level of persecution — no one was injured, the incidents passed quickly, and the robbery/extortion were criminal and economically motivated with no evidence of ethnic targeting. School discrimination, while unacceptable, did not deny education and was not escalated to higher authorities. The harm faced was a generalized risk broadly shared across Argentine society.
firac.conclusion: The RAD found the panel did not err; the discrimination and harassment did not amount to persecution, and no sufficient nexus to a Convention ground was established, even cumulatively.

firac.issue: Did the Appellants rebut the presumption of state protection in Argentina?
firac.facts: The Appellants alleged police refused to help them because they were Chinese, demanded bribes, took merchandise, and that the Chinese community knew police would not help. They often chose not to involve police. Police did respond to the 2009 robbery; they did not contact police regarding the 2015 extortion despite embassy advice.
firac.rule: A claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect to rebut the presumption of state protection. Country documentary evidence (NDP: US Department of State, Amnesty International, Freedom House) is weighed against the claimant's evidence.
firac.application: The RAD found the Appellants did not provide clear and convincing evidence they sought and were denied protection; they could have approached higher police authorities and reported bribe demands. Country evidence showed federal authorities investigate, prosecute and convict abusive officers, and that Argentine and Chinese police jointly combated criminal groups preying on Chinese business owners. The RAD rejected the claim that police universally refuse to help ethnic Chinese; the mixed evidence on police conduct reflected a generalized problem, not ethnic-based denial of protection.
firac.conclusion: The RAD held the panel did not err; the Appellants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection.

firac.issue: Are the Appellants excluded under Article 1E, and was the claim against Argentina properly assessed?
firac.facts: The principal, female and minor female Appellants are citizens of China and permanent residents of Argentina; the minor male Appellant is an Argentine citizen. The Minister submitted they were entitled to return to Argentina, triggering the 1E exclusion. The Appellants did not contest their status.
firac.rule: Article 1E of the Refugee Convention, incorporated by s. 98 of the IRPA, excludes persons who have status substantially similar to nationals in a country of residence; the panel first assesses any claim against the 1E country before applying the exclusion.
firac.application: The panel found the Appellants entitled to return to Argentina and, before applying 1E, assessed their claim against Argentina, finding no serious possibility of persecution nor risk under s. 97. The minor male Appellant likewise failed to establish a claim against Argentina, his country of nationality. Only if the Argentina claim failed against China would that be considered.
firac.conclusion: The Appellants were excluded under s. 98/Article 1E and were found to be neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection; the appeals were dismissed under s. 111(1)(a).

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the core claim under ss. 96/97. K079 (persecution) is central because the determinative question was whether discrimination rose to persecution. K080 (state protection) reflects the second contested issue. K069 (discrimination) and K065 (racism) capture the alleged anti-Chinese prejudice and the persecution-vs-discrimination analysis. K014 (standard of review) applies because the RAD expressly discussed the Huruglica correctness standard governing its review of the RPD. Article 1E exclusion had no dedicated keyword; inadmissibility (K077) was considered but is not apt since 1E is an exclusion, not inadmissibility, so it was omitted.
location_rationale: The decision states 'Appeal considered / heard at Toronto, Ontario', establishing the city and province.
registry_rationale: The Refugee Appeal Division considered the appeal at Toronto, Ontario; the file bears RAD File Nos. TB6-04723 et al. Toronto is the office where the matter was handled.

name_verification.name_in_document: Richard Warman v. Northern Alliance and Jason Ouwendyk

defining_issues: Did the Canadian Human Rights Commission's withdrawal from the hearing (or the respondent's Consumer Proposal or the delay in filing) deprive the Tribunal of jurisdiction to continue the inquiry?
Were the impugned website messages likely to expose identifiable persons to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground within the meaning of s. 13(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act?
Were the communications made repeatedly, in whole or in part, by means of a telecommunication undertaking within Parliament's legislative authority?
Did Jason Ouwendyk and the Northern Alliance, acting in concert, communicate or cause to be communicated the impugned messages?
What remedies, if any, should be ordered, given the complainant's own conduct and the cessation of the impugned activity?

firac.issue: Did the Commission's withdrawal, the respondent's Consumer Proposal, or the pre-complaint delay deprive the Tribunal of jurisdiction to continue the inquiry?
firac.facts: One week before the hearing the Commission advised it would no longer participate, citing that the impugned material was off the internet, the website had been sold, and Ouwendyk's Consumer Proposal under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act stayed the financial claims. The respondent Ouwendyk asked that the complaints be dismissed, also on the basis that the conduct predated the complaint by more than a year.
firac.rule: Under s. 44(3)(a) and s. 49(1)-(2) of the Canadian Human Rights Act the Commission's request obliges the Chair to institute an inquiry; s. 51 permits the Commission to decline further participation where not in the public interest but does not undo the request; ss. 41(1)(e) and 44(3) contemplate inquiries into conduct occurring more than a year before the complaint.
firac.application: Once the Commission had requested the inquiry, the Tribunal was statutorily bound to hold a hearing, and the Commission's later withdrawal did not remove that obligation. The Consumer Proposal stayed only financial claims (which the complainant then removed by amending his particulars) and did not bar the inquiry. The one-year timing issue was expressly contemplated by the Act. The complainant was present and prepared to proceed.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal retained jurisdiction and proceeded with the hearing; the requests to dismiss were rejected, though the Tribunal found the late withdrawal 'troubling'.

firac.issue: Were the impugned messages likely to expose identifiable persons to hatred or contempt under s. 13(1)?
firac.facts: The Northern Alliance Website forum and photo gallery contained numerous posts and images targeting Roma, Eastern Europeans, gays and lesbians, the disabled, Hispanics, Chinese/East Asians, Blacks, Aboriginal persons, and Jews, Muslims and Arabs, portraying them as inferior, dangerous, or deserving of elimination, and denying the Holocaust.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) CHRA; the meaning of 'hatred', 'contempt', 'likely' and 'expose' as set in Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor [1990] 3 SCR 892, Nealy v. Johnston, and the Taylor/Western Guard decision; hallmarks of hate material from Warman v. Kouba, 2006 CHRT 50.
firac.application: The messages expressed that people should be hated because of who they are, deploying stereotypes and the recognized hallmarks (powerful menace, predator, sub-human, banishment, call to violence, trivializing past tragedy). They created conditions for hatred to flourish against the targeted groups on prohibited grounds of religion, sexual orientation, race, colour, national or ethnic origin, and disability.
firac.conclusion: The material was likely to expose the targeted persons to hatred or contempt within the meaning of s. 13(1).

firac.issue: Were the communications made repeatedly by means of a telecommunication undertaking within Parliament's authority?
firac.facts: The material was posted on the publicly accessible Northern Alliance Website, which Warman was able to view and download simply by navigating to the site's forum, with no obstacles to access.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) and s. 13(2) CHRA; Tribunal jurisprudence holding internet material is by its nature a repeated communication (Warman v. Beaumont, Harrison, Kulbashian, Tremaine).
firac.application: Because the material was posted on an unrestricted website accessible to anyone on the internet, it constituted a repeated communication by telecommunication, and s. 13(2) confirms s. 13(1) applies to internet communications.
firac.conclusion: The communications were made repeatedly by a telecommunication undertaking within Parliament's legislative authority, contrary to s. 13(1).

firac.issue: Did Ouwendyk and the Northern Alliance act in concert to communicate the messages?
firac.facts: Ouwendyk admitted being a member, elected spokesperson, webmaster and administrator of the site, and posted some impugned material under the pseudonym 'Jay'; he appeared but gave no evidence. Photos, letterhead, a postal box, e-mail, newsletter and financial account evidenced the Northern Alliance as an organized group.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) CHRA requires a person or group acting in concert; jurisprudence including Smith v. Western Guard Party, Taylor, Khaki v. Canadian Liberty Net, Nealy, Chilliwack Anti-Racism Project, Warman v. Western Canada For Us.
firac.application: The uncontradicted evidence established Ouwendyk's personal responsibility and that the Northern Alliance, though unincorporated, functioned as a group acting in concert when the messages were communicated. Ouwendyk did not rebut the evidence.
firac.conclusion: Ouwendyk individually, and Ouwendyk and the Northern Alliance acting in concert, communicated or caused the messages to be communicated within the meaning of s. 13(1); the complaints were substantiated.

firac.issue: What remedies should be ordered given the complainant's own conduct and cessation of activity?
firac.facts: Warman sought a cease-and-desist order and, against the Northern Alliance, a $7,500 penalty and $6,000 compensation. On cross-examination he admitted posting on similar hate sites under pseudonyms ('Pogue Mahone', 'Axetogrind'), including content quoting antisemitic material. The website had been sold and the activity had ceased years earlier.
firac.rule: Section 54(1)(a) (cease and desist), s. 54(1)(b) (compensation) and s. 54(1)(c) (penalty) CHRA; Tribunal discretion informed by remedial purpose; Chair Sinclair's earlier ruling deferring any order pending the constitutional outcome in Warman v. Lemire.
firac.application: A cease-and-desist order was made as a precaution, but not to be issued until final court determination of the constitutional question in Lemire. The Tribunal declined the penalty and compensation because the impugned activity had long ceased and because Warman's own participation on similar hate sites diminished his credibility and was 'disappointing and disturbing'.
firac.conclusion: Only a deferred cease-and-desist order under s. 54(1)(a) was granted; no penalty or compensation was awarded.

keywords_rationale: K007 (Human rights) is the tier-1 practice area. K061 (hate speech) and K063 (online hate/social media) capture the core subject: hate messages posted on a website. K113 (CHRA s. 13) and K108 (Canadian Human Rights Act) are the governing statute and provision. K072 (human rights tribunal) reflects the CHRT forum. K070 (discriminatory messages) matches the s. 13 'discriminatory practice' framing. K062 (Holocaust denial) is engaged by the 'Holohoax' posts minimizing the Holocaust, and K058 (antisemitism) by the anti-Jewish content; both are strong given the targeted material. K069 (discrimination) is the general underlying concept. Antisemitism/Holocaust denial are somewhat narrower given the messages targeted many groups, but they are squarely present in the evidence.
location_rationale: The reasons are signed 'OTTAWA, Ontario March 13, 2009', and the parties-of-record note the hearing took place in Hamilton, Ontario. City is given as Ottawa (place of signing); province Ontario.
registry_rationale: The Canadian Human Rights Tribunal is a national tribunal with no local registry; the decision identifies only tribunal file numbers (T1216/2807, T1217/2907), so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: [Claimant names redacted] — file nos. TA1-08064 / TA1-08065 / TA1-08066 / TA1-08067

defining_issues: Was there an objective basis for the claimant's fear of persecution in Syria on the ground of his Christian (Armenian) faith, or did the treatment amount only to discrimination?
Were the specific incidents of abuse alleged by the claimant and his wife credible?
Did the claimant face a risk on return to Syria as a failed asylum seeker who left without authorization?
Did the dependent claims of the wife and children succeed, given that they were based on the principal claimant's claim?

firac.issue: Was there an objective basis for the claimant's fear of persecution in Syria on account of his Christian faith?
firac.facts: The claimant, a 41-year-old Armenian Christian from Aleppo, alleged that Syrian authorities and the Sunni majority persecuted his family, including harassment of his children at school, mistreatment of his wife, non-payment by clients of his auto-electrical business, and general hostility toward Christians.
firac.rule: To ground a refugee claim, discrimination must rise to the level of persecution; per para. 54 of the UNHCR Handbook, discrimination amounts to persecution only where it produces consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature, such as serious restrictions on the right to earn a livelihood, to practise religion, or to access normally available education.
firac.application: Documentary evidence showed Christians in Syria practise their faith openly, are well protected by the regime, face no employment discrimination, and that schools accommodate Christian religious instruction and even liturgical languages such as Armenian. The claimant completed high school, his children attended elementary school without restriction, and he had been gainfully employed for eight years as a technical expert. Non-payment by some clients was a challenge faced by businessmen universally and unconnected to later employment. The panel found the treatment did not reach the substantially prejudicial threshold.
firac.conclusion: There was no valid objective basis for the fear; the claimant would not face a serious possibility of persecution for his Christian faith on return.

firac.issue: Were the specific incidents of abuse alleged by the claimant and his wife credible?
firac.facts: The claimant alleged a 1999 church-window smashing that cut him, a 1995 assault by a printing-factory owner, a mid-1980s car theft later seen driven by a policeman, and repeated assaults on his wife including men grabbing and squeezing her breasts and throwing garbage and water at her.
firac.rule: A claimant must establish the alleged incidents with credible and trustworthy evidence; late additions to a PIF narrative, internal inconsistencies, vagueness, and silence in objective country documentation on significant events may undermine credibility.
firac.application: The alleged church vandalism was unsupported by any human-rights documentation, which reliably reported comparable events (e.g., a Damascus synagogue vandalism in 2000), so its absence indicated the event did not occur. The factory-owner assault was a single isolated event seven years earlier with no recurrence. The car theft occurred over 15 years earlier with no link to faith. The most serious allegations concerning the wife (grabbing and squeezing) were added only at the hearing and in oral testimony, and the couple's accounts were inconsistent and vague; the panel found them to be embellishments.
firac.conclusion: The incidents were not credible or lacked probative value and did not establish a well-founded fear.

firac.issue: Did the claimant face a risk on return to Syria as a failed asylum seeker who left without authorization?
firac.facts: The claimant raised, but led no evidence on, the treatment of failed asylum seekers returned to Syria, and could not recall any such incidents.
firac.rule: Where a claimant raises a risk category, the objective country documentation and available evidence must support a serious possibility of harm; silence in recent human-rights monitoring reports may indicate the absence of serious problems.
firac.application: The claimant put forward no evidence of harm to returnees, and the documentary record was silent on the issue, which the panel took as an indication of no serious problems for those returned.
firac.conclusion: The claimant did not have a well-founded fear of persecution as a returnee leaving without authorization.

firac.issue: Did the dependent claims of the wife and children succeed?
firac.facts: The wife and two minor children based their claims entirely on the principal claimant's claim, which incorporated incidents relating to them.
firac.rule: Where dependents' claims rely wholly on the principal claimant's claim, they stand or fall with it.
firac.application: As the principal claimant's claim failed on both objective basis and credibility, the same analysis applied to the wife and children.
firac.conclusion: The dependent claims also failed; all claimants were found neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the nature of the claim under s. 96/97. K079 (persecution) is central, as the determinative issue was whether an objective, well-founded fear of persecution existed. K069 (discrimination) is engaged by the UNHCR Handbook discrimination-vs-persecution analysis. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the deciding tribunal. K025 (freedom of religion) is included because the persecution ground was the claimant's Christian faith, though it is used descriptively rather than as a Charter analysis, making it a slightly weaker pick. Credibility was central but has no dedicated vocabulary term.
location_rationale: The decision closes with "DATED at Toronto this 23rd day of October 2002," identifying Toronto as the sitting location; Ontario follows as the province in which Toronto lies.
registry_rationale: No registry is separately named, but the file prefix 'TA' and the 'DATED at Toronto' notation indicate the matter was heard and decided in the Board's Toronto office.

defining_issues: Should the appellant's proposed new documentary evidence be admitted on appeal under s. 110(4) of the IRPA?
Did the appellant establish a serious possibility of persecution by reason of his Bamileke ethnicity, including through the cumulative effect of discrimination?

firac.issue: Should the appellant's proposed new documentary evidence be admitted on appeal under s. 110(4) of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The appellant tendered nine documents on appeal, seven published after the RPD decision reporting recent events (including violence and hate speech against the Bamileke community and remarks by a government minister), and two published before the decision but said to illuminate the current context.
firac.rule: Under s. 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD may admit only evidence that arose after the RPD decision, was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected to present; if a document meets a criterion, the RAD must also assess whether it is new, credible and relevant (Canada (MCI) v. Singh, 2016 FCA 96).
firac.application: The seven post-decision documents arose after the RPD ruling and were clearly relevant to understanding the seriousness of the current situation and treatment of Bamilekes; the two earlier documents helped explain the current context in light of the others. All appeared to be from credible sources, being reports by renowned journalists and reputable organizations. An oral hearing was refused as unnecessary to assess credibility.
firac.conclusion: All nine documents were admitted as new evidence and the request for an oral hearing was denied.

firac.issue: Did the appellant establish a serious possibility of persecution by reason of his Bamileke ethnicity, including through the cumulative effect of discrimination?
firac.facts: The appellant, a Francophone Bamileke from Douala, cited three 2017-2018 incidents (an assault while travelling in an Anglophone region, an assault linked to a workplace complaint, and the burning of his daughter's Anglophone school) and pointed to escalating tensions between Bamilekes and the majority Beti group, including a minister comparing Bamilekes to Holocaust-era Jews, assaults at Sangmélima, and hate speech targeting Bamilekes.
firac.rule: A refugee claimant must establish a serious possibility of persecution; discrimination that individually appears minor may, through its cumulative effect, amount to persecution, but there must be evidence that the situation goes beyond isolated incidents.
firac.application: While the new evidence showed heightened tension and verbal and behavioural outbursts between Bamilekes and Betis, it did not establish a political climate producing discrimination or violence against Bamilekes to a significant degree; the incidents remained isolated and society had not descended into collective hatred. The cumulative-effect threshold was not met, the broader Anglophone and Boko Haram conflicts were not shown to affect Bamilekes more than other Cameroonians, and the 2017-2018 incidents disclosed no prospective ethnicity-based risk, particularly in Douala.
firac.conclusion: The appellant failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution as a Bamileke, or on a balance of probabilities a personalized risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment; the appeal was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the refugee claim framework, and K079 (persecution) is the core substantive test analysed. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the deciding tribunal (RAD). K069 (discrimination) reflects the cumulative-discrimination argument central to the persecution analysis. K061 (hate speech) is engaged because the new evidence concerned hate speech targeting the Bamileke community. Antisemitism keywords were considered given the minister's Holocaust comparison but were not selected as they are only a peripheral factual detail, not an issue in the case.

defining_issues: Did the claimants provide clear and convincing evidence rebutting the presumption of adequate state protection in Hungary?
Were the claimants credible in their allegations of persecution as Roma?
Did the harm alleged against the minor children and other family members amount to persecution or a s. 97 risk?

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption that Hungary is able to provide adequate state protection to Roma citizens?
firac.facts: The principal claimant, half Roma and half Jewish, his Hungarian common-law partner, their four children and his mother sought protection citing incidents including a 2010 Magyar Garda assault, a 2008 car arson, a 2006 car accident, and Facebook threats. In several incidents the police took reports, conducted witness interviews, the arsonist was apprehended and sentenced to 5.5 years, and investigations occurred.
firac.rule: There is a presumption that a state can protect its citizens, absent complete breakdown, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence (Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689). The onus increases with the state's degree of democracy (Kadenko). Protection need only be adequate, not perfect or effective per se; local failures do not establish overall failure (Villafranca; Zhuravlvev). The claimant must exhaust reasonable avenues of protection.
firac.application: The Board found Hungary a functioning multiparty democracy with police, courts, an Independent Police Complaints Board, Minority Ombudsman, Equal Treatment Authority, and Roma anti-discrimination legal services. In each incident authorities responded—reports taken, witness interviews conducted, the arsonist prosecuted, and the Magyar Garda dissolved by the courts. The claimants failed to pursue available recourse and did not take reasonable steps to seek protection. Despite acknowledged imperfections and police corruption, the preponderance of objective evidence showed adequate, serious state efforts.
firac.conclusion: The claimants did not rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence; adequate state protection is available in Hungary.

firac.issue: Were the claimants credible in their allegations of persecution based on Roma ethnicity?
firac.facts: The principal claimant gave inconsistent accounts about returning to police after the 2010 assault, the reason for the 2006 investigation, and whether perpetrators knew he was Roma. He acknowledged not resembling a Roma. He maintained an active Facebook account despite alleged threats and initially had no security settings.
firac.rule: Sworn testimony is presumed true unless there is reason to doubt it (Maldonado, (1994) 23 Imm. L.R. (2d)). Contradictions, omissions and implausibilities can rebut that presumption.
firac.application: The Board found contradictions between testimony and the amended PIF and corroborative evidence regarding the 2010 police contact, concluding he embellished his claim. It found it implausible that racial slurs identified him as Roma while driving. The maintenance of an unsecured Facebook account contradicted his claimed fear. These undermined the ethnicity-based fear, and the wife (ethnic Hungarian) and mother added little substantive support.
firac.conclusion: The Board drew adverse credibility findings and concluded the ethnicity-based fears were not substantiated.

firac.issue: Did the alleged harm to the minor children and other family members amount to persecution or a s. 97 risk?
firac.facts: The claimants feared future discrimination against their children; son XXXX XXXX was traumatized in the 2010 assault but no psychological evidence was filed for him. The mother alleged discrimination and being pushed off a bus but gave scant detail. The wife is ethnic Hungarian.
firac.rule: Fears must be more than speculative; an isolated incident, absent corroboration, does not constitute persecution. Sections 96 and 97 IRPA require a well-founded fear or risk, and the state protection presumption applies to each claimant.
firac.application: The children's fears were largely future and speculative; the one 2010 incident affecting the son, without psychological corroboration, did not amount to persecution. The mother provided insufficient evidence and did not rebut state protection. The wife's claim rested on her husband's allegations, which failed.
firac.conclusion: None of the family members established persecution or a s. 97 risk; all claims failed on state protection and evidentiary grounds.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K080 (state protection) is the determinative legal issue—the availability and adequacy of Hungarian state protection under Ward. K079 (persecution) and K078 (refugee protection) capture the ss. 96/97 claim based on Roma ethnicity. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the deciding tribunal (RPD). K081 (stay of removal) is a weaker/borderline pick—no stay was actually sought—but it is the closest available removal-related term; the case is better characterized by refugee determination rather than removal, so it is flagged as marginal. Credibility, the other determinative issue, has no dedicated vocabulary keyword, so it is captured through the persecution and refugee-protection terms.

registry_rationale: The Refugee Protection Division heard the matter in Toronto, Ontario, as indicated in the 'Place of Hearing' field; the RPD registry is Toronto.

case_name: R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.

defining_issues: Does an accused corporation have standing to challenge the Lord's Day Act as violating the s. 2(a) guarantee of freedom of conscience and religion?
Does the Lord's Day Act infringe the freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed by s. 2(a) of the Charter, and is constitutionality to be assessed by the legislation's purpose or its effect?
If the Act limits freedom of religion, is it a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
Was the Lord's Day Act validly enacted under the federal criminal law power in s. 91(27) of the Constitution Act, 1867?

firac.issue: May a corporation defend a criminal charge by arguing that the Lord's Day Act violates freedom of conscience and religion, even though a corporation cannot itself hold religious belief?
firac.facts: Big M Drug Mart Ltd., a corporation, was charged under s. 4 of the Lord's Day Act for selling goods on a Sunday. The Attorney General for Alberta argued a corporation cannot claim s. 2(a) rights and that the Provincial Court lacked jurisdiction to declare the Act invalid.
firac.rule: Section 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 makes the Constitution supreme, so no one can be convicted under an unconstitutional law. Standing to challenge the validity of a law under which one is prosecuted is the same whether the challenge rests on ss. 91–92 of the Constitution Act, 1867 or the Charter. Recourse to the s. 24(1) remedy is unnecessary where the attack is on the constitutionality of the legislation itself.
firac.application: Big M did not come to court as a public-interest litigant seeking a prerogative declaration; it was compelled to defend a prosecution and sought only dismissal of the charges. Whether a corporation can hold religious belief is irrelevant: it is the nature of the impugned law, not the status of the accused, that is in issue. A law that itself infringes religious freedom is inconsistent with s. 2(a) regardless of whether the accused is Christian, non-believer, individual or corporation. Provincial courts have always been able to hold legislation invalid in criminal cases.
firac.conclusion: Big M had standing and the Provincial Court had jurisdiction; any accused may raise the constitutional invalidity of the law under which it is charged.

firac.issue: Does the Lord's Day Act infringe s. 2(a), and is constitutionality tested by legislative purpose or effect?
firac.facts: The Lord's Day Act, whose historic and consistently recognized purpose is to compel observance of the Christian Sabbath, prohibits work and commercial activity on Sunday under penal sanction. Non-Christians and those observing other days of rest are thereby compelled to conform to a Christian religious observance.
firac.rule: Freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) means, at minimum, that government may not coerce individuals to affirm a religious belief or manifest a religious practice for a sectarian purpose; freedom is characterized by absence of coercion, including indirect coercion (Hunter v. Southam purposive approach). Constitutionality is assessed first by legislative purpose; effects need only be considered if the purpose is valid. Purpose is fixed at enactment and does not shift with changing social conditions; the 'shifting purpose' argument is rejected. Robertson and Rosetanni (Canadian Bill of Rights) is distinguishable because it concerned application, not constitutional validity, of the legislation.
firac.application: The acknowledged purpose of the Act is compulsion of sabbatical observance, a religious purpose. Binding all to a sectarian Christian ideal works a coercion inimical to the Charter and gives the appearance of discrimination against non-Christians; the protection of one religion with concomitant non-protection of others produces disparate impact destructive of religious freedom, contrary also to the multicultural interpretive guide in s. 27. Since the purpose offends s. 2(a), it is unnecessary to weigh the Act's secular effects; legislation with an invalid purpose cannot be saved by inoffensive effects. (Wilson J. would begin with effect rather than purpose, but reached the same result.)
firac.conclusion: The Lord's Day Act, especially s. 4, infringes s. 2(a) of the Charter.

firac.issue: Is the infringement a reasonable limit demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society under s. 1?
firac.facts: The Attorneys General argued that public convenience and the value of a uniform day of rest justified the Act, citing a UN study and comparable legislation in Britain, Australia and New Zealand.
firac.rule: Section 1 requires the government objective to be sufficiently important to override a Charter right and the means to be reasonable and proportionate (impairing the right as little as possible). Parliament cannot rely on an ultra vires or colourable purpose to justify a limit under s. 1 (cf. Quebec Association of Protestant School Boards).
firac.application: The secular 'uniform day of rest' objective was never found to be the legislation's purpose; the Act's pith and substance is the compulsion of a Christian religious duty. Parliament cannot assert a secular objective under s. 1 to validate legislation that in substance compels religious observance, as this would permit doing indirectly what it cannot do directly and would legitimize curtailing religious freedom for the very purpose of curtailing it.
firac.conclusion: The Act is not justified under s. 1; the infringement cannot be saved.

firac.issue: Was the Lord's Day Act validly enacted under the federal criminal law power in s. 91(27)?
firac.facts: The Act compels observance of the Christian Sabbath through prohibitions backed by summary-conviction penalties. All five Alberta Court of Appeal judges, and both parties before the SCC, treated it as criminal legislation.
firac.rule: Legislation compelling a religious obligation by prohibition and penalty is directed to maintenance of public order and safeguarding public morality, an 'ordinary end' of the criminal law (Reference re Dairy Industry Act; Hamilton Street Railway).
firac.application: Because the Act's purpose is compelling Sunday observance for its religious significance under penal sanction, it is aimed at safeguarding public morality and falls within s. 91(27). Had its purpose been the secular goal of a uniform day of rest, it would have fallen under provincial jurisdiction (s. 92(13)).
firac.conclusion: The Act was validly enacted under the criminal law power, but is nonetheless of no force or effect for violating s. 2(a).

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 practice area. K025 (freedom of religion) and K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) are the core of the decision — the Act's compulsion of Sabbath observance. K030 (reasonable limits, s. 1) covers the s. 1 justification analysis. K107 (Canadian Charter) and K121 (s. 27 multiculturalism) reflect the interpretive materials expressly relied on by Dickson J. K004 (Criminal law) is engaged because the Act was upheld as valid under the s. 91(27) criminal law power. K011 (judicial review) is a weaker/borderline pick, included to capture the constitutional-invalidity challenge and standing/jurisdiction discussion, though the case is not a classic administrative-law judicial review.
location_rationale: The Supreme Court of Canada does not state a sitting city in the text. The decision is 'on appeal from the court of appeal for alberta', and the prosecution arose in Calgary, Alberta, so the province of origin is Alberta; the SCC's own seat (Ottawa) is not stated in the judgment.
registry_rationale: No court registry is identified in the decision; the SCC file number (18125) is given but no registry office, so registry is left null.

case_name: Committee for the Commonwealth of Canada v. Canada

name_verification.name_in_document: Committee for the Commonwealth of Canada v. Canada

defining_issues: Does the government's proprietary ownership of airport property give it an unlimited right to prohibit expressive activity on that property, or does freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter extend to expression on some government property?

Did the airport officials' order that the respondents cease distributing political pamphlets and soliciting members infringe the respondents' freedom of expression guaranteed by s. 2(b) of the Charter?

Do ss. 7(a) and 7(b) of the Government Airport Concession Operations Regulations apply to the respondents' political activities, and if the infringement flowed from those provisions or from an internal policy, was the limit 'prescribed by law' and justifiable under s. 1 of the Charter?

firac.issue: Does the government's ownership of airport property confer an unlimited right to control expression, or does s. 2(b) protect expression on some government property?
firac.facts: The respondents attempted to promote the Committee for the Commonwealth of Canada and recruit members inside Dorval airport, a federally owned property, when they were ordered to stop. The Crown argued that as owner it had the same exclusive rights as any private owner to control activity on its property.
firac.rule: Freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter cannot be defeated merely by the government's proprietary rights, given the 'quasi-fiduciary' nature of government ownership (Hague v. Committee for Industrial Organization). Government property is held for the benefit of citizens, not for the state's own private benefit. The Court divided on the precise test: Lamer C.J. proposed a 'compatibility with the function of the place' test at the s. 2(b) stage; L'Heureux-Dubé J. would treat nearly all expression on public property as protected with balancing under s. 1; McLachlin J. proposed a values-based test drawn from Irwin Toy asking whether the expression in the forum promotes the purposes underlying free expression.
firac.application: All members of the Court rejected the Crown's absolutist property argument. The special nature of government ownership means it cannot alone authorize an infringement of s. 2(b). Freedom of expression necessarily requires physical space; confining it to places owned by the speaker would deny its foundation. However, the Court agreed that s. 2(b) does not extend to all government property (e.g., private offices, control towers, prison cells, judges' chambers). Airport public areas, being modern thoroughfares with large and varied audiences, are appropriate forums for expression.
firac.conclusion: The government's ownership does not authorize unlimited control of expression; expressive activity in the public areas of an airport falls within the protection of s. 2(b) of the Charter.

firac.issue: Did ordering the respondents to cease distributing pamphlets and soliciting members infringe their s. 2(b) freedom of expression?
firac.facts: On March 22, 1984, respondents Lépine and Deland peacefully approached travellers at Dorval airport to discuss the Committee's political aims and recruit members, distributing leaflets and magazines. An RCMP officer and the assistant airport manager ordered them to stop, relying on a policy prohibiting political propaganda activities.
firac.rule: Under Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (Attorney General), any activity that conveys or attempts to convey meaning has expressive content and prima facie falls within s. 2(b), unless it takes a proscribed form such as violence. Content of the message is irrelevant to whether s. 2(b) is engaged.
firac.application: The respondents' conduct clearly conveyed a political message and took a peaceful form. The distribution of pamphlets and discussion with the public were in no way incompatible with the airport's primary function of accommodating the travelling public, which as a thoroughfare with open and waiting areas can readily accommodate expression. The order to cease these activities limited the respondents' freedom of expression.
firac.conclusion: The respondents' freedom of expression under s. 2(b) was infringed by the airport manager's order to cease their activities.

firac.issue: Did ss. 7(a) and 7(b) of the Regulations apply, and was the limit 'prescribed by law' and justifiable under s. 1?
firac.facts: Section 7 of the Government Airport Concession Operations Regulations prohibited conducting 'any business or undertaking, commercial or otherwise' and 'advertising or soliciting' at an airport except as authorized in writing by the Minister. The airport officials relied on an established internal policy prohibiting political propaganda.
firac.rule: A limit must be 'prescribed by law' to be justified under s. 1 (R. v. Therens; R. v. Thomsen). Legislation open to more than one interpretation should be read consistently with the Charter (Slaight Communications; presumption of constitutionality). A limit that is unduly vague or overbroad cannot be a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 (R. v. Oakes; R. v. Edwards Books). The Court fractured on both the interpretation of s. 7 and the s. 1 analysis.
firac.application: Lamer C.J. (with Sopinka J.), applying statutory interpretation and the presumption of constitutionality, held that s. 7 covers only commercial activity and does not reach political propaganda; the limit therefore flowed from an unpublished internal policy, which is not a 'law' capable of s. 1 justification. La Forest J. held s. 7 did not apply, but the officials exercised the Crown's legal right to manage its property, so the limit was prescribed by law though not justified. L'Heureux-Dubé J. and McLachlin J. held that 'advertise' and 'solicit' in s. 7(b) were broad enough to catch the respondents' non-commercial conduct; the Regulation was a limit prescribed by law but was fatally vague and overbroad, failing the s. 1 minimal impairment and proportionality analysis. Either way, no valid justification under s. 1 was established, as the blanket exclusion of political activity bore no rational connection to any legitimate airport-related objective.
firac.conclusion: The limitation on the respondents' expression could not be justified under s. 1, whether because it did not arise from a 'law' or because the Regulation was too vague and overbroad; the appeal was dismissed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Amram Elkayam v. Attorney General of Canada

defining_issues: Was the Canadian Human Rights Commission's decision under paragraph 44(3)(b) of the Canadian Human Rights Act to dismiss the complaint reasonable and supportable on the evidence before it?
Did the time the Commission took to process and dismiss the complaint amount to an unreasonable administrative delay warranting the Court's intervention?

firac.issue: Was the Commission's decision to dismiss the complaint under paragraph 44(3)(b) of the CHRA supportable on the evidence?
firac.facts: Elkayam, a Jewish electrician working on contract for the Department of National Defence at the Longue Pointe Base, complained of discrimination on account of religion and age, harassment (including two 'Heil Hitler' remarks by a colleague), unequal treatment in contract renewals, and reprisals. Three investigation reports (June 2001, August 2001, February 2003) found the Department had reprimanded the offending employee, distributed its harassment policy, held a sensitivity meeting, and implemented procedural changes; the evidence indicated the applicant was competent but had difficulty working in a team. The Commission dismissed the complaint on the ground that the additional evidence did not support the allegations and that the Department had done everything possible to resolve the matter.
firac.rule: Under s. 44(3)(b)(i) of the Canadian Human Rights Act the Commission dismisses a complaint where, having regard to all the circumstances, an inquiry is not warranted. The Commission's role is a screening function assessing the sufficiency of the evidence, not adjudication (Cooper v. Canada (CHRC), [1996] 3 S.C.R. 854; Syndicat des employés de production du Québec et de l'Acadie, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 879). The Commission enjoys a remarkable degree of latitude (Bell Canada, [1999] 1 F.C. 113 (C.A.)) and its dismissal attracts a high level of deference, subject to review only for breach of natural justice or where the decision is not supportable on the evidence (Bourgeois v. CIBC; Murray v. Canada (CHRC)).
firac.application: The applicant alleged no breach of procedural fairness and did not argue the investigation was defective under Slattery. He offered no evidence for his claims that the investigators were manipulated or that the Commission acted at the Department's behest. On the merits, the three reports showed the Commission considered the Textus report, the anti-Semitic incident, the reprisals and the contract-award issues, and reasonably concluded the evidence was insufficient to convene a tribunal. The applicant was in substance asking the Court to reweigh the evidence, which it cannot do given the deference owed.
firac.conclusion: The Commission's decision was supportable on the evidence; the applicant's allegations were without merit or unsupported.

firac.issue: Did the Commission's processing time constitute an unreasonable administrative delay?
firac.facts: The applicant said he filed his complaint in early January 2000 and that the Commission took roughly three and a half years to dismiss it in May 2003. He signed the formal complaint form on May 15, 2000, after working with Commission officers to clarify it, and the file involved multiple investigation reports, a conciliation attempt, and examination of numerous witnesses.
firac.rule: Administrative delay may in some circumstances constitute an abuse of process, but must be assessed against all the circumstances (Blencoe v. British Columbia (Human Rights Commission), [2000] 2 S.C.R. 307). Court intervention at the screening stage will not rectify prejudice caused by delay in the investigation (Murray v. Canada (CHRC)).
firac.application: The complaint was not signed until May 15, 2000, not early January. The elapsed time was explained by the applicant's own clarification work, attempts at mediation and conciliation, and the Commission's justified desire to complete a thorough investigation involving numerous witnesses at various stages. Taking all circumstances into account, the delay was not unreasonable.
firac.conclusion: There was no unreasonable administrative delay warranting the Court's intervention.

case_name: Pressler v. Lethbridge and Westcom TV Group Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: Pressler v. Lethbridge and Westcom TV Group Ltd.
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The metadata name and citation match the style of cause and neutral citation printed in the decision. One internal inconsistency worth flagging: the style of cause names the male plaintiff 'CLIVE PRESSLER', while the body of the reasons repeatedly refers to him as 'Claus Pressler' — an internal spelling discrepancy in the judgment, not a mismatch with the supplied metadata.

defining_issues: Was the television broadcast defamatory of the plaintiffs?
Is Dr. Lethbridge liable for the defamatory sting of the whole broadcast when only edited portions of his interview were aired?
Can the defendants defeat the claim through the defences of qualified privilege and fair comment?
Were the compensatory damages properly assessed?
Should punitive damages be awarded against Dr. Lethbridge on the plaintiffs' cross-appeal?

firac.issue: Was the television broadcast defamatory of the plaintiffs?
firac.facts: A CHBC/Westcom broadcast about the Presslers' newly constructed rural property near Salmon Arm juxtaposed images, rumours and interview clips to suggest the Presslers were building a fortified compound with underground bunkers, perimeter fences, its own telecommunications, and a possible paramilitary training ground, and were deceiving municipal officials, rather than building a retirement home and honey farm. The trial judge found these imputations false and defamatory, though the portrayal of Mrs. Pressler as a racist and anti-Semite was true.
firac.rule: A trial judge in a defamation action first asks whether the publication is capable of a defamatory meaning (a question of law) and then whether it was in fact defamatory — i.e., whether it held the plaintiffs up to hatred, ridicule and contempt (the jury question). A television broadcast must be taken as a whole: words and images cannot be artificially separated (disagreeing with the Ontario CA approach in Colour Your World Corp. v. CBC).
firac.application: The Court held the broadcast was capable of a defamatory meaning and found no reversible error in the trial judge's conclusion that it was defamatory. Right-thinking Canadians view paramilitary activity with contempt, and accusing someone of cheating municipal land-use rules holds them up to odium. The appellate court is not free to interfere with the 'jury question' findings absent error, and Westcom's argument that words alone should govern was rejected: the publication must be read whole, so that images and words together carried the defamatory sting.
firac.conclusion: The broadcast was defamatory; the trial judge's finding stands.

firac.issue: Is Dr. Lethbridge liable for the defamatory sting of the whole broadcast when only edited excerpts of his interview were aired?
firac.facts: Dr. Lethbridge gave a recorded interview to Westcom's reporter Gaffney, in which he repeated construction 'rumours' (bunkers, telecommunications, paramilitary training) while claiming not to believe them. Westcom broadcast only selected excerpts. His counsel argued his broadcast words alone were not defamatory and he could not be liable for Westcom's juxtaposition.
firac.rule: Publication is the essence of defamation. A person who communicates defamatory material to a reporter is deemed to have authorized its publication and is liable as though he published it himself (Douglas v. Tucker, [1952] 1 S.C.R. 275; Hay v. Bingham; R. v. Cooper (1846); Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada). An interviewee is liable for a broadcast where, by his antecedent dealings, he authorized publication of its substance and sting and the broadcaster published that substance and sting.
firac.application: The Court compared the interview transcript with the broadcast and found the sting and substance of Dr. Lethbridge's remarks and of the broadcast were the same — the broadcast reflected him fairly. Having disclaimed belief in paramilitary intentions, he nonetheless repeated the false construction rumours; saying 'there are rumours but I do not believe them' is capable of a defamatory meaning where the rumour's sting exposes the subject to odium. There was ample evidence he impliedly, if not expressly, authorized publication; the pleadings alleged he 'conspired' with Westcom and Mrs. Pressler was quoted calling him the source of the rumours.
firac.conclusion: Dr. Lethbridge is liable for the defamatory broadcast; his liability appeal fails.

firac.issue: Can the defendants defeat the claim on the defences of qualified privilege and fair comment?
firac.facts: Lethbridge pleaded qualified privilege and fair comment (without proper particulars); Westcom pleaded qualified privilege grounded in the public importance of the subject and its role as a news broadcaster. The trial judge found an occasion of qualified privilege but held it, and fair comment, defeated by express malice on the part of both defendants.
firac.rule: Qualified privilege requires a legal, social or moral duty to publish to persons with a corresponding interest to receive it (Blackshaw v. Lord; Globe and Mail Ltd. v. Boland — a journalist's privilege is 'no other and no higher' than any subject's). Fair comment requires that the underlying facts be true; a rumour that is untrue cannot support the defence (Speidel v. Plato Films). Malice defeats qualified privilege where an improper motive is dominant (Horrocks v. Lowe).
firac.application: Southin J.A. held there was no occasion of qualified privilege: a citizen's right of free speech gives no duty or right to ruin the reputations of persons holding objectionable opinions; the true 'story' lay only in the false imputations about the buildings. Fair comment failed because rumours are not facts and the false construction imputations were untrue; only the imputation that Mrs. Pressler was anti-Semitic and racist was true and fair comment. Esson J.A. would have upheld a qualified-privilege occasion for Westcom on the ground of interest but agreed it was vitiated by express malice (Westcom deliberately edited and juxtaposed material to create misleading impressions — akin to Vogel v. C.B.C.), and agreed no privilege arose for Lethbridge.
firac.conclusion: The defences fail; the defendants remain liable.

firac.issue: Were the compensatory damages properly assessed?
firac.facts: The trial judge awarded Mrs. Pressler $10,000 against Westcom and $1,500 against Lethbridge, and Mr. Pressler $50,000 against Westcom and $10,000 against Lethbridge, taking into account harm to Mr. Pressler's pharmacy career. The appellants argued the awards ignored the plaintiffs' pre-existing reputation for extremist views and improperly compensated business loss the plaintiffs said they were not claiming.
firac.rule: Damages must bear some relation to the plaintiff's actual reputation in the relevant sector of life (Neeld v. Western Broadcasting; Speidel v. Plato Films). Compensatory damages in defamation include insult and pain, vindication, injury to pride, and possible economic damage that cannot be expressly proven, particularly in mass-media defamation (Brown v. Cole).
firac.application: The relevant reputation was in land-use/citizenship, not the plaintiffs' unpopular opinions; there was no evidence they had a reputation for flouting land-use laws, so ordinarily that opinion-based reputation would be irrelevant. However, the plaintiffs put their reputations in issue by their broad pleading and had to bear the consequence. The Court was not persuaded the trial judge gave insufficient weight to his findings; assessing defamation damages is not a science. As to Mr. Pressler's pharmacy losses, Lethbridge's avowed aim was to destroy the business, and economic damage that cannot be expressly proven is a permissible component.
firac.conclusion: No error in the damages assessment; the awards stand and the damages appeals are dismissed.

firac.issue: Should punitive damages be awarded against Dr. Lethbridge on the plaintiffs' cross-appeal?
firac.facts: Dr. Lethbridge's avowed aim was to drive the Pressler family from Salmon Arm by destroying the pharmacy business; he orchestrated hate calls and a demonstration and repeated the false rumours after the broadcast. The trial judge declined to award punitive damages against either defendant.
firac.rule: A proper purpose of punitive damages is to warn off others who assert that ends justify means or who take the law into their own hands; malice and high-handed conduct may attract them (Cassell & Co. v. Broome).
firac.application: As to Westcom, the Court found no profit motive and that the reporter was blinded by Mrs. Pressler's opinions, so it declined to interfere with the refusal. As to Dr. Lethbridge, no private citizen has the right to drive anyone out of a community; if Mrs. Pressler committed a crime, prosecution is for the Attorney General. His laudable anti-racism aim did not justify his means — 'a lynch mob is still a lynch mob even if the person lynched committed the crime.' The Court could not understand why no punitive award was made against him and fixed $15,000 as sufficient.
firac.conclusion: Cross-appeal allowed to the extent of awarding $15,000 punitive damages against Dr. Lethbridge; otherwise the cross-appeal (including against Westcom) is dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a tort action in defamation. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. K016 (fair comment) and K018 (qualified privilege) are the two pleaded defences the Court analysed and rejected as unavailable/defeated by malice. K024 (freedom of expression) reflects the free-speech tension running through the reasons and the s. 2(b) Charter plea; K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) is included because Westcom expressly pleaded s. 2(b) though a pre-trial motion left the case to be decided on the common law — a borderline/weak pick since it was not ultimately decisive. K058 (antisemitism), K061 (hate speech / 'hate literature') and K062 (Holocaust denial / revisionism) are genuinely engaged: the plaintiffs' anti-Semitic and Holocaust-revisionist activities, and 'literature on the border of hate literature,' are central factual context bearing on truth, fair comment and reputation. I did not select group defamation (K017) as the claim was individual, not collective.
