name_verification.name_in_document: Richard Warman v. Jessica Beaumont

defining_issues: Did Beaumont communicate or cause to be communicated the impugned messages by means of the Internet within the meaning of s. 13 of the Canadian Human Rights Act?
Were the communications made 'repeatedly' within the meaning of s. 13?
Was the material likely to expose members of the targeted groups to hatred or contempt on the basis of a prohibited ground of discrimination under s. 13(1)?
What remedies should follow — a cease and desist order, special compensation, and a penalty?

firac.issue: Did Beaumont communicate or cause to be communicated the impugned messages via the Internet within s. 13?
firac.facts: Beaumont admitted posting on the Stormfront.org forum under the pseudonym 'Jessy Destruction,' with over 1,000 posts by May 2006. She acknowledged posting nearly all of the impugned messages except Messages 2 and 3, which she did not recall.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) requires that a person communicate or cause to be communicated, repeatedly, by telecommunication facilities, matter likely to expose persons to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground; s. 13(2) confirms s. 13(1) applies to Internet communications.
firac.application: Beaumont conceded authorship of almost all messages. For Messages 2 and 3, the identical margin notes and signature blocks, the consistency of the views expressed, and her failure to delete them supported an inference on the balance of probabilities that she posted them too.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal was satisfied Beaumont communicated all the impugned messages by means of the Internet within the meaning of s. 13.

firac.issue: Were the communications made 'repeatedly' within s. 13?
firac.facts: The messages were posted on publicly accessible Internet forums (Stormfront.org and BloodandHonour.com) requiring no password or pre-registration to view. Beaumont's agent argued each posting was a discrete private conversation among like-minded individuals, analogous to personal telephone calls in Taylor.
firac.rule: Material communicated via the Internet is, by that medium's characteristics, a repeated communication where no obstacles prevent access (Warman v. Harrison; Warman v. Kulbashian; Warman v. Tremaine). Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892 distinguished private personal telephone calls.
firac.application: Postings on an open message board are available to anyone on the Internet, not just friends. Beaumont herself understood the distinction between public posting and private messaging, having invited others to 'PM' her, and stated she posted material 'for other people to read.' The public circulation of her messages was not equivalent to private telephone calls among acquaintances.
firac.conclusion: The material was communicated repeatedly within the meaning of s. 13.

firac.issue: Was the material likely to expose the targeted groups to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground?
firac.facts: The postings used derogatory epithets ('nigger,' 'chink,' 'chug,' 'fags'), described Jews as 'spawn of Satan' and 'dirty Jewish animals,' called for AIDS to 'die off' targeted persons, promoted segregation and all-white schools/neighbourhoods, and blamed Jews as a controlling menace, targeting groups by race, religion, national/ethnic origin and sexual orientation.
firac.rule: 'Hatred' means extreme ill will and 'contempt' means treating as inferior (Nealy v. Johnson); 'likely' does not require proof anyone was actually victimized; the terms refer to unusually strong emotions of detestation, calumny and vilification (Taylor). Recurring hallmarks include epithets, animal comparisons, blaming the group for society's problems, portraying the group as a menace, and advocating segregation/deportation (Kouba, Kulbashian, Nealy). Intent is not required (Taylor).
firac.application: Most messages used inflammatory epithets in hostile contexts, compared Jews to vermin/animals, depicted Jews as a controlling menace, blamed non-whites for crime and social decay, and advocated racial segregation via the '16 Facts' and 'Bill of Racial Rights.' The Tribunal excepted certain items (e.g. the Norman Rockwell description and uses of 'retarded' as a synonym for 'absurd') where context did not expose groups to hatred, but found the bulk of the material offended s. 13.
firac.conclusion: Most of the impugned messages were likely to expose the targeted groups to hatred or contempt; the complaint was substantiated.

firac.issue: What remedies should follow?
firac.facts: Warman sought a permanent cease and desist order, $10,000 special compensation and a $7,500 penalty. Beaumont referenced Warman as 'that retarded jew,' 'disgraceful animal,' posted a doctored 'Dead Warman Society' image with swastikas, and quoted a message calling him a 'kyke.' She was 21, living with parents, earning $10.50/hour, with no proven prior discriminatory practice.
firac.rule: Section 54(1)(a) permits a cease and desist order; s. 54(1)(b) permits special compensation up to $20,000 where a victim is specifically identified and the respondent acted wilfully or recklessly; s. 54(1)(c) and 54(1.1) permit a penalty up to $10,000, assessed on the nature/gravity of the practice, wilfulness, prior practices, and ability to pay. Perceived membership in a protected group suffices (Jubran; Quebec v. Montreal (City)).
firac.application: A cease and desist order merely reiterates the statute and poses no unfair peril, so it was granted. Warman, though perceived as Jewish, was specifically identified and targeted wilfully via hate messages, warranting special compensation; s. 54(1)(b)/53(3) do not distinguish types of victim. However the messages were less grave than in other cases — shorter, less frequent epithets, no vivid violence, no dedicated hate website — and she had limited means and no proven prior practice, reducing the penalty.
firac.conclusion: A permanent cease and desist order was issued; $3,000 special compensation and a $1,500 penalty (payable within 120 days) were ordered.

case_name: Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Canadian Liberty Net

name_verification.name_in_document: Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Canadian Liberty Net

defining_issues: Does the Federal Court have jurisdiction, under s. 44 of the Federal Court Act, to issue an interlocutory injunction in support of the prohibitions in the Canadian Human Rights Act pending a human rights tribunal's final determination?
Was it appropriate to apply the American Cyanamid test in deciding whether to grant an injunction restraining pure (hate) speech?

Can a party who violates an injunction be held in contempt of court by asserting that the granting court lacked jurisdiction, or wrongly exercised jurisdiction, or that the impugned conduct occurred outside Canada?

firac.issue: Does the Federal Court have jurisdiction under s. 44 of the Federal Court Act to issue an interlocutory injunction in support of the Canadian Human Rights Act while a tribunal's decision on the merits is pending?
firac.facts: The Canadian Human Rights Commission, having referred telephone hate-message complaints to a tribunal under s. 13(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act, applied to the Federal Court, Trial Division for an injunction restraining Canadian Liberty Net and Tony McAleer from making such messages available until the tribunal rendered its final order. Muldoon J. granted the injunction; the Federal Court of Appeal set it aside for want of jurisdiction.
firac.rule: The three-part jurisdictional test from ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc., [1986] 1 S.C.R. 752 requires a statutory grant of jurisdiction, an existing body of federal law nourishing that grant, and a valid 'law of Canada' under s. 101 of the Constitution Act, 1867. Section 44 of the Federal Court Act permits injunctions 'in addition to any other relief.' Inherent jurisdiction (a feature of provincial superior courts, not the statutory Federal Court) is residual and does not justify reading federal jurisdiction-granting statutes narrowly (Roberts v. Canada; Board v. Board; Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way Employees v. Canadian Pacific).
firac.application: The majority (Bastarache J., L'Heureux-Dubé and Gonthier JJ.) held s. 44 is a power-conferring provision, not merely a limitation clause. Read with s. 3 (Federal Court as a superior court of record) and its extensive supervisory powers over federal tribunals (ss. 18, 18.1, and Human Rights Act ss. 57–58), the Federal Court has plenary jurisdiction over interim measures related to the control of administrative decision-makers; these supervisory powers constitute 'other relief' for s. 44 purposes. The doctrine of inherent jurisdiction does not require narrowing federal grants; jurisdiction is concurrent with the provincial superior court's inherent jurisdiction (Idziak; Pringle v. Fraser require 'clear and direct' language to oust s. 96 court jurisdiction). Federal law (s. 13(1)) nourishes the grant. However, the Court rejected any implied grant in the Human Rights Act itself, since an injunctive power is not a necessary incident of the tribunal's functions (New Brunswick Electric Power). The dissent (McLachlin and Major JJ.) held s. 44's opening words are ancillary, requiring pre-existing jurisdiction the Federal Court lacked, so no jurisdiction existed.
firac.conclusion: By majority, the Federal Court had jurisdiction under s. 44 to issue the injunction; the appeal on jurisdiction was allowed (McLachlin and Major JJ. dissenting). The issue was ultimately moot because the tribunal had rendered its final order.

firac.issue: Was the American Cyanamid three-stage injunction test the appropriate test for granting an injunction restraining pure (non-commercial) speech such as alleged hate speech?
firac.facts: The injunction sought would restrain telephone messages alleged to expose persons to hatred or contempt under s. 13(1). The speech had no commercial element; the speaker's only interest was expression itself, engaging s. 2(b) of the Charter.
firac.rule: American Cyanamid Co. v. Ethicon Ltd. (serious question, irreparable harm, balance of convenience), as adopted in Metropolitan Stores and RJR-MacDonald. Jurisprudence on injunctions against defamatory speech (Rapp v. McClelland & Stewart; Herbage v. Pressdram; Champagne v. CEGEP de Jonquière) requires that injunctions restraining speech issue only in the rarest and clearest cases where the words are manifestly unlawful and impossible to justify.
firac.application: The Cyanamid test developed in a commercial context where 'balance of convenience' and 'irreparable harm' are measurable; applied to pure speech it stacks the deck against the non-commercial speaker, who has no tangible interest other than the expression, thereby undermining s. 2(b). The defamation analogy is closer and shows Cyanamid is displaced for restraint of speech. The constitutionality of s. 13(1) in Taylor was predicated on the absence of such interlocutory remedies, so any test must be mindful of freedom of expression. Because the tribunal had already ruled, the injunction appeal was moot on this point and the Court declined to fix the precise test.
firac.conclusion: The Cyanamid test is inappropriate for cases of pure speech; a stricter approach modelled on defamation-injunction principles applies, but the point was moot and left for another day.

firac.issue: Can persons who breach an injunction escape a contempt finding by arguing the granting court lacked or wrongly exercised jurisdiction, or that the offending conduct occurred outside Canada?
firac.facts: After the injunction, a Commission investigator found the Liberty Net line advertised a new U.S. (Washington State) number carrying messages proscribed by the order. Liberty Net argued the messages emanated from outside Canada and that the injunction was void for want of jurisdiction. Teitelbaum J. found them in contempt; the Federal Court of Appeal affirmed.
firac.rule: A court order stands and must be obeyed until set aside by legal process; its ultimate invalidity is no defence to contempt (Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor, per McLachlin J.). For territorial jurisdiction, Canadian courts have jurisdiction where a 'real and substantial link'—a significant portion of the activity—occurs in Canada (Libman v. The Queen).
firac.application: Since the Federal Court had jurisdiction to make the order, at most it was wrongly exercised; such an order is neither void nor nugatory, and breach is contempt. Even the dissent, having found no jurisdiction, agreed the contempt conviction stood. On territoriality, the gravamen was communication of the offending messages, effected by the advertisement placed in Canada on the old Liberty Net line referring callers to the U.S. number, done with knowledge of the content and of the order. A significant portion of the activity thus occurred in Canada, satisfying Libman.
firac.conclusion: The contempt finding was upheld; the contempt appeal was dismissed unanimously.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally about the Federal Court's jurisdiction to grant an injunction in the administrative-law context, so Administrative law (K001) is the primary practice area, with judicial review/supervisory jurisdiction (K011) and interpretive standard (K014) engaged. Interlocutory injunction (K021) is the central remedy. The subject matter of the injunction was telephone hate messages under s. 13(1) CHRA, so hate speech (K061), Holocaust denial (K062, given the Holocaust-denial content), CHRA s. 13 (K113), and freedom of expression under s. 2(b) (K024) all apply directly. Human rights (K007) is engaged as the underlying statutory framework, and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (K107) because s. 2(b) framed the injunction analysis. K014 (standard of review) is a slightly weak pick—the case concerns statutory interpretation of jurisdiction rather than reasonableness review—so it is borderline; K011 is included as the supervisory/judicial-review jurisdiction was central to the s. 44 reasoning.

name_verification.discrepancy_note: The case name matches, but the supplied citation (2021 BCSC 512) does not match the citation printed in the decision, which is 2021 BCSC 226 (the header and para. of the decision consistently show 'Beaudoin v. British Columbia, 2021 BCSC 226', dated 20210210).

defining_issues: Should ARPA Canada be granted leave to intervene in a Charter challenge to COVID-19 public health orders restricting religious gatherings, and if so on what terms?

Can an intervention application be decided before the parties' substantive written submissions are filed, where the proposed intervenor's usefulness (non-duplicative, non-'hijacking' perspective) cannot yet be assessed?

firac.issue: Should ARPA Canada be granted intervenor status in the petition challenging the provincial COVID-19 orders restricting religious gatherings?
firac.facts: ARPA Canada, a non-profit organization representing Canada's Reformed Christian community, sought leave to intervene in a petition brought by individuals and churches challenging Ministerial and Provincial Health Officer orders restricting religious gatherings as unjustifiable Charter infringements. ARPA claimed no direct interest but asserted a unique perspective on the essential nature of in-person corporate worship and the proportionality analysis under s. 1. The petitioners supported the application; the respondents opposed it, arguing ARPA's submissions would be duplicative of the petitioners' and would expand the litigation (e.g., on s. 2, which the Crown had conceded was infringed).
firac.rule: Applications to intervene are guided by the court's inherent jurisdiction; an applicant must show either a direct interest or that the case raises public law issues, legitimately engages the applicant's interests, and that the applicant offers a perspective that will assist the court. Per Equustek Solutions Inc. v. Google Inc., 2014 BCCA 448, an intervenor offering a special perspective must show it is in the court's/public interest for it to be heard, must present a perspective not already before the court, must not expand or 'hijack' the litigation, and intervention is discretionary and not granted as of course (see also Squamish Nation, Trans Mountain).
firac.application: The Chief Justice noted that the Court of Appeal authorities relied on by the respondents concerned interventions where the record and evidence had been settled, whereas here the parties' substantive submissions were not yet known. ARPA had provided only a 'thumbnail sketch' of its proposed submissions on ss. 1, 2 and 15. Without the parties' filed submissions, the court could not determine whether ARPA's proposed submissions would 'hijack' the litigation, be irrelevant or academic (as on the conceded s. 2 issue), or simply duplicate the petitioners' arguments (as suggested for the s. 15 and s. 1 points).
firac.conclusion: The court declined to grant or refuse the application at that stage, adjourning ARPA's intervention application to March 1, 2021.

firac.issue: Could the intervention application be determined before the parties filed their substantive written submissions?
firac.facts: The Chief Justice hoped to have the parties file written submissions before the March 1, 2021 petition hearing so ARPA could demonstrate its submissions offered a distinct, non-duplicative perspective. Petitioners' counsel could only commit to filing by February 22 (endeavouring for February 19); respondents' counsel declined to agree to any filing schedule or to file before the hearing date.
firac.rule: The advisability of an intervention depends on whether the proposed submissions add a perspective not otherwise before the court without duplicating a supported party or expanding the litigation (Equustek). Assessing this requires knowledge of the parties' positions.
firac.application: Because the respondents would not agree to a pre-hearing filing schedule, the court could not assess the utility and uniqueness of ARPA's proposed submissions. The court was unwilling to decide the application on speculation about what ARPA might offer in response to submissions not yet filed.
firac.conclusion: The application was adjourned to March 1, 2021, when the parties' positions would be clearer.

keywords_rationale: The decision is an intervention application within a Charter challenge, so Constitutional law (K003) is the anchor tier-1 area and the underlying substantive rights drive the relevance of freedom of religion (K025) and Charter s. 2(a) (K110), which the Crown conceded was infringed. The proposed intervenor submissions concerned the s. 1 proportionality analysis, making reasonable limits (K030) and the Doré/Loyola framework (K010) directly engaged, and equality rights (K023) reflects the s. 15 'religious equality' argument discussed. Civil litigation (K002) captures the procedural intervention character of the ruling, and judicial review (K011) reflects that the underlying proceeding is a petition/judicial review of public health orders. There is no controlled keyword for 'intervention' specifically, so these are the closest available; K023 and K011 are somewhat weaker as they relate to the underlying merits rather than the narrow procedural issue actually decided.

registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: XXXXX XXXXX (Claimant) — Private Proceeding, RPD File No. AA5-00211

defining_issues: Was the claimant's evidence credible so as to establish a well-founded fear of persecution or risk of harm in Peru or Israel?
Did the claimant, a dual citizen, establish an absence of adequate state protection in her countries of nationality?
Was the claimant's conduct — including renewing her Israeli passport, returning to Peru, and delaying her refugee claim — consistent with a genuine subjective fear of persecution?

firac.issue: Was the claimant's evidence credible enough to establish a well-founded fear of persecution or risk of harm in Peru or Israel?
firac.facts: The claimant, a 47-year-old dual citizen of Peru and Israel from a Jewish family who converted to Christianity, alleged persecution in Peru by the SOGNUT emigration agency and by her family and the local Jewish community, and harassment in Israel following her conversion. She offered no explanation for why SOGNUT (a body assisting Jewish emigration to Israel) would target her, produced no objective evidence, and continued visiting her allegedly abusive father in Peru.
firac.rule: To qualify as a Convention refugee under s. 96 IRPA or a person in need of protection under s. 97(1) IRPA, a claimant must provide credible and trustworthy evidence of a well-founded fear of persecution or risk.
firac.application: The panel found the account implausible and internally inconsistent: the claimant could not explain why an emigration agency would break into her home or leave animal blood at her door, produced no corroboration, and behaved inconsistently by repeatedly returning to her father's home. Documentary evidence showed Israel respects full social and political equality regardless of religion, undercutting the alleged Israeli persecution during her decade-long residence there.
firac.conclusion: The panel found the claimant not credible and held she failed to establish a well-founded fear of persecution or risk of harm.

firac.issue: Did the claimant establish an absence of adequate state protection in Peru?
firac.facts: The claimant filed only one police report, made just before departing for Canada, and asserted the Peruvian police were all corrupt and would not assist her.
firac.rule: A claimant must rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.
firac.application: The panel found that a single detailed report followed by prompt departure did not amount to clear and convincing evidence; general corruption did not establish that Peru could not protect her.
firac.conclusion: The claimant did not establish an absence of state protection.

firac.issue: Was the claimant's conduct consistent with a genuine subjective fear of persecution?
firac.facts: Despite alleging fear of Israel and its agents, the claimant did not renounce her Israeli citizenship and renewed her Israeli passport in Lima before travelling to Canada. She entered Canada as a visitor in February 2004, repeatedly extended her visitor status, pursued a live-in caregiver program, and claimed refugee protection only in April 2005 after being refused a US visa.
firac.rule: Conduct inconsistent with subjective fear — including reavailment of the protection of the alleged persecuting state and unexplained delay in claiming — undermines a refugee claim.
firac.application: Renewing the Israeli passport while claiming Israeli agents were persecuting her was contradictory, and the delay in claiming while pursuing other immigration avenues was inconsistent with genuine fear; the explanation of ignorance of the refugee program was rejected given her inquiries into permanency.
firac.conclusion: The claimant's behaviour was inconsistent with a subjective fear of persecution, reinforcing the negative credibility finding.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K075 (convention refugee) and K078 (refugee protection) capture the s. 96/s. 97 IRPA determination. K079 (persecution) reflects the alleged religion- and family-based persecution central to the claim. K080 (state protection) is engaged by the finding that the claimant failed to rebut the presumption of Peruvian state protection. K093 (Jewish) is apt given the claimant's Jewish-family origin, conversion to Christianity, and the Jewish-community and SOGNUT dimensions. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the deciding tribunal. Credibility and dual nationality are central but have no dedicated vocabulary term; K075/K078/K079 are the closest fits.
location_rationale: The decision states "Place of Hearing / Lieu de l'audience: Halifax, Nova Scotia." The reasons were, however, "Dated at Montreal this 6th day of April, 2006"; the hearing location (Halifax, Nova Scotia) is used as the sitting location.
registry_rationale: The document identifies only "Refugee Protection Division" and RPD File No. AA5-00211, with no specific registry office named, so registry is left null.

case_name: Pavlov v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)

name_verification.name_in_document: IGOR PAVLOV and SVETLANA GELTONOZKO PAVLOVA v. THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: What is the applicable standard of review for the Board's determination that the applicants are not Convention refugees?
Did the Board err in law by relying on the applicants' failure to seek asylum in Israel under the Israeli Law of Return to make a negative credibility finding on their subjective fear of persecution?

firac.issue: What standard of review applies to the Board's determination that the applicants are not Convention refugees?
firac.facts: The Board determined that Igor Pavlov, a Russian Jew, and his non-Jewish spouse were not Convention refugees, finding they had not established a well-founded fear of persecution. The applicants challenged this determination on judicial review, raising questions of both law and fact.
firac.rule: Per Conkova v. Canada (MCI), [2000] F.C.J. No. 300, the standard of review of CRDD decisions is generally patent unreasonableness, except for questions involving the interpretation of a statute, where the standard becomes correctness.
firac.application: The Court found the Board was faced with a question of law—whether the applicants fell within the definition of 'Convention refugee' in s. 2(1) of the Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-12. Because the disposition turned on the correct interpretation and application of that statutory definition, correctness governed.
firac.conclusion: The applicable standard of review was correctness.

firac.issue: Did the Board err in law by treating the applicants' failure to seek asylum in Israel under the Israeli Law of Return as undermining the subjective element of their fear of persecution?
firac.facts: The Board concluded that the applicants' failure to go to Israel as full citizens under the Israeli Law of Return, with a generous absorption package, indicated a lack of subjective fear and undermined the credibility of their claim. The male applicant had the option under the Law of Return but did not wish to go to Israel.
firac.rule: A refugee claimant must first seek the protection of countries in which the claimant can assert nationality as a basis of citizenship before claiming in Canada (Canada (A.G.) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689; M.E.I. v. Akl (1990), 140 N.R. 323 (F.C.A.); Grygorian). However, there is no requirement to pursue status in a country where the claimant has no right to qualify for citizenship (Basmenji v. Canada (MCI), [1998] F.C.J. No. 39). The Israeli Law of Return depends upon a desire to settle in Israel (Katkova v. Canada (MCI), [1997] F.C.J. No. 549).
firac.application: The Board mistakenly assumed the applicants were required to seek protection in Israel before claiming in Canada and linked their failure to do so to a negative credibility finding. The applicants had no right to qualify for citizenship in Israel because the Law of Return depends on a desire to settle there, and the male applicant did not wish to go. Following Basmenji and Katkova, the Board could not draw an adverse inference from the failure to invoke the Law of Return.
firac.conclusion: The Board erred in law in relying on the Israeli Law of Return to reach a negative credibility finding on the subjective element of the applicants' fear; the application was allowed and the matter remitted to a differently constituted panel.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) capture the procedural posture and the determinative correctness analysis. K075 (convention refugee), K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) reflect the core refugee-determination issue and the alleged fear of persecution. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) apply because the claim was based on the male applicant's Jewish nationality and anti-Semitism in Russia. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the tribunal under review. K103 (Israel) is central because the case turned on the Israeli Law of Return. State protection (K080) was borderline and omitted as the decision focused on the Law of Return rather than state protection analysis.
location_rationale: The decision states 'PLACE OF HEARING: OTTAWA, ONTARIO'. The reasons were signed at Toronto, Ontario, but the matter was heard in Ottawa. Province is Ontario in both instances.
registry_rationale: No specific court registry office is named in the decision; the Federal Court of Canada issued the decision under docket IMM-4401-00, but no registry is designated, so it is left null.

name_verification.discrepancy_note: The case name matches, but the supplied citation (2025 FPSLREB 101) does not match the citation in the decision text, which is 2024 FPSLREB 168 (File 561-02-39259, decided December 5, 2024).

defining_issues: Does the Board have jurisdiction to dismiss a duty of fair representation complaint on written submissions, without an oral hearing, where the complaint discloses no arguable case?

Is a union's decision not to refer a grievance to adjudication subject to a correctness or reasonableness standard of review, or only to the arbitrary, discriminatory, or bad-faith test under s. 187 of the Act?
Should the complainant be granted a further extension of time to raise a constitutional challenge to ss. 187 and 190 of the Act and ss. 6 and 34(1) of the FPSLREBA?

firac.issue: Does the Board have jurisdiction to summarily dismiss a duty of fair representation complaint without an oral hearing where no arguable case is made out?
firac.facts: Abi-Mansour, an AS-03 employee at the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, complained under s. 190 that the union breached its s. 187 duty of fair representation by refusing to refer to adjudication his grievance over a denial of leave without pay. The union sought summary dismissal; the complainant argued the Board had no statutory power to dismiss without a hearing and that applying an arguable-case analysis created an unauthorized 'leave step'.
firac.rule: Section 22 of the FPSLREBA provides that the Board may decide any matter before it without holding an oral hearing. Procedural fairness does not require an oral hearing in every case (Baker v. Canada, 1999 CanLII 699 (SCC); Osman v. PSAC, 2021 FCA 227; Boshra v. CAPE, 2011 FCA 98). The Board applies an 'arguable case' test — taking the alleged facts as true and disregarding any defence, whether there is an arguable case of a s. 187 breach (Quadrini v. CRA, 2008 PSLRB 37; Grant v. Unifor, 2022 FCA 6).
firac.application: The complainant's lack of awareness of an enabling provision did not deprive the Board of jurisdiction. The Board's long-established arguable-case jurisprudence has never been overturned on judicial review, and it creates jurisprudence rather than legislating. The parties were notified the dismissal request would proceed in writing and were invited to address whether an arguable case existed. Applying that analysis is not a 'leave step'; it simply requires the complainant to show his allegations, if proven, could amount to a breach. Five allegations met that threshold and were set down for hearing.
firac.conclusion: The Board has jurisdiction to dismiss without an oral hearing; the request for summary dismissal was granted except for the five allegations reserved for an oral hearing.

firac.issue: Is a union's refusal to refer a grievance to adjudication reviewable on a correctness or reasonableness standard, or only on the s. 187 arbitrary/discriminatory/bad-faith standard, and does it vary by grievance type?
firac.facts: The complainant argued that refusal to refer a s. 209(1)(a) grievance (which forecloses the grievor's own recourse) should be assessed on a reasonableness standard per Vavilov, while other grievance types could be assessed on the s. 187 standard, and that the union's decision was incorrect or unreasonable.
firac.rule: Section 187 of the Act sets a single duty of fair representation test: a union must not act in a manner that is arbitrary, discriminatory, or in bad faith. Judicial standards of review (Canada (MCI) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65) are distinct from that statutory test.
firac.application: Neither the legislation nor the jurisprudence distinguishes between grievance types for the purpose of the duty. The Board does not sit as a review or appeal court over union decisions and does not assess their correctness or reasonableness. A union's decision whether to refer a grievance to adjudication is its own to make, provided it is not arbitrary, discriminatory, or in bad faith.
firac.conclusion: There is only one test — the s. 187 standard — regardless of grievance type; the complainant's argument for a correctness/reasonableness review was rejected.

firac.issue: Should the complainant receive a further extension of time to raise a constitutional challenge to the governing statutory provisions?
firac.facts: The complainant had flagged a constitutional issue in his 2018 complaint and again in 2019, and in his November 30, 2022 submission sought a further 1.5-month extension to file a notice of constitutional question against ss. 187 and 190 of the Act and ss. 6 and 34(1) of the FPSLREBA. He had already been granted two prior month-long extensions.
firac.rule: Extensions of time require an adequate justification; the statutory objective is the fair, credible and efficient resolution of disputes.
firac.application: The complainant had four years since first alluding to the constitutional issue in 2018, plus three months from August to November 2022 and two extensions, without offering an appropriate reason for further delay. He had ample time to serve and file a notice of constitutional question and prepare the challenge.
firac.conclusion: The request for a further extension of time to raise a constitutional challenge was denied.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns a duty of fair representation complaint about a grievance. K084 (labour arbitration/grievance) captures the underlying grievance and refusal to refer to adjudication. K012 (procedural fairness) is central to the ruling that no oral hearing was required. K014 (standard of review) reflects the complainant's rejected argument confusing judicial standards of review with the s. 187 test. K001 (Administrative law) is the tier-1 parent for the procedural-fairness and standard-of-review reasoning by this tribunal. K003 (Constitutional law) is engaged by the denied request to mount a constitutional challenge to the enabling statutes. K011 (judicial review) is a weaker/borderline pick, included because the complainant repeatedly invoked judicial review concepts, though the Board clarified it does not sit as a review court.
location_rationale: The decision is that of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations and Employment Board, a national tribunal, and no city or province is stated in the text; it was decided on the basis of written submissions.
registry_rationale: No registry or office is identified. Only the Board file number (561-02-39259) appears, which is not a geographic registry.
