Nuttall, 2018 BCCA 479, dated 20181219.

defining_issues: Did the trial judge err in finding that the RCMP entrapped the accused and in staying the terrorism charges on that basis?
Did the trial judge err in directing an acquittal on the facilitation count (s. 83.19 of the Criminal Code) on the basis that principals cannot facilitate their own terrorist activity?
Did the trial judge err in instructing the jury not to consider the second conspiracy count (count 2) if it convicted on the first conspiracy count (count 1), and in staying count 2?

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in finding that the RCMP entrapped the accused and in staying the terrorism charges on that basis?
firac.facts: Following a months-long RCMP INSET undercover operation involving 28 scenarios, Nuttall and Korody placed inert pressure cooker bombs (containing police-supplied C-4) outside the Victoria Parliament Buildings on Canada Day 2013. A jury convicted them of conspiracy to commit murder for a terrorist group and of making/possessing an explosive with intent for a terrorist group. The trial judge stayed the charges for entrapment on three bases: lack of reasonable suspicion when C-4 was offered, that the average person would have committed the offences (partly because the couple feared they would be killed), and a residual finding that the police manufactured the crime.
firac.rule: R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903 establishes an objective test: entrapment exists where (a) police provide an opportunity to commit an offence without reasonable suspicion or a bona fide inquiry, or (b) having reasonable suspicion, they go beyond providing an opportunity and induce the offence; a residual category applies where police conduct otherwise exceeds propriety and manufactures the crime. Reasonable suspicion is more than mere suspicion but less than reasonable and probable grounds (R. v. Kang-Brown, 2008 SCC 18; R. v. Gingras, 2013 BCCA 293). Findings of fact are reviewed for palpable and overriding error (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33); stays are reviewed deferentially (R. v. Regan, 2002 SCC 12; R. v. Babos, 2014 SCC 16); questions of law for correctness.
firac.application: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge made two errors: she wrongly found the police lacked reasonable suspicion when C-4 was offered on June 16, 2013 (Nuttall's active bomb-planning, downloaded Inspire instructions, shopping list and requests presumptively supplied reasonable suspicion per Gingras), and she wrongly found the average person would have planted the bombs, a conclusion resting on a finding that the couple feared they would be killed—a finding inconsistent with her own self-defence ruling (2015 BCSC 963) and based impermissibly on the accused's subjective beliefs rather than the objective police conduct. However, the Court held the third, residual basis was unassailable: the police knew the couple lacked the ability to commit terrorism, yet pushed them relentlessly, supplied the explosive, tools, transportation, location, and direction, chose the date and target, and manufactured the crime. Balancing fairness against the need to protect the public from serious terrorism offences, the police misconduct amounted to a manufactured crime and a travesty of justice.
firac.conclusion: Appeal from the stays entered on counts 1 and 4 dismissed; despite errors in two of the three bases, the residual manufactured-crime finding supported the stay of proceedings.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in directing an acquittal on the s. 83.19 facilitation count on the basis that principals cannot facilitate their own terrorist activity?
firac.facts: Count 3 charged the accused with knowingly facilitating a terrorist activity, particularized as the placing of an explosive device at the Parliament Buildings. The trial judge directed a verdict of not guilty, reasoning that s. 83.19 targets persons on the periphery of terrorist groups and that principals cannot facilitate their own activity, so the Crown's principal-liability theory was not captured.
firac.rule: Section 83.19 of the Criminal Code makes it an offence to knowingly facilitate a terrorist activity. 'Facilitate' means to make a matter easier, or to make it easier for another to commit a crime (R. v. Lindsay, 2009 ONCA 532; R. v. Legare, 2009 SCC 56; R. v. Khawaja, 2012 SCC 69). Where counts overlap, the trier of fact should deliver verdicts on all counts and the judge applies the rule against multiple convictions (R. v. Kienapple, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729; R. v. Provo, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 3).
firac.application: The Court held the trial judge misread the particulars: the terrorist activity that was facilitated was the placing of the devices, so preparatory acts (buying pressure cookers and materials, scouting targets) could constitute facilitation. While a person cannot be convicted as both principal and facilitator of the same activity, and generally facilitation involves aiding another, where two people act in concert each could facilitate the other's act, and self-facilitation is not foreclosed. The count should have gone to the jury; any overlapping conviction would then be addressed by Kienapple. Because count 1 (conspiracy to murder) resulted in a conviction, a guilty facilitation verdict would have been conditionally stayed, and the entrapment finding would apply in any event, so a new trial would be an abuse of process (relying on s. 686(4), (8) and R. v. Hinse, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 597).
firac.conclusion: Appeal allowed to the extent of setting aside the acquittal on count 3 and substituting a stay of proceedings; the trial judge erred but a new trial would be abusive.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in instructing the jury not to consider count 2 if it convicted on count 1, and in staying count 2?
firac.facts: Counts 1 and 2 both charged conspiracy—count 1 to murder persons unknown, count 2 to place an explosive with intent to cause death or serious bodily injury—both for a terrorist group and limited by the Crown to placing the pressure cooker devices at the Parliament Buildings. The trial judge treated the counts as one conspiracy with two objects, instructed the jury not to consider count 2 if it convicted on count 1, and entered a stay on count 2.
firac.rule: Where there is one agreement with multiple unlawful objects there is a single conspiracy and the Crown need only prove one object (Cox and Paton v. The Queen, [1963] S.C.R. 500). Overlapping counts should be left to the jury with the judge applying the Kienapple principle and entering a conditional stay on the lesser count (R. v. Provo). On a Crown appeal from an acquittal or stay, the Crown must show a legal error and a reasonable degree of certainty that the result would not necessarily have been the same (Cullen v. The King, [1949] S.C.R. 658; R. v. Graveline, 2006 SCC 16; R. v. Jewitt, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 128).
firac.application: Because the two counts alleged different objects (intent to murder versus intent to cause serious bodily injury), there was a route to acquittal on count 1 and conviction on count 2; the trial judge should have left both counts to the jury and applied Kienapple to any guilty verdicts, staying the lesser. Her instruction removing count 2 was an error. However, the result would be the same—a stay—whether under Kienapple or the entrapment finding, so the Crown could not show a real likelihood of a different outcome.
firac.conclusion: Although the instruction was erroneous, the appeal from the stay of proceedings on count 2 was dismissed because the result remains a stay.

case_name: Mugesera v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)

name_verification.name_in_document: Mugesera v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)

defining_issues: Did the Federal Court of Appeal, sitting at the secondary level of appellate review, exceed its judicial review function by substituting its own assessment of the evidence for the IAD's findings of fact rather than reviewing them for reasonableness?

Did Mr. Mugesera's speech, on the facts found by the IAD, constitute incitement to murder, incitement to genocide, and incitement to hatred within the meaning of the Criminal Code, such that he is inadmissible under s. 27(1) of the Immigration Act?

Are there reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Mugesera committed a crime against humanity within the meaning of s. 7(3.76) of the Criminal Code, rendering him inadmissible under ss. 27(1)(g) and 19(1)(j) of the Immigration Act?

firac.issue: Did the Federal Court of Appeal exceed the scope of its judicial review function by reassessing the IAD's findings of fact?
firac.facts: The IAD (per Duquette) upheld the deportation order based on a detailed interpretation of Mugesera's 1992 speech. The FCTD upheld the incitement findings but set aside the crime-against-humanity finding. The FCA reversed several IAD findings of fact, rejected the reliance on the ICI Report and the rejection of Professor Angenot's interpretation, reweighed witness credibility, and set aside the deportation order.
firac.rule: Judicial review of decisions under the Immigration Act proceeds under s. 18.1(4) of the Federal Court Act: questions of law are reviewed for correctness (para. (c)); findings of fact may be set aside only if made in a perverse or capricious manner or without regard to the material (para. (d)), the standard being patent unreasonableness (Aguebor). At the secondary level of appellate review, the appellate court's role is limited to determining, on a correctness standard, whether the reviewing judge selected and applied the correct standard of review (Dr. Q v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of B.C.).
firac.application: The FCA showed no deference to the IAD's factual findings and conducted its own broad-ranging reassessment of the evidence, effectively applying a correctness standard to questions of fact. Duquette's interpretation of the speech was based on a careful review of all evidence, was well reasoned, and was reasonable. Since no reviewable error on the reasonableness standard had been demonstrated, the FCA should have proceeded on the facts as found by the IAD. By contrast, Nadon J. properly rejected as patently unreasonable the findings of Bourbonnais and Champoux Ohrt that murders resulted and that Mugesera was an Akazu/death-squad member, since no evidence supported them.
firac.conclusion: The FCA erred by exceeding its judicial review function; the analysis must proceed on the IAD's findings of fact, including its interpretation of the speech.

firac.issue: Did the speech constitute incitement to murder, genocide and hatred rendering Mugesera inadmissible under s. 27(1) of the Immigration Act?
firac.facts: On 22 November 1992 Mugesera, a prominent MRND member, addressed about 1,000 people at Kabaya. Using violent language, he urged the audience not to be 'invaded,' to 'exterminate' opponents and Tutsi ('Inyenzi'), referenced sending Tutsi corpses down the Nyabarongo River (the 'river passage'), and warned that 'anyone whose neck you do not cut is the one who will cut your neck.' Roughly 2,000 Tutsi had been massacred between 1990 and 1992.
firac.rule: Under ss. 27(1)(a.1)(ii) and (a.3)(ii) of the Immigration Act the Minister must prove on a balance of probabilities that the act would constitute an offence abroad and in Canada. Counselling murder not committed: s. 464(a) Criminal Code; the actus reus is met where statements, viewed objectively, are likely to incite and are made with a view to inciting the offence (Dionne; Sharpe), with intent to bring about the result. Incitement to genocide: s. 318(1) (incorporating the Genocide Convention); requires direct and public incitement plus specific intent to destroy an identifiable group; no proof of resulting genocide required (Akayesu; Media Case). Incitement to hatred: s. 319 requires promotion of the most intense forms of detestation (Keegstra), assessed objectively in social/historical context and by reference to the target audience (Buzzanga).
firac.application: On the IAD's findings, the speech objectively was likely to incite and was made with a view to inciting murder of Tutsi and opponents; Mugesera intended that result given his knowledge of ongoing ethnic massacres. The 'river passage,' understood by the audience, directly and publicly advocated killing Tutsi with intent to destroy the group in part, satisfying incitement to genocide. The speech's violent language and references to past massacres promoted intense hatred of the Tutsi, satisfying incitement to hatred. The FCA erred by applying an abstract 'reasonable listener' standard (Prud'homme) and ignoring the target audience.
firac.conclusion: All three offences were made out on a balance of probabilities; Mugesera is inadmissible under s. 27(1)(a.1)(ii) and (a.3)(ii).

firac.issue: Are there reasonable grounds to believe Mugesera committed a crime against humanity?
firac.facts: The same speech was alleged to be a crime against humanity. The IAD could not establish that murders actually resulted from the speech. Between October 1990 and November 1992 systematic, government/military-linked massacres and mass arrests targeted Tutsi and moderate Hutu, many in and around Gisenyi prefecture where the speech was given.
firac.rule: Section 19(1)(j) of the Immigration Act requires 'reasonable grounds to believe'—more than suspicion, less than balance of probabilities, an objective basis grounded in compelling and credible information (Sivakumar; Chiau; Sabour)—applicable only to questions of fact; whether the facts meet the legal definition is a question of law. Under s. 7(3.76) Criminal Code, interpreted in light of customary international law (ICTY/ICTR jurisprudence), a crime against humanity requires: (1) a proscribed act with its physical and mental elements; (2) committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack; (3) directed against a civilian population; and (4) knowledge of the attack and that the act forms part of it. Persecution requires a gross or blatant denial of fundamental rights on discriminatory grounds equal in gravity to other enumerated acts, with discriminatory intent (Tadic; Kupreskic; Media Case). Finta is overruled to the extent it required discriminatory intent for all crimes against humanity.
firac.application: Counselling murder could not qualify because no murders were proven to have resulted, as international law requires for instigation. However, persecution by hate speech qualified: the speech, advocating extermination in a volatile, massacre-prone environment, was a gross or blatant denial of fundamental rights equal in gravity to other enumerated acts, committed with discriminatory intent against Tutsi and moderate Hutu. A systematic attack (government/military-sanctioned pattern of massacres and arrests) was under way, directed against the civilian Tutsi and moderate Hutu population. The persecutory speech objectively furthered and fit the pattern of that attack, including geographic proximity in Gisenyi. Mugesera, educated and politically prominent, knew of the attack and that his speech formed part of it.
firac.conclusion: Reasonable grounds exist to believe Mugesera committed a crime against humanity; he is inadmissible under ss. 27(1)(g) and 19(1)(j). The appeal is allowed and the deportation order restored.

name_verification.name_in_document: Louis Adam Wolfson v. Jennifer Rebecca Wolfson
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The party names match (Wolfson v. Wolfson), but the supplied citation (2021 NSSC 260) and court (NSSC) refer to the trial-level merits decision of Justice Forgeron. The document provided is the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal decision, 2023 NSCA 57 (CA 514322), which reviews that trial decision. The 2021 NSSC 260 decision is cited within the appeal as the 'merits decision' but is not the decision being analysed.

defining_issues: Does the Matrimonial Property Act permit a court to classify an asset as having 'two primary but equal purposes' (part business, part matrimonial), or must an asset be classified as either business or matrimonial?
Was the trial judge's finding that the rental-property companies were held for the equal primary purpose of a retirement vehicle a palpable and overriding error?
Did the trial judge err in her analysis and quantification of the unequal-division award under s. 13 of the MPA?
Should the trial costs award be adjusted, and should the appellant's fresh-evidence motion be admitted?

firac.issue: Does the MPA permit a 'two primary but equal purposes' hybrid classification of an asset, or must an asset be classified as either a business asset or a matrimonial asset?
firac.facts: Mr. Wolfson owned controlling shares in a group of companies owning 21 rental buildings (257 units), with agreed equity ultimately valued at $13,908,662. He sought exclusion of the shares as business assets under s. 4(1)(e); Ms. Wolfson sought matrimonial classification. The trial judge found the companies were held for 'two primary but equal purposes'—an income-producing vehicle and a retirement vehicle—and split the value 50/50. Neither party proposed this approach and the judge did not alert them to it before releasing her decision.
firac.rule: Under the MPA (R.S.N.S. 1989, c. 275) all property is presumptively matrimonial unless it falls within a s. 4(1) exception; business assets (defined in s. 2(a) as property 'primarily used or held for' a commercial/income-producing purpose) are excepted under s. 4(1)(e). Section 16 permits a declaration whether property 'is a matrimonial asset or a business asset'. Statutory interpretation follows Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes Ltd. (Re), [1998] 1 SCR 27 (words read in context, grammatical and ordinary sense). The classifying party bears the balance-of-probabilities burden (Clarke v. Clarke, [1990] 2 SCR 795; Tibbetts v. Tibbetts). Interpretation of the MPA is a question of law reviewed for correctness (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33).
firac.application: The Court held the judge, while correctly recognizing the need to determine the 'primary purpose', erred by creating a novel category of assets that are equally matrimonial and non-matrimonial. 'Primarily' in s. 2(a) means principal or chief—only one purpose can be primary. The disjunctive 'or' in s. 16(1)(b) and 16(2)(b) links mutually exclusive alternatives, and the standalone structure of s. 4(1)(e) (unlike ss. 4(1)(a),(b),(c)) shows no legislative intent to permit a divisible business asset. Sections 13(f) and 18 presuppose that business assets are not divisible as such. No authority supported a dual-primary classification. Amending the business-asset exemption is for the legislature.
firac.conclusion: The judge erred in law; the hybrid classification cannot stand. The classification was set aside.

firac.issue: Was the finding that the companies were held for the equal primary purpose of a retirement vehicle a palpable and overriding error?
firac.facts: The record contained extensive evidence that the properties were operated to generate income in an entrepreneurial sense and kept separate from family finances. Evidence of retirement intention was sparse—limited to affidavit statements about possibly living in one penthouse unit and contested testimony; Mr. Wolfson denied ever discussing 'cashing out' and spoke instead of a 'legacy' for his children.
firac.rule: Factual findings and inferences are reviewed for palpable and overriding error—an error plain to see that has a material impact on the outcome (Laframboise v. Millington, 2019 NSCA 43). To qualify as a business asset the primary purpose must be income/profit generation in an entrepreneurial sense.
firac.application: The sparse retirement evidence could not reasonably establish a 'primary' retirement purpose. The judge conflated 'legacy' with 'retirement' and over-relied on a discussion about personal use of one of 257 units. The record overwhelmingly showed the companies were owned, operated and managed to generate income; the retirement-vehicle finding was plain error affecting nearly $7 million in classification, hence overriding.
firac.conclusion: Palpable and overriding error established; on the record Mr. Wolfson proved the disputed shares are business assets, excluded from division.

firac.issue: Did the judge err in her s. 13 unequal-division analysis and in quantifying the award?
firac.facts: The judge found equal division would be unfair or unconscionable and awarded $4,477,165 (or $1,000,000 if her hybrid classification stood), crafting the award to preserve the effect of her classification. She relied on s. 13(a) (unreasonable impoverishment) and s. 13(e) (date/manner of acquisition), among others.
firac.rule: Section 13 permits unequal division or division of non-matrimonial property only where equal division would be unfair or unconscionable, proven by strong, convincing evidence (Donald v. Donald; Volcko v. Volcko, 2015 NSCA 11; Young v. Young, 2003 NSCA 63). Section 13 requires a two-step analysis (Donald; Archibald v. Archibald): first whether equal division is unfair/unconscionable, then what division would be fair and conscionable. The purpose is to alleviate unfairness, not redistribute wealth. It is an error to consider irrelevant factors, unenumerated factors, or to misclassify assets affecting the analysis.
firac.application: Section 13(a) was irrelevant—the judge wrongly made it a comparative inquiry (business equity outpacing matrimonial assets) rather than asking objectively whether matrimonial assets were unreasonably impoverished, and made no finding of unreasonableness. Section 13(e) was tainted by the erroneous retirement-vehicle finding. The judge completed only the first Donald step and never determined what amount was needed to neutralize the unfairness, instead importing the quantum from her improper classification. The award was therefore not entitled to deference. Having the full record, the Court reassessed, weighing undisturbed factors including Ms. Wolfson's disproportionate domestic/child-care contributions (s. 13(f)) and overlap with ss. 13(g) and (i), and declining to factor tax consequences or the compensatory spousal-support component.
firac.conclusion: Reversible error established; the s. 13 award reduced from $4,477,165 to $1,500,000.

firac.issue: Should the trial costs award be adjusted and should the fresh-evidence motion be admitted?
firac.facts: The judge awarded $422,567 in costs, including $168,117 for expert fees, citing Mr. Wolfson's egregious non-disclosure of share values. Mr. Wolfson sought to adduce fresh evidence (counsel communications and pre-trial conference transcripts) to undermine the non-disclosure finding.
firac.rule: Costs are discretionary but where an appeal succeeds the underlying award may be reassessed anew (Doncaster v. Field, 2016 NSCA 25; O'Brien v. Clark). Divided success generally means parties bear their own costs (Keddy; Doncaster). Non-disclosure is the 'cancer' of family litigation warranting costs against the non-disclosing party (Michel v. Graydon, 2020 SCC 24; Leskun v. Leskun, 2006 SCC 25). Fresh evidence requires 'special grounds' under Civil Procedure Rule 90.47(1), governed by the Palmer test (Palmer v. The Queen; Barendregt v. Grebliunas, 2022 SCC 22).
firac.application: With success now divided at trial and on appeal, each party should bear its own costs except the $168,117 expert-fee reimbursement, which was justified by Mr. Wolfson's disclosure deficits and the eleventh-hour valuation agreement did not negate that. The fresh evidence failed Palmer: it was not fresh, was available with due diligence, and would not have affected the result on the expert-fee award.
firac.conclusion: Fresh-evidence motion dismissed; costs reduced from $422,567 to $168,117, with each party otherwise bearing its own costs at trial and on appeal.

defining_issues: Did the claimants rebut the presumption that Israel, as a functioning democracy, is able to protect its citizens?
Did the male claimant's refusal to perform Israeli military service establish a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground?
Were the claimants credible, and did their allegations of religious/ethnic discrimination amount to persecution?

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption that Israel can protect its citizens?
firac.facts: The Russian-origin Orthodox Christian family alleged assaults by a neighbour and abuse of their children, and that police refused to help because they were not Jewish. The male claimant did not obtain medical certificates, did not pursue a police complaint, and had never heard of the Ombudsman. Country documentation showed Israel has a police-complaints division, an Ombudsman's office with Russian-speaking staff, and functioning democratic institutions.
firac.rule: A state is presumed able to protect its citizens absent clear and convincing evidence to the contrary; the burden of rebutting the presumption is heavier where the state is a functioning democracy (Canada (MCI) v. Kadenko; Hinzman v. MCI, 2007 FCA 171).
firac.application: The panel found the claimant not credible (in particular regarding the medical report), and found he had failed to seek recourse through the police-complaints division, the Ombudsman, or the public prosecutor. Given Israel's democratic institutions and available complaint mechanisms, the claimants bore a heightened burden they did not meet.
firac.conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection, which was fatal to the claim.

firac.issue: Did the male claimant's refusal to serve in the Israeli military ground a Convention claim?
firac.facts: The male claimant was called for military duty during a period of heightened readiness. He was not a conscientious objector in general (he had served in the Russian military) but refused to take up arms against Palestinians. Immigrants are informed of the service obligation upon immigrating via the Absorption Basket.
firac.rule: A requirement to perform military service is a law of general application; refusal to serve based on objection to particular operations, absent conscientious-objector status, does not constitute persecution.
firac.application: The panel found that mandatory military service in Israel is a law of general application of which immigrants are notified, that the claimant was not a conscientious objector, and that a selective refusal to fight Palestinians did not amount to persecution.
firac.conclusion: The refusal to serve did not establish a well-founded fear of persecution; the claimant must fulfil his military obligation if required.

firac.issue: Were the claimants credible and did the alleged discrimination amount to persecution?
firac.facts: Allegations included verbal/physical abuse of the children at school, discriminatory treatment by police and teachers, inability to practice religion, and fear of a Kahanist organization not mentioned in the narrative. Much of this was unsupported by the National Documentation Package.
firac.rule: Claimants must establish credibility on a balance of probabilities; allegations unsupported by documentary evidence and embellishments added at hearing may undermine credibility, and discrimination must rise to the level of persecution.
firac.application: The panel found the claimant embellished his account (adding the medical-report explanation and the fear of the Kahanist group at hearing), that country documents contradicted key allegations, that Russian-speaking communities and Christian religious practice exist freely in Israel, and that a children's Ombudsman and other mechanisms addressed school abuse.
firac.conclusion: The claimants were found not credible and the alleged mistreatment did not amount to persecution; no s. 97 risk was established.

defining_issues: Was the Refugee Protection Division's decision that the applicants were not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection reasonable, including its credibility, internal flight alternative and state protection findings?

firac.issue: Was the Board's determination that the applicants were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection reasonable, given its credibility, IFA and state protection findings?
firac.facts: The Loshkariev family, Russian-born Israeli citizens, claimed protection based on the father's experience running a construction business in Israel where he hired Palestinian subcontractors. After the Intifada began in 2000, he and his workers were beaten, threatened and harassed by Jewish settlers and Orthodox Jews, and the police allegedly did little. The Board found the father not credible, preferred country documentation, found no evidence that Jews who supported the Palestinian cause were targeted otherwise than in situ, found the police had dispersed the settlers, and determined there was an internal flight alternative in Haifa with available state protection.
firac.rule: On judicial review the decision is reviewed for reasonableness following Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9; reasonableness concerns justification, transparency and intelligibility and whether the outcome falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes defensible on the facts and law. Findings of fact and inferences are not to be disturbed absent palpable and overriding error (Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc., [1997] 1 S.C.R. 748; Stein v. 'Kathy K', [1976] 2 S.C.R. 802; Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33), and inferences drawn from evidence are permissible where not mere speculation (Canada (M.E.I.) v. Satiacum).
firac.application: The Court rejected the applicants' argument that the credibility findings were really unsupported plausibility findings. It held that the factual findings on credibility, the IFA and state protection were inferences properly drawn from the evidentiary record, not speculation or conjecture. Applying the deferential reasonableness standard, the Court found the decision reasonable in all respects, noting that a reasonable balance of probabilities suffices and that courts must not interfere with inferential fact-finding absent palpable and overriding error.
firac.conclusion: The Board's decision was reasonable; the application for judicial review was dismissed and no serious question of general importance was certified.

case_name: Board of School Trustees of School District No. 44 (North Vancouver) v. Jubran

name_verification.name_in_document: Board of School Trustees of School District No. 44 (North Vancouver) v. Jubran et al

defining_issues: What is the standard of review applicable to the Human Rights Tribunal's interpretation of s. 8 of the Human Rights Code?

Did the students' harassing conduct — directed at a complainant who is not homosexual and whom the students did not believe to be homosexual — fall within s. 8 as discrimination 'because of the sex or sexual orientation of that person'?
Should the matter be remitted to the Tribunal or should the administrative proceedings be ended?

firac.issue: What standard of review applies to the Tribunal's interpretation of s. 8 of the Human Rights Code?
firac.facts: On judicial review, the Board challenged the Tribunal's April 8, 2002 finding that the students' conduct fell within s. 8. The material facts found by the Tribunal raised a question of law general in nature about the reach of s. 8.
firac.rule: A question of law that is general in nature is reviewed on a standard of correctness (U.B.C. v. Berg, 102 D.L.R. (4th) 665 at 676-677). Human rights legislation must be given a broad, liberal and purposive construction, but courts must not read legislation loose from the words chosen by the legislature.
firac.application: Stewart J. found that whether s. 8 captured the students' conduct was a general question of law attracting correctness. He added that, even if it were the application of law to particular facts (reviewable for reasonableness per Canada (A.G.) v. Mossop), the result would be the same because the Tribunal's conclusion that s. 8 captured the conduct was itself unreasonable.
firac.conclusion: The applicable standard is correctness; alternatively, on reasonableness the outcome is unchanged.

firac.issue: Did harassment by homophobic epithets of a complainant who is not homosexual and not believed to be homosexual fall within s. 8's prohibition on discrimination 'because of the sex or sexual orientation of that person'?
firac.facts: Jubran endured years of homophobic taunts and assaults at Handsworth Secondary; the Tribunal proceeded on the basis that Jubran is not homosexual and that the students who attacked him did not believe he was homosexual. The Tribunal nonetheless found the conduct contravened s. 8.
firac.rule: Section 8(1)(b) of the Human Rights Code prohibits discrimination against a person 'because of the ... sex or sexual orientation of that person or class of persons.' Legislation must be applied in accordance with the words chosen by the legislature (U.B.C. v. Berg at 678).
firac.application: Reading the concluding words of s. 8, Stewart J. held that discrimination by hurtful words of a sexual nature is not the same as discrimination 'because of the sex or sexual orientation OF THAT PERSON.' While the two may coincide, they do not in every case. Because Jubran is not homosexual and the students did not believe he was, the conduct fell wholly outside the words of the Act. Equating harassment through sexual epithets with discrimination because of the victim's own sexual orientation slipped the anchor of the statutory language.
firac.conclusion: The conduct did not fall within s. 8; the Tribunal's contrary finding was incorrect (and, alternatively, unreasonable).

firac.issue: Should the matter be remitted to the Tribunal or should the proceedings be ended?
firac.facts: Having quashed the finding that the Board contravened s. 8, the court had to decide the disposition. Counsel for the Board urged there was no basis for reasons 'in the alternative'.
firac.rule: On judicial review the court may quash a decision and, where appropriate, decline to remit and instead end the administrative proceedings.
firac.application: Stewart J. concluded the flaw was fatal and that this was a case to bring a halt to the proceedings, subject to reversal on appeal, rather than remit the matter to the Tribunal.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal's decision was quashed and the administrative proceedings were ended; the matter was not remitted.

keywords_rationale: The operative BCSC decision is a judicial review quashing a human rights tribunal ruling, so Administrative law (K001), judicial review (K011) and standard of review (K014) are directly engaged — Stewart J. expressly applied correctness under U.B.C. v. Berg. Human rights (K007), discrimination (K069) and human rights tribunal (K072) capture the substantive s. 8 Human Rights Code question. registry_rationale: The document header expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

defining_issues: Does the claimant, an ethnic Jewish man from western Ukraine, face an objectively well-founded fear of persecution based on current country conditions for Jews in Ukraine?
Given the passage of almost a decade since he left, is there a serious possibility of persecution by any past agent of persecution on return?

firac.issue: Is there an objectively well-founded fear of persecution for an ethnic Jewish man returning to Ukraine given current country conditions?
firac.facts: The 58-year-old ethnic Jewish claimant left Ukraine in 2008 after being beaten by Ukrainian nationalists in 2007, having his door defaced and his car stolen. His original claim was denied in 2012, then quashed on judicial review and remitted for redetermination. Counsel argued anti-Semitic violence had surged and no part of Ukraine, including a Kiev IFA, was safe.
firac.rule: Under s. 96 of the IRPA, a claimant must establish a well-founded fear of persecution, which requires an objective basis. Per Sukhraj Singh (F.C.T.D.), documentary evidence may be contradictory, and the panel must weigh conflicting sources.
firac.application: The panel weighed conflicting country-condition evidence. It preferred reporting from local/regional Jewish minority monitoring groups (NMRMG, cited in the 2017 U.S. State Department Religious Freedom Report, and the Va'ad Association researcher Likhachov) over the Israeli Ministry for Diaspora Affairs figures, which a Ukrainian anti-Semitism researcher called 'flawed and amateurish.' The preferred evidence showed no anti-Semitic violence recorded in 2017 and only isolated prior violent incidents, alongside documented vandalism (24 cases in 2017), against an estimated Jewish population of 360,000, and noted Ukraine had a Jewish Prime Minister.
firac.conclusion: The panel concluded that while unfortunate anti-Semitic incidents occur, they are not so pervasive as to amount to persecution; the claimant's fear was not objectively well-founded.

firac.issue: Is there a serious possibility of persecution by a past agent given the passage of nearly a decade?
firac.facts: The claimant had not lived in Ukraine since November 2008, almost ten years before the hearing. His agents of persecution were the nationalists who attacked him in 2007.
firac.rule: A blended assessment of well-foundedness under s. 96/s. 97 of the IRPA considers present and prospective risk, including whether past agents of persecution retain continued interest in the claimant, on a balance of probabilities.
firac.application: The panel considered the passage of almost a decade and found, on a balance of probabilities, a resultant lack of continued interest in the claimant by any past agent of persecution.
firac.conclusion: There is no serious possibility of persecution should the claimant return to Ukraine.

case_name: The Jewish Community Council of Montreal v. Canada (Attorney General)

name_verification.name_in_document: THE JEWISH COMMUNITY COUNCIL OF MONTREAL, KASHRUTH COUNCIL OF CANADA, RABBI ABRAHAM BANON, 4412532 CANADA INC (D/B/A KOSHER MEHADRIN), 1458935 ONTARIO LTD (D/B/A SHEFA MEATS) v THE ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA

defining_issues: Should the application for judicial review be treated and proceeded with as an action (conversion) under s 18.4(2) of the Federal Courts Act?
Is affidavit evidence adequate to establish the factual record, or is viva voce evidence necessary given the interplay of scientific, religious and Charter issues?

firac.issue: Should the application for judicial review be converted to an action under s 18.4(2) of the Federal Courts Act?
firac.facts: The applicants challenge CFIA Guidelines governing ritual (shechita) slaughter as an unreasonable interpretation of the Safe Food for Canadians Regulations and as infringing Charter ss 2(a) and 15(1). They moved to have their judicial review proceed as an action so that viva voce evidence and a statement of defence would be available; the Attorney General opposed, arguing affidavit evidence sufficed and conversion would cause unnecessary cost and delay.
firac.rule: Section 18.4(2) of the Federal Courts Act gives the Court discretion to direct that a judicial review be treated and proceeded with as an action. The applicant bears the burden of justifying conversion (Association des crabiers acadiens at para 35). Conversion is appropriate where the summary nature of judicial review is too constraining, and is guided by non-conjunctive factors including inadequacy of affidavit evidence, procedural safeguards, access to justice, and remedial inadequacy (Association des crabiers at paras 38-39); conversion is 'most rare' (Tsleil-Waututh Nation).
firac.application: The Court found the determinative factor to be whether the facts could be adequately established through affidavit evidence. It rejected the Respondent's siloed approach, emphasizing the mutual influence between conflicting scientific testimony on humane slaughter and religious testimony on kosher tradition, where the credibility of one set of witnesses affects the reliability of the other. Unlike a review of a tribunal decision, there was no prior decision or defined record, so the Court would be the first instance to adjudicate the facts, law and constitutionality. Access to justice and the constitutional stakes favoured conversion.
firac.conclusion: The motion was granted in part; the claim is to be treated and proceeded with as an action allowing viva voce evidence at trial, with costs in the cause.

firac.issue: Is affidavit evidence adequate to establish the factual record for the Charter claims, or is viva voce testimony necessary?
firac.facts: The applicants had already filed some 9,100 pages of affidavit evidence, including cross-examined expert witnesses, for the interlocutory injunction. They argued this was generated for an emergency injunction and that sincerity of religious belief (s 2(a)) and perpetuation of stereotypes/disadvantage (s 15(1)) required live testimony and credibility assessment.
firac.rule: Conversion is appropriate only where affidavit evidence would be inadequate, not merely where viva voce evidence would be preferable (Macinnis). Viva voce evidence may be needed to assess credibility or give the Court a full grasp of the evidence. A complete factual foundation is essential for Charter adjudication; s 15(1) claims require more than 'a web of instinct' (Taypotat), and sincerity under s 2(a) is a question of fact based partly on the credibility of the claimant's testimony (Amselem at para 53).
firac.application: The Court held that assessing sincerity of belief and historical disadvantage, intertwined with potentially biased or conflicting scientific evidence, could not be fairly resolved on affidavits alone. The interplay of oral history of Jewish tradition and expert scientific evidence created evidentiary challenges analogous (though not identical) to Aboriginal-rights cases (Houle, Barlow, Delgamuukw) where oral history warrants live testimony. Affidavits do not permit rigorous examination of witnesses' assumptions, methodologies and biases.
firac.conclusion: Affidavit evidence was found inadequate; viva voce evidence is necessary to adjudicate the constituent elements of the alleged Charter breaches, supporting conversion.

defining_issues: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Hungary with clear and convincing evidence?
Were the claimants' allegations of persecution based on Jewish ancestry credible?

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption that Hungary could provide adequate state protection?
firac.facts: The principal claimant, of distant Jewish ancestry, alleged threats, hateful letters and physical attacks by anti-Semitic neighbours and members of the Hungarian Guard. He did not report all incidents, did not give the police the threatening letters he had kept, and did not bring forward neighbour-witnesses who allegedly knew of the plot against him. Hungary was found to be a functioning multiparty democracy with security forces reporting to civilian authorities.
firac.rule: There is a presumption that a state can protect its citizens except in cases of complete breakdown (Canada (AG) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689); the claimant must rebut it with clear and convincing evidence on a balance of probabilities. The burden is directly proportional to the level of democracy (Kadenko; Sanchez), and the claimant bears the evidentiary burden of showing protection is inadequate (Carrillo v. Canada, 2008 FCA 94).
firac.application: The panel found Hungary a functioning democracy actively combating anti-Semitism — condemning incidents, banning and prosecuting the Hungarian Guard, and amending the Criminal Code to protect targeted groups. The claimants failed to report all incidents, withheld corroborating letters from police, and produced no witnesses, so the police could not be faulted for an inconclusive investigation. The one report the claimant did make was received and recorded but he could not identify his attackers.
firac.conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection; adequate state protection was available, which was determinative.

firac.issue: Were the claimants' allegations of targeted anti-Semitic persecution credible?
firac.facts: The claimants self-identified as Roman Catholic; the husband's father was of Jewish origin but he did not practise Judaism, belong to Jewish organizations, or face problems in adulthood until after a single anti-Semitism demonstration. The wife claimed her attackers wore Hungarian Guard insignia, but her police report described only a hooded sweater. The alleged pursuit of the claimant 120 km outside Budapest was unexplained.
firac.rule: Credibility findings turn on internal consistency and consistency with documentary and contemporaneous evidence; material omissions from prior statements (such as police reports) may undermine an allegation.
firac.application: The panel doubted that attackers bearing Hungarian Guard insignia would go unmentioned in the wife's police report, and rejected her explanation. It found it not credible that assailants would pursue the claimant to a distant town when the family had already left the neighbourhood, and found the minor child's non-selection for an advanced pre-school class was not shown to be linked to distant Jewish ancestry.
firac.conclusion: Key allegations were not credible, reinforcing the finding of no established risk, though state protection remained the determinative issue.

name_verification.name_in_document: LIDIA RYVINA v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Did the Board Member err in designating the applicant's son as her designated representative, contrary to the requirements of procedural fairness and the RPD Rules?
Were the Board's negative credibility findings reasonable?
Was the Board's finding that adequate state protection was available in Russia reasonable?

firac.issue: Did the Board err in appointing the applicant's son as her designated representative during the RPD hearing?
firac.facts: The 83-year-old applicant, represented by counsel, had difficulty answering basic questions through an interpreter. After she struggled to testify, her own counsel proposed that her son Yakov, who was present and said he knew the facts, be designated to testify on her behalf. The Board Member designated Yakov, had him sworn, and kept the applicant seated beside him with proceedings in Russian so she could follow and supplement his evidence.
firac.rule: Section 167(2) IRPA requires the Division to designate a representative where a person is unable to appreciate the nature of the proceedings; Rule 20 of the RPD Rules sets out designation criteria (age, understanding, willingness to act in best interests, no conflict) and the responsibilities of a designated representative. Procedural fairness issues are reviewed on correctness with deference to the Board's procedural choices (Forest Ethics Advocacy Association v National Energy Board, 2014 FCA 245; Khela, 2014 SCC 24). Espinoza v Canada (1999), 164 FTR 194 requires the Board to ensure the representative understands the role and its consequences.
firac.application: The Court found the designation arose only after the applicant experienced difficulty testifying, so many Rule 20 responsibilities (retaining/instructing counsel, gathering evidence, appeals) had no application; the son's limited role was to testify in her place and protect her interests under Rules 20(10)(d) and (e). The Board Member assessed her inability to appreciate the proceedings under s. 167(2), a view her counsel expressly endorsed, ensured the son understood his role and could act in her best interests, and kept the applicant engaged. Espinoza was distinguished because the son clearly understood he was to testify in his mother's place and the consequences of doing so.
firac.conclusion: No breach of procedural fairness or Rule 20; the designation was proper.

firac.issue: Were the Board's negative credibility findings reasonable?
firac.facts: The applicant alleged her husband was murdered by skinheads and that she and her late husband suffered ongoing anti-Semitic persecution. Her son testified he had been told his father died of kidney failure and only learned of a murder when his mother arrived in Canada months later; medical documentation was not produced and various details (police statements, prosecutor complaints, threatening letters) were inconsistent or absent from the PIF.
firac.rule: Credibility findings are reviewed on reasonableness with significant deference, as tribunals are ideally placed to assess credibility (Aguebor v Canada (1993), 160 NR 315 (FCA)); the decision must be read as a whole, not scrutinized in isolation (Caicedo v Canada, 2010 FC 1092).
firac.application: The son's evidence significantly contradicted the applicant's central claim that her husband was murdered, including that he believed his father died of kidney failure until his mother told a different story, and that supporting medical documents referencing the kidneys were never produced. These and other inconsistencies amply supported the adverse findings.
firac.conclusion: The credibility findings were reasonable and disclosed no reviewable error.

firac.issue: Was the Board's state protection analysis reasonable?
firac.facts: The Board acknowledged rising discrimination and anti-Semitism in Russia and inconsistent police responses, but found the state was taking legislative and operational steps to combat anti-Semitism and extremism and to address police misconduct.
firac.rule: State protection assessments are questions of mixed fact and law reviewed on reasonableness (Hinzman v Canada, 2006 FC 420, aff'd 2007 FCA 171); a claimant must rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.
firac.application: The Board's review of governmental action at the legislative and operational level supported its conclusion that adequate state protection exists in Russia, and the son's testimony about efforts to seek protection contained similar inconsistencies. The applicant had not provided clear and convincing evidence that protection would be inadequate.
firac.conclusion: The state protection finding was reasonable; no reviewable error.

name_verification.name_in_document: Ingram v. Kulynych Estate

defining_issues: Which limitation period governs an equitable trust (constructive trust / unjust enrichment) claim brought against a deceased person's estate — the ten-year period under s. 4 of the Real Property Limitations Act or the two-year period under s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act?
Does a claim for unjust enrichment / constructive trust against an estate constitute a 'wrong' within the meaning of s. 38(2) of the Trustee Act?
Is the respondent's equitable trust claim an 'action to recover any land' within s. 4 of the RPLA?

firac.issue: Which limitation period governs an equitable trust claim against a deceased's estate — the ten-year period under s. 4 of the RPLA or the two-year period under s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act?
firac.facts: Henry Kulynych died in February 2017 leaving his estate to his children; his will left nothing to the respondent, who claimed to have been his common-law partner and to have supported him. She commenced her application in March 2021, more than four years after his death, asserting a constructive/resulting trust and unjust enrichment over the estate assets. The estate trustee had distributed most assets by 2020.
firac.rule: Statutory interpretation seeks legislative intent by reading words in context and harmoniously with the scheme and object of the statute (Canada (Information Commissioner) v. Canada (Minister of National Defence), 2011 SCC 25). Where two limitation periods may apply, Iskenderov, 2023 ONCA 528 directs consideration of historical/legislative purpose, judicial treatment, nature of relief, and statutory language. The presumption of coherence and generalia specialibus non derogant (special legislation prevails over general) apply (R. v. Greenwood (1992)). Standard of review on this pure question of law is correctness (Beaudoin Estate, 2021 ONCA 57).
firac.application: Applying the Iskenderov framework (unavailable to the motion judge), the court reviewed the legislative history and purpose of s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act — its strict two-year cap, inapplicability of discoverability (Waschkowski; Ryan v. Moore), and the policy of prompt, final estate administration (Levesque; Appleyard). The presumption of coherence with the SLRA, FLA, Estates Act and EAA reinforced a short limitation regime for estate claims. The repeal of the former Limitations Act ss. 43-44 trust exemptions showed the legislature intended s. 38(3) to capture all equitable trust claims against estates except discrete RPLA exceptions (express trusts of land, dower). As the more specific provision, s. 38(3) prevails over the general s. 4 RPLA.
firac.conclusion: The two-year limitation period under s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act applies; the ten-year RPLA period does not.

firac.issue: Does an unjust enrichment / constructive trust claim against an estate constitute a 'wrong' under s. 38(2) of the Trustee Act?
firac.facts: The respondent alleged Mr. Kulynych benefited financially at her expense by living rent-free in her home while renting out his own and keeping the income, and sought a constructive/resulting trust over the estate assets on that basis.
firac.rule: A 'wrong' under s. 38(2) is not confined to tort; it covers all actionable wrongs regardless of how framed and is determined by the nature of the injury, not the pleading (Smallman v. Moore, [1948] SCR 295; Roth v. Weston Estate; Bikur Cholim; Lafrance Estate). Unjust enrichment requires a benefit, a corresponding deprivation, and absence of juristic reason (Kerr v. Baranow, 2011 SCC 10), resting on unjust retention of a benefit at another's loss.
firac.application: The motion judge's construction of 'wrong' was too narrow. Unjust enrichment — the unjust retention of a benefit to another's loss — connotes a 'wrong'. The respondent expressly framed her claim as Mr. Kulynych's enrichment 'at her expense', i.e. a wrong to her, remedied by a constructive or resulting trust, falling neatly within s. 38(2).
firac.conclusion: The equitable trust claim is a 'wrong' within s. 38(2) and is therefore subject to the two-year limitation period in s. 38(3).

firac.issue: Is the respondent's equitable trust claim an 'action to recover any land' within s. 4 of the RPLA?
firac.facts: The respondent sought 'an interest in the Estate by virtue of Constructive Trust and Resulting Trust in relation to all estate assets on the basis of contribution of money or money's worth', not merely an interest in the deceased's real property.
firac.rule: Section 4 of the RPLA applies to an 'action to recover any land or rent'. McConnell v. Huxtable, 2014 ONCA 86 held equitable trust claims can be claims to recover land, but did not involve a claim against an estate. Upon death, a deceased's assets vest in the executor and become estate assets (EAA s. 2(1); s. 9(1) vesting after three years).
firac.application: The claim targets all estate assets, not just the Ajax house, and crystallized on death when the assets vested in the estate; it is thus an estate claim, not a claim to recover land. McConnell is distinguishable as it did not concern an estate, and Wilkinson v. Robinson, 2020 ONSC 91 (which applied McConnell to an estate) was wrongly decided for failing to analyze s. 38's history, purpose and judicial treatment.
firac.conclusion: The claim is not an 'action to recover any land' under s. 4 of the RPLA; it is an estate claim governed by s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a civil estates limitations dispute. K054 (wills/estates) is the most specific applicable keyword — the case concerns a claim against a deceased's estate, estate administration, distribution by the estate trustee, and the Trustee Act/SLRA. K006 (Family law) is included as the vocabulary's parent area for K054 and because the claim arose from an alleged common-law spousal relationship and touched dependant support and FLA elections. K049 (marriage/cohabitation agreement) is a borderline/weak pick, engaged only loosely because the claim stemmed from a cohabitation relationship and equitable contribution claims typical of unmarried partners — no actual agreement existed. K014 (standard of review) is a weak/borderline pick reflecting the court's express correctness standard for the pure question of law. The controlled vocabulary is a poor fit for a limitation-period/estates statutory-interpretation case, so several picks are flagged as approximate; there is no vocabulary entry for limitation periods, unjust enrichment or constructive trust.
