name_verification.name_in_document: Doug Collins v. Harry Abrams, British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal, Deputy Chief Commissioner of the British Columbia Human Rights Commission, and Attorney General of British Columbia

defining_issues: Does the British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal have jurisdiction to adjudicate the constitutional validity of s. 7(1)(b) of the Human Rights Code and claims of institutional bias and lack of independence under s. 11(d) of the Charter?

Did the chambers judge err in exercising her discretion under the Judicial Review Procedure Act to remit the constitutional and bias issues to the Tribunal rather than deciding them on judicial review?

firac.issue: Does the B.C. Human Rights Tribunal have jurisdiction to decide the constitutional validity of s. 7(1)(b) of the Human Rights Code and Charter-based claims of institutional bias and lack of independence?
firac.facts: A discrimination complaint was made against Collins and the North Shore News for publishing articles alleged to expose Jewish persons to hatred and contempt. The Tribunal severed and decided that s. 7(1)(b) had been breached, ordering $2,000 compensation. Collins then sought judicial review, arguing the Tribunal could not adjudicate the constitutional validity of the section or the bias/independence issues, which should be decided by the Court.
firac.rule: An administrative tribunal given the power to decide questions of law also has the power to decide the Charter validity of the law it is to apply while discharging its statutory function (Douglas/Kwantlen Faculty Association v. Douglas College, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 570; Tétreault-Gadoury v. Canada (E.I.C.), [1991] 2 S.C.R. 22; Cuddy Chicks Ltd. v. Ontario (LRB), [1991] 2 S.C.R. 5). Jurisdiction is a question of statutory interpretation. Cooper v. Canada (Human Rights Commission), [1996] 3 S.C.R. 854 holds only that a tribunal cannot invalidate a provision that limits its own jurisdiction.
firac.application: The Court held that Cooper did not support the proposition that constitutionality is generally beyond statutory tribunals; it was authority to the contrary. Berscheid was distinguishable and did not establish that a court must always hear declaratory relief. Because the B.C. Human Rights Tribunal is empowered to decide questions of law, it had the power to consider and decide the Charter issues while discharging its statutory function.
firac.conclusion: The chambers judge did not err in holding the Tribunal had jurisdiction to hear and decide the constitutional issues raised.

firac.issue: Did the chambers judge err in exercising her discretion to remit the outstanding constitutional and bias issues to the Tribunal rather than deciding them?
firac.facts: Collins' judicial review application was brought before the Tribunal had held a hearing on the s. 1 justification, jurisdiction, and bias/independence issues. He argued that bringing the matter directly to the Supreme Court would avoid duplication and achieve judicial efficiency; the Attorney General argued the Tribunal was better placed to conduct a full evidentiary hearing, producing a record for any later review.
firac.rule: Under s. 2(2) of the Judicial Review Procedure Act the granting of relief is discretionary. Such discretion must be exercised judicially — considering all relevant factors, excluding irrelevant ones, and reaching a reasonable conclusion.
firac.application: The chambers judge considered judicial efficiency, fragmentation, and the fact that a full evidentiary hearing was required on the constitutional validity, jurisdiction and bias questions that the Tribunal had not yet completed. She reasonably concluded the Tribunal should be given the opportunity to complete its task and generate a record. The Court of Appeal found no error in this exercise of discretion.
firac.conclusion: The chambers judge did not err; the decision to remit the matter to the Tribunal was reasonable.

keywords_rationale: The case turns on administrative law: the jurisdiction of a statutory tribunal and the discretionary exercise on judicial review, so K001 (Administrative law, primary tier 1) and K011 (judicial review) are central; K014 (standard of review/discretion) applies to the reasonableness review of the chambers judge's discretion. K003 (Constitutional law) and K107 (Charter) reflect the tribunal's authority to decide Charter validity and s. 11(d) bias claims. K007 (Human rights) and K119 (Human Rights Code) capture the statutory framework and s. 7(1)(b). K024 (freedom of expression) and K061 (hate speech) reflect the underlying complaint about articles exposing Jewish persons to hatred and contempt, and K093 (Jewish) identifies the targeted group. K014 is a borderline pick since the judgment does not use formal standard-of-review labels, but the appellate deference to discretionary exercise justifies it.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'COURT OF APPEAL FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA' and 'Victoria, B.C.', and the oral reasons were delivered in Victoria.
registry_rationale: The heading expressly states 'Registry: Victoria' and docket 'V03571'.

name_verification.name_in_document: A.M. v. M.S.

defining_issues: Should the March 2016 consent divorce order and/or the April 2015 separation agreement be set aside as significantly unfair under s. 93(5) of the Family Law Act?
What did the requirement that title be transferred 'upon the approval of mortgage' mean — did it require the respondent's approval or only a lender/bank's approval?
Is the claimant entitled to $20,000 in damages for the deposit she lost when the respondent refused to cooperate in the sale of the family property?
Can the court determine the value of the mehr in the Iranian marriage deed on the evidence tendered?
Can the court order both parties to attend before the appropriate authority to complete their agreed Iranian (Sharia) divorce, and does doing so infringe freedom of religion?
Should the existing 60/40 parenting-time arrangement be changed under s. 47 of the FLA?

firac.issue: Should the divorce order and/or separation agreement be set aside as significantly unfair under s. 93(5) of the Family Law Act?
firac.facts: The parties' April 2015 separation agreement was 'rolled into' a March 2016 consent divorce order under which the respondent's interest in the Coquitlam family home was to be transferred to the claimant. Neither document contemplated the 2017 sale of the home, which yielded about $110,000 in equity. The respondent sought to set the agreement aside so he could claim one-half of the sale proceeds, arguing the documents were incomplete and unfair because the property had increased in value.
firac.rule: Section 93 of the FLA permits the Supreme Court to set aside a written agreement respecting property division, including under s. 93(5) where the agreement is 'significantly unfair' considering the passage of time, the intention to achieve certainty, and reliance on the terms; s. 93 applies to agreements, not court orders. Section 214(3) provides that a later order replaces conflicting parts of an agreement. A final property order can be varied only for fraud, duress, a 'slip', or a failure to express the manifest intention of the parties (Pond v. Pond, 2017 BCCA 243; Ting v. Wong, 2015 BCSC 1808). Section 215(2) bars variation of Part 5 property orders except as provided in that Part.
firac.application: The operative document was the divorce order, which s. 93(5) cannot reach because that provision applies only to agreements. The respondent did not rely on fraud, duress or a slip, and there was no evidence of any manifest intention that future increases (or decreases) in the property's value would be shared. That neither document anticipated the later sale did not make them significantly unfair; parties must rearrange their affairs for unforeseen events absent agreement to reopen. No windfall was even established, and the mehr the claimant gave up was part of the consideration.
firac.conclusion: The application to set aside the divorce order and/or separation agreement under s. 93(5) was dismissed; the respondent had no entitlement to a half-share of the sale proceeds.

firac.issue: Did 'approval of mortgage' require the respondent's approval or only a lender's approval?
firac.facts: The divorce order stated title 'will be transferred upon the approval of mortgage of the Claimant', without saying whose approval. The respondent claimed his approval was needed (and later that he had to approve any sale), and asserted a beneficial interest, refusing to sign transfer/sale documents.
firac.rule: Settlement agreements on marriage breakdown must meet contractual formation requirements, though less rigorously, and are interpreted objectively, with resort to genesis, aim and the parties' subsequent conduct where language is unclear (Reid v. Reid, 2011 BCSC 231; Stanbridge v. Stanbridge, 2015 BCSC 1468).
firac.application: Although the order was ambiguous, its genesis — the separation agreement — expressly said the transfer was 'subject to lender(s)/bank(s) approval'. The parties' July 2016 texts showed the respondent accepted the claimant's statement that she had mortgage approval without demanding documents. Third-party affidavits (the realtor and translator) confirmed he treated the home as hers and never mentioned a beneficial interest. Giving one spouse a veto over the other's new home would be a novel and untenable term.
firac.conclusion: The required approval was that of a lender or bank, which the claimant obtained; the respondent's claim to approval rights and to a beneficial interest was dismissed, and the trust funds were ordered released to the claimant.

firac.issue: Is the claimant entitled to $20,000 damages for her lost deposit?
firac.facts: The claimant could no longer afford the mortgage, found an apartment and paid a $20,000 deposit, but lost it when the respondent refused to sign the documents needed to sell the Coquitlam property, insisting the Iranian divorce be completed first. Justice Sharma had initially ordered the $20,000 (later stayed for argument).
firac.rule: A party in breach of an order/agreement is liable for resulting loss; relief against oppressive penalties under s. 24 of the Law and Equity Act (MTK Auto West Ltd. v. Allen, 2003 BCSC 1613) applies only to penalties exceeding actual loss.
firac.application: The respondent was required to permit the transfer/sale once the claimant had mortgage approval and breached that obligation, telling her the deposit 'is not my problem'. The claimant acted reasonably and prudently; the sale was court-ordered, not a unilateral negligent decision. MTK Auto was inapposite because the claimant sought only her actual loss, not a penalty.
firac.conclusion: Damages of $20,000 were awarded against the respondent to restore the claimant to her position had he complied.

firac.issue: Can the court value the mehr on the tendered evidence?
firac.facts: The Sharia marriage deed included a mehr of, inter alia, 5 kg of 24-carat gold. The claimant valued it at $270,000; the respondent at $45,100, relying on a claimed entitlement to discharge it for 110 gold coins. The evidence included a lawyer's affidavit, a Google translation of Iranian law, and online gold prices.
firac.rule: A mehr may be enforceable as a marriage agreement where the evidence supports it (Mohammadi v. Mohammadi, 2016 BCSC 1873; Delvarani; Amlani; N.M.M.). Expert evidence on foreign law must comply with the Supreme Court Family Rules (Part 13); unreliable hearsay/opinion is inadmissible.
firac.application: The respondent's affidavit relied on inadmissible Google-translated hearsay and an unexplained per-coin valuation; the claimant's figure rested on an unverified online source. The $264,900 gap could not be resolved reliably — 'akin to flipping a coin'. Proper expert evidence on Iranian divorce law and gold valuation was required.
firac.conclusion: The court declined to value the mehr and directed that any determination proceed by application supported by expert evidence complying with Part 13.

firac.issue: Can the court order the parties to complete their agreed Iranian divorce, and does this breach freedom of religion?
firac.facts: The parties made an oral April 2015 agreement to obtain a Sharia divorce; both still wanted one, but it had not occurred, largely because the respondent insisted the divorce precede the property transfer. The respondent sought to withdraw his request for an order; the claimant opposed withdrawal.
firac.rule: The religious dimension of a dispute does not make it non-justiciable; a civil agreement to obtain a religious divorce is enforceable by the civil courts (Bruker v. Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54). An oral contract is as enforceable as a written one where its terms are proven (Hik v. Redlick, 2012 BCSC 1684).
firac.application: The parties agreed there was a valid oral civil contract to divorce; both accepted its essential terms. Unlike Bruker, neither challenged jurisdiction and no doctrinal religious issue arose — only completion of an agreed civil obligation. There was no need to weigh religious freedom against democratic values, and ordering attendance did not violate freedom of religion. The claimant faced real prejudice (inability to travel to Iran).
firac.conclusion: The adjournment/withdrawal was refused; both parties were ordered to attend the appropriate Sharia authority to apply for a divorce, unconditionally, the court not itself granting the divorce.

firac.issue: Should the parenting-time arrangement be changed under s. 47 of the FLA?
firac.facts: Under the existing arrangement the claimant had N. about 60% of the time. The respondent sought to reverse it, citing N.'s absences (23.75 days) from French-immersion kindergarten and other concerns.
firac.rule: Under s. 47 of the FLA a parenting order may be changed only if, since it was made, there has been a change in the child's needs or circumstances.
firac.application: N.'s absences were during an illness in late 2016; he had missed no school since February 2017 and his report card was 'glowing'. Any change in circumstances benefited the child. The room-rental concern was reasonably explained.
firac.conclusion: The application to change parenting time was dismissed; the existing arrangement was confirmed, with additional guardianship, exchange, passport and counselling directions.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K049 (marriage/cohabitation agreement) captures the mehr in the Iranian marriage deed and the separation agreement — dowry/mehr is expressly within this concept. K051 (religious divorce) is applied by analogy: the case concerns an agreed Iranian/Sharia divorce and relies squarely on Bruker v. Marcovitz; the vocabulary's religious-divorce keyword is Jewish-centred (get), so this is flagged as an analogical, though central, pick. K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) cover the s. 47 parenting-time dispute over N. K025 (freedom of religion) reflects the court's Bruker analysis of whether ordering a religious divorce infringes s. 2(a) — borderline because the court ultimately found no infringement, but it is a genuinely engaged legal question. K053 (spousal support) is confirmed/continued in the order, a minor but real element. K086 (co-ownership) reflects the jointly owned Coquitlam family home whose transfer and sale drove the property and damages issues.
location_rationale: The header states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA', 'Registry: Vancouver', and gives the place of hearing and judgment as 'Vancouver, B.C.'
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly lists 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: X (Re) — RPD File No. MB4-00921 (claimant name redacted)

defining_issues: Was the claimant credible with respect to the essential elements of his refugee claim?
Does the treatment of Jewish people in Mexico amount to persecution such that the claimant faces a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground?
Does the Article 1E exclusion apply, and must the panel consider the claimant's possible Israeli or Polish citizenship?

firac.issue: Was the claimant credible with respect to the essential elements of his refugee claim?
firac.facts: The claimant, a Mexican citizen who converted to (Messianic) Judaism after learning he was allegedly born in Israel to a Holocaust-survivor mother, alleged extortion, assaults and anti-Semitic threats by criminal groups (Los Pelones, Zetas). His BOC Form contained anachronisms about the age (33 vs 45) at which he learned his heritage, and two amendments added major new allegations, including a denunciation leading to the arrest of a former state governor and a 2007 assault by the Zetas. He returned to Mexico after a 2008 trip to Canada, failed to claim in the United States, and delayed claiming for over 18 months after arriving in Canada.
firac.rule: Under sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA the claimant bears the burden of establishing his claim. A panel may examine the BOC Form both before and after amendments (Villarroel v. M.C.I., 2014 FC 417). Major omissions and inconsistencies, return to the country of alleged persecution, failure to claim at the first opportunity and delay in claiming may support negative credibility inferences.
firac.application: The panel found the amendments were not minor: the conversion date is foundational to the claim and the added denunciation/assault allegations are direct persecution, not cosmetic. The claimant was university-educated, fluent in English, needed no interpreter, and signed a declaration that his BOC was complete and true; his explanations (lawyer error, fear of information-sharing, ignorance of confidentiality) were unsatisfactory. His return to Mexico, adjusting testimony, failure to claim in the US or on re-entry, and the implausible account of border crossings without document checks all undermined credibility.
firac.conclusion: The panel disbelieved the claimant's account of persecution, torture, threats and mistreatment, drawing negative inferences on overall credibility.

firac.issue: Does the treatment of Jewish people in Mexico amount to persecution engaging a Convention ground?
firac.facts: The claimant feared persecution in Mexico because of his Jewish faith. The objective country evidence disclosed anti-Semitic incidents and demonstrations.
firac.rule: To qualify under section 96, there must be a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground; harassment and discrimination falling short of persecution are insufficient.
firac.application: The panel, while condemning anti-Semitic attitudes, found the documented incidents constituted harassment and discrimination rather than persecution. It also found that any assault (Exhibit C-31) reflected a generalized risk faced by other Mexican citizens, not risk tied to the claimant's faith.
firac.conclusion: There was no serious possibility the claimant would face persecution merely because of his Jewish faith on return to Mexico.

firac.issue: Does the Article 1E exclusion apply and must possible Israeli/Polish citizenship be considered?
firac.facts: The Minister intervened seeking exclusion under Article 1E, arguing the claimant, as a Jewish person, could obtain status in Israel. The claimant alleged he was born in Israel to a Jewish, Israeli and Polish mother.
firac.rule: Article 1E of the Refugee Convention excludes persons recognized as having the rights and obligations of nationality in a country where they have established residence.
firac.application: The panel found the claimant never 'established his residence' in Israel, so Article 1E did not apply. Because it disbelieved the underlying account of persecution/risk in Mexico, the panel found it unnecessary to consider whether the claimant could obtain Israeli or Polish citizenship.
firac.conclusion: The Article 1E exclusion did not apply, and consideration of possible Israeli/Polish citizenship was unnecessary.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) capture the sections 96/97 claim and the finding that treatment fell short of persecution. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) reflect the claimant's faith and the anti-Semitic threats and country-condition analysis. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the deciding tribunal (RPD). K077 (inadmissibility) is a weaker pick used to capture the Minister's Article 1E exclusion argument, as there is no dedicated exclusion keyword; it is flagged as borderline since 1E exclusion is not strictly statutory inadmissibility.
location_rationale: The decision states 'Place of hearing: Montréal, Quebec', establishing the hearing city and province.
registry_rationale: The Refugee Protection Division heard the matter in Montréal, Quebec; the file number (MB) and hearing location indicate the Montréal registry of the RPD.

name_verification.name_in_document: XXXX XXXX (claimant) — RPD File No. TB0-17375

defining_issues: Was the claimant a credible witness such that her allegations of anti-Semitic persecution in Russia could be believed?
If a risk existed, was adequate state protection available to the claimant as a Jewish person in Russia, rebutting the claim under ss. 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA?

firac.issue: Was the claimant a credible witness such that her allegations of anti-Semitic persecution in Russia could be believed?
firac.facts: The 83-year-old claimant, a Jewish citizen of Russia, alleged threatening letters, swastika graffiti, and a skinhead attack in 2010 that killed her husband, plus a later assault on herself. Her son acted as Designated Representative. His testimony about the husband's death (attributed by a friend and a doctor to kidney failure) contradicted the murder allegation; no medical report, death-certificate cause, threatening letters, or police documents were produced, and the PIF omitted the alleged approach to the prosecutor's office that the DR later asserted.
firac.rule: Sworn testimony is presumed true unless there is valid reason to doubt it (Maldonado v. Canada (MEI), [1980] 2 F.C. 302 (C.A.)); truthfulness is assessed against the preponderance of probabilities a practical, informed person would recognize as reasonable (Faryna v. Chorny, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 354 (B.C.C.A.)); evidence must be probably, not just possibly, so (Orelien v. Canada (MEI), [1992] 1 F.C. 592 (C.A.)).
firac.application: The panel found the DR's account that the father died of kidney failure and was without refrigeration contradicted the claim that he was murdered by skinheads. Key documents were absent, the PIF omitted the prosecutor's-office complaint central to state protection, and the DR gave vague, shifting answers ('not sure', 'I don't know') and appeared to be filling gaps to bolster the story. The panel concluded the husband died of natural causes and that the threatening letters, graffiti and assaults were fabricated or exaggerated.
firac.conclusion: The claimant and her DR were found not credible; the central allegations of persecution were fabricated or embellished and were not believed.

firac.issue: Was adequate state protection available to the claimant as a Jewish person in Russia, rebutting the claim under ss. 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA?
firac.facts: Documentary evidence showed persistent societal anti-Semitism and inconsistent police responses in Russia, but also a special unit to investigate police abuses, multiple avenues for complaints against police, prosecutions of anti-Semitic acts, hundreds of registered Jewish organizations, and improving conditions especially in Moscow and St. Petersburg.
firac.rule: A claimant must rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence, on a balance of probabilities, that the state would not provide adequate protection (ss. 96 and 97(1), IRPA).
firac.application: The panel preferred the wide-ranging documentary evidence over the discredited testimony, finding that Russia is making serious efforts to combat anti-Semitism and extremism, that oversight bodies exist for police misconduct, and that Jews in larger centres could reasonably expect protection. Even assuming local failures, the claimant did not provide clear and convincing evidence protection would not be forthcoming.
firac.conclusion: State protection was found to be available; the claimant failed to rebut the presumption, and neither a serious possibility of persecution nor a s. 97 risk was established.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 refugee protection and K079 persecution reflect the ss. 96/97 claim of feared persecution. K080 state protection is the determinative ground on which protection is denied. K058 antisemitism and K093 Jewish capture the claimed persecution ground. K038 vandalism (swastika graffiti, desecration) and K122 swastika reflect the specific alleged incidents. K100 Immigration and Refugee Board identifies the deciding tribunal (RPD). K112 (Charter s. 7 / risk to life analog) is borderline — s. 97 concerns risk to life and cruel treatment, though the Charter itself was not argued; it is a weak pick and could be dropped, but reflects the s. 97 risk assessment. Credibility, though central, has no dedicated vocabulary term.
location_rationale: The decision states 'Place of Hearing: Toronto, Ontario', establishing the city and province.
registry_rationale: The Refugee Protection Division is a national tribunal; no distinct court registry is named beyond the hearing location in Toronto, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: [no public name] (RPD File No. TB0-02950)

defining_issues: Did the claimant establish, with credible evidence, past persecution or discrimination amounting to persecution on account of his Roma ethnicity?
Did the claimant demonstrate a genuine subjective fear of persecution given his conduct and delay in departure?
Did the claimant rebut the presumption of state protection available to Roma in Hungary?

firac.issue: Did the claimant establish, with credible evidence, past persecution or discrimination amounting to persecution on account of his Roma ethnicity?
firac.facts: The claimant, a Hungarian Roma, alleged a 2003 ethnically motivated assault (unreported, no medical evidence), police stops in 2006, denial of access to nightclubs/malls/restaurants, and workplace problems. His POE notes, first narrative, and amended narrative contained differing allegations, and no violence was mentioned in his sworn POE evidence.
firac.rule: Sworn testimony is presumed true unless there is valid reason to doubt it (Maldonado v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1980] 2 F.C. 302 (C.A.)); credibility is assessed on a balance of probabilities (Orelien v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1992] 1 F.C. 592 (C.A.)). To amount to persecution, mistreatment must be serious and generally repetitive, persistent or systematic; discrimination does not necessarily equal persecution (UNHCR Handbook, para. 54).
firac.application: The claimant gave inconsistent testimony about why he failed to report the 2003 assault (first blaming 2006 police stops, then recanting), and omitted any violent events from his sworn POE statement. The panel found the assault embellished to bolster the claim. The incidents of discrimination described did not seriously constrain his ability to work, pursue education, or exercise religion, and thus did not reach the threshold of persecution.
firac.conclusion: The claimant failed to establish past persecution or discrimination amounting to persecution with credible evidence.

firac.issue: Did the claimant demonstrate a genuine subjective fear of persecution?
firac.facts: The claimant continued to reside and work at the same location until his departure, delayed leaving for years after the pivotal events, had previously lived and worked in Budapest, and claimed he was too poor to relocate internally while nonetheless saving money to come to Canada.
firac.rule: A Convention refugee must have both a subjective fear and an objectively well-founded fear (Canada (A.G.) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689); absence of the subjective element is itself sufficient for the claim to fail (Kamana v. M.C.I.). The system is not a convenient route to landed status (Urbanek v. M.E.I.).
firac.application: His continued residence, ability to relocate to Canada but not internally, prior time in Budapest, and lengthy delay were inconsistent with genuine subjective fear and more consistent with a long-term relocation plan born of dissatisfaction with life in Hungary rather than a need for international protection.
firac.conclusion: The claimant did not establish a genuine subjective fear of persecution.

firac.issue: Did the claimant rebut the presumption of state protection available to Roma in Hungary?
firac.facts: The claimant never approached the police or any Hungarian institution for any alleged problem and offered no reasonable explanation. Hungary is a functioning multi-party parliamentary democracy with extensive anti-discrimination laws, ombudsman and complaint mechanisms, prosecution of racist attacks, and numerous Roma inclusion programs, though local implementation remains imperfect.
firac.rule: States are presumed capable of protecting citizens; the presumption is rebutted only by clear and convincing proof (Ward). Protection need not be perfect (Zalzali; Villafranca). In a democratic state the onus is proportional to the level of democracy, requiring the claimant to exhaust available avenues (Kadenko). Local failures do not equal state-wide failure unless part of a broader pattern (Zhuravlvev).
firac.application: Given Hungary's democratic institutions, functioning security forces, prosecution of police misconduct and racist murders, and array of protective programs and recourse mechanisms (Equal Treatment Authority, ombudsmen, anti-discrimination legal network), the panel found adequate, operationally effective protection available. The claimant's total failure to seek any domestic protection, without reasonable explanation, meant he did not discharge his onus.
firac.conclusion: The claimant failed to rebut the presumption of state protection; adequate protection is available in Hungary.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the ss. 96/97 IRPA claim. K080 (state protection) is the determinative issue, engaging Ward/Kadenko/Villafranca. K079 (persecution) reflects the credibility and persecution-threshold analysis. K069 (discrimination) covers the finding that discrimination against Roma did not amount to persecution. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the deciding tribunal (RPD). Subjective fear is discussed but has no dedicated keyword, so it maps to persecution/refugee protection.
location_rationale: The decision states 'Place of Hearing: Toronto, Ontario', identifying the city and province where the RPD sat.
registry_rationale: The Refugee Protection Division heard the matter in Toronto, Ontario, which serves as the registry/hearing office for this file (TB0-02950).

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Sears

defining_issues: Does the challenge to the summary conviction appeal judge's decision to hear the appeal by videoconference rather than in person raise a question of law alone warranting leave under s. 839(1) of the Criminal Code?
Does the challenge to the findings on the elements (actus reus and mens rea) of the s. 319(2) offences raise a question of law alone?
Does s. 718.2(a)(i) of the Criminal Code apply to offences under s. 319(2), and did treating hate motivation as aggravating disclose an arguable error of law?
Does the imposition of consecutive sentences on the two counts raise a question of law alone warranting leave to appeal?

firac.issue: Does the challenge to holding the summary conviction appeal by Zoom videoconference raise a question of law alone justifying leave under s. 839(1)?
firac.facts: Because of rising COVID-19 infections in Toronto, the case management judge (Akhtar J.) directed that the self-represented applicant's summary conviction appeal proceed by Zoom over his objection that he was entitled to an in-person hearing per a Notice to Profession. A short adjournment was granted, the applicant participated throughout, and his ineffective-assistance-of-counsel claim was heard and dismissed.
firac.rule: Under s. 839(1) Criminal Code a second-level summary conviction appeal lies to the Court of Appeal only, with leave, 'on any ground that involves a question of law alone'; leave principles are set out in R. v. Lam, 2016 ONCA 850 and R. v. R.R., 2008 ONCA 497. Sections 683(2.1) and 822(1) empower a summary conviction appeal court to order appearance by videoconference. A challenge to a procedural decision made within jurisdiction does not raise a question of law alone: R. v. Bresnark, 2013 ONCA 110.
firac.application: The applicant did not dispute the power to order a videoconference, only its exercise given the Notice to Profession. A challenge to a discretionary procedural decision within jurisdiction is not a question of law alone. Even if characterized as a procedural fairness breach, the merits were very weak: the order responded to unique public-health conditions and the feared prejudice (viva voce evidence/cross-examination on ineffective assistance) did not materialize, as that claim was heard and not appealed. The issue had no significance beyond the case.
firac.conclusion: The ground did not meet even a relaxed application of the R.R. principles; leave refused on this ground.

firac.issue: Does the challenge to the trial judge's findings on the elements of the s. 319(2) offences raise a question of law alone?
firac.facts: The 22 issues of 'Your Ward News' (Exhibit 2) were treated by the trial judge as direct evidence of the statements from which he inferred intent to promote hatred against Jews and women. The Appeal Judge affirmed, finding the trial judge applied R. v. Keegstra and correctly treated the publications as direct evidence, consistent with R. v. Villaroman.
firac.rule: On a second appeal only questions of law alone may be advanced (s. 839(1)); the governing principles for the offence are in R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697 (mens rea usually inferred from the statements made), and circumstantial-evidence reasoning is governed by R. v. Villaroman, 2016 SCC 33. The leave judge assesses whether the summary conviction appeal judge properly applied appellate review principles.
firac.application: The Appeal Judge correctly identified the scope of review, the Keegstra and Villaroman principles, and found ample evidence supporting the trial judge's findings. The applicant identified no error of law; he merely repeated disagreement with how the law was applied to the facts, which is fact-focused.
firac.conclusion: The ground does not engage a question of law alone; leave refused.

firac.issue: Does s. 718.2(a)(i) apply to s. 319(2) offences and did its use disclose an arguable legal error?
firac.facts: The trial judge treated hate motivation under s. 718.2(a)(i) as an aggravating factor. The applicant argued the provision was intended only for violent crimes against individuals and should not 'redundify' s. 319, relying on Parliamentary debate.
firac.rule: Statutory interpretation is a question of law of general significance. Section 718.2(a)(i) applies to all Criminal Code offences and states no exception. Characterizing an element of the offence as an aggravating factor can be reviewable error (R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64; R. v. Adan, 2019 ONCA 709), but courts have found no error where statutory aggravating factors overlap with offence elements (Tejeda-Rosario; B.S.; S.C.W.; J.A.S.); appellate intervention still requires impact on the sentence.
firac.application: The provision on its face admits no exception and the applicant offered no plausible interpretive argument. Even reframed as double-counting an element, the Appeal Judge found the sentence not demonstrably unfit, and no arguable error of law was shown in that review.
firac.conclusion: The ground fails the R.R. principles; leave refused.

firac.issue: Does the imposition of consecutive six-month sentences on the two counts raise a question of law alone?
firac.facts: The trial judge imposed maximum consecutive sentences, relying on R. v. Gummer, finding hatred against women and against Jews involved separate legally-protected interests promoted over three years across many issues. The Appeal Judge upheld this, deferring absent an error in principle or demonstrably unfit sentence.
firac.rule: Sentencing decisions attract deference absent an error in principle or a demonstrably unfit sentence. Whether offences warrant consecutive or concurrent sentences turns on the closeness of the nexus between them — a fact-specific inquiry (Ruby, Sentencing, 10th ed., §14.18; R. v. Gummer).
firac.application: The Appeal Judge correctly identified the review principles; the applicant identified no jurisprudential conflict. Whether the offences were sufficiently distinct to justify consecutive sentences is a fact-specific inquiry, not a question of law alone.
firac.conclusion: The ground does not amount to a question of law alone; leave refused.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area. K067 (wilful promotion of hatred) and K115 (Criminal Code s. 319(2)) capture the substantive convictions, with K061 (hate speech) as the broader doctrine. K060 (hate motivation) reflects the disputed s. 718.2(a)(i) aggravating-factor sentencing ground. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) reflect that one identifiable group targeted was Jews. K012 (procedural fairness) covers the contested videoconference/mode-of-hearing ground. K063 (online hate/social media) is a slightly weaker pick reflecting that Your Ward News was distributed online as well as in print. No leave-to-appeal-specific keyword exists in the vocabulary; the procedural nature is captured through K012.
location_rationale: The decision is styled 'COURT OF APPEAL FOR ONTARIO', establishing the province as Ontario. No city is stated for the court's sitting; the hearing was held 'by video conference'. References to Toronto relate to where 'Your Ward News' was distributed, not the court's location, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: No registry office is identified in the decision beyond the Court of Appeal for Ontario docket numbers (M52559 & M52561); registry left null.
