name_verification.name_in_document: Ryan Richards v. Correctional Service Canada

defining_issues: Should the impugned portions of the complainant's and Commission's Statements of Particulars be struck on a preliminary basis as being beyond the scope of the complaints referred to the Tribunal?
Should the Commission's proposed expert witness be prevented from providing evidence on the basis that racial and systemic discrimination evidence exceeds the scope of the complaints?

firac.issue: Should the impugned portions of the SOPs be struck as being beyond the scope of the complaints?
firac.facts: CSC moved to strike passages of Ryan Richards' SOP and Amended SOP and the Commission's Amended SOP dealing with security classification, systemic mistreatment of Black and Muslim inmates, and related public-interest remedies, arguing they lacked a sufficient nexus with the three joined complaints (grounded principally in religious discrimination) and were disproportionate. The complaints, referred by the Commission without any stated scope limitation, alleged discrimination on grounds of religion, sex, race, colour and disability, plus harassment and retaliation. CSC never sought judicial review of the referral decisions.
firac.rule: Under ss. 49, 50(1)-(2) and 48.9 CHRA the Tribunal inquires into complaints referred by the Commission and must give each party a full and ample opportunity to be heard. The Tribunal may determine or amend the scope of a complaint and strike portions of an SOP that exceed it (Connors; Postmasters Association), but the power to strike on a preliminary basis is exercised cautiously and only in the 'clearest of cases' (Desmarais; Buffet). The test is whether the impugned particulars have a reasonable nexus or connection to the complaints, examined together with the Commission's referral letters (AA; Casler; Gaucher). Human rights legislation is quasi-constitutional and interpreted broadly, and intersecting grounds must be considered together (s. 3.1 CHRA; Turner v. Canada; Moore).
firac.application: Reviewing the three joined complaints globally and purposively together with the referral letters, the Tribunal found real references to racial and systemic mistreatment of Black and Muslim inmates, including security classification, discipline, use of force and diet issues. The impugned particulars, though including newer and ongoing instances, flowed from and were sufficiently linked to the essence of the complaints and elaborated, particularized and updated them. Systemic allegations are notoriously difficult to prove and appropriately supported by context. The Quebec courts' adjudication of a single security-classification decision did not oust the Tribunal's authority, and the availability of the CCRA process did not either, since the CHRA is quasi-constitutional and the Commission had declined the s. 41(1) diversion. CSC's credibility and proportionality arguments could not be resolved without a hearing, and CSC had not shown unfairness, prejudice or surprise. Requests to strike public-interest remedies were premature (s. 53(2) CHRA; Emmett).
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal declined to strike any of the impugned portions of the SOPs; a sufficient nexus existed and this was not one of the clearest of cases warranting a preliminary strike.

firac.issue: Should the Commission be prevented from calling its proposed expert witness on the basis the evidence exceeds the scope of the complaints?
firac.facts: The Commission gave notice it would call Dr. Akwasi Owusu-Bempah to testify on institutional discipline, use of force, security classification, segregation, restrictive confinement and culturally relevant programming and their impacts on federally incarcerated Black inmates. CSC sought to exclude the evidence as disproportionate and lacking a nexus, especially where no racial discrimination had been proven.
firac.rule: Admissibility of expert evidence is governed by the White Burgess/Mohan framework (relevance, necessity, absence of exclusionary rule, properly qualified expert, then a cost-benefit discretion) (Christoforou; White Burgess). Systemic evidence may support an individual discrimination claim and there is no requirement to prove individual discrimination before adducing systemic evidence (Moore; Desmarais).
firac.application: The Tribunal had not yet received the expert report and it was inappropriate to conduct a substantive review of the merits at a preliminary stage. The proposed testimony related directly to the referred allegations of racial and systemic discrimination and could assist the inquiry into whether alleged personal discrimination against Mr. Richards resulted from systemic problems. Allowing delivery of the report did not mean the Tribunal accepted or would rely on it; admissibility and relevance would be tested at the hearing where CSC could challenge it and lead rebuttal evidence.
firac.conclusion: CSC's request to exclude the expert evidence was premature and was dismissed; the report may be delivered, with admissibility to be determined at the hearing.

keywords_rationale: K007 (Human rights) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case arises under the CHRA before the CHRT. K072 (human rights tribunal) captures the adjudicative forum and its procedural powers. K069 (discrimination) and K074 (systemic discrimination) are central, as the dispute turns on whether individual and systemic discrimination allegations fall within the complaints. K065 (racism) reflects the racial-discrimination allegations against Black inmates that CSC sought to exclude. K012 (procedural fairness) is engaged by CSC's fairness/proportionality arguments and the s. 50(1) full-and-ample-opportunity standard. K031 (religious accommodation) reflects the Muslim religious-diet and worship accommodation allegations. K083 (harassment) reflects the harassment ground pleaded in the complaints. Weaker/borderline picks: K031 and K083 are contextual grounds rather than the ruling's focus, which was scope and procedure; judicial review was mentioned only as the route CSC failed to take, so no K011 was added.
location_rationale: The ruling is signed 'Edward P. Lustig, Tribunal Member, Ottawa, Ontario, August 14, 2020', identifying the seat as Ottawa, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The Canadian Human Rights Tribunal is a national tribunal that does not operate through provincial registries; the decision identifies only Tribunal file numbers (T2218/4017, T2282/3718, T2395/5419) and no registry office, so registry is left null.

name_verification.discrepancy_note: No public style of cause exists; this is a private (huis clos) refugee appeal identified only by RAD file numbers VB9-07285 and VB9-07286, which match the supplied citation.

defining_issues: Should the tendered new evidence be admitted under s. 110(4) IRPA and should an oral hearing be held under s. 110(6)?
Did the RPD commit a procedural fairness error by not resuming the hearing?
Was the RPD's rejection of the parents' claim tainted by homophobia, and can family unification / humanitarian considerations ground refugee protection?
Did the RPD correctly find no prospective risk of persecution or s. 97 risk on return to Russia?

firac.issue: Should the tendered new evidence be admitted under s. 110(4) IRPA and should an oral hearing be held under s. 110(6)?
firac.facts: The unrepresented Appellants filed several documents post-dating the August 27, 2019 RPD rejection: letters from themselves and their son, a physician's letter, a case manager's letter, an employment letter, and a psychiatric/disability application concerning their son. They also asked for an oral hearing without explaining the basis.
firac.rule: Section 110(4) IRPA permits only evidence arising after, not reasonably available before, or that could not reasonably have been expected to be presented at the rejection; the Singh and Raza tests of newness, credibility and relevance also apply. Rule 29 requires an explanation of how the evidence meets s. 110(4). An oral hearing under s. 110(6) requires admitted new evidence raising a serious credibility issue central to and determinative of the claim.
firac.application: Most documents post-dated the rejection and met the criteria, so the panel admitted them, exercising leniency given the Appellants were unrepresented; the employment letter was excluded as irrelevant. Because none of the admitted new evidence raised a serious determinative credibility issue, the s. 110(6) threshold for an oral hearing was not met.
firac.conclusion: All new evidence except the employment letter was admitted; no oral hearing was held.

firac.issue: Did the RPD commit a procedural fairness error by failing to resume the hearing?
firac.facts: The Appellants claimed the July 30, 2019 hearing was to resume August 20, 2019 but never did, and they were not notified. In fact the RPD had directed counsel to research the Principal Appellant's possible Ukrainian status and file written submissions by August 20; counsel filed them August 7-8, 2019.
firac.rule: Procedural fairness in RPD proceedings; a party must have been misled or denied an opportunity to be heard.
firac.application: The recording showed no resumption of the hearing was ever discussed or scheduled; the August 20 date was a written-submission deadline, which counsel met early. The Appellants, though represented and fully interpreted at the hearing, simply misunderstood the proceedings.
firac.conclusion: No procedural fairness error occurred.

firac.issue: Was the RPD decision tainted by homophobia, and can family unification or humanitarian considerations ground refugee protection?
firac.facts: The Appellants argued the RPD ignored that their refugee-recognized gay son cannot live without their care and that its decision was distorted by homophobia; they stressed their inseparability from their son.
firac.rule: Refugee protection under ss. 96 and 97 IRPA requires a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or, on a balance of probabilities, s. 97 risk. Family unification is one IRPA objective but not a governing factor in ss. 96/97 determinations (Akinfolajimi 2018 FC 722; Douillard 2019 FC 390); the RPD/RAD cannot decide on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.
firac.application: However difficult the family's situation, dependence of an adult son and the desire to remain together are humanitarian considerations outside the RPD's and RAD's mandate. Recognizing these limits reflected the statutory scope, not homophobia.
firac.conclusion: No homophobia was shown; family unification/H&C considerations cannot ground refugee protection.

firac.issue: Did the RPD correctly find no prospective risk of persecution or s. 97 risk on return to Russia?
firac.facts: The Principal Appellant said he was perceived as an LGBT supporter, lost work after hosting an injured gay activist, held anti-Putin views, refused to vote, and is a Jew of Ukrainian origin. A Jewish Family Services letter asserted relatives of homosexuals are persecuted in Russia.
firac.rule: A claimant must show more than a mere possibility of persecution (s. 96) or, on a balance of probabilities, s. 97 risk; discrimination by a single employer does not amount to persecution; assertions must be supported by objective country documentation.
firac.application: The National Documentation Package did not corroborate that family members of LGBT persons face persecution; loss of a single job was discrimination, not persecution; the Principal Appellant had no public anti-Putin profile despite 20 years of the regime and had faced no consequences; and the son who owned the business linked to the activist had left Russia for the U.S., reducing any perceived LGBT association.
firac.conclusion: The RPD correctly found no prospective risk; the Appellants face neither a serious possibility of persecution nor s. 97 risk.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 refugee protection and K075 convention refugee capture the ss. 96/97 determination at the heart of the appeal, and K079 persecution reflects the determinative prospective-risk analysis. K012 procedural fairness is engaged by the alleged RPD hearing-resumption error. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) reflects the RPD/RAD institutional context. K093 (Jewish) is a weaker, tier-3 pick included because the Principal Appellant's Jewish and Ukrainian origins were raised as contributing factors, though they were not developed and are borderline.
location_rationale: The decision states 'Appeal considered / heard at Ottawa, ON', establishing the city as Ottawa and the province as Ontario.
registry_rationale: The Refugee Appeal Division is a national tribunal and no separate registry office is named beyond the RAD file numbers; left null.

case_name: Deline v. Vancouver Talmud Torah Association

name_verification.name_in_document: Deline v. Vancouver Talmud Torah Association

defining_issues: Does the plaintiff's proposed defamation pleading state a reasonable cause of action against VTT and the proposed additional defendants such that leave to amend and join them should be granted?
Should VTT's application for summary judgment dismissing the negligence action be granted on the basis that VTT owed the plaintiff no duty of care?

firac.issue: Should leave be granted to amend the pleadings to add a defamation claim and join additional defendants, or is the proposed pleading deficient for failing to state a reasonable cause of action?
firac.facts: Mr. Deline, a self-employed chess instructor, sought leave to add a defamation claim against VTT, Ms. Lowenstein, Ms. Shecter, and four unknown persons, centred on reports allegedly made to the Vancouver Police Department. The proposed pleading referred generally to 'a pattern of misconduct' and cross-referenced paragraphs 14, 19, 20 and 23 of the existing pleading, none of which specified whether the alleged communications were oral or written, or whether the claim was for libel or slander, and did not properly plead special damages.
firac.rule: Leave to amend should be granted where the proposed pleading states a reasonable cause of action; a claim fails only if it is plain and obvious it has no reasonable chance of success (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42). Defamation pleadings are technical and must specify the publication, the words published, the time, place and manner of publication, and to whom it was made (Christian Advocacy Society v. Arthur, 2013 BCSC 1542; Nu Fibre Inc. v. Ishkanian, 2013 BCSC 1255). Libel (written) is actionable per se; slander (spoken) requires proof and pleading of special damages unless the words are actionable per se (Libel and Slander Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 263, s. 2; Brown on Defamation).
firac.application: The proposed paragraph 47's reference to a 'pattern of misconduct' did not meet defamation pleading requirements. Paragraphs 19 and 23 did not properly plead defamatory communications to a third party. Paragraphs 14 and 20 identified VTT as publisher and VPD as recipient with dates but failed to state whether the communications were oral or written and did not identify the claim as libel or slander — a fatal deficiency. If slander, no proper special damages were pleaded, since the investigator and lawyer expenses had nothing to do with what was said to the VPD. The email of April 7 relied on to found claims against Lowenstein and the Doe defendants was not defamatory, and Shecter's alleged misrepresentations were not themselves pleaded as defamatory communications. The deficiencies were fundamental, going to the existence of a cause of action, not merely the exact words, so no further chance to plead was warranted, especially as Mr. Deline said he could pursue a separate action.
firac.conclusion: The proposed pleading did not state a reasonable cause of action against VTT or any proposed defendant; leave to amend and join the defendants was refused.

firac.issue: Did VTT owe Mr. Deline a duty of care obliging it to inform him of the one-digit telephone number discrepancy, such that the negligence action should proceed?
firac.facts: In July 2016 Mr. Deline declined to provide chess instruction and offered, without obligation, to try to find a replacement. VTT independently retained Mr. Chan. In January 2017 Mr. Deline raised concerns about Mr. Chan, showing Ms. Shecter a text he wrongly believed came from Mr. Chan; Ms. Shecter noticed the one-digit phone discrepancy and confirmed Mr. Chan had not sent it. Mr. Deline claimed VTT negligently failed to promptly advise him of the discrepancy, causing him loss including forensic investigator fees.
firac.rule: On a summary judgment application under Supreme Court Civil Rule 9-6, the court reviews the evidence to determine whether the plaintiff is bound to lose, without weighing evidence beyond incontrovertible facts (Beach Estate v. Beach, 2019 BCCA 277; Canada v. Lameman, 2008 SCC 14). A negligence claim requires a duty of care, which depends on a recognized legal relationship or sufficient proximity.
firac.application: The correspondence showed Mr. Deline had not contracted with VTT nor been appointed its agent; he merely volunteered to try to find a replacement. By January 2017 any such role was spent, and Mr. Chan had been retained independently. When Mr. Deline raised his concerns he was not assisting VTT but trying to persuade it to terminate Mr. Chan. The parties were strangers in law with no recognized relationship, so VTT owed no duty to correct unsolicited communications. Even if a duty existed, it was satisfied by Ms. Lowenstein's April 7 email confirming Mr. Chan did not send the text; Mr. Deline was an independent adult, not a child under instruction.
firac.conclusion: VTT owed no duty of care; the negligence claim was legally misconceived, bound to fail, and was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a civil action involving negligence and defamation pleading/procedure. K015 (defamation) directly engages the proposed defamation claim and the extensive analysis of libel/slander pleading requirements. K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) apply because the defendant is a Jewish day school (Vancouver Talmud Torah Association) and the underlying text message concerned 'Jewish schooling.' There is no closer keyword for negligence/duty of care or for summary judgment/pleading amendments in the vocabulary, so only four strong picks exist; the entity keywords are somewhat peripheral to the legal reasoning but reflect the parties involved.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Registry: Vancouver' and lists the place of hearing and judgment as 'Vancouver, B.C.' The court is the Supreme Court of British Columbia, so the province is British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

case_name: Christian Medical and Dental Society of Canada v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario

name_verification.name_in_document: The Christian Medical and Dental Society of Canada v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario

defining_issues: What standard of review and analytical framework (Doré/Loyola or Oakes) applies to the constitutional challenge to the College's policies?
Do the effective referral requirements infringe physicians' freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
Do the effective referral requirements infringe physicians' equality rights under s. 15(1) of the Charter?
If the effective referral requirements infringe s. 2(a), are they justified under s. 1 of the Charter?

firac.issue: What standard of review and analytical framework (Doré/Loyola or Oakes) applies to the constitutional challenge to the College's policies?
firac.facts: The College enacted two policies requiring objecting physicians to make an 'effective referral.' The appellants challenged the constitutionality of the policies of general application, rather than individual decisions. The Divisional Court applied a correctness standard and the Oakes framework; the College argued for reasonableness and the Doré/Loyola framework.
firac.rule: Housen v. Nikolaisen governs appellate review; questions of law are reviewed for correctness. The Oakes framework (R. v. Oakes) applies to laws of general application, while the Doré/Loyola framework applies to administrative decisions engaging the Charter. The purpose of both frameworks is to determine whether the measure unreasonably limits Charter rights (Doré, at para. 6).
firac.application: The parties agreed the outcome was unaffected by the choice of framework, since both ask whether the policies unreasonably limit Charter rights. The court declined to definitively resolve which framework applied, applying the Oakes framework chosen by the Divisional Court while noting it would reach the same result under a reasonableness standard and the Doré/Loyola framework.
firac.conclusion: The court left the standard of review question for another day, applying the Oakes framework as the Divisional Court had, and confirming the result would be the same under Doré/Loyola.

firac.issue: Do the effective referral requirements infringe physicians' freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
firac.facts: The individual appellants sincerely believe human life is sacred, that abortion and MAiD are sinful, and that providing an effective referral makes them complicit in those procedures and is equally sinful. Sincerity of belief and interference were conceded; the College argued the interference was trivial or insubstantial.
firac.rule: The two-part test from Trinity Western (2018 SCC 32) and Amselem: (1) the claimant sincerely believes in a practice with a nexus to religion; and (2) the impugned state conduct interferes in a more than trivial or insubstantial manner with the ability to act in accordance with that belief. Freedom of religion is internally limited but contextual limits generally belong in the s. 1 analysis.
firac.application: With sincerity and interference conceded, the only question was triviality. The court held the contextual features the College raised (regulated profession, single-payer system, gatekeeper role) belong to the s. 1 analysis, not the delineation of the right. Given the centrality of the appellants' beliefs and that at least some appellants could not practice medicine in accordance with those beliefs, the interference was neither trivial nor insubstantial. The court declined to rule on freedom of conscience given the insufficient evidentiary record and the religion-grounded nature of the claim.
firac.conclusion: The effective referral requirements infringe the appellants' s. 2(a) freedom of religion; the interference is more than trivial or insubstantial. The freedom of conscience argument was not decided.

firac.issue: Do the effective referral requirements infringe physicians' equality rights under s. 15(1) of the Charter?
firac.facts: The appellants argued the policies impose a burden on religious physicians not imposed on others, forcing them to give up direct patient care rather than sacrifice their beliefs. The policies apply to all conscientious objectors, whether religious or secular.
firac.rule: The two-part test from Kahkewistahaw First Nation v. Taypotat: (1) whether the law creates a distinction on an enumerated or analogous ground; and (2) whether the law imposes burdens or denies benefits in a manner that reinforces, perpetuates or exacerbates disadvantage, perpetuating arbitrary disadvantage.
firac.application: Without deciding whether a distinction on religion existed, the court held the second branch was not met. The policies represent an attempt to balance equitable access to care with physicians' beliefs; they do not reinforce, perpetuate or exacerbate disadvantage, promote prejudice, restrict access to a fundamental social institution, or impede full membership in Canadian society. Physicians who find the Fact Sheet options unacceptable can transition to other areas of medicine.
firac.conclusion: The effective referral requirements do not infringe s. 15(1). The appeal on this ground was dismissed.

firac.issue: If the effective referral requirements infringe s. 2(a), are they justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The policies aim to facilitate equitable patient access to health care, including MAiD, abortion and reproductive services, given physicians' gatekeeper role in a single-payer system. Vulnerable patients depend on family physicians as navigators. The appellants proposed a 'generalized information'/self-referral model as a less impairing alternative.
firac.rule: The Oakes framework: the limit must be prescribed by law; the objective must be pressing and substantial; and the means must be proportionate (rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality of salutary and deleterious effects). A reasoned apprehension of harm may suffice (Harper); the government need not choose the least restrictive means, only one within a range of reasonable alternatives (RJR-MacDonald; Hutterian Brethren; Irwin Toy).
firac.application: The policies were prescribed by law (Greater Vancouver Transportation Authority). The objective—equitable patient access to health care—was pressing and substantial, addressing a real risk of deprivation for vulnerable populations. There was a rational connection given physicians' gatekeeper function. On minimal impairment, the appellants' generalized information/self-referral model was fatally flawed because it was directed at protecting physicians' rights rather than advancing equitable access, and would compromise the objective by leaving vulnerable patients to navigate the system alone (as in Hutterian Brethren). Other jurisdictions' policies were not shown to be less impairing and equally effective, and deference was owed to the College's institutional expertise. On balancing, patients' interests (engaging s. 7) prevailed; physicians have no right to practice medicine and can restructure their practice; the salutary effects outweighed the deleterious effects even taking the burden at its most onerous.
firac.conclusion: Any infringement of s. 2(a) is justified under s. 1. The effective referral requirements are reasonable limits demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. Appeal dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns on Charter analysis. K025 (freedom of religion) is central—the s. 2(a) infringement finding. K023 (equality rights) captures the s. 15(1) claim. K030 (reasonable limits/Oakes test) is core to the dispositive s. 1 analysis. K010 (Doré/Loyola framework) and K014 (standard of review) reflect the contested framework/standard issue. K013 (professional discipline) applies as the College is the self-governing medical regulator whose binding policies were at issue. K011 (judicial review) is engaged as the constitutional review of the policies. K042 (code of conduct) fits the College's normative policy statements/professional standards. K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) precisely identifies the operative provision. Religious accommodation (K031) was considered but the court framed the analysis under s. 1 rather than statutory accommodation, so it was omitted as weaker.
location_rationale: The decision is of the Court of Appeal for Ontario, which sits in Toronto. Evidence and affidavits reference Toronto institutions (Women's College Hospital in Toronto, Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre in Toronto). Province is Ontario, as the appeal is from the Ontario Divisional Court and concerns the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.
registry_rationale: No specific court registry office is stated in the decision beyond the docket number (C65397); the Court of Appeal for Ontario does not identify a separate registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor

defining_issues: Does s. 13(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act, prohibiting repeated telephonic communication of matter likely to expose persons to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground, infringe the guarantee of freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter?
If s. 13(1) infringes s. 2(b), is it a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter (including whether it is a 'limit prescribed by law' given alleged vagueness)?
Is the Tribunal's cease and desist order unconstitutionally vague, and can the appellants avoid a contempt finding by attacking the order collaterally?
Was the Tribunal's order invalid for reasonable apprehension of bias arising from the Commission's appointment of the tribunal, and did the appellants waive that objection?

firac.issue: Does s. 13(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act infringe freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter?
firac.facts: The appellants operated a Toronto telephone service delivering pre-recorded messages denigrating Jewish people, found by the Tribunal to constitute a discriminatory practice under s. 13(1). Section 13(1) prohibits repeated telephonic communication of matter likely to expose persons to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground.
firac.rule: Under Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (Attorney General), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 927, any activity conveying or attempting to convey a meaning through a non-violent form has expressive content within s. 2(b); s. 2(b) protects all content regardless of message. The guarantee is infringed where the government's purpose is to restrict expressive activity. The Irwin Toy violence exception applies only to physical violence.
firac.application: Telephonic communication of matter inherently conveys meaning, and Parliament's purpose in enacting s. 13(1) was expressly to restrict such expression by censuring particular conveyances of meaning. Hate propaganda is not excluded from s. 2(b) on a content basis, and the violence exception extends only to physical violence, not analogous expression. The point was conceded by the Commission.
firac.conclusion: Section 13(1) infringes s. 2(b); the protected activity falls within freedom of expression (unanimous on this point).

firac.issue: Is s. 13(1) a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
firac.facts: Section 13(1) uses the terms 'hatred or contempt,' contains no intent requirement, provides no defence of truth, and can reach private telephone communications. It operates within a conciliatory human rights scheme, with imprisonment possible only through a contempt order following a filed cease and desist order.
firac.rule: R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103 requires a pressing and substantial objective and proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionate effects); the limit must first be 'prescribed by law.' Context and ss. 15 and 27 of the Charter and international instruments (ICCPR Art. 20, CERD Art. 4) inform the analysis, per Keegstra.
firac.application: The Court unanimously held s. 13(1) is sufficiently precise to be 'prescribed by law.' The majority (Dickson C.J.) found the objective of preventing harm from hate propaganda pressing and substantial, magnified by ss. 15 and 27 and international commitments; 'hatred or contempt' refers only to extreme detestation and vilification; the absence of intent is justified by human rights law's focus on effects; imprisonment only follows an intentional breach of a filed order; the lack of a truth defence and reach to telephone use are acceptable given the conciliatory scheme. The dissent (McLachlin J.) found s. 13(1) overbroad and vague, lacking rational connection and minimal impairment, catching much defensible speech, with no truth defence or freedom-of-expression safeguard, thus failing proportionality.
firac.conclusion: Majority: s. 13(1) is justified under s. 1 and is constitutional. Dissent (La Forest, Sopinka, McLachlin JJ.): s. 13(1) is not justified and is invalid.

firac.issue: Is the Tribunal's cease and desist order unconstitutionally vague, and may the appellants attack it collaterally in contempt proceedings?
firac.facts: The Tribunal ordered the appellants to cease communicating 'the subject matter which has formed the contents of the tape-recorded messages.' The appellants argued this was too vague to support a contempt finding and that the unconstitutionality of s. 13(1) invalidated the order.
firac.rule: The test for vagueness of an order is whether its intention and import are ascertainable to a person of average intelligence reading it in good faith. An order of a court must be obeyed while it remains in force regardless of alleged flaws; it must be challenged by due process, not disobeyed (Canada Metal Co. v. CBC (No. 2); R.J. Sharpe, Injunctions and Specific Performance).
firac.application: Read with the Tribunal's expansive reasons, the order clearly identified the enjoined subject matter (messages exposing Jews to hatred or contempt). The appellants could have had no bona fide doubt about what was prohibited. Even the dissent, which found s. 13(1) invalid, held the order remained valid for contempt purposes until quashed effective the date of judgment, so invalidity was no defence to the contempt citation.
firac.conclusion: The order was not unconstitutionally vague; the majority upheld the contempt findings, and the dissent likewise affirmed the convictions (reducing Taylor's sentence to three months).

firac.issue: Was the Tribunal's order invalid for reasonable apprehension of bias, and did the appellants waive the objection?
firac.facts: The Tribunal was appointed by the Commission, which investigated, substantiated and prosecuted the complaint. The appellants raised bias for the first time before the Federal Court of Appeal, nearly eight years after the Tribunal's order.
firac.rule: Bias must be alleged at the earliest practical opportunity; failure to do so amounts to implied waiver (In re Human Rights Tribunal and Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd., [1986] 1 F.C. 103), distinguishing MacBain v. Lederman, [1985] 1 F.C. 856 where bias was raised at the outset.
firac.application: The appellants participated in the proceedings for years without raising bias, raising it only on appeal. This constituted implied waiver. Moreover, they had not directly challenged the order but sought to attack it collaterally in contempt, which is impermissible.
firac.conclusion: The apprehension-of-bias argument was rejected; the objection was waived (unanimous).

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally a Charter freedom-of-expression challenge, so K003 (Constitutional law, tier-1) and K024 (freedom of expression, s. 2(b)) are central, with K111 pinpointing Charter s. 2(b). K061 (hate speech) captures the subject matter—telephonic hate propaganda against Jews. K030 (reasonable limits, s. 1/Oakes) is core to the majority/dissent split on justification. The provision at issue is s. 13(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act, so K007 (Human rights, tier-1) and K072 (human rights tribunal/commission) apply, and K093 (Jewish) reflects the targeted group. K012 (procedural fairness) covers the apprehension-of-bias/waiver issue argued as an administrative-law point. K107 identifies the Charter as the governing statute. Borderline: K007 competes with K003 as the primary area, but the impugned instrument is human-rights legislation; K012 is a secondary but genuinely contested issue.
location_rationale: The decision is a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, which sits in Ottawa, Ontario. Although the text does not expressly state 'Ottawa', it is the seat of the SCC; the appeal was 'on appeal from the federal court of appeal.'
registry_rationale: No court registry is stated in the decision. As an SCC appeal, no registry office is identified (File No. 20462 is the Court's docket number, not a registry).

name_verification.name_in_document: Steven McKee v. Honourable Mike Farnworth

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff's notice of civil claim be struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action and as frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process?
Should leave to amend be denied and the action dismissed in its entirety?
Was a lump-sum costs award appropriate?

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's notice of civil claim be struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action and as frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process?
firac.facts: Self-represented plaintiff Steven McKee filed a notice of civil claim against the Honourable Mike Farnworth seeking $50,000,000, pleading as 'facts' definitions of words like 'mandate', 'dictatorship' and 'tyrant', news stories about mandates, and examples of tyrants, and asserting as its legal basis that Canadian law enforcement enforced mask/vaccination 'rules that are not laws'. He explained his purpose was to 'make a statement' that vaccine passports amount to a dictatorship.
firac.rule: Under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules, a claim may be struck where it is 'plain and obvious', assuming the pleaded facts are true, that it discloses no reasonable cause of action, has no reasonable prospect of success or is certain to fail (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 SCR 959; R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42). A pleading is frivolous, vexatious or unnecessary where it does not establish a cause of action, advances no claim known in law, cannot succeed, or wastes the court's time and public resources (Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083; Mohebbi v. North Vancouver RCMP, 2015 BCSC 2083).
firac.application: Master Robertson found the notice of civil claim, on its face, met each definition: the pleaded 'facts' (dictionary definitions, news stories) and 'legal basis' disclosed no recognized cause of action and had no prospect of success. The plaintiff's stated goal of making a political statement was not a proper use of civil process and merely wasted judicial time and resources.
firac.conclusion: The claim was struck as frivolous, vexatious and disclosing no reasonable cause of action.

firac.issue: Should leave to amend be denied and the action dismissed in its entirety?
firac.facts: The defects lay in the very substance of the claim, which advanced no legal cause of action and rested on the assertion that public health mandates were 'not laws'.
firac.rule: Where the errors in a pleading are irredeemable, the court may dismiss the action without leave to amend rather than allow correction (Parhar v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2021 BCSC 700 at para. 34).
firac.application: The Master was satisfied the deficiencies were irredeemable, so amendment would serve no purpose; the entire action should be dismissed.
firac.conclusion: Leave to amend was refused and the action dismissed in its entirety.

firac.issue: Was a lump-sum costs award appropriate?
firac.facts: The defendant sought costs assessed on a lump-sum basis at $500 to avoid the expense of a formal assessment.
firac.rule: Rule 14-1(15) permits the court to award costs as a lump sum.
firac.application: The Master agreed that a lump-sum award was appropriate to avoid the further cost of an assessment and fixed costs in the amount sought.
firac.conclusion: Lump-sum costs of $500 were awarded to the defendant, and approval as to form of the order by the plaintiff was dispensed with.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the correct tier-1 practice area — the case concerns striking a civil pleading under Rule 9-5. K001 (Administrative law) and K011 (judicial review) are engaged obliquely because the cited authorities treat challenges to government/administrative decisions as matters properly pursued by judicial review rather than a novel civil claim, and the plaintiff's grievance is against a government minister over public-health mandates. K087 (protest/demonstration) is a weak pick reflecting the plaintiff's stated aim to 'make a statement' against COVID mask/vaccination mandates. K107 (Canadian Charter) is a borderline pick — the plaintiff's 'free world vs dictatorship' rhetoric implicates rights arguments though no Charter section was actually pleaded or decided. The controlled vocabulary (oriented toward antisemitism/religion cases) is a poor fit for this pleadings-strike decision, so K087 and K107 are flagged as tenuous and are included only to reach the minimum count.
location_rationale: The style of cause states 'Registry: Vancouver' and the place of hearing and judgment is given as 'Vancouver, B.C.' The court is the Supreme Court of British Columbia, so the province is British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The heading expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: [no public name] (RPD File No. TB1-14252, TB1-14310, TB1-14320, TB1-14321)

defining_issues: Did the claimants establish a well-founded fear of persecution under s. 96 of the IRPA such that they are Convention refugees?
Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection in Israel with clear and convincing evidence?
Are the claimants persons in need of protection under s. 97(1) of the IRPA facing a risk to life, cruel and unusual treatment, or torture?

firac.issue: Did the claimants establish a well-founded fear of persecution under s. 96 of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The claimants, a mixed Russian Jewish and Catholic family from Israel, alleged discrimination and harassment by Orthodox Jews, including stones thrown at their home and cars and threats at the minor claimants' school, because the male claimant is Catholic and the family celebrates Christmas.
firac.rule: Under s. 96 of the IRPA, a claimant must have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground. Discrimination does not necessarily amount to persecution; the acts must reach the level of persecution and the objective element requires that the state be unable or unwilling to protect.
firac.application: The panel recognized that discrimination exists in Israel between religious and ethnic groups, but found that the acts committed against the claimants as a mixed family did not come within the realm of persecution. There was no clear and convincing evidence that Israeli officials condone such discrimination. The claimants could freely practise their faith as Jews or Christians in Israel.
firac.conclusion: The claimants did not establish a well-founded fear of persecution and are not Convention refugees.

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection in Israel?
firac.facts: The claimants alleged they sought police protection in 2007 and 2009 with little or no action, and consulted a lawyer for Russian-speaking people who told them it was useless where Orthodox Jews were involved. They did not complain to the Ombudsman's office, saying they could not afford to.
firac.rule: Per Canada (AG) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689, a claimant must show on a balance of probabilities that the state is unable or unwilling to protect; there is a presumption of state protection unless there is a complete breakdown of the state apparatus. State protection need not be perfect (Villafranca; Zalzali). Doubting effectiveness without truly testing protection does not rebut the presumption (Ramirez); local policing failures do not amount to a lack of protection unless part of a broader pattern (Zhuravlvev).
firac.application: The panel found Israel is a functioning multiparty democracy with effective mechanisms to investigate abuse, an Ombudsman's office with branches serving FSU immigrants, and NGOs (SHATIL, IRAC) assisting immigrants. The claimants only briefly attempted to seek protection, did not pursue the Ombudsman, and could not corroborate their attempts. This subjective reluctance and untested doubt did not rebut the presumption.
firac.conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection; adequate state protection was available in Israel.

firac.issue: Are the claimants persons in need of protection under s. 97(1) of the IRPA?
firac.facts: The claimants alleged a risk to their lives, cruel and unusual treatment, and danger of torture if returned to Israel arising from the same discrimination and harassment.
firac.rule: Under s. 97(1) IRPA, a claimant must show on a balance of probabilities a risk to life, cruel and unusual treatment/punishment, or danger of torture. Per Li v. Canada, there must be persuasive evidence establishing it is more likely than not that the claimant would be tortured; per Bouaouni, a s. 97 claim must be evaluated against the country's human rights record.
firac.application: Given the availability of state protection and the country's human rights record, the panel was not persuaded that the claimants faced a substantial danger of torture or that it was more likely than not they would suffer cruel or degrading treatment. There was insufficient evidence to support a finding of danger of torture.
firac.conclusion: The claimants are not persons in need of protection under s. 97(1).

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the ss. 96/97 claim. K080 (state protection) is the determinative issue, tied to the Ward analysis. K079 (persecution) reflects the s. 96 well-founded fear analysis. K069 (discrimination) captures the alleged mistreatment of the mixed family that the panel found fell short of persecution. K025 (freedom of religion) is engaged given the religious-freedom country evidence and the family's Catholic/Jewish practice. K103 (Israel) is the country of reference and K093 (Jewish) reflects the family's mixed Jewish/Catholic identity central to the claim. Borderline: K025 is somewhat peripheral since the case turned on state protection rather than a Charter freedom-of-religion analysis, but religious identity underlies the claim.
location_rationale: The decision states 'Place of Hearing: Toronto, Ontario', establishing city and province.
registry_rationale: The hearing was held in Toronto, Ontario before the Refugee Protection Division; the Toronto office is the applicable registry as indicated by the place of hearing.

case_name: Ont. Human Rights Comm. v. Simpsons-Sears

name_verification.name_in_document: Ontario Human Rights Commission and Theresa O'Malley (Vincent) v. Simpsons-Sears Limited

defining_issues: Is proof of an intention to discriminate a necessary element of a contravention of the anti-discrimination provisions of the Ontario Human Rights Code?

Can a neutral employment rule adopted for legitimate business reasons but applied equally to all employees constitute discrimination because of its adverse effect on an employee on a prohibited ground such as creed?
Where adverse effect discrimination on the basis of creed is established, what duty does the employer bear to accommodate the employee, and who bears the burden of proof?

firac.issue: Is proof of an intention to discriminate a necessary element of a contravention of the anti-discrimination provisions of the Ontario Human Rights Code?
firac.facts: Simpsons-Sears required full-time sales staff to work Friday evenings and two Saturdays out of three for sound business reasons, with no intent to discriminate against O'Malley or her faith. After her conversion to the Seventh-Day Adventist Church she could no longer work Saturdays. The Divisional Court and Court of Appeal held that intent to discriminate was essential to a breach of s. 4(1)(g).
firac.rule: Human rights legislation is of a special, quasi-constitutional nature to be interpreted broadly to advance its purposes (Insurance Corporation of British Columbia v. Heerspink). The Code aims to remove discrimination and provide relief to victims, not to punish discriminators; it is the result or effect of the impugned action that is significant, not the motive (Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Borough of Etobicoke; Gay Alliance Toward Equality v. Vancouver Sun).
firac.application: The Court held that requiring proof of intent would place a virtually insuperable barrier before complainants, since motive is difficult to prove and easily cloaked in facially neutral rules (Griggs v. Duke Power Co.). Human rights remedies are essentially civil, concerned with consequences of conduct rather than punishment, so criminal-law notions of intent should not govern. The courts below erred in treating intent as a necessary element.
firac.conclusion: Intent to discriminate is not a necessary element; the courts below erred on this point.

firac.issue: Can a neutral employment rule adopted for legitimate business reasons but applied equally to all employees constitute discrimination because of its adverse effect on an employee on a prohibited ground such as creed?
firac.facts: The Saturday-work rule applied equally to all sales staff and was adopted for genuine business reasons, but it conflicted with O'Malley's Sabbath observance and thus affected her differently from other employees.
firac.rule: A distinction exists between direct discrimination (a facially discriminatory rule) and adverse effect discrimination, where a neutral rule applying equally to all imposes, because of some special characteristic of an employee or group, obligations or restrictive conditions not imposed on others (concept drawn from Griggs v. Duke Power Co.). Section 4(1)(g) of the Ontario Human Rights Code prohibits discrimination in a term or condition of employment because of creed.
firac.application: The Saturday-work rule, though neutral and business-justified, imposed on O'Malley because of her creed a burden not borne by other employees, requiring her to choose between her religious principles and full-time employment. This constitutes adverse effect discrimination contrary to the Code, and the appellant established a prima facie case of discrimination based on creed.
firac.conclusion: Yes; adverse effect discrimination is a contravention of the Code and a prima facie case was made out.

firac.issue: Where adverse effect discrimination on the basis of creed is established, what duty does the employer bear to accommodate the employee, and who bears the burden of proof?
firac.facts: After being told to resign, O'Malley was offered part-time work, which she accepted, with reduced hours and benefits, and was told she would be considered for other suitable jobs. The employer called no evidence about the difficulty or expense of further accommodation. The Board of Inquiry placed the onus on the Commission and found it had not shown the employer acted unreasonably.
firac.rule: In adverse effect discrimination the rule, if rationally connected to the employment, need not be justified; instead the employer has a duty to take reasonable steps to accommodate the employee short of undue hardship (i.e., without undue interference in the business or undue expense). Following Etobicoke, the complainant must first establish a prima facie case; the onus then shifts to the employer to show reasonable accommodation short of undue hardship, since the employer possesses the necessary information.
firac.application: Once O'Malley made out a prima facie case, the burden shifted to Simpsons-Sears to prove it had accommodated her short of undue hardship. The employer led no evidence about the expense or problems of rearranging schedules or providing further accommodation, so there was no basis to find undue hardship. The Board erred in fixing the Commission with the burden of proof; the employer failed to discharge its onus.
firac.conclusion: The employer bears the onus to show reasonable accommodation short of undue hardship; here it failed to do so, so the appeal succeeds.

keywords_rationale: K007 (Human rights) is the primary tier-1 area, as the case turns on the Ontario Human Rights Code. K009 (Labour and employment law) is engaged because the discrimination arose in a condition of employment. K069 (discrimination) captures the core subject, and K031 (religious accommodation) is central given the newly-articulated duty to accommodate short of undue hardship. K025 (freedom of religion) applies given the Sabbath-observance conflict discussed by the Court. K068 (bona fide occupational requirement) is relevant because the Court contrasts the BFOR/justification defence for direct discrimination with the accommodation approach; it is somewhat borderline but directly discussed. K072 (human rights tribunal) fits the Board of Inquiry / Human Rights Commission machinery. K119 (Human Rights Code) identifies the governing statute. K034 (sincerity of belief) applies to the finding that O'Malley's conversion was genuine and sincere. Borderline: K068 and K034 are minor but genuinely engaged.
location_rationale: As a Supreme Court of Canada judgment, the decision does not state a sitting city or registry. The heading states 'on appeal from the court of appeal for ontario', identifying the province of origin as Ontario.
registry_rationale: No court registry is stated; the SCC decision heading gives only the file number (17328) and the appellate origin, with no registry office named.

name_verification.name_in_document: Laurier Saumur (Plaintiff) Appellant; and The City of Quebec (Defendant) Respondent and The Attorney General for Quebec Intervenant

defining_issues: Was By-law 184 of the City of Quebec — prohibiting distribution of any book, pamphlet or tract in the streets without the written permission of the Chief of Police — within the legislative competence conferred on the province (use of streets / property and civil rights / local matters), or did it trench on matters beyond provincial power such as religion, freedom of the press and criminal law?

Did the by-law conflict with the guarantee of the free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession and worship contained in the pre-Confederation Freedom of Worship Act (14-15 Vict., c. 175; now R.S.Q. 1941, c. 307), so that it could not validly restrain the appellant, a member of Jehovah's Witnesses, from distributing his religious literature?

firac.issue: Was By-law 184 within provincial/municipal legislative competence, or did it invade federal jurisdiction over religion, the press and criminal law?
firac.facts: By-law 184, passed in 1933, forbade distributing any book, pamphlet, booklet, circular or tract in the streets of Quebec City without the prior written permission of the Chief of Police, with fine and imprisonment for breach. In practice the police examined the contents of proposed material and refused permission for objectionable writings; distribution had been refused only to Jehovah's Witnesses. Saumur, a Jehovah's Witness, challenged the by-law and the enabling provincial legislation as ultra vires. He abandoned the argument that the delegation of discretion to the Chief of Police was invalid.
firac.rule: Under ss. 91 and 92 of the B.N.A. Act legislative power is exhaustively divided between Parliament and the provinces; the validity of an enactment turns on its true nature and character ('pith and substance'). Provinces may legislate on the use of highways, municipal institutions, property and civil rights and local matters (s. 92(8),(13),(16)); Parliament has exclusive jurisdiction over criminal law (s. 91(27)) and residual peace, order and good government. The Court referred to Reference re Alberta Accurate News and Information Act, [1938] SCR 100, Bank of Toronto v. Lambe, and Provincial Secretary of PEI v. Egan, [1941] SCR 396.
firac.application: For the majority the true nature of the by-law was not regulation of the streets but censorship of the contents of written and religious matter, since the licence turned on what the document said, not on any obstruction, litter or traffic concern. Rand, Kellock, Estey and Locke JJ. held that legislation in relation to religion and free public discussion is not a matter of property and civil rights or a merely local matter, but concerns Canada as a whole and, so far as suppression is concerned, lies with Parliament under the criminal law power and by necessary implication of the constitution; a general licensing power that could be applied indifferently to matters outside provincial competence could not be sustained. Kerwin J. held the by-law not necessarily ultra vires on its face but inoperative against the appellant. The dissenters (Rinfret C.J., Taschereau, Cartwright and Fauteux JJ.) viewed the pith and substance as control of the use of the streets and police regulation to prevent disorder, a valid provincial subject that could incidentally affect press and religion.
firac.conclusion: By a majority the by-law could not stand as applied: it was either ultra vires (Rand, Kellock, Estey, Locke JJ.) or did not extend to prohibit the appellant's distribution (Kerwin J.). Appeal allowed.

firac.issue: Did the by-law conflict with the statutory guarantee of freedom of religious profession and worship, so as to protect the appellant's distribution of religious literature?
firac.facts: The 1852 statute (continued by s. 129 of the B.N.A. Act and re-enacted as R.S.Q. 1941, c. 307, s. 2) declared the free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession and worship, without discrimination or preference, subject to acts not being an excuse for licentiousness or practices inconsistent with the peace and safety of the province. Jehovah's Witnesses regarded distribution of printed sermons from door to door and in the streets as a vital part of their worship; their literature contained harsh attacks on other religions, particularly Roman Catholicism.
firac.rule: Freedom of religious profession and worship is protected by the Freedom of Worship Act; the saving words ('licentiousness'... 'practices inconsistent with the peace and safety of the Province') remove protection only from acts already unlawful and do not authorize prior censorship. Kerwin J. found freedom of worship and of the press to be civil rights in the province but not abrogated by general municipal charters; other majority judges held the right was a constitutional right not a s. 92(13) civil right.
firac.application: The majority held that spreading beliefs by printed and written word is part of religious worship and that the Witnesses' attacks, though offensive to the majority religion, did not amount to licentiousness or endanger the peace and safety of the province so as to fall within the exception. A general charter power could not override the specific statutory guarantee of freedom of worship. Kerwin J. therefore declared the by-law did not extend to prohibit the appellant, a Jehovah's Witness, from distributing the writings in the exhibits. The dissent held the Witnesses' provocative literature could be seen as inconsistent with peace and safety and that in any event the appellant, having never applied for a permit, could not complain.
firac.conclusion: The by-law could not lawfully restrain the appellant's distribution of his religious literature; the City and its officers were enjoined from interfering with that distribution.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 practice area — the case turns on division of powers under ss. 91–92 of the B.N.A. Act. K025 (freedom of religion) captures the freedom of worship guarantee central to the majority's reasoning, and K024 (freedom of expression) covers the freedom-of-the-press dimension (censorship of pamphlets and public discussion) heavily relied on from the Alberta Press reference. name_verification.name_in_document: Bruker v. Marcovitz

defining_issues: Is an agreement with a religious dimension (a promise to obtain a Jewish get) justiciable in the civil courts, or is its religious character a bar to adjudication?

Does clause 12 of the Consent to Corollary Relief satisfy the requirements of a valid and binding contract under Quebec civil law (in particular, does it have an object and is it contrary to public order)?
Can the husband invoke his freedom of religion under s. 3 of the Quebec Charter to escape liability in damages for breaching the agreement, when balanced under s. 9.1?
Was the trial judge's award of damages, interest and additional indemnity appropriate?

firac.issue: Is an agreement with a religious dimension justiciable in the civil courts?
firac.facts: The parties, each represented by counsel, signed a Consent to Corollary Relief on divorce; clause 12 obliged them to appear before rabbinical authorities to obtain a get. The husband argued the obligation's religious nature made it non-justiciable.
firac.rule: Justiciability turns on whether a subject-matter is suitable for judicial determination (Sossin). Courts will not decide strictly spiritual or doctrinal matters, but will intervene where civil or property rights are engaged (Ogilvie; Lakeside Colony of Hutterian Brethren v. Hofer; McCaw v. United Church of Canada; Re Morris and Morris).
firac.application: The Court was not asked to review doctrinal religious principles such as the validity of a particular get, but to determine whether a voluntarily negotiated commitment intended to have legally enforceable consequences was binding. The religious element does not immunize an obligation from judicial scrutiny where it engages civil rights.
firac.conclusion: The dispute was justiciable; the religious aspect did not by itself remove it from the courts' purview.

firac.issue: Does clause 12 satisfy the requirements of a valid and binding contract under Quebec civil law?
firac.facts: Clause 12 was negotiated between two consenting, legally capable adults as part of a voluntary exchange of commitments and mutual releases; the husband argued its object—attendance before the rabbinical court—was contrary to public order and hence null.
firac.rule: Arts. 1373, 1378, 1385, 1412 and 1413 C.C.Q.: a contract requires consent, capacity, cause and object; the object is the juridical operation envisaged by the parties and is invalid only if prohibited by law or contrary to public order (art. 1413). Nothing prevents transforming a moral obligation into a civil one.
firac.application: Capacity, consent and cause were not in dispute. The object fell within the broad scope of 'juridical operation' and was not contrary to public order; on the contrary, the 1990 Divorce Act amendments (s. 21.1) show Parliament's intention to discourage religious barriers to remarriage, so an agreement to give a get harmonizes with public policy, equality and religious freedom.
firac.conclusion: Clause 12 was a valid and legally binding contractual obligation under Quebec law.

firac.issue: Can the husband rely on freedom of religion to avoid damages for breaching the agreement?
firac.facts: The husband refused to provide the get for 15 years, admitting his refusal was because he was angry at the wife (harassment, alienation of children, money), not a religious tenet. The wife remained an agunah, unable to remarry in her faith between ages 31 and 46.
firac.rule: Section 3 of the Quebec Charter guarantees freedom of religion; s. 9.1 requires that fundamental freedoms be exercised with proper regard for democratic values, public order and the general well-being of Quebec citizens. Freedom of religion is not absolute and must be balanced against competing rights and harm (Big M Drug Mart; Amselem; Multani; comparative authority from Israel, France, UK, US).
firac.application: The husband showed little sincere religious basis for refusing; even assuming a non-trivial infringement, any impairment to his religious freedom was significantly outweighed by the harm to the wife and to the public interest in equality, dignity, autonomous choice in marriage/divorce, and enforcement of valid contracts. Enforcing an agreement to provide a get is consistent with public policy in Canada and other democracies.
firac.conclusion: The husband could not rely on the Quebec Charter to escape liability; his freedom-of-religion claim did not survive the s. 9.1 balancing.

firac.issue: Was the trial judge's award of damages, interest and additional indemnity appropriate?
firac.facts: The trial judge awarded $2,500 per year for each of the 15 years the wife could not remarry ($37,500) plus $10,000 for the inability to have 'legitimate' children, with interest and indemnity from the 1996 amended claim.
firac.rule: Art. 1607 C.C.Q. allows damages for injury that is an immediate and direct consequence of the debtor's default; arts. 1618 and 1619 govern interest and additional indemnity. Appellate courts will not interfere absent palpable and overriding error.
firac.application: The husband's breach was the exclusive cause of the wife's loss; the trial judge considered the evidence and committed no error of principle. Interest and indemnity ran from the date the amended damages claim was served, an exercise of discretion warranting no interference.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge's award was upheld; no basis to disturb quantum, interest or indemnity.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary practice area given the divorce/corollary-relief context and enforcement of a marital agreement. K003 (Constitutional law) reflects the freedom-of-religion analysis, a co-subject noted by the Court. K051 (religious divorce (get)) is the central specific doctrine—the get refusal and agunah problem. K025 (freedom of religion) captures the s. 3 Quebec Charter defence and the s. 9.1 balancing. K026 (halacha/Jewish law) applies given the extensive treatment of Jewish religious law (beth din, mamzerim). K049 (marriage/cohabitation agreement) fits the Consent to Corollary Relief being enforced as a contract. K120 (Quebec Charter) is the governing rights instrument. K117 (Divorce Act) is engaged via s. 21.1, heavily relied on. K093 (Jewish) identifies the community and religious framework at issue. K002 (Civil litigation) reflects the contract/damages dimension. Borderline: K002 is a weaker tier-1 pick since the case straddles family and civil-contract law, but the action was a contractual damages claim; K093 is an entity tag but strongly engaged.
location_rationale: The Supreme Court of Canada sits in Ottawa; the decision is 'on appeal from the court of appeal for quebec', so the underlying province is Quebec. No express statement of a hearing city appears beyond the SCC's status as the national court, hence Ottawa is inferred as the seat of the Court.
