name_verification.name_in_document: Anton Paul Andres v. Canada Revenue Agency (Indexed as Andres v. Canada Revenue Agency)

defining_issues: Did the employer meet its duty to accommodate the grievor's religious observance of Orthodox Good Friday and Easter Monday?

Did the grievor discharge his own obligation in the accommodation process by making his proposed accommodation (working Western Good Friday/Easter Monday in exchange for paid Orthodox holidays) known to the employer?

Did the employer's reliance on clause 17.19 of the collective agreement, requiring the grievor to use vacation, compensatory or make-up leave, constitute adverse-effect discrimination on the ground of religion?

firac.issue: Did the employer meet its duty to accommodate the grievor's religious observance of Orthodox Good Friday and Easter Monday?
firac.facts: The grievor, an Orthodox Christian, observed Good Friday and Easter Monday one week after the Western dates designated as paid holidays (DPHs) under the collective agreement. Clause 17.19 offered options for religious observance: annual leave, compensatory leave, leave without pay, or discretionary time off with pay to be made up hour-for-hour within six months. The grievor was aware of and had used these options in prior years but chose vacation leave in 2009, then sought conversion to paid leave, which was refused.
firac.rule: The duty to accommodate requires reasonable, not perfect, accommodation (Central Okanagan (Renaud), [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970; Campbell v. AG Canada). An employer need not accommodate to the point of undue hardship where another reasonable means of accommodation is available (Richmond v. Canada, [1997] 2 F.C. 946). Scheduling changes without loss of pay can satisfy the duty (Tratnyek; Markovic), and there is no obligation to grant additional paid leave for religious observance (Richmond).
firac.application: The adjudicator found the collective agreement's clause 17.19 provided a menu of reasonable options — including compensatory leave and discretionary make-up time — that allowed the grievor to observe his holy days without necessarily losing vacation credits. The grievor was not forced to take vacation and was reminded of alternatives when refused. Reasonable accommodation was available and offered; the law does not compel additional paid leave.
firac.conclusion: The employer met its duty to accommodate; the accommodation offered satisfied the applicable jurisprudence.

firac.issue: Did the grievor discharge his own obligation in the accommodation process by making his proposed accommodation known to the employer?
firac.facts: The grievor requested vacation on April 9, 2009 (hours before the Western long weekend), then on April 14 sought conversion to paid leave. At the hearing he argued he should have been permitted to work Western Good Friday and Easter Monday in exchange for paid Orthodox holidays. No document or email mentioned this proposal, and there was no evidence of when, with whom, or whether such a discussion occurred; Mr. Taylor testified he never discussed it.
firac.rule: The search for accommodation is a multi-party inquiry; the complainant must facilitate the search and his conduct must be considered (Central Okanagan (Renaud), [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970, paras 43–44). If the employer does not know an accommodation is being sought, it cannot respond.
firac.application: The adjudicator found insufficient evidence that the exchange-of-days proposal was ever raised before the vacation request. Since the grievor did not make his proposed accommodation known at a point when the employer could respond, he failed in his part of the accommodation process.
firac.conclusion: The grievor did not discharge his obligation in the accommodation process; for this reason alone the grievance failed.

firac.issue: Did requiring the grievor to use vacation or make-up leave rather than granting paid leave amount to adverse-effect discrimination on the ground of religion?
firac.facts: Employees observing Western Good Friday and Easter Monday receive those DPHs off with pay, while the grievor, observing the Orthodox dates one week later, had to use leave options under clause 17.19. He alleged this breached the no-discrimination clause 43.01 and s. 7(b)/s. 3 of the Canadian Human Rights Act.
firac.rule: Adverse-effect discrimination arises where a facially neutral rule imposes obligations on an employee because of a protected characteristic (O'Malley, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536). However, the remedy is reasonable accommodation, which does not require paid leave where reasonable scheduling/leave options exist (Richmond; Tratnyek; Chambly distinguished).
firac.application: The adjudicator accepted that DPHs like Good Friday and Easter Monday can have a discriminatory effect on non-Western-Christian employees, but held that clause 17.19 addressed this potential adverse effect by providing reasonable options. Chambly was distinguished because teachers there could not use scheduling alternatives; here reasonable options existed and the Supreme Court did not establish a general principle that employers must pay for time off for religious observance. Clause 17.23(b) was inapplicable because clause 17.19 specifically governed religious leave.
firac.conclusion: No compensable discrimination was established; the collective agreement's accommodation options were reasonable and adequate.

name_verification.name_in_document: [no public name — anonymized Refugee Protection Division decision]

defining_issues: Did the claimants establish a well-founded, objectively reasonable fear of persecution or risk on return to Hungary as (half-)Roma?
Did the claimants rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Hungary with clear and convincing evidence, and did they take all reasonable steps to seek that protection before fleeing?

firac.issue: Did the claimants establish an objectively reasonable fear of persecution or risk on return to Hungary?
firac.facts: The principal claimant is half-Roma; her husband is ethnic Hungarian and their minor child is a co-claimant. She alleged discrimination in housing, employment and education, plus two skinhead assaults in 2001 and 2009. She worked from 1999–2009, received government child and health benefits, and obtained medical treatment in Hungary. Both adult claimants had been gainfully employed for many years.
firac.rule: Sections 96 and 97(1) IRPA require a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or, on a balance of probabilities, a personal risk of torture, risk to life, or cruel and unusual treatment. A sworn allegation is presumed true absent reason to doubt it (Maldonado v. Canada, [1980] 2 F.C. 302 (C.A.)); credibility is assessed on a balance of probabilities (Orelien v. Canada, [1992] 1 F.C. 592 (C.A.)).
firac.application: The panel accepted that the PC is half-Roma and that Roma in Hungary face discrimination and, at times, violence from right-wing extremists. However, the claimants' own circumstances—continuous employment, receipt of social assistance and medical care—undercut a finding of personalized persecution. The determinative question was not the existence of societal discrimination but whether the fear was objectively reasonable given available state protection.
firac.conclusion: The claimants did not establish a serious possibility of persecution or a personalized risk; the fear was not objectively reasonable in light of available protection.

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of adequate state protection and take all reasonable steps to seek it?
firac.facts: The 2001 assault of the husband and the 2009 assault of the PC were both reported to police, who collected data and searched for witnesses but could not identify the offenders. The PC did not follow up on her 2009 report because she left for Canada, and she sought no other avenue of assistance beyond the police.
firac.rule: States are presumed capable of protecting their citizens; the claimant bears the burden of rebutting that presumption with clear and convincing evidence on a balance of probabilities (Canada (AG) v. Ward, [1993] S.C.R. 689; Flores Carrillo v. Canada, [2008] 4 F.C.R. 636 (F.C.A.)). A claimant must take all reasonable steps to seek protection (Peralta, 2002 FCT 989); fleeing before police can respond does not establish lack of protection (Montemayor Romero, 2008 FC 977); the state's efforts need not always succeed (Villafranca (1992), 18 Imm. L.R. (2d) 130 (F.C.A.)); subjective reluctance is insufficient (Camacho, 2007 FC 830); local failures do not amount to lack of protection absent a broader pattern (Zhuravlvev, [2000] 4 F.C. 3 (T.D.)).
firac.application: Hungary is a functioning EU-member democracy in effective control of its territory with a functioning security force. Police investigated both reported assaults. The PC left before the 2009 investigation could conclude and pursued no other recourse such as the Minorities Ombudsman, the Independent Police Complaints Board, the Equal Treatment Authority, or the Roma Police Officers' Association. The documentary record showed serious central-government efforts on Roma education, employment, housing and health, though imperfectly implemented locally—amounting to mixed evidence, not a broader pattern of inability or refusal to protect.
firac.conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and did not exhaust reasonable avenues before fleeing; adequate state protection is available in Hungary.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K080 (state protection) is the determinative issue—whether the presumption of state protection was rebutted. K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) capture the ss. 96/97 claim and the alleged fear of persecution. name_verification.name_in_document: XXXX XXXX (RAD File No. MB4-04300)

defining_issues: What is the RAD's role and the degree of deference owed to the RPD when reviewing a question of mixed law and fact such as an internal flight alternative and country conditions?
Should the appellant's proposed new evidence be admitted under s. 110(4) of IRPA?
Did the RPD err in concluding that the appellant had a viable internal flight alternative in Kherson or Mykolayiv, both as to safety (first prong) and reasonableness of relocation (second prong)?

firac.issue: What is the RAD's role and standard of review when reviewing an RPD finding on IFA and country conditions?
firac.facts: The appellant, a 68-year-old Russian-speaking citizen of Ukraine of Bulgarian ethnicity, appealed the RPD's rejection of her refugee claim, which turned on the availability of an internal flight alternative and an assessment of country conditions.
firac.rule: Per Huruglica v. M.C.I. (2014) FC 799 and Njeukam v. M.C.I. (2014) FC 859, the RAD must review all aspects of the RPD decision and reach an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or person in need of protection; deference may be shown on credibility findings or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage, but not on matters such as country-conditions evidence.
firac.application: Because the appeal turned on a question of mixed law and fact — the IFA and country-conditions assessment — where the RPD had no particular advantage, the panel undertook its own independent assessment of the evidence rather than deferring to the RPD.
firac.conclusion: The RAD conducted an independent review of the evidence and reached its own conclusion on the IFA issue.

firac.issue: Should the appellant's new evidence concerning the sale of her property and cost of relocation be admitted?
firac.facts: The appellant sought to file new evidence relating to the sale of her property in Belgorad-Dniestrovski and the cost of purchasing an apartment in Kherson or Mykolayiv.
firac.rule: Section 110(4) of IRPA permits new evidence on appeal where it could not reasonably have been presented earlier (the decision cites 's. 104(4)', an evident typographical reference to the new-evidence provision).
firac.application: The panel accepted that the appellant could not reasonably have provided the material earlier and therefore admitted it.
firac.conclusion: The new evidence was admitted.

firac.issue: Did the RPD err in finding a viable IFA in Kherson or Mykolayiv?
firac.facts: The appellant feared Ukrainian nationalists/militias seeking to drive Russians from her area. The RPD found she was credible but that her situation was anomalous, that documentary evidence showed harmonious inter-ethnic relations, and that as a retired Russian-speaking woman of Bulgarian ethnicity she did not fit a risk profile. She conceded no serious possibility of persecution in the proposed cities but disputed the reasonableness of relocating given administrative and financial constraints.
firac.rule: The two-prong IFA test requires (1) no serious possibility of persecution/risk in the proposed location and (2) that relocation not be objectively unreasonable in all the circumstances. The RPD's use of 'impossible' was challenged as applying the wrong test.
firac.application: The panel found the RPD's second use of 'impossible' was rhetorical, mirroring the appellant's own language, and that the RPD correctly articulated the second prong. On the first prong, the appellant did not contest safety, and the documentary evidence (including a UN Special Rapporteur report) showed no targeting of persons of her profile. On the second prong, the panel found registration of relocation was administratively possible (her former husband could assist) and that although housing costs were substantial, her son in Canada could potentially assist; the loss of her property was not a necessary consideration. The panel found no error.
firac.conclusion: The RPD did not err; a viable and reasonable IFA existed in Kherson or Mykolayiv.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the substance of the s. 96/97 claim. K079 (persecution) reflects the alleged fear of Ukrainian nationalists driving Russians out. K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) identifies the deciding institution (RAD/RPD). K014 (standard of review) applies because the panel expressly addressed the RAD's role and degree of deference under Huruglica and Njeukam. case_name: Canadian Doctors for Refugee Care v. Canada (Attorney General)

name_verification.name_in_document: Canadian Doctors for Refugee Care, The Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers, Daniel Garcia Rodrigues, Hanif Ayubi and Justice for Children and Youth v. Attorney General of Canada and Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

defining_issues: Should the applicant organizations (CDRC, CARL and JFCY) be granted public interest standing?
Were the 2012 Orders in Council ultra vires the prerogative/executive powers of the Governor in Council?
Did the Governor in Council owe and breach a duty of procedural fairness (including any legitimate expectation) by making the 2012 IFHP changes without notice or consultation?
Do the 2012 changes to the IFHP violate section 7 of the Charter by depriving affected persons of life, liberty and security of the person?
Do the 2012 changes to the IFHP constitute 'cruel and unusual treatment' contrary to section 12 of the Charter?
Do the 2012 changes to the IFHP violate section 15 of the Charter by discriminating on the basis of national origin (DCO/non-DCO) or immigration status?
If sections 12 and 15 are breached, are those breaches justified under section 1 of the Charter?
What is the appropriate remedy?

firac.issue: Should the applicant organizations be granted public interest standing?
firac.facts: CDRC (refugee physicians), CARL (refugee lawyers) and JFCY (children's legal clinic) sought public interest standing to challenge the 2012 IFHP changes; two directly affected individuals (Ayubi and Garcia Rodrigues) already had standing as of right, but no directly affected DCO claimants, non-DCO claimants or PRRA-only applicants had come forward, many being too ill, too poor, facing removal, or reluctant to sue the government whose protection they sought.
firac.rule: The three-factor discretionary test for public interest standing from Canada (AG) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45, and Manitoba Métis Federation v. Canada, 2013 SCC 14: (1) a serious justiciable issue; (2) a genuine interest; (3) whether the proposed action is a reasonable and effective means of bringing the matter to court; the factors are weighed cumulatively and generously.
firac.application: The respondents conceded serious justiciable issues. JFCY, with its demonstrated history of advocacy for children (e.g. Canadian Foundation for Children), had a genuine interest despite relying on the other applicants' evidence. The organizations assembled a substantial evidentiary record exceeding what individual vulnerable claimants could realistically produce, avoided a multiplicity of proceedings, and brought distinct useful perspectives (medical, legal, child-focused).
firac.conclusion: Public interest standing was granted to all three organizations.

firac.issue: Were the 2012 Orders in Council ultra vires the Governor in Council?
firac.facts: The IFHP had always operated by Order in Council rather than statute. The applicants argued the payments were not truly ex gratia and that any Crown prerogative to fund refugee health care had been extinguished by IRPA and the Canada Health Act.
firac.rule: The Crown prerogative is the residue of discretionary authority left in the Crown (Khadr, 2010 SCC 3), and includes the natural-person/executive power to make spending decisions to which no one has an enforceable entitlement (Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Assn. v. BC). Prerogative goes into abeyance only where a statute occupies the field expressly or by necessary implication (Black v. Canada; Interpretation Act, s. 17).
firac.application: Neither IRPA (which contains nothing about health care for those it governs) nor the Canada Health Act (which addresses provincial insured persons, not refugees) occupied the field of funding health insurance for those seeking Canada's protection. The mere borrowing of IRPA terminology in the OICs did not extinguish the prerogative. Once created, providers had a right to payment, but the executive retained authority to define and restrict the scheme.
firac.conclusion: The 2012 OICs were intra vires the executive branch, though remaining subject to Charter and fairness review.

firac.issue: Did the Governor in Council breach a duty of procedural fairness by acting without notice or consultation?
firac.facts: The 2012 changes were announced in the federal budget and enacted by OIC without advance notice or stakeholder consultation, despite 55 years of prior practice and consultations with provinces.
firac.rule: No general duty of fairness attaches to legislative functions (Authorson). Whether a duty arises depends on whether the decision is 'legislative and general' versus 'administrative and specific' (Wells v. Newfoundland; Inuit Tapirisat). Legitimate expectation requires clear, unambiguous and unqualified representations (Mavi; Baker).
firac.application: The applicants adduced no clear, unqualified representations grounding a legitimate expectation of participatory rights. The 2012 OICs were 'legislative and general', affecting a large, amorphous, not-readily-identifiable group of stakeholders, unlike the specific citizenship revocation in Oberlander. Even the more compelling contractual situation in Hospitality House attracted no duty of fairness.
firac.conclusion: No duty of procedural fairness was owed; this ground failed.

firac.issue: Do the 2012 IFHP changes violate section 7 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The applicants argued the cuts exposed impoverished refugees to risks to life and psychological security by withdrawing previously available health coverage.
firac.rule: Section 7 requires a deprivation of life, liberty or security of the person not in accordance with fundamental justice (Chaoulli; Gosselin). Canadian law does not recognize a free-standing or positive constitutional right to state-funded health care (Chaoulli; Flora; Toussaint FCA; Covarrubias); a mere change in a discretionary benefit does not ground a s. 7 violation (Flora; Ferrel; Gosselin).
firac.application: What the applicants sought was, in substance, to impose a positive obligation on the government to fund health care. The 2012 IFHP does not prohibit anyone from obtaining care with their own resources; the barrier is economic. The change to a discretionary program does not become reviewable under s. 7 merely because benefits were reduced, and the Dunmore test failed at its first element (no underlying fundamental right to state-funded health care).
firac.conclusion: The section 7 claim was dismissed.

firac.issue: Do the 2012 IFHP changes constitute cruel and unusual treatment under section 12?
firac.facts: The changes intentionally targeted a poor, vulnerable, disadvantaged group of persons under immigration control, denying coverage for life-saving medications, prenatal/paediatric care and, for PRRA-only claimants, all care, expressly to deter 'bogus' claims and hasten departures.
firac.rule: 'Treatment' under s. 12 may extend beyond the penal context where there is an active state process exercising control over the individual (Rodriguez; Chiarelli). Treatment is 'cruel and unusual' where it is so excessive as to outrage standards of decency, assessed through factors including necessity, arbitrariness, social value, public acceptance and degradation of human dignity (R. v. Smith); reasonable hypotheticals are permissible (Goltz).
firac.application: Persons seeking Canada's protection are under the administrative control of the state, and the government intentionally targeted them for adverse treatment, distinguishing them from Ms. Rodriguez. The cuts were arbitrary (unrelated to health needs), of limited social value, met with widespread condemnation by 21 medical bodies and provinces, and inflicted predictable suffering—especially on innocent children (asthma, ear infections, HIV, tuberculosis, suicidal trauma) and on individuals such as Ayubi, Akhtar and Garcia Rodrigues—forcing sick people to beg for care, degrading human dignity.
firac.conclusion: The 2012 changes subject affected persons to 'treatment' that is 'cruel and unusual', violating section 12.

firac.issue: Do the 2012 IFHP changes violate section 15 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The 2012 IFHP provided lesser coverage to refugee claimants from Designated Countries of Origin than to non-DCO claimants, and provided lesser coverage than that available to low-income Canadians; the applicants alleged discrimination on national origin and on immigration status.
firac.rule: Section 15 protects substantive equality; the test is whether the law draws a distinction on an enumerated or analogous ground that creates disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping (Andrews; Kapp; Withler; Quebec v. A.). Section 15(2) saves genuinely ameliorative programs where the distinction serves the ameliorative object (Kapp; Cunningham). Immigration status is not an analogous ground (Toussaint FCA).
firac.application: Subsection 4(3) of the April 2012 OIC expressly denied coverage based on the claimant's DCO nationality—a distinction on national origin. It was not saved by s. 15(2): the respondents conceded the program did not respond to health needs and there was no evidence DCO claimants were less needy, so the distinction did not advance any ameliorative purpose. The distinction put lives at risk and perpetuated the stereotype that DCO claimants are 'bogus' queue-jumpers, worsening the disadvantage of a vulnerable group. However, 'immigration status' is not an analogous ground and that binding Federal Court of Appeal holding was dispositive.
firac.conclusion: Section 15 is violated by the DCO/non-DCO distinction based on national origin; the immigration-status claim was dismissed.

firac.issue: Are the section 12 and 15 breaches justified under section 1?
firac.facts: The government advanced objectives of cost containment, fairness to Canadians, protecting public health and safety, and protecting the integrity of the immigration system.
firac.rule: Section 1 justification under R. v. Oakes requires a pressing and substantial objective and proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, and balancing of deleterious and salutary effects); budgetary considerations alone are rarely pressing and substantial (Martin; N.A.P.E.).
firac.application: Cost containment (as one of several goals), public health/safety, and integrity of the immigration system were accepted as pressing and substantial, but 'fairness to Canadians' was not, since the pre-2012 IFHP was not unfair. Rational connection failed for fairness and partly for public health (denying PRRA-only claimants coverage for communicable diseases undermines that goal). Minimal impairment failed: no reliable evidence isolated IFHP savings from other reform measures, less drastic alternatives (faster processing, more IRB members, quicker removals) existed, and the 'pull factor' deterrence rested on unverified perceptions. The profoundly deleterious effects—illness, disability, death, and risk to children—greatly outweighed any unproven salutary effects.
firac.conclusion: The respondents failed to justify the breaches under section 1.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the primary tier-1 area, as the case turns on Charter analysis. case_name: Kempling v. BC College of Teachers

name_verification.name_in_document: Kempling v. The British Columbia College of Teachers

defining_issues: Was there procedural unfairness in the Hearing Panel's finding of conduct unbecoming, given the adequacy of reasons and use of the appellant's private writings?
What is the appropriate standard of review for the Hearing Panel's finding of conduct unbecoming, and was that finding sustainable on that standard?
What is the appropriate standard of review for the Council's penalty decision, and was the one-month suspension sustainable on that standard?
Were the appellant's Charter rights under ss. 2(a), 2(b), 7 and 15 infringed by the disciplinary action?
If any Charter right was infringed, was the infringement justified under s. 1 of the Charter?

firac.issue: Was there procedural unfairness in the Hearing Panel's finding of conduct unbecoming, given the adequacy of its reasons and its use of the appellant's private writings?
firac.facts: The appellant did not attend the disciplinary hearing. The Panel's reasons listed exhibits, set out submissions, and made findings of fact referencing particular newspaper writings. During the investigation the appellant voluntarily produced private correspondence and essays. The appellant and intervener argued the reasons failed to identify which writings grounded the offence and that private correspondence may have been improperly used.
firac.rule: Administrative tribunals are not strictly bound by the rules of evidence. Procedural fairness requires reasons that adequately indicate the evidence and reasoning on which a decision is based; unfairness would arise from reliance on irrelevant, prejudicial evidence such as private correspondence.
firac.application: The court found the Panel's reasons sufficiently identified the evidence and reasoning. The Panel quoted exclusively from and relied upon the newspaper publications in finding conduct unbecoming and did not rely on the private letters or memorandum. The private writings were non-conscriptive, having been produced on the appellant's own initiative, and the appellant chose not to challenge any evidence. At the penalty stage the two essays intended for free distribution were properly considered as part of the broader context.
firac.conclusion: There was no procedural unfairness; the reasons were adequate and no improper use was made of the private correspondence.

firac.issue: What is the appropriate standard of review for the finding of conduct unbecoming, and was it sustainable?
firac.facts: The BCCT Hearing Panel found the appellant, a secondary teacher and counsellor, guilty of conduct unbecoming based on published discriminatory writings about homosexuals which he linked to his professional status.
firac.rule: The pragmatic and functional approach in Pushpanathan and Dr. Q governs: privative clause/appeal right, relative expertise, statutory purpose, and nature of the question. Reasonableness review under Law Society of New Brunswick v. Ryan asks whether the reasons, taken as a whole, are tenable to support the decision. Standard of proof is 'clear and cogent evidence' (Jory). Off-duty teacher conduct may be sanctioned where it harms the school system (Ross v. New Brunswick School District No. 15; Shewan).
firac.application: Though the broad appeal right in s. 40 of the Teaching Profession Act militated against deference, the Panel's specialized expertise, the balancing statutory purpose, and the fact-intensive nature of 'conduct unbecoming' pointed to deference, yielding reasonableness simpliciter. Applying a somewhat probing examination, the appellant's newspaper writings consistently associated homosexuals with immorality, abnormality, perversion and promiscuity, and he expressly linked these views to his teaching/counselling role. Harm to the school system was both per se and reasonably inferable (loss of confidence, impaired impartiality, community controversy). Speech can constitute discrimination under the Human Rights Code.
firac.conclusion: The standard is reasonableness simpliciter, and the finding of conduct unbecoming was reasonable and affirmed.

firac.issue: What is the appropriate standard of review for the Council's penalty decision, and was the one-month suspension sustainable?
firac.facts: The Council adopted the Panel's recommendation of a one-month suspension, notification to licensing authorities, and publication of the appellant's name and a case summary.
firac.rule: Pragmatic and functional approach (Dr. Q); a statutory purpose requiring selection among remedial choices, protecting the public and balancing interests commands greater deference. Sections 4 and 35 of the Teaching Profession Act confer discretion on sanction. Reasonableness review does not permit substitution of the court's opinion.
firac.application: Absence of a privative clause militated against deference but the other three factors—superior expertise of practising teachers in choosing sanctions, the public-protection and balancing purpose, and the mixed fact/law nature of the decision—called for considerable deference. The Council considered the appellant's unblemished career, community service, gravity of conduct, public protection and deterrence. A genuine public-protection issue existed given the vulnerability of homosexual students. Ross was not a helpful comparator as the penalty here was far less drastic.
firac.conclusion: The standard is reasonableness simpliciter, and the penalty was reasonable and affirmed.

firac.issue: Were the appellant's Charter rights under ss. 2(a), 2(b), 7 and 15 infringed?
firac.facts: The appellant claimed the discipline infringed his freedom of expression, freedom of religion, liberty/security, and equality rights, arguing he could be silenced or lose his profession.
firac.rule: Correctness governs administrative decisions on constitutional issues (Cuddy Chicks). Section 2(b) protects non-violent expression conveying meaning (Irwin Toy) but not expression purporting to carry the authority of a professional capacity one is not authorized to use (Walker v. PEI). Section 2(a) protects sincerely held religious expression in a personal capacity (R. v. Jones). Section 7 does not extend to a right to exercise one's chosen profession (Prostitution Reference; Blencoe). Section 15 requires an appropriate comparator group and evidence of differential treatment.
firac.application: The content of the appellant's views was protected expression, but what was sanctioned was his off-duty expression of discriminatory views purportedly with the authority of a teacher/counsellor, causing harm—following Walker, no s. 2(b) infringement. For the same reasons s. 2(a) does not protect expression in a professional capacity one is not authorized to use. Section 7 does not protect the right to practise teaching. For s. 15, the proper comparator was other disciplined teachers, not the general public, and no differential treatment was shown.
firac.conclusion: No Charter rights were infringed; all Charter claims were dismissed.

firac.issue: If any Charter right had been infringed, would the infringement be justified under s. 1?
firac.facts: The BCCT disciplined the appellant to protect students and uphold a non-discriminatory school system.
firac.rule: Section 1 justification is assessed under R. v. Oakes, applied flexibly with attention to contextual factors (Ross): pressing and substantial objective, rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality of effects. A 'reasoned apprehension of harm' suffices rather than scientific proof (RJR-MacDonald; Sharpe; Butler).
firac.application: Contextual factors—protection of vulnerable children, an historically disadvantaged group, enforcement of professional standards, and the low value of discriminatory expression—favoured a less stringent application. The objectives of a discrimination-free school environment, protecting gay and lesbian students, and restoring confidence were pressing and substantial. Sanctioning discriminatory conduct linked to professional status was rationally connected. The one-month suspension, far less drastic than in Ross, was minimally impairing, and its salutary effects outweighed its deleterious effects, which left the appellant free to express views in a private capacity.
firac.conclusion: Any infringement would be justified under s. 1; the appeal was dismissed with costs.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally an administrative-law judicial review/statutory appeal of a professional regulator's decision, so K001 (Administrative law), K014 (standard of review—reasonableness/pragmatic and functional), K011 (judicial review) and K013 (professional discipline—BCCT is a self-regulating body) all apply directly. K046 (teacher misconduct/conduct unbecoming) is the specific disciplinary subject. K045 relates to the school/education discipline context, though it is a slightly weaker fit as it targets student discipline; it is included because education law and school-system harm are central. K024 (freedom of expression, s. 2(b)) and K025 (freedom of religion, s. 2(a)) are the core Charter freedoms litigated, with K110 (s. 2(a)) and K111 (s. 2(b)) as the specific statutory provisions, and K107 (Canadian Charter) as the governing instrument. K069 (discrimination) captures the finding that the appellant's statements against homosexuals were discriminatory under the Human Rights Code. Procedural fairness (K012) was considered but the s.15 equality and s.7 claims were peripheral, so those were not chosen as primary picks.

registry_rationale: The decision expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Salager v. Dye & Durham Corporation
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The case name matches, but the supplied citation (2018 BCSC 438) does not match the citation printed in the decision, which is 2017 BCSC 470 (dated 20170323). The party names are consistent; only the neutral citation is wrong.

defining_issues: Did the law firm Harris concurrently represent clients whose interests were directly adverse without informed consent, so as to engage the 'bright line' rule?
Did Harris receive confidential information attributable to a solicitor–client relationship with Dye & Durham that is relevant to this action and at risk of misuse?
Is there a disqualifying conflict of interest warranting removal of Harris as counsel and an injunction?

firac.issue: Did Harris concurrently represent clients whose immediate legal interests were directly adverse without their informed consent, engaging the bright line rule?
firac.facts: Harris acted for Mr. Salager in ongoing defamation and breach-of-settlement litigation against OneMove/Mr. Proud. It had also, between 2005 and September 2015, intermittently given Dye & Durham employment-law advice with no written retainer and no monetary retainer. In March 2016 OneMove acquired Dye & Durham and they amalgamated on July 1, 2016. Harris had done no work for Dye & Durham for about 10 months before the amalgamation.
firac.rule: The 'bright line rule' from Canadian National Railway Co. v. McKercher LLP, 2013 SCC 39 (citing R. v. Neil): a lawyer may not represent one client whose interests are directly adverse to the immediate interests of another current client, even in unrelated matters, without both clients' informed consent. The rule does not apply where it would be unreasonable to expect the lawyer not to act against the client in unrelated matters, assessed case-by-case (McKercher, para. 37).
firac.application: The Court found that when the two companies merged, Harris was not concurrently providing advice to both Mr. Salager and Dye & Durham; Harris had given Dye & Durham no advice for roughly 10 months. The relationship was intermittent, involved occasional phone/e-mail advice on discrete employment matters, with no ongoing retainer. The conflict arose only from the amalgamation, not from Harris knowingly taking on an adverse client. This made it one of the exceptional cases where it was unreasonable for Dye & Durham to expect Harris would not act against it in an entirely unrelated matter.
firac.conclusion: The bright line rule had no application; there was no impermissible concurrent representation.

firac.issue: Did Harris obtain relevant confidential information from Dye & Durham that is at risk of being misused in this action?
firac.facts: Dye & Durham's former corporate operations officer deposed that Harris had access to internal strategy and executive decision-making on legal disputes. Harris's partner deposed there was never litigation work, no litigation strategy advice, and only summary employment advice. The present claims are for defamation and breach of the settlement agreement.
firac.rule: MacDonald Estate v. Martin, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1235: (1) did the lawyer receive confidential information attributable to a solicitor–client relationship relevant to the matter at hand, and (2) is there a risk it will be used to the client's prejudice, assessed from the standpoint of a reasonably informed member of the public. A 'bald assertion' of access to litigation philosophy is insufficient; information must be 'capable of being used against the client in some tangible manner' (McKercher, para. 54). Courts take a cautious approach and require compelling evidence of real mischief (Brookville Carriers; Stewart v. Stewart, 2016 BCSC 2256).
firac.application: Any confidential information Harris received related to employment/HR matters, which are unrelated to the defamation and breach-of-settlement claims. Harris last advised Dye & Durham 10 months before the acquisition, so it could not have obtained information specific to this action. The defendants offered only a bare assertion of access to strategic decision-making, which is insufficient. The deponent had also retired, and any insight into Mr. Proud's decision-making came from acting for Salager, not Dye & Durham.
firac.conclusion: Harris received no relevant confidential information, and a reasonably informed person would be satisfied there is no risk of misuse.

firac.issue: Is there a disqualifying conflict of interest justifying removal of counsel and an injunction?
firac.facts: The defendants sought a declaration of conflict, an order removing Harris, and an injunction restraining Harris from acting for the plaintiff.
firac.rule: Disqualification is a discretionary, equitable remedy warranted only where the bright line rule is breached or there is a real risk of misuse of confidential information (McKercher; MacDonald Estate; Stewart v. Stewart). Courts interfere with a party's chosen counsel only in clear cases and must guard against tactical use of disqualification applications.
firac.application: Having found no concurrent adverse representation engaging the bright line rule and no relevant confidential information at risk of misuse, there was no basis for disqualification.
firac.conclusion: No disqualifying conflict of interest; the application was dismissed with costs to the plaintiff at Scale B as costs in the cause.

K013 (professional discipline / law society) is the closest available keyword touching conflict-of-interest and lawyer conduct standards, though it is a weak fit since this is a court disqualification motion rather than a regulatory discipline proceeding. defining_issues: Did the chambers judge err by failing to consider the legal nature of the Surrey Knights as a partnership in analysing the procedural fairness and oppression issues?
Did the Pacific Junior Hockey League breach the principles of procedural fairness by failing to give adequate notice and by having a biased decision maker involved in preliminary rulings?
Did the chambers judge err by considering the interests of the players in her oppression analysis under s. 102 of the Societies Act?
Was the remedy prohibiting any further proceedings against the respondents in respect of the September 24, 2015 incident an appropriate exercise of discretion under s. 102 of the Societies Act?
Should the chambers judge have recused herself, or reopened the hearing, on the basis of a reasonable apprehension of bias arising from her son playing in the league?

firac.issue: Did the chambers judge err by failing to consider the legal nature of the Surrey Knights as a partnership in analysing the procedural fairness and oppression issues?
firac.facts: The Surrey Knights team was owned by Mr. Craighead and Mr. Gill. PJHL argued that because they operated as a partnership, the wrongful acts of one partner (Craighead) were imputed to the other, so no separate notice or particulars were required for the team or Mr. Gill.
firac.rule: Partnership liability principles (Partnership Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 348, ss. 7, 8, 11, 12; Coal Harbour Properties Partnership v. Liu; Strother v. 3464920 Canada Inc.) concern a partnership's liability for debts, obligations and losses. Oppression relief under s. 102 of the Societies Act turns on reasonable expectations and fairness, not partnership liability.
firac.application: The Court held partnership-liability principles were of little assistance. PJHL's own bylaws made membership varied: Craighead was also an employee (coach/general manager) and an 'Associated Person'; Operating Member eligibility extends to individuals, corporations and partnerships. The chambers judge defined 'Operating Member' to include the franchise and both owners, an interpretation PJHL did not appeal. The franchise/team has an interest in maintaining membership independent of partnership liability, and PJHL itself described teams as the 'actual members'.
firac.conclusion: No error. The existence of the partnership did not limit the analysis of oppression, unfair prejudice and natural justice; ground of appeal rejected.

firac.issue: Did the PJHL breach procedural fairness by failing to give adequate notice and by having a biased decision maker involved in preliminary rulings?
firac.facts: The Eaton complaint and subsequent communications described conduct only of Mr. Craighead, yet the proceedings could expel the team and Mr. Gill. President Stonehouse, who witnessed the incident and had strong views on Craighead's guilt, recused himself as chair but still convened the Governors' preliminary vote and decided preliminary applications on jurisdiction and document production before the hearing.
firac.rule: Courts may intervene in voluntary-association decisions where legal, property or contractual rights are at stake (Highwood Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses v. Wall, 2018 SCC 26; Lakeside Colony of Hutterian Brethren v. Hofer). Natural justice requires notice of the nature of the charge and consequences (Hofer at 195-196) and an unbiased tribunal, tested by whether a reasonably informed bystander could perceive bias (Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 623 at 636). Early-stage defects may be cured by a fair subsequent hearing (Histed v. Law Society (Manitoba)), but only where the later hearing is full and fair.
firac.application: Property and contractual rights were engaged. The Court found PJHL was never clear who it was pursuing: notices, the chair's opening remarks and instructions focused on Craighead alone, and the team was never told its liability rested on 'guilt by association' until the close of the case. The July 11, 2017 letter and Eaton complaint did not constitute proper particulars. Stonehouse, having acknowledged bias, improperly administered the Governors' preliminary vote (held before particulars were provided) and rendered the preliminary jurisdiction and disclosure rulings; the chair relied on those rulings, so the defect was not cured by the subsequent hearing. Whether the rulings were reasonable was irrelevant to the apprehension of bias.
firac.conclusion: No error; PJHL breached both the notice and unbiased-tribunal requirements, and the defect was not cured by the hearing.

firac.issue: Did the chambers judge err by considering the interests of the players under s. 102 of the Societies Act, and was that issue properly before her?
firac.facts: PJHL argued the players were non-members and that impact on players had not been pleaded, relying on an affidavit prepared for an injunction application that was never proceeded with but which entered the petition record. The judge made one finding that players could lose their opportunity to play junior hockey if the team was expelled.
firac.rule: Section 102 relief is assessed on the reasonable expectations of the affected member in context (Dalpadado v. North Bend Land Society, 2018 BCSC 835; BCE Inc. v. 1976 Debentureholders, 2008 SCC 69). An issue is properly before the court if relevant to the relief claimed, raised at hearing, and the parties had an opportunity to address it.
firac.application: The Court found the impact on players did not take a central role; the judge's reasonable-expectations findings focused on the team. Because PJHL framed the complaint as against the Surrey Knights team, the players' interests were necessarily engaged as it is difficult to separate a team from its players. The dispersal-draft evidence was in the record and referred to without objection, and PJHL had opportunity to (and did) tender further evidence on reconsideration.
firac.conclusion: No error; the issue was relevant, raised, and addressable, and the judge did not overweigh player interests.

firac.issue: Was the remedy prohibiting further proceedings in respect of the September 24, 2015 incident an appropriate exercise of discretion under s. 102?
firac.facts: The judge ordered PJHL to cease and take no further action against the respondents relating to the incident. PJHL argued the procedural findings did not justify a permanent bar and that the matter should have been remitted with directions.
firac.rule: Section 102(2) confers a broad discretion to grant equitable orders 'with a view to remedying or bringing to an end the matters complained of'; remedies are discretionary and owed deference unless based on error of law, wrong principle, irrelevant considerations, or are unjust (Khela v. Phoenix Homes; Wilson v. Alharayeri, 2017 SCC 39). Re-litigation of matters already decided elsewhere may be abuse of process (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63).
firac.application: The judge found more than minor failures: PJHL's treatment lacked probity and fair dealing, ignored the interests of the team and Mr. Gill, and targeted only Craighead, who had already received a substantial penalty from BC Hockey and Hockey Canada. Given PJHL's persistent focus on the same individual for the same conduct, ending the proceedings was the only way to remedy the unfairness.
firac.conclusion: No error in principle; the discretionary remedy was upheld.

firac.issue: Should the chambers judge have recused herself, or reopened the hearing, on the basis of a reasonable apprehension of bias because her son played in the league?
firac.facts: After the reasons were released but before entry of the order, PJHL sought disqualification on the basis that the judge's son played in the PJHL when judgment was rendered, or alternatively to reopen the hearing on the players'-impact issue.
firac.rule: The test is whether a reasonable, informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically, would conclude the judge's conduct gives rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias (Yukon Francophone School Board v. Yukon (A.G.), 2015 SCC 25; Wewaykum Indian Band v. Canada, 2003 SCC 45). There is a strong presumption of impartiality; the interest must be substantial, not trifling or shared by the whole community (Liszkay v. Robinson). Reopening before entry of order requires a probable miscarriage of justice or a probable change in result (Grewal v. Grewal; Moradkhan v. Mofidi).
firac.application: Considering the size of the league, the eligible age group, and the substantial turnover and transitory connection of players, the judge concluded her son's participation gave rise to no interest in the outcome and no reasonable apprehension of bias. On reopening, she found no probable miscarriage of justice and no probable change in result, as the players'-impact issue was inherent in PJHL's own framing of the complaint. PJHL alleged no error of law or principle, only disagreement with the outcome.
firac.conclusion: No error; the applications to recuse and to reopen were properly dismissed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Clancy v. Farid

defining_issues: Did the Registrar err in dismissing the appeal for failure to perfect it within the judicial deadline set by Thorburn J.A.?
Should the Registrar's dismissal order be set aside and the time to perfect the appeal extended in the interests of justice?

firac.issue: Did the Registrar err in dismissing the appeal for failure to perfect it within the judicially set deadline?
firac.facts: Thorburn J.A. had extended the time to perfect on condition that perfection of the appeal on both liability and damages be completed within 30 days of receipt of the motion judge's decision on damages; those reasons were released June 27, 2023, making the deadline July 26, 2023. Mr. Farid did not perfect, and on March 15, 2024 the Registrar dismissed the appeal under r. 61.13(3.1). Mr. Farid argued the deadline ran from Brownstone J.'s February 23, 2024 decision and complained of prejudgment and ex parte communications, but filed no affidavit.
firac.rule: Rule 61.13(3.1) of the Rules of Civil Procedure requires the Registrar to dismiss an appeal not perfected within the time prescribed by an order of a judge of the appellate court. Under r. 3.02(3) the Registrar has no power to vary a time provided by the Rules, and nothing gives the Registrar power to vary a time set by a judge's order.
firac.application: Thorburn J.A. set a 'strict timeline' of 30 days from receipt of the damages reasons; that the June 27, 2023 reasons also granted injunctive/mandatory relief did not change the clear starting point for the count. Mr. Farid's collateral attempt to challenge the copyright-assignment portion in the Superior Court did not alter the deadline. The unsupported allegations of prejudgment and ex parte contact had no evidentiary basis. The Registrar had no discretion and was bound to dismiss.
firac.conclusion: There was no error in the Registrar's interpretation of the deadline or in the dismissal order.

firac.issue: Should the Registrar's dismissal order be set aside and the time for perfection extended in the interests of justice?
firac.facts: Mr. Farid moved to set aside the dismissal, relying on his self-represented status and alleged advice from unnamed pro bono counsel that he need not perfect until Superior Court proceedings concluded. He never amended or filed a further notice of appeal covering the June 27, 2023 orders. One respondent, Ms. Clancy, filed an affidavit deposing to ongoing reputational harm and inability to find work while the defamatory posts remained online.
firac.rule: A Registrar's order may be set aside under r. 61.16(5). The governing factors are those in Issasi v. Rosenzweig, 2011 ONCA 112: bona fide intention to appeal, length of and explanation for the delay, prejudice to the responding parties, merit of the appeal, and the overriding 'justice of the case'. Where the missed deadline was itself a tailored judicial extension set to limit prejudice, heightened attention to delay/explanation and to prejudice is warranted. Merit is assessed by whether the appeal so lacks merit that it is just to deny the right to proceed (Issasi, para. 10; 1250264 Ontario Inc. v. Pet Valu Canada Inc., 2015 ONCA 5).
firac.application: The delay was lengthy given more than two years had elapsed and the deadline was already a one-year extension; the claimed reliance on counsel's advice lacked evidentiary support and Mr. Farid pressed on despite a clear warning. The respondents faced real prejudice, as shown by Ms. Clancy's affidavit and the need for finality. On the merits, the liability findings (authorship and the limitation-period discoverability finding) attracted deference and were supported by the Duquette forensic report and spoliation reasoning; the notice-of-appeal grounds—inadequate reasons, bias, Charter challenge to the Anton Piller Order, jurisdiction, abuse of process, and the Jordan/s. 11(b) contempt argument—were unsupported by any record and lacked arguable merit.
firac.conclusion: The justice of the case did not support an extension; the motion to set aside the dismissal was dismissed with $5,000 costs to the responding parties.

defining_issues: Was the RPD's finding of adequate state protection in Hungary for the Roma applicants reasonable?
Was the RPD's finding that the applicants had a viable Internal Flight Alternative in Debrecen reasonable?

firac.issue: Was the RPD's finding of adequate state protection in Hungary for the Roma applicants reasonable?
firac.facts: The applicants, Roma citizens of Hungary, alleged persecution: the male applicant was beaten by police after complaining about his son's medical treatment; the female applicant suffered domestic violence from a former partner linked to the racist Hungarian Guard, and police were reluctant to intervene. The RPD accepted the specific incidents but found the applicants had not rebutted the presumption of state protection and had not taken all reasonable steps to seek it, relying heavily on the Hungarian government's 'efforts' and complaint mechanisms such as the IPCB and the Minorities Ombudsman.
firac.rule: A refugee claimant must rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence (Canada (AG) v. Ward, [1993] 2 SCR 689); state protection findings are reviewed for reasonableness (Carillo v. Canada, 2008 FCA 94). Protection must be assessed at the operational level for effectiveness, not merely on the state's good intentions or 'serious efforts' (Bors, Hercegi, Rezmuves, Katinszki 2012 FC 1326, Orgona 2012 FC 1438); where protection is not reasonably forthcoming there is no requirement to seek it (Ward).
firac.application: Justice Russell found the RPD acknowledged horrendous conditions and rising racist violence against Roma yet concluded protection was adequate based on the government's efforts and complaint bodies whose mandate is to make recommendations after the fact, not to provide operational protection. The evidence, including Amnesty International and US DOS reports, indicated police failure to investigate hate crimes and that the head of the National Police neglected 90% of IPCB recommendations. The RPD relied selectively on the investigation of nine notorious attacks and failed to establish 'operational adequacy' or that police were willing and able to protect Roma. Consequently it failed to seriously test the applicants' claim that protection would not be reasonably forthcoming.
firac.conclusion: The state protection analysis was unreasonable; the Court adopted the reasoning in Katinszki and Orgona and quashed the decision.

firac.issue: Was the RPD's finding that the applicants had a viable IFA in Debrecen reasonable?
firac.facts: The RPD held the male applicant could relocate to Debrecen to escape the harassing police officer and that the female applicant's former partner would not be motivated to pursue her there over two years after last contact. The applicants argued no part of Hungary is safe for Roma given generalized racism and the reach of the Hungarian Guard.
firac.rule: An IFA requires, per Rasaratnam v. Canada, [1992] 1 FC 706, that there be no serious possibility of persecution in the proposed location and that relocation not be unreasonable; the analysis must consider the claimant's particular circumstances and, where applicable, the Gender Guidelines.
firac.application: The IFA and state protection issues were intertwined because the applicants' fear of generalized racism formed part of the second prong of the IFA analysis. Since the RPD's assessment of the availability of protection against racist violence anywhere in Hungary was flawed, its conclusion that the applicants could safely relocate to Debrecen could not stand independently.
firac.conclusion: The IFA finding could not survive the flawed state protection analysis; the decision was quashed and remitted for redetermination by a differently constituted RPD.

keywords_rationale: The case is an immigration/refugee judicial review, so K008 (Immigration law, tier-1) and K078 (refugee protection) apply. The determinative issue was K080 (state protection) and the underlying claim rested on K079 (persecution) of Roma; K075 (convention refugee) reflects the s.96/97 claim. The judicial review posture engages K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review — reasonableness under Dunsmuir/Carillo). K100 (Immigration and Refugee Board) is the tribunal whose decision was reviewed. case_name: Herrera v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)

name_verification.name_in_document: Oscar Marquez Herrera v. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

defining_issues: Did the Board's reliance on the applicant's lack of an "allure efféminée" to disbelieve his homosexuality give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias, and was that basis for the credibility finding patently unreasonable?
Did the Board breach procedural fairness by making adverse credibility findings on inconsistencies it noticed only after the hearing, without confronting the applicant?

Did the Board make erroneous findings of fact and fail to conduct a proper state protection analysis, particularly regarding the applicant's inability to complain against police who allegedly assaulted him?

firac.issue: Did the Board's reliance on the applicant's lack of an "allure efféminée" to reject his claimed homosexuality raise a reasonable apprehension of bias and constitute a patently unreasonable credibility finding?
firac.facts: The applicant, a Mexican citizen, claimed a fear of persecution based on his homosexuality. The Board disbelieved that he was gay, noting in particular that he did not appear to have an "allure efféminée", and used this to impugn his credibility.
firac.rule: The test for reasonable apprehension of bias from Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 369 and R. v. R.D.S., [1997] 3 S.C.R. 484 asks what an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically, would conclude. Credibility findings cannot rest on inappropriate stereotypes (R.D.S.; Vodics v. Canada, 2005 FC 783; Kotkova v. Canada, 2004 FC 1706), and sworn testimony is presumed true absent cogent reasons (Maldonado v. MEI, [1980] 2 F.C. 302).
firac.application: The Court held there was no reason for the Board to mention effeminacy unless it assumed a homosexual must be effeminate — a thoroughly discredited stereotype. Applying the Kotkova reasoning ("what does a Jewish person look like?"), the Court found the comment revealed ignorance and prejudice especially astonishing in a decision-maker adjudicating sexual-orientation claims. Basing a credibility finding on external appearance, contrary to Maldonado and Vodics, was also patently unreasonable, and the bias could not have been raised at the hearing since it emerged only in the released reasons.
firac.conclusion: A reasonable apprehension of bias existed and the credibility finding was patently unreasonable, vitiating the entire decision.

firac.issue: Did the Board breach procedural fairness by relying on inconsistencies it identified only after the hearing without giving the applicant an opportunity to explain them?
firac.facts: The Board acknowledged ("a constaté") that it noticed most of the discrepancies only during deliberation, after reviewing exhibits including some produced the day of the hearing, and did not confront the applicant or re-open the inquiry because it already found him not credible.
firac.rule: Whether a duty to confront arises depends on the factors set out in Ngongo v. Canada (M.C.I.), [1999] F.C.J. No. 1627: whether the contradiction was obvious or found on careful later analysis, whether it followed a direct question, whether it was a real contradiction, whether counsel was present, whether an interpreter was used, and whether the decision rested on one or many contradictions.
firac.application: Applying Ngongo, the contradictions were found only on later analysis, not in response to direct questions, and counsel was not present to address them. The Court noted the Board contradicted itself by faulting the applicant both for oral testimony contradicting the PIF and for being too repetitive of it, and treated non-inconsistent matters (e.g. unmentioned medical treatment after beatings) as inconsistencies, contrary to the principle that the PIF gives bare facts explained at the hearing (Basseghi; Grinevich). If the credibility finding preceded the noticing of most inconsistencies, its basis was unclear, reinforcing the bias finding.
firac.conclusion: The Board breached procedural fairness in failing to confront the applicant on the inconsistencies it relied upon.

firac.issue: Did the Board make erroneous findings of fact and fail to properly analyse state protection?
firac.facts: The applicant testified he could not complain about being attacked in 2000 by police officers because he could not identify them, being told a complaint against police required a name. The Board treated this as a general statement that no complaint could be made in Mexico about crimes by unknown perpetrators, and did not address documentary evidence on police treatment of homosexuals, nor question the applicant on matters a gay person would know.
firac.rule: The claimant bears the burden of showing the state cannot protect him (Canada (A.G.) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689). A decision may be set aside where based on erroneous findings of fact made without regard to the evidence, and a proper state protection analysis is required.
firac.application: The Court found the Board mischaracterized the testimony, conflating a complaint against police officers with reporting a crime by an unknown perpetrator — distinct processes even in Canada. The Board failed to analyse what protection could realistically follow from complaining to the very police alleged to be the aggressors, ignored corroborating documentary evidence on police conduct toward homosexuals, never tested the applicant's sexual orientation in the usual manner (e.g. questions about gay venues, as in Polyakov and Zamanibakhsh), and gave no reasons for disbelieving his explanation about the labour Secretariat's summons.
firac.conclusion: The Board made patently unreasonable and erroneous findings of fact and failed to conduct a proper state protection analysis.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the underlying refugee claim; K079 (persecution) reflects the claimed fear of persecution based on sexual orientation; K080 (state protection) is squarely engaged by the third issue on whether Mexican police could protect him. K011 (judicial review) is the procedural vehicle, and K014 (standard of review) reflects the patent unreasonableness applied to the fact/credibility findings. K012 (procedural fairness/natural justice) covers both the reasonable apprehension of bias and the duty-to-confront analyses. There is no controlled keyword specific to sexual-orientation persecution, so that dimension is captured through the persecution and refugee-protection terms.

registry_rationale: The Federal Court is a national court with no distinct registry stated in the decision; only the file number (IMM-9323-03) and place of hearing (Montreal) appear, so registry is left null.

defining_issues: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection in Ukraine, particularly in Kiev, with clear and convincing evidence?
Is Ukraine in a state of complete breakdown such that state protection is unavailable, whether generally or for religious minorities?

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection in Ukraine, particularly in Kiev, with clear and convincing evidence?
firac.facts: The claimants, Evangelical Baptist converts from Kiev, alleged persecution (vandalism, hateful graffiti, violence) because of their religion and claimed the police were unresponsive. They filed multiple police reports, medical and insurance records. In several instances they withheld the religious/hate motivation from police, declined to testify to enable a criminal investigation, sought police reports only for insurance purposes, or did not report bodily-harm incidents at all.
firac.rule: States are presumed capable of protecting their citizens (Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689). To rebut the presumption, a claimant must provide 'clear and convincing' evidence of the state's inability to protect (Ward), must take all reasonable steps to seek protection (Peralta), provide police with sufficient evidence to mount a successful investigation (Karaseva), and give authorities a sufficient opportunity to respond (Montemayor Romero). Adequacy is assessed objectively (Martinez) and the claimant must persuade on a balance of probabilities with reliable and probative evidence (Flores Carrillo); protection need not be perfect (Villafranca; Zalzali; Smirnov). A claimant cannot rely on inadequacy where the failure flows from their own reluctance to pursue matters (Rio Ramirez).
firac.application: The Panel examined each police report and found the police were in fact responsive given the information provided. The claimants repeatedly withheld the hate/religious motivation, declined to testify when police offered to open an investigation, obtained reports solely for insurance purposes, and failed to report bodily-harm incidents, reflecting a subjective reluctance to engage the state rather than an objective failure of protection. The summonses and initiated criminal proceedings contradicted the assertion that police did nothing. The claimants submitted no objective evidence of inadequate protection specific to Kiev.
firac.conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection; their personal evidence did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection in Kiev was inadequate.

firac.issue: Is Ukraine in a state of complete breakdown such that state protection is unavailable, whether generally or for religious minorities?
firac.facts: The claimants alleged the 2014 upheaval made Ukraine dangerous, with pro-Russians targeting Baptists as alleged pro-American agents. Objective evidence (US DOS reports, UNHCR July 2014 update, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reports) showed armed conflict concentrated in the eastern regions and Crimea, with Kiev receiving internally displaced persons fleeing the east.
firac.rule: The presumption of state protection fails only where the state is in complete breakdown (Ward). Where the state effectively controls its territory, has military, police and civil authority and makes serious efforts to protect citizens, occasional failures do not rebut the presumption (Villafranca).
firac.application: The Panel found the conflict isolated to the eastern regions; Kiev, in north-central Ukraine, was a place of refuge for IDPs. The government remained mindful of its human-rights obligations and police were managing violence, including in Kiev. Objective evidence showed that in non-eastern regions it was persons perceived as pro-Russian separatists (not Baptists) who were targeted, and where Jewish minorities were threatened the police deterred protestors. There was no evidence Evangelical Baptists were being targeted or that Kiev was in breakdown.
firac.conclusion: Kiev and the non-eastern regions were not in a state of complete breakdown; Ukraine effectively controls its territory there and makes serious efforts to protect citizens, so the presumption of state protection was not displaced.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K080 (state protection) is the determinative issue and the core of both confirmed issues. K078 (refugee protection) and K075 (convention refugee) capture the ss. 96/97 claim. K079 (persecution) reflects the alleged religious persecution underlying the claim. K025 (freedom of religion) is engaged because the claimants alleged persecution as Evangelical Baptist converts and the analysis turned on treatment of religious minorities. Vandalism (K038) was considered as a possible tag but is a passing factual detail rather than a legal issue, so it was omitted.

registry_rationale: The Refugee Protection Division heard and decided the matter at Toronto, Ontario, so the registry/office is Toronto.

defining_issues: Was the female claimant's fear of persecution objectively well-founded, given the availability of adequate state protection in Hungary for Roma?
Did the female claimant rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence, including by taking all reasonable steps to seek protection?
Do the claimants qualify as persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA?
Do the male claimant and the children's claims succeed independently of the female claimant's claim?

firac.issue: Was the female claimant's fear of persecution objectively well-founded, given the availability of adequate state protection in Hungary for Roma?
firac.facts: The principal female claimant, of Roma ethnicity, and her ethnic Hungarian husband and three children fled Hungary in 2009 after years of harassment, school segregation, workplace abuse, threats, and violent attacks by the Hungarian Guard and others; family members were also attacked. She rarely reported incidents to police, believing they did not care about Roma.
firac.rule: Under s. 96 IRPA a claimant must establish a serious possibility of persecution. There is a presumption that a state can protect its citizens, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence (Ward; Flores Carillo). The test is whether protection is adequate, not perfect, measured by 'serious efforts' (Villafranca); the burden is proportional to the level of democracy (Kadenko); local failures do not equal state failure absent a broader pattern (Zhuravlvev).
firac.application: The panel reviewed extensive documentary evidence and found that, despite significant ongoing discrimination against Roma and reported racially motivated violence and an increase in anti-Roma marches, Hungary is a functioning democracy in effective control of its territory. Discrimination did not cumulatively rise to persecution, and there was no systematic failure of protection. Police in the majority of cases investigate, arrest, and prosecute crimes against Roma, and effective oversight mechanisms exist (Minority Ombudsman, Equal Treatment Authority), though the Independent Police Complaints Body was found less effective.
firac.conclusion: The panel found adequate state protection is available in practice; the claimant's fear was not objectively well-founded on a Convention ground.

firac.issue: Did the female claimant rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence, including by taking all reasonable steps to seek protection?
firac.facts: The claimant reported only some incidents (her husband's 2006 assault, her brother's 2005 firebombing) and failed to report others (2004 home invasion, 2007 assault on her son, 2009 threatening calls, 2009 Guard break-in), citing fear and belief police would not help. She gave limited and at times contradictory details of police responses.
firac.rule: A claimant must approach the state where protection might reasonably be forthcoming and cannot merely show unsuccessful past efforts; in a democracy the onus is heavy (Villafranca; Kadenko; De Baez). Testimony of similarly situated persons may rebut the presumption.
firac.application: The panel found the claimant did not provide persuasive evidence that police failed to investigate reported incidents, and that her failure to report other serious incidents was objectively unreasonable. Family members were not shown to be similarly situated given the sparse detail. She took no further steps to complain of alleged police inaction.
firac.conclusion: The claimant did not make diligent efforts to seek protection and failed to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection; her s. 96 claim failed.

firac.issue: Do the claimants qualify as persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA?
firac.facts: Same facts as the s. 96 analysis; no additional distinct risk was established.
firac.rule: Section 97(1) IRPA requires proof, on a balance of probabilities, of a personalized risk to life or of torture or cruel and unusual treatment; state protection findings apply equally.
firac.application: For the same reasons — availability of adequate state protection — the panel found no such personalized risk established on a balance of probabilities.
firac.conclusion: The claimant is not a person in need of protection under s. 97.

firac.issue: Do the male claimant and the children's claims succeed independently of the female claimant's claim?
firac.facts: The male claimant and the three children's claims were joined and were largely dependent on the female claimant's narrative, with no evidence differentiating them.
firac.rule: Joined claims (Rule 49(1) RPD Rules) stand or fall on their own evidence; dependent claims fail where the principal claim fails and no distinguishing evidence exists.
firac.application: Since no persuasive evidence significantly differentiated the male claimant's or children's claims from the female claimant's, the same state-protection conclusion applied.
firac.conclusion: The male claimant and children are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection; all claims rejected.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) capture the s. 96/97 refugee claim. K080 (state protection) is the determinative issue. K069 (discrimination) and K065 (racism) reflect the anti-Roma discrimination and racially motivated violence at the heart of the country-conditions analysis. K076 (deportation/removal) is a weaker pick reflecting the consequence of return to Hungary but is included as the claim concerns risk on return; it is borderline. No Charter or hate-speech offence keywords apply since this is an administrative refugee determination.

defining_issues: Did the chambers judge err by declining to impose a permanent (unvariable) publication ban rather than one that either party could apply to vary or vacate?
Did the chambers judge err in ordering the appellant to post $15,000 security for costs based on a finding that she held accessible equity in Ontario property?

firac.issue: Did the chambers judge err by declining to impose a permanent publication ban that could never be varied or vacated?
firac.facts: On I.J.'s application, a chambers judge initialized the style of cause, extended a Supreme Court trial publication ban to the appeal, and sealed the appeal file, while providing that either party could apply to vary or vacate the ban. I.J. sought review, arguing the ban should be permanent and unvariable.
firac.rule: On a review of a chambers order, the applicant must establish that the chambers judge erred in law or principle or misconceived the material facts; a review is not a rehearing (Semenoff v. Bridgeman, 2015 BCCA 139; DeFehr v. DeFehr, 2002 BCCA 139; Haldorson v. Coquitlam (City), 2000 BCCA 672).
firac.application: Assuming without deciding that a chambers judge has jurisdiction to impose a permanent ban, I.J. showed no error of law or principle in the judge's decision to make a variable ban instead. The Court noted I.J. remains entitled to be heard should any application to vary or vacate the ban be brought.
firac.conclusion: No error was established; the order making a variable publication ban was upheld.

firac.issue: Did the chambers judge err in ordering security for costs based on the appellant's equity in Ontario property?
firac.facts: The respondents obtained an order requiring I.J. to post $15,000 security for costs within 30 days, staying the appeal in the interim. The judge relied on evidence that I.J. was the registered owner of Ontario property; I.J. asserted her son was the beneficial owner but provided no supporting evidence, and on review claimed the property had since been transferred to her son, again without evidence.
firac.rule: The applicant must show the chambers judge misconceived the material facts or erred in law or principle to succeed on review (Semenoff v. Bridgeman, 2015 BCCA 139).
firac.application: The judge based his finding on the evidence before him, which showed I.J. as registered owner. Because she offered no evidence of beneficial ownership by her son, it could not be said the judge misconceived the facts; the same evidentiary gap persisted on the review.
firac.conclusion: No error was established; the security-for-costs order was upheld.
