firac.issue: Was the impugned online material likely to expose members of the targeted groups to hatred or contempt within the meaning of s. 13(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act?
firac.facts: The CNP Forum contained postings by 'Rocket440' and others attacking Jews, Blacks, Arabs, Asians, homosexuals and other groups with dehumanizing slurs, Holocaust denial, calls to kill or eradicate minorities, and claims that Jews controlled the American media.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) CHRA prohibits communicating matter likely to expose persons to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground. In Nealy v. Johnson and Canada (HRC) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892, 'hatred or contempt' means unusually strong and deep-felt emotions of detestation, calumny and vilification; 'likely' means no proof of actual effect is required. Warman v. Kouba, 2006 CHRT 50 sets out hallmarks of hate messages.
firac.application: The material displayed numerous Kouba hallmarks: portraying targeted groups as innately evil and deserving eradication, dehumanizing comparisons to animals and vermin, highly inflammatory slurs, trivialization of the Holocaust and slavery, calls to violence, and portrayal of Jews as a menace controlling institutions. The media-control posting, read in context, was not legitimate discourse but vilification.
firac.conclusion: The material was likely to expose the targeted groups to hatred or contempt within s. 13(1).

firac.issue: Were the hate messages communicated 'repeatedly' as required by s. 13(1)?
firac.facts: The messages were posted on a publicly accessible Internet message board that any member of the public could view at any time.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) requires that the matter be communicated 'repeatedly'; s. 13(2) confirms application to Internet communication. Warman v. Kulbashian, 2006 CHRT 11; Schnell v. Micka; Canada (HRC) v. Winnicki, 2005 FC 1493.
firac.application: Because the messages remained on the CNP Forum and could be viewed at any time by anyone using the Internet, they were being communicated repeatedly.
firac.conclusion: The repeated-communication requirement was satisfied.

firac.issue: Did the evidence establish that the respondent Bobby Wilkinson communicated or caused to be communicated the impugned messages?
firac.facts: Postings under 'Rocket440' signed 'Forum Administrator' were linked to the email bobby.wilkinson@sympatico.ca and an Ottawa location; on Stormfront.org 'MeinStruggle'/'Bobby' admitted running the Canadian Nazi/Socialist ezboard forum until it was shut down for hate speech, and referenced a s. 13(1) complaint served on his grandfather Robert P. Wilkinson.
firac.rule: A prima facie case, if believed, is complete and sufficient in the absence of an answer (Ontario (HRC) v. Simpsons-Sears (O'Malley)). Under s. 13, a person may be liable for messages authored by others if he 'caused' them to be communicated; a forum administrator with power to edit/delete/screen posts can be liable (Warman v. Kulbashian).
firac.application: The Tribunal drew inferences that Bobby Wilkinson was 'Rocket440' and the forum administrator who authored some messages and, having power to remove and having viewed others' posts, allowed them to remain. Wilkinson did not appear and offered no answer, so the uncontradicted prima facie case stood.
firac.conclusion: Wilkinson communicated and/or caused the impugned messages to be communicated; a prima facie case of discrimination against him was established.

firac.issue: Was a discriminatory practice established against the Canadian Nazi Party as a group acting in concert?
firac.facts: The forum's web address incorporated 'canadiannaziparty' and a discussion invited people to 'Join the National Nazi Movement,' listing one supposed new member and two moderator monikers.
firac.rule: Section 13(1) applies to a group of persons acting in concert; the group need not be a formal legal entity (Nealy v. Johnston), but there must be evidence of persons acting in concert.
firac.application: There was no evidence the CNP existed as a legal entity or that anyone other than Wilkinson administered the forum; the alleged 'member' and second moderator did not establish two or more persons acting in concert. The CNP was found to be nothing more than Wilkinson's alter ego.
firac.conclusion: The complaint against the Canadian Nazi Party was not substantiated and was dismissed.

firac.issue: What remedies, including a penalty, should be ordered?
firac.facts: The Commission and Warman sought a cease-and-desist order and a $6,000 penalty against each respondent. The content was vicious and extreme, advocating extermination of minorities. Wilkinson appeared to be a young person of modest means with no proven prior discriminatory practice.
firac.rule: Section 54(1)(a) permits a cease-and-desist order; s. 54(1)(c) permits a penalty up to $10,000, with s. 54(1.1) factors: nature/gravity of the practice, wilfulness/intent, prior practices, and ability to pay.
firac.application: A cease-and-desist order was appropriate. The extreme, wilful nature of the messages favoured a significant penalty, but Wilkinson's modest means and absence of prior discriminatory practice moderated the amount.
firac.conclusion: Wilkinson was ordered to cease and desist and to pay a $4,000 penalty within 120 days.

keywords_rationale: K007 (Human rights) is the tier-1 practice area. K061 (hate speech) and K063 (online hate/social media) capture the core subject — hate messages on an Internet forum. K070 (discriminatory messages) and K113 (CHRA s. 13), with K108 (Canadian Human Rights Act), are the specific statutory basis of the complaint. K072 (human rights tribunal) reflects the adjudicating body. K066 (white supremacism) and K065 (racism) capture the Nazi/white-power content; K058 (antisemitism) and K062 (Holocaust denial) capture the anti-Jewish and Holocaust-denial material; K122 (swastika) reflects the swastika image on the forum home page. Borderline picks are K122 (a single factual detail) and K065 (overlaps with the broader hate-speech terms), but both are genuinely engaged by the record.
location_rationale: The decision states the hearing was 'conducted at the Tribunal's offices in Ottawa' and is signed 'OTTAWA, Ontario July 10, 2007'; the Parties of Record list the place of hearing as 'Ottawa, Ontario.'
registry_rationale: The Canadian Human Rights Tribunal is a national body but the hearing was held and decision signed at its offices in Ottawa, Ontario, under Tribunal file T1095/7605.

name_verification.name_in_document: ALEXANDRE KHODOS, TATIANA JIJINA, IOULIA KHODOS v. THE SOLICITOR GENERAL OF CANADA

defining_issues: Did the PRRA Officer err by failing to adequately assess the risk to the applicants arising from their status as successful business people, focusing instead on their Jewish ethnicity?
Did the PRRA Officer err in concluding that adequate state protection was available to the applicants in the face of allegedly contrary evidence?

firac.issue: Did the PRRA Officer err by failing to adequately assess the risk arising from the applicants' successful business, focusing instead on their Jewish ethnicity?
firac.facts: The applicants, Russian Jews whose refugee claim had been rejected by the CRDD (with Khodos found not credible), sought a PRRA claiming they feared for their safety because of their Jewish ethnicity and their successful business, having faced extortion by anti-Semitic skinheads. The PRRA decision referred extensively to ethnicity. The applicants argued the Officer failed to focus on their business status.
firac.rule: Section 113(c) of the IRPA requires a PRRA Officer to consider risk assessments under sections 96-98. Under s. 96 the Officer may take into account CRDD findings, particularly where no new evidence is adduced. The reviewable standard for such factual weighing was patent unreasonableness.
firac.application: The Court found the Officer's references to ethnicity occurred within an analysis of risk and state protection, and it was the applicants themselves who cast every event in terms of ethnicity/religion, making Jewish identity the common thread through which business-related risk was alleged. Having failed on ethnicity, the applicants could not fault the Officer for insufficient attention to their business status. The Officer was aware of corruption and extortion in Russia, and the real complaint was about the weighing of the evidence, which was not patently unreasonable.
firac.conclusion: The Officer committed no reviewable error; the challenge to the risk assessment failed.

firac.issue: Did the PRRA Officer err in concluding that adequate state protection existed despite allegedly ignored contrary evidence?
firac.facts: The applicants argued the Officer ignored the police's failure to return a telephone call, a threatening telephone call, and the events surrounding the beating of Khodos's stepson Artem. Country reports indicated state protection, while imperfect, was adequate and applied to business people as well as the general public.
firac.rule: A decision-maker need not mention every fact examined. There is a presumption of adequate state protection which an applicant must displace with clear and convincing evidence. The standard of review for this finding was reasonableness.
firac.application: Although the Officer's analysis on state protection was sparse, significant country evidence confirmed adequate protection extending to business people. It was reasonably open to the Officer to conclude, on all the evidence, that despite events specific to the applicants, adequate state protection was available, and that the evidence was insufficient to displace the presumption. More written analysis would have been helpful but the conclusion was not unreasonable.
firac.conclusion: The state protection finding was reasonable; the application for judicial review was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a judicial review of a PRRA decision. K081 (stay of removal) and K078 (refugee protection) reflect the pre-removal risk assessment context; K079 (persecution) and K080 (state protection) are central to the s. 96/97 risk analysis and the presumption of adequate state protection. K093 (Jewish) and K065 (racism) capture the applicants' claimed anti-Semitic/skinhead extortion basis. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) reflect the procedural posture and the patent unreasonableness/reasonableness standard applied. K081 is a somewhat weak pick as the case concerns a PRRA rather than a stay motion, but no closer PRRA-specific keyword exists in the vocabulary.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Toronto, Ontario, March 24th, 2004' and 'PLACE OF HEARING: TORONTO, ONTARIO'.
registry_rationale: The Federal Court sat and heard the matter at Toronto, Ontario, as stated in 'PLACE OF HEARING: TORONTO, ONTARIO'.

name_verification.name_in_document: [no public name] (Private Proceeding / Huis clos), Claimant citizen of Sweden

defining_issues: Did the harassment and racist violence the claimant experienced in Sweden amount to persecution establishing a well-founded fear under the Convention refugee definition?
Was adequate state protection available to the claimant in Sweden such that his claim must fail even if he faced a risk?
Was the claimant a person in need of protection facing a danger of torture or risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment?

firac.issue: Did the racist harassment and violence the claimant experienced over his years in Sweden amount to persecution?
firac.facts: Over roughly nine years' residence (1986–1995, briefly 1998), the claimant, a Black Christian originally from Zaire, alleged four skinhead/neo-Nazi attacks (two in 1986–1989, two in 1994, one of which followed ignoring a warning to avoid a racist town) plus threats and harassment by racist Muslims. During the same period he obtained asylum, became a Swedish citizen, was continuously employed, obtained further education, raised a family and benefited from social welfare; his ex-wife and children continue to live in Sweden without particular race-based problems.
firac.rule: Persecution requires an 'element of repetition and relentlessness' (Valentin v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1991] 3 F.C. 390 (C.A.)). Discrimination and harassment, even cumulatively, may fall short of persecution.
firac.application: The panel found the incidents were episodic rather than systematic or relentless, and that the claimant otherwise led a productive, relatively harassment-free life. He provided no evidence that conditions on return would be worse than those he had faced. The events constituted discrimination and harassment not amounting to persecution.
firac.conclusion: The claimant did not face more than a mere possibility of persecution on race or any other Convention ground; not a Convention refugee.

firac.issue: Did the claimant rebut the presumption that Sweden was able to protect him?
firac.facts: On the various occasions the claimant or a social/camp worker filed police reports, there was no follow-up, and some officers made rude comments (e.g., asking whether he wanted a bodyguard). Country documentation showed Sweden has a neo-Nazi/skinhead problem but treats it as a high priority, with effective law and judiciary, an independent ombudsman, hate-motivation as an aggravating sentencing factor since 1994/1995, and government support for anti-racism efforts. Sweden is a stable constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy.
firac.rule: States are presumed able to protect their citizens absent complete breakdown, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence (Canada (A.G.) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689). In democratic states, a claimant must exhaust all reasonable courses of action; refusal of some officers to act does not itself show state inability (Kadenko v. Canada). Protection need only be adequate, not perfect (Zalzali v. Canada, [1991] 3 F.C. 605 (C.A.)).
firac.application: The claimant did not pursue matters after initial reports or complain to the police hierarchy or ombudsman, and thus did not exhaust available avenues in a democratic state. The rude police comments reflected imperfect but adequate protection. His evidence was insufficient to rebut the Ward presumption.
firac.conclusion: Adequate state protection was available in Sweden; the claim fails on this ground in the alternative.

firac.issue: Was the claimant a person in need of protection under the danger-of-torture / risk-to-life standard?
firac.facts: The claimant asserted continued risk from neo-Nazis and from his former teacher's ex-husband and associates; the same evidentiary record concerning past events and state protection applied.
firac.rule: A person in need of protection must show, on removal, a personal danger of torture or a risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment (IRPA s. 97).
firac.application: Based on the same evidence establishing only discrimination/harassment and the availability of state protection, the panel found the claimant would not personally face such dangers on removal to Sweden.
firac.conclusion: The claimant is not a person in need of protection.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 refugee protection and K079 persecution are central to the first issue (whether harassment/discrimination amounted to persecution). K080 state protection is the determinative alternative ground, applying Ward and Kadenko. K065 racism and K066 white supremacism (neo-Nazi/skinhead) reflect the factual basis of the feared harm. K076 deportation reflects the removal context. K100 identifies the Immigration and Refugee Board / RPD as the deciding institution. Borderline: K076 is weak since the case is a refugee determination rather than a removal challenge, but the claimant had complied with a removal order and removal to Sweden was assessed.
location_rationale: The decision states 'Place of Hearing / Lieu de l'audience: Ottawa, Ontario' and is 'Dated at Ottawa this 10th day of June 2003.'
registry_rationale: The Refugee Protection Division heard and decided the matter at Ottawa, Ontario; the hearing location and dating clause both identify Ottawa.

case_name: J.F.M. v. Canada Employment Insurance Commission

name_verification.name_in_document: J. F. M. v. Canada Employment Insurance Commission

defining_issues: Did the Appellant voluntarily leave his employment, such that the Commission met its onus under the Employment Insurance Act?
If the departure was voluntary, did the Appellant have just cause for leaving under paragraph 29(c) of the Employment Insurance Act?

firac.issue: Did the Commission prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant voluntarily left his employment?
firac.facts: The Appellant, an accounting assistant of 14 years, submitted a resignation letter on July 25, 2013 effective August 9, 2013, while suffering from work-related stress, insomnia, an adjustment disorder and anxiety. Days later, on August 1 and 5, 2013, he sought medical attention and attempted to withdraw his resignation. The Employer refused the withdrawal, having decided to abolish his position for financial/administrative reasons. Medical notes corroborated his condition at the time of resignation.
firac.rule: Under jurisprudence (White 2011 FCA 190; Patel 2010 FCA 95; Tanguay A-1458-84), the Commission must first prove voluntary departure on a balance of probabilities before the burden shifts to the claimant to prove just cause under s. 29(c). A line of CUB decisions treats a tendered and accepted resignation as voluntary even where later retracted, but the Tribunal is not bound by CUB decisions and found a rebuttable presumption of voluntariness arises.
firac.application: The Tribunal found the Appellant's own evidence and the medical records showed he was reacting involuntarily to trauma caused or exacerbated by workplace stress, and was not operating with a clear or sound mind when he resigned. His attempt to withdraw the resignation and his long employment history showed the act was out of character. The presumption of voluntariness was rebutted in these exceptional circumstances; his conduct was not sufficiently deliberate or reckless to constitute voluntary separation or misconduct, and the Employer refused the withdrawal for its own economic reasons, not because of the Appellant's conduct.
firac.conclusion: The Commission proved the Appellant departed his employment but did not prove he did so voluntarily on a balance of probabilities.

firac.issue: If the departure were voluntary, would the Appellant have had just cause for leaving under paragraph 29(c) of the Act?
firac.facts: The Appellant left due to overwhelming workplace stress and a documented adjustment disorder, anxiety and insomnia. He did not discuss the situation with the Employer, seek sick leave, a leave of absence, vacation, or other employment before resigning.
firac.rule: Paragraph 29(c) EI Act: just cause exists where, having regard to all circumstances, the claimant had no reasonable alternative to leaving, including working conditions dangerous to health or safety (29(c)(iv)). Section 30(1) disqualifies claimants who voluntarily leave without just cause.
firac.application: Because the Commission failed to prove voluntary departure, the Tribunal was not required to decide just cause. It observed, in the hypothetical, that it would have found just cause under s. 29(c)(iv), and that no reasonable alternatives existed given the Appellant's inability to cope or communicate with his Employer, the situation being 'manifestly intolerable' to him.
firac.conclusion: Not necessary to decide; obiter, just cause would have been found had the departure been voluntary.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the core subject matter — an employment insurance dispute turning on voluntary leaving and misconduct in the employment relationship. K001 (Administrative law) applies because the decision is a Social Security Tribunal administrative adjudication reviewing a Commission decision. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is a weak/borderline pick capturing the termination/resignation dynamic (the Employer accepted the resignation and abolished the position) but the case is about EI entitlement, not a dismissal claim. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) are weak procedural picks flagged as such — the Tribunal weighed burden of proof and CUB jurisprudence but this was a statutory appeal, not judicial review. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated employment insurance / voluntary leaving keyword, so these five are the closest available matches; K085, K011 and K014 are flagged as approximate.
location_rationale: The decision does not state the seat of the Tribunal. The hearing was held by teleconference and the Social Security Tribunal is a national body. Although the Appellant's medical treatment took place in Montréal and Verdun (Jewish General Hospital, Verdun Family Medical Clinic), this reflects the Appellant's location, not the Tribunal's, so city and province are left null.
registry_rationale: No court registry or office is identified in the decision; the SST General Division heard the matter by teleconference under reference number GE-13-1754, with no registry stated.

case_name: Petrova v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)

name_verification.name_in_document: Olga Petrova and Vadim Petrov v. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

defining_issues: Did the CRDD err by focussing on the issue of Jewish ethnicity/identity and not addressing the other issues it had identified at the outset of the hearing?
Did the CRDD err in its assessment of the evidence, including the re-issued birth certificate and the adverse inference drawn from the son's testimony?
Did the CRDD fail to consider whether Ms. Petrova was perceived by her persecutors to be Jewish?

firac.issue: Did the CRDD err by focussing on ethnicity and not determining the other issues it had identified at the start of the hearing?
firac.facts: The claim of well-founded fear of persecution in Russia rested solely on Ms. Petrova's Jewish ethnicity. At the outset the CRDD told the applicants and counsel it would begin by focussing on ethnicity and 'move on from there, if we need to'. The CRDD concluded the applicants had not established Jewish ethnicity.
firac.rule: To qualify as a Convention refugee, a claimant must establish a well-founded fear of persecution by reason of one of the five recognized grounds. Where identity/ground is dispositive, a tribunal need not address other issues.
firac.application: The applicants were clearly advised of the importance of ethnicity. Once the CRDD properly concluded that identity had not been established, it was unnecessary to consider the remaining evidence, because failure to establish identity made it impossible to establish that any fear of persecution was by reason of a Convention ground.
firac.conclusion: No reviewable error; the CRDD was entitled to dispose of the claim on the ethnicity/identity issue alone.

firac.issue: Did the CRDD err in its assessment of the evidence, including the re-issued birth certificate and the adverse inference from the son's testimony?
firac.facts: Ms. Petrova relied on a recently re-issued birth certificate. There was evidence that authentic birth certificates attesting Jewish parentage can be obtained with ease even where untrue. The 15-year-old son, who had attended a Jewish school and taken weekly religious instruction, could give only garbled accounts of Jewish belief and did not know the term 'bar mitzvah'.
firac.rule: Findings of fact and the weighing of evidence by the CRDD are entitled to deference and will not be disturbed where they are supported by, and rationally connected to, the evidence before the tribunal.
firac.application: On review of the transcript and documents, the CRDD's findings were rationally connected to the evidence. Given the evidence about easily obtained certificates, and the son's inability to demonstrate Jewish knowledge despite attending a Jewish school, the CRDD could reasonably discount the birth certificate and draw an adverse inference from the son's testimony.
firac.conclusion: No reviewable error in the assessment or weighing of the evidence.

firac.issue: Did the CRDD fail to consider whether Ms. Petrova was perceived to be Jewish by her persecutors?
firac.facts: Perceived Jewish identity was not advanced as the basis of the claim before the CRDD, and counsel did not argue it, conceding the onus on the claimant regarding credibility and ethnic identity. The CRDD's reasons nonetheless addressed whether the applicants 'would be perceived to be Jewish'.
firac.rule: A tribunal is not required to decide an issue not advanced before it; and an argument not raised at the hearing generally cannot ground judicial review. Perceived membership in a Convention ground can be relevant where properly raised.
firac.application: The perceived-identity argument was not the basis of the claim as advanced and was not argued by counsel. In any event, the CRDD expressly considered whether the applicants would be perceived to be Jewish based on their identity documents and found no persuasive evidence.
firac.conclusion: No reviewable error; the argument was not raised below and was in any event addressed by the CRDD.

keywords_rationale: K008 (Immigration law) is the tier-1 practice area. K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) capture the Convention refugee claim and alleged anti-Semitic persecution in Russia. K011 (judicial review) reflects the procedural posture — an application for judicial review of a CRDD decision. K014 (standard of review) applies because the Court deferred to the CRDD's findings of fact where rationally connected to the evidence. K093 (Jewish) is central because the claim turned on establishing Jewish ethnicity/identity. K027 (Jewish holidays) is a weaker/borderline pick — the case touches on Jewish religious knowledge (bar mitzvah, religious instruction) as evidence of identity, but is not squarely about holidays; it is included as the closest identity-culture keyword available. Antisemitism keywords were considered but the case concerns proof of ethnicity rather than adjudicating hate conduct.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Vancouver, British Columbia, Thursday the 14th day of March 2002' and the 'PLACE OF HEARING: Vancouver BC' confirms the location.
registry_rationale: The hearing was in Vancouver, BC ('PLACE OF HEARING: Vancouver BC'), and the reasons are dated at Vancouver, British Columbia; the Federal Court sat there.

name_verification.name_in_document: JACQUES ABENAIM v HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN

defining_issues: Does the entire settlement amount received by Mr. Abenaim constitute a taxable retiring allowance under subsection 248(1) and subparagraph 56(1)(a)(ii) of the Income Tax Act, or is part of it non-taxable moral damages?
Are Mr. Abenaim's signing of the release characterizing the amount as a retiring allowance and his reporting of it as such on his tax return determinative of the amount's true nature?
If the payment has a dual purpose, how should it be apportioned between taxable and non-taxable components?

firac.issue: Does the entire settlement amount constitute a taxable retiring allowance, or is a portion non-taxable moral damages?
firac.facts: After being dismissed twice (1990 and 2006), Mr. Abenaim filed an oppression action under s. 241 CBCA, and alternatively actions for damages and an injunction, against the Konica Minolta group. A 2009 judicial-mediation settlement produced a lump sum paid in exchange for a release. No breakdown of the amount was agreed at the settlement conference; the sum was arbitrary and far exceeded any pay in lieu of notice available on the case-law scale (max ~18 months, about $390,000, or even 36 months at ~$780,000 on a $260,000 average salary).
firac.rule: Subparagraph 56(1)(a)(ii) ITA requires a retiring allowance to be included in income; subsection 248(1) defines a retiring allowance as an amount received in respect of a loss of office or employment. Per Overin and Merrins, only damages relating to a loss of employment fall within s. 248(1); the test is 'but for the loss of employment would the amount have been received?' Moral damages not linked to loss of employment are not taxable as a retiring allowance.
firac.application: The Court found the entire amount could not be pay in lieu of notice, since even 36 months' notice fell well below the sum paid. The proceeding was principally an oppression action; counsel testified that without the oppression action Mr. Abenaim would never have received the amount, and that the Minolta/KM groups' relationship with him had always been oppressive, humiliating and marked by broken promises, twice depriving him of his life's work. The Court concluded the payment had a dual purpose: part compensating loss of employment/contractual damages (taxable) and part compensating moral damages unrelated to loss of employment (non-taxable).
firac.conclusion: The payment had a dual character; a portion constitutes non-taxable moral damages while the remainder is taxable as pay in lieu of notice/contractual damages.

firac.issue: Are the release and the tax return filed reporting the amount as a retiring allowance determinative of its nature?
firac.facts: KM Group drafted a release treating the whole amount as taxable and made source deductions to protect itself from tax authorities. Facing financial pressure and unable to fund continued litigation, Mr. Abenaim signed the release on his lawyer's advice to instead contest the characterization with the tax authorities. His accountant reported the amount as a retiring allowance because it appeared as such on the T4.
firac.rule: The characterization stated in a release or tax return is not determinative of the true nature of a payment; the case law consistently permits taxpayers to object to an assessment that reflects their own return (Schwartz; general TCC jurisprudence).
firac.application: The Court held that signing the release and reporting the amount as a retiring allowance were not determinative given Mr. Abenaim's financial circumstances, which left signing and later disputing with the tax authorities as his only realistic option. The lawyer's invoice referring to recovery of salary and severance also did not settle the matter, as omitted terms showed it dealt only 'in particular' with such recovery.
firac.conclusion: The release and tax return did not fix the true nature of the payment; the Court looked to the substance and the underlying civil proceeding.

firac.issue: How should a lump sum with a dual purpose be apportioned between taxable and non-taxable amounts?
firac.facts: No breakdown was agreed during the settlement; Mr. Abenaim's evidence that half was moral damages was confused and contradicted, and counsel confirmed no allocation was ever agreed. His pleadings claimed $1,500,000 in moral damages.
firac.rule: Per Schwartz v. Canada, once a payment is shown to have a dual purpose the bar for establishing the breakdown must not be set too high; there must be some evidence from which the court can infer on a balance of probabilities the portion attributable to each type of damages. Per Dumas and Mohawk Oil, the pleadings and settlement documents may be examined to determine why the amount was paid.
firac.application: The Court used the civil proceeding pleadings as the best guide to apportionment, noting the significant moral-damages claim and that the case-law scale had no influence on the amount actually paid (which also inflated the pay-in-lieu component). It fixed the taxable portion as pay in lieu of notice/contractual amounts and the balance as non-taxable moral damages.
firac.conclusion: A portion was allocated as non-taxable moral damages and the difference as taxable pay in lieu of notice/contractual damages, following the civil pleadings.

keywords_rationale: The case turns on characterizing a settlement flowing from Mr. Abenaim's dismissals and an oppression action, so Labour and employment law (K009) and wrongful dismissal / pay in lieu of notice (K085) are directly engaged, as is Civil litigation (K002) since it is a Tax Court appeal contesting an assessment and relies heavily on the underlying civil pleadings. The Income Tax Act retiring-allowance characterization is the true subject but tax is not available in the controlled vocabulary. K058 (antisemitism) and K065 (racism) are weak/flagged picks included only because the reasons reference a California action over anti-Semitic remarks and alleged racist remarks against Mr. Abenaim; they are background context, not determinative issues.
location_rationale: The judgment states "PLACE OF HEARING: Montreal, Quebec" and is "Signed at Montreal, Quebec"; the appeal was heard at Montreal, Quebec.
registry_rationale: The Tax Court of Canada heard the matter at Montreal (place of hearing Montreal, Quebec); no separate registry office is named beyond this, so Montreal is used.

name_verification.name_in_document: BRANISLAV DJORDEVIĆ v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Did the PRRA officer misinterpret paragraph 113(a) of the IRPA by treating the provision as barring new evidence of risks previously considered by the RPD, rather than barring only evidence not newly arising?
Did the officer err in failing to assess the new evidence (release of the kidnappers and the mother's affidavit) bearing on the ongoing risk to the applicant?

firac.issue: Did the PRRA officer misinterpret paragraph 113(a) of the IRPA regarding what constitutes admissible new evidence?
firac.facts: Mr. Djordevic, a rejected refugee claimant, filed a PRRA raising risks tied to his Jewish ethnicity, HIV-positive status and ongoing threat from his kidnappers. The officer stated the correct test twice but, between those statements, wrote that the identified risks 'could have reasonably been presented to the RPD' because they were 'known to the applicant at the time of his hearing.'
firac.rule: Paragraph 113(a) IRPA limits a rejected claimant to presenting 'only new evidence that arose after the rejection or was not reasonably available' at the time of rejection. Under Raza v Canada (MCI), 2007 FCA 385, a PRRA officer may consider new evidence arising after, or not reasonably available at, the RPD hearing, even where it addresses risk factors the RPD already considered; an application cannot be rejected solely because it addresses the same risk.
firac.application: The officer's conflicting statements meant the Court could not determine which formulation of the test was applied. The inaccurate middle statement suggested the officer focused on whether new grounds of risk were raised, rather than whether new evidence had arisen. Under Dunsmuir, a court may review the record to see if a decision is justified but cannot perform the analysis the decision-maker failed to do. Given the complete absence of analysis of the 350 pages of submissions, the decision lacked transparency and intelligibility.
firac.conclusion: The officer erred; the decision was not transparent or intelligible, and this was reason alone to set it aside.

firac.issue: Did the officer err in failing to assess the new evidence relevant to the ongoing risk from the kidnappers?
firac.facts: After the RPD hearing, the last of the kidnappers (Mr. Dejan and Mr. Oljeg, who received the longest sentences) were released from prison, evidenced by official Municipal Court documents, and the applicant's mother swore an affidavit that the family continued to receive anonymous phone calls seeking the applicant while police refused to act.
firac.rule: New evidence under paragraph 113(a), per Raza, must be credible, relevant, new and material. Evidence relating to events occurring after the RPD hearing could not reasonably have been presented earlier.
firac.application: The release of the kidnappers and the mother's affidavit related to post-hearing events, were credible (official court documents), relevant and material because they could contradict the RPD's finding that the criminal organization posed no ongoing threat. Had these leaders been at large at the time of the RPD hearing, the RPD might have found the applicant in need of protection. The officer failed to refer to this evidence at all, and the Respondent's 'includes' argument was rejected as nonsensical since the kidnapping risk was the principal risk originally presented to the RPD.

defining_issues: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence that Hungary is unable or unwilling to protect Roma citizens?
Did the discrimination and mistreatment experienced by the claimants (including the children) amount to persecution under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA?

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence that Hungary is unable or unwilling to protect its Roma citizens?
firac.facts: The claimants, ethnic Roma from Hungary, described numerous incidents of racist violence and harassment by guardsmen, skinheads and extremists, as well as abuse by police. In most incidents they either did not report to police, fled before police arrived, or could not identify perpetrators. Where police were contacted (broken windows/swastikas, the wife's assault), the police did respond, took reports and increased patrols. The claimants never approached higher police authorities, the Independent Police Complaints Board, the Equal Treatment Authority, the Minority Ombudsman or NGOs, though the principal claimant had contact with a Roma-rights figure (Mr. XXXX).
firac.rule: A state is presumed capable of protecting its citizens except in complete breakdown (Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689). The claimant must rebut the presumption with clear and convincing evidence and must approach the state where protection might reasonably be forthcoming. Local failures do not equal state failure absent a broader pattern (Zhuravlvev). The onus is proportional to the level of democracy (Kadenko). The test is adequacy of protection, not perfect effectiveness (Villafranca; Flores), and the claimant must take all reasonable steps to seek protection.
firac.application: The panel accepted historic and ongoing discrimination and rising extremism against Roma, but found Hungary, a democratic EU member, was making serious operational, legal and institutional efforts — the IPCB, the Equal Treatment Authority, the Minority Ombudsman, dissolution of the Hungarian Guard, prosecutions of the 2008–2009 attackers, police discipline and Roma-integration programs. The claimants had largely failed to seek redress: they did not report incidents to higher authorities, drove off before police could respond, and did not pursue available complaint mechanisms. Their interactions with police did not establish inadequate protection.
firac.conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and did not take all reasonable steps to seek protection; adequate state protection is available in Hungary.

firac.issue: Did the discrimination and mistreatment suffered by the claimants and their children amount to persecution?
firac.facts: The claimants' children faced bullying and segregation at school (one daughter needed psychiatric counselling, one son was beaten); the family's windows were broken and swastikas painted; the son was excluded from soccer by a racist coach; the principal claimant lost his job. The children were partly home-schooled.
firac.rule: To qualify under s. 96/97 IRPA, harm must rise to the level of persecution rather than mere discrimination; incidents falling short of persecution do not ground a claim.
firac.application: The panel found the broken windows and painted walls did not amount to persecution, exclusion by a racist soccer coach was discrimination not persecution, and the children were not denied education even though the family could not afford tutors for all of them. The mistreatment, while regrettable, did not cross the threshold of persecution.
firac.conclusion: The discriminatory treatment experienced by the claimants and their children did not amount to persecution.

defining_issues: Should the Court grant a Crown application to seal the materials filed on the appeal, displacing the open court presumption?
Was it appropriate to anonymize the style of cause in the appeal even though no party sought that relief?

firac.issue: Should the Court grant a Crown application to seal the materials filed on the appeal, displacing the open court presumption?
firac.facts: On an appeal from conviction, the Crown applied to seal the transcript, appeal book, both factums, and other materials. The trial had been heard in camera, a sealing order had been made over certain witnesses' evidence, and a publication ban under s. 486.5 of the Criminal Code protecting the appellant's identity remained in force. The appellant did not oppose and supported the sealing order.
firac.rule: The open court presumption may be displaced under the analytical framework of Dagenais v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp., [1994] 3 S.C.R. 835, R. v. Mentuck, 2001 SCC 76, and the two-step test summarized in Sierra Club of Canada v. Canada (Minister of Finance), 2002 SCC 41 at para. 53. A prior publication ban under s. 486.5 of the Criminal Code that has not been set aside remains in force (R. v. K. (V.) (1991), 68 C.C.C. (3d) 18 at 21 (B.C.C.A.)).
firac.application: Applying the Dagenais/Mentuck framework and the Sierra Club two-step test, the Court was satisfied that the Crown had shown that the presumption of public access to court records must give way. Given that the trial was in camera, that witness evidence was already sealed, and that a s. 486.5 publication ban protecting the appellant's identity remained in force, sealing was necessary. The Court declined to limit the order to the specific materials the Crown listed, since the file contained other documents that also had to be sealed to give effect to the order's rationale.
firac.conclusion: Application granted. The Court's file was sealed; no materials may be disclosed to anyone except counsel and court personnel, save by further order on two days' notice.

firac.issue: Was it appropriate to anonymize the style of cause even though no party sought it?
firac.facts: Neither the Crown nor the appellant sought anonymization of the style of cause, but a publication ban protecting the appellant's identity was in force.
firac.rule: A court may make ancillary orders necessary to give effect to an existing publication ban and to protect against disclosure of identifying information.
firac.application: To make the sealing order and existing publication ban effective, the Court found it necessary to anonymize the style of cause so that identifying information would not appear on publicly available court lists.
firac.conclusion: The appeal was ordered to proceed as Regina v. A.B., with that style of cause used on all publicly available lists relating to the matter.

name_verification.name_in_document: TATYANA LEBEDEVA v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

defining_issues: Did the Board err in finding that a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) was available to the applicant in Russia?
Should the Court entertain the applicant's new procedural fairness argument raised for the first time at the hearing, and was the applicant denied her right to counsel before the Board?
Did the Board err in its application of the Gender Guidelines?
Should any of the five proposed questions be certified as serious questions of general importance?

firac.issue: Did the Board err in finding that a viable internal flight alternative was available to the applicant in Russia?
firac.facts: The applicant, a Russian citizen of Russian Orthodox faith, was harassed and attacked by skinheads in Orenburg who perceived her as Jewish because her daughter married a Jewish man and lived in Israel and because she had travelled to Israel. The Board accepted her credibility but found a viable IFA in Yekaterinburg, noting she had lived in Moscow for eight months without incident and that her mistreatment was localized to Orenburg.
firac.rule: Whether an IFA exists is integral to a refugee determination (Rasaratnam). Once raised, the claimant bears the burden of proving the IFA does not exist or is unreasonable (Thirunavukkarasu). The two-part test asks (1) whether there is no serious possibility of persecution or s. 97 risk in the proposed IFA on a balance of probabilities, and (2) whether it would be reasonable in the claimant's circumstances to relocate there. IFA findings are reviewed on the reasonableness standard (Dunsmuir; Rodriguez Diaz; Sivasamboo), with reasons read as a whole and not microscopically (Medina; Ahmed).
firac.application: The Board did not discount the applicant's Orenburg experience but reasonably found it unique and localized—arising from information spreading through her local community—with no country conditions evidence of similarly based persecution of non-Jews elsewhere. The applicant did not carry the usual risk factors (she is not Jewish, is fair-skinned and Orthodox). The Court found the phrase 'no evidence' meant 'no additional evidence' when read in context. The applicant could have adduced evidence of similarly situated persons, of skinhead networks exchanging information, or that rumours had spread beyond Orenburg, but did not. Her incident-free eight-month stay in Moscow supported the localized-risk finding. Her argument that gossip would spread and her request that the Court re-weigh evidence were rejected, as re-weighing is not the Court's role.
firac.conclusion: The Board did not err; the IFA finding was reasonable and the application for judicial review was dismissed on this ground.

firac.issue: Should the Court entertain the new procedural fairness argument raised for the first time at the hearing, and was the right to counsel denied?
firac.facts: At the hearing before the Federal Court, counsel raised for the first time an allegation that the applicant's right to counsel was denied because she was prevented from asking her counsel a question during the Board hearing. This issue was absent from the memorandum of fact and law and from the leave application.
firac.rule: Rule 309(1) of the Federal Courts Rules requires arguments to be canvassed in the memorandum of fact and law, but the Court retains discretion to allow new arguments, guided by the factors in Al Mansuri v Canada (MPSEP), 2007 FC 22 (knowledge of facts at leave stage, prejudice, completeness of record, relation to issues granted leave, apparent strength, and delay). Greater caution applies where the argument is raised only at the hearing, depriving the respondent of any opportunity to respond.
firac.application: The new issue was entirely unrelated to the issues on which leave was granted, was never raised in the memoranda, and the respondent would be prejudiced by having no opportunity to file responsive evidence or argument. On the merits, the Court read the entire transcript and found the applicant was told she would be questioned by the Board Member and that her counsel could question her later; she was not forced to answer, was not penalized for declining, and was not prevented from telling her story. The argument had no merit.
firac.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the new argument and, in any event, found no breach of procedural fairness.

firac.issue: Did the Board err in its application of the Gender Guidelines?
firac.facts: The applicant argued the Board applied the Gender Guidelines incompletely by concluding her feared harm was not gender-based simply because her son faced similar targeting, ignoring her heightened vulnerability as a woman.
firac.rule: The Guidelines on Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution provide that where the risk factor is not sexual status, the substantive analysis does not vary as a function of gender; the Guidelines are engaged only where the claimant suggests her fear is gender-related (Walcott; Plaisimond). In an IFA assessment, the Guidelines require the Board to consider a woman's ability to travel to and remain in the IFA safely without undue hardship.
firac.application: The applicant never claimed persecution based on her gender; she described her son and his family facing similar treatment and even said she feared more for her son. The Board nonetheless considered her personal circumstances and found she would not face gender-related difficulties relocating within Russia, satisfying the Guidelines' requirement in the IFA reasonableness analysis.
firac.conclusion: The Board did not err in applying the Gender Guidelines.

firac.issue: Should any of the five proposed questions be certified as serious questions of general importance?
firac.facts: Counsel proposed five questions for certification concerning IFA evidence, perceived group membership across localities, right to counsel, leading questions by non-lawyer counsel, and application of the Gender Guidelines.
firac.rule: Paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA permits certification only of a 'serious question of general importance.' The test (Zazai) requires a serious question that would be dispositive of an appeal and that transcends the interests of the immediate parties (Boni; Liyanagamage).
firac.application: The first two questions were factually driven, inseparable from the specific facts, and would not be determinative given the Board did not disregard the applicant's past experience. The procedural fairness questions were not dispositive because they arose only at the hearing and were factually driven. The fifth question would not be determinative because the Board did consider whether the fear was gender-related and did assess gender in the IFA reasonableness analysis; the Guidelines are not engaged where the claimant does not allege gender-related persecution.
firac.conclusion: None of the proposed questions met the certification test; no questions were certified.

defining_issues: Did the adult claimants establish a well-founded fear of persecution on the basis of their evangelical Christian religion in Hungary?
Did the discrimination and harassment the Roma female claimant and her ethnic-Hungarian husband experienced in Hungary rise to the level of persecution under s. 96?
Did the adult claimants rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Hungary with clear and convincing evidence?

firac.issue: Did the adult claimants establish a well-founded fear of persecution based on their practice of evangelical Christianity in Hungary?
firac.facts: The claimants preached publicly and went door to door; skinheads and nationalists attacked their prayer group in 2008 and a Guardist assaulted the male claimant in 2010. They alleged discrimination as evangelical Christians.
firac.rule: Section 96 IRPA requires a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground; discriminatory acts by non-state actors do not amount to religious persecution where the state protects freedom of religion. The panel relied on the US DOS International Religious Freedom Report for Hungary (2016).
firac.application: The panel found that neither the state nor its agents ever prevented the claimants from worshipping or preaching; Hungary's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, penalizes violence against religious communities, and nearly 73% of the population is Christian. The 2008 skinhead attack was discriminatory but did not rise to persecution, and state protection was available for religious freedom.
firac.conclusion: The claimants' religious experiences did not constitute persecution; freedom of religion exists in Hungary and state protection is available on that basis.

firac.issue: Did the discrimination and harassment experienced on the basis of Roma ethnicity amount to persecution under s. 96?
firac.facts: The female claimant is Roma and the male claimant is perceived as Roma by association. They experienced multiple incidents over years: killed dogs, a knocked-down gate, fireworks causing a miscarriage, menacing by uniformed men, and an arson at a relative's home. The male claimant nonetheless worked full-time and provided for his family.
firac.rule: Discrimination becomes persecution only where it is serious or systematic (Sagharichi v. Canada (MEI)); mere Roma ethnicity does not establish more than a mere possibility of persecution (Balogh 2016 FC 426; Csonka; Ahmad); a claimant must link general country conditions to personal circumstances; persecution may be shown through similarly situated individuals (Salibian).
firac.application: The panel found that documentary evidence shows Roma face discrimination in many spheres but are not, as a group, persecuted; no NGO or monitoring report characterizes the situation as persecutory. The claimants' personal experiences — including the male claimant's steady employment — amounted to discrimination and harassment that did not, individually or cumulatively, meet the threshold of serious and persistent harm.
firac.conclusion: The treatment experienced was discrimination, not persecution; there was no forward-looking risk of persecution simply because they are Roma.

firac.issue: Did the adult claimants rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Hungary?
firac.facts: The female claimant called police 5–6 times; police responded to some calls and to the arson (investigators from Budapest confirmed arson, case still open when they left) and to the fallen gate. The male claimant personally contacted police only about the arson; other incidents went unreported or involved unidentifiable perpetrators.
firac.rule: Countries are presumed capable of protecting citizens (Canada (AG) v. Ward); the claimant bears the burden of rebutting this presumption with clear and convincing evidence on a balance of probabilities (Flores Carrillo); the burden is proportional to the level of democracy (Kadenko; Hinzman); state protection need only be adequate at the operational level, not perfect (Villafranca; Racz; Mudrak), and police oversight agencies (IPCB, Commissioner for Fundamental Rights, Equal Treatment Authority) form part of that protection.
firac.application: Hungary is a functioning multi-party democracy in control of its territory with functioning police and courts. The claimants received operationally adequate protection when police responded to the arson and the gate incident; they left before the arson investigation concluded and failed to report most incidents. The panel reviewed the disbanding of the Hungarian Guard, Jobbik's move toward the centre, prosecutions of racist murders, and mechanisms such as the ETA (with documented decisions favouring Roma) and the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights, finding operational adequacy despite imperfections.
firac.conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection with clear and convincing evidence; operationally adequate state protection would be reasonably forthcoming if they sought it.

defining_issues: Did the claimants provide clear and convincing evidence to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Hungary for Roma?
Did the claimants take all reasonable steps to seek state protection before claiming refugee protection in Canada?

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption that Hungary is able to provide adequate state protection to its Roma citizens?
firac.facts: The claimants, Roma citizens of Hungary, alleged discrimination and harm on the grounds of their race across employment, education, housing and public life. Documentary evidence showed a history of discrimination, worsening conditions, right-wing extremism (Jobbik Party, Hungarian Guard) and police excesses against Roma, but also showed anti-discrimination laws, complaint mechanisms (IPCB, Minorities Ombudsman, Equal Treatment Authority), police investigations of anti-Roma attacks, and disciplinary action against officers.
firac.rule: A state is presumed capable of protecting its citizens; the claimant bears the burden of rebutting that presumption with clear and convincing, reliable and probative evidence on a balance of probabilities (Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689; Flores Carrillo, 2008 FCA 94). Local failures do not constitute state failure unless part of a broader pattern (Zhuravlvev). State protection need not be perfect; where a state controls its territory and makes serious efforts, occasional failures do not rebut the presumption (Villafranca). Efforts must actually translate into adequate protection at the operational level (Hercegi; Jaroslav).
firac.application: The panel acknowledged widespread discrimination and persecution of Roma but found the objective documentary evidence showed Hungary, a functioning democracy in effective control of its territory, is making serious operational-level efforts: police investigated anti-Roma attacks (ERRC/Amnesty reports), disciplined and prosecuted officers, and provides oversight bodies (IPCB, Minorities Ombudsman, Equal Treatment Authority) and anti-discrimination legislation. The claimants did not rebut this documentary evidence, and the panel preferred it as drawn from a wide range of reliable sources.
firac.conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection with clear and convincing evidence; protection, though imperfect, was found to be adequate at the operational level.

firac.issue: Did the claimants take all reasonable steps to avail themselves of state protection before seeking refugee status?
firac.facts: The principal claimant reported only one incident (an assault where he was beaten and hospitalized) to the police, who took a written report. He did not follow up, and there were no other incidents reported. His wife made no complaints. His main grievance was employment discrimination he attributed to being Roma. He believed police treat Roma differently based on what he had heard from others.
firac.rule: Refugee protection is surrogate protection invoked only where the claimant has unsuccessfully sought home-state protection; the onus is on the claimant to approach the state where protection might reasonably be forthcoming (Ward; Hinzman). A subjective reluctance or doubting protection without testing it does not rebut the presumption (Camacho; Ramirez). A claimant must approach higher authorities or oversight bodies if dissatisfied with police response (De Baez).
firac.application: The principal claimant made only a single police report and never followed up; he did not pursue available higher recourses such as the Minorities Ombudsman or the Independent Police Complaints Board. His belief that the process would go nowhere was based on hearsay and not on testing the available mechanisms, which the evidence showed do take and act on complaints.
firac.conclusion: The claimants did not take all reasonable steps to seek state protection before claiming in Canada, and no compelling explanation excused the failure.

name_verification.name_in_document: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration v. Yuri Dinaburgsky

defining_issues: Did the defendant obtain lawful admission to Canada for permanent residence in 1989 by false representation, fraud, or by knowingly concealing material circumstances (his foreign criminal convictions), thereby engaging the deeming provision of s. 10(2) of the Citizenship Act?
Could the defendant defeat the reference by arguing that his foreign convictions were wrongful, fabricated, and the product of anti-Semitism, and that he was a minor at the time?

firac.issue: Did the defendant obtain lawful admission for permanent residence by false representation, fraud, or concealment of material circumstances, engaging s. 10(2) of the Citizenship Act?
firac.facts: Before immigrating, Dinaburgsky had been convicted in the Belorussian SSR of attempted rape and gang rape of a minor (committed at ages 15 and 17), theft, escaping prison, and breach of supervision, serving roughly 12 years. On his 1989 permanent residence application and to the visa officer in Rome he answered 'No' to whether he had ever been convicted of any crime, and gave false information about his addresses, employment and education during the years he was actually imprisoned.
firac.rule: Under s. 10(2) of the Citizenship Act, a person is deemed to have obtained citizenship by false representation, fraud, or concealment of material circumstances where they were 'lawfully admitted to Canada for permanent residence' by such means and thereby obtained citizenship. A person who lies or withholds material facts from immigration officers is not 'lawfully admitted' (Bogutin; Skomatchuk, 2006 FC 994). The Minister bears the burden on the civil balance of probabilities, applied with great care given the serious consequences (Odynsky, Obodzinsky). Under s. 19(1)(c) of the Immigration Act a person convicted of an offence punishable in Canada by ten years or more is inadmissible; attempted/gang rape corresponds to sexual assault (Criminal Code s. 271, ten-year maximum), rendering the defendant prima facie inadmissible.
firac.application: The Court accepted the visa officer's evidence of her consistent practice of check-marking answers and found she recorded a 'No' to the conviction question. It found the defendant not credible: he admitted large portions of his application were untrue and shifted his explanations. The Court found he did not tell the officer he 'had troubles with the law when young'; had he disclosed the convictions, the officer would have flagged the matter for investigation of inadmissibility (including his minority). His serious convictions made him prima facie inadmissible, and his concealment meant he was not lawfully admitted.
firac.conclusion: The Court held that the defendant gained admission by false representation, fraud, or concealment of material circumstances, and is therefore deemed under s. 10(2) to have obtained citizenship by those means.

firac.issue: Could the defendant avoid the deeming provision by asserting his foreign convictions were fabricated, wrongful, and anti-Semitic, or that he was a minor?
firac.facts: The defendant and his wife testified the rape convictions were fabricated by Bobruisk authorities because he was Jewish; an undated Minsk newspaper article corroborated this claim. The offences were committed at ages 15 and 17, though he was tried and convicted in adult court and served the sentence.
firac.rule: A revocation reference under s. 18 determines whether admission/citizenship was obtained by misrepresentation; the Court cannot re-try foreign convictions. A conviction in adult court is a conviction within the meaning of the Immigration Act even where the person was a minor (De Freitas). The proper forum to raise wrongful-conviction and minority factors was the visa interview.
firac.application: The Court found the detailed 17-page foreign verdict more credible than the self-serving allegations and newspaper article, and held it could not re-try the defendant 33 years later. His minority might have been a relevant factor for the visa officer, but only if disclosed; because he concealed the convictions entirely, no such assessment occurred. Whether to forgive or condone the concealment was a matter for the Minister and Governor in Council, not the Court.
firac.conclusion: The defence failed; the alleged wrongfulness of the convictions and his minority did not displace the finding of concealment or the operation of s. 10(2).

K077 (inadmissibility) is central — the defendant's serious foreign convictions rendered him prima facie inadmissible under s. 19(1)(c). case_name: CL v Canada Employment Insurance Commission

name_verification.name_in_document: CL v Canada Employment Insurance Commission

defining_issues: Does the Claimant's appeal have a reasonable chance of success such that leave to appeal should be granted?
Is there an arguable case that the General Division made an important factual error or applied the wrong legal test for misconduct by discounting the Claimant's workplace safety concerns?
Is there an arguable case that the General Division member was biased or prejudiced (anti-Semitic) or used an unfair process?

firac.issue: Should leave to appeal be granted where the applicant must show the appeal has a reasonable chance of success?
firac.facts: The Claimant was dismissed after refusing to comply with her employer's requirement to return to full-time in-office work. The General Division found this was misconduct under the EI Act and she was disqualified from benefits. She sought leave to appeal to the Appeal Division.
firac.rule: Under s. 58(2) of the Department of Employment and Social Development Act (DESD Act), leave may be granted only where the appeal has a reasonable chance of success, meaning an arguable ground on which the appeal might succeed (Osaj v Canada (AG), 2016 FC 115; Paradis v Canada (AG), 2016 FC 1282). The four grounds under s. 58(1) are procedural fairness, jurisdictional error, legal error, and important factual error.
firac.application: The member reviewed the Claimant's reasons for appeal, the documentary record, and the hearing recording, and also considered whether the self-represented Claimant might have other unidentified grounds. He found no arguable case under any of the four grounds.
firac.conclusion: The appeal had no reasonable chance of success, so leave to appeal was refused.

firac.issue: Is there an arguable case that the General Division made an important factual error or misapplied the misconduct test by discounting the Claimant's safety concerns?
firac.facts: The Claimant worked at a Jewish organization and, post-October 7, 2023, feared anti-Semitic attacks and wanted armed security and hybrid work. She refused full-time office work; her employer would not compromise and dismissed her after she requested a severance package.
firac.rule: An important factual error under s. 58(1)(c) DESD Act arises where the decision is based on a finding made by ignoring or misunderstanding legally relevant evidence. Misconduct focuses on the employee's conduct and entitlement to benefits, not the employer's conduct; the only question is whether the employee knew or ought to have known of the requirement and its consequences and engaged in conduct that objectively could lead to dismissal (Lance v Canada (AG), 2025 FCA 41). Where an employer's prior conduct caused the alleged misconduct, the conduct may not be wilful (Astolfi v Canada (AG), 2020 FC 30).
firac.application: The General Division applied the correct legal test, citing binding authority. Evidence about the employer's failure to address safety concerns was not legally relevant to whether the Claimant's conduct was misconduct. Astolfi did not apply because the evidence did not show she refused after harassment or threats; she requested a severance package the day before the meeting and refused office work believing she knew better than her employer. Her refusal was a deliberate, wilful choice that caused her unemployment.
firac.conclusion: No arguable case of an important factual error or misapplication of the misconduct test; the finding was supported by the relevant evidence and the purpose of EI benefits.

firac.issue: Is there an arguable case that the General Division member was biased or used an unfair process?
firac.facts: The Claimant alleged the individuals reviewing her case were anti-Semitic because they did not understand the point of her claim regarding workplace safety after October 7, 2023.
firac.rule: A tribunal member is presumed impartial. The person alleging bias must show a reasonably informed person, viewing the matter realistically and having thought it through, would conclude it more likely than not the decision-maker would not decide fairly (Committee for Justice and Liberty v National Energy Board, [1978] 1 SCR 369; Canadian Pacific Railway v Canada (AG), 2018 FCA 69; Kuk v Canada (AG), 2024 FCA 74).
firac.application: The member reviewed the decision and hearing recording and found nothing suggesting anti-Semitism, bias, or prejudice. The refusal to accept the Claimant's argument reflected the law of misconduct, not bias. The General Division gave her a full and fair opportunity to know and meet the case, present evidence, call a witness, and respond to the Commission's materials.
firac.conclusion: No arguable case of bias or procedural unfairness.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns dismissal and EI benefit entitlement turning on misconduct. K085 (wrongful dismissal/termination) reflects the termination context, though here framed as EI misconduct disqualification. Borderline picks: K085 is somewhat imperfect since this is EI misconduct rather than a wrongful dismissal suit, but it is the closest labour keyword; the vocabulary has no dedicated employment-insurance/misconduct term.

name_verification.name_in_document: The Minister of Justice of Canada v. Jozsef Pataki a.k.a. Mike Harrison
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The style of cause in the reasons names 'The Minister of Justice of Canada' as respondent and Jozsef Pataki (a.k.a. Mike Harrison) as applicant/appellant, whereas the metadata uses the conventional 'Canada (Attorney General)' form; these designate the same federal respondent and the citation matches, so the reference is consistent.

defining_issues: Did the extradition judge err in the committal order by mis-assessing the reliability of the Record of the Case, excluding certain defence evidence, and finding sufficient evidence to commit?

Did the Supreme Court's decision in Németh change the legal principles governing the Minister's surrender decision so as to bind the Minister when the person sought is a Canadian citizen who has never held refugee status?
Was the Minister's decision that Mr. Pataki's unconditional surrender would not be unjust or oppressive under s. 44(1) of the Extradition Act reasonable?

firac.issue: Did the extradition judge err in ordering committal for extradition?
firac.facts: Hungary sought Pataki's extradition on two counts of fraud arising from the purchase of oil without intent to pay. Pataki challenged the reliability of the Record of the Case, sought to lead evidence that another person shared his name, and argued the evidence was insufficient.
firac.rule: An extradition judge may reject evidence found manifestly unreliable; the person sought need not undermine the entire Record of the Case; committal requires evidence upon which a properly instructed jury could convict. Exculpatory evidence going to trial issues (e.g., identity) is not admissible to show manifest unreliability.
firac.application: The judge understood she could reject manifestly unreliable evidence and considered only 'sourced' statements; the transcript evidence was not manifestly unreliable. The proposed defence identity evidence was proper trial exculpatory evidence, not proof of manifest unreliability. There was ample evidence to infer Pataki purchased the oil without intending to pay.
firac.conclusion: No error; the appeal of the committal order was dismissed.

firac.issue: Did Németh alter the onus and standard the Minister must apply where the person sought is a non-refugee?
firac.facts: Pataki is a dual Canadian and Hungarian citizen who is Jewish, never came as a refugee, and has never held refugee status. He argued Németh v. Canada (Justice), 2010 SCC 56 changed the law governing the Minister's surrender decision under s. 44(1)(b).
firac.rule: Under s. 44(1)(b) of the Extradition Act the Minister must refuse surrender where the request is made to prosecute by reason of protected grounds. Németh and Gavrila v. Canada (Justice), 2010 SCC 57 hold that for a person with subsisting refugee status the onus shifts to the Minister to show on a balance of probabilities that the circumstances justifying refugee status no longer exist; Németh (para. 113) expressly does not affect the burden on a person without refugee status. Slovenia v. Soba, 2011 ONCA 206 confirmed Németh changed the law only for certified convention refugees.
firac.application: Németh rested on the Refugee Convention and IRPA cessation provisions, which govern obligations to persons holding refugee status, not citizens. Pataki is a Canadian citizen who never held refugee status, so Németh's shifted onus does not apply to him. The Minister correctly declined to apply Németh's principles.
firac.conclusion: Németh did not change the legal principles governing a non-refugee; the Minister acted correctly.

firac.issue: Was the Minister's decision that unconditional surrender was not unjust or oppressive reasonable?
firac.facts: Pataki argued surrender would be unjust or oppressive because he would not receive a fair trial in Hungary given lack of respect for the rule of law and significant anti-Semitism, and that the Minister should obtain assurances on speciality and bail.
firac.rule: Under s. 44(1)(a) surrender must be refused if it would be unjust or oppressive; the Minister's assessment attracts substantial deference and is reviewed for reasonableness (per United States of Mexico v. Hurley). The person sought bears the onus of showing the risk of unfair trial.
firac.application: There was ample material before the Minister to support the conclusion that Pataki had not met his onus to show he would not get a fair trial. He established no basis to fear a speciality violation, and Hungary's functioning bail system made a bail assurance unnecessary.
firac.conclusion: The Minister's decision was reasonable; the application for judicial review was dismissed.

defining_issues: Did the claimants establish an objectively well-founded fear of persecution, or a risk under s. 97, such that they qualify as Convention refugees or persons in need of protection?
Did the claimants rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Hungary with clear and convincing evidence?

firac.issue: Did the claimants establish an objectively well-founded fear of persecution or a s. 97 risk given the situation of Roma in Hungary?
firac.facts: The claimants, a woman, her brother and her minor son, are Roma from a Hungarian city near the Austrian border. They alleged continuous persecution, abuse and harassment on account of their ethnicity, including assaults by the Hungarian Guard and a Molotov cocktail thrown at their house. Documentary evidence confirmed widespread discrimination and violent attacks against Roma.
firac.rule: Sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act require a claimant to establish a serious possibility of persecution for a Convention ground, or on a balance of probabilities a danger of torture or risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment. A well-founded fear has both subjective and objective components.
firac.application: The panel accepted that Roma in Hungary face discrimination and live in a climate of fear, and that the claimants may have suffered discrimination and harassment. However, the male claimant's testimony about the assaults was inconsistent (differing dates), there were no claim-specific corroborating documents, and the determinative question turned on whether the fear was objectively reasonable — i.e., whether state protection was available. Because adequate state protection existed, the objective basis for the fear was not made out.
firac.conclusion: The claimants did not establish a serious possibility of persecution or a s. 97 risk; they are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

firac.issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Hungary with clear and convincing evidence?
firac.facts: The claimant said she did not report the Hungarian Guard assaults to police, citing a childhood incident where police sided with a teacher, and gave inconsistent evidence about whether the incidents were reported. Police did attend when the Molotov cocktail was thrown, took a report, but could not proceed because the perpetrators were unknown. Counsel argued discrimination against Roma is institutionalized and police fail Roma from the first report.
firac.rule: Countries are presumed capable of protecting their citizens; the claimant bears the burden of rebutting that presumption with clear and convincing evidence establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate (Canada (AG) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689; Flores Carrillo, 2008 FCA 94). A claimant must take all reasonable steps to seek protection, and mere subjective distrust of police in a functioning democracy does not rebut the presumption (Camacho, 2007 FC 830).
firac.application: The panel found no reliable evidence that the claimants sought police protection, and even if they had reported, the perpetrators were unidentified so no investigation could realistically proceed. Reviewing extensive country documentation, the panel found the evidence on Hungary's efforts 'mixed' but concluded that, as an EU member bound to certain standards, Hungary is making serious efforts through mechanisms such as the Independent Police Complaints Board, the Equal Treatment Authority, the Minorities Ombudsman and various Roma integration and anti-discrimination programs. Distrust alone did not suffice, and the claimants failed to approach available higher authorities or complaint mechanisms.
firac.conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection; adequate, though not perfect, state protection is available to Roma victims in Hungary.

defining_issues: Did the claim qualify for expedited determination without a hearing under s. 170(f) of the IRPA?
