name_verification.name_in_document: S. K. (Plaintiff) c. B. S. et al (Defendant)

defining_issues: Should the court exercise its discretion under s. 21.1 of the Divorce Act to dismiss the defendant's proceedings because he withholds consent to the ghet?
Does the defendant's coerced 'willingness' to consent to the ghet constitute removal of the barriers to the plaintiff's religious remarriage?
Has the defendant established genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature (desire for reconciliation) for refusing to remove the barriers?
Must a motion under s. 21.1 of the Divorce Act meet the criteria for a safeguard order, including urgency, and is the rabbi's expert opinion admissible?
Can the court suspend the separate proceedings for separation as to bed and board to render its s. 21.1 order effective?

firac.issue: Should the court exercise its discretion under s. 21.1 of the Divorce Act to dismiss the defendant's proceedings because he withholds consent to the ghet?
firac.facts: The parties are observant Orthodox (Satmar) Jews married civilly and religiously, with three children. The plaintiff filed for divorce and served the defendant with a s. 21.1 affidavit confirming she had asked him in writing to remove all barriers to her religious remarriage and that he had failed to do so. Without the ghet she remains an 'agunah', unable to remarry in her faith.
firac.rule: Section 21.1 of the Divorce Act permits a deponent spouse to file an affidavit setting out barriers to remarriage within the deponent's religion; where the served spouse does not confirm removal of the barriers, the court may dismiss any application filed by that spouse under the Act and strike its pleadings and affidavits. Bruker v. Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54, confirms it is public policy to discourage such barriers and to 'level the playing field' (per Tannenbaum J., Droit de la famille – 2296).
firac.application: The plaintiff satisfied her burden under s. 21.1(2). The defendant did not file an affidavit confirming removal of the barriers, and the court found he was likely using his refusal to grant the ghet as leverage to obtain concessions on financial and custodial matters — precisely the mischief s. 21.1 was designed to remedy.
firac.conclusion: The court exercised its discretion to dismiss the defendant's proceedings and personal affidavits in the divorce file and foreclosed him from filing further proceedings under the Act.

firac.issue: Does the defendant's coerced 'willingness' to consent to the ghet constitute removal of the barriers to the plaintiff's religious remarriage?
firac.facts: The defendant stated in affidavits that he was 'willing' to consent to the ghet only in order to protect his relationship with his children and his right to exercise his civil recourses, and conceded that a ghet requires his free and enlightened consent, which he said was not realistic 'at the present time'.
firac.rule: Under s. 21.1(3)(a) the served spouse must file an affidavit indicating that all barriers referred to in para. 2(e) have been removed; a valid ghet requires the husband's free and wilful consent. Coerced willingness to consent, given only to protect one's rights, is not a genuine consent (Droit de la famille, 3558, [2000] R.D.F. 268).
firac.application: The defendant filed no affidavit confirming removal of the barriers and admitted his purported consent was not the free, enlightened consent required by the Rabbinical Court. His conditional willingness, aimed at preserving his own procedural rights, could not enable the ghet to be validly granted.
firac.conclusion: The defendant had not removed, and had not shown he would remove, the barriers to the plaintiff's religious remarriage.

firac.issue: Has the defendant established genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature (a desire for reconciliation) for refusing to remove the barriers?
firac.facts: The defendant claimed a religious and community obligation to attempt reconciliation and relied on Rabbi Poupko's opinion that Jewish faith requires efforts at reconciliation. Yet he had filed a Motion for Separation as to Bed and Board pleading that the parties' will to live together was 'gravely undermined' and that they were 'at an impasse', and the plaintiff, who had already attended counselling, adamantly ruled out any reconciliation and alleged mental cruelty.
firac.rule: Section 21.1(4) allows the court to refuse to exercise its powers where the served spouse shows 'genuine grounds' ('un motif sérieux' in the French text) of a religious or conscientious nature. A genuine belief must be authentic, rooted in reality, and reflected in the person's conduct — not mere words uttered to avoid the law.
firac.application: Reconciliation can in principle be a genuine ground, but the court found it was not genuine here: the plaintiff firmly refused reconciliation (which requires two people), the high level of animosity and volume of proceedings made it unrealistic, and, most tellingly, the defendant's own Motion for Separation as to Bed and Board asserted the marriage was over, contradicting his reconciliation claim. The court concluded he was shielding himself from dismissal of his proceedings.
firac.conclusion: The defendant did not satisfy the court that his refusal rested on a genuine religious or conscientious ground; his refusal was leverage.

firac.issue: Must a s. 21.1 motion meet the criteria for a safeguard order (including urgency), and is the rabbi's expert opinion admissible?
firac.facts: The defendant argued the motion to dismiss was akin to an injunction/safeguard order requiring urgency, appearance of right, irreparable harm and balance of convenience, and relied on Rabbi Poupko's opinion that ghet and civil proceedings normally evolve and conclude together.
firac.rule: Section 21.1 contains no urgency criterion; its 15-day response period indicates the motion should be dealt with efficiently and, following Darel v. Darel, 1999 ABQB 881, as a preliminary objection. Expert opinion must meet the relevance and necessity criteria of R. v. Mohan, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 9, affirmed in White Burgess v. Abbott and Haliburton, 2015 SCC 23.
firac.application: The court held s. 21.1 imposes no safeguard-order test; the motion was filed and treated as an interlocutory motion to be resolved before the merits so that each party could advance rights free of the ghet threat. The court applies domestic law, not Jewish religious law, and Rabbi Poupko's opinion on Jewish law and on how civil proceedings should evolve was neither relevant nor necessary to the issues.
firac.conclusion: The safeguard-order/urgency argument was rejected and the rabbi's expert opinion was ruled inadmissible.

firac.issue: Can the court suspend the separate proceedings for separation as to bed and board to render its s. 21.1 order effective?
firac.facts: The defendant had filed an Introductive Motion for Separation as to Bed and Board (file 500-04-066333-155) raising the same custody, access and nesting claims as in the dismissed divorce proceedings. Section 21.1 only permits dismissal of proceedings filed under the Divorce Act.
firac.rule: Section 21.1 of the Divorce Act limits dismissal/striking to proceedings under that Act. However, arts. 2, 20 and 46 of the Code of Civil Procedure give the court power to control its process; where orders in a divorce file and a separation file would concern the same parties and object, divorce orders take precedence (Gobeille v. Savard, [1975] C.A. 94).
firac.application: The court could not dismiss the separation proceedings, as they were not filed under the Divorce Act, but to give effect to its s. 21.1 order it invoked its C.c.p. powers to suspend those proceedings, since they duplicated the custody/access claims and could circumvent the foreclosure.
firac.conclusion: The separation as to bed and board proceedings were suspended until the defendant files an affidavit confirming the ghet has been granted.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K051 (religious divorce/get) is the central subject — the s. 21.1 refusal of the ghet. K117 (Divorce Act) is the governing statute and s. 21.1 its key provision. K025 (freedom of religion) and K034 (sincerity of belief) capture the defendant's asserted genuine religious/conscientious ground and the court's assessment of its authenticity. K097 (Orthodox/Hasidic community) and K093 (Jewish) reflect that the parties are observant Satmar Orthodox Jews. K098 (rabbi) reflects the disputed and ultimately inadmissible expert opinion of Rabbi Poupko. K048 (custody/access) is engaged because the withheld ghet was found to be leverage over custody, access and nesting claims. K026 (halacha) captures the role of Jewish law governing the ghet. Borderline: K048 and K026 are secondary but genuinely engaged.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'SUPERIOR COURT (Family Division), CANADA, PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC, DISTRICT OF MONTRÉAL', identifying the city as Montréal and the province as Quebec.
registry_rationale: The 'DISTRICT OF MONTRÉAL' and file number 500-12-326305-152 indicate the Montréal registry of the Superior Court.

name_verification.name_in_document: Christopher Hudspeth and George Smitherman v. William Whatcott et al. (Hudspeth v. Whatcott)

defining_issues: Are the defendants estopped, for the purposes of the motions, from denying that the pamphlets distributed at the 2016 Pride Toronto Parade constitute hate speech?
Should the plaintiffs' proposed class action be dismissed under the anti-SLAPP provisions of s. 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act?
Is the proposed class action an abuse of process warranting dismissal?

Do the pleadings disclose reasonable causes of action for defamation, civil conspiracy to injure, and intentional infliction of mental distress that can be advanced as a class action on behalf of a collective, or only as individual claims?
Should a Norwich order be granted compelling Mr. Whatcott to identify the unidentified co-defendants?

firac.issue: Are the defendants estopped, for the purposes of the motions, from denying that the pamphlets distributed at the 2016 Pride Toronto Parade constitute hate speech?
firac.facts: In Saskatchewan (Human Rights Commission) v. Whatcott, 2013 SCC 11, the Supreme Court found that two of Mr. Whatcott's flyers were hate speech and enjoined similar distribution. In 2016 Mr. Whatcott and his 'Gay Zombies' distributed similar anti-gay pamphlets at the Pride Toronto Parade. The plaintiffs invoked issue estoppel/res judicata; Mr. Whatcott argued the parties, statutes and content differed.
firac.rule: Res judicata, issue estoppel (Danyluk v. Ainsworth Technologies Inc., 2001 SCC 44) and the flexible abuse-of-process doctrine (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63) may preclude re-litigation; issue estoppel requires same parties, same question, finality and necessity, and its application is discretionary (Penner v. Niagara, 2013 SCC 19). Abuse of process can bar re-litigation where the strict requirements of estoppel are not met.
firac.application: The co-defendant Gay Zombies are Mr. Whatcott's privies, and the pamphlets were similar enough to the Saskatchewan flyers that, although the parties were not identical, the doctrine of abuse of process precluded re-litigation of the hate-speech characterization for the limited, technical purpose of the preliminary motions. The court exercised its discretion to invoke this bar for the motions only, expressly leaving the merits (including any distinguishing features of a political-event context) to the trial judge.
firac.conclusion: For the purposes of the two motions, Mr. Whatcott and his privies are estopped from denying that the pamphlets are or could be hate speech; whether estoppel binds at trial is left to the trial judge.

firac.issue: Should the proposed class action be dismissed under the anti-SLAPP provisions of s. 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act?
firac.facts: Mr. Whatcott moved to dismiss the action as a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation, arguing his distribution of the pamphlets at a political event was expression on a matter of public interest being suppressed by litigation.
firac.rule: Under ss. 137.1–137.5 CJA the moving party must first show the proceeding arises from expression on a matter of public interest; the onus then shifts to the responding party to show substantial merit, no valid defence, and that the harm outweighs the public interest in protecting the expression (1704604 Ontario Ltd. v. Pointes Protection Assn.; Platnick v. Bent; Able Translations). Hate speech is, by its nature, not in the public interest (Saskatchewan (HRC) v. Whatcott).
firac.application: Because Mr. Whatcott was estopped from denying the pamphlets were hate speech, he could not meet the threshold of showing expression on a matter of public interest, as hate speech interferes with rather than contributes to public discourse. In the alternative, even if he met the threshold, the plaintiffs showed substantial merit, no valid defence, and serious harm sufficient to outweigh any protected expression.
firac.conclusion: The anti-SLAPP motion was dismissed.

firac.issue: Is the proposed class action an abuse of process?
firac.facts: The Statement of Claim was intemperate, contained irrelevant and prejudicial historical material, and at a press conference the plaintiffs said they wished to 'stamp out' and punish Mr. Whatcott with a $100 million judgment.
firac.rule: Courts may stay or dismiss for abuse of process under Rule 21.03(3)(d) and inherent jurisdiction; abuse includes proceedings brought for an improper purpose such as harassment (Canam Enterprises v. Coles; Lang Michener v. Fabian). The power is exercised only in the clearest of cases (Temilini v. Ontario (OPP)).
firac.application: Though the tone of the pleadings and press conference lent some traction to the abuse allegation, the claim revealed a genuine grievance and possible civil wrongs, and raised important juridical questions about the civil law's response to hate speech against a marginalized group. A properly pleaded opt-in joinder action would not be abusive.
firac.conclusion: The action was not dismissed as an abuse of process.

firac.issue: Do the pleadings disclose reasonable causes of action for defamation, civil conspiracy, and intentional infliction of mental distress advanceable by a collective as a class action?
firac.facts: The claims were framed on behalf of the LGTBTQ2SI Community and large classes (500,000 Marchers, a 500-person Liberal Subclass, and 9,000 Recipients), seeking to remedy harm caused by hate speech through common law torts.
firac.rule: Defamation is a personal action; a group claim lies only where each member is 'singled out' (Knupffer v. London Express; Seafarers International Union v. Lawrence; Bou Malhab v. Diffusion Métromédia CMR, 2011 SCC 9). The Class Proceedings Act, 1992 is procedural and creates no substantive collective rights (s. 5(1)(a)). Conspiracy requires targeting of individuals (Canada Cement Lafarge); intentional infliction of mental suffering requires flagrant conduct, intent/knowledge and provable illness (Boucher v. Wal-Mart). Tort law compensates individual injury; harm to a community from hate speech is the province of criminal/public law.
firac.application: The claims were, in pith and substance, an attempt to have the court act as public prosecutor for hate speech against a collective. Given the size, heterogeneity and generality of the allegations, no individual could be shown to have been singled out across the whole class, and a class action cannot supply a missing element of the cause of action. However, individual members (e.g., named politicians in the Liberal Subclass) may have personal claims capable of joinder.
firac.conclusion: It was plain and obvious the pleadings disclosed no reasonable collective cause of action; the Statement of Claim was struck in its entirety, with leave to deliver a Fresh as Amended Statement of Claim for an opt-in joinder action (which may seek declaratory and injunctive relief) rather than a class action.

firac.issue: Should a Norwich order be granted compelling identification of the unidentified co-defendants?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs did not know the identities of the Gay Zombies or Mr. Whatcott's financial backers; Mr. Whatcott was the only source and refused to disclose them.
firac.rule: A Norwich order requires: a bona fide claim; the respondent's involvement beyond mere witness; the respondent being the only practical source; a balancing of interests; and that the interests of justice favour disclosure (GEA Group AG v. Ventra Group Co.; 1654776 Ontario Ltd. v. Stewart).
firac.application: Mr. Whatcott was involved in the wrong and was the only practical source of the identities, which would in any event have to be disclosed at discovery. The interests of justice, and natural justice permitting the co-defendants to defend themselves, favoured disclosure, subject to first allowing the co-defendants to identify themselves.
firac.conclusion: The Norwich motion was granted on terms: substituted service on Mr. Whatcott, an opportunity for co-defendants to self-identify, failing which Mr. Whatcott must disclose their identities.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, since the case turns on tort pleadings, class-proceeding procedure and remedies. K015 (defamation) and K017 (group defamation) are central, as the Liberal Subclass's claim failed for want of individual 'singling out' under Knupffer/Bou Malhab. K020 (class action) captures the core holding that the Class Proceedings Act is procedural and cannot create collective rights, leading to conversion into an opt-in joinder action. K061 (hate speech) is engaged throughout via the Whatcott 2013 SCC hate-speech findings and issue estoppel. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) reflect the anti-SLAPP analysis and the extensive discussion of freedom of expression limits; K111 is somewhat secondary because the court held the Charter does not directly apply between private parties. K107 (Canadian Charter) is included given the sustained Charter-values discussion, though it is a borderline/background pick. Abuse of process and the Norwich order lacked dedicated vocabulary entries and are covered under Civil litigation.
location_rationale: The heading states only 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE' without naming a city or registry office; the province is therefore Ontario. Although the court file number 'CV-16-558424CP' (a Toronto-region class-proceeding number), Perell J.'s bench, and the Toronto-based parties strongly suggest Toronto, the decision text itself never states the sitting city, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: No registry office is named in the decision. The file number CV-16-558424CP implies the Toronto region, but as the text does not expressly state a registry, this field is left null.

case_name: Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. A.U.

name_verification.name_in_document: Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. A.U.

defining_issues: Was the child S. a child in need of protection within the meaning of s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
What disposition best served the child's best interests — Crown wardship with no access for adoption as sought by the Society, or return to the mother under a supervision order?
Was an order of Crown wardship justified where less disruptive alternatives were available?

firac.issue: Was the child S. a child in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
firac.facts: S., born in 2002, was apprehended in June 2008 after her father complained of neglect. At the time the mother, Ms. U., was using marijuana in large quantities, was the surety for and living with Mr. RR, a man with a violent criminal record, and S. had missed significant school and reported concerning living conditions. The mother had a history of untreated depression and there was evidence of ongoing adult conflict/domestic violence witnessed by S.
firac.rule: Under s. 37(2)(b),(f),(g) CFSA a child is in need of protection where there is physical harm or risk of harm and emotional harm or risk of emotional harm. The need-for-protection question is decided without reference to best interests; the relevant date runs from apprehension forward to the hearing. Risk of harm must be real and likely, not speculative (Children's Aid Society of Rainy River v. B.(C.)). Exposure to a pattern of domestic violence can create a risk of emotional harm (CAS of Toronto v. S.A.C.).
firac.application: The court found S.'s statements about her living conditions, the mother's marijuana use, and particularly the mother's remaining surety for Mr. RR until February 2009 put S. at risk under s. 37(2)(b). Given the overwhelming evidence of historical volatility between the parents and the agreed facts, the court found emotional harm and risk of emotional harm established under s. 37(2)(f) and (g).
firac.conclusion: S. was found to be, and to continue to be, a child in need of protection under s. 37(2)(b), (f) and (g).

firac.issue: What disposition served the child's best interests — Crown wardship for adoption or return to the mother under supervision?
firac.facts: S. had been in care nearly three years. The mother had completed numerous programs (parenting, anger management, Jean Tweed addiction counselling, Strengthening Families, the Thistletown Interface assessment, dyadic therapy), was compliant with antidepressant medication, had ended the relationship with Mr. RR, secured stable housing, and had consistent, positive, largely unsupervised access. S. consistently expressed a wish to return to her mother and to keep contact with her father and extended family, and did not want to be adopted. Assessors identified insight and capacity for change. The mother had, however, relapsed on marijuana on New Year's Eve 2010 and had not obtained a recent hair-strand test.
firac.rule: The paramount purpose of the CFSA (s. 1) is the best interests, protection and well-being of the child, with best-interest factors in s. 37(3). Sections 57(2)-(3) require the court to consider the Society's efforts to assist and to be satisfied that less disruptive alternatives (e.g. a supervision order) would be inadequate before removing a child. The test is whether the parent has in fact changed and can now meet the minimum standard of care (Children's Aid Society of Winnipeg v. R.); parenting need not be perfect (minimum-standard test). Marijuana use is not in itself a protection concern absent evidence it impairs parenting (CAS of Toronto v. T.R.; CCAS of Toronto v. SS).
firac.application: The court found the mother had made great strides, that a strong, meaningful and beneficial bond existed between mother and daughter, and that her fundamental parenting was adequate. The Society's evidence lacked direct observation of the mother-child relationship in her home and was treated with caution (per CAS of Toronto v. H.(B.)). Marijuana use, without evidence of impaired parenting, did not require removal; the residual risk of occasional use could be managed through a supervision order with drug testing, counselling, safety-plan and monitoring conditions. Crown wardship with no access, given S.'s age and wishes, would leave her in limbo.
firac.conclusion: Crown wardship was refused; S. was ordered returned to her mother under a ten-month Society supervision order with detailed conditions, including a graduated transition and continued father access.

firac.issue: Was an order of Crown wardship justified where less disruptive alternatives existed?
firac.facts: The Society sought the most profound order available, Crown wardship with no access for adoption, on the basis of the length of time in care and the mother's historically sporadic engagement.
firac.rule: Crown wardship is the most profound order a court can make and must be exercised with the highest degree of caution, on compelling evidence, and only after careful examination of alternatives (CCAS of Hamilton-Wentworth v. G.(J.)). The Society bears the onus, on the balance of probabilities but with clear and compelling evidence where access is to be denied (CAS of Oxford County v. D.T.). Section 57(3) bars removal unless less disruptive alternatives are inadequate.
firac.application: The court held the Society had not shown that a supervision order would be inadequate, criticized it for not increasing access to test the mother's parenting and for failing to reassess as circumstances evolved, and found returning S. home with tailored supervision conditions adequately met any residual risk.
firac.conclusion: Crown wardship was not justified; the least disruptive appropriate alternative — return under supervision — was ordered.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area — this is a child protection proceeding under the Child and Family Services Act. K047 (best interests of the child) is the paramount statutory test applied throughout the disposition analysis. K048 (custody/access) captures the contested access and placement questions, including the father's access and the presumption against access on Crown wardship. K112 (Charter s. 7) is engaged because the court expressly held that child protection proceedings implicate parents' s. 7 liberty interests. K050 (parental support) is a weaker pick — child support is mentioned (the father's offer to pay $124/month) but is peripheral. K023 (equality rights) is also borderline but genuinely engaged: the court discussed the disproportionate impact of protection proceedings on poor single mothers, the feminization of poverty and Moge v. Moge, raising equality concerns. No controlled keyword squarely captures 'child protection' or substance abuse, which are the case's real drivers.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'IN THE ONTARIO COURT OF JUSTICE' and bears 'Toronto Registry No. C 45139/08', establishing Toronto, Ontario as the location.
registry_rationale: The document states 'Toronto Registry No. C 45139/08', identifying the Toronto registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: MICHAEL GELUCH (Plaintiff) v. ROSEDALE GOLF ASSOCIATION, LIMITED (Defendant)

defining_issues: Did the employer establish just cause to summarily dismiss the general manager for alleged fiscal impropriety, theft, and abusive conduct/sexual harassment?
If the dismissal was wrongful, what is the reasonable notice period?
Is the employee entitled to Wallace, aggravated, or punitive damages, and to compensation for accumulated vacation and mitigation expenses?
Is the employer entitled to recover on its counterclaim?

firac.issue: Did Rosedale establish just cause for the summary dismissal of Mr. Geluch?
firac.facts: Geluch, hired in 1985 as General Manager and Secretary/Treasurer, was fired on the spot on October 31, 1997 after board members interviewed a former employee (Anne Taylor) who described abusive and belittling conduct. Rosedale later alleged fiscal impropriety (a split salary advance, personal use of the club credit card, an unauthorized clothing allowance, and unadjusted financial entries), theft (furniture built by staff, food and wine taken), and abusive conduct including sexual harassment of staff. Geluch was given no reasons at the time and no opportunity to respond.
firac.rule: An employer bears the onus of proving cause on a balance of probabilities, with heightened scrutiny for allegations of theft/dishonesty (Homer v. Roccha; Havens). Whether misconduct justifies dismissal is assessed by the contextual approach in McKinley v. BC Tel, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 161 — the misconduct must give rise to a breakdown in the employment relationship. Sexual harassment (Janzen v. Platy) may justify dismissal, but employers generally must investigate serious allegations and give the employee an opportunity to respond, and may need to warn before dismissing for lesser or condoned conduct (Wallace; Gonsalves; Simpson).
firac.application: The court found the salary advance and clothing allowance were errors in judgment or bookkeeping, fully recorded and reviewed by auditors over years, not dishonesty; the auditor's credit-card report was unreliable and general ledgers were missing, so personal misuse was unproven. The alleged theft of furniture/food/wine was undesirable practice but not sufficiently serious or proven. Geluch's volatile, sometimes abusive style and the sporadic sexual innuendo toward Ms. Buell (1992) were deserving of a warning but not systematic abuse warranting dismissal. Rosedale ignored its own sexual-harassment policy, conducted no investigation, and never warned or disciplined Geluch, who received regular raises. The incidents did not amount to cause individually or cumulatively.
firac.conclusion: Rosedale failed to prove just cause; Geluch was wrongfully dismissed.

firac.issue: What is the appropriate period of reasonable notice?
firac.facts: Geluch was 54, had served twelve years as General Manager, earned roughly $129,000, and took thirteen months to secure comparable employment in Vancouver.
firac.rule: Reasonable notice is determined on the fact-based Bardal v. Globe and Mail factors — character of employment, length of service, age, and availability of similar employment — adopted in Wallace v. United Grain Growers.
firac.application: Applying the Bardal factors to Geluch's senior position, long service, age, and the difficulty finding comparable work in a small industry, the court set the notice period at 15 months, noting the office manager had received 15 months' severance.
firac.conclusion: Reasonable notice fixed at 15 months, with earnings from his subsequent job deducted.

firac.issue: Is Geluch entitled to Wallace, aggravated, or punitive damages, and to vacation and mitigation compensation?
firac.facts: Geluch was fired without warning, escorted out in front of staff during a colleague's retirement party, offered ten minutes to resign, given no reasons until February 1998, no reference or outplacement, and the President's later letter to members referred critically to former senior management. He also claimed 21 weeks of untaken vacation and moving/mitigation expenses.
firac.rule: Bad-faith or unfair manner of dismissal extends the notice period (Wallace v. United Grain Growers). Aggravated and punitive damages require a separate, independently actionable wrong (Vorvis v. ICBC; Wallace); punitive damages require harsh, vindictive, reprehensible conduct (Whiten v. Pilot). The Employment Standards Act prohibits a 'use it or lose it' vacation policy.
firac.application: The insensitive, hasty manner of dismissal and the negative message to members warranted a two-month Wallace extension. No separate actionable wrong (the only candidate, defamation, was not pleaded) supported aggravated or punitive damages. The statutory bar on forfeiting vacation entitled Geluch to $50,000 for 21 weeks; reasonable relocation/mitigation expenses were allowed at $8,000 (home-sale costs offset against capital gain).
firac.conclusion: Two months' Wallace damages ($24,725) awarded; aggravated and punitive damages refused; vacation pay ($50,000) and mitigation ($8,000) granted.

firac.issue: Is Rosedale entitled to recover on its counterclaim?
firac.facts: Rosedale counterclaimed for the clothing allowance, personal airfare, and $500 for furniture built for Geluch with club materials on club time.
firac.rule: A counterclaiming employer must prove its claim on the balance of probabilities.
firac.application: Only the furniture claim was proven; Rosedale established that Geluch owed $500 for items built on club time using club materials.
firac.conclusion: Counterclaim allowed in the amount of $500.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the core issue — whether just cause existed and the reasonable notice/Wallace analysis. K083 (harassment) applies because sexual harassment and abusive treatment of staff were central to the alleged cause. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) are borderline/weak picks: the case discusses the 'blackball' membership system that potentially discriminated against a prominent member of the Jewish community (George Cohon), which Geluch alleged as the real reason for his firing, though the court found it irrelevant to the dismissal. They are included only because that theme is expressly canvassed; they are not central to the holding.
location_rationale: The header identifies the court as the 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE' (province = Ontario). No sitting city is stated in the reasons; the matter concerns a Toronto golf club but the decision does not expressly name the city where the court sat, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: No registry office is named in the decision. Only the court file number (98-CV-152133) and the court name appear, so registry is left null.

case_name: Unrau v National Dental Examining Board

name_verification.name_in_document: Unrau v National Dental Examining Board

defining_issues: Should Unrau's Statement of Claim be struck out as an abusive and vexatious proceeding under Rule 3.68 / the CPN7 'show cause' procedure?

Does a superior court of inherent jurisdiction have authority (independent of statute) to impose prospective court access restrictions (a vexatious litigant order) reaching beyond the immediate dispute?

Does procedural fairness (per Lymer v Jonsson) require a separate hearing or further process before the Court may impose indefinite court access restrictions on Unrau, or could the Court proceed immediately?
Should Unrau be declared a vexatious litigant and made subject to ongoing (global) court access restrictions?

firac.issue: Should Unrau's Statement of Claim be struck out as an abusive and vexatious proceeding?
firac.facts: Unrau filed a Statement of Claim making bald allegations (defamation, theft of IP, abuse of process) that named none of the eleven defendants in its statement of facts, sought $5 million plus impossible remedies such as 'retroactive licensure', 'more open mindedness' and 'respect'. The Court, via Civil Practice Note 7, gave Unrau 14 days and up to ten pages to show a valid basis for the action. Unrau made no reply.
firac.rule: Rule 3.68 of the Alberta Rules of Court permits striking out pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim, are frivolous/irrelevant/improper, or are an abuse of process. Pleadings composed only of 'bald allegations' (GH v Alcock, 2013 ABCA 24) that leave defendants unable to respond are vexatious and an abuse of process (kisikawpimootewin v Canada, 2004 FC 1426). CPN7 permits a paper-only show-cause procedure.
firac.application: The Court had already found (Unrau #1) that the Statement of Claim was prima facie composed only of bald allegations, failed to identify the defendants, advanced unsubstantiated conspiratorial complaints, and sought impossible and disproportionate remedies. Given the opportunity to rebut, Unrau said nothing. Per CPN7 para 3(c), the pleading was therefore struck.
firac.conclusion: The Statement of Claim was struck out as an abusive, hopeless and vexatious proceeding.

firac.issue: Does the Court possess inherent jurisdiction, independent of statute, to impose vexatious litigant orders extending beyond the current dispute?
firac.facts: The Court needed to determine the source of its authority to restrict Unrau's future litigation. Two competing lines of authority existed: a 'Traditional Jurisdiction' view (statute-only) and a 'Modern Approach' (statute and inherent jurisdiction co-exist).
firac.rule: A superior court of inherent jurisdiction may act to prevent abuse of its processes (Jacob, 'The Inherent Jurisdiction of the Court'; BCGEU v British Columbia, 1988; R v Caron, 2011 SCC 5). Inherent jurisdiction is not ousted by statute unless in clear and unambiguous terms (Rose, 1998; Amato). Judicature Act s. 23.1(9) preserves the Court's authority. The Modern Approach (Ebert v Venvil; Bhamjee v Forsdick (No 2); Tupper; Grenier; adopted in Hok v Alberta #2) holds courts may screen anticipated/threatened litigation under inherent jurisdiction.
firac.application: The Court surveyed extensive Commonwealth and Canadian authority, concluding the historical 'gap' in inherent jurisdiction was an error and that Judicature Act ss. 23-23.1 (with its 'persistence' requirement, no interim-order power, single remedy, and notice requirement) is inadequate for the post-Hryniak 'culture shift'. Section 23.1(9) shows the Legislature intended inherent jurisdiction to co-exist. The Court adopted the Modern Approach, under which prospective, proportionate court access restrictions are available under inherent jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: The Court's inherent jurisdiction provides a complete, flexible, and superior basis to impose vexatious litigant orders; statutory and inherent authority co-exist.

firac.issue: Does procedural fairness require a separate vexatious-litigant process before restricting Unrau, or may the Court proceed immediately?
firac.facts: Unrau had already been told in Unrau #1 that his pleading appeared abusive and exhibited multiple indicia; he was invited to respond and did nothing; he was also aware interim court access restrictions had been imposed. The question was whether Lymer v Jonsson required a further Hok v Alberta #2 two-step process.
firac.rule: Natural justice requires an opportunity to be heard before an adverse decision (Lymer v Jonsson, 2016 ABCA 32; Kallaba). Procedural fairness is contextual and calibrated to the importance/impact of the decision (Baker v Canada, 1999). A leave requirement is a minimal, gatekeeping imposition, not an extraordinary denial of rights (Wong; Olumide v Canada; Trial Lawyers - no one has a right to abusive litigation).
firac.application: Applying Baker, the Court held that a simple leave requirement only minimally affects rights (it screens, not bars, access), that legislative intent (Rule 14.5(1)(j)) treats such restrictions as proportionate, and that the audi alteram partem principle was already satisfied because Unrau had a full chance to respond in Unrau #1 and declined. A further step would be 'undue process' contrary to Hryniak. Lymer v Jonsson, resting on pre-culture-shift authority, was not treated as binding, and in any event Unrau was not 'surprised'.
firac.conclusion: No separate process was required; the Court could proceed immediately to impose a leave-based vexatious litigant order (though more intrusive restrictions would generally require the two-step Hok process).

firac.issue: Should Unrau be declared a vexatious litigant and subjected to global court access restrictions?
firac.facts: Unrau's litigation record showed a 20-year campaign to practise dentistry without a licence: he had been enjoined (Alberta Dental Assn v Unrau, 2001 ABQB 24), found in contempt twice (2001, 2006), refused to acknowledge the Court's jurisdiction, and used litigation to seek delay. His 2018 claim expanded targets to NAIT, the City of Calgary, the FBI and Amazon, and added IP/hacking complaints, with no discernible pattern.
firac.rule: A vexatious litigant order is appropriate where anticipated abusive litigation extends beyond a single dispute (threshold test). Orders must be explicit and enforceable by Court Clerks; where a narrow scope cannot be reliably enforced, the Court should 'default broad' (Biley v Sherwood; Tupper). Rule 14.5(1)(j) automatically extends restrictions to appeals.
firac.application: Unrau's disobedience of orders, refusal to accept jurisdiction, expanding and unfocused target list, and obsessive objective made future abusive litigation across multiple disputes plausible, satisfying the threshold test. Because his targets were unpredictable, no narrow enforceable order was possible, so a global leave requirement across all three Alberta courts was warranted. A simple leave requirement (no additional intrusive steps) was proportionate; fee waivers were revoked and ancillary clauses added.
firac.conclusion: Unrau was declared a vexatious litigant and made subject to a global leave-based court access restriction order; the interim order was vacated and no costs were imposed as the matter proceeded on the Court's own motion.

keywords_rationale: This is fundamentally a civil-procedure/administrative-law decision about managing abusive litigation. K002 (Civil litigation) is the closest tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns civil litigation conduct, striking out pleadings under the Rules of Court, and vexatious litigant orders. K001 (Administrative law) is included because the decision turns heavily on the superior court's inherent jurisdiction, its supervisory role over inferior courts and tribunals, and legislative-interpretation of the Judicature Act. K011 (judicial review) is a weaker/borderline pick — chosen because the reasons repeatedly engage the court's supervisory jurisdiction and standard of appellate review of discretionary court-access decisions; it is not a classic judicial review case, so it is flagged as borderline. K012 (procedural fairness) squarely applies: a defining issue was whether natural justice (Baker; Lymer v Jonsson) required a further hearing before restricting Unrau. K013 (professional discipline) is engaged because the underlying dispute arises from Unrau's decades-long unlicensed dentistry and regulation by the Alberta Dental Association under the Dental Profession Act, and the vocabulary maps 'professional regulation' to this ID. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated 'vexatious litigant / abuse of process / inherent jurisdiction' keyword, so the five selected are the closest available; K011 and K013 are the weakest and are flagged accordingly.
location_rationale: The header states 'Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta', 'Registry: Calgary', and the decision closes 'Dated at the City of Calgary, Alberta this 25th day of April, 2019.' Province is Alberta from the court name.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly lists 'Registry: Calgary' and the docket 1801 12350, and the reasons are dated at Calgary.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Althorpe

defining_issues: What is the fit and proportionate global sentence for a leader of neo-Nazi militant accelerationist terrorism whose propaganda and instructions inspired real-world killings?
Should the presumption of parole ineligibility of one-half of the sentence under s. 743.6(1.2) of the Criminal Code be applied or displaced?

firac.issue: What is the fit and proportionate global sentence for the offender's terrorism offences?
firac.facts: Mr. Althorpe pleaded guilty to facilitating terrorist activity (s. 83.19(1)), instructing terrorist activity (s. 83.22), and wilfully promoting hatred as a terrorism offence (s. 319(2)/s. 83.2). Over roughly a decade he was a leading proponent of militant accelerationism, produced three Atomwaffen Division propaganda/recruitment videos, co-authored and published three influential Terrorgram manifestos (Militant Accelerationism, Do It for the 'Gram, The Hard Reset) advocating mass-casualty attacks and genocide against Jewish, Muslim, Black, LGBTQ+ and other groups, and led a neo-Nazi 'Active Club'. At least six attacks or plots, including fatal shootings, were inspired by the Terrorgram publications. He pleaded guilty, expressed remorse, had no record, was 18 when he began, suffered childhood abuse and had borderline personality disorder, but Dr. Iosif questioned the depth of his reform and noted he admitted 'I am the same racist guy.'
firac.rule: Sentencing is governed by ss. 718–718.2 of the Criminal Code, with proportionality under s. 718.1 and aggravation for hate motivation (s. 718.2(a)(i)) and terrorism (s. 718.2(a)(v)). Terrorism cases are not a distinct class (R. v. Khawaja, 2012 SCC 69), but denunciation and deterrence are paramount because of the unusual gravity of terrorism (R. v. Esseghaier; R. v. Khawaja). Where terrorist activity is designed to or likely to result in the indiscriminate killing of innocent people, serious consideration should be given to life sentences, and where life is not called for, to sentences exceeding 20 years (R. v. Khalid, 2010 ONCA 861, para. 34). Rehabilitation is a mitigating factor but rigid ideology may support an inference of ongoing dangerousness. Consecutive sentences are required by s. 83.26 and the totality principle applies (R. v. Ahmed, 2017 ONCA 76).
firac.application: The court rejected defence counsel's characterization of the offender as a mere 'ideologist,' finding his talk and messages actually caused death and injury and that his materials were designed to or likely to result in indiscriminate killing. Aggravating factors included his leadership role, decade-long commitment, recruitment and instruction of others, six documented inspired attacks, and continuing risk. Mitigating factors included the guilty plea, expressed remorse and claimed renunciation, absence of a record, youth at onset, difficult upbringing, personality disorder (no causal link found), family support, and harsh custodial conditions. The court distinguished Ahmed (12 years), Ahmad (16 years) and MacDonald (10 years, no proven consequences) as less serious. It found the starting point and appropriate range to be 20 years to life; a trial conviction would likely have attracted life. It imposed a global 20 years (Count 2: 6 years; Count 5: 10 years consecutive; Count 7: 4 years consecutive), less 48 months' combined Summers and Duncan credit, leaving 16 years to serve.
firac.conclusion: A global sentence of 20 years' imprisonment (240 months) was imposed, reduced by 48 months' pre-sentence credit to 16 years (192 months) remaining, with ancillary lifetime weapons prohibition, DNA, non-communication and forfeiture orders.

firac.issue: Should the mandatory-parole-ineligibility presumption in s. 743.6(1.2) be applied or displaced?
firac.facts: Mr. Althorpe received a terrorism sentence exceeding two years, engaging the presumption that he serve one-half of the sentence (or ten years, whichever is less) before full parole eligibility. He had participated in numerous institutional programs, showed motivation to reintegrate, had no misconduct infractions, and Dr. Iosif opined he was not antisocial, was not without remorse, and would benefit from therapy not yet available to him.
firac.rule: Section 743.6(1.2) creates a presumption of one-half parole ineligibility for terrorism sentences, displaceable where the court is satisfied that denunciation and specific/general deterrence would be adequately served by ineligibility under the Corrections and Conditional Release Act; s. 743.6(2) makes denunciation and deterrence paramount with rehabilitation subordinate. The offender bears the onus on a balance of probabilities (R. v. Khalid; R. v. Ahmed).
firac.application: The court found the offender met the onus. Dr. Iosif's assessment that he was not antisocial, led a responsible lifestyle apart from these offences, was not without remorse, and would do well in therapy, together with his extensive programming and apparent motivation to be pro-social, satisfied the court that deterrence objectives would be adequately met without the extended ineligibility. It reasoned that the Parole Board would be best positioned to assess his rehabilitative progress, noting this did not guarantee early release but only allowed an earlier application.
firac.conclusion: The presumption was displaced; Mr. Althorpe is not required to serve one-half of his sentence before applying for parole under s. 743.6(1.2).

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area. K037 (terrorism) is central — the offences are all terrorism offences and the case turns on terrorism sentencing principles. K067 (wilful promotion of hatred) and K115 (Criminal Code s. 319(2)) map directly to Count 7. K061 (hate speech) and K060 (hate motivation) capture the s. 718.2(a)(i) hate aggravation and the hateful propaganda. K066 (white supremacism) reflects the neo-Nazi/Atomwaffen/accelerationist ideology. K063 (online hate/social media) fits the Telegram publication and distribution. K058 (antisemitism) and K055 (advocating genocide) reflect the express calls to kill and 'erase' Jewish and other persons in the manifestos. All are firmly engaged; none are weak picks, though K058 and K055 are among several targeted groups (Muslim, Black, LGBTQ+) rather than the sole focus.
location_rationale: The decision is styled 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE' and bears court file no. CR-24-90000280-0000, establishing the province as Ontario. No sitting city is stated in the reasons (references to Thorold, St. Catharines and the Toronto South Detention Centre relate to the offender's residence and place of pre-sentence custody, not the court's seat), so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The reasons do not identify a court registry or office; only the court file number and 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' appear, so registry is left null.

case_name: Organisation mondiale sikhe du Canada c. Procureur général du Québec

name_verification.name_in_document: Organisation mondiale sikhe du Canada c. Procureur général du Québec / World Sikh Organization of Canada v. Attorney General of Quebec

defining_issues: Is the Act respecting the laicity of the State (Bill 21) intra vires the province under the division of legislative powers in ss. 91-92 of the Constitution Act, 1867?
Can pre-Confederation statutes (the Quebec Act 1774, the Rectories Act 1852, the Hart Act 1832) or unwritten constitutional principles be used to invalidate the Act?

Were the notwithstanding clauses in ss. 33 and 34 of the Act validly invoked, and does Ford v. Quebec remain binding such that only requirements of form apply to s. 33 of the Canadian Charter and s. 52 of the Quebec Charter?
Where a statute validly invokes the override, may courts nonetheless review and declare that it infringes the overridden Charter provisions and grant declaratory or pecuniary remedies?
Does s. 28 of the Canadian Charter (sexual equality) limit or neutralize the use of s. 33, thereby preventing the override from affecting sexual equality?
Does the Act infringe s. 23 of the Canadian Charter (minority language education rights) of Quebec's English linguistic minority?

Does the requirement that members of the National Assembly exercise their functions with their face uncovered (s. 8 para. 1 read with para. 1 of Schedule III) infringe s. 3 of the Canadian Charter, which is not subject to override?

firac.issue: Is the Act respecting the laicity of the State intra vires the province under the division of legislative powers?
firac.facts: Bill 21 affirms the laicity of the Quebec State, prohibits certain state agents (Schedule II) from wearing religious symbols, and requires certain persons to exercise functions and receive services with their face uncovered. It contains no penal or criminal sanctions. Opponents argued it is criminal law (s. 91(27)) or falls under Parliament's residual POGG power.
firac.rule: A statute challenged under ss. 91-92 of the Constitution Act, 1867 must be characterized by its pith and substance (purpose and effects, using intrinsic and extrinsic evidence) and then classified under a head of power (Murray-Hall v. Quebec (A.G.), 2023 SCC 10; References re Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act, 2021 SCC 11). There is no general or inherent connection between religion and criminal law.
firac.application: The Court held the Act's pith and substance is to affirm state laicity as a fundamental principle of Quebec public law, establish its requirements and regulate the conditions for exercising certain state functions. The trial judge erred in characterizing ss. 6 and 8 as criminal-law-like, confusing purpose with means; the Act contains no penalty. The Act connects to s. 92(4) (provincial offices), s. 92(13) (property and civil rights) and s. 92(16) (matters of a local or private nature), and certain provisions to s. 45 of the Constitution Act, 1982.
firac.conclusion: The Act is intra vires; the division-of-powers appeals fail.

firac.issue: Can pre-Confederation statutes or unwritten constitutional principles invalidate the Act?
firac.facts: Opponents relied on the Quebec Act (1774), the Rectories Act (1852) and the Hart Act (1832), asserting they enshrine supra-legislative principles of religious equality and freedom of worship that the Act violates, and on the notions of 'constitutional architecture' and unwritten principles.
firac.rule: The supra-legislative character of imperial and colonial statutes was progressively eroded through devolution (Constitutional Act 1791, Union Act 1840, Colonial Laws Validity Act 1865, Statute of Westminster 1931, Canada Act 1982). Unwritten constitutional principles cannot serve as an independent basis to invalidate legislation; their role is interpretive and structural (Toronto (City) v. Ontario (A.G.), 2021 SCC 34). One part of the Constitution cannot invalidate another.
firac.application: The Court traced the constitutional history and found none of these statutes retains supra-legislative status; they were never used on their own to invalidate legislation and have become obsolete or metamorphosed into ordinary statutes (e.g., the Freedom of Worship Act). Section 129 of the Constitution Act, 1867 is transitional and confers no constitutional status. The vagueness/rule-of-law argument failed because s. 6 provides sufficient guidance for legal debate (R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society).
firac.conclusion: Neither the pre-Confederation statutes nor unwritten principles/constitutional architecture invalidate the Act; these grounds fail.

firac.issue: Were the notwithstanding clauses validly invoked and does Ford remain binding?
firac.facts: Sections 33 and 34 of the Act override, respectively, ss. 1-38 of the Quebec Charter and ss. 2 and 7-15 of the Canadian Charter, using standard wording. Opponents argued the use is subject to substantive requirements, must satisfy s. 1/Oakes, is barred by international law, and that Ford should be revisited.
firac.rule: Under Ford v. Quebec (A.G.), [1988] 2 S.C.R. 712, s. 33 of the Canadian Charter lays down requirements of form only; there is no substantive review of the legislative policy behind the override. Stare decisis may be departed from only for a new legal issue or a change fundamentally shifting the parameters of debate (Bedford; Carter).
firac.application: The trial judge correctly applied Ford. Section 1 does not apply to s. 33; the override defeats judicial declarations of inoperability. The simultaneous 'wholesale' use of both charters, the override of judicial/legal rights, and international-law arguments raise no new legal issue; the presumption of conformity cannot rewrite clear text. Alleged 'populism' and legislative attitudes do not fundamentally shift the debate and would require impermissible political judgment. Section 52 of the Quebec Charter requires only formal expression and is broader in scope than s. 33.
firac.conclusion: Sections 33 and 34 satisfy the requirements of form; Ford remains binding; the challenge to the override fails.

firac.issue: May courts review and declare infringements of overridden provisions and grant remedies despite a valid override?
firac.facts: Opponents sought declarations that the Act infringes freedoms of religion and expression and equality rights, and the Lauzon Group sought damages, notwithstanding ss. 33-34.
firac.rule: A valid override under s. 33 of the Canadian Charter or s. 52 in fine of the Quebec Charter removes the statute from the application of the overridden provisions and exempts it from judicial review of conformity with them; s. 24(1) and arts. 142 and 529 C.C.P. cannot ground a remedy where the underlying rights do not apply. Section 33 operates as a kind of 'constitutional privative clause' limiting s. 96 review. The doctrine of mootness (Borowski; Doucet-Boudreau) bars deciding questions with no practical effect.
firac.application: Because the Act is exempt from the overridden provisions, the Court cannot review its conformity with them or grant declaratory or pecuniary relief; to do so would indirectly do what cannot be done directly. Subsidiarily, the question is moot: a finding of infringement would have no legal effect, and the adversarial context was deficient (the AGQ presented no s. 1 justification), so it is not in the interests of justice to answer. Pecuniary relief is also unavailable against the AGQ for constitutionally valid legislation.
firac.conclusion: No judicial review of conformity with the overridden provisions and no remedy (declaratory or pecuniary) can be granted; these claims are rejected.

firac.issue: Does s. 28 of the Canadian Charter (sexual equality) override s. 33?
firac.facts: Opponents argued s. 28, operating 'notwithstanding anything in this Charter,' shields sexual equality from any override and prevents s. 33 from being used in a manner that disproportionately affects women (mainly Muslim women).
firac.rule: Section 28 is an interpretive provision ensuring that the rights and freedoms in ss. 2-23 are guaranteed equally to male and female persons; it has no standalone normative value and is grafted onto those provisions. Its text, placement under 'General' provisions, and jurisprudence (Hess; Nguyen) confirm its interpretive purpose.
firac.application: Since s. 33 permits the override of ss. 2 and 7-15, and s. 28 attaches to those very rights, once those rights are overridden s. 28 is stripped of its foundation and cannot substitute for them regarding sexual equality. Reading s. 28 as limiting s. 33 would create an insoluble logical contradiction (s. 28 cannot bar an override yet permit justification under s. 1) and would incongruously privilege sex over other s. 15 grounds. Section 50.1 of the Quebec Charter is treated the same way.
firac.conclusion: Section 28 does not limit s. 33; it cannot stand in the way of the full application of s. 34 of the Act.

firac.issue: Does the Act infringe s. 23 of the Canadian Charter (minority language education rights)?
firac.facts: The trial judge held that several provisions, by restricting the recruitment of teachers/principals who wear religious symbols, infringed the English minority's right of management and control over its schools, tied to a 'culture' of celebrating religious diversity. Nothing in the Act affects the language of instruction; the quality and facilities of English schooling remain substantively equivalent.
firac.rule: Section 23 is preventive, remedial and unifying, interpreted generously but faithfully to its text (Mahe; Arsenault-Cameron; Rose-des-vents; CSFCB). It protects the linguistic dimension of culture through the medium of the minority language, not all cultural manifestations; the right of management and control pertains to aspects of education affecting the minority's language and culture.
firac.application: No s. 23 rights holder is deprived of a right; nothing in the Act touches the use of English in schools or the quality of instruction. The asserted 'culture' of promoting religious diversity is unrelated to language and would artificially constitutionalize a recent practice, extending s. 23 beyond its scope. Multiculturalism (s. 27) must be reconciled with s. 23, which protects only linguistic minorities. The trial judge gave s. 23 a scope it does not have.
firac.conclusion: The Act does not infringe s. 23; the Trial Judgment is reversed on this point (making s. 1 analysis unnecessary).

firac.issue: Does requiring members of the National Assembly to have their face uncovered infringe s. 3 of the Canadian Charter?
firac.facts: Section 8 para. 1, read with para. 1 of Schedule III, requires MNAs to exercise their functions with their face uncovered, which would prevent a person wearing a niqab or burqa from sitting once elected. Section 3 is not subject to s. 33. The AGQ led no evidence and made no submissions to justify any infringement under s. 1.
firac.rule: Section 3 protects not only the right to vote and to be a candidate but the right to sit once elected, and contains no internal limits; any restriction must be justified under s. 1 (Harvey v. New Brunswick (A.G.); Sauvé; Frank). A stringent justification standard applies.
firac.application: The combined provisions would prevent a person whose sincere beliefs require a face-covering from exercising the functions of an MNA, negating meaningful participation in the electoral process. A sufficient factual basis existed to decide the issue. The AGQ adduced no evidence and offered no s. 1 justification, so the Court could not undertake a s. 1 analysis on its own motion. By contrast, s. 6 with paras. 1 and 6 of Schedule II (President/Vice-Presidents, Minister of Justice) does not infringe s. 3, as those appointments/elections lie outside the electoral process protected by s. 3.
firac.conclusion: Section 8 para. 1 with para. 1 of Schedule III unjustifiably infringes s. 3 and is of no force or effect; the trial judge's finding is upheld, while s. 6/Schedule II is found not to infringe s. 3.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns entirely on constitutional interpretation. K029 (notwithstanding clause) is the central doctrine — the validity and scope of ss. 33/52 overrides. K025 (freedom of religion) and K032 (religious symbols/dress) capture the substance of Bill 21's prohibition on wearing religious symbols. K023 (equality rights) is engaged by the s. 28/s. 15 sexual-equality analysis. K031 (religious accommodation) reflects the Act's prohibition on accommodation (s. 14). K011 (judicial review) captures the extensively analyzed question of whether courts can review a statute shielded by the override. K107 (Canadian Charter) and K120 (Quebec Charter) are the governing instruments. K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) and K109 (Charter s. 15) are the specific overridden guarantees at issue. The s. 23 minority-language-education and s. 3 democratic-rights holdings are significant but lack precise vocabulary entries; K043 (denominational schools) was considered but rejected as the s. 23 issue is linguistic, not denominational. K093 (Jewish) was considered given the Hart Act and Lord Reading Law Society but is too peripheral to the ratio.
location_rationale: The decision's header states 'COURT OF APPEAL / CANADA / PROVINCE OF QUEBEC / REGISTRY OF MONTREAL' and identifies the court sitting in the district of Montreal; the underlying Superior Court judgment was rendered in the District of Montreal.
registry_rationale: The header expressly reads 'REGISTRY OF MONTREAL', and the appeal file numbers (500-09-...) are Montreal registry numbers.

name_verification.name_in_document: Waxman v. Waxman
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The style of cause in the decision ('Waxman v. Waxman') matches the supplied case name. The decision text carries only the hearing/judgment dates and docket numbers (33234/88, 36583/89, 37616/89, 42114/89, 44142/89); the neutral/database citation '2002 CanLII 49644 (ONSC)' does not appear within the reasons themselves, which is normal for a trial judgment of this vintage.

defining_issues: Did Chester Waxman owe fiduciary duties to his brother and 50% co-owner Morris, and did he breach them in connection with the 1983 share sale, the corporate bonuses, and the diversion of profits to companies owned by his sons?
Should the December 1983 share sale and lease be set aside on the grounds of breach of fiduciary duty, undue influence, and unconscionability?
Is Morris entitled to relief under the oppression remedy in s. 248 of the Ontario Business Corporations Act, and are Chester's sons liable for knowing receipt of the bonuses?
Did Chester, Robert and IWS induce Philip Enterprises to breach its contract with Solid Waste Reclamation Inc. (SWRI)?
Was Morris wrongfully dismissed / oppressively removed from IWS?
Did the solicitor Paul Ennis breach his fiduciary and contractual duties to Morris in documenting the share sale, and were the auditors Taylor Leibow liable to Morris personally?

firac.issue: Did Chester owe and breach fiduciary duties to Morris in connection with the share sale, the bonuses, and the profit diversions?
firac.facts: Morris and Chester built IWS from a horse-and-wagon scrap operation into a multi-million-dollar business as 50/50 partners and later equal shareholders. By long custom Morris ran operations and Chester controlled all financial and legal matters; Morris trusted Chester absolutely, signed whatever documents Chester put before him without reading them, and never monitored the finances. Without telling Morris, Chester declared $6.6M in 1981–82 bonuses (and $250,000 in 1979) largely to himself and his sons, permitted Robert to divert IWS profits to Greycliffe and other related companies, and orchestrated the purchase of Morris's shares.
firac.rule: Partners owe each other fiduciary duties of good faith, disclosure of material facts, and avoidance of conflict of duty and self-interest (Lac Minerals; Hodgkinson v. Simms; MacDonald Estate v. Martin; Norberg v. Wynrib). A fiduciary relationship may also be found outside traditional categories where, given all the circumstances, one party could reasonably expect the other to act in his best interests, the touchstone being vulnerability/dependence.
firac.application: As 50/50 partners and brothers, Chester prima facie owed Morris fiduciary duties, a point his counsel conceded until final argument. Applying Hodgkinson, Morris could reasonably expect Chester to protect his interests in financial matters in which Morris was wholly dependent and vulnerable. Chester breached those duties by declaring undeserved and undisclosed bonuses stripping IWS equity, by permitting and concealing profit diversions to Greycliffe and related companies, and by procuring Morris's signature on share-sale documents without disclosing that Morris was selling his shares or any of the material facts affecting value.
firac.conclusion: Chester owed and flagrantly breached his fiduciary duties to Morris with respect to the share sale, the bonuses, and the profit diversions.

firac.issue: Should the December 1983 share sale and lease be set aside for breach of fiduciary duty, undue influence, and unconscionability?
firac.facts: In December 1983, while Morris was ill, preoccupied with an impending angiogram and open-heart surgery, and unaware that share-sale documents were even being prepared, he was called to the office of the family lawyer Ennis and signed a share sale of all his IWS shares for a nominal $3 million (of which he really received about $1.6M) and a 50-year lease at $2,000/month, far below market. IWS shares were then conservatively worth $8.7–$9M apart from stripped bonuses. Chester funded much of the price with Morris's own money (a gifted dividend and a reallocated bonus).
firac.rule: Contracts may be set aside for breach of fiduciary duty, for undue influence (actual or presumed where a relationship of trust and a disadvantageous transaction exist: Geffen v. Goodman Estate; Barclays Bank v. O'Brien), and for unconscionability (inequality of bargaining power plus an improvident bargain: Morrison v. Coast Finance; Norberg).
firac.application: The deal was manifestly unfair, improvident and one-sided. Morris reposed exceptional trust in Chester, was situationally weak and received no independent legal, valuation or tax advice; a presumption of undue influence arose and was not rebutted. Chester exploited an overwhelming imbalance of power to obtain a grossly improvident bargain, satisfying the test for unconscionability. Chester failed to rebut any of the presumptions.
firac.conclusion: The share sale, lease and ancillary documents are set aside as products of breach of fiduciary duty, undue influence and unconscionability; the deal was patently unfair and manifestly disadvantageous to Morris.

firac.issue: Is Morris entitled to an oppression remedy under s. 248 OBCA, and are Chester's sons liable for knowing receipt of the bonuses?
firac.facts: Chester operated IWS as if he were sole owner, causing the corporation to declare a $1M dividend and reallocate $412,000 of Morris's bonus to fund his own share purchase, to lend him $500,000 interest-free, and to pay excessive bonuses to himself and his sons while excluding Morris and his son Michael from the business. Chester's sons received large 1981-82 bonuses funded by the Laidlaw/Lasco sale proceeds.
firac.rule: Section 248 OBCA permits relief where corporate conduct is oppressive, unfairly prejudicial to or unfairly disregards a complainant's interests, protecting reasonable expectations, especially in closely held incorporated partnerships (Brant Investments; Naneff; Ballard; Ebrahimi). Knowing receipt requires a trust/fiduciary breach, beneficial receipt of property, and actual or constructive knowledge of the breach (Citadel; Gold v. Rosenberg).
firac.application: Morris and Morriston had standing. Chester used IWS's resources to secure control and stripped its equity, conduct that was oppressive and unfairly prejudicial to Morris's reasonable expectation of 50% participation. The sons, active in the business and aware of the sale proceeds, had at least constructive knowledge that the bonuses were an unjustifiable distribution of Morris's equity, so they knowingly received them.
firac.conclusion: Morris is entitled to oppression relief against Chester and IWS; Robert, Warren and Gary are liable for knowing receipt of the 1981–82 bonuses ($622,000; $936,000; $500,000 respectively).

firac.issue: Did Chester, Robert and IWS induce Philip Enterprises to breach its contract with SWRI?
firac.facts: SWRI (owned by Morris's sons) had a well-established subcontracting relationship with Philip. After Morris's dismissal and the litigation, Robert tampered with the Lasco documents to make it appear SWRI had cheated Philip, and IWS refused to release Philip from its counterclaim unless Philip stopped doing business with SWRI, also promising not to compete for the business. Philip terminated SWRI on 7 March 1989, the same day IWS discontinued its counterclaim against Philip.
firac.rule: Inducing breach of contract requires a valid contract, the defendant's knowledge of it, an intentionally procured breach effected by wrongful interference, and resulting damage (Posluns v. TSE; Gainers/369413 Alberta v. Pocklington).
firac.application: There was a valid, mutually beneficial contract of which the defendants were aware. Robert forged documents and, with Chester's involvement, used economic pressure and inducements to procure the breach; but for these acts Philip would have continued. SWRI's revenues collapsed from ~$3M to ~$267,000 the following year.
firac.conclusion: Robert, Chester and IWS induced the breach; damages assessed at large at $2.5 million plus $100,000 punitive damages against Chester and Robert.

firac.issue: Was Morris wrongfully dismissed / oppressively removed from IWS?
firac.facts: On 26 October 1988 Linton handed Morris a termination letter ending his position as President and cutting off all family health benefits (Morris had a heart condition and his wife had just been diagnosed with cancer). No genuine cause was given; the alleged theft of accounts and diversion to SWRI was rejected because Chester/IWS had consented to SWRI's activities.
firac.rule: An employer dismissing without cause must give reasonable notice (Bardal; Wallace v. United Grain Growers). Where dismissal forms part of a pattern of oppression it may also ground s. 248 relief (Naneff).
firac.application: Morris was dismissed without cause; his employment was inextricably tied to his ownership, and the dismissal was part of Chester's pattern of oppressive conduct. Given his 45-year tenure, age, presidency and manner of discharge, a two-year notice period was appropriate; to avoid double recovery only salary (not drawings) was awarded.
firac.conclusion: Morris was wrongfully dismissed / oppressively removed; damages awarded on a two-year notice period (salary only).

firac.issue: Did the solicitor Ennis breach his duties to Morris, and were the auditors Taylor Leibow liable to Morris personally?
firac.facts: Ennis had acted for Morris, Chester and IWS for over a decade. He took instructions on the share sale solely from Chester, never explained the documents or advised Morris to obtain independent legal advice, and obtained a waiver of independent advice only after the documents were signed. The auditors, engaged by IWS, omitted material related-party (Greycliffe) disclosure and prepared Morris's tax returns treating the staged share sale as completed.
firac.rule: A solicitor owes fiduciary and contractual duties of care, disclosure and loyalty and must decline to act, or advise independent representation, in a conflict (Davey v. Woolley, Hames, Dale & Dingwall). Auditors generally owe their duty of care to the corporation collectively, not to individual shareholders, absent a specific assumption of a duty (Hercules Management v. Ernst & Young; Caparo; Roman Corp.).
firac.application: Ennis should have refused to act; he breached his fiduciary and contractual duties by failing to disclose that Morris was selling his shares, failing to advise, and lending the transaction a veneer of normalcy — but for which Morris would not have signed. The auditors, by contrast, owed their audit duty to IWS, not to Morris personally, so policy considerations ousted any prima facie duty; the related-party claims were also barred by an agreement/undertaking, though negligence in the tax filings (had the sale stood) would have been made out.
firac.conclusion: Ennis is liable to Morris for the same amounts as Chester on the share sale; the claims against the auditors are dismissed (they owed no personal audit duty to Morris).

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area: this is a sprawling commercial/corporate dispute among family co-owners involving fiduciary duty, oppression, undue influence, unconscionability, inducing breach of contract, and professional negligence. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is squarely engaged by Action #36583/89, and K009 (Labour and employment law) is its tier-1 parent. The controlled vocabulary lacks terms for the case's core doctrines (fiduciary duty, oppression remedy, breach of contract), so several central concepts cannot be tagged. K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) reflect that the Waxmans are a prominent Jewish family (Chester was 'Hamilton's Jewish Man of the Year') and K105 (synagogue) reflects repeated synagogue references (e.g., meetings there); these three tier-3 tags are borderline/weak, included only because more specific commercial-law keywords are unavailable in the vocabulary.

The Waxman family business (I. Waxman & Sons Ltd.) and virtually all events occurred in Hamilton, Ontario, but because the seat of the court is not expressly stated the city is left null.
