firac.issue: What standard governs the 'appearance of right' criterion where the requested injunction may indirectly affect freedom of expression?
firac.facts: McGill sought a prohibitory injunction restraining the blocking/obstruction of buildings and paths, excessive noise, and the intimidation/harassment/threatening of persons associated with McGill's policies. Union interveners argued the order would chill picketing and expression and therefore engage the heightened free-speech standard.
firac.rule: Under art. 511 C.C.P. and Groupe CRH Canada Inc. v. Beauregard, the appearance-of-right criterion is normally low (claim neither frivolous nor vexatious). A heightened standard — issuance only in 'the most manifest and rare cases' — applies where an injunction seeks to restrain free speech (Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Canadian Liberty Net; Association étudiante de l'Université McGill v. X, 2025 QCCA 475).
firac.application: The Court found McGill did not seek to enjoin any specific message, protest, banner or slogan; it sought to prohibit physical blocking, excessive noise, and intimidation/harassment. These orders may indirectly affect expression, but are not comparable to injunctions restraining defamatory or hateful speech. The chilling effect is properly weighed at the balance-of-convenience stage, not through a heightened first-step standard. Universities have a right and duty to ensure access to classes and to control their property (multiple prior Quebec authorities), and McGill's apparent right had been recognized four times in prior proceedings.
firac.conclusion: The ordinary prima facie standard applies, and McGill satisfied it — a serious question to be tried was demonstrated.

firac.issue: Did McGill demonstrate that the injunction is 'necessary to prevent serious or irreparable prejudice' under art. 511 C.C.P.?
firac.facts: McGill relied on a series of past violent events (2024 blockades, encampment, building occupation, April 2025 strike disruptions, property damage) and on SPHR Instagram posts vowing 'no business as usual until divestment.' However, those posts were over a year old and SPHR had published nothing since April 2025. Professor Campbell's vague reference to a possible second-anniversary mobilization lacked specifics.
firac.rule: Art. 511 C.C.P. requires that the injunction be 'necessary to prevent' the harm. For a quia timet/precautionary injunction, courts must adopt a cautious approach requiring 'a high degree of probability' that the harm will occur (Sharpe, Injunctions and Specific Performance; Operation Dismantle; Association générale des étudiants... v. Roy Grenier, 2016 QCCA 86).
firac.application: Past events undoubtedly caused serious and irreparable harm, but the issue was likelihood of recurrence. The record contained no evidence of who is behind SPHR or their intentions, no post since April 2025, and no probative evidence of imminent action. There was no 'forte probabilité' or 'probabilité sérieuse' of recurrence in the short or medium term. Nor was there evidence that the injunction would alleviate the antisemitic/harmful campus climate, since McGill expressly disclaimed any intent to restrain expression. Urgency is not required at the interlocutory stage, but an injunction cannot rest on hypothetical harm.
firac.conclusion: McGill failed to demonstrate that the injunction is necessary to prevent serious or irreparable prejudice.

firac.issue: Does the balance of convenience favour granting the injunction?
firac.facts: The order would apply to 'any person having knowledge of' it, cover the entire lower campus and any building used for McGill's operations, and remain in force indefinitely. Unions feared it would chill picketing and mobilization (e.g., the April 2024 AMPFA gathering that 'pretty much blocked' an entrance).
firac.rule: Balance of convenience must always be assessed (Groupe CRH; HRM Projet Children). Courts must consider an injunction's overall impact including its chilling effect, must be reluctant to enjoin conduct unrelated to the claims advanced (Re Brake, 2019 NLCA 17), and must not bind non-parties who act independently (Sharpe; Aetna Financial Services v. Feigelman).
firac.application: Three features tipped the balance against McGill: (1) no identifiable defendant — SPHR is a non-existent entity and the order would apply indiscriminately to anyone on campus regardless of motivation, though McGill could likely have identified individuals; (2) the vast geographic scope (all of lower campus, and no geographic limit for the harassment orders); and (3) the indeterminate temporal duration, which magnifies the inconvenience and chilling effect. McGill's laudable narrowing of the wording did not resolve the uncertainty. Unlike short provisional injunctions where overbreadth is tolerable, the indefinite duration made the inconvenience substantial.
firac.conclusion: The balance of convenience does not favour granting the injunction.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, the case being an interlocutory injunction application. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the central remedy and legal test. K087 (protest/demonstration) captures the campus blockades, encampment and strike disruptions at issue. K024 (freedom of expression) reflects the contested question of the applicable standard and chilling effect on picketing/expression. K041 (campus/university) situates the dispute at McGill. K058 (antisemitism) reflects the troubling antisemitic incidents relied on as part of the alleged harm. K038 (vandalism) captures the smashed windows, thrown paint and desecration-type damage. K059 (boycott) reflects the divestment/academic boycott (BDS-style) agenda driving the protests. K102 (Gaza) and K104 (Palestine) situate the underlying cause. K038 and K059 are somewhat secondary but genuinely engaged by the factual record; the core doctrinal keywords are K021 and K024.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'SUPERIOR COURT', 'PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC', 'DISTRICT of Montreal', and identifies the lower campus as being 'in downtown Montreal.'
registry_rationale: The 'DISTRICT of Montreal' and court file no. 500-17-133705-254 identify the Montreal registry of the Superior Court.

case_name: Frontenac Children's Aid Society v. C. N.

name_verification.name_in_document: Frontenac Children's Aid Society v. C. N. (mother)

defining_issues: Should the respondent mother's Answer and pleadings be struck out for failure to obey court orders in a child protection proceeding?
Should the court grant summary judgment (an uncontested/summary trial) making disposition orders in the children's best interests without a full trial?
Should the file be transferred from Kingston to Brantford where the mother now resides?

firac.issue: Should the respondent mother's Answer be struck out for failure to obey court orders in a child protection proceeding?
firac.facts: Over almost two years and 25 court appearances, the self-represented mother repeatedly disobeyed orders: she was found to have participated in the disappearance of both children, published prohibited material contrary to s. 45(8) CFSA, was found in contempt and incarcerated 30 days, boycotted the court, and stopped filing material or attending. The children were already found in need of protection.
firac.rule: The Family Law Rules, O. Reg. 114/99 (Courts of Justice Act), permit a court to strike out pleadings where a party fails to follow the rules, obey a court order, or where the pleadings disclose no reasonable claim or defence. Rule 14(23) allows striking a party's Answer where a party does not obey an order made on motion. Courts are reluctant to strike pleadings in child protection matters because it forecloses a parent's ability to assist in determining best interests.
firac.application: The court found the mother was not influenced by court orders, had been found in contempt and punished yet continued to defy directions, and conceded the school and health concerns. It weighed the prejudice to the mother against the prejudice to the children of further delay, emphasizing the need for permanency and finality in child welfare disputes. The court preserved her affidavit material to keep her viewpoint before the court, but struck the Answer as the litigation itself was harming the children.
firac.conclusion: The mother's Answer was struck out (though her affidavits were not), and the matter was allowed to proceed by summary/uncontested trial.

firac.issue: Should the court grant summary judgment making disposition orders without a full trial?
firac.facts: The younger child C. (13) had been missing over seven months, not in school, at risk of inappropriate medication; the older child T. (16) had attended only two days of school in seven months under an interim supervision order. Psychiatric and clinic assessments documented the mother's delusional belief system and its serious harm to the children. The mother filed nothing and did not oppose the motion.
firac.rule: Rule 16 (Family Law Rules) allows summary judgment; Rule 10(5) provides that where an Answer is struck the respondent is not entitled to further notice or participation. The moving party (the Society) bears the burden of showing no triable issue (Children's Aid Society of Halton Region v. K.L.A., 2006 CanLII 33538 (ON CA)), and the jurisdiction must be exercised with caution, taking a 'good, hard look' at the full evidentiary record (Children's Aid Society of Waterloo v. R.S., 2000 CanLII 22902; F.B. v. S.G.). Disposition is governed by ss. 57, 57(2), 57(3), 57(4) and 70(1) CFSA, requiring decisions in the child's best interests, consideration of less disruptive alternatives, and observance of wardship time limits.
firac.application: The court reviewed the voluminous record and found compelling, credible, uncontradicted evidence of overwhelming protection concerns. Community placement for T. had been tried and failed through the mother's interference; no less restrictive plan existed for C.; the mother's prognosis for change was bleak and statutory time limits were running. The relief sought was temporary and less intrusive than the assessor's recommendation of Crown wardship. The court found no genuine issue requiring a trial regarding the children's health and educational needs.
firac.conclusion: Summary judgment granted: C. made a ward of the Society until the later of June 29, 2007 or three months after his return; T. placed with the mother under a three-month supervision order with detailed conditions.

firac.issue: Should the child protection file be transferred from Kingston to Brantford?
firac.facts: The mother had relocated to Brantford and both parties now appeared to consent to a transfer. However, the younger child C. remained missing, and his assessments, medical resources, lawyer, foster home, school and familiar workers were all in the Kingston area.
firac.rule: A court may transfer a proceeding where appropriate, but the governing consideration in child protection remains the child's best interests and the balance of convenience.
firac.application: Despite the unopposed request, the court found the substantial convenience remained in Kingston and that transfer while C. was still missing would be counterproductive to his security. His support network and resources were all in Kingston, and the mother's non-cooperation and disregard for the legal system made transfer inappropriate at this time; the motion could be renewed by C.'s counsel once he was returned to care.
firac.conclusion: The motion to transfer the case to the Ontario Court of Justice in Brantford was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a child protection/child welfare proceeding under the Child and Family Services Act. K047 (best interests of the child) is central: the disposition, striking of pleadings, and transfer were all decided on the best-interests standard (ss. 57, 57(3) CFSA). K048 (custody/access) applies because the orders addressed wardship, placement with the mother under supervision, and access arrangements. K002 (Civil litigation) is a supporting pick capturing the procedural dimensions — striking pleadings under the Family Law Rules and summary judgment (Rule 16) — and is somewhat weak as a standalone. K005 (Education law) is a borderline/weak pick reflecting that school attendance was a core protection concern and a term of the supervision order, though no education statute was directly litigated. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated child-protection/wardship term, so these are the closest available.
location_rationale: The heading states 'COURT FILE NO.: Kingston 342/05' and 'SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE – FAMILY COURT', identifying Kingston, Ontario as the location. Ontario is confirmed by references to Ontario statutes (Child and Family Services Act, R.S.O. 1990) and the Superior Court of Justice.
registry_rationale: The court file number 'Kingston 342/05' and the concluding style of cause naming the 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE' indicate the Kingston registry; the transfer motion to Brantford was refused, keeping the file in Kingston.

case_name: Gould v. Yukon Order of Pioneers

name_verification.name_in_document: Gould v. Yukon Order of Pioneers (No. 2)
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The style of cause in the decision adds "(No. 2)" but is otherwise identical to the supplied name. No neutral citation is printed in the text (the decision predates and does not display the CanLII citation); the appealed-from decision is cited as (1989), 1989 CanLII 9102 (YK HRC), 10 C.H.R.R. D/5812 (Y.T. Bd.Adj.).

defining_issues: On a statutory appeal limited to questions of law, what degree of deference does the reviewing court owe to a human rights board of adjudication's interpretation of its enabling statute?

Did the refusal of Madeleine Gould's membership application, because she is female, constitute "discrimination" within the meaning of ss. 6 and 11 of the Yukon Human Rights Act, and did the Board err by failing to balance the right to equality against the competing right to freedom of association?

Did the Pioneers' collection and preservation of Yukon history amount to "offering or providing services... to the public" under s. 8(a) of the Act such that the male-only membership rule constituted prohibited discrimination?
Did the Board err in law by failing to consider the reasonable-cause defence in s. 9 and the social-organization group exemption in s. 10 of the Act?
Could the Board find as a fact, on a "common sense" basis, that history recorded only by males is distorted, in the absence of sufficient evidence?

firac.issue: On a statutory appeal on questions of law, how much deference is owed to the Board's interpretation of the Human Rights Act?
firac.facts: The Pioneers appealed the Board's decision under ss. 26(3)-(4) of the Human Rights Act, which permit appeals on questions of law only. The Board's task involved statutory interpretation and evidentiary questions it was addressing for the first time.
firac.rule: Sections 26(3)-(4) confer a statutory right of appeal on questions of law and make appeal the only means to set aside a Board decision. Where a legislature grants an appeal on "law or jurisdiction," the patently unreasonable standard does not apply; the court must correct all errors of law (Jones & de Villars; Bell Canada v. Canada (CRTC), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1722). Curial deference is limited to matters squarely within the tribunal's expertise.
firac.application: The court held that appellate jurisdiction is broader than judicial review. Matters of statutory interpretation and evidence do not fall squarely within the Board's expertise, especially on its first occasion addressing them; the court was therefore entitled and obliged to determine the law and correct errors of law without deference.
firac.conclusion: The court would review the Board's legal and evidentiary determinations for correctness and correct any error of law.

firac.issue: Was the exclusion of Gould "discrimination" under ss. 6/11, and did the Board fail to balance equality against freedom of association?
firac.facts: Gould was refused membership solely because she is female. The Pioneers is a century-old male-only fraternal order whose primary objects are the mutual protection and brotherhood of its members. The Yukon Human Rights Act expressly protects, in its Bill of Rights (s. 5), the right to form associations of any character.
firac.rule: Discrimination under ss. 6 and 11 must be assessed by effect, not intent (O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536; Andrews v. Law Society of B.C., [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143). Human rights legislation is quasi-constitutional and given a fair, large and liberal interpretation, but no right is absolute and competing rights (including freedom of association, expressly guaranteed by the Act and s. 2 Charter) must be balanced in their social, political and legal context.
firac.application: The Board declared discrimination "in the abstract" had been established without properly determining whether the conduct fell within ss. 6 or 11 in context, and without recognizing that not all differential treatment is discriminatory. Critically, the Board failed to weigh the Pioneers' countervailing right to associate against Gould's right to equality. The genuine membership screening, congeniality, absence of commercial activity and private character all had to be considered.
firac.conclusion: The Board erred in law; the membership policy may not be discriminatory within the meaning of the Act, and the failure to balance the competing rights was an error requiring a rehearing.

firac.issue: Did the collection and preservation of history amount to providing "services to the public" under s. 8(a)?
firac.facts: The Pioneers' historian, Mr. Cyr, a volunteer, gathered and preserved records about members and provided historical information to anyone in the public who requested it. The intervener conceded there was no discrimination in the distribution of information but argued the male-only preparation of history was inherently discriminatory.
firac.rule: Section 8(a) prohibits discrimination "when offering or providing services, goods or facilities to the public." The word "services" is unqualified; "public" modifies to whom services are offered, not the nature of the services. Legislation must be given the meaning its words can bear (Action travail des femmes).
firac.application: The court held the Board wrongly used "public" to modify "services" and confused "public services" with "services to the public." Even if the historical activity were a service, it was offered to all members of the public without discrimination in distribution. Creating information, however one-sided, shared freely with all who request it, is not conduct caught by the Act; the activity was also expressive conduct protected by freedom of expression under the Act and s. 2(b) of the Charter.
firac.conclusion: The Board erred in law; the creation of information provided without discrimination to the public is not prohibited discrimination under s. 8(a).

firac.issue: Did the Board err by not considering the s. 9 defence and the s. 10 group exemption?
firac.facts: The Pioneers is fairly characterized as a social organization. The Board did not consider s. 9 at all and applied a narrow, restrictive construction to s. 10, concluding the people the Order exists to serve was the whole community.
firac.rule: Section 9 provides that treatment based on factors establishing reasonable cause is not discrimination. Section 10 provides that a religious, charitable, educational, social, cultural or athletic organization may give preference to its members or those it exists to serve. Group-exemption provisions confer and protect associational rights and are not to be read restrictively like BFOR defences (Caldwell v. St. Thomas Aquinas; Brossard (Ville) v. Québec (CDP)).
firac.application: The court held s. 9 should have been considered (freedom of association and expression may be reasonable cause). Section 10 is not a mere BFOR-type limit but a provision integral to defining the Act's scope, establishing the primacy of group rights in specified circumstances, and should be given the ordinary meaning of its words. The Yukon provision, unlike Quebec's, requires no showing that the exclusion is "justified." The Pioneers likely fit within s. 10 as a social organization, and "the people the organization exists to serve" is arguably its members.
firac.conclusion: The Board erred in law in failing to consider s. 9 and in its restrictive treatment of s. 10; both must be considered on rehearing.

firac.issue: Could the Board find history is distorted when recorded only by males without sufficient evidence?
firac.facts: The Board accepted "from a common sense standpoint" that history recorded solely by males would be distorted, while acknowledging the evidence on that point "could not be accorded much weight." This finding grounded its conclusion of prohibited discrimination.
firac.rule: A complaint must be proven on a balance of probabilities (s. 23), and hearings must accord with fundamental justice (s. 22). While the Board may receive relevant evidence beyond strict court rules (s. 11 Regulations), a finding must rest on material with probative value (R. v. Deputy Industrial Injuries Commissioner, Ex p. Moore; Blanchard v. Control Data). A finding of fact with no evidence is an error of law; social/legislative facts require more than common-sense reasoning.
firac.application: The court held the Board reached a critical factual conclusion in the absence of evidence, relying on unsubstantiated opinion and academic writings whose excerpts may not support the propositions urged. Distinguishing admissibility from weight, and cautioning about the danger of over-broad legislative facts in narrowly focused litigation, the court found the complainant had not proven her case even under the relaxed evidentiary standard.
firac.conclusion: The Board erred in law by finding distortion of history without sufficient probative evidence; this independently justified setting aside the decision.

keywords_rationale: K007 (Human rights) is the primary practice area — the case turns on the Yukon Human Rights Act. K069 (discrimination) is the core substantive issue (sex-based refusal of membership, ss. 6/11/8). K072 (human rights tribunal) captures the Board of Adjudication whose decision was appealed. K014 (standard of review) reflects the court's extensive analysis of deference on a statutory appeal on questions of law; K001 (Administrative law) is its tier-1 parent, engaged by the appeal/deference and evidentiary/fundamental-justice analysis. K024 (freedom of expression) is genuinely engaged — the court held the history-recording activity was protected expression under the Act and s. 2(b). K023 (equality rights) reflects the equality-versus-association balancing at the heart of the case. K107 (Canadian Charter) is cited throughout as an interpretive aid. A weakness: the pivotal countervailing right is freedom of association, for which the vocabulary has no dedicated keyword, so K023/K024 and the administrative-law tags carry the analytical weight instead.
location_rationale: The decision is headed "Yukon Supreme Court" and "Supreme Court of the Yukon Territory, Allan H. Wachowich J.", establishing the territory as Yukon. No sitting city (e.g., Whitehorse) is stated in the text, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: No court registry or office is identified anywhere in the decision, so registry is left null.

case_name: X c. Students' Society of McGill University

name_verification.name_in_document: X c. Students' Society of McGill University

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff be permitted to litigate anonymously under a confidentiality order despite the open-court principle?
Should an interlocutory injunction be granted restraining the SSMU from ratifying and implementing the Policy Against Genocide in Palestine pending trial?

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff be permitted to litigate anonymously under a confidentiality order despite the open-court principle?
firac.facts: The plaintiff, a McGill student who chaired the anonymous online 'No' campaign against the SSMU's Policy Against Genocide in Palestine, sought a confidentiality order. She adduced social-media messages branding 'No' campaigners as 'pro genociders' and 'genocide supporters', an anonymous user boasting of belonging to an 'evil gang', and newspaper articles and a McGill affidavit describing rising tensions and antisemitic incidents in Montreal after October 7, 2023. The SSMU argued her fears were subjective, that the newspaper articles were inadmissible hearsay, and that she had renounced anonymity.
firac.rule: The open-court principle is constitutionally protected under s. 2(b) of the Charter and s. 3 of the Quebec Charter, and codified in arts. 11 and 12 C.C.P. A confidentiality order may issue only where the applicant establishes the three cumulative Sherman/Sierra Club prerequisites: (1) court openness poses a serious risk to an important public interest; (2) the order is necessary because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; and (3) the benefits of the order outweigh its negative effects. Physical safety is an important public interest and serious risk may be established by logical inference from objective circumstantial facts, not mere speculation (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25; J.C. c. Douville, 2022 QCCA 958).
firac.application: The court found the social-media messages were thinly veiled threats designed to harass, intimidate and silence the plaintiff, and that it was not fanciful to infer she could be further threatened or harmed if named; this was more than negligible or speculative and beyond mere discomfort. Newspaper articles were admissible only to show a broader climate of disquiet, and the McGill affidavit corroborated the tensions. She had not renounced anonymity by filing the injunction application or by disclosing her name in an exhibit filed in support of confidentiality (Exhibit P-2 ordered sealed). Anonymity was preferable to in camera hearings or sealing orders, but the requested order was too broad, so the court adopted Douville-style non-publication/non-dissemination orders while requiring disclosure of her name to instructing SSMU members through counsel.
firac.conclusion: The confidentiality application was granted in part; the plaintiff may litigate anonymously with non-publication and non-dissemination of identifying information, Exhibit P-2 sealed, and her name disclosed only to authorized SSMU members through counsel.

firac.issue: Should an interlocutory injunction be granted restraining the SSMU from ratifying and implementing the Policy pending trial?
firac.facts: A referendum adopted (by roughly 25% of members) the Policy Against Genocide in Palestine, which condemned Israel and demanded that McGill and the SSMU cut ties, divest and take pro-Palestinian positions for five years. McGill's Deputy Provost warned that adoption would breach the SSMU Constitution and constitute an event of default under the Memorandum of Agreement, and that the Policy invoked antisemitic tropes. The plaintiff sought to enjoin ratification and implementation, alleging violations of the Constitution, the Equity Policy and the Antisemitism Motion. The SSMU argued the application was premature (the Board had not yet ratified) and that the Policy was mere political expression protected by student democracy.
firac.rule: Under art. 511 C.C.P. and Groupe CRH Canada inc. c. Beauregard, 2018 QCCA 1063, an interlocutory injunction requires: (1) an appearance of right (a serious question to be tried, neither frivolous nor vexatious); (2) serious or irreparable harm; and (3) a balance of inconvenience favouring the applicant. Sufficient interest is governed by art. 85 C.C.P. Freedom of expression is fundamental (Pepsi-Cola, R.W.D.S.U. Local 558), and courts are reluctant to interfere in the internal affairs of student associations (Presch v. AMS of UBC, 2017 BCSC 963).
firac.application: The application was not premature or moot: its gravamen was the unconstitutionality of the Policy tied to the referendum itself, and the SSMU had undertaken only not to ratify pending the hearing, distinguishing Fried where the Board had refused to ratify. On appearance of right, the court distinguished Presch (a mere 'loaded question' on procedural/contractual grounds) — here a detailed 'loaded policy' omitting October 7 arguably breached constitutional principles requiring the SSMU to facilitate interaction among all communities and respect human dignity regardless of national, ethnic or religious origin; the claim was serious. The court found no appearance of right on the Equity Policy (the plaintiff failed to use the available complaints procedure) or the Antisemitism Motion (not a policy). It found serious harm: the Policy's cascading call to action would exacerbate division and, if antisemitic and unconstitutional, would violate the human dignity of Jewish students with no rescission mechanism until 2028. The balance of inconvenience favoured the plaintiff, as ratifying a possibly unconstitutional four-year policy was more prejudicial than delaying it.
firac.conclusion: The injunction application was granted in part; an interlocutory injunction issued restraining the SSMU from ratifying or implementing the Policy until trial on the merits, without security, and not declared executory notwithstanding appeal.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns a private civil proceeding for an injunction and a confidentiality order. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the central remedy under art. 511 C.C.P. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) anchor both the open-court analysis and the SSMU's student-democracy/free-expression defence. K058 (antisemitism) and K061 (hate speech) reflect the plaintiff's core allegation that the Policy invoked antisemitic tropes and constituted hate literature. K093 (Jewish) and K096 (Jewish students) capture the affected group. K041 (campus/university) situates the dispute in a student-association referendum. K104 (Palestine) and K107 (Charter) reflect the Policy's subject matter and the constitutional framework relied on. Borderline: K061 (hate speech) is a weaker pick since the court did not decide the hate-speech question, but the allegation drove the appearance-of-right analysis.
location_rationale: The header states 'SUPERIOR COURT', 'PROVINCE OF QUEBEC', 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL', No. 500-17-127703-232, and the disposition notes the Defendant's principal office in Montreal, Quebec.
registry_rationale: The proceeding was filed in the District of Montreal (court file 500-17-127703-232), identifying the Montreal registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: Soliman v. Bordman

defining_issues: Was the case appropriate for disposition by summary judgment under Rule 20?
Did Bordman's statements defame Soliman, making out the elements of the tort of defamation?
Did the defence of fair comment succeed?
Did the defence of responsible communication on a matter of public interest succeed?
What remedies — damages and injunctive relief — were appropriate?

firac.issue: Was the case appropriate for disposition by summary judgment under Rule 20 of the Rules of Civil Procedure?
firac.facts: Soliman moved for summary judgment in his defamation action. Bordman resisted, arguing numerous genuine issues required a trial, particularly whether his statements were hate speech and whether he was a racist. The record was extensive: video recordings, examinations for discovery, cross-examinations and two factums; Bordman had abandoned the justification defence.
firac.rule: Rule 20.04(2)(a) directs summary judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; Rule 20.04(2.1) permits weighing evidence, assessing credibility and drawing inferences unless it is in the interest of justice to reserve those powers for trial (Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7). In defamation matters availability of summary judgment requires a case-by-case analysis (Skafco Ltd. v. Abdalla, 2020 ONSC 136).
firac.application: Perell J. found a fulsome evidentiary record allowing fair and just determination of defamation, the fair comment and responsible communication defences, and remedies. Credibility concerns evaporated on close review of the evidence. Only the collateral questions of whether Bordman's speech was hate speech and whether he was a racist raised genuine issues requiring a trial, but Soliman did not need those findings to succeed.
firac.conclusion: Except for the hate-speech/racist allegations, the case was appropriate for summary judgment; a trial was not required to determine liability, defences and remedies.

firac.issue: Did Bordman's statements defame Soliman?
firac.facts: Bordman, an alternative-media journalist, published Internet videos and posts asserting that Soliman, a prominent lawyer and Conservative campaign chair, was a supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood and extremist/terrorist Islamic organizations, a closet anti-Semite and Al Quds Day supporter, and a covert advocate of Sharia law in Canada. Publication and reference to Soliman were admitted.
firac.rule: Defamation requires: (1) the defendant made a statement; (2) the words were defamatory (would lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person); (3) the words referred to the plaintiff; and (4) they were published (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). Grave imputations such as being a terrorist or terrorist supporter are so obviously harmful that harm and general damages may be inferred.
firac.application: Bordman's many statements synthesized into three assertions, each of which would lower Soliman's reputation. Bordman never argued the statements were non-defamatory, publication was undisputed, and he abandoned justification. The statements plainly referred to and were published about Soliman.
firac.conclusion: Soliman established all elements of defamation; the statements were defamatory.

firac.issue: Did the defence of fair comment succeed?
firac.facts: Bordman relied on the Al-Qazzaz open letter, the Soliman-Safavi meeting, the Soliman-Singh transcript (which he said recorded Soliman as 'a Muslim Brotherhood guy'), Soliman's children's parochial school, and a 2007 Globe and Mail interview on Sharia financing to support his statements.
firac.rule: Fair comment requires the impugned statement to be (a) comment/opinion not fact, (b) on a matter of public interest, (c) based on true facts, (d) objectively fair (any person could honestly express it on the proved facts), and (e) made without malice (WIC Radio v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Cherneskey v. Armadale). Malice includes reckless disregard for the truth (Platnick v. Bent, 2020 SCC 23).
firac.application: The statements were presented as investigated true facts, not comment, so fair comment was unavailable. Even if comment, though on a matter of public interest, they were not based on true facts (Bordman relied on inadmissible double/triple hearsay and illogical inferences), were not objectively fair (no person could honestly draw those conclusions on the proved facts), and were made with malice — Bordman never interviewed Soliman, relied on rumour and unreliable hearsay, and spoke with reckless disregard for the truth.
firac.conclusion: The fair comment defence failed.

firac.issue: Did the defence of responsible communication succeed?
firac.facts: Bordman published serious allegations without contacting Soliman for comment, without notes or records of investigation, and with no formal training in journalism or national security.
firac.rule: Responsible communication requires (a) a matter of public interest and (b) responsible publication — reasonable steps to ensure the accuracy of factual assertions and the fairness of the publication (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61).
firac.application: Although the statements concerned a matter of public interest, Bordman took no reasonable steps to verify accuracy or ensure fairness, and spoke with reckless disregard for the truth. He was not a responsible journalist.
firac.conclusion: The responsible communication defence failed.

firac.issue: What remedies were appropriate?
firac.facts: Soliman claimed general, aggravated and punitive damages and injunctive relief. He advanced no claim for special or pecuniary damages; his reputation remained largely intact, but he and his family suffered anguish and the defamatory Internet material continued to circulate. It was doubtful Bordman could pay a damages award.
firac.rule: Defamation damages restore reputation and provide vindication and consolation (Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto, 1995); Internet publication is an aggravating factor (Rutman v. Rabinowitz, 2018 ONCA 80). A permanent injunction may issue where the defendant is likely to continue defaming or where recovery of damages is doubtful.
firac.application: Having regard to Soliman's standing, the seriousness of the imputations, the pernicious Internet medium, the absence of any retraction or apology, and Bordman's conduct, the court assessed general and aggravated damages at $500,000; punitive damages were not warranted. Given Bordman's demonstrated inability to distinguish defamatory from non-defamatory statements about Soliman, an absolute injunction against any statements (other than an approved apology) was justified.
firac.conclusion: Summary judgment granted: $500,000 in general and aggravated damages and a permanent injunction requiring removal of the material and barring further statements about Soliman.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a civil defamation tort action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. K016 (fair comment) and K019 (responsible communication) are the two substantive defences the court analysed and rejected. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the closest controlled term for the injunctive relief granted, though here the injunction was permanent rather than interlocutory — a slight mismatch flagged as such. K024 (freedom of expression) is engaged because Bordman framed his defences around free speech on matters of public interest. K063 (online hate / social media) is apt because the defamation was published through Internet videos and social media, which the court treated as an aggravating factor. Antisemitism/Israel keywords were considered but are only incidental context (the allegations were largely Islamophobic and the parties' faiths were background), so they were omitted.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE' and cites the Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, so the province is Ontario. No city is stated in the text; the court file number (CV-20-00636658-0000) and Perell J. are consistent with Toronto but the judgment does not expressly name a sitting city, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision does not name a court registry or office; only the court file number appears. Registry is therefore left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Di Franco v. Bueckert

defining_issues: Should some or all of the defendant's supporting affidavit be struck under r. 25.11 as scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or for containing opinion evidence, references to unproduced materials, or speculation?
Did the defendant establish that the defamation action arises from an expression relating to a matter of public interest under s. 137.1(3) of the Courts of Justice Act?
Did the plaintiff show that the defamation action has substantial merit under s. 137.1(4)(a)(i)?
Did the plaintiff show that the defendant has no valid defence (fair comment, justification) under s. 137.1(4)(a)(ii)?

Did the plaintiff show that the harm suffered is sufficiently serious that the public interest in permitting the action to continue outweighs the public interest in protecting the expression under s. 137.1(4)(b)?

firac.issue: Should some or all of the defendant's supporting affidavit be struck under r. 25.11 or as improper opinion, unproduced-source, speculative, or inflammatory evidence?
firac.facts: Mr. Di Franco moved to strike part or all of Mr. Bueckert's 94-paragraph affidavit, arguing it contained impermissible opinion evidence (Bueckert not qualified as an expert), referred to websites and academic texts not reproduced, contained speculation about people's beliefs and motivations, and included inflammatory antisemitic material.
firac.rule: R. 25.11 permits striking scandalous, frivolous or vexatious pleadings; r. 4.06(2) limits affidavits to facts within personal knowledge, but r. 39.01(4) allows information and belief on a motion if the source and belief are specified; r. 4.06(3) governs exhibits; preliminary motions to strike affidavits are discouraged and granted only for special reasons (Allianz Global Risks). 'Nothing can be scandalous which is relevant' (McNabb).
firac.application: The affidavit satisfied r. 39.01(4) because Bueckert identified his sources; the opinion portions were explicitly framed as opinion and were relevant to the viability of his defence and absence of malice on the s. 137.1 analysis. Bueckert could not be qualified as an independent expert, but that went to weight, not admissibility. Failure to reproduce publicly available online/academic sources went to weight (9646035 Canada Ltd. v. Hill). His inferences were grounded in cited material and not unduly speculative. The antisemitic references were relevant to good faith belief and absence of malice, so not scandalous.
firac.conclusion: Motion to strike dismissed; the objections went to weight, not admissibility.

firac.issue: Did the expression relate to a matter of public interest under s. 137.1(3)?
firac.facts: Bueckert's tweets, article and podcast criticized the Ontario government's education policies (campus free-speech mandate and Student Choice Initiative) and the students consulted.
firac.rule: Section 137.1(3) CJA: the moving party must show the proceeding arises from an expression relating to a matter of public interest.
firac.application: Mr. Di Franco conceded that the tweets, interview and podcast related to a matter of public interest, namely the provincial government's education policies.
firac.conclusion: Threshold met; the analysis proceeded to stage two.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff show the defamation action has substantial merit under s. 137.1(4)(a)(i)?
firac.facts: Bueckert posted a series of tweets, an article and a podcast associating Mr. Di Franco (or his student club, often accompanied by the group photo with Premier Ford) with the 'alt-right', 'extremist alt-right fringe', 'Nazis', 'white supremacists' and 'MAGA chuds'; several did not name Di Franco directly.
firac.rule: Defamation requires words that would tend to lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person, that referred to the plaintiff, and that were published (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). Under s. 137.1 the judge asks only whether a trier could reasonably conclude the claim has substantial merit, avoiding a 'deep dive' into the merits (Pointes Protection).
firac.application: Read in context as a connected series, a court could reasonably find the tweets, including those not naming Di Franco but placed beside his photo, referred to him and imputed extreme views. Given Bueckert's own concession that 'alt-right' can include persons with extreme views, and his use of 'extremist alt-right' and 'alt-right fringe', a trier could reasonably find the statements defamatory; the article and podcast could similarly be found defamatory.
firac.conclusion: Substantial merit established.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff show the defendant has no valid defence of fair comment or justification under s. 137.1(4)(a)(ii)?
firac.facts: Bueckert pleaded fair comment and justification, relying on Di Franco's appearances with and endorsements of commentators such as Gavin McInnes, and social media posts; Di Franco characterized his views as 'centre right' and said a Holocaust post was a joke in poor taste.
firac.rule: Fair comment requires a matter of public interest, a factual basis, recognizability as comment, that a person could honestly express the opinion on the proved facts, and no malice (Simpson v. Mair, 2008 SCC 40). The plaintiff need only show it is possible the defence would not succeed—that it 'could go either way' (Lascaris v. B'nai Brith Canada, 2019 ONCA 163; Bondfield).
firac.application: While a trier could reasonably accept the defences, a trier could equally conclude the 'alt-right fringe'/'extreme alt-right' characterizations were stated as fact not opinion, that endorsing someone's free-speech right does not endorse their views, and that Di Franco's statements were not extreme—paralleling Lascaris. The justification defence failed for the same reasons, turning on contested meaning and credibility.
firac.conclusion: Plaintiff met his onus; the defences might reasonably fail.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff show the harm is sufficiently serious that the public interest in continuing the action outweighs the public interest in protecting the expression under s. 137.1(4)(b)?
firac.facts: Di Franco, now a law student, claimed ongoing reputational harm and future income loss because the impugned statements remain accessible online and could affect law-firm hiring. The action lacked the classic SLAPP hallmarks.
firac.rule: Section 137.1(4)(b) requires balancing the seriousness of the harm against the public interest in the expression; hallmarks of a SLAPP and the presumption of general damages in libel are considered (Pointes Protection; Platnick v. Bent; Hill v. Church of Scientology). Public-interest value of speech is diminished by vitriol or falsehoods.
firac.application: The action lacked SLAPP hallmarks—no litigation history, no power imbalance (both students), no punitive purpose. A lawyer's reputation is of paramount importance and the accessible statements could affect job prospects, so more than nominal damages were possible; Bueckert's 'nominal damages only' argument improperly presupposed findings on meaning and credibility unavailable on a s. 137.1 motion. Although the topics were of important public interest, the vitriolic Twitter medium made the protective value of the speech uncertain.
firac.conclusion: Balance favoured allowing the action to proceed; the anti-SLAPP motion was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a civil defamation suit resolved on procedural/screening motions. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. K016 (fair comment) and the defence of justification are central to stage 2(ii). K024 (freedom of expression) captures the public-interest expression balancing that underlies the anti-SLAPP framework. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is included as the closest procedural-remedy vocabulary term for the anti-SLAPP/interlocutory motion context—this is a weak/borderline fit since the motion was a s. 137.1 dismissal rather than an injunction, and no better procedural keyword exists in the vocabulary. K066 (white supremacism) and K058 (antisemitism) reflect the impugned content ('white supremacists', 'Nazis', antisemitic material referenced), engaged in assessing the defences; these are moderate-strength picks tied to the substance of the statements.
location_rationale: The decision is of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice. Court file no. CV-19-79414 and the parties (a University of Ottawa undergraduate and a Carleton University graduate student, both located in Ottawa) together with counsel Jean-François Lalonde/Yavar Hameed indicate an Ottawa proceeding. Province is expressly 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE'.
registry_rationale: The registry is inferred as Ottawa from the Ottawa-based parties, counsel, and the nature of the proceeding; the decision does not print the registry location expressly, but the CV-19 file number and Ottawa context support it.

case_name: Waldman v. The Medical Services Commission of British Columbia

name_verification.name_in_document: Deborah Judith Waldman v. The Medical Services Commission of British Columbia and The Attorney General of British Columbia (and Anita Kafai Wong and Andrew Biro v. same)

defining_issues: Did the Commission have statutory authority under the Medicare Protection Act to enact measures that discriminate (in the administrative-law sense) among physicians on the basis of province of residence, and could it re-enact such measures retroactively?
Did the billing measures violate the Canada Health Act and thereby fall outside the authority conferred by the Medicare Protection Act?
Did the interim and permanent measures infringe the petitioners' mobility rights under s. 6 of the Charter?
Does s. 7 of the Charter protect the right to practise a profession, so that the billing restrictions engage it?
Did the measures infringe the petitioners' equality rights under s. 15 of the Charter, and is 'province of previous residence' an analogous ground?
If Charter rights were infringed, were the measures justified as a reasonable limit under s. 1?

firac.issue: Did the Commission have statutory authority to enact residence-based discriminatory measures, and could it apply them retroactively?
firac.facts: The Commission created a 'new biller' category (interim measures) and 13 categories (permanent measures) limiting new applicants to reduced billing, while grandfathering B.C.-trained and established physicians. Section 4(1)(r.1), authorizing supply-management measures, came into force July 14, 1995, after the petitioners had applied for billing numbers; Minutes 96-0033 and 96-0015 were passed in 1996 but purported to apply to physicians who applied after February 11, 1994.
firac.rule: A delegated body may only discriminate where expressly or impliedly authorized by its enabling statute (Shell Canada Products Ltd. v. Vancouver; R. v. Sharma). Administrative bodies possess only powers authorized by statute and cannot act retroactively unless the statute so provides explicitly or by necessary implication (Côté; Driedger; Quebec (A.G.) v. Healey).
firac.application: Section 21's general language did not authorize discrimination between residents and non-residents; only s. 4(1)(r.1) provided that authority. Because s. 4(1)(r.1) took effect only on July 14, 1995, the interim measures were unauthorized when enacted, and applying the 1996 Minutes to the petitioners required giving s. 4(1)(r.1) retroactive/retrospective effect, which was neither expressly nor impliedly authorized. Section 21(5) showed the legislature granted retroactive power only where it chose to (expressio unius).
firac.conclusion: The interim measures are invalid and the permanent measures have no retroactive effect; the petitioners are entitled to billing numbers under the rules in force before February 11, 1994.

firac.issue: Did the measures violate the Canada Health Act and thus exceed the Commission's authority under s. 4(2) of the Medicare Protection Act?
firac.facts: A 50% billing number was found not financially viable. Section 4(2) prohibits the Commission from acting in a manner that does not satisfy s. 7 of the Canada Health Act, which requires (via s. 12(1)(c)) 'reasonable compensation for all insured health services rendered by medical practitioners.' The Master and Working Agreements provided only single-arbitrator dispute resolution alterable by the courts.
firac.rule: Section 4(2) of the Medicare Protection Act; ss. 7 and 12 of the Canada Health Act, including the s. 12(2) deeming provision requiring a representative 'panel' with an 'independent chairman' and finality alterable only by legislation.
firac.application: A 50% billing number does not provide reasonable compensation. The agreements did not satisfy s. 12(2): a single arbitrator is not a 'panel,' the Master Agreement did not provide binding arbitration, and awards were alterable under the Commercial Arbitration Act. Compliance with the Canada Health Act is a precondition to the valid exercise of the Commission's powers, distinguishable from cases treating funding consequences as non-justiciable (Collett).
firac.conclusion: By enacting measures that do not provide reasonable compensation, the Commission acted contrary to s. 4(2) and exceeded its jurisdiction; the measures are void.

firac.issue: Did the measures infringe s. 6(2)(b) mobility rights, and were they saved by s. 6(3)(a)?
firac.facts: All petitioners trained and resided in Ontario before coming to B.C. and were restricted to locum or single-hospital practice; equally qualified B.C.-trained physicians were exempt. Evidence showed most 'new billers' come from outside B.C. and the measures were designed to limit such migration.
firac.rule: Section 6(2)(b) protects the right to pursue the livelihood of choice on the same conditions as residents where inter-provincial mobility is involved (Black v. Law Society of Alberta; Skapinker; Mia). Section 6(3)(a) saves laws of general application that do not discriminate primarily/principally on the basis of province of present or previous residence.
firac.application: Extra-provincial training is an aspect of residence; the exemptions/grandfathering for B.C.-trained physicians rendered the petitioners' livelihood of choice 'practically ineffective and essentially illusory.' Even after grandfathering expires, the measures were designed to and would most severely affect out-of-province physicians, distinguishing them from Walker v. P.E.I. The measures are not laws of general application because they impair the capacity of 'new billers' as a group.
firac.conclusion: The interim and permanent measures violate s. 6, and s. 6(3)(a) does not save them.

firac.issue: Does s. 7 protect the right to practise a profession so as to be engaged by the billing restrictions?
firac.facts: Earlier B.C. decisions (Mia; Wilson) had held that s. 7 liberty included the right to practise medicine. The facts here were indistinguishable from Wilson.
firac.rule: Section 7 of the Charter. Lamer J. in the Soliciting Reference held s. 7 does not protect the right to practise a profession, a view adopted by numerous appellate courts and effectively affirmed by the Supreme Court in Walker v. P.E.I.
firac.application: The weight of authority since Wilson—including the Supreme Court's affirmation of Walker—establishes that s. 7 does not protect the right to practise a profession. Wilson has effectively been overruled.
firac.conclusion: Section 7 has no application; the petitioners' s. 7 rights are not violated.

firac.issue: Did the measures infringe s. 15 equality rights, with province of previous residence as an analogous ground?
firac.facts: The petitioners were denied 100% billing numbers compared with established and B.C.-trained physicians because of where they had trained/resided. Dr. Waldman additionally alleged discrimination on age, sex and religion.
firac.rule: Section 15(1) (Andrews; Symes; Miron trilogy): the claimant must show denial of a benefit and that the denial is discriminatory on an enumerated or analogous ground; analogous grounds turn on whether the characteristic is an irrelevant, often immutable basis of exclusion affecting a discrete and insular minority (Turpin; S.(S.); Haig left province of residence open).
firac.application: The age, sex and religion claims failed for lack of proof of differential impact. However, out-of-province physicians are denied the benefit of an unrestricted billing number based on prior residence—a characteristic more immutable than citizenship, tied to a group unrepresented by the B.C.M.A., and unrelated to merit. This was the 'appropriate case' to recognize province of previous residence as an analogous ground.
firac.conclusion: Section 15(1) is infringed on the analogous ground of province of previous residence.

firac.issue: Were the infringements justified under s. 1?
firac.facts: The stated objectives were quality health care and cost control; the measures used financial disincentives to deter physicians and redistribute them. Expert evidence (Coyte vs. Hanvelt) conflicted on whether the measures would work; the supply template showed no under-serviced regions for GPs.
firac.rule: R. v. Oakes / Edwards Books: pressing and substantial objective plus proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionate effects); onus on the state on a balance of probabilities (RJR-MacDonald).
firac.application: Quality care and cost control are pressing and substantial. But the measures created obstacles to practising in under-serviced areas, contradicting the access objective, and the respondents provided no evidence connecting the financial disincentives to reduced numbers or cost savings; the petitioners in fact did not stay away. The impairment was not minimal given the fundamental nature of mobility and equality rights and the lengthy training involved. Severance would not save the measures.
firac.conclusion: The respondents failed to establish rational connection or minimal impairment; the measures are not justified under s. 1 and are of no force and effect.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) and K001 (Administrative law) are the two tier-1 areas engaged, since the measures were struck down both on ultra vires/retroactivity/Canada Health Act grounds (administrative law) and under the Charter (constitutional law). K023 (equality rights) and K109 (Charter s. 15) reflect the central holding recognizing province of previous residence as an analogous ground. K107 (Canadian Charter) anchors the Charter analysis generally, and K112 (Charter s. 7) is warranted by the substantial analysis of whether Wilson was overruled. K011 (judicial review) fits the petition challenging the validity of the Commission's Minutes. K025 (freedom of religion) and K093 (Jewish) are weaker/borderline: Dr. Waldman argued her Jewish faith required living in a large community, but this s. 15 religion argument failed and 'Jewish' is only an incidental entity reference; they are included for completeness but flagged as minor. Note that the case's most prominent issue—s. 6 mobility rights—has no corresponding keyword in the controlled vocabulary.
location_rationale: The heading states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA' and the 'Date and Place of Hearing' line reads 'Vancouver B.C.'; the registry block also names 'Vancouver'.
registry_rationale: The decision's caption expressly lists 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Grosz v. Jones

defining_issues: Should the claim against the Lawyer defendants and Mr. Mackey be dismissed under R. 9-6(5)(a) as raising no genuine issue for trial?

Should the pleadings be struck and the proceeding dismissed against all defendants under R. 9-5(1)(a), (b) and (d) as disclosing no reasonable claim and being frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process?
Should Mr. Grosz be declared a vexatious litigant under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act?
What terms should be imposed on any vexatious litigant order?

firac.issue: Should the claim against the Lawyer defendants and Mr. Mackey be dismissed under R. 9-6(5)(a) as raising no genuine issue for trial?
firac.facts: Grosz, a self-represented former paralegal, sued six lawyers and a proposal trustee arising out of his earlier employment dispute with Guo Law Corporation. His allegations against the lawyers were that Mr. Jones filed a false RCMP statement, attended court to pressure him, and breached solicitor-client privilege by attaching a medical report; that Mr. McLean informed a master his partner acted for the trustee; and that Mr. Brousson and Mr. Louman-Gardiner were part of an unparticularized conspiracy. The defendants filed affidavit evidence, notably Mr. Jones's, contradicting the allegations.
firac.rule: Under R. 9-6(5)(a) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules the court must dismiss a claim that raises no genuine issue for trial; unlike R. 9-5(1)(a) it permits consideration of evidence, though the judge does not weigh evidence but may draw inferences strongly supported by undisputed facts (Kerfoot v. Richter, 2018 BCCA 238). The applicant bears the evidentiary burden of showing there is no genuine issue to be tried.
firac.application: The court found the allegations against the lawyers were speculative or non-actionable: advising a master of who represented the trustee, appearing in court, and negotiating a settlement as opposing counsel raise no genuine issue, and counsel owe no duty to an adverse party. Mr. Jones's uncontradicted evidence established he had no contact with the RCMP before Grosz's detention, was in Kamloops on the alleged court date, and received the medical report outside any solicitor-client relationship. Grosz provided no evidence to support his assertions.
firac.conclusion: The claims against the Lawyer defendants and Mr. Mackey were dismissed under R. 9-6(5)(a) as raising no genuine issue for trial.

firac.issue: Should the pleadings be struck and the proceeding dismissed against all defendants under R. 9-5(1)(a), (b) and (d)?
firac.facts: The notice of civil claim repleaded and attached the notice of civil claim from the settled First Guo Action, made broad allegations of fraud, conspiracy, extortion, malicious prosecution and defamation against all defendants, and sought consolidation with prior proceedings. Grosz had settled the First Guo Action for $5,000 with a mutual release and consent dismissal order, and his application to set aside that order had been dismissed. He did not obtain leave to sue Mr. Munro, a licensed trustee.
firac.rule: R. 9-5(1) permits striking pleadings that (a) disclose no reasonable claim, (b) are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or (d) are otherwise an abuse of process. The test under (a) is whether it is plain and obvious the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42); conspiracy must be pleaded with heightened precision (Ontario Consumers Home Services, 2014 ONSC 4154); abuse of process protects judicial economy, consistency and finality (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63). Section 215 of the BIA bars actions against a trustee without leave of the court.
firac.application: The court held it plain and obvious the claims offended R. 9-5(1)(a), (b) and (d). The allegations were inflammatory, unparticularized and based on pure speculation; the claim against Mr. Munro required BIA leave that was never sought and disclosed no cause of action; and the action was an attempt to relitigate the settled First Guo Action and to disqualify or punish opposing counsel. Given the deficiencies, vexatious nature and improper purpose, amendment was refused.
firac.conclusion: The pleadings were struck and the proceeding dismissed against all defendants.

firac.issue: Should Mr. Grosz be declared a vexatious litigant under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act?
firac.facts: Grosz was party to approximately 17 proceedings and had sought to add himself to 19 others, had brought or threatened actions and complaints against numerous lawyers, law firms, the Law Society, judges, police, the trustee and various bodies, rolled forward allegations from earlier actions into new ones, sued opposing counsel to disqualify them, disregarded case-management orders, and overwhelmed registry staff.
firac.rule: Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 443 empowers the court to prohibit a person who has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds instituted vexatious legal proceedings from bringing further proceedings without leave. Key indicators are summarized in Rafique v. AWM-Alliance, 2019 BCSC 247 (citing Carten v. Carten) and Re Lang Michener and Fabian; the power must balance open court access against preventing abuse (Semenoff Estate v. Semenoff, 2017 BCCA 17). Vexatious litigant orders should be used only where other procedural techniques are ineffective (Jonsson v. Lymer, 2020 ABCA 167).
firac.application: The court found practically all indicators present: relitigating decided issues, rolling forward allegations, suing opposing lawyers to disqualify or punish them, bringing actions for improper purposes, and disregarding court directions. Case-management orders and cost sanctions had proven ineffective, and Grosz indicated he would appeal every order. His self-represented status and frustration did not excuse the conduct.
firac.conclusion: Grosz was declared a vexatious litigant under s. 18 and prohibited from instituting proceedings in the Supreme Court, or filing in proceedings where he is not a party, without leave.

firac.issue: What terms should be imposed on the vexatious litigant order?
firac.facts: The defendants sought broad additional terms: stays of the First Guo and Minoru Actions, a bar on all courts and statutory tribunals, a requirement that Grosz act only through counsel, and security for costs of leave applications. Grosz had consistently been granted indigent status.
firac.rule: A litigant may be restricted to filing through a solicitor (Household Trust Co. v. Golden Horse Farms, 1992 CanLII 420), but vexatious litigant orders are tolerable only because they perform a gatekeeping function and must not create insurmountable barriers to court access (Jonsson v. Lymer, 2020 ABCA 167). Absent express language such orders do not reach the filing of private informations (A.G.B.C. v. Lindsay, 2007 BCCA 165), and jurisdiction under s. 18 over other courts is doubtful (Parchment v. British Columbia, 2015 BCSC 1006).
firac.application: The court declined to stay the First Guo Action (already dismissed) or the Minoru Action (managed by another judge), refused to require counsel or security for costs as an insurmountable barrier to an indigent litigant, and limited the order to the BC Supreme Court, requiring leave only to institute proceedings or to file in proceedings where Grosz is not a party. Special costs were awarded given his reprehensible conduct, but lump-sum special costs were refused for lack of an evidentiary basis.
firac.conclusion: A narrowly tailored leave requirement confined to the BC Supreme Court was imposed, with special costs to the defendants.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing practice area — this is a civil action struck under the Supreme Court Civil Rules with a vexatious litigant declaration. K015 (defamation) applies because slander/libel/defamation were among the pleaded causes of action. K085 (wrongful dismissal) and K083 (harassment) are engaged indirectly through the underlying First Guo Action (unpaid wages, alleged sexual harassment, wrongful dismissal) which forms the factual matrix repleaded here — both are weak/borderline picks as this decision concerns the collateral action, not the merits of those claims. K013 (professional discipline / law society) is engaged because Grosz's threats to have lawyers disciplined by the Law Society and disqualification tactics were central to the vexatious-litigant analysis, though borderline. K054 (wills/estates) is not applicable and is excluded. The controlled vocabulary lacks direct terms for 'vexatious litigant', 'striking pleadings' or 'abuse of process', so the closest available terms were selected and the weak ones flagged. I have removed K054 as inapplicable.
location_rationale: The header states 'Registry: Vancouver' and 'Place and Date of Hearing: Vancouver, B.C.' and 'Place and Date of Judgment: Vancouver, B.C.', and the court is the Supreme Court of British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly lists 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Paramount Fine Foods et al. v. Johnston et al. [Indexed as: Paramount Fine Foods v. Johnston]

defining_issues: Did Banerjee's impugned expression relate to a matter of public interest so as to qualify for dismissal of the defamation action under s. 137.1(3) of the Courts of Justice Act (anti-SLAPP)?
Should the defamation action against Banerjee be dismissed under rule 21.01(3)(d) as frivolous, vexatious, or an abuse of process?

firac.issue: Did Banerjee's impugned expression relate to a matter of public interest so as to qualify for dismissal under s. 137.1(3) of the Courts of Justice Act?
firac.facts: During a protest outside Fakih's Paramount Fine Foods restaurant in Mississauga against the federal government's settlement of Omar Khadr's lawsuit, Banerjee, standing next to Johnston who was filming, said patrons had to be a 'jihadist' and had to have 'raped [their] wife at least a few times' to be allowed into the Muslim-owned restaurant. The 7.5-second clip formed part of eight videos widely distributed online. Banerjee argued his brief comments, viewed in the context of the whole protest, related to the Khadr settlement, a matter of public interest.
firac.rule: Section 137.1(3) CJA requires a judge to dismiss a proceeding if the moving party shows it arises from an expression relating to a matter of public interest. The judge acts as gatekeeper; the focus is on the substance of the expression as a whole, assessed objectively, not the occasion (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). Hate speech—expression that exposes a group to detestation and vilification bearing the 'hallmarks of hate'—is by its nature not in the public interest (Saskatchewan (HRC) v. Whatcott, 2013 SCC 11; Hudspeth v. Whatcott, 2017 ONSC 1708; R. v. Keegstra, 1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)).
firac.application: The court held it is the expression giving rise to the proceeding—Banerjee's statements about Paramount and Fakih—that must relate to a matter of public interest, not his mere participation in the protest. Reviewing all eight videos, the court found the early videos targeted the plaintiffs and communicated that they and their patrons were terrorists, criminals and part of a secret conspiracy because they were Muslims. Banerjee's comments went beyond offensive expression and bore the hallmarks of hate, inspiring extreme ill-will and delegitimizing the plaintiffs. Merely uttering something at a forum where public-interest matters are discussed does not make the expression itself of public interest; hate communication raises no public-interest subject matter regardless of its setting. Banerjee therefore failed to discharge his initial onus under s. 137.1(3).
firac.conclusion: The expression did not relate to a matter of public interest and was unworthy of protection; the s. 137.1 motion was dismissed. It was unnecessary to consider s. 137.1(4), though the court noted that analysis would have favoured the plaintiffs.

firac.issue: Should the defamation action against Banerjee be dismissed under rule 21.01(3)(d) as frivolous, vexatious, or an abuse of process?
firac.facts: Banerjee argued he was sued as a co-producer/co-publisher to punish him for past anti-Islamic conduct rather than for the 7.5-second remarks, pointing to the cross-examination focused on his past statements and to Fakih's comments about frustration with the defendants sowing discord.
firac.rule: Rule 21.01(3)(d) permits dismissal where a cause of action is clearly not bona fide, cannot succeed, or where no reasonable person could expect relief (Currie v. Halton (Region) Police Services Board, 2003 CanLII 7815 (ON CA)). Defamation sets a low prima facie threshold: a statement tending to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society (Sim v. Stretch; Vander Zalm v. Times Publishers; Gatley on Libel and Slander). Publication may arise from knowingly making statements to a recording camera, and joint tortfeasors may be liable for a common design (Crookes v. Wikimedia, 2011 SCC 47; Hill v. Church of Scientology, 1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)).
firac.application: The statement of claim clearly set out a prima facie case of defamation; Banerjee's comments were facially defamatory and directed at the plaintiffs. Publication was established because he knowingly made the statements to Johnston's camera, and it could reasonably be proven that he and Johnston acted as joint tortfeasors in a common design to injure the plaintiffs. The relevance of past-conduct evidence and Fakih's expressions of frustration fell far short of showing the suit was brought to harass, oppress or abuse Banerjee.
firac.conclusion: There was no merit to the rule 21.01(3)(d) motion; it was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a defamation tort action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action, engaging the low prima facie threshold and joint-tortfeasor/publication analysis. K061 (hate speech) is central: the court applied the Whatcott/Keegstra 'hallmarks of hate' framework to hold the expression unworthy of anti-SLAPP protection. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) reflect the balancing of expressive freedom against reputation that framed the s. 137.1 analysis. K063 (online hate/social media) fits the videos distributed via YouTube, Twitter and Freedomreport.ca. K065 (racism) captures the racist/anti-Muslim tropes the court identified. The anti-SLAPP s. 137.1 CJA provision has no dedicated vocabulary ID, so it is captured through the defamation and free-expression keywords. K065 is a slightly broad pick since the target was religious (Muslim) rather than strictly racial, but the court expressly described 'racist tropes.'
location_rationale: The decision identifies the court as the 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' but does not state the city where the court sits or its registry. The events occurred at the Mississauga location of the Paramount restaurant, but the sitting location of the court is not given, so city is left null; province is Ontario from the court name and the citation (ONSC).
registry_rationale: No registry or court office is named anywhere in the reported decision, so it is left null.

case_name: CUPW v. B’nai Brith Canada et. al

name_verification.name_in_document: CUPW v. B'nai Brith Canada et. al

defining_issues: Did the impugned press releases concern a matter of public interest so as to engage s. 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act?
Were there grounds to believe the defamation proceeding had substantial merit and that the defendants had no valid defence under s. 137.1(4)(a)?
Did the balancing under s. 137.1(4)(b) favour permitting the action to continue rather than dismissing it as a SLAPP?

firac.issue: Did the impugned press releases concern a matter of public interest so as to engage the anti-SLAPP provision in s. 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act?
firac.facts: B'nai Brith published press releases criticizing CUPW's affiliation with the Palestinian Postal Service Workers Union and CUPW's support of the BDS movement, accusing the union of aligning with terrorism and being motivated by antisemitism. These matters relate to union spending, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the BDS movement.
firac.rule: Section 137.1(3) of the Courts of Justice Act permits dismissal where the expression relates to a matter of public interest; 1704604 Ontario Ltd. v. Pointes Protection Association, 2018 ONCA 685, establishes a screening process, not a bar to all actions.
firac.application: The court accepted that the use of union funds for political causes, positions on the Middle East conflict, and support of organizations that might support attacks on Israel are matters of public interest, and legitimate criticism would be protected speech.
firac.conclusion: The expression concerned a matter of public interest, so s. 137.1 was engaged and the burden shifted to the analysis under s. 137.1(4).

firac.issue: Were there grounds to believe the defamation proceeding had substantial merit and that the moving parties had no valid defence?
firac.facts: The press releases stated CUPW aligned with 'the path of violence and extremism' and partnered with a 'terror-supporting organization,' branding its leadership as radical and antisemitic. CUPW pointed to its published policies opposing terrorism, violence and antisemitism and supporting a peaceful two-state solution, and argued B'nai Brith's conclusions rested on a cursory internet/Facebook search.
firac.rule: Section 137.1(4)(a) requires the responding party to show grounds to believe the proceeding has substantial merit and the moving party has no valid defence; Lascaris v. B'nai Brith Canada, 2019 ONCA 163, interprets this to mean a reasonable trier could conclude the pleaded defences would fail. Defamation elements are drawn from Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61, and malice principles from Hill v. Church of Scientology, 1995 CanLII 59 (SCC).
firac.application: The three defamation elements were easily met: the words were published, referred to CUPW by name, and would lower the union's reputation. The court found serious flaws in the defences of truth, justification, fair comment and responsible communication, noting evidence that PPSWU did not officially support terrorism, that B'nai Brith ignored CUPW's own policies, exercised little due diligence, and that malice could be inferred from the branding of the leadership as antisemitic and the prior history of litigation.
firac.conclusion: There were grounds to believe the action had substantial merit and that the defences were not certain to succeed, so the action could not be dismissed on this basis.

firac.issue: Did the public-interest balancing under s. 137.1(4)(b) favour allowing the action to continue?
firac.facts: CUPW alleged the press releases were designed to create dissension among its membership and disrupt its operations, causing serious harm; B'nai Brith contended the suit was an illegitimate attempt to suppress public-interest expression.
firac.rule: Section 137.1(4)(b) requires that the harm to the responding party be sufficiently serious that the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue outweighs the public interest in protecting the expression; the legislation targets litigation of doubtful merit brought to stifle debate.
firac.application: The court found the defamation action appeared meritorious and that CUPW's principal objective was not to stifle criticism. The harm—suggesting a union misuses dues, supports terrorism and is racist—was serious, and this was a legitimate action rather than the doubtful-merit litigation the statute was meant to weed out.
firac.conclusion: The balancing favoured allowing the action to continue; the anti-SLAPP motion was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: The case is a civil defamation matter, so K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area and K015 (defamation) is the core doctrine. The court analysed the defences of fair comment (K016) and responsible communication (K019), and the anti-SLAPP framework turns on freedom of expression (K024). The dispute arose from CUPW's support of the BDS movement (K059 boycott) and its alleged anti-Israel/anti-Zionist stance (K056), with B'nai Brith accusing the union of antisemitism (K058) and links to terrorism (K037). Entity keywords capture B'nai Brith (K089) and Israel (K103). Palestine (K104) was considered but omitted to stay within limits, though the PPSWU connection makes it a borderline candidate; anti-Zionism (K056) is slightly indirect but reflects the BDS/anti-Israel framing central to the accusations.
