name_verification.name_in_document: Rosenberg c. Lacerte

defining_issues: Did the defendant's blog posts, newspaper articles, caricatures and photomontages constitute a fault amounting to defamation of the plaintiffs under art. 1457 C.c.Q. and the Quebec Charter?
Did the material infringe the plaintiffs' right to privacy or amount to harassment based on religion?
Did the plaintiffs prove concrete injury to their reputation and a causal link with the defendant's conduct?
Should the court grant a final injunction ordering removal of all posts concerning the plaintiffs and imposing prior judicial screening of future posts?
Was the plaintiffs' action an abusive SLAPP suit (poursuite-bâillon) under arts. 54.1 ff. C.p.c., entitling the defendant to damages and a provision for costs?

firac.issue: Did the defendant commit a fault amounting to defamation of the plaintiffs?
firac.facts: Lacerte ran a blog denouncing alleged religious accommodations granted by Outremont authorities to the Hasidic community, targeting among others Michael and Martin Rosenberg and Alex Werzberger — leaders/spokespersons of that community who sat on municipal committees. Over five years he published 314 columns (plus caricatures, photomontages, hyperlinks and newspaper articles) on parking violations, illegal synagogue renovations, buses, Hasidic schools, a New York trip financed in part by Rosenberg, and removal petitions against Rosenberg and Werzberger.
firac.rule: Defamation is civil liability under art. 1457 C.c.Q.: fault, injury and causation (Prud'homme). Fault is assessed against the reasonable-person standard and may be malicious or merely negligent (St-Ferdinand; Bou Malhab). True facts and honest opinion on matters of public interest are generally not faulty; public figures must tolerate greater criticism (WIC Radio; Torstar; Société Saint-Jean-Baptiste). Words are read in their full context.
firac.application: The court reviewed each theme. The facts diffused (parking infractions, unpermitted renovations supervised by the Rosenbergs, unauthorized buses, the New York trip) were true and diligently gathered from observation and government/media sources; the epithets ('nabab', 'intégriste', 'lobbyiste', 'théocrate', 'secte') were, in context, non-defamatory commentary or opinion. The plaintiffs were public figures engaged in public-interest debates (religious accommodation, municipal governance, removal petitions), so an ordinary citizen aware of the context would not find their reputation discredited, and a reasonable person would not view publication as faulty.
firac.conclusion: No fault proven; the impugned material did not defame the plaintiffs.

firac.issue: Did the material infringe privacy or constitute religious harassment?
firac.facts: Plaintiffs complained of photos taken of them and their vehicles, references to their religious dress, and a five-year 'fixation'; they alleged harassment based on their religion.
firac.rule: Arts. 35–36 C.c.Q. and ss. 5, 10.1 Quebec Charter; photos taken in public with rational surveillance grounds, or of persons not the principal subject, may be published (Aubry; Bridgestone). Harassment requires objective gravity.
firac.application: Photos were taken from the defendant's home or street, served to document infractions relevant to public-interest debate, and were not obtained in breach of privacy. References to Hasidic dress were not hateful and could not be both claimed and shielded. Judge Ouimet had already found no criminal harassment; on the same balance-of-probabilities standard that finding had res judicata effect, and the abundance of columns did not constitute harassment given the plaintiffs' own provocation.
firac.conclusion: No breach of privacy and no religious harassment or discrimination established.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiffs prove injury to reputation and causation?
firac.facts: Plaintiffs testified to frustration, stress and feared social consequences; a monitor (Delisle) and banker/community witnesses announced did not testify. Rosenberg remained on the committee over two years and Werzberger continued as spokesperson.
firac.rule: The victim must prove concrete injury by the ordinary-citizen standard plus proof of actual dissemination and its penetration in the milieu (Bou Malhab; Fabien; Lapierre); mere posting online raises no presumption of harm; hearsay is inadmissible.
firac.application: No third party testified to a diminished esteem; evidence was hearsay and general. Rosenberg's fears (lost contracts, difficulty marrying his daughter) were unsupported and undermined his credibility. Any harm would more plausibly flow from media reports the defendant merely linked. Testimony showed annoyance, not a proven attack on reputation or dignity, and no proof of extent of dissemination.
firac.conclusion: No injury or causation proven; the damages claim would fail even had a fault been found.

firac.issue: Should a final injunction removing all posts and imposing prior judicial screening be granted?
firac.facts: Plaintiffs sought removal from the blog of everything concerning them and an order requiring court permission before future posts.
firac.rule: Injunctions restraining expression are exceptional; only precise defamatory statements may be enjoined, requiring appearance of right, irreparable harm and a favourable balance of convenience (Prud'homme c. Rawdon; Ward c. Labelle).
firac.application: Having found no defamation, there was no basis; moreover the sweeping relief sought resembled censorship or a prior restraint (bâillon) with no precedent.
firac.conclusion: Injunction refused.

firac.issue: Was the action an abusive SLAPP entitling the defendant to relief?
firac.facts: Plaintiffs escalated from a $100,000 demand letter, to criminal complaints offered to be withdrawn if the blog closed, to a $375,000 civil action seeking removal of posts and judicial screening.
firac.rule: Arts. 6, 7, 1457 C.c.Q. and arts. 54.1 ff. C.p.c.; a SLAPP is a suit designed to limit public participation; rejection requires conduct so abusive as to show bad faith or a diversion of justice; an excessive quantum and disparity of means are mere indicia (Acadia Subaru; Dalla Riva).
firac.application: Although the escalating strategy gave the suit the appearance of a SLAPP and the plaintiffs clearly wished to silence the blog, the pleadings raised genuine, arguable questions that had to be decided on the merits; the plaintiffs' limited French and reliance on out-of-context translations made recourse to a court understandable. Losing on the merits does not make the action abusive. The defendant also failed to prove causation for lost jobs, lacked standing for family damages, and did not meet the Little Sisters test for a provision for costs.
firac.conclusion: Cross-demand dismissed; action not declared abusive and no damages or provision for costs awarded.

keywords_rationale: The case is a civil defamation action, so K002 (Civil litigation, tier-1 practice area) and K015 (defamation) are central. K024 (freedom of expression) is the countervailing right that decided the case, and the court weighed the collective/individual dimension of the posts, engaging K017 (group defamation) via the heavy reliance on Bou Malhab. K021 (injunction) covers the sought final injunction/prior-restraint relief. K031 (religious accommodation) reflects the very subject of the blog ('accommodements'). K120 (Quebec Charter) is the statutory source of the rights invoked (ss. 4, 5, 10.1, 49). K097 (Orthodox/Hasidic community) and K094 (Jewish community) identify the group at the centre of the dispute. Borderline picks: K017 (plaintiffs framed harm personally, though collectivity analysis featured) and K094 (overlaps with K097).
location_rationale: The header states «COUR SUPÉRIEURE», «DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL», file no. 500-17-045603-084, situating the court in Montréal, Quebec.
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the «DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL» as the judicial district/registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: Lisa Ellen Libbus v. William Francis Libbus

defining_issues: In deciding which school the children should attend, what does the best interests of the children require given the parents' shared goal of raising them in the Jewish faith?
Was the mother required to demonstrate a material change in circumstances under the Gordon v. Goertz framework before the schooling/residential arrangement could be revisited?
How should the expert opinion evidence on the development of Jewish identity be treated?

firac.issue: What do the best interests of Abby and Ben require regarding choice of school, given both parents' agreement to raise them as Jews?
firac.facts: Both parents, though the father is Roman Catholic and the mother Jewish, agreed to raise the two children (ages 8 and 7) in the Jewish faith. The children attended Uxbridge Public School (UPS) in a rural community with no other Jewish families or Jewish classmates, while the mother had moved to Thornhill, a heavily Jewish area, and sought to enrol them at Woodland Public School (WPS). Both parents were found to be excellent parents; the only unresolved issue was schooling.
firac.rule: Section 16(8) of the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.) requires the court to consider only the best interests of the child by reference to the child's condition, means, needs and other circumstances. The court also had regard to the non-exhaustive factors in s. 24(2) of the Children's Law Reform Act, weighing no single factor as determinative. The standard is what is 'best' for the children, not merely good or better.
firac.application: The court accepted expert evidence that fostering Jewish religious, cultural and ethnic identity depends heavily on peer groups and a supportive wider community, not just parental effort. Remaining at UPS, without a Jewish peer group or community, would likely leave the children conflicted about their identity as they aged, notwithstanding the parents' efforts. Thornhill/WPS (also a French immersion school) offered a critical mass of Jewish community life. The father's plan was 'good' but the mother's plan best served the identity goal both parents shared, while the children's stability could be preserved through continued substantial contact with the father and grandmother.
firac.conclusion: The court held it was in the best interests of Abby and Ben to attend Woodland Public School in Thornhill beginning September 2008.

firac.issue: Was the mother required to prove a material change in circumstances under Gordon v. Goertz before the arrangement could be reviewed?
firac.facts: The parties were governed by a 2005 'store-bought' separation agreement providing joint custody, shared residency and a mobility clause requiring residence within a 20-minute radius of Uxbridge, with a review mechanism. The mother's proposed move to Thornhill was roughly a 10-minute drive beyond that radius. The father argued she had to meet the Gordon v. Goertz threshold of a material change.
firac.rule: Under Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27 and Young v. Young (2003), a two-stage test applies where a court order is being varied: first a material change not reasonably foreseen, then a fresh best-interests inquiry. Review clauses (per Baggs v. Baggs, Choquette, Leskun) allow reconsideration without proving material change.
firac.application: The court held the parties were bound by a separation agreement, not a court order requiring variation under s. 17 of the Divorce Act, so no threshold onus applied; the 2005 agreement itself provided for review. The distance involved was de minimis and the mobility cases relied upon by the father were fact-specific and distinguishable. In any event, the emerging issue of the children's religious and ethnic identity as they grew older was not contemplated when the 2005 agreement was signed, so a material change would have been made out.
firac.conclusion: No threshold onus of proving material change applied; the analysis proceeded directly to the best interests of the children.

firac.issue: How should the court treat the expert opinion evidence on the development of Jewish identity?
firac.facts: The mother called Dr. Karen Mock (educational psychologist) and Dr. Randall Schnoor (sociologist of Jewish life). The father's counsel conceded their qualifications but attacked their opinions as biased and as usurping the trial judge's function.
firac.rule: Expert evidence must be relevant and necessary to assist the trier of fact. Section 30 of the Children's Law Reform Act legislatively recognizes the use of experts in custody-related matters. An expert may not opine on the ultimate issue reserved to the court.
firac.application: The court found the experts qualified and their evidence necessary because the judge had no independent knowledge of how Jewish identity is fostered. Allegations of bias (reviewing only the mother's affidavits, not interviewing the parties) were rejected because this was not a custody assessment and the central opinion — that peer groups and community are pivotal to maintaining identity — was unshaken on cross-examination. Dr. Mock's view that relocation served the identity goal did not usurp the court's role, since the ultimate decision on school choice remained the judge's alone.
firac.conclusion: The expert evidence was admitted and given weight; it materially supported the conclusion that a change of school was in the children's best interests.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test under s. 16(8) of the Divorce Act and the central rule. case_name: Adam (Family of) Davidson v. Cummer Avenue United Church et al.

name_verification.name_in_document: Adam (Family of) Davidson v. Cummer Avenue United Church et al.

defining_issues: Did CAUC, as occupier, owe and breach a duty of care under the Occupiers' Liability Act to the plaintiff?
Were Ms. Seepaul and CAUC negligent — did they owe a duty of care, breach the applicable standard of care, and cause the plaintiff's injuries?
Is the plaintiff entitled to damages (including for mental distress and aggravated damages) and in what amount?
Was the plaintiff contributorily negligent for the assault?

firac.issue: Did CAUC, as occupier of the drop-in centre, owe and breach a duty of care under the Occupiers' Liability Act?
firac.facts: CAUC operated a weekly drop-in centre for vulnerable adults. On October 21, 2015, the plaintiff, a user of the centre, reported antisemitic abuse by a guest named Joe to the program director, Ms. Seepaul, who invited the plaintiff to walk with her toward Joe. Joe then assaulted the plaintiff. The defendants argued the assault was an unforeseeable act of a third party.
firac.rule: Section 3(1) of the Occupiers' Liability Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.2 requires an occupier to take such care as is reasonable in the circumstances to see that persons entering the premises are reasonably safe; the standard is not perfection (Waldick v. Malcolm, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 456; Kerr v. Loblaws, 2007 ONCA 371). Liability is fact-specific, and where a debate arises as to reasonable conduct recourse to expert evidence is appropriate.
firac.application: The court distinguished Coleiro and Omotayo (no duty where injury flows from an unpredictable third-party act with no proximity created by the occupier), finding that here Ms. Seepaul created the proximity between the plaintiff and Joe by inviting the plaintiff to accompany her. The defendants' own expert established a six-element standard of care for a small drop-in centre, endorsed by the plaintiff's expert. On the direct evidence heard, CAUC failed to meet at least two elements: assigning staff/volunteers to supervise the space (#2) and maintaining a meaningful anti-harassment policy that employees felt bound by (#6), and training of employees (#5) was insufficient. Not having cameras or security guards was not a breach.
firac.conclusion: CAUC breached the standard of care and is liable under the Occupiers' Liability Act.

firac.issue: Were Ms. Seepaul and CAUC negligent in duty, standard of care, and causation?
firac.facts: Ms. Seepaul, holding an MSW and crisis-intervention training, invited the plaintiff to accompany her toward Joe without instructing him to stay back or separating the parties, and CAUC had not trained her to handle a discrimination complaint despite adopting an anti-harassment policy in February 2014.
firac.rule: Negligence requires a duty of care, breach of the applicable standard, damage, and causation (Canadian Tort Law, 12th ed.). The standard is that of a reasonable and prudent director/operator (Krawchuk v. Scherbak, 2011 ONCA 352); expert evidence generally informs the standard but is not always required.
firac.application: A duty was owed to the plaintiff as a service user injured on the premises while denouncing discrimination. Both experts and the anti-harassment policy confirmed that de-escalation requires separating disputing parties. Ms. Seepaul breached the standard by leading the plaintiff to confront Joe rather than keeping them apart; CAUC breached by failing to train her to manage a discrimination complaint. The foreseeable reaction of an accused person materialized and caused the plaintiff's non-remote injuries.
firac.conclusion: Both Ms. Seepaul and CAUC were negligent and their breaches caused the plaintiff's injuries.

firac.issue: Is the plaintiff entitled to damages, including mental distress and aggravated damages, and in what amount?
firac.facts: The plaintiff was sucker-punched, fell, hurt his back and head, attended hospital (released with ice and Tylenol), and suffered significant anxiety, aggravated by being on the Autism spectrum. He never returned to CAUC — a place where he had socialized, eaten and obtained haircuts — and was banned for one month.
firac.rule: Expert evidence is not required to prove compensable mental distress, but the distress must be more than mere inconvenience and must impair one's ability to carry on daily life (Saadati v. Moorhead, 2017 SCC 28; Bothwell v. London Health Sciences Centre, 2023 ONCA 323). Aggravated damages compensate additional harm to the plaintiff's dignity.
firac.application: Unlike Bothwell, the plaintiff established impairment of his daily activities: he could no longer attend CAUC, which had been part of his routine. He was humiliated by the one-month ban he considered unjust, contrary to the policy's protection of good-faith complainants, warranting aggravated damages.
firac.conclusion: Damages of $7,500 awarded: $2,500 for the assault/physical injuries, $2,500 for mental distress, and $2,500 aggravated damages.

firac.issue: Was the plaintiff contributorily negligent for the assault?
firac.facts: The defendants claimed the plaintiff was 75% responsible because he raised his voice and pointed his finger at Joe, provoking the assault.
firac.rule: Contributory negligence requires that a reasonable person in the plaintiff's circumstances would have acted differently or foreseen the harm.
firac.application: The court found the breach flowed from the defendants placing the plaintiff in proximity to Joe without caution or instruction; the plaintiff did not strike Joe, merely raised his finger while voicing concerns, and did not know what was expected of him. If he was agitated, that made it more incumbent on the defendants to caution him.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiff was not contributorily negligent.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 anchor — the case is a tort/occupiers'-liability and negligence claim. K057 (antisemitic slurs) and K058 (antisemitism) capture Joe's abuse ("filthy Jews", telling the couple to go back to Russia) that triggered the events. K093 (Jewish) reflects the plaintiff's Jewish descent and the discriminatory conduct denounced. K072 (human rights tribunal) reflects the earlier HRT complaint the plaintiff had brought and which was dismissed, discussed in the facts. K059 (boycott) reflects the plaintiff's BDS-related allegation against the United Church, though weak since no evidence supported it. K083 (harassment) reflects the anti-harassment policy central to the standard-of-care analysis. K069 (discrimination) reflects the discrimination complaint the plaintiff was denouncing. K059 and K069 are the more borderline picks, included because they frame the factual context though the ratio turns on tort principles.
location_rationale: The header identifies the Ontario Superior Court of Justice. The city is not printed in the header, but the venue is inferable from the Toronto locus of the events and institutions referenced — the Cummer Avenue United Church drop-in centre, the Toronto Drop-in Network (TDIN), Toronto North Support Services, and the Toronto Conference of the United Church.
registry_rationale: No registry is expressly stated. Given the Toronto locus of the parties and events and the ONSC file no. 17-583951, the Toronto registry is the reasonable inference; treated as inferential rather than expressly stated.

case_name: Ross v. Board of School Trustees, District No. 15

name_verification.name_in_document: Attis c. Board of Education of District 15 et al.
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The decision's printed style of cause is 'Attis c. Board of Education of District 15 et al.' (with Court File 27/92/CA), naming the complainant Attis first, whereas the supplied name is 'Ross v. Board of School Trustees, District No. 15,' which puts the appellant teacher first and renames the school authority. The neutral citation 1993 CanLII 5613 (NBCA) does not appear in the text (only the court file number is given). The two refer to the same proceeding but the party naming/order and body designation differ.

defining_issues: Did the board of inquiry's order removing Malcolm Ross from teaching (leave of absence, redeployment to a non-teaching post, and eventual termination) infringe his Charter s. 2(a) and 2(b) freedoms of religion and expression?
If the classroom-removal order infringed those freedoms, was it a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
Should the 'gag order' (s. 2(d)), which would trigger dismissal if Ross published anti-Jewish material, be reinstated as a justified limit under s. 1?

firac.issue: Did the board of inquiry's order removing Ross from teaching infringe his Charter s. 2(a) and 2(b) freedoms?
firac.facts: A human rights board of inquiry found the school board had discriminated contrary to s. 5(1) of the Human Rights Act by failing to meaningfully discipline Ross, whose off-duty anti-Jewish writings and public statements created a poisoned educational environment. The board ordered Ross placed on leave, offered a non-teaching position, and terminated if none was accepted. Ross sincerely held and publicly expressed his views; there was no evidence of classroom proselytizing.
firac.rule: Section 2 of the Charter guarantees freedom of conscience and religion (2(a)) and freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression (2(b)). A state-imposed sanction that penalizes an individual for publicly expressing sincerely held views engages these freedoms.
firac.application: The Court agreed with Creaghan J. that penalizing Ross by ending his teaching career for publicly expressing his sincerely held (though discriminatory) views offended his s. 2(a) and 2(b) rights; the infringement was not in dispute.
firac.conclusion: The classroom-removal order (s. 2(a),(b),(c)) infringed Ross's s. 2(a) and 2(b) Charter freedoms.

firac.issue: Was the classroom-removal order a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1?
firac.facts: The board found no evidence of any direct classroom activity by Ross and no connection between his expressed views and anti-Jewish remarks made by children in another school's playground. Ross never used his classroom or school property to further his views, and the school board had not acquiesced. His status as teacher and role model was central to the board's rationale.
firac.rule: Under R. v. Oakes and R. v. Zundel, a limit on a Charter freedom requires a purpose 'so pressing and substantial as to be capable of overriding the Charter's guarantees,' and the limiting measure must satisfy proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportional effect). Denial of freedom of expression should occur only in the clearest of cases.
firac.application: The majority held that, on the evidence, silencing Ross's off-duty views to prevent a public perception of condonation was not so pressing and substantial as to override his freedom of expression. The links to actual harm (playground remarks at another school) were too tenuous; Ross had not used his position to spread his views. Upholding the sanction would risk condoning suppression of unpopular views (the 'slippery slope' noted in Keegstra), and the case did not meet the clearest-of-cases test.
firac.conclusion: The order was not justified under s. 1; s. 2(a),(b) and (c) could not be saved and were quashed.

firac.issue: Should the publication ban ('gag order') in s. 2(d) be reinstated?
firac.facts: Creaghan J. had quashed s. 2(d), which would trigger immediate dismissal if Ross published or distributed specified anti-Jewish works, as an unjustified violation of s. 2 that failed proportionality. Attis, the Human Rights Commission and the Canadian Jewish Congress cross-appealed to reinstate it.
firac.rule: Same Oakes/Zundel s. 1 framework; a limit on expression must be demonstrably justified and proportionate.
firac.application: Having concluded that even the lesser classroom-removal restriction failed the s. 1 test, the majority necessarily found the broader publication ban unjustified. Ryan J.A., dissenting, would have reinstated it, reasoning that a teacher-role-model's off-duty promotion of discrimination could be restrained and that the ban was minimally impairing given the pervasiveness of modern communication.
firac.conclusion: Cross-appeals dismissed; the gag order was not reinstated (Ryan J.A. dissenting).

keywords_rationale: The appeal turned on the Charter, so Constitutional law (K003) is the tier-1 anchor, with freedom of expression (K024) and freedom of religion (K025) as the engaged freedoms and reasonable limits (s. 1)/Oakes (K030) as the dispositive analytical framework; Charter s. 2(b) (K111) and s. 2(a) (K110) are the specific provisions. Human rights (K007) is included because the underlying order arose under the New Brunswick Human Rights Act, with discrimination (K069) and the human rights board of inquiry (K072, tribunal) directly engaged. Teacher misconduct/off-duty conduct as a role model (K046) is central to the sanction. The complaint concerned anti-Jewish (antisemitism, K058) conduct affecting Jewish students (K096). K058 and K096 are contextually strong; K046 sits at the education/labour boundary but reflects the core dispute over disciplining a teacher for off-duty expression. I omitted hate-speech IDs because the case was decided on Human Rights Act discrimination, not hate-propaganda offences.
location_rationale: The header identifies the court as the 'New Brunswick Court of Appeal' and the coram (Hoyt C.J.N.B., Angers and Ryan JJ.A.), so the province is New Brunswick. No city is stated in the text; the appeal is from the Court of Queen's Bench, but the appellate registry/sitting location is not specified, so city is left null.

case_name: HSCAS v. M.S., C.D.S., and C.A.D.

name_verification.name_in_document: Highland Shores Children's Aid Society v. M.N.S., C.D.P., and C.A.D. (cited as "HSCAS v. M.S., C.D.S., and C.A.D.")
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied case name and citation match the citation line printed on the decision ("HSCAS v. M.S., C.D.S., and C.A.D., 2026 ONSC 3038"). There is, however, an internal inconsistency within the document: the citation line uses the initials M.S. and C.D.S., while the style of cause names the respondents as M.N.S. (the Mother) and C.D.P. (T.'s Father). This is a discrepancy internal to the judgment and does not affect consistency with the supplied metadata.

defining_issues: Was the mother entitled to any Charter remedy on her constitutional challenge alleging breaches of ss. 2(b), 7 and 15, and does the Court have jurisdiction to restrain her internet activity?
Were the disputed video and audio recordings (the Ring camera videos, the mother's video of H., and the 40 hours of access-visit audio) admissible?
Are the two children in need of protection under ss. 74(2)(b)(i),(ii) and 74(2)(h) of the CYFSA?
What disposition is in the children's best interests — a supervision order or final custody orders to the fathers under s. 102 of the CYFSA?
Should the mother's access be terminated or continued on a supervised basis, and should restrictions be placed on future litigation?

firac.issue: Was the mother entitled to a Charter remedy for alleged breaches of her freedom of expression (s. 2(b)), security of the person (s. 7) and equality (s. 15) rights, and did the Court have jurisdiction to restrain her internet activity?
firac.facts: The mother served a Notice of Constitutional Question challenging ss. 74, 87 and Part X of the CYFSA and the Child Protection Standards. She complained her social media had been improperly restricted, that disclosure was inadequate and the removal unlawful, and that the Society discriminated against her mental/physical health. She had been subject to McCarty J.'s June 5, 2025 consent order barring posting about the case, which she breached mid-trial by posting about a testifying psychologist and witness F.
firac.rule: Section 24(1) of the Charter permits a remedy for infringed rights; s. 52(1) Constitution Act, 1982 renders inconsistent laws of no force. The open court principle is protected by s. 2(b) but discretionary publication limits may be imposed where openness poses a serious risk to an important interest, no reasonable alternative exists, and benefits outweigh negative effects (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25). Courts may regulate a parent's internet activity and order removal of offensive material under ss. 87(8), 94, 101, 102 and 104 CYFSA and ss. 28 and 35 CLRA (B.M. v. J.G., 2025 ONCJ 72; Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. N.E., 2023 ONCJ 156). Section 7 rights are engaged in child protection but not necessarily deprived contrary to fundamental justice (New Brunswick v. G.(J.), 1999; Winnipeg Child and Family Services v. K.L.W., 2000 SCC 48). Consideration of a parent's mental health focused on impact on children does not breach s. 15.
firac.application: The Court found most of the mother's complaints did not require the Charter at all — they were requests for factual findings. The disclosure complaint failed on the evidence: the mother received full party disclosure throughout, only more heavily redacted duplicates under Part X. The removal was warrant-based, followed by prompt hearings at which the mother was represented; s. 7 was engaged but not violated. Considering the mother's mental health in relation to the children's welfare was not discrimination under s. 15. Applying Sherman Estate, non-publication and removal orders were necessary to protect the children, witnesses and the integrity of the trial, with no reasonable alternative given the mother's repeated, defiant breaches.
firac.conclusion: The constitutional challenge was dismissed in full as devoid of merit; no Charter remedy was warranted, and the Court confirmed jurisdiction to restrain the mother's internet activity.

firac.issue: Were the disputed recordings admissible?
firac.facts: The Society sought to admit two Ring camera videos recorded by the mother's brother's partner F. showing the mother striking, shaking and throwing T. during a school morning. The mother sought to admit a video (Exhibit B) of H. stating his father hit his penis, and roughly 40 hours of audio she recorded at supervised access visits.
firac.rule: The party tendering a recording bears the onus of proving admissibility (Hameed v. Hameed). Recordings must be authenticated — accurately depicting acts, verified by the recorder, without intent to mislead (Rodger v. Strop; Webster v. Suteu). Secret recordings are presumptively inadmissible as their prejudice outweighs probative value unless serious misconduct, risk to a child, or another compelling interest is shown (Van Ruyven v. Van Ruyven, 2021 ONSC 5963); recordings evidencing family violence may be admitted (T.I. v. C.B., 2025 ONCJ 392; F.(A.) v. A.(B.J.), 2017 ONCJ 108).
firac.application: The Ring videos were authenticated by F., were not illegally or surreptitiously obtained, were made to show the mother her own conduct, and were highly probative of family violence and the mother's parenting, corroborating extensive other evidence. The gaps in the footage did not defeat admissibility. Exhibit B was admitted only as evidence of the mother coaching H., not for the truth of its contents, given serious authenticity and public-policy concerns. The 40 hours of access audio were excluded on policy grounds, as evidence-gathering at visits should be discouraged and the mother sought to have the Court simply review them wholesale.
firac.conclusion: The Ring videos were admitted (re-marked Exhibit 122); the mother's video of H. was admitted only as proof of coaching (re-marked Exhibit 123); the 40 hours of access audio were ruled inadmissible.

firac.issue: Are the children in need of protection under ss. 74(2)(b)(i),(ii) and 74(2)(h) of the CYFSA?
firac.facts: The children T. (9) and H. (5) were exposed to extreme parental conflict and family violence, the mother's physical discipline (captured on video), her coaching of H. to make false sexual abuse allegations, neglect of T.'s education (129 absences, 223 lates), mismanagement of the children's health care, incessant lawsuits/complaints against those in the children's lives, harmful internet conduct, and the mother's untreated Borderline Personality Disorder and ADHD.
firac.rule: Under s. 74(2)(b) the risk of physical harm must be real and likely (more probable than not) with a causal connection to parental conduct; family violence, inappropriate discipline and untreated mental illness are recognized bases (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. R.M., 2019 ONSC 2251). Under s. 74(2)(h) the risk of emotional harm of the kind in (f) must be shown on a balance of probabilities; expert evidence is not required (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. N.N., 2019 ONCJ 8). Courts may consider evidence up to the date of trial (Children's Aid Society of Brant v. T.(J.A.), 2005 ONCJ 302).
firac.application: The Court found an overwhelming and multi-faceted record of risk: exposure to family violence, an assault of T. on video, coached false sexual abuse allegations subjecting H. to unnecessary examinations, educational neglect impacting T., health-care mismanagement, and the mother's untreated BPD with no insight and no continuity of treatment. The mother's claim of rehabilitation through post-2023 medication and therapy was found not credible. The protection concerns persisted at trial and had not resolved except through the removal itself.
firac.conclusion: Both children were found in need of protection under ss. 74(2)(b)(i),(ii) and 74(2)(h).

firac.issue: What disposition is in the children's best interests — a supervision order or final custody orders to the fathers under s. 102?
firac.facts: The Society, both fathers and the OCL sought final s. 102 custody orders placing each child with his respective father, pointing to marked improvements since removal. The mother sought return of the children or, alternatively, expanded supervised access. T. is a First Nations, Inuit and Métis child through his father.
firac.rule: Section 101(1) sets disposition options where intervention is necessary; s. 102(1) permits a custody order to a non-foster parent, with consent, where it is in the child's best interests. The best interests test is in s. 74(3) CYFSA, and for T. the augmented best interests test under ss. 10 and 16 of An Act respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families (S.C. 2019, c. 24) applies, with a s. 16(1) placement priority. A supervision order is limited to 12 months. Where a s. 102 order varies an existing final CLRA order, a material change in circumstances must be shown (Children's Aid Society of London and Middlesex v. S.A.R., 2015 ONSC 2534).
firac.application: A supervision order with the mother was not viable — her required treatment exceeded 12 months, she lacked insight, refused treatment, and would not work with the Society. Both fathers had strong plans, the children had improved, and T.'s placement preserved his Indigenous heritage. A custody order was preferred over supervision to end the litigation the children had endured (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. A.M., 2024 ONCJ 607). The material change threshold was met given the accumulated events since the prior CLRA orders.
firac.conclusion: Final s. 102 custody orders were made placing each child with his respective father, with specific terms and continued Society involvement for T.'s father to set up services.

firac.issue: Should the mother's access be terminated or continued on a supervised basis, and should future litigation be restricted?
firac.facts: The mother's supervised visits had significant problems (passive engagement, interrogation of children, inappropriate conversations, missed and late visits), and a pre-trial community visit and a post-trial visit generated conflict and police calls. No party sought termination. The children expressed missing their mother; some positive visit evidence existed. The mother had launched a barrage of lawsuits and complaints against those in the children's sphere.
firac.rule: Access is governed by s. 104 CYFSA; under s. 105(2) an access order must be made unless continued contact is not in the children's best interests. Supervised access is generally not a long-term solution and termination must be considered where supervision proves unworkable (V.S.J. v. L.J.G., 2004 CanLII 17126; M.(B.P.) v. M.(B.L.D.E.)). Courts may impose conduct and restraining orders (ss. 28 and 35 CLRA via s. 102 CYFSA) and, through rules 1(6), 14(21) and 15(27) of the Family Law Rules, restrict future motions.
firac.application: The Court seriously considered terminating access but balanced the risks against the children's interest in maintaining some relationship and the fact that no party sought termination. Only tightly controlled, monthly supervised access at access centres was found workable; community and family-supervised access were rejected as unworkable. A restraining order was granted for H.'s father, conduct orders restricting internet use and communication were imposed, disclosure of the children's records to the mother was constrained, and a two-year moratorium with a leave requirement on future motions to change was ordered.
firac.conclusion: The mother's access was continued only on a strictly supervised basis at access centres; a restraining order, conduct orders, and a two-year moratorium (with leave screening) on motions to change were imposed. The mother's post-trial 14B motion was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally a child protection proceeding, so K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area, with K047 (best interests of the child) central to the s. 74(3)/Federal Act analysis and K048 (custody/access) engaged by the s. 102 custody orders and supervised access determination. The mother's Notice of Constitutional Question makes K003 (Constitutional law) genuinely engaged, and the specific Charter provisions litigated support K024 (freedom of expression), K111 (Charter s. 2(b)), K112 (Charter s. 7) and K109 (Charter s. 15), with K107 (Canadian Charter) as the umbrella statute. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward a specialized collection with no bearing here, so I omitted those. Borderline picks I declined: religious upbringing (K052) arose only as a minor best-interests factor (Muslim/Catholic upbringing), and online hate/social media (K063) is framed around hate speech rather than the mother's family-law social media misuse, so neither was strong enough to include.
location_rationale: The decision header states "BELLEVILLE COURT FILE NO.: FC-24-420" and "ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE". Numerous references situate the proceeding in Belleville (e.g., the Belleville Police Service, exchanges at the Belleville police station, and the direction that future motions be brought in the Family Court in Belleville).
registry_rationale: The registry is identified by the file number line "BELLEVILLE COURT FILE NO.: FC-24-420", indicating the Belleville registry of the Superior Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Regina v. Zundel

defining_issues: Is s. 177 of the Criminal Code (spreading false news) unconstitutional as an infringement of freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter, and if so, is it saved by s. 1 or void for vagueness/overbreadth?
Did the trial judge err in refusing to permit the accused to challenge prospective jurors for cause on the basis of prejudicial pretrial publicity and the accused's notoriety?
Was the expert opinion evidence of Dr. Hilberg concerning the Holocaust admissible despite being based largely on hearsay documentary material?
Did the trial judge err in declining to take judicial notice of the existence of the Holocaust?

Did the trial judge misdirect the jury by equating proof of the absence of an honest belief in the truth of the pamphlet with proof of knowledge of its falsity, the required mental element under s. 177?
Did the trial judge err in the admission and rejection of certain evidence (the Red Cross document, the film narrative, and the accused's photographs, models and German-language sources)?

firac.issue: Does s. 177 of the Criminal Code infringe freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter, and if so is it justified or overbroad?
firac.facts: Zundel was charged under s. 177 with wilfully publishing a statement he knew to be false and likely to cause injury or mischief to the public interest in social and racial tolerance, arising from his publication of the pamphlet 'Did Six Million Really Die?'. He challenged the section's constitutionality.
firac.rule: Section 2(b) of the Charter guarantees freedom of expression; a freedom is defined by the residual unregulated area, with restrictions for decency and public order (including criminal libel and sedition) forming the regulated area (Re Alberta Legislation; Saumur; Big M Drug Mart). Section 1 permits reasonable limits under the Oakes proportionality test. Vagueness/overbreadth analysis follows Morgentaler and Luscher.
firac.application: The essence of s. 177 is the wilful publication of assertions of fact known to be false that cause or are likely to cause injury or mischief to a public interest. Knowingly spreading falsehoods is the antithesis of seeking truth through free exchange, has no social or moral value, and does not serve parliamentary democracy or self-fulfilment; it therefore lies within the permissibly regulated area and is not protected by s. 2(b). In the alternative, s. 177 is a reasonable limit under s. 1: its objective is pressing, lesser measures would be ineffective, and it impairs expression as little as possible and proportionately. The wording is not too vague or overbroad, being confined to statements of fact known to be false and tied to injury or mischief to a public interest.
firac.conclusion: Section 177 is constitutionally valid; it does not infringe s. 2(b), and even if it did it would be saved by s. 1 and is not void for vagueness or overbreadth.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in refusing to allow a challenge for cause based on pretrial publicity and the accused's notoriety?
firac.facts: Zundel and his trial had attracted extensive adverse publicity and repeated public confrontations. Defence counsel sought to challenge prospective jurors for cause under s. 567(1)(b) with a list of questions, many focused on race, religion and moral belief; the trial judge rejected all questions, stressing the absence of a 'notorious episode' and the lack of an evidentiary connection, and instead cautioned the panel to self-disqualify.
firac.rule: Section 567(1)(b) entitles an accused to challenge jurors on the ground that a juror is not indifferent between the Crown and the accused; the validity of a challenge is determined by the triers, not the judge (s. 569(2)); R. v. Hubbert; R. v. Crosby. A notorious episode is a relevant factor but not an absolute prerequisite.
firac.application: The judge erred in elevating a 'notorious episode' to a sine qua non (the well-publicized confrontations qualified in any event) and in requiring an evidentiary connection, which is for the triers to assess, not the judge. While many of counsel's proposed questions (targeting Jews and Freemasons on general grounds of race/religion) were properly rejected, the judge ought to have advised counsel that he could rephrase certain questions in accordance with Hubbert. Foreclosing all challenge denied the accused the fundamental right to determine juror impartiality; the self-disqualification caution was insufficient.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge erred; the accused was effectively denied his right to a jury selected according to law, a ground of merit contributing to the order for a new trial.

firac.issue: Was Dr. Hilberg's expert opinion, based largely on hearsay documents, admissible?
firac.facts: The Crown called Dr. Raul Hilberg, qualified as an expert on the Holocaust, who opined that over five million Jews were systematically annihilated pursuant to Nazi policy, based primarily on documents (many used at Nuremberg) and secondarily on witness accounts. The Crown also called eyewitness survivors.
firac.rule: Expert opinion based on unproven hearsay is of no weight (R. v. Abbey), but this is inapplicable where an exception to the hearsay rule applies. Two relevant exceptions: (1) events of general history may be proved by accepted historical treatises where living witnesses are unlikely and the matter is of general interest; and (2) an expert may rely on material of a general nature widely used and acknowledged as reliable in the field. Hearsay exceptions rest on necessity and trustworthiness (Ares v. Venner; Myers).
firac.application: The Holocaust occurred over 40 years earlier, making living policy-makers unavailable, and was self-evidently of general interest, satisfying the historical-treatise rationale; an expert historian's testimony is superior because he can be cross-examined. The documents relied on were contemporaneous, not created for litigation, and formed source material any competent historian would use—satisfying trustworthiness—so the opinion was admissible even though primarily documentary. It also fell within the second exception. In any event the Crown's case did not rest solely on Hilberg, given the eyewitness survivors.
firac.conclusion: The evidence was admissible; the courts may expand the hearsay exceptions to admit such expert opinion evidence.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in refusing to take judicial notice of the Holocaust?
firac.facts: The Crown twice asked the judge to take judicial notice that millions of Jews were annihilated as a matter of Nazi policy; the judge declined, reasoning it would eliminate part of the Crown's burden and impair the accused's ability to make full answer and defence.
firac.rule: A court may take judicial notice of a fact so generally known or verifiable that it cannot reasonably be questioned (R. v. Potts), including historical facts, and even of a fact in issue, but the judge has a wide discretion. The modern view is that judicial notice, once taken, is final and the jury must be directed accordingly.
firac.application: Had the judge taken judicial notice, he would have had to direct the jury to find the Holocaust existed, which would have been gravely prejudicial to the defence that the accused honestly believed it had not occurred, by influencing the inference as to his knowledge of the pamphlet's falsity. The existence of the Holocaust could instead be treated as a circumstance from which the jury might, but need not, infer knowledge of falsity.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge exercised his discretion judicially in refusing to take judicial notice; no error.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge misdirect the jury on the mental element by equating absence of honest belief with knowledge of falsity?
firac.facts: Section 177 requires that the statement be false to the accused's knowledge at the time of publication. In his charge, and particularly in his final re-charge answering the jury's question, the judge told the jury the basic issue was whether the accused published the pamphlet with 'no honest belief in the essential truth' of it.
firac.rule: The offence under s. 177 requires proof of actual knowledge of the falsity of the statement; recklessness is insufficient (R. v. Havard). Wilful blindness equals knowledge (Sansregret) but was not charged. Absence of an honest belief in truth, with indifference, is recklessness—not knowledge. The test is the impression the words might reasonably convey to the jury (Bigaouette).
firac.application: Publishing with no honest belief in truth, not caring whether true or false, is recklessness as to falsity, not knowledge of falsity. Although the judge elsewhere correctly stated the Crown had to prove knowledge, the charge as a whole—especially the final instruction—might reasonably have conveyed that absence of honest belief equalled knowledge. The prejudice was compounded by the failure to instruct that a belief need not be reasonable to be honest.
firac.conclusion: The misdirection was a serious error gravely prejudicial to the accused, a principal ground for ordering a new trial.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in admitting or rejecting certain evidence?
firac.facts: The judge admitted an excerpt of a 1978 International Committee of the Red Cross document (via a Canadian Red Cross witness) and the narrative accompanying the film 'Nazi Concentration Camps'; he refused to let the accused file photographs taken by Felderer, scale models of Auschwitz, and German-language books he claimed to have relied on.
firac.rule: Business records are admissible under s. 30 of the Canada Evidence Act only if made in the usual and ordinary course of business. The public-document exception admits statements made by public officers under a duty (Finestone), but is narrow. Evidence relevant to the accused's honest belief is admissible.
firac.application: There was no evidence the Red Cross document was made in the ordinary course of the ICRC's business, so it was inadmissible under s. 30. The film's narrative was hearsay from unknown narrators and sources beyond what the film depicted and did not fall within the narrow public-duty or ancient-document exceptions, so it was wrongly admitted (though the film itself was admissible). The photographs, models and German books were relevant to the accused's honest belief in the truth of the pamphlet and should have been admitted; the judge erred in excluding them. Cross-examination on the accused's National Socialist views was properly allowed as relevant to credibility and motive.
firac.conclusion: The judge erred in admitting the Red Cross excerpt and film narrative and in rejecting the defence photographs, models and German sources; these errors contributed to the order for a new trial.

case_name: Lethbridge and District Pro-Life Association v Lethbridge (City)

name_verification.name_in_document: Lethbridge and District Pro-Life Association v Lethbridge (City)

defining_issues: Should the applicant's affidavit evidence be admitted on judicial review despite the general rule against affidavit evidence?
Did the City's refusal to post the five proposed advertisements infringe the applicant's s. 2(b) Charter freedom of expression?
Was the City's decision reasonable under the Doré/Loyola framework — i.e., did it proportionately balance and minimally impair the applicant's freedom of expression against its statutory objectives?
Was the City's decision tainted by a reasonable apprehension of bias?
What is the appropriate remedy — mandamus compelling posting, or quashing and remitting for reconsideration?

firac.issue: Should the applicant's affidavit (the Konynenbelt affidavit) be admitted on judicial review?
firac.facts: The applicant filed the affidavit of its president, containing a history of dealings with the City and Pattison, including events before April 2018 and characterizations of complainants as 'lobbyists.' The City objected, arguing leave had not been obtained under Rule 3.22 and that opinion evidence is inadmissible.
firac.rule: Rule 3.22 of the Alberta Rules of Court limits evidence on judicial review; affidavits are generally not allowed, especially on the merits, but may be admitted in exceptional circumstances (Alberta Liquor Store Assn v Alberta (Gaming and Liquor Commission), 2006 ABQB 904; Alberta College of Pharmacists v Sobeys West Inc, 2017 ABCA 306). Three recognized exceptions: breach of natural justice not apparent on the record; background/standing; and where no transcript exists.
firac.application: The affidavit largely duplicated the certified Record, established background facts, and was relevant to the alleged breach of natural justice (bias). There was no transcript of the impugned decision. The court disregarded personal opinions and material not before the decision-maker, but allowed the affidavit for context and to support the bias allegation.
firac.conclusion: The affidavit was admitted subject to the stated limitations.

firac.issue: Did the refusal to post the advertisements infringe s. 2(b) of the Charter?
firac.facts: The applicant, a registered pro-life charity, sought to post five advertisements on City transit property; the City refused on November 7, 2018. Section 2(b) protects freedom of expression, including unpopular and controversial content.
firac.rule: Section 2(b) is given a broad, purposive interpretation protecting all communications conveying meaning regardless of content, including false, unpopular or disturbing speech (R v Zundel, [1992] 2 SCR 731; Irwin Toy; Greater Vancouver Transportation Authority, 2009 SCC 31). Transit authorities are government actors subject to the Charter.
firac.application: The City conceded that the Charter applied and that its decision infringed the applicant's s. 2(b) rights. The real contest was over justification/reasonableness.
firac.conclusion: The s. 2(b) infringement was conceded and established.

firac.issue: Was the City's decision reasonable under the Doré/Loyola framework?
firac.facts: The City's written reasons cited the Canadian Code of Advertising Standards, the applicant's branding/website, community response to a previously posted (and removed) advertisement, its statutory objective to maintain 'safe and viable communities,' and case law. The reasons contained only a single sentence referring to the Charter.
firac.rule: Where an administrative decision limits a Charter right, the reviewing court asks whether the decision reflects a proportionate balancing of the Charter protection against the statutory objectives, limiting the right no more than necessary (Doré v Barreau du Québec, 2012 SCC 12; Loyola High School, 2015 SCC 12; Law Society of BC v Trinity Western, 2018 SCC 32; Canadian Centre for Bio-Ethical Reform v Grande Prairie (City), 2018 ABCA 154; Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65). Public upset and offence are insufficient to displace freedom of expression (Bracken v Fort Erie; Bracken v Niagara Parks Police).
firac.application: The reasons revealed no actual minimal impairment analysis — merely an assertion that Charter rights had been weighed. Reliance on the applicant's logo/website was misplaced since no web address appeared on the ads and the website was informational, unlike the shocking, graphic material in Grande Prairie. Factual accuracy is not a precondition to protection; opinion and even inaccurate expression are protected (Zundel). The eight complaints about the prior (different) advertisement did not establish a rational connection to a safety objective or a high probability of harm; the City ignored the substantial favourable public response. The Code was a relevant factor only, but the City placed undue reliance on it, failed to consider the political-advertising exemption, and ignored the inconclusive ASC opinion. The ads were far less graphic and 'hateful' than in Grande Prairie.
firac.conclusion: The City failed to conduct the required minimal impairment/proportionality analysis; the decision was unreasonable and must be set aside.

firac.issue: Was the decision tainted by a reasonable apprehension of bias?
firac.facts: The City considered only negative community response, treating support for the applicant's expression as 'irrelevant,' relied on alleged Code breaches despite an inconclusive ASC opinion, assumed harm, and referenced 'public outcry.'
firac.rule: The test is whether an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and having thought it through, would conclude it more likely than not the decision-maker would not decide fairly (Committee for Justice and Liberty v Canada (NEB), [1978] 1 SCR 369); standards vary with context (Baker v Canada, [1999] 2 SCR 817; Newfoundland Telephone).
firac.application: The City considered only one side of the public response, relied on Code non-compliance contrary to the ASC opinion, failed to conduct any genuine Doré/Loyola analysis, and assumed harm the record did not support. An informed person would conclude the City did not undertake an independent, open-minded evaluation.
firac.conclusion: A reasonable apprehension of bias was established, providing a further basis to set aside the decision.

firac.issue: What is the appropriate remedy?
firac.facts: The applicant sought mandamus to compel posting, or alternatively quashing and remission with directions; the City argued for quashing and remission only.
firac.rule: Section 24(1) of the Charter provides remedies for government acts; mandamus is reserved for exceptional cases where only one outcome is possible (Canada (AG) v PHS Community Services, 2011 SCC 44; Giguère v Chambre des notaires, 2004 SCC 1; South Coast, 2018 BCCA 344).
firac.application: As in South Coast, this was not a case where any refusal of the advertisements would necessarily be unreasonable, so mandamus was inappropriate. Given the bias finding, the court recommended the City appoint an alternative decision-maker on reconsideration.
firac.conclusion: The decision was quashed and remitted to the City for reconsideration, with a strong recommendation to use a different decision-maker; the applicant was awarded costs.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the primary tier-1 area — this is a judicial review of a municipal decision. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) capture the review of the City's decision for reasonableness. K010 (Doré/Loyola framework) is central, as the case turns on the proportionate balancing/minimal impairment analysis the City failed to perform. K003 (Constitutional law) and K024 (freedom of expression) reflect the s. 2(b) right at the heart of the dispute, with K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) and K107 (Canadian Charter) as the specific statutory anchors. K012 (procedural fairness) covers the reasonable apprehension of bias finding. The affidavit-admissibility issue is procedural and adequately captured within administrative law/judicial review rather than a distinct keyword.
location_rationale: The heading states 'Registry: Lethbridge' and the decision closes 'Dated at the City of Lethbridge, Alberta this 29th day of October, 2020.' The application was 'heard by me on October 10, 2019, at Lethbridge, Alberta.' The court is the Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly lists 'Registry: Lethbridge.'

name_verification.name_in_document: Paramount v. Kevin J. Johnston

defining_issues: Are the impugned statements published by the Johnston defendants defamatory of the plaintiffs?
Are any defences (justification, fair comment, responsible communication, or Charter freedom of expression) available to the Johnston defendants?
What quantum of general, aggravated, and special (compensatory) damages should be awarded?
Is an award of punitive damages warranted?
Are permanent restraining orders (injunctions) appropriate?

firac.issue: Are the impugned statements published by the Johnston defendants defamatory of the plaintiffs?
firac.facts: Mr. Johnston, through FreedomReport.ca and numerous social media accounts, published a series of videos and posts falsely portraying Mr. Fakih and Paramount as funding terrorism, being a 'front', requiring patrons to be 'jihadists' or rapists, and calling for a boycott, expressly naming and depicting the plaintiffs, including a photo of Mr. Fakih altered to show blood on his hands.
firac.rule: The tort of defamation has three elements: (1) the words were published to at least one other person; (2) the words referred to the plaintiff; and (3) the words are defamatory in that they would tend to lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person. Once established, falsity and damages are presumed (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61).
firac.application: The statements were posted online worldwide to thousands of followers (publication); they expressly named and depicted Mr. Fakih and Paramount (reference); and they associated the plaintiffs with terrorists, rapists and child killers, which would lower their reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person (defamatory). Justice Nakatsuru had already found the event videos to be facially defamatory and to bear the hallmarks of hate speech, and the other statements were substantially similar.
firac.conclusion: The impugned statements are defamatory; all three elements are met.

firac.issue: Are any defences available to the Johnston defendants?
firac.facts: The Johnston defendants filed no responding materials and provided few particulars in their defence, alluding to 'satire', and relied primarily on freedom of expression under s. 2 of the Charter. They led no evidence of any factual basis for their remarks.
firac.rule: Particulars of justification/truth must be pleaded and the defendant bears the burden of proving truth. Fair comment and responsible communication require the statements to concern a matter of public interest and are defeated by malice (WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Grant v. Torstar). The Charter does not apply to litigation between private citizens; violent, threatening and hateful expression falls outside s. 2(b) protection (R v. Keegstra; Whatcott v. Saskatchewan HRT, 2013 SCC 11).
firac.application: No factual basis for justification was offered, and the defendants called their comments 'satire', which by definition is not fact. Hate communication raises no public-interest subject matter, defeating fair comment and responsible communication, and any such defences are further defeated by malice. The Charter does not apply to private litigation, and even if it did, the defendants' violent, threatening and hateful expression would fall outside protected expression.
firac.conclusion: No defences are available to the Johnston defendants.

firac.issue: What quantum of compensatory (general, aggravated, and special) damages is appropriate?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs are prominent, philanthropic public figures whose reputation was central to Paramount's mission to destigmatize halal food; the internet-based hate campaign caused lost employees, customer concern, family distress, and the loss of a UAE master-franchise deal worth roughly $2.6 million per year. The defendants never apologized and bragged about the harm caused.
firac.rule: General damages are presumed once defamation is made out; factors include the plaintiff's standing, seriousness of statements, mode/extent of publication, absence of apology, and the defendant's conduct and motive (Barrick Gold Corp. v. Lopehandia). Internet defamation is aggravated by its ubiquity and reach. Aggravated damages arise where the defendant's conduct is high-handed, malicious or oppressive (Hill v. Church of Scientology). Special damages compensate for proximate, measurable business loss.
firac.application: The allegations of terrorism and rape were among the most serious possible, published widely online with no way to measure reach; the defendants refused any apology, continued the campaign, and accosted Mr. Fakih and his children, all supporting aggravated damages. The lost UAE deal alone exceeded $2.6 million per year, more than the compensatory damages claimed. The court awarded a global sum encompassing general, aggravated, and special damages.
firac.conclusion: Substantial compensatory damages (general, aggravated and special) are warranted, forming part of the $2.5 million total award.

firac.issue: Is an award of punitive damages warranted?
firac.facts: The defendants evaded service, lied to process servers, breached multiple court orders and cost awards, publicly maligned the court and the 'white woman judge' as being 'in on' a conspiracy, and persisted in hate speech targeting Muslims solely on the basis of religion.
firac.rule: Punitive damages punish rather than compensate and express the court's outrage at egregious conduct (Focus Graphite Inc. v. Douglas, 2015 ONSC 1104). Hate speech is a special category of expression deserving of sanction given its grave psychological and social harm (Whatcott v. Saskatchewan HRT).
firac.application: The defendants' repeated contempt for the court process, breaches of orders, and unrelenting hateful campaign, combined with the pressing societal harm caused by hate speech that marginalizes a vulnerable group, justified punishment beyond compensation.
firac.conclusion: Punitive damages are warranted and form part of the $2.5 million award.

firac.issue: Are permanent restraining orders (injunctions) appropriate?
firac.facts: The defendants continued their defamatory and harassing campaign for nearly three years without abatement, ignored and breached court orders, refused to pay costs awards, harassed the plaintiffs' family and counsel, and gave no indication they would stop.
firac.rule: Permanent injunctions may be granted in defamation actions where (a) there is a likelihood the defendant will continue to publish defamatory statements despite a liability finding, or (b) there is a real possibility the plaintiff will not receive compensation because enforcement of a damages award may be impossible (Sustainable Development Technology Canada v. Sigurdson, 2018 ONSC 7320).
firac.application: Both grounds were met: the defendants' persistent campaign made continued publication highly likely, and their history of ignoring orders and refusing to pay costs made non-payment of any judgment a real possibility. The court therefore restrained contact with, recording of, and defamatory publications about Mr. Fakih, his family, the plaintiffs, and their counsel, including proximity restrictions.
firac.conclusion: Permanent injunctions were granted against the Johnston defendants.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 practice area as this is a defamation tort action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. K016 (fair comment) and K019 (responsible communication) are the specific defences the court considered and rejected. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the closest vocabulary term for the permanent injunctions/restraining orders granted. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) address the defendants' unsuccessful Charter defence. K061 (hate speech) is central, as the impugned statements were found to bear the hallmarks of hate speech per Whatcott/Keegstra. K058 (antisemitism) is a weak/borderline pick — the case concerns anti-Muslim (Islamophobic) hate rather than antisemitism, but the vocabulary lacks an Islamophobia term; it is included only because the judgment references the rise of hate crimes targeting Muslim, Jewish and Black people. K093 (Jewish) similarly appears only in that statistical context and is borderline. The hate targets Muslims, for which the controlled vocabulary provides no specific term.

name_verification.name_in_document: Condominium Corporation No 8722942 v Buck

defining_issues: Did the property managers commit civil fraud (or otherwise wrongfully) pay themselves vacation pay on termination?
Did the Management Agreement create an employment relationship, and were Mr. and Mrs. Buck each individual employees?
Did the condominium corporation have just cause to terminate the Agreement on the basis of insubordination?
What damages are the wrongfully dismissed employees entitled to under a fixed-term contract, and was there any duty to mitigate?

firac.issue: Did the Bucks fraudulently or wrongfully pay themselves vacation pay upon termination?
firac.facts: Under s. 10 of the Agreement the Bucks were entitled to three weeks' paid vacation per year with carry-over, and Oakwood Towers did not dispute the contractual or statutory entitlement. The Bucks took only 5 working days' vacation, had the corporation's accountant calculate the payout, and presented the calculation and cheques to the two designated board members (Roberge and Bigelow) who reviewed, initialed and signed them in accordance with the established practice. Oakwood Towers alleged the Bucks 'paid themselves' $8,094 fraudulently and threatened criminal charges.
firac.rule: Civil fraud/deceit requires (1) a false representation by the defendant; (2) knowledge or recklessness as to its falsity; (3) that the representation caused the plaintiff to act; and (4) resulting loss (Bruno Appliance and Furniture Inc. v. Hryniak, 2014 SCC 8; HSBC Bank Canada v. Lourenco, 2012 ABQB 380). The plaintiff bears the onus and must prove fraud with clear and convincing evidence. The Employment Standards Code, RSA 2000, c. E-9, ss. 34–44 and 42(2) require an employer to pay out vacation pay on termination and to keep vacation records.
firac.application: The Court found no false representation: the Bucks were both contractually and statutorily entitled to vacation pay, the accountant's unchallenged calculation was accurate, and payment was made by the two designated board members following the same approval process used for all Oakwood Towers expenses. Stenzel's evidence that the Bucks took more vacation was vague, unreliable and inconsistent with the documentary record; Oakwood Towers failed to keep or produce vacation records as the Code required. The board president had confirmed to Service Canada there was 'no fraud'. Oakwood Towers suffered no loss by paying an entitlement.
firac.conclusion: Oakwood Towers proved no element of civil fraud; its claim for fraud and for 'wrongfully' paid vacation pay was dismissed in its entirety.

firac.issue: Did the Agreement create an employment relationship, and were the Bucks each individual employees?
firac.facts: Oakwood Towers 'appointed' the Bucks as resident managers, paid them a monthly gross salary subject to statutory withholdings, controlled the work, and retained the power to dismiss under s. 13. The Agreement referred to the Bucks collectively as 'the Manager' but was signed by both and contained an express plurality clause (s. 14). Oakwood Towers argued they should be treated as a single employment unit.
firac.rule: An employment relationship is assessed on four indicia: authority to select, payment of wages, control over the method/what work is done, and ability to suspend or dismiss (Levitt, The Law of Dismissal in Canada). Contracts are interpreted to give effect to the parties' intention, reading the contract as a whole with surrounding circumstances (Sattva Capital Corp. v. Creston Moly Corp., 2014 SCC 53). Employees must be individuals; a full-time worker who is not a partner/shareholder is presumed an employee; 'employee' is defined in the Employment Standards Code s. 1(1)(k).
firac.application: All four indicia were met, so the Agreement created an employment relationship. The 'single employment' argument ignored the express plurality clause and the evidence of Stavropoulos that Mr. Buck insisted Mrs. Buck be a party and that they were intended to be joint managers. Both signed the Agreement, which contemplated more than one employee.
firac.conclusion: Oakwood Towers was the employer; Mr. and Mrs. Buck were each individual employees entitled to the common law and statutory protections owed to employees.

firac.issue: Did Oakwood Towers have just cause to terminate for insubordination?
firac.facts: Oakwood Towers terminated the Agreement about 13 months before its fixed term expired, relying on either a pivotal act of insubordination (Mr. Buck's second July 6, 2016 email after a 'cease and desist' direction) or cumulative minor acts (September 2015 board meeting, December 2015 tenant letters, January 2016 roofing invoice/reserve fund transfer, June 2016 reserve fund report). Much of the friction stemmed from an interpersonal dispute between Mr. Buck and board member/Treasurer Stenzel, arising from a separate suite-management agreement.
firac.rule: The employer bears the onus of proving just cause on a balance of probabilities. Cause is assessed contextually under the three-step McKinley v. BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38 framework (nature/extent of misconduct; surrounding circumstances; proportionality of dismissal). Insubordination requires either willful and deliberate disobedience of a clear, authorized, lawful and reasonable work order (Karmel v. Calgary Jewish Academy, 2015 ABQB 731; Amos v. Alberta) or behaviour amounting to a deliberate challenge; usually more than one instance is required, and cumulative cause requires clear warnings and a chance to improve (Dawson v. Bridge Brand Food Services Ltd., 2007 ABQB 15; Kokilev v. Picquic Tool Company Inc., 2010 BCSC 1412). Employers owe a duty of good faith and fair dealing (Bhasin v. Hrynew, 2014 SCC 71).
firac.application: Working through each incident, the Court found no willful disobedience and no deliberate challenge. The September 2015 conflict ended with an accepted apology and no warning; the December 2015 communication directives were unauthorized, unlawful and unreasonable because they interfered with the Bucks' duties under s. 4 and arose from Stenzel's uninvestigated complaint about a separate contract; the January 2016 work orders were all completed; the June 2016 reserve report was partially completed with no deliberate disobedience; and the July 2016 'cease and desist' order was unclear, unauthorized, unlawful, unreasonable, and not disobeyed, since Mr. Buck's reply addressed legitimate board business. Stavropoulos' evidence was found unreliable and unbalanced. The two weeks' working notice given was itself inconsistent with a genuine claim of just cause.
firac.conclusion: Oakwood Towers failed to prove insubordination or just cause; the termination was wrongful and the Bucks' counterclaims for wrongful dismissal succeeded.

firac.issue: What damages are owed for wrongful dismissal under a fixed-term contract, and was there a duty to mitigate?
firac.facts: The Agreement was a fixed-term contract running May 1, 2014 to August 31, 2017. The Bucks were terminated effective July 31, 2016. Each filed a separate counterclaim. Oakwood Towers did not challenge the damages calculation and did not raise mitigation.
firac.rule: An employee under a fixed-term contract is entitled to the full contractual amount to the end of the term, and has no duty to mitigate (Lovely v. Prestige Travel, 2013 ABQB 457; Bowes v. Goss Power Products Ltd., 2012 ONCA 425). Counterclaims are independent actions (Baig v. Guarantee Co. of North America, 2007 ONCA 847). Vacation pay of 6% applies under the Employment Standards Code.
firac.application: The Bucks had no duty to mitigate, and Oakwood Towers led no evidence on mitigation. The unchallenged calculation (salary to August 31, 2017, gas and laundry allowances, and vacation pay) totalled $85,989.30, divided equally between the two independent counterclaims. Statutory deductions were reserved.
firac.conclusion: Judgment for $42,994.65 to each of Mr. and Mrs. Buck, with pre-judgment interest from July 31, 2016 under the Judgment Interest Act; costs awarded to the Bucks, with enhanced-costs and statutory-deduction issues reserved.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the core dispute concerns an employment relationship, just cause and dismissal. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the most specific and central keyword—the Bucks succeeded on wrongful-dismissal counterclaims. K002 (Civil litigation) captures the plaintiff's civil fraud/deceit claim over vacation pay, decided on the Hryniak elements. K086 (co-ownership) is included because the plaintiff/employer is a condominium corporation and the Court touched on the Condominium Property Act jurisdiction question, though it is a weak/contextual pick rather than a decided issue. K083 (harassment) is a weak pick, reflecting the characterization of board member Stenzel's threatening texts and 'harassment' emails, which formed part of the factual backdrop but were not an independently adjudicated cause of action. The controlled vocabulary lacks precise terms for civil fraud, just cause, employment contract interpretation and fixed-term damages, so K002, K086 and K083 are the closest available proxies and are flagged as borderline.

registry_rationale: The decision expressly lists 'Registry: Edmonton'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Catholic Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto v. S.(T.)
