defining_issues: Does the Child Welfare Act (and its successor the Child and Family Services Act) contain sufficient ambiguity to permit a court to grant birth parents access that continues after the children's adoption by foster parents?

If the legislation requires termination of birth-parent access upon placement for adoption, do those provisions violate freedom of association (s. 2(d)), the right to life, liberty and security of the person (s. 7), or equality rights (s. 15(1)) of the Charter?

Was the appellate (District Court) judge entitled to overrule the reviewing judge and find that adoption without access, rather than continued Crown wardship with access, was in the best interests of the children?

firac.issue: Does the Child Welfare Act contain ambiguity permitting an order for birth-parent access to continue after adoption by foster parents?
firac.facts: Two children apprehended in 1981 had lived with the same foster parents since infancy. The foster parents wished to adopt but opposed continued access by the birth parents. The reviewing judge (Nasmith Prov. Ct. J.) held the statute was ambiguous—particularly because s. 69(15) conflicted with s. 38—and that no physical 'placement' was needed since the children already lived with the prospective adopters, so a 'deemed placement' allowed adoption with continuing access.
firac.rule: Child Welfare Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 66, ss. 38(5),(7),(8)(d), 69(15), 86(1) (and concordant provisions of the Child and Family Services Act, 1984). Section 38(7) bars an access order once a Crown ward is placed and residing in an approved adoption home; s. 38(8)(d) and s. 69(15) require any outstanding access order to be terminated before placement; s. 86(1) provides that on adoption the child ceases to be the child of the birth parents.
firac.application: The court held s. 38 is paramount and requires a choice between continued Crown wardship with access or adoption without access. 'Placement' is an abstract concept and includes a 'deemed placement'; it occurs when the decision to adopt coincides with the child's residence with the prospective adopters, so the fact the children already lived with the foster parents did not create ambiguity. The primary purpose of terminating access is family stability, not merely secrecy: granting access after adoption would put the adoptive relationship on an unequal footing with a natural family because access would be controlled by a judicial or administrative official rather than within the family unit.
firac.conclusion: No genuine ambiguity exists; the legislation requires termination of birth-parent access by the time the children are placed for adoption. Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. erred in law; Lissaman D.C.J. was correct.

firac.issue: Do provisions requiring termination of birth-parent access upon placement for adoption violate ss. 2(d), 7 or 15(1) of the Charter?
firac.facts: The birth mother argued that terminating her access to prepare for adoption violated her freedom of association, her liberty/security of the person, and her equality rights.
firac.rule: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1, 2(d), 7, 15(1); Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143; Reference re Workers' Compensation Act, 1983 (Nfld.), [1989] 1 S.C.R.; Reference re s. 94(2) of the Motor Vehicle Act, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 486.
firac.application: Section 2(d): freedom of association is public and collective in nature and protects associations pursuing common economic, political, religious, social or similar goals; the desire of a parent to be with a child has no such purpose and family relationships fall outside the guarantee, consistent with Re White, Shingoose and Nova Scotia (Minister of Community Services) v. S.(M.K.). Section 7: barring access to a particular person is not confinement; the existence of places one may not go and people who may refuse contact does not deprive another of liberty or security of the person. Section 15: under Andrews, recourse requires that the claimant's situation be analogous to the enumerated grounds; the situation of birth parents is 'in no way analogous' to those listed, following Reference re Workers' Compensation Act.
firac.conclusion: None of ss. 2(d), 7 or 15(1) is infringed, so it was unnecessary to consider s. 1. The statutory provisions are constitutionally valid.

firac.issue: Could the appellate judge overrule the reviewing judge and find that adoption without access was in the children's best interests?
firac.facts: On appeal from the status review, Lissaman D.C.J. received the review-hearing evidence plus a follow-up assessment and further testimony, and concluded adoption without access served the children's best interests.
firac.rule: Child Welfare Act, ss. 37, 43(8) (further evidence on appeal), 1(1)(b) (definition of 'best interests of the child'); Children's Aid Society of Renfrew County v. L.P.W. (appellate function, not a hearing de novo).
firac.application: Because the reviewing judge erred in law by assuming adoption could be combined with continued access, the appellate court could review the decision. All expert witnesses, including the birth parents' expert, favoured adoption, and any value ascribed to continuing access was hypothetical and lost relevance once combination was legally impossible. The best-interests factors in s. 1(1)(b)—the parent-child relationship, disruption of continuity, the merits of the adoption plan, and delay—all favoured adoption; the foster parents had become the children's psychological parents over nearly six years, and imposing unwanted relationships threatened family stability.
firac.conclusion: Lissaman D.C.J. was entitled to and correctly found that Crown wardship with a view to adoption and no birth-parent access was in the children's best interests.

K003 (Constitutional law) is the second tier-1 area given the Charter challenges. K048 (custody/access) directly captures the central dispute over post-adoption access. K047 (best interests of the child) reflects the governing statutory test applied on the third issue. K107 (Canadian Charter) is the umbrella statute engaged. The s. 2(d) freedom-of-association argument is significant but the controlled vocabulary has no freedom-of-association keyword, so it is not tagged; this is the one notable gap.

name_verification.name_in_document: Crystal Lynne Meads v. Dennis Larry Meads

defining_issues: Can a litigant escape the jurisdiction and authority of a superior court by advancing 'Organized Pseudolegal Commercial Argument' (OPCA) theories?
Do 'foisted unilateral agreements' such as fee schedules and copyright/trademark notices create binding legal obligations on the court, opposing counsel or state actors?
Does the 'double/split person' concept (separating a 'flesh and blood man' from a capital-letters 'corporate' persona) relieve a litigant of legal obligations?
Can an 'Accept for Value' / A4V 'money for nothing' scheme be used to discharge child and spousal support obligations?
Was it appropriate to appoint a case management justice and order financial disclosure from Mr. Meads in the divorce and matrimonial property action?

firac.issue: Can a litigant escape the jurisdiction and authority of a superior court by advancing OPCA theories (admiralty court, 'God's Law', freeman-on-the-land, 'I have not consented', etc.)?
firac.facts: In a divorce and matrimonial property action, the respondent Dennis Larry Meads denied the Court's authority, asserting it was an admiralty court, that he was a 'flesh and blood man' subject only to 'God's Law' or the 'Maximus of Law', that legislation did not apply to him, and that he had not consented to the Court's jurisdiction; he left the hearing before it concluded.
firac.rule: Provincial superior courts are courts of inherent jurisdiction descended from the English Royal Courts; where a justiciable right exists there must be a court to vindicate it, and only an explicit statutory ouster removes jurisdiction (Board v. Board; Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Canadian Liberty Net). Inherent jurisdiction cannot be defeated even by privative clauses (Pasiechnyk; Dunsmuir). Belief-based immunity is not a Charter defence and religious belief is subject to reasonable limits (Charter s. 1; Hutterian Brethren).
firac.application: Every OPCA 'magic hat' (exempt group, self-declared immunity, misidentification, different law, admiralty/military court, defective oaths, God's Law) fails because the Court's inherent jurisdiction reaches every Alberta matter not assigned to another tribunal. No Canadian court has ever accepted an OPCA concept; a litigant may argue he is in the wrong court but cannot claim no court has authority over him.
firac.conclusion: Such arguments cannot succeed; they are intrinsically frivolous and vexatious, may be struck without further analysis, and may amount to contempt of court. Mr. Meads is subject to the Court's authority regardless of his assertions.

firac.issue: Do foisted unilateral agreements — fee schedules, copyright/trademark notices, appointments of fiduciaries — bind their recipients?
firac.facts: Mr. Meads served a 'fee schedule' purporting to charge officials $2,000,000 per 'occurrence' of conduct such as arrest or 'disrespect'; a copyright/trademark notice claiming $100,000,000 per use of his name; and documents purporting to appoint a court clerk and Justice Rooke as his fiduciaries, all stating that silence constituted agreement.
firac.rule: A binding contract requires consensus ad idem and communicated acceptance; one cannot foist a contract on another without consent, and silence generally cannot constitute acceptance (Silver's Garage Ltd. v. Bridgewater; Felthouse v. Bindley; Ron Ghitter Property Consultants v. Beaver Lumber). Liquidated damages must be reasonable and not a penalty in terrorem (Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre; H.F. Clarke).
firac.application: None of Mr. Meads's documents could bind their recipients; failure to rebut does not create obligation, and the sums claimed were grossly disproportionate penalties. Such 'fee schedules' are tools of intimidation and may satisfy the actus reus/mens rea of intimidation of a justice system participant (Criminal Code s. 423.1) and the criminal interest rate prohibition (s. 347).
firac.conclusion: The foisted agreements have no legal effect; they are evidence of vexatious conduct and may attract punitive damages, elevated costs and criminal sanction.

firac.issue: Does the 'double/split person' concept relieve a litigant of legal obligations?
firac.facts: Mr. Meads asserted he was two entities — the 'flesh and blood' Dennis-Larry: Meads and a state-created 'corporate' persona DENNIS LARRY MEADS — and executed intra-personal contracts assigning all property to one and all debts to the other, arguing that the support obligations attached only to the corporate persona.
firac.rule: Canadian law recognizes only one legal identity per person; a purported second capacity or entity is a pure fiction not sanctioned by law (Canada (MNR) v. Stanchfield; R. v. Lindsay). A person wishing to add a legal layer must incorporate.
firac.application: Whatever nomenclature Mr. Meads adopted, it is the person before the Court who is bound. The split-person contracts, powers of attorney and indemnities were 'rubbish' with no legal effect.
firac.conclusion: The double/split person strategy fails; Mr. Meads is one legal person fully subject to the Court's orders.

firac.issue: Can an 'Accept for Value' / A4V scheme discharge child and spousal support obligations?
firac.facts: Mr. Meads claimed a secret government bank account linked to his birth certificate and social insurance number, and instructed the Court and the Bank of Canada to pay his support obligations and $100 billion in gold or silver from that account.
firac.rule: The A4V 'money for nothing' concept has no basis in law and has been rejected (Underworld Services Ltd. v. Money Stop Ltd.; Mercedes-Benz Financial v. Kovacevic).
firac.application: There is no secret account and no mechanism by which the Court could discharge obligations in this way; the A4V documents are 'legal alchemy'.
firac.conclusion: The A4V scheme is rejected as absurd; any litigation or defence based on it is inherently frivolous and vexatious.

firac.issue: Was it appropriate to appoint a case management justice and order financial disclosure?
firac.facts: Ms. Meads's counsel could not meaningfully communicate with Mr. Meads because of his OPCA documents and sought a case management justice; Mr. Meads had generally paid interim support ordered by Veit J. but had not disclosed his financial records.
firac.rule: Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, s. 4.11(c) authorizes appointment of a case management justice; family law proceedings carry mutual and reciprocal disclosure obligations, enforceable including by contempt.
firac.application: OPCA-inflected litigation warrants close single-judge supervision; the requested disclosure (tax returns, earnings, investments, precious metals, sworn statement of income/assets) was routine and had not been provided voluntarily.
firac.conclusion: Case management was appropriate and Justice Rooke appointed himself; Mr. Meads was ordered to provide the specified disclosure by 31 August 2012, failing which the Court's powers, including contempt, could be exercised.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area: the reasons are a treatise on vexatious pseudolegal litigation, court procedure, costs, punitive damages and vexatious-litigant status. K006 (Family law) captures the underlying divorce and matrimonial property action in which the OPCA conduct arose. K050 (parental support) and K053 (spousal support) reflect the interim child and spousal support obligations Mr. Meads sought to evade and the disclosure ordered to quantify them. K004 (Criminal law) is engaged by the extended analysis of contempt of court and potential Criminal Code offences (intimidation of a justice system participant, s. 347 criminal interest rate). K025 (freedom of religion) is a weak/borderline pick — included only because one OPCA category addressed was the claim that 'God's Law' and religious belief trump the courts, which the Court dismissed under Charter s. 2(a)/s. 1; it is not a genuine religious-freedom holding. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward antisemitism/hate-speech topics that this case does not engage, so several picks are the closest available rather than precise matches.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta', gives 'Registry: Edmonton', and closes 'Dated at the City of Edmonton, Alberta this 18th day of September, 2012.' Province is therefore Alberta and city Edmonton.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly states 'Registry: Edmonton', and Associate Chief Justice Rooke describes himself as the senior administrative judicial official of the Court of Queen's Bench in Edmonton.

case_name: Attis v. New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15

name_verification.name_in_document: Ross v. New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15 (style of cause: David Attis, Complainant, and Human Rights Commission, Commission, v. Board of School Trustees, District 15, Respondent, and Malcolm Ross, Department of Education, New Brunswick Teachers' Federation, and Canadian Jewish Congress, Parties)
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The metadata names the case 'Attis v. New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15' and cites '1991 CanLII 12184 (NBQB)', but the decision is a New Brunswick Board of Inquiry decision (before Brian D. Bruce), not a Court of Queen's Bench judgment. The header reads 'Ross v. New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15' while the actual complainant/respondent style of cause is David Attis v. Board of School Trustees, District 15. The 'Attis' in the metadata correctly identifies the complainant, but the court designation (NBQB) and the header party name (Ross) diverge from the tribunal that rendered this decision.

defining_issues: Does public education provided in public schools constitute an 'accommodation, service or facility available to the public' under s. 5 of the New Brunswick Human Rights Act, and is a school board a 'person' capable of discriminating?

Did Malcolm Ross's off-duty anti-Semitic writings and public statements create a discriminatory 'poisoned environment' in School District 15 in breach of s. 5(1) of the Act, notwithstanding the free-expression clause in s. 6(2) and the religious-freedom protection in s. 3?

Is the School Board statutorily liable for the discriminatory conduct of its teacher-employee under s. 5, and did the Board also directly discriminate by failing to discipline Ross and thereby condoning his views?
What remedy is appropriate where a teacher's off-duty conduct violates the Act?

firac.issue: Is public education a 'service available to the public' under s. 5 and is a school board a 'person' under the Act?
firac.facts: David Attis, a Jewish parent of children in School District 15, complained that the Board of School Trustees breached s. 5 in the provision of educational services. Preliminary objections questioned whether public education was a covered service and whether the School Board qualified as a 'person'.
firac.rule: Section 5 of the Human Rights Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11 prohibits denial of or discrimination in accommodation, services or facilities available to the public on grounds including religion and ancestry. Human rights legislation receives a broad, purposive interpretation (O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears; Interpretation Act s. 17). 'Person' includes the extended meaning under the Interpretation Act, s. 38.
firac.application: The New Brunswick Court of Appeal had already held that public education under the Schools Act is a service available to the public within s. 5. The Board of Inquiry followed that direction and found a school board established under the Schools Act is a 'person'; the use of 'employer' in s. 3 alongside 'or other person' confirmed employers fall within the general term 'person' used in s. 5, consistent with Memorial University v. Rose.
firac.conclusion: Public education is a service available to the public and the School Board is a 'person' capable of discriminating under s. 5.

firac.issue: Did Ross's off-duty anti-Semitic writings and statements create a discriminatory poisoned environment breaching s. 5(1), and do s. 6(2) or s. 3 shield the conduct?
firac.facts: Between 1978 and 1989 Ross, a teacher in District 15, published books (Web of Deceit, The Real Holocaust, Spectre of Power, Christianity vs. Judeo-Christianity), letters to the editor and gave a television interview alleging an international Jewish conspiracy and denigrating Judaism and the Holocaust. There was no recent evidence of classroom remarks, but Jewish students including Yona Attis experienced name-calling, swastikas and 'Heil Hitler' salutes and felt fear and isolation.
firac.rule: Section 5(1)(b) prohibits discrimination in a public service; discrimination is assessed by effect, not intent (Simpsons-Sears). Teachers are role models and off-duty conduct having a negative effect on the employer's operation is disciplinable (Peterson; Etobicoke Board of Education; Abbotsford v. Shewan; Fraser). Section 6(2)'s free-expression clause applies only to 'this section' (s. 6), not s. 5. Freedom of religion does not entitle attacking or condemning another religion (Boucher; Taylor v. CHRC; Dufour).
firac.application: The Board found Ross's writings were prima facie discriminatory against persons of Jewish faith and ancestry, not scholarly discourse, and that the extensive publicity contributed over years to a poisoned educational environment interfering with the complainant's children's right to non-discriminatory education. The reasonable-effect test, applied from the perspective of a reasonable child/parent, was met; the students' evidence was credible. Section 6(2) was confined to s. 6 and could not exempt s. 5 conduct; there was no evidence Ross's religion required his writings, and even if s. 3 were engaged, a reasonable balance favoured protection from discrimination since attacking another religion exceeds legitimate religious freedom.
firac.conclusion: Ross's off-duty conduct violated s. 5(1) with no reasonable cause to excuse the discriminatory effect; neither s. 6(2) nor s. 3 provided a defence.

firac.issue: Is the School Board liable for Ross's conduct and did it also directly discriminate by failing to discipline him?
firac.facts: The School Board became aware of controversy over Ross's publications as early as 1978, monitored his classroom, established a Review Committee in 1987, but took no disciplinary action until March 1988, then removed the record in September 1989 and gave only a severe reprimand after his 1989 television appearance.
firac.rule: Under s. 5, employers are statutorily liable for discriminatory acts of employees related to employment (Robichaud v. Canada (Treasury Board)); the word 'indirectly' in s. 5 imports employer liability. A school board must maintain a positive, non-discriminatory environment and take a proactive role.
firac.application: Because Ross's off-duty conduct breached s. 5, the School Board as employer was liable. Separately, the Board's reluctance and slow, ineffectual response—failing to act until 1988 despite established authority to discipline off-duty conduct, an inadequate Review Committee that ignored Jewish community submissions, and defensive resistance to the Commission—created the effect of condoning Ross's views, which a reasonable person would anticipate would injure the complainant and his children. Two failed motions were not shown to be discriminatory, and there was no evidence of intent, but effect governs.
firac.conclusion: The School Board discriminated against the complainant contrary to s. 5(1), both indirectly through Ross and directly through its own inaction, with no reasonable cause to excuse the effect.

firac.issue: What remedy is appropriate?
firac.facts: Ross remained committed to publishing his views even after School Board direction. The complainant indicated he would not oppose Ross being placed in a non-teaching position.
firac.rule: Human rights remedies aim to remove discrimination and provide relief, not to punish (Simpsons-Sears). Section 20(6.2) permits an order against any party found to have violated the Act.
firac.application: The Board found monitoring, apology, or restricting Jewish students' access inadequate; the only viable relief was to remove Ross from the classroom while minimizing punitive effect. It ordered systemic measures for the Department of Education and directed the School Board to place Ross on an 18-month unpaid leave, appoint him to a non-teaching position if available, terminate him if none arose, and terminate immediately if he published or distributed the identified anti-Semitic materials.
firac.conclusion: Comprehensive remedial order made, including leave of absence, possible non-teaching reassignment, and conditional termination; the Board reserved jurisdiction over implementation.

name_verification.name_in_document: Hugh Owens v. Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission et al.

defining_issues: What standard of review applies to a human rights board of inquiry's determination that a publication contravened s. 14(1)(b) of The Saskatchewan Human Rights Code?

What is the proper meaning and scope of the prohibition in s. 14(1)(b) against publications that expose or tend to expose to hatred, ridicule, belittle or affront dignity, read in light of the Charter guarantees of freedom of expression and religion?
Did Mr. Owens' newspaper advertisement, properly characterized in its full context, contravene s. 14(1)(b) of the Code?
Did the Board of Inquiry and Court of Queen's Bench err by failing to give effect to Mr. Owens' freedom of religion?

firac.issue: What is the applicable standard of review of the board of inquiry's finding that the advertisement violated s. 14(1)(b)?
firac.facts: A human rights board of inquiry found Owens contravened s. 14(1)(b) and the Court of Queen's Bench upheld that result. The Code (s. 32) provides an appeal on questions of law. Boards were ad hoc, staffed by private-practice lawyers without full-time human rights expertise, and operated without a privative clause.
firac.rule: The functional and pragmatic analysis (Pushpanathan; Dr. Q v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of BC) governs standard of review even on statutory appeals: privative clause, tribunal expertise, purpose of the scheme, and nature of the question. Questions of statutory interpretation and general legal reasoning attract correctness (Gould v. Yukon Order of Pioneers; Mossop; Berg).
firac.application: No privative clause and a statutory right of appeal on questions of law; boards had no special expertise; the adjudicative process was not polycentric; and the meaning of 'hatred,' 'ridicule,' 'belittlement' and 'affronts to dignity' are legal concepts informed by constitutional values of equality, freedom of religion and expression. Whether the advertisement offended the Code is not a purely factual question warranting deference.
firac.conclusion: The correctness standard applies; the Court is free to make its own assessment of whether the advertisement offended s. 14(1)(b).

firac.issue: What is the proper meaning and scope of s. 14(1)(b) read consistently with the Charter?
firac.facts: Section 14(1)(b) prohibits publications that expose or tend to expose to hatred, ridicule, belittle or otherwise affront dignity on a prohibited ground; s. 14(2) preserves freedom of expression. The provision directly constrains expression and the dissemination of religious belief.
firac.rule: Statutes are read consistently with the Charter where possible (R. v. Zundel; Rizzo Shoes). In Canada (HRC) v. Taylor the Supreme Court read comparable hate-speech language as reaching only 'unusually strong and deep-felt emotions of detestation, calumny and vilification' of an 'ardent and extreme nature.' Saskatchewan (HRC) v. Bell applied this same threshold to s. 14, including its 'ridicule, belittle or affront dignity' language. Freedom of religion is not absolute (Amselem; Multani; Ross) and religiously motivated speech that harms others is subject to reasonable limits.
firac.application: To be constitutionally valid, s. 14(1)(b) reaches only genuinely extreme expression meeting the Taylor/Bell standard, not merely offensive, distressing or belittling speech, which a robust democracy must tolerate. The provision must be applied objectively—from the perspective of a reasonable person aware of the context—not by the subjective reaction of complainant or publisher. Freedom of religion does not alter this, since s. 14(1)(b) limits religious speech in the same justifiable way it limits speech generally.
firac.conclusion: Section 14(1)(b) captures only speech reaching the extreme threshold of hatred/detestation described in Taylor and Bell, assessed objectively in context.

firac.issue: Did the advertisement, objectively characterized in context, contravene s. 14(1)(b)?
firac.facts: The 1997 ad, published during gay pride week amid an active national debate over sexual orientation rights, cited four Bible passages and depicted two stickmen holding hands overlaid with a 'not permitted' symbol, offered as a bumper sticker. Sexual orientation had only recently become a prohibited ground and an analogous Charter ground.
firac.rule: The objective Bell standard: whether a reasonable person aware of context would understand the speech as exposing the target group to hatred etc. of an ardent and extreme nature; human rights legislation receives a generous, purposive interpretation, and courts must not authoritatively interpret sacred texts.
firac.application: The stickmen were neutral, unlike the demeaning caricatures in Bell, and the 'not permitted' symbol was ambiguous. The Bible citations, though strongly worded, are part of a larger work also associated with love and forgiveness, are open to varied interpretations, and were understood by many to condemn conduct rather than identity. The Board and Chambers judge erred by taking the passages at face value as equivalent to a modern statement that homosexuals should be killed and by ignoring the wider public-debate context. Read as a whole, the ad reads as a position in an ongoing public policy debate, not a message of extreme detestation.
firac.conclusion: The advertisement did not meet the Bell threshold and did not contravene s. 14(1)(b).

firac.issue: Did the tribunals err by failing to consider Mr. Owens' freedom of religion?
firac.facts: All parties accepted Owens published the ad from a sincere, bona fide religious conviction, engaging s. 2(a) of the Charter; the Board said nothing about freedom of religion and the Chambers judge gave it minimal attention.
firac.rule: Freedom of religion includes the right to disseminate belief (Big M) but is not absolute and may be limited where religiously motivated speech harms others (Amselem; Multani; Ross).
firac.application: Although the tribunals gave freedom of religion little or no attention, the validity of s. 14(1)(b) does not change once religion is added, since it justifiably limits religious speech the same way it limits speech generally. The failure did not alter the outcome because the advertisement, properly characterized, did not offend the Code in any event.
firac.conclusion: The tribunals gave freedom of religion inadequate consideration, but the appeal succeeds on the characterization of the advertisement rather than on a distinct religious-freedom ground.

keywords_rationale: K007 (Human rights) is the tier-1 practice area — the case turns on a statutory human rights complaint under The Saskatchewan Human Rights Code. K061 (hate speech) is central: s. 14(1)(b) is a hate-speech style prohibition interpreted through Taylor and Bell. K024 (freedom of expression) and K025 (freedom of religion) are the competing Charter freedoms shaping the interpretation of s. 14(1)(b). K014 (standard of review) was a distinct, decided issue (correctness). K070 (discriminatory messages) captures the specific prohibited practice of publishing a discriminatory representation. K119 (Human Rights Code) identifies the governing statute. K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) are the specific Charter provisions engaged. Weak/borderline: K070 overlaps with K061 but is retained because it names the statutory practice; the antisemitism-focused vocabulary otherwise offered no better fit for a sexual-orientation hate-speech case.

registry_rationale: The court is identified in the header as 'THE COURT OF APPEAL FOR SASKATCHEWAN,' sitting at Regina; there is no separate registry office named beyond that court.

defining_issues: Were the impugned statements capable of, and did they bear, a defamatory meaning?
Were the statements published on an occasion of qualified privilege?
Were the statements fair comment on a matter of public interest?
Were the statements made with malice, defeating the defences of privilege and fair comment?
Were the statements justified in the sense of being substantially true?
Was the plaintiff entitled to Wallace damages for the manner of the termination of her employment?

firac.issue: Were the impugned statements capable of, and did they bear, a defamatory meaning?
firac.facts: Ms. Lane, terminated as Superintendent of School District 68 after issuing a 'Christmas Notice' renaming seasonal school concerts, sued in defamation over six statements by trustees and the Board (the First and Second Harrison, Cowling, Montgomery and Saunders statements, and the Board's press release).
firac.rule: A defamatory statement tends to lower a person in the estimation of right-thinking members of society (Salmon on Torts; Vander Zalm v. Times Publishers). Words injuring one in one's calling must impute a quality detrimental (or the absence of a quality essential) to one's office or profession (Gately on Libel and Slander). The judge decides first whether words are capable of a defamatory meaning, then whether they in fact defamed the plaintiff, construing words in their natural and ordinary meaning as understood by an ordinary person.
firac.application: The court held that the First and Second Harrison, Cowling, Montgomery and Saunders statements merely criticized a single decision or expressed disagreement without imputing any detrimental personal characteristic, and so were not capable of defamatory meaning. The Board Statement, by contrast, went beyond criticism of one decision and implied Ms. Lane was responsible for low staff morale, lack of cooperation and instability, imputing a quality detrimental to her as an education administrator; it was capable of and did defame her.
firac.conclusion: Only the Board Statement was defamatory; the other five statements were not capable of a defamatory meaning.

firac.issue: Were the statements published on an occasion of qualified privilege?
firac.facts: Trustees are elected officials; several statements were made to local newspapers, at a public Board meeting, and (Montgomery) to the National Post; the Board Statement was a press release announcing the search for a new superintendent.
firac.rule: Qualified privilege arises where the maker has a duty or interest to communicate and the recipient a reciprocal interest to receive (Adam v. Ward; Hill v. Church of Scientology). Publication to the world may exceed the privilege absent proper reason (Moises; Parlett v. Robinson). A person answering an attack has privilege limited to matters germane to the attack (Douglas v. Tucker; RTC Engineering).
firac.application: Elected trustees had a duty to keep constituents informed on the publicly controversial Christmas Notice and Ms. Lane's employment; the First and Second Harrison, Cowling and Saunders statements were made on privileged occasions to local media/meetings. The Montgomery Statement to a national newspaper exceeded the privilege as the matter was not of national interest. The Board Statement was not a trustee responding to attack but the employer announcing a termination and was not privileged.
firac.conclusion: Qualified privilege applied to the First and Second Harrison, Cowling and Saunders statements, but not to the Montgomery Statement or the Board Statement.

firac.issue: Were the statements fair comment on a matter of public interest?
firac.facts: Some statements were letters to the editor or comments on the Christmas Notice controversy; others (Second Harrison, Saunders, Board) were statements of fact without stated underlying facts.
firac.rule: Fair comment requires (1) recognizable comment on true facts, not a bare statement of fact, (2) a matter of public interest, and (3) an honest expression of the maker's real view (Vander Zalm v. Times Publishers; Brown, Law of Defamation).
firac.application: The First Harrison and Cowling statements were recognizable comment on true public-interest facts and honestly held, so fair comment applied. The Second Harrison, Saunders and Board statements contained no indication of the facts commented on and were treated as statements of fact, failing the first requirement.
firac.conclusion: Fair comment protected the First Harrison and Cowling statements but not the Second Harrison, Saunders or Board statements.

firac.issue: Were the statements made with malice?
firac.facts: Ms. Lane alleged the defendant trustees harboured personal spite, relying on long lists of prior events; Chair Montgomery and the trustees testified their motives were to inform constituents or express genuine disagreement.
firac.rule: Malice defeats qualified privilege and fair comment. For privilege, malice means a dominant improper motive—desire to injure, or speaking dishonestly or with reckless disregard for truth (Hill; Horrocks v. Lowe). For fair comment, the defence fails only if the maker did not genuinely hold the view expressed (Cheng v. Tse Wai Chun).
firac.application: The court found each defendant's dominant motive was to express genuine disagreement or inform the public, not to injure Ms. Lane; relationships were poor but the evidence did not establish ill-will as the dominant motive for any statement.
firac.conclusion: Malice was not proven for any statement; the applicable defences were not defeated.

firac.issue: Were the statements justified as substantially true?
firac.facts: The defendants pleaded justification for all statements except the Second Harrison Statement, providing extensive particulars (Appendices A and B) regarding poor morale, lack of cooperation and instability during Ms. Lane's tenure.
firac.rule: Truth (justification) is a complete defence; the defendant bears the burden of proving the 'sting' substantially true (Brown, Law of Defamation). The defendant may justify its own pleaded meaning (Miller v. CBC) and is confined to its particulars.
firac.application: The court found it was not inappropriate or an error for Ms. Lane to issue the Christmas Notice, so the First Harrison, Cowling and Montgomery meanings were not proven true. However, on the proven particulars, Ms. Lane did cause poor morale, a lack of cooperation and instability, so the Saunders Statement's poor-morale meaning and the Board Statement were substantially true.
firac.conclusion: The Board Statement was justified as substantially true and the poor-morale sting of the Saunders Statement was true; justification failed for the other statements.

firac.issue: Was the plaintiff entitled to Wallace damages for the manner of her termination?
firac.facts: Ms. Lane was dismissed without cause under an employment contract permitting termination on 12 months' notice or pay; she was informed by telephone on a weekend and claimed the manner was callous, seeking six additional months' salary.
firac.rule: Wallace v. United Grain Growers Ltd. permits an extension of the notice period for bad-faith conduct in the manner of dismissal, but only where the employee was wrongfully dismissed and no express contractual notice term governs; employers must be candid, reasonable, honest and forthright and not unduly insensitive.
firac.application: Ms. Lane was not wrongfully dismissed; her contract expressly fixed 12 months' notice/pay, which she received, precluding an implied reasonable-notice term (Barnard v. Testori). Further, the Board acted honestly and, though telephoning on a weekend was somewhat insensitive, it was not unduly insensitive given the circumstances and prior warning.
firac.conclusion: No Wallace damages were available; the claim failed on all three grounds.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally a defamation action, so K015 (defamation) and its two central defences K016 (fair comment) and K018 (qualified privilege) are core; justification and malice are analysed within these. K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area. The termination claim engaged Wallace/manner-of-dismissal law, supporting K085 (wrongful dismissal) and its tier-1 parent K009 (Labour and employment). The defendants were school trustees and the Board, and the trustees' duties under the School Act framed the privilege analysis, supporting K044 (school board) and its parent K005 (education law). K005 and K044 are somewhat secondary since the legal doctrines are defamation/employment, but the school-governance context is genuinely engaged.

registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: Nanaimo'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Sabbah v Sabbah

defining_issues: Did the respondent have genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove barriers to religious remarriage, such that the court should decline to exercise its powers under s. 21.1(3) of the Divorce Act?
If not, what is the appropriate remedy for the respondent's refusal to provide a Get?

firac.issue: Did the respondent establish genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to give the Get, so as to bar relief under s. 21.1(3)?
firac.facts: The parties married in 2012 and separated in 2020. Ms Sabbah requested a Get in May 2021 and complied with the s. 21.1(2) affidavit procedure. Mr. Sabbah refused to grant the Get until the civil divorce was granted, asserting deeply held religious beliefs, citing passages from Exodus, Deuteronomy and Maimonides and alleging his wife's adultery. However, he provided no independent or expert evidence of the objective content of Jewish law, and his correspondence repeatedly threatened to make the Get 'more expensive' and conditioned it on the outcome of the civil proceedings.
firac.rule: Section 21.1 of the Divorce Act gives the court discretion to refuse relief to a spouse who fails to remove barriers to the other spouse's religious remarriage; under s. 21.1(4) the court may decline to strike pleadings where the refusing spouse establishes 'genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature'. Bruker v Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54 holds that a mere ability to refuse under religious law differs from being prevented by a genuine tenet of belief, and that withholding a Get as leverage is contrary to public policy. Zoughaib v El-Mokadem, 2024 ONSC 292 and S(K) v B(S), 2015 QCCS 3717 apply the same analysis, and H(K) v S(J), 2000 CanLII 18733 (QCCS) treats willingness to give the Get only after civil divorce as evidence of using it as a negotiating weapon.
firac.application: The court found Mr. Sabbah's March 15, 2024 affidavit did not assert religious or conscientious grounds, and his June 11, 2024 affidavit raised them only after being served with the s. 21.1 application. He offered no independent or expert evidence establishing the objective content of the scriptural passages he cited, so his stated beliefs appeared only subjectively binding. Following Zoughaib, the court found the refusal had less to do with genuine religious belief than with anger and leverage: uncontroverted correspondence showed Mr. Sabbah threatening to increase the Get's 'cost', linking it to legal fees and the civil outcome, and stating he might die without signing it. He never denied or addressed this leveraging evidence, and made clear he would give the Get only bundled with conclusion of the civil divorce.
firac.conclusion: The court held Mr. Sabbah failed to establish genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature; his position amounted to using the Get as a bargaining tool contrary to the purpose of s. 21.1.

firac.issue: What remedy should the court grant under s. 21.1(3) given the respondent's failure to remove the barriers?
firac.facts: Ms Sabbah sought an order striking Mr. Sabbah's pleadings and prohibiting further applications until he agrees to give the Get. She also sought significantly enhanced costs.
firac.rule: Section 21.1(3)(c) and (d) of the Divorce Act allow the court to dismiss applications and strike pleadings and affidavits of a non-compliant spouse, subject to appropriate terms; H(K) v S(J) modelled a conditional order allowing refiling once barriers are removed. Costs follow Schedule C of the Rules of Court absent authority justifying enhanced costs.
firac.application: The court allowed the application but abeyanced the actual striking until February 14, 2025 to give Mr. Sabbah an opportunity to file an affidavit confirming all barriers to the religious divorce were removed. Meanwhile no existing or new applications could proceed. On costs, the court was not persuaded the case resembled DN v BN, 2022 BCSC 2029, and found no authority justifying enhanced costs.
firac.conclusion: Application allowed; pleadings to be struck if no compliance affidavit filed by February 14, 2025, with no further participation permitted thereafter; costs awarded per Schedule C, Column One.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a Divorce Act application. K051 (religious divorce (get)) is the central subject — the withholding of a Jewish Get and s. 21.1 of the Divorce Act. K117 (Divorce Act) is the governing statute. K025 (freedom of religion) and K034 (sincerity of belief) are engaged because the respondent invoked deeply held religious beliefs and the court assessed whether his grounds were genuine versus subjectively/objectively valid, drawing on Bruker v Marcovitz. K093 (Jewish) and K098 (rabbi) reflect the religious context and the correspondence with a Rabbi. K048 (custody/access) is a weaker pick, flagged: custody is referenced only as the type of concession the legislation guards against, not directly litigated here — included because the s. 21.1 rationale expressly concerns leveraging custody and support.

registry_rationale: The decision header expressly states 'Registry: Edmonton'.

case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Haldimand and Norfolk v. K.H. (mother) and R.J. (father)

name_verification.name_in_document: Children's Aid Society of Haldimand and Norfolk v. K.H. (mother) and R.J. (father)

defining_issues: Is the child in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b) of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017?
If the child is in need of protection, what disposition is in the child's best interests — a return to the prior CLRA order, a supervision order under s. 101, or a custody order under s. 102?
What access should the father have, and should it be supervised at a third-party facility?

firac.issue: Is the child in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b) CYFSA because of a risk of physical harm?
firac.facts: The father, subject to a criminal harassment/assault charge, resides with paternal grandparents who have long-term opioid addiction (crushing and sniffing medication) and recent cocaine use; a drug-using paternal uncle lives in an unsecured basement; there are firearms and an unverified gun safe in the home; the father would not permit the CAS to fully tour the home and showed no insight into the risks, refusing to complete recommended programming.
firac.rule: Under s. 74(2)(b) CYFSA a child is in need of protection where there is a risk the child is likely to suffer physical harm from the person's failure to adequately care for/supervise/protect, or a pattern of neglect. The risk must be real and likely, not speculative (Children's Aid Society of Rainy River v. B.(C.), 2006 ONCJ 458); intention need not be proven (Jewish Family and Child Service v. K.(R.), 2008 ONCJ 774, aff'd 2009 ONCA 903); a child may be at risk even if conduct is not directed at that child; limited parental capacity may create risk (CAS of Hamilton v. O.(E.), 2009 CanLII 72087).
firac.application: The court found the home unsafe: nascent-at-best recovery from long-term addiction, recent cocaine use by the paternal grandfather, contaminated surfaces accessible to a child, an unsecured area occupied by a drug-using uncle, and unverified storage of medications and firearms. The father, despite parenting strengths in supervised settings, showed no insight into these hazards and failed to complete programming to build capacity, creating a real and likely risk of physical harm. The court declined to find a risk of emotional harm under s. 74(2)(h), holding the specific enumerated harms were not established, and rested the finding on s. 74(2)(b) alone.
firac.conclusion: The child is in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b)(i) and (ii) CYFSA.

firac.issue: What disposition is in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: All parties agreed the child should live full-time with the mother, whose parenting was not in question. The father sought a return to the February 20, 2019 CLRA order (permitting immediate overnight access) or a supervision order so the CAS would remain involved and afford him more access.
firac.rule: Sections 101 and 102 CYFSA govern disposition; s. 101 permits a supervision order (3–12 months), s. 102 permits a custody order deemed made under s. 28 CLRA. Section 101(8) allows no disposition order where unnecessary. Best interests under s. 74(3) govern placement.
firac.application: A supervision order was unnecessary because the mother's parenting required no supervision and continued CAS involvement would unduly burden her; the father did not seek a supervision order to address his own issues and had not complied with the prior temporary supervision order's programming terms. Simply returning to the CLRA order was inappropriate because it imposed no limits on the location of parenting time and would trigger immediate overnight access while the father still lived in the unsafe home. A custody order to the mother with tailored terms best served the child's needs, developmental stage, security within a family, and ties to her mother.
firac.conclusion: The child is placed in the mother's custody under s. 102(1) CYFSA, with protective terms; no supervision order is made.

firac.issue: Should the father's access be supervised at a third-party facility?
firac.facts: The father had only ever parented in supervised settings since May 2019, missed numerous visits, could identify no suitable alternative access location or supervisor, resides in an unsafe home, has anger-regulation difficulties and made inappropriate communications to and about the mother, and did not complete recommended anger/parenting programming.
firac.rule: Access must be determined in the child's best interests under s. 74(3) CYFSA, consistent with the protection concerns underlying the finding.
firac.application: The father's lack of insight into home risks and appropriate access locations, absence of any alternative location or supervisor, history of unsupervised care being non-existent, failure to complete programming, and difficulties regulating emotions all favoured supervised access; direct exchanges risked exposing the child to inappropriate conduct toward the mother. The court ordered weekly two-hour supervised access at Dalhousie Place where accommodable, noting supervision need not be long-term if the father addresses his housing, anger and communication issues.
firac.conclusion: The father shall have weekly (two-hour) supervised access at a third-party facility (Dalhousie Place), subject to availability.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a child protection application under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is central, as disposition and access were decided under the s. 74(3) best-interests test. K048 (custody/access) directly captures the custody order to the mother and the supervised access ruling for the father. K050 (parental support) is weak — child support was discussed but expressly not ordered and left for the parties; included only as the closest available term. K083 (harassment) is a borderline fit — the father's criminal harassment charge, following/surveillance of the mother, and abusive communications were material to the protection and access analysis, though the canonical term leans toward workplace harassment. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated child-protection/CYFSA keyword, so several picks are approximations flagged as weak.

case_name: Trinity Western University v. British Columbia College of Teachers

name_verification.name_in_document: TRINITY WESTERN UNIVERSITY and DONNA GAIL LINDQUIST v. THE BRITISH COLUMBIA COLLEGE OF TEACHERS

defining_issues: Did the BCCT exceed its jurisdiction under the Teaching Profession Act by considering TWU's Community Standards and the religious beliefs of its graduates as discriminatory practices contrary to the public interest?
Was the BCCT's decision patently unreasonable because it was made without any evidence that TWU's Community Standards led or could lead to intolerant conduct by its graduates?

firac.issue: Did the BCCT exceed its jurisdiction by treating TWU's Community Standards (including the requirement to refrain from 'homosexual behaviour') as discriminatory practices contrary to the public interest under s. 4 of the Teaching Profession Act?
firac.facts: TWU, a private evangelical university, requires students to sign Community Standards forbidding conduct 'biblically condemned,' including homosexual behaviour. It applied for approval of its teacher education program. The BCCT Council denied approval on the ground the program followed 'discriminatory practices which are contrary to the public interest and public policy,' relying on its s. 4 mandate to set standards 'having regard to the public interest.'
firac.rule: An administrative body must interpret its enabling statute correctly; a decision based on irrelevant considerations, an improper purpose, or a misinterpretation of jurisdiction-limiting provisions is a nullity (U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault, [1988] 2 SCR 1048; Nipawin, [1975] 1 SCR 382; Roncarelli v. Duplessis, [1959] SCR 121; Prince George v. Payne, [1978] 1 SCR 458). 'Public interest' must be construed in the context of the statute (Lindsay v. Manitoba). The Wednesbury principle requires exclusion of irrelevant matters.
firac.application: The Court held that s. 4 limits the BCCT to those aspects of the public interest bearing on the education, professional responsibility and competence of teachers; it does not confer unlimited authority to promote all public policy. If an applicant meets the BCCT's standards, the College cannot refuse certification merely because of a teacher's religious belief that homosexual behaviour is sinful. However, the Community Standards were not per se irrelevant: the BCCT was entitled to examine the actual conduct of TWU graduates and to consider whether any inappropriate conduct was tied to those Standards.
firac.conclusion: The BCCT was entitled to consider the Community Standards, but only in connection with evidence of graduates' conduct; it could not deny certification based simply on the beliefs expressed in those Standards.

firac.issue: Was the Council's decision patently unreasonable because it rested on no evidence that TWU's Community Standards produced or could produce intolerant teachers?
firac.facts: The BCCT concluded it was 'entitled to anticipate' that graduates who promised to refrain from behaviour labelled sinful might be biased against homosexual students. No evidence supported this. In contrast, the Program Approval Team found TWU graduates competent, roughly 70% taught in public schools, many taught in multicultural, First Nations and other diverse settings, and there was no evidence of problems with pupils.
firac.rule: A tribunal's decision must have a factual basis; a decision based on no evidence, or resting on a premise that cannot withstand rational analysis, is patently unreasonable and made without jurisdiction (Dairy Producers Co-operative v. Teamsters (1993) (Sask CA); Hicks v. Langley Memorial Hospital (1992) (BCSC)).
firac.application: The Council's premise—that TWU graduates would be intolerant because they promised not to engage in homosexual behaviour—required unfounded assumptions. Evidence actually before the Council (the Approval Team report and TWU's submissions on its graduates' successful public-school placements) contradicted the conclusion of intolerance, and further evidence was readily obtainable given the many TWU graduates already teaching. The Council failed to consider the evidence before it and reached a conclusion it could not have reached had it done so.
firac.conclusion: The decision was made without any reasonable evidentiary foundation, was patently unreasonable, and was quashed; the Court declined to address the remaining Charter and natural-justice issues.

keywords_rationale: The case is a judicial review of a professional body's decision, so K001 (Administrative law, the primary tier-1 area), K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review — the patently unreasonable / jurisdiction analysis) are central. K005 (Education law) and K042 (code of conduct) capture the teacher-certification and TWU Community Standards context. K025 (freedom of religion) and K069 (discrimination — here on sexual orientation) reflect the substantive values at stake, and K107/K110 (Charter, s. 2(a)) engage the freedom-of-religion arguments raised. The Charter/s.2(a) picks are somewhat weaker because the Court expressly declined to decide the Charter grounds, but they were squarely argued and frame the dispute; discrimination is engaged because the BCCT's rationale rested on the sexual-orientation discrimination of the Standards.

name_verification.name_in_document: Droit de la famille — 241452

defining_issues: Was the Application for Revocation time-barred under article 347 C.C.P. because it was served beyond the 30-day limit after the defendant became aware of the divorce judgment?
Was the defendant prevented from attending the divorce trial by fraud, surprise or any other cause considered sufficient under article 346 C.C.P., including alleged physical illness?

Does letting the divorce judgment stand tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute under article 345 C.C.P. by reason of the defendant's religious beliefs prohibiting divorce (or the alleged unfairness of the judgment)?

firac.issue: Was the Application for Revocation served within the strict 30-day time limit of article 347 C.C.P.?
firac.facts: The divorce judgment was rendered March 13, 2024 and emailed the same day to the defendant at an address she confirmed was hers and used regularly; she admitted receiving it that day but deletes all emails. A bailiff later served it personally on March 26, 2024, after she initially denied being herself. She served her Application for Revocation on April 22, 2024.
firac.rule: Article 347 C.C.P. requires the application for revocation to be served within 30 days after the party became aware of the judgment; these are strict ('de rigueur') time limits.
firac.application: The preponderance of evidence established that the defendant became aware of the judgment on March 13, 2024 when it was emailed to her and acknowledged received. Serving the application on April 22, 2024 was beyond the 30-day limit; her denial of identity to the bailiff showed she attempted to avoid service.
firac.conclusion: The application was time-barred, and for this reason alone it had to be dismissed.

firac.issue: Was the defendant prevented from defending on the merits by fraud, surprise or any other sufficient cause under article 346 C.C.P.?
firac.facts: The defendant was repeatedly and duly notified of the March 12, 2024 trial date (by court staff, by opposing counsel, and by two judges), had earlier been represented and filed a defence and cross-demand, then ceased to follow her file. She did not attend the trial, which proceeded by default. She alleged a physical illness but produced only old medical documents predating the trial by over a year and gave no testimony or expert report on incapacity.
firac.rule: Article 346 C.C.P. permits revocation of a default judgment where the party was prevented from defending by fraud, surprise or any other cause considered sufficient; carelessness, negligence or laxity is not a sufficient cause. Where health-based incapacity is alleged, expert testimony is generally required (Luft v. Greif; Olivier v. Canada).
firac.application: The evidence showed the defendant knew of the trial date but chose not to attend; her medical documents did not establish any incapacity on the trial date and no expert evidence was adduced. Her failure resulted from her own negligence and carelessness, which cannot ground revocation.
firac.conclusion: No fraud, surprise or other sufficient cause was proven; article 346 was not satisfied.

firac.issue: Does maintaining the divorce judgment bring the administration of justice into disrepute under article 345 C.C.P. because of the defendant's religious beliefs against divorce, or its alleged unfairness?
firac.facts: The defendant claimed deeply held religious beliefs prohibiting divorce prevented her attendance and made the judgment unfair. Yet she had earlier filed an answer, case protocol and cross-demand herself seeking a divorce and partition, never raising religious objections. The judgment partitioned the family patrimony and partnership of acquests equally, based on the plaintiff's full disclosure, while the defendant filed no statements.
firac.rule: Article 345 C.C.P. allows revocation only where letting the judgment stand would tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute; the flaw must be serious and irreparable (Allianz v. SNC-Lavalin; Fabrikant). Marriage and divorce fall under federal jurisdiction; every Canadian has the right to obtain a civil divorce under the Divorce Act. Bruker v. Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54 confirms religious belief cannot defeat the public interest in equality and the right to divorce; s. 21.1 of the Divorce Act prevents using religious-divorce refusal as leverage.
firac.application: The plaintiff had a fundamental right to obtain a divorce notwithstanding the defendant's beliefs. Her belief could not prevent that right and, since she still holds the same belief, revocation would be futile (a new trial would again proceed by default). Her past conduct in seeking a divorce herself undermined the credibility of her religious objection, which was a pretext. The judgment conformed to the public-order partition rules of the Civil Code, and she failed to show any unfairness.
firac.conclusion: Maintaining the judgment does not bring the administration of justice into disrepute; the basis of the judgment is not seriously or irreparably flawed.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area, as the matter concerns revocation of a divorce judgment and partition of the family patrimony. K025 (freedom of religion) and K034 (sincerity of belief) apply because the defendant argued religious beliefs prohibiting divorce and the court assessed—and doubted—the sincerity/probative value of that belief. K117 (Divorce Act) and K120 (Quebec Charter) are engaged because the court relied on the federal right to divorce (including s. 21.1) and the Charter/Quebec Charter analysis from Bruker and Droit de la famille — 22187. K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) reflects the freedom-of-religion constitutional dimension. K051 (religious divorce (get)) is a borderline pick—the case is the inverse (objection to civil divorce rather than get refusal) but the court's reasoning rests squarely on the get/Bruker line of authority; flagged as weaker. No procedural-revocation keyword exists in the vocabulary, so those tier-2 doctrinal points are not captured.
