case_name: Ontario Public School Boards' Association v. Ontario (Attorney General)

name_verification.name_in_document: Ontario Public School Boards' Association et al. and Attorney General of Ontario; Association des conseillers (ères) des écoles publiques de l'Ontario et al., Interveners (heard with Ontario English Catholic Teachers' Association et al. v. Attorney General of Ontario)

defining_issues: Does Bill 160's removal of the local property-taxation power from separate school boards prejudicially affect a right or privilege of the Roman Catholic community with respect to denominational schools contrary to s. 93(1) of the Constitution Act, 1867?
Are the provisions of Bill 160 (Division D) providing for supervision of boards' financial affairs and vesting orders unconstitutional under s. 93(1)?
Does Bill 160 contravene s. 93(1) as it applies to the public school system, i.e. does the public system enjoy 'mirror equality' constitutional protection?
Can the applicants rely on a constitutional convention to preserve the boards' power to levy and determine property taxes?
Do the broad regulation-making and delegation provisions of Bill 160 offend the rule of law by reason of excessive delegation or vagueness?
Does conferring on the Minister of Finance the power to set tax rates by regulation offend ss. 53 and 54 of the Constitution Act, 1867 ('taxation without representation')?

firac.issue: Does Bill 160's removal of the local property-taxation power from separate school boards prejudicially affect Roman Catholic denominational rights under s. 93(1) of the Constitution Act, 1867?
firac.facts: For over 150 years separate school boards could levy local property taxes (a power rooted in s. 7 of the Scott Act of 1863) to supplement provincial grants. Bill 160 repealed the boards' independent power to set and levy school taxes, centralizing all revenue in the province while guaranteeing proportional per-pupil funding.
firac.rule: Section 93(1) protects rights or privileges affecting denominational schools enjoyed by a class of persons by law at Union that are prejudicially affected (Greater Hull; Bill 30 Reference; GMPSB). Protection extends to the means necessary to achieve denominational education (GMPSB), and the right to levy taxes without limit is itself a 'right or privilege with respect to denominational schools' protected by s. 93(1) (Greater Hull).
firac.application: Section 7 of the Scott Act conferred a stand-alone, unqualified right to tax, separate from the s. 20 proportionality right. Though facially non-denominational, that independent financing power was constitutionally guaranteed at Union. Bill 160's proportional funding does not exhaust that right; it leaves the Catholic community hostage to provincially-imposed funding ceilings without any independent means to enhance resources. A 'separate' system implies a means of financing from within the community, so eliminating the taxing power impinges a constitutional right.
firac.conclusion: The taxation power is constitutionally protected; Bill 160, insofar as it removes the taxation power from the Roman Catholic educational community, is unconstitutional as a violation of s. 93(1) and of no force and effect to that extent.

firac.issue: Are Bill 160's Division D supervision and vesting-order provisions unconstitutional under s. 93(1)?
firac.facts: Division D allows the Minister to investigate boards' financial affairs and seek vesting orders where there is a deficit, default, or likelihood thereof, with mandatory revocation where no deficit exists, and a statutory clause protecting denominational aspects.
firac.rule: The test is whether authority to withdraw a right or privilege necessarily operates to the prejudice of the class affected (Ottawa Separate School Trustees v. Ottawa; Re Ottawa Separate Schools). Sufficiently defined standards for imposition and removal of supervision save such provisions.
firac.application: Unlike the indefinite, standardless power struck down in the earlier Ottawa case, Division D imposes supervision only on defined financial grounds and mandates revocation once no deficit exists; it also statutorily reiterates s. 93(1) protection of denominational aspects. The absence of an express court-review invitation is not fatal, and any attempt to preclude review of a s. 93(1) violation would itself be invalid. A separate factual foundation is unnecessary where prejudice would be per se.
firac.conclusion: Division D is, on its face, constitutionally valid; the applicants' submissions are rejected.

firac.issue: Does Bill 160 contravene s. 93(1) as applied to the public school system through a doctrine of 'mirror equality'?
firac.facts: OPSBA argued that because the separate system's rights are measured against the public system, the public system enjoys reciprocal constitutional protection that Bill 160 infringes.
firac.rule: Section 93(1) is protective legislation for the denominational minority (Re Calgary Board of Education; Alberta Public School Boards' Assn.). Adler v. Ontario holds the public system is 'impliedly contemplated' by s. 93 only as a backdrop, immune from Charter attack, but public school rights are not themselves constitutionally entrenched.
firac.application: The 'reciprocity/mirror equality' argument rests on a false syllogism: shared constitutional recognition does not confer identical rights. The public system is contemplated only as a reference point/means to preserve the separate system's Catholicity, not as an independent constitutional goal; the majority may protect itself through the ballot box. Adler is a shield, not a sword to win denominational rights for public schools (following Campbell J. in Fewer School Boards).
firac.conclusion: The mirror-image argument is rejected; the public school system enjoys no entrenched rights under s. 93(1) (except perhaps a right of existence, not necessary to decide).

firac.issue: Can the applicants rely on a constitutional convention to preserve the boards' taxing power?
firac.facts: The applicants argued a constitutional convention protects boards' power to levy and determine property taxes and that Bill 160 breaches it.
firac.rule: Constitutional conventions are not enforced by the courts and cannot invalidate express legal rules (Reference re: Amendment of the Constitution of Canada); s. 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982 did not make conventions justiciable; implicit powers (New Brunswick Broadcasting) are distinct from conventions.
firac.application: Even if such a convention existed, it could not strike down clear legislation. The distinction between non-justiciable conventions and implicit but justiciable constitutional powers defeats the argument; a convention expanding s. 93 against the province's plenary education power is highly unlikely to exist and, in any event, unenforceable.
firac.conclusion: The constitutional-convention submission is rejected.

firac.issue: Do Bill 160's broad delegation and regulation-making powers offend the rule of law through excessive delegation or vagueness?
firac.facts: Bill 160 confers extensive regulation-making powers on the executive, including the Minister of Finance's power to set tax rates, across numerous enumerated subjects.
firac.rule: Wide legislative delegation is constitutionally permissible provided it is explicitly set out (Hodge v. The Queen; Re Gray; Chemicals Reference; A.G. Nova Scotia v. A.G. Canada). A provision is unconstitutionally vague only if it provides no adequate basis for legal debate (Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society).
firac.application: The enabling provisions specify the subjects of regulation with defined headings, satisfying the requirement of explicit delegation. The tax-rate power identifies its object (school purposes) and the collecting bodies, providing an ascertainable basis for legal debate; it is not vague.
firac.conclusion: The rule-of-law/delegation submission is rejected; the delegation is valid and the provisions are not vague.

firac.issue: Does the Minister of Finance's power to set tax rates by regulation offend ss. 53 and 54 of the Constitution Act, 1867?
firac.facts: Section 257.12(1)(b) empowers the Minister of Finance to prescribe school tax rates by regulation without a money bill; the applicants said this is taxation without representation contrary to ss. 53-54 (applied to provinces by s. 90).
firac.rule: Bills imposing taxes must originate in and be recommended to the legislative chamber (ss. 53-54). Case law (National Fish Co.; Chemicals; Canada Assistance Plan Reference) suggests taxing power may not be delegated casually; implicit repeal of constitutional provisions is rejected (R. v. Mercure; Manitoba Language Reference).
firac.application: The court rejected the implicit-repeal theory but held ss. 53-54 are satisfied where the delegation of the taxing power in a legislature-approved bill is clear and explicit, as here. Municipalities and school boards have always validly exercised delegated taxing powers, reinforcing that express delegation suffices.
firac.conclusion: The ss. 53-54 challenge is rejected; the express delegation satisfies those sections.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the primary practice-area keyword: the case turns entirely on s. 93(1), ss. 53-54 and constitutional convention analysis. K005 (Education law) is the co-tier-1 area because the dispute concerns education funding and school governance under the Education Act/Bill 160. K043 (denominational schools) is the most specific keyword for the core holding on Roman Catholic separate school rights and the s. 7 Scott Act taxing power. K044 (school board) captures the governance and financial-supervision issues central to Issues 1-3 and 5. K025 (freedom of religion) is included because the s. 93(1) protection is historically rooted in religious-minority protection, though it is borderline since the court stresses s. 93 is not a general guarantee of religious freedom. K107 (Canadian Charter) is a weaker/borderline pick, engaged only through the discussion of Adler and the Charter s. 2(a)/s. 15 arguments considered in Issue 3.
location_rationale: The heading identifies the court as 'Ontario Court (General Division) Cumming J.' and the entire dispute concerns Ontario legislation (Bill 160/Education Act) and s. 93 rights in Ontario, so the province is Ontario. No sitting city is stated in the decision, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision gives only the Court File Nos. (97-CV-137668; 98-CV-139317) and does not name a registry office or court location, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Her Majesty the Queen v. James Sears and Leroy St. Germaine

defining_issues: Does the six-month procedural maximum for a summarily prosecuted hybrid offence operate as the ceiling, or must the court first determine the fit sentence and then apply the procedural cap?
Should the two counts of wilful promotion of hatred (against women and against Jews) be served concurrently or consecutively?
What is the fit sentence for James Sears for wilfully promoting hatred, and may the requested publication-restricting probation terms be imposed consistent with his Charter freedom of expression?
What is the fit sentence for Leroy St. Germaine, given the Gladue factors and his personal circumstances?

firac.issue: Does the six-month procedural maximum for a summarily prosecuted hybrid offence operate as the ceiling, or must the court first determine the fit sentence and then apply the procedural cap?
firac.facts: Wilful promotion of hatred under s. 319(2) is a hybrid offence; the Crown elected summary conviction, capping the maximum at six months per count. The Crown argued the fit sentence should be determined independently, then limited by that procedural maximum.
firac.rule: Section 718.1 requires proportionality to the gravity of the offence and the offender's responsibility. R. v. Cheddesingh, 2004 SCC 16, holds a maximum sentence need not be reserved for the worst offender. R. v. Solowan, 2008 SCC 62, holds a fit sentence for a summarily prosecuted hybrid offence is neither a function nor a fraction of what could have been imposed on indictment and should not be 'scaled down' from the summary maximum.
firac.application: The Court accepted the Crown's position, concluding it must first determine the appropriate sentence under s. 718.1 and then apply the procedural limitation truncating that sentence. The fit sentence per count (18 months) far exceeded the summary maximum, so the six-month cap applied.
firac.conclusion: The court determines the fit sentence first and then applies the six-month summary procedural cap per count.

firac.issue: Should the two counts of wilful promotion of hatred be served concurrently or consecutively?
firac.facts: Over three years, YWN promoted hatred against two distinct identifiable groups—women and Jews—through many issues, not a single incident. Defence argued the hate publication was 'one continuous transaction' warranting concurrent sentences.
firac.rule: R. v. Grummer, 1983 CanLII 5286 (ON CA): although offences from the same transaction are normally concurrent, that rule does not apply where the offences invade different legally-protected interests.
firac.application: Women and Jews have separate, legally-protected interests; the defendant could have promoted hatred against one and not the other but chose both, repeatedly over three years. Each group's interest was separately invaded.
firac.conclusion: The sentences on the two counts are to be served consecutively.

firac.issue: What is the fit sentence for James Sears, and may publication-restricting probation terms be imposed consistent with his Charter freedom of expression?
firac.facts: Sears, in his mid-fifties, edited YWN over a lengthy period, reaching a purported readership over one million with an online presence, glorifying Nazism, denying the Holocaust, demonizing Jews and dehumanizing women. He authored post-trial editions continuing the same themes. The Crown sought the maximum plus three years' probation prohibiting publishing activities.
firac.rule: Section 718.1 (proportionality); s. 718(2)(a)(ii) (hate-motivation as aggravating). Appellate guidance: R. v. Keegstra, 1996 ABCA 308 (one-year term appropriate) and R. v. Lelas (ONCA) (six months increased to one year for anti-Semitic vandalism). Probation terms must not unduly infringe the Charter right to freedom of expression.
firac.application: Given circumstances far more serious than Lelas, the fit sentence was 18 months per count, but truncated to the six-month summary maximum per count, consecutive, totalling one year. The Court found the proposed publication ban too broad, infringing freedom of expression; Sears remains free to publish lawful content, risking re-charge only if he again promotes hate.
firac.conclusion: Sears sentenced to one year (six months per count, consecutive); no probation imposed.

firac.issue: What is the fit sentence for Leroy St. Germaine given the Gladue factors and his personal circumstances?
firac.facts: St. Germaine, nearly 78 and in poor health, published YWN but did not create the hateful content authored under Sears's editorship. He is Metis, cooperated with police via a videotaped statement, expressed regret, and had a history of positive community work. Gladue report was unavailable; restorative justice proved unhelpful.
firac.rule: Section 718.2(e) and R. v. Gladue, 1999 CanLII 679 (SCC): sanctions other than imprisonment reasonable in the circumstances should be considered, with particular attention to Aboriginal offenders. Section 742.1 conditional sentence preconditions; s. 718.1 proportionality.
firac.application: Gladue factors (intergenerational trauma, institutional discrimination), cooperation, regret, age and ill health reduced his moral blameworthiness, though the gravity of the offence remained high. Denunciation and deterrence could be met by a conditional sentence with a punitive component; he posed no danger serving it at home.
firac.conclusion: St. Germaine sentenced to a 12-month conditional sentence (six months per count, consecutive) served under house arrest with conditions; no probation.

keywords_rationale: The case is a criminal sentencing (K004) for wilful promotion of hatred under s. 319(2) (K115, K067), engaging hate speech generally (K061) and its content: antisemitism (K058), Holocaust denial (K062), and Nazi/white-supremacist glorification (K066). Hate motivation as an aggravating factor engages K060. Freedom of expression (K024) was central to rejecting the publication ban. The targeted group Jews (K093) and the intervening/impacted organizations Friends of Simon Wiesenthal Center (K099) and CIJA (K091) are named. K115 pinpoints the specific charging section. Borderline: K060 overlaps with the s. 718(2)(a)(ii) discussion but is genuinely engaged; the entity picks (K099, K091) are supporting but appear expressly in the community impact statements.
location_rationale: The court file number reads 'Toronto 4817 998' and the Ontario Court of Justice heard the matter in Toronto, as indicated in the court file heading.
registry_rationale: The court file number 'Toronto 4817 998 18-70010807-01;-02' identifies the Toronto registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Watson v. TrojanOne Ltd.

defining_issues: Should the constructive dismissal / harassment action against the individual corporate officers (Harrison and Lee) be struck out on the basis that officers are not personally liable for acts done on behalf of the corporation?
Are the defendants entitled to an order compelling the plaintiff to deliver further particulars?

firac.issue: Should the action against the individual officers be struck out because officers are not personally liable for acts done within their authority on behalf of the corporation?
firac.facts: Watson sued his former employer TrojanOne for constructive dismissal and also named its President/CEO Harrison and Chief Creative Officer Lee. The Statement of Claim alleged that over nine months the two officers subjected him to bullying, racially insensitive, homophobic and sexist remarks, a public physical/verbal altercation, and a poisoned work environment causing anxiety and depression. The officers moved to strike the claim against them personally.
firac.rule: A corporation is a separate legal person; at common law officers are not liable for acts done within their authority on the corporation's behalf. Under the Rule in Said v. Butt, [1920] 3 K.B. 497, and Normart Management, ScotiaMcLeod and Schembri v. Way, an officer may nonetheless be personally liable where there is conduct on the officer's part that is tortious in itself or independent misconduct from that of the corporation; the pleading must specifically address the cause of action asserted against the officer. The elements of intentional infliction of mental distress (Piresferreira v. Ayote; Correia v. Canac Kitchens) are flagrant/outrageous conduct, intent or knowledge of harm, and a visible and provable illness.
firac.application: Perell J. read the Statement of Claim as suing TrojanOne for breach of the employment contract, but suing Harrison and Lee not for inducing that breach but for their own conduct that was tortious in itself or independent misconduct. Although not named, all constituent elements of intentional infliction of mental distress were pleaded: flagrant and outrageous conduct, intent or knowledge of harm, and a resulting visible and provable illness (anxiety and depression requiring treatment). Independent wrongdoing by the officers was therefore alleged.
firac.conclusion: The claim against Harrison and Lee disclosed independent actionable wrongdoing and should not be struck out; the motion to strike was dismissed.

firac.issue: Are the defendants entitled to an order requiring the plaintiff to deliver further particulars?
firac.facts: The defendants served a Demand for Particulars with roughly 100 questions, deemed the response inadequate, and continued to demand more, seeking, for example, all facts 'supportive' of specific allegations about Harrison's and Lee's own conduct.
firac.rule: An order for particulars is discretionary and must be just (Fairbairn v. Sage). Particulars are normally ordered only if they are not within the demanding party's knowledge and are necessary to enable a response (Fairbairn; Physicians' Services Inc. v. Cass). The court takes a realistic, pragmatic approach (Ontario v. Rothmans Inc.), the standard is the same in simplified procedure (Big Green Property Services), and the motion usually fails unless supported by an affidavit that particulars are not known and are needed to plead, unless the allegations are so bald that particulars are obviously necessary (Steiner v. Lindzon).
firac.application: The defendants filed no affidavit deposing that they needed the particulars to plead, and since the allegations concerned the conduct of Harrison and Lee themselves, they could not claim the facts were outside their own knowledge. Most demands sought facts supportive of allegations, which are matters for examinations for discovery, not proper demands for particulars. The objection that the claim exceeded the monetary limit for simplified procedure was answered by Rule 76 and had no bearing on the motion.
firac.conclusion: The defendants failed to make out a case for particulars; the demand for particulars was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the primary tier-1 area, the action being for constructive dismissal. K085 (wrongful dismissal) captures the constructive dismissal claim at the heart of the pleading. K083 (harassment) reflects the pleaded bullying and poisoned work environment. K002 (Civil litigation) covers the procedural core actually decided — the motion to strike pleadings and the demand for particulars. K119 (Human Rights Code) is engaged because damages were claimed under the Ontario Human Rights Code for a poisoned work environment. K082 (employment discrimination) is a borderline/weaker pick tied to the pleaded discriminatory remarks and poisoned environment, but is secondary since the decision turned on pleadings principles rather than the merits of any discrimination claim.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'ONTARIO / SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE', establishing the province as Ontario. No city is stated in the heading or reasons; although the corporate defendant's headquarters are in Toronto and the court file number (CV-15-534821) is consistent with a Toronto civil filing, the text does not expressly identify the sitting city, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision gives the court file number CV-15-534821 but does not expressly name a registry office, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Warman v. The National Post Company et al. [Indexed as: Warman v. National Post Co.]

defining_issues: What is the governing default rule for documentary discovery under the amended Rules of Civil Procedure — 'broad and liberal' relevancy or proportionality?
Is a defendant in a defamation action who pleads justification entitled to production of a mirror image of the plaintiff's computer hard drive, or to broad electronic discovery of it?
To what extent may a defamation defendant use discovery to support a plea of justification or to establish the plaintiff's bad character in mitigation of damages?

firac.issue: What is the governing default rule for documentary discovery under the amended Rules of Civil Procedure — 'broad and liberal' relevancy or proportionality?
firac.facts: The action was commenced under the simplified procedure (Rule 76) for an apology and damages capped at $50,000, yet one of ten defendants delivered a 145-paragraph defence and moved for an extensive forensic analysis of the plaintiff's hard drive, raising the question of what discovery is proportionate.
firac.rule: Rule 1.04(1.1) requires orders proportionate to the importance and complexity of the issues and the amount involved; Rules 29.1 (discovery plan), 29.2 (proportionality in discovery) and 29.2.03 set out the considerations; the Master adopted the eight-factor proportionality test from Rowe Entertainment, Inc. v. William Morris Agency, Inc. (S.D.N.Y. 2002) supplementing U.S. Federal Rule 26(b)(2)(C), and endorsed the Sedona Canada Principles and the analysis of Netzorg and Kern.
firac.application: The Master held that the amendment from documents 'relating to' to those 'relevant to' a matter in issue signalled the abandonment of 'broad and liberal' discovery. Proportionality must be the starting point, not an afterthought, with relevancy remaining only a threshold requirement rather than a licence to unlimited production. He applied the eight Rowe factors and the Rule 29.2.03 considerations to the request.
firac.conclusion: The default rule of discovery is proportionality; the 'broad and liberal' standard is abandoned, so that relevancy is part of, but not the starting point of, the test for permissible discovery.

firac.issue: Is a defamation defendant who pleads justification entitled to production of a mirror image of the plaintiff's computer hard drive?
firac.facts: Levant sought a mirror image of Warman's personal computer hard drive (or examination by an expert) to test his theory that Warman authored the 'Hateful Posting' and used false personas; Warman produced an expert report stating his computer was not on when the posting was made and denied authorship.
firac.rule: A 'document' includes electronic data (Rule 1.03, Rule 30.01(1)(a); s. 31.8 Canada Evidence Act). Case law (Nicolardi v. Daley; Vector Transportation v. Traffic Tech; Northwest Mettech; Innovative Health Group v. Calgary Health Region) requires convincing evidence of a real likelihood of undisclosed relevant documents before a hard-drive inspection; a mirror image is generally not producible, and any examination must be tightly circumscribed to protect irrelevant/private data.
firac.application: Applying proportionality and the Rowe factors, and mindful that the plaintiff had deliberately limited his claim to a simplified, economical proceeding and that Levant appeared to seek the data for collateral uses, the Master refused sweeping access. He allowed only very limited, defined searches (specified personas, IP addresses, related metadata) of a mirror image by an independent, mutually acceptable expert bound by a non-disclosure agreement and Form 53 undertaking, with Levant to fund the expert initially.
firac.conclusion: No mirror-image production or broad access was granted; only a narrowly circumscribed forensic examination of very limited areas of the hard drive by an independent expert was ordered.

firac.issue: To what extent may a defamation defendant use discovery to support justification or to establish the plaintiff's bad character in mitigation?
firac.facts: Levant pleaded a broad justification with detailed particulars and sought documents about Warman's false personas and reputation, arguing his knowledge of Warman's conduct predated the pleading; Warman argued this was a fishing expedition to found new defences and attack his character.
firac.rule: Longstanding defamation-discovery limits (Care Canada v. CBC; I.B.E.W. v. Pacific Newspaper Group; Kent v. Kehoe; Pizza Pizza v. Toronto Star adopting Polly Peck; Scott v. Sampson; Di Poce v. Simpson; Cameron v. Pacific Press; Brown, The Law of Defamation): a defendant pleading justification bears the onus to prove substantial truth, may not use discovery to find a defence unknown at pleading, cannot justify by proof of other reprehensible conduct, and in mitigation may adduce only general bad-reputation evidence, not specific acts of misconduct; the court retains discretion to protect the plaintiff from oppression.
firac.application: The Master declined to treat a broad, generalized plea of justification with particulars as equivalent to a properly particularized specific defence, refusing to let a party 'pry open Pandora's box (or hard drive)' through mitigation-based pleading. Documents concerning Warman's other complaints, litigation threats, employment, funding, and reputation were held irrelevant or of marginal relevance, and most requests were answered as 'no such documents' or requiring no further response.
firac.conclusion: A defendant is not entitled to sweeping discovery by virtue of a broad, generalized plea of justification; discovery was confined to material relevant to whether Warman authored the posting, and character/mitigation-based requests were refused.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area: the decision turns on civil-procedure discovery and proportionality. K015 (defamation) is central — this is a libel action and the analysis concerns defamation-specific discovery limits. K016 (fair comment) applies because Levant pleaded both justification and fair comment. K024 (freedom of expression) is engaged through Levant's free-speech posture and the epilogue's discussion of Charter values (Warman v. Wilkins-Fournier). K061 (hate speech), K063 (online hate/social media) and K066 (white supremacism) capture the factual backdrop — the 'Hateful Posting', neo-Nazi/white-supremacist websites and CHRC hate-messaging complaints; these are contextual rather than doctrinally decided, so they are somewhat weaker picks. K072 (human rights tribunal) reflects the CHRT/CHRC proceedings underlying the dispute, again more background than holding. No controlled-vocabulary term precisely captures 'discovery/proportionality/electronic documents', so K002 carries the procedural core.
location_rationale: The decision identifies the court as the 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' and applies Ontario's Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, confirming the province is Ontario. No city or hearing location is stated in the text.
registry_rationale: No court registry or office location is stated anywhere in the endorsement; only the court (Ontario Superior Court of Justice) and the presiding officer (Master Short) are identified.

case_name: C.A.S. of London and Middlesex v. T.Y.

name_verification.name_in_document: Children's Aid Society of London and Middlesex v. T.Y.

defining_issues: Was the infant A.D.Y. a child in need of protection within the meaning of s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
What evidence may the court consider on the protection (finding) phase — is post-apprehension evidence admissible?

If protection is found, was a supervision order returning the child to the mother adequate, or was a s. 57.1 custody order to the father and paternal grandparents warranted in the child's best interests?
What access order to the mother was in the child's best interests?

firac.issue: Was the infant A.D.Y. a child in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
firac.facts: A.D.Y. was apprehended three days after birth. The mother, T.Y., had a lengthy history of aligning herself with physically and emotionally abusive men (M.S., L.B., E.P.), was assaulted by her co-tenant E.P. days after the baby's apprehension, made unverifiable claims about previously deceased twins, refused a fresh psychiatric assessment initially, and had a very weak personal support system. Dr. Sudermann's parenting capacity assessment found no strong attachment, poor conflict-resolution patterns, and a real risk the child would be exposed to unsafe or problematic people.
firac.rule: Section 37(2) CFSA defines a child in need of protection to include a child who has suffered or is at risk of physical harm, or is at risk of emotional harm, resulting from the parent's failure to care for, supervise or protect the child, or pattern of neglect. Risk of harm must be real and not speculative (Jewish Family and Child Service of Toronto v. R.K., 2008 ONCJ 774, aff'd 2009 ONCA 903; Children's Aid Society of Ottawa-Carlton v. T. and T.). A pervasive pattern of exposing a child to domestic abuse is sufficient. Expert evidence may support a finding of risk of emotional harm (N.V.C. v. CCAS of Toronto, 2017 ONSC 796).
firac.application: Relying on Dr. Sudermann's assessment, the court found the risk of harm to A.D.Y. was real and not speculative. The mother's demonstrated pattern of forming relationships with violent, unpredictable men exposed the child to a real risk of physical harm, and her instability, poor judgment and absence of a stable support network created a risk of emotional harm. The court found strong similarities to Jewish Family and Child Service v. R.K.
firac.conclusion: A.D.Y. was found to be a child in need of protection.

firac.issue: May the court consider post-apprehension evidence on the protection (finding) phase of a child protection hearing?
firac.facts: Much of the evidence supporting protection concerns arose after the apprehension, including the E.P. assault days after the baby was taken and the mother's continued conduct during access and parenting programs. Counsel objected to certain hearsay paragraphs in the social worker's affidavit.
firac.rule: Following Children's Aid Society of Hamilton-Wentworth v. K.R. and C.W., [2001] O.J. No. 5754, and the reasoning approved in Children's Aid Society of Brant v. J.A.T., 2005 ONCJ 302 and Catholic Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto v. C.M., [1994] 2 S.C.R. 165, the relevant time period for facts on a finding of protection is flexible; only facts related solely to disposition are statutorily excluded. The child-centred, best-interests purpose of the Act supports admitting accurate, updated information.
firac.application: The court adopted the flexible approach, permitting post-apprehension evidence to be assessed alongside pre-apprehension evidence. Hearsay paragraphs in the affidavit were admitted for the limited purpose of showing the statements were made and formed the basis for the Society's investigation and action.
firac.conclusion: Post-apprehension evidence was properly admissible on the protection phase and was considered in reaching the finding.

firac.issue: Was a supervision order returning the child to the mother adequate, or was a s. 57.1 custody order to the father and paternal grandparents warranted?
firac.facts: The Society, joined by the father J.M.1, sought a s. 57.1 custody order placing A.D.Y. with J.M.1 and his parents. The child had thrived in the paternal family's care since July 2016. The mother had shown inconsistent parenting, resisted coaching, and had a weak support system; Dr. Sudermann remained guarded about her prognosis. J.M.1, though diagnosed with stable long-term schizophrenia, was stable, medication-free, symptom-free and provided attentive care with grandparental support.
firac.rule: Section 57(3) CFSA requires the least disruptive alternative; the court must not remove a child unless satisfied less disruptive alternatives would be inadequate. Per Windsor-Essex CAS v. T.B., [2012] O.J. No. 4481, a s. 57.1 custody order may not be considered until the court is satisfied that leaving the child with the pre-intervention caregiver under supervision would be inadequate. Principles of fundamental justice apply (New Brunswick (Minister of Health) v. G.(J.), 1999 SCC), and courts must avoid imposing middle-class standards (Re Brown; CAS of Hamilton v. E.O., 2009 CanLII 72087).
firac.application: The court found a supervision order returning A.D.Y. to T.Y. inadequate because her impulsivity and poor judgment could result in quick, sudden risk to the child leaving no time for Society intervention, and because supervision depends on willing acceptance of monitoring which T.Y. resisted. Having found supervision inadequate, the court proceeded to the custody request and found joint custody with J.M.1 and grandparents best met A.D.Y.'s needs, ensuring continuity, safeguarding his settled family placement and obviating the risks identified by Dr. Sudermann.
firac.conclusion: A supervision order was rejected; a s. 57.1 order placing A.D.Y. in the joint custody of J.M.1, J.M.2 and B.M. was made in the child's best interests.

firac.issue: What access order to the mother was in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: There was significant antipathy between T.Y. and the grandparents, who wished to avoid contact with her. T.Y. lived in London while the paternal family lived in Woodstock; she was willing to bus to Woodstock and stay with W.E. Dr. Sudermann recommended supervised, biweekly access at the Merrymount facility, cautioning against overnight/weekend access and over-frequent exchanges.
firac.rule: Section 58(1) CFSA authorizes an access order with conditions following disposition; the test is the child's best interests (Children's Aid Society of Haldimand & Norfolk v. D.(R.), 2011 ONSC 4857).
firac.application: Adopting Dr. Sudermann's recommendations and weighing the parties' commitments, the antipathy between T.Y. and the grandparents, and the distance between cities, the court ordered supervised biweekly access for three hours at the Woodstock Merrymount centre (or Oxford CAS), with costs shared, and endorsed a gradual relaxation of supervision over time upon successful visits.
firac.conclusion: T.Y. was granted supervised biweekly access of three hours, with conditions and provision for future relaxation of supervision in the child's best interests.

name_verification.name_in_document: Hedy Blank v. Howard Blank

defining_issues: Do the defendant's acts — publishing family and privileged documents on a website, calling his sister's employer, and leaving menacing voicemail messages — constitute civil faults under the Civil Code of Québec and unlawful interference with rights protected by the Quebec Charter?
Did those faults cause compensable moral damages to the plaintiff?
Was the unlawful interference with the plaintiff's Charter rights intentional so as to justify an award of punitive damages, and in what amount?

firac.issue: Do the defendant's acts constitute civil faults and unlawful interference with the plaintiff's rights under the Civil Code and Quebec Charter?
firac.facts: After their mother's will favoured Hedy, her brother Howard, angry that she would not submit the estate to the Rabbinical Court (Beth Din), created a website ('Hedy's troubles') posting the will's bequests, a Beth Din letter naming Hedy and her home address, a privileged letter to her lawyer, and other private correspondence; he also telephoned the principal of the Orthodox Jewish school where she taught to ask what would happen to her for defying Jewish law, and left menacing, malicious voicemail messages.
firac.rule: Arts. 3, 7, 35 and 36(2) and 36(6) C.c.Q. protect reputation, privacy, and private communications/correspondence, and prohibit exercising a right with intent to injure or in bad faith; art. 1457 C.c.Q. establishes extracontractual liability for fault. Sections 4, 5 and 9 of the Quebec Charter protect the safeguard of dignity, honour and reputation, respect for private life, and non-disclosure of confidential information.
firac.application: The court found the website targeted Hedy's tight-knit Orthodox community and disclosed private and even privileged, address-bearing information; posting the lawyer's privileged letter was an indefensible invasion of privacy under arts. 35 and 36; posting the will and Beth Din letter breached her privacy and dignity; even documents Howard received were used with intent to injure contrary to art. 7. The call to the principal was a deliberate attempt to jeopardize her employment and reputation, a fault under art. 1457 and ss. 4, 5 and 9. The malicious messages, though private, were left with intent to injure under arts. 7 and 1457 and s. 4.
firac.conclusion: Each set of acts constituted a civil fault and an unlawful interference with Hedy's Charter rights.

firac.issue: Did the faults cause compensable moral damages?
firac.facts: Hedy testified to horror and shame, fear of losing her job (her family's sole income given her husband's terminal leukemia), fear that her six children could not marry in the community, social ostracism and possible excommunication, plus loss of sleep, trembling, paranoia, hives, migraines and teeth-gnashing; her mother had died less than a year earlier and her husband was dying.
firac.rule: Art. 1457 C.c.Q. permits recovery of moral damages caused by fault; the 'thin skull rule' provides that a wrongdoer takes the victim in the state she is in when the harm is caused (Baudouin & Deslauriers, La responsabilité civile).
firac.application: The court found her testimony credible and the harm real; even had Howard been unaware of her vulnerable circumstances, he would remain liable for the aggravated damages, and here he was fully aware. No defamation claim was needed as the harm to her emotional wellbeing was established.
firac.conclusion: Hedy was awarded the full $25,000 claimed in moral damages, with interest and the additional indemnity from the date of service, September 28, 2006.

firac.issue: Was the interference intentional so as to warrant punitive damages, and in what amount?
firac.facts: Howard, an experienced businessman, deliberately chose the website's contents despite his brothers telling him he was going too far; he acted out of hate, malice and a desire for revenge, and knew of Hedy's other hardships.
firac.rule: Section 49, para. 2 of the Quebec Charter allows punitive damages for unlawful AND intentional interference; the test is intentionality of the consequences (the interference with the right), not merely of the act (St-Ferdinand, 1996 CanLII 172 (SCC)). Art. 1621 C.c.Q. requires assessing the gravity of the fault and the debtor's patrimonial situation.
firac.application: The court held the interference was clearly intentional: Howard knew his conduct would harm Hedy's dignity, honour, reputation, privacy and confidential information, and intended exactly that to achieve revenge. The fault was very serious and aggravated by his knowledge of her grief and her husband's illness, but in light of the moral damages already awarded the $50,000 claimed was excessive.
firac.conclusion: Punitive damages were set at $25,000, with interest and the additional indemnity running only from the date of judgment.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 area: the case is a civil claim for extracontractual liability (art. 1457 C.c.Q.), invasion of privacy and Charter damages. K083 (harassment) captures the core wrong — a campaign of harassing conduct against the sister. K054 (wills/estates) reflects that the entire dispute arises from the mother's will and the estate. K120 (Quebec Charter) is central because liability and both damage awards rest on ss. 4, 5, 9 and 49 of the Charter. K071 (human dignity) maps to the s. 4 right to safeguard of dignity, honour and reputation. K026 (halacha) applies given the Beth Din/Rabbinical Court and the demand to resolve the estate under Jewish law. K093 (Jewish) and K097 (Orthodox/Hasidic community) situate the parties and explain why targeting Hedy's community caused the harm. K071 is a slightly loose fit since it sits under statutory human rights, but the dignity concept is directly engaged.
location_rationale: The header states 'SUPERIOR COURT', 'PROVINCE of QUÉBEC', 'DISTRICT of MONTREAL' and court file No. 500-17-033071-062, indicating the Quebec Superior Court sitting in Montreal.
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the 'DISTRICT of MONTREAL' as the judicial district, so the registry is Montreal.

case_name: Ontario (Minister of Health) v. Grassroots for Affordable Jewish Education Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: Ontario (Minister of Health) v. Grassroots for Affordable Jewish Education Inc.

defining_issues: Did the motion judge err in concluding that the respondents had a reasonable prospect of satisfying the Bedford/Carter test for revisiting the binding precedent of Adler v. Ontario, such that their application to fund Jewish day schools should not be struck?
Did the motion judge err by relying on facts and circumstances that were not new or that did not fundamentally shift the parameters of the debate?
Did the motion judge err by relying on the dissenting opinions in Adler to question the force of the majority's s. 93 analysis?
Did the motion judge err in concluding that developments in international law (the presumption of conformity) had a reasonable prospect of meeting the Bedford/Carter test?
Did the motion judge err in concluding that the addition of s. 93A to the Constitution Act, 1867 had a reasonable prospect of meeting the Bedford/Carter test?

firac.issue: Was it an error to conclude the respondents had a reasonable prospect of meeting the Bedford/Carter test to revisit Adler on a motion to strike?
firac.facts: Members of the Jewish community sought public funding for Jewish day schools, arguing that funding Roman Catholic separate schools while not funding Jewish day schools breaches ss. 2(a) and 15(1) of the Charter. Ontario moved to strike, relying on Adler v. Ontario, which directly determined these issues. The motion judge refused to strike, finding a reasonable prospect the respondents could satisfy the test to revisit binding precedent.
firac.rule: Under Canada (Attorney General) v. Bedford, 2013 SCC 72 and Carter v. Canada, 2015 SCC 5, a lower court may revisit binding precedent only where (1) new legal issues are raised or (2) a change in circumstances or evidence fundamentally shifts the parameters of the debate. R. v. Comeau, 2018 SCC 15 stresses the exception is narrow, requiring a profound alteration of the underlying social context. On a motion to strike the court must identify a reasonable prospect the record could establish such a shift.
firac.application: The Court found that Adler directly decided the issues raised, and none of the facts, circumstances, or alleged legal developments had a reasonable prospect of meeting the strict Bedford/Carter test. The motion judge's reliance on cumulative but individually insufficient factors, on the Adler dissents, on international law, and on s. 93A each constituted error, leaving no reasonable prospect of revisiting Adler.
firac.conclusion: Yes; it was an error to find a reasonable prospect of success. The appeal was allowed and the application dismissed.

firac.issue: Was it an error to rely on facts and circumstances that were not new?
firac.facts: The respondents relied on evidence of the threat to the long-term survival of the Jewish community, the importance and rising cost of Jewish day school education, and a growing recognition of the benefits of diversity. The motion judge acknowledged these facts were not individually sufficient but found them 'relevant' as part of an overall matrix of changes.
firac.rule: The Bedford/Carter/Comeau standard requires evidence that fundamentally shifts the parameters of the debate—a profound alteration of the social context; small shifts in various facts are insufficient.
firac.application: The evidence replicated the circumstances already before the Court in Adler, where the survival of the religious community and s. 27 multicultural/diversity considerations were squarely addressed, including in L'Heureux-Dubé J.'s dissent. Cumulating individually insufficient factors could not meet the strict test.
firac.conclusion: Yes; it was an error to treat these non-new facts as relevant to meeting the Bedford/Carter test.

firac.issue: Was it an error to question the force of the majority analysis in Adler by relying on its dissents?
firac.facts: The motion judge declined to accept that s. 93 together with s. 29 of the Charter could bear no other interpretation, noting four of nine justices in Adler had reached a different conclusion, and relied on proposed developments (state neutrality expanding s. 2(a); positive obligations to legislate under s. 15(1)).
firac.rule: Vertical stare decisis binds lower courts to the majority reasons of the Supreme Court of Canada (Carter, para. 44). Adler held that s. 93 of the Constitution Act, 1867 is a comprehensive code of denominational school rights immune from Charter (s. 2(a) and s. 15(1)) scrutiny; one part of the Constitution cannot invalidate another (Reference re Bill 30).
firac.application: No subsequent appellate authority had adopted or developed the Adler dissents, so the majority analysis remained binding. Because s. 93 is a comprehensive code, proposed developments in s. 2(a) and s. 15(1) were irrelevant absent a significant change in the interpretation of s. 93 itself. Treating the Court of Appeal's Charter analysis as still relevant was likewise an error given the binding SCC decision.
firac.conclusion: Yes; questioning the majority's s. 93 analysis via the dissents was an error, and the proposed Charter developments had no reasonable prospect of meeting the test.

firac.issue: Was it an error to conclude developments in international law had a reasonable prospect of meeting the Bedford/Carter test?
firac.facts: The motion judge found the 'presumption of conformity' in international law was a new development applied at the start of the interpretive process, capable of affecting the interpretation of ss. 2(a), 15(1), s. 93 and s. 29.
firac.rule: Constitutional interpretation follows the purposive approach in R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., beginning with text, history and Charter objects. Per Quebec (AG) v. 9147-0732 Québec Inc., 2020 SCC 32, international law only supports or confirms an interpretation reached through Big M; it does not define the scope of Charter rights.
firac.application: It was an error to apply the presumption of conformity at the outset. Given Adler's interpretation of s. 93 as a complete code rooted in the historical Confederation compromise, international instruments on the right to education without discrimination could not invalidate s. 93—just as s. 15(1) cannot—so they offered no reasonable prospect of revisiting Adler.
firac.conclusion: Yes; the treatment of international law was a separate error with no reasonable prospect of meeting the test.

firac.issue: Was it an error to conclude the addition of s. 93A had a reasonable prospect of meeting the Bedford/Carter test?
firac.facts: In 1997, by bilateral amendment under s. 43 of the Constitution Act, 1982, s. 93A was added providing that paragraphs (1)–(4) of s. 93 do not apply to Quebec. The respondents argued the historical compromise underlying s. 93 no longer exists because Quebec has exited it.
firac.rule: Section 43 permits amendments applying to one or more but not all provinces only with authorization of Parliament and the legislative assembly of each province to which the amendment applies. A province cannot alter the constitutional rights of another province's residents without its assent (Havercroft v. Ontario, 2022 ONSC 6651).
firac.application: Section 93A applies only to Quebec. The Confederation history and wording of s. 93 remain unchanged for Ontario; only Quebec exempted itself. To hold that Quebec's exemption changes Ontario residents' rights would let Quebec and Ottawa alter Ontario's constitutional position without its input, which cannot be correct. Ontario could pursue its own amendment but has not.
firac.conclusion: Yes; it was an error to find s. 93A raised a reasonable prospect of changing the effect of s. 93 on Ontario residents.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the primary practice area, as the case turns on s. 93 of the Constitution Act, 1867 and its interplay with the Charter. K005 (Education law) and K043 (denominational schools) capture the subject matter—public funding of Jewish day schools versus Roman Catholic separate schools. K025 (freedom of religion) and K023 (equality rights) are the underlying Charter rights invoked, with K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) and K109 (Charter s. 15) the specific provisions, and K107 (Canadian Charter) the governing instrument. K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) reflect the claimant group and the community-survival evidence central to the record. I did not add a stare decisis/precedent keyword because the vocabulary lacks one; the Bedford/Carter revisiting-precedent framework is the doctrinal core but has no dedicated ID. K094 is slightly weaker but supported by the community-survival evidence discussed.
location_rationale: The decision states 'HEARD at Toronto: June 11, 2024' and is issued by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Divisional Court, placing it in Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The Divisional Court file no. 521/23 is recorded and the matter was heard at Toronto; the Divisional Court of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice sitting at Toronto is the registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: REGINA v. ADAMS
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The style of cause matches. No neutral citation appears in the reported text; the decision is that of the County Court of the County of Halifax, Nova Scotia, whereas the supplied citation designates '(NS SC)'.

defining_issues: Were the four seized magazines 'obscene' within the meaning of ss. 150(8) and 150A of the Criminal Code so as to justify forfeiture?
What legal test governs obscenity — the Hicklin 'tend to deprave and corrupt' test, the community-standards test, or both — and is s. 150(8) an exhaustive definition?
Is the determination of contemporary Canadian community standards a question of law or of fact, and how is it to be established?

firac.issue: Were the four seized magazines obscene within ss. 150(8) and 150A of the Criminal Code, warranting forfeiture?
firac.facts: A Halifax detective purchased and then seized 30 copies of designated 'girlie magazines' (Ecstasy, Misty, Blaze and Flirt) kept for sale at the Maritime Campus Book Store; each consisted overwhelmingly of nude and semi-nude photographs of women emphasizing breasts and buttocks, with brief stories aimed at erotic wish-fulfilment.
firac.rule: Section 150(8) deems a publication obscene where a dominant characteristic is the undue exploitation of sex; the Crown bears the onus of proving obscenity (R. v. Brodie; R. v. Dominion News & Gifts). Undue exploitation is measured against contemporary Canadian community standards and, where relevant, the internal necessities of the work.
firac.application: Examining each magazine as a whole, the judge found the sole purpose of each was erotic stimulation directed at the sexually inadequate or immature; the sexual exploitation pervaded and dominated each publication, exceeding anything borderline and going well beyond the 'flippant, saucy, risqué' material tolerated. The minor stories, cartoons and reportage did not displace the dominant pornographic character.
firac.conclusion: Each of the four magazines was held obscene within ss. 150(8) and 150A; the Court ordered the material forfeited to Her Majesty in right of Nova Scotia.

firac.issue: What test governs obscenity and is s. 150(8) exhaustive?
firac.facts: The respondent, appearing in person, relied on an up-to-date Criminal Code and the UK Obscene Publications Act, 1959. The judge undertook an extensive review of R. v. Curl, R. v. Hicklin, Brodie and Dominion News.
firac.rule: In R. v. Munster (N.S.S.C. in banco) it was held that s. 150(8) does not purport to be an exhaustive definition and that matter not caught by it may still be obscene, and that the Hicklin test ('tendency to deprave and corrupt those into whose hands it may fall') remains applicable. That decision binds the County Court, whereas contrary Ontario authority (R. v. C. Coles Co.) does not.
firac.application: Following Munster, the judge treated s. 150(8) as non-exhaustive and applied both the statutory community-standards analysis and the Hicklin test. He reconciled propositions 4.1 (internal necessities) and 5.1 (community standards) so that community standards form the ultimate measure of undueness.
firac.conclusion: Section 150(8) is not exhaustive; the magazines were obscene both under the statutory community-standards test and, on the alternative Hicklin analysis, as tending to corrupt those likely to receive them.

firac.issue: Is contemporary Canadian community standards a question of law or fact, and how is it determined?
firac.facts: The judge had only the seized material and evidence of sale; no expert or opinion evidence of community standards was tendered.
firac.rule: Community standards must be contemporary and Canadian, reflecting a general average of community thinking, not the standards of the most permissive or most puritan (Brodie; Dominion News). Where close to the borderline, tolerance is preferred to proscription.
firac.application: Given the expanded appeal rights under s. 150A(5) allowing appeals on fact, the primacy of the impugned material as 'real evidence', and the reasoning in Brodie, the judge concluded the content of community standards is a question of fact, ascertainable through judicial notice supplemented by wide reading rather than through party evidence. Surveying various commentators, he concluded the Canadian average condemns pornography deliberately designed as an aphrodisiac.
firac.conclusion: Community standards are a question of fact, established by the tribunal's general knowledge; measured against them the magazines constituted undue exploitation of sex.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary practice area — this is a Criminal Code s. 150A forfeiture proceeding for obscene publications. K024 (freedom of expression) is genuinely engaged: the judge frames the case as balancing free expression against preservation of moral standards. K003 (Constitutional law) reflects that public-policy free-expression analysis. The controlled vocabulary is oriented to antisemitism/hate-speech and Jewish-law matters and contains no 'obscenity' or 'community standards' term, so no closer fit exists. defining_issues: What is the standard of review applicable to the Board of Arbitration's decision that it lacked jurisdiction to award aggravated and/or punitive damages?

Did the Board of Arbitration have jurisdiction to award aggravated and/or punitive damages to the grievor after finding the college dismissed him without just cause in breach of the collective agreement?

firac.issue: What is the standard of review applicable to the Board's ruling that it lacked jurisdiction to award aggravated and/or punitive damages?
firac.facts: After reinstating Mr. Olivo and finding an unjust dismissal, the tripartite Board in its Second Award concluded it had no jurisdiction to award aggravated or punitive damages, treating those claims as tort claims outside the collective agreement. The Union sought judicial review of that jurisdictional determination.
firac.rule: A tribunal's decision about whether it has jurisdiction (i.e. deciding upon jurisdiction rather than acting within it) must be correct: Dayco (Canada) Ltd. v. C.A.W.–Canada (1993); Royal Oak Mines Inc. v. Canada (LRB) (1996). Questions of law of general applicability outside a labour board's core expertise, including whether external rights are incorporated into a collective agreement, are reviewed for correctness: Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79; Parry Sound (District) SSAB v. O.P.S.E.U., Local 324 (2003).
firac.application: The Court held that the Board's conclusion that it lacked jurisdiction to award aggravated/punitive damages was a question of law and jurisdiction that the Board was required to decide correctly. It was not a discretionary remedial choice within jurisdiction (which would attract deference) but a determination of the existence of jurisdiction itself.
firac.conclusion: The applicable standard of review is correctness.

firac.issue: Did the Board have jurisdiction to award aggravated and/or punitive damages arising from the manner of the grievor's dismissal without cause?
firac.facts: Mr. Olivo, a unionized Seneca professor, was discharged in 1998 for allegedly sending anti-Semitic material to a manager years earlier. The grievance alleged unjust, bad-faith and malicious dismissal and sought reinstatement, lost compensation, and damages for defamation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings. The Board reinstated him with full compensation but, in the Second Award, declined jurisdiction over aggravated and punitive damages, holding these tortious claims did not arise out of the collective agreement and directing Mr. Olivo to sue in court.
firac.rule: Under s. 46(1) of the Colleges Collective Bargaining Act (mirroring s. 45(1) of the Labour Relations Act), disputes arising from the interpretation, application, administration or alleged contravention of a collective agreement go to final and binding arbitration. The exclusive jurisdiction model in Weber v. Ontario Hydro (1995) requires the decision-maker to assess the 'essential character' of the dispute; disputes expressly or inferentially arising out of the collective agreement are foreclosed to the courts, and arbitrators apply the law of the land (common law, statute, Charter) and may grant remedies the legislation empowers. Labour arbitrators have broad remedial power including damages (Polymer Corp. (1959); Allen v. Alberta (2003); Gaignard v. Canada (2003); Giorno v. Pappas (1999)).
firac.application: The essential character of the dispute was an unjust dismissal and the appropriate remedy for it. Once Mr. Olivo was discharged, his only avenue was to grieve; the claim for aggravated and punitive damages arose directly or inferentially from the collective agreement and fell within the Board's exclusive jurisdiction. The Court held the aggravated/punitive damage claims were remedial 'loose threads' of the dismissal grievance, not independent tort claims, and the facts had already been canvassed over a twelve-day hearing. The Board erred in treating them as separate tort claims requiring a civil action; arbitrators apply the same law as courts and have broad power to award damages.
firac.conclusion: The Board had exclusive jurisdiction to determine the aggravated and/or punitive damages claim and erred in declining jurisdiction. The Second Award was quashed to that extent and remitted to the same Board to decide whether such damages should be awarded (applying Vorvis and Whiten) and, if so, the quantum.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) and K011 (judicial review) reflect that this is a judicial review of a tribunal award. K009 (Labour and employment law) is the primary practice area; K084 (labour arbitration) captures the grievance/collective agreement arbitration under the Colleges Collective Bargaining Act; K085 (wrongful dismissal) reflects the underlying unjust dismissal grievance. K002 (Civil litigation) is a borderline pick, included because the case turns on the Weber line distinguishing arbitral from court jurisdiction over tort-type damages claims (aggravated/punitive damages). firac.issue: Did the conduct of the chambers judge give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias?
firac.facts: Mr. M alleged that Justice Dario had been biased and hostile toward the M family since 2015, claiming she had refused repeated recusal requests, made a stereotypical 'Jewish community deep pockets' comment from the bench, and had the word 'Jewish' deleted from the transcript. In fact his own counsel had asked her to remain seized of the matter, her 'deep pockets' reference simply paraphrased the appellants' own letter, and an unaltered audio recording confirmed she never used the word 'Jewish'.
firac.rule: A party alleging a reasonable apprehension of bias must establish an evidentiary basis for the claim; mere assertion or misrepresentation of the record will not suffice.
firac.application: The Court reviewed the record, including an untampered audio recording, and found Mr. M's allegations were based on misrepresentations with no basis in fact. Far from being biased, the judge had been extremely lenient toward the appellants over years of defiance.
firac.conclusion: The ground was dismissed for want of any supporting evidence; the bias claim was spurious.

firac.issue: Was the evidence relied upon by the chambers judge to support the finding of contempt unreliable?
firac.facts: Mr. M had posted information on social media since at least 2014 claiming his grandchildren had been 'abducted' by the Director, some posts bearing his name and photograph. On April 12, 2019, represented by counsel, he admitted posting the offending messages. The September 6 posts were consistent with the earlier ones, though he equivocated about whether he had posted them.
firac.rule: Factual findings of contempt, including attribution of authorship of postings, are entitled to appellate deference absent palpable and overriding error.
firac.application: The posts at issue were consistent with his earlier admitted conduct, and his own position that they did not violate s. 126.2 because the children were no longer in care supported the finding that he was responsible for them. The chambers judge's finding was owed deference.
firac.conclusion: The Court saw no basis to interfere; the ground was dismissed.

firac.issue: Was the contempt hearing procedurally unfair?
firac.facts: The Court reviewed transcripts of both the September 6 and April 12 hearings. The appellants had violated a court order and s. 126.2 of the Act since 2016 without sanction until April 2019, and the judge gave Mr. M two months to produce evidence of impecuniosity to potentially reduce the $5,000 fine, which he never provided.
firac.rule: Procedural fairness requires notice, an opportunity to respond, and an impartial hearing.
firac.application: The transcripts revealed no procedural unfairness; the appellants had in fact been treated fairly and with considerable leniency, including the opportunity to demonstrate inability to pay.
firac.conclusion: The ground was dismissed; the appeal was dismissed with $5,000 costs to the respondents.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the dispute arises from a child protection/adoption context under the Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act. K012 (procedural fairness) captures the reasonable-apprehension-of-bias and procedural-unfairness grounds, which were the core of the appeal. K047 (best interests of the child) reflects the judge's emphasis on protecting the grandchildren's privacy and emotional interests. K048 (custody/access) reflects the underlying custody/adoption dispute and the closed adoption denying the grandparents access. K063 (online hate/social media) applies because the contempt consisted of prohibited social media postings identifying children who had received intervention services — flagged as a partial fit since it concerns social media publication rather than hate. K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) appear because the appellants framed the dispute around returning 'Jewish children to the Jewish fold' and made repeated references to the Jewish community; these are contextual entity tags of moderate weight.
