case_name: 2538520 Ontario Limited v Eastern Platinum Limited

name_verification.name_in_document: 2538520 Ontario Limited v. Eastern Platinum Limited

defining_issues: Do the plaintiffs have standing to bring an oppression claim under s. 227 of the Business Corporations Act when they were neither shareholders nor 'appropriate persons' at the time of the alleged oppressive conduct?

Do the pleadings for unlawful act conspiracy raise a genuine issue for trial, given the alleged unlawful act (breach of a confidentiality agreement) and the requirement to plead conduct directed at the plaintiffs?
Is the loss alleged by the plaintiffs non-compensable pure economic loss falling outside the recognized categories of recoverable economic loss?
Does re-injecting the previously withdrawn Union Goal allegations into the Oppression Action constitute an abuse of process by relitigation?
Are the Great Wall Proceedings in substance a derivative claim requiring leave under the BCA, and are they vexatious and an abuse of process?

firac.issue: Do the plaintiffs have standing to seek an oppression remedy when they were not shareholders or appropriate persons when the alleged oppression occurred?
firac.facts: Mr. Hong never personally held EPL shares; 253 Ont. Ltd. was not incorporated until September 2016 and became a shareholder only in September 2017. The alleged oppressive conduct (failure to enforce a confidentiality agreement, giving competitors an advantage in the 2016 proxy battle) occurred in July–August 2016, before 253 Ont. Ltd. held shares.
firac.rule: Under s. 227(2) of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, only a shareholder (including a beneficial owner and 'any other person whom the court considers to be an appropriate person') may seek an oppression remedy. Oppression protects wrongs suffered qua shareholder (Yen v. Ghahramani, 2023 BCCA 403; Dubois v. Milne, 2020 BCCA 216), reasonable expectations are assessed at the time shares were acquired (Ford Motor; Hollinger), and harm to the company as a whole must be pursued derivatively under s. 232 (Tassone v. Smith; Pasnak v. Chura).
firac.application: The reasonable expectations alleged pre-dated 253 Ont. Ltd.'s acquisition of shares, so it had no standing as a shareholder. Ninth Square Capital did not assist because there the claimant was a beneficial shareholder under a binding contract, unlike the plaintiffs. The asserted 'continuing' oppression was unpleaded and, in any event, alleged share-value diminution is a derivative harm. As an unsuccessful bidder for control, Mr. Hong did not fall within the narrow class of 'appropriate persons', and the plaintiffs offered no substantive answer despite notice.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiffs lack standing; the oppression claim raises no genuine issue for trial and was struck under R. 9-6, a defect that cannot be cured by amendment.

firac.issue: Do the conspiracy pleadings raise a genuine issue for trial?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs alleged that Horizon, Ka An and EPL's officers acted in concert to acquire control of EPL and that Horizon breached a January 2016 confidentiality agreement, unfairly defeating Mr. Hong in the proxy battle. Ka An was not a party to the agreement, which did not prohibit acquiring EPL shares and permitted purchases from named entities (Invesco, Harrington), from whom Ka An acquired shares.
firac.rule: The elements of unlawful act conspiracy are combination, an unlawful act, conduct directed at the plaintiff, knowledge of likely injury, and resulting injury (LeRoy v. Timberwest, 2021 BCCA 326). Conspiracy must be pleaded with heightened precision and full particulars (H.M.B. Holdings, 2021 BCCA 142; Gong v. O'Neill). On R. 9-6 the defendant must show beyond a reasonable doubt the plaintiff is bound to lose (Beach Estate v. Beach, 2019 BCCA 277).
firac.application: The pleadings offered only a bald conclusory assertion that conduct was directed at Mr. Hong, with no material facts. More fundamentally, the confidentiality agreement did not prohibit share acquisition and Ka An was not a party, so no unlawful act was made out. The court declined, however, to strike on the privity ground alone, finding the law on whether breach of a third-party contract can constitute unlawful means (Latifi; XY, LLC) insufficiently settled.
firac.conclusion: The conspiracy claim raises no genuine issue for trial and was struck under R. 9-6 (and, being bound to fail, also under R. 9-5(1)(a)).

firac.issue: Is the alleged loss non-recoverable pure economic loss?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs claimed loss of the opportunity to acquire a controlling interest in EPL, allegedly caused by misuse of confidential information; Mr. Hong conceded 253 Ont. Ltd.'s loss arose from diminution in share value after it became a shareholder.
firac.rule: There is no general right in tort protecting against negligent or intentional infliction of pure economic loss; loss from ordinary marketplace competition is damnum absque injuria (1688782 Ontario Inc. v. Maple Leaf Foods, 2020 SCC 35; A.I. Enterprises v. Bram). Recovery is confined to recognized categories (negligent misrepresentation/service, shoddy goods/structures, relational loss), and courts are reluctant to extend tort protection to failed commercial negotiations (Martel Building v. Canada, 2000 SCC 60).
firac.application: The loss of opportunity to control EPL is pure economic loss; Mr. Hong had no right to acquire control and the pleadings disclosed no facts showing the loss arose from anything other than market competition. The claim fell within none of the recognized categories and the plaintiffs advanced no policy basis for a new one.
firac.conclusion: The alleged losses are non-compensable pure economic loss, reinforcing that the claim is bound to fail.

firac.issue: Does reviving the withdrawn Union Goal allegations constitute an abuse of process?
firac.facts: By a June 2021 consent order (deemed adjudged on the merits) the Union Goal allegations were removed from the Oppression Action; leave to bring a derivative action over the Union Goal Transaction had earlier been denied (2019 BCSC 1446, aff'd 2020 BCCA 313). Mr. Hong nonetheless re-asserted the Union Goal Transaction in his response materials, and Ms. Hu's role in that transaction is being litigated in the ongoing Ren Derivative Action.
firac.rule: Relitigation may be an abuse of process where the prior decision is final, the second proceeding seeks to relitigate a decided issue, and relitigation would impugn the finality and integrity of the earlier judgment (Skender v. Farley, 2007 BCCA 629; Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., 2003 SCC 63). Courts have inherent jurisdiction to prevent abuse and protect judicial economy, consistency and finality.
firac.application: Reviving the Union Goal allegations circumvented the consent order and was an 'end run' around the Smith Decision denying leave (cf. Daum v. Gorrell). It would also duplicate the Ren Derivative Action. Despite an opportunity to withdraw them, Mr. Hong did not, supporting an inference the conduct was intended to vex the defendants and continue his retribution campaign.
firac.conclusion: Raising the Union Goal Transaction in response to the strike motions was an abuse of the court's process.

firac.issue: Are the Great Wall Proceedings in substance a derivative claim requiring leave, and are they vexatious and an abuse of process?
firac.facts: 253 Ont. Ltd. framed the Great Wall matter as an oppression claim after EPL, on advice, declined to sue over the 2022 Great Wall transactions and after Mr. Hong had threatened a derivative action. The pleadings alleged share-price depreciation, diversion of assets, and failure to disclose related-party transactions, repeating the proxy-battle and Union Goal allegations. Mr. Hong admitted he chose oppression to avoid the cost of counsel and the 'uphill battle' of the good-faith leave requirement.
firac.rule: A shareholder seeking oppression must show particular prejudice beyond diminution in share value (1043325 Ontario Ltd. v. CSA, 2016 BCCA 258); harm to the company generally must be pursued by derivative action with leave under s. 232 (Pasnak; Robak Industries v. Gardner, 2007 BCCA 61; Foss v. Harbottle). Directors owe fiduciary duties to the company, not shareholders, absent a special relationship (BCE Inc., 2008 SCC 69; Yen). Pleadings may be struck under R. 9-5(1)(a)–(d) where they disclose no reasonable claim, are vexatious, or are an abuse of process.
firac.application: The harms alleged—loss of share value, Ka An's increased shareholding, non-disclosure—were suffered by EPL and shareholders generally, not uniquely by 253 Ont. Ltd.; the corporate-opportunity claim failed because Ka An was not pleaded as a majority shareholder on adequate facts. The claim was therefore derivative and required leave. The conspiracy, fiduciary and negligence claims rested on the same corporate loss and bald allegations. The repetition of failed allegations, the improper choice of oppression to avoid leave, and threats to sue advising law firms established a vexatious, retributive proceeding.
firac.conclusion: The Great Wall Action and Petition disclose no reasonable oppression claim, are derivative claims requiring leave, and were struck in their entirety as vexatious and an abuse of process.

name_verification.name_in_document: Her Majesty the Queen v. Artur Pawlowski

defining_issues: Are the impugned bylaw and traffic provisions (placing material on a street, operating an amplification system in a park, loud and unnecessary noise from a motor vehicle, and 'stunting') void for vagueness or overbreadth?
Did enforcement of these provisions infringe the accused's freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
Did enforcement of these provisions infringe the accused's freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter?
Where an infringement was found, could the provision be justified as a reasonable limit under s. 1 of the Charter?
Did the conduct of City Bylaw Officers and police amount to an abuse of process warranting a remedy?
Did the Crown prove the accused guilty beyond a reasonable doubt of 'stunting'?

firac.issue: Are the impugned provisions void for vagueness or overbreadth?
firac.facts: Pawlowski, leader of Street Church Ministries, was ticketed for placing 'material' on a street, operating an 'amplification system' in a park, causing 'loud and unnecessary noise' from a motor vehicle, and 'stunting' while ministering to homeless and impoverished people in downtown Calgary in 2007.
firac.rule: A law must be sufficiently precise to give fair notice and to constrain enforcement discretion; overbreadth and vagueness offend s. 7 and may prevent a provision from being a 'limit prescribed by law' (R. v. Heywood; Prostitution Reference; Osborne v. Canada; R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical). A law is void for vagueness only where it fails to provide an 'intelligible standard' or 'sufficient guidance for legal debate'; 'stunting' had been judicially narrowed in R. v. Jones and R. v. Tremblay.
firac.application: The Street Bylaw definition of 'material' ('any object or article') was so broad it could capture a shoe sole or briefcase, providing no intelligible standard. 'Unnecessary' noise in s. 82 of the Regulation gave no intelligible standard and was overbroad, especially applied to a parked vehicle used only as a speaker stand. By contrast, 'amplification system' in the Parks Bylaw gave adequate notice (the accused had previously held permits), and 'stunting', as interpreted in Jones, provided a workable standard.
firac.conclusion: 'Material on a street' and 'loud and unnecessary noise' were unconstitutionally vague/overbroad; the amplification-in-a-park and 'stunting' provisions were not.

firac.issue: Did enforcement infringe the accused's freedom of religion under s. 2(a)?
firac.facts: Pawlowski sincerely believed his ministry — preaching with amplified sound and distributing food to the poor — was a religious obligation drawn from his personal reading of the Bible, and the tickets interfered with these activities.
firac.rule: An s. 2(a) infringement is established where the claimant sincerely believes in a practice with a nexus to religion and the impugned measure interferes in a more than trivial or insubstantial way (Alberta v. Hutterian Brethren; Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem; Multani). The court assesses sincerity, not validity or mandatory nature.
firac.application: The Court accepted the accused's sincere belief that using amplified sound and feeding congregants had a nexus with his faith. Enforcement of the City bylaws (permit requirements, ticketing while saying grace) more than trivially interfered with his religious practice. The provincial provisions (noise/stunting) had only an indirect, trivial effect and, given the Jones interpretation of 'stunting', the accused conceded no s. 2(a) breach arose from that charge.
firac.conclusion: The City bylaw provisions infringed s. 2(a); the provincial provisions did not.

firac.issue: Did enforcement infringe freedom of expression under s. 2(b)?
firac.facts: The accused's amplified preaching, banners, and a cross conveyed religious and political meaning; all charges arose from activity on public parks, streets and sidewalks.
firac.rule: Activity that attempts to convey meaning is protected unless violent in form (Irwin Toy). Expression on government property is protected only where the form is compatible with the principal function of the place (Committee for the Commonwealth of Canada v. Canada).
firac.application: The accused's activity conveyed meaning tied to social and political participation. On the sidewalks pedestrian flow was not significantly impeded, so his expression was compatible with the space; Triangle Park had ceased to function as a general-public space (dominated by drug activity), so amplified preaching was not incompatible with its function. The noise provision infringed expression through overbreadth; properly interpreted 'stunting' did not affect expression.
firac.conclusion: The Street Bylaw, Parks Bylaw and the noise Regulation infringed s. 2(b); the 'stunting' provision did not.

firac.issue: Could the infringing provisions be saved under s. 1?
firac.facts: The City relied on interests in safe, accessible streets and parks and reducing noise; a permit regime existed but the City had refused to accept the accused's permit applications and applied no clear standards.
firac.rule: R. v. Oakes: the limit must serve a pressing and substantial objective and be proportionate (rational connection, minimal impairment, and net proportionality); the state bears the burden on a balance of probabilities.
firac.application: Although the objectives were pressing and substantial and rationally connected, the vague/overbroad 'material' and 'unnecessary noise' provisions were not minimal impairments. The Parks Bylaw permit scheme became arbitrary once the City applied no known criteria and refused to consider the accused's applications, so it failed minimal impairment; deleterious effects outweighed benefits.
firac.conclusion: None of the infringing provisions was saved by s. 1; each was of no force or effect in these circumstances.

firac.issue: Did the officials' conduct amount to an abuse of process?
firac.facts: Enforcement escalated from noise complaints (for which the accused was never charged) to numerous tickets and an increasing officer presence, culminating in the City refusing even to accept the accused's permit applications.
firac.rule: Abuse of process (R. v. Scott; R. v. O'Connor) permits a stay only in the 'clearest of cases' where proceedings are oppressive/vexatious and offend the community's sense of fair play and the integrity of the justice system.
firac.application: The Court found the accused acted in good faith to comply while continuing his ministry, and that the City's intransigence, including refusing his applications, fell 'precariously close' to an abuse of power, but did not reach the 'clearest of cases' threshold.
firac.conclusion: Abusive conduct was found but did not warrant a stay; it could bear on penalty if the accused were convicted.

firac.issue: Was the accused guilty of 'stunting' beyond a reasonable doubt?
firac.facts: On June 18, 2007 the accused preached with an amplified public-address system and a cross at a street corner; the officer testified drivers slowed but no photograph showed distraction, and the Court rejected the claim of danger or distraction.
firac.rule: Section 115(2)(e) of the Traffic Safety Act, interpreted in R. v. Jones/Tremblay, requires a 'stunt' or other activity likely to distract, startle or interfere with highway users — more than merely attracting attention.
firac.application: The accused's conduct was not a 'stunt', and the Court rejected the officer's evidence that drivers were distracted or endangered, finding such a gathering unlikely to distract, startle or interfere with users of the highway.
firac.conclusion: The Crown failed to prove an essential element; the accused was found not guilty of stunting.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally a Charter analysis, so K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 anchor. K025 (freedom of religion) and K024 (freedom of expression) are the two central rights, with their specific Charter provisions K110 (s. 2(a)) and K111 (s. 2(b)). K034 (sincerity of belief) captures the Amselem/Hutterian Brethren test the Court applied. K030 (reasonable limits/Oakes) is central to the s. 1 stage. K107 (the Charter) is engaged throughout. K112 (Charter s. 7) reflects the vagueness/overbreadth and abuse-of-power framing argued under s. 7. K087 (protest/demonstration) fits the street-ministry gatherings and the accused's characterization of standing up for his rights. Borderline picks: K087 is somewhat weak (the activity is religious rather than pure protest but the accused framed events as demonstrations), and there is no dedicated keyword for abuse of process, so K112 stands in for that dimension.
location_rationale: The heading states 'In the Provincial Court of Alberta', gives 'Registry: Calgary', and the decision closes 'Dated at the City of Calgary, Alberta this 7th day of December, 2009.'
registry_rationale: The case header expressly lists 'Registry: Calgary'.

case_name: Pembroke Civic Hospital v. Ontario (Health Services Restructuring Commission)

name_verification.name_in_document: Pembroke Civic Hospital v. Ontario (Health Services Restructuring Commission)
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The style of cause and indexed name match the supplied name. The decision is that of the Ontario Court (General Division), Divisional Court; the supplied metadata labels the court 'ONCA', but the reported decision under review is the Divisional Court's (the Court of Appeal later dismissed leave to appeal per the editorial note). The neutral citation 1997 CanLII 16241 corresponds to this reported Divisional Court judgment.

defining_issues: Did the Health Services Restructuring Commission exceed its jurisdiction by considering policy relating to the preservation of denominational (Roman Catholic) health care in Ontario?

Did the Commission breach the duty of procedural fairness in the disclosure it provided, in the 'case to meet' it gave the applicant, in its consultations with Roman Catholic interests, or through prejudgment or bias?
Were the applicants' Charter challenges under ss. 2(a), 7 and 15 premature and without an evidentiary foundation?

firac.issue: Did the Commission exceed its jurisdiction by taking into account the tradition and role of denominational hospitals in Ontario?
firac.facts: The Commission ordered the closure of the non-denominational Pembroke Civic Hospital and the restructuring of the Pembroke General Hospital, a Roman Catholic institution operated by the Grey Sisters. Of 209 Ontario public hospitals, 32 are denominationally owned. The applicant argued the Commission wrongly considered preservation of denominational health care.
firac.rule: Under ss. 6 and 9(10) of the Public Hospitals Act, the Ministry of Health Act and O. Regs. 87/96 and 88/96, the Commission stands in the Minister's shoes with virtually unfettered powers, with no right of appeal to the court. On the political/judicial spectrum it sits near the political/legislative extreme (Knight v. Indian Head School Division No. 19; Whitley v. United States). The court reviews only whether the Commission acted according to law, not the wisdom of its decisions.
firac.application: The Commission was required to consider the public interest in local health systems, including the appropriate role of denominational providers. Considering representations from the Roman Catholic Health Association and accepting a role for Roman Catholic hospitals was a policy decision within the widest area of non-reviewable discretion. Ontario's long tradition of denominational hospital governance was a reality the Commission was entitled to weigh.
firac.conclusion: The Commission did not exceed its jurisdiction by considering denominational health care; the jurisdictional argument failed.

firac.issue: Did the Commission deny the applicant procedural fairness in disclosure, notice of the case to meet, its consultations, or through prejudgment or bias?
firac.facts: The Commission invited public and group submissions but refused to produce lists and copies of all submissions. The applicant said it was not told the case to meet, that a parallel undisclosed process with Roman Catholic interests existed, and that the Commission prejudged and was biased (relying partly on staff drafts and the executive director's statement that the Commission did not analyze the by-laws).
firac.rule: The content of fairness depends on the nature of the body. A policy-making and implementation body is not an adversarial forum and need not adopt court procedures of discovery and production; it must give affected parties a fair opportunity to make their views known. The 'case to meet' principle (Webb, Nicholson, Downing, Consolidated Bathurst) applies fully to adversarial lites but far less to complex polycentric decisions.
firac.application: The Commission's December 3, 1996 notice expressly set out the option of sole governance by the Grey Sisters with the Civic directed to close, clearly disclosing the case to meet. The Civic engaged repeatedly and in a face-to-face meeting with the very denominational-governance issues it now raised, so there were no undisclosed 'new grounds.' Consultation with the Roman Catholic Health Association was the Commission's duty and was proper. Staff discussion drafts did not evidence a closed mind; the Commission rejected the General's governance proposal and required a representative board, showing an open mind. The by-law point disclosed no bias.
firac.conclusion: There was no procedural unfairness, prejudgment, bias or wrongful exercise of discretion; these grounds failed.

firac.issue: Were the Charter challenges under ss. 2(a), 7 and 15 premature and unsupported by evidence?
firac.facts: The applicant alleged the restructuring would infringe freedom of conscience and religion, security of the person and equality, focusing on health services involving sexuality, reproduction and abortion, and on the presence of crosses/crucifixes and a requirement that elected board candidates respect the hospital's values. No present infringement was alleged.
firac.rule: A Charter challenge is generally to be brought when there is an actual infringement, not on speculation of future infringement; standing of a corporation and of a person without a demonstrated need for the services is doubtful. To succeed on adverse-effect claims a claimant must prove the alleged effects will occur or are highly probable. Silent religious symbols do not compel religious practice and do not infringe s. 2(a).
firac.application: The challenge was premature and speculative as no present infringement existed. On the merits, uncontradicted evidence (including Dr. Sharma, Chief of Obstetrics and Gynaecology) showed no religious interference in care; crosses and crucifixes did not coerce anyone; no abortions had been performed in Renfrew county for at least 14 years for reasons unrelated to the closure, so future availability effects were speculative; equality claims lacked any showing of disproportionate disadvantage to a disadvantaged group; and requiring board candidates to respect (not adhere to) the hospital's values infringed no Charter right.
firac.conclusion: The Charter challenges were dismissed on prematurity and, in the alternative, for want of any evidentiary basis.

keywords_rationale: The case is a judicial review of an administrative tribunal, so K001 (Administrative law, tier-1) and K011 (judicial review) are core, with K012 (procedural fairness) covering the disclosure, case-to-meet, consultation, prejudgment and bias arguments. The constitutional dimension supports K003 (Constitutional law) with the specific Charter grounds argued: K025 (freedom of religion) for the s. 2(a) claim, K023 (equality rights) for s. 15, and the entity-statute tags K110 (Charter s. 2(a)), K112 (Charter s. 7), K109 (Charter s. 15) plus K107 (Canadian Charter) which frame the challenges. Standard of review is engaged conceptually (limited court role) but K014 was omitted as the court framed its role in jurisdiction/fairness terms rather than a formal SOR analysis; the tier-3 Charter section tags are somewhat granular but reflect the precise grounds pleaded.
location_rationale: The decision states it was rendered by the 'Ontario Court (General Division), Divisional Court', which locates it in Ontario, but no city is stated in the text, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: No registry or court office is named in the decision; the header identifies only the court and panel, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Her Majesty the Queen v. James Sears and LeRoy St. Germaine

defining_issues: Does the six-month summary-conviction ceiling operate as the true 'maximum sentence', or must the court fix the appropriate sentence first and only then apply the procedural cap?
Should the sentences on the two counts of wilful promotion of hatred (against women and against Jews) be served concurrently or consecutively?
What is the fit sentence for Mr. Sears's wilful promotion of hatred, and how do aggravating and mitigating factors and community impact bear on it?
Should the court impose probation with terms restricting the defendant's publishing activities, given his Charter freedom of expression?

firac.issue: Does the six-month summary-conviction ceiling function as the 'maximum sentence' to be reserved for the worst cases, or must the appropriate sentence be determined first and the procedural cap applied afterward?
firac.facts: Wilful promotion of hatred under s. 319(2) is a hybrid offence; the Crown elected to proceed summarily, so the statutory maximum was six months per count. The Crown argued this procedural maximum is not the 'maximum sentence' engaged when weighing all sentencing factors.
firac.rule: Under s. 718.1 of the Criminal Code the fundamental principle is proportionality to gravity of the offence and degree of responsibility. R. v. Cheddesingh, 2004 SCC 16, rejects reserving the maximum only for the worst offender/worst offence. R. v. Solowan, 2008 SCC 62, holds a fit sentence for a hybrid offence prosecuted summarily is neither a function nor fraction of what could have been imposed on indictment and must not be scaled down.
firac.application: The court held it must first determine the appropriate sentence on ordinary sentencing principles and only then apply any procedural limitation that would truncate that sentence, rather than treating the six-month summary cap as a benchmark to be discounted.
firac.conclusion: The court determined the fit sentence independently, then applied the six-month procedural maximum per count.

firac.issue: Should the two counts of promoting hatred (against women and against Jews) be served consecutively or concurrently?
firac.facts: Over three years YWN promoted hatred against both Jews and women through many issues; the defence argued the publication was 'one continuous transaction' warranting concurrent sentences.
firac.rule: R. v. Grummer, 1983 CanLII 5286 (ON CA): offences from the same transaction are normally concurrent, but that rule does not apply where the offences invade different legally-protected interests.
firac.application: Women and Jews are identifiable groups with separate, legally-protected interests; the defendant could have promoted hatred against one and not the other but chose both, repeatedly and consistently over three years, through many incidents rather than one.
firac.conclusion: The sentences on the two counts are to be served consecutively.

firac.issue: What is the fit sentence for wilful promotion of hatred in these circumstances?
firac.facts: Sears, in his mid-fifties, edited YWN, a publication with a purported readership over one million and an online presence, glorifying Nazism and Hitler, denying the Holocaust, demonizing Jews, and dehumanizing women while counselling violence against them. A Winter 2019 issue continued these themes after trial. He had 1992 sexual-assault convictions (not appearing on his CPIC record) given little weight. Seven community impact statements were tendered.
firac.rule: s. 718.1 (proportionality); s. 718(2)(a)(ii) (hate motivation as aggravating); s. 722.2 (community impact statements); R. v. Keegstra, 1996 ABCA 308 (one-year appropriate for anti-Semitic hate-mongering by a teacher); R. v. Lelas (ON CA 1990) (one year for anti-Semitic vandalism).
firac.application: Aggravating factors included the vast breadth and online reach of the material and its continuation after trial; the 1992 convictions were given little weight. The community impact statements complied with s. 722.2 and reflected real harm, though harm to the community was in any event universal and obvious. Compared to Lelas (one year in 1990) and Keegstra, Sears's conduct was significantly more serious, warranting at least 18 months on each count. The procedural maximum, however, capped each count at six months.
firac.conclusion: The fit sentence was 18 months per count, but limited by the six-month procedural maximum, served consecutively, for a total of one year's incarceration.

firac.issue: Should probation with terms restricting the defendant's publishing be imposed?
firac.facts: The Crown sought three years' probation prohibiting all publishing, including editing or publishing YWN, to reduce recidivism. The defence argued this infringed the Charter right to freedom of expression.
firac.rule: Charter freedom of expression; probation terms must not unduly curtail lawful expression.
firac.application: The court agreed the proposed prohibitions were far too broad. Sears remains free to publish whatever he wishes, even if unpopular or objectionable, so long as it does not offend the Criminal Code; if he again promotes hatred he risks re-prosecution.
firac.conclusion: No probation was imposed.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area, this being a sentencing decision. K067 (wilful promotion of hatred) is the precise offence under s. 319(2) (K115). K061 (hate speech) and K060 (hate motivation, s. 718(2)(a)(ii)) capture the nature of the conduct and the statutory aggravating factor. K058 (antisemitism), K062 (Holocaust denial) and K066 (white supremacism/Nazi glorification) describe the content of YWN, and K093 (Jewish) identifies the targeted group. K024 (freedom of expression) is engaged by the refusal to impose publication-restricting probation on Charter grounds. Misogyny/dehumanization of women is a central theme but has no dedicated vocabulary term, so it is not separately coded; that is the main gap.
location_rationale: The header identifies the 'Ontario Court of Justice' and the court file number 'Toronto 4817 998 18-70010807-01;-02', and submissions were heard in Toronto; province is Ontario as the court is the ONCJ.
registry_rationale: The court file number is prefixed 'Toronto', indicating the Toronto registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

case_name: Marriage Commissioners Appointed Under The Marriage Act (Re)

name_verification.name_in_document: In the Matter of Marriage Commissioners appointed under The Marriage Act, 1995, S.S. 1995, c. M-4.1 (Reference Re The Marriage Act, 1995 (Sask.))

defining_issues: Would the proposed amendments to The Marriage Act, 1995 (the Grandfathering Option and the Comprehensive Option) infringe the equality rights of gay and lesbian persons under s. 15(1) of the Charter?

If the amendments infringe s. 15(1), can that infringement be justified under s. 1 of the Charter as a reasonable limit, given the competing s. 2(a) freedom-of-religion interests of marriage commissioners?

firac.issue: Would the proposed amendments permitting marriage commissioners to decline to solemnize marriages contrary to their religious beliefs infringe s. 15(1) equality rights based on sexual orientation?
firac.facts: Following recognition of same-sex marriage, some Saskatchewan marriage commissioners refused to solemnize same-sex unions on religious grounds. The Lieutenant Governor in Council referred two possible amendments to the Court: a 'Grandfathering Option' (for commissioners appointed on or before November 5, 2004) and a 'Comprehensive Option' (all commissioners). Marriage commissioners are public officials and the only route to a non-religious civil marriage, which many same-sex couples must rely on since many faiths will not marry them.
firac.rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter guarantees equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination. Per Andrews, Kapp and Ermineskin, a claimant must show (1) a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground, and (2) that the distinction creates a disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping. Sexual orientation is an analogous ground (Vriend, Hislop). A facially neutral law can violate s. 15(1) by its effects (Andrews, Eldridge).
firac.application: Neither Option's purpose was to deny rights, but their effect would be to allow commissioners to refuse same-sex couples, drawing a negative distinction on the analogous ground of sexual orientation. The majority rejected the 'someone else will help you' argument, analogizing to refusing service to a person because they are Black, First Nations or Jewish, and noted the significant personal hurt, geographic obstacles, and risk that many commissioners would opt out. Given the historical marginalization of gays and lesbians (Egan), the distinction perpetuated disadvantage and stereotyping.
firac.conclusion: Both Options would, by their effect, create a discriminatory distinction based on sexual orientation contrary to s. 15(1).

firac.issue: Can the s. 15(1) infringement be justified under s. 1, balanced against the marriage commissioners' s. 2(a) freedom of religion?
firac.facts: Compelling commissioners to solemnize same-sex marriages engages the sincerely held religious beliefs of at least some commissioners (s. 2(a)). The amendments were aimed at accommodating those beliefs. During argument the Court raised a 'single entry point' system as a less restrictive alternative, which counsel conceded was less restrictive and operates in Ontario.
firac.rule: Section 1 permits reasonable limits demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society, assessed under R. v. Oakes: (1) a pressing and substantial objective, and (2) proportionality — rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality between salutary and deleterious effects. Charter rights are reconciled at s. 1, with no hierarchy of rights (Dagenais). Freedom of religion is broadly defined (Big M, Amselem) but is not absolute.
firac.application: The majority accepted accommodating commissioners' s. 2(a) freedoms as a pressing and substantial objective and found rational connection, but held the Options failed minimal impairment because a 'single entry point' system could accommodate beliefs behind the scenes without any couple being refused. On final proportionality, the deleterious effects — perpetuating recently-overcome discrimination, genuine harm to same-sex couples, and undermining the principle that the state serves everyone equally — outweighed the limited salutary benefits, since the religious interest concerned acting on beliefs in public office rather than the core of religious freedom. Smith J.A. (concurring) would characterize the objective more narrowly and doubted it was pressing and substantial, stressing that the unprecedented notwithstanding clause would strip gays and lesbians of Human Rights Code protection.
firac.conclusion: The infringement is not justified under s. 1. Both Options would be unconstitutional and of no force or effect.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a Charter reference. K023 (equality rights) and K109 (Charter s. 15) capture the s. 15(1) sexual-orientation discrimination analysis, which is the core holding. K025 (freedom of religion) and K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) reflect the competing religious-freedom interests of marriage commissioners. K030 (reasonable limits s. 1) is central because the outcome turned on the Oakes justification analysis. K031 (religious accommodation) fits the stated objective of accommodating commissioners' beliefs. K034 (sincerity of belief) applies because the court accepted the commissioners' sincerely held beliefs under the Amselem framework — a slightly weaker pick but genuinely engaged. K107 (Canadian Charter) anchors the governing instrument. Sexual orientation itself has no dedicated vocabulary ID, so it is captured via the equality-rights keywords.
location_rationale: The decision is rendered by the 'Saskatchewan Court of Appeal', so the province is Saskatchewan. No city is stated in the text (appellate reference), so city is left null.
registry_rationale: No registry office is identified in the decision beyond the court itself; the reference proceeds under The Constitutional Questions Act before the Court of Appeal, with no registry named.

name_verification.name_in_document: MARCELLO ARAUJO v. JEWS FOR JESUS/JUIFS POUR JESUS

defining_issues: Under Rule 31.06 of the Rules of Civil Procedure, is the identity of the employees who emailed the plaintiff a copy of the non-solicitation policy and a list of donors relevant to a matter in issue in the action, such that the plaintiff must disclose it on discovery?
May a party redact identifying information from an otherwise relevant produced document where that information is irrelevant and its disclosure could cause harm?
If the informants' identities were relevant, does the Wigmore case-by-case privilege protect them from disclosure on the basis of confidentiality?

firac.issue: Is the identity of the employees who supplied the plaintiff with the non-solicitation policy and donor names relevant to a matter in issue under Rule 31.06?
firac.facts: In a wrongful dismissal action against Jews for Jesus (JFJ), JFJ counterclaimed that the plaintiff solicited its donors after termination in breach of contractual and fiduciary duties. Two JFJ employees had emailed the plaintiff a copy of the non-solicitation policy and a list of donors the plaintiff had cultivated. JFJ moved to compel the plaintiff to identify those senders (discovery questions 695 and 893), relying on Rule 31.06(2).
firac.rule: Rule 31.06(1) requires answers to any 'proper question relevant to any matter in issue'; the 2010 amendments replaced the 'semblance of relevance' test with a stricter simple relevance test (Justice Reform Project; Noble v. York University Foundation, 2010 ONSC 399; Brand Name Marketing v. Rogers Communications, 2010 ONSC 1159). Rule 31.06(2) permits disclosure of names of persons who might reasonably be expected to have knowledge of transactions or occurrences in issue. Pleadings determine relevance (Noble).
firac.application: The Master held the new stricter relevance test applied. The transactions or occurrences in issue were the plaintiff's sending of solicitation letters to former JFJ donors and any resulting breach of duty — facts flowing from the plaintiff and documents held by the plaintiff and CPM. The senders of the policy and the donor names could not be expected to have knowledge of what the plaintiff did after receiving that material. Whether an employee independently breached a duty to JFJ was not an issue framed by the pleadings.
firac.conclusion: The identity of the senders is not relevant to any matter in issue; questions 695 and 893 need not be answered.

firac.issue: May identifying information be redacted from a produced relevant document where the information is irrelevant and disclosure could cause harm?
firac.facts: The plaintiff produced (at Tab 13) the email enclosing the non-solicitation policy but redacted the sender's identity. The sender was a current JFJ employee; the plaintiff feared JFJ would discipline that employee for assisting him, and JFJ refused to give a written undertaking not to do so.
firac.rule: The whole of a relevant document must ordinarily be produced and irrelevant portions cannot simply be redacted, except where clearly irrelevant material is of a nature giving good reason for non-disclosure and disclosure could cause considerable harm while serving no legitimate purpose in resolving the issues (McGee v. London Life, 2010 ONSC 1408; North American Trust v. Mercer International).
firac.application: The identity of the policy sender was already found irrelevant; disclosing it would in no way help resolve the issues. There was a genuine risk of discipline of the employee, reinforced by JFJ's refusal to undertake not to discipline and its factum's stance. Although the deemed undertaking rule (30.1.01) offered some protection, that protection could cease if the evidence were filed or used at trial, or upon relief from the undertaking.
firac.conclusion: The redacted identifying information may remain redacted; disclosure could cause considerable harm and serve no legitimate purpose.

firac.issue: If relevant, would the Wigmore case-by-case privilege protect the informants' identities?
firac.facts: The plaintiff sought to withhold the senders' identities on grounds of confidentiality, but filed no affidavit of his own establishing that the communications were made in confidence.
firac.rule: There is no free-standing privilege for confidential information; the four-part Wigmore test (Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254) applies on a case-by-case basis, the first condition being that the communication originated in a confidence that it would not be disclosed (see Cadillac Fairview v. Standard Parking).
firac.application: The plaintiff provided no evidence that either communication originated in confidence; a mere fear of reprisal is not evidence of confidentiality. Without proof of the essential first condition, the remaining conditions could not be assessed, though the Master noted that on the fourth condition disclosure would have little benefit to the litigation.
firac.conclusion: Had the identities been relevant, the plaintiff failed to establish confidentiality under Wigmore; the point was academic given the relevance ruling.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary practice area — this is an interlocutory discovery motion in a civil action turning on Rule 31.06 relevance, document redaction (McGee), and Wigmore privilege. K009 (Labour and employment law) and K085 (wrongful dismissal) reflect the underlying action for wrongful dismissal and the post-employment non-solicitation/fiduciary counterclaim. K013 (professional discipline) is a weak/borderline pick, included because the risk that JFJ would discipline the employee informant was central to the redaction and confidentiality analysis, though it is not disciplinary regulation in the administrative-law sense. K093 (Jewish) is also weak — it captures the defendant 'Jews for Jesus,' a self-described Jewish evangelistic society, but the religious dimension was not a live legal issue. The controlled vocabulary is thematically oriented toward antisemitism/Charter matters and fits this procedural civil-litigation decision poorly; no keyword exists for discovery, relevance, redaction, or the Wigmore privilege, so the five closest were selected.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE - ONTARIO', establishing the province as Ontario. No city or municipal sitting location is stated in the endorsement (the court file number 06-CV-309783 is given but no registry city is named), so city and registry are left null.
registry_rationale: The endorsement identifies the court (Ontario Superior Court of Justice) and a court file number but does not name a registry office or city, so registry is left null.

case_name: Catalyst Capital Group Inc. v. West Face Capital Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: The Catalyst Capital Group Inc. v. West Face Capital Inc.

defining_issues: Did the moving parties establish a strong prima facie case on the merits of their counterclaims, including personal liability of Mr. Glassman?
Does the test for a Mareva injunction require proof of intent to remove or dissipate assets for the purpose of defeating creditors or judgment, and did the moving parties meet that requirement?
Did the moving parties establish irreparable harm and that the balance of convenience favoured granting the injunction?
Did the delay in bringing the motion (the absence of urgency) undermine the entitlement to Mareva relief?

firac.issue: Did the moving parties establish a strong prima facie case on the merits of their counterclaims, including the personal liability of Mr. Glassman?
firac.facts: West Face and Boland allege Catalyst and Glassman hired Black Cube and Psy Group to conduct covert 'sting' operations and defamation/harassment campaigns against them and against former Justice Newbould. Glassman created a handwritten 'Bonus Legend' offering up to US$11.5 million in success fees, and personally directed dissemination of false material. Glassman claimed he acted only as officer/director and that Tamara Global retained the operatives.
firac.rule: A strong prima facie case is more stringent than a serious issue to be tried; the moving party must be 'clearly right and almost certain to succeed at trial' (Lee v. Chang, 2018 ONSC 930; Quizno's Canada Restaurant Corp., 2009 CanLII 20708). Officers/directors are shielded from personal liability for acts under a corporate name unless their conduct is itself tortious, fraudulent, deceitful or dishonest, exhibiting a separate identity or interest (ScotiaMcLeod Inc. v. People's Jewellers Ltd., 1995 CanLII 1301; Khursheed v. Benedig Capital; Guru Eak Transport).
firac.application: The court found the Catalyst Parties' conduct 'despicable' and rooted in deceit. Glassman could not hide behind his corporate capacity because his direction of the false social-media campaign and creation of the Bonus Legend constituted independent tortious, deceitful and fraudulent activity, consistent with prior findings by Boswell J. and McEwen J. that he was the directing mind. The 'dollar for dollar' damages argument was rejected because the counterclaim pleaded conspiracy, breach of confidence, inducing breach of contract/fiduciary duty and unlawful means, not merely defamation, and no authority requires dollar-for-dollar proof.
firac.conclusion: The West Face Parties established a strong prima facie case, including against Glassman personally. Mr. Langstaff, however, did not meet this threshold, his claim's prospects being less clear cut.

firac.issue: Does the Mareva test require proof of intent to remove or dissipate assets to defeat creditors, and did the moving parties meet it?
firac.facts: Glassman relocated to the Bahamas (property first purchased there in 2014, before litigation), listed his Ardwold Gate house on MLS in 2024, and Catalyst surrendered its OSC registration. However, Catalyst renewed its 181 Bay Street lease for five years in 2021, retains over US$1 billion in assets, and Boland admitted on cross-examination he could not identify any asset Catalyst had moved out of Ontario. Glassman retains a house and cottage in Ontario.
firac.rule: The six-part Chitel v. Rothbart test governs (1982 CanLII 1956). On the removal/dissipation element, the majority in R. v. Consolidated Fastfrate Transport Inc. (1995 CanLII 1527) per Galligan J.A. holds the decisive question is the purpose of the arrangement: relief lies only where assets are arranged with intent to defeat creditors. Intent to put assets beyond reach is the 'sine qua non' (10390160 Canada Ltd. v. Casey, 2022 ONSC 628; RBC Dexia; Ghaeinizadeh; Di Menza; Aetna Financial Services Ltd. v. Feigelman, 1985 CanLII 55).
firac.application: The court held the preponderance of authority, including recent cases, requires intent to defeat creditors. There was no evidence Catalyst had moved or intended to move assets; the lease renewal contradicted removal. Glassman's relocation reflected a longer-term plan predating the litigation, and substantial Ontario assets remained. The house had long been on the market and its MLS listing was not revelatory. The court refused to infer intent from Glassman's general bad character, which would lower the high threshold and encourage mudslinging. Ms. MacDonald's evidence about the cottage was contradicted by uncross-examined affidavits (e.g., Mr. Scully) and could not be relied on.
firac.conclusion: The moving parties failed to show a real risk of removal or dissipation, and failed to show the requisite intent to defeat creditors; this element was not met.

firac.issue: Did the moving parties establish irreparable harm and that the balance of convenience favoured the injunction?
firac.facts: Expert evidence indicated Ontario judgments can generally be enforced in the Bahamas and Cayman Islands. The moving parties argued enforcement would be a 'whack-a-mole' exercise. Considerable Catalyst assets remain in Ontario; the moving parties sought to enjoin only $50 million of assets worth multiples of that.
firac.rule: The need to pursue normal means to enforce a judgment abroad is not the type of irreparable harm contemplated for an interlocutory injunction (Khan v. Coloma, 2019 ONSC 7202); mere difficulty or expense enforcing outside Ontario does not entitle a party to Mareva relief absent a genuine risk of disappearance of assets (Aetna).
firac.application: Because ample assets remain in Ontario to satisfy any judgment and there was no clear evidence of intent to shield assets, the difficulty of pursuing hypothetical foreign assets did not meet the stringent irreparable-harm threshold. Tying up Catalyst's assets pending judgment would inappropriately inconvenience the Catalyst Parties; the balance of convenience favoured the status quo.
firac.conclusion: Irreparable harm was not established and the balance of convenience favoured the Catalyst Parties.

firac.issue: Did the delay in bringing the motion defeat the claim for Mareva relief?
firac.facts: An August 23, 2022 letter from West Face counsel already asserted the same risk that Glassman would have insufficient assets and referenced the house sale and asset removal. The motion was not delivered until March 1, 2024. The purported new triggers—the MLS listing and OSC deregistration—were either already known or independently explained (OSC surrender advised by counsel, unrelated to relocation).
firac.rule: Mareva injunctions must be pursued with dispatch; delay may itself show the risk is not significant enough to warrant relief, and injunctions are not awarded to parties showing no sense of urgency (Original Traders Energy Ltd. (Re), 2024 ONSC 325, citing Sharpe, Injunctions and Specific Performance; Lee v. Chang, 2018 ONSC 2091).
firac.application: The court found the same items and conduct relied on now were enumerated in the August 2022 letter; Boland confirmed he held the same view of the risk then. The purported new triggers were unpersuasive—the house-sale efforts were already known and the OSC surrender was explained by unchallenged evidence (Foster affidavit). The over-18-month delay with no compelling explanation was fatal.
firac.conclusion: The lack of demonstrated urgency was a second significant, independent reason the motions failed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the correct tier-1 practice area—this is a commercial civil action and counterclaim seeking an interlocutory freezing order. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is central, as the motion is for a Mareva-type injunction, the core subject of the decision. K015 (defamation) applies because the underlying counterclaim largely sounds in defamation (the Black Cube/Psy Group campaign). K017 (group defamation) is borderline/weak—the defamation targeted West Face and Boland specifically rather than a collectivity, so it is a weaker pick but the closest defamation-flavour keyword after K015; it is flagged as marginal. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is included because Mr. Langstaff's counterclaim alleges he lost his Canaccord position due to pressure from the Catalyst Parties (termination of employment), engaging employment/termination concepts, though it is a secondary aspect. The controlled vocabulary lacks precise keywords for Mareva/asset dissipation, conspiracy or the six-part test, so the selection is constrained; the injunction and defamation keywords capture the genuinely engaged doctrines.
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the Superior Court of Justice – Ontario (Commercial List), court file CV-17-587463-00CL. The Commercial List sits in Toronto and the assets/premises at issue (181 Bay Street, 17 Ardwold Gate) are in Toronto; West Face is described as 'based in Toronto'. Province is Ontario as expressly stated ('SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE – ONTARIO').
