name_verification.name_in_document: Shoolestani v. Ichikawa

defining_issues: Is the defamation counterclaim statute-barred under the Limitation Act, or is it saved by s. 4(1) as a claim related to or connected with the subject matter of the original action?
Do the pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action against Ms. Pour for defamation and malicious prosecution, such that the counterclaim should not be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a)?
Does the imprecise paraphrasing of the allegedly defamatory emails in the counterclaim render the pleading deficient and warrant striking rather than amendment?
Can the Amnis defendants maintain a claim for malicious prosecution when Ms. Pour's original claim has not terminated in their favour?

firac.issue: Is the defamation counterclaim statute-barred, or saved by s. 4(1) of the Limitation Act as related to the subject matter of the original action?
firac.facts: The alleged defamatory statements were made March 19 and 29, 2009; the counterclaim was filed March 25, 2015, nearly six years later. Defamation carries a two-year limitation under s. 3(2)(c) of the Limitation Act. Ms. Pour argued the counterclaim was untimely and unrelated to her claim for unpaid food services.
firac.rule: Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 3(2)(c) (two-year limitation for defamation) and s. 4(1), which provides that lapse of time is no bar to proceedings by counterclaim relating to or connected with the subject matter of the original action. ASM Capital Corp. v. Mercer International Inc., 1999 BCCA 353, and Lui v. West Granville Manor Ltd., 1987 CanLII 164 (BC CA), interpret s. 4(1); the 'relation back' theory was rejected in Lui.
firac.application: The court found the counterclaim's theory—that Ms. Pour and the other family members conspired to pressure the Amnis defendants through defamatory statements and an improper action—was related to and connected with Ms. Pour's action, given the interrelationship of the claims and the plaintiffs' decision to advance them together against all 12 defendants. The 'relation back' argument was rejected per Lui, since s. 4(1) eliminates the limitation defence entirely for related counterclaims.
firac.conclusion: Section 4(1) applies; the limitation period does not bar the defamation counterclaim. The first two arguments failed.

firac.issue: Do the pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action against Ms. Pour under Rule 9-5(1)(a)?
firac.facts: The defamatory emails were sent by Amir Yashar Shoolestani, not Ms. Pour, and related to engineering work; her own claim was for food services. The counterclaim alleged she concurred in and was equally responsible for the emails and conspired with the other plaintiffs in bringing the action.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1)(a): a claim is struck only if, assuming pleaded facts to be true, it is 'plain and obvious' the claim cannot succeed; novel or complex claims should not be struck (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., 1990 CanLII 90 (SCC); R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada, 2011 SCC 42; Watson v. Bank of America Corporation, 2014 BCSC 532).
firac.application: Taking the pleaded facts as true—that Ms. Pour participated in a conspiracy involving publication of defamatory statements and improper litigation for an improper purpose—the counterclaim raised a triable issue. Complexity or novelty is not a basis to strike. No affidavit merely contradicting the pleadings could displace this on a 9-5(1)(a) application.
firac.conclusion: It was not plain and obvious the claim could not succeed; the counterclaim disclosed a triable issue. This argument failed.

firac.issue: Does the failure to quote the defamatory emails accurately render the pleading fatally defective?
firac.facts: The counterclaim paraphrased rather than quoted the March 2009 emails; counsel conceded the emails were not accurately quoted but said this was done for conciseness and was a fair reading.
firac.rule: Striking is a draconian remedy that should not be granted where the deficiency can be cured by amendment or a less severe order (Sahyoun v. Ho, 2015 BCSC 392, aff'd 2017 BCCA 96; Royal Bank of Canada v. Roberts, 2014 BCSC 1797).
firac.application: The court agreed the emails should have been quoted accurately but held the deficiency was not fatal and could be cured by a more proportionate remedy—leave to amend to properly quote the emails.
firac.conclusion: Pleading not struck on this ground; leave to amend granted.

firac.issue: Can a malicious prosecution claim stand where the underlying proceeding has not terminated in the claimant's favour?
firac.facts: Ms. Pour's claim for monies owed was ongoing when the counterclaim was filed and remained extant. She had discontinued her action against some corporate defendants but continued against Mr. Ichikawa.
firac.rule: Nelles v. Ontario, 1989 CanLII 77 (SCC), sets four elements for malicious prosecution, including that the proceedings must have terminated in favour of the plaintiff. Abuse of process, by contrast, does not require termination (311165 B.C. Ltd. v. Canada (A.G.), 2017 BCCA 196).
firac.application: When the counterclaim was filed the Amnis defendants had no cause of action for malicious prosecution because Ms. Pour's claim was ongoing. Her discontinuance against related corporate entities—done to clarify her claim was against Mr. Ichikawa—was not a 'termination in favour of the plaintiff'. The defect was not cured.
firac.conclusion: No cause of action for malicious prosecution existed; paragraph 4 of the prayer for relief (damages for malicious prosecution) was struck against Ms. Pour.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally civil litigation (K002), so that is the tier-1 practice area. The counterclaim at issue was principally for defamation (K015), the central substantive cause of action analysed for both limitation and cause-of-action purposes. The dispute arose in the context of a class-style joint family action, but more accurately it involves procedural machinery; K020 (class action / collective recovery) is a weak/borderline pick and is flagged—the case is not truly a class proceeding, so it is included only loosely to capture the multi-plaintiff/counterclaim procedural dimension. K021 (interlocutory injunction) does not apply and should not be used. The strongest genuinely engaged keywords are K002 and K015; the application concerns striking pleadings, limitation of counterclaims, and the tort of malicious prosecution, for which the vocabulary offers no precise tier-2 term. I limited selection to those that genuinely fit rather than inventing IDs. Note: fewer than five strongly applicable keywords exist in this controlled antisemitism-focused vocabulary, so K020 is flagged as weak and K021 is not appropriate—the truly applicable picks are K002 and K015.

registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Richard Warman v. Michael Veck

defining_issues: Were the words published by Mr Veck defamatory of Mr Warman, and did the plaintiff establish publication of and concerning him?
Did Mr Veck have any defence in law — fair comment, qualified privilege, or responsible communication — for publishing the defamatory statements?
What quantum of general damages is appropriate?
Did Mr Veck's retraction and apology serve to reduce or eliminate the damages?

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff establish that Mr Veck published defamatory statements of and concerning Mr Warman?
firac.facts: Mr Veck, a WAIS website member, posted an article in March 2009 that reproduced the entire text of a retracted National Post article and amplified it, stating in effect that Mr Warman was 'corrupt', 'surreal', 'strange', a 'radical anti-racist' who had fabricated a racist article about Senator Cools and manufactured 'phony-racism', asserting the National Post allegations were true.
firac.rule: To make out defamation the plaintiff must show the words were defamatory, referred to the plaintiff, and were published; posting on the internet constitutes publication (Barrick Gold Corp. v. Lopehandia, 2004 CanLII 12938 (ON CA)). Repetition is not a defence — one who repeats a defamatory statement is answerable as if he had started it (Associated Newspapers Ltd. v. Dingle, [1964] A.C. 371).
firac.application: The court found the article clearly imputed dishonest and quasi-criminal conduct to Mr Warman — creating hate speech to advance anti-hate complaints — which was obviously defamatory, was clearly of and about Mr Warman, and was published by posting to the WAIS website. That much of the content was drawn from Mr Kay's National Post article did not assist Mr Veck.
firac.conclusion: The three elements of defamation were established; the article was defamatory of Mr Warman.

firac.issue: Did Mr Veck have a legal defence of fair comment, qualified privilege, or responsible communication?
firac.facts: Mr Veck argued his post was fair comment on a matter of public interest, was made on an occasion of qualified privilege, and was responsible communication. He was not a journalist, had read only the National Post article, did not learn it had been retracted, did no further research, and did not contact Mr Warman.
firac.rule: Fair comment protects statements of opinion, not assertions of fact, and comment must appear as comment (WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40). Qualified privilege attaches to an occasion where the publisher has a legal, moral or social duty to communicate and the recipient a corresponding interest (Hill v. Church of Scientology, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130); publication to 'the world' on the internet is generally overpublication (Vigna v. Levant, 2010 ONSC 6308). Responsible communication generally applies to journalists acting professionally (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61).
firac.application: The post was a statement of facts, not opinion; the epithets were rhetorical responses to defamatory facts rather than distinguishable comment, so fair comment failed. There was no reciprocal duty/interest and publication to the entire internet was overpublication, so no occasion of qualified privilege arose. Mr Veck was not a journalist, there was no urgency, he did not seek Mr Warman's side, and the matters were already public — responsible communication did not apply.
firac.conclusion: None of the defences succeeded; Mr Veck was liable.

firac.issue: What quantum of general damages should be awarded?
firac.facts: The article was posted to the entire internet but remained on WAIS for about 18 months without Mr Warman, who vigilantly monitored statements about himself, becoming aware of it. Mr Veck was a lawyer but not identified as such in the post; there was no claim for economic loss or special damages, and no malice.
firac.rule: General damages in defamation are assessed on all the circumstances, including extent of publication; a lawyer's defamatory statement can aggravate damages only where professional status lends credibility, and aggravated damages require malice or egregious conduct.
firac.application: The court inferred from the lack of detection that few persons actually read the article. Mr Veck's status as a lawyer was immaterial since he was not identified as one. He acted without malice, reacting to a reputable newspaper article he believed true, so aggravated damages were not warranted.
firac.conclusion: General damages of $10,000 were awarded; no aggravated damages.

firac.issue: Did Mr Veck's retraction and apology reduce the damages?
firac.facts: After receiving the libel notice Mr Veck removed the article and posted a statement noting that Mr Warman said the allegations were false and retracting and apologizing on that basis, without acknowledging the article was without foundation.
firac.rule: Under the Libel and Slander Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.12, s. 9, a full and effective retraction and apology may mitigate or eliminate damages; the adequacy of the apology is assessed on its substance.
firac.application: The retraction amounted only to a withdrawal because Mr Warman disagreed, and stopped short of acknowledging the article lacked foundation. Mr Veck could at least have stated that the source article had been withdrawn by its author and that he had no personal knowledge of the matters, but did not. The apology fell so short of a full and effective one that no reduction was warranted.
firac.conclusion: The apology and retraction did not reduce the damages; judgment for Mr Warman for $10,000.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a defamation tort action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. name_verification.name_in_document: Sylvia Katerina Josephe Boss v. The Heirs to the Estate of the Late Valentine Boss -and- Milica Krivokapic, and Helen Heslop

defining_issues: Did Professor Boss possess the mental capacity required to make the notarial will of November 12, 2010?
Was the will vitiated by undue influence (captation) exercised by his second wife, Milica?
Should the plaintiff's expert report be excluded for lack of objectivity and procedural defects?
Should the defendant's cross-demand for damages for libel/defamation arising from the pleadings succeed?

firac.issue: Did the testator have the required capacity to make the November 12, 2010 will?
firac.facts: Professor Boss, an intellectually distinguished McGill historian, suffered a series of medical incidents (prostate cancer, a June/July 2010 bout of pancreatitis causing encephalopathy and delirium, gall-bladder surgery) and was later diagnosed (2011-2014) with Lewy Body/Parkinson's dementia. He nonetheless continued teaching two courses in fall 2010 and gave the will instructions directly to the notary.
firac.rule: Art. 703 and 707 C.C.Q.: every person with the required capacity may make a will, capacity assessed at the moment of execution. There is a presumption of capacity; the contestant bears the initial burden and, on prima facie proof of a serious (not merely simple) doubt on the balance of probabilities, the burden shifts to the proponent (Paquin v. Trottier; Succession de Charette, 2017 QCCS 1381). Capacity requires the power to hold the essential field of the mind in appreciation as a whole (McEwen v. Jenkins; Thibodeau v. Thibodeau).
firac.application: The Court rejected the plaintiff's expert (Dr. Brock) for bias and accepted the neurologist Dr. Verret, who concluded that the delirium was transient and reversible, that Lewy Body disease was diagnosed only a year later, and that Boss was near his pre-delirium cognitive state in November 2010. The notary Rapp and numerous affiants confirmed his lucidity, though the Court found some cognitive diminution had occurred by then.
firac.conclusion: Professor Boss had the requisite capacity to execute the will; the incapacity argument was rejected.

firac.issue: Was the will the product of undue influence (captation) by Milica?
firac.facts: The will effectively disinherited Sylvia (Boss's only child, whom he loved despite her bipolar illness), leaving essentially the whole estate to Milica. Independent witnesses described Milica's hostility toward Sylvia, statements that Sylvia deserved to inherit nothing, her control of Boss's social contacts (lawyers' cease-and-desist letters, supervised final visit), her management/censoring of his correspondence, and Boss's growing physical and emotional dependence on her amid some cognitive decline.
firac.rule: Captation requires fraudulent manoeuvres (improper schemes, lies, deceit) that were determinative of the testator's dispositions (Succession de Charette; Brusenbauch v. Young). Capacity does not preclude coercion where weakened faculties reduce the testator's resistance (Brière; Tewkesbury v. Ouellet; Thibault v. Auger). Proof may rest on serious, precise and concordant presumptions (arts. 2846, 2849 C.C.Q.; Longpré v. Thériault), the precision test being one of probability, not near-certainty (Ducharme).
firac.application: The Court found the near-total exclusion of a beloved daughter unexplained and out of character; Milica's antipathy, sense of entitlement to the whole estate, control over Boss's contacts and correspondence, and his dependence and diminished cognition together formed a concordant pattern. Milica's credibility was rejected as she contradicted eight independent witnesses. These facts founded a serious and precise presumption of undue influence.
firac.conclusion: Undue influence was established; the will was annulled and the succession devolves ab intestat under art. 666 C.C.Q.

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's expert report be excluded?
firac.facts: Dr. Brock's reports lacked the art. 235 C.C.P. declaration initially, he had not been recognized as an expert, and he attended trial acting as a coach/advocate for the plaintiff, speculating on Milica's motives and overstepping the Court's limits.
firac.rule: Art. 22 C.C.P. requires experts to act objectively and impartially; the acid test is whether the opinion would be the same regardless of who retained the expert (White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co., 2015 SCC 23). Arts. 235, 293 C.C.P. govern the declaration and recognition of experts.
firac.application: The declaration defect was cured by refiling; Brock was recognized as an expert in medicine for the aged but not on delirium. However, his manifest bias and advocacy destroyed his usefulness and credibility.
firac.conclusion: All evidence authored by Dr. Brock was rejected except where corroborated by Milica's expert; the exhibit filing objection (P-81.1-.3) was maintained.

firac.issue: Should Milica's cross-demand for defamation succeed?
firac.facts: Milica claimed damages for allegedly false, outrageous and malicious allegations in Sylvia's pleadings (that she abused, controlled and manipulated Boss) and for counsel's use of the word 'greedy' in a case-management conference.
firac.rule: Allegations consistent with and supportive of a genuine claim, made in the context of legal proceedings, are not actionable defamation.
firac.application: The impugned statements were neither outrageous nor malicious but were consistent with a supportable claim of coercion; moreover, para. 110's allegation of manipulation was found proven. Milica's exaggerated claim bordered on abuse.
firac.conclusion: The cross-demand was dismissed with costs; Helen would not have been liable in any event.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 area under which wills/estates falls in the vocabulary, and K054 (wills/estates) is the most specific term for this succession dispute over testamentary capacity and undue influence/captation. K002 (Civil litigation) captures the civil action, expert-evidence and abuse-of-process dimensions. K015 (defamation) is engaged by the defendant's cross-demand for damages for libel/defamation. name_verification.name_in_document: Richard Warman v. The National Post Company, Jonathan Kay, Ezra Levant, Kathy Shaidle, fivefeetoffury.com, smalldeadanimals.com, Catherine McMillan, Mark Fournier, freedomInion.ca, Constance Wilkins-Fournier

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff be ordered to produce the unredacted appendices to the Independent Computer Expert (ICE) Report, or were relevance-based redactions permissible under the ICE Protocol and the proportionality principles governing discovery?
Must the plaintiff provide fuller particulars of his solicitor-client and litigation privilege claims over the redacted appendices?
Had the plaintiff satisfied the ICE Protocol and the Court's original production order, and were all relevant documents produced?

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff be compelled to produce the unredacted 12,000+ page appendices to the ICE Report, or were relevance redactions justified under the protocol and proportionality?
firac.facts: In a defamation action alleging Warman authored a 'Hateful Posting', the Court had earlier ordered an Independent Computer Expert to examine a mirror image of Warman's hard drive to determine whether he authored the posting. Single-word searches generated over 12,000 pages of raw data in appendices, which Warman's counsel vetted and heavily redacted for relevance and privilege. Levant moved to obtain the unredacted appendices.
firac.rule: Rule 76 (Simplified Procedure) and Rule 29.2 of the Rules of Civil Procedure require proportionality in discovery; the court must consider time, expense, prejudice, interference with the orderly progress of the action, and overall volume of documents (r. 29.2.03). Parties need only produce relevant documents (Rule 30). Privacy interests in personal computers are heightened: R. v. Vu, 2013 SCC 60; R. v. Morelli, 2010 SCC 8.
firac.application: The Master found the single-word searches produced an enormous, unforeseen volume of raw data, most of it irrelevant to the narrow question of authorship of the Hateful Posting. The protocol, though silent on relevance, was implicitly intended to narrow, not expand, production. Ordering disclosure of 12,000+ pages, requiring further multi-party review, would defeat the Simplified Procedure's goals of economy and speed, was disproportionate, and would sweepingly invade Warman's heightened privacy interest in his personal computer. The core purpose of the order had been achieved: no evidence of the Hateful Posting existed on the drive.
firac.conclusion: Production of the unredacted appendices was refused; relevance redactions were permitted and proportionality favoured denying the motion.

firac.issue: Must the plaintiff provide fuller particulars of his solicitor-client and litigation privilege claims?
firac.facts: Warman redacted appendices citing solicitor-client privilege, litigation privilege and irrelevancy, providing a revised list of objections that did not always identify document type, date, or the related proceedings. Levant argued he could not assess or challenge the claims.
firac.rule: Schedule 'B' privilege claims must identify the privilege, the parties to the communication, its author, and a description sufficient to show relevance (Shibish v. Honda of Canada Inc., 2010 ONSC 3770); factual information in privileged documents that would otherwise be disclosable is not shielded. Litigation privilege endures only to the end of related litigation and yields more readily than solicitor-client privilege (Kaymar Rehabilitation Inc. v. Champlain CCAC, 2013 ONSC 1754).
firac.application: The Master accepted that counsel had reasonably established that all relevant files—those establishing whether Warman authored the Hateful Posting or relating to other issues—had been produced. Requiring Warman to re-review 12,000+ pages to further particularize privilege claims over predominantly irrelevant material would be wasteful, delay the action, and serve only the 'fishing expedition' Levant had sworn he was not pursuing. Levant's own Schedule B was itself devoid of particulars.
firac.conclusion: The request for full particulars of the privilege claims was dismissed.

firac.issue: Had the plaintiff satisfied the ICE Protocol and the Court's original production order?
firac.facts: The ICE Report and earlier Digital Wyzdom reports confirmed no evidence on Warman's hard drive of the Hateful Posting, the pseudonym used, or the registering email address.
firac.rule: An order must be complied with according to its spirit and intent, applying common sense and logic where the literal outcome was unanticipated.
firac.application: The order's purpose—a second opinion on whether Warman could have authored the Hateful Posting—had been fulfilled; the redactions to the appendices did not affect that conclusion. The order was designed to limit, not expand, Levant's access; handing over 12,000+ pages of raw data was contrary to its intent and to the Simplified Procedure Rule. With discoveries now available under amended Rule 76, Levant's original justification for computer access no longer held.
firac.conclusion: The order's spirit and intent had been satisfied; the motion was dismissed with costs to Warman on a partial indemnity basis.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as the decision turns on discovery, production, proportionality (Rule 29.2/Rule 76) and privilege in a civil action. K015 (defamation) is central: the underlying action is a defamation claim over internet postings. name_verification.name_in_document: Bouchard c. Succession de Zalac

defining_issues: Was the late Slavoljub Zalac subjected to undue influence (captation) by Boris Zalac such that the 2020 Will must be declared null?
Should Boris Zalac be declared unworthy of inheriting from his father's estate?

firac.issue: Was the 2020 Will the product of undue influence (captation) by Boris Zalac, rendering it null?
firac.facts: After a 35-year loving relationship, the testator made mirror wills with his spouse Ms. Bouchard in 2015, naming her sole universal legatee. In 2019-2020 his health collapsed (legally blind, hip pain, hearing impairment, depression, isolation, heavy drinking). During the COVID lockdown Boris Zalac, his son, retained his own notary, booked and followed up on appointments, reviewed the draft will and mandate, brought his father to sign, chose his own spouse as witness, and became sole heir and liquidator under the 2020 Will. Ms. Bouchard was never informed; she even unknowingly paid the notary's invoice.
firac.rule: Under the Civil Code of Quebec and Stoneham and Tewkesbury v. Ouellet, [1979] 2 SCR 172, captation consists of fraudulent maneuvers that determine how a testator bequeaths; currying favour is not illegal but seizing the testator's will is. Per Brusenbauch v. Young, 2019 QCCA 914, the party alleging undue influence must prove fraud, defect in consent and causation on a balance of probabilities (arts. 2803, 2804 C.c.Q.), often through serious, precise and concordant presumptions of fact (art. 2849 C.c.Q.). Section 48 of the Quebec Charter protects aged persons against exploitation.
firac.application: The Court found the testator vulnerable, isolated and dependent, and rejected Boris Zalac's portrayal of a 'toxic' marriage as unsupported (all corroborating texts postdated 2019). Numerous indicia from M.P. c. F.D. were present: the heir chose the notary, drove the process, approved drafts, selected the witness, and became sole heir/liquidator, with a complacent notary who missed the testator's impairments. The powerful and only reasonable inference was that Boris exploited his father's weakened state to redirect the estate to himself, contrary to s. 48 of the Quebec Charter.
firac.conclusion: The Plaintiff discharged her burden; the 2020 Will was declared null and void and the estate devolved under the 2015 Will, with Boris ordered to reimburse amounts he paid himself and his lawyers from the Estate.

firac.issue: Should Boris Zalac be declared unworthy of inheriting under arts. 621-623 C.c.Q.?
firac.facts: The Plaintiff added a conclusion in her Modified Application of July 22, 2022 seeking a declaration of unworthiness against Boris Zalac; the succession opened on the testator's death on March 5, 2021.
firac.rule: Articles 621-623 C.c.Q. allow a successor to apply, within one year after the opening of the succession or becoming aware of a cause of unworthiness, to have an heir declared unworthy.
firac.application: Because the 2020 Will was nullified and the 2015 Will (which does not name Boris as a legatee) governs, the unworthiness question is moot. Additionally, the conclusion was added more than one year after the succession opened, so it was time-barred under art. 623.
firac.conclusion: The Court declined to declare Boris unworthy; the conclusion failed as both moot and out of time.
