name_verification.name_in_document: S.S.1 v. S.S.2

defining_issues: Should the mother be granted sole custody of the children, and what parenting/access regime is in the best interests of A.E.S.?
Should income be imputed to the father on the basis of intentional under-employment, and in what amount?
What table child support and section 7 expenses are payable, including retroactive amounts and post-secondary expenses?
Has there been a material change in circumstances warranting variation or termination of the spousal support the mother pays the father?
Should the father be ordered to obtain life insurance to secure his child support obligation?
Was the transfer of the father's shares in the numbered company valid?

firac.issue: Should the mother have sole custody of the children and what residential/access arrangement serves the best interests of the youngest child, A.E.S.?
firac.facts: The parties are highly conflicted; the four oldest children have no or minimal relationship with the father, and the father consented to the mother having custody of the three girls. Only the youngest son, A.E.S., who has ADHD and a learning disability, still follows an access schedule. The father sought parallel parenting and alternating-week residence; the mother sought sole custody and reduced access. Voice of the Child reports, a psycho-educational assessment and CAS reports emphasized A.E.S.'s need for stability and the harm of ongoing parental conflict.
firac.rule: Custody is governed by the best interests of the child. Joint custody requires evidence that parties can communicate effectively (Kaplanis v. Kaplanis, 2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)). The court considers each parent's role, the child's needs, wishes and stability.
firac.application: Given the toxic relationship and inability to communicate, joint or parallel parenting was inappropriate; one parent had to be the decision-maker. The mother had been the primary parent managing A.E.S.'s medical, educational, tutoring and extracurricular needs. A.E.S. required a calm, predictable environment; the father was found to be negatively influencing him. The court declined to disrupt stability with an alternating-week schedule and adopted the mother's proposed access with a detailed multidirectional order.
firac.conclusion: The mother was granted sole custody of all four remaining children. A.E.S. resides primarily with the mother with defined access to the father, governed by a comprehensive multidirectional order; the child is to attend a public school chosen by the mother.

firac.issue: Should income be imputed to the father for intentional under-employment, and if so how much?
firac.facts: The father, a mechanical engineer with a Master's degree, was terminated in October 2013. He applied mostly for jobs well below his qualifications, never applied in construction or dental office work despite experience, and abandoned building-inspector certification one course short. He received large dividend distributions in 2015 but lent $185,000 to his sister and rerouted rental income to his brother's company to avoid creditors, while on social assistance yet taking vacations.
firac.rule: Section 19 of the Federal Child Support Guidelines permits imputing income where a spouse is intentionally under-employed. The three-part Drygala v. Pauli (2002) test applies; there is no need for bad faith (Drygala), the payor bears the onus once intentional under-employment is shown (Jackson v. Mayerle), and the court has broad discretion to fix an amount on a rational basis (D.D. v. H.D.).
firac.application: The father chose to earn less than he was capable of, applying for jobs below his abilities and declining reasonable avenues (construction, dental office, building inspector). His financial manoeuvres to avoid creditors reinforced intentional under-employment. The court rejected the food-industry figure and rejected the mother's speculative building-inspector and dividend figures, but added benefits paid by his brother's company and RRSP income.
firac.conclusion: Income of $60,000 was imputed to the father effective January 1, 2015 and for 2016, comprising imputed employment income plus housing/personal benefits and other amounts.

firac.issue: What table child support and section 7 expenses are payable, including retroactive amounts and post-secondary costs?
firac.facts: Four children reside primarily with the mother; the eldest, M.I.S., attends university. The mother incurred all section 7 expenses (medical, health insurance, tutoring, Hebrew school, camps, extracurriculars, university costs). The father argued he was not consulted and could not pay while denied interest on equalization.
firac.rule: Table support is set under the Federal Child Support Guidelines based on income. A child continuing full-time education remains a 'child of the marriage' under the Divorce Act. Section 7 expenses must meet the three-part necessity/reasonableness test and fall within the enumerated categories.
firac.application: Using imputed income of $60,000 and mother's income of $139,260, the court set table support amounts and found M.I.S. a child of the marriage whose university costs are section 7 expenses. The court scrutinized each expense, disallowing excessive summer camps and non-qualifying extracurriculars, allowed a child contribution from M.I.S.'s income, and recalculated the father's percentage share (35.7% in 2015; 36% in 2016). Retroactive section 7 arrears were set off against interest accruing on the equalization payment.
firac.conclusion: The father must pay specified table support and $28,725.96 toward section 7 expenses (retroactive portion set off against equalization interest); future arrears to be deducted from the equalization payment.

firac.issue: Has there been a material change in circumstances permitting variation of the spousal support the mother pays the father?
firac.facts: The Divisional Court had ordered the mother to pay the father $800/month needs-based spousal support from January 1, 2015. Since then the mother's income dropped from $172,664 to $139,260, the father's income was imputed at $60,000, and M.I.S. ceased to attract table support.
firac.rule: Spousal support may be varied on a material change in circumstances. Entitlement here was non-compensatory (need-based). Quantum is assessed against the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines.
firac.application: The changes in the parties' incomes and support obligations constituted a material change. The father remained entitled to needs-based support given the 19-year marriage and income disparity. Using DivorceMate calculations with corrected incomes, the court fixed mid-range SSAG amounts.
firac.conclusion: Support was varied to $1,018/month effective January 1, 2015 and $989/month effective January 1, 2016; no termination or end date imposed, subject to future material change.

firac.issue: Should the father be ordered to obtain life insurance to secure his child support obligation?
firac.facts: The mother sought a $1,000,000 life insurance designation as security, citing A.E.S.'s special needs. The father owns no life insurance, and there was no evidence of his insurability or insurance cost.
firac.rule: Under the Divorce Act the court has broad discretion to impose terms securing support, including insurance and binding the estate (Katz v. Katz, 2014 ONCA 606); insurability, cost and required quantum must be established.
firac.application: Without evidence of insurability, cost, or the amount needed, the court could not order insurance, but it could bind the estate.
firac.conclusion: No life insurance ordered; instead, the father's child support obligation is declared binding on his estate, limited to support owing over the duration of entitlement.

firac.issue: Was the June 3, 2013 transfer of the father's shares in the numbered company valid?
firac.facts: Both parties admit the father was a shareholder. The share register shows his 10 class C shares transferred to the mother on June 3, 2013, but the father never consented or signed, and the mother conceded he should retain a 10% interest.
firac.rule: A share transfer requires the shareholder's consent; an unauthorized transfer is void.
firac.application: As the father never consented and did not sign, and the mother conceded his interest, the transfer and related director's resolution were nullified.
firac.conclusion: The share transfer and 2013 director's resolution were declared null and void; corporate records to be corrected; sale/valuation issues remain with Justice Roger.

keywords_rationale: The case is squarely family law (K006). Custody and access determinations turned on best interests of the child (K047) and custody/access arrangements (K048), the core of the decision. Child support and section 7 expenses, including imputation of income and post-secondary support, engage parental/child support (K050). Variation of spousal support engages spousal support (K053). Religious upbringing (K052) applies because the detailed order addresses Hebrew school and the child's religious education. Jewish holidays (K027) is directly engaged by the extensive holiday access schedule (Shavuot, Sukkot, Rosh Hashanah, Hanukkah, Purim, Pesach, Yom Kippur). Marriage/separation agreement (K049) is a weaker pick — the parties' prior orders and equalization arose from the divorce rather than a negotiated agreement, so it is borderline and included mainly for the property/equalization aspect.
location_rationale: The decision is of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice. Numerous references locate the family in Ottawa (e.g., Children's Aid Society of Ottawa, Ottawa Police Service, Ottawa-Carleton District School Board, schools 'in Ottawa'), establishing the city as Ottawa.
registry_rationale: Court file no. is FC-11-927-1 but no specific court registry office is named in the decision, so registry is left null.

case_name: Z.H. v. Huron-Perth Children’s Aid Society

name_verification.name_in_document: Z.H. v. Huron-Perth Children's Aid Society

defining_issues: Is an openness order in favour of the birth parents in the best interests of the two Métis children being placed for adoption, under s. 196(7) of the CYFSA and the Federal Act?
Will openness permit the continuation of a relationship with the birth parents that is both beneficial and meaningful to the children?
If some openness is warranted, what form should the order take given the birth parents' aggressive conduct and the need to protect the adoptive placement?

firac.issue: Is an openness order in favour of the birth parents in the best interests of the two Métis children being placed for adoption?
firac.facts: T.H. (10) and Z.H. (9), found to be of Métis heritage, were placed in extended care in 2020 and then placed for adoption in 2023 with their two younger siblings. They wish to keep in-person contact with their birth parents, which the parents consent to but the Society opposes. The Office of the Children's Lawyer brought openness applications on the children's behalf.
firac.rule: Section 196(7) CYFSA permits an openness order where it is in the best interests of the child, will permit continuation of a beneficial and meaningful relationship, and (for children 12+) the child consents. 'Best interests' for openness is defined in s. 179(2), which mandates consideration of the child's views and, for a First Nations, Inuit or Métis child, the importance of preserving cultural identity and connection to community. The Federal Act (ss. 9, 10, 17) makes cultural continuity essential and the best interests the primary consideration. Kawartha-Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316, requires special considerations for Indigenous children in every decision, including openness.
firac.application: The children are only 9 and 10, so consent under s. 196(7)(c) does not apply. The court found the children clearly and consistently wished to maintain in-person contact, and that preservation of their Métis culture was a paramount factor since the specific Métis community could not be identified despite reasonable efforts by the Society and OCL. The birth parents may be the children's only real link to their specific Indigenous community. However, these cultural and best-interests considerations had to be balanced against the primary need for the security and permanency of the adoptive placement.
firac.conclusion: Some openness is in the children's best interests, principally because contact with the birth parents is the children's main link to their specific Métis heritage.

firac.issue: Will openness permit the continuation of a relationship with the birth parents that is both beneficial and meaningful to the children?
firac.facts: The children love their parents and enjoy visits (rating them highly), but Z.H. wanted another adult present because 'his dad gets mad.' The birth father engaged in sustained aggressive conduct: threatening voicemails and social media posts calling the adoptive parents 'kidnappers,' a conviction for uttering threats, picketing at the adoptive family's church leading to arrest and a peace bond, and telling the children the adoptive parents were kidnappers. The birth mother, though more cooperative, could not control the father and did not accept the adoption.
firac.rule: Under s. 196(7)(b), the relationship must be both beneficial and meaningful, assessed from the child's perspective (Re SM, 2009 ONCJ 317). A relationship may be meaningful but not beneficial; it is not beneficial where the birth parent's conduct could undermine the adoption. Courts list attributes—aggression/poor impulse control, lack of support for the caregiver, dishonesty, litigiousness—that impair adoption prospects (CAS of Toronto v. A.F., 2015 ONCJ 678).
firac.application: The court found the relationship meaningful because the children love their parents and would be sad without contact. On benefit, the father exhibited essentially all the attributes courts identify as undermining adoption, and the mother could not control him or accept the adoptive placement. Direct contact therefore posed a serious risk of destabilizing the placement. The benefit lay not in the contact itself but in the cultural connection to the children's Métis community that the birth parents could provide.
firac.conclusion: The relationship is meaningful, and beneficial only insofar as it provides the children's main connection to their specific Métis culture; direct in-person contact is not beneficial.

firac.issue: What form should the openness order take given the birth parents' conduct and the need to protect the adoptive placement?
firac.facts: The adoptive parents had to move communities for safety and obtained police protection; a peace bond restrains the father. The Society would support only written updates. In-person visits historically triggered the father and worsened the children's behaviours. The OCL sought a detailed, supervision-like in-person openness order with numerous protective terms.
firac.rule: Openness must be structured so it does not undercut the security and success of the adoption; the biological parent's interests are secondary to the adoption succeeding (B.R. v. K.R., 2017 ONSC 5402). The court may order indirect contact (letters, pictures, video) and must weigh the adoptive parents' ability to comply (s. 196(8)); the Society cannot be compelled to participate without consent (s. 196(9)). The applicant bears the onus of presenting a viable plan for in-person openness (CCAS of Toronto v. A.P., 2019 ONCJ 631).
firac.application: The 'road testing' of access since 2020 showed in-person contact was unworkable and destabilizing, and no viable supervised in-person plan was presented. In-person visits, even with the mother alone, would jeopardize the placement given the father's uncontrollable conduct. The court instead ordered indirect openness: annual written updates from caregivers to the parents, annual video/letter/card messages from each parent (subject to review and appropriateness), non-contact and no-attendance terms, plus a consent sibling-access provision. The parents were encouraged to share Métis cultural information.
firac.conclusion: An indirect openness order was made—annual updates and screened annual messages, with protective no-contact terms—rather than the intrusive in-person order sought by the OCL.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a child-protection/adoption openness proceeding under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is central: the s. 179(2) and Federal Act best-interests tests, including the special Indigenous cultural-continuity considerations, drive the outcome. K048 (custody/access) is the closest available term for the openness/contact regime the court crafted. K024 (freedom of expression) and its parent K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) are weaker picks—flagged as borderline—but the birth father expressly invoked a 'right to freedom of expression' and 'civil liberties' to justify his social-media posting and protesting, which the court weighed against the children's placement security. The controlled vocabulary lacks dedicated terms for Indigenous/Métis child welfare, openness orders, or child protection, so no more precise keywords were available.
location_rationale: The court file numbers are given as 'City of Stratford F023-881' and 'City of Stratford F023-882', and the proceeding is before the Ontario Court of Justice, placing the matter in Stratford, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The court file heading 'City of Stratford' identifies the Stratford registry/office of the Ontario Court of Justice.

case_name: CAS of S.D.G. v. A.A., J.M., A.E., T.S., J.W.

name_verification.name_in_document: CAS of S.D.G. v. A.A., J.M., A.E., T.S., J.W.

defining_issues: Did the Society meet the two-part test under s. 94 CYFSA to establish that the child could not be returned to the pre-intervention caregiver (Ms. M), with or without a supervision order?

As between the competing placements of the kin caregiver (Mr. W) and the biological father (Mr. S), which placement is in the child's best interests, having regard to the risk of harm arising from Mr. S's outstanding criminal allegations?
What interim access arrangements should be ordered for Mr. S and Ms. M under s. 94(8) CYFSA?

firac.issue: Did the Society meet the two-part test under s. 94 CYFSA to show the child could not be returned to the pre-intervention caregiver?
firac.facts: J, born 2023, is a child with significant special needs (leg braces, physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy). Ms. M was principally caring for J on weekdays before the Society's intervention; concerns arose about unmet developmental and medical needs and maternal drug use, leading to J's removal from Ms. M's care on September 5, 2025. Communication between Ms. M and Mr. W had since improved and Ms. M was meeting conditions for her four other children.
firac.rule: At a temporary care and custody hearing the onus is on the Society to establish, on credible and trustworthy evidence, reasonable grounds to believe there is a real possibility that if returned the child will more probably than not suffer harm, and that the child cannot be adequately protected by a supervision order (Children's Aid Society of Ottawa-Carleton v. T., 2000 CanLII 21157). The court must choose the least disruptive placement consistent with adequate protection (s. 1(2) CYFSA); ss. 94(2)(a)/(b) are the least intrusive options, and s. 94(4) requires reasonable grounds of risk before a placement under (c) or (d).
firac.application: The court found Ms. M had charge of J immediately before intervention and that his medical needs were unmet at that time. While recent progress was acknowledged, the judge found it premature to return J: there were reasonable grounds to believe a real possibility that if returned J would more probably than not suffer harm through unmet medical needs, and that a supervision order could not adequately protect him.
firac.conclusion: The Society met its two-part onus under s. 94 CYFSA; J could not be returned to Ms. M's care, with or without a supervision order.

firac.issue: As between Mr. W and Mr. S, which placement is in J's best interests given Mr. S's criminal allegations?
firac.facts: J had been in Mr. W's kin care for over 200 days and was thriving. Mr. S, the biological father, had recently developed a positive relationship with J under supervision by paternal grandparents (approved kin caregivers). However, Mr. S faces two charges of sexual interference and two of sexual assault involving a six-year-old complainant, allegedly committed when he was about 15, with trial set for September 29, 2026; his affidavit did not disclose the charges and there was no evidence of bail conditions or of an independent Society risk assessment.
firac.rule: Where only one person had charge before intervention, competing placements under s. 94(2)(c) are decided on the child's best interests, protection and well-being (s. 74(3) CYFSA factors). Courts prioritize continuity of care and biological parents among viable plans (Catholic CAS of Toronto v. R.A., 2016 ONCJ 880) but must consider criminal history and potential exposure to harm in assessing risk (Children's Aid Society of Algoma v. W.(B.)). The inquiry is forward-looking and protective on a balance of probabilities, not a retrospective criminal-standard determination of fault.
firac.application: The judge found J was bonded to all caregivers and that Mr. W and Ms. M were his psychological parents since February 2023. She rejected the claim Mr. S was prevented from parenting earlier, and was not satisfied the safety plan mitigated the risk of sexual harm given the nature of the allegations and the absence of any independent Society assessment or verification. The uncertainty of the criminal trial's outcome also posed a risk of emotional harm and instability. Continuity favoured Mr. W, whose care concerns were largely mitigated or explained (only three missed appointments in over 200 days). Shared custody with Ms. M was rejected as premature and risking instability, and the grandparents' independent plan was not the least disruptive option.
firac.conclusion: J is to remain in Mr. W's care as the least disruptive placement consistent with his best interests; Mr. S's relief and the shared-custody proposal were dismissed.

firac.issue: What interim access should be ordered for Mr. S and Ms. M?
firac.facts: Mr. S already had every-second-weekend overnight access; Ms. M had one overnight per week. Mr. W sought to limit Mr. S to supervised daytime access twice weekly, while Mr. S sought an accelerated trajectory to expanded parenting time.
firac.rule: Section 94(8) CYFSA permits access orders on such terms as the court considers appropriate, guided by the paramount purpose of the child's best interests, protection and well-being and the secondary purpose of maintaining family integrity (s. 1(1)-(2), s. 74(3) CYFSA).
firac.application: Despite concerns about overnight visits with Mr. S, the court noted J enjoyed the time and that three attentive adults were present, and permitted one supervised overnight per week (with a door-alarm safety mechanism), ideally including a weekday so Mr. S could assist with appointments. Ms. M's access trajectory could continue to expand at the Society's discretion. Access to Mr. S could be revisited on motion after an independent Society assessment and the criminal trial.
firac.conclusion: Mr. S granted one overnight visit per week with safety conditions; Ms. M's access trajectory to continue expanding at the Society's discretion; J with Mr. W at all other times.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a child protection proceeding under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test for the competing-placement decision under s. 74(3). K048 (custody/access) captures both the temporary care and custody determination and the access order under s. 94(8). K004 (Criminal law) is a borderline pick included because the father's outstanding sexual offence allegations were central to the risk-of-harm analysis, though the case is not itself a criminal prosecution. K012 (procedural fairness) is a weak/borderline pick reflecting the judge's concern about the information gap created by the absence of disclosure of criminal charges/bail conditions in child protection court; it is more a commentary than a decided ground. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated child-protection term, so no closer keyword exists.
location_rationale: The decision states at para. 14 that "All the families reside in Cornwall, Ontario," and the applicant is the Children's Aid Society of the United Counties of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry (of which Cornwall is the seat). Province is Ontario (Superior Court of Justice, CYFSA, S.O. 2017).
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the court as the Ontario Superior Court of Justice with court file no. 25-233 but does not expressly name a court registry office, so it is left null.

defining_issues: What parenting order (primary residence, decision-making, and parenting time) is in the best interests of the child, given the father's family violence and harmful conduct?
Should income be imputed to the respondent father for the purpose of retroactive and ongoing child support and section 7 expenses, and if so in what amount?
Has the applicant established reasonable grounds to fear for her safety so as to justify a restraining order under s. 46 of the Family Law Act?

firac.issue: What parenting order is in the best interests of the six-year-old child, given the father's history of family violence and harmful conduct toward the child?
firac.facts: The parties separated in August 2022 and have one child, J.C. (six at trial). The father engaged in a pattern of rage, physical intimidation and verbal abuse of the mother, often in the child's presence, and directed psychological and physical abuse at the child (repeatedly telling her she 'smells'/'stinks', a lemon-juice 'ritual' on her armpits, scrubbing her genital area raw, bathing her in public men's washrooms, and cutting a chunk of her hair). He refused to disclose his current address, breached numerous court orders, refused to participate in the court-ordered s. 30 CLRA assessment and mediation, and failed to attend trial though granted leave to address parenting. The child nonetheless has a strong loving bond with him.
firac.rule: Sections 16(1)-(6) of the Divorce Act require the court to consider only the best interests of the child, with the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being as the primary consideration; s. 16(3) lists non-exhaustive factors including family violence (s.16(3)(j)); s. 2 defines 'family violence' broadly to include psychological and physical abuse and a child's direct/indirect exposure to it; s. 16(4) governs the impact-of-violence analysis. Barendregt v. Grebliounas, 2022 SCC 22 and V.K.G. v. I.G., 2023 ONSC 6329 guide the individualized, discretionary determination and the supervision analysis.
firac.application: The court accepted the largely uncontested evidence (including admissions deemed under r. 22(4) FLRs, affidavits, the s. 30 assessment and the mother's testimony) and found the father's conduct constituted psychological and physical abuse and family violence, revealing a lack of insight and an inability to place the child's needs ahead of his own conflict with the mother. Although the court gave weight to the child's love for her father, a strong bond is not necessarily a healthy one; the child could not be exposed to the father's instability and harmful behaviours without controls. The court gave limited weight to some of the assessor's recommendations given the more fulsome trial record and the father's non-participation. Joint decision-making was untenable given the father's refusal to communicate.
firac.conclusion: Primary residence remains with the mother; the mother has sole (final) decision-making over health, education and religion subject to notice/consultation via AppClose. The father's in-person parenting time is suspended immediately pending disclosure of his address with proof, then resumes on a professionally supervised basis, reviewable after 90 days and completion of parenting and anger-management programs; interim videoconference parenting continues. Specific prohibitions (no lemon-juice ritual, no telling the child she smells, no bathing in public washrooms, no cutting her hair) are imposed.

firac.issue: Should income be imputed to the father for child support and s. 7 expenses, and in what amount?
firac.facts: The father refused to comply with financial disclosure obligations despite court orders. He has a University of Toronto degree, a sporadic work history (soccer coaching, entry-level sales), quit jobs after two to three months, is director of Panodigm Inc. (no disclosure), told the child he is a 'no work daddy', and had recorded income/expenses in a 2022 financial statement (spousal support of $2,950/month; expenses of $35,112; rent of $2,300/month). He has paid no child support or s. 7 expenses since separation.
firac.rule: Section 15-20 of the Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97; s. 19(1) permits imputation where a spouse is intentionally unemployed/underemployed or fails to provide required income information. Imputation must be evidence-based, not arbitrary: Drygala v. Pauli (2002), 61 O.R. (3d) 711 (C.A.); Jeevanantham v. Thiruchelvam, 2023 ONCJ 487.
firac.application: Drawing an adverse inference from the father's non-disclosure and finding him capable of graduate-level employment, the court concluded he was intentionally unemployed/underemployed and imputed the amount submitted by the mother ($62,712, grossed-up to $78,604), derived from his recorded expenses plus rent. DivorceMate calculations produced table support of $732/month effective February 1, 2025, plus retroactive support from separation and a proportionate (46%) share of s. 7 expenses (daycare, camp, therapy).
firac.conclusion: Income of $62,712 (grossed-up $78,604) imputed; father to pay $732/month ongoing, $20,215 in retroactive child support arrears and $11,205.21 in s. 7 arrears, enforceable by the Family Responsibility Office via a Support Deduction Order, with annual disclosure obligations.

firac.issue: Has the applicant shown reasonable grounds to fear for her safety warranting a restraining order?
firac.facts: The father had threatened to kill and harm the mother, physically attacked and intimidated her (pinning her against a wall, shoving her), smashed her phone, made repeated false reports to police, the CAS and JFCS, contacted her employer to jeopardize her job by disclosing her medical condition, and continued acts of intimidation after separation (forcing his way into her apartment lobby).
firac.rule: Section 46 of the Family Law Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3 permits a restraining order where the applicant has 'reasonable grounds to fear' for her or a child's safety — a standard lower than the balance of probabilities: L.A.B. v. J.A.S., 2020 ONSC 3376. Such orders are not granted lightly given the liberty impairment and potential quasi-criminal/criminal consequences (r. 31 FLRs; s. 127(1) Criminal Code): Stave v. Chartrand, 2004 ONCJ 79; J.K. v. R.K., 2021 ONSC 1136. Section 46(3) permits appropriate terms (Marshall v. Reid, 2018 ONSC 648).
firac.application: The court found the father had committed past psychological and physical family violence and repeated post-separation intimidation, giving the mother's subjectively held fears a reasonable basis, while balancing the need to preserve meaningful parenting contact. Some requested terms (barring false institutional complaints; extending protection to non-party family members) were refused as unwieldy or beyond jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: A restraining order issued: the father must stay 200 metres from the mother's residence and workplace and not contact her directly or indirectly (except AppClose communications about the child), with a 10-metre exception for parenting exchanges. It is reviewable after one year absent breach.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area. K047 (best interests of the child) is central to the parenting determination under s. 16 of the Divorce Act. K048 (custody/access) captures the residence and supervised parenting-time orders. K050 (parental support) covers the child support and imputation-of-income analysis under the Child Support Guidelines. K052 (religious upbringing) applies because major decisions about the child's religion were allocated and the child's Jewish/Roman Catholic heritage featured in the best-interests analysis. K093 (Jewish) reflects the child's Jewish maternal heritage and the father's objections to Jewish professionals. K058 (antisemitism) is a borderline pick, flagged as weak: it is engaged only through the father's objection to the s. 30 assessor and counsel being Jewish and his claim the mother was 'faking being Jewish', not a central legal issue. There is no controlled-vocabulary keyword for family violence or restraining orders, which are otherwise significant to the case.
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice and the events are situated in Toronto (e.g., parenting exchanges 'in front of the Shoppers Drug Mart located at 2345 Yonge Street Toronto', involvement of the Toronto Police Service, Children's Aid Society of Toronto, and the Applicant's Toronto employer). Province is Ontario as the court is the ONSC applying Ontario statutes.
registry_rationale: The decision names the Ontario Superior Court of Justice and court file no. FS-22-32470 but does not expressly identify the registry office; given the Toronto locus it is likely Toronto, but as the text does not state it, the field is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Paramount Fine Foods v Johnston

defining_issues: What is the appropriate sanction for civil contempt of court where the contemnor repeatedly breached a permanent defamation injunction?
Does the fact that the contumacious conduct constituted hate speech motivated by religion aggravate the sentence?
Is a custodial (jail) sentence warranted, or would non-custodial options such as a fine or community service suffice?

firac.issue: What is the appropriate sanction for civil contempt of court where the contemnor repeatedly breached a permanent defamation injunction?
firac.facts: After Ferguson J. found Johnston liable for defaming Fakih and Paramount Fine Foods and granted a permanent injunction (2019 ONSC 2910), Johnston, between February and May 2021, again publicly branded Fakih a 'terrorist,' 'baby killer,' 'murderer' and 'terror funder.' Myers J. found six acts of contempt (2021 ONSC 5285). Johnston delivered no mitigating evidence, refused to purge his contempt, and repeated the allegations twice more in an affidavit and new statement of claim days before sentencing.
firac.rule: Rule 60.11(5) of the Rules of Civil Procedure sets out the range of sanctions for contempt. Sentencing factors include the gravity of the offence, need to deter, past record and character, protection of the public, ability to realize on judgment, and intent (Estate of Paul Penna, 2010 ONSC 6993, adopting Law Society of BC v. Hansen, 2004 BCSC 825). The primary purpose is to compel compliance and uphold the rule of law (United Nurses of Alberta v. Alberta, 1992 CanLII 99 (SCC); Duncan v. Buckles, 2021 ONSC 5567). Sentences must be proportionate (Chiang (Re), 2009 ONCA 3).
firac.application: The court found no mitigating factors: this was not Johnston's first contempt, he showed no contrition, denied wrongdoing, mis-quoted his own broadcasts, and actively delegitimized the court. He repeated the defamation six times, including after the contempt motion was brought, for profit and to build his political audience. Monetary penalties were pointless as he had paid nothing and organized his affairs to avoid enforcement; community service without contrition would achieve neither compliance nor punishment.
firac.conclusion: The court imposed jail terms of three months for each of the six acts, running consecutively in two groups, for a total of 18 months, with a review after 15 months to allow purging of the contempt.

firac.issue: Does the fact that the contumacious conduct constituted hate speech motivated by religion aggravate the sentence?
firac.facts: Johnston's statements branded Fakih, a Muslim, a terrorist and baby-killer, drawing on Islamophobic tropes. Two prior judges characterized his words as classic hate speech. Johnston had also pleaded guilty in Brampton to wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group. The National Council of Canadian Muslims filed a Community Impact Statement.
firac.rule: Section 718.2(a)(i) of the Criminal Code directs that a sentence be increased where the offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on race, national or ethnic origin, or religion. Hate propaganda is 'wholly inimical to the democratic aspirations of the free expression guarantee' (R v Keegstra, 1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)). Sections 722 and 722.2 permit consideration of victim and community impact statements, applied here by analogy.
firac.application: The court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Johnston's acts of contempt were motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on religion, drawing on ugly stereotypes branding Muslims as terrorists. This social context, combined with his attacks on the rule of law and his profit/power-seeking motives, made the contempt especially odious and aggravating.
firac.conclusion: The hate-speech, religiously-motivated character of the conduct was an aggravating factor under s. 718.2(a)(i), justifying a sentence longer than prior precedents.

firac.issue: Is a custodial (jail) sentence warranted, or would non-custodial options suffice?
firac.facts: Johnston asked the court to impose 100 hours of community service so he could be a 'central figurehead of love,' and repeatedly asked for a list of prohibited words. He had paid nothing on the damages or costs awards, was already serving a contempt jail term in Alberta, and continued to undermine the court in his broadcasts and pleadings.
firac.rule: The court should consider sanctions other than jail (Criminal Code s. 718(2)(d),(e); Sussex Group Ltd. v. Sylvester). But where court orders can be ignored with impunity, 'the road to civil anarchy is close at hand' (Sussex Group Ltd. v Sylvester, 2003 CanLII 49336). Proper penalties must make the community take notice that disobedience will not be tolerated (Penna Estate).
firac.application: The court rejected Johnston's claims of good faith; he had already been given lists of defamatory statements yet repeated them. A monetary penalty was futile, and community service in the absence of contrition would achieve nothing. Given the ongoing danger to Fakih and the public and the affront to the rule of law, only removing Johnston from the public for a time would compel compliance and protect the public.
firac.conclusion: No sentencing option short of a jail term would secure compliance, protect Fakih and the public, or vindicate the rule of law; a custodial sentence of 18 months was imposed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a civil contempt proceeding arising from a defamation action. K015 (defamation) is central: the underlying tort and the injunction breached both concern defamatory statements. K061 (hate speech) and K060 (hate motivation) apply because the court expressly treated Johnston's words as classic hate speech and found the contempt aggravated under s. 718.2(a)(i) as motivated by religious bias. K063 (online hate / social media) fits, as Johnston's statements were made through internet broadcasts and podcasts. K024 (freedom of expression) is engaged through the Keegstra analysis and Johnston's claim to be exercising free-speech/political rights. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the closest vocabulary match for the injunction whose breach founded the contempt — a slightly weak pick since the order was a permanent, not interlocutory, injunction, but it is the nearest available term for injunctive relief.
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice. Court File No. CV-17-580326. The judge orders Mr. Johnston to surrender himself 'at the University Avenue entrance to the 361 University Avenue courthouse,' which is the Toronto courthouse, indicating the proceeding sits in Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: No registry is expressly labelled, but the reference to the 361 University Avenue courthouse (Toronto) where Mr. Johnston must turn himself in, combined with the Ontario Superior Court of Justice heading, supports Toronto as the registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: Her Majesty the Queen v. Sleiman El-Merhebi

defining_issues: How should the offence be characterized for sentencing — as vandalism or as a terrorist and hate-motivated act?
What aggravating and mitigating factors bear on the sentence for arson of a Jewish school library?
What is a fit and proportionate sentence given the priority of denunciation and general deterrence over rehabilitation?

firac.issue: How should the offence be characterized for sentencing purposes — as mere vandalism or as a terrorist and hate-motivated act?
firac.facts: The accused pleaded guilty to arson under s. 434 for firebombing the library of the United Talmud Torah Jewish elementary school, leaving a tract signed 'The Sheik Ahmed Yasine Brigade' threatening harder strikes against 'Israelis and Zionists' if Middle East conflict continued. In a taped conversation he told a friend 'This isn't vandalism, it's terrorism.'
firac.rule: Section 718.2(a)(v) of the Criminal Code makes it an aggravating circumstance that an offence was a terrorism offence, and s. 718.2(a)(i) that it was motivated by prejudice or hate based on national or ethnic origin or religion. Terrorism is distinguished from vandalism in that it aims to intimidate and spread fear for political ends.
firac.application: The tract's threats and the accused's own words showed intent to sow fear for political ends, aimed at Montréal's Jewish community whom he held responsible for Israel's acts. This was terrorism, not mindless destruction, and was motivated by hate/prejudice based on religion and ethnic origin, engaging both aggravating circumstances.
firac.conclusion: The Court characterized the crime as a terrorist act motivated by hate and prejudice toward the Jewish community, engaging s. 718.2(a)(i) and (v).

firac.issue: What aggravating and mitigating factors bear on the appropriate sentence?
firac.facts: Aggravating: maximum 14-year penalty; targeting an elementary school library; over $600,000 in damage; premeditation (kerosene bought two days ahead, alibi fabricated); the intimidating tract; severe trauma to the school and Jewish community. Mitigating: accused was 18½ at the offence, 19 at sentencing; no criminal record; guilty plea (though delayed seven months); expressed remorse; isolated act with no proven link to any terrorist or racist organization; supportive functional family; low assessed dangerousness per Dr. Morissette.
firac.rule: Section 718.2(a) requires a sentence to be increased or reduced to account for relevant aggravating and mitigating circumstances, and s. 718.1 requires proportionality to the gravity of the offence and the offender's degree of responsibility.
firac.application: The Court weighed the numerous serious aggravating factors — terrorism, hate motivation, targeting children, extensive damage, premeditation — against the youth, absence of record, guilty plea, remorse and isolated nature of the act. It gave the accused the benefit of the doubt on sincerity of remorse but noted the plea was not at the earliest opportunity and the evidence was overwhelming.
firac.conclusion: The balance of factors, dominated by the gravity of a hate-motivated terrorist act, supported a substantial custodial sentence while the mitigating factors kept it to the minimum consistent with the governing principles.

firac.issue: What is a fit and proportionate sentence when denunciation and general deterrence take priority over rehabilitation?
firac.facts: The Crown sought a minimum of two years' imprisonment (denunciatory), while the defence sought two years less a day to be served in the community. The accused had spent 8 months in preventive detention.
firac.rule: Sections 718, 718.1 and 718.2 of the Criminal Code; for terrorist acts denunciation and general deterrence are paramount (R. v. Sandouga, 2002 ABCA 196; R. v. Atwal (1990) 57 C.C.C. (3d) 143; R. v. Lelas, 1990 CanLII 6836). Per R. v. Proulx, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 61, where denunciation and deterrence are particularly pressing, incarceration is generally the favoured sanction despite the availability of a conditional sentence.
firac.application: A community-based sentence would not satisfy the priority criteria of seriousness, denunciation and general deterrence. Comparable terrorism/hate cases warranted real imprisonment. Crediting the 8 months of pre-trial detention at double (16 months), a global 40-month term was appropriate and represented the most lenient sentence consistent with the governing principles.
firac.conclusion: The Court imposed 40 months' imprisonment, less 16 months' credit for pre-trial custody, leaving two years' imprisonment from the date of judgment, plus a 10-year s. 109 weapons prohibition and exemption from the victim surcharge.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a sentencing decision. K037 (terrorism) is central: the court expressly characterized the firebombing as a terrorist act engaging s. 718.2(a)(v). K060 (hate motivation) and K058 (antisemitism) capture the hate/prejudice aggravating factor under s. 718.2(a)(i) targeting the Jewish community. K061 (hate speech) reflects the threatening tract. K036 (mischief) and K038 (vandalism) are engaged by the court's discussion distinguishing vandalism from terrorism and the comparator cases (Lelas, Soles). K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) identify the targeted group; K105 (synagogue) is borderline but relevant given the comparator cases about synagogues though the actual target was a school library — weak pick, included because of the recurring religious-property context; K116 (Criminal Code s. 430) is a slightly weak pick given the charge was arson under s. 434 rather than mischief, but the reasoning draws heavily on mischief jurisprudence. K066 (white supremacism) is not apt here — I exclude it. I replaced it conceptually; note K105 and K116 are the weakest picks.
location_rationale: The decision names the 'COURT OF QUEBEC', 'PROVINCE OF QUEBEC', 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and 'Criminal and Penal Division', identifying the sitting in Montréal, Quebec.
registry_rationale: The heading states 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' with court file No. 500-01-006651-043, indicating the Montréal registry of the Court of Quebec.

name_verification.name_in_document: Yee v WestJet

defining_issues: Does the Alberta Court of Justice have jurisdiction over a wrongful dismissal claim whose supporting facts are largely allegations of discriminatory failure to accommodate?

Did the employer establish just cause to terminate for non-compliance with its mandatory COVID-19 vaccination policy, including whether it reasonably applied the policy and denied the religious exemption?
Even if the religious exemption denial was reasonable, was dismissal for cause a proportionate response?
Does the termination clause in the employment agreement limit the employee to statutory severance?
If wrongfully dismissed, what is the reasonable notice period and did the employee fail to mitigate?
Is the employee entitled to moral or aggravated damages?

firac.issue: Does the Court have jurisdiction over a wrongful dismissal claim founded largely on allegations of discriminatory failure to accommodate a religious exemption?
firac.facts: Mrs. Yee's civil claim pleaded wrongful termination but its factual foundation was WestJet's denial of her religious exemption from the vaccination policy. She had filed and then discontinued a human rights complaint with the Canadian Human Rights Commission. WestJet argued the claim was in substance a human rights complaint that belonged before the Commission.
firac.rule: Courts have jurisdiction over wrongful/constructive dismissal claims founded in contract even where the underlying facts also engage discrimination, provided the discrimination allegations are 'tethered to' an independent cause of action (Lewis v WestJet, 2019 BCCA 63; Stomp v 3M Canada, 2023 ONSC 5180; Garner v Bank of Nova Scotia, 2015 NSSC 122). A standalone tort of discrimination is not actionable (Seneca College v Bhadauria, [1981] 2 SCR 181).
firac.application: The civil claim expressly referenced wrongful dismissal; the absence of the words 'breach of contract' was not fatal. The discrimination facts were pleaded in support of a valid cause of action (wrongful termination) and damages were sought for wrongful termination, not for discrimination per se. The Defendant's authorities (Bhadauria, Harun, Hamilton) all involved standalone discrimination claims and were distinguishable, while Lewis, Stomp and Garner were directly analogous.
firac.conclusion: The Court has jurisdiction to decide the wrongful dismissal claim even though it engages issues that could have been heard by the Commission.

firac.issue: Did WestJet establish just cause by reasonably applying its vaccination policy and reasonably denying the religious exemption request?
firac.facts: Mrs. Yee, an 11-year accounting employee working from home, sought a religious exemption as a bible-believing Christian, supported by her pastor's letter. WestJet accepted her beliefs were sincere but denied the exemption in a final, non-appealable letter, reasoning that her expressed vaccine-safety concerns 'cast doubt' on religion being the true ground and made her objection secular/personal. It never sought clarifying information.
firac.rule: The employer bears the burden of proving just cause (Haack v Secure Energy, 2021 ABQB 82; McDonald v Sproule, 2023 ABKB 587). Workplace policies must be reasonable, unambiguous, well published and consistently enforced (Stonham v Recycling Worx, 2023 ABKB 629) and must be applied reasonably. Sincerely held religious beliefs must be given deference (Syndicat Northcrest v Amselem, 2004 SCC 47). The employer must demonstrate the reasonable and fair application of the rule (KVP; Henrikson v WestJet, 2024 CIRB 1157).
firac.application: The vaccination policy itself was found reasonable and enforceable, responsive to the federal mandate and health-and-safety duties. However, WestJet did not properly consider the accommodation request: it accepted her beliefs were sincere yet treated a coexisting safety concern as negating the religious ground without explaining why the two could not coexist, could not articulate what the form needed to contain to qualify, and never sought additional information though its own policy permitted this and its decision led to termination for cause.
firac.conclusion: WestJet did not reasonably apply its vaccination and accommodation policies; because the exemption denial set the termination in motion, the employer could not establish just cause. It was unnecessary to decide whether the denial was also discriminatory per se.

firac.issue: Even if the exemption denial had been reasonable, was dismissal for cause a proportionate response?
firac.facts: After her exemption was denied Mrs. Yee kept working professionally and met deadlines until placed on unpaid leave on November 1, then terminated December 1, 2021. She worked exclusively from home; the federal Regulations (COVID-19 Order 43) applied only to employees accessing aerodrome property. WestJet did not consider allowing her to continue working from home.
firac.rule: Dismissal for cause must be contextually proportionate to the misconduct, striking a balance between severity and sanction (McKinley v BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38; Motta v Davis Wire, 2019 ABQB 899), assessed against the Haack factors and whether the misconduct is irreconcilable with continued employment (McDonald).
firac.application: Her non-compliance did not affect job performance, endanger employees or the public, or damage the employer's trust; it was not the type of insubordination irreconcilable with continued employment. The Regulations would not have applied to her while working from home, and continued remote work was a viable alternative to dismissal (contrast Parmar and Van Hee, where unpaid leaves struck a reasonable balance). WestJet did not demonstrate why she could not keep working remotely.
firac.conclusion: Dismissal for cause was not a proportionate response; the just cause defence failed on this alternative ground as well.

firac.issue: Does the termination clause limit the Plaintiff to statutory severance?
firac.facts: The employment agreement's without-cause clause provided statutory-minimum notice/severance under the Canada Labour Code and concluded that the employee had no additional claim 'provided WestJet terminates your employment without just cause in accordance with the provision of this paragraph.' WestJet purported to dismiss for cause and paid no statutory minimums.
firac.rule: Without-cause termination provisions are a question of construction and are strictly construed (Singh v Clark Builders, 2025 ABKB 3; Humphrey v Mene, 2021 ONSC 2539). An employer's failure to prove cause does not automatically bar reliance on a valid without-cause clause, subject to the clause's wording.
firac.application: The clause only extinguished further claims if termination occurred 'in accordance with the provision of this paragraph,' i.e. payment of the statutory minimums. Because WestJet dismissed for cause and never paid those minimums, the triggering condition was never met. Singh was distinguishable, both on its facts and its clause wording.
firac.conclusion: The termination clause cannot serve as a defence and does not limit the Plaintiff to statutory severance.

firac.issue: What is the reasonable notice period and did the Plaintiff fail to mitigate?
firac.facts: Mrs. Yee was 36, had 11 years' service, held a specialized industry-specific accounting role without a formal designation, and was the most junior team member. Her only salary evidence was a 2019 T-4 of $71,550.28 likely including benefits. She testified she looked for work but was unqualified while unvaccinated; WestJet led no evidence of available alternative jobs.
firac.rule: Reasonable notice is set by the Bardal factors—nature of employment, length of service, age, availability of similar employment (Bardal v Globe & Mail, 1960 CanLII 294). To prove failure to mitigate the employer must show the employee failed to take reasonable steps and that such steps would probably have produced employment (Plotnikoff v Associated Engineering, 2023 ABCJ 200).
firac.application: Weighing length of service and specialized position against her age and junior status, and against a submitted range of 10-12 months, the Court fixed 11 months. On mitigation, even if reasonable steps were not taken, WestJet led no evidence that comparable employment would have been found, so the second branch of the test failed.
firac.conclusion: Damages equivalent to 11 months' notice ($65,587.72) awarded with interest from December 1, 2021; the failure-to-mitigate defence was not established.

firac.issue: Is the Plaintiff entitled to moral or aggravated damages?
firac.facts: Mrs. Yee sought $21,500 in moral damages, relying on the alleged insensitivity of the exemption denial and the termination letter inviting her to reapply if she became compliant. She led virtually no evidence of the impact of the dismissal on her.
firac.rule: Aggravated damages require conduct in the manner of dismissal that is unfair or in bad faith—'untruthful, misleading or unduly insensitive'—with proof of actual damages beyond the normal distress of termination (Elgert v Home Hardware, 2011 ABCA 112; Honda v Keays, 2008 SCC 39).
firac.application: Although the dismissal was wrongful, the surrounding circumstances did not show an unduly insensitive or egregious manner of dismissal, and the Plaintiff led almost no evidence of harm flowing from the manner of termination.
firac.conclusion: The claim for moral/aggravated damages was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case is a wrongful dismissal action; K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the core cause of action and just-cause analysis. K031 (religious accommodation) and K025 (freedom of religion) are central because the termination flowed from denial of a religious exemption, and K034 (sincerity of belief) captures the Amselem sincerity analysis applied to Mrs. Yee's beliefs. K069 (discrimination) reflects the alleged discriminatory failure to accommodate underlying the jurisdiction and just-cause arguments. K068 (bona fide occupational requirement) is engaged by the pleading that vaccination was not a BFOR. K108 (Canadian Human Rights Act) applies since the accommodation duty was framed under the CHRA. Borderline: K068 is a weaker pick as the BFOR point was pleaded but not decisive; K069 is used generally rather than as a decided discrimination finding, since the Court declined to rule on discrimination per se.
location_rationale: The heading states 'In the Alberta Court of Justice', 'Registry: Calgary', and the judgment is 'Dated at the City of Calgary, Alberta this 13th day of May, 2025.'
registry_rationale: The decision expressly lists 'Registry: Calgary' and was heard and dated at Calgary.

name_verification.name_in_document: Ontario (Electrical Safety Authority) v. Broomfield

defining_issues: Did the cumulative effect of the prosecutor's conduct during the trial constitute an abuse of process under s. 7 of the Charter, either by prejudicing the defendant's right to a fair trial (main category) or by undermining the integrity of the judicial process (residual category)?

Did the prosecution prove beyond a reasonable doubt the actus reus of 'operating an electrical contracting business without holding a valid electrical contractor licence' contrary to s. 3 of O. Reg. 570/05 for each of the three counts?
Did the defendant establish the defence of due diligence on a balance of probabilities for the counts whose actus reus was proven?
Did the prosecution's failure to disclose a witness's (Ali Nabbouh's) pre-testimony conversation with the ESA investigator breach s. 7, and what was the appropriate remedy?

firac.issue: Did the prosecutor's conduct during the trial amount to an abuse of process under s. 7 of the Charter warranting a stay of proceedings or a new trial?
firac.facts: The self-represented defendant (unrepresented for 9 of 12 trial days) alleged the ESA prosecutor engaged in egregious misconduct: asking leading questions of Crown witnesses; eliciting hearsay, lay opinion and bad character evidence; giving evidence himself; getting the defendant to comment on witnesses' veracity; questioning him about his relationship with counsel, his lifestyle and unsavoury associations, and his failure to cooperate with ESA inspectors; inserting editorial commentary and personal opinions; using sarcastic and demeaning language; and threatening to seek the maximum penalty.
firac.rule: Under R. v. O'Connor and R. v. Babos, abuse of process under s. 7 falls into two categories: (1) prosecutorial conduct affecting trial fairness (main category), and (2) conduct that contravenes fundamental notions of justice and undermines the integrity of the judicial process (residual category). The claimant bears the burden on a balance of probabilities (R. v. Anderson), while a stay requires the 'clearest of cases.' The three-part Babos test requires prejudice manifested through the trial or its outcome, no alternative remedy, and a balancing of interests. In a non-jury strict liability trial, the trier is presumed able to disabuse itself of inadmissible or prejudicial evidence (R. v. T.B., R. v. Sekhon), and the prosecution may adduce rebuttal evidence in chief to anticipate a due diligence defence.
firac.application: The court examined each impugned category of conduct in context. Because this was a non-jury trial of strict liability regulatory offences, any prejudicial effect of leading questions, hearsay, bad character, or opinion evidence was lessened, as the trier could disabuse its mind and attach no weight to inadmissible material. Much of the evidence was relevant to genuine issues (the relationships with the homeowners, rebutting a claim of inadequate investigation, credibility). The prosecutor's sarcastic and demeaning comments, though not ideal or professional, did not cross the line from aggressive to abusive and did not intimidate the defendant or prevent full answer and defence. The prosecutor's giving of evidence about 'Winmar' concerned a minor non-controversial fact, and the maximum-penalty comment, though inappropriate, caused no unfairness in a non-jury trial.
firac.conclusion: The defendant failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the cumulative effect of the prosecutor's conduct rendered the trial unfair or undermined the integrity of the judicial process. The abuse of process application was dismissed.

firac.issue: Did the prosecution prove beyond a reasonable doubt the actus reus of operating an electrical contracting business without a valid licence for each count?
firac.facts: The defendant, unlicensed by the ESA, was hired to renovate three homes. At 22 Vespahills Crescent (Jairam) and 291 Boon Avenue (Khan), the homeowners testified they saw the defendant running/pulling wire; he told them he was an electrician; no permits had been taken out. At 94 Narrow Valley Crescent (Bacchus), the homeowner did not see the defendant do electrical work and understood he would bring in properly licensed people for work he could not do.
firac.rule: Section 3 of the Licensing of Electrical Contractors and Master Electricians Regulation (O. Reg. 570/05) prohibits operating an electrical contracting business without a licence, an offence under s. 113.20(1)(d) of the Electricity Act, 1998. 'Electrical work' is defined as work within the Ontario Electrical Safety Code consisting of constructing, installing, extending, altering or connecting any electrical installation. For strict liability offences (R. v. Sault Ste. Marie) the Crown must prove the prohibited act beyond a reasonable doubt.
firac.application: Running or pulling wire constitutes 'electrical work.' Scott Eason's evidence proved the defendant was never licensed. The credible testimony of Jairam and Khan (including Khan's memorable account of the defendant wiring while standing in water) established the defendant personally performed electrical work at their homes, and no permits were taken out. For Bacchus, there was no credible evidence the defendant performed electrical work or that no permit existed; she only saw a young man drilling holes for pot lights.
firac.conclusion: The actus reus was proven beyond a reasonable doubt for counts 1 and 2, but not for count 3. An acquittal was entered on count 3.

firac.issue: Did the defendant establish the defence of due diligence on a balance of probabilities for counts 1 and 2?
firac.facts: The defendant claimed he did not personally do the electrical work, that an unnamed electrician did the work at 22 Vespahills, and that he did not know Steve Duff (who assisted at 291 Boon) was unlicensed.
firac.rule: Under R. v. Sault Ste. Marie, once the Crown proves the actus reus of a strict liability offence, the accused must prove on a balance of probabilities that he took all reasonable care or reasonably believed in a mistaken set of facts that would render the act innocent.
firac.application: There was no evidence any licensed electrician did the work at 22 Vespahills, nor evidence the defendant took reasonable steps. At 291 Boon, the defendant was observed doing electrical work himself before Duff was involved, and he took no steps to verify Duff's qualifications or to have Duff obtain a permit, so his claimed belief was not a reasonable mistake of fact.
firac.conclusion: The defendant failed to establish due diligence for counts 1 and 2; convictions were entered on both counts.

firac.issue: Did the Crown's failure to disclose a defence witness's pre-testimony conversation with the ESA investigator breach s. 7, and what remedy applied?
firac.facts: Ali Nabbouh, called by the defence to support the claimed partnership, testified he had already told ESA Investigator Corbett that morning that he was not the defendant's partner. That conversation had not been disclosed to the defendant before Nabbouh testified.
firac.rule: The Crown has an ongoing obligation to disclose all relevant evidence (R. v. Stinchcombe); non-disclosure breaches s. 7 where it causes actual prejudice to full answer and defence (R. v. Bjelland). Exclusion of evidence may be an appropriate s. 24(1) remedy where an adjournment cannot cure the prejudice.
firac.application: Had the conversation been disclosed, the defendant might not have called Nabbouh. The non-disclosure prejudiced the defendant's ability to make an informed decision on calling the witness, and an adjournment or costs could not remedy this.
firac.conclusion: Section 7 was infringed; Nabbouh's testimony was excluded and given no weight.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area: although these are regulatory/strict liability offences under the Electricity Act, they are penal proceedings governed by criminal-law doctrines (abuse of process, disclosure, burden of proof). K112 (Charter s. 7) and K107 (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms) are directly engaged by the abuse of process and disclosure claims and the s. 24(1) remedy sought. K012 (procedural fairness/natural justice) captures the fair-trial dimension central to the abuse of process analysis. K013 (professional discipline / professional regulation) is a borderline pick reflecting the electrical contractor licensing regime administered by the ESA, though this was a prosecution rather than a disciplinary proceeding. K001 (Administrative law) is a weaker, borderline pick reflecting the regulatory/licensing statutory context; it is included because the controlled vocabulary lacks a specific keyword for regulatory prosecutions, abuse of process, or provincial offences. The vocabulary is poorly suited to this regulatory prosecution, so several picks are approximations.
