name_verification.name_in_document: A.B. v. N.L.A.

defining_issues: Did the case conference judge have jurisdiction, and was it appropriate under rule 17(8)(b.1) of the Family Law Rules, to make final, non-consensual substantive orders on custody, access and child support at a case conference?

Did the case conference judge deny the unrepresented father procedural fairness by refusing an adjournment and disposing of all substantive issues without adequate notice or a meaningful opportunity to be heard?
Were the final orders (including the imputed income for child support) supported by admissible evidence?

firac.issue: Did the case conference judge have jurisdiction, and was it appropriate under rule 17(8)(b.1) of the Family Law Rules, to make final non-consensual substantive orders at a case conference?
firac.facts: At the second case conference the judge, without consent, made final orders disposing of custody, access and child support, largely mirroring the mother's draft order and offer to settle, adding terms neither party requested. The only materials were case conference briefs, an offer to settle, an OCL s. 112 report, the mother's financial statement and the father's tax documents.
firac.rule: Rule 17(8)(b.1) of the Family Law Rules permits a conference judge, on notice and 'if it is appropriate to do so', to make a final or temporary order. Rules 2(2)-(5) set the primary objective of dealing with cases justly and fairly. Rules 17(22), 17(24) and 18(8) keep conference briefs and offers to settle out of the trial record and bar the conference judge from later hearing the issue. Robinson v. Morrison, [2000] O.J. No. 2973; W.W. v. X.X., 2013 ONSC 879.
firac.application: The court held that while rule 17(8)(b.1) allows final orders on notice, it is virtually never appropriate to make an opposed, non-consensual final substantive order at a conference. Conferences exist to explore settlement, ensure disclosure and achieve trial readiness (rule 17(4)), not to adjudicate contested issues. The judge relied on the conference briefs and the mother's offer to settle as if they were evidence and expressed views on the merits, contrary to the scheme of the Rules; summary judgment under Rule 16 (with affidavit evidence and a right of reply) was the proper route if the mother's case were that strong.
firac.conclusion: The final orders were made inappropriately and incorrectly in law; the making of them exceeded what was appropriate at a case conference.

firac.issue: Was the unrepresented father denied procedural fairness by the refusal of an adjournment and the disposition of all substantive issues?
firac.facts: The father, unrepresented, had filed a 14B adjournment motion (dated February 6, 2012) to retain a family lawyer that apparently was never ruled on; he renewed the request at the conference and was refused. He repeatedly said he expected only settlement discussion, not a final disposition, and did not intend to make submissions. Most of the transcript was dialogue between the judge and the father; the mother was not questioned similarly.
firac.rule: Dealing with cases justly requires that procedure be fair to all parties (rule 2(3)(a)). The duty of fairness ensures a party affected is given a proper opportunity to be heard (Canadian Union of Postal Workers v. Canada Post Corp., [2007] O.J. No. 4629 (C.A.); Farm Credit Corp. v. Pipe (1993), 16 O.R. (3d) 49 (C.A.)). Before any substantive order, a litigant is entitled to notice, an opportunity to respond and to be heard (Robinson v. Morrison).
firac.application: The father had no reasonable expectation that final orders would be made; both the mother's own brief and her counsel's submissions confirmed they expected the judge's assistance in settling, not an imposed final order. The father was denied a chance to retain counsel and to challenge the OCL report and other material. The issues were not urgent given the history, and an adjournment with costs would not have prejudiced the mother or child, since the orders essentially maintained the status quo.
firac.conclusion: The process was procedurally unfair; the father was denied a meaningful opportunity to be heard.

firac.issue: Were the final orders, including the imputed income used for child support, supported by admissible evidence?
firac.facts: Child support was fixed on an imputed income of $35,000, but the father's tax documents disclosed lower income (and he disputed the imputation as based on a misrepresentation of his employment). The OCL report recommended maintaining the status quo and flagged a pending psychological referral for the child; there were no current affidavits, no financial statement from the father verified for this purpose beyond tax data, and no motion or exchange of affidavits.
firac.rule: Findings amount to palpable and overriding error where made in the absence of evidence, in conflict with accepted evidence, or based on misapprehension (Waxman v. Waxman, 2004 CanLII 39040 (ON CA)). Appellate standard from Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33. An OCL s. 112 report forms part of the evidence but is not determinative (s. 112(3), Courts of Justice Act).
firac.application: The tax documents did not support the child-support figure, and the OCL report recommended no change and identified unresolved medical/psychological issues. The final orders were thus unsupported by the admissible evidence and rested on materials (conference briefs, offer to settle) not properly evidentiary at a hearing.
firac.conclusion: The orders, unsupported by the evidence, constituted palpable and overriding error and could not stand.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary practice area — the appeal concerns custody, access and child support. K048 (custody/access) and K050 (parental support / child support) are the substantive orders under review. K047 (best interests of the child) underpins the OCL report and custody analysis. K012 (procedural fairness) is the central legal ground — the father's right to notice and an opportunity to be heard, and the natural-justice reasoning from Robinson v. Morrison. K014 (standard of review) reflects the appellate framework applied (Housen; palpable and overriding error). name_verification.name_in_document: Morgenthau v. Toronto Metropolitan University

defining_issues: Should the Divisional Court exercise its discretion to decline to hear the application for judicial review because adequate alternative forums exist for the applicant's complaint?
Do the Strickland factors and the balance of convenience favour the alternative forums (grievance/labour arbitration and the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario) over judicial review?
Are there exceptional circumstances justifying judicial review despite the availability of alternative remedies?

firac.issue: Should the Divisional Court exercise its discretion to decline to hear the application for judicial review of TMU's decision not to proceed with the applicant's complaint?
firac.facts: Morgenthau, a Jewish adjunct professor at TMU's Lincoln Alexander School of Law, complained under the Student Code of Conduct and the Discrimination and Harassment Prevention Policy about 72 students who signed an Open Letter concerning the Israel–Hamas conflict, which she considered antisemitic. TMU appointed an independent External Reviewer (former Chief Justice MacDonald), who concluded the students had not breached the Code. TMU then declined to proceed with Morgenthau's complaint on the basis the MacDonald Report had addressed its substance. She sought judicial review to have that decision quashed and the students disciplined.
firac.rule: Judicial review is a discretionary public-law remedy; a reviewing court must first decide whether to exercise its discretion to review, and may decline where a discretionary bar is present (Yatar v. TD Insurance Meloche Monnex, 2024 SCC 8; Strickland v. Canada (AG), 2015 SCC 37). Even where a case for review on the merits is made out, the court retains an overriding discretion to refuse relief; there is no right to judicial review.
firac.application: The Panel found it inappropriate for the court to second-guess TMU's decision not to discipline the students. TMU, a self-governing university under the Toronto Metropolitan University Act, 1977, adopted a reasonable, resourced process (the External Review) to address a matter affecting the whole community. The applicant's real objective—reopening the investigation and disciplining students—amounted to an indirect/collateral attack on the MacDonald Report, which was not a decision about her complaint and which she had no standing to challenge.
firac.conclusion: The Panel exercised its discretion to decline to hear the judicial review application.

firac.issue: Do the Strickland factors and the balance of convenience favour the alternative forums over judicial review?
firac.facts: TMU argued the applicant had alternative avenues: a grievance under the faculty collective agreement (available while employed), an application to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario, and private tort/contract claims against the students. Morgenthau argued none could deliver her preferred remedy—discipline of the students—so judicial review must proceed.
firac.rule: Strickland sets out non-exhaustive factors for assessing whether an alternative remedy is adequate (convenience, nature of error, nature and remedial capacity of the other forum, existing recourse, expeditiousness, relative expertise, economical use of judicial resources, cost), followed by a balance-of-convenience analysis considering the statutory scheme and impact on third parties. The alternative need not be the claimant's preferred remedy or identical to that sought on review; labour arbitrators and the HRTO can enforce human-rights obligations (Parry Sound; Weilgosh).
firac.application: The Panel found a grievance (before she left TMU) and an HRTO application (still available, with time extensions under s. 34(2) HRC) to be convenient, expeditious, and before expert decision-makers who could address her workplace-safety, harassment and discrimination concerns, including her procedural-fairness and bias allegations. Judicial review, by contrast, would proceed without the record or the participation of directly affected third parties (the students and the External Review Team member whose impartiality was impugned), and would be disrespectful of the university's autonomous, self-governing statutory framework (Canadian Federation of Students, 2021 ONCA 553).
firac.conclusion: The Strickland factors and balance of convenience favoured the alternative forums, which more appropriately addressed the applicant's concerns than judicial review.

firac.issue: Are there exceptional circumstances justifying judicial review despite the availability of adequate alternative remedies?
firac.facts: The applicant alleged procedural unfairness, errors of law in the MacDonald Report, and bias on the part of a member of the External Review Team.
firac.rule: Absent exceptional circumstances, courts should not interfere with administrative processes until completed or available effective remedies are exhausted; the threshold for exceptionality is high and denials of procedural fairness typically do not qualify (C.B. Powell Ltd., 2010 FCA 61; Harelkin; Gupta v. Canada (AG), 2021 FCA 202).
firac.application: The applicant provided no indication of exceptional circumstances that would justify exemption from the requirement to pursue suitable alternative redress mechanisms.
firac.conclusion: No exceptional circumstances were established; the discretionary refusal to hear the application stood.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns entirely on discretionary refusal of judicial review. K011 (judicial review) and K012 (procedural fairness) capture the core remedy sought and the alleged errors. K041 (campus/university) and K042 (code of conduct) reflect the TMU setting and the Student Code of Conduct at issue. K084 (labour arbitration) and K072 (human rights tribunal) are the two adequate alternative forums (grievance and HRTO) that drove the outcome, with K083 (harassment) reflecting the workplace harassment/discrimination substance of her complaint. K058 (antisemitism), K093 (Jewish) and K024 (freedom of expression) ground the underlying subject matter—the Open Letter, the applicant's antisemitism allegations, and the free-speech basis of the MacDonald Report's findings. Antisemitism/Jewish and freedom of expression are contextual rather than the decided legal issue, so they are somewhat weaker picks, but they are central to the factual matrix.
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Divisional Court, and states 'HEARD at Toronto: June 26, 2025', establishing Toronto, Ontario as the location.
registry_rationale: The header identifies 'DIVISIONAL COURT FILE NO.: 601/24-JR' and the panel sits as the Divisional Court of the Superior Court of Justice, so the registry is the Divisional Court.

case_name: Association étudiante de l'Université McGill c. X

name_verification.name_in_document: Association étudiante de l'Université McGill c. X

defining_issues: Did the Superior Court err in finding that the respondent established a serious risk to her physical safety justifying a confidentiality order derogating from the open court principle under the Sherman test?

Did the Superior Court apply the correct legal test and err in concluding there was an apparent right (apparence de droit) supporting an interlocutory injunction that would prevent ratification of a democratically adopted policy engaging freedom of expression?
Did the Superior Court err in finding irreparable harm and that the balance of convenience favoured granting the interlocutory injunction?

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in finding that the respondent established a serious risk to her physical safety justifying a confidentiality order?
firac.facts: X, a Jewish student who led the 'No' campaign against a referendum policy on Palestine, sought to litigate anonymously, invoking fear for her physical safety based on offensive social-media comments received during the campaign, a general climate of tension and rising antisemitism, and an affidavit from a McGill vice-provost. No threats followed the filing of proceedings, and her identity as 'No' campaign president was already publicly known on campus.
firac.rule: The open court principle is enshrined in art. 11 C.p.c. and tied to freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter, creating a strong presumption of openness. Exceptions require the three cumulative Sherman (Succession) c. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 criteria; protection from physical harm is an important public interest, but the applicant must show an objectively discernible risk linked to the publicity of the proceedings, based on logical inference beyond mere assertion or a general climate. The standard of review is palpable and overriding error, or correctness for errors of law.
firac.application: The Court found the social-media comments, while offensive and to be denounced, were too vague to ground a genuine risk to physical safety and were sent during the campaign, before the proceedings. No threatening or improper messages arose after the proceedings were filed, even though the authors knew her identity, and the University confirmed it knew of no direct threat. The newspaper articles and vice-provost's affidavit addressed a general climate, not a risk tied to the publicity of this case. The judge could not link the openness of the judicial debate to any risk or increased risk to her safety.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge committed a palpable and overriding error; the respondent failed to satisfy the first Sherman criterion, and the confidentiality request should have been dismissed.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge apply the correct test for an interlocutory injunction restraining expression and err in finding an apparent right?
firac.facts: X sought an interlocutory injunction preventing the student Association from ratifying and implementing the 'Policy Against Genocide in Palestine' adopted by referendum (78.7% in favour), arguing it breached the Association's Constitution and was antisemitic. The judge applied the ordinary Beauregard/American Cyanamid test, treating the threshold as a serious, non-frivolous question.
firac.rule: Where an interlocutory injunction seeks to restrain expression, the ordinary serious-question test does not apply; per Canada (HRC) v. Canadian Liberty Net, [1998] 1 SCR 626, and Champagne c. CEGEP de Jonquière, an injunction may issue only in the clearest and rarest cases where the impugned words are so manifestly defamatory or impossible to justify that a defamation action would almost certainly succeed. Courts should also avoid interfering in the internal affairs of private legal persons absent compelling reasons, especially where internal recourse (here arbitration under the Memorandum of Agreement) is not exhausted.
firac.application: The judge used the wrong prism, treating the matter as a contractual question of Constitution compliance rather than as a restriction on the Association's and members' political expression. The Policy strongly criticized Israeli actions but bound no one and left dialogue open; it was on a different spectrum from Keegstra hate propaganda and was, at most, 'possibly antisemitic' — merely arguable, not clearly indefensible. By saying further evidence would be needed at trial, the judge implicitly conceded the Policy was not manifestly impossible to justify and improperly reversed the burden onto the Association. Even framed as a Constitution question, the preamble's universal values could not bar debate on divisive topics, and courts should not interfere before internal remedies were exhausted.
firac.conclusion: The judge erred in law; there was no apparent right justifying the injunction, and the injunction should have been refused.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in finding irreparable harm and a balance of convenience favouring the injunction?
firac.facts: X claimed the Policy would harm her and the Jewish community's dignity, while also suing for $100,000 in moral and $25,000 in punitive damages arising from the referendum. She pleaded a fear largely tied to the campaign and asserted a harm general to her community, not distinct from it.
firac.rule: Irreparable harm refers to harm not quantifiable or curable by damages; injunctions cannot rest on hypothetical considerations and require an actual or imminent breach of an apparent right. A person cannot claim, merely as a group member, a collective harm; the interest must be direct and personal (Bou Malhab c. Diffusion Métromédia CMR, 2011 SCC 9).
firac.application: The harm X alleged was compensable in money, as shown by her own damages claim, and reflected a subjective fear tied to the referendum process. She demonstrated no personal, distinct harm from ratification and instead asserted a harm general to her community, which is insufficient to found standing for injunctive relief. The balance of convenience clearly favoured the Association, which was being prevented from ratifying a democratically adopted policy of political expression, while the judge's finding of a possibly antisemitic dignity harm was unsupported.
firac.conclusion: The judge erred; no irreparable harm was established and the balance of convenience favoured the appellant.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 area, as the case turns on injunction, open court and standing doctrines. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the core remedy at issue, engaging the special rule for injunctions restraining speech. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) are central both to the open court principle and to the restraint on the Association's political expression. K017 (group defamation/collectivity) captures the Bou Malhab personal-versus-collective harm analysis applied to standing. K058 (antisemitism) and K061 (hate speech, via the Keegstra/hate-literature argument) reflect the respondent's characterization of the Policy. K093 (Jewish) and K104 (Palestine) identify the parties and subject matter, and K041 (campus/university) situates the dispute in a student-association/university context. The hate-speech and antisemitism picks are somewhat borderline since the Court expressly declined to characterize the Policy as hateful, but the arguments were squarely raised and analyzed.
location_rationale: The header states 'COUR D'APPEL', 'PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC', 'SIÈGE DE MONTRÉAL', identifying the Quebec Court of Appeal sitting in Montréal.
registry_rationale: The decision indicates 'SIÈGE DE MONTRÉAL' with file no. 500-09-031059-249, the Montréal seat of the Court of Appeal.

case_name: Ontario English Catholic Teachers' Assn v. Ontario (Attorney General)

name_verification.name_in_document: Ontario English Catholic Teachers' Assn v. Ontario (Attorney General)

defining_issues: Do Bill 160 and its funding model prejudicially affect a s. 93(1) right or privilege of the Roman Catholic community with respect to denominational schools by removing the local taxing power?
Are the provisions supervising school boards' financial affairs and authorizing vesting orders unconstitutional under s. 93(1)?
Does Bill 160 contravene s. 93(1) as it applies to the public school system on a 'mirror equality' theory?
Can the applicants rely on an unwritten constitutional convention to preserve boards' power to levy and determine property taxes?
Do the delegations of taxing and regulatory power to the executive violate the rule of law or render the legislation unconstitutionally vague?
Does empowering the Minister of Finance to set tax rates by regulation constitute 'taxation without representation' contrary to ss. 53 and 54 of the Constitution Act, 1867?

firac.issue: Do Bill 160 and its funding model prejudicially affect a s. 93(1) right or privilege of the Roman Catholic community with respect to denominational schools by removing the local taxing power?
firac.facts: Bill 160 (the Education Quality Improvement Act, 1997) replaced 150 years of local property-tax funding by centralizing all school-board revenue in the province, repealing separate boards' power to set and levy tax rates. Section 7 of the Scott Act of 1863 had conferred on separate school trustees a stand-alone, unqualified right to levy taxes, in force at Confederation.
firac.rule: Section 93(1) of the Constitution Act, 1867 protects any right or privilege with respect to denominational schools enjoyed by a class of persons by law at the Union (Greater Hull; Bill 30 Reference; GMPSB). The protection extends to non-denominational 'aspects' where they are necessary to give effect to denominational guarantees, and the right to tax recognized in s. 7 of the Scott Act is a right 'with respect to denominational schools' (Greater Hull; OHBA; Bill 107 Reference).
firac.application: Although Bill 160 preserved proportional funding (s. 20 Scott Act carried into s. 234) and the managerial/denominational discretion of Catholic boards, s. 7's right to tax was created separately and independently of the proportionality right. Cumming J. held it guarantees an independent financing mechanism allowing the Catholic community itself to determine adequate funding for its separate system, and its removal is prejudicial per se, leaving the community hostage to the province's assessment of adequacy.
firac.conclusion: Bill 160 is unconstitutional insofar as it removes the taxation power from the Roman Catholic educational community, violating the s. 93(1) guarantee; the Education Act as amended is of no force and effect to that extent.

firac.issue: Are the provisions supervising school boards' financial affairs and authorizing vesting orders unconstitutional?
firac.facts: Division D of Part IX allows the Minister to investigate a board's finances and seek a vesting order on grounds of deficit, default, or concern about ability to meet obligations; no board was under supervision. Division D also reiterates the denominational protections of s. 93(1).
firac.rule: The test is whether authority to withdraw a right necessarily operates to the prejudice of the affected class (Ottawa Separate School Trustees v. Ottawa); indefinite, discretionary removal is invalid, but supervision tied to defined standards with mandatory restoration is valid (Re Ottawa Separate Schools). A factual foundation is required only where prejudice is not per se (McEvoy; Danson).
firac.application: The preconditions (deficit/default or likelihood) and the mandatory revocation once no deficit exists provide adequate, assessable standards, and s. 257.52 preserves denominational aspects. The privative clause could not oust review of a s. 93(1) violation. The scheme therefore does not necessarily prejudice separate-school supporters.
firac.conclusion: Division D is, on its face, constitutionally valid; the challenge is rejected.

firac.issue: Does Bill 160 contravene s. 93(1) as it applies to the public school system on a 'mirror equality' theory?
firac.facts: The public-school applicants argued the public system enjoys reciprocal constitutional protection because separate-school rights were defined by reference to it and Roman Catholics could choose between the two publicly funded systems (Adler).
firac.rule: Adler v. Ontario holds the public system is impliedly contemplated by s. 93 only as a backdrop/reference point immunizing it from Charter attack; it is not itself entrenched, and the province's plenary education power is what is protected (Adler; Fewer School Boards; Calgary Board of Education; Alberta Public School Boards' Assn.).
firac.application: Cumming J. found the 'constitutional reciprocity' argument rested on a false syllogism: implicit contemplation of the public system does not confer identical rights. The ultimate purpose of s. 93(1) is preserving denominational (Catholic) schooling; the public system serves only as a means/reference point, and the majority can protect itself through the ballot box.
firac.conclusion: The mirror-equality argument is rejected; the public system holds no entrenched rights under s. 93(1) beyond possibly a right of existence, which need not be decided.

firac.issue: Can the applicants rely on an unwritten constitutional convention to preserve boards' power to levy and determine property taxes?
firac.facts: The applicants argued a convention protecting local taxing power, said to be enforceable via s. 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982.
firac.rule: Constitutional conventions are not enforceable by courts and cannot override clear legal rules (Reference re Amendment of the Constitution of Canada, 1981); implicit powers grounded in constitutional text differ from conventions (New Brunswick Broadcasting).
firac.application: Section 52 did not alter the non-justiciability of conventions. The claimed convention would improperly expand s. 93 against the province's plenary power; unwritten but implicit powers (as in New Brunswick Broadcasting) are distinct and inapplicable here.
firac.conclusion: The convention argument is rejected; it is doubtful any such convention exists and, if it did, it would be unenforceable.

firac.issue: Do the delegations of taxing and regulatory power to the executive violate the rule of law or render the legislation unconstitutionally vague?
firac.facts: Bill 160 delegates broad regulation-making powers, including the Minister of Finance's power to set tax rates, to the executive.
firac.rule: Legislatures may delegate widely provided the delegation is explicit (Hodge v. The Queen; Re Gray; Chemicals Reference); vagueness is measured by whether the provision provides a basis for legal debate (R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society).
firac.application: The impugned provisions specify their objects (e.g., tax rates for school purposes for s. 257.7) with sufficient particularity, so the delegation is explicit and the objects are ascertainable, permitting legal debate.
firac.conclusion: The rule-of-law/vagueness challenge is rejected.

firac.issue: Does empowering the Minister of Finance to set tax rates by regulation constitute 'taxation without representation' contrary to ss. 53 and 54?
firac.facts: Section 257.12(1)(b) empowers the Minister of Finance to prescribe school tax rates by regulation; ss. 53 and 54 (applied to provinces by s. 90) govern money bills.
firac.rule: Sections 53 and 54 require an explicit, clear delegation of the taxing power in legislation; implicit repeal of these constitutional provisions is not permitted (National Fish Co.; Chemicals; Mercure; rejecting Pigeon J.'s obiter in Agricultural Products Marketing Reference).
firac.application: Though not entrenched, ss. 53-54 have real, if limited, effect and cannot be impliedly repealed; their requirements are satisfied where the enabling delegation of the taxing power is express and clear, as it is here, consistent with the accepted delegation of taxing power to municipalities.
firac.conclusion: The ss. 53-54 challenge is rejected; the express delegation satisfies those provisions.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the primary tier-1 area because the case turns entirely on interpreting s. 93(1) and ss. 53-54 of the Constitution Act, 1867. K005 (Education law) is the co-engaged tier-1 area, as the dispute concerns the governance and funding of Ontario's school systems. K043 (denominational schools) is the most specific applicable keyword: the core holding protects Roman Catholic separate-school taxing rights. K044 (school board) applies because the litigation is about the powers and financing of separate and public school boards. K118 (Education Act) is the statute amended by Bill 160 and central to the analysis. K107 (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms) is a weaker/borderline pick — the Charter is discussed mainly through Adler's holding that s. 93 schooling is immune from Charter attack, so it is included only for that contextual engagement. No freedom-of-religion keyword was chosen because the judgment expressly distinguishes s. 93(1) rights from Charter religious freedom.
location_rationale: The heading identifies the tribunal as the 'Ontario Court (General Division)' with Cumming J. presiding, so the province is Ontario. No hearing city is stated in the decision (counsel affiliations and party names such as the Toronto District School Board do not establish where the court sat), so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision records 'Court File Nos. 97-CV-137668; 98-CV-139317' but does not name a registry office or court location, so registry is left null.

case_name: Kaplan-Myrth v. Ottawa Carlton District School Board

name_verification.name_in_document: Kaplan-Myrth v. Ottawa Carlton District School Board

defining_issues: Did the Board's decision sanctioning the trustee reflect a reasonable and proportionate balancing of her freedom of expression under the Doré framework?
Was the applicant denied procedural fairness in the complaint and sanctioning process?
Were the sanctions imposed by the Board reasonable?
Should the proposed fresh evidence be admitted and did it affect the outcome?

firac.issue: Did the Board's decision sanctioning the trustee reflect a reasonable and proportionate balancing of her freedom of expression under the Doré framework?
firac.facts: Dr. Kaplan-Myrth, an elected OCDSB trustee, made statements on social media and at/after a September 11, 2023 Board meeting that disparaged fellow trustees and the Board's Code of Conduct process (e.g. calling it a 'kangaroo court', accusing conservative trustees of abusing the process). The Integrity Commissioner found breaches of ss. 3.5, 3.7, 3.8, 3.15, 3.17 and 3.18 of the Code, and the Board voted to find breaches and impose sanctions. The parties agreed the decision limited her freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter.
firac.rule: Judicial review of administrative decisions engaging the Charter is governed by Doré v. Barreau du Québec, 2012 SCC 12: a court first asks whether the decision limits Charter protections, then whether the decision reflects a proportionate balancing of the Charter right/values against the statutory objectives (Commission scolaire francophone des TNO, 2023 SCC 31, at para. 73). Reasonableness is the standard (Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65). The Education Act (ss. 218.1, 218.2, 218.3) requires boards to adopt and enforce a Code of Conduct.
firac.application: The Court found the IC report addressed the Doré arguments directly and at length, weighing Charter values against the objectives of the Education Act and the Code. The Code does not restrict trustees from expressing views but limits the manner of expression, requiring civility and respect. The applicant was sanctioned for how she spoke out, not the substance of her views. Following Ramsay, Del Grande and Peterson, deference is owed to a board interpreting and enforcing its own Code, which is presumed to have expertise. The decisions represented a reasonable, proportionate balancing of expressive rights against the Act's objectives.
firac.conclusion: The decision was a reasonable and proportionate balancing under Doré; the applicant showed no basis to intervene.

firac.issue: Was the applicant denied procedural fairness in the complaint and sanctioning process?
firac.facts: The applicant was not permitted to participate in the in-camera meeting or to vote, could not make oral representations to the Board, and complained that the IC reformulated the complaint and included prejudicial material. She had, however, filed two 39-page written responses to the IC and a 15-page appeal submission, all before the Board.
firac.rule: Procedural fairness requirements are assessed on a correctness/fairness standard (Abrametz, 2022 SCC 29). Baker sets the factors, and considerable weight is given to the agency's choice of procedures and institutional constraints, particularly where the statute leaves the decision-maker to choose its procedures (Baker, paras. 23, 27; Del Grande, 2023 ONSC 349).
firac.application: The Education Act leaves boards to determine their own Code and procedures. The Code provided for an independent Integrity Commissioner, written submissions, private meetings, deliberation and appeal — a process the applicant herself voted to approve. The reformulated complaint introduced no new allegations and she had opportunity to respond. Inclusion of contextual material did not amount to unfairness; complaints about it were a prohibited line-by-line search for error. The modest impact on her reputation did not warrant heightened fairness beyond what the Code provided.
firac.conclusion: The process was not structurally unfair; no denial of procedural fairness was established.

firac.issue: Were the sanctions imposed by the Board reasonable?
firac.facts: The Board barred the applicant from one regular Board meeting and from participating in committees for three months. No censure or apology was required.
firac.rule: A court must defer to the Board on sanctions unless the applicant establishes an error in principle or that the sanctions are clearly unfit — 'manifestly deficient or excessive and a substantial and marked departure from penalties in similar cases' (Khan v. Law Society of Ontario, 2022 ONSC 1951, at para. 77; Del Grande, at para. 88).
firac.application: The sanctions are provided for under s. 218.3(3) of the Act and are similar to those given in comparable cases. The applicant provided little reason to support her assertion that they were excessive.
firac.conclusion: The sanctions were not excessive or disproportionate; the applicant failed to establish an error in principle or that they were clearly unfit.

firac.issue: Should the proposed fresh evidence be admitted and did it affect the outcome?
firac.facts: The applicant sought to introduce a letter from the Information and Privacy Commissioner confirming that Board staff had released her personal information to Rebel News, supporting her explanation for her upset over the events underlying her impugned conduct.
firac.rule: Fresh evidence is admissible only in exceptional circumstances — to provide background, show an absence of evidence on an essential point, or show a breach of procedural fairness not provable on the record (Re Keeprite, 1980 CanLII 1877 (ON CA); Windrift Adventures, 2023 ONSC 4501, at para. 34).
firac.application: The evidence was new, uncontroversial and added weight to the applicant's explanation of why she was upset, so it was admitted for a complete record. However, the conduct of concern was the accusatory manner in which she raised her concerns, not whether the concern was true; standards of civility apply whether or not a trustee is reasonably upset. The evidence therefore did not change the disposition.
firac.conclusion: The motion for fresh evidence was granted, but the evidence did not affect the outcome of the application.

keywords_rationale: The case is a judicial review (K011) in administrative law (K001, the primary practice area) applying the reasonableness standard of review (K014) and, because the decision limited a Charter right, the Doré/Loyola proportionate-balancing framework (K010). The engaged Charter right is freedom of expression (K024), specifically s. 2(b) of the Charter (K111) under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (K107). Procedural fairness (K012) was squarely contested. The dispute concerned a trustee's breach of a school board code of conduct (K042) enforced by a school board (K044) under the Education Act, engaging education law (K005). K005 is a secondary tier-1 area but genuinely applies given the school-board statutory context; the dominant classification remains administrative law.
location_rationale: The decision states it was 'HEARD at Toronto: May 22, 2024' and identifies the court as the 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE DIVISIONAL COURT', establishing Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The header identifies 'DIVISIONAL COURT FILE NO.: DC-24-00002849-0000' and the panel sitting in the Divisional Court of the Superior Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Ahmed v. Assu

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff's Notice of Civil Claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1) as disclosing no reasonable claim, or as frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process where it re-litigates matters already decided?
Was it necessary to make an order under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act declaring the plaintiff a vexatious litigant?
Should the defendants be awarded special costs?

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1) as vexatious and an abuse of process?
firac.facts: Mr. Ahmed sued the defendants for $100,000, alleging conspiracy to file a false lawsuit, fraud, forgery, blackmail, defamation and threats. The claim stemmed from a 2007 landlord-tenant fire dispute already litigated in Provincial Court, where the defendants obtained judgment against Mrs. Ahmed and Mr. Ahmed's counterclaim was dismissed. Appeals had failed for non-compliance with transcript and security-for-costs orders. The pleading contained no material facts supporting allegations such as fraud, forgery and blackmail and gave no proper legal basis.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim (a), are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious (b), or are an abuse of process (d). The 'plain and obvious' test from Hunt v Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 SCR 959 governs (a). Under (b) a pleading is vexatious where it advances no claim known in law or cannot succeed (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish Congress). Abuse of process under (d) prevents re-litigation of decided issues (Toronto (City) v CUPE Local 79, 2003 SCC 63; Babavic v Babowech). Material facts must be pleaded (Young v Borzoni, 2007 BCCA 16).
firac.application: The Court found the claim was an attempt to re-litigate matters already decided and a collateral attack on the Provincial Court judgment, the additional allegations flowing from Mr. Ahmed's belief he was wrongly sued and that judges acted improperly. His appeal was never heard on the merits due to his own failure to file transcripts. The pleading was also deficient, containing no material facts for fraud, forgery and blackmail and no proper legal basis, and was too defective to save by amendment.
firac.conclusion: It was plain and obvious the claim was vexatious and an abuse of process; the claim was struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b) and (d).

firac.issue: Was a s. 18 vexatious-litigant order necessary?
firac.facts: Mr. Ahmed had a history of repeated actions arising from the same dispute. In Ahmed v. Vancouver (City), 2012 BCSC 301, Sewell J. had already made a s. 18 order against him, though that order post-dated the filing of this action.
firac.rule: Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act permits ordering that proceedings not be instituted without leave where a person has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds instituted vexatious legal proceedings, applying the Re Lang Michener v Fabian (1987) factors.
firac.application: Because an order under s. 18 had already been made against Mr. Ahmed by Sewell J., the Court found it unnecessary to make another, though it described the basis for the existing order (re-litigation, meritless actions, unfounded allegations against parties, counsel and judges).
firac.conclusion: No further s. 18 order was made; it was unnecessary given the existing order.

firac.issue: Should special costs be awarded against the plaintiff?
firac.facts: Mr. Ahmed persisted in re-litigating a concluded dispute and made serious, unfounded allegations against the defendants, their counsel and various judges, and disregarded court orders.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) allows costs of the application to be paid as special costs. Special costs are warranted where conduct is reprehensible and worthy of rebuke (Garcia v Crestbrook Forest Industries Ltd.); attempting to re-litigate with reckless indifference to prior orders is reprehensible (Muller v Muller, 2010 BCSC 1381).
firac.application: While striking a claim as vexatious does not automatically justify special costs, Mr. Ahmed had behaved badly, making baseless allegations against the defendants, counsel and judges and continuing to disregard court orders, amounting to reprehensible conduct.
firac.conclusion: Special costs were awarded to the defendants on the application.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area and the core of the case, which concerns striking a civil claim under the Supreme Court Civil Rules, abuse of process and special costs. K015 (defamation) applies because defamation over a web log was one of the pleaded (struck) causes of action. K065 (racism), K063 (online hate/social media) and K061 (hate speech) are weak, tangential picks: the pleading alleged that the defendant used 'abusive, obscene, degrading and racially motivated language' on a web log over the internet, but these allegations were never adjudicated and the claim was struck as vexatious. They are flagged as weak — the controlled vocabulary lacks direct terms for the true subject matter (abuse of process, vexatious litigant, striking pleadings, special costs), so no strongly-matching procedural keywords exist beyond the tier-1 area.

registry_rationale: The decision expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation v. James Keegstra

defining_issues: Was there a real and substantial risk that a fair trial would be impossible if the broadcast were allowed, so as to justify a quia timet injunction restraining publication on the ground that it might interfere with the administration of justice?

firac.issue: Should an injunction restraining the CBC from broadcasting a drama said to characterize Keegstra be granted on the basis that it might prejudice a possible future retrial of his hate-promotion conviction?
firac.facts: The CBC proposed to broadcast, in Alberta on December 8, 1985, a television drama set in Ontario about a teacher who advocated anti-semitism, said to be a thinly-disguised characterization of Keegstra, who had been convicted by a jury in July 1985 of wilfully promoting hatred of Jews and had a pending, not-yet-heard appeal. On December 6, 1985 Keegstra sued in defamation and, in an emergent chambers application, obtained an injunction. The chambers judge treated the matter as a quia timet injunction against feared sub judice contempt affecting any new trial, reasoning 'better not to publish than be damned later.' The CBC appealed.
firac.rule: An injunction against a proposed publication on the ground that it might interfere with the administration of justice is granted only where 'there is a real and substantial risk that a fair trial will be impossible in the circumstances of the case if publication is allowed' (A-G Alta. v. Plantation Indoor Plants (1982) 34 A.R. 348 (Alta. C.A.)). Not every potentially criminal or contemptuous act may be enjoined (Attorney-General v. Times Newspapers [1973] 3 All E.R. 54, per Lord Diplock). Other safeguards of a fair trial exist: challenge for cause in jury selection, change of venue, delay, and jury warnings; sub judice contempt is invoked only when those are unlikely to be effective.
firac.application: The Court held the chambers judge applied the wrong test. The risk of interference depended on a lengthy chain of contingencies: that Keegstra win his appeal, that a new trial be ordered, that potential jurors saw and were inflamed by the program, that they remained so at jury selection, that they could not be successfully challenged, and that no disinterested array could be found. Any new trial would not begin for at least six months and likely not before 1988. Nothing in the material persuaded the Court that prejudiced jurors could not be challenged for cause or that a disinterested array could not be found. Accordingly, the risk of interference with the administration of justice was not real or substantial. The Court did not decide the defamation claim, nor whether the sub judice rule was a reasonable limit on free speech.
firac.conclusion: The requirements for the injunction not being made out on the correct test, the appeal was allowed and the order vacated; the Court emphasized this was not an order permitting publication, which the CBC undertakes at its own risk.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally a civil litigation matter about restraining publication, so K002 (Civil litigation, tier-1) and K021 (interlocutory injunction — the quia timet injunction sought) are central. K024 (freedom of expression) is engaged because the Court noted but expressly declined to decide whether the sub judice rule is a reasonable limit on free speech. K015 (defamation) applies to Keegstra's underlying statement of claim, though the Court did not decide it. K067 (wilful promotion of hatred) and K061 (hate speech) reflect Keegstra's underlying conviction for wilfully promoting hatred of Jews, which framed the risk to a fair trial; these are contextual/background picks. K093 (Jewish) captures the group targeted in the drama and conviction. The hate-related keywords are somewhat peripheral since the ruling turned on the injunction test, but they identify the substantive backdrop.
location_rationale: The header of the decision identifies the Court of Appeal of Alberta and states 'Registry: Calgary', placing the court in Calgary, Alberta.
registry_rationale: The decision expressly states 'Registry: Calgary'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Her Majesty the Queen v. William Whatcott

defining_issues: Does the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms apply to the University of Calgary's action in banning Mr. Whatcott and issuing a trespass ticket under provincial legislation?
Did the University's use of trespass legislation to stop and ban Mr. Whatcott from distributing flyers infringe his freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter?
If s. 2(b) was infringed, was the infringement a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter?

firac.issue: Does the Charter apply to the University of Calgary's conduct in banning Mr. Whatcott and enforcing the Trespass to Premises Act against him?
firac.facts: Mr. Whatcott was banned indefinitely from University of Calgary property in 2005 for distributing graphic anti-abortion leaflets and was ticketed for trespass in 2008 while distributing flyers. The University is a statutory body governed by the Post-Secondary Learning Act. The challenge was to the University's application of trespass legislation, not the legislation itself.
firac.rule: Under s. 32(1) of the Charter, as interpreted in RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery, the Charter binds government actors and actions. McKinney v. University of Guelph held universities are not generally part of government, but Eldridge v. British Columbia (AG) held the Charter applies to a private/autonomous entity when it implements a specific governmental policy or program. Pridgen v. University of Calgary applied this to the University in exercising its educational mandate.
firac.application: The court adopted Streklaf J.'s reasoning in Pridgen: while a university's day-to-day operations (like hiring/firing) are non-governmental, the University acts as the agent of the province in providing accessible post-secondary education under the PSL Act. Regulating a person's freedom of expression as a condition of access to a public educational institution is integrally connected to that governmental program, so the University's conduct attracts Charter scrutiny.
firac.conclusion: The Charter applies to the University of Calgary's impugned actions.

firac.issue: Did the University's enforcement of the trespass legislation infringe Mr. Whatcott's s. 2(b) freedom of expression?
firac.facts: Mr. Whatcott peacefully distributed pamphlets on campus; his activity presented no harm to persons or property. The 2005 ban and the 2008 ticket arose from complaints about the content of his flyers.
firac.rule: Ross v. New Brunswick School District No. 15 and Irwin Toy establish a two-step test: (1) does the activity convey meaning and thus fall within s. 2(b); and (2) does the purpose or effect of the impugned action restrict that expression. Truth or unpopularity of content is irrelevant.
firac.application: Distributing flyers conveys meaning and falls within s. 2(b) regardless of the content's unpopularity. Campus security used the trespass legislation to respond to complaints about the content of the flyers, so the effect of the action was to restrict protected expression.
firac.conclusion: Mr. Whatcott's s. 2(b) rights were infringed.

firac.issue: Was the infringement justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The University banned Mr. Whatcott indefinitely and enforced the ban with a trespass ticket because attendees found his peaceful leafleting offensive.
firac.rule: R. v. Oakes requires a pressing and substantial objective and a proportionality analysis (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionate effects); the party invoking s. 1 bears the onus.
firac.application: Preventing peaceful distribution of leaflets that some attendees find offensive is not a pressing and substantial objective sufficient to override a constitutional right. The indefinite ban was arbitrary, unfair and disproportionate, so the s. 1 justification failed at the first stage and on proportionality.
firac.conclusion: The infringement was not justified under s. 1; a stay of proceedings was entered on the trespass ticket.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns entirely on Charter analysis. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) capture the core right at issue in distributing flyers. K030 (reasonable limits s. 1) reflects the Oakes analysis undertaken. K107 (Canadian Charter) is the governing statute. K041 (campus/university) situates the dispute at the University of Calgary and the s. 32 application question. K011 (judicial review) is a borderline pick — the case addresses whether the University's action attracts Charter scrutiny (s. 32 government-action analysis under McKinney/Eldridge), which is administrative-law adjacent though the decision is a provincial-offence prosecution; it is included as the closest term for the government-actor analysis but is weaker than the others.
location_rationale: The header states 'In the Provincial Court of Alberta', 'Registry: Calgary', and the judgment is 'Dated at the City of Calgary, Alberta'.
registry_rationale: The decision expressly lists 'Registry: Calgary' in its header.

case_name: Ontario Nurses' Association v. Orillia Soldiers Memorial Hospital

name_verification.name_in_document: Ontario Nurses' Association v. Orillia Soldiers Memorial Hospital et al. [Indexed as: Ontario Nurses' Assn. v. Orillia Soldiers Memorial Hospital]

defining_issues: Do collective-agreement provisions that stop employer contributions to benefit premiums for nurses on long-term disability discriminate on the basis of handicap contrary to s. 5 of the Human Rights Code?
Do the provisions limiting service accrual for disabled nurses on unpaid leave discriminate on the basis of handicap?
Do the provisions limiting seniority accrual for disabled nurses violate s. 5 of the Code, and if so is the violation excused under s. 17?
If the benefit/service provisions amount to constructive (adverse-effect) discrimination under s. 11, is the employer entitled to the bona fide occupational qualification justification?

firac.issue: Do collective-agreement provisions ending employer contributions to benefit premiums for nurses on long-term disability constitute direct discrimination because of handicap under s. 5 of the Human Rights Code?
firac.facts: Under the ONA full-time collective agreement, the hospital paid benefit premiums for active nurses and for a limited period for nurses on unpaid leave; after 30 months on long-term disability the nurse paid 100% of premiums. The grievers were nurses whose disabilities fell within 'handicap' in s. 10(1).
firac.rule: Section 5(1) guarantees equal treatment in employment without discrimination because of handicap. Employer benefit contributions are a form of compensation (Brooks v. Canada Safeway). Discrimination exists only where a distinction is based on a prohibited ground; the appropriate comparator group is determined by the purpose of the benefit (Gibbs v. Battlefords; War Amputations of Canada).
firac.application: The purpose of employer premium contributions is to provide compensation in exchange for work. Disabled nurses did not receive it because they were not providing services, not because of handicap. The correct comparator is other employees not providing work; disabled nurses received benefits equal to or more generous than that group. Distinguishing compensation between those working and those not working is not prohibited discrimination.
firac.conclusion: No s. 5 discrimination; the benefit-premium provision does not contravene the Code, so s. 17 need not be considered.

firac.issue: Do provisions limiting service accrual for disabled nurses discriminate on the basis of handicap under s. 5?
firac.facts: Continuous service determines vacation pay and place on the wage grid; a nurse on unpaid leave accrued service only for 30 days regardless of disability status.
firac.rule: Same s. 5 analysis: identify the purpose of the benefit and the appropriate comparator group.
firac.application: The purpose of service accrual is to fix compensation on the salary grid and vacation pay, so the comparator is other employees on unpaid leave of absence. All members of that group, handicapped or not, were treated identically. As disabled nurses could provide no service, no accommodation could overcome their inability to work.
firac.conclusion: No s. 5 or s. 11 discrimination; the service-accrual provision does not breach the Code.

firac.issue: Do provisions limiting seniority accrual for disabled nurses violate s. 5, and can any violation be excused under s. 17?
firac.facts: Seniority accrued only for one year for nurses on long-term disability or workers' compensation. Under the agreement seniority was a competitive tie-breaker for vacancies, layoffs and recalls where skill, ability, experience and qualifications were relatively equal.
firac.rule: Section 5(1) equal treatment; the comparator depends on the purpose of the right (Gibbs). Section 17(1) excuses infringement only where a person is incapable of performing the essential duties attending the right because of handicap. Seniority is 'labour's premier equity tool' (Abella Report) at the core of human-rights protection for the disabled (Eldridge; Eaton).
firac.application: Unlike compensation, seniority is triggered simply by the status of being an employee, a status long-term disabled nurses retained, so the comparator is all other employees. Denying seniority accrual disadvantaged disabled nurses on returning to work, affecting access to promotion and protection from layoff. Section 17 did not excuse the violation because accruing seniority required nothing more than the passage of time as an employee — no essential duty the disabled nurse was incapable of performing. Analogous to automatic-termination cases (Etobicoke General Hospital).
firac.conclusion: The seniority provisions directly discriminate under s. 5 and are not saved by s. 17; they must be struck down and disabled employees exempted from the curtailment while they remain employees within the Code definition of handicap.

firac.issue: If the impugned provisions amount to constructive discrimination under s. 11, does the bona fide occupational qualification defence in s. 11(1)(b)/(2) apply?
firac.facts: The ONA argued adverse-effect discrimination, contending the neutral rule (employer contributes only for nurses in active employ) burdened disabled nurses. The employer led no evidence on undue-hardship factors of cost, funding or health and safety.
firac.rule: Section 11 codifies constructive/adverse-effect discrimination (Simpsons-Sears); the s. 11(1)(a)/(2) defence requires showing the group's needs cannot be accommodated without undue hardship (Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud). Accommodation means adjusting to actual characteristics, not 'reverse stereotyping' or wage top-ups (Eaton). Section 11 applies to handicap and to compensation, rejecting the Versa Services participation/compensation split.
firac.application: For benefits and service accrual, requiring work in exchange for compensation is a reasonable and bona fide requirement and no accommodation could enable non-working nurses to earn it, so the BFOQ defence applies. For seniority, however, no undue hardship was shown; both employer and union share the accommodation duty (Renaud), and adjusting seniority causes at most minor impact on other employees, insufficient to defeat the right.
firac.conclusion: The BFOQ defence saves the benefit and service provisions but not the seniority provisions, which alternatively constitute unjustified constructive discrimination; the appropriate accommodation is to exempt disabled nurses from the seniority curtailment.

keywords_rationale: The case turns on discrimination because of handicap under the Ontario Human Rights Code, so K007 (Human rights, tier 1) and K069 (discrimination) are core, with K119 (Human Rights Code) as the governing statute. The distinction between direct discrimination and the bona fide occupational qualification / duty-to-accommodate defence engages K068 (BFOR) and K073 (prima facie discrimination). Because the discrimination arises in the workplace via a collective agreement and grievance arbitration, K009 (Labour and employment, tier 1), K082 (employment discrimination) and K084 (labour arbitration) apply. The matter reached the court on judicial review of an arbitration award on a correctness standard, supporting K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review). K031 is included for the duty-to-accommodate/undue-hardship analysis, though it is flagged as a borderline pick because its canonical label is 'religious accommodation' while the accommodation here concerns disability.
location_rationale: The decision is rendered by the Court of Appeal for Ontario (Doherty, Laskin and Rosenberg JJ.A.), which sits in Toronto; the province is Ontario, confirmed by references to the Ontario Human Rights Code and the Divisional Court. The precise city is not stated in the text but is the seat of the ONCA.
registry_rationale: No court registry/office is stated in the decision; the document identifies only the court and docket number (C28113), so registry is left null.

case_name: R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. BIG M DRUG MART LTD.

defining_issues: Was the Lord's Day Act validly enacted under Parliament's criminal law power (s. 91(27) of the Constitution Act, 1867)?
Does a corporation have standing and the benefit of the guarantee of freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
Does s. 4 of the Lord's Day Act infringe freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter, and if so is it saved as a reasonable limit under s. 1?
May a trial court reconsider higher-court authority (the Hamilton Street Ry. line) in light of changed social conditions and the enactment of the Charter, despite stare decisis?

firac.issue: Was the Lord's Day Act validly enacted under Parliament's criminal law power (s. 91(27) of the Constitution Act, 1867)?
firac.facts: Big M Drug Mart was charged under s. 4 of the Lord's Day Act with unlawfully carrying on the sale of goods on Sunday, 30 May 1982, in Calgary. The Act's constitutional foundation rested on A.G. Ont. v. Hamilton Street Ry., which had characterized Sunday-observance legislation as 'criminal law in its widest sense,' resting on the notion that Christianity was part of the common law.
firac.rule: Under s. 91(27), criminal law was originally defined as 'criminal law in its widest sense' (Hamilton Street Ry.), but Canadian authorities (P.A.T.A. case, per Duff J.; Margarine Reference, per Rand J.) narrowed it: a valid criminal law must be enacted for a public purpose to suppress human conduct that is an evil or menace to public peace, order, security, health or morality.
firac.application: The court found the criminal law power has been substantially narrowed since 1902, and that Sunday-observance legislation compelled a religious/moral obligation stemming from the erroneous premise that Christianity was part of the common law—a premise doubted since Bowman v. Secular Soc. The proscribed acts (Sunday selling) are intrinsically innocent, and in a multi-religious Canada with no state church there is no public evil or menace to suppress. The Act was thus deprived of its constitutional underpinnings.
firac.conclusion: The court held the Lord's Day Act ultra vires the Parliament of Canada.

firac.issue: Does a corporation have standing and the benefit of the guarantee of freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
firac.facts: The accused was a subsisting Alberta corporation charged under s. 4. The Crown questioned whether a corporation could claim freedom of religion and whether it had standing.
firac.rule: 'Everyone' in s. 2 is at least as wide as 'person,' which by the Interpretation Act, the Criminal Code and Union Colliery Co. v. R. includes corporations. Standing is established (Borowski) where a party is directly affected or has a genuine interest and there is no other reasonable and effective way to bring the issue forward; whether a law infringes religious freedom depends on the nature of the law, not the accused's beliefs (Cartwright J., dissenting, in Robertson).
firac.application: The court concluded 'everyone' and 'person' are synonymous and include corporations, noting s. 2(b) protects media vehicles typically owned by corporations. The corporate accused was directly affected by the prosecution, had a genuine interest in the Act's validity, and had no other effective means to raise the issue; the accused's own religious persuasion was irrelevant to whether the law infringed freedom of religion.
firac.conclusion: The corporation had standing and could invoke s. 2(a) to challenge s. 4 of the Lord's Day Act.

firac.issue: Does s. 4 of the Lord's Day Act infringe freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter, and if so is it saved under s. 1?
firac.facts: Section 4 forbids selling goods on Sunday, recognizing Sunday as the Sabbath of certain Christian denominations. The Charter preamble recognizes 'the supremacy of God' without reference to a Christian God, reflecting Canada's multicultural, multi-denominational make-up.
firac.rule: A law which compels a course of conduct for a purely religious purpose infringes freedom of religion (Cartwright J. in Robertson). Under s. 1, once a prima facie infringement is shown, the state must prove on a balance of probabilities that the limit is reasonable, prescribed by law, not more excessive than necessary, and not arbitrary or capricious (drawing on MacKay v. R.).
firac.application: The court found the purpose of s. 4 is to recognize Sunday as a Christian day of rest, which adversely affects the religious freedoms of non-observers and even non-Sunday-observing Christians; the entrenched, broadly interpreted Charter reaches further than the earlier Canadian Bill of Rights considered in Robertson. Commercial regulation falls to the provinces under s. 92(13) and (16), so forced Sunday observance is no longer a valid federal objective, and enforcing it under penalty is an excessive limit. The court also noted the selective application of the Act's enforcement (s. 16). The Crown failed to discharge the s. 1 onus.
firac.conclusion: Section 4 infringes freedom of religion, is not saved by s. 1, and must be struck down; it is of no force and effect under s. 52(1).

firac.issue: May a trial court reconsider binding higher-court authority in light of changed social conditions and the Charter?
firac.facts: The Attorney General's agent argued the court lacked authority to revisit established Supreme Court and Privy Council authority (the Hamilton Street Ry. line) as social conditions change.
firac.rule: Section 1 of the Charter, by its terms, invites courts to consider changing social values in assessing 'reasonable limits...demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society'; courts may consider extrinsic evidence (Re Anti-Inflation Act).
firac.application: The court held it could take account of changed and changing social conditions both on precedent and by virtue of the newly enacted Canada Act/Charter, which had altered the legal landscape since the Boardwalk Merchandise Mart appellate decision.
firac.conclusion: The court was entitled to reconsider the prior authority in light of the Charter and evolving social conditions.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) and K004 (Criminal law) capture the two constitutional axes—division of powers under s. 91(27) criminal law power and Charter review. K025 (freedom of religion) and K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) are the core Charter guarantee at issue. K107 (Canadian Charter) reflects the newly enacted instrument driving the result. K030 (reasonable limits s. 1) applies because the court conducted an s. 1 analysis in the alternative. K033 (shabbat/sabbath) is a reasonable content tag since the Act concerns compulsory Sabbath (Sunday) observance; it is a slightly weaker pick as the vocabulary term leans toward the Jewish Sabbath, but it best captures the Sabbath-observance subject matter.
