name_verification.name_in_document: Rex v. James Butler (and companion accused Timothy Champ, Immanuel Covenant Reformed Church, John Koopman, Riverside Calvary Chapel, Brent Phillip Smith)

defining_issues: On a Vukelich hearing, do the accused's Charter challenges to the Provincial Health Officer's Gatherings and Events Orders have a reasonable prospect of success such that a full evidentiary hearing is warranted?

Are the Charter challenges, brought at trial after the accused allegedly breached the public health orders, an impermissible collateral attack on those administrative orders under the Maybrun framework?

Is the court bound by the constitutional validity of the same Orders as determined in Beaudoin (upheld by the BCCA), and does the additional evidence proposed meet the threshold to revisit binding precedent?
Is Beaudoin determinative of the challenges of accused (Champ and Butler) who were not petitioners in that case, and of the ss. 7 and 15 Charter claims?

firac.issue: On a Vukelich hearing, do the accused's Charter challenges to the PHO's Gatherings and Events Orders have a reasonable prospect of success justifying a full evidentiary hearing?
firac.facts: Nineteen tickets were issued against pastors and churches for breaching the PHO's Gatherings and Events Orders limiting in-person worship during COVID-19. The accused sought to challenge the constitutional validity of the Orders under ss. 2(a)(b)(c)(d), 7 and 15(1) of the Charter at trial. The Crown moved to summarily dismiss the Charter applications without a full evidentiary hearing.
firac.rule: Under R. v. Vukelich (1996) and R. v. Cody, 2017 SCC 31, a court may summarily dismiss an application that has no reasonable prospect of success and no basis upon which it could succeed; Vukelich screening extends to challenges to legislation and stays (Trans Mountain Pipeline ULC v. Mivasair, 2020 BCCA 255). The court must assume the applicant's proffered facts are true and ask whether they disclose a legal basis for the remedy sought (R. v. Frederickson, 2018 BCCA 2).
firac.application: The court heard four days of argument and a voluminous record. Assuming the applicants' facts to be true, it found the challenges raised identical questions to those already heard and decided in Beaudoin and were an impermissible collateral attack, leaving no reasonable prospect of success. Summary dismissal did not deprive the accused of the ability to defend the charges by other means, as they remained presumed innocent (save the one already tried).
firac.conclusion: The Charter applications were summarily dismissed as having no reasonable prospect of success.

firac.issue: Are the Charter challenges an impermissible collateral attack on the administrative Orders?
firac.facts: The accused sought to challenge the validity of PHO Orders at trial after allegedly breaching them, rather than through the s. 43 reconsideration process of the Public Health Act or judicial review. Most of the alleged breaches pre-dated any reconsideration request; some letters to the PHO were demands to rescind Orders with promises of non-compliance.
firac.rule: The general rule against collateral attack (R. v. Bird, 2019 SCC 7; Wilson v. The Queen) requires a distinct analysis for administrative orders under R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd., 1998 CanLII 820 (SCC), weighing the statutory scheme, availability of review, penalty, and legislative intent. Horizontal stare decisis (Re Hansard Spruce Mills; R. v. Sullivan, 2022 SCC 19) binds the court to R. v. Lucier, 2022 BCPC 191, absent narrow exceptions.
firac.application: The court held Lucier — which applied Maybrun to identical Gatherings Orders — was binding, having not been undermined by appellate authority, decided in haste, or reached per incuriam. The Public Health Act creates a comprehensive regime with a s. 43 reconsideration process and judicial review; the legislature did not intend to permit challenges to orders in later prosecutions after breach. Whether an accused used those avenues was immaterial to the ratio. The correspondence relied on did not constitute reconsideration requests, and s. 43(6) means an order is not suspended during reconsideration.
firac.conclusion: The challenges were impermissible collateral attacks and dismissed on that basis as well.

firac.issue: Is the court bound by the finding of constitutional validity in Beaudoin, and does the proposed additional evidence meet the threshold to revisit that precedent?
firac.facts: Four of the six applicants were petitioners in Beaudoin v. British Columbia, 2021 BCSC 512, aff'd 2022 BCCA 427, where the same Orders survived Charter challenge on the same grounds. The applicants proposed additional evidence (affidavits of Drs. Kettner and Warren, a newspaper article, excerpts from Dr. Henry's book) said to be essential to the s. 1 analysis.
firac.rule: Lower courts may not revisit binding rulings on constitutional validity absent a fundamental shift in the legal or factual matrix (Canada (AG) v. Bedford, 2013 SCC 72, paras 38-47; Carter v. Canada, 2015 SCC 5). The standard is high; even significant developments do not warrant revisiting (R. v. Topham, 2017 BCSC 259). The BCCA in Beaudoin conducted an Oakes analysis (in addition to Doré) that was authoritative guidance under R. v. Henry, 2005 SCC 76.
firac.application: The nature of the alleged breaches was identical to Beaudoin. The proposed evidence, even if accepted, represented at most an alternate view of risk already considered; the Chief Justice had noted such opinions would not render the Orders unreasonable, and the BCCA had knowingly conducted a full Oakes analysis finding the Orders justified. Constitutional rulings on judicial review bind criminal courts (Suresh; Whatcott; Ktunaxa cited as precedent in criminal contexts). No fundamental shift was shown.
firac.conclusion: Beaudoin was determinative; the challenges had no reasonable possibility of success and could not be re-litigated.

firac.issue: Is Beaudoin determinative for accused who were not petitioners (Champ and Butler) and for the ss. 7 and 15 claims?
firac.facts: Champ and Butler were not petitioners in Beaudoin but provided affidavits in that record; their factual basis for the alleged infringements was identical. In Beaudoin the courts found the s. 7 and s. 15 claims were subsumed by the s. 2 analysis and would not alter the s. 1 result.
firac.rule: A ruling on the constitutional validity of orders applies to any person charged under those orders alleging the same kind of violation. The BCCA in Beaudoin held that even if s. 15 or additional breaches were established, no analytical route would change the proportionality/s. 1 analysis (paras 234, 238).
firac.application: Nothing distinguished the challenges of Champ and Butler from the petitioners. The ss. 7 and 15 claims were framed as in Beaudoin, where they were subsumed by s. 2 and did not affect the s. 1 justification. The court found the constitutional validity decision determinative of all alleged breaches.
firac.conclusion: Beaudoin bound the non-petitioner accused and was determinative of the ss. 7 and 15 claims; all applications dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 anchor: the applications turned on Charter challenges to the PHO Orders. K025 (freedom of religion) and K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) capture the core asserted right — in-person worship. K030 (reasonable limits s. 1) and K010 (Doré/Loyola framework) reflect the s. 1 / Oakes and Doré analyses the court discussed as governing the justification of the Orders. K011 (judicial review) is central because the binding precedent (Beaudoin) arose on judicial review and the collateral-attack analysis pointed to that avenue. K014 (standard of review) reflects the reasonableness/deference discussion applied to the PHO's expert judgment. K023 (equality rights) covers the s. 15(1) claims addressed. K004 (Criminal law) is included because the matters were quasi-criminal ticket prosecutions decided on a Vukelich screening device; it is a somewhat secondary but genuine dimension. There is no controlled-vocabulary term for 'collateral attack' or 'Vukelich', which were central doctrines, so those are reflected through the judicial review / standard of review picks.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'IN THE PROVINCIAL COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA' and lists 'Registries: Chilliwack, Abbotsford'. The 'Place of Hearing' is stated as 'Abbotsford, B.C.', which is used for the city.
registry_rationale: The header expressly lists two registries — 'Registries: Chilliwack, Abbotsford' — with individual tickets assigned to Chilliwack or Abbotsford; both are recorded.

name_verification.name_in_document: Baumgartner v. Jamieson

defining_issues: Was the plaintiff dismissed for just cause, or was she wrongfully dismissed?
If wrongfully dismissed, what is the appropriate notice period and should it be extended for bad-faith conduct in the manner of dismissal?
Is the plaintiff entitled to future commissions, overtime, and vacation/statutory holiday pay, and did she fail to mitigate her damages?

firac.issue: Did the employer establish just cause for the summary dismissal of the plaintiff, or was she wrongfully dismissed?
firac.facts: Baumgartner, a commissioned salesperson at AIP from May 2000, was dismissed on January 9, 2003 with the explanation 'insubordination...there's a list.' The employer alleged a long, shifting list of grounds (insubordination to sales manager Findlay, the WCB meeting outburst, the Dr. Pezim account, the January 7 email copied to colleagues, racial slurs including 'Jew me down', theft of a client list, etc.). The dismissal followed shortly after the plaintiff raised an employment-standards issue about vacation and statutory holiday pay.
firac.rule: An employer bears the onus of proving cause on a balance of probabilities (Geluch v. Rosedale Golf Assn.; McKinley v. BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38). The test is two-step: establish the misconduct, then establish that its nature or degree warranted dismissal, assessed contextually within the whole employment relationship. Cumulative minor misconduct may suffice, but employers often must warn employees, condoned misconduct cannot later be relied upon, and after-discovered/after-alleged grounds carry less weight (Wallace v. United Grain Growers).
firac.application: Justice Cohen preferred the plaintiff's witnesses, finding Jamieson's evidence badly conflicted across three discoveries and trial as to the actual grounds. There were no contemporaneous notes, emails or memoranda corroborating the alleged staff revolt or the plaintiff's poisoning of the workplace; the administrative staff never left; the plaintiff was never disciplined or warned; the November 1 memorandum was found not to be aimed at her; the Dr. Pezim incident posed no risk to AIP and Jamieson had conceded the client's complaint was not a ground; and the January 7 email dispute was 'a tempest in a teapot.' The court found the employment-standards issue put strain on AIP's tight finances and that Jamieson's antagonism toward the plaintiff, corroborated by Kane and Rodrigue, showed the real reason for dismissal.
firac.conclusion: The defence failed to prove just cause. The plaintiff was dismissed mainly because she raised legitimate Employment Standards Act issues; the after-the-fact grounds could not defeat her claim. She was wrongfully dismissed.

firac.issue: What is the reasonable notice period, and should it be extended for the manner of dismissal?
firac.facts: The plaintiff had roughly 2.5 years' service, was the second-highest salesperson, was dismissed without warning and told only 'insubordination...there's a list.' She was devastated, and her family doctor confirmed a significant clinical depression tied to the dismissal.
firac.rule: Reasonable notice is assessed on the Bardal factors (Bardal v. Globe and Mail Ltd.) — character of employment, length of service, age, and availability of similar employment (Ansari). An employer must act with good faith and fair dealing in the manner of dismissal; breach is compensated by extending the notice period (Wallace v. United Grain Growers, 1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)).
firac.application: Applying Bardal, the court set the base notice at 3 months. Because Jamieson dismissed the plaintiff for raising employment-standards rights, without warning and with a bare accusation of insubordination, the court found bad faith in the manner of discharge warranting a Wallace extension of 2 months.
firac.conclusion: Notice period fixed at 5 months, yielding damages of $18,750 on annual earnings of $45,000.

firac.issue: Is the plaintiff entitled to future commissions, overtime and vacation/holiday pay, and did she fail to mitigate?
firac.facts: The Policy and Procedures Manual, which the plaintiff accepted ('Sounds good to me'), provided that on termination account executives receive no compensation for advertising booked into the future. The plaintiff claimed future commissions, overtime she chose to work, and vacation/statutory holiday pay. She sought only part-time replacement work after dismissal.
firac.rule: Contract terms accepted by an employee govern entitlements; overtime is compensable only where required by the employer. On mitigation the employer must prove both a lack of reasonable effort and that comparable employment was available (Litster v. British Columbia Ferry Corp.).
firac.application: The clear Manual clause, understood and accepted by the intelligent and articulate plaintiff, barred future commissions. Jamieson never demanded overtime and encouraged staff to leave at quitting time, so the overtime claim failed. The defence proved neither a lack of effort nor availability of comparable work, and it was reasonable for the depressed plaintiff, who had always wanted part-time work, not to seek full-time replacement. Vacation and statutory holiday pay were not contested.
firac.conclusion: Future commissions and overtime claims dismissed; no failure to mitigate; the plaintiff awarded $3,421.94 for vacation and statutory holiday pay in addition to the notice damages.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, and K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the central issue — the court found no just cause and awarded pay in lieu of notice with a Wallace extension. K083 (harassment) reflects the plaintiff's allegation, accepted in substance, that Jamieson became antagonistic and harassed her after she raised the employment-standards issue, but it is a supporting characterization rather than a distinct legal claim (weak). K057 (antisemitic slurs) and K065 (racism) are engaged only because the plaintiff's admitted use of the phrase 'Jew me down' and remarks about Asians were among the after-the-fact grounds the employer alleged; these are tangential to the outcome and flagged as weak picks reflecting factual mentions rather than the legal ratio.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA', 'Registry: Vancouver', and the trial was held in 'Vancouver, B.C.'
registry_rationale: The header expressly reads 'Registry: Vancouver'.

case_name: O.W.L. (Orphaned Wildlife) Rehabilitation Society v Day

name_verification.name_in_document: O.W.L. (Orphaned Wildlife) Rehabilitation Society v. Day

defining_issues: Did Ms. Day receive unauthorized payments for rent, salary and vacation pay such that O.W.L. was unjustly enriched and entitled to reimbursement?
Did O.W.L. have just cause to dismiss Ms. Day without notice?
What damages, including notice period, lost benefits, and aggravated/punitive damages, is Ms. Day entitled to for wrongful dismissal?

firac.issue: Was Ms. Day paid unauthorized amounts (rent, salary, vacation pay) entitling O.W.L. to recover on the basis of unjust enrichment?
firac.facts: O.W.L., a charitable raptor-rehabilitation society, alleged that its founder and executive director, Ms. Day, misappropriated funds by having O.W.L. pay the rent for her on-site residence and by receiving unauthorized salary increases and vacation pay. O.W.L. abandoned the misappropriation claim at the start of closing argument and relied solely on unjust enrichment. Board minutes going back to 1988, and evidence of four former board members and two bookkeepers, showed the Board decided and authorized all aspects of Ms. Day's remuneration, including payment of her rent (required because she was O.W.L.'s live-in caretaker), and treatment of part of the rent as a taxable benefit.
firac.rule: A claim in unjust enrichment requires an enrichment, a corresponding deprivation, and the absence of any juristic reason. Contemporaneous documents are more reliable than later reconstruction (Faryna v. Chorny; Chudy v. Merchant Law Group, 2007 BCSC 279).
firac.application: The Board minutes and the credible, consistent evidence of former directors and bookkeepers established that O.W.L. had always agreed and remained obliged, as part of Ms. Day's employment contract, to pay the rent for her on-site housing, and that her salary and vacation payments were all Board-authorized and carried out by bookkeepers who took no instruction from Ms. Day. The court rejected the reconstructed evidence of Ms. Wheatley and Ms. Wells as unreliable. There was thus a juristic reason (the employment contract and Board authorization) for all payments and no unjust enrichment.
firac.conclusion: O.W.L.'s claim for unauthorized rent, salary and vacation pay, and its unjust enrichment claim, were dismissed in their entirety.

firac.issue: Did O.W.L. establish just cause to dismiss Ms. Day summarily?
firac.facts: O.W.L. dismissed Ms. Day on October 23, 2014 without notice, relying at the time on three grounds (a comment to Martina Versteed, her dismissal of Rob Hope, and alleged misappropriation of rent) and later adding grounds including insubordination and neglect of duties. Ms. Day had authority to hire and fire; she dismissed Mr. Hope for cause after prior warnings and an incident involving a sexually explicit book shown in front of minors. The Board, without investigation, exonerated Mr. Hope and voted him severance, then directed Ms. Day to open a cabinet to produce the chequebook, which she refused once.
firac.rule: An employer must prove just cause; the onus is a heavy one (Staley v. Squirrel Systems, 2013 BCCA 201). Misconduct must be seriously incompatible with the employee's duties and, applying proportionality, dismissal must be balanced against the misconduct (McKinley v. BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38; Leung v. Doppler Industries). Progressive discipline and proper investigation are expected (Porta v. Weyerhaeuser). A single isolated act of insubordination, especially where the employer provokes an avoidable confrontation, generally does not justify dismissal (Henry v. Foxco; Stein v. BC Housing).
firac.application: The court found each ground factually inaccurate or insufficient. The rent issue was meritless and, even if proven, would not be cause. Ms. Day had investigated and had authority to dismiss Mr. Hope, and her statements were protected or non-defamatory. Her single refusal to open the cabinet was an isolated act provoked by the Board where other means existed to issue the cheque, and did not go to the root of the contract. Allegations of neglect (arising during a period of personal tragedy that the Board had encouraged her to take time for) and the Versteed comment, though inappropriate, were not cause absent warnings. O.W.L. gave no warnings, failed to investigate, and ignored proportionality.
firac.conclusion: None of the grounds constituted just cause; Ms. Day was wrongfully dismissed.

firac.issue: What damages is Ms. Day entitled to for wrongful dismissal, including notice, mitigation, and aggravated/punitive damages?
firac.facts: Ms. Day, aged 63 at dismissal (68 at trial), founded and ran O.W.L. for about 30 years, including 18 years as paid executive director, in a narrow field of expertise. She had not sought other work, citing surgery, grief and the litigation. O.W.L. pursued unfounded misappropriation and mismanagement allegations publicly through to trial and threatened to have her arrested if she attended the premises.
firac.rule: Reasonable notice is determined by the Bardal factors (character of employment, length of service, age, availability of similar employment) (Keays v. Honda Canada, 2008 SCC 39). The employer bears a heavy onus to prove failure to mitigate (Evans v. Teamsters Local 31; Red Deer College v. Michaels). Aggravated damages are available where the manner of dismissal or subsequent conduct is unfair or in bad faith and causes harm beyond ordinary upset (Honda; Wallace; Bailey v. Service Corporation International, 2018 BCSC 235). Punitive damages require harsh/malicious conduct, an actionable wrong, and rational need to punish (Whiten v. Pilot Insurance; Honda).
firac.application: Given her lengthy senior service, specialized field and age, her case was exceptional, warranting 26 months, reduced by 2 months for her likely intention to reduce hours, yielding 24 months' salary plus vacation pay and specified lost benefits. O.W.L. failed to prove availability of similar employment and thus failed to establish failure to mitigate. O.W.L.'s bad-faith conduct — unfounded, publicly maintained dishonesty allegations, callous treatment, and manufactured grounds — justified $30,000 in aggravated damages. Punitive damages were declined to avoid double-recovery, as the conduct was better reflected in aggravated damages and Ms. Day intended to seek special costs.
firac.conclusion: Judgment for Ms. Day: 24 months' salary plus 6% vacation pay, employer-paid rent (net of amounts already paid), $650 internet, $936 MSP premiums, and $30,000 aggravated damages; no punitive damages; costs to Ms. Day, with certain benefit losses left for further submissions.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area; K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the core doctrine, covering just cause, notice and dismissal damages. K002 (Civil litigation) captures O.W.L.'s civil claim advanced against Ms. Day. K022 (restitution) is the closest available match to the abandoned/alternative unjust enrichment claim over the rent, salary and vacation payments — a borderline pick as the vocabulary has no dedicated unjust enrichment term. K083 (harassment) is a weak/borderline pick tied to the workplace-conduct grounds asserted for cause (the Hope incident and the 'spread her legs' comment); it is flagged as marginal because those were largely characterizations of others' or isolated conduct rather than a harassment finding. The controlled vocabulary is heavily oriented to human-rights/antisemitism themes and is a poor fit for this employment case, so fewer than a full set of strongly applicable terms exists.
location_rationale: The header states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA', 'Registry: Vancouver', and the place of trial and judgment as 'Vancouver, B.C.'
registry_rationale: The decision expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver' and docket 'S150247'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Sara Trotta, Applicant AND Dustin Kyle Chung, Respondent

defining_issues: Should the court appoint the proposed s. 30 assessor over the father's objection that the assessor and mother are Jewish and only a Black assessor is acceptable?

Should the respondent's Answer on financial, property and damages claims be struck under Family Law Rule 1(8) for persistent non-compliance with court orders and disclosure obligations, while allowing him to continue participating on parenting issues?
Should the court order therapy for the child over the father's race-based objection to the therapist?
Should full-recovery costs be awarded against the respondent for bad-faith conduct?

firac.issue: Should the court appoint the proposed s. 30 assessor over the father's race-based objection?
firac.facts: Justice Akazaki had appointed Howard Hurwitz as the s. 30 assessor without objection, but Hurwitz resigned after the father engaged in threatening behaviour toward his staff. The mother proposed Susan Lieberman, a highly qualified, consenting assessor able to finish in three months, with the mother paying subject to reallocation. The father objected that Lieberman is Jewish (like the mother) and that only a Black, specifically 'Black Caribbean' or 'Black Chinese Caribbean' assessor like himself, would be appropriate; the child is Black.
firac.rule: Under s. 30 of the Children's Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12, the court may appoint an expert assessor to report on the needs of the child and the parties' ability and willingness to meet them. Parenting issues under the Divorce Act and the CLRA turn on the best interests of the child, which includes the child's cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual upbringing and heritage. Section 30(5) allows the court to require attendance for assessment, and s. 30(6) permits adverse inferences where a party refuses to participate.
firac.application: The court held it does not, and cannot, appoint or refuse to appoint professionals based solely on race; assessors are appointed for their technical and professional skills and routinely assess families of diverse heritage. There is no requirement that an assessor share the child's or parent's heritage, though sensitivity to that heritage informs recommendations. The father could raise his identity concerns through participation. He filed no materials and proposed no alternate assessor. Lieberman was qualified and available. The court appointed her, authorized psychological testing, and permitted the assessment to proceed without the father, warning that s. 30(6) allows adverse inferences from a refusal to participate.
firac.conclusion: Susan Lieberman was appointed as the s. 30 assessor, with authority to conduct testing and proceed without the father's participation.

firac.issue: Should the respondent's Answer on financial issues be struck for non-compliance, while preserving his participation on parenting issues?
firac.facts: The father breached four orders: the Form 8.0.1 Automatic Order (financial disclosure), two orders of Justice Kraft (attend mediation; pay $3,000 costs), and Justice Akazaki's order (answer a Request for Information within 30 days). Almost a year into an equalization case he never served a sworn Form 13.1 statement, produced no income tax returns for 2019–2022, and provided no corporate financials. He filed no responding materials on the motion to strike.
firac.rule: Family Law Rule 1(8) permits striking pleadings for non-compliance. The framework in Sheresht v. Abadi, 2021 ONSC 1665, para. 48 (citing Mullin v. Sherlock, 2018 ONCA 1065; Kovachis v. Kovachis, 2013 ONCA 644; Manchanda v. Thethi, 2016 ONCA 909) requires the court first to find non-compliance, then to fashion a proportionate remedy weighing the extent and persistence of non-compliance, wilfulness, reasonable efforts/explanations, ability to pay (for support), and proportionality. For parenting, Burke v. Poitras, 2018 ONCA 1025, para. 18, requires the utmost caution before striking pleadings, as a full evidentiary record including both parents is generally needed.
firac.application: The court found the non-compliance pervasive and wilful, with no explanation, no reasonable efforts, and no plan to comply despite repeated demands and unpaid costs — an abuse of process. Striking the Answer on financial, property and damages claims (equalization, damages, spousal and child support) was proportionate and necessary. However, applying Burke v. Poitras, the father's conduct did not yet warrant excluding him from parenting issues, which must be decided on the best interests of the child with both parents' participation, conditional on his compliance with orders, payment of costs, filing of briefs, and refraining from attacks on counsel.
firac.conclusion: The Answer was struck except for parenting paragraphs; the applicant may proceed to an uncontested trial on financial, property and damages claims under Rule 1(8.4), while the father may participate only on parenting issues once outstanding costs are paid.

firac.issue: Should the court order therapy for the child over the father's race-based objection?
firac.facts: The mother sought an order that the child attend closed play therapy, which the evidence showed to be in the child's best interests. The father refused consent, objecting that the therapist is not Black, and proposed no alternative therapist.
firac.rule: Decisions concerning the child are governed by the best interests of the child; as with assessors, the court does not appoint or refuse to appoint professionals based solely on race.
firac.application: The therapy was in the child's best interests on the evidence, and the father's race-based objection was rejected for the same reasons as his objection to the assessor. He supplied no evidence of a preferred alternative therapist.
firac.conclusion: The court ordered the child to attend closed play therapy with the designated therapist, records inadmissible, fees paid by the applicant.

firac.issue: Should full-recovery costs be awarded against the respondent?
firac.facts: The mother sought $18,186.22 in full-recovery costs. The father's persistent financial non-disclosure and non-compliance with orders forced multiple motions and mounting fees; he made overtly racist outbursts attacking applicant's counsel and objected to professionals solely on the basis of race, while filing no motion materials.
firac.rule: Costs are discretionary under s. 131(1) of the Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43. Mattina v. Mattina, 2018 ONCA 867, para. 10, identifies indemnification, encouraging settlement, sanctioning inappropriate behaviour, and dealing with cases justly (Rule 2(2)) as the purposes of family costs, with reasonableness and proportionality as touchstones. Trudel v. Trudel, 2010 ONSC 5177, paras. 17–18, holds that a 'catch-me-if-you-can' approach to disclosure amounts to bad faith warranting full-recovery costs.
firac.application: The father's continuing failure to make disclosure in the face of orders amounted to bad faith under Trudel, and his race-based objections and racist attacks, combined with filing no materials, constituted bad-faith conduct warranting sanction. The bill of costs, time and rates were reasonable and the motion necessary.
firac.conclusion: The respondent was ordered to pay $18,000 in costs (inclusive of HST) to the applicant by January 5, 2024, with participation in the case barred until outstanding costs are paid.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area — this is a matrimonial proceeding involving equalization, support and parenting. K047 (best interests of the child) is the operative test for appointing the s. 30 assessor and ordering therapy. K048 (custody/access) captures the parenting-time and decision-making dimension preserved for the father under Burke v. Poitras. K065 (racism) is squarely engaged: the father repeatedly objected to professionals solely on racial grounds and made overtly racist attacks on counsel, which the court condemned. K093 (Jewish) reflects the father's specific objection that the assessor and mother are Jewish — a genuine, though secondary, factual basis of the dispute. K117 (Divorce Act) is a supporting statutory framework the court cites for the best-interests analysis; it is the weakest pick, engaged as background law rather than a contested issue. There is no controlled-vocabulary keyword for striking pleadings/financial disclosure, which is otherwise a central procedural issue.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE' and states 'HEARD: At Toronto by videoconference September 21, 2023', establishing Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The matter was heard 'At Toronto' and bears court file no. FS-22-32470; Toronto is the applicable Superior Court of Justice registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: BROUILLETTE & ASSOCIÉS, S.E.N.C.R.L. v. IAN HALPERIN

defining_issues: Is the law firm entitled to the legal fees it claims for services rendered under the signed mandate?
Did an alleged verbal agreement or the lawyer's breaches of the Code of ethics of advocates preclude or reduce the fees claimed?
Did the firm commit a fault in the management of its trust account causing damages to Mr. Halperin, and what is the quantum?

firac.issue: Is the law firm entitled to the legal fees it claims for professional services rendered under the signed mandate?
firac.facts: Halperin signed a mandate dated June 10, 2009 with Brouillette & associés setting hourly rates and interest for files concerning Guy Laliberté, CJAD and Radio Canada. The firm claimed $26,470.82 for services rendered, which were completed and about which Halperin never complained as to quality.
firac.rule: A client who alleges a verbal agreement relieving him of the obligation to pay fees bears the burden of proving that agreement by preponderant evidence; the Code of ethics of advocates (art. 3.08.02) requires fees to be fair and reasonable.
firac.application: A signed mandate governed the relationship and legal services were provided and files resolved. Halperin, Me Frenière and Me Brouillette each described different, contradictory versions of the alleged verbal agreements, so Halperin failed to prove that Transit would pay his fees. However, the invoices showed excessive research and demand-letter time and were not fair and reasonable.
firac.conclusion: The firm rendered compensable services, but the fees required scrutiny; entitlement was established subject to reduction.

firac.issue: Did an alleged verbal agreement or the lawyer's breaches of the Code of ethics preclude or reduce the fees?
firac.facts: Me Brouillette was simultaneously the firm's senior partner, counsel to Halperin, and co-shareholder/director/signing officer of Transit, the publisher. He drafted the Halperin-Transit publishing contract, registered hypothecs against Transit's assets shortly after Halperin's notice to arbitrate, sold his shares days after the arbitral award, and transferred trust funds to pay Transit's accounts, all while Halperin was a client.
firac.rule: Where a lawyer breaches duties under the Code of ethics of advocates (arts. 3.03.04(e), 3.05.08, 3.06.05, 3.06.05.01, 3.06.06, 3.06.07, 3.08.02), the appropriate sanction in a fee claim is a discretionary reduction based on fairness (Mathieu c. Marchand; Jonathan J. Robinson et associés c. Goldberg).
firac.application: The verbal-agreement defence failed for lack of proof. But Me Brouillette failed to maintain professional independence, placing his personal interest above his client's and putting himself in a brazen conflict of interest; combined with fees that were not fair and reasonable, this justified a reduction.
firac.conclusion: The fees were reduced by $10,654.03 to $15,816.79; after compensation with the cross-demand award, no fees were payable by Halperin.

firac.issue: Did the firm commit a fault in managing its trust account causing damages to Halperin, and in what amount?
firac.facts: Brouillette & associés held $148,740 (US) from the Simon & Schuster advance for the Michael Jackson book in trust, to be split 50/50 between Transit and Halperin after expenses. The firm made deductions labelled 'Legal' and 'Other' totalling $41,369.52 that neither Turgeon, the Transit accountant, nor Me Brouillette could explain, and transferred trust funds to unrelated Transit obligations.
firac.rule: A law firm holding funds in trust for a beneficiary must account for the movements of those funds; it cannot transfer trust money without right to the detriment of a beneficiary, and cannot claim to act merely on a client's instructions where it is not at arm's length from that client.
firac.application: Me Brouillette was not at arm's length from Transit but an integral part of it, so he could not justify releasing funds solely on Transit's instructions. He failed to explain the 'Legal' and 'Other' deductions or transfers to unrelated files, and could account only for $3,500 and $592.60 in legitimate Michael Jackson expenses. From $144,647.40 (after those expenses) each party was owed $72,323.70; Halperin received only $57,632.27.
firac.conclusion: The firm committed a fault; it was ordered to pay Halperin the shortfall of US$14,691.43, converted to $15,816.79 Canadian at judgment date.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area: this is a civil action for fees with a cross-demand for damages. K013 (professional discipline) is the closest match for the central conflict-of-interest and Code of ethics of advocates breaches that drove the reduction of fees and the trust-account fault. K015 (defamation) is engaged because the underlying legal services were defamation matters (Laliberté, CJAD, Radio Canada). K093 (Jewish) and K058 (antisemitism) reflect the Radio Canada file, in which anti-Semitic remarks were made about Halperin, who is Jewish; these are genuine but contextual/tangential picks flagged as weaker, and are included partly because the controlled vocabulary offers no closer terms for trust-account or lawyer-fee disputes.

registry_rationale: The decision is filed in the District of Montreal, Civil Division, court file No. 500-22-184914-110, indicating the Montreal registry of the Court of Quebec.

case_name: Re Clark et al. and Attorney-General of Canada

name_verification.name_in_document: Re Clark et al. and Attorney-General of Canada

defining_issues: When should an intervention amicus curiae be permitted?
Does the Supreme Court of Ontario have jurisdiction, or does the Federal Court have exclusive jurisdiction under ss. 17 and 18 of the Federal Court Act?
Are the Uranium Information Security Regulations authorized by s. 9 of the Atomic Energy Control Act (intra vires)?
Is s. 2(a)(ii) of the Regulations, exempting persons acting with the Minister's consent, ultra vires as an unlawful subdelegation (delegatus non potest delegare)?
Do the Regulations abridge parliamentary privilege, and can a court adjudicate the scope of that privilege?
Do the Regulations override the solicitor-client privilege?
Do the Regulations violate s. 1(a) (due process) or s. 1(d) (freedom of speech) of the Canadian Bill of Rights?

firac.issue: When should an intervention amicus curiae be permitted?
firac.facts: The Canadian Civil Liberties Association moved for leave to intervene amicus curiae in the application challenging the Uranium Information Security Regulations. The parties were represented by experienced senior counsel who had fully covered the issues in their facta.
firac.rule: Subject to statutory or court-made rules, intervention amicus curiae is discretionary and should be restricted to cases where the court is clearly in need of assistance because the issues have not been fully presented (e.g., where one side of the argument is missing). It should not be allowed where it would merely widen the lis or introduce a new cause of action (discussing Re Drummond Wren, R. ex rel. Rose v. Marshall, Re Chateau-Gai Wines).
firac.application: Because both parties were ably represented and the issues were squarely and completely canvassed, the intervention would serve no useful purpose and would only widen the issues the parties chose to present. Counsel for the association conceded there was no right of intervention.
firac.conclusion: The application to intervene was denied as an exercise of the Court's discretion.

firac.issue: Does the Supreme Court of Ontario have jurisdiction, or is jurisdiction exclusively in the Federal Court under ss. 17 and 18 of the Federal Court Act?
firac.facts: Applicants, six federal Progressive Conservative MPs, sought declarations about regulations made by the Atomic Energy Control Board and approved by the Governor in Council. The Court raised whether ss. 17 (relief against the Crown) or 18 (relief against a federal board) of the Federal Court Act ousted its jurisdiction.
firac.rule: Section 17(1) gives the Federal Court Trial Division exclusive jurisdiction where relief is claimed against the Crown; s. 18 gives it exclusive jurisdiction over declaratory relief against a federal board (Denison Mines, Hamilton Harbour Com'rs). However, a statute should not be construed to oust the jurisdiction of a superior court absent clear and unambiguous language (Maxwell; Gibson's critique of Denison Mines).
firac.application: The application did not attack the validity of a statute (distinguishing Denison Mines) but reviewed both the Board's power under s. 9 and the Governor in Council's approval; the complementary decision-making of the Board and the Governor in Council took the matter outside s. 18. It was unclear that s. 17 was designed for this situation. In the absence of the clearest words to the contrary, the Court's jurisdiction must be assumed to continue.
firac.conclusion: The Supreme Court of Ontario retained jurisdiction to hear the application.

firac.issue: Are the Uranium Information Security Regulations authorized by s. 9 of the Atomic Energy Control Act?
firac.facts: SOR/76-644 imposed secrecy on information relating to uranium transactions between 1972 and 1975, in response to sweeping U.S. subpoenas. The applicants argued s. 9(d) and (e) were too narrow and s. 9(g) was merely procedural.
firac.rule: Section 9(g) empowers the Board, with the Governor in Council's approval, to make regulations it 'may deem necessary for carrying out any of the provisions or purposes of this Act'; the necessity is a subjective determination for the Board, not reviewable absent bad faith (following Robins J. in Re Westinghouse/Duquesne; Pronto Uranium Mines; Re Chemicals Reference). The intent of the statute governs the reach of the regulation-making power (Driedger).
firac.application: The Act's preamble declares atomic-energy control to be in the national interest, and s. 9(g) confers substantive, not merely procedural, power. Adopting Robins J.'s reasoning, the secrecy regulations fell within the Act's purposes; no bad faith was shown and the necessity or expediency was for the Board to judge.
firac.conclusion: The Regulations, apart from s. 2(a)(ii), are intra vires the Board and the Governor in Council.

firac.issue: Is s. 2(a)(ii) of the Regulations an unlawful subdelegation offending delegatus non potest delegare?
firac.facts: Section 2(a)(ii) allowed release of uranium information where a person 'does so with the consent of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources', with no guidelines and no supervisory control by the Board.
firac.rule: Delegatus non potest delegare bars a body vested with discretionary powers from vesting them in another authority it cannot control, unless expressly empowered (de Smith; A.-G. Can. v. Brent). The war-time Chemicals Reference, permitting subdelegation, is distinguishable as arising from wartime exigencies of an over-burdened Executive.
firac.application: The exemption effectively vested the Board's regulation-making power in the Minister, who could grant exemptions to everyone and nullify the Regulations. Nothing in the Act authorizes the Board to delegate to a Cabinet Minister, and no principal-agency arrangement or guidelines existed. This was not a wartime situation, and the Board of experts was best suited to exercise its own powers.
firac.conclusion: Section 2(a)(ii) is ultra vires and struck out; the balance of the Regulations remains valid.

firac.issue: Do the Regulations abridge parliamentary privilege, and can the Court adjudicate its scope?
firac.facts: MPs sought a declaration that they could use the proscribed uranium information in Parliament and release it to the media and constituents. The respondent argued Parliament alone judges the extent of its privileges.
firac.rule: Courts have jurisdiction to determine the existence and extent of parliamentary privilege as part of the law of the land (Erskine May; Re Parliamentary Privilege Act 1770; Roman Corp. v. Hudson's Bay Oil & Gas). Privilege attaches to 'proceedings in Parliament' — the 'real' or 'essential' functions of a Member (Bill of Rights 1689 art. 9; Ex parte Wason; R. v. Bunting; A.-G. Ceylon v. de Livera; Roman Corp.), extending to matters ancillary to parliamentary business such as press releases echoing statements in the House, but not the general informing of constituents (Official Secrets Act Select Committee report).
firac.application: Interpreting SOR/76-644 required deciding whether it overrode privilege, which the Court could do without infringing Parliament's role. A Member may use the information in Parliament and release it to the media, but privilege is finite: it stops at the press and does not cover release to constituents, which is not an essential parliamentary function.
firac.conclusion: MPs are privileged to use the information in Parliament and release it to the media, but not to their constituents.

firac.issue: Do the Regulations override the solicitor-client privilege?
firac.facts: Applicants sought declarations that they could disclose the information to their solicitors for legal advice and to initiate legal proceedings.
firac.rule: Solicitor-client privilege reflects a fundamental principle of the judicial system and is prima facie paramount; clear and unequivocal statutory language is required to abridge it (Re Director of Investigation & Research and Shell Canada; Re Presswood). The privilege does not protect communications made to further a crime, but bona fides cannot be assessed in advance.
firac.application: SOR/76-644 contained no precise language abridging the privilege and referred to 'any person, government, crown corporation, agency or other organization', which does not encompass the administration of justice. Clients could therefore disclose to their solicitors for bona fide advice and could institute court proceedings, provided confidentiality was maintained (e.g., by sealing pleadings or in camera proceedings). The privilege does not allow release of the information to the public or to the Director under the Combines Investigation Act, though an investigation may still be triggered under ss. 7-8 using public information.
firac.conclusion: The Regulations do not override solicitor-client privilege; disclosure for legal advice and confidential court proceedings is permitted.

firac.issue: Do the Regulations violate s. 1(a) or s. 1(d) of the Canadian Bill of Rights?
firac.facts: Applicants argued SOR/76-644 deprived citizens of security of the person and enjoyment of property without due process and infringed freedom of speech.
firac.rule: Under Curr v. The Queen, courts must exercise extreme caution before using the statutory 'due process' standard in s. 1(a) to negate validly enacted substantive federal legislation, and must not substitute their judgment for Parliament's absent objective, manageable standards. Freedom of speech under s. 1(d) is not absolute but governed by law.
firac.application: The Act was enacted in the national interest (Pronto), and the necessity of the Regulations was a subjective matter for the Board not to be second-guessed (Duquesne). No standards or evidence were offered to justify striking the legislation. The Regulations were properly promulgated by due process; abridging freedom of speech in the national interest, with the Governor in Council's approval, did not offend the Bill of Rights.
firac.conclusion: Neither the Act nor SOR/76-644 is invalidated by the Canadian Bill of Rights.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the primary practice area: the case is a judicial review of subordinate legislation turning on the vires of regulations and the maxim delegatus non potest delegare. K011 (judicial review) captures the procedural vehicle (application under the Judicial Review Procedure Act to review the Regulations). K003 (Constitutional law) is engaged by the parliamentary-privilege analysis and the Canadian Bill of Rights challenge. K024 (freedom of expression) applies to the s. 1(d) Bill of Rights freedom-of-speech argument, though it is secondary. K002 (Civil litigation) is a borderline pick reflecting the declaratory-relief/jurisdiction dispute; it is the weakest of the five. The controlled vocabulary is heavily oriented to Charter/hate-speech matters and offers no specific term for ultra vires regulations, subdelegation, solicitor-client privilege, parliamentary privilege, or the Canadian Bill of Rights, so the closest available terms were selected and the weaker ones flagged.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'ONTARIO / HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE' and decided by Evans, C.J.H.C., establishing the province as Ontario. No city is named in the text, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision names only the court ('Ontario High Court of Justice') and gives no registry or court office, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: City of Westmount v. Sam (Salim) Fattal

defining_issues: Should a permanent injunction issue restraining Fattal from communicating with the City, its employees, elected officials and lawyers, and requiring him to remove his website and posters?
Should Fattal be declared a vexatious (quarrelsome) litigant and subjected to a leave requirement before instituting proceedings against the City?

firac.issue: Should a permanent injunction issue restraining Fattal's communications with the City and requiring removal of his website and posters?
firac.facts: Over roughly 15 years Fattal, a Westmount property owner required to comply with municipal by-laws and building/fire codes, sent hundreds of derogatory faxes, letters and text messages to City employees, elected officials and the City's lawyer, mailed offensive materials to employees' homes, appeared at their residences, brandished a baseball bat while wearing a Saddam Hussein mask, appended Nazi/concentration-camp imagery, and posted derogatory statements and photos of officials on a website and on posters on his building. He falsely accused officials of anti-Semitism and harassment; multiple tribunals found no basis for the accusations.
firac.rule: Under article 751 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Court may issue a permanent injunction where the circumstances demonstrate the necessity of such a remedy. Freedom of expression does not extend to defamatory language, repeated false accusations, or repetitive communications intended to disrupt and annoy, which constitute harassment.
firac.application: The Court found Westmount merely required Fattal to comply with by-laws and codes and that officials acted properly; Fattal produced no evidence of unfair or malicious treatment or discrimination. His conduct was abusive and exceeded reasonable free speech, amounting to harassment, and he demonstrated he would not change unless restrained.
firac.conclusion: A permanent injunction was necessary; the Court prohibited direct contact and ordered removal of all references to Westmount officials from his website and property.

firac.issue: Should Fattal be declared a vexatious litigant and required to obtain leave before instituting proceedings?
firac.facts: Fattal brought eight Small Claims actions against City inspectors, security officers and contractors, artificially reducing claims to $7,000 to deny defendants counsel; served numerous subpoenas then abandoned suits; filed lengthy incoherent pleadings filled with insults; appealed and sought revocation of adverse rulings; accused a municipal judge of bias; and reported the City's lawyer to the Bar. Human Rights Commission (2002) and Justices Denis (2004), Brossard (2005) and Pinsonneault (2009) had all rejected his abuse and discrimination claims.
firac.rule: Articles 84 to 90 of the Rules of Practice of the Superior Court permit the Court, where a person exercises litigious rights in an excessive or unreasonable manner, to prohibit instituting proceedings without prior authorization. The characteristics of a quarrelsome litigant are those described by Yves-Marie Morissette and applied in Barreau du Québec c. Srougli, 2007 QCCS 685 (narcissism/stubbornness, multiplication of vexatious recourses against justice participants, reiteration of the same claims despite failures, inventive but irrational arguments, self-representation, insults in pleadings).
firac.application: Fattal displayed narcissism and stubbornness, abused the legal system through repeated and abandoned suits and complaints against judges and lawyers, persisted despite repeated adverse rulings, and represented himself while filing insulting pleadings — matching multiple hallmarks of a quarrelsome litigant.
firac.conclusion: Fattal was declared a vexatious litigant and prohibited from instituting any proceeding against the City, its employees or officials without prior written approval.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, this being a civil action for injunction and a vexatious-litigant declaration. K021 (injunction) is the closest controlled term for the permanent injunction granted under art. 751 C.p.c. K024 (freedom of expression) reflects the Court's holding that Fattal's expressive rights did not cover defamatory and harassing communications. K015 (defamation) captures the false, derogatory accusations. K083 (harassment) reflects the finding that his repetitive communications constituted harassment. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) apply because Fattal alleged the City acted out of anti-Semitism against him as a Jewish resident, though these were rejected. K088 (Holocaust) reflects his repeated use of Nazi and concentration-camp imagery. There is no controlled keyword for 'vexatious/quarrelsome litigant', the core doctrine, so it is captured only through the tier-1 civil litigation term; K058/K093/K088 are thematic rather than doctrinal picks.
location_rationale: The header states 'SUPERIOR COURT ... PROVINCE OF QUEBEC, DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and the court sits in Montreal.
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and file numbers in the Montreal registry (500-17-...).

name_verification.name_in_document: CAS of S.D.G. v. A.R., S.C., and D.A.
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied short form 'CAS of S.D.G. v. A.R.' is an abbreviated version of the full style of cause 'CAS of S.D.G. v. A.R., S.C., and D.A.' printed in the decision; the citation 2021 ONSC 712 matches exactly.

defining_issues: Are the children in need of protection under s. 74(2) of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017?
What findings and procedural steps were required in respect of J's First Nations (Cree) heritage before a protection finding could be made?
What disposition is in the children's best interests — return to the mother (with or without supervision) or Extended Society Care?
What access order, if any, is in the best interests of children placed in Extended Society Care?

firac.issue: Are the children in need of protection under s. 74(2) CYFSA on the basis of risk of physical or emotional harm?
firac.facts: Eight-year-old G and nearly three-year-old J had a long history of Society involvement. The Society alleged domestic conflict/violence between the mother and D.A., suspected drug use, G's poor school attendance, and the parents' lack of engagement. G disclosed to workers in October 2019 that he had overheard D.A. verbally abusing and threatening his mother, that he was scared and worried, and that he feared being taken away. The mother repeatedly partnered with abusive or toxic men, disappeared from the children's lives from late July to November 2020, and D.A. never attended a single access visit.
firac.rule: Under s. 74(2)(b) and (h) CYFSA a child is in need of protection where there is a risk of physical harm from a caregiver's failure to care/pattern of neglect, or a risk of serious emotional harm (anxiety, depression, withdrawal, self-destructive/aggressive behaviour, delayed development) resulting from the parent's actions, failure to act or pattern of neglect. The Society bears the burden on a balance of probabilities; the risk must be real, not speculative (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. R.M., 2019 ONSC 2251; Children's Aid Society of Algoma v. J.B., 2019 ONCJ 6). Exposure to domestic violence and a year-long absence from a child can ground a finding of risk of emotional harm.
firac.application: The court found the drug-use and school-attendance allegations not proven on the current evidence and declined to find a risk of physical harm. However, it accepted contemporaneous evidence that G was repeatedly exposed to D.A.'s verbal and emotional abuse of the mother, that G expressed serious fear and worry, and that both children exhibited behavioural difficulties. The three-part emotional-harm test was met: risk of a listed harm, seriousness of the harm, and a causal connection to the parents' conduct and failure to protect, compounded by the mother's roughly twelve-month absence and D.A.'s failure to see J for over twelve months.
firac.conclusion: The children continue to be in need of protection under s. 74(2)(h); the finding of risk of physical harm under s. 74(2)(b) was not established. Both fathers consented to the protection finding.

firac.issue: What First Nations findings and procedural steps were required given J's Cree heritage?
firac.facts: J is of Cree, First Nations heritage through his father D.A. The prior January 30, 2019 consent finding had not properly confirmed J's particulars or First Nations status.
firac.rule: Kawartha-Haliburton Children's Aid Society v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316 requires a finding as to a child's First Nations status before a protection finding; failure to do so is an appealable error. However, under s. 79(1)4 CYFSA only communities identified by regulation (O. Reg. 159/18) are necessary parties entitled to service, and no First Nations community (only Inuit Tapariit Kanatami) is identified, so no First Nations community can be served (Simcoe Muskoka Child, Youth and Family Services v. A.M.B. and N.M., 2020 ONSC 7953; Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S.T., 2019 ONCJ 207).
firac.application: The court corrected the defective 2019 finding by making a new statutory finding that J is First Nations under s. 90(2)(b) CYFSA. It concluded that because no First Nations community is identified under the CYFSA regulations, no service or notice on a band was required, though J's Cree heritage remained a relevant best-interests consideration.
firac.conclusion: J was found to be First Nations under s. 90(2)(b) CYFSA; no service on a band or First Nations community was necessary.

firac.issue: Is Extended Society Care, rather than return to the mother with or without supervision, in the children's best interests?
firac.facts: G had been outside his mother's care about 1059 days; J had been in care about 578 days and with kin S.R. for fourteen months. The mother had strong parenting abilities and a genuine bond with the children, but had moved roughly twelve times in eleven months, disappeared for months, missed access visits (including two during the ten-day trial despite a simple check-in condition), lacked insight, and proposed an untested plan to live with her father J.R. (on the road 5–6 days a week) and step-mother T.C., neither of whom had seen G since 2017 or met J.
firac.rule: Section 101 CYFSA requires, where a child is in need of protection and court intervention is necessary, an order in the child's best interests per s. 74(3); the court must inquire into Society efforts, be satisfied less restrictive alternatives failed, and consider extended family/community placement. Extended Society Care is the most profound order and requires compelling evidence and caution (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto v. M.(C.), 1994 CanLII 83; Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. Y.M., 2019 ONCJ 489). A supervision order requires confidence the parent will comply (CAS v. J.D., 2018 ONSC 3298).
firac.application: The court found the Society had made more than reasonable efforts to support the mother. A supervision order was rejected because the mother could not demonstrate consistency or engagement, continued to associate with abusive/toxic men, disappeared from the children's lives, and presented an untested last-minute plan; the court had no confidence she would comply. An extension under s. 122(5) was refused as more time would not remedy the mother's lack of engagement. G wished to remain with S.R. and not be separated from J, and both children were stable and thriving in kin care.
firac.conclusion: The least intrusive option consistent with the children's best interests was Extended Society Care for both G and J.

firac.issue: What access is in the best interests of the children placed in Extended Society Care?
firac.facts: The mother enjoyed inconsistent supervised virtual access; her inconsistency emotionally affected G. Both fathers consented to access at the Society's discretion and wished to be access holders. G wished to continue seeing his mother and father and not to be separated from J.
firac.rule: Sections 104–105 CYFSA govern access; for a child in extended society care access is terminated unless the court is satisfied it is in the child's best interests (s. 74(3), s. 105(5)–(6)). The test is now a holistic best-interests analysis, not the former presumption against access (Kawartha-Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316; Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. J.G., 2020 ONCA 415). The court must specify access holders and recipients (s. 105(7)).
firac.application: Balancing G's wishes, the children's bonds, and the need not to destabilize the placement, the court crafted graduated supervised virtual access for the mother with escalation to in-person visits contingent on consistency and COVID-19 protocols, with suspension provisions for missed visits. Access for each father was ordered at the Society's discretion, and monthly sibling access was ordered should the children ever be separated.
firac.conclusion: Specified graduated access to the mother (mother, G and J as access holders); access to D.A. and to S.C. at the Society's discretion; and sibling access at least monthly if the children cease living together.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area — this is a child protection proceeding under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is the central legal test governing both the disposition and access analyses under s. 74(3). K048 (custody/access) captures the extensive access determinations and placement/care disposition. K002 (Civil litigation) is included as a borderline procedural/parent classification for a contested civil trial with credibility and hearsay rulings, but is weak. K052 (religious upbringing) is a weak/borderline pick used only as the closest available proxy for the case's treatment of J's cultural background — in truth the case turns on J's Cree/First Nations heritage under the CYFSA, for which the controlled vocabulary has no dedicated keyword; there is likewise no keyword for domestic violence exposure or child protection specifically, so the vocabulary fits this case poorly and the last two picks are flagged as weak.
location_rationale: The decision is styled 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' and applies Ontario legislation (the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017), so the province is Ontario. The applicant is the Children's Aid Society of the United Counties of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry and the text references Cornwall Police Services and the SD&G jurisdiction, but the decision never expressly states the city where the court sits, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision shows only 'COURT FILE NO.: 18-103' and does not name a specific court registry or office, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: B.T. v. N.T.

defining_issues: Is it in the child's best interests to continue the status quo shared/joint custody, or should one parent be granted sole custody, and if so which parent?
What weight, if any, should be given to the court-appointed assessor's custody and access report, given challenges to its neutrality and the delay in its completion?

firac.issue: Should the alternating-week joint custody arrangement continue, or should one parent be awarded sole custody in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: A.T. (born 1996) lived on an alternating weekly shared-parenting schedule with both parents since their February 2000 separation, an arrangement confirmed in a December 2000 separation agreement pending court order. The mother applied for sole custody; the father sought continuation of the status quo or, alternatively, sole custody to himself. A.T. was outwardly happy and doing well at school, but repeatedly voiced confusion and distress about the weekly transitions to her aunt/caregiver, daycare staff, a CAS worker and the assessor, and the father had communicated strongly negative views of the mother to the child.
firac.rule: Custody is determined by the best interests of the child. On court-ordered joint custody, Kruger v. Kruger (1979), 25 O.R. (2d) 673 (Ont. C.A.) requires that each parent accept the other as fit and that they can genuinely cooperate; such willingness cannot be imposed by a court. The law has since developed (Kappler v. Beaudoin, 2000 CanLII 22579 (ON SC); Orth-Lashley v. Lashley) so that joint custody may be ordered without both parents' consent only where the evidence shows they can and will make it work, with past experience a cogent factor. Ongoing and worsening conflict and lack of cooperation may warrant departing from an existing arrangement (Wreggit v. Belanger, [2001] O.J. No. 477 (C.A.)). The status quo is important but not determinative.
firac.application: The court found both parents adequate, but that the mother provided more effective structure and routine, dealt better with third parties (school, daycare), and was far more respectful of the other parent, whereas the father, whether intentionally or not, communicated his strongly held negative views of the mother to A.T. The parents' communication was frequently acrimonious and they were unable to agree on numerous important parenting decisions (school, daycare, busing, flu shot, field trips), demonstrating an absence of the cooperation required for viable joint custody. The child's expressed distress at the transitions and her being drawn into an alliance with her father against her mother could not be allowed to continue. Sole custody to the father risked entrenching that alliance and marginalizing the mother.
firac.conclusion: The status quo was altered; sole custody was awarded to the mother, with defined alternate-weekend and midweek access to the father and a detailed holiday schedule, and the father was ordered to pay Table child support of $621 per month based on income of $77,400.

firac.issue: How much weight should be given to Dr. Munt's court-ordered assessment given challenges to its neutrality and completion delay?
firac.facts: Dr. Munt, an experienced clinical psychologist, was appointed to conduct a custody and access assessment. His report was excessively delayed (dated January 2003, begun July 2001), the meetings appeared skewed toward the mother's side (22 interviews to 14), he conducted workplace interviews of both parents, and he issued an addendum changing his access recommendation on input from the mother alone. The father called Dr. Leonoff, who testified to best practices without critiquing Dr. Munt's actual conclusions.
firac.rule: An assessor's report must both preserve the appearance of neutrality (its 'moral authority' to the parties) and produce valid, balanced conclusions; procedural deficiencies may undermine the former without necessarily impairing the latter (per Dr. Leonoff's uncontradicted evidence on assessment methodology). The court, not the assessor, is the fact-finder.
firac.application: The court found the length of the assessment excessive, the meetings insufficiently symmetrical in appearance, the workplace interviews unjustified, and the addendum a breach of neutrality — departures from best practices that negated the perception of neutrality. However, on careful review the court concluded Dr. Munt's observations of A.T. and of each parent were accurate, balanced (noting strengths and weaknesses of both) and corroborated by other trial evidence; he had not actually lost his neutrality nor had the delay rendered the report unhelpful. Minor factual inaccuracies did not undermine its weight, and the alleged pressure from the mother's side was not made out.
firac.conclusion: Despite procedural shortcomings undermining the report's persuasive/moral authority, its substantive observations and conclusions were accepted as helpful and reliable and were given weight, though the court ultimately rejected both of Dr. Munt's specific access recommendations as impractical.

name_verification.name_in_document: Konstan v Berkovits, 1539058 Ontario Inc. v. 212503 Ontario Inc., Berkovits v. Gerstel, Gerstel v. Toronto Sun Newspaper, Gerstel v. 1539058 Ontario Inc.

defining_issues: Did Maria establish the tort of malicious prosecution against Jack Berkovits and Saeed Hosseini for the criminal charges laid against her?
Did Maria establish conspiracy to injure, abuse of process and intentional infliction of mental distress against Jack and Hosseini?
Should Jack's 'murder for hire' counterclaim against Harold and Maria succeed?
Did the Omni corporations establish nuisance and intentional interference with economic relations (but not conspiracy) against Harold and HJB, and what damages flow?
Were the statements in the Town Crier, CFRB and Toronto Sun publications defamatory of the parties, and were any defences made out?
Did Harold personally have a viable claim for misappropriation of personality?

firac.issue: Did Maria establish malicious prosecution against Jack Berkovits and Saeed Hosseini?
firac.facts: Following a street altercation, Hosseini told Jack of an alleged plot by Maria to have him harmed or killed. Jack and Hosseini gave sworn statements and Maria was charged with uttering threats and counselling offences; charges were withdrawn, then she was charged again for a technical breach of recognizance, also later withdrawn. The court found no murder-for-hire plot actually occurred and that Jack was motivated by a desire to implicate his business rival Harold.
firac.rule: The four elements of malicious prosecution from Miazga v. Kvello Estate, 2009 SCC 51: (i) proceedings initiated by the defendant; (ii) terminated in the plaintiff's favour; (iii) initiated without reasonable and probable cause; and (iv) malice or a primary purpose other than carrying the law into effect.
firac.application: Both defendants initiated the proceedings and the charges terminated in Maria's favour. Jack was found to have acted with malice, using the criminal process to try to rope in Harold. However, as of the date Jack swore his statement there was objective reasonable and probable cause because Hosseini had in fact reported a plot and Jack subjectively believed his life was at risk; Jack had no independent duty to investigate. Against Hosseini, since the plot never happened, there could be no reasonable and probable cause and his malice/improper purpose (self-enrichment) was made out.
firac.conclusion: Maria's malicious prosecution claim against Jack was dismissed (reasonable and probable cause existed); her claim against Hosseini was granted.

firac.issue: Did Maria establish conspiracy to injure, abuse of process and intentional infliction of mental distress?
firac.facts: Maria advanced these torts against Jack and Hosseini arising from the criminal charges, media coverage, her humiliation, diagnosed PTSD, anxiety, depression and a suicide attempt after the second set of charges.
firac.rule: Conspiracy to injure (Agribrands Purina Canada Inc. v. Kasamekas, 2011 ONCA 460) requires combination/common design and unlawful conduct causing injury; abuse of process (Harris v. GlaxoSmithKline, 2010 ONCA 872) requires a legal process used predominantly for an improper collateral objective with a definite act and special damage; intentional infliction of mental distress (Merrifield v. Canada (A.G.), 2019 ONCA 205) requires flagrant/outrageous conduct calculated to produce harm resulting in a visible and provable illness.
firac.application: Conspiracy failed for lack of common design—Jack sought to ruin Harold while Hosseini sought only personal payment, 'two ships passing in the night.' Abuse of process was made out against both: Jack used the criminal process for the collateral purpose of harming Harold's reputation and pursuing settlement leverage, and had Maria charged a second time on moot recognizance terms; Hosseini's collateral purpose was to extract payment. IIMD failed against Jack (his conduct did not reach flagrant/outrageous given reasonable and probable cause) but succeeded against Hosseini, whose knowingly false statements were calculated to cause harm and produced provable illness.
firac.conclusion: Conspiracy dismissed against both. Abuse of process granted against Jack and Hosseini. IIMD dismissed against Jack, granted against Hosseini. Damages of $75,000 general, $46,775 legal fees, $50,000 aggravated and $50,000 punitive awarded jointly and severally against Jack and Hosseini.

firac.issue: Should Jack's 'murder for hire' counterclaim against Harold and Maria succeed?
firac.facts: Jack counterclaimed against Harold and Maria for conspiracy, assault and intentional infliction of mental suffering, alleging they hired Hosseini to harm him for money.
firac.rule: The counterclaim depended on proof, on a balance of probabilities, that Harold and Maria met with Hosseini and agreed to inflict harm on Jack for payment.
firac.application: The court found no such request or agreement occurred. At most Maria uttered angry words that Jack deserved to have his legs broken; Hosseini acted alone, seizing the opportunity to enrich himself by fabricating a plot.
firac.conclusion: Jack's counterclaim was dismissed.

firac.issue: Did the Omni corporations establish nuisance and intentional interference with economic relations against Harold and HJB, and what damages flow?
firac.facts: In response to Omni entering the cash-for-gold business, Harold hired 'sandwichboarders' to patrol and divert customers, blocked parking and access, conducted surveillance and had an employee cycle around Omni's premises, harassing staff and customers over several years.
firac.rule: Nuisance requires substantial and unreasonable interference with use and enjoyment of property (Antrim Truck Centre Ltd. v. Ontario, 2013 SCC 13; 1317424 Ontario Inc. v. Chrysler Canada, 2015 ONCA 104). Intentional interference with economic relations requires intention to injure, interference by unlawful means, and economic loss (Pro-Sys Consultants Ltd. v. Microsoft Corp., 2013 SCC 57). Conspiracy per Agribrands.
firac.application: The obstruction, harassment, surveillance and diversion tactics amounted to substantial and unreasonable interference with Omni's commercial property, satisfying nuisance; Harold was vicariously liable for the sandwichboarders acting within his instructions. The same unlawful conduct, coupled with intent to injure and economic loss, established intentional interference. Conspiracy failed—the sandwichboarders merely followed instructions with no common design. On damages, Omni's expert relied on unreliable assumptions and incomplete, unsegregated financial records; adverse inferences were drawn and damages assessed at no more than a 10% revenue loss.
firac.conclusion: Nuisance and intentional interference granted; conspiracy dismissed. Damages of $200,000 awarded jointly and severally against Harold and 210.

firac.issue: Were the impugned media statements defamatory, and were defences established?
firac.facts: Three defamation actions were pursued: Jack's Town Crier action (Harold showed reporters fabricated text messages suggesting Jack bribed witnesses, and alleged a threatening gesture at Maria); Harold's CFRB action (Jack said Harold 'chose not to show up' at a discovery hearing); and Harold's Toronto Sun action ('avoid the bullets that keep coming my way').
firac.rule: Defamation requires words that lower the plaintiff's reputation, referring to the plaintiff, and published to a third party (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). Truth/justification requires the defamatory statement be entirely true; damages in defamation are at large and presumed (Rutman v. Rabinowitz, 2016 ONSC 5864).
firac.application: Town Crier: the first excerpt (fabricated bribery texts) was defamatory and Harold's justification defence failed because the texts were fabricated; the second excerpt (threatening gesture) was justified. General damages of $50,000 awarded; aggravated/punitive refused as Harold did not know the texts were false. CFRB: Jack's statement was substantially true (Harold was ordered to pay costs for non-attendance; service on counsel is service on Harold), so not defamatory—claim dismissed. Toronto Sun: 'bullets coming my way' was a common figurative phrase not conveying that Harold was behind violence—not defamatory, claim dismissed.
firac.conclusion: Jack's Town Crier action succeeded in part ($50,000 general damages). Harold's CFRB and Toronto Sun actions dismissed.

firac.issue: Did Harold personally have a viable misappropriation of personality claim?
firac.facts: Jack erected signs and displays using Harold's name and image ('Compare Harold to Omni', 'Harold Jewellery Buyer') to divert customers. Justice Spence had earlier granted an interlocutory injunction. The 'Harold the Jewellery Buyer' business name is registered solely to 210 (Harold's corporation).
firac.rule: The tort of misappropriation of personality protects a proprietary right to commercially exploit one's personality by endorsement (Gould Estate v. Stoddart Publishing Co., 1996 CanLII 8209; Krouse v. Chrysler Canada; Athans v. Canadian Adventure Camps).
firac.application: Although Harold's name and image underlie the HJB brand, Harold admitted the business name and brand are assets owned by 210, and the pleaded proprietary interest was the goodwill of the HJB brand, not Harold's right to sell his own endorsement. The cause of action therefore vested in 210, which was not a plaintiff; Harold chose not to plead passing off.
firac.conclusion: Harold's personal misappropriation of personality claim was dismissed for want of standing in the proper party.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, this being a suite of tort actions. K015 (defamation) is central to the three media actions and the Grant v. Torstar framework applied. K021 (interlocutory injunction) reflects Justice Spence's injunction restraining misappropriation of Harold's name.
