defining_issues: Did the court exceed its jurisdiction or err in its discretion by adjourning the child protection trial for more than 30 days and by not scheduling the remaining trial days consecutively, having regard to s. 51(1) of the CFSA, Rule 33 and Rule 2 of the Family Law Rules?
Did the scheduling delay violate the father's rights under s. 7 of the Charter (security of the person and fundamental justice)?
Did the scheduling delay violate the father's equality rights under s. 15 of the Charter?
If a Charter breach were established, would any of the remedies sought by the father under s. 24(1) be appropriate and just?

firac.issue: Did the court exceed its jurisdiction or err in discretion by adjourning the trial more than 30 days and refusing to schedule the balance of trial on consecutive days?
firac.facts: A child protection application concerning two children (aged 10 and 8) sought a 12-month supervision order with the mother, with the father seeking dismissal. Trial time was allocated 'off the grid' by the case management judge and repeatedly expanded from 3 weeks to 5 weeks, then a further 43 days were set from April to December 2014 because counsel's estimates of required trial time kept growing. The father objected only near the end of the November 2013 sittings, though he had earlier himself sought an adjournment.
firac.rule: Section 51(1) CFSA bars adjournments of more than 30 days without consent or over an absent party's objection. Rule 33 of the Family Law Rules sets a 120-day timetable, extendable under subrules 33(3)/(5) where the best interests of the child require. Rule 2 makes the primary objective dealing with cases justly, including 'giving appropriate court resources to the case while taking account of the need to give resources to other cases.' Sections 72 and 75 CJA vest control of sittings and assignment of judicial duties in the judiciary. Authorities: Kenora-Patricia CFS v. M.(A.), 2005 ONCJ 39; CAS of Halton v. C.(S.), 2004 ONCJ 54; L.(R.) v. CAS Niagara, 2002 CanLII 41858 (ONCA); CAS Thunder Bay v. S.P.; L.H. v. CCAS Toronto, 2011 ONCA 385.
firac.application: No breach of s. 51(1) had actually occurred, as all parties had agreed to return dates in January and February 2014; the true question was a prospective breach. The court held that exceeding the Rule 33 timetable does not oust jurisdiction where the best interests of children are considered, distinguishing C.N. The scheduling reflected Rule 2 balancing: the North Toronto Family Court carries one of the highest family caseloads in Canada (each judge responsible for ~568 cases), this trial already consumed a disproportionate share of resources (25% of 2014 sitting days for 0.0018% of the caseload), and consecutive scheduling was impossible given four counsel's commitments, vacations and religious holidays. Under the CJA the judiciary, not the Attorney General, controls sittings.
firac.conclusion: Both the length of the adjournment and the non-consecutive scheduling were within the court's jurisdiction and discretion and were set in accordance with the primary objective under Rule 2.

firac.issue: Did the scheduling delay violate the father's s. 7 Charter rights?
firac.facts: The father claimed the delay in completing the trial impaired his security of the person. He filed three affidavits (283 paragraphs) largely focused on the children's alleged best interests and access, with only bare references to stress on himself.
firac.rule: Section 7 requires (1) that state action have a serious and profound effect on psychological integrity, objectively assessed, being more than ordinary stress, and state-imposed with a sufficient causal connection; and (2) that any deprivation not accord with the principles of fundamental justice, which require a fair hearing (reasonable notice, meaningful participation, neutral arbiter). Authorities: New Brunswick v. G.(J.), [1999] 3 SCR 46; Blencoe v. B.C., 2000 SCC 44; Charkaoui, 2007 SCC 9; Winnipeg CFS v. K.L.W., 2000 SCC 48.
firac.application: The delay was only partly state-caused, being also attributable to counsel's other commitments and to the father, who had himself earlier sought an adjournment and raised no objection to the scheduling until months later. The father failed to show his stress rose above ordinary stress to a serious and profound effect, or a sufficient causal connection to the delay. The hearing was fair: the father had experienced counsel, reasonable notice of the allegations, three prompt post-apprehension hearings, neutral arbiters, and unfettered cross-examination.
firac.conclusion: No breach of s. 7; that portion of the motion was dismissed.

firac.issue: Did the scheduling delay violate the father's s. 15 equality rights?
firac.facts: The father argued that as a respondent parent in a child protection proceeding he was discriminated against compared with parties governed by shorter timelines under the YCJA, other CFSA provisions and other statutes.
firac.rule: Section 15 requires (1) a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground, and (2) a disadvantage perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping. Analogous grounds concern immutable inherent attributes, not behaviour. Authorities: R. v. Kapp, 2008 SCC 41; Withler, 2011 SCC 12; Quebec v. A., 2013 SCC 5; Corbiere; Auton, 2004 SCC 78; Penner v. Danbrook; Sagkeeng CFS v. A.R.W.; Wareham.
firac.application: Being a respondent in a child protection proceeding is not an immutable characteristic but arises from alleged behaviour, so no enumerated or analogous ground was engaged. Comparisons between federal and provincial legislation, or between different provisions within the CFSA directed at different objectives, cannot ground a s. 15 claim. The father did not show he was denied a benefit or saddled with a burden not imposed on similarly situated parents.
firac.conclusion: The father failed both parts of the test; no breach of s. 15, and that portion of the motion was dismissed.

firac.issue: Would any of the s. 24(1) remedies sought by the father be appropriate and just if a Charter breach existed?
firac.facts: The father sought orders resuming the trial within 30 days on consecutive days, compelling the Attorney General to make arrangements, or alternatively dismissing/staying the application, placing the children in his care, or transferring access supervision to an outside agency.
firac.rule: Section 24(1) permits remedies a court considers 'appropriate and just in the circumstances.' In prospective child-protection breaches the only remedies are limited; a stay returning children is inappropriate where they may need protection. Authorities: New Brunswick v. G.(J.), [1999] 3 SCR 46 (para 101); R. v. Imona-Russell, 2011 ONCA 303; CAS Hamilton v. E.O.
firac.application: Resuming on consecutive dates was impossible without injustice to the other 567 cases; the court cannot order the Attorney General to assign another judge (no authority, and it would defeat single-judge case management and lacks physical infrastructure). A stay or dismissal would return the children before any merits determination, contrary to the paramount purpose of the CFSA. Removing the society's statutory access-supervision role in favour of a private agency, absent proof of society misconduct, was inappropriate, especially since access was itself a live trial issue already ruled on twice by Justice Sherr.
firac.conclusion: None of the sought-after remedies would be appropriate or just; the constitutional motion was dismissed in its entirety.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area — this is a child protection proceeding under the CFSA. K003 (Constitutional law) is the second tier-1 area, as the entire motion is a Notice of Constitutional Question. K047 (best interests of the child) is the paramount statutory purpose the court repeatedly invoked to justify extending timelines and refusing to return the children. K112 (Charter s. 7) and K109 (Charter s. 15) are the two specific Charter provisions litigated; K023 (equality rights) pairs with the s. 15 analysis. K012 (procedural fairness) captures the fundamental-justice / fair-hearing branch of the s. 7 analysis. K107 (Canadian Charter) is the governing instrument. K093 (Jewish) is a weak/borderline entity tag reflecting only that the applicant agency is the 'Jewish Family and Child Service'; the case has no substantive Jewish-law or antisemitism content, so it is included solely for entity indexing.
location_rationale: The decision header states "Ontario Court of Justice, North Toronto Family Court, 47 Sheppard Avenue East, Toronto, Ontario M2N 5N1", establishing Toronto, Ontario as the location.
registry_rationale: The heading identifies the court as the "North Toronto Family Court" of the Ontario Court of Justice; the body of the reasons repeatedly refers to the caseload and scheduling practices of the North Toronto Family Court.

case_name: Manitoba Human Rights Commission et al. v.JewishCommunity Campus of Winnipeg Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: Manitoba Human Rights Commission et al. v. Jewish Community Campus of Winnipeg Inc.

defining_issues: What is the applicable standard of review of an adjudicator's determination under s. 37.1 of The Human Rights Code that a settlement offer was reasonable?
Did the adjudicator in fact proceed on the basis of assuming the allegations in the complaint were proven, as he stated?
Was the adjudicator's finding that the offer reasonably addressed compensation for financial loss reasonable, despite an error in stating the law on measuring damages?
Was the adjudicator's finding that the $5,250 offer reasonably addressed damages for injury to dignity, feelings and self-respect reasonable?

firac.issue: What standard of review applies to an adjudicator's decision under s. 37.1 of The Human Rights Code that a settlement offer is reasonable?
firac.facts: An adjudicator appointed under The Human Rights Code found a rejected settlement offer reasonable under s. 37.1 and terminated the adjudication. The Commission argued for correctness on questions of law; the JCC argued reasonableness because the adjudicator was interpreting his home statute.
firac.rule: Per Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, and subsequent authorities (Alberta Teachers' Association, McLean, CNR, Smith v. Alliance Pipeline), reasonableness is presumed when a tribunal interprets or applies its home statute, including questions of law; correctness applies only to four categories (constitutional issues, questions of central importance outside expertise, jurisdictional lines between tribunals, true questions of vires). The Manitoba Court of Appeal in Korsch v. Human Rights Commission (Man.), 2012 MBCA 108, applied reasonableness to an analogous provision.
firac.application: The adjudicator was interpreting and applying s. 37.1, squarely within his specialized expertise and his home statute. The Commission's argument that the alleged error was so serious as to make the decision of central importance conflated the degree of error with the nature of the decision; the standard depends on the nature of the decision, not the outcome. Korsch was directly on point.
firac.conclusion: Reasonableness is the correct standard of review; the court must defer to the adjudicator's decision.

firac.issue: Did the adjudicator actually assess the offer on the basis of assuming the complaint's allegations to be proven, as he had stated?
firac.facts: The adjudicator's written reasons repeatedly stated he assumed the complaint's allegations to be proven (following Mancusi). The Commission argued that, based on the JCC's arguments and the adjudicator's questions at the hearing, he really assessed credibility and considered the reply.
firac.rule: Interlocutory remarks made by a decision-maker during a hearing are not part of the decision and cannot be relied upon to contradict the written reasons (Faryna v. Chorny, 1951 CanLII 252 (BC CA)). The parties agreed that assuming the complaint proven was a reasonable approach.
firac.application: The written decision consistently showed the adjudicator accepted the complaint as proven and rejected nothing in it. Nothing in the reasons indicated he considered the reply or assessed credibility, nor could that be inferred from submissions or comments at the hearing.
firac.conclusion: The adjudicator proceeded as stated, assuming the allegations proven; the Commission's first alleged error was not made out.

firac.issue: Was it reasonable for the adjudicator to find the offer reasonably addressed compensation for financial loss, despite misstating the law?
firac.facts: The offer allocated nothing to financial loss (with up to $2,000 for proven expenses). The complainant remained employed 16 months after filing, was later terminated for performance reasons and paid in lieu of notice. The complaint never alleged the termination was connected to the harassment or a reprisal. The adjudicator relied on employment-standards notice principles to reject financial loss.
firac.rule: Damages under s. 43(2)(b) of the Code aim to restore the complainant to the position she would have been in but for the discriminatory act, and are not limited to reasonable-notice/wrongful-dismissal measures (Piazza, 1989 CanLII 4071 (ON CA); Korsch v. Manitoba Human Rights Commission, 2011 MBQB 222). Under Dunsmuir, a decision is reasonable if the outcome falls within a range of acceptable outcomes defensible on the facts and law.
firac.application: The adjudicator incorrectly stated the law by applying employment-standards notice principles. However, the complaint contained no allegation, express or implied, of financial loss connected to the harassment. Assuming the complaint proven, it was open to the adjudicator to find the offer reasonably addressed financial loss without relying on the legal error. Unlike Mancusi, where lost wages were alleged, here there was no basis to speculate about evidence that might arise at a hearing on an allegation absent from the complaint.
firac.conclusion: Despite the misstatement of law, the outcome fell within a range of acceptable outcomes and was reasonable.

firac.issue: Was the adjudicator's finding that $5,250 reasonably addressed injury to dignity, feelings and self-respect reasonable?
firac.facts: The JCC allocated the entire $5,250 to injury to dignity under s. 43(2)(c). The adjudicator compared prior awards (Korsch noting a $1,000–$4,000 range; Budge, $4,000; Garland v. Tackaberry, $7,750) and found the offer at the higher end.
firac.rule: Section 37.1 requires adjudicators to assess the quantum likely to be awarded if the complaint were proven — a matter within their expertise. Prior awards have precedential value though the range is not a cap; awards turn on the facts of each case.
firac.application: The adjudicator assumed the allegations proven, reviewed comparable awards, and applied a sensible test, finding the offer approximated what would be ordered. This determination was within his expertise and open to him on the facts and law.
firac.conclusion: The finding that this part of the offer was reasonable was itself reasonable.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case is a judicial review of a tribunal decision. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) are central — the entire analysis turns on Dunsmuir reasonableness. K072 (human rights tribunal) fits the adjudicator/Commission under The Human Rights Code, and K119 (Human Rights Code) is the governing statute (Manitoba's Code is within this canonical entry). K083 (harassment) reflects the underlying sexual-harassment complaint. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is engaged because the financial-loss analysis turned on termination/pay in lieu of notice and the distinction between employment-law and human-rights damages measures; it is somewhat borderline since dismissal was not itself the complaint, but the legal reasoning squarely addressed notice/termination principles.
location_rationale: The docket header reads 'CI 13-01-86158 (Winnipeg Centre)' and identifies the Court of Queen's Bench of Manitoba; the citation 2015 MBQB 47 confirms Manitoba. Winnipeg is the centre named.
registry_rationale: The docket notation '(Winnipeg Centre)' indicates the registry/judicial centre of the Court of Queen's Bench.

name_verification.name_in_document: Droit de la famille — 21827

defining_issues: Did the Wife satisfy the requirements of s. 21.1(2) of the Divorce Act so as to trigger the Court's discretionary power under s. 21.1(3) to dismiss the Husband's proceedings for his failure to remove a barrier to religious remarriage?

Where a spouse claims 'genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature' under s. 21.1(4) for refusing to give a get, must the Court refuse to exercise its power to dismiss, or does it retain discretion to do so?
Can the Court's power under s. 21.1 of the Divorce Act extend to proceedings (the 04 file) that were not brought under the Divorce Act?

firac.issue: Did the Wife satisfy s. 21.1(2) so as to trigger the Court's power to dismiss the Husband's proceedings?
firac.facts: Both parties are observant Jews married in 2006 with four children. After separation the Wife sought a civil divorce but requires a get, which only the Husband can give. She served him with a s. 21.1(2) affidavit on September 14, 2020 requesting removal of the barrier; the Husband acknowledged he was unwilling to give the get.
firac.rule: Section 21.1(2) of the Divorce Act permits a spouse to serve and file an affidavit attesting to the marriage, the barrier to religious remarriage within the other spouse's control, and the written request to remove it. Under s. 21.1(3), if the other spouse fails within 15 days to remove the barrier, the court may dismiss any application and strike out pleadings filed by that spouse.
firac.application: The Court found it undisputed that the Husband alone controlled the barrier to the Wife's religious remarriage and had not agreed to give the get, and that the Wife's September 14, 2020 affidavit conformed to s. 21.1(2). The Husband's argument about lack of urgency (the Wife not yet being civilly divorced) was rejected, as the Act imposes no urgency requirement and the 15-day reply period signals an intention that the process move quickly.
firac.conclusion: The Wife met her burden; the Court was satisfied it could exercise its powers under s. 21.1(3).

firac.issue: Does an assertion of genuine religious grounds under s. 21.1(4) require the Court to decline to dismiss, or does discretion remain?
firac.facts: The Husband, an Orthodox Hassidic Jew, swore he could not validly give the get while litigation and conflict persisted because consent must be free and peaceful; he filed two rabbis' letters stating a get given under threat would be void. The Wife alleged the refusal was a pretext to extract concessions.
firac.rule: Section 21.1(4) provides the court 'may' refuse to exercise its s. 21.1(3) powers where a spouse establishes 'genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature'. The provision's purpose, per Bruker v. Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54 and Droit de la famille – 112747, 2011 QCCA 1589, is to prevent a spouse from using refusal of the get as leverage to extract concessions in a civil divorce. The rabbis' letters, not filed as expert reports and unsworn, were given no probative weight.
firac.application: The Court held that even assuming the Husband's refusal rested on a genuine religious ground, s. 21.1(4) is permissive, not binding. The Husband's position—that pending civil proceedings themselves prevented free consent—would apply to any Jewish spouse and would defeat the very purpose of s. 21.1 by turning the provision on its head. Endorsing it would render the section ineffective and would not be a judicious exercise of discretion.
firac.conclusion: The Court retained discretion and chose to exercise its s. 21.1(3) powers to dismiss the Husband's proceedings regardless of the claimed religious justification.

firac.issue: Can the s. 21.1 power extend to the 04 file not brought under the Divorce Act?
firac.facts: The Husband's 04 file sought interim access and child care benefits and was not taken under the Divorce Act. The Wife's Application, based solely on the Act, sought to dismiss proceedings in both files.
firac.rule: Section 21.1(3)(c) and (d) expressly limit the court's power to dismissing applications and striking pleadings filed 'under this Act'.
firac.application: Because the 04 file proceedings were not taken under the Divorce Act and the Application relied only on the Act (not the Code of Civil Procedure), the Court held it lacked power to extend its order to those proceedings.
firac.conclusion: The Application was granted only as to the Divorce file, not the 04 file.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K051 (religious divorce (get)) is the central subject—the Husband's refusal to give the get and s. 21.1 of the Divorce Act. K117 (Divorce Act) is the governing statute. K025 (freedom of religion) and K034 (sincerity of belief) are engaged by the Husband's asserted religious/conscientious grounds under s. 21.1(4), though the Court noted no Charter/Quebec Charter argument was actually raised, making these somewhat supporting rather than decisive. K026 (halacha/Jewish law) reflects the analysis of what Jewish law requires for a valid get. K093 (Jewish), K097 (Orthodox/Hasidic community) and K098 (rabbi) identify the parties as observant/Orthodox Hassidic Jews and the two rabbis whose letters were tendered. K034 is a slightly weaker pick since sincerity was assumed rather than adjudicated.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'SUPERIOR COURT ... PROVINCE OF QUEBEC ... DISTRICT OF TERREBONNE', and the file numbers (700-...) are Terrebonne district files. Province is Quebec; the judicial district/registry is Terrebonne.
registry_rationale: The heading expressly states 'DISTRICT OF TERREBONNE', identifying the judicial district/registry where the proceedings were filed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Kinnarath v. Choiselat et al.

defining_issues: Were Ms. Choiselat's social media and media statements defamatory, and can she rely on the defence of fair comment?
Was Mr. Henderson's comment ('both were extreme views') defamatory, whether directly or by innuendo?
Is the People's Party of Canada vicariously liable for Ms. Choiselat's defamatory publications?
Should the court recognize a new tort of 'doxxing' and does the tort of publication of private facts apply?
What quantum of general, aggravated and punitive damages is appropriate?

firac.issue: Were Ms. Choiselat's statements defamatory, and does the fair comment defence apply?
firac.facts: After the plaintiff caused the cancellation of a PPC candidate meet-and-greet, Ms. Choiselat posted on Facebook and Twitter calling the plaintiff a 'terrorist', a 'vile person', and implying he was responsible for arson, along with his photograph and personal contact details. She reposted after Facebook removed the material and later posted on the PPC Winnipeg Centre Twitter account.
firac.rule: Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61 sets the three-part defamation test: (1) words were defamatory (would lower reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person); (2) words referred to the plaintiff; (3) words were published. Falsity and damage are then presumed. The fair comment defence (Grant, para. 31; WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40) requires: (a) matter of public interest; (b) based on fact; (c) recognizable as comment; (d) could any person honestly express that opinion on the proved facts; (e) defeated by malice.
firac.application: The court found the words defamatory, referring directly to the plaintiff (with photo and contact details) and published on multiple occasions. Although the statements arose during a federal election (public interest), the accusations of terrorism and arson were unproven statements of fact, not honest comment, and could not satisfy the objective test. Ms. Choiselat was found to be actuated by malice: she reposted after Facebook removed the material, ignored a warning the post was defamatory, posted on the PPC Twitter account knowing she lacked authority under PPC policy, and refused to withdraw the comments through to trial.
firac.conclusion: The statements were defamatory and the fair comment defence was rejected; Ms. Choiselat was found liable.

firac.issue: Was Mr. Henderson's comment defamatory directly or by innuendo?
firac.facts: When asked by a journalist about Ms. Choiselat's posts, Mr. Henderson, the PPC candidate, commented that 'both were extreme views', referring to the plaintiff's and Ms. Choiselat's actions.
firac.rule: Grant v. Torstar Corp. defamation test and the fair comment defence (Grant; WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson).
firac.application: The court found the words merely expressed Mr. Henderson's opinion on how he viewed both parties' conduct during an election campaign and were not defamatory, whether by fact or innuendo. Even if defamatory, they were clearly his opinion based on the fact of the posts, attracting the protection of fair comment.
firac.conclusion: The comment was not defamatory; the claim against Mr. Henderson was dismissed.

firac.issue: Is the People's Party of Canada vicariously liable for Ms. Choiselat's publications?
firac.facts: Ms. Choiselat was the CEO of the PPC Winnipeg Centre EDA and had limited authority to post positive content on the EDA Twitter account. PPC policy in the Handbook restricted personal comments and attacks. She posted defamatory material on her personal Facebook and then on the PPC EDA Twitter account contrary to policy.
firac.rule: Brown on Defamation: a principal is not liable where the agent exceeds the scope of authority or departs from the principal's business for their own purpose; liability requires ratification, authorization, or acting within the scope/furtherance of the employer's business or apparent authority.
firac.application: The court accepted evidence that the PPC's policies expressly instructed candidates and EDAs to refrain from such posts, that Ms. Choiselat's authority was limited to positive posts, and that she exceeded and acted without apparent authority. The PPC did not ratify her acts—it removed the posts, no further posts were made, and she was removed from her position. Extending vicarious liability would improperly create strict liability for political parties for every member comment.
firac.conclusion: The PPC was not vicariously liable; the claim against it was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should a new tort of 'doxxing' be recognized and does the tort of publication of private facts apply?
firac.facts: Ms. Choiselat published the plaintiff's photograph, home address and contact details; however, the physical and email addresses were incorrect at the time. The photograph was taken from the plaintiff's publicly available social media page. No harassing calls or texts were shown to have been received.
firac.rule: The Privacy Act, C.C.S.M. c. P125, s. 2(1) creates a statutory tort for substantial, unreasonable violation of privacy without claim of right. Publication of private facts (ES v Shillington, 2021 ABQB 739) concerns publishing private/intimate material without consent.
firac.application: The court found no need to create a new tort of doxxing because the Privacy Act already provides a statutory privacy tort. On publication of private facts, the photograph was already publicly available on the plaintiff's own social media, distinguishing the case from Shillington (non-consensual intimate images).
firac.conclusion: The court declined to recognize a tort of doxxing and rejected the publication-of-private-facts claim.

firac.issue: What quantum of damages should be awarded?
firac.facts: The defamatory statements were widely published on social media and the internet during an election period, but there was no evidence of actual reputational harm; the plaintiff continued his activism, won an activist award, and the media focus was largely on his own prior anti-Semitic and misogynist posts. Ms. Choiselat never apologized and maintained her 'terrorist' characterization through trial.
firac.rule: Bibeau v. Chartier, 2022 MBCA 5 (leading Manitoba case on defamation damages); Hill v. Church of Scientology (aggravated and punitive damages principles): aggravated damages for high-handed/oppressive conduct increasing distress; punitive damages only where conduct is so malicious, oppressive and high-handed as to offend the court's sense of decency and where general/aggravated awards are insufficient.
firac.application: Given the absence of proven reputational harm and the plaintiff's continued unabated activism, the court found minimal damages appropriate and distinguished larger awards (Paramount, Supel). It awarded nominal general damages of $5,000. Because Ms. Choiselat never apologized and maintained her defamatory characterization five years later, aggravated damages of $5,000 were warranted. Her conduct was not so malicious or high-handed as to offend the court's sense of decency, so punitive damages were refused.
firac.conclusion: General damages of $5,000 and aggravated damages of $5,000 awarded against Ms. Choiselat; no punitive damages. Costs to the plaintiff against Ms. Choiselat, and to the PPC and Mr. Henderson against the plaintiff.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a civil defamation tort action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action and the subject of the Grant v. Torstar test. K016 (fair comment) is the central defence advanced by both Ms. Choiselat and Mr. Henderson and analyzed in detail. K024 (freedom of expression) is engaged because the court framed defamation as a limitation on Charter-protected free expression per Grant. The vicarious liability question does not map neatly to the vocabulary; there is no direct keyword for vicarious liability or privacy tort. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is not applicable and was not selected. Note that only four strongly on-point keywords exist in the vocabulary for this defamation/privacy case; I flag that the controlled vocabulary lacks specific entries for vicarious liability, privacy/doxxing tort, and damages assessment, so coverage is thin. To reach the minimum I include K085's parent-area concept only weakly—it does not fit—so I instead relied on the closest genuine matches; the selection is intentionally limited to genuinely engaged concepts.
location_rationale: The header identifies the 'COURT OF KING'S BENCH OF MANITOBA' and the docket notes '(Winnipeg Centre)', establishing Winnipeg, Manitoba as the location.
registry_rationale: The docket line reads 'Docket: CI 20-01-28613 (Winnipeg Centre)', indicating the Winnipeg Centre registry of the Manitoba Court of King's Bench.

case_name: Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd. c. Québec (Procureure générale)

name_verification.name_in_document: Imperial Tobacco Canada Limited v. Attorney General of Quebec

defining_issues: Did the trial judge err in concluding that the Tobacco-related Damages and Health Care Costs Recovery Act does not violate section 23 of the Quebec Charter, in particular the right to a fair hearing and the right to be heard?

Does the expression 'en pleine égalité' (full and equal) in section 23 of the Quebec Charter incorporate a broad 'equality of arms' principle that bars the legislature from altering rules of evidence, procedure and prescription in pending civil actions?

firac.issue: Does the Tobacco-related Damages and Health Care Costs Recovery Act infringe the right to a full and fair hearing guaranteed by section 23 of the Quebec Charter?
firac.facts: The Act, modelled on British Columbia legislation upheld in British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2005 SCC 49, alters civil-liability rules of evidence and prescription to facilitate recovery of tobacco-related health care costs. It creates rebuttable presumptions (ss. 16-19), permits proof of causation by statistical or epidemiological evidence (s. 15), exempts the government from identifying individual recipients (s. 13), and eliminates prescription (s. 27). The manufacturers argued the cumulative effect denies them a fair trial and full defence.
firac.rule: Section 23 of the Quebec Charter guarantees a full, equal, public and fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. Quebec Court of Appeal authority (Béliveau; Crane Canada; SCFP v. Jonquière) holds that s. 23 constitutionalizes natural justice — the right to an independent tribunal and the right to be heard — and confers only procedural, not substantive, guarantees. Per Wells v. Newfoundland and Imperial Tobacco (SCC), parliamentary sovereignty permits the legislature to amend substantive and procedural law, including retroactively, within constitutional limits; courts do not review the wisdom of legislative choices.
firac.application: The Court found the Quebec Act practically identical to the British Columbia statute, so the SCC's judicial-independence analysis applies fully. Section 23 protects only procedural fairness; concluding it guarantees only procedural rights simply means the Quebec Charter does not preclude amendment of substantive general-law rules. The Act does not compromise the tribunal's independence or impartiality, does not deny access to the evidence against the manufacturers, and preserves their right to respond. The presumptions are rebuttable and require the government first to prove failure and general causation; the privacy provisions are counterbalanced by s. 14 sampling; and prescription changes, expressly made retroactive by s. 31, are within legislative competence. Although the Act is strict and removes some defences, that does not render the trial unfair.
firac.conclusion: The Act does not violate section 23; the trial judge did not err in dismissing the motion for a declaration of invalidity.

firac.issue: Must 'en pleine égalité' in section 23 be read to incorporate an 'equality of arms' principle precluding legislative interference with pending civil actions?
firac.facts: The manufacturers relied on European Court of Human Rights jurisprudence and the singular Court of Quebec decision Restaurant Brossard to argue that 'full and equal' incorporates equality of arms, barring statutory changes that advantage the government or apply retroactively to their pending litigation.
firac.rule: The Quebec Charter is quasi-constitutional and commands a large and liberal interpretation (Bombardier), but international and foreign law inform interpretation only where consistent with the provision and domestic case law. ECHR jurisprudence recognizes that legislatures may enact retroactive civil provisions and set differing prescription rules, prohibiting only legislative 'judging' of the government's own case absent compelling public interest.
firac.application: Nothing in the Quebec Charter's legislative history supports importing equality of arms with the scope urged; neither the principle nor the words 'en pleine égalité' were debated at enactment. The appellants misread the ECHR case law, which does not prevent the legislature from amending general rules of evidence, procedure and prescription to craft a specific remedy. The Act does not definitively and retroactively settle the merits of the pending dispute, and Imperial Tobacco identifies a sufficiently compelling public interest justifying the measures.
firac.conclusion: Section 23 protects equal procedural treatment only; it does not embody the broad equality-of-arms bar the appellants asserted, and the ground fails.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns on the constitutional validity of a statute. K120 (Quebec Charter) is the central instrument, specifically s. 23. K012 (procedural fairness / natural justice) captures the s. 23 guarantee that the Court held to be purely procedural. K107 (Canadian Charter) is engaged as a pleaded and comparative instrument. K020 (class action) reflects the collective-action machinery the Act facilitates and to which the impugned rules apply. K002 (Civil litigation) is a secondary tier-1 area because the dispute concerns tobacco civil-liability/damages rules; it is a weaker, supporting pick given the constitutional focus.
location_rationale: The header states 'COURT OF APPEAL / CANADA / PROVINCE OF QUEBEC / REGISTRY OF MONTREAL' and the matter arose from the Superior Court, District of Montreal.
registry_rationale: The decision expressly bears 'REGISTRY OF MONTREAL' with file no. 500-09-024341-141.

case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. C.M.

name_verification.name_in_document: Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. C.M.

defining_issues: Is intervention through a court order still necessary to protect the child in the future on a status review under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017?
If intervention is necessary, what disposition (return to mother under supervision versus custody to the maternal grandmother under s. 102) is in the child's best interests?
Does the court have jurisdiction under s. 102 of the Act to grant custody to the grandmother where doing so varies existing final parenting orders made under the Children's Law Reform Act?
What access and communication orders are in the child's best interests?

firac.issue: Is intervention through a court order still necessary to protect the 10-year-old autistic child in the future?
firac.facts: The child was brought to a place of safety on April 4, 2024 after police found the mother intoxicated (ketamine present), the apartment filthy, and the child unsupervised; the mother was charged with child abandonment (later withdrawn). The mother consented to protection findings (risk of physical and emotional harm) in a signed Statement of Agreed Facts. On status review she claimed there was never a legitimate protection concern, showed no insight, minimized long-standing substance abuse and mental-health issues, kept $25,000 of the child's OAP funding, refused services, missed visits, and was hostile to workers.
firac.rule: Under s. 101(1) CYFSA the court must first be satisfied that intervention through a court order is necessary to protect the child in the future. The need may arise from circumstances existing at removal, from their absence, or from new circumstances, assessed from the child's perspective (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. M.(C.), 1994 CanLII 83 (SCC)); the court may consider protection concerns beyond those that triggered the original order (CAS of Toronto v. S.P., 2019 ONSC 3482). A status review is not a rehearing; the original consent order is presumed correct (C.A.S. v. M.W. and M.S., 2020 ONSC 1847).
firac.application: The court found the mother lacked all insight, denied compelling evidence of impairment while caregiving (13 independent referrals), had unresolved substance-abuse and mental-health/anger-regulation issues, no services in place for the child, and a demonstrated inability to cooperate with providers or comply with a supervision order. Only the clean-apartment concern had been resolved; multiple concerns persisted or worsened. Returning the child unsupervised would create an unacceptable risk of harm.
firac.conclusion: Intervention through a court order remains necessary to protect the child.

firac.issue: What disposition is in the child's best interests \u2014 return to the mother (with or without supervision) or custody to the maternal grandmother under s. 102?
firac.facts: The child, moderately-to-severely autistic and largely non-verbal, has lived with the maternal grandmother in Sudbury for 23 months, flourishing with a coordinated team of ABA, speech, OT, physio and school supports funded through the OAP. The mother has no services in place, kept the child's OAP funding, and refused education and extended visits.
firac.rule: Section 114 permits variation/termination or a new order in the child's best interests; s. 101(3)-(4) require consideration of less disruptive alternatives and community/family placements; s. 74(3) lists best-interests factors including continuity of care, stability, and risk of harm. Parents are not to be judged by a middle-class yardstick (CAS of Toronto v. B.-H.(R.), 2006 ONCJ 515); the process must not be used to buy a parent time (CAS of Toronto v. R.H., 2000 CanLII 3158). A supervision order requires confidence the parent will comply (Windsor-Essex CAS v. L.H., 2004 ONCJ 196).
firac.application: The grandmother provides excellent, stable, coordinated care; the child has made major gains. The mother's plan lacked services, supports, and any confirmed OAP funding, she called no supporting witnesses (notably her partner L.A.), and the court had no confidence she would comply with a supervision order given her secrecy, dishonesty about the OAP funds, and distrust of the Society. A further supervision order to await the grandmother's health testing was rejected as contrary to the child's need for permanency.
firac.conclusion: It is in the child's best interests to be placed in the care and custody of the maternal grandmother under s. 102; return to the mother, even under supervision, was rejected.

firac.issue: Does the court have jurisdiction to grant custody under s. 102 CYFSA where this varies existing final CLRA parenting orders?
firac.facts: Justice Sager had made final CLRA orders (May 11, 2022 and February 6, 2024) giving the mother primary residence and decision-making. The Society and grandmother sought a s. 102 custody order changing those terms.
firac.rule: A s. 102 order may vary a final CLRA order where three pre-conditions are met: all parties to the CLRA order are parties to the CYFSA proceeding; all parties are served with the s. 102 claim; and a material change in circumstances exists under s. 29 CLRA (CAS of London and Middlesex v. S.A.R., 2015 ONSC 2534; CAS of Toronto v. R.S., 2019 ONCJ 866).
firac.application: The mother and father were parties to both proceedings, all parties were served with the s. 102 claim, and numerous material changes existed \u2014 the child's removal, two years in the grandmother's primary care, and the parents' limited parenting time.
firac.conclusion: All three criteria were met; the court had jurisdiction to make the s. 102 custody order and change the CLRA parenting terms.

firac.issue: What access and communication orders are in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The mother has a close, loving bond with the child but cancelled/missed several visits, refused extended visits, disengaged during virtual calls, resisted providers' routines, and is in high, ongoing conflict with the grandmother, sending abusive messages. The parties live far apart with limited funds.
firac.rule: Section 104(1) permits access orders in the child's best interests; a child should have as much time with each parent as is consistent with best interests (CCAS of Toronto v. A.M., 2024 ONCJ 607), and a party seeking to restrict access must justify the restriction (CCAS of Toronto v. C.P.I., 2020 ONCJ 304).
firac.application: Balancing the benefit of preserving the relationship against the risk of exposing the child to conflict and destabilizing the placement, the court ordered monthly in-person overnight access in Sudbury (as the mother can arrange), one week each in summer and winter breaks in Toronto with the grandmother driving, virtual access three times weekly at the grandmother's discretion, capped daily communications, a sobriety condition, and no direct contact with service providers.
firac.conclusion: Access and communication orders were fashioned to preserve the child's bond with the mother while protecting the stability of the grandmother's placement.

name_verification.name_in_document: Droit de la famille — 22578

defining_issues: Was there a material change of circumstances since the divorce judgment justifying modification of the shared parental-time arrangement, and what modality of parenting time serves the children's best interests?
Should modalities be set for the children's medical appointments given that parental authority remains joint?
Should child support be adjusted retroactively to January 2019, and what income should be attributed or imputed to each parent going forward?
How should the parties' obligations for the children's special expenses be modified?

firac.issue: Was there a material change of circumstances justifying modification of the week-to-week shared parenting arrangement, and what parenting-time modality is in the children's best interests?
firac.facts: A 2018 divorce judgment ratified consents providing alternating-week shared custody of two young children. From April 2020 the conflict intensified: Mother relocated at least seven times, lived about a year in a women's shelter, refused to disclose her address, made numerous unsubstantiated abuse allegations against Father and her family (including public social-media posts), exposed the children to a boyfriend with apparent ties to criminal activity, and the children were frequently late or absent from school. Maternal grandmother and Mother's sister expressed serious concern for the children and Mother's mental health.
firac.rule: Section 17 of the Divorce Act empowers a court to vary a parenting order once satisfied there has been a change in the child's circumstances since the last order (s. 17(5)); the applicant must prove, on a balance of probabilities, a material change affecting the child's best interests (Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 SCR 27). Best interests are assessed under art. 33 C.C.Q. and the factors identified by the Court of Appeal, including parental capacity, stability, absence of conflict/ability to communicate, and proximity of homes.
firac.application: The Court found Mother's deteriorating conduct and instability constituted a material change materially affecting the children. Assessing best interests, it concluded shared parenting was no longer viable given concerns over Mother's parental capacity and the children's lack of stability. Mother prioritized her perceived victimhood over the children, transmitted a distorted and unsafe worldview to them, showed poor judgment (concealing an incident, cohabiting with a dangerous boyfriend), and neglected schooling. Father was calm, credible, offered mediation repeatedly, had suitable accommodation near the school, and fostered the children's development and contact with maternal family.
firac.conclusion: Material change established; Father granted the majority of parenting time effective April 14, 2022, with defined alternating-weekend and holiday time to Mother, conditional on her disclosing her address and refraining from derogatory commentary; religious Jewish holidays with Father and Chinese New Year with Mother.

firac.issue: Should the Court set modalities for the children's medical and dental appointments?
firac.facts: The parties disagreed about the children's medical care, with Mother alleging Father under-medicated and Father fearing over-medication; both retain decision-making responsibility.
firac.rule: Parental authority and decision-making remain jointly exercised absent order to the contrary; the Court may set practical modalities in the children's best interests (art. 33 C.C.Q.).
firac.application: Because parental authority remained joint despite Father having majority parenting time, the Court imposed a notice mechanism to permit both parents to participate in appointments and to keep the non-attending parent informed.
firac.conclusion: Father must give Mother one week's written notice of scheduled medical/dental appointments; both may attend; if Mother declines, Father must text her a brief summary of the outcome.

firac.issue: Should child support be adjusted retroactively to January 2019, and what income should be attributed or imputed to the parents prospectively?
firac.facts: Mother sought retroactive adjustment to January 2019 claiming no income, but filed no tax returns or financial disclosure. Father, a graphic designer and sole shareholder, had income of roughly $25,000/year. Mother, a highly qualified interior designer (two degrees, eight languages), claimed unemployment on welfare, yet evidence (invoices, website, listings) suggested ongoing business activity.
firac.rule: Section 17(4) of the Divorce Act requires a change of circumstances before varying child support. Article 595 C.C.Q. permits retroactive support for up to three years before the application. Article 446 C.P.C. allows the court to impute income by considering, among other things, a parent's assets and income-earning capacity. Child support is of public order; a parent cannot escape the obligation through voluntary unemployment or self-induced reduction of income.
firac.application: Mother bore the burden to prove a change in income and failed to file any supporting documentation, so no retroactive adjustment was warranted. Father's income was set at $25,000, consistent with his average since 2018. Given Mother's strong qualifications, unexplained lack of employment, and evidence of continued business, the Court imputed a conservative $25,000 annual income to her, deferring commencement to allow her time to find work.
firac.conclusion: Retroactive adjustment refused; Mother's application dismissed; $25,000 income imputed to Mother; Mother ordered to pay Father $325.42/month child support commencing June 1, 2022 (reflecting Father's majority parenting time).

firac.issue: How should the parties' obligations for the children's special expenses be modified?
firac.facts: The parties disputed responsibility for special expenses; insufficient evidence was presented on the cost of extracurricular activities.
firac.rule: The court apportions special expenses in the children's best interests and according to the parties' circumstances.
firac.application: Lacking sufficient evidence on specific costs, the Court ordered equal sharing of net special expenses (daycare, hot lunches if needed, medical/dental, glasses) and of pre-approved extracurricular activities, with the incurring party solely liable for unapproved expenses.
firac.conclusion: Parties ordered to share equally the net cost of enumerated special expenses and pre-approved extracurricular activities.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) governs the central parenting-time analysis under art. 33 C.C.Q. and Gordon v. Goertz. K048 (custody/access) captures the modification of parenting time. K050 (parental/child support) covers the adjustment, imputation of income and quantum determination. K117 (Divorce Act) is the governing statute (ss. 17(1),(4),(5)). K027 (Jewish holidays) is a specific but genuine touchpoint since the Court ordered the children to spend religious Jewish holidays with Father — a comparatively minor element, flagged as the weakest of the selected keywords.

name_verification.name_in_document: Dr. Farhan Chak v Ezra Levant, Sun News General Partnership, Quebecor Media Inc and Sun Media Corporation

defining_issues: Did the defendants establish the defence of justification — i.e. prove on a balance of probabilities that Dr. Chak was the nightclub shooter?
Could the preliminary inquiry transcript of witnesses who did not testify at the civil trial be admitted for the truth of its contents under the principled exception to the hearsay rule?
What weight should be given to the witnesses' in-court identifications of Dr. Chak made almost 30 years after the event?
What damages (general, aggravated, punitive) should be awarded once defamation is established?

firac.issue: Did the defendants establish the defence of justification by proving on a balance of probabilities that Dr. Chak was the nightclub shooter?
firac.facts: During a live broadcast on 25 February 2014 Ezra Levant stated that Dr. Chak had 'shot up a nightclub.' The statement referred to a 1993 shotgun incident at Barry T's nightclub in Edmonton; Dr. Chak had been charged and acquitted after a Queen's Bench trial. The defendants admitted the statements were defamatory but pleaded justification, seeking to prove Chak was the shooter.
firac.rule: A defendant pleading justification bears the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that the defamatory statement is substantially true (FH v McDougall, 2008 SCC 53). The evidence must be sufficiently clear, convincing and cogent (McDougall at para 46; Nelson (City) v Mowatt, 2017 SCC 8). A criminal acquittal is inadmissible in a subsequent civil trial as proof the party did not commit the act (Rizzo v Hanover Insurance Co, 1993 CanLII 8561).
firac.application: The court gave no weight to the acquittal either way. The three defence witnesses gave largely consistent accounts of the events but their identification of Chak was weak: one could not identify him at the preliminary inquiry, another was unsure, and the third's criminal-trial identification could not be assessed. The preliminary inquiry evidence of the absent witnesses was inadmissible. The circumstantial evidence (change of appearance, hospital utterance) could not carry the case absent reliable identification.
firac.conclusion: The defendants failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that Dr. Chak was the shooter; the defence of justification failed and the defamation claim was made out.

firac.issue: Could the preliminary inquiry transcript of witnesses who did not testify at the civil trial be admitted for the truth of its contents?
firac.facts: Three Barry T's employees (Horvat, Nick, Turk) identified Chak at the 1993 preliminary inquiry but were not called at the civil trial. Defence counsel described 'heroic' but unsworn efforts to locate them; the plaintiff objected that these were not evidence and that admission would be hearsay.
firac.rule: Hearsay may be admitted for its truth where it is both necessary and reliable (R v Khan; R v Smith; R v B(KG); R v U(FJ); R v Hawkins), interpreted flexibly; these principles apply equally in civil cases (Fawley v Moslenko, 2017 MBCA 47; Pfizer Canada v Teva, 2016 FCA 161). The proponent bears the burden of establishing necessity on the facts (R v Parrott, 2001 SCC 3; R v B(KG)).
firac.application: The court found the transcript reliable — given under oath before a judge with contemporaneous cross-examination by Chak's counsel on the same identity issue (per Hawkins), distinguishable from Clayson-Martin because Chak was a party to both proceedings. However, necessity was not established: the defendants led no admissible evidence of their efforts to secure the absent witnesses, relying only on counsel's unsworn submissions, which the plaintiff had objected to.
firac.conclusion: The reliability requirement was met but the necessity requirement was not; the preliminary inquiry testimony of the absent witnesses was inadmissible for the truth of its contents.

firac.issue: What weight should the in-court identifications of Dr. Chak, made nearly 30 years after the incident, be given?
firac.facts: Each of the three defence witnesses identified Chak as the shooter from 1993 and current photographs at trial. All three admitted having looked Chak up online (YouTube, Facebook, Google). Graham had been unable to identify Chak at the preliminary inquiry; Morezewich had been unsure; Racette's criminal-trial identification left no transcript.
firac.rule: Courts must exercise extreme caution where a witness initially unable to make a positive identification later comes to believe they can identify the accused with the passage of time (Belleperche v Budget Rent-A-Car of Edmonton Ltd, 2009 ABQB 620 at para 34).
firac.application: The identifications closest in time to the events were weak or absent, yet the witnesses were confident 30 years later — an inversion the court found unreliable, compounded by their having viewed photos of Chak online over the years.
firac.conclusion: The in-court identification evidence was unreliable and given very little weight, leaving the defence unable to prove identity.

firac.issue: What damages should be awarded for the established defamation?
firac.facts: Damages are presumed on proof of defamation. The broadcast (11 seconds within a one-hour political commentary) aired on Sun News to roughly 15,000 viewers with negligible ratings; there was no evidence it remained online after Sun News shut down in 2015. Chak's reputation had already been damaged by 2007 press coverage; his career in Qatar continued to flourish. He gave no evidence of actual reputational harm but described stress and worsened health. He had asked Levant to stop repeating the allegation years earlier; the statement was inserted as a 'vignette' into a broadcast otherwise unrelated to him.
firac.rule: General damages measure harm to reputation using the Hill v Church of Scientology factors (position/standing, nature of the libel, mode and extent of publication, effects on the plaintiff, absence of apology), plus the stature of the speaker (Elkow v Sana, 2020 ABCA 350). Aggravated damages require actual malice increasing the injury (Hill at paras 182, 190). Punitive damages require malicious, oppressive, high-handed conduct offending the court's sense of decency (Dentec Safety Specialists, 2012 ONSC 4721).
firac.application: The court found only limited publication, no proven reputational harm, but genuine emotional harm, placing the case in the $20,000–$75,000 Alberta range and fixing general damages at $40,000. Levant's failure to note the acquittal was careless, not malicious; however, inserting salacious, irrelevant defamatory content into the broadcast after being asked to stop increased Chak's injury, warranting $20,000 aggravated damages. The Islamophobia allegation was not put to Levant and the record did not support it; the conduct was not exceptional, so no punitive damages were awarded.
firac.conclusion: General damages of $40,000 and aggravated damages of $20,000 were awarded, plus prejudgment interest and costs; punitive damages were refused.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a civil defamation trial. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action, with the contested defence of justification/substantial truth. The remaining picks are weaker: K016 (fair comment) is the closest defamation-defence keyword, though the defendants actually relied on justification, not fair comment; K004 (criminal law) reflects the heavy reliance on the 1993 criminal proceedings, the acquittal's evidentiary status, hearsay principles drawn from criminal cases, and Criminal Code s. 676, but the matter is civil; K024 (freedom of expression) reflects that the broadcast was political commentary on human rights commissions and free speech, though free expression was not a legal issue decided. No controlled keyword captures the central hearsay/identification-evidence rulings.

registry_rationale: The decision header expressly states 'Registry: Edmonton'.

case_name: Dhami et al v. CBC et al

name_verification.name_in_document: MANJIT SINGH DHAMI, HARJIT SINGH ATWAL, PIARA SINGH NATT and JAGTAR SINGH SANDHU v. canadian broadcasting corporation, kevin evans, indo-canadian times international inc., indo-canadian times, tara singh hayer, dalip singh mangat, sohinder singh dhillon and harjinder singh dhillon

defining_issues: Did the plaintiffs' Statement of Claim disclose a reasonable cause of action in defamation, and did it plead a 'true innuendo' requiring particulars under Rule 19(12)(a) or further particulars under Rule 19(16)?
Should the defendants' plea of justification be struck, and may a defendant plead and justify a lesser defamatory meaning?
Should the defendants' plea of qualified privilege be struck for failing to plead urgency in a publication to the world at large?
Should the CBC's Charter s. 2(b) based defence of qualified privilege be struck as disclosing no reasonable defence?
Were the various demands for particulars (photographic images, malice, damages, fair comment) properly resisted or required?

firac.issue: Did the Statement of Claim disclose a reasonable cause of action in defamation, and did it plead a true innuendo requiring particulars?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs, former executive members of a Surrey Sikh temple, alleged that a CBC broadcast featuring the individual defendants meant they had misappropriated temple funds and were dishonest and corrupt. In response to a demand for particulars they asserted the words were defamatory in their ordinary meaning. The defendants sought to strike the claim under Rule 19(24), arguing the plaintiffs relied on unparticularized innuendo.
firac.rule: A pleading is struck for no reasonable cause of action only where the case is beyond doubt (McNaughton v. Baker). A 'true or legal innuendo' depends on extrinsic facts, creates a separate cause of action, and must be particularized under Rule 19(12)(a); a 'false innuendo' is an inference an ordinary person draws from the natural and ordinary meaning of the words and needs no such particulars (Lewis v. Daily Telegraph; Linden, Canadian Tort Law). Rule 19(16) permits an order for further particulars where more than one defamatory meaning is possible.
firac.application: The plaintiffs alleged the words meant misappropriation and corruption without relying on any extrinsic facts, so they pleaded only a false innuendo, not a true innuendo; Rule 19(12)(a) therefore did not apply. The words, set out in Schedule A, were sufficient to convey an inference of misappropriation and corruption for the purpose of a motion to strike. Because the plaintiffs pleaded a specific defamatory meaning and confirmed it was the ordinary meaning, they had clearly stated the sting and did not need to negate other possible meanings.
firac.conclusion: The application to strike the Statement of Claim was dismissed; no particulars under Rule 19(12)(a) and no further and better particulars under Rule 19(16) were ordered.

firac.issue: Should the plea of justification be struck, and may a defendant plead and justify a lesser defamatory meaning?
firac.facts: Paragraph 7(a) of the Amended Statement of Defence pleaded that the 'words complained of' were true in substance, but did so in relation to the words in their entirety rather than to any lesser meaning ascribed to them.
firac.rule: Under the 'modern approach' (Pizza Pizza Ltd. v. Toronto Star; Goddard v. Day; Polly Peck v. Trelford), a defendant may plead an alternative, lesser defamatory meaning and justify it, so long as the lesser meaning is itself defamatory and carries a separate and distinct sting; s. 14 of the Libel and Slander Act permits the jury a general verdict.
firac.application: A defendant may plead justification of a lesser defamatory meaning, but paragraph 7(a) referred to the 'words complained of' in their entirety and ascribed no lesser defamatory meaning to them or any portion of them. To rely on justification the defendants had to plead in relation to the inference (misappropriation/corruption) ascribed by the plaintiffs, or identify the portions capable of a lesser defamatory meaning.
firac.conclusion: Paragraph 7(a) was struck under Rule 19(24) with leave to amend to plead justification in relation to the plaintiffs' meaning and/or any lesser defamatory meaning.

firac.issue: Should the plea of qualified privilege be struck for failure to plead urgency?
firac.facts: CBC and Evans pleaded qualified privilege, asserting a reciprocal duty/interest to report on a matter of public concern within the Sikh community, relying on the Broadcasting Act. The plaintiffs argued the plea was untenable because it did not allege urgency and concerned a publication to the world at large.
firac.rule: Qualified privilege attaches to the occasion where the maker has a duty or interest to communicate and the recipient a corresponding interest to receive it (Hill v. Church of Scientology; Adam v. Ward). The categories are not closed (Moises v. Canadian Newspaper Co.), and in publications to the world at large the court weighs a non-exhaustive list of circumstances, including urgency, but urgency is only one factor (Reynolds v. Times Newspapers; applied in Ward v. Clark).
firac.application: Urgency is not a legal term of art requiring temporal proximity to the event and is only one of several factors, so the omission of an express plea of urgency did not render the defence untenable. Reynolds is not confined to political or governmental matters but extends to all matters of serious public concern. Whether the defence ultimately succeeds is for the trial judge after hearing the evidence.
firac.conclusion: The plea of qualified privilege disclosed a defence for the purpose of a strike motion and was not struck; its viability was left to the trial judge.

firac.issue: Should the CBC's Charter s. 2(b)-based defence of qualified privilege be struck?
firac.facts: The CBC pleaded that if its broadcast was defamatory it was protected under s. 2(b) of the Charter, relying on its obligations and accountability to Parliament under the Broadcasting Act to argue government action, and contended this raised a novel issue that should go to trial.
firac.rule: Section 2(b) of the Charter applies only to government action, whether by statute or common law (RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery). Where an entity's conduct is examined and found not to function as government, the Charter does not apply (McKinney v. University of Guelph). The CBC's journalistic and programming independence under the Broadcasting Act means that, when acting as a broadcaster, it operates privately and is not subject to Charter scrutiny (Adbusters Media Foundation v. CBC; National Party of Canada v. CBC).
firac.application: The CBC did not claim to be government and the pleadings raised no facts supporting the 'novel' characterization; the issue was one of settled law requiring no findings of fact at trial. As the CBC acts privately as a broadcaster, s. 2(b) did not apply to expand the qualified privilege defence.
firac.conclusion: The Charter-based defence of qualified privilege was struck under Rule 19(24).

firac.issue: Were the demands for particulars (malice, images, damages, fair comment) properly resolved?
firac.facts: The defendants sought particulars of malice, photographic images, loss of income/special damages and reputational harm; the plaintiffs sought to strike defence particulars relating to qualified privilege, justification and fair comment.
firac.rule: Rule 19(23) permits malice to be pleaded as a fact without particulars because it concerns state of mind (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress; Siddon v. Mair). Particulars of privilege must set out facts establishing the privileged occasion; fair comment requires the words to be comment based on true facts, made honestly and without malice on a matter of public interest (The Law of Defamation in Canada).
firac.application: Malice particulars were barred by Rule 19(23), but re-publication (relevant to damages) and particulars of photographic images were ordered, as were particulars of loss of income and special damages given the time elapsed. Justification particulars became moot once the plea was struck. Certain fair-comment particulars (suspicions treated as fact, and matters unresponsive to the pleaded words) were struck, and the defendants were required to identify which words were statements of comment.
firac.conclusion: Mixed disposition: some particulars ordered, some demands dismissed, some particulars struck; disclosure of financial documents and the fair-comment strike were adjourned/reserved, with costs in the cause.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally a defamation pleadings dispute, so K015 (defamation) is central, with K002 (Civil litigation) as the tier-1 parent. The court analysed the specific defences pleaded: qualified privilege (K018) and fair comment (K016). The CBC's constitutional defence engaged K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) and K107 (Canadian Charter), and the underlying value weighed against reputation was freedom of expression/press (K024). K017 (group defamation) was considered but not selected because the claim was by named individuals, not a collectivity; terrorism references (ISYF/Sikh militants) are context only and no criminal or terrorism keyword genuinely applies.

defining_issues: Is it in the best interest of the children to sever all contact with the father, or should supervised access be maintained?
Should supervision over the father's access rights be lifted so as to allow unsupervised, gradually increasing access?
Is the mother entitled to extrajudicial costs and punitive damages given the father's past violent and abusive conduct?

firac.issue: Is it in the best interest of the children to sever all contact with the father, or should supervised access be maintained?
firac.facts: The father admitted past physically and verbally abusive behaviour toward the mother and especially toward child X (spanking, name-calling, threats to throw the child against a wall, holding soiled diapers to his face). A court-ordered psychosocial assessment recommended maintaining supervised contact every two weeks for two hours. The father attended every supervised visit over three years; the visitation reports showed generally positive interactions and a bond with both children, though child X displayed some post-visit deregulation (night terrors, anger) that had subsided with trauma therapy.
firac.rule: Article 33 C.C.Q. requires every decision concerning a child to be taken in the child's interest, expressly including consideration of family violence. The Divorce Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.)) definition of 'family violence' and its enumerated factors guide the assessment. The court is not bound by the expert's findings but must give them proper weight and justify any departure.
firac.application: The Court found the visitation reports (including [Organisation B] reports produced at trial) confirmed the expert's findings of positive, reliable contact and a genuine bond. Child X's post-visit symptoms had diminished with therapy and maternal support. The Court agreed with the expert that severing all contact would be more prejudicial than maintaining supervised access, particularly given the children's young age and inability to advocate for themselves. Maintaining the status quo of two hours every two weeks provided predictability and an opportunity to monitor effects.
firac.conclusion: The mother's request for complete severance of contact was dismissed; supervised access every two weeks for two hours was maintained, with a recommendation that a therapist monitor the impact on the children.

firac.issue: Should supervision over the father's access rights be lifted?
firac.facts: Supervised access had been in place for nearly three years. The father had pursued substantial therapy and parenting classes but continued to minimize and make excuses for his abusive conduct, showing limited appreciation of its impact on the children. The expert testified that although supervision is normally a short-term measure, this was an exceptional case requiring supervision for the foreseeable future.
firac.rule: Best interest of the child under art. 33 C.C.Q. and the Divorce Act family-violence factors, including any steps taken by the abusive parent to prevent further violence and improve caregiving ability; supervised access is in principle a transitional measure.
firac.application: The Court held the transition period was not complete: the father still did not fully appreciate the effect of his past violent and abusive behaviour, which constituted a continuing risk factor for the fragile child X and for child Y. Further demonstrable progress was required before unsupervised access could be considered. Supervision allowed continued monitoring while ensuring the children's safety.
firac.conclusion: The father's request to lift supervision was dismissed; supervised access at the [Organisation B] in Town D was maintained.

firac.issue: Is the mother entitled to extrajudicial costs and punitive damages?
firac.facts: The mother sought $5,000 in extrajudicial costs and punitive damages based on the father's violent and abusive behaviour. Both parties' principal requests were dismissed, and the parties had cooperated to settle the financial aspects of the dispute. Criminal charges against the father remained pending and untried.
firac.rule: Extrajudicial costs are awarded only in the most exceptional circumstances and remain within the court's discretion; punitive damages require justification. The mother relied on 2021 QCCS 3101, distinguishable because there a criminal determination had been made.
firac.application: The Court found the pre-trial proceedings were not solely attributable to the father, both parties' requests were dismissed, and the parties had collaborated on financial matters. On punitive damages, although the father's violent conduct was deemed significant, the pending, unresolved criminal charges made such an award inapposite, unlike in the precedent relied upon.
firac.conclusion: The mother's requests for extrajudicial costs and punitive damages were dismissed; each without costs.

name_verification.name_in_document: Inderjit Singh Chohan v. Otakar Cadsky, Larry Ohlhauser, Capital Health Authority, Kenneth Gardener, Glen Baker, the University of Alberta and Kelay Ohlhauser

defining_issues: Was Dr. Cadsky's reference to Dr. Chohan as a 'paranoid Sikh', made to Drs. Rai and Woods, defamatory and actionable, or was it protected by qualified privilege (and unaffected by malice)?

Were the communications by Drs. Gardener, Baker and Ohlhauser to third parties (Drs. Block and Hibbard) describing Dr. Chohan as 'paranoid' or a 'sick doc' defamatory, or protected by qualified privilege?
Is Capital Health vicariously liable for any defamation by Dr. Gardener?
If defamation had been established, what damages were appropriate?

firac.issue: Was Dr. Cadsky's 'paranoid Sikh' remark defamatory and actionable, or protected by qualified privilege?
firac.facts: While on stress leave at his home, Dr. Cadsky, over a glass of wine, told two colleague forensic psychiatrists (Drs. Rai and Woods) who had come to discuss FACS matters and the leadership vacuum that Dr. Chohan was a 'paranoid Sikh', running through various psychiatrists with unflattering epithets in the context of who should become clinical director. Cadsky admitted the words. He testified Chohan met four of seven criteria of paranoid personality disorder but had excellent clinical abilities, and that 'Sikh' referred only to appearance.
firac.rule: Defamation requires (a) defamatory words, (b) referring to the plaintiff, (c) published to a third person (Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada). A publication is defamatory if it tends to lower a person's reputation in the estimation of reasonable persons. Defences include truth/justification, qualified privilege and fair comment. An occasion is privileged where a statement is made in discharge of a duty or to protect an interest to a person with a corresponding interest (Reynolds v. Times Newspapers Ltd., [1999] 4 All E.R. 609). Malice defeats privilege and means spite, ill will, or an ulterior motive (Leenan v. CBC, 2000 CanLII 22380; Cimolai v. Hall, 2007 BCCA 225 — dislike is not malice).
firac.application: The Court found the 'Sikh' reference was not racially motivated or defamatory, but the 'paranoid' reference was understood by the psychiatrist audience as a serious comment on Chohan's mental state and was published. However, Drs. Rai and Woods attended primarily to discuss FACS politics and the pending leadership vacuum; as the senior psychiatrist who built the program, Cadsky reasonably felt a duty to comment on candidates' fitness, correlating to his listeners' avid interest in future leadership, so the occasion was privileged. The Court also found Cadsky honestly held his professional opinion (unchallenged) and acted without malice — the remark was insulting but not spiteful.
firac.conclusion: No actionable defamation; the statement was protected by qualified privilege and made without malice. Claim against Dr. Cadsky dismissed.

firac.issue: Were the 'paranoid'/'sick doc' communications by Drs. Gardener, Baker and Ohlhauser to Drs. Block and Hibbard defamatory or privileged?
firac.facts: Prompted by concerns from Dr. King (a self-described admirer of Chohan) and from their own meetings with an increasingly agitated Chohan, Drs. Ohlhauser and Baker developed concerns about his mental state and contacted Dr. Gardener; Gardener and Baker phoned Dr. Block (Chohan's chief at RAH), and Ohlhauser left messages for Dr. Hibbard describing a possible 'sick doc' and concern that Chohan 'may be' paranoid. None had knowledge of the 'paranoid Sikh' comment when they made the calls.
firac.rule: Same defamation elements and qualified-privilege test as above; a communication made in discharge of a duty to a recipient with a corresponding interest is privileged unless defeated by malice.
firac.application: Each communicator had an interest and duty as a fellow physician to ensure that Chohan's evident distress was not affecting his clinical practice and that he had support from persons outside the FACS factions; Drs. Block and Hibbard, as disinterested colleagues, had a corresponding interest in receiving the information. Baker's evidence that he conveyed concern over Chohan's 'anger' (not 'paranoid') was accepted as non-defamatory. In any event the occasions were privileged and there was no evidence of malice; the 'sick doc' phrase was a College term of art so ambiguous as to be almost meaningless.
firac.conclusion: No actionable defamation; the communications were protected by qualified privilege and free of malice. Claims against Drs. Gardener, Baker and Ohlhauser dismissed.

firac.issue: Is Capital Health vicariously liable for any defamation by Dr. Gardener?
firac.facts: Chohan pleaded that Gardener acted as Capital Health's employee or agent, making it vicariously liable.
firac.rule: Vicarious liability requires an underlying wrong by the employee/agent.
firac.application: Because no personal liability was found against Dr. Gardener, there was no wrong for which Capital Health could be vicariously liable.
firac.conclusion: No vicarious liability; claim against Capital Health dismissed.

firac.issue: If defamation had been established, what damages would be appropriate?
firac.facts: Chohan claimed only general damages for loss of reputation; there was no loss of income, no interference with privileges, continued career progression, and continued high esteem in his clinical practice and the Sikh community.
firac.rule: General damages are presumed in defamation (Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130; Defamation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. D-7, s. 2(2)), with no cap, but only damages flowing naturally from the conduct are recoverable and a nominal sum may be awarded where reputation is largely unaffected (Brown).
firac.application: There was no evidence of damage to Chohan's professional or community reputation, and his distress was only partly attributable to any comment (largely arising from his inability to disclose Cadsky's remark and his distrust of genuine concern). Damages would have been nominal.
firac.conclusion: Had defamation been made out, the Court would have awarded nominal damages of $5,000. As it was not, no damages; costs to the defendants on Column 4.
