registry_rationale: The decision identifies the 'Judicial Centre: Regina', which is the Court of Queen's Bench registry hearing the matter.

name_verification.name_in_document: IBM Canada ltée c. D... C...

defining_issues: Did the trial judge err in awarding a 24-month reasonable notice period (délai-congé) for the disguised dismissal?
What is the proper starting date for calculating the notice period?
Did the employee satisfy his duty to mitigate his damages?
Was the employee entitled to the employer's virtual SERP retirement-plan contributions accrued before he reached the plan's vesting age of 55?
Was the employee entitled to compensation for stock options (forced exercise, and RSUs/Buy-First-Options that would have vested during the notice period)?
Was the award of $35,000 in moral damages justified, and was it excessive or duplicative of the notice indemnity?
Could exemplary (punitive) damages be awarded under s. 49 of the Quebec Charter for discrimination based on the employee's cancer, and if so in what amount?

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in fixing a 24-month reasonable notice period for the disguised dismissal?
firac.facts: C..., a director-level IBM executive earning about $327,000/year, supervising some 250 people, over 50 years old with roughly 12 years of service, was disguised-dismissed. The trial judge awarded 24 months' notice; IBM argued this was excessive and that she wrongly considered the absence of serious cause.
firac.rule: Articles 2091, 2092 and 2094 C.c.Q.; the notice must be reasonable given the nature of the employment, circumstances and length of service (Standard Broadcasting Corp. c. Stewart). Appellate courts intervene only for error as to applicable criteria or a clearly excessive duration (Transforce c. Baillargeon).
firac.application: IBM was right that absence of serious cause is not a factor going to the duration of notice, but the judge relied primarily on the proper Stewart criteria—seniority, importance of responsibilities, age, and difficulty of finding comparable work. Although generous and at the upper end of the range, the award was not unreasonable, and the incidental reference to absence of cause did not vitiate it.
firac.conclusion: No reviewable error; the 24-month notice period was upheld.

firac.issue: What is the proper starting date for calculating the notice period?
firac.facts: IBM argued the notice should run from September 20, 2006 (or January 12, 2007), when C... learned of the substantial changes. C... continued working and negotiations continued; IBM had insisted throughout that no dismissal had occurred and that C... had resigned.
firac.rule: The determination of when an employee must understand he has no choice but to seek other employment is a highly factual question reviewable only for palpable and overriding error.
firac.application: IBM never gave, expressly or implicitly, any notice of termination; it maintained C... remained employed. The judge found the dismissal crystallized on May 25, 2007, when IBM insisted he take the inferior position. IBM showed no palpable and overriding error.
firac.conclusion: The starting date of May 25, 2007 was upheld.

firac.issue: Did the employee satisfy his duty to mitigate?
firac.facts: C... refused the offered inferior position and, after job-searching, started his own consulting business in early 2008. IBM argued he should have kept looking and that his actual income was understated, seeking a larger deduction ($102,579.75 rather than $60,281.51).
firac.rule: Mitigation is a highly factual question; a reasonable person is not required to accept a humiliating demotion. Appellate deference applies to the trial judge's assessment of the evidence.
firac.application: The judge accepted C...'s testimony and evidence of a thorough job search showing he could not find equivalent work; refusing the degrading post was reasonable. IBM merely asked the court to reweigh the evidence without demonstrating error.
firac.conclusion: Mitigation was satisfied; the deduction of $60,281.51 stood.

firac.issue: Was C... entitled to the employer's virtual SERP contributions accrued before the age-55 vesting condition?
firac.facts: C... participated in a notional SERP retention plan requiring continuous employment until age 55 to receive benefits. He was 51 at dismissal and 53 at the end of the notice period. IBM ended the plan in 2008. The trial judge awarded $52,333.12 for IBM's contribution; C... claimed the full $257,191.62 arguing the age-55 clause was abusive.
firac.rule: IBM could terminate without cause subject only to reasonable notice (art. 2091 C.c.Q.). A clause is not abusive (art. 1437 C.c.Q.) where it pursues a legitimate retention objective known and accepted by all.
firac.application: The age-55 condition legitimately aimed to retain key executives and was not abusive. Even had C... remained employed to the end of the notice period he would not have reached 55, so he never acquired any right to the SERP funds; his situation was identical to any employee leaving before 55, and no proof showed the dismissal was aimed at depriving him of SERP.
firac.conclusion: Appeal allowed on this point; the $52,333.12 award was set aside.

firac.issue: Was C... entitled to compensation for stock options—both the forced exercise of vested options and the RSUs/BFOs that would have vested during the notice period?
firac.facts: Vested options had to be exercised within 90 days of the alleged resignation; C... realized over $70,000 and claimed the difference against the stock's peak price during the notice period. He also claimed for RSUs and BFOs that would have vested during the notice period; the trial judge awarded $18,702.70 (BFO) and $31,243.05 (RSU).
firac.rule: Loss on securities must be assessed without speculation, typically using the average trading price over the relevant period (Nurun c. Deschênes); loss of chance is not compensable in Quebec (Laferrière c. Lawson). Incentive award clauses that are not abusive apply according to their terms.
firac.application: Using the ~$105 average price, C... would have earned less than he actually realized, so no compensable loss existed. As for RSUs/BFOs, they were discretionary retention incentives; had IBM given proper notice it would have ceased offering incentives designed to retain him, so no injury flowed from the insufficient notice or abusive termination.
firac.conclusion: Both option claims failed; appeal allowed to strike the $18,702.70 and $31,243.05 awards, incidental appeal dismissed.

firac.issue: Was the award of $35,000 in moral damages justified and appropriate?
firac.facts: The trial judge found IBM, particularly Ms Keating, engaged in humiliating, degrading and hurtful conduct over many months (perverted performance evaluation, mishandled harassment complaint, later interference with C...'s new business), coinciding with his cancer diagnosis, and awarded $35,000.
firac.rule: Moral harm that is merely the ordinary consequence of dismissal is not compensable; damages are available only where faulty conduct aggravates the normal negative consequences (Stewart, Hoeckner, Saulnier). Care must be taken to avoid duplication with the notice indemnity.
firac.application: The majority (St-Pierre, Gagnon JJ.A.) held the abusive, insidious conduct caused injury beyond the ordinary consequences of termination, and $35,000 was consistent with the jurisprudence and warranted deference. Pelletier J.A., dissenting on this point, would have reduced it to $20,000 as partly duplicative of the large notice indemnity.
firac.conclusion: Majority upheld the $35,000 moral-damages award (Pelletier J.A. would have reduced it).

firac.issue: Could exemplary damages be awarded under s. 49 of the Quebec Charter, and in what amount?
firac.facts: IBM declined to transfer C... to a U.S. post, and the trial judge found IBM used his cancer to justify imposing an inferior position—unlawful, intentional discrimination based on handicap—awarding $300,000, based essentially on IBM's ability to pay.
firac.rule: Section 49 (para. 2) of the Quebec Charter permits punitive damages for unlawful and intentional interference; intentionality exists where the actor acts with knowledge of the immediate and natural, or at least extremely probable, consequences (Curateur public c. St-Ferdinand). Quantum is governed by art. 1621 C.c.Q. (gravity of fault, patrimonial situation, other reparation already owed) and must not exceed what suffices for the preventive purpose (Cinar c. Robinson).
firac.application: The majority held the finding of intentional, unlawful discrimination affecting C...'s dignity was reasonably supported and that Honda c. Keays (a common-law case) should be treated cautiously and applies only at the quantum stage. However, the trial judge erred by fixing $300,000 almost solely on IBM's ability to pay, ignoring gravity of fault and the substantial other reparation owed; $300,000 was disproportionate. Pelletier J.A. would have struck the award entirely.
firac.conclusion: Majority reduced exemplary damages to $25,000; compensatory indemnity reduced by $117,278.87 to $684,488.44; incidental appeal dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns termination of an indeterminate employment contract. K085 (wrongful dismissal) captures the central finding of congédiement déguisé (constructive dismissal). K082 (employment discrimination) and K069 (discrimination) apply to the finding that IBM used C...'s cancer/handicap to justify an inferior post, grounding the Charter claim. K071 (human dignity) reflects the s. 4 Quebec Charter dignity finding underlying moral and exemplary damages. K120 (Quebec Charter) is the statutory basis (arts. 10, 16, 49) for the punitive damages analysis. K002 (Civil litigation) is a secondary tier-1 tag for the quantum/damages assessment (notice indemnity, mitigation, art. 1621 C.c.Q. punitive damages), though it is a weaker, borderline pick given the labour focus.
location_rationale: The header states 'COUR D'APPEL, PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC, GREFFE DE MONTRÉAL', establishing Montréal, Quebec as the seat and registry.
registry_rationale: 'GREFFE DE MONTRÉAL' in the header identifies the Montréal registry; the underlying Superior Court judgment was rendered in 'district de Montréal'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Henri Hazan c. Fédération CJA

defining_issues: Should the court grant an interlocutory injunction ordering the Fédération CJA to lift the ban preventing Hazan from accessing the Cummings building?
Did Hazan establish a sufficient appearance of right, given the seriously contested legal questions about whether the premises are public and whether the access ban was justified?
Would Hazan suffer irreparable harm and does the balance of convenience favour granting the injunction?

firac.issue: Should the court grant an interlocutory injunction ordering the Fédération CJA to lift the access ban imposed on Hazan?
firac.facts: Hazan, a member of Montréal's Jewish community and a former Jewish General Hospital employee, waged a prolonged campaign of harsh, accusatory correspondence against hospital and CJA figures, notably Steven Cummings, invoking comparisons to Hitler, the Holocaust, Nazis and Valery Fabrikant. In mid-September 2001, upon Cummings becoming CJA president, administrator Cantor banned Hazan from the Cummings building over safety fears. Hazan sought an interlocutory injunction to lift the ban.
firac.rule: On an interlocutory injunction the court applies the three-part test: appearance of right (serious question), irreparable harm, and balance of convenience; where the right is doubtful the balance of convenience becomes decisive. At the interlocutory stage the court must avoid resolving contested factual and legal questions reserved for the trial judge and generally preserves the existing situation.
firac.application: The court found numerous serious, contested legal questions (whether the premises are public, whether freedom of movement was validly restricted, whether the ban was reasonable) that must be left to the trial judge. Granting the injunction would substitute the court's view for Cantor's assessment of a sufficient fear, which was not manifestly unjustified. The court noted objective grounds for fear reinforced by Hazan's conduct at the hearing (pulling opposing counsel's hair, keeping a knife at the witness stand). It preferred to preserve the status quo and prioritize security.
firac.conclusion: The court granted the request only in part, preserving the ban but carving out limited access.

firac.issue: Did Hazan establish a sufficient appearance of right?
firac.facts: Hazan claimed the building housed public services and that his exclusion trampled truth, freedom of expression and democratic rights; the CJA is a private Jewish philanthropic organization owning the Cummings building, with security controls at entry.
firac.rule: To succeed the applicant must demonstrate a sufficient appearance of right; where the right is seriously contested, the court proceeds cautiously and weighs the balance of convenience.
firac.application: The public character of the premises was not proven — non-members' access appeared to be a privilege, not a right. Granting relief would improperly substitute the court's opinion for Cantor's genuine and not manifestly unjustified fear. The court assessed fear on an objective standard and found Hazan's own conduct inspired objective fear.
firac.conclusion: The appearance of right was insufficient given the serious contested questions, favouring preservation of the ban.

firac.issue: Would Hazan suffer irreparable harm and does the balance of convenience favour the injunction?
firac.facts: Hazan sought access to social services, the Gelber Centre, the not-yet-open Holocaust Museum, and the library. He was not a library member and used another library; the museum was not open.
firac.rule: Irreparable harm and balance of convenience components of the interlocutory injunction test; caution favours security over unrestricted access.
firac.application: The court recognized Hazan would suffer irreparable harm if denied social services, and that he might wish to attend Gelber Centre events. It fashioned limited access: social services by appointment, and Gelber Centre conferences with written authorization from Cantor, whom the court found to be acting in good faith. The balance of convenience favoured caution and security.
firac.conclusion: The court ordered partial lifting of the ban: access to social services by appointment only, and to Gelber Centre conferences upon written authorization from Cantor.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, this being a civil interlocutory injunction proceeding. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the central doctrine applied via the appearance-of-right/irreparable-harm/balance-of-convenience test. K015 (defamation) reflects the defamatory character of Hazan's correspondence, which underpinned the dispute (an earlier defamation injunction against him was refused). K094 (Jewish community) and K093 (Jewish) are engaged because the defendant is a Jewish philanthropic organization and the parties are within the Jewish community. K088 (Holocaust) is engaged by Hazan's repeated Holocaust/Nazi comparisons and the building's Holocaust Memorial Centre; it is a somewhat contextual pick.
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the Cour supérieure, 'PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC, DISTRICT DE de Montréal', file No. 500-05-072458-027, confirming Montréal, Quebec.
registry_rationale: The header identifies the 'DISTRICT DE de Montréal', which is the judicial district/registry of the Superior Court where the file was filed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Feldman c. Lande

defining_issues: Should the amended claim against Lande and Pion be dismissed on the basis of res judicata and lis pendens under art. 168 C.C.P.?
Is the claim prescribed either under the one-year defamation prescription of art. 2929 C.C.Q. or the six-month prescription of s. 586 of the Cities and Towns Act?
Does the amended application constitute an abuse of procedure under art. 51 C.C.P. warranting its dismissal against all nine defendants and an award of extrajudicial fees?

firac.issue: Should the amended claim against Lande and Pion be dismissed on the basis of res judicata and lis pendens under art. 168 C.C.P.?
firac.facts: Feldman's accusations that Lande inherited a fortune from Nazi-stolen gold, submerged him in litigation, and caused the liquidation of jointly owned properties had already been the subject of judgments (including Feifer v. Feldman, 2024 QCCS 643, and Feldman c. Succession de Lande, 2021 QCCS 2949) and of a pending defamation action set for trial in 2025.
firac.rule: Under art. 168 C.C.P. an application may be dismissed for lis pendens or res judicata; art. 2848 C.C.Q. requires identity of persons, object and cause. For res judicata the court examines the prior judgment; for lis pendens it compares the pleadings, taking allegations as proven, exercising caution (Rocois Construction Inc. v. Québec Ready Mix Inc.).
firac.application: The court found identity of persons, object and cause between the amended application and the numerous prior and pending proceedings, concluding that Feldman was relitigating claims already decided or before another court, save the false-arrest allegations.
firac.conclusion: The court would dismiss most of the claim against Lande and Pion under art. 168(1) C.C.P., but chose to dispose of the entire claim under art. 51 C.C.P.

firac.issue: Is the claim prescribed under art. 2929 C.C.Q. or s. 586 of the Cities and Towns Act?
firac.facts: Feldman's damages flowed from arrests on December 20, 2019 and June 24, 2020; he sent a demand letter and pursued disciplinary complaints in 2020-2021, but filed his originating application only in December 2022 (and January 2022 against the City).
firac.rule: Art. 2929 C.C.Q. imposes a one-year prescription for defamation, to be read restrictively (Desbiens c. Standish, 2024 QCCA 725, holding that a claim founded on false denunciation attacking liberty falls under the three-year prescription of art. 2925 C.C.Q.). S. 586 of the Cities and Towns Act imposes a six-month prescription for claims against a municipality except for bodily injury.
firac.application: Given the restrictive scope of art. 2929 and Desbiens, the court could not conclude the claim was purely defamatory and thus prescribed as against Lande, Pion and the lawyers. Against the SPVM and Leclerc, however, the six-month municipal prescription applied and had expired well before filing, with no bodily-injury exception.
firac.conclusion: The defamation-based prescription argument was not retained for most defendants, but the claim against the SPVM and Leclerc was found prescribed (and also unfounded and abusive).

firac.issue: Does the amended application constitute an abuse of procedure under art. 51 C.C.P.?
firac.facts: Feldman, a lawyer, claimed 39.5 million dollars against nine defendants over 89 paragraphs, describing a conspiracy led by his former partner Lande, with the lawyers, a business associate (Alavi) and the police cast as enablers; the allegations were largely opinions and conjecture, contradicted by prior civil, disciplinary and criminal outcomes, including his own guilty plea to criminal harassment.
firac.rule: Arts. 51 and 168 C.C.P. permit declaring a proceeding abusive; abuse includes clearly unfounded, frivolous, vexatious or excessive pleadings and disproportionate claims (Bohémier; Gravel c. Orlup; Boggia c. Maiello). Once abuse is summarily established the burden shifts to the plaintiff to justify the proceeding. Lawyers enjoy relative immunity and can be liable only for an independent fault marked by recklessness or bad faith (Chionis c. Gaudet).
firac.application: The exorbitant, unexplained quantum, the recycling of dismissed accusations, and the absence of pure facts establishing fault, causation and damage against the lawyers, Alavi, and the police (mere secret recording and handing it to police being no fault) all pointed to abuse. Feldman offered no substantive rebuttal, merely repeating his allegations.
firac.conclusion: The court held the amended application abusive against all defendants, dismissed it, and condemned Feldman to reimburse Alavi's extrajudicial fees (rectified to $17,978.57) with costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area, as the case turns on motions to dismiss for abuse of procedure and prescription under the C.C.P. and C.C.Q. K015 (defamation) is squarely engaged by the prescription analysis under art. 2929 C.C.Q. and the Desbiens c. Standish discussion. K024 (freedom of expression) applies because that same authority frames defamation as the fault-based limit on free expression. K013 (professional discipline) is a moderate pick reflecting the Barreau du Québec syndic complaints against the defendant lawyers and against Feldman that informed the abuse finding. K088 (Holocaust) and K093 (Jewish) capture the factual core of Feldman's accusations that Lande's fortune derived from Nazi gold stolen from Jewish victims; these are thematic/background picks and are the weakest, included because the accusation drives the whole litigation but the case is not itself about antisemitism.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'COUR SUPÉRIEURE (Chambre civile) ... PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC ... DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL' and lists file No. 500-17-123406-228, placing the Superior Court sitting in Montréal, Quebec.
registry_rationale: The 'DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL' designation and the 500-17 Montréal court file number identify the Montréal registry of the Superior Court.

case_name: D.M. v Alberta (Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, Director)

name_verification.name_in_document: D.M. v Alberta (Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, Director)

defining_issues: Does the grandfather have a recognized cause of action under the Family Law Act to terminate or obtain guardianship of grandchildren who are under a Permanent Guardianship Order to the Director?
Does the doctrine of res judicata / issue estoppel bar the grandfather from re-litigating the guardianship question?
Should the grandfather be declared a frivolous and vexatious litigant and prohibited from bringing further applications without leave?

firac.issue: Does the grandfather have a recognized cause of action under the Family Law Act to terminate or obtain guardianship of grandchildren who are under a Permanent Guardianship Order to the Director?
firac.facts: The children were placed under a Permanent Guardianship Order (PGO) to the Director under s. 34 of the Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act by Judge Shaw on October 22, 2014. The grandfather filed a Family Law Act claim purporting to terminate guardianship, and at the leave hearing stated he was actually applying for guardianship of the grandchildren; his earlier guardianship application had been dismissed.
firac.rule: Section 25(1) of the Family Law Act permits termination of guardianship only where there is a guardian in place under that Act and either the guardian consents or the court considers it necessary or desirable. Guardianship of children subject to a PGO is governed by the Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, not the Family Law Act.
firac.application: The children are not subject to guardianship under the Family Law Act; the Director holds permanent guardianship under the CYFEA. The grandparents had already been repeatedly denied access under s. 34(8). It is therefore not possible to use the Family Law Act to terminate the Director's PGO, so no cause of action exists.
firac.conclusion: There is no cause of action available to the grandfather under the Family Law Act.

firac.issue: Does the doctrine of res judicata / issue estoppel bar the grandfather from re-litigating the guardianship question?
firac.facts: The grandparents' guardianship applications were dismissed at a 20-day trial before Judge Shaw; their appeals to the Court of Queen's Bench were dismissed by Justice Dario, an application to reinstate was denied after a substantive review of over 2,000 pages of transcript, and a final appeal to the Court of Appeal to reinstate was denied.
firac.rule: Res judicata makes a final judgment on the merits conclusive between the parties as to matters litigated or that could have been litigated (CAG v. SG, 2012 ABQB 529; Hill v. Hill, 2016 ABQB 49). Issue estoppel (Angle v. MNR, [1975] 2 SCR 248; Toronto (City) v. CUPE Local 79, 2003 SCC 63) requires the same question decided, a final decision, and the same parties or privies.
firac.application: The same guardianship question, involving the same children and the same parties, was decided and exhaustively reviewed on the merits by Justice Dario, whose decision was final after appeal avenues were exhausted. The grandfather's assertion that the merits were never heard was rejected; the reinstatement proceeding was a thorough substantive review of every ground of appeal.
firac.conclusion: Re-litigation is barred; the matter has been conclusively decided and finality applies.

firac.issue: Should the grandfather be declared a frivolous and vexatious litigant and prohibited from bringing further applications without leave?
firac.facts: There had been 54 Family Law Act and 57 CYFEA appearances in Provincial Court, plus Queen's Bench and Court of Appeal proceedings. The grandparents made repeated defamatory accusations (calling various agencies and individuals anti-Semitic, comparing Child and Family Services to Nazi Germany, alleging conspiracy), attempted to locate the children in foster care causing a placement to break down, and published the children's identities contrary to the CYFEA.
firac.rule: Section 91(1) of the Family Law Act allows the court to prohibit a person who has made frivolous or vexatious applications from further applications without leave. Indicia of vexatious conduct include re-litigating decided issues and abuse of process (Kavanagh v. Kavanagh, 2016 ABQB 107; Gauthier v. Starr, 2016 ABQB 213; 420093 B.C. Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal; s. 23 of the Judicature Act).
firac.application: The grandfather persistently pursued applications on matters already decided, engaged in bizarre, inflammatory and defamatory conduct in and outside court, breached publication restrictions, and tried to locate the children. This course of conduct constitutes abuse and misuse of legal process.
firac.conclusion: The grandfather is a frivolous and vexatious litigant; he is prohibited from further applications without leave and ordered to pay $5,000 costs.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area, as the application arises under the Family Law Act and Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act. K047 (best interests of the child) captures the guiding concern of protecting the children from abuse that underlay the guardianship refusal. K048 (custody/access) covers the guardianship and access dimension of the dispute. K058 (antisemitism) and K094 (Jewish community) reflect the grandparents' recurring (and rejected) allegations of anti-Semitism against the Director, the Calgary Jewish Academy and Jewish Family Services, and their inappropriate requests regarding Gentile relatives; K093 (Jewish) captures the community context. The antisemitism-related picks are weaker/tangential — the allegations were made by the litigant and found baseless — but are the closest vocabulary matches to the recurring subject matter, and there is no controlled term for res judicata or vexatious-litigant designation.

registry_rationale: The docket block expressly lists 'Registry: Calgary'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Michael Hendricks et René Leboeuf c. Le Procureur général du Québec et La Procureure générale du Canada

defining_issues: Does Parliament have legislative competence under s. 91(26) of the Constitution Act, 1867 to modify the meaning of 'marriage' to include same-sex couples?

Does the opposite-sex requirement for marriage (s. 5 of the Federal Law–Civil Law Harmonization Act and s. 1(1) of the Modernization of Benefits and Obligations Act) infringe the equality guarantee under s. 15(1) of the Canadian Charter?
If there is an infringement of s. 15(1), is it justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
Is art. 365 C.c.Q. (requiring marriage between a man and a woman) within provincial competence, and is it the source of the discriminatory treatment?
What remedy is appropriate where the impugned provisions are found unconstitutional?

firac.issue: Does Parliament have jurisdiction under s. 91(26) to redefine marriage to include same-sex couples?
firac.facts: Marriage predates the Constitution Act, 1867, which conferred exclusive authority over 'marriage and divorce' on Parliament (s. 91(26)) while leaving 'solemnization of marriage' to the provinces (s. 92(12)). Neither the common law nor the C.c.B.C. ever expressly defined marriage, but both understood it as the union of one man and one woman.
firac.rule: Sections 91 and 92 of the Constitution Act, 1867 are attributive of legislative competence over classes of subjects. The Constitution is a 'living tree capable of growth and expansion within its natural limits' (Edwards) to be interpreted broadly and dynamically to meet new social realities.
firac.application: The Court disagreed with Egale (Pitfield J.) that redefinition would require a constitutional amendment. Applying evolutive interpretation—used for 'banks', telephony and 'Indians'—the Court held the meaning of 'marriage' in s. 91(26) can be modulated without amending the Constitution. Section 5 of the Harmonization Act (2001) shows Parliament actively legislating on a substantive condition of marriage.
firac.conclusion: Parliament has the legislative competence to modify the original meaning of marriage to include same-sex couples.

firac.issue: Does the opposite-sex requirement for marriage infringe s. 15(1) of the Charter?
firac.facts: Hendricks and Leboeuf, a same-sex couple in a nearly 30-year conjugal relationship, were refused a marriage licence because the law confines marriage to a man and a woman. Recent federal and Quebec laws extended benefits and (in Quebec) civil union to same-sex couples, but not access to marriage.
firac.rule: The three-part analysis in Law v. Canada: (1) differential treatment; (2) based on an enumerated or analogous ground; (3) that is truly discriminatory by offending human dignity. Sexual orientation is an analogous ground (Egan; M. v. H.).
firac.application: Excluding same-sex couples from marriage imposes differential treatment based on sexual orientation, an analogous ground. Considering the contextual factors—historical disadvantage of homosexuals, the fact procreation is not a condition of civil marriage, and the fundamental importance of the institution—the exclusion sends a message that such unions merit less respect, undermining the couple's dignity. Civil union and economic benefits do not cure this ('separate but equal' rejected, per Linden J. in Egan).
firac.conclusion: The definition of marriage in s. 5 of the Harmonization Act discriminates against same-sex couples contrary to s. 15(1).

firac.issue: Is the s. 15(1) infringement justified under s. 1?
firac.facts: The Attorney General of Canada argued the law preserves traditional marriage, an institution with social, historical and religious roots that the State merely recognized. Interveners argued redefinition would threaten religious freedom.
firac.rule: Oakes test: a pressing and substantial objective, plus proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality of effects); the government bears the burden.
firac.application: The State failed at the first step. Preservation of the traditional/religious conception of marriage cannot justify denying equality; a religious majority cannot impose its conception of marriage on a civil institution (Big M Drug Mart). Complementarity of the sexes and procreation are not conditions of civil marriage. Religious freedom (s. 2(a)) is not threatened, since no minister of religion can be compelled to celebrate a marriage contrary to his faith (art. 367 C.c.Q.). No pressing objective was established; the harmonization exercise was not urgent.
firac.conclusion: The infringement is not justified under s. 1.

firac.issue: Is art. 365 C.c.Q. ultra vires or the source of the discrimination?
firac.facts: The registrar refused the licence citing art. 365 C.c.Q., which requires marriage between a man and a woman. The Attorney General of Quebec conceded a province cannot enact substantive conditions of marriage, which fall to Parliament.
firac.rule: A substantive condition of marriage (capacity, impediments) is within exclusive federal competence; a province may only legislate on solemnization. Section 15 does not alter the division of powers (Haig; s. 31 of the Charter).
firac.application: If art. 365 al. 2 imposes a substantive condition it is ultra vires; if it merely obliges the celebrant to verify the federally-imposed condition it is intra vires. Either way, since the opposite-sex requirement now flows from s. 5 of the Harmonization Act, art. 365 is not the true legal source of the discrimination, and the province cannot grant the remedy sought. The Quebec Charter (art. 10) argument likewise fails.
firac.conclusion: Art. 365 al. 2 is not the source of the discrimination, but its 'man and a woman' portion, being merely a verification of the federal condition, is declared inoperative to follow the fate of s. 5.

firac.issue: What is the appropriate remedy?
firac.facts: The impugned provisions were found to violate s. 15 and be unjustified. The reform of a fundamental social institution engaging strongly divergent values was at stake; Ontario's Halpern judges had adopted differing remedies.
firac.rule: Section 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982. Courts act as guardians of Charter rights (Vriend) but must show restraint before radically changing established law (Watkins v. Olafson), leaving major reform with ramifications to the legislature.
firac.application: Although the Court could simply read in 'two persons', it held the choice of remedy for so profound a reform belongs to Parliament, which has consultation mechanisms to weigh social, religious and cultural impacts. A legal vacuum cannot be left, so the declaration of invalidity is suspended for 24 months.
firac.conclusion: The application is allowed; s. 5 of the Harmonization Act, s. 1(1) of the Modernization Act, and the 'man and a woman' part of art. 365 al. 2 C.c.Q. are declared inoperative, with the declarations of invalidity suspended for two years, costs against the co-respondents.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns on the division of powers and Charter equality. K023 (equality rights) and K109 (Charter s. 15) are central: the exclusion of same-sex couples was held discriminatory under s. 15(1). K030 (reasonable limits s. 1) covers the Oakes justification analysis. K069 (discrimination) captures the finding of discriminatory treatment on the analogous ground of sexual orientation. K107 (Canadian Charter) is the governing instrument. K025 (freedom of religion) is engaged by the interveners' arguments and the Court's discussion of s. 2(a) and art. 367 C.c.Q. K120 (Quebec Charter) reflects the alternative claim under art. 10 of the Quebec Charter. A family-law marriage tag would be borderline; the case is decided as a constitutional matter, so it was omitted.
location_rationale: The header states 'COUR SUPÉRIEURE / PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC / DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL' and gives file no. 500-05-059656-007, establishing the Quebec Superior Court sitting in Montréal.
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the 'DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL', so the registry is Montréal.

case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. J.F.

name_verification.name_in_document: Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. J.F.

defining_issues: Was the letter from the Jean Tweed Centre admissible evidence on a summary judgment motion in a child protection proceeding?

Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial such that the summary judgment motion should be dismissed, or could the court fairly determine the matter summarily under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules and Hryniak?

Does the child continue to be in need of protection so that a further court order is required, and if so, is placement in the extended care of the Society (rather than return to the mother or placement with Ms JD) in the child's best interests?
Should the court order access to the child in extended society care, and can it instead make an order 'silent' as to access?

firac.issue: Was the letter from the Jean Tweed Centre admissible on the summary judgment motion?
firac.facts: The mother sought to rely on a letter from Marcie Pekar of the Jean Tweed Centre, attached as an exhibit to her affidavit, offering opinions from Ms Pekar and unnamed staff about the mother's parenting and attachment. The Society did not object but urged limited weight; the mother urged considerable weight.
firac.rule: On a summary judgment motion the evidence presented must be 'trial worthy' (Children's Aid Society of Ottawa v. J.B. and H.H., 2016 ONSC 2757; Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. B.B., 2012 ONCJ 646). The same admissibility standard applies to parents and to the Society; a court acts as gatekeeper and should not admit inadmissible evidence merely to give it no weight.
firac.application: The letter contained hearsay opinions from unidentified staff, no explanation why an affidavit could not be sworn, no information on the author's qualifications to opine on attachment or parenting, and facts contrary to both the Society's and the mother's own evidence. Admitting it would deprive the opposing party of cross-examination. Even if admitted it would carry no weight, being nearly a year old and predating the mother's termination of involvement with Jean Tweed.
firac.conclusion: The letter was inadmissible; exclusion was not unduly prejudicial since there was no dispute the mother attended the programs and other admissible evidence showed positive interactions.

firac.issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial, or could the matter be decided summarily?
firac.facts: The Society moved for summary judgment on its status review application; the mother argued there were triable issues about returning the child to her care, but pleaded no specific facts and largely admitted or did not dispute the Society's evidence over 17 months of involvement.
firac.rule: Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules: the moving party must show no genuine issue requiring a trial (r. 16(4)); the responding party may not rest on mere allegations but must set out specific facts showing a genuine issue (r. 16(4.1)) and must 'put its best foot forward.' Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, as applied to child protection in Kawartha-Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2018 ONSC 2783 and L.M. v. CAS of Peel, 2019 ONSC 1566, governs; summary judgment is granted sparingly in protection cases but the pre-Hryniak higher-threshold jurisprudence no longer applies.
firac.application: The judge found she could make the necessary findings of fact, apply the law, and reach a fair and just determination on the record without the expanded powers or oral evidence, and that doing so was proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive. The mother identified no specific triable issues and offered no description of evidence she would call; merely advancing a plan does not entitle a parent to a trial.
firac.conclusion: There was no genuine issue requiring a trial; the matter was properly determined summarily on its merits.

firac.issue: Does the child continue to be in need of protection, and is extended society care in his best interests?
firac.facts: The child was apprehended at six days old in November 2017 after a safety plan failed; he had been in care 17 months, exceeding statutory timelines. The mother had persistent unaddressed issues: mental health/depression, inability to meet her own medical and financial needs, keeping her home clean, safe and bug-free, lack of supports, and sporadic access. Alternative plans were her care with supervision or placement with Ms JD.
firac.rule: Status review under ss. 113-114 CYFSA; the original order is presumed correct and the court assesses whether protection concerns persist (CCAS of Metropolitan Toronto v. M.(C.), [1994] 2 SCR 165) and the best interests of the child under s. 74(3), from the child's perspective (CAS of Niagara Region v. B.P. and B.W., 2018 ONSC 4371). Section 122 limits interim care duration; extensions only if in the child's best interests. A parent's plan must be plausible on the whole record (CAS of Sudbury and Manitoulin v. T.S., 2011 ONCJ 745).
firac.application: The same concerns that led to apprehension continued; the mother showed no insight and no sustained improvement despite 17 months of Society and Jean Tweed support. Her plan merely restated what she had consistently failed to do and lacked reality and detail. Ms JD's plan was last-minute, ill-conceived, and already showing tension on the first visit. No evidence supported extending timelines.
firac.conclusion: The child continues to need protection; the only viable plan in his best interests is placement in the extended care of the Society, with a view to adoption.

firac.issue: Should access be ordered, and can an order be 'silent' as to access?
firac.facts: The Society sought an order silent as to access for adoption flexibility; the mother sought access. She had attended roughly one-fifth of offered visits by early 2019, with lengthy absences.
firac.rule: Following CAS of Toronto v. D.P., [2005] O.J. No. 930, a court cannot make an order 'silent' as to access to circumvent the statutory scheme; it must decide the access question. Under s. 105(5)-(6) CYFSA the court shall not order access to a child in extended care unless satisfied it is in the child's best interests, considering whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and whether access would impair adoption; the onus is on the person seeking access (CAS of Niagara Region v. B.P. and B.W.).
firac.application: The court had to decide access rather than remain silent. Applying s. 74(3) best interests factors, the mother led no evidence that access was beneficial and meaningful from the child's perspective; that visits were pleasant and the mother loved the child was insufficient. The young child needed permanency; access would delay and impair adoption, and severing ties would be minimally disruptive given no distress over her long absences.
firac.conclusion: No access was ordered; the child is placed in extended society care with no access to permit prompt permanency.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area, as this is a child protection proceeding under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test for both disposition and access under s. 74(3) and s. 105 CYFSA. K048 (custody/access) captures the contested access determination and the refusal of access to a child in extended care. K002 (Civil litigation) reflects the substantial procedural dimension — a Rule 16 summary judgment motion applying Hryniak and evidentiary admissibility/gatekeeping. K012 (procedural fairness) is a borderline pick, engaged by the discussion of deprivation of a parent's day in court, cross-examination rights, and the gatekeeper role on summary judgment. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated child-protection/child-welfare term, so K002 and K012 are somewhat broad proxies and are flagged as the weaker choices.
location_rationale: The applicant is the 'Children's Aid Society of Toronto' and the decision is styled 'ONTARIO COURT OF JUSTICE' with court file No. C11883/17. The Society and the proceedings are situated in Toronto, and events (Etobicoke General Hospital, Rexdale, Mimico) are within the Toronto area, supporting Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The heading identifies the Ontario Court of Justice and court file No. C11883/17; the applicant is the Children's Aid Society of Toronto, indicating the Toronto registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Dr. Frank Fowlie v. David Spinney, Ahmed Shamiya, and Mara Schiavulli

defining_issues: Did the defendants show that the defamation proceeding arises from an expression that relates to a matter of public interest under s. 137.1(3) of the Courts of Justice Act?
Did the plaintiff show, under s. 137.1(4)(a), that there are grounds to believe the proceeding has substantial merit and that the defendants have no valid defence?

Did the plaintiff show, under s. 137.1(4)(b), that the harm suffered is sufficiently serious that the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue outweighs the public interest in protecting the expression?

firac.issue: Did the defendants establish that the action arises from an expression relating to a matter of public interest under s. 137.1(3)?
firac.facts: Between February and December 2021, coaches David Spinney and Ahmed Shamiya, and Mara Schiavulli (mother of wrestler Madison Parks), sent numerous emails to figures in the wrestling and amateur-sport communities and to government officials criticizing Dr. Fowlie's conduct and suitability as Complaints and Appeals Officer (CAO) of Wrestling Canada Lutte (WCL), a largely publicly funded national governing body. The emails concerned his handling of complaints, alleged breaches of confidentiality, and his prior public record.
firac.rule: 'Expression' is broadly defined in s. 137.1(2). Under s. 137.1(3) and 1704604 Ontario Ltd. v. Pointes Protection Association, 2020 SCC 22, the moving party need only show that some segment of the community would have a genuine interest in receiving information on the subject; 'public interest' is given a broad, generous interpretation with no qualitative assessment of the expression (Buttar, 2023 ONCA 539; Sokoloff, 2020 ONCA 730).
firac.application: All the impugned emails related to Dr. Fowlie's decision-making, conduct and suitability as CAO. The CAO role was central to WCL's independent complaints and discipline process created after the 2018 Bennett Report found systemic abuse in Canadian wrestling. Athlete safety in a publicly funded Olympic sport, and confidence in the complaints system, are matters in which the wrestling community and the broader public have a genuine interest. Dr. Fowlie himself conceded on cross-examination that the emails related directly to his CAO role and that the public has an interest in athlete safety.
firac.conclusion: The defendants met their burden under s. 137.1(3); the action arises from expression relating to a matter of public interest.

firac.issue: Did Dr. Fowlie show grounds to believe the proceeding has substantial merit and that the defendants have no valid defence under s. 137.1(4)(a)?
firac.facts: Dr. Fowlie's statement of claim reproduced emails from all three defendants describing him as, among other things, abusive, deceitful, a bully, a misogynist, and racist, and referencing a Canadian Transportation Agency finding against him. The defendants pleaded qualified privilege, fair comment and (for Spinney and Schiavulli) justification.
firac.rule: Substantial merit requires a real prospect of success (Pointes, para. 49). Defamation requires publication to a third party, reference to the plaintiff, and words tending to lower reputation in a reasonable person's eyes (Bent v. Platnick, 2020 SCC 23). The plaintiff must show the defences have no real prospect of success; a defence that 'could go either way' is not defeated (Buttar; Bondfield). Qualified privilege attaches to a reciprocal duty/interest occasion and is defeated by malice or exceeding scope (Bent; Thatcher-Craig, 2023 ONCA 96). Fair comment requires public interest, factual basis, recognizable comment, an objective honesty test, and can be defeated by malice (WIC Radio v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Hansman, 2023 SCC 14).
firac.application: Some emails from each defendant contained words that would tend to lower Dr. Fowlie's reputation, so the defamation claim had substantial merit. As advocates for wrestlers and, for Schiavulli, a parent, the defendants had an interest/duty to communicate their concerns to recipients with a corresponding interest, establishing qualified privilege. However, some record evidence of ill-will (Spinney's threat that Fowlie would 'feel some lasting effects'; Shamiya's threat to bring protesters to Fowlie's IRB workplace) meant the qualified privilege and fair comment defences of Spinney and Shamiya could go either way. There was no evidence of malice by Schiavulli, and her factual bases and the justification defence (supported by admissions and the record) were not shown to fail. The abandoned internet-harassment and false-light claims were found meritless.
firac.conclusion: Dr. Fowlie showed grounds to believe the defamation claim had substantial merit and that Spinney and Shamiya had no valid defence, but failed to do so as against Schiavulli, whose motion was granted at this stage.

firac.issue: Did the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue outweigh the public interest in protecting the expression under s. 137.1(4)(b)?
firac.facts: Dr. Fowlie claimed over $800,000, asserting the emails cost him his WCL contract, tarnished his reputation and caused health problems. WCL's executive director testified the contract was terminated for WCL's own reasons based on Fowlie's own conduct, not the defendants' emails. Dr. Fowlie continued as an IRB member and held other sports roles; he relied only on the presumption of general damages and led no medical evidence (a supporting affidavit was struck).
firac.rule: The weighing exercise is the crux of the analysis (Pointes, para. 18, 53). The plaintiff must show harm that is 'serious' and causally linked to the expression; presumed general damages and bare assertions are insufficient (Hansman, 2023 SCC 14; Gill v. Maciver, 2024 ONCA 126; Park Lawn, 2023 ONCA 129). Harm is assessed against any pre-existing blemishes on reputation (Levant, 2022 ONCA 79). Quality of and motivation behind the expression, and the chilling effect, are weighed (Pointes, paras. 73-74; Hansman, paras. 76-77).
firac.application: Dr. Fowlie provided no evidence permitting an inference of serious harm; the loss of the WCL contract was attributable to his own performance, not the defendants. His reputation was already blemished by the 2010 CTA decision and a 2019 SDRCC decision, both public. The expression addressed important issues of athlete safety and integrity of a complaints process in a publicly funded sport, and the defendants had no history or animus toward him. Allowing the suit would chill others from speaking out. Fowlie's numerous retaliatory steps (RCMP complaint, complaints to regulators, employers and Ministry of Labour) indicated the action bore the hallmarks of a SLAPP seeking retribution.
firac.conclusion: Dr. Fowlie failed to show serious harm outweighing the public interest in protecting the expression; the balance favoured the defendants and the action was dismissed in its entirety.

keywords_rationale: The case is a civil defamation action, so K002 (Civil litigation, tier-1 practice area) and K015 (defamation) are core. The defences analysed were fair comment (K016) and qualified privilege (K018), both central to the s. 137.1(4)(a) 'no valid defence' inquiry. K024 (freedom of expression) is engaged because anti-SLAPP legislation exists to protect expression on matters of public interest and the weighing exercise turned on that value. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is a weaker pick — the anti-SLAPP dismissal motion is a screening/procedural remedy and the vocabulary has no dedicated SLAPP or dismissal-motion term; it is included as the closest procedural-remedy keyword but is flagged as borderline. There is no controlled-vocabulary term for anti-SLAPP or 'strategic lawsuit against public participation,' which would otherwise be the most specific tag.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE - ONTARIO', establishing the province as Ontario. No city or sitting location is stated in the text, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision bears court file no. CV-22-88853 but does not name a specific court registry or office, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Garrick v. Saporowski

defining_issues: What access order is in the child's best interests?
Should income be imputed to the father and what should the ongoing table amount of child support be?
Should the outstanding child support arrears be reduced or rescinded?

firac.issue: What access order is in the child's best interests, given the father's lengthy history of fraud convictions and repeated incarcerations?
firac.facts: The father sought roughly equal 'week about' parenting time, or liberal overnight access, to the child Wolf (born 2004). The mother had sole custody (unappealed 2012 order) and sought to maintain the existing alternate-Sunday daytime access with supervised exchanges. The father had been repeatedly incarcerated for fraud, spent significant portions of Wolf's early years in custody, faced a possible further two-year default sentence, showed no remorse, and had emotionally harmed the mother's older son Denzil by posing as his biological father and then abandoning him. Wolf was thriving in the mother's stable home; he enjoyed his father and paternal grandparents.
firac.rule: Access is determined by the best interests of the child under ss. 24(2), (3) and (4) of the Children's Law Reform Act, with past conduct considered where relevant to ability to parent. Maximum contact with both parents is encouraged where consistent with best interests (Gordon v. Goertz; Young v. Young); a non-custodial parent's regular access is presumptively beneficial and forfeited only in extreme circumstances (Jafari v. Dadar); the party seeking to restrict normal access must justify the restriction, and access may be limited to minimize risk from a parent's conduct or lifestyle (M.A. v. J.D.; W.(B.H.) v. W.(S.M.)).
firac.application: Weighing the statutory factors, the court found Wolf lived in a stable home with the mother as primary caregiver and was doing well. The father's incarcerations and risk of future imprisonment (including a possible default sentence when Wolf would be about 15) made a shared or greatly expanded schedule potentially traumatic and disruptive. The court preferred the mother's credible evidence over the father's grandiose, evasive and contradictory testimony, and found the profound harm the father caused Denzil, his lack of remorse, and his beginning to tell Wolf he was wrongfully convicted, all counselled caution. Nonetheless Wolf loved his father and grandparents and the existing order had gone well, so modest expansion was warranted.
firac.conclusion: Access was modestly expanded to include a Saturday overnight on alternating weekends (plus specified holiday, summer and telephone access), with supervised exchanges, conditional on the father residing with the paternal grandparents; the father's request for equal/50% parenting time was refused.

firac.issue: Should income be imputed to the father and what should the ongoing table amount of child support be?
firac.facts: The father claimed no income and inability to work owing to incarceration, bail conditions, lack of identity documents and his criminal record. However he was a beneficiary of a substantial trust set up by his grandfather (from which he testified he had accessed up to $3.5 million and bought a $1.8 million New York apartment), had funded a comfortable lifestyle and over $500,000 in legal fees, and disclosed nothing about the trust. His CRA assessments showed prior income up to $146,000. He was intelligent, educated and, at the time of judgment, not incarcerated and free to work.
firac.rule: Under ss. 19(1) and (2) of the Child Support Guidelines (O. Reg. 391/97) the court may impute income, including where a payor is intentionally under-employed (s. 19(1)(a)) or is a beneficiary receiving benefits from a trust (s. 19(1)(i)). Drygala v. Pauli sets the test for intentional under-employment; adverse inferences may be drawn for failure to disclose (Smith v. Pellegrini; Maimone v. Maimone).
firac.application: The court found the father was a beneficiary of and had access to the grandfather's trust under s. 19(1)(i), and had failed entirely to disclose it. He was also intentionally under-employed given his capacity, education and freedom to work. Considering trust access, earning capacity and the pre-separation lifestyle funded by the trust, income of $75,000 per year was reasonably imputed. The prior $1,000 temporary figure (on imputed income of $66,900) was unexplained and appeared simply incorrect.
firac.conclusion: Income of $75,000 was imputed; ongoing child support was set at the Ontario table amount for one child ($782/month, commencing November 1, 2015), with annual disclosure including the trust settlement and financial statements.

firac.issue: Should the father's accumulated child support arrears be reduced or rescinded?
firac.facts: The father had paid only one $1,000 payment since the December 22, 2009 temporary order and nothing for years before, leaving arrears of roughly $70,000. He asserted inability to pay; his father testified he avoided depositing funds because accounts would be seized by the Family Responsibility Office. The mother had struggled financially, relied on social assistance and her parents, and had her credit destroyed by the father's identity misuse.
firac.rule: The discretion to reduce arrears must be exercised judicially per DiFrancesco v. Couto (nature of obligation, ongoing capacity, ongoing need, delay in enforcement, delay by payor, and undue hardship). Mere accumulation without proven past and future inability to pay does not justify relief (Haisman v. Haisman); the D.B.S. factors also inform reduction/rescission (Galloway v. Cassino; H.F. v. P.F.).
firac.application: Applying the DiFrancesco factors, the court found a court-ordered obligation never followed, no payments for years, prompt enforcement efforts by the mother, apparent avoidance of enforcement by the father, genuine financial need of the mother and child, and no evidence that payment would cause hardship given the father's trust access. The father was willing to fund private school and gifts but refused table support. Arrears were recalculated on the corrected table amount for imputed income of $75,000 over five years and ten months, less a $1,000 credit.
firac.conclusion: Relief was largely refused; arrears were fixed at $53,740 (exclusive of interest), payable within 30 days, reflecting the corrected table amount rather than any rescission for hardship.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) and K048 (custody/access) capture the central access determination under the Children's Law Reform Act. K050 (parental support) covers the child-support determination, imputation of income under s. 19 of the Guidelines, and the arrears analysis. K052 (religious upbringing) is engaged by the contested question of whether Wolf should be raised Jewish (father) or Catholic (mother), a recurring theme though not outcome-determinative. K093 (Jewish) is a weak/borderline entity pick reflecting the father's claimed conversion to Judaism and desire to raise the child in the Jewish faith; it is included only because that dispute recurs, but it is peripheral to the ratio.
location_rationale: The decision is a judgment of the Ontario Court of Justice bearing court file 'Halton 188/09' and the parties reside in Oakville, Ontario, with the supervised access facility located on Brant St., Burlington, Ontario. No single sitting city is expressly stated, so city is left null; the province is Ontario (Ontario Court of Justice, Children's Law Reform Act).
registry_rationale: The court file number is stated as 'Halton 188/09', identifying the Halton registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. S.C.M.K.

name_verification.name_in_document: Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S.C.M.K.

defining_issues: Should the court adjourn the trial and/or extend the statutory time limit under s. 122(5) of the CYFSA to allow the grandmother's late-advanced plan to be assessed?
Does the child continue to be a child in need of protection on the status review?
Which disposition — placement with the grandmother on a supervision order, further interim society care, or extended society care — is in the child's best interests?
What form of access should be ordered following extended society care, and who should be designated the access holder?

firac.issue: Should the court adjourn the trial or extend the statutory time limit under s. 122(5) of the CYFSA to allow the grandmother's plan to be assessed?
firac.facts: T.K. had been in the society's continuous care since December 6, 2019 (from about two weeks old), 18 months by trial — six months beyond the 12-month limit in s. 122(1)(a) for a child under six. The maternal grandmother advanced her plan only about three days before trial, after the great-grandmother's kin plan had been withdrawn months earlier.
firac.rule: Section 122(1) of the CYFSA caps interim society care at 12 months for a child under six; s. 122(5) permits a single six-month extension only if it is in the child's best interests. Extensions require 'unusual, exceptional, or equitable considerations' and should not be routinely used (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. LU, 2008 CanLII 26661 (ON SC)). Delay in child protection is measured from the child's perspective (CAS of Toronto v. T.(L.), 2016 ONCA 146).
firac.application: Family relationship is only one of the s. 74(3) best-interests factors and does not trump the effect of delay on a toddler. The grandmother came forward at the eleventh hour despite knowing no other kin plan existed; permitting a last-minute relative to halt trial 'is not the law.' Adding another six months to 18 months of litigation limbo was contrary to the Act's permanency objectives (ss. 1(2), 122(1)).
firac.conclusion: The adjournment motion and any s. 122(5) extension were refused; the trial proceeded.

firac.issue: Does T.K. continue to be a child in need of protection?
firac.facts: T.K. was found in need of protection on August 26, 2020 under s. 74(2)(n) (mother unable to care) per a signed statement of agreed facts. At trial the mother had no stable housing, was transient, had cognitive limitations (mild intellectual disability, suspected FASD), had not taken a parenting program or COVID test, and conceded she could not parent alone; no community supports were proven.
firac.rule: On a status review under ss. 113–114, the court applies the two-step test in Children's Aid Society of Oxford v. W.T.C., 2013 ONCA 491: it must first determine whether a court order is necessary to protect the child in future, considering present circumstances and any new concerns (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S.P., 2019 ONSC 3482), guided by the paramount best-interests purpose in s. 1(1).
firac.application: The parties agreed protection continued. The mother's situation had not materially changed since the SAF: no stable housing, no demonstrated supports, continuing cognitive limitations and transiency. She remained unable to care for T.K.
firac.conclusion: T.K. continues to be a child in need of protection.

firac.issue: Which disposition is in T.K.'s best interests — grandmother supervision, further interim care, or extended society care?
firac.facts: The grandmother lived in a shelter, had had virtually no contact with T.K. for about nine months, missed the Family Group Conference, declined virtual visits, never returned the worker's calls, was in unresolved conflict with the mother, and knew little about the child. The mother's alternative was six more months of interim care to assess that plan.
firac.rule: Section 101(1) requires the court to select the order in the child's best interests, after considering efforts to assist (s. 101(2)), less disruptive alternatives (s. 101(3)) and community/relative placement (s. 101(4), s. 102), applying the s. 74(3) best-interests factors and the paramount purpose (s. 1(1)); relative placement is weighed like any other factor (CAS of Northumberland v. D.P.).
firac.application: The grandmother's proposal was 'little more than a plan to make a plan,' revealing little insight and a serious lack of commitment. Further interim care would require an unwarranted s. 122(5) extension absent the 'unusual, exceptional, or equitable' circumstances described. The society had made reasonable efforts, considered less disruptive alternatives and pursued kin placements up to trial, leaving extended society care as the only option consistent with T.K.'s need for permanency.
firac.conclusion: T.K. placed in the extended care of the society; the supervision and further interim-care requests were dismissed.

firac.issue: What access should be ordered after extended society care, and who should be the access holder?
firac.facts: In-person visits ceased in March 2020; virtual visits were sporadic and short, and the mother chose to stop all visits after April 8, 2021, two months before trial. T.K. was 18 months old with only minor special needs and good adoptive prospects.
firac.rule: Under s. 105(5)–(7), access to a child in extended society care is ordered only if in the child's best interests, considering whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and whether access would impair future adoption (s. 105(6)); the new CYFSA removed the presumption against access and makes best interests predominant (CAS of Toronto v. J.G., 2020 ONCA 415), with access meant only to preserve an existing beneficial relationship (CAS of Toronto v. Y.M., 2019 ONCJ 489). Only the access holder may apply for an openness order (ss. 195–196).
firac.application: There was no meaningful relationship to preserve given the thin, discontinued contact; in-person visits and video calls would confuse rather than benefit T.K. Written/photo contact preserved his ability to know his story without impairing adoption. Making the mother a joint access holder risked, given her lack of insight, an openness application that could unduly delay adoption.
firac.conclusion: Ordered non-visit contact (letters, cards, photos, videos by email), with T.K. as sole access holder and the mother as access recipient.

case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. J.T.

name_verification.name_in_document: Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. J.T.

defining_issues: Was summary judgment appropriate, i.e. was there no genuine issue requiring a trial, given the heightened caution required in child protection proceedings?
What disposition order is in the child's best interests — return to the parent under supervision, or extended society care?
What access order is in the child's best interests once the child is placed in extended society care?
Should the parent be an access holder or only an access recipient?

firac.issue: Was summary judgment appropriate under rule 16 of the Family Law Rules, given the exceptional caution required in child protection cases?
firac.facts: The matter had twice been set for trial but was adjourned when the parent was hospitalized and later when he refused to participate. The parent was found a special party and the PGT appointed. The society moved for summary judgment relying on trial affidavits, joint document briefs, medical/police records and a psychological assessment; the material facts were largely uncontested. The parent did not attend the motion.
firac.rule: Rule 16 Family Law Rules and the two-step test in Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7: there is no genuine issue requiring a trial where the judge can make necessary findings of fact, apply the law, and do so in a proportionate, expeditious and less expensive way. In child protection, exceptional caution is required and the objectives of the CYFSA and the child's best interests govern, per Kawartha Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316; L.M. v. CAS Peel, 2019 ONCA 841. The moving party bears the burden; the court must still be satisfied on the evidence even if the respondent fails to raise a genuine issue.
firac.application: The court screened out inadmissible evidence and found the record comprehensive, with material facts either undisputed or not meaningfully contested. It could make the necessary findings without weighing evidence or assessing credibility, and cross-examination would add little. Given the child had been in care over 26 months, summary disposition was not merely efficient but necessary to achieve the Act's objectives.
firac.conclusion: There was no genuine issue requiring a trial; the society established a prima facie case and the parent failed to show any triable issue. Summary judgment was granted.

firac.issue: What disposition order is in the child's best interests — supervised return to the parent or extended society care?
firac.facts: The six-year-old child has Autism Spectrum Disorder and Intellectual Disability with significant special needs. The parent has a primary psychotic disorder with two major involuntary hospitalizations, delusional and aggressive behaviour, criminal charges and convictions (including threatening society workers), and shows little insight or engagement with treatment. The child showed neglect (not attending school, matted hair, dirty) when apprehended. A prior supervision-order return in 2023 broke down.
firac.rule: CYFSA ss. 101(1) (menu of orders), 101(2)-(4) (efforts to assist, least disruptive alternatives, community/family placements), s. 1 (paramount purpose — best interests, protection and well-being), and best-interests factors in s. 74(3). Mental illness alone does not establish need for protection (CAS Toronto v. R.S., 2019 ONCJ 866); court assesses severity, insight, treatment compliance and impact on parenting. A supervision order requires confidence the parent will comply (Windsor-Essex CAS v. L.H.).
firac.application: The court found the risks of physical/emotional harm remained unacceptably high; the parent's severe untreated mental health, lack of insight, hostility and inability to work with the society made a supervision order unworkable. No family/community plan materialized. The child needs stability and a caregiver able to collaborate with service providers. The statutory two-year care limit (ss. 122(1),(3)) had been exceeded, leaving only return or extended society care.
firac.conclusion: Extended society care is the least disruptive alternative consistent with the child's best interests; the child is placed in extended society care.

firac.issue: What access order is in the child's best interests for a child in extended society care?
firac.facts: Since April 2025 the parent has had weekly virtual access, generally positive and beneficial, though visits often end early due to the child's attention span and the parent has recently missed some. In-person access is problematic due to the parent's mental health, aggression and refusal to engage with the society. The society sought a minimum of six visits per year in its discretion; the PGT sought weekly in-person and weekly virtual visits.
firac.rule: CYFSA ss. 105(4)-(6): once extended society care is ordered prior access terminates; access may be ordered only if in the child's best interests, considering s. 74(3) factors, whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful, and (if relevant) impairment of adoption opportunities. Kawartha (2019 ONCA 316) removed the presumption against access and the burden shift. Access discretion may be delegated to the society only if significantly circumscribed by minimum rights (J.S.R. v. CAS Ottawa, 2021 ONSC 630; CAS Toronto v. J.G., 2020 ONCA 315).
firac.application: The court found access beneficial and meaningful, and that the child became dysregulated when visits lapsed, so the society's proposed six visits a year was insufficient. But the parent's untreated mental health, aggression, lack of transparency, missed visits and the need to preserve a limited adoption pool weighed against frequent access. The court balanced these by ordering a minimum of once every other week, with the society given discretion over location, duration, supervision and method, and safeguards (early termination; reduction to monthly if four visits missed in two months).
firac.conclusion: Access is ordered at a minimum of once every other week, supervised, with defined society discretion and safeguards.

firac.issue: Should the parent be an access holder or only an access recipient?
firac.facts: The parent loves the child and has not undermined the foster placement, and had not been dysregulated at a virtual visit since October 2025. However he has anger/aggression/impulse-control problems, a conviction for threatening two workers, serious untreated mental health, a chaotic life, non-transparency, and his condition had repeatedly delayed the proceeding (vacated trial dates, refusal to participate).
firac.rule: CYFSA s. 105(7) requires identifying access holder vs recipient; only an access holder may bring an openness application on a Notice of Intent to place for adoption. Impairment of adoption opportunity (including undue delay) takes heightened importance; attributes suggesting impairment include aggression/anger, lack of support for alternate caregivers, dishonesty, litigiousness, and mental health/chaotic lifestyle (CAS Toronto v. A.F., 2015 ONCJ 678; CCAS v. A.P., 2019 ONCJ 631; affirmed CAS Toronto v. R.E., 2025 ONCA 623).
firac.application: Weighing the A.F./A.P. attributes, the court found the parent's aggression, lack of transparency, ungovernability and chaotic mental health likely to deter a limited pool of prospective adoptive parents and to delay any openness application, outweighing the factors favouring holder status. Protection was provided by ordering that any Notice of Intent be served on the PGT (and the Office of the Children's Lawyer), and the child, given his age and bond, would likely bring an openness application.
firac.conclusion: The child is the access holder and the parent is the access recipient; any Notice of Intent to place for adoption must be served on the PGT.

case_name: Jones v. Industrial Wood and Allied Workers of Canada (Local 1-3567)

name_verification.name_in_document: Jones v. Industrial Wood and Allied Workers of Canada (Local 1-3567)

defining_issues: Whether the impugned paragraphs of the petition and the petitioner's affidavit should be struck under Rule 19(24) as disclosing no reasonable claim, being unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, or as containing argument rather than admissible fact in a judicial review proceeding.

firac.issue: On an application to strike under Rule 19(24), which of the challenged paragraphs of a petition and affidavit filed in support of judicial review of a labour board decision are inadmissible because they are irrelevant, unnecessary, or amount to argument rather than fact?
firac.facts: Remond Jones sought judicial review of an LRB decision (and its reconsideration) dismissing his s. 12 Labour Relations Code complaint that the Union had failed to represent him fairly against his employer, Canfor. The Union applied to strike paras. 59, 60 and 62 of the petition and various paragraphs of Jones's affidavit, arguing they disclosed no reasonable claim, were scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, or contained argument rather than fact. Much of the impugned material described the personal/reputational impact of the events on Jones and characterized the LRB's findings in inflammatory, adjective-laced terms.
firac.rule: Rule 19(24) of the Rules of Court permits striking pleadings (and, per Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860, affidavits) that disclose no reasonable claim, are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, may prejudice or delay, or are an abuse of process. Rule 51(10) confines affidavits to what a deponent could state in evidence at trial. Affidavits must state facts only, not adjectival opinion or argument (Creber v. Franklin; Kennedy v. Kennedy, 2006 BCSC 190; Chamberlain v. Surrey School District No. 36). On judicial review the materials are generally restricted to the record before the tribunal; evidence going to procedural fairness may be admissible but must not amount to a reinterpretation of the record or a rehearing on the merits (Kinexus Bioinformatics Corp. v. Asad, 2010 BCSC 33). The court cannot award damages on judicial review (Judicial Review Procedure Act, s. 2; McLean v. British Columbia).
firac.application: The live issues on the judicial review were whether the LRB decisions met the standard of review and whether Jones was denied procedural fairness. Measured against these, the court struck material dealing only with the personal, emotional and reputational impact on Jones (paras. 59 of the petition; 29-33 of the affidavit) as irrelevant and, in the case of para. 59, argument for which no damages could be awarded. Paragraphs mixing fact with argument were partially cured: 'incorrectly' was deleted from para. 19 and an argumentative phrase from para. 21, preserving the relevant factual allegations about the fairness of the LRB process and absence of cross-examination. Paragraphs 23 and 24 were struck entirely as predominantly argumentative and inflammatory, seeking to re-argue inferences from the record. Paragraph 60 (nature of the employer's conduct as disciplinary) and para. 62 (the 2005 internal Union report) of the petition, and paras. 26-28 of the affidavit (alleged bias/improper purposes of Union officials, already before the LRB), were held potentially relevant to the standard-of-review question and were not struck.
firac.conclusion: Application granted in part: para. 59 of the petition and paras. 23-24, 29, 30-33 of the affidavit struck; 'incorrectly' struck from para. 19 and the specified phrase from para. 21, with the balance saved; the applications to strike paras. 60 and 62 of the petition and paras. 26-28 of the affidavit denied. Given divided success, each party bears its own costs.

keywords_rationale: The ruling arises in a judicial review of a Labour Relations Board decision, so K001 (Administrative law) and K011 (judicial review) are core, as is K014 (standard of review) and K012 (procedural fairness) since the court framed relevance around whether the LRB decision met the standard of review and whether Jones was afforded a fair process. K009 (Labour and employment) and K084 (labour arbitration — grievance/duty of fair representation) capture the underlying s. 12 fair-representation complaint about the Union's handling of Jones's grievance against Canfor. K083 (harassment) is engaged because the substrate is a sexual-harassment investigation and allegations of harassment by Union officials, though it is borderline as the ruling does not decide those merits. K002 (civil litigation) reflects the procedural nature of the motion to strike pleadings/affidavit evidence; it is a supporting/weak pick since no dedicated 'strike pleadings' keyword exists in the vocabulary.
