name_verification.name_in_document: Droit de la famille — 162274

defining_issues: When separated parents with joint custody cannot agree on their child's secondary school, on what basis must the court decide?
How much weight should the court give to the wishes previously expressed by a 12-year-old child regarding her choice of school?
Which school best serves the child's best interest, considering academic quality, artistic development, and continuation of her Jewish education?

firac.issue: On what legal basis must the court resolve a dispute between parents over the choice of their child's secondary school?
firac.facts: The divorced parents share custody of their 12-year-old daughter X and have amicably resolved past disagreements, but they are at an impasse over whether she should attend [School A] (arts focus) or [School B] (strong academics with Jewish studies).
firac.rule: Under art. 604 C.C.Q., where difficulties arise in the exercise of parental authority, the court decides 'in the interest of the child' after fostering conciliation. Art. 33 C.C.Q. requires all decisions concerning a child to be made in light of the child's interests and rights, considering the child's moral, intellectual, emotional and physical needs, age, health, personality and family environment.
firac.application: The choice of school ordinarily falls under parental authority and is best left to the parents in consultation with the child, but because the parents remained deadlocked despite court-fostered conciliation, the court had to decide. It applied the sole criterion of the child's best interest under arts. 33 and 604 C.C.Q.
firac.conclusion: The court proceeded to determine, on the evidence, which school placement was in X's best interest.

firac.issue: How much weight should be given to the child's previously expressed preference for [School A]?
firac.facts: Between February and June 2015, when she was 11, X expressed a preference for [School A], including in a letter (GK-1). By July 2015 she stepped back, saying she would be happy at either school, and by 2016 she told her lawyer she had no preference and wanted the judge to decide.
firac.rule: An informed wish freely expressed by a child aged 12 or more, without undue influence, is a largely determining factor because it often corresponds to the child's interest (Droit de la famille – 1883; Droit de la famille – 07832; Droit de la famille – 15754). Art. 34 C.C.Q. requires giving the child an opportunity to be heard where age and discernment permit. However, the court is not bound by the child's choice where other factors show it is not in her best interest, and parental authority is not transferred to the child.
firac.application: The court found X's 2015 preference was not fully informed or grounded: she was only 11, her enthusiasm shifted after each school visit, she chose [School A] before visiting [School B], her motivation was limited to the arts program, and she was influenced (unintentionally) by her father's enthusiasm; part of the GK-1 letter was written in defiance and frustration toward her mother. By 2016 she expressed no clear or definite preference. Allegations that the mother had bribed or coerced X rested on inadmissible hearsay and, in any event, were outweighed by the mother's credible denials.
firac.conclusion: X's wish could not be a determining or decisive factor, as it was neither fully informed nor currently clear and definite; the decision had to be made on best-interest grounds.

firac.issue: Which school best serves X's best interest?
firac.facts: Both schools are private, government-accredited and follow the Quebec curriculum. X is a bright, hardworking student interested in sciences and maths, passionate and talented in the arts, and aspires to become a neuroradiologist. She attended a Jewish elementary school; both parents are Jewish, the mother being more observant. [School B] offers high-standard secular studies plus Jewish studies as one of four pillars, along with arts opportunities; [School A] has an excellent arts program but is non-denominational.
firac.rule: The best interest of the child under arts. 33 and 604 C.C.Q. governs, assessed on the child's abilities, character, needs and family environment.
firac.application: The court found [School B] a step above academically and better suited to X's needs, based on the school officials' testimony and the mother's carefully considered understanding of her daughter. X could continue developing her artistic interests at either school, as arts is a pillar at [School B] and the mother would continue supporting her artistic pursuits. The evidence showed X's Jewish education, begun in elementary school, was incomplete and important to her (interest in her Jewish identity, kosher eating), and Jewish studies at [School B] would complete it in a balanced, non-insular environment; the father's proposed after-school program was not equivalent. Attending [School B] would also facilitate continued joint custody between a secular father and observant mother.
firac.conclusion: It was in X's best interest to attend [School B]; the father's motion to modify was dismissed and provisional execution ordered.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a parental-authority dispute under the C.C.Q. K047 (best interests of the child) is the central governing test (arts. 33, 604 C.C.Q.). K052 (religious upbringing) is squarely engaged since a key factor was completing X's Jewish education through Jewish studies at [School B]. K048 (custody/access) applies given the joint custody arrangement that framed the analysis. K093 (Jewish) identifies the family's identity and the religious dimension. K027 (Jewish holidays) and K028 (kosher/dietary law) are weaker, entity-level picks reflecting the discussion of the child's observance of Jewish holidays and her choice to eat only kosher meat — included as they evidence the sincerity/importance of her Jewish practice, though they are peripheral to the ratio.

name_verification.name_in_document: J.S. v. G.J.S.

defining_issues: Should custody of the children be joint (with equal parenting time) as the father seeks, or sole to the mother with defined access?
What access arrangement is in the best interests of the children?
What amount of child support should be ordered given the father's income?
Is either party entitled to spousal support?

firac.issue: Should custody be joint with equal parenting time, or sole custody to the mother?
firac.facts: After a 3.5-year marriage the parents separated. The father sought joint custody and guardianship with alternating weeks; the mother had held sole interim custody since 2001 and sought to keep it. The parties were locked in high-conflict relations, generating nine prior court orders, repeated frightening scenes at access exchanges, and an inability to communicate without rancour.
firac.rule: Under s. 16 of the Divorce Act and s. 24 of the Family Relations Act, the best interests of the child govern custody; the analysis is wide-ranging and free of any presumption for or against joint custody (Robinson v. Filyk; Gordon v. Goertz). Joint custody requires a degree of consultation and cooperation between parents (Lucken v. Hopkins; Ness v. Ness), though it can be ordered even where communication is difficult (P.Y.Y.M. v. D.M.; Carr v. Carr).
firac.application: The Court found the parties consistently unable to prevent tension and strife over access exchanges, causing trauma to the children, and unable to cooperate or agree on a schedule without recourse to the courts. A joint custody order would increase opportunities for conflict and expose the children to greater stress. The mother had been the primary caregiver and provided a stable home; the father, though a good parent to the children directly, showed uncontrolled, frightening behaviour at exchanges and lacked insight into it.
firac.conclusion: Joint custody was refused; the mother was granted continued sole custody and sole guardianship with the children's primary residence with her.

firac.issue: What access arrangement is in the children's best interests?
firac.facts: Dr. Elterman recommended alternating-week care (Wednesday to Monday). The children (ages 7 and 5) attended school in Langley, while the father lived in Vancouver, requiring 45–90 minutes of driving each way. The father's outbursts at exchanges risked psychological harm, though he posed no risk of physical harm.
firac.rule: Access is intended to facilitate a meaningful, continuing post-divorce relationship between children and the access parent, to the extent consistent with the children's best interests (Young v. Young; Anson v. Anson).
firac.application: The Court declined the expanded alternating-week arrangement, citing the burdensome travel from Langley to Vancouver on school days and, more importantly, concern about the father's emotional stability and the risk of psychological harm from his outbursts. The current arrangement, with adjustments, was found optimal to allow the children to know their father while preserving their stable environment.
firac.conclusion: The father was granted alternating weekend access (Friday to Monday), specified Jewish-holiday days (up to seven), birthday, Father's Day, long-weekend Mondays, summer weeks, half of spring break, and daily telephone access; the restraining injunction and police-clause order were continued.

firac.issue: What amount of child support should the father pay?
firac.facts: The father, a manufacturer's representative, ran nearly all expenses through his company and had been paying only $7 per month. The defendant calculated his average income plus 75% of operating expenses at about $39,925; his business had suffered from market conditions and an uncollectible receivable.
firac.rule: Child support is set under the Federal Child Support Guidelines according to the payor's income; a reasonable portion of business expenses may be reallocated as personal income where the evidence supports it.
firac.application: With little evidence distinguishing personal from business expenses but agreement that some reallocation was warranted, the Court imputed a total income of $25,000, yielding a guideline amount of $375 per month for two children.
firac.conclusion: The father was ordered to pay $375 per month in child support effective the first of the month following judgment.

firac.issue: Is either spouse entitled to spousal support?
firac.facts: The parties cohabited about 3.5 years. Neither showed substantial means; the father expected to rebuild his business once litigation ended, and the mother was a fitness trainer with a private clientele about to marry a capable, comfortably situated man.
firac.rule: Spousal support turns on the conditions, means, needs and other circumstances of each spouse, the length of cohabitation and each party's obligation to become self-sufficient (Divorce Act ss. 15.2(4) and (6); F.R.A. s. 89). Marriage alone does not entitle a spouse to support (Moge v. Moge; Bracklow v. Bracklow); a new relationship does not automatically disentitle (Boudreau v. Bradbury).
firac.application: Given the short marriage, the absence of compensatory economic loss, the modest means of both parties, and the mother's successful business and impending marriage providing a comfortable lifestyle, the Court found neither party had substantial means or great need for support.
firac.conclusion: No spousal support was ordered to either party; each party to bear its own costs.

K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) are the core of the custody and access determination under the Divorce Act s. 16 and F.R.A. s. 24. K050 (parental/child support) and K053 (spousal support) cover the two support claims decided. K021 (interlocutory injunction) captures the continued restraining/police-clause order restraining the father's contact. name_verification.name_in_document: Birju Dattani v. Melissa Lantsman et al.

defining_issues: Should the proposed interveners (Independent Jewish Voices Canada and the National Council of Canadian Muslims) be granted leave to intervene under Rule 13 in the anti-SLAPP motions?
Does s. 137.1(5) of the Courts of Justice Act prohibit any intervention in an anti-SLAPP motion?
In what order should oral argument on the anti-SLAPP motions proceed?

firac.issue: Should the proposed interveners (IJV and NCCM) be granted leave to intervene as parties or friends of the court under Rule 13 in the anti-SLAPP motions?
firac.facts: IJV and NCCM sought, at the eleventh hour after all evidence and 100-page factums had been exchanged, to intervene in defamation anti-SLAPP motions concerning statements that the plaintiff, a former Chief Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, was a 'terror supporter' and 'Jew-hater'. Both wished to file affidavits and make submissions on the meaning of anti-semitism (NCCM also on the impact of such accusations on Muslims). The plaintiff consented; the defendants opposed.
firac.rule: Rule 13.01 requires a proposed party-intervener to show they may be adversely affected by the judgment or share a common question of law or fact, subject to considering undue delay or prejudice; Rule 13.02 allows a friend of the court to render assistance by argument. The overarching question is whether the applicant can make a useful contribution without causing injustice to the parties (Animal Justice v. Ontario (AG), 2024 ONCA 941; Bedford v. Canada (AG), 2009 ONCA 669; Solmar Inc. v. Hall, 2025 ONCA 570; Peel v. Great Atlantic & Pacific). Intervention is granted sparingly in private disputes, even those with public-interest components, and anti-SLAPP motions under s. 137.1 CJA are meant to be a limited, expeditious screening exercise decided on a limited record (Pointes Protection, 2020 SCC 22; Benchwood Builders, 2025 ONCA 171; Hamer v. Jane Doe, 2024 ONCA 721).
firac.application: The court held these were private defamation actions between two parties each, not constitutional or public-interest litigation, so the intervention test applies more rigorously. Neither intervener had a legal interest at stake; IJV's concern about being called anti-semitic in cross-examinations was collateral and it had not sued. Their submissions on the meaning of anti-semitism would constitute a 'deep dive' into factual issues inconsistent with the limited anti-SLAPP weighing exercise, would augment an already extensive record, and were brought too late for the defendants to respond, risking prejudice and injustice. The plaintiff was well-represented and had already filed extensive evidence on the same issues.
firac.conclusion: The motions to intervene were dismissed.

firac.issue: Does s. 137.1(5) of the Courts of Justice Act bar interventions in an anti-SLAPP motion?
firac.facts: The defendants argued that s. 137.1(5)'s stay on further steps in the proceeding once an anti-SLAPP motion is made prohibits interventions.
firac.rule: Section 137.1(5) provides that once an anti-SLAPP motion is made, no further steps may be taken 'by any party' until the motion and any appeal are finally disposed of.
firac.application: The court disagreed: the provision restricts only parties, and potential interveners are not parties; there is a distinction between steps in the underlying proceeding and steps within the anti-SLAPP motion itself (Catalyst Capital, 2021 ONSC 125); and interveners have participated in anti-SLAPP motions and appeals before (Rainbow Alliance Dryden v. Webster, 2023 ONSC 7050; 40 Days for Life v. Dietrich; Buttar; Hansman v. Neufeld, 2023 SCC 14).
firac.conclusion: Section 137.1(5) does not prohibit interventions; the argument was rejected, though the motions were dismissed on the merits of the Rule 13 test.

firac.issue: Which party should present oral argument first on the anti-SLAPP motions?
firac.facts: The defendants (moving parties) argued the plaintiff should go first because he conceded the expression concerned a matter of public interest, shifting the burden to him under s. 137.1(4). The plaintiff objected, noting the defendants are the moving parties.
firac.rule: On an anti-SLAPP motion, the moving party need only establish that the proceeding arises from expression on a matter of public interest, after which the burden shifts to the plaintiff; ordinarily the party bringing the proceeding argues first even where it bears the persuasive burden, as in defamation trials.
firac.application: The court found that although the plaintiff bears the persuasive burden, the defendants are the moving parties whose materials and submissions address all issues and were delivered first, with the plaintiff responding; there was no reason to alter that order.
firac.conclusion: The defendants proceed first and address all issues.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is procedural civil litigation (interventions and order of argument). K015 (defamation) and K024 (freedom of expression) are central because the underlying actions are defamation claims subject to anti-SLAPP motions under s. 137.1 CJA, whose purpose is protecting expression on matters of public interest. K016 (fair comment), K018 (qualified privilege) and K019 (responsible communication) are the pleaded defamation defences expressly noted by the court. K058 (antisemitism) reflects the central contested issue of what constitutes 'anti-semitism' and the impugned statements ('Jew-hater'). K091 (CIJA) applies because the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs is a named defendant. Borderline: the fair comment/privilege/responsible communication defences are only mentioned, not adjudicated, so those are supporting rather than dispositive; there is no controlled-vocabulary term for intervention or anti-SLAPP procedure itself, nor for NCCM or IJV.
