case_name: Islamic Schools Federation of Ontario v. Ottawa Board of Education

name_verification.name_in_document: Islamic Schools Federation of Ontario v. Ottawa Board of Education

defining_issues: Does Regulation 304's designation of Christmas, Good Friday and Easter Monday as school holidays infringe Muslims' freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter, in purpose or effect?

Does Regulation 304 discriminate against Muslim students contrary to s. 15 of the Charter by creating adverse effect discrimination, given that Christian holy days coincide with school holidays while Muslim holy days do not?
If any Charter right is infringed, is the limit justified under s. 1?
Did the Ottawa Board of Education have a duty to close schools on the two Muslim high holy days, or to study/accommodate that request, and did it fulfil any duty to accommodate?

firac.issue: Does Regulation 304's designation of Christmas, Good Friday and Easter Monday as school holidays infringe freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
firac.facts: Regulation 304 under the Education Act designates a Christmas vacation, Good Friday and Easter Monday (and Saturdays/Sundays) as school holidays. The applicants argued these holidays have a religious purpose recognizing Christian holy days, contrary to Muslims' s. 2(a) rights.
firac.rule: Following R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713, Peel (Regional Municipality) v. Great Atlantic & Pacific Co. (1991), 2 O.R. (3d) 65 (C.A.), and CSR de Chambly v. Bergevin, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 525, days such as Sundays, Christmas and Easter, though of religious origin, have become secular common pause days; a calendar including them is secular and neutral on its face. Section 2(a) is engaged only where a state-imposed cost is capable of interfering with religious belief or practice.
firac.application: The court found no evidence that the impugned holidays were chosen for a religious rather than secular purpose; Easter Monday is not a holy day and Good Friday is not a day of obligation in the Roman Catholic Church. The holidays are secular common pause days chosen to coincide with community-wide rest days. Moreover, s. 21(2)(g) of the Education Act excuses a child from attendance on a day regarded as a holy day of the child's religion, so Muslim students may be absent on their holy days without penalty. Any embarrassment flows from the student's own religious obligations, not from the secular legislation.
firac.conclusion: Regulation 304 does not infringe s. 2(a) in purpose or effect.

firac.issue: Does Regulation 304 create adverse effect discrimination contrary to s. 15 of the Charter?
firac.facts: Muslim students must miss two school days each year for Eid-al-Fitr and Eid-al-Adha, while Christian holy days fall on existing school holidays. There was no evidence about how many Christian students actually observe Christmas or Good Friday religiously.
firac.rule: Section 15 equality guarantee; adverse effect discrimination requires a comparator group receiving a significant advantage (per Peel and Bergevin). Absent evidence of real advantage to Christians, discrimination is not established.
firac.application: The court doubted discrimination could be found on the record, noting the absence of evidence that Christian students observe these days religiously, but was prepared to assume adverse effect discrimination arose from Muslim students having to miss school while Christians did not.
firac.conclusion: No adverse effect discrimination was proven, but the court proceeded on the assumption that it existed.

firac.issue: If Regulation 304 infringes s. 15, is the limit demonstrably justified under s. 1?
firac.facts: The legislature chose school holidays coinciding with secular common pause days enjoyed by the wider community, including those in the Retail Business Holidays Act.
firac.rule: Section 1 Oakes-type analysis as summarized in Edwards Books: the objective must be pressing and substantial, and the means proportional (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionate effects).
firac.application: Providing school holidays is a pressing and substantial objective. Choosing holidays coinciding with community-wide pause days minimally impairs religious rights; the only alternative—making every holy day of every student a holiday—was impossible and would itself be unconstitutional by favouring religion over atheists, agnostics and the non-affiliated (more than 12% of Canadians). Christmas and Good Friday must remain school holidays for Ontario to align with the rest of the western world.
firac.conclusion: Any infringement is a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1; Regulation 304 does not offend the Charter.

firac.issue: Did the Board have a duty to close schools on Muslim holy days or to study the request, and did it fulfil any duty to accommodate?
firac.facts: The applicants asked the Board to make one or both Muslim high holy days school holidays (or professional-activity days) and to study accommodation. The Board had permitted absences on holy days, distributed multi-faith calendars, directed teachers not to schedule tests on holy days, provided prayer rooms and make-up tests, and operated a Multiculturalism Advisory Committee. In 1994 it delayed the school start by two days for Rosh Hashanah as a one-time event.
firac.rule: Assuming adverse effect discrimination, there is a duty to accommodate by reasonable means short of undue hardship (Bergevin). Accommodation need not extend to closing schools; professional activity days are not throw-away days.
firac.application: The court held closing schools for religious observance would itself breach the Charter, and there were too few available days for the many holy days of all religions. The Board had already taken numerous reasonable steps to relieve the disadvantage. The Rosh Hashanah delay was a rare, non-precedential accommodation of an orientation problem, not recognition of a holy day. The Board considered and rejected the applicants' request and communicated its decision.
firac.conclusion: The Board had no obligation to close schools or study the request, and it had already provided reasonable accommodation; the application was dismissed with costs of $7,500.

keywords_rationale: The case is a Charter challenge, so K003 (Constitutional law, tier-1) anchors it. K025 freedom of religion and K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) capture the s. 2(a) analysis of the secular-holiday holding. K023 equality rights and K109 (Charter s. 15) capture the adverse-effect discrimination claim. K030 reasonable limits (s. 1) reflects the Oakes/Edwards Books justification analysis. K031 religious accommodation captures the duty-to-accommodate discussion (make-up tests, prayer rooms, Bergevin). K118 Education Act and K044 school board reflect the statutory setting (Regulation 304, s. 21(2)(g), and the Board's decision). K107 Canadian Charter is the governing instrument. Jewish-holiday keywords were considered (Rosh Hashanah delay) but are only contextual, so were omitted.
location_rationale: The decision is that of the Ontario Court (General Division), Divisional Court, applying the Ontario Education Act, so the province is Ontario. No city is expressly stated in the text; Ottawa is inferred because the respondent is the Ottawa Board of Education and the matter concerns Ottawa schools, but the seat is not confirmed in the text so this is treated with caution.
registry_rationale: The only file reference is 'Court File: 1082/96'; the decision does not name a court registry or office, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Jama v. The Speaker

defining_issues: Do the debate on and passage of a censure motion in the Legislative Assembly, and the resulting censure of an MPP, fall within parliamentary privilege so as to oust the court's jurisdiction over the application for judicial review?

Do the recognized categories of parliamentary privilege — control over debates and proceedings and disciplinary authority over members — remain necessary in the contemporary context at the provincial level?
Does the fact that the MPP's impugned statements were made outside the legislature, or that Charter rights are invoked, remove the matter from parliamentary privilege and permit judicial review?

firac.issue: Do the debate and passage of a censure motion, and the resulting censure of an MPP, fall within parliamentary privilege so as to oust the court's jurisdiction?
firac.facts: Sarah Jama, MPP for Hamilton Centre, was censured by the Legislative Assembly of Ontario after Motion 19, moved by Government House Leader Paul Calandra, was debated and passed, authorizing the Speaker not to recognize her until she retracted and apologized for social-media statements about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. She sought judicial review to quash the Speaker's decision to allow the motion, to have the motion ruled out of order, to quash the censure, and a declaration the measures were unconstitutional.
firac.rule: Courts have no jurisdiction to review matters falling within parliamentary privilege, which is a rule of curial jurisdiction conferring immunity from judicial review (Canada (House of Commons) v. Vaid, 2005 SCC 30; Chagnon, 2018 SCC 39; Duffy v. Canada (Senate), 2020 ONCA 536). Control over debates and proceedings and disciplinary authority over members are established categories of privilege. Motions to dismiss for want of jurisdiction proceed under rr. 21.01(1)(b) and 21.01(3)(a) of the Rules of Civil Procedure; s. 52.1(1) of the Legislative Assembly Act affirms the Assembly holds the same privileges as the U.K. House of Commons as of 1867.
firac.application: The relief sought targeted steps taken within the Legislative Assembly — allowing, debating, voting on and adopting Motion 19 and its disciplinary consequences. These squarely engaged the categories of control over debates and proceedings and disciplinary authority over members. Once a category of privilege is recognized, the court cannot examine the merits or exercise of the privilege; the starting point is the existence and scope of the category, not the fairness of the censure.
firac.conclusion: The subject matter fell within parliamentary privilege; the court had no jurisdiction and the application was dismissed.

firac.issue: Do the categories of control over debates and proceedings and disciplinary authority over members remain necessary in the contemporary context?
firac.facts: The applicant argued Motion 19 and the censure were not necessary in the contemporary context and relied on Chagnon, an employment case about dismissed National Assembly security guards.
firac.rule: Under Vaid, at para. 29, necessity is read broadly and tied to the autonomy legislative assemblies require; the test is what the dignity and efficiency of the legislature require. At the provincial level the court may consider whether a category continues to be necessary. The activity must be so closely connected with the assembly's functions that outside interference would undermine its required autonomy (Vaid, para. 46; Chagnon, paras. 29-31).
firac.application: The correct question was not whether the specific censure was necessary but whether the categories relied on remain necessary. Control over debates and proceedings has been recognized since 1689 and remains central to legislative autonomy; disciplinary authority over members likewise remains necessary, as confirmed in Duffy. Chagnon did not involve a legislative motion or discipline of an elected member and was distinguishable. External intervention would create delays, disruption and costs holding up the legislature's business.
firac.conclusion: Both categories remain necessary in the contemporary context; privilege applied.

firac.issue: Does the location of the statements outside the legislature or the invocation of Charter rights remove the matter from privilege?
firac.facts: The applicant made her impugned statements on X (outside the chamber) and argued her political speech and her Charter freedom of expression, plus impacts on her constituents, warranted judicial review; she also invoked the Legislative Assembly Act and Members' Integrity Act.
firac.rule: Parliamentary privilege is not confined to conduct within the legislature (Harvey; Michaud; Zundel; Saunders). Where privilege applies, the legislature has exclusive competence to adjudicate alleged Charter breaches; judicial review even for Charter compliance would nullify the immunity (Chagnon, para. 24; Vaid, para. 30; Duffy, para. 110). Privilege is as much part of the Constitution as the Charter, and one part cannot abrogate another.
firac.application: The privilege extends to sanctioning conduct occurring outside the chamber, and the applicant had captioned her post by referencing her role as a politician. The Members' Integrity Act was not a comprehensive code waiving privilege, and s. 46 authority over criminal matters is additional to, not a limitation on, privilege. Impact on constituents was considered but, as in New Brunswick Broadcasting where s. 2(b) did not prevail, did not displace privilege. The Charter arguments presumed privilege did not apply; since it did, the court lacked jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: Neither the extramural location of the statements nor the Charter claims removed the matter from privilege; the applicant's remedy lay with the Legislative Assembly and, ultimately, the electorate.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the primary practice area — the case turns on parliamentary privilege as part of the constitutional separation of powers. K011 (judicial review) captures the procedural vehicle the court declined to entertain for want of jurisdiction. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) are engaged because the applicant relied on political-speech and free-expression arguments (and the court cited New Brunswick Broadcasting on s. 2(b) not prevailing over privilege); K107 (Charter) reflects the broader Charter claims held to be within the legislature's exclusive competence. K058 (antisemitism) and K056 (anti-Zionism) reflect the substance of Motion 19, which censured the MPP for statements characterized as anti-Semitic and concerning the existence of the State of Israel. K103 (Israel), K104 (Palestine) situate the underlying social-media controversy (Gaza/Israeli-Palestinian conflict). The antisemitism/anti-Zionism and place keywords are contextual rather than central to the legal holding, so they are somewhat weaker picks, but they reflect the factual matrix. There is no controlled-vocabulary term for 'parliamentary privilege' itself, so constitutional law and judicial review carry the doctrinal weight.
location_rationale: The heading identifies the 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE DIVISIONAL COURT' and the decision states it was 'HEARD at Toronto: February 22, 2024', establishing Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The decision is styled as a 'DIVISIONAL COURT' matter (Court File No. 652/23) of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, heard at Toronto.

name_verification.name_in_document: Fidler v. Burns Lake (Village)

defining_issues: Is the Corporation of the Village of Burns Lake vicariously liable for the alleged torts of RCMP officers policing a municipality of fewer than 5,000 persons?

Are the plaintiff's claims (assault, kidnapping, forcible confinement, trespass, unreasonable search and seizure, defamation, cruel and unusual punishment and Charter breaches) statute-barred, and was the limitation period postponed?
Should the pleadings regarding sexual assault and malicious prosecution be struck for failing to disclose a reasonable cause of action?

firac.issue: Is the Village of Burns Lake vicariously liable for the alleged torts of RCMP officers policing a municipality with a population under 5,000?
firac.facts: Burns Lake had a population of approximately 3,649 in 2006 and played no role in hiring, training, supervising or disciplining the defendant RCMP officers. Policing was provided by the RCMP acting as the provincial police force under a 1992 federal-provincial agreement to which Burns Lake was not a party.
firac.rule: Under s. 3(1)(b) of the Police Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 367, the provincial government must provide policing for municipalities of up to 5,000 persons; s. 14 allows the RCMP to serve as the provincial police force. Municipal joint-and-several tort liability under s. 20 applies only to municipalities over 5,000 with municipal constables; liability for provincial constables lies with the Province (s. 11; Quinn v. Dubnyk, 2011 BCSC 792; Roy v. British Columbia (AG), 2005 BCCA 88).
firac.application: Because Burns Lake had fewer than 5,000 residents, the officers were provincial constables, not municipal constables. Burns Lake had no statutory or contractual role in their policing and thus could not be vicariously liable; any such liability rested with the Province.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiff had no basis for a claim against Burns Lake and the action against it was dismissed under Rule 9-6(4).

firac.issue: Are the plaintiff's tort and Charter claims statute-barred, and was the two-year limitation period postponed?
firac.facts: The impugned conduct occurred on October 19-20, 2006; the notice of civil claim was filed April 29, 2011. The plaintiff had already commenced two Vancouver actions (November 2006 and December 2008) advancing mirror allegations. He claimed postponement due to periods of psychiatric hospitalization and incarceration and medication effects, but tendered no expert evidence of incapacity.
firac.rule: The Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266 imposes a two-year period running from when damage was sustained and the tortfeasor is known (Levitt v. Carr; Craig v. ICBC, 2005 BCCA 275). Postponement under s. 6(4)/(6) requires, per Ounjian v. St. Paul's Hospital and Novak v. Bond, [1999] 1 SCR 808, that a reasonable person with the known facts and appropriate advice could bring an action; the onus is on the plaintiff. Trespass, forcible confinement and defamation are not among the s. 6(3) categories capable of postponement.
firac.application: There was no discoverability issue: the plaintiff knew of his injuries and could readily have learned the officers' identities, as shown by his earlier Vancouver actions naming the RCMP and John Does. He unreasonably declined to seek legal advice despite being urged to do so. Even if incapacity or incarceration were established, commencing the action in 2011 would still fall outside the limitation period.
firac.conclusion: The claims for assault, kidnapping, forcible confinement, trespass, illegal search and seizure, defamation and cruel and unusual punishment (and related Charter breaches) were statute-barred and dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the pleadings alleging sexual assault and malicious prosecution be struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action?
firac.facts: The 18-page, 67-paragraph notice of civil claim quoted the Magna Carta and religious material, described the RCMP as a 'standing army' and used scandalous invective. The sexual assault allegation was based only on being struck on the 'stomach, ribs and genitals'; the malicious prosecution claim was pleaded without its constituent elements. Malicious prosecution and sexual assault claims were not time-barred (s. 3(4)(k); D.E. v. British Columbia, 2005 BCCA 134).
firac.rule: Under Rule 9-5(1) a pleading may be struck where it discloses no reasonable claim or is scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, assuming pleaded facts are true (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 SCR 959; R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42). Sexual assault requires conduct of a sexual nature violating sexual integrity (R. v. Chase, [1987] 2 SCR). Malicious prosecution requires four elements: proceedings initiated by the defendant, terminated in the plaintiff's favour, absence of reasonable and probable cause, and malice/improper purpose (Miazga v. Kvello Estate, 2009 SCC 51; Nelles v. Ontario, [1989] 2 SCR 170).
firac.application: The sexual assault pleading alleged an assault but no facts establishing a sexual context or motive; this was not a mere drafting deficiency. The malicious prosecution claim failed to plead the four required elements. The overall pleadings were prolix, embarrassing and largely incomprehensible.
firac.conclusion: The sexual assault allegation was struck; the plaintiff was granted 60 days to file an entirely new notice of civil claim particularizing malicious prosecution, failing which that claim would also be dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area: the case turns on summary judgment, vicarious liability, limitation defences and the striking of pleadings. K107 (Canadian Charter) and K112 (Charter s. 7) reflect the plaintiff's pleaded Charter breaches concerning liberty, cruel and unusual punishment and due process, which were addressed in the limitation analysis. K015 (defamation) is one of the specific pleaded causes of action that was dismissed as time-barred. K004 (Criminal law) is a weaker but genuine pick — the court applied criminal-law tests (R. v. Chase on sexual assault; the Miazga/Nelles malicious prosecution elements) arising from the plaintiff's arrest and acquittal. The controlled vocabulary lacks precise terms for the core doctrines here (limitation periods, vicarious liability of police, striking pleadings, summary judgment), so several picks are approximations flagged as such.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Registry: Smithers' and lists 'Place and Date of Hearing: Smithers, B.C.' and 'Place and Date of Judgment: Smithers, B.C.', so the court sat in Smithers, British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly indicates 'Registry: Smithers'.

name_verification.name_in_document: LENNIE RYER C.A. v. STEPHEN R. POTTEN and S.R. POTTEN ENTERPRISES LTD

defining_issues: Did Potten or the Company breach their obligation to negotiate and cooperate in good faith toward the conclusion of the acquisition contemplated by the Letter of Intent?
If a breach were found, what damages flow from it and are they proven?
Can Ryer claim Greenspoon's share of the alleged losses when Greenspoon is not a party and the holding company was never incorporated?
Is Ryer's action abusive, or did his conduct during the litigation (repeated emails) trigger extracontractual liability toward Potten?

firac.issue: Did the defendants breach the obligation of good faith in negotiating and cooperating toward completion of the acquisition set out in the Letter of Intent?
firac.facts: Ryer and his partner Greenspoon negotiated to buy Potten's seasonal barbecue company. A Letter of Intent signed December 22, 2010 set a $11.75M price, a $7.7M minimum Net Book Value at closing, and a February 22, 2011 closing. Potten cancelled a February 17 meeting, and the parties then deadlocked over ownership of the strong 2011 profits, with Potten later proposing revised terms the buyers rejected before walking away.
firac.rule: Arts. 6, 7 and 1375 C.C.Q. require good faith in the exercise of rights and in contract formation and performance. The duty to negotiate in good faith is not an absolute obligation to conclude a contract; a party may terminate negotiations over a material disagreement provided it does so reasonably and not abusively (Greenberg v. Capital d'Amérique CDPQ inc., 2011 QCCA 958; Friedman v. Ruby, 2012 QCCS 1778; Pegasus Partners Inc. v. Groupe Laurem inc., 2007 QCCS 476).
firac.application: The Court found Potten cooperated in good faith with due diligence—giving access to his consultant, bankers and auditors and supplying extensive financial documentation sufficient for the buyers to obtain two financing offers; Ryer himself wrote that due diligence was 'progressing well with no surprises.' The failure resulted from a genuine, material disagreement over ownership of the 2011 profits, an issue the ambiguous NBV Clause did not unequivocally resolve (the three protagonists each read it differently). Potten flagged the profit issue early, and both sides made reasonable good-faith attempts to bridge it before the buyers walked away. Delaying closing legitimately affected the deal's economics.
firac.conclusion: No breach: the defendants acted in good faith throughout; the deal failed because of a legitimate, unresolved disagreement, not bad faith. The main action is dismissed with costs.

firac.issue: If there were a breach, are the claimed damages proven?
firac.facts: Ryer's damages claim shifted from $3.24M to $6.24M to $3.69M, comprising lost 2011/2012 profits, consulting fees, and loss of time.
firac.rule: A claimant must prove damages with a causal link and account for offsetting obligations; parties bear their own transaction costs where the contract so provides.
firac.application: Even though the action failed, the Court noted the lost-profits claim ignored the $9M–$11.75M purchase price the buyers would have had to pay, and improperly incorporated alleged unreported cash sales raised only at trial. Consulting fees were payable by each party under the LOI, were partly unpaid, were partly incurred for optional renegotiations, and were billed to a non-party holding company. The loss-of-time claim was overstated—Ryer would have earned about $67,000 over the four relevant months, not $200,000, and he showed no lost future earnings.
firac.conclusion: The damages were unproven and overstated; obiter, they would not have supported recovery in any event.

firac.issue: Can Ryer recover Greenspoon's share of the alleged losses?
firac.facts: Ryer and Greenspoon were to be equal (50/50) partners through a holding company for the acquisition. Greenspoon chose not to sign the LOI and is not a party; the holding company was never incorporated.
firac.rule: A party cannot advance a claim belonging to another who has chosen not to sue; standing requires the claimant hold the right asserted.
firac.application: Greenspoon, for his own strategic reasons, declined to sign the LOI and to bring a claim, and must bear that choice. The intended holding company never existed and is not a party, distinguishing Pegasus Partners Inc. v. Groupe Laurem inc.
firac.conclusion: Ryer cannot claim Greenspoon's share of the alleged losses.

firac.issue: Was Ryer's action abusive, or did his litigation conduct give rise to extracontractual liability entitling Potten to damages on the cross-claim?
firac.facts: Potten sought $350,000 in moral and punitive damages, alleging an abusive suit and a lengthy series of emails Ryer personally sent him during the litigation (invoices, invitations, articles, Holocaust survivor pictures, Jewish New Year wishes, health links) apparently intended to annoy.
firac.rule: An unfounded action is abusive only where brought in a manner 'so patent, or so frivolous or dilatory as to be an abuse of process' (Acadia Subaru v. Michaud, 2011 QCCA 1037); extracontractual liability requires proof of fault, damage and causation.
firac.application: Although weaker than the defence, Ryer's claim was not so frivolous as to be an abuse of right. The Court found Ryer's persistent emails did amount to harassment and intimidation and were grossly inappropriate, but Potten's evidence of resulting damage (stress, sleeplessness) was minimal and could not be attributed to Ryer's fault as opposed to the failed deal or the litigation itself.
firac.conclusion: The cross-claim is dismissed with costs; harassment was found but causally linked damages were not proven.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the correct tier-1 area: this is a commercial dispute over good faith in contract negotiations under arts. 6, 7 and 1375 C.C.Q. K083 (harassment) is genuinely engaged because the court expressly found Ryer's repeated emails 'amounted to harassment and intimidation,' a central plank of the cross-claim. The remaining picks are peripheral and reflect only the content of the harassing emails cataloged by the court: K093 (Jewish) and K027 (Jewish holidays, i.e. the 'Jewish New Year wishes'/Rosh Hashanah email) and K088 (Holocaust, i.e. the 'pictures depicting... Holocaust survivors' email). These three are weak, incidental references rather than substantive legal issues, and are flagged as such; the controlled vocabulary offers no keywords for good-faith negotiation, contract formation or abuse of process, so the closest genuinely applicable terms were selected.
location_rationale: The header states 'SUPERIOR COURT', 'PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC', 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL', file no. 500-17-065609-110, confirming the court sits in Montreal, Quebec.
registry_rationale: The 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' designation and Montreal file number indicate the Montreal registry of the Superior Court.

name_verification.name_in_document: Justin Shaundor Kozma v. Island Health

defining_issues: Is it plain and obvious that the plaintiff's notice of civil claim discloses no reasonable cause of action such that it should be struck under R. 9-5(1)(a)?
Is the notice of civil claim an abuse of process amounting to a collateral attack on the Mental Health Act review panel's decision, warranting striking under R. 9-5(1)(d)?
If the pleading is deficient, should it be struck outright or should the self-represented plaintiff be granted leave to amend?

firac.issue: Is it plain and obvious that the plaintiff's notice of civil claim discloses no reasonable cause of action under R. 9-5(1)(a)?
firac.facts: Kozma, self-represented, was brought to hospital by police, involuntarily detained under s. 22 of the Mental Health Act on two physician certifications, and treated; his detention was confirmed by a review panel. He later filed a poorly drafted NOCC alleging human rights violations, defamation, and intentional infliction of emotional distress, among other matters.
firac.rule: Under R. 9-5(1)(a) evidence is inadmissible and the court assumes the pleaded facts are true (Kripps v. Touche Ross). A claim can only be struck where it is 'plain and obvious' it discloses no reasonable cause of action, has 'no reasonable prospect of success', or is 'certain to fail' (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.; Imperial Tobacco). Pleadings, including as they might be amended, are read generously to accommodate drafting deficiencies (Operation Dismantle; Chang Estate).
firac.application: Although the NOCC was difficult to understand and lacked particulars, the Court read it generously and identified facts capable of supporting established causes of action: false imprisonment (Kovacs), assault and battery (Norberg; Kearns), breach of Charter rights, and breach of fiduciary duty. The defamation allegation, though un-particularized, pleads a known cause of action that could be cured by amendment. The Court could not say these claims were bound to fail.
firac.conclusion: It was not plain and obvious the NOCC disclosed no reasonable claim; the pleading was not struck on this ground, save that any Human Rights Code complaint must proceed through the statutory process.

firac.issue: Does the NOCC constitute an abuse of process as a collateral attack on the review panel's detention decision under R. 9-5(1)(d)?
firac.facts: The defendant argued the claim was essentially a challenge to the involuntary certification and the review panel's confirmation of detention, brought in the wrong forum. Kozma had not sought judicial review of the review panel decision.
firac.rule: A collateral attack occurs where a party challenges the validity of a binding order in the wrong forum rather than by direct attack (Garland v. Consumers' Gas Co.; Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79). Where the object of the action is not to invalidate the order but to recover damages allegedly flowing from it, the doctrine does not apply (Garland; Canada (AG) v. TeleZone Inc.).
firac.application: The Court found the NOCC was not confined to the fact of detention but alleged that the detention and treatment violated the plaintiff's civil and constitutional rights and caused him damage. Following TeleZone, the plaintiff sought damages, not to set aside the review panel decision, so the collateral attack doctrine did not apply.
firac.conclusion: The claim was not a collateral attack and was not struck as an abuse of process.

firac.issue: Should the deficient pleading be struck outright or should leave to amend be granted?
firac.facts: The plaintiff is self-represented, has a history of vulnerability due to mental health issues, and drafted a very poorly worded NOCC alleging wrongdoing while he was in a highly vulnerable state in the defendant's care.
firac.rule: The court has discretion under R. 9-5 to strike, stay, dismiss, or allow amendment; pleadings should be read generously and drafting inadequacies of self-represented litigants accommodated where a just and equitable outcome favours amendment.
firac.application: Given the plaintiff's self-represented status and vulnerability, and that identifiable causes of action could be properly particularized with amendment, the Court exercised its discretion to allow amendment rather than strike, ordering 60 days to file an amended NOCC, failing which the claim would stand dismissed. The order was without prejudice to renewing the application to strike.
firac.conclusion: Application dismissed; the plaintiff was granted 60 days to file an amended NOCC, with no order as to costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a civil motion to strike pleadings involving tort claims (false imprisonment, assault, battery, breach of fiduciary duty). K015 (defamation) is engaged because the NOCC pleads defamation and the Court analyzed its sufficiency. K107 (Canadian Charter) and K112 (Charter s. 7, security of the person) apply because the plaintiff alleged Charter breaches including security of the person and cruel and unusual treatment. K024/K111 (freedom of expression / s. 2(b)) and K110 (s. 2(a) freedom of conscience) reflect the plaintiff's pleaded freedom of thought, conscience, and expression claims. K119 (Human Rights Code) is a borderline/weaker pick, engaged only because the Court noted any Human Rights Code complaint must be pursued through the statutory process. The controlled vocabulary lacks a specific term for 'motion to strike', 'collateral attack', 'abuse of process', 'false imprisonment', or 'mental health detention', which are the case's true centre of gravity, so keyword coverage is necessarily approximate.
location_rationale: The decision states 'Place and Date of Hearing: Vancouver, B.C.' and 'Place and Date of Judgment: Vancouver, B.C.', and the court is the Supreme Court of British Columbia, so the province is British Columbia and the city where judgment was delivered is Vancouver.
registry_rationale: The header of the decision expressly states 'Registry: Victoria' (Docket S202555), reflecting that the action was filed in the Victoria registry even though the teleconference hearing was heard out of Vancouver.

name_verification.name_in_document: Euriphile Joseph v. Omar Washington

defining_issues: Is it in the children's best interests, under the Divorce Act, to permit the mother to relocate them to Brooklyn, New York?
Who bears the burden of proof on the relocation application given that the parties were operating under an interim equal shared-parenting order (ss. 16.93 and 16.94)?
Should the court decline jurisdiction over property division under s. 106(4) of the Family Law Act because New York is the more appropriate forum?
What amount of income should be attributed to the father for child support, and how should support be calculated?

firac.issue: Is the proposed relocation of the children from Victoria to Brooklyn in their best interests under the Divorce Act?
firac.facts: The parents of two young children (aged 8 and 6) separated in 2020 in Victoria after years living in Brooklyn and Costa Rica. The mother wished to move the children back to their former Brooklyn neighbourhood, where the family has deep roots and a supportive, racially and culturally diverse community; the father opposed relocation but conceded he would move to New York with the children if relocation were allowed. Both parents were found to be loving, capable, equally involved co-parents.
firac.rule: Under the Divorce Act, relocation is governed by the best interests of the child (s. 16(2) primary consideration: the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being), assessed through the factors in s. 16(3), the maximum contact principle (s. 16(6)) and the additional relocation factors in s. 16.92(1), including the reasons for the move and its impact (Duggan v. White, 2019 BCCA 200; K.W. v. L.H., 2018 BCCA 204; Stav v. Stav, 2012 BCCA 154). Paramountcy directs use of the Divorce Act (T.T. v. S.Z.T., 2020 BCSC 1628).
firac.application: Because the father would relocate too, the only realistic options were shared parenting in New York or in Victoria. The children's basic needs, schooling, health care and friendships could be met in either city, and financial circumstances would be similar, so those factors were neutral. The reasons for the move (financial and emotional stability and, weighing heavily, the opportunity to nurture the children's racial and cultural identities within a Black and diverse community) were reasonable and advanced in good faith. The mother would be more professionally and emotionally fulfilled in New York, benefiting the children, and the large supportive community there would enhance their stability. The move would not reduce the father's time with them, and any short-term disruption was minor given the children's demonstrated adaptability.
firac.conclusion: Relocation to Brooklyn was found to be in the children's best interests and was permitted, with equal shared parenting to continue in New York on a 2-2-5-5 schedule and shared decision-making.

firac.issue: Who bears the burden of proving the relocation is or is not in the children's best interests where an interim equal-parenting order is in place?
firac.facts: An interim order of February 2, 2021 provided for equal shared parenting (4-3-3-4), which the parties complied with. The mother's desire to relocate had prompted the proceeding, and the interim order was granted after that issue was known.
firac.rule: Section 16.93(1) of the Divorce Act places the burden on the relocating parent where the parties substantially comply with an equal-time order, but s. 16.94 gives the court discretion not to apply that burden where the order is an interim order (analogy drawn to K.W. v. L.H., 2018 BCCA 204).
firac.application: The interim order did not reflect any determination of where the children should reside and was merely a holding arrangement pending trial; the proceeding was effectively an initial determination of parenting arrangements, so deference to the interim order was not warranted.
firac.conclusion: The court exercised its discretion under s. 16.94 not to impose the s. 16.93(1) burden on the mother; in any event the relocation was found to be in the children's best interests.

firac.issue: Should the court decline jurisdiction over property division in favour of New York?
firac.facts: The most valuable asset was the jointly owned Brooklyn family home. The parties' first common habitual residence was New York and most property and debt was acquired and located there. No admissible expert evidence established New York law on community of property.
firac.rule: Section 106(2) FLA gives jurisdiction, but s. 106(4)-(6) permits declining it where more appropriate for jurisdiction to be exercised elsewhere, weighing the s. 106(5) factors. Section 108 mandates applying the law of the first common habitual residence where a 'regime of community of property' applies. Foreign law is a question of fact requiring admissible expert evidence (X.W.L. v. J.L., 2021 BCSC 860; Rule 13-2 Supreme Court Family Rules).
firac.application: Most s. 106(5) factors favoured exercising jurisdiction, but the court could not determine whether New York operated a community-of-property regime because no qualified expert evidence was tendered; statutory excerpts were insufficient. Since s. 108 would compel applying New York law if such a regime existed, and the point could not be resolved, it was more appropriate for jurisdiction to be exercised in New York.
firac.conclusion: The court declined under s. 106(4) FLA to make property division orders, leaving those issues to be resolved in New York.

firac.issue: What income should be used for the father and how should child support be set?
firac.facts: The mother sought to impute income to the father equal to his former HBO salary. After trial he obtained a full-time Victoria job earning $90,000 CAD. The parties share parenting equally.
firac.rule: The Federal Child Support Guidelines under the Divorce Act; imputation requires a finding of intentional under-employment; equal parenting time supports a set-off approach.
firac.application: The father was not found intentionally under-employed given his new $90,000 CAD position; his Guideline obligation was $1,388/month and the mother's $1,827/month. With equal parenting a straight set-off was appropriate.
firac.conclusion: The mother pays the father $439/month child support, with s. 7 expenses shared proportionally; the father having abandoned his spousal support claim, that claim was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area. K047 (best interests of the child) is the central legal test applied to the relocation. K048 (custody/access) captures the parenting-time and shared-parenting determinations that the relocation decision turned on. K050 (parental support/child support) covers the child support and imputation-of-income analysis. K053 (spousal support) is engaged though weakly, since the father's spousal support claim was abandoned and dismissed. K117 (Divorce Act) is the statute under which the divorce, relocation and support were decided. The vocabulary has no keyword for relocation or for property-division forum non conveniens, so those significant issues could not be tagged; K053 is the weakest pick given the claim was dropped.
location_rationale: The header states 'Registry: Victoria' and lists the place of trial and judgment as 'Victoria, B.C.' The court is the Supreme Court of British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly records 'Registry: Victoria' and Docket E203870.

name_verification.name_in_document: Allan Einstoss (Petitioner/Husband) and Dawn Starkman (Respondent/Wife)

defining_issues: Did Ms. Starkman deliberately disobey the access provisions of the court orders and thereby commit contempt of court not in the face of the court, proven beyond a reasonable doubt?
What sanctions should be imposed for the contempt, having regard to the best interests of the child?

firac.issue: Did Ms. Starkman commit contempt ex facie by intentionally breaching the access orders regarding her son Jake?
firac.facts: Access, custody and support were fixed by Minutes of Settlement incorporated into Chapnik J.'s judgment of May 2, 2000, and refined by orders of Lane J. (Aug. 30, 2001) and Ferrier J. (Nov. 29, 2001) specifying pick-up and drop-off at Ms. Starkman's home. Ms. Starkman was subject to criminal non-communication conditions but, rather than returning to court, unilaterally varied the location for access and, through her lawyer and later self-representation, frustrated Mr. Einstoss's court-ordered access. She admitted intentional non-compliance with the specified locations but claimed she complied with the 'spirit' of the orders.
firac.rule: Rules 60.05 and 60.11 of the Rules of Civil Procedure confer jurisdiction over contempt not in the face of the court. Following Re Sheppard and Sheppard (1976 CanLII 710 (ON CA)) and applied in cases such as Genua v. Genua and McMillan v. McMillan, contempt for breach of an access order requires: (1) the order is clear and unambiguous; (2) the defendant knew of the order; and (3) the defendant intentionally did or failed to do something in contravention of the order. It is not necessary to intend to disobey the order — only to intend the prohibited act. The standard of proof is beyond a reasonable doubt given the possible penalty of fine or imprisonment.
firac.application: The court found the orders clear and unambiguous, that Ms. Starkman knew them (she had helped settle them), and that she intentionally refused to make Jake available at the specified location. Her belief that she only had to provide access, not comply with the location, afforded no defence. Her non-communication bail conditions did not require breach because sincere pick-up/drop-off needed no communication; the proper course was to return to court, not unilaterally vary the orders. The judge found Mr. Einstoss credible and Ms. Starkman combative, evasive and the 'fomenter' on access, and that her conduct in fact deprived Jake of contact with his father.
firac.conclusion: The court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Ms. Starkman was in contempt of the orders of Chapnik J., Lane J. and Ferrier J.; the November 8, 2001 and January 7, 2002 motions were granted.

firac.issue: What sanction was appropriate for the contempt, consistent with the best interests of the child?
firac.facts: Jake, a 6½-year-old only child, was in therapy owing to his parents' conflict. Both parents claimed to act in his best interests; Ms. Starkman repeatedly asserted she wanted Mr. Einstoss to have more time with Jake. Counsel for Mr. Einstoss sought pre-set penalties for future breaches, including change of custody, reduced support and a fine.
firac.rule: Subrule 60.11(5) of the Rules of Civil Procedure grants wide discretion in penalizing contempt, including ordering the person to 'comply with any other order that the judge considers necessary.' Any sanction must be proportionate to the breach and, in a family context, consistent with the best interests of the child. Pre-determined future penalties would offend the presumption of innocence and due process.
firac.application: Rather than punitive measures, the court crafted a remedial access regime to reduce conflict and promote the father-child relationship: alternating week-on/week-off access with pick-up and drop-off at Jake's school (removing the parents' need to interact), equal sharing of summer, holidays, and equal division of Jewish holidays. The court declined to impose automatic future penalties, holding that any future breach must be determined in fresh proceedings with full due process, though it warned Ms. Starkman such sanctions were real possibilities.
firac.conclusion: The court varied the access arrangements as a proportionate, best-interests-focused sanction, refused to impose pre-set penalties for future breaches, and reserved and awarded costs of the trial and related motions to Mr. Einstoss to be fixed on written submissions.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a matrimonial dispute over access enforcement. K048 (custody/access) is central: the contempt arose from breaches of access provisions. K047 (best interests of the child) drove both the credibility analysis and the sanction, which was crafted around Jake's interests. K049 (marriage/separation agreement) is a borderline pick reflecting that access terms originated in Minutes of Settlement incorporated into judgment. K027 (Jewish holidays) is weak/borderline — engaged only because the remedial access schedule divides the Jewish holidays equally between the parents, signalling a Jewish family, but it is peripheral to the legal reasoning. No dedicated 'contempt of court' keyword exists in the vocabulary, so the civil-procedure enforcement dimension is under-captured.
location_rationale: The heading reads 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE (TORONTO REGION)', establishing the court sits in Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The decision is styled under the 'TORONTO REGION' of the Superior Court of Justice, with Court File No. 97-FP-138047, indicating the Toronto registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: Kohuch and Loewen v. Wilson

defining_issues: Were the defendant's statements about the school principal and Director of Education defamatory?
Did the defences of justification, fair comment, or qualified privilege succeed, or were they defeated by malice?
Was publication of the defamatory statements established?
What damages, and of what character (compensatory, aggravated, or punitive), should be awarded?
Should the defendant's counterclaim in defamation against Loewen succeed?
Should a permanent injunction issue restraining further defamation?

firac.issue: Were the defendant's statements about the plaintiffs in their professional capacities defamatory?
firac.facts: Over several years the defendant, a parent, made numerous statements about the principal Kohuch and Director of Education Loewen through open-line radio calls, letters to editors, school boards, the Department of Education, teachers, students and handmade postcards, imputing hypnotism of students, drug problems, child molestation, locking children in closets, incompetence, corruption and Nazi/Hitler-like conduct.
firac.rule: A statement is defamatory if it imputes any unfitness or want of ability on the part of a professional person to discharge his or her duties and responsibilities.
firac.application: The court held the statements plainly imputed unfitness and misconduct in the plaintiffs' professional roles as educator and administrator, satisfying the definition.
firac.conclusion: The statements were defamatory.

firac.issue: Were the defences of justification, fair comment and qualified privilege available, or were they defeated by falsity and malice?
firac.facts: The defendant pleaded truth (justification), fair comment on a matter of public interest, and qualified privilege as a taxpayer/parent with a duty to communicate. The evidence showed the allegations (forced resignation from Val Marie, drug use, hypnotism, drinking from toilets, death threats, arson) were untrue, and independent witnesses (Bath, Legault, Adams, Weibe) contradicted her. She admitted she was 'not a woman of gentle opinions' and boasted she 'got the bugger just about out'.
firac.rule: Justification requires the statements to be true. Fair comment must be honest comment on true facts. Qualified privilege and fair comment both fail if the plaintiff proves the defendant acted from actual malice — an indirect or dishonest motive other than a sense of duty (Gatley on Libel and Slander, 8th ed.).
firac.application: The court found the underlying assertions false, so justification failed and fair comment had no true factual foundation. The defendant's conduct sprang from spite and ill will arising out of the initial confrontations over her son's truancy; the malicious tone of the statements ('blacker devil', 'Hitler-like', 'Geek') and her triumphant admissions established actual malice, defeating both qualified privilege and fair comment.
firac.conclusion: No defence was established; the defences were defeated by falsity and malice.

firac.issue: Was publication of the defamatory statements established?
firac.facts: Statements were made on province-wide open-line radio, in letters to editors, school boards, the Department of Education, the Minister, the STF and the RCMP, on handmade postcards, and in conversations recorded by Loewen's friend Coombs after the defendant published her phone number in a newspaper.
firac.rule: The plaintiff bears the onus of proving publication, an essential element of defamation. Publication occurs where a third party reads or hears the material; postcards designed to be read in transit, and letters to a business where others open the mail, are published. Each communication is a separate publication.
firac.application: Publication was clearly established for the radio broadcasts, letters to editors, boards, department and RCMP; the postcards were published when read at the post office, school and board office; and Loewen was justified in having Coombs place the call, so those remarks were published and not the product of entrapment.
firac.conclusion: There was publication of all the defamatory statements, its extent varying by mode.

firac.issue: What damages should be awarded and of what character?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs remained employable (the board would rehire them) but left the community; Kohuch found the attacks unbearable and Loewen described them as pervasive. Many acquaintances knew the defendant was prone to ridiculous statements. Kohuch was the principal target.
firac.rule: Defamation of a professional ordinarily attracts substantial damages (McElroy v. Cowper-Smith and Woodman, [1967] S.C.R. 425). Compensatory damages may include injury to feelings and aggravation from high-handed or insulting conduct (Gatley; Waddams, The Law of Damages). Punitive damages are more apt against media defendants as a deterrent.
firac.application: The court treated the statements as a continuous course of conduct warranting a single award per plaintiff, found injury more to feelings and confidence than reputation, and treated the defendant's conduct as aggravating rather than deserving punishment, declining punitive damages. Special damages for house sale/rental losses were too remote and unproven.
firac.conclusion: Kohuch awarded $50,000 and Loewen $25,000 in compensatory (including aggravated) damages, plus costs; special and punitive damages refused.

firac.issue: Should the defendant's counterclaim in defamation against Loewen succeed?
firac.facts: Loewen conceded calling the defendant a 'crazy lady' at a teachers' meeting and wrote a letter to the Herbert Herald responding to her accusations.
firac.rule: A defamatory statement is not actionable where made without malice and causing no injury; and statements that are true are justified.
firac.application: The 'crazy lady' remark, though defamatory, was made in exasperation without malice and caused no discernible injury to the defendant's reputation or feelings; the letter's statements, if defamatory, were true and justified.
firac.conclusion: The counterclaim was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should a permanent injunction issue restraining further defamation?
firac.facts: The defendant told Coombs she was judgment proof, and her pattern of conduct persisted over years.
firac.rule: An injunction will not normally issue where damages are an adequate remedy, but may issue where there is a reasonable apprehension of repetition and damages are inadequate.
firac.application: Because the defendant was effectively judgment proof and the court had a reasonable apprehension of continued defamation, monetary compensation was inadequate and the personal vendetta had to be ended.
firac.conclusion: An injunction issued restraining the defendant from publishing any further remarks concerning the plaintiffs.

case_name: Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. J.G.

name_verification.name_in_document: The Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. J.G. [Indexed as: Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. G. (J.)]

defining_issues: Did the enactment of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017 change the meaning of a 'beneficial and meaningful' relationship for the purpose of determining access to a child in extended society care?
In assessing a child's best interests for access, may a court consider the benefits of a future relationship rather than only the existing relationship?
Did the trial judge err in law by referring to the child's medical information and family history as a benefit of continued access?

firac.issue: Did the CYFSA change the meaning of a 'beneficial and meaningful' relationship for access to a child in extended society care?
firac.facts: The mother's youngest child was placed in the extended care of the Society, which she did not contest; she sought only continued supervised access. The trial judge rejected the Society's argument to apply the narrow pre-CYFSA test and adopted an expansive best-interests inquiry, granting access at the Society's discretion. The appeal judge reversed, holding the old 'significantly advantageous' interpretation survived because the statutory words 'beneficial and meaningful' were unchanged.
firac.rule: Statutes are read in their entire context, in their grammatical and ordinary sense, harmoniously with the scheme and object of the Act and the intention of the legislature (Bell ExpressVu Limited Partnership v. Rex, 2002 SCC 42, citing Driedger). Under the CYFSA, ss. 105(5)-(6) and the best-interests definition in s. 74(3), access to a child in extended society care turns on the child's best interests, with the beneficial-and-meaningful nature of the relationship being only one factor. As held in Kawartha-Haliburton CAS v. W. (M.), 2019 ONCA 316 and M. (L.) v. Peel CAS, 2019 ONCA 841, the CYFSA effected a significant shift, removing the presumption against access.
firac.application: The court held the CYFSA is remedial legislation to protect vulnerable children and must be liberally construed. The old 'significantly advantageous' gloss from Niagara CAS v. J. (M.) applied dictionary definitions untethered from context and cannot survive the new best-interests framework. Huron-Perth CAS v. L. (J.) did not endorse the old test as it concerned different issues. The access analysis is now a holistic best-interests test in which 'beneficial and meaningful' is one aspect and impairment of adoption is relevant only where the court considers it so; there is no longer a presumption against access and no helpful role for a formal onus.
firac.conclusion: The test changed: the appeal judge erred in applying the restrictive pre-CYFSA interpretation; the trial judge's expansive best-interests approach was correct.

firac.issue: May the benefits of a future relationship be considered in the access best-interests analysis?
firac.facts: The trial judge considered that the child's best interests include all relevant factors, past, present or future. The appeal judge held this was an error because the statute asks whether the relationship 'is' beneficial and meaningful, relying on the Manitoulin decision.
firac.rule: Section 74(3) of the CYFSA requires consideration of, among other things, any other relevant circumstance, the development of a positive relationship, continuity of care and the possible effect of disruption, and the risk the child may suffer harm — all forward-looking considerations. Best interests are not static.
firac.application: The 'beneficial and meaningful' inquiry is no longer a separate precondition but a consideration within the best-interests analysis. The plain wording of s. 74(3) demands considerations that continue through time, and there is nothing to suggest access must be decided without reference to the future; custody and access decisions inherently involve a predictive element.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge did not err in taking future considerations into account.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err by referring to the child's medical information and family history as a benefit of access?
firac.facts: The trial judge listed, as one of ten benefits of access, that continued contact could make the child's medical information and family history more readily available. The child had significant medical issues arising from a premature birth. The appeal judge found this to be speculation unsupported by evidence and thus an error of law.
firac.rule: Best interests include future considerations; a court may draw common-sense conclusions grounded in the evidence, and no single factor is determinative in a best-interests weighing.
firac.application: It was not speculative because the child had significant medical issues from a premature birth, making it a common-sense conclusion that continuing contact with the biological mother could be beneficial. The factor was only one of ten the trial judge identified, and the future-oriented nature of the analysis was proper.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge did not err in referring to the child's medical information and family history.

K047 (best interests of the child) is central: the case turns on the CYFSA's best-interests framework under s. 74(3). name_verification.name_in_document: Droit de la famille — 191353

defining_issues: How should the 2007 Final Consent be interpreted with respect to custody, child support and spousal support?
Is the Father entitled to child support payable to him by the Mother?
Is the Mother entitled to reinstatement of spousal support after her renunciation effective July 2012?
Are the Mother's claims for reimbursement of expenses and for damages well-founded?
Were the Father's repeated proceedings abusive under arts. 51–55 C.c.p., justifying damages and a quarrelsome-litigant declaration?

firac.issue: How should the 2007 Final Consent be interpreted regarding custody and support?
firac.facts: The divorced, self-represented parents of four children signed a July 10, 2007 consent, homologated July 12, 2007, providing for joint custody with the children residing roughly 60% with the Father and 40% with the Mother; the Father undertook to pay all children's expenses 'without contribution by Plaintiff', paid spousal support until July 2012, and child support was contemplated only as payable to the Mother if the residential schedule changed in her favour and once she was working.
firac.rule: A homologated consent constitutes the law between the parties and must be interpreted according to its clear and unambiguous terms; joint custody remains in force absent a subsequent varying judgment.
firac.application: The Court found the joint custody arrangement remained in force for the only minor child (A, 17), no motion or judgment having overturned it since the 2010 Perrault Judgment. Paragraph 3.1 clearly obliged the Father to pay all children's expenses without any contribution from the Mother, and paragraph 6 contemplated child support only to the Mother, never to the Father.
firac.conclusion: The 2007 Final Consent governs; joint custody subsists and any support analysis must proceed on that basis, with the Father bearing all children's expenses.

firac.issue: Is the Father entitled to child support payable to him by the Mother?
firac.facts: The Father claimed child support from the Mother based on her notional income retroactive to 2007/2008, asserting de facto sole custody; he had made identical claims dismissed by Justice Richer (interim) and Justice Perrault (2010 merits).
firac.rule: Child support is for the children and is calculated on custody arrangements and respective incomes; res judicata and the terms of a homologated consent apply; a party cannot benefit from custody circumstances created by his own alienating conduct.
firac.application: The 2007 Consent never contemplated support payable to the Father; his prior identical claim was dismissed in 2010; the increased residential time with him resulted from his own alienating behaviour; and the Court's own calculations for 2013–2018 showed that under either a 50-50 or 60-40 schedule it is the Father, whose income vastly exceeded the Mother's, who would have owed support.
firac.conclusion: The Father's 2016 Motion for child support is dismissed as unfounded in fact and law.

firac.issue: Is the Mother entitled to reinstatement of spousal support after her 2012 renunciation?
firac.facts: In the 2007 Consent the Mother agreed spousal support would cease July 31, 2012 and renounced any future support regardless of changed circumstances; her 2010 claim for increased support was dismissed by Justice Perrault.
firac.rule: A renunciation of spousal support may be varied only in rare circumstances, such as a radical, unpredictable change linked to the marriage (Droit de la famille – 3066, [1998] R.D.F. 546); art. 17 Divorce Act.
firac.application: The issue was already decided in 2010, and the Mother offered no evidence of a radical change linked to the marriage; her difficulties stemmed from the Father's conduct rather than a marriage-linked change.
firac.conclusion: The claim for reinstatement of spousal support is dismissed.

firac.issue: Are the Mother's claims for reimbursement of expenses and damages well-founded?
firac.facts: The Father collected roughly $6,000 in medical reimbursements from his insurer without paying the Mother, and failed to fund summer camps, the nanny and clothing he had undertaken to provide; the Mother sought reimbursement, legal fees, and moral and punitive damages.
firac.rule: Homologated obligations must be honoured; arts. 51 and 54 C.c.p. permit the court to award damages, reimbursement of costs and professional fees where proceedings are abusive.
firac.application: The Court found the $6,000 medical reimbursement clearly owing and other expenses (camps, nanny, clothing) owed but hard to quantify because when the Father failed to fund them the children stayed with him. Given the abusive nature of the Father's conduct, the Court summarily fixed damages at $25,000 and awarded $7,000 in substantiated legal fees.
firac.conclusion: Reimbursement of $6,000, damages of $25,000 (art. 54 C.c.p.) and $7,000 legal fees are ordered; the Mother's Motion is granted in part.

firac.issue: Were the Father's proceedings abusive, warranting a quarrelsome-litigant declaration?
firac.facts: Since November 2007, three months after signing the Consent, the Father repeatedly moved to vary accessory measures and claim child support, largely re-litigating dismissed matters over 12 years while alienating the children from the Mother.
firac.rule: Art. 51 C.c.p. allows a court, even on its own initiative, to declare an application abusive where clearly unfounded, frivolous or vexatious; art. 54 permits damages; art. 55 permits prohibiting a quarrelsome party from proceeding without authorization.
firac.application: The Father's repeated, unfounded and frivolous claims, coupled with his efforts to keep the children from the Mother to manufacture de facto sole custody, were declared abusive. Given the 15-year 'guerilla warfare' detrimental to the children, both parties were declared quarrelsome litigants.
firac.conclusion: The Father's Motion is declared abusive; both parties are declared quarrelsome litigants under art. 55 C.c.p. and prohibited from further applications regarding their marriage, divorce and children without judicial authorization.

case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa v S.K.

name_verification.name_in_document: Children's Aid Society of Ottawa v. S.K.

defining_issues: Was summary judgment an appropriate procedure to determine this child protection application, or was there a genuine issue requiring a trial?
Is K.K. a child in need of protection within the meaning of s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
Is an order of sole custody to the mother under s. 57.1 of the CFSA in the child's best interests?
Is any access to the father in the child's best interests, or should access be terminated?

firac.issue: Was summary judgment appropriate in this child protection application, or was there a genuine issue requiring a trial?
firac.facts: The CAS moved for summary judgment. The record consisted of voluminous affidavits, text messages, emails, police reports and two competing expert reports (Dr. Ward and Dr. Sutton). The father, self-represented, declined an offered adjournment to obtain counsel and argued the volume of material and disputed facts mandated a trial.
firac.rule: Under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules the court must grant summary judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; Rule 16(6.1) permits weighing evidence, assessing credibility and drawing inferences unless the interests of justice require these powers be used only at trial. Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, whose principles are of general application, guides the analysis; courts have applied it to child protection cases while cautioning that a 'good hard look' is required given the high stakes and the parent's loss of a day in court.
firac.application: The court found the evidence—largely documentary text messages, emails and police reports contextualized by affidavits—made credibility non-critical and cross-examination unlikely to alter the essence of the evidence. Applying Rule 16(6.1), the court weighed the competing expert reports, discounted Dr. Ward's report (she had not interviewed S.K. or the CAS, reviewed the police history or conducted testing) and adopted Dr. Sutton's concerns. The father's reliance on the sheer volume of material 'missed the point'—the volume and nature of the material is what permitted summary determination.
firac.conclusion: The process met proportionality and timeliness requirements and the CAS's prima facie case shifted the onus to the father, who failed to raise a genuine issue for trial. Summary judgment was granted.

firac.issue: Is K.K. a child in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the CFSA?
firac.facts: The father had a 2000 assault conviction against the mother, a documented 13-year history of threatening and aggressive conduct toward police, officials and others, sent violent threatening texts (including 'I would sooner slice ur throat'), assaulted the mother in the child's presence in March 2013, and told the two-year-old child 'you're pissing me off' and to recite that 'Poppa will destroy all opposition'.
firac.rule: Section 37(2)(b) (risk of physical harm) and s. 37(2)(g) (risk of emotional harm) of the CFSA; the CAS bears the onus on a balance of probabilities. 'Risk' means harm more likely than not to occur; expert evidence generally assists, and harm need not be directed specifically at the child (assessment considers likelihood of positive change given the parent's mental health and hostility to services).
firac.application: The court found the documented pattern of physical aggression and threats, the assault in the child's presence, and the father's emotional abuse of the mother (which would inevitably affect the child) established real, non-speculative risk. Dr. Ward's contrary conclusions were rejected for lack of collateral information; Dr. Sutton's assessment of the father's chronic difficulties and lack of insight was adopted.
firac.conclusion: K.K. was found to be a child in need of protection under both s. 37(2)(b) and s. 37(2)(g).

firac.issue: Is sole custody to the mother under s. 57.1 of the CFSA in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The relationship was dysfunctional, acrimonious and at times violent. The CAS had no protection concerns regarding the mother alone. Both experts agreed shared custody was impossible; the mother consented and the father did not dispute that sole custody to the mother was in the child's best interests.
firac.rule: Section 57.1 of the CFSA permits a custody order where it serves the child's best interests as an alternative to other protection dispositions.
firac.application: Given the history and the father's personality disorders, the experts concluded sole custody was the only workable option, and the father conceded it was in the child's best interests.
firac.conclusion: Sole custody was granted to the mother; no genuine issue for trial existed on this point.

firac.issue: Should the father have any access, or should access be terminated as being contrary to the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The father professed love for the child and offered to accept supervised access, but insisted supervisors act only as passive 'observers', repeatedly stated he would never comply with CAS or court directions, described workers as 'terrorists' and 'witches', and lacked insight into his conduct. The only supervised visit went well. No third-party evidence showed his parenting course or treatment had improved his insight.
firac.rule: Termination of access is a last resort; the best interests of the child under s. 37(3) of the CFSA govern and prevail where they clash with the parent's interests (Young v. Young, [1993] 4 SCR 3). The court must consider supervised access before terminating access, weighing the benefit to the child of terminating against continued contact.
firac.application: The court accepted the father loves the child but found he lacked insight into the harm his behaviour causes, that no supervisor acceptable to him could realistically be found, and that he would not abide by conditions. Dr. Ward's optimistic view was rejected; Dr. Sutton's concerns about physical and psychological harm were adopted. Supervised access was therefore not viable and continued contact would be contrary to the child's best interests.
firac.conclusion: Access to the father was terminated; a restraining order and permission to relocate out of province without disclosing the address were granted; child support was deferred to family court for lack of financial evidence.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area, as this is a child protection proceeding under the Child and Family Services Act. K047 (best interests of the child) is central to the protection finding, custody and access analysis. K048 (custody/access) captures the s. 57.1 sole-custody order and the termination-of-access determination. K050 (parental support) reflects the mother's child support request, though it is a weaker pick since support was deferred to family court for want of financial evidence. K002 (Civil litigation) is included as a borderline tier-1 tag for the Hryniak/Rule 16 summary judgment procedure that framed the decision; it is weak because the controlled vocabulary has no dedicated summary-judgment, child-protection, restraining-order or domestic-violence keyword. Fewer than five keywords apply strongly, so K050 and K002 are flagged as the closest available but weak matches.

defining_issues: Was there a material change in circumstances justifying a variation of Justice Roger's March 9, 2017 final order granting sole custody to the mother with supervised access to the father?
What parenting arrangement (decision-making authority and primary residence) is in the best interests of the two children under the Children's Law Reform Act?

firac.issue: Was there a material change in circumstances justifying a variation of the 2017 final custody order?
firac.facts: The 2017 order gave Shanna sole custody with supervised access to Zackery. On October 11, 2018, an incident led to Shanna being charged with assault and the children being placed in Zackery's primary care, where they remained for over four and a half years. Zackery brought a motion to change; both parties sought sole decision-making and primary residence.
firac.rule: A final parenting order may be varied where a material change in circumstances affecting the child has occurred since the order was made, triggering a fresh best-interests determination under the Children's Law Reform Act.
firac.application: The court found the October 11, 2018 event and the subsequent relocation of the children into the father's primary care constituted a clear material change from the arrangement contemplated by Justice Roger's 2017 order, which had assumed the children would remain with the mother with only supervised paternal access.
firac.conclusion: A material change was established, requiring a new best-interests analysis.

firac.issue: What parenting arrangement best serves the children's best interests under s. 24 of the Children's Law Reform Act?
firac.facts: For 4 years 8 months in the father's care, the children had chronic school absences, were expelled, received no maintained counselling or ADHD treatment despite repeated professional recommendations, and were fostered by the father to fear their mother (believing she tried to kill K.). The father accused the mother of poisoning the children and other unsupported allegations, obstructed her parenting time, and exposed the children to adult conflict. The mother consistently advocated for services, addressed her own mental-health issues through DBT, and had generally warm, loving interactions with the children.
firac.rule: Under s. 24(1)-(3) of the Children's Law Reform Act, the court must consider only the best interests of the child, giving primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being, and weighing the enumerated factors including each parent's willingness to support the child's relationship with the other parent, the history of care, ability to meet the child's needs, capacity to communicate and cooperate, and any family violence or conflict.
firac.application: The court found the father utterly incapable of meeting the children's educational, medical and psychological needs, of supporting their relationship with their mother, of communicating and cooperating, and of sheltering them from conflict, most damagingly by instilling an unfounded fear of their mother. The mother, by contrast, had persistently sought services, worked on her mental health, and maintained affectionate relationships despite forced absences. On credibility, the court preferred the mother's evidence, corroborated by documentary records, over the father's deflective and at times incredible testimony.
firac.conclusion: It was in the children's best interests to reside primarily with the mother with sole decision-making authority; the father's parenting time was reserved for a further two-day hearing, with supervised parenting continuing in the interim per the June 23, 2023 temporary order.
