name_verification.name_in_document: ROSLYN GOTHELF PHILLIPS v. MAUREEN ROSEN DOUEK, NICOLE MAGDER DOUEK, BERTHA GOLIGER DOUEK and THE ESTATE OF THE LATE ALBERT DOUEK

defining_issues: Were the notarial wills made in September 2012 the product of undue influence by Mr. Douek's daughters and therefore void?
Was the April 2012 will invalid on grounds of undue influence by Ms. Phillips or unworthiness, and had Ms. Phillips misappropriated funds so as to defeat her claim?
Was the $275,000 sum a valid gift, or a null gift made mortis causa?
Should the 2012 transfer of Mr. Douek's interest in the Côte-Saint-Luc property to Ms. Phillips be revoked for coercion or ingratitude?

firac.issue: Were the September 2012 notarial wills the product of undue influence by Mr. Douek's daughters, rendering them void?
firac.facts: Six months before his death from acute myeloid leukemia, the wealthy 91-year-old Albert Douek made an April 2012 will bequeathing $700,000 to his de facto spouse, Ms. Phillips. While hospitalized and briefly in the ICU in September 2012, he signed new wills (Sept. 2 and Sept. 29) leaving his estate to his wife and daughters and omitting Ms. Phillips. A handwritten note to notary Derhy showed he believed Ms. Phillips was having an affair with a tennis pro. An independent witness, Ms. Santullo, overheard Ms. Rosen Douek say the family had to convince the father to change his will by telling him Ms. Phillips had been unfaithful.
firac.rule: Undue influence has two elements: (1) proof of 'improper schemes, disgraceful devices, lies, slander, deceit and trickery, or deliberate misrepresentations,' and (2) proof that those machinations caused the testator to make the impugned will (Brusenbauch v. Young, 2019 QCCA 914; Stoneham and Tewkesbury v. Ouellet, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 172). The standard is the balance of probabilities, and undue influence may be established by serious, precise and concordant presumptions of fact (art. 2849 C.C.Q.).
firac.application: Given the daughters' demonstrated willingness to resort to questionable means, Mr. Douek's weakened condition, Ms. Santullo's credible independent testimony, rumours of an affair circulating in the family, Ms. Rosen Douek's evasive and implausible discovery answers, and the note to Mtre Derhy, the Court found it more likely than not that Mr. Douek's false belief resulted from deceit primarily by Ms. Rosen Douek. Logic, common sense and Mtre Derhy's testimony established that this belief was the probable reason Ms. Phillips was excluded; the defendants' countervailing circumstantial facts supported an equally consistent narrative and did not rebut causation.
firac.conclusion: Both September 2012 wills were annulled on grounds of undue influence.

firac.issue: Was the April 2012 will invalid for undue influence or unworthiness, and had Ms. Phillips misappropriated funds from Mr. Douek?
firac.facts: The defendants argued in the alternative that the April 2012 will resulted from undue influence by Ms. Phillips and that she was unworthy (art. 621 C.C.Q.) because she had misappropriated close to $430,000 through cheques and credit-card payments. They initially alleged forged signatures, filing an expert report, but abandoned the forgery theory mid-trial and shifted to a theory of pre-signed cheques used without authorization.
firac.rule: Same undue-influence framework; unworthiness under art. 621 C.C.Q.; circumstantial proof must meet the serious, precise and concordant standard (art. 2849 C.C.Q.).
firac.application: The facts advanced fell short of supporting an inference of undue influence, and the compelling testimony of the notaries and advisers showed the will reflected Mr. Douek's true intentions. The misappropriation theory lacked direct evidence; the circumstantial evidence was weak, Ms. Phillips's imperfect recollection was attributable to the passage of seven years, and it was implausible that a sophisticated businessman would not have noticed large-scale theft, especially given his broader pattern of generosity to her. The daughters' abandoned forgery allegation reflected an inclination to resort to questionable means.
firac.conclusion: The April 2012 will was declared Mr. Douek's true last will; the unworthiness and misappropriation claims were dismissed and the succession was ordered to pay Ms. Phillips $700,000.

firac.issue: Was the $275,000 a valid gift, or a null gift made mortis causa?
firac.facts: Ms. Phillips deposited a $275,000 cheque bearing Mr. Douek's signature on August 31, 2012; the funds were later returned to his account after a bank verification. She claimed the sum from the succession as a valid gift by delivery.
firac.rule: A gift of movable property may be validly made where consent is accompanied by delivery and immediate possession (art. 1824, para. 2 C.C.Q.). However, a gift made during the donor's 'deemed mortal illness' is null unless it would have been made notwithstanding the donor's impending death (art. 1820, para. 1 C.C.Q.); the test is both objective (death objectively imminent) and subjective (donor aware death was likely imminent) (Michaud-Caron c. Dufour, 2004 CanLII 65628 (QC CS)).
firac.application: Mr. Douek was terminally ill with acute myeloid leukemia, having been given two to six months to live, and died less than two months later. He was highly intelligent and in all likelihood aware of the gravity of his condition; Ms. Phillips admitted he made the gift to protect her because he knew he was ill. Nothing showed he would have made the gift regardless of his impending death.
firac.conclusion: The gift was null as having been made mortis causa; the $275,000 claim was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the 2012 transfer of Mr. Douek's interest in the Côte-Saint-Luc property to Ms. Phillips be revoked for coercion or ingratitude?
firac.facts: In April 2012 Mr. Douek transferred his undivided half-interest in the co-owned Côte-Saint-Luc house to Ms. Phillips for one dollar. The defendants alleged she had harassed and coerced him and sought revocation for ingratitude (art. 1836, para. 2 C.C.Q.).
firac.rule: A gift may be revoked for ingratitude under art. 1836, para. 2 C.C.Q.; coercion requires proof that consent was vitiated.
firac.application: The coercion assertion found no support in the evidence; the notaries' and adviser's testimony showed the transfer reflected Mr. Douek's true intentions, and Ms. Rosen Douek could offer no specifics. The ingratitude argument depended on the misappropriation allegations, which failed.
firac.conclusion: The claim to revoke the property transfer was dismissed; the April 2012 transaction stood.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area under which wills and estates fall, and K054 (wills / estates) is the central subject — the validity of successive notarial wills, undue influence, unworthiness and a gift alleged to be mortis causa. K002 (Civil litigation) captures the private-law adversarial nature of the estate litigation, including the abuse-of-process and solicitor-client-fee arguments under arts. 51 ff. C.C.P. K086 (co-ownership) is engaged by the disputed transfer of Mr. Douek's undivided half-interest in the co-owned Côte-Saint-Luc residence. K093 (Jewish) is a weak, contextual pick reflecting the Douek family's background and hospitalization at the Jewish General Hospital; it is flagged as borderline since it is not a defining legal issue. The controlled vocabulary lacks specific terms for undue influence, gifts, or mortis causa dispositions, so the closest available keywords were selected.

registry_rationale: The decision expressly identifies the 'DISTRICT OF Montreal' with file no. 500-17-078480-137, indicating the Montreal registry of the Superior Court.

name_verification.discrepancy_note: The neutral citation matches. The supplied style of cause 'Taperek c. Taperek' captures the parties (Teresa Taperek v. Richard Taperek and Jadwiga Taperek Ciochon) but the decision is formally styled 'Konysz-Taperek (Succession de)', after the deceased mother's estate. Minor discrepancy in the style of cause rather than a mismatched case.

defining_issues: Did the testator (the mother) have the testamentary capacity required to make the four wills and codicils executed between March 2009 and March 2010?
Were the contested wills and codicils the product of undue influence (captation) exercised by the siblings?
Were out-of-court statements, particularly those of the deceased mother, admissible under the hearsay exceptions of the Civil Code of Québec?

firac.issue: Did the mother have the testamentary capacity required to execute the four contested wills and codicils?
firac.facts: The mother, over 18 and never placed under protective supervision, executed four testamentary documents between March 2009 and March 2010 while suffering various physical ailments and fluctuating cognitive test scores (MMSE and CASE). Two experts who never met her drew opposite conclusions; treating doctors, social workers and two notaries interacted with her.
firac.rule: Arts. 703 and 707 C.C.Q. require the 'required capacity', assessed at the time the will is made; the notion of 'sound intellect' (sain d'esprit) developed under art. 831 C.C.L.C. continues to apply. Every person is presumed of sound intellect and the burden lies on the party contesting the will; if a general state of unsoundness is proven prima facie, the burden shifts to the party upholding the will to show a lucid interval (Bertrand c. Opération Enfant Soleil). Expert, medical, lay and notarial evidence are all admissible.
firac.application: No professional ever diagnosed Alzheimer's or concluded the mother lacked capacity; only one physician suggested possible cognitive impairment. The court accepted that the two anomalously high MMSE scores (administered by family doctors) should be excluded, leaving a pattern of mild, worsening impairment, but Dr. Friedman only expressed 'concerns' requiring follow-up that was never done. Social workers, an ergotherapist, family friend MacDonald and both notaries found her lucid and able to make decisions. The court found impairment short of incapacity.
firac.conclusion: Teresa failed to prove on the balance of probabilities that the mother lacked testamentary capacity; the mother had capacity to make valid wills.

firac.issue: Were the contested wills and codicils the product of undue influence by the siblings?
firac.facts: After April 2009 Teresa had little contact with the mother, who was isolated from her and lived in three care institutions where the siblings instructed staff that she did not want to see Teresa. The mother progressively reduced and finally, in March 2010, eliminated Teresa's inheritance, after a December 2009 letter drafted by Richard.
firac.rule: Undue influence (captation) requires dolosive manoeuvres (isolating the testator, intercepting mail, denigrating family) beyond mere flattery, and must be the cause of the disposition; the burden rests on the party alleging it, with no shift, though courts may draw inferences from circumstances (J. Beaulne; Stoneham v. Ouellet; Blain (Succession de)). Mere suspicion or vague allegation is insufficient.
firac.application: The siblings had opportunity, the mother was cognitively impaired, the final will was harsh and benefited them. However, the mother's anger stemmed from Teresa's own conduct in April 2009 (changing locks, unplugging the telephone, attempting to keep the mother from siblings), expressed consistently to disinterested doctors, social workers and notaries whether or not siblings were present, and she never phoned Teresa though able to. The events described in the December 2009 letter had a rational foundation, and both notaries met the mother alone and were satisfied the decisions were hers.
firac.conclusion: While undue influence was possible, it was not established on the balance of probabilities; the burden on Teresa was not met, and the action was dismissed.

firac.issue: Were out-of-court statements, particularly the deceased mother's, admissible as evidence?
firac.facts: Numerous witnesses (Teresa, the siblings, friends) repeated statements made to them, chiefly by the mother concerning her will and her relationships. Objections were made on both sides.
firac.rule: Arts. 2870 and 2871 C.C.Q. codify the hearsay exceptions: a statement of a person who does not testify is admissible where it is impossible or unreasonable for the declarant to appear and the reliability of the statement is sufficiently guaranteed by the circumstances (spontaneous, contemporaneous statements presumed reliable); reliability focuses on the declarant, not the reporting witness (R. v. Smith).
firac.application: The mother could not testify. Most of her statements were spontaneous and contemporaneous, made in circumstances negating mistake or untruth, and she had nothing to gain by lying. The credibility of the reporting witness goes to weight, not admissibility. Statements by the children in their own interest were unnecessary (all testified); statements against their interest were admissible as declarations against interest.
firac.conclusion: The statements, particularly the mother's, were admissible; weight depended on the credibility of the reporting witness.

name_verification.name_in_document: Regina v. Parks [Indexed as: R. v. Parks]

defining_issues: Was the trial judge correct to refuse the proposed challenge-for-cause question relating to the credibility of witnesses involved in drugs?

Did the trial judge err in refusing to permit defence counsel to ask prospective jurors whether their ability to judge the evidence impartially would be affected by the fact that the accused was black and the deceased white?
Did the trial judge's inaccurate recollections of the evidence in the jury charge, and the s. 9(2) Canada Evidence Act ruling, warrant a new trial?

firac.issue: Was the trial judge correct to refuse the proposed challenge-for-cause question about jurors' ability to judge witnesses involved in drugs?
firac.facts: Defence counsel sought to ask prospective jurors whether their ability to judge witnesses without bias would be affected by the fact that people involved in cocaine and other drugs were part of the case.
firac.rule: On a challenge for cause under s. 638(1)(b) of the Criminal Code, proposed questions must go to a matter relevant to a juror's potential partiality; matters properly bearing on witness credibility are not a basis for challenge.
firac.application: A witness's involvement in the drug trade and personal use of illicit drugs are legitimate considerations for a jury in assessing credibility and reliability, not sources of impermissible partiality. The question wrongly implied such involvement should be irrelevant to judging witnesses.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge correctly refused the first question; the appellate court found no merit in this ground.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in refusing to permit a challenge-for-cause question directed at anti-black racial partiality of prospective jurors?
firac.facts: The accused was a black drug dealer convicted of manslaughter in the death of a white cocaine user; the violence was interracial and occurred during a drug transaction. Defence counsel proposed a single race-neutral question asking whether a juror's ability to judge the evidence impartially would be affected by the accused being black and the deceased white. The trial judge relied on the presumption that sworn jurors decide on the evidence without regard to personal prejudice and refused the question.
firac.rule: The right to challenge for cause based on partiality (Criminal Code s. 638(1)(b)) is essential to the constitutional right to a fair trial and to trial by jury. Under R. v. Sherratt, [1991] 1 S.C.R. 509, a challenge may proceed where (a) the question is relevant to potential partiality and (b) there is a "realistic potential for the existence of partiality" on a sufficiently articulated ground. Partiality has both an attitudinal and a behavioural component (bias plus discrimination in reaching a verdict); it is not equated with mere bias (R. v. Hubbert; R. v. Barrow).
firac.application: The single, focused question captured both components of partiality — attitude and its effect on the verdict — and was therefore relevant. Drawing on numerous studies and reports (including the Lewis report and human rights commission data), the court found widespread anti-black racism a grim reality in Metropolitan Toronto, creating a realistic possibility that one or more jurors would consciously or subconsciously discriminate against a black accused. The interracial nature of the violence and the accused's involvement in a criminal drug transaction heightened that possibility. Post-selection safeguards (oath, jury dynamics, judicial warnings) were held insufficient to displace this realistic potential where subconscious, engrained bias was at issue.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge erred in refusing the question; a trial judge in Metropolitan Toronto should permit such a question in any case involving a black accused who requests it, and it was essential to a fair trial here.

firac.issue: Did the s. 9(2) Canada Evidence Act ruling and the errors in the jury charge warrant a new trial?
firac.facts: The Crown was permitted to cross-examine witness Dobson on a verbatim transcript of his videotaped statement. The trial judge also misstated one piece of evidence and mislabelled one witness's credibility as uncontested, but corrected these after further submissions and jury questions.
firac.rule: Section 9(2) of the Canada Evidence Act requires the prior statement to be "in writing, or reduced to writing." A misdirection warrants reversal only where it causes prejudice not cured by correction or by the overall balance of the charge (cf. R. v. Wood).
firac.application: A verbatim transcript of a videotape satisfies s. 9(2) even though the videotape itself does not, consistent with Wood. The two factual misstatements did not relate to the applicable law, were subject to repeated instruction that the jury's recollection prevailed, and were expressly corrected; the court declined to speculate that the jury ignored the corrections.
firac.conclusion: These grounds failed; no prejudice warranting reversal arose from them.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area — a manslaughter conviction and jury-selection procedure under the Criminal Code. K065 (racism) is central: the court's reasoning turns on documented anti-black racism in Metropolitan Toronto. K074 (systemic discrimination) fits the court's discussion of institutional/systemic racism and its persistence in the criminal justice system. K069 (discrimination) captures the operative test — whether a biased juror would discriminate against the black accused in reaching a verdict. K071 (human dignity) and K107 (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms) reflect the constitutional right to a fair trial and trial by jury underpinning the challenge for cause. K112 (Charter s. 7) is a borderline pick — the court grounds the challenge right in the constitutional right to a fair trial, though it does not cite a specific section; it is flagged as weak. The controlled vocabulary lacks a specific 'jury / challenge for cause' term, so the closest applicable keywords were selected.

The city is not expressly stated in the text; Toronto is given as the seat of the Ontario Court of Appeal (its registry), and the case itself repeatedly concerns juries drawn from "Metropolitan Toronto."
registry_rationale: The heading names the deciding body as the "Court of Appeal for Ontario" (Krever, Doherty and Abella JJ.A.), which is the registry through which the appeal proceeded.

case_name: R. v. Westfair Foods Ltd. and Canada Safeway Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Westfair Foods Ltd. and Canada Safeway Ltd.

defining_issues: Do the Sunday-closing provisions of the Urban Municipality Act, 1984 and the Saskatoon Store Hours Bylaw infringe the freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed by s. 2(a) of the Charter?
If those provisions infringe s. 2(a), is the infringement a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
If the Sunday-closing provisions are unconstitutional, should they be wholly of no force or effect or merely unenforceable against Saturday observers (a constitutional exemption)?
Does the overall store-hours regulatory scheme, which classifies businesses by type and store size, infringe the equality guarantee in s. 15(1) of the Charter?

firac.issue: Do the Sunday-closing provisions of the Act and the Store Hours Bylaw infringe s. 2(a) of the Charter?
firac.facts: Section 121 of the Urban Municipality Act, 1984 and the City of Saskatoon Store Hours Bylaw required larger retail stores to close on Sundays. Westfair Foods and Canada Safeway operated stores exceeding 1100 square metres and kept them open in defiance of the bylaw, leading to charges. The respondents argued the Sunday-closing requirement coerced retailers who observe Saturday as their Sabbath (such as those of the Jewish and Seventh-day Adventist faiths) into closing an extra day or trading on their own religious holiday.
firac.rule: Freedom of religion under s. 2(a) protects against coercion and constraint, including indirect forms that limit conduct (R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295). A purpose-and-effects test applies; legislation with a valid secular purpose may still infringe s. 2(a) by its effects (R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713). A court may take judicial notice of society's history and values (Jones v. The Queen) and must recognize Canada's multicultural heritage (s. 27).
firac.application: The court found the legislation had a valid secular purpose of providing a common pause day for retail workers. Although, unlike in Edwards Books, there was no evidence of Saskatchewan Saturday observers, the court took judicial notice that Jewish and Seventh-day Adventist persons in Saskatoon observe Saturday as their Sabbath and engage in retail trade. The Sunday-closing provisions therefore had the same adverse effect on Saturday observers as the Ontario statute in Edwards Books.
firac.conclusion: The Sunday-closing provisions infringe s. 2(a) of the Charter.

firac.issue: Is the s. 2(a) infringement justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
firac.facts: Unlike the Ontario statute in Edwards Books, which contained a Sabbatarian exemption for Saturday-observing retailers with limited staff and floor area, neither the Saskatchewan legislation nor the Saskatoon bylaw contained any exemption or measure to alleviate the effects on Saturday observers.
firac.rule: Under s. 1 (Oakes; Edwards Books) a limit must serve a pressing and substantial objective and be proportionate: rationally connected, minimally impairing, and not disproportionate in effect. A legislature enacting Sunday-closing laws must 'attempt very seriously to alleviate the effects of those laws on Saturday observers' (Dickson C.J. in Edwards Books).
firac.application: The common pause day objective was sufficiently important and the measures rationally connected, but the analysis failed at minimal impairment: the absence of any Sabbatarian exemption meant no effort was made to mitigate the infringement of Saturday observers' religious freedom. That omission was fatal.
firac.conclusion: The infringement is not demonstrably justified under s. 1.

firac.issue: Should the invalid Sunday-closing provisions be wholly of no force or effect, or merely subject to a constitutional exemption for Saturday observers?
firac.facts: The laws were enacted for a valid secular purpose but incidentally interfered with the religious tenets of some. The court considered whether a case-by-case constitutional exemption (canvassed but left open in Big M Drug Mart and Edwards Books) was preferable to full invalidity.
firac.rule: Section 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 renders inconsistent laws of no force or effect to the extent of the inconsistency. A constitutional exemption for individuals whose religious freedom is infringed is a possible alternative remedy.
firac.application: The court reasoned that exemptions would breed uncertainty (who qualifies; corporations that cannot hold beliefs; retailers who do not actually close Saturdays), would require intrusive and possibly demeaning inquiries into religious beliefs that might themselves violate the Charter, and could collide with s. 15(1). Tailoring the law to the Constitution is a task for legislators, not courts.
firac.conclusion: The Sunday-closing provisions are declared of no force or effect in their entirety.

firac.issue: Does the store-hours regulatory scheme infringe s. 15(1) equality rights by classifying businesses by type and store size?
firac.facts: The scheme treated retail businesses differently from other businesses, different retailers differently by the goods sold, and similar retailers differently by store size (over/under 1100 square metres).
firac.rule: Section 15(1) guarantees equality before and under the law without discrimination. Discrimination means any distinction, exclusion, restriction or preference whose purpose or effect nullifies or impairs forms of equality connected to human dignity and worth (Reference re Use of French in Criminal Proceedings, per Cameron J.A.). The inquiry asks whether a protected form of equality is engaged and, if so, whether the measure discriminates.
firac.application: The court held that the forms of equality protected by s. 15(1) are those connected to human dignity and worth. Regulation of businesses as such is not so connected and is not governed by s. 15 absent some trespass on human-rights objectives. The distinctions drawn by the store-hours scheme did not engage any protected form of equality.
firac.conclusion: Section 15(1) has no application; the scheme does not infringe equality rights, so those charges are referred back for trial.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally constitutional (K003). The central holding is that Sunday-closing laws infringe freedom of religion (K025) of Saturday observers, engaging Charter s. 2(a) (K110). The s. 1 reasonable-limits/Oakes analysis (K030) is decisive because of the missing Sabbatarian exemption. The equality argument invokes Charter s. 15 (K109) and equality rights (K023), though rejected. The affected observers keep the Sabbath on Saturday, engaging shabbat (K033), and are described as Jewish and Seventh-day Adventist faiths (K093, a borderline but supported tier-3 group tag given the Jewish Sabbath reference). The Canadian Charter (K107) is the governing instrument, and the court expressly relied on s. 27 multiculturalism (K121). K093 and K121 are the weaker, more peripheral picks.
location_rationale: The header states 'Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench, Judicial Centre of Saskatoon,' and the reasons refer to bylaws of the City of Saskatoon and persons 'in the City of Saskatoon, in the Province of Saskatchewan.'
registry_rationale: The decision issues from the 'Judicial Centre of Saskatoon,' identifying Saskatoon as the registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: Tara S. Olfert (Petitioner) and Korvin Arthur Grant Olfert (Respondent)

defining_issues: Which parent should be designated the primary caregiver of the two children in their best interests?
Should the mother be permitted to relocate the children from Swift Current to Indianapolis?
Should the parents continue as joint legal custodians?
How should religious instruction of the children be addressed?

firac.issue: Which parent should be designated the primary caregiver of the two children in their best interests?
firac.facts: Both parents were found to be loving and competent, but had different parenting styles — the mother more permissive/moderate, the father more authoritative and prone to spanking. A jointly-commissioned clinical psychologist (Mr. Stewart) administered an extensive battery of psychometric tests and interviews, concluding the children (especially eight-year-old Bianca) gravitated toward and relied more on their mother.
firac.rule: Under s. 16(8) of the Divorce Act and ss. 6 and 8 of The Children's Law Act, 1997, the court considers only the best interests of the child, including the quality of relationships, the child's personality and emotional needs, each parent's capacity, home environment and the child's wishes; past conduct is relevant only if it bears on parenting ability.
firac.application: The court accepted Mr. Stewart's uncontradicted expert evidence, corroborated by the trial testimony, that the children's individual personalities, emotional needs and preferences were more readily met by the mother's parenting style. The father's admitted pornography habit was noted as a potential risk but given little weight due to the absence of evidence about its nature.
firac.conclusion: The mother was designated primary caregiver of Bianca and Sophia.

firac.issue: Should the mother be permitted to relocate the children from Swift Current to Indianapolis?
firac.facts: The mother, born and raised in Indianapolis, wished to return there with the children to be near her family and take a hospital position. The father was rooted in Swift Current with his family farm (his father having recently died), church and community. The mother testified she would remain in Swift Current if relocation were refused.
firac.rule: Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27 governs mobility: after a material change, the court conducts a fresh best-interests inquiry with no presumption favouring either parent, considering existing arrangements, maximizing contact with both parents, the child's views, and disruption. The maximum-contact principle in s. 16(10) of the Divorce Act and s. 6(5) of The Children's Law Act is mandatory though not absolute (Berry v. Berry, 2011 ONCA 705).
firac.application: Because the parents shared de facto custody under one roof, the 'classic double bind' did not apply. The mother's reasons for moving — professional/social opportunity and escaping her in-laws' intrusiveness — were not exceptional; her privacy concerns would be resolved by the divorce regardless of where she lived, and the children's needs could be met in either city. Relocation would seriously jeopardize the children's relationship with their father, extended family and community, offending the maximum-contact principle without justification.
firac.conclusion: The application to relocate the children to Indianapolis was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the parents continue as joint legal custodians?
firac.facts: Both parents were well-educated, capable and actively involved; no evidence of inability to communicate on major decisions or of abusive behaviour warranting sole custody.
firac.rule: Schick v. Woodrow, 2012 SKCA 1: even where one parent is designated the parent of primary residence, it is presumptively in the child's best interests to have as much contact with each parent as possible and for each to play an active role, favouring joint custody absent a contrary reason.
firac.application: There was no evidentiary basis to disenfranchise either parent; major decisions on education, health and activities were to be collaborative, with the mother's discretion prevailing on education disagreements as primary parent.
firac.conclusion: The parents were ordered to continue as joint legal custodians, with the mother as primary caregiver and a defined parenting schedule maximizing the father's contact.

firac.issue: How should religious instruction of the children be addressed?
firac.facts: Both parents were devout Christians of different denominations (father evangelical Mennonite/Brethren, mother Methodist); religion had contributed to marital conflict.
firac.rule: Young v. Young, [1993] 4 S.C.R. 3: custody/access decisions must not be based on a parent's faith, but religion may be a relevant circumstance; exposure to a parent's faith is appropriate so long as not detrimental to the child, and the custodial parent's authority over religious activities must be secured where religion is a source of conflict.
firac.application: The court found it consonant with the children's best interests to be exposed to each parent's faith in reasonable moderation, leaving them free to choose their own faith in adolescence, with no evidence justifying restraint of either parent.
firac.conclusion: Both parents may share their respective faiths with the children within reasonable limits.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test under both the Divorce Act and The Children's Law Act and drives every issue. K048 (custody/access) captures the primary-care determination, joint-custody order and parenting schedule, and is the closest controlled term for the mobility/relocation question. K050 (parental/child support) applies because the court ordered child support under the Federal Child Support Guidelines. K052 (religious upbringing) reflects the discrete section on religious instruction analysed under Young v. Young. K117 (Divorce Act) is the primary governing statute (s. 16). No specific 'mobility/relocation' keyword exists in the vocabulary, so K048 serves that function.
location_rationale: The heading states 'QUEEN'S BENCH FOR SASKATCHEWAN' and 'Judicial Centre: Swift Current, Family Law Division', establishing the city as Swift Current and the province as Saskatchewan.
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the Judicial Centre as 'Swift Current, Family Law Division', which is the registry/office.

name_verification.name_in_document: Warman v. Grosvenor

defining_issues: Were the elements of the tort of defamation established by the defendant's Internet postings?
Were the elements of the tort of assault established by the defendant's postings and e-mails threatening the plaintiff?
Could the plaintiff recover separate damages for the tort of invasion of privacy?
Did deficiencies in the notice under the Libel and Slander Act bar the plaintiff's defamation claims?
What quantum of general, aggravated and punitive damages, and what injunctive relief, was appropriate?

firac.issue: Were the elements of the tort of defamation established by the defendant's Internet postings?
firac.facts: The defendant, an Edmonton resident, made repeated Internet postings about the plaintiff, an Ottawa lawyer engaged in human rights work on Internet hate propaganda, calling him a dishonest man, liar, scumbag, pimp and disgusting maggot, alleging he was part of organized crime financed by 'mobs', and falsely alleging a conviction for child molestation, while attacking his professional credibility.
firac.rule: Per Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press Publications Ltd., [1995] 3 S.C.R. 3, a publication that lowers a person in the estimation of right-thinking members of society or exposes them to hatred, contempt or ridicule is defamatory. The plaintiff must prove on a balance of probabilities that (1) the words are defamatory, (2) they were published, and (3) they referred to the plaintiff (Rainaldi, Remedies in Tort).
firac.application: The postings were clearly defamatory on their ordinary meaning, being calculated to be personally and professionally insulting and exposing the plaintiff to hatred, contempt and ridicule. Publication was established because the Internet disseminates words worldwide and each re-posting created a new publication. The plaintiff was named in all fourteen postings and identified by photographs, so he was clearly the person defamed.
firac.conclusion: All three elements were met; the defendant defamed the plaintiff.

firac.issue: Were the elements of the tort of assault established by the postings and e-mails?
firac.facts: The defendant posted the plaintiff's residential address, phone numbers, aerial photos and a map, urged readers to 'pay him a visit,' called for his 'execution at the hands of a people's government,' referred to him as a 'dead Jew walkin',' wrote 'I AM GOD AND I HAVE A RUGER P-90 AND IT'S BULLETS HAVE YOUR NAME ON THEM,' and e-mailed 'Your day of reckoning is coming.' The conduct continued for over two years, causing the plaintiff to move residences.
firac.rule: Assault is the intentional creation of the apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact; damages are recoverable by someone made apprehensive of immediate physical contact even if it never occurs, but only where the feared event is imminent (Linden & Feldthusen, Canadian Tort Law).
firac.application: The persistent, detailed and malevolent messages, combined with the disclosure of the plaintiff's whereabouts and repeated invitations to others to harm him, were not mere general threats. Given the wide Internet publication and the real possibility that someone would act on the invitations (people had already contacted his co-op management), the plaintiff was reasonably apprehensive of imminent physical harm.
firac.conclusion: The elements of assault were established; the plaintiff was entitled to damages for assault.

firac.issue: Could the plaintiff recover separate damages for the tort of invasion of privacy?
firac.facts: The defendant published the plaintiff's personal information, including an aerial photograph and map of his residence, invading the privacy the plaintiff had tried to maintain by removing his address and using an unlisted number.
firac.rule: Assuming a common-law right to privacy exists in Canada (an unsettled question per Nitsopoulos v. Wong, 2008 CanLII 45407), recoverable damages must flow from harm not subsumed by other torts; a statutory tort such as under the B.C. Privacy Act (Griffin v. Sullivan) was distinguishable.
firac.application: The postings did invade the plaintiff's privacy, but the harm claimed was not distinct from that flowing from the defamation and assault. Unlike Wong, there was no separate tortious conduct producing separate harm, and no statutory privacy tort applied in Ontario.
firac.conclusion: No separate damages for invasion of privacy were awarded.

firac.issue: Did deficiencies in the notice under the Libel and Slander Act bar the plaintiff's defamation claims?
firac.facts: The plaintiff served a Notice of Libel under s. 5(1) of the Libel and Slander Act for only eight of the fourteen postings and none of the e-mails. The relevant servers were believed to be in California, Italy and Germany.
firac.rule: Section 5(1) requires notice for libel in a newspaper or broadcast, and s. 7 limits this to broadcasts from a station in Ontario. Per Weiss v. Sawyer, 2002 CanLII 45064 (ON CA), and Warman v. Fromm, whether Internet postings and e-mails are a 'broadcast' from an Ontario station requires an adequate evidentiary record.
firac.application: There was no evidentiary record establishing that the postings and e-mails were 'broadcasts' or that they emanated from a station in Ontario; the servers appeared to be outside Ontario. The court concluded there was no proof s. 5(1) applied, so the action was unaffected by notice. In any event, the fifth and ninth-to-thirteenth postings were covered by the Notice of Libel and were sufficient to sustain the defamation claim, and the defendant had actual notice but chose not to mitigate.
firac.conclusion: The notice deficiencies did not bar the plaintiff's claims.

firac.issue: What quantum of damages and injunctive relief was appropriate?
firac.facts: The postings and e-mails were vicious, profane, extreme and malicious, falsely portraying the plaintiff as a convicted pedophile and organized-crime figure. The defendant refused to retract or apologize and continued after service of the claim. The plaintiff waived any excess over $50,000 to proceed under the Simplified Rules.
firac.rule: Damages in libel depend on the nature of the publication, the victim's position, effects on the plaintiff, and the defendant's motivations (Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130). Aggravated damages follow from malice causing additional injury; punitive damages (Whiten v. Pilot Insurance Co., 2002 SCC 18) are awarded exceptionally where other penalties do not achieve retribution, deterrence and denunciation.
firac.application: Given the seriousness of the allegations, the frightening threats, the borderless reach of the Internet (Barrick Gold Corp. v. Lopehandia), and the extreme malice shown by dishonest and reckless disregard of truth, an award of $175,000 in general and aggravated damages was appropriate. Punitive damages were unnecessary because general and aggravated damages plus injunctive relief adequately achieved the objectives, and the point was academic given the $50,000 cap. A broadly-worded injunction was necessary given the defendant's use of multiple identities.
firac.conclusion: Damages capped at $50,000 were awarded ($20,000 general and $10,000 aggravated for defamation; $15,000 general and $5,000 aggravated for assault), with no punitive damages, plus injunctive relief, interest and substantial indemnity costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns tort claims in defamation, assault and invasion of privacy. K015 (defamation) is the central cause of action. K021 (injunction) captures the permanent injunctive relief granted, though the canonical term is interlocutory injunction — a slightly imperfect fit but the closest available for injunctive relief. K057 (antisemitic slurs), K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) reflect the antisemitic character of the postings targeting Warman as Jewish ('dead Jew walkin',' 'Jew hatemonger,' 'kike'). K061 (hate speech) and K063 (online hate / social media) capture that the defamatory and threatening content was hate-laden material disseminated on the Internet. Assault and invasion of privacy have no dedicated vocabulary entries, so they are represented through the tier-1 civil litigation keyword.
location_rationale: The decision identifies the court as the 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' before Ratushny J., establishing the province as Ontario. No sitting city is stated for the court itself; the plaintiff resides in Ottawa and the defendant in Edmonton, but neither is identified as the court's location, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision does not name a specific court registry or office, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: SNYDER v. MONTREAL GAZETTE LTD.

defining_issues: Could the newspaper escape liability by relying on the statutory press privileges/immunities under the Press Act of Québec?
Did the plaintiff establish defamation (fault, prejudice and causal link) under arts. 1053-1054 of the Civil Code?
Was the jury's award of $135,000 in moral damages 'unreasonable' within the meaning of art. 380 C.C.P. such that the Court should decline to enter judgment in conformity with the verdict?

firac.issue: Whether the Montreal Gazette could avail itself of the press immunities and privileges under the Press Act of Québec.
firac.facts: The Gazette did not plead the truth of the statements but relied on the Press Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 48. The article was ruled in law to be a report of a court (the Quebec Police Commission) sitting not held in camera. The jury nonetheless found the report inaccurate (Q.5) and not made in good faith (Q.8); it also found the retraction was not published in as conspicuous a place as the offending article (Q.19) and the plaintiff's reply was published with further comment (Q.24).
firac.rule: Section 10 of the Press Act grants complete immunity only where the report is (a) accurate, (b) in good faith, (c) of a court sitting, and (d) not in camera. Sections 3-9 grant a second immunity conditional on eleven requirements including publication of a full retraction, without comment, in as conspicuous a place, within the prescribed (but extendable) delay. Sections 4-5 give partial immunity through retraction.
firac.application: Because the jury found the report inaccurate and not in good faith, the s.10 privilege failed. The second privilege failed because the retraction was not as conspicuously placed and the reply was published with comment. The partial-immunity defence under ss.4-5 failed for the same want of conspicuousness. Ample evidence supported these findings, drawn from the issues of March 13, 14 and May 9, 1975.
firac.conclusion: All three aspects of the statutory press privilege were negatived and could not shield the newspaper from liability.

firac.issue: Whether the plaintiff proved defamation under the general law of civil liability.
firac.facts: The front-page article of March 13, 1975 labelled a 'former city official' a member of the 'Jewish Mafia', linked to an alleged underworld figure. The jury found the allegations untrue (Q.25), that a reasonably informed reader could identify the plaintiff (Q.11), that the plaintiff did not identify himself (Q.12), and that he was defamed (Q.26) and suffered damage as a direct result (Q.27).
firac.rule: Under arts. 1053 and 1054 of the Civil Code the plaintiff must prove (a) a fault of the defendant or its reporter, (b) a prejudice, and (c) a causal relationship between them.
firac.application: The jury found in the plaintiff's favour on all three elements, and the Court held there was ample evidence to support those conclusions.
firac.conclusion: Defamation was established; this part of the verdict was sustained.

firac.issue: Whether the $135,000 moral-damages award was unreasonable under art. 380 C.C.P.
firac.facts: The jury awarded nothing for career/earnings damage but $135,000 for moral damages (pain, suffering, anguish, humiliation) suffered by a public figure (Olympic organizing-committee vice-president) widely and viciously libelled during the pre-Olympic period. Seven similar actions against other media remained pending. The trial judge had instructed the jury, following Lewis v. Daily Telegraph, to compensate only for damage caused by the Gazette and not to award punitive damages.
firac.rule: Article 380 C.C.P. requires the judge to render judgment in conformity with the verdict unless it appears unreasonable. Quebec courts award real but non-punitive general damages for injury to reputation (Langlois v. Drapeau et Plante; Larouche v. Bonneville); juries express the community's valuation of reputation.
firac.application: After surveying Quebec, Canadian, French and U.K. jurisprudence (Appendices A-D), the Court found awards had historically been kept low but that reputation deserved higher valuation in modern times, analogising to the upward personal-injury adjustments in Andrews and Thornton. The jury, aware of the pending parallel actions, gave the situation proper consideration; the amount, while high, was not so grossly inflated as to be unreasonable.
firac.conclusion: The award was not unreasonable; the verdict was confirmed, with 10% interest from May 27, 1975, costs, and an order to publish the judgment in the Gazette.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a civil damages action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. K018 (qualified privilege) is used for the statutory press privilege/immunity defence under the Press Act, the closest controlled term for the press-privilege issue that was central to liability. K024 (freedom of expression) captures the court's extended discussion of freedom of the press and the balance against reputation. K093 (Jewish) reflects that the plaintiff is Jewish and the defamatory phrase was 'Jewish Mafia', and K057 (antisemitic slurs) reflects that offensive characterisation; both are somewhat borderline because the case is decided as ordinary defamation rather than as an antisemitism matter, so they are flagged as weaker, contextual picks.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'Quebec Superior Court, Deschênes, C.J.' and repeatedly references the article published in Montreal, the sitting of the Quebec Police Commission 'held in Montreal', and the English-speaking jury empanelled at Montreal; the Superior Court of Quebec sat at Montreal.
registry_rationale: The proceeding, jury trial and Quebec Police Commission sitting all took place in Montreal, indicating the Montreal registry of the Quebec Superior Court; no other registry is named.

name_verification.name_in_document: Regina v. John Michael Kapp et al

defining_issues: Do the Aboriginal Communal Fishing Licences Regulations and the pilot sales program of the Aboriginal Fishing Strategy, which authorize an exclusive commercial fishery limited to members of three Indian bands, infringe the s. 15(1) Charter equality rights of the excluded commercial fishers?
Is the differential treatment saved as an ameliorative program under s. 15(2) of the Charter?
If the program infringes s. 15, is the limit justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
What is the appropriate and just remedy under s. 24(1) of the Charter given that the accused admitted the fishing offence?

firac.issue: Do the ACFLR and the pilot sales program, authorizing an exclusive commercial fishery restricted to members of the Musqueam, Burrard and Tsawwassen bands, infringe the s. 15(1) equality rights of excluded commercial fishers?
firac.facts: During a 24-hour opening on August 19-20, 1998, only designated fishers of the three bands could fish for sockeye in Area 29 under Communal Fishing Licence No. FRD-98-CL278/MBT, which permitted the sale of the catch. The accused, non-designated Area 'E' gillnetters, fished in protest to bring a constitutional challenge and admitted the actus reus and mens rea.
firac.rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter guarantees equality without discrimination; the three-stage analysis in Law v. Canada, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 497 asks (1) whether the law draws a distinction on a personal characteristic, (2) whether it is based on an enumerated or analogous ground, and (3) whether it discriminates by imposing a burden reflecting stereotype or demeaning dignity, assessed against the four contextual factors (Andrews; Corbiere; Egan; Lovelace).
firac.application: The court found the program drew a distinction between those with a bloodline connection to the three bands and everyone else — a distinction analogous to race — thereby withholding from the claimant fishers the general public right to participate equally in the commercial fishery. Although no stereotype had yet formed, the program severely affected the fishers financially and emotionally, generated racial discord in a formerly integrated fishing community, and promoted the view that the excluded fishers were less worthy of concern and respect. The DFO was treated as effectively an employer imposing restrictive conditions on one group on a prohibited ground.
firac.conclusion: The pilot sales program offends s. 15(1) and violates the accused's equality rights.

firac.issue: Is the differential treatment saved as an ameliorative program under s. 15(2) of the Charter?
firac.facts: The Crown argued the program had an ameliorative purpose for a disadvantaged Aboriginal community, though it conceded the program was not designed to be ameliorative but coincidentally conferred benefits. Evidence showed the Musqueam and Tsawwassen bands were not financially disadvantaged, no economic study was done, and the benefits flowed only to individual designated fishers who kept the profits.
firac.rule: Section 15(2) requires a rational connection between the preferential treatment and the disadvantage, and a real nexus between the declared object and the program's form and implementation (Lovelace; MacVicar; Willocks; Schafer); the party invoking it bears the burden and a bald declaration is insufficient (Apsit).
firac.application: The court found no rational connection: financial disadvantage was not a real problem for these bands, the 'communal' label was misleading since individuals kept all profits, Sparrow did not mandate a commercial fishery, and the courts had generally rejected Aboriginal commercial-fishing claims. The program was misconceived, illogical and ineffective in remedying any genuine disadvantage, and grossly unfair to the excluded fishers.
firac.conclusion: The program is not a genuine ameliorative program and is not saved by s. 15(2).

firac.issue: Is the s. 15 infringement justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
firac.facts: Various shifting rationales were offered for the program — poaching control, experimentation, Sparrow compliance, treaty testing, economic development — with no consistent objective and no evidence considering less drastic alternatives such as the buyback program.
firac.rule: Under R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103, the objective must be pressing and substantial and the means proportionate (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionality of salutary to deleterious effects per Dagenais); the Crown bears the burden.
firac.application: The inconsistent rationales undermined any pressing-and-substantial objective; poaching was speculative and better addressed by enforcement; the program was not rationally connected to remedying band disadvantage; it failed minimal impairment because the buyback program could achieve any change with compensation; and its questionable benefits were vastly outweighed by lost income, damaged dignity, and government-sponsored racial discord.
firac.conclusion: The limit is not justified under s. 1; there is no justification for the program on the Oakes test.

firac.issue: What is the appropriate remedy under s. 24(1), and should the declaration be suspended?
firac.facts: The accused admitted knowingly fishing during a closure, having done so to litigate the program's validity. The Crown sought a ten-day suspension of the ruling to allow DFO to respond; the defence pointed to years of prior notice of the regulations' questionable validity.
firac.rule: Section 24(1) permits a remedy that is appropriate and just; suspensions of invalidity derive from a superior court's inherent jurisdiction, which provincial courts lack, though a transitional period could be built into a s. 24(1) remedy.
firac.application: A judicial stay of proceedings was the only remedy that addressed and condemned the discriminatory program. The court declined to suspend the effect, citing DFO's long-standing notice of the problem, the experimental program's eleven-year duration, and the paramount principle that identified racial discrimination — especially government-sponsored — should not be permitted to continue.
firac.conclusion: A stay of proceedings is entered, effective immediately; the suspension application is denied.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns entirely on Charter analysis. K023 (equality rights) and K109 (Charter s. 15) capture the core s. 15(1) claim and the Law framework applied. K030 (reasonable limits s. 1) reflects the extensive Oakes analysis. K107 (Canadian Charter) is the governing instrument. K069 (discrimination) and K065 (racism) are engaged because the court found the bloodline-based distinction analogous to race and repeatedly characterized the program as racially discriminatory. Criminal/regulatory keywords were not used because the Fisheries Act offence was admitted and non-contested; the case is substantively constitutional. K065 (racism) is somewhat borderline as a controlled term drawn from the hate-speech cluster, but it fits the court's express findings of racial discrimination.
location_rationale: The header states 'IN THE PROVINCIAL COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA (Criminal Division)', gives 'Registry: Vancouver', and lists 'Place of Hearing: Vancouver, B.C.'
registry_rationale: The decision expressly records 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Yves Michaud v. Michel Bissonnette, in his capacity as President of the National Assembly of Quebec

defining_issues: Did the National Assembly exceed its powers by adopting the December 14, 2000 motion denouncing a private citizen's remarks, or was it protected by the parliamentary privilege of freedom of speech?
Does section 21 of the Quebec Charter (right of petition to the National Assembly) empower the courts to compel the National Assembly to rule on a citizen's petition?

firac.issue: Was the National Assembly's unanimous motion denouncing the appellant's remarks a valid exercise of parliamentary privilege beyond judicial review, or an ultra vires act?
firac.facts: After Michaud made controversial remarks about the Jewish people at hearings of the Commission des États généraux on the French language, the National Assembly unanimously (109 MNAs) carried a motion on December 14, 2000 denouncing his 'unacceptable remarks'. Michaud sought a declaratory judgment that the Assembly lacked constitutional authority to reprove remarks of a non-Member absent a breach of privilege, invoking Standing Order 324.
firac.rule: Legislative assemblies hold inherent constitutional parliamentary privileges necessary to their functioning, including freedom of speech (New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 319; Canada (House of Commons) v. Vaid, 2005 SCC 30; Bill of Rights 1689, art. 9). Freedom of speech is a privilege of the House as a whole, not merely individual members, and permits the Assembly to declare its opinions by resolution (Standing Orders 185-186). Courts inquire only into the existence and extent of a privilege, not its exercise.
firac.application: The Court held that freedom of speech protects motions collectively adopted by the Assembly, which are resolutions expressing opinion with no normative effect, distinct from legislation. Standing Order 324 governs only motions impugning conduct that breaches the Assembly's privileges and does not limit the broad privilege to express diverging opinions on current political issues. The Assembly acts as a deliberative body, not solely a legislative/supervisory one; here it expressed an opinion on a live Québec political issue in which the appellant had freely joined. Since privilege existed and applied, the courts could not review the motion's merits, timeliness or appropriateness.
firac.conclusion: The National Assembly acted within its purview; the motion was protected by the privilege of freedom of speech and beyond judicial review.

firac.issue: Can the courts, under s. 21 of the Quebec Charter, order the National Assembly to rule on a citizen's petition?
firac.facts: Michaud presented petitions (May 3 and December 13, 2001) seeking redress; the December 13, 2001 petition lapsed when the Legislature was dissolved before a proposed amendment passed. He argued s. 21 of the Charter gave the right of petition normative, quasi-constitutional force enforceable by the courts.
firac.rule: Section 21 of the Charter of human rights and freedoms guarantees every person a right of petition to the National Assembly for redress of grievances. The Assembly has the inherent privilege of exclusive control over its proceedings (s. 42, Act respecting the National Assembly). Absent specific Charter language, the Charter cannot override inherent parliamentary privileges of constitutional status (New Brunswick Broadcasting Co.).
firac.application: The Court found the right of petition is a very old right whose exercise has always been delimited by the Assembly's privileges. Section 21 merely codifies the historical principle without debate and creates no new judicially enforceable right; it can be applied only by the National Assembly itself (Brun and Tremblay, Droit constitutionnel). Ordering the Assembly to rule on the petition would breach its privilege of exclusive control over its own debates.
firac.conclusion: Section 21 does not permit the courts to compel the Assembly to act; the trial judge rightly declined to order it to rule on the petition.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 area, as parliamentary privilege is a matter of constitutional status. K024 (freedom of expression) captures the central privilege of freedom of speech invoked by the Assembly. K011 (judicial review) reflects the courts' limited role in reviewing existence/extent but not exercise of privilege, and the declaratory-judgment challenge to a legislative act. K120 (Quebec Charter) is directly engaged through s. 21 and s. 42. K058 (antisemitism), K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) reflect the factual context — the remarks about the Jewish people that triggered the Assembly's motion; these are contextual rather than doctrinal, so weaker picks. K089 (B'nai Brith) appears in the recapped remarks and is a borderline/context pick.
location_rationale: The heading states 'COURT OF APPEAL / CANADA / PROVINCE OF QUEBEC / QUÉBEC / REGISTRY' with file No. 200-09-005100-059, indicating the Québec registry of the Quebec Court of Appeal sitting in Québec City.
registry_rationale: The style of cause identifies the 'QUÉBEC REGISTRY' expressly.

name_verification.name_in_document: Sydel v. HMTQ

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff's action be struck under Rule 19(24) as an abuse of process because it constitutes a collateral attack on her criminal convictions?
Should the plaintiff's request for an adjournment pending her conviction appeal be granted?
Does the invalidity of the Income Tax Act and the alleged lack of jurisdiction of the Provincial Court save the claim from being characterized as a collateral attack?

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's action be struck under Rule 19(24) as an abuse of process because it constitutes a collateral attack on her criminal convictions?
firac.facts: Sydel was convicted in Provincial Court of making false statements in tax returns and evading income tax under the Income Tax Act, sentenced to 18 months and fined. She abandoned her conviction appeal, then commenced a civil action seeking $300,000,000 in damages and declarations that the Income Tax Act is invalid and her convictions a nullity, alleging a conspiracy involving CRA employees, Justice lawyers and Provincial Court judges, including allegations about a Jewish judge and prosecutor and Freemason sign language.
firac.rule: Rule 19(24) of the Rules of Court permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim, are frivolous or vexatious, or are otherwise an abuse of process. A civil action that collaterally challenges a criminal conviction is an abuse of process (Rule 19(24)(d)); Hainsworth v. Ontario (A.G.); Arthur J.S. Hall and Co. v. Simons; R. v. Wilson [1983] 2 S.C.R. 594; Benji v. Keefer, 2008 BCSC 1721; V.H. v. British Columbia (A.G.), 2005 BCSC 139.
firac.application: The court found the gravamen of Sydel's claim was to relitigate issues determined at her criminal trial and to challenge the investigation and conduct of the proceedings. These matters were fully addressed and rejected by Judge Meyers. The proper and only recognized course to attack a conviction is an appeal, not a civil damages action. Following Benji and V.H., the action was actuated by the improper purpose of collaterally attacking the criminal process.
firac.conclusion: The action was struck in its entirety as a collateral attack constituting an abuse of process under Rule 19(24)(d); the action was dismissed with costs at Scale B (special costs refused).

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's request for an adjournment pending her conviction appeal or answers to interrogatories about Freemasonry be granted?
firac.facts: Sydel sought an adjournment until her appeal from conviction was heard or until defendants answered interrogatories about their association with Freemasonry.
firac.rule: An adjournment may be refused where it would serve no meaningful purpose and is incapable of changing the outcome: Rose v. University of British Columbia, 2008 BCSC 1661.
firac.application: Because the court found the claims fundamentally flawed and incapable of amendment, an adjournment would only delay the inevitable and increase costs for all parties.
firac.conclusion: The adjournment application was denied.

firac.issue: Does the alleged invalidity of the Income Tax Act and the claimed lack of jurisdiction of the Provincial Court prevent the claim from being characterized as a collateral attack?
firac.facts: Sydel argued she was not mounting a collateral attack because the Income Tax Act is invalid legislation, making the Provincial Court proceedings a nullity and void ab initio; she also relied on her status as a 'natural person' and the 'detax movement'.
firac.rule: For Rule 19(24)(d) purposes the court need not assume that arguments of law dressed up as material facts are true or treat presumptively valid legislation as non-existent. The Income Tax Act has repeatedly been held valid: Canada (A.G.) v. Hanover, 2007 BCSC 1378. Even if a court acted without jurisdiction, a civil damages action is not the appropriate forum; the remedy is an appeal.
firac.application: No Canadian court has found the Income Tax Act void or non-existent, and Judge Meyers expressly held it valid. The court declined to treat the invalidity argument as fact. Even assuming a jurisdictional defect, the proper recourse remained an appeal, not a civil action.
firac.conclusion: The invalidity/jurisdiction argument failed; the claim remained a collateral attack and abuse of process.

K004 (Criminal law) is engaged because the entire matter turns on a collateral attack against tax-evasion convictions. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) reflect the plaintiff's allegation that selection of a Jewish judge and prosecutor, given her German descent, violated her rights — a conspiracy theory grounded in antisemitic reasoning. case_name: Scotford Electrical et al v. Blue Mountain Log Sales et al

name_verification.name_in_document: Scotford Electrical & Technical Services Ltd. v. Blue Mountain Log Sales Ltd., doing business as North American Wood Treating, Rae Fujikawa

defining_issues: What is the test for ordering security for costs against a corporate plaintiff under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act?
Where the plaintiff's alleged impecuniosity is caused by the defendant's conduct that is itself the subject matter of the litigation, does that bar an award of security or merely affect its quantum?
What effect does the defendant's counterclaim arising from the same dispute have on an application for security for costs against the plaintiff?
What is the proper amount of security to be ordered?

firac.issue: What is the test for ordering security for costs against a corporate plaintiff under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act?
firac.facts: Scotford, a corporate plaintiff suing Blue Mountain for unpaid accounts on a planer mill, had only about $8,700 in accounts receivable and $5,300 in hard assets, and had incurred a $40,153.91 obligation to CCRA arising from the disputed contract. Blue Mountain sought $25,000 in security for costs.
firac.rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c.57 permits the court to require security where it appears a corporate plaintiff will be unable to pay the defendant's costs if the defence succeeds. The governing framework is set out in Kropp v. Somerset Bay (1997) and applied in Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress (1999): (1) does it appear the plaintiff cannot pay costs if the action fails; (2) has the plaintiff shown exigible assets sufficient to satisfy costs; (3) do the defendants have an arguable defence; (4) would an order visit undue hardship that would stifle the plaintiff's case. The first three are preconditions to discretion, the fourth is the exercise of discretion (Scopeset Technology).
firac.application: Scotford's nominal cash flow and receivables showed it would likely be unable to pay costs, and its $5,300 in hard assets was insufficient. The pleadings disclosed an arguable defence for Blue Mountain. On the fourth branch, there was no evidence that an order would stifle Scotford's claim, and little evidence about the principals' ability to raise funds.
firac.conclusion: The first three preconditions were met and no evidence established that an order would stifle the claim; the discretionary framework was therefore engaged and security could be considered.

firac.issue: Where the plaintiff's alleged impecuniosity is caused by the defendant's conduct that is the subject matter of the litigation, does that bar an award or affect quantum?
firac.facts: Scotford's inability to pay stemmed from the CCRA debt, which arose because Blue Mountain allegedly failed to pay the accounts that are the subject of the litigation. Scotford led no evidence that it could not raise funds for security.
firac.rule: Where a corporate plaintiff's impecuniosity is linked to the defendant's impugned conduct, the court may take this into account either in declining security (Grant, Gold River, Gray) or in reducing quantum (Apex Mountain v. British Columbia). Under Kropp/Keary, a plaintiff seeking to show a claim would be stifled must prove it has no means of raising money for security, not merely that it lacks assets.
firac.application: Because Scotford provided no evidence that it or its principals could not raise funds, the court preferred the Apex Mountain approach over Gray: absent proof the claim would be stifled, the court could not decline security outright, but the connection between the CCRA debt and the underlying dispute was a proper factor in reducing the amount awarded.
firac.conclusion: The link between impecuniosity and the defendant's alleged conduct did not bar security but justified reducing the quantum.

firac.issue: What effect does the defendant's counterclaim from the same dispute have on the security application?
firac.facts: Blue Mountain counterclaimed for breach of contract, negligence, negligent misrepresentation and wrongful filing of a lien, arising from the same facts as Scotford's claim.
firac.rule: Per Gray v. Powerassist Technologies Inc., where claim and counterclaim are intertwined and based on the same dispute, it may be unjust to require one party to post security and stay its action while permitting the other to continue litigating the same dispute; the presence of a counterclaim may be considered in setting quantum.
firac.application: Although the roles were reversed (security sought against the plaintiff), the same consideration applied: an oppressive amount of security could stifle Scotford's ability to prosecute its claim and defend the counterclaim while Blue Mountain remained free to pursue the counterclaim.
firac.conclusion: The intertwined counterclaim was a factor weighing toward a moderate security award.

firac.issue: What is the proper amount of security to be ordered?
firac.facts: The defendants' bill of costs supported approximately $25,000 at scale 3, an amount Scotford did not seriously dispute.
firac.rule: There is no obligation to award the full amount requested (Kropp); the amount must be more than nominal, assessed relative to the sum claimed (Wright Parry); awards of 15–25% of the amount sought have been held not nominal (Wright Parry, Cambridge International); an award that would halt litigation may be reduced (Galaxy Sports); and a link between impecuniosity and the cause of action may reduce quantum (Apex Mountain).
firac.application: Weighing the connection between Scotford's impecuniosity and the underlying dispute, the presence of Blue Mountain's counterclaim, and the risk of stifling the claim, the court found $25,000 excessive while requiring more than nominal security.
firac.conclusion: Scotford was ordered to post $6,000 security — $3,000 before the pending Rule 18A application and a further $3,000 before any trial; each party to bear its own costs of the application.

keywords_rationale: This is a commercial civil-procedure dispute about security for costs, so K002 (Civil litigation) is the clear tier-1 practice area. The controlled vocabulary contains no term for 'security for costs', so the remaining picks are the closest procedural/remedies neighbours and are flagged as weak: K021 (interlocutory injunction) and K020 (class action) and K022 (restitution) sit in the Civil procedure/remedies cluster nearest to the procedural remedy at issue but do not squarely apply. K015 (defamation) and K089 (Canadian Jewish Congress) appear only because the leading authority cited is Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, a defamation case — these are passing citations, not issues engaged, and should be treated as very weak. Only K002 genuinely applies; the vocabulary lacks apt terms for this cost-security matter.
