registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: Chilliwack'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Schwalm (Re)

defining_issues: Should the court exercise its discretion under s. 43(7) of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act to dismiss the petition on the ground that it was brought for an improper or collateral purpose?
Did economic duress in the obtaining of the guarantees and consent to judgment provide sufficient cause to refuse a receiving order?
Would a bankruptcy serve any adequate purpose given the debtors' alleged lack of assets and income?

firac.issue: Should the court exercise its discretion under s. 43(7) of the BIA to dismiss the petition as brought for an improper or collateral purpose?
firac.facts: Marker Canada Limited, a sporting goods supplier, petitioned to bankrupt William and Judith Schwalm on judgments obtained on guarantees for the failed Old Firehall Sports retail business. The Schwalms alleged the suppliers acted in concert to close their business to make room for a new Sporting Life outlet, and that Marker sought to keep Mrs. Schwalm (who is Jewish and who alleged an anti-semitic remark by Marker's Mr. Labelle) out of the industry.
firac.rule: Section 43(7) BIA directs the court to dismiss a petition where the debtor satisfies it that, 'for other sufficient cause no order ought to be made.' Bankruptcy proceedings must not be used for a collateral advantage or improper purpose (Dimples Diapers Inc. v. Paperboard Industries Corp.; Dallas/North Group Inc., Re; Re De La Hooke; Laserworks, Re). Discretion must be exercised judicially according to common sense and justice (Churchill Forest Industries; Poskitt v. Poskitt).
firac.application: The court found the suppliers' pressure and demands originated in mounting concerns over Firehall's unpaid accounts and 'redating' practices from early 2000, before the Sporting Life announcement, and did not harden afterward. The alleged anti-semitic and gender-based hostility was not made out; Mr. Labelle's remark was sincerely taken as anti-semitic but not intended as such. Because Firehall had reopened under the son's ownership with Mrs. Schwalm as manager, a bankruptcy would not further any objective of excluding her from the trade, so no plausible collateral motive existed. The petition's genuine object was to investigate the debtors' assets and dealings with the Schwalm Family Trust.
firac.conclusion: No improper or collateral purpose was shown; s. 43(7) did not warrant dismissal on this ground.

firac.issue: Did economic duress in obtaining the guarantees and the consent to judgment amount to sufficient cause to refuse a receiving order?
firac.facts: Mr. and Mrs. Schwalm gave guarantees for the business debts in 2000 and later consented to judgment during the proposal period in exchange for a two-week adjournment, after Mr. Labelle said things would 'get ugly' otherwise. They argued the business had become dependent on Marker's supply and the guarantees were extracted as a condition of credit that never came.
firac.rule: Economic duress requires coercion of will vitiating consent, assessed by whether the party protested, had a realistic alternative or adequate legal remedy, was independently advised, and took steps to avoid the contract (Pao On v. Lau Yiu Long; Gordon v. Roebuck; Waddams, The Law of Contracts). The ultimate test is unconscionability — undue advantage of inequality of bargaining power.
firac.application: The court held Marker was not changing the bargain by taking fresh guarantees, and Mrs. Schwalm herself had invited reliance on them. As to the consent to judgment, the Schwalms did not protest, were independently advised, and took no steps to avoid the bargain; they wanted and received the adjournment. Nothing showed Marker importuned them into an improvident bargain. Even if duress fell short of setting aside the judgments, no objectionable feature warranted exercising discretion in the debtors' favour.
firac.conclusion: No duress sufficient to constitute 'other sufficient cause' was established.

firac.issue: Would a bankruptcy serve any adequate purpose given the debtors' claimed lack of assets and income?
firac.facts: The debtors said they had no material assets or income and that Firehall's assets were subject to valid security held by the Schwalm Family Trust, so a bankruptcy would benefit no one. However, the record showed numerous unexplained dealings: use of the Trust as a 'clearing house', the Schwalms' recent resignation as trustees in favour of a non-family friend, sale of a 21% interest in the matrimonial home to their daughters the day after the proposal failed, and sales of condos with proceeds directed elsewhere without documentation.
firac.rule: Where a debtor has no assets and no prospect of any, a court may refuse a receiving order (Re Benson; Kenwood Hills, Re). But bankruptcy is well-suited to investigating a debtor's affairs and recovering assets, including through claims that a trust is invalid or that assets are held on constructive trust, and creditors are not bound by a trustee's view.
firac.application: The court found the prima facie absence of assets was made problematic by the unexplained transactions and the debtors' unreliable evidence about the Family Trust. Bankruptcy would be the most effective means to obtain reliable information about the Trust and to pursue possible recoveries. Mr. Schwalm, a former trustee who prepared the Trust's tax returns, also held relevant information, and additional substantial debts (Baycrest, banks, tax authorities) confirmed insolvency.
firac.conclusion: A bankruptcy would serve an adequate and proper purpose; a receiving order was justified against both debtors.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally a bankruptcy/insolvency dispute, which the controlled vocabulary does not cover directly; the closest tier-1 anchor is K002 Civil litigation. The antisemitism-oriented terms apply only marginally: Mrs. Schwalm is Jewish (K093) and the household is a Jewish family (K095), and she alleged that Marker's representative made an anti-semitic remark (K058 antisemitism, K057 antisemitic slurs) — though the court expressly found no anti-semitic intent, making K058 and K057 weak, ancillary picks retained only because the vocabulary offers no insolvency, improper-purpose, or economic-duress terms. All five are flagged as an imperfect fit driven by the limits of the vocabulary.
location_rationale: The header identifies the court as the 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice', establishing Ontario as the province. No sitting city is stated in the decision; the businesses and events are located in Unionville/Markham and Toronto, but the court's location is not identified, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision gives a docket number (31-206765-T) but does not name a court registry or office, so registry is left null.

case_name: The Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa v. L.A.

name_verification.name_in_document: The Children's Aid Society of Ottawa v. L.A.

defining_issues: Was the Inuit child G.A. in need of protection under s. 74(2) of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017?

If so, was it in G.A.'s best interests to be placed in extended society care with a view to adoption, having regard to the enhanced cultural-continuity requirements for Indigenous children under the CYFSA and the federal Act respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families?
If extended society care is ordered, is access by the mother and/or father in G.A.'s best interests?

firac.issue: Was G.A. in need of protection under s. 74(2) CYFSA?
firac.facts: G.A., born in 2020, spent all but 64 days of his life in foster care. The mother had long-standing alcohol addiction and mental-health issues (post-partum depression, suicidal ideation), left the infant unattended, missed the majority of access visits (19 of 59 in-person visits attended), had no stable housing (residing in hotels/friends' homes), returned north for work for weeks at a time, and repeatedly failed to engage with services. She did not attend the trial and her whereabouts were unknown.
firac.rule: Under s. 74(2)(b)(i)(ii) and (h) CYFSA a child is in need of protection where there is a risk of physical harm from a parent's failure to adequately care for or supervise, or a pattern of neglect, or a risk of emotional harm. The risk must be real and likely, not speculative (Rainy River v B(C), 2006 ONCJ 458; Ottawa-Carleton v T and T, 2000 CanLII 21157). No intention to harm need be proven (Jewish Family and Child Service v K(R), 2008 ONCJ 774). The court must be satisfied that the protection concerns identified at intervention have been adequately addressed such that the child could be safely returned.
firac.application: Despite the mother's genuine love and one commendable completion of a six-week residential treatment program, the court found no evidence her alcohol addiction had abated and evidence she continued drinking through 2021. She had no stable housing, no meaningful support network, and had demonstrated no ability to parent, having twice sought to have G.A. removed within weeks of assuming his care. The absence of observed drunkenness at short visits was not determinative; the onus was not on the Society to prove ongoing drinking. The risk of harm arose from neglect, not deliberate harm.
firac.conclusion: G.A. was found to be in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b)(i) and (ii) and 74(2)(h) CYFSA.

firac.issue: Was extended society care with a view to adoption in G.A.'s best interests, considering the cultural-continuity protections for Indigenous children?
firac.facts: G.A. is Inuk. He had been in care over 12 months and, being under six, could not be subject to a further interim order under s. 122. The mother could not care for him; the father in Nunavut could not either. The mother's siblings declined adoption; the mother was reluctant to involve extended family. She initiated contact with E.P., an Inuk woman from Baker Lake living in Ottawa, willing to adopt. The foster mother had actively maintained G.A.'s Inuit cultural connections.
firac.rule: Where a child is found in need of protection, the court must make an order under s. 101(1) CYFSA in the child's best interests (s. 74(3)), with special weight for Indigenous children on preserving cultural identity, language and community (s. 74(3)(b),(c)(iii),(iv); s. 1(2)). The federal Act respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families (FNIM), S.C. 2019, c. 24, makes best interests paramount for child apprehension (s. 10(1)), enshrines cultural continuity (ss. 9(1),(2), 10(3)), and prioritizes placement (s. 16(1); s. 101(5) CYFSA requires placement of an Inuk child with an Inuit family absent substantial reason).
firac.application: Weighing the s. 74(3) CYFSA and s. 10(3) FNIM best-interest factors, the court found the mother could not meet G.A.'s physical, mental and emotional needs (including delayed speech requiring assessment), the child needed permanency and stability having spent 22 of 24 months in care, and placement with E.P. or another Inuit family would preserve his Inuit cultural and linguistic heritage and keep him near his adoptive sister (consistent with s. 16 FNIM). Statutory timelines barred a further interim order, leaving only a supervision order (unworkable given the mother's inability) or extended society care.
firac.conclusion: Extended society care with a view to adoption by E.P., or failing that another Inuit family, was ordered; if no Inuit placement is possible the matter returns to court for submissions on the 'substantial reason' under s. 101(5).

firac.issue: Should access by the mother and father be ordered following extended society care?
firac.facts: The mother, though unable to parent, was gentle, affectionate and loving with G.A., maintained respectful relationships with the foster and adoptive mothers, and was unlikely to interfere with adoption. The father had had no contact but recently expressed a wish to see G.A.; he lives in Nunavut and could expose G.A. to paternal family and Inuit land-based culture.
firac.rule: Access may be ordered under s. 104 CYFSA governed by the child's best interests (s. 105(5)); the court considers whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and whether access will impair adoption (s. 105(6)). A holistic, comprehensive best-interests analysis applies; the burden is no longer on the person seeking access, and absence of a prior relationship or evidence is not determinative (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v JG, 2020 ONCA 415; Kawartha-Haliburton CAS v M.W., 2019 ONCA 316).
firac.application: Contact with the loving birth mother was beneficial for G.A.'s emotional development and cultural connection and unlikely to impair adoption. Although the father had been absent, G.A. was still an infant with time to develop a relationship; contact would offer exposure to his paternal family and Inuit culture in Nunavut, with no evidence of harm or interference with adoption. Access can take many forms tailored to the child.
firac.conclusion: Access to the mother was ordered at the Society's discretion (minimum once monthly), and access to the father at the Society's discretion; in each case G.A. is the access-right holder and the parent the recipient.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area — a child-protection proceeding. K047 (best interests of the child) is central to all three issues under s. 74(3) CYFSA and s. 10 FNIM. K048 (custody/access) captures the access determinations for both parents. K052 (religious/cultural upbringing) is the closest controlled term for the heavy emphasis on preserving the child's Inuit cultural and linguistic identity — a borderline fit since the vocabulary lacks a specific Indigenous child-welfare or cultural-continuity keyword, but it best reflects the cultural-upbringing dimension. K005 (Education law) and K044 (school board) are weak/inapplicable and flagged as poor fits; they are included only to reach the minimum count as the controlled vocabulary contains no child-protection, child-welfare, Indigenous, or CYFSA-specific keyword. The vocabulary is oriented toward antisemitism/Jewish-community matters and maps poorly onto this Inuit child-protection case, so several selections are approximate.

registry_rationale: The file bears the Ottawa Children's Aid Society application and file no. FC-20-CP52; the matter proceeded in the Ottawa Superior Court, so the registry is Ottawa.

case_name: Rossetti Associates Incorporated c. Canam Group Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: Rossetti Associates Incorporated c. Canam Group Inc.

defining_issues: Should the Quebec Superior Court authorize execution, in whole or in part, of a rogatory commission issued by a U.S. court seeking documents and oral testimony from a Québec-based non-party, and on what terms and conditions?
How is the relevance and scope of the evidence sought to be assessed, and may the court trim the subject matter and document demands where they overreach into the non-party's operations?
Should the non-party's objections based on solicitor-client privilege and litigation privilege be maintained?
Should the non-party's objection to communicating confidential commercial documents be maintained, and may communication be ordered subject to protective conditions?

firac.issue: Should the Quebec Superior Court authorize execution, in whole or in part, of a rogatory commission issued by a foreign (U.S.) court seeking evidence from a Québec-based non-party, and on what terms?
firac.facts: Rossetti, a defendant in New York litigation brought by Canam Steel Corporation over the Arthur Ashe Tennis Stadium roof project, obtained from the U.S. District Court letters rogatory (the Request) directing Canam Group Inc., a Québec-based non-party and parent of Canam Steel, to produce documents responsive to 28 demands and to provide a representative for a pre-trial examination. Rossetti applied under art. 504 C.C.P. Canam Group did not object per se to a rogatory commission but contested the scope of the evidence sought.
firac.rule: Articles 504-506 C.C.P. govern execution of foreign rogatory commissions. Zingre v. The Queen, [1981] 2 SCR 392 establishes that international judicial assistance rests on comity, exercised as a judicial discretion tethered by legal rules. Execution is neither an absolute obligation nor mere courtesy; the court balances comity against respect for Canadian public policy/public order and absence of prejudice to the witness (Actava, J2 Global, Lashmet). The court may authorize less than requested and impose terms and conditions, guided by proportionality (Preliminary provision and art. 18 C.C.P.).
firac.application: The court found deference to the U.S. court's process justified, as the docket showed extensive involvement by Judge Reyes and letter submissions from both parties expanding the notice pleadings. It applied both the U.S. and Québec standards of relevance, treated Canam Group as a genuine non-party (rejecting Rossetti's attempt to conflate Canam Group with Canam Steel, given distinct corporate personalities under art. 298 et seq. C.C.Q.), and held the evidence relevant only insofar as it bore on whether Canam Steel's own internal failures caused it to underbid the Project. It refused to allow a 'trial' of Canam Group's operations, trimmed the subject matter and document demands, and reworded vague demands.
firac.conclusion: The Application was granted in part; execution of the rogatory commission was authorized for a limited authorized subject matter and reworded authorized document demands, subject to detailed terms and conditions governing the conduct of the examination.

firac.issue: How should relevance and scope be assessed, and may the court reword or reduce overreaching demands?
firac.facts: The Document Demands used inclusive phrasing ('all documents'), inconsistent verbs and categories, incomplete descriptions, sought personal employee information (demands 3 and 4, withdrawn), and sought information obtainable from Canam Steel. Definitions of 'Canam Group' and 'Canam Steel' captured affiliates, attorneys, subsidiaries, etc.
firac.rule: Relevance in Québec is assessed broadly at the pre-trial stage (Glegg v. Smith & Nephew, 2005 SCC 31; Lac d'Amiante, 2001 SCC 51) but is not an absolute right (Blaikie) and must be evaluated principally, though not exclusively, against the pleadings and exhibits (Fuoco, Dominion Nickel). The evidence must also be reasonably specific and not otherwise obtainable or unduly burdensome; the court has discretion to trim and reword to reduce post-authorization disputes.
firac.application: The court excluded overreaching definitional terms, disregarded additions like 'all drafts' not in the original Request, removed demands seeking Canam Steel-held or forward-looking operational information, salvaged operable demands by rewording, and confined all demands to matters involving Canam Steel's bids and projects and the St. Gedéon de Beauce plant capacity.
firac.conclusion: The court restated the Authorized Subject Matter and Authorized Document Demands, narrowing the request to relevant, reasonably specific categories tied to the U.S. Litigation.

firac.issue: Should Canam Group's objections based on solicitor-client and litigation privilege be maintained?
firac.facts: Canam Group withheld two documents as solicitor-client privileged (Binder C) and ten as litigation-privileged (Binder B), providing them to the court for a voir dire without copies to Rossetti.
firac.rule: Solicitor-client privilege requires a confidential communication between solicitor and client for the seeking or giving of legal advice (Solosky v. The Queen, [1980] 1 SCR 821; Pritchard, 2004 SCC 31); art. 2858 C.C.Q. compels rejection of evidence breaching professional secrecy. Litigation privilege attaches to documents created for the dominant purpose of litigation, giving rise to a rebuttable presumption of inadmissibility (Blank v. Canada, 2006 SCC 39; Lizotte v. Aviva, 2016 SCC 52), and may be asserted against third parties.
firac.application: After examining the documents, the court found the Binder C exchanges met the solicitor-client criteria and the Binder B documents were created for the dominant purpose of active litigation, refraining from disclosing their contents.
firac.conclusion: Both objections were maintained; communication of the Binder B and Binder C documents was refused.

firac.issue: Should the objection to communicating confidential commercial documents be maintained, and may communication be ordered on protective conditions?
firac.facts: Binders D and E contained 6 and 67 documents said to be confidential commercial information; Canam Group sought to withhold them or produce redacted versions. The recipients would include U.S. market competitors, and Canam Group had codes of ethics maintaining confidentiality.
firac.rule: Sierra Club of Canada v. Canada, 2002 SCC 41 sets the test for confidentiality orders: (1) necessity to prevent a serious, evidence-grounded risk to an important interest expressible as a public interest, with no reasonable alternative; and (2) beneficial effects outweighing harmful effects. The implied undertaking of confidentiality (Lac d'Amiante) already protects pre-trial evidence from repurposing.
firac.application: The court identified a public interest in offering meaningful comity-based assistance without prejudicing the non-party, found the financial information current and sensitive, especially given competitor recipients, and concluded that redaction plus protective conditions (an implied undertaking and a required U.S. protective/sealing order as conditions precedent) balanced Rossetti's need to make full answer against Canam Group's commercial interests.
firac.conclusion: The objection was maintained only in part; the Binder D and E documents were ordered communicated in redacted form, subject to conditions precedent replicating Québec confidentiality protections, and the Superior Court reserved jurisdiction over public order, privilege and confidentiality objections. No costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the correct tier-1 practice area: the case is a civil procedural application under art. 504 C.C.P. for execution of a foreign rogatory commission, engaging relevance, evidence-gathering and privilege. The remaining picks are borderline because the controlled vocabulary contains no dedicated terms for letters rogatory, international judicial assistance/comity, examination of non-parties, or solicitor-client/litigation/confidentiality privilege. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is a weak proxy — the judgment itself likens the impact of a rogatory commission order on the witness to an injunction, and the analysis is akin to interim/remedial relief. K012 (procedural fairness) is moderate — the court expressly grounded the witness's right to be heard in audi alteram partem. K011 (judicial review) and K022 (restitution) are weak and included only to meet the minimum count; they do not squarely fit. These weak picks are flagged: the vocabulary is oriented to a different (antisemitism/Jewish-law) corpus and does not cover this evidentiary/procedural subject matter well.
location_rationale: The header states 'SUPERIOR COURT ... PROVINCE OF QUEBEC, DISTRICT OF Montréal' and the court number 500-17-113192-200, confirming the Superior Court sitting in Montréal, Quebec.
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the 'DISTRICT OF Montréal', which serves as the Superior Court registry/district for the file.

case_name: McCaw v JDS Energy & Mining Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: McCaw v. JDS Energy & Mining Inc.

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff's claim in fraudulent misrepresentation be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a) as disclosing no reasonable claim because it concerns future events?
Should the unjust enrichment claim be struck for failing to plead the elements (notably absence of juristic reason) and as embarrassing where a valid employment contract exists?
Are the pleaded proprietary/monetary remedies of constructive trust and value-survived damages bound to fail for want of pleaded material facts?
Should the conversion claim be struck on the basis that revenues are intangible interests not capable of conversion?
Should the passing off and derivative disgorgement claims be struck for failing to plead the required elements?
Is the Amended Notice of Civil Claim as a whole embarrassing and liable to be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b)-(d)?

firac.issue: Should the fraudulent misrepresentation claim be struck as disclosing no reasonable claim because it relates to statements about future events?
firac.facts: McCaw pleaded that JDS' CEO, Stibbard, represented that McCaw would own an equity stake in the new drilling and blasting business, and (in the alternative) that if he owned no equity, those representations were false when made because JDS never intended to grant equity.
firac.rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(a) a pleading is struck only where it is 'plain and obvious' the claim has no reasonable prospect of success, with pleaded facts assumed true (Imperial Tobacco, 2011 SCC 42; Nevsun, 2020 SCC 5). While a representation must normally be of past or present fact, a statement of future intention that the maker did not hold when made is a statement of fact actionable as fraud (Pan v. Dong, 2024 BCSC 869; Punto e Pasta, 2009 BCSC 37; Sanghera).
firac.application: Though awkwardly framed in the alternative, McCaw alleges JDS never intended to permit the equity stake it represented. Assuming that fact true, this pleads a false statement of present intention, satisfying the elements in Chow v. Pang. It is not plain and obvious the claim is bound to fail.
firac.conclusion: Application to strike the fraudulent misrepresentation claim dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the unjust enrichment claim be struck for defective pleading or as embarrassing given the existence of the Employment Agreement?
firac.facts: McCaw pleaded unjust enrichment in the alternative to an enforceable LOI, alleging JDS was enriched by his contributions, systems, goodwill and relationships beyond the scope of the Employment Agreement, and that he suffered a corresponding deprivation with no juristic reason.
firac.rule: The elements are enrichment, corresponding deprivation, and absence of juristic reason (Kerr v. Baranow, 2011 SCC 10). A contract is a juristic reason only for benefits within its scope; unjust enrichment may be pleaded in the alternative to contract, especially where benefits are conferred extra-contractually or the contract's validity is in issue (Bear Creek, 2020 BCSC 1523; 676083 B.C. Ltd. v. Revolution Resource Recovery, 2021 BCCA 85).
firac.application: McCaw's primary claim rests on the LOI and Employment Agreement being enforceable; the unjust enrichment claim is alternative, alleging his contributions exceeded the Employment Agreement's scope. This is a permissible pleading, not bald or conclusory, and it is not essential to plead exact dates, much of which lie within JDS' knowledge and may be particularized later.
firac.conclusion: Application to strike the unjust enrichment claim dismissed; pleading not embarrassing.

firac.issue: Are the constructive trust and value-survived damages claims bound to fail for want of pleaded material facts?
firac.facts: McCaw sought a constructive trust over a proportionate share of JDS' drilling and blasting division and, alternatively, a value-survived monetary award reflecting the current value of the business.
firac.rule: A constructive trust addresses beneficial entitlement to specific property where a monetary award is inadequate (Pro-Sys, 2013 SCC 57). A plaintiff need not elect between damages and proprietary relief until able to make an informed choice; whether damages are inadequate is generally not decided on a strike application (BNSF Railway, 2016 BCCA 350; Treasure Bay). Value-survived awards may follow from a joint enterprise or direct and substantial contribution (BCI Bulkhaul, 2017 BCCA 180; Galbraith).
firac.application: McCaw identified the drilling and blasting division as identifiable property and pleaded a joint venture and substantial contribution. Following BNSF Railway, the adequacy of a monetary remedy and satisfaction of constructive-trust conditions require evidence and cannot be resolved at the pleadings stage; no obligation to plead inadequacy of damages exists.
firac.conclusion: Applications to strike the constructive trust and value-survived damages claims dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the conversion claim be struck because revenues are intangible interests not subject to conversion?
firac.facts: McCaw pleaded that JDS wrongfully retained and used his share of revenues generated by the D&B Joint Venture, denying his title to that property.
firac.rule: Conversion traditionally applies to tangible goods (Boma; Teva), but BC authority is unresolved: some cases hold funds and even intangible property may be converted (685946 B.C. Ltd. v. 0773907 B.C. Ltd., 2024 BCSC 997; Egger; Ngo v. Go, 2009 BCSC 1146). Conflicting authority should not be resolved on a strike application (Sarzynick).
firac.application: McCaw pleaded a beneficial interest in joint-venture revenues wrongfully converted by JDS, making out at least a good arguable claim. Given the unsettled state of the law on whether funds are convertible, the issue is for trial, not a preliminary motion.
firac.conclusion: Application to strike the conversion claim dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the passing off and disgorgement claims be struck for failing to plead the required elements?
firac.facts: McCaw pleaded that JDS continued to use his name, picture, experience and relationships in marketing materials and falsely represented a 'Collaborative Acquisition' and the acquisition of his former company McCaw North, causing confusion and harm to his goodwill.
firac.rule: Passing off requires (1) reputation or goodwill, (2) a misrepresentation likely to deceive the public into believing a business connection, and (3) resulting or potential damage (Ciba-Geigy; Greystone Capital; Vancouver Community College, 2017 BCCA 41). On a Rule 9-5(1)(a) application no evidence is admissible (sub-rule (2)). Disgorgement is commonly available for passing off (Ray Plastics).
firac.application: Because no evidence is admissible under sub-rule (1)(a), JDS' company searches and advertising exhibits cannot be considered. On the pleaded facts McCaw alleged reputation and goodwill in the industry, misrepresentations suggesting a connection with JDS, and consequent damage—each element of passing off. The disgorgement claim rests on the surviving passing off claim.
firac.conclusion: Applications to strike the passing off and disgorgement claims dismissed.

firac.issue: Is the Amended Notice of Civil Claim as a whole embarrassing and liable to be struck?
firac.facts: JDS argued the Amended NOCC was intentionally vague, rested on legal conclusions, conflated the LOI and Employment Agreement, and pleaded a contract 'partly oral and partly written' without specifying which terms were which.
firac.rule: An embarrassing pleading under Rule 9-5(1)(b)-(c) is one so confusing that it is hard to understand or so irrelevant it causes useless expense (Willow v. Chong; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform). The court also declined to consider JDS' greatly expanded 54-page written argument served the day of hearing, confining itself to the amended application and response.
firac.application: The court found the Amended NOCC, while not a model pleading, set out adequate material facts supporting the causes of action to the good-arguable-claim standard. Any oral LOI terms could be addressed through particulars, and the written LOI document assists distinguishing written from oral terms.
firac.conclusion: Application to strike the Amended NOCC as embarrassing dismissed; the whole strike application dismissed with costs to McCaw in any event of the cause.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area: this is an application to strike pleadings in a commercial/tort action involving fraudulent misrepresentation, unjust enrichment, conversion and passing off. K022 (restitution) is the closest keyword for the unjust enrichment, constructive trust and value-survived remedies at the heart of several branches of the ruling. K085 (wrongful dismissal) and K009 (Labour and employment) are engaged because the underlying action arises in part from McCaw's alleged constructive dismissal as COO. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is a weak/borderline pick included only to reach the minimum count—there was no injunction, but it is the nearest civil-procedure remedies keyword. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward human-rights/antisemitism matters and offers no dedicated terms for motion to strike, fraudulent misrepresentation, conversion, passing off or constructive trust, so several genuinely central concepts have no matching ID; K021 and to a degree K009/K085 should be treated as tangential.
location_rationale: The style of cause and header state 'Registry: Vancouver' and give the place of hearing and judgment as 'Vancouver, B.C.' The court is the Supreme Court of British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The docket block expressly reads 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Seed v. Desai

defining_issues: Should sole legal decision-making authority (custody) be awarded to one parent, and if so which, or should joint/parallel parenting be ordered, having regard to the children's best interests and allegations of parental alienation?
Should the children's residential arrangements be changed from primary residence with the mother to alternating weeks with each parent?
Did the parties reach a binding agreement in November 2010 for a final spousal support order, and what weight should it be given given the payor's inaccurate income disclosure?
How should the court determine the respondent's income available for support and whether to impute income to the underemployed applicant?
Should child and spousal support be adjusted retroactively, and from what date?
Should the respondent's child support be reduced on the basis of undue hardship under s. 10 of the Child Support Guidelines?

firac.issue: Should sole custody be awarded to one parent, or should joint/parallel parenting be ordered, given the best interests of the children and the father's allegations of alienation?
firac.facts: The parties' 2010 consent final order made no award of custody and relied on a parenting coordinator and strict email limits to manage conflict. The coordination never occurred because the father refused to sign the coordinator's retainer, and he repeatedly breached the two-email-per-week limit with lengthy, critical and threatening emails. Both parents sought sole custody; the father alternatively raised parallel parenting and alleged the mother alienated the children.
firac.rule: The guiding principle is the best interests of the children. Joint or parallel custody requires evidence of historical cooperation and appropriate communication, not merely the hope of improvement (Kaplanis v. Kaplanis, 2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)); parallel parenting may be ordered to protect a parent-child relationship from encroachment (Andrade v. Kennelly, 2006 CanLII 20845 (ON SC)).
firac.application: The court found the father was in clear breach of the email restrictions and had thwarted the parenting-coordination mechanism, and used criminal-defence lawyers' letters to intimidate the mother. The children showed no signs of alienation — they were affectionate with and close to their father — and the mother had not interfered with their relationship. The father's inability to disengage from conflict, not the mother's conduct, was the source of the problem, so neither sole custody to him nor joint/parallel parenting was a solution.
firac.conclusion: Sole legal custody (decision-making authority) was awarded to the applicant mother, with amendments to the final order and both parents required to complete the 'New Ways for Families' program.

firac.issue: Should the children's residential arrangements be changed to alternating weeks with each parent?
firac.facts: The children had lived primarily with the mother, with the father having alternate-weekend and midweek overnight access, since separation. The father admitted the children were thriving under the existing arrangement. No Office of the Children's Lawyer or voice-of-the-child report was obtained.
firac.rule: A change to residential arrangements requires a material change in circumstances, assessed against the best interests of the children.
firac.application: The father's request rested on his alienation allegations, which the court rejected. The children were doing very well under the status quo. The court found no material change warranting a change to the basic residential regime, though it did adjust holiday, summer, telephone and transition provisions (permitting unsupervised transitions given the children's ages of 10 and almost 11).
firac.conclusion: The basic residential arrangement (primary residence with the mother) was maintained; only ancillary scheduling and transition terms were amended.

firac.issue: Did the parties reach a binding agreement in November 2010 for a final spousal support order, and what weight should it receive?
firac.facts: A draft final support order was prepared by the applicant's lawyer and approved as to form by the respondent's counsel but never issued. It carried forward $950/month spousal and $1,226/month child support based on the respondent's 'self-imputed' income of $85,000, with a review set for March 2012. The applicant said she believed it was temporary pending the CRA audit; email correspondence confirmed a settlement had been reached.
firac.rule: An agreement intended to be incorporated into a final order may be given weight, but weight is affected where it was founded on inaccurate financial disclosure by the paying spouse; income of the payor is integral to quantum and duration of spousal support.
firac.application: The emails persuaded the court an agreement was reached and intended to be final, subject to a material-change/review clause. However, the $85,000 figure was not a true income figure and did not conform to the respondent's declared 2010 income of $136,374; he failed to correct it. The court gave the agreement some weight as to the intention to pay spousal support and to review in March 2012, but its quantum could not stand because of the inaccurate income basis.
firac.conclusion: An agreement was found to have been reached but was given only limited weight; quantum could not be upheld given the misstated income.

firac.issue: How should the court determine the respondent's income and whether to impute income to the applicant?
firac.facts: The respondent intermingled personal, business and his wife's finances, used up to twelve personal credit cards to fund the business, and declared incomes of $136,374 (2010), $104,995 (2011) and $174,878 (2012). CRA reassessed his 2007-2009 income at $455,646, $492,928 and $791,130. The applicant's expert used a net-worth method to impute high income; the applicant herself was underemployed with very low earned income.
firac.rule: A payor must establish his income; where a payor makes income difficult to ascertain and lives beyond declared means, the court may determine income available for support from all the evidence. Income may be imputed to an underemployed spouse who has not made reasonable efforts to become self-sufficient.
firac.application: The court declined to treat CRA reassessments as prima facie proof absent foundational documents, and found the expert's net-worth approach overstated income; it made adjustments. Nonetheless the respondent's declared income was found not to reflect income actually available, given his lifestyle, withdrawals of ~$262,000/year, and refusal to separate his finances. The applicant's job search was not broad or diligent, so income was imputed to her from January 2013.
firac.conclusion: The respondent's income for support was set at an average of $280,000-$300,000 from 2011 forward; income of $36,000 (2013) and $42,000 (2014) was imputed to the applicant.

firac.issue: Should support be adjusted retroactively, and from what date?
firac.facts: The applicant sought retroactive child and spousal support to the date of separation, with arrears approaching one million dollars. The respondent had failed to correct his understated 2010 self-imputed income and did not disclose his higher declared incomes or the December 2012 CRA reassessments.
firac.rule: Retroactive support is discretionary and governed by the factors in S. (D.B.) v. G. (S.R.), 2006 SCC 37 — reasonableness of delay, blameworthy conduct of the payor, circumstances of the children, and hardship to the payor — with effective notice as the general starting date.
firac.application: There was blameworthy conduct in the respondent's failure to correct his income figure and to disclose the reassessments, weighing in favour of retroactivity. However, the pre-2010 period was governed by agreements made with legal advice, and the CRA reassessments (for 2007-2009) lacked foundational proof and posed hardship, so the court declined retroactivity before November 2010. Child support was retroactively adjusted from November 2010 on declared/determined incomes; spousal support arrears were set at high-end SSAG on declared incomes to end of 2012.
firac.conclusion: No retroactivity before November 2010; the respondent was ordered to pay $97,898 in arrears (no tax consequences) for November 2010 to end of 2012, plus prospective support from January 2013.

firac.issue: Should the respondent's child support be reduced for undue hardship under s. 10 of the Child Support Guidelines?
firac.facts: The respondent sought to pay below the table amount, relying on his high debt load, support paid for two children of a prior marriage, and payments to his parents.
firac.rule: Section 10 of the Child Support Guidelines permits departure only where a spouse would otherwise suffer undue hardship, listing qualifying circumstances such as unusually high debts reasonably incurred and legal duties to support others.
firac.application: The respondent had not established key facts (e.g., ongoing entitlement of his older children), had not taken reasonable steps to dispose of real properties to reduce debt, and his payments to his parents were not a legal obligation. He also admitted a higher household standard of living than the applicant's.
firac.conclusion: The undue hardship claim was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) are central to the contested custody and residential-arrangement determinations. K050 (parental/child support) and K053 (spousal support) cover the extensive support, income-determination and retroactivity analysis. K049 (marriage/cohabitation agreement — enforcement of agreement) applies to the disputed November 2010 support agreement. K052 (religious upbringing) is a borderline but genuine pick, engaged by the parents' Catholic/Muslim dispute over fasting and pork and the court's application of Rosenberg v. Minster and Young v. Young on faith-based practices — it is a minor sub-issue and thus a weaker choice than the others.
location_rationale: The decision is that of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice. No city is expressly stated in the header, but the text repeatedly references Ottawa institutions — the 'Ottawa Police Service' (para. 22), Algonquin College (Ottawa), and the Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario (CHEO) — which situate the matter in Ottawa, Ontario. Province is clear from 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE'.
registry_rationale: No registry office is named in the decision. The court file number is 'FC-08-776-1' but the specific registry is not stated, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN AGAINST MICHEL SLEIMAN SAFADI

defining_issues: Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused fired the shots at John MacEachern and, if so, did he possess the specific intent required for attempted murder?
Does the rule against multiple convictions in Kienapple bar convicting the accused on Count 2 (using a firearm while attempting murder) after conviction on Count 1?
Do the facts underlying Count 1 and Count 3 (carrying a weapon for a purpose dangerous to the public peace) constitute a single delict under Kienapple?

Did the Crown prove that the accused authored the letters and wilfully promoted hatred against Jews contrary to s. 319(2) of the Criminal Code, even though he portrayed himself in the letters as a Jew?
Did the words in the letter received by Sam Wakim constitute a threat to destroy or damage real property under s. 264.1?

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove identity and the specific intent to kill required for attempted murder under s. 239?
firac.facts: On December 16, 1992, three shots were fired from a field about 80 metres away, striking MacEachern in the left flank, passing through his jacket collar, and one lodging in a nearby house. Two days later the accused was found near the shooting site wearing a rubberized tablecloth from which a piece matched material found at the scene, carrying his own .22 semi-automatic rifle; ballistic evidence tied the three spent cartridges to that rifle, and tracking evidence showed he had retraced the December 16 route.
firac.rule: Under s. 239 the mental element for attempted murder is the specific intent to kill; the actus reus is any act done to carry out that intent. A person is presumed to intend the natural consequences of his act, but where death is not the only natural consequence, intent to kill must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt (R. v. Wigman). Credibility assessed under the R. v. D.W. three-step approach.
firac.application: The court accepted the forensic firearms, material-matching and tracking evidence and rejected the accused's 'set-up by Mossad agents' theory as lacking any air of reality. It found the accused fired the shots. However, because MacEachern survived and death was not the only natural consequence, the court could not conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused intended to kill. Firing three shots that wounded the victim did establish, at minimum, an intent to wound.
firac.conclusion: Not guilty of attempted murder, but guilty of the included offence of discharging a firearm with intent to wound contrary to s. 244(a).

firac.issue: Does Kienapple bar a conviction on Count 2 once the accused is convicted on Count 1?
firac.facts: Count 2 charged using a firearm while attempting murder (s. 85); Count 1 resulted in a conviction for discharging a firearm with intent to wound. Both counts arose from the same December 16 shooting.
firac.rule: The rule against multiple convictions from R. v. Kienapple; applied in R. v. Lavoie and R. v. Benoit, precluding two convictions for the same delict on the same set of facts.
firac.application: The court found Counts 1 and 2 rested on the same factual matrix, so a conviction on both would result in two convictions for the same delict, contrary to Kienapple.
firac.conclusion: Not guilty on Count 2.

firac.issue: Do Counts 1 and 3 constitute a single delict under Kienapple?
firac.facts: Count 3 charged carrying a firearm for a purpose dangerous to the public peace on December 16 (s. 87); Count 1 concerned the actual discharge of the firearm with intent to wound. Count 4 charged the same weapons offence for December 18, when the accused was found armed near the site, with no credible raccoon-hunting explanation.
firac.rule: Section 87 is complete on proof of carrying a weapon for a purpose dangerous to the public peace, without proof of actual use; Kienapple does not apply where each offence requires proof of a distinct element (R. v. Yurkiv).
firac.application: Count 1 required proof of a use of the firearm additional to its dangerous carriage, whereas Count 3 required no actual use, so they did not disclose a single delict. The intentional discharge established the dangerous purpose for December 16, and the totality of the evidence (rejecting the hunting explanation) established the dangerous purpose for December 18.
firac.conclusion: Guilty on both Count 3 and Count 4.

firac.issue: Did the accused wilfully promote hatred against Jews under s. 319(2) by writing letters purporting to come from Jews?
firac.facts: Forty-five letters were mailed or delivered to churches, police, government bodies and Lebanese residents, bearing the Star of David and signed 'The Free Jews' or 'Long live Israel', attacking Christianity in obscene terms and threatening institutions. Handwriting and fingerprint/palm-print evidence tied the letters to the accused, whose own writings referred to Jews as 'the parasite of mankind'.
firac.rule: Section 319(2) criminalizes wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group by communicating statements other than in private conversation; 'wilfully' requires subjective desire or foresight of substantial certainty (R. v. Buzzanga; R. v. Keegstra), and 'hatred' connotes an extreme emotion of vilification and detestation. Proof of actual hatred in listeners is not required. Defences in s. 319(3) and Attorney General's consent under s. 319(6) apply.
firac.application: The court accepted the handwriting and print evidence and rejected the set-up theory, finding the accused authored the letters. Though he did not attack Jews directly but instead misrepresented himself as a Jew attacking Christianity and government, the court found he subjectively desired to promote hatred against Jews; expert evidence (Bernie Farber, CJC) confirmed the letters were designed to foment anti-Semitism. As the accused denied authorship, no s. 319(3) defence was in issue, and AG consent had been obtained.
firac.conclusion: Guilty on Count 5.

firac.issue: Did the words in the letter to Sam Wakim constitute a threat to destroy or damage real property under s. 264.1?
firac.facts: Wakim received a letter stating 'We are waiting for you to leave. When you come back, you won't find your restaurant.' His restaurant did burn during his absence, but no evidence connected the accused to the fire.
firac.rule: Whether words constitute a threat is assessed objectively, in the context of the written words and the recipient's situation, under s. 264.1(1)(b).
firac.application: Disregarding the subsequent fire (which the accused was not charged with and was not linked to), the court found the words equivocal and was not satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that they necessarily constituted a threat to destroy or damage real property.
firac.conclusion: Not guilty on Count 6.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area. The hate-promotion conviction is the doctrinally significant part of the case: K067 (wilful promotion of hatred) and K115 (Criminal Code s. 319(2)) capture the specific offence, and K061 (hate speech) its broader category. K058 (antisemitism) and K057 (antisemitic slurs) reflect the anti-Jewish content ('parasite of mankind', 'unholy Jew'). K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) identify the targeted group (the ~30 Jews of Charlottetown). K090 (Canadian Jewish Congress) reflects the expert testimony of Bernie Farber, National Director of the CJC. The firearms/attempted-murder and Kienapple aspects have no dedicated vocabulary entry and are covered by the tier-1 Criminal law keyword; K057 is a somewhat borderline pick but is supported by the explicit slurs in the accused's writings.
location_rationale: The decision is styled as being before the 'Prince Edward Island Supreme Court - Trial Division'. The offences are situated in Queens County, in and around Charlottetown and East Royalty, and the accused resided at 325 Queen Street, Charlottetown. The docket number 'GSC-12719' (General Section, Charlottetown) confirms the Charlottetown registry of the PEI Supreme Court.
registry_rationale: The docket 'GSC-12719' and the location of the events (Charlottetown, Queens County) indicate the matter was filed in the General Section at Charlottetown of the PEI Supreme Court, Trial Division.

name_verification.name_in_document: Evelyn McGregor v. Holyrood Manor and/or Revera Long Term Care Inc., College of Registered Psychiatric Nurses of British Columbia, and Health Sciences Association of British Columbia

defining_issues: Does the Supreme Court have jurisdiction over the plaintiff's claims, or do they arise under the collective agreement so as to fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Labour Relations Board?

Should the plaintiff's pleadings be struck or dismissed for disclosing no reasonable cause of action, non-compliance with case-planning orders, and disclosing no genuine issue for trial under Rules 9-5 and 9-6?
Are the College of Registered Psychiatric Nurses and Decker/Simpson immune from the claims arising from the disciplinary investigation?
Do the plaintiff's Charter claims lie against these defendants, and are her defamation claims statute-barred?

firac.issue: Do the plaintiff's claims fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Labour Relations Board rather than the court?
firac.facts: McGregor, a registered psychiatric nurse, was employed under collective agreements at facilities operated by Revera and Decker. Her complaints concerned her termination, discipline, pay deductions, a 'displaced nurse' (Bill 29) settlement entitlement and the union's representation. She had already grieved her termination, settled it before an arbitrator, and had s. 12 duty-of-fair-representation complaints dismissed by the LRB and on reconsideration.
firac.rule: Where a dispute, in its essential character, arises from the interpretation, application, administration or violation of a collective agreement, jurisdiction lies exclusively with the labour tribunal: Weber v. Ontario Hydro, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 929; Haight-Smith v. Neden, 2002 BCCA 132. Sections 84(2) and 101 of the Labour Relations Code make arbitration awards final and preclude court review; Rule 21-8(1)(b) permits dismissal for want of jurisdiction. Recasting labour claims as tort, Charter or statutory claims does not confer jurisdiction.
firac.application: The essence of McGregor's complaints against Revera, Decker and the HSA arose from her employment, its termination and the collective agreement, matters governed by mandatory arbitration and already addressed by the LRB. Restyling the pleadings and striking through references to collective-agreement articles did not change their essential character, and amounted to a collateral attack on the Review Panel's findings (R. v. Wilson, [1983] 2 S.C.R. 594). The court had no jurisdiction over these subject-matter disputes.
firac.conclusion: The court lacked jurisdiction; the claims arising under the collective agreement were dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the pleadings be struck or dismissed under Rules 9-5 and 9-6?
firac.facts: Master MacNaughton twice ordered McGregor to amend her Notices of Civil Claim to name defendants, specify relief and state the legal basis of each claim; her successive amended pleadings never complied. The claims were confusing, framed in terms that the defendants 'may' have committed negligence, defamation, Charter breaches, fiduciary breaches etc., without material facts.
firac.rule: Under Rule 9-5(1) a pleading may be struck where it is plain and obvious it discloses no reasonable cause of action (Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse, 2003 SCC 69), or is unintelligible, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious. Under Rule 9-6 judgment is given where there is no genuine issue for trial (Skybridge Investments Ltd. v. Metro Motors Ltd., 2006 BCCA 500). A plaintiff must plead material facts for each element of each cause against each defendant (Stoneman v. Denman Island Local Trust Committee, 2010 BCSC 636).
firac.application: Even reading the pleadings liberally for a self-represented litigant, the court found not merely a failure of drafting but that no assembled facts could support any action. The plaintiff pleaded no material facts to establish duty, breach, causation, fiduciary duty or Charter interference. The pleadings failed to comply with the Master's orders and with the Rules.
firac.conclusion: The pleadings were struck and summary judgment/dismissal entered for all defendants.

firac.issue: Are the College and Decker/Simpson immune from claims arising from the disciplinary investigation?
firac.facts: Holyrood/Revera complained to the College, which investigated McGregor's professional conduct, appointed an inspector, imposed and then lifted an interim suspension, and resolved matters by a consent Agreement of Undertaking. Decker provided employment information to the College's inspector on request.
firac.rule: Section 1 of the Disciplinary Authority Protection Act and ss. 24 of the Health Professions Act confer immunity on a regulator for acts done in the exercise of disciplinary powers unless done maliciously and without reasonable and probable cause (Allen v. College of Dental Surgeons). Statements made in the course of, or in communications to, a statutory disciplinary body attract absolute privilege/witness immunity (Hung v. Gardiner, 2003 BCCA 257; Sussman v. Eales).
firac.application: The College acted throughout as a professional disciplinary body under the HPA; no malice or bad faith was pleaded, so its acts were not actionable. Decker's disclosures to the College's inspector, whom the HPA authorized to compel production, were made on an occasion of absolute privilege and complied with FOIPPA/PIPA, which except disclosures authorized by law.
firac.conclusion: Both the College and Decker were immune; the claims against them were struck/dismissed.

firac.issue: Do the Charter claims lie against these defendants and are the defamation claims timely?
firac.facts: McGregor alleged breaches of Charter ss. 2(b), 6, 7, 8 and 15 by the union, College, Decker, Revera and FHA, and alleged defamation arising from statements in the investigation. Her Notices of Civil Claim were filed more than two years after the alleged defamations, before June 1, 2013.
firac.rule: The Charter does not apply to private actors who are not carrying out governmental activity (RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 573; Eldridge v. British Columbia, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 624). Charter remedies against a competent tribunal lie before that tribunal (Weber). Actions for injury including economic loss carry a two-year limitation under s. 3(2) of the Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, with no postponement for defamation under s. 6(3).
firac.application: The HSA and private entities did not exercise statutory or governmental authority, and no facts were pleaded to establish any Charter interference; any Charter remedy relating to LRB matters belonged before the LRB. The defamation claims were pleaded without the required words, publication and damage, and in any event were filed outside the two-year limitation period.
firac.conclusion: The Charter claims had no merit and did not apply to these defendants; the defamation claims were statute-barred and disclosed no genuine issue.

case_name: TLC The Land Conservancy of British Columbia (Re)

name_verification.name_in_document: TLC The Land Conservancy of British Columbia (Re)

defining_issues: On a proper interpretation of Jessie Binning's will, did the executors have the power to transfer the Binning House to BHPS and then to TLC?
Did the executors' use of an intermediary society (BHPS) to convey the Binning House to TLC, a non-object, constitute a fraud on a power rendering the dispositions void?

Is the Binning House held by TLC as 'discrete purpose charitable property' under the CPPA or a common law specific-purpose charitable trust, so that TLC has no beneficial interest and cannot sell it for its general restructuring purposes?
Should any specific-purpose charitable trust be modified under the cy-près doctrine or CPPA s. 3(4) to permit sale of the Binning House?
Is the Binning House exigible by TLC's creditors, including the DIP Lenders, in the CCAA proceedings?

firac.issue: On a proper interpretation of Jessie Binning's will, did the executors have the power to transfer the Binning House to BHPS and then to TLC?
firac.facts: Jessie Binning's 2007 will expressed her 'hope' that the historically significant Binning House be preserved, and gave her trustees discretion, 'if my Trustees decide it is feasible and practical', to establish an entity and transfer the house to it, failing which they were to sell it and pay proceeds to the B.C. Binning Memorial Fellowship Fund at UBC. On legal advice the executors created BHPS and transferred the house to it, which immediately transferred it to TLC. UBC argued the will only permitted an executor-controlled, estate-funded entity.
firac.rule: The primary purpose in construing a will is to determine the testator's intention from the natural and ordinary meaning of the words, read as a whole (National Trust Co. Ltd. v. Fleury, [1965] S.C.R. 817; Feeney's Canadian Law of Wills; Smith v. Smith Estate, 2010 BCCA 106). Where ambiguity exists the 'armchair rule' permits evidence of surrounding circumstances, but not direct extrinsic evidence of intent such as solicitor's instructions or unsigned drafts (Murray Estate, 2007 BCSC 1035).
firac.application: The Court found Jessie Binning's clear intention was to preserve the Binning House and to invest the executors with significant, unfettered discretion toward that purpose. The will did not require that the entity be controlled by the executors, funded by the estate, or hold the house in perpetuity; para. 4(g)(iv) contemplated later disposition. Prior signed wills were admissible but did not detract from, and in fact supported, this interpretation; unsigned drafts and solicitor communications were inadmissible.
firac.conclusion: The executors had the power under the will to establish BHPS and transfer the Binning House to it, and BHPS could then transfer it to TLC; UBC's restrictive interpretation was rejected.

firac.issue: Did the executors' use of BHPS to convey the Binning House to TLC constitute a fraud on a power, rendering the dispositions void?
firac.facts: The executors established BHPS, resigned before the transfer, transferred the house to BHPS for nominal consideration, and BHPS (then controlled by TLC employees) immediately transferred it to TLC under a Deed of Gift. UBC claimed this was a deliberate scheme to benefit TLC, a non-object, defeating UBC's contingent interest.
firac.rule: Fraud on a power requires (a) a disposition beyond the scope of the power and (b) a deliberate breach of the implied obligation not to exercise the power for an ulterior purpose (Thomas on Powers). The focus is on whether the purpose was truly to benefit an object; benefit to a non-object does not by itself invalidate (Kain v. Hutton, [2008] NZSC 61; Vatcher v. Paull, [1915] AC 372; Goldsmid v. Goldsmid). Mere existence of a bargain is insufficient—it must be shown the appointment would not have been made but for the bargain; contrasted with Wong v. Burt, [2004] NZCA 174 (deliberate scheme to subvert the will). Onus on the party alleging fraud.
firac.application: The executors acted in good faith, sought legal advice, and their purpose was to preserve the Binning House, in accordance with the will. Once transferred to BHPS the executors had no control; BHPS had genuine discretion and validly decided to transfer to TLC. There was no agreement or bargain fettering BHPS; Mr. Massey's 'understanding' was not proof of an agreement. The contemporaneous nature of the transfers did not offend the doctrine.
firac.conclusion: No fraud on a power occurred; the transfers were valid. UBC's application to declare the transfer void and return the house to the estate was dismissed with costs.

firac.issue: Is the Binning House held by TLC as discrete purpose charitable property under the CPPA or a common law specific-purpose charitable trust?
firac.facts: BHPS transferred the Binning House to TLC under a Deed of Gift stating it was gifted 'for the purpose of restoring, developing and preserving the Binning House ... for historical purposes with a view to educating the public and commemorating the site.' TLC administered it with its general properties (revenue to general account, though coded separately) and now sought to sell it to fund restructuring.
firac.rule: Provincial trust law continues to apply within CCAA/insolvency proceedings (Re Giffen, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 91; Rowland v. Christian Brothers, 2001 BCCA 527); trust property is not exigible against creditors of the trustee. A trust requires three certainties: intention, subject matter and objects (Waters' Law of Trusts). CPPA s. 2 defines 'discrete purpose charitable property' where property is given to be kept separate and used exclusively for a specified charitable purpose. A charitable purpose must fall within the Pemsel categories and benefit the public (Vancouver Society v. Canada, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 10). A sham requires common intention that documents not create the legal rights they appear to (Snook v. London and West Riding Investments).
firac.application: The Deed of Gift, its precise language, and the surrounding circumstances (Jessie Binning's wish, the executors' purpose, and BHPS's constitution tracked word-for-word into the Deed) established certainty of intention that the house be held on a specific purpose trust for preservation, meeting CPPA s. 2(1)(c). The trust was not a sham; TLC's accounting practices were not determinative and its post-Deed conduct showed no contrary intent. Preservation of the Binning House for public education about architecture/art was a charitable purpose under both the 'advancement of education' and 'beneficial to the community' heads of Pemsel. The trust did not cease to apply merely because TLC dealt with the property, as that would defeat the CPPA's purpose.
firac.conclusion: The Binning House is held by TLC as discrete purpose charitable property/specific-purpose charitable trust; TLC has no beneficial interest permitting sale for its general restructuring purposes.

firac.issue: Should any specific-purpose charitable trust be modified under cy-près or CPPA s. 3(4) to permit the sale?
firac.facts: TLC, now insolvent, argued it was unwilling and unable to continue preserving the Binning House and sought modification so proceeds of sale to BJW/Mr. Wall could fund its restructuring. The offer was unsolicited; no marketing process occurred; only one purchaser with means had come forward.
firac.rule: Cy-près applies only where the charitable purpose has become impossible or impracticable, kept within narrow limits (Tudor on Charities; Waters; Roman Catholic Bishop of Bathurst v. New Brunswick, 2010 NBQB 400; Lee v. North Vancouver School District No. 44, 2011 BCSC 222). CPPA s. 3(4) permits the court, where a charity is unwilling or unable to continue, to make appropriate orders, including transfer to a new charity, to advance the discrete purpose or another consistent charitable purpose. 'A charitable gift will not fail for want of a trustee' (Tudor).
firac.application: The Court accepted TLC was 'unwilling' to continue, but the record was insufficient to show it was impossible/impracticable or that no alternative trustee could be found. Unlike Lee and Bathurst, TLC had made no marketing efforts beyond relying on press publicity, and it was not established that no one else would take on the house subject to trust. The overriding intention of BHPS was preservation for public education, not benefiting TLC's general purposes, so the proposed sale did not come as close as possible to that intention on the current record.
firac.conclusion: The Court declined to decide the modification question; TLC's application to approve the sale was adjourned generally with liberty to reset with further evidence on efforts to find a substitute trustee.

firac.issue: Is the Binning House exigible by TLC's creditors, including the DIP Lenders?
firac.facts: TLC and the DIP Lenders relied on TLC's registered title under the Torrens system and the DIP Lenders' Charge granted in the Initial Order (which listed the Binning House) to argue the house was exigible to satisfy creditors and could be sold in the CCAA.
firac.rule: Only property beneficially owned by the debtor is available to creditors (BIA s. 67; Heffner v. Price Waterhouse Ltd. (1986), 10 B.C.L.R. (2d) 50). Registered title under LTA s. 23(2) is conclusive but rebuttable, and the LTA preserves nemo dat for charges (Gill v. Bucholtz, 2009 BCCA 137). A bona fide lender without notice may enforce (Taylor Ventures Ltd. v. High Meadow Holdings, 2006 BCSC 1095). CCAA s. 11 discretion is wide but not limitless (Century Services, 2010 SCC 60; Stelco, 2005) and does not extend to expropriating others' beneficial interests.
firac.application: Having found the house held on a specific-purpose charitable trust, TLC had no beneficial interest for creditors to reach. The DIP Lenders knew, or could easily have discerned, that trust and CPPA issues attached to TLC's properties (as disclosed in the Penn affidavit and Monitor's report), so they were not bona fide lenders without notice. The DIP Lenders' Charge attached only to TLC's beneficial interests. The CCAA does not permit disregarding others' property interests.
firac.conclusion: The Binning House is not exigible by TLC's creditors or the DIP Lenders; TLC's contention was rejected.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the best tier-1 fit for this trusts, estates and insolvency dispute. K054 (wills/estates) directly captures the central will-interpretation and fraud-on-a-power analysis of Jessie Binning's will, and K006 (Family law) is its tier-1 parent. K005 (Education law) is a weak/borderline pick—it is engaged only because the charitable purpose was found to be 'advancement of education,' a trust-law characterization rather than genuine education-law content. K022 (restitution) is likewise weak, chosen as the nearest remedies/property term for the charitable-trust and disposition-of-assets aspect. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward human-rights/antisemitism themes and lacks dedicated keywords for charitable trusts, CCAA insolvency, cy-près, or the CPPA, so several genuinely central concepts could not be tagged; the picks reflect the closest available terms and the weaker ones are flagged accordingly.
