registry_rationale: The decision header expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Her Majesty the Queen and David Ahenakew

defining_issues: Were the impugned statements made 'other than in private conversation' as required by s. 319(2) of the Criminal Code?
Did the accused, in making the statements, wilfully promote hatred against an identifiable group (people of the Jewish faith)?

firac.issue: Were the statements made to the reporter 'other than in private conversation' within the meaning of s. 319(2)?
firac.facts: After his conference speech, Ahenakew gave a recorded interview to James Parker, a Saskatoon Star Phoenix reporter known for critical coverage of First Nations affairs. Ahenakew knew Parker was a reporter, had participated in roughly 1000 media interviews, and characterized the exchange as a 'confrontation' rather than an interview, though he had agreed to be interviewed.
firac.rule: Section 319(2) of the Criminal Code criminalizes wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group by 'communicating statements, other than in private conversation.' A private conversation involves two people talking discreetly without intending to be overheard or reported.
firac.application: The court found Ahenakew was well aware Parker was a reporter whose job was to report what he was told, knew reporters investigate and publish, and had agreed to be interviewed. The presence or absence of a tape recorder was irrelevant. The demeanor evidence showed he was confident, not ambushed. The exchange was an interview intended for publication, not a private conversation.
firac.conclusion: The interview was not a private conversation within the meaning of s. 319(2).

firac.issue: Did Ahenakew wilfully promote hatred against people of the Jewish faith?
firac.facts: The accused did not dispute making the statements or that Jewish people are an identifiable group. His conference remark that 'the Second World War was created by the Jews' and his interview statements described Jews as owning/dominating the world, characterized them as a 'disease' that had to be gotten rid of, and expressed approval that Hitler 'fried six million of those guys' to 'clean up the world.'
firac.rule: Under s. 319(2), as interpreted in R. v. Keegstra, R. v. Buzzanga and Durocher, R. v. Harding and R. v. Andrews, the Crown must prove both actus reus and mens rea beyond a reasonable doubt. 'Wilful' requires that the accused subjectively desire or foresee as substantially certain the promotion of hatred; 'promote' requires active stimulation of hatred; 'hatred' means an extreme emotion of detestation and vilification. Intent may be inferred from the statements and surrounding circumstances. Section 319(3) provides defences (truth, religious opinion, public interest, good-faith removal of hatred).
firac.application: For the conference speech and several interview statements (distortions, lies, bigoted outbursts), the court found the Crown had not proven the wilful intent to promote hatred beyond a reasonable doubt, given the unfocused nature of the speech. However, the statements equating Jews to a 'disease' to be gotten rid of, approving that Hitler 'fried six million,' and endorsing Hitler cleaning up the world dehumanized the group and justified their killing. The fury and passion in the audio-taped delivery convinced the court the sole intent was to promote hatred. The court rejected the suggestion the comments were caused by diabetes, wine or medication.
firac.conclusion: Those specific statements met the stringent requirements of s. 319(2); the accused wilfully promoted hatred against people of the Jewish faith and was found guilty.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area. K115 (Criminal Code s. 319(2)) and K067 (wilful promotion of hatred) are the precise offence provision and doctrine at issue. K061 (hate speech) captures the subject matter. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) identify the targeted group and nature of the remarks. K088 (Holocaust) is directly engaged by the statements approving the killing of six million Jews. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) reflect the court's discussion of the Keegstra balance between free expression and the hate-propaganda prohibition. Holocaust denial (K062) was considered but not selected, as the accused justified rather than denied the Holocaust.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'IN THE PROVINCIAL COURT OF SASKATCHEWAN AT SASKATOON', identifying both the city (Saskatoon) and the province (Saskatchewan).
registry_rationale: The Provincial Court sitting is identified as 'AT SASKATOON', which serves as the registry/location of the sitting.

case_name: P.B. v. Jewish Family & Child Services

name_verification.name_in_document: P.B. v. Jewish Family & Child Services

defining_issues: Did the Children's Aid Society (Jewish Family and Child Services) act lawfully and without negligence or bad faith when it apprehended the plaintiff's children into protective custody without a warrant?
Was the Society's conduct in imposing supervised and limited access to the children wrongful or improper?
Did the Society owe a fiduciary duty to the plaintiff that could ground his claim for damages?

firac.issue: Did the Society act lawfully and without negligence or bad faith in apprehending the children without a warrant?
firac.facts: Following repeated violent, alcohol-fuelled altercations witnessed by the two young children, a bite mark on N.B. and old bruises on T.B., and apparent lack of parental control at the home and hospital, child protection workers apprehended the boys after consulting their supervisor and advising the parents they would seek a protection order.
firac.rule: Under the Child and Family Services Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-11, a Children's Aid Society has the functions set out in s. 15.3 (including investigating and protecting children); s. 40(1) allows an application to court, while s. 40(7) permits a child protection worker with reasonable and probable grounds to bring a child to a place of safety without a warrant. The guidelines in Children's Aid Society of Durham (Region) v. W.(K.) (1990), 72 O.R. (2d) 711, adopted in B.(D.) v. Children's Aid Society of Durham (Region), assess whether the Society investigated thoroughly, worked with police, considered alternatives, treated both parents fairly and used skilled workers.
firac.application: The court found the workers interviewed both parents, made repeated home visits, gathered substantial background, arranged a hospital examination, kept the parents advised at all times and sought a court order (obtained on consent before Judge Nelson on a signed statement of agreed facts). Unlike B.(D.), the parents were notified and did not dispute the order. The investigation was thorough and the statutory grounds for apprehension were met.
firac.conclusion: The Society acted fairly, within its statutory powers under s. 40(7), and without negligence or bad faith; the apprehension was justified.

firac.issue: Was the supervised and limited access wrongful or improper?
firac.facts: Access was supervised so workers could observe how each parent interacted with the children; the plaintiff resented the supervision, disregarded safety suggestions, waved a knife near a worker, and disrupted a parenting course by recording it. The supervised-access regime flowed from a consent order and a statement of agreed facts the plaintiff signed while represented by counsel.
firac.rule: A court hearing a damages claim will not review or set aside the orders of other judges made in the child protection proceedings, which were open to appeal; access terms agreed to on consent bind the party who signed them.
firac.application: The plaintiff had consented, through counsel, to being observed during access and to completing anger-management and parenting programs. The workers' observations were accepted over the plaintiff's evidence. It was not this court's role to second-guess the earlier protection orders, which the plaintiff could have appealed.
firac.conclusion: The supervision and limited access were fair and adequate, not wrongful; this branch of the claim fails.

firac.issue: Did the Society owe a fiduciary duty to the plaintiff?
firac.facts: The plaintiff pleaded that the Society owed him a fiduciary duty and had breached it, along with derivative and children's claims.
firac.rule: Any fiduciary duty of a Children's Aid Society runs to the children in its care, not to a parent; derivative claims require a properly pleaded claim on behalf of family members.
firac.application: The court held that any fiduciary obligation was owed to the children and, in any event, was exercised properly and in accordance with professional principles. The derivative and children's damages claims were not properly pleaded and lacked supporting evidence.
firac.conclusion: No fiduciary duty was owed to the plaintiff; all heads of damages were dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area because the case turns on child protection under the Child and Family Services Act. K002 (Civil litigation) is included because the proceeding is a parent's tort/damages action alleging negligence, bad faith and breach of fiduciary duty. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing standard for the apprehension and protection order. K057 (antisemitic slurs) and K058 (antisemitism) reflect the plaintiff's repeated anti-Semitic remarks ('Jew boy', 'beat the Hebrew out of him'), which featured in the evidence, and K093 (Jewish) captures that the defendant is a Jewish agency and the boys were found Jewish for the protection proceeding. K052 (religious upbringing) is a weaker, borderline pick — the plaintiff's concern about the boys being raised Jewish and circumcised was mentioned but not decided.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice', which fixes the province as Ontario. The events took place in Richmond Hill and at Musselman's Lake, but the judgment does not state the city or courthouse where the court sat, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: No court registry or office is named anywhere in the decision, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Michelle Roth v. Luke Halstead

defining_issues: Has there been a material change in circumstances since the 2014 Final Order affecting or likely to affect the child's best interests?
If so, what custody and access arrangement (sole vs. joint/parallel custody, and the schedule and conditions of the father's access) is now in the child's best interests?
Should child support be varied and can the mother re-open the question of retroactive child support arrears?

firac.issue: Has there been a material change in circumstances since the 2014 Final Order of Justice Murray that affects or is likely to affect the best interests of the child?
firac.facts: The parties consented to a joint custody, parallel-parenting Final Order in May 2014 while the father lived full-time in Pembroke, roughly five hours from Toronto. Since 2016 the father obtained work as a Toronto paramedic and now divides his time between Toronto and Pembroke, living with the paternal grandmother when in Toronto. The divided decision-making authority under the joint custody regime, especially over Thomas's ADHD medication and psychiatric treatment, had caused confusion among the parents and service providers and delayed treatment (a roughly five-month delay in ADHD medication).
firac.rule: Section 29 of the Children's Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12 bars variation of a custody or access order unless there has been a material change in circumstances affecting or likely to affect the child's best interests. Under Gordon v. Goertz, 1996 CanLII 191 (SCC), the moving party must first show a change, not foreseen or reasonably contemplated when the last order was made, to the child's condition, needs, means or circumstances or to the parent's ability to meet them; the change must be material, not trivial (Docherty v. Beckett).
firac.application: The court found two material changes: (1) the father's relocation of much of his time and new employment in Toronto, allowing more regular, consistent and predictable access than was possible when he lived in Pembroke; and (2) the demonstrated unworkability of the divided decision-making under the joint custody order, which had produced confusion for professionals and delays in Thomas's medical treatment that were not contemplated when the consent order was made.
firac.conclusion: The threshold was met: material changes in circumstances affecting Thomas's best interests were established, permitting a fresh inquiry into custody and access.

firac.issue: What custody and access order is now in the best interests of the child?
firac.facts: Thomas, 12, has a generalized anxiety disorder, ADHD and a learning disability. He has lived primarily with the mother since infancy. The relationship between the parents is high-conflict, with seven years of litigation and three child protection investigations initiated by the mother and her partner, none of which verified abuse. The OCL clinician found the father was not abusive but had shown poor judgment (e.g., detonating a Tannerite explosive at a shooting range with Thomas after being told not to expose him to firearms). The mother and her partner Mr. Coey labelled the father abusive, restricted access, terminated the paternal grandmother's independent time, programmed child-protection numbers into Thomas's phone, and Mr. Coey held himself out as Thomas's father. The OCL recommended sole custody to the mother with structured alternating-weekend and midweek access to the father, subject to firearm and exercise conditions.
firac.rule: Section 24 of the Children's Law Reform Act requires the court to determine best interests by reference to the enumerated factors, including the child's views and preferences, stability, each parent's ability to parent and to facilitate the child's relationship with the other parent, and any violence or abuse (s. 24(3),(4)). Maximum contact with both parents is favoured where consistent with best interests (Gordon v. Goertz). Joint custody requires a history of effective communication and cannot be ordered merely in the hope communication will improve (Kaplanis v. Kaplanis); there is no default in favour of joint custody. A parent's failure to support the child's relationship with the other parent is relevant to parenting ability (Leggatt v. Leggatt; Moreira v. Garcia Dominguez).
firac.application: Given the entrenched conflict and inability to communicate, and the treatment delays caused by divided decision-making, joint custody was not viable and would only perpetuate conflict and Thomas's anxiety. Because Thomas had been in the mother's responsible primary care since birth, sole custody to the mother was appropriate, but tempered by clear provisions allowing the father to obtain information directly from professionals, since the mother could not be trusted to support the father's relationship with Thomas. The court accepted the OCL evidence that Thomas wants a relationship with his father, is not afraid of him, but dislikes firearms and strenuous exercise; the father was not abusive but had exercised poor judgment. A consistent, structured access schedule (alternating weekends plus a midweek visit, shared holidays) with conditions barring firearm exposure and excessive exercise was in Thomas's best interests; the mother's proposal of two overnights was unduly restrictive and the father's ten-day proposal exceeded the status quo and would heighten anxiety.
firac.conclusion: The mother was granted sole custody with a duty to consult and with the father entitled to direct access to information; the father received structured alternating-weekend and midweek access in Toronto, shared holidays, and grandmother involvement, subject to firearm and exercise restrictions.

firac.issue: Should child support be varied and may the mother re-open retroactive child support arrears?
firac.facts: The parties entered a Final Consent Order on April 29, 2016 fixing child support at $724/month based on imputed income of $80,000 and settling all arrears. After the father amended his motion to change, the mother sought to re-open child support and claim retroactive support back to 2006.
firac.rule: A motion to change requires a material change in circumstances; a matter already finally determined by consent is res judicata and cannot be re-litigated absent a material change.
firac.application: The ongoing support figure was left in place subject to annual disclosure. The arrears had been resolved by the Final Consent Order; there was no material change, so the issue was res judicata and the mother's attempt to re-open retroactive support failed.
firac.conclusion: Ongoing child support of $724/month continued; the mother's request to re-open retroactive arrears was dismissed as res judicata.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) is central — the case turns on varying a custody and access order. K047 (best interests of the child) is the operative legal standard under s. 24 CLRA and Gordon v. Goertz. K050 (parental/child support) covers the child support and retroactive arrears issue. K049 (marriage/cohabitation / separation agreement) is a weaker pick, included because the disputed orders were consent orders/agreements being varied and the arrears settlement was treated as res judicata — flagged as borderline. The vocabulary is oriented toward hate-speech/Jewish-community topics and offers few family-law terms, so no tier-3 entity keywords were engaged (Jewish Family and Child Services appears only as the incidental child-protection agency and does not make the case about the Jewish community).
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the Ontario Court of Justice and bears 'COURT FILE No.: Toronto FO-12-11002', indicating the Toronto registry; the parties and child reside in Toronto and the access is to be exercised in Toronto.
registry_rationale: The court file number is expressly identified as 'Toronto FO-12-11002', establishing the Toronto registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Turpel-Lafond v. British Columbia

defining_issues: Does the doctrine of parliamentary privilege deprive the court of jurisdiction to adjudicate the plaintiff's contract and negligent misrepresentation claims arising from her appointment as Representative for Children and Youth?

If privilege does not apply, should the plaintiff's amended notice of civil claim against the Government be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a) as disclosing no reasonable claim — because the alleged verbal contract is contrary to the RCY Act, the Government is not a proper party, it cannot be vicariously liable for the Deputy Clerk's representations, and it cannot be a common employer?
Is the claim unnecessary or frivolous under Rule 9-5(1)(b) given the written agreements limiting the plaintiff's CYO remuneration?
Is there no genuine issue for trial such that the claim should be dismissed under Rule 9-6?

firac.issue: Does parliamentary privilege oust the court's jurisdiction over the plaintiff's claims concerning her remuneration and benefits as an officer of the Legislative Assembly?
firac.facts: Turpel-Lafond, appointed the first Representative for Children and Youth (an officer of the legislature) and briefly the Child and Youth Officer, alleged a verbal contract and negligent misrepresentations by the Deputy Clerk, Attorney General and others regarding enhanced pension entitlement and relocation reimbursement. The Legislative Assembly and the Government sought to strike the claim, arguing that inquiring into a legislative officer's remuneration falls within a recognized category of parliamentary privilege.
firac.rule: Parliamentary privilege renders decisions within its scope immune from judicial review (New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia; Canada (House of Commons) v. Vaid, 2005 SCC 30; Chagnon v. Syndicat de la fonction publique, 2018 SCC 39; Legislative Assembly Privilege Act, s. 1(1)). Courts first ask whether the matter falls within an established category, then apply the necessity test: the sphere of activity must be 'so closely and directly connected with the fulfilment by the assembly or its members of their functions as a legislative and deliberative body ... that outside interference would undermine the level of autonomy required.' There is no blanket privilege over all employment relations (Vaid; Chagnon), and enforcing contracts entered into with legislative officers may fall to the courts (Roberts v. Commissioner of the NWT; Wells v. Newfoundland).
firac.application: The court distinguished Marin and March, which concerned appointment/reappointment and removal decisions and debating/passing resolutions — activities at the core of legislative function. The plaintiff's claim was fundamentally a private-law contract and misrepresentation claim about remuneration for a role once appointed, which would not require inquiry into the Assembly's internal proceedings, motives, or management of her. The defendants bore the burden but did not demonstrate that adjudicating whether contractual remuneration terms were fulfilled would interfere with legislative and deliberative functions or offend the separation of powers. The RCY's independence, tied to financial security (Wells), supported reviewability rather than immunity.
firac.conclusion: Parliamentary privilege does not apply; the privilege asserted was cast too broadly. The Legislative Assembly's application (resting entirely on privilege) was dismissed, and the Government's application was dismissed to the extent it relied on privilege.

firac.issue: Does the amended notice disclose a reasonable claim against the Government under Rule 9-5(1)(a)?
firac.facts: The Government argued the alleged verbal contract was unenforceable as contrary to the RCY Act (which limits pension entitlement), that it was not a proper party since the RCY is an officer of the legislature, that it could not be vicariously liable for the Deputy Clerk's representations, and that it could not be a common employer.
firac.rule: A claim is struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a) only where it is plain and obvious, assuming pleaded facts true, that no reasonable cause of action is disclosed (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42; Hunt v. Carey). Courts must be generous and permit novel but arguable claims to proceed. Statute supersedes contract only by clear express language (Wells v. Newfoundland).
firac.application: Wells did not assist the Government because the RCY Act contains no language expressly removing the right to sue for breach or precluding remuneration beyond the statutory scheme (e.g., vacation days were negotiated though not in the Act). The failure of the Act to permit the claimed pension did not doom the negligent misrepresentation claim. Because of the unique transition and two written agreements involving the Attorney General, the plaintiff's claim of a partial contractual relationship with the Government was reasonable. The Government offered no reason the Deputy Clerk could not act as its agent, and the plaintiff's uncontradicted evidence was that the Attorney General and other government employees participated in negotiating her entitlements. The common employer argument based on separation of powers was insufficient to strike a novel but arguable claim.
firac.conclusion: None of the four grounds succeeded; the court declined to strike any aspect of the claim under Rule 9-5(1)(a).

firac.issue: Is the plaintiff's claim unnecessary or frivolous under Rule 9-5(1)(b)?
firac.facts: The Government relied on the written agreements stating the plaintiff's only CYO remuneration would be her RCY salary and benefits, and characterized her claim to have worked as CYO past March 30, 2007 as untenable.
firac.rule: A pleading is unnecessary or frivolous if it does not go to establishing a cause of action or advance a claim known in law (Woolsey v. Dawson Creek).
firac.application: There was a single set of negotiations and one benefits package for both roles, so her CYO compensation was intimately tied to her RCY compensation; the written agreements did not clearly dispose of the alleged verbal promises of additional remuneration.
firac.conclusion: The claim is neither unnecessary nor frivolous.

firac.issue: Is there no genuine issue for trial warranting dismissal under Rule 9-6?
firac.facts: The Government argued the signed written agreements were conclusive that the plaintiff had no reasonable prospect of success. The plaintiff admitted the agreements' authenticity but alleged verbal promises of additional pension and reimbursement, and that her CYO duties continued past March 30, 2007.
firac.rule: Under Rule 9-6 the applicant bears a heavy burden to show no genuine issue of material fact requiring trial (McLean v. Law Society of BC; Canada (AG) v. Lameman, 2008 SCC 14). The judge does not weigh contested evidence (Skybridge Investments Ltd. v. Metro Motors Ltd.).
firac.application: The Government adduced no evidence disputing the alleged verbal agreement or representations and did not assert they were not made. The wording of the written agreements did not necessarily overcome the breach of contract or negligent misrepresentation claims, and sufficient material facts were pleaded.
firac.conclusion: A genuine legal and factual issue exists for trial; dismissal under Rule 9-6 refused.

name_verification.name_in_document: Her Majesty the Queen v. Everette Shannon Carman

defining_issues: What is a fit term of imprisonment for the robbery of a financial institution and the other offences committed by this youthful offender?

Are the statutory prerequisites and sentencing principles for a conditional sentence order under the Proulx framework satisfied, so that a conditional sentence (plus probation) rather than a penitentiary term is appropriate?

firac.issue: What is a fit term of imprisonment for the robbery of a financial institution together with the theft, obstruction and fail-to-appear offences committed by this youthful offender?
firac.facts: The 18-year-old accused robbed a Scotiabank by presenting a note claiming he had a gun and threatening to kill, though he had no gun; he obtained cash but threw it away and was immediately caught after being chased by three people. While on judicial interim release he committed two thefts under $5,000, obstructed a security guard and failed to attend court. He had a minor youth record (assault, assault with a weapon) but no adult record, pled guilty, was genuinely remorseful, and had spent about four months in pretrial custody. His motive was found to be rescuing his father's failing hair salon rather than greed.
firac.rule: R. v. Earl (1985) A.J. 168 sets a four-year starting point for 'robbery by note' of a financial institution, adjustable for aggravating and mitigating factors. Sentencing principles in ss. 718–718.2 of the Criminal Code, including proportionality and restorative objectives (as discussed in R. v. Proulx, 2000 SCC 5 and R. v. Gladue), govern the fit sentence.
firac.application: The court weighed strong mitigating factors — youth, unsophisticated offence 'destined to fail,' no personal gain, guilty pleas, remorse, no adult record, a chaotic and unstable home life, being forced from home into the influence of a bad family, and four months of difficult first-time pretrial custody — against the aggravating robbery of a financial institution with a threat of violence and reoffending on release. A probationary term would be too lenient, but a penitentiary term risked making a slight, bully-prone youth more dangerous. The court fixed a fit global sentence below the Earl starting point.
firac.conclusion: A fit global sentence was determined to be a term of incarceration of two years less a day.

firac.issue: Are the Proulx prerequisites and sentencing principles met so that a conditional sentence order (followed by probation) is appropriate rather than actual incarceration?
firac.facts: None of the offences carry a minimum term; the fit sentence was set at two years less a day; the accused was assessed as posing no serious risk to the community, unlikely to reoffend and, if he did, only in a minor way. The offence was a robbery of a financial institution requiring denunciation and deterrence.
firac.rule: R. v. Proulx, 2000 SCC 5 sets four criteria for a conditional sentence: (1) no minimum term of imprisonment; (2) a term of less than two years imposed; (3) community safety not endangered (assessing risk of reoffence and gravity of potential harm); and (4) consistency with ss. 718–718.2. There is no presumption for or against conditional sentences for particular offences; where both punitive and restorative objectives can be met, a conditional sentence may be preferable; onerous conditions can supply denunciation and deterrence (see also R. v. Millward and R. v. Watkinson).
firac.application: The court found the first three prerequisites satisfied: no minimum term, a fit sentence of two years less a day, and no serious danger to the community. On the fourth, denunciation and deterrence for robbing a financial institution could be achieved through an onerous conditional sentence — house confinement day and night except for work/education, restitution of $1,547, anger-management assessment and counselling, and 240 hours of community service — reinforced by a further year of probation on the same restrictive terms, extending the curtailment of liberty to three years. The stigma of serving the sentence in plain view of peers, and the risk that penitentiary would worsen this vulnerable youth, favoured a community sentence.
firac.conclusion: A conditional sentence of two years less a day, followed by one year of probation on restrictive terms, was found appropriate; counsel were invited to address the final terms.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the core practice area — this is a sentencing decision for robbery, theft, obstruction and failure to attend. The vocabulary lacks specific keywords for robbery, sentencing or conditional sentences, so no tier-2 criminal offence keyword fits precisely. The Jewish-related keywords reflect genuinely material mitigation facts: the accused is from a Jewish family (K093 Jewish, K095 Jewish family), and his youth record and difficulties are explained by racial slurs against him — he was called a 'dirty Jew' (K057 antisemitic slurs), reflecting antisemitism (K058) and racial prejudice (K065 racism). These identity/hate keywords are contextual rather than central legal issues and are flagged as weaker picks; they are included because the slurs were expressly weighed as a mitigating circumstance in the sentence.

registry_rationale: No separate registry designation is given beyond the Provincial Court of Alberta sitting in Calgary; the concluding line places the court in the City of Calgary, so Calgary is taken as the registry.

case_name: Streng v. Northwestern Utility Construction Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: Streng v. Northwestern Utility Construction Ltd.

defining_issues: Did Northwestern have just cause to dismiss Mr. Streng without notice on the grounds of insubordination, conflict of interest, or insolence?
If there was no just cause, what is the appropriate measure of damages, including the reasonable notice period and any set-off for mitigation earnings and lost benefits?

firac.issue: Did Northwestern have just cause to summarily dismiss Mr. Streng for insubordination, conflict of interest, or insolence?
firac.facts: Mr. Streng, a 55-year-old lineman with roughly 3.5 years' service and no written contract or prior discipline, was terminated on July 14, 2015. The employer alleged he disobeyed a direct order to 'park the truck' (leading to a 'near miss' at a rail crossing), that he threatened to take the company's work elsewhere, and that he directed a profanity-laden outburst at his manager Mr. Morgan in the yard after being handed a discipline letter and told he was suspended. The truck was actually driven by his co-worker Mr. Ferch, and the outburst followed the suspension.
firac.rule: In wrongful dismissal, once employment and dismissal are proven, the employer bears the onus of proving just cause on a balance of probabilities (McKinley v. BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38). Cause requires a contextual, proportionality analysis of the nature/extent of the misconduct, the surrounding circumstances, and whether dismissal is proportional (Dowling v. Ontario (WSIB)). Insubordination (intentional refusal to obey lawful orders) is distinct from and generally more serious than insolence (abusive language toward a superior); a single insolent act justifies dismissal only in the three circumstances set out in Henry v. Foxco, 2004 NBCA 22. An employer may rely on pre-termination after-discovered cause, and suspension without pay is not available absent an express or implied contractual term (Potter v. NB Legal Aid, 2015 SCC 10).
firac.application: The court rejected Mr. Morgan's account as not credible, finding he had authorized the trip to Fort St. John and gave no 'park the truck' order, so no insubordination occurred; the near-miss was caused by Mr. Ferch, not Mr. Streng, and no opportunity to file a report was given. The 'conflict of interest' claim failed because there was no non-competition agreement, the duty of loyalty ended on termination, and the words were merely 'blowing off steam.' The court found the yard outburst was insolence and employee misconduct, but it was not pleaded in the Termination Letter or Reply, the manager showed no reaction and did not testify the relationship was irreparable, profanity was common in the workplace, and Mr. Morgan (not the owner) was the target. An adverse inference was drawn from Northwestern's failure to disclose the Discipline Letter. Applying McKinley, dismissal was not a proportional response to a single act of insolence.
firac.conclusion: Northwestern failed to prove insubordination or conflict of interest, and although one incident of insolence was made out, it did not warrant dismissal. Mr. Streng was wrongfully dismissed.

firac.issue: What damages flow from the wrongful dismissal, given the reasonable notice period, mitigation, and claimed lost benefits?
firac.facts: There was no fixed-term contract. Mr. Streng found comparable full-time work with CMH within three weeks. The parties agreed a four-month notice period was appropriate. His T4 showed monthly earnings of about $5,815.40; his actual earnings during the notice period totalled $21,782.95. He also claimed lost RRSP matching contributions and benefit premiums.
firac.rule: Absent a fixed term, reasonable notice is implied (Bardal factors; Honda Canada v. Keays, 2008 SCC 39). Damages equal the salary the employee would have earned during the notice period (Wallace v. United Grain Growers, 1997). The employee must mitigate, with the employer bearing the onus on failure to mitigate (Red Deer College v. Michaels). Lost benefits are recoverable only where the employee proves actual out-of-pocket loss (Wilks v. Moore Dry Kiln, per McLachlin J.).
firac.application: The court used the T4 figure to set notional four-month salary at $23,400, deducted actual mitigation earnings of $21,782.95, leaving $1,618. The RRSP matching contributions would not have vested within the four-month notice period and were not recoverable. Benefit premiums were disallowed because Mr. Streng adduced no evidence he purchased replacement coverage or incurred actual losses. Mitigation was reasonable, so no failure-to-mitigate reduction applied.
firac.conclusion: Mr. Streng was awarded $1,618 for loss of salary over the four-month notice period, plus $176 in costs; the benefit and RRSP claims were dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the core doctrine, directly engaged by the just-cause analysis and damages for lack of reasonable notice. name_verification.name_in_document: Carson v. Knucwentwecw Society

defining_issues: Did the complainants lack standing to bring the human rights complaint?
Did the complaint fall within exclusive federal jurisdiction under s. 91(24) of the Constitution Act, 1867, depriving the provincial Tribunal of jurisdiction?
Is it an essential element of a complaint under s. 7(1)(a) of the Human Rights Code that the discriminatory publication relate to a field of activity otherwise covered by the Code?
Did the Tribunal err in refusing to dismiss the complaint under s. 27(1)(b) and (c) on the basis that there was no reasonable prospect of success?

firac.issue: Did the complainants lack standing to bring the human rights complaint?
firac.facts: The complaint was brought by Gerald Koehler on behalf of the Knucwentwecw Society, its members, members of the Bands it represents, and youth who would reside at the proposed care home. The petitioners argued the Code protects only personal rights, so the Society could not be a complainant. A prior Tribunal decision of January 30, 2006 had substituted Koehler as representative complainant, and that decision was never challenged.
firac.rule: Section 21(4) of the Human Rights Code specifically provides for representative complaints. Standing objections must be raised by way of review of the decision naming the complainant.
firac.application: The complaint was not brought by the Society directly but by Koehler on its behalf under s. 21(4). The Tribunal found Koehler clearly had standing, and that was all that was required. The January 30, 2006 decision constituted a finding that Koehler was a proper complainant; any objection had to be brought by an application to review that decision, and none was made.
firac.conclusion: The standing objection could not succeed.

firac.issue: Did the complaint fall within exclusive federal jurisdiction under s. 91(24), depriving the provincial Tribunal of jurisdiction?
firac.facts: The petitioners argued that because the complaint related to a care home for First Nations adolescents and was brought by Native complainants, s. 91(24) ('Indians, and lands reserved for Indians') placed the matter in exclusive federal jurisdiction. The subject matter was actually publications (signs, letters, statements) made by the non-Native Seven Respondents.
firac.rule: Standard of review on jurisdiction under s. 27(1)(a) of the Code is correctness (s. 59 Administrative Tribunals Act). Division of powers over speech turns on the aspect/pith and substance of the regulation, not the topic of the speech (Canadian Jewish Congress v. North Shore Free Press Ltd.; A.G. (Canada) and Dupond v. Montreal).
firac.application: The Tribunal was not inquiring into the conduct of First Nations people but into whether the non-Native respondents breached s. 7 of the Code. Regulation of speech about 'Indians' is not beyond provincial competence; the topic of speech does not determine jurisdiction. The fact that Native people initiated the complaint did not constitutionally immunize the respondents' publications from provincial scrutiny. Any resulting overlap with federal jurisdiction was a feature of Canada's constitutional framework, not a defect in the reasoning.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal was correct that it had jurisdiction; the ground failed.

firac.issue: Is it an essential element of a complaint under s. 7(1)(a) of the Human Rights Code that the discriminatory publication relate to a field of activity otherwise covered by the Code?
firac.facts: The petitioners argued, relying on Stacey v. Campbell and Khanna v. Common Ground Publishing, that s. 7(1)(a) prohibits only publications discriminatory in respect of a field of activity otherwise protected by the Code (e.g. employment, services). The Tribunal expressly departed from Stacey.
firac.rule: Standard of review is correctness. The current s. 7(1)(a) contains no limiting words comparable to the repealed s. 2(1) of the former Code ('in any manner prohibited by this Act'). The Code is to be construed purposively.
firac.application: The Tribunal analysed Stacey and the authorities it relied upon (Konyk, Singer, Engineering Students' Society, Black United Front, Kane) and found they did not necessarily support Stacey's interpretation, noting Stacey overlooked contrary authority (Kane v. Church of Jesus Christ Christian-Aryan Nations). Because s. 7(1)(a) contains no limiting language and the Code must be read purposively, a plain-language reading applied and no field-of-activity limitation should be read in. Tribunal members are not bound by prior Tribunal decisions.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal correctly interpreted s. 7(1)(a); the complaint could not be dismissed under s. 27(1)(b) on this basis.

firac.issue: Did the Tribunal err in refusing to dismiss the complaint under s. 27(1)(b) and (c) for having no reasonable prospect of success?
firac.facts: The respondents argued there was no reasonable prospect of success, asserting safety-based (non-discriminatory) motives and that the high threshold for 'hate publications' could not be met. They filed submissions but no affidavit evidence. They said the Tribunal failed to analyse the record individually as to each respondent.
firac.rule: A s. 27(1)(c) dismissal is a discretionary decision reviewable only for patent unreasonableness (s. 59(3)-(4) Administrative Tribunals Act). Section 27(1)(c) requires the respondent to show no reasonable prospect of success; a complainant need not establish a prima facie case, and intent is not necessary to a breach of the Code. Context is critical to assessing the meaning of a publication (Abrams v. North Shore Free Press Ltd.).
firac.application: The Tribunal found the respondents' submissions merely offered a different version of the facts and did not establish that the allegations were not a Code contravention or had no reasonable prospect of success. Determining the discriminatory nature of publications required contextual factual findings best made at a hearing with individual, expert and documentary evidence tested by cross-examination. Nothing suggested the discretion was exercised arbitrarily, in bad faith, for an improper purpose, on irrelevant factors, or in disregard of statutory requirements.
firac.conclusion: The refusal to dismiss was not patently unreasonable; the ground failed.

keywords_rationale: The case is a judicial review (K011) of a BC Human Rights Tribunal (K072) summary-dismissal decision, so Administrative law (K001) is the primary tier-1 area and standard of review (K014) was central (correctness for jurisdiction/interpretation, patent unreasonableness for the discretionary s. 27(1)(c) call). Human rights (K007) is engaged because the underlying complaint concerns discrimination (K069) via publications, i.e. discriminatory messages (K070) under s. 7 of the Human Rights Code (K119). Section 7(1)(b) targets publications likely to expose a group to hatred or contempt, supporting hate speech (K061). Constitutional law (K003) applies because the division-of-powers argument under s. 91(24) was a defining issue. Hate speech (K061) is somewhat borderline since the merits were not decided, but the statutory basis of the complaint squarely engages it.
location_rationale: The header states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA', 'Registry: Vancouver', and the trial/hearing took place in 'Vancouver, B.C.'
registry_rationale: The decision expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

case_name: Board of Education of District No. 15 v. Human Rights Board of Inquiry (N.B.)

name_verification.name_in_document: New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15 v. New Brunswick (Human Rights Board of Inquiry)
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied name calls the party 'Board of Education of District No. 15', whereas the decision names it the 'Board of School Trustees, District No. 15' (also styled 'New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15'). The neutral citation 1989 CanLII 208 (NBCA) does not appear in the text; the text cites the appeal court file numbers and the appealed decision (1989 CanLII 7931 (NB QB), 10 C.H.R.R. D/5800). The parties and subject matter otherwise clearly correspond to the same case.

defining_issues: Is judicial review by way of prohibition available to prevent a Human Rights Board of Inquiry from proceeding with a hearing before it has found facts?

Does public education in the New Brunswick public school system fall within 'accommodation, services, or facilities available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted' under s. 5 of the Human Rights Act?
Is David Attis a proper complainant as a 'person claiming to be aggrieved' under s. 17 of the Act?
Was Attis's written complaint sufficiently precise to constitute a valid complaint under the Act?

firac.issue: Is judicial review by way of prohibition available to prevent a Human Rights Board of Inquiry from proceeding with its hearing?
firac.facts: The Minister of Labour appointed a Board of Inquiry to hear Attis's discrimination complaint against the School Board. Before the Board held its first hearing, the School Board and the Teachers' Federation obtained a stay and applied for judicial review to prohibit the Board from proceeding, raising the questions whether education is a 'service' and whether Attis was a proper complainant.
firac.rule: Prohibition is available where there is a clear question of law, not depending on particular facts, on which the tribunal's jurisdiction turns (Bell v. Ontario Human Rights Commission, [1971] S.C.R. 756; R. v. Tottenham and District Rent Tribunal, [1957] 1 Q.B. 103). Courts must exercise restraint and curial deference and not usurp a tribunal's statutory role (Re CIP Paper Products v. Saskatchewan HRC; CUPE Local 963 v. N.B. Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227), but must intervene where a tribunal acts beyond jurisdiction.
firac.application: The Court held the three main grounds (meaning of s. 5, status of the complainant, sufficiency of the complaint) were questions of law determinable on uncontested affidavit facts without deciding the merits of the Attis complaint. Miller J. had not attempted to decide the merits. The Teachers' Federation had not acquiesced in the Board's jurisdiction, having sought party status and then promptly challenged jurisdiction, so it retained standing to seek review.
firac.conclusion: Judicial review by prohibition was available; the reviewing judge properly exercised his discretion to entertain the application, though the correct remedy was to prohibit the Board from proceeding rather than to quash the Minister's administrative order.

firac.issue: Does public education fall within the 'accommodation, services, or facilities available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted' under s. 5 of the Human Rights Act?
firac.facts: Attis alleged the School Board condoned teacher Malcolm Ross's anti-Semitic and Holocaust-denying statements, thereby depriving Jewish and other minority students of equal opportunity within the public education system provided as a service to the public. Miller J. had held that school facilities and education programs were not covered by s. 5.
firac.rule: Human rights legislation is quasi-constitutional and must be given a 'fair, large and liberal' purposive interpretation (Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17; O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536; Heerspink, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 145; Robichaud v. Canada (Treasury Board), [1987] 2 S.C.R. 84; Gay Alliance v. Vancouver Sun). A service offered to the public need not be offered to all members of the public and may carry eligibility criteria (Saskatchewan HRC v. Saskatchewan (Social Services)).
firac.application: Applying a purposive construction, the Court found the Act cast in wide terms and that reading education out of s. 5 would frustrate the legislative intent and permit, e.g., exclusion of children on prohibited grounds. Alternatively, public education under the Schools Act is a service provided to a client group meeting statutory eligibility requirements, which cannot discriminate among the group on prohibited grounds.
firac.conclusion: Public education in New Brunswick falls within s. 5(1) of the Human Rights Act; Miller J. erred in holding otherwise.

firac.issue: Is David Attis a 'person claiming to be aggrieved' entitled to complain under s. 17 of the Act?
firac.facts: Attis is a member of the Jewish community with three children enrolled in School District No. 15. He complained that the Board's condoning of Ross's conduct harmed his and his children's equality of opportunity. The trial judge noted neither Attis nor his children had direct contact with Ross as a teacher.
firac.rule: Section 17 permits 'any person claiming to be aggrieved' to complain; the phrase is to be given a wide interpretation, especially at the preliminary stage. Human rights law looks to effect rather than intent, and a 'victim' is not limited to the direct target (Re Singh, 86 N.R. 69 (F.C.A.)).
firac.application: Attis made a written complaint on the prescribed form claiming to be aggrieved. Whether the claim has merit is for the Commission and Board of Inquiry, not the reviewing court. The Société des Acadiens parental-standing precedent addressed court standing, not complainant status under the Act, and was inapposite. The representative-complaint concern need not be resolved since Attis's principal claim was personal to him and his children.
firac.conclusion: Attis met the s. 17 standard and has legal status as a complainant. (Ryan J.A. concurred in the result but viewed this as a question of fact, or mixed fact and law, best left to the Board.)

firac.issue: Was Attis's written complaint sufficiently precise to constitute a valid complaint under the Act?
firac.facts: Attis's form set out his identity, the alleged offender's conduct, the period (1976-77 to 1988), the School Board's inaction, examples of effects, and the alleged violation of s. 5. Miller J. found it insufficiently specific, relying on Mackin v. Judicial Council (N.B.).
firac.rule: The word 'complaint' in s. 17 must be interpreted to advance the broad purposes of the Act. A valid complaint generally identifies the complainant, victim, time, place, nature of the practice, relevant section, and an affirmation of reasonable grounds (Canada (CHRC) v. Bell Canada). Particulars can be demanded later; a Board of Inquiry controls its own procedure (Act s. 20(3); Industrial Relations Act s. 66(2)).
firac.application: The standard for a complaint under the Provincial Court Act in Mackin differs from that under the remedial Human Rights Act. Attis's submission was in writing on the prescribed form and contained most of the essential elements, satisfying s. 17 on judicial review; any further detail could be obtained through particulars before the Board.
firac.conclusion: The complaint was sufficient to qualify as a valid complaint under the Act; Miller J. erred in holding it too imprecise.

Administrative law (K001) and judicial review (K011) capture the central procedural holding on prohibition of a tribunal.
