registry_rationale: The decision expressly names 'GREFFE DE MONTRÉAL' (Montréal registry of the Court of Appeal).

case_name: Canada Trust Co. v. Ontario Human Rights Commission (C.A.)

name_verification.name_in_document: Canada Trust Co. v. Ontario Human Rights Commission

defining_issues: Did the superior court have jurisdiction to determine the validity of the charitable trust, and was doing so premature given a pending complaint before the Ontario Human Rights Commission?
Were the discriminatory eligibility provisions of the charitable trust void for contravening public policy (or void for uncertainty)?
If the discriminatory provisions were void, could the cy-près doctrine be applied to preserve the charitable trust?

firac.issue: Did the superior court have jurisdiction to rule on the validity of the trust rather than deferring to the Ontario Human Rights Commission, and was such a ruling premature?
firac.facts: The Ontario Human Rights Commission filed a formal complaint in August 1986 alleging the Leonard Foundation trust contravened the Human Rights Code, 1981. The trustee, Canada Trust Company, then applied under s. 60 of the Trustee Act and rule 14.05 for the court's advice and direction on the trust's validity. The Commission argued the questions concerning the Code fell within its exclusive primary jurisdiction.
firac.rule: Under Seneca College v. Bhadauria, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 181, the Human Rights Code provides a comprehensive scheme that must be pursued before resort to the courts for a breach of the Code. However, superior courts retain inherent jurisdiction over the administration of charitable trusts, reinforced by s. 60 of the Trustee Act, and may determine questions of law where no facts are in dispute (Bell v. Ontario Human Rights Commission, [1971] S.C.R. 756).
firac.application: The court distinguished Bhadauria: this was not an attempt to create a common-law tort of discrimination but the administration of a charitable trust, a matter of centuries-old inherent equitable jurisdiction invoked by the trustee itself. The Commission's remedial powers under s. 40(1) of the Code could not alter or void the terms of a trust, so recourse to the court was necessary in any event; and the matter turned on a question of law with no disputed facts. A determination before the Commission investigated was therefore not premature.
firac.conclusion: The court had jurisdiction to determine the validity of the trust, and the determination was not premature. This preliminary objection was dismissed.

firac.issue: Were the trust's provisions restricting eligibility, management and benefits by race, religion and sex void as contrary to public policy (or void for uncertainty)?
firac.facts: The 1923 indenture recited the settlor's beliefs in the superiority of the 'White Race' and Christianity and restricted scholarships, committee membership and eligible institutions to white, British, Protestant Christians; a further clause capped income spent on female students at one-quarter of the total. The trust had operated for over 65 years and drew sustained public criticism.
firac.rule: Public freedom to dispose of property (Blathwayt v. Lord Cawley, [1976] A.C. 397) is limited by public policy, to be invoked only in clear cases where harm to the public is substantially incontestable (Re Millar, [1938] S.C.R. 1). The public policy against discrimination is drawn from the Human Rights Code, 1981, the Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, other statutes, ss. 15, 27 and 28 of the Charter, and ratified international conventions (per Tarnopolsky J.A.). A charitable trust must be wholly charitable and confer a public benefit; a condition precedent defining beneficiaries is not void for uncertainty if some person can satisfy it (Jones v. T. Eaton Co.; McPhail v. Doulton).
firac.application: Robins J.A. read the recitals together with the operative clauses, finding the trust premised on notions of racism and religious superiority patently at odds with contemporary values of racial and religious equality guaranteed constitutionally and reflected in Canada's multicultural heritage; its continued operation in that form was inimical to the public interest. Tarnopolsky J.A. held the eligibility clause was a sufficiently certain condition precedent (severing only the 'allegiance' language if needed) so the trust did not fail for uncertainty, but was void on public policy grounds to the extent it discriminated by race, religion and sex — while cautioning that not all restrictive charitable trusts (e.g. ameliorative or needs-based ones) are void.
firac.conclusion: The provisions confining management, judicial advice, eligible institutions and benefits on grounds of race, colour, ethnic origin, creed/religion and sex were void as contravening public policy; it was unnecessary to decide the uncertainty question (Robins J.A.), and Tarnopolsky J.A. found the trust sufficiently certain.

firac.issue: If the discriminatory provisions were void, could the cy-près doctrine be applied to preserve the charitable trust?
firac.facts: The trust was valid when created in 1923; changed social attitudes rendered its discriminatory terms contrary to public policy. The settlor's stated object was the advancement of education/leadership through education, and para. 13 allowed alteration of objects for purposes conducive to promoting education.
firac.rule: A charitable trust that becomes impracticable or fails will be applied cy-près where the settlor had a general (paramount) charitable intention, as distinct from a particular intention tied to a specific mode (Re Lysaght; Re Dominion Students' Hall Trust; National Anti-Vivisection Society v. IRC, [1948] A.C. 31 — 'a charity once established does not die, though its nature may be changed').
firac.application: Both judges found the settlor's paramount intention was charitable — the advancement of education/leadership through education — and that the discriminatory scheme was merely the machinery for carrying it out, not an essential part of the paramount intention. As changing public policy had made the original scheme impracticable and offensive, the court exercised its inherent jurisdiction to bring the trust into accord with public policy.
firac.conclusion: Cy-près was applied. The recitals and all restrictions as to race, colour, creed/religion, ethnic origin and sex (for beneficiaries, committee members, judicial advice and eligible institutions) were struck out, preserving the charitable trust; the preferences for children of clergymen, teachers, service members, etc. were left intact.

keywords_rationale: The case turns on discrimination and the public policy of equality, so K069 (discrimination) and K023 (equality rights) are central, with K007 (Human rights) as the tier-1 practice-area anchor and K003 (Constitutional law) as parent since the court relied on Charter equality values. K065 (racism) captures the race-based restrictions (with religion and sex discrimination also engaged). K072 (human rights tribunal/commission) reflects the OHRC's role and the jurisdiction issue. K054 (wills/estates — includes 'public policy void bequest' and estate litigation) is the closest vocabulary match for the charitable trust/cy-près subject matter, as the list has no dedicated trusts heading. K005 (Education law) reflects that the trust funds educational scholarships. K121 (s. 27 multiculturalism) is a weaker but genuine pick — the court expressly grounded public policy in Canada's multicultural heritage and s. 27. There is no perfect tier-2 keyword for charitable trusts or cy-près, which is a limitation flagged here.

registry_rationale: The decision does not name a court registry or office; appellate decisions of the Court of Appeal for Ontario typically do not, so registry is left null.

case_name: Benarroch c. Sir. Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital

name_verification.name_in_document: Yohann Benarroch c. Sir. Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital

defining_issues: Was the plaintiff illegally dismissed, or did the employment relationship end because of his own conduct in refusing to report to his reassigned position?
Was the disputed exhibit D-9 admissible in evidence?

firac.issue: Was the plaintiff illegally dismissed, or did the employment relationship end because of his own conduct in refusing to report to his reassigned position?
firac.facts: Benarroch, a 22-year-old supervisor in laundry and sterilization services, was transferred to a supervisor position in housekeeping. He characterized the transfer as a demotion and an illegal dismissal, linking it to his discovery of alleged misappropriation of funds by a superior, Claude Bensmihen. The employer argued Benarroch had accepted the transferred position but never reported to it. Testimony from HR officer Mallet (30 years' experience), supervisor Elbas, and colleague Audrey Bennaroche established chronic lateness, poor performance, failure to cooperate, personal internet use at work, and that a co-worker often covered his duties. The employer had offered him a way to keep his job at the same salary ($38,000), which he refused.
firac.rule: Under Quebec employment/contract law, where an employee refuses to report to a validly reassigned position after accepting it, the ending of employment may constitute a rupture of the employment relationship by the employee's own conduct rather than an illegal dismissal. Where witness versions conflict, the court assesses credibility and probability.
firac.application: Faced with contradictory versions, the Court preferred the defendant's credible and probable account, relying particularly on Mallet's serious investigation and Bennaroche's disinterested, courageous testimony. The evidence showed Benarroch had accepted the lateral transfer, then changed his mind and reportedly said he would stay in the laundry and that they could fire him if they wished. His performance was declining and the alleged 'targeting' after the Bensmihen incident was not made out, since Bennaroche—also involved in denouncing Bensmihen—was not targeted. The Court found the end of employment resulted from the plaintiff's presumptuous conduct.
firac.conclusion: The Court found there was a rupture of the employment relationship caused by the plaintiff's own acts, not an illegal dismissal; the claim for $48,000 in damages was rejected.

firac.issue: Was the disputed exhibit D-9 admissible in evidence?
firac.facts: The defendant sought to introduce exhibit D-9, a document confirming the employee's status, over the plaintiff's objection that it had not been pleaded in the proceedings and was irrelevant. The objection had been taken under reserve.
firac.rule: Evidence that is relevant to the issues and at least indirectly alleged in the proceedings may be admitted.
firac.application: The Court considered D-9 relevant and not foreign to the litigation, being indirectly alleged and inferable from the whole of the evidence. It confirmed the employee's status.
firac.conclusion: D-9 was admitted; it established that at hiring the plaintiff held a temporary full-time position, not a permanent one.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns an alleged illegal dismissal and job reassignment. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the core substantive issue—whether the plaintiff was illegally dismissed or the employment ended by his own conduct. K002 (Civil litigation) applies as the matter was a civil claim for damages tried in the Cour du Québec, including a contested evidentiary ruling. Only three keywords genuinely apply; the case has no religious, human rights, or discrimination dimension despite the defendant hospital's name, so no antisemitism/Jewish-community keywords are warranted.

registry_rationale: The judgment identifies the court as 'COUR DU QUÉBEC', District and Locality of Montréal, file no. 500-02-113128-024, indicating the Montréal registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: CAS v. N.A.-M.

defining_issues: Should the law clerk's affidavits, sworn on information and belief and tendered as the mother's evidence, be admitted and, if so, what weight should they receive?
Should an adverse inference be drawn from the mother's failure to provide direct evidence in response to the summary judgment motion?
Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial that the child is in need of protection under the Child and Family Services Act?
Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial for a disposition other than crown wardship?
Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether the mother should have access to a crown ward?

firac.issue: Should the law clerk's affidavits, sworn on information and belief and tendered as the mother's substantive evidence, be admitted and what weight should they carry?
firac.facts: The mother filed no responding affidavit of her own. Her counsel instead relied on two affidavits sworn by counsel's law clerk purporting to set out the mother's circumstances in Dubai, her plan of care, her income, and family support. No source for the attributed statements was identified, no contact information or names of supporting relatives were given, and the exhibits (passport copies, 'medical report', employment documents) were largely unreadable and of uncertain authenticity.
firac.rule: Rule 14(18) of the Family Law Rules expresses a preference for personal-knowledge affidavits; Rule 14(19) permits information-and-belief evidence only where the source is named and the deponent states a belief in its truth (conjunctive requirements). A judge retains discretion to refuse hearsay led for its truth (Berger v. Berger, 2016 ONCA 884). Lawyers'/staff affidavits are generally inappropriate on summary judgment except to summarize record or uncontested facts (Ferreira v. Cardenas, 2014 ONSC 7119; Children's Aid Society of Ottawa v. B.(J.), 2016 ONSC 2757). Weight is governed by the best-evidence rule, direct evidence outweighs hearsay, and the more dispositive the hearsay the more scrutiny it attracts.
firac.application: The clerk never indicated she had communicated with the mother or why direct affidavits from the mother, her husband, or his family could not be obtained. The attributed statements were contentious and went to the heart of the mother's response, yet no source or particulars were provided, making trustworthiness impossible to assess, and the exhibits were inherently unreliable. There was no necessity shown for the clerk to give substantive evidence.
firac.conclusion: The court gave the law clerk's evidence as to the mother's circumstances in Dubai no weight, while not striking the affidavits.

firac.issue: Should an adverse inference be drawn from the mother's failure to lead direct evidence?
firac.facts: The mother did not attend the motion, filed no responsive affidavit, and provided only hearsay through her counsel's law clerk. She had never sought temporary care and control and offered no direct evidence from herself or the family said to support her plan.
firac.rule: Rule 16(5) of the Family Law Rules permits the court to draw conclusions unfavourable to a party whose evidence is not from a person with personal knowledge of the disputed facts; the rule is permissive (Jewish Child and Family Services v. S.K., 2015 ONCJ 246). A responding party must 'lead trump or risk losing' (Sweda Farms).
firac.application: Given the absence of any direct evidence and the unexplained failure to obtain affidavits from the mother or her supporters, the circumstances supported drawing an adverse inference that the missing evidence would have harmed her case.
firac.conclusion: The court drew an adverse inference from the mother's failure to depose direct evidence.

firac.issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial that the child is in need of protection?
firac.facts: R.S.A., born 2015, was apprehended at almost 10 months old, having lived only in shelters and hotels; she was developmentally delayed and later diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder, needs the mother had not recognized. The mother had a long history with child welfare agencies, chronic instability, repeated misrepresentations of her identity, occupation and whereabouts, refused mental health assessment, and left Canada, not seeing the child since January 31, 2017.
firac.rule: On a Rule 16 summary judgment motion the moving party must show no genuine issue for trial; the responding party must set out specific facts showing a triable issue (CAS of Toronto v. T.(K.), 2000 CanLII 20578). 'No genuine issue for trial exists where there is no realistic possibility of an outcome other than that sought by the applicant' (CAS of Niagara Region v. S.C., 2008 CanLII 52309). Protection grounds under ss. 37(2)(b)(i),(ii) and 37(2)(g) of the Child and Family Services Act.
firac.application: The mother's own June 2016 affidavit conceded instability and untruthfulness; her plan of care was predicated on remaining in Ontario, which no longer applied. The child's significant unmet needs at apprehension and the mother's departure left no realistic alternative outcome. The hearsay clerk affidavit could not raise a triable issue.
firac.conclusion: The court found no genuine issue requiring a trial and made the protection findings under ss. 37(2)(b)(i),(ii) and 37(2)(g).

firac.issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial for a disposition other than crown wardship?
firac.facts: After apprehension the mother rebuffed the Society's supports, attended access sporadically, then disappeared for extended periods, relocating to Dubai. She provided no verified travel documents, no viable plan, and no kin options. The child had been in care over two years and required substantial ongoing support.
firac.rule: Child protection timelines are paramount; a child's need for permanency planning must be respected, with a one-year statutory limit for children under six under clause 70(1)(a) of the Act. The parent's evidence must disclose an arguable notion of better prospects than at removal (CCAS of Toronto v. G.O., 2014 ONCJ 523).
firac.application: The only proposed trial witness was the law clerk, whose information-and-belief evidence was insufficient. The mother offered no direct or reliable evidence of an improved situation, and no alternative disposition was realistically available given the timelines and permanency needs.
firac.conclusion: The court found no genuine issue requiring a trial for any disposition other than crown wardship.

firac.issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether the mother should have access to the crown ward?
firac.facts: The mother had not seen the child since January 31, 2017 and had ceased residing in Canada. Her counsel made no submissions on access.
firac.rule: Section 59(2.1) of the Child and Family Services Act creates a presumption against access to a crown ward; the person seeking access must prove the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and that access will not impair the child's future opportunities for adoption.
firac.application: With no submissions and no evidence that the relationship was beneficial and meaningful or that access would not impair adoption prospects, the presumption against access was not displaced.
firac.conclusion: The court found no genuine issue requiring a trial on access; crown wardship with no access was ordered for the purpose of adoption.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area — this is a child-protection/crown wardship proceeding under the Child and Family Services Act. K047 (best interests of the child) is central: permanency planning and statutory timelines drove the disposition. K048 (custody/access) applies squarely to the s. 59(2.1) analysis of whether the mother should have access to the crown ward. K002 (Civil litigation) is a weaker, procedural pick reflecting the Rule 16 summary judgment and hearsay/affidavit-weight analysis that dominates the reasons, for which the controlled vocabulary has no dedicated evidence keyword. K052 (religious upbringing) is a borderline/weak pick tied only to the statutory finding that the child's religion is Islam; it is included for completeness but is peripheral. The vocabulary is oriented toward antisemitism/Jewish-law themes not engaged here, so several picks are necessarily approximate.

registry_rationale: The court file number is preceded by 'NEWMARKET', indicating the Newmarket registry of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Budgell v. British Columbia

defining_issues: Does the plaintiff's statement of claim disclose a reasonable cause of action, in particular for misfeasance in public office, so as to survive an application to strike under Rule 19(24)(a)?
Are the pleadings unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious under Rule 19(24)(b)?
Does the action constitute an abuse of the process of the court, including an impermissible collateral attack on the administrative/judicial review process, under Rule 19(24)(d)?

firac.issue: Does the statement of claim disclose a reasonable cause of action for misfeasance in public office?
firac.facts: Mr. Budgell, after losing a wrongful dismissal grievance and multiple Labour Relations Board and judicial review proceedings, sued the Attorney General, the Minister of Labour and the Crown alleging that a 1996 statutory-revision change to s. 13 of the Labour Relations Code (replacing 'prima facie' with 'sufficient evidence that the contravention has apparently occurred') was surreptitious and illegal and that ministers deceptively covered it up, causing him to lose his career.
firac.rule: Under Rule 19(24)(a) and Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, a claim is struck only where, assuming the pleaded facts true, it is plain and obvious it discloses no reasonable cause of action. Pleadings must set out the material facts constituting each element of a recognized cause of action (Rule 19(1); Delaney; Alford). Misfeasance in public office (Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse, 2003 SCC 69) requires deliberate unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions and awareness the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff, plus causation and compensable injury. Lawmakers and officials enforcing legislation are not liable in damages for the effects of legislation (Welbridge Holdings v. Winnipeg; Guimond v. Quebec (A.G.)); the Crown is not vicariously liable for the Board's functionaries (Speckling v. Kearney).
firac.application: The employer, union and Board alleged to have caused harm were not made parties; the Crown is not vicariously liable for the Board's functionaries. Lawmakers and officials cannot be liable in damages for enacting or implementing legislation, so even a pleading of invalidity could not ground a claim. Critically, the statement of claim failed to plead the material facts establishing the two essential elements of misfeasance in public office; the bare assertion of an 'unlawful exercise of statutory powers' was unsupported by material facts, as in A.L. v. Ontario.
firac.conclusion: The pleadings disclose no reasonable claim; struck under Rule 19(24)(a).

firac.issue: Are the pleadings unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious?
firac.facts: The statement of claim mixed allegations against ministers, ministry staff, the Board's adjudicators, the union and employer, without clearly identifying who was at fault or which acts founded the claim.
firac.rule: Rule 19(24)(b); Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress (1999) — pleadings are irrelevant/embarrassing where so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is pleaded, and unnecessary or vexatious where they do not establish a cause of action or advance a claim known in law.
firac.application: The pleadings were confusing as to who was at fault and why, and did not establish any recognized cause of action, rendering them irrelevant, embarrassing, unnecessary and vexatious.
firac.conclusion: The pleadings are also liable to be struck under Rule 19(24)(b).

firac.issue: Does the action constitute an abuse of process or an impermissible collateral attack on the administrative and judicial review process?
firac.facts: Mr. Budgell had already litigated his fair-representation complaint through the Board, reconsideration panels, two judicial review petitions and the Court of Appeal, all unsuccessfully, and now sought compensatory damages for loss of career on issues that were or could have been raised in those proceedings.
firac.rule: Rule 19(24)(d); Young v. Borzoni, 2007 BCCA 16 (abuse of process where court used unfairly/for improper purpose or through multiple successive related proceedings). A party cannot obtain by civil action a remedy available through the statutory judicial review process; such evasion is a prohibited collateral attack (Berscheid v. Ensign; R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines).
firac.application: Although the court accepted Mr. Budgell acted sincerely and not dishonestly, he was seeking substantially the same relief and raising the same or available issues (including the proper s. 13 test) as in the earlier Board and judicial review proceedings. This was another in a series of multiple successive related proceedings amounting to a collateral attack.
firac.conclusion: The action is an abuse of the process of the court under Rule 19(24)(d).

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area: the action is a tort claim (misfeasance in public office) and the decision turns on the civil-procedure test for striking pleadings under Rule 19(24). name_verification.name_in_document: Seymour Avrith v. Paul Ayoub

defining_issues: Were the statements Mr. Ayoub made in his complaint to the Quebec Bar Association defamatory and a wrongful act, and did they cause Mr. Avrith compensable damages?
Were Mr. Ayoub's statements in Small Claims Court that Mr. Avrith had 'lied to the judge' defamatory and wrongful, and did they cause compensable damages?

firac.issue: Were the statements in Mr. Ayoub's complaint to the Quebec Bar Association defamatory, wrongful, and productive of compensable damages?
firac.facts: After Mr. Avrith described himself in Small Claims Court as the 'administrator' of Phillip Avrith Investments Inc., Mr. Ayoub filed a written complaint with the Syndic of the Quebec Bar alleging Mr. Avrith had falsely presented himself as an administrator. The Syndic, noting Mr. Avrith was the duly authorized representative and signatory of the lease, found he had not lied and closed the file. The complaint was confidential and known only to the parties and the Syndic.
firac.rule: An action in defamation rests on the ordinary rules of civil liability under art. 1457 C.c.Q.; the plaintiff must prove injury, fault and a causal link. Whether remarks are defamatory is assessed objectively — whether an ordinary person would believe the remarks brought discredit on the person's reputation (Prud'homme v. Prud'homme, 2002 SCC 85). Fault may be malicious or merely negligent; a scandalmonger who makes unfavourable statements without valid reason may be liable. Compensatory damages are evaluated on the multi-factor criteria including gravity, extent of dissemination and effect on the victim (Hill; Fabien; Gagné c. Galand). Punitive damages require an intentional and illicit interference under s. 49 of the Quebec Charter.
firac.application: The Court found the complaint's allegation impugning Mr. Avrith's honesty was defamatory. Since 'administrator' in English properly describes a manager, Mr. Avrith's statement was not false, and there was no valid reason for the complaint, so Mr. Ayoub's conduct was unjustified though not malicious. However, the complaint was confidential with no publicity or diffusion; Mr. Avrith remained a member in good standing of the Bar and showed no actual effect on his reputation. He therefore established no injury and no compensable damages, and there was no intentional illicit violation warranting punitive damages.
firac.conclusion: Although the complaint was defamatory and unjustified, Mr. Avrith proved no damages; no compensation was awarded.

firac.issue: Were Mr. Ayoub's statements in Small Claims Court that Mr. Avrith had lied defamatory, wrongful, and productive of compensable damages?
firac.facts: At the February 19, 2007 Small Claims hearing, Mr. Avrith himself first raised the Bar complaint while seeking a postponement, telling the judge Mr. Ayoub had accused him of being a liar. In response to the judge's questions, Mr. Ayoub explained that Mr. Avrith had presented himself as an administrator and 'lied to the judge.' The courtroom was said to be full of unidentified litigants awaiting their own cases.
firac.rule: Defamation arising in the course of judicial proceedings requires proof of five elements (Terreault c. Bigras, 2005 QCCA 1243; Gagné c. Galland, 2008 QCCS 5083): that the allegations are defamatory, false, not pertinent to the litigation, made without reasonable motive, and malicious or recklessly so. Witnesses must be able to speak freely without fear of subsequent liability, and unrepresented litigants in Small Claims Court are held to a lower standard, requiring particularly convincing evidence of malice or malicious recklessness.
firac.application: It was Mr. Avrith, not Mr. Ayoub, who introduced the subject; Mr. Ayoub, whose mother tongue was not English, merely responded to the Court's questions using the same 'lied' terminology Mr. Avrith had used. He could reasonably believe the judge wanted to understand the Bar issue, and was defending himself against a legally trained opponent. No malice or malicious recklessness was shown. In any event there was no evidence identifying anyone in the courtroom or showing any impact on Mr. Avrith's employment, revenue or reputation.
firac.conclusion: Mr. Ayoub committed no wrongful act during the hearing, and no damages were established; the claim failed.

case_name: Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton v R.M. and N.M.

name_verification.name_in_document: Catholic Children's Aid Society of Hamilton v. R.M. and N.M.

defining_issues: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether the child G.M. continues to be in need of protection?
Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial regarding the placement and access terms in G.M.'s best interests?
Is a trial required to determine whether a restraining order should issue against N.M.?

firac.issue: On a summary judgment motion in a Status Review application, is there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether the child continues to be in need of protection?
firac.facts: The Society had been involved with the family since 2010 based on serious domestic violence by the father N.M. against the mother R.M. Over several years N.M. was convicted of assaults, breached probation and restraining terms, failed to complete the PAR domestic-violence program, showed borderline intellectual functioning and emotional volatility, made rambling and incoherent communications, was inconsistent in access, undermined the mother during visits, and failed to advance a clear plan of care. The mother had ended the relationship and was competently caring for G.M. N.M.'s affidavit did not address the ongoing concerns.
firac.rule: Under s. 64-65 of the Child and Family Services Act and Catholic Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto v. M.(C.), [1994] S.C.J. No. 37, a Status Review involves a two-part test: (1) whether the child continues to require a court order for protection, and (2) the child's best interests (ss. 37(3)-(4)). On summary judgment under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules and Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, the court grants final judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; the responding party must put its best foot forward with specific facts.
firac.application: The Court found no ongoing protection concern regarding R.M., who was meeting all of G.M.'s needs. However, it found numerous persisting concerns regarding N.M.: unaddressed history of domestic violence and abusive attitudes, cognitive and emotional instability, unreliable access, undermining conduct toward the mother during visits, inability to cooperate with the Society, and no viable plan of care. N.M.'s affidavit merely minimized these concerns and offered bald assertions, providing no material facts giving his case a real chance of success. The Court could make the necessary findings on the affidavit record without the enhanced fact-finding powers.
firac.conclusion: No genuine issue requiring a trial; the Court found G.M. continues to be in need of protection because of the ongoing concerns respecting N.M.

firac.issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial regarding the placement and access terms in G.M.'s best interests?
firac.facts: R.M. had been G.M.'s primary caregiver since birth, addressed her historical concerns, and cared competently for him. N.M. had never been a primary caregiver, missed numerous visits, made unsettling comments to the child about coming to live with him, disparaged the mother's care, and had no consistent plan. G.M. showed anxiety and oppositional behaviour after visits.
firac.rule: Section 57.1 of the CFSA permits a custody order to a non-foster person where it is in the child's best interests; s. 58 governs access; best interests are assessed under s. 37(3). The child-centred focus requires permanency planning within a timeframe sensitive to the child's needs (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. R.H.).
firac.application: The evidence clearly supported granting R.M. sole custody under s. 57.1, as she was meeting all of G.M.'s needs and the child had a close, loving relationship with her. Placement with N.M. would not be in G.M.'s best interests given the serious protection concerns and N.M.'s never having been a caregiver. Access with N.M. was found contrary to G.M.'s best interests because the negatives (undermining the placement, inconsistency, anxiety-inducing comments) far outweighed the positives, and supervised access was not practicable long-term.
firac.conclusion: No trial required; sole custody granted to R.M. under s. 57.1 with no access to N.M. except one goodbye visit; the supervision order was terminated.

firac.issue: Is a trial required to determine whether a restraining order should issue against N.M.?
firac.facts: N.M. had a longstanding history of domestic violence, emotional abuse and intimidation of R.M., convictions for assault, breaches of no-contact terms, cognitive/psychological concerns, and had told G.M. he would take him by force. The Society's involvement, which had buffered R.M., was ending.
firac.rule: Section 57.1(3) of the CFSA allows a restraining order in accordance with s. 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act where the applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for his/her safety or that of a child in lawful custody; guidance in Children's Aid Society of Halton Region v. C.(C.L.) requires evidence of threats, assault, stalking or harassment and consideration of alternative protections.
firac.application: The Court found R.M. had reasonable grounds to fear for her own and G.M.'s safety given the history of violence, breaches of no-contact orders, N.M.'s emotional instability and his threat to take the child by force. With the Society's protective involvement ending, no adequate alternative protection existed.
firac.conclusion: No trial required; a restraining order issued against N.M. restraining contact and prohibiting him from coming within 100 metres of specified locations.

defining_issues: In the children's best interests, should custody be granted to the father, to the mother (full custody sought), or remain shared as previously agreed?
Should the father be permitted to leave Canada and take the children to Pakistan given the imminent expiry of his work permit?
Should the perception of child support and spousal alimony (and arrears) be suspended pending the divorce on the merits?

firac.issue: In the children's best interests, should custody be granted to the father, to the mother, or remain shared?
firac.facts: The parties, Pakistani citizens living in Montreal, agreed through mediation in 2001 to a 50/50 shared custody of their two children. In 2002 the mother repudiated the agreement and sought full custody, alleging she had left the children only because of daycare costs and denying youth-protection allegations, while the father sought custody. Youth protection had intervened, the children were entrusted to the father, and both parents signed voluntary measures recognizing the children's security or development was endangered by the mother leaving them alone, yelling and using physical discipline. The children repeatedly expressed a wish to live with their father.
firac.rule: Under s. 16(8),(9),(10) of the Divorce Act and arts. 32, 33, 514, 599, 600, 604, 605, 612 C.C.Q., the sole criterion is the best interests of the child, not parental interests; a prior consent is strong evidence that each parent found it adequate. Gordon v. Goertz sets a two-stage inquiry (material change, then fresh best-interests inquiry); Young v. Young and W.(V.) v. S.(D.) confirm the child's-interest focus.
firac.application: The Court found the earlier mediated agreement strong proof that both are loving, capable parents and that shared custody served the children. It found the mother exaggerated abuse, coached and pressured the children to take sides, and offered no compelling best-interests reason to abandon shared custody. It found the father credible, his parental capacity uncontested, and no evidence of alienation or bad faith. Given the impending loss of legal status in Canada, shared custody was no longer workable.
firac.conclusion: Custody of both children was granted to the father, with extensive defined access rights to the mother; the mother's motion for full custody was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the father be permitted to leave Canada and take the children to Pakistan?
firac.facts: The father's work permit, which allowed the family to remain legally in Canada, expired November 30, 2002 and would not be renewed after he lost his job; the family could not stay legally, could not access schooling or health insurance, and their immigration file through Mexico remained pending. Pakistan was the only country where the father could work legally, obtain family support, and monitor the son's latent tuberculosis, and the mother's family also lived there. The father undertook to return to Canada and to keep the mother on the immigration file, and had sought the Court's permission as required.
firac.rule: Section 16(6),(7) of the Divorce Act permits the Court to impose terms and conditions, including notice of a change of the child's place of residence; the determining criterion remains the child's best interests (Gordon v. Goertz), the custodial parent having the right to determine the child's residence (W.(V.) v. S.(D.)).
firac.application: The Court found no bad faith or sinister intent by the father, who had properly asked permission to relocate. Given the family's loss of legal status and the practical impossibility of remaining in Quebec, and the father's undertakings to facilitate the mother's contact and to keep her on the immigration file, relocation with the children served their best interests.
firac.conclusion: The father was permitted, if need be, to return to Pakistan with the children; the mother and her counsel were ordered to remit the children's identity documents and passports by November 26, 2002.

firac.issue: Should the perception of child support and spousal alimony and arrears be suspended?
firac.facts: The father had lost his employment, faced departure from Canada, and moved to suspend perception of child support, spousal alimony, and all arrears, referring cancellation and future fixation to the trial judge on the merits.
firac.rule: Under s. 17 of the Divorce Act and arts. 514, 605 C.C.Q., support may be varied or suspended in light of changed means, needs and circumstances, subject to the best interests of the children.
firac.application: Given the parties' changed financial situation and the father's loss of income and imminent departure, the Court suspended perception pending the divorce on the merits and referred the questions of cancellation of arrears and fixation of support to the trial judge, reserving the parties' right to file further provisional motions.
firac.conclusion: Perception of child support, spousal alimony and all arrears was suspended; cancellation of arrears and fixation of support were referred to the judge hearing the divorce on the merits.

defining_issues: Was the security and development of the six children compromised within the meaning of section 38 of the Youth Protection Act?

firac.issue: Was the security and development of the six children compromised under s. 38 of the Youth Protection Act?
firac.facts: The parents, of Russian origin, immigrated to Canada from Slovakia in June 2002 with their six children (aged 4 to 15). The father regularly beat the mother, especially after drinking, and struck the children, notably A..., to discipline them, sometimes with a stick, and threatened to kill them. On 6 February 2003 he pushed and struck the mother when she wanted to take two sons to hospital following a circumcision performed by rabbis, and threatened her with death. The father, through counsel, admitted the children's situation of compromise under paragraphs g) and e) of s. 38. The Director declared it had no evidence on the ground of lack of appropriate care (para. c).
firac.rule: Section 38 of the Youth Protection Act sets out the grounds on which a child's security or development is deemed compromised, including physical ill-treatment (para. e) and serious risk from a parent's conduct/behaviour (para. g).
firac.application: The Tribunal accepted the evidence of the four eldest children and the mother's earlier statements describing physical abuse and threats by the father, as well as the father's own admission of compromise under paragraphs e) and g). The psychological assessment did not exclude impulsive and aggressive reactions toward the family. The Director offered no evidence on the lack-of-care ground, so that ground was not retained.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal declared that the security and development of the children were in danger (compromised) under s. 38.

firac.issue: What measures should be ordered under s. 91 to end the situation of compromise?
firac.facts: On 27 August 2003 the Director recommended returning the children to both parents, the father's active participation in an anger management program, family access to the Family Preservation Program, individual psychological therapy for both parents, and social follow-up for one year. The psychological report recommended family reunification, finding the father was not a dangerous or abusive profile and could parent adequately with therapeutic help, taking account of migratory/acculturation stress. The father, mother and children all consented to the proposed measures.
firac.rule: Section 91 of the Youth Protection Act empowers the Tribunal, once compromise is established, to order the measures required to put an end to the situation and protect the child, guided by the child's interest.
firac.application: Given the psychological recommendation of reunification, the strong emotional and solidarity bonds within the family, the children's wish for their father's return, and the consent of all parties, the Tribunal entrusted the children to both parents subject to protective conditions: no exposure to violence, no physical discipline, participation in an anger management program, individual psychological therapy, medical follow-up, the Family Preservation Program, full cooperation with the DYP, and aid/counsel/assistance, all for one year.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal entrusted the children to their parents with a suite of supervisory and therapeutic measures for one year, entrusting oversight to the Ville Marie Child and Youth Protection Centre Director.

firac.issue: Should the mother's trial retraction of her earlier denunciations be accepted?
firac.facts: The mother initially denounced the father's violence to police, DYP workers, JIAS workers and immigration officials, admitted all allegations at the provisional-measures hearing, and said she wanted a divorce and custody. At trial on 20 June she recanted, claiming she had denounced him only because she panicked over the children's suffering after their circumcision by rabbis rather than by a doctor.
firac.rule: The trier of fact assesses credibility and may prefer earlier consistent statements over a later retraction where the retraction appears motivated by external considerations.
firac.application: The Tribunal found the mother retracted solely because she wanted her husband home, as she could not manage six children alone and the children still loved and missed their father. It therefore rejected the trial retraction and retained her prior statements made to various persons at different times.
firac.conclusion: The retraction was not accepted; the earlier statements were retained as reliable.

firac.issue: What weight should be given to children's expressed refusal of contact where parental alienation is present?
firac.facts: E. and G., adopted children aged 11 and 13, saw their father regularly and happily until May 1998 (holiday ski photos showed them cheerful), after which they categorically refused to see or speak to him, not even answering the dedicated phone line installed for them. The court-appointed psychologist Dr. Worenklein concluded this was a clear case of parental alienation, meeting nearly all of Dr. Gardner's criteria, with the mother tending to devalue the father despite claiming to want the relationship maintained.
firac.rule: Under s. 16(8) of the Divorce Act the court considers only the best interests of the child, and under s. 16(10) it applies the maximum-contact principle. Article 33 C.c.Q. requires decisions to be made in the child's interest and respect of rights. Jurisprudence (Droit de la famille — 2829; — 1485; — 1242) holds that a child's expressed wish is an important factor, but where there is undue influence of a parent bordering on parental alienation, the court must assess the child's interest beyond the expressed wish.
firac.application: The court accepted Dr. Worenklein's uncontradicted finding of parental alienation, reinforced by the children's testimony. Applying the cited case law, the court held that the children's refusal did not reflect their genuine best interests but resulted from the parental conflict and the mother's insufficiently exercised authority. The children needed to see their father regularly and frequently and had to understand they had no choice.
firac.conclusion: The children's stated refusal was overridden; the court looked beyond it to their true best interests, which required restoring the relationship with the father.

firac.issue: Should the court grant access to the father and order the family to undergo therapy in the children's best interests?
firac.facts: Both parents now wanted regular, frequent access, and both, along with the children, undertook to participate in a therapeutic process. Dr. Worenklein recommended frequent access in the former family home and family therapy at the Jewish General Hospital's Multi-Family Therapy Unit, warning that a change of custody could be considered if the situation was not normalized. A therapist, Mme L.G., specialized in parental alienation, agreed to conduct the follow-up.
firac.rule: Section 16 of the Divorce Act and art. 33 C.c.Q. authorize access orders in the child's best interests; the court may order therapeutic measures and dispense with the oath and notice requirements (arts. 418, 419 C.p.c.) for a witness therapist.
firac.application: Finding the children's psychological stability already shaken and the mother now sincerely willing to remedy the situation, the court set a detailed access schedule (Tuesdays, Sundays, holidays), ordered the mother to facilitate and not undermine access, took note of the parents' undertakings, and mandated a ten-week therapeutic follow-up with Mme L.G., dispensing her from oath and notice under arts. 418–419 C.p.c.
firac.conclusion: The motion for access was allowed; access rights were granted to the father and a ten-week family therapeutic process was ordered.

name_verification.name_in_document: Baglow v. Smith

defining_issues: Did the operators of an online message board (the Fourniers) 'publish' allegedly defamatory words posted by another user on their forum?

Were the impugned words ('one of the Taliban's more vocal supporters') defamatory of the plaintiff — did they refer to him and would they tend to lower his reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person, having regard to the context of political blogging?
Did the defence of fair comment apply to the impugned words?
Was the fair comment defence defeated by proof that the defendants were actuated by express malice?

firac.issue: Did the operators of an online message board 'publish' the allegedly defamatory words posted by another user?
firac.facts: Roger Smith (a.k.a. 'Peter O'Donnell') posted the impugned words on Free Dominion, a conservative message board moderated and administered by Connie and Mark Fournier. The Fourniers did not write, edit or endorse the post but declined to remove it after Dr. Baglow complained. They argued that, like a content-neutral hyperlink, provision of message-board software should not amount to publication, and relied on Crookes v. Newton and U.S./U.K. statutory immunities.
firac.rule: Publication requires that the defendant, by any act, conveyed defamatory meaning to a third party who received it (Crookes v. Newton, 2011 SCC 47; McNichol v. Grandy). In Crookes a mere hyperlink was held not to be publication because it is content neutral and exerts no control over content. Carter v. B.C. Federation of Foster Parents Association, 2005 BCCA 398, held a forum operator with knowledge and control could be a publisher.
firac.application: The Court held Crookes was distinguishable — 'apples to oranges'. A message board exists precisely to provide content; the Fourniers were not passive bystanders but posted themselves, set terms of service, and had the ability to delete posts and ban users. Given that nearly all users posted anonymously, treating operators as non-publishers would leave plaintiffs with no way to correct reputational harm and would upset the balance the law of defamation strikes. Canadian legislatures have not enacted the U.S./U.K. immunity schemes.
firac.conclusion: The impugned words were published by both the Fourniers and Mr. Smith.

firac.issue: Were the impugned words defamatory of the plaintiff given the political-blog context?
firac.facts: The post referred to 'Dr. Dawg', the plaintiff's pseudonym, as 'one of the Taliban's more vocal supporters', published while Canadian forces were at war with the Taliban. Dr. Baglow's identity as Dr. Dawg was widely known and had been linked to his real name repeatedly, including on Free Dominion. The defendants and the CCLA argued the rough-and-tumble, hyper-partisan blog context meant a reasonable reader would not think less of him.
firac.rule: A plaintiff must prove the words (1) refer to the plaintiff, (2) were published, and (3) are defamatory, i.e. would tend to lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). This is a low threshold (WIC Radio v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40). Meaning is assessed contextually including audience and manner of presentation (Crookes).
firac.application: Reference and publication were established. Although context on partisan blogs is important, the Court rejected the notion that little could ever be defamatory in that medium; in WIC Radio even 'shock-jock' statements were defamatory. Expert evidence showed lurkers' views were unknowable and anonymous online actors could gain credibility over time. The impugned words nearly stood alone, with no prior Free Dominion debate on Khadr to supply context. The words were reasonably capable of meaning the plaintiff supported an Islamist terrorist organization and thereby tended to lower his reputation.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiff established all three elements; the words were defamatory.

firac.issue: Did the defence of fair comment apply?
firac.facts: The words concerned the well-known Omar Khadr controversy, on which public opinion was split and about which Dr. Baglow had written extensively, taking the position that Khadr should be repatriated. Smith honestly believed that supporting Khadr amounted to supporting the Taliban. The post appeared in a subforum 'Opinions are Like Clymers' and was a rambling political rant.
firac.rule: Fair comment requires: (1) the comment is on a matter of public interest; (2) it is based on fact; (3) it is recognizable as comment (which may include inferences of fact); and (4) any person could honestly express that opinion on the proved facts (WIC Radio v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Grant v. Torstar). Words appearing factual may, in pith and substance and context, be comment.
firac.application: Public interest was easily met (the Khadr case). The factual substratum — Khadr's detention and Dr. Baglow's notorious pro-repatriation, anti-mission views — was sufficiently known. The context (a conservative opinion forum, an 'Opinions' subforum, a rambling rant, and the hyperbolic phrase 'one of the Taliban's more vocal supporters') showed the words were recognizable comment, not fact. Applying the honest-belief test (not a reasonableness test), a person could honestly hold the view that support for Khadr amounted to support for the Taliban, as Smith and others in fact did.
firac.conclusion: The defence of fair comment was established.

firac.issue: Was the fair comment defence defeated by express malice?
firac.facts: Malice was alleged only against the Fourniers, based on their refusal to retract, two mocking responsive posts ('FD gets libel notice…' and 'John Baglow puts on his frilliest internet dress'), and their spoliation allegations.
firac.rule: Fair comment is defeated only if the plaintiff proves malice was the dominant motive for the publication (Simpson v. Mair, 2004 BCSC 754; WIC Radio). Ill will or anger alone does not establish malice where the dominant purpose is a proper one.
firac.application: The Fourniers investigated the complaint and gave non-malicious reasons for leaving the post up (the Ms. Mew sock-puppet, the ongoing debate, the public-interest nature, Dr. Baglow's own similar conduct). The responsive posts were reactions to the sock-puppet and were no harsher than Dr. Baglow's own commentary about them. Their spoliation suspicions were understandable given the disappearance of the old comments. None of this showed malice as the dominant motive. The related spoliation claim itself failed on the evidence.
firac.conclusion: Malice was not proven; the fair comment defence stood and the action was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area since this is a private defamation action. K015 (defamation) and K016 (fair comment) are the core doctrines — the case turns on the elements of defamation and the fair comment defence. K024 (freedom of expression) and its parent K003 (Constitutional law) are engaged because the judgment repeatedly frames defamation as a balance between reputation and Charter-protected free expression (Grant, WIC Radio, Crookes). K107 (Canadian Charter) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) reflect the court's reliance on the s. 2(b) free-expression jurisprudence in shaping the common law; these are somewhat secondary/supporting picks since no Charter claim was formally adjudicated. Group defamation, injunctions and hate-speech keywords were considered but do not fit the actual holdings.
location_rationale: The header reads 'CITATION: Baglow v. Smith, 2015 ONSC 1175 OTTAWA' and 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE', and the decision notes it was 'HEARD AT OTTAWA'.
registry_rationale: The matter bears court file no. CV-10-49803 and was heard at Ottawa in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, indicating the Ottawa registry.

case_name: Camp Development Corporation v. Greater Vancouver (Transportation Authority)

name_verification.name_in_document: Camp Development Corporation v. Greater Vancouver Transportation Authority

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff be granted leave to amend its statement of claim to challenge the validity of the expropriation, or is such a challenge barred by s. 51 of the Expropriation Act after the land has vested?
Are the proposed validity amendments impermissible because they are inconsistent with the plaintiff's original pleading seeking statutory compensation?

Should the plaintiff be granted leave to amend to allege bad faith and breach of s. 21 of the Expropriation Act (failure to offer surplus land back), and are those claims statute-barred or lacking a cause of action?

firac.issue: Should leave be granted to amend the claim to attack the validity of the expropriation despite s. 51 of the Expropriation Act?
firac.facts: GVTA expropriated about 89 acres in Maple Ridge for the Golden Ears Bridge; the expropriation notice was filed June 21, 2005 and title vested about June 29, 2005. Camp accepted roughly $9 million in advance payments and in 2006 sued only for enhanced statutory compensation. Nearly four years after vesting Camp sought to amend to allege the taking was ultra vires and void because the notice misstated the true purpose and excess land was taken.
firac.rule: Amendments/pleadings are struck only where it is 'plain and obvious' the claim cannot succeed (Hunt v. T&N plc; Extra Gift Exchange; Dempsey v. Envision). Section 51(1) of the Expropriation Act provides that legal proceedings to challenge the validity of an expropriation must not be brought after land vests under s. 23, and s. 51(2) (30-day judicial review window) is subject to s. 51(1) (Rella v. Village of Montrose; Seaside Acres; Roadmaster). Adding a new cause of action after a limitation period has expired is inappropriate (City Construction Co. v. Salmon's Transfer).
firac.application: The court found the notice stated the purpose as the Golden Ears Bridge Project Transportation System constituting a linear development; the whole/partial taking question had been canvassed between the parties beforehand. The 'no notice' and tax-sale authorities (Costello, Van Kam, Gray) did not assist Camp, and following Gray/McLachlin J.A., the legislative scheme evinces an intent that an expropriation stand after vesting notwithstanding defects. Since vesting occurred nearly four years earlier, s. 51(1) is a complete answer and any validity challenge is bound to fail; the expropriated party retains statutory compensation as redress.
firac.conclusion: Leave to amend to challenge the validity of the expropriation was refused; those amendments raise an issue bound to fail.

firac.issue: Are the validity amendments barred as inconsistent with the original pleading?
firac.facts: The original statement of claim asserted the land had been expropriated and sought additional statutory compensation for an inadequate advance payment; Camp accepted the payments and stood by while the bridge was built. The proposed amendment recharacterized the taking as merely 'purported' and void.
firac.rule: Rule 19(7) prohibits pleading a claim inconsistent with a previous pleading, subject to the right to plead alternatively (R. 19(8); Gabbs v. Bouwhuis). More significantly, the substantive law of election applies: where a person has, with full knowledge, done an unequivocal act choosing one of two inconsistent rights, he cannot later pursue the other (United Australia v. Barclays Bank; M.E.P.C. Canadian Properties v. The Queen; Molander v. Cranbrook; Erickson v. Kamloops).
firac.application: By accepting advance payments, commencing an action for enhanced compensation within the Act's time limits, and standing by during construction, Camp made an unequivocal election to treat the expropriation as valid. Asserting the taking is now void is inconsistent and precluded by the substantive law of expropriation election, distinguishable from Gabbs where amendments were merely alternate theories on the same facts.
firac.conclusion: The validity amendments were also impermissible as inconsistent with the position on which the action was commenced.

firac.issue: Should leave be granted to amend to allege bad faith and breach of s. 21, and are those claims barred?
firac.facts: Camp sought to add that GVTA failed to offer surplus land back to it as required by s. 21 of the Act, breaching a statutory duty on or before June 28, 2007, and acted in bad faith. GVTA argued no cause of action, statute-bar, and that it had not 'disposed' of the property.
firac.rule: The 'plain and obvious' test governs (Hunt). Under the Limitation Act, 'injury to property' in s. 3(2)(a) means physical harm by external force (410727 B.C. Ltd. v. Dayhu Investments); pure economic loss falls under the six-year period in s. 3(5) (Alberni District Credit Union; Armstrong v. West Vancouver). Breach of statutory duty is a recognized tort.
firac.application: The claim was for economic loss, so the applicable period was six years and had not expired. Camp pleaded breach of the statutory duty in s. 21, a recognized cause of action; whether a separate cause of action is needed, whether the remedy is confined to s. 21, and the meaning of 'disposed' are arguable matters properly resolved on the pleadings, not plain and obvious losers.
firac.conclusion: Leave to amend to plead breach of s. 21 and related bad faith was granted (amendments similar to proposed paragraphs 48-52 allowed).

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the core: the case turns on pleading-amendment principles under Rule 19 and the 'plain and obvious' test. K001 (Administrative law) and K011 (judicial review) are engaged because the validity challenge concerns the exercise of a statutory expropriation power and s. 51(2)/the Judicial Review Procedure Act. K022 (restitution) reflects Camp's waiver-of-tort, disgorgement and unjust-enrichment theories. K014 (standard of review) is a weak, borderline pick included only to reach five; it is not squarely engaged. The controlled vocabulary is a poor fit for an expropriation/civil-procedure matter, so several choices are approximations rather than precise matches.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Registry: Vancouver' and lists the 'Place and Date of Hearing' and 'Place and Date of Judgment' as 'Vancouver, B.C.', so the court sits in Vancouver, British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly records 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Elise Attar (Amos) v. Joe Attar

defining_issues: Was it in the best interests of the three children to relocate with their mother from the Thornhill area to Montréal?
Which parent's home should be the children's primary residence, and what custody/access arrangement is in the children's best interests?

firac.issue: Was it in the best interests of the children to move with their mother to Montréal?
firac.facts: The applicant mother, the children's primary caregiver, wished to relocate the three young children (ages 8, 7 and 5) to Montréal, where her family resided, offering free accommodation and better employment and schooling prospects. The children had lived in Thornhill all their lives, attended school there, had their synagogue and most of the father's extended family in the area, and had a strong and growing relationship with their father through a well-established access regime.
firac.rule: On a mobility application the test is the best interests of the child under s. 16(8) of the Divorce Act, applying the framework in Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27: where there is a material change, the court conducts a fresh best-interests inquiry considering, among other factors, the existing custody and access arrangements, the desirability of maximizing contact with both parents, the child's views, the reason for moving (only where relevant to parenting ability), and the disruption from a change in custody or from removal from family, school and community.
firac.application: The court found there was no final order so the threshold step did not apply, and proceeded to weigh the Gordon v. Goertz factors. A move to Montréal would effectively cut the children off from frequent contact with their father, from whom they derived great benefit, and the applicant's proposed bi-weekly driving plan was unrealistic and would alienate the children. The children wished to see both parents (Daniel wished to see more of his father); the mother's reason for moving (financial support from her father) did not establish she could not provide adequately in Ontario; and the move would remove the children from their family, schools, friends, synagogue and community.
firac.conclusion: The court held it was not in the children's best interests to move to Montréal; they should remain in the Thornhill area.

firac.issue: Which parent's home should serve as the children's primary residence and what custody/access arrangement best serves the children?
firac.facts: Both parents sought sole custody. The mother was consumed by hatred and resentment toward the father, hired a private investigator, hacked his computer, made slanderous statements to the Children's Lawyer and tried to sabotage his new relationship. The father, though initially immature, had stabilized with a committed partner (Ms. March) and his parents' support; the Children's Lawyer found the children's relationship with the father stronger and their routine more stable in his home. The three children had special needs requiring substantial attention and homework help.
firac.rule: Custody is determined under s. 16 of the Divorce Act by reference solely to the best interests of the child; s. 24(2) of the Children's Law Reform Act provides a useful checklist including love and emotional ties, the child's views, stability of the home, each parent's ability and willingness to provide guidance, education, necessaries and to meet special needs, the parties' plans, the permanence and stability of each family unit, and the blood relationship.
firac.application: Applying the checklist, the court found the extended-family factor even but the children looked first to the father for affection and their relationship with the mother was more distant. The father's household, aided by Ms. March and his parents, provided more stable routine, discipline, and consistent help with homework and David's learning disability, whereas the mother's home was more chaotic and she was preoccupied by the litigation. The mother's household lacked permanence (no employment, dependent on gifts). Shared custody could not succeed given the mother's persistent animosity and attempts to undermine the father. The children needed to continue seeing their mother substantially, achieved through alternate-weekend and weekly access.
firac.conclusion: The court ordered joint custody with daily care and control to the father as primary residence, education/medical/dental decision-making to the father, and a defined access schedule for the mother including alternate weekends, weekly evenings, alternating holidays and Jewish High Holidays, and four summer weeks.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test under both the Divorce Act and Gordon v. Goertz and is central to both issues. K048 (custody/access) captures the joint-custody, primary-residence and access dispute (including the mobility question, which the vocabulary lacks a discrete term for and which folds into custody/best interests). K117 (Divorce Act) is the statute under which custody was decided. K052 (religious upbringing) is a modest fit given the parties' disputes over Jewish schooling and the allowance made for the children's Jewish education; K095 (Jewish family) reflects that both parties come from observant Jewish families; K027 (Jewish holidays) is a weaker, borderline pick reflecting the access order alternating the Jewish High Holidays — flagged as minor.
location_rationale: The heading states 'Newmarket Registry' and identifies the 'SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE FAMILY COURT'; the parties are Ontario residents and the matter is decided under Ontario legislation, so the province is Ontario.
registry_rationale: The decision opens with 'Newmarket Registry, No. 20211/04', identifying the registry as Newmarket.

case_name: Canadian Jewish Congress v. Board of School Trustees, District No. 15

name_verification.name_in_document: Canadian Jewish Congress v. The Minister of Labour and The Board of School Trustees, District No. 15 and The New Brunswick Teachers' Federation et al.
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied case name matches the lead parties (Canadian Jewish Congress as intervenor/appellant and the Board of School Trustees, District No. 15 as a respondent). The neutral/CanLII citation does not appear in the text.
