defining_issues: Was judicial review by way of prohibition available to prevent a Human Rights Act Board of Inquiry from proceeding with a hearing?

Does subsection 5(1) of the Human Rights Act ('accommodation, services, or facilities available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted') encompass education provided by the New Brunswick public school system?
Did David Attis have status as a 'person claiming to be aggrieved' and thus as a valid complainant under the Act?
Was Mr. Attis' written complaint sufficiently precise to constitute a valid complaint under the Act?

firac.issue: Was judicial review by way of prohibition available to prevent a Human Rights Act Board of Inquiry from proceeding with its hearing?
firac.facts: The Human Rights Commission recommended, and the Minister of Labour appointed, a Board of Inquiry to investigate Attis' complaint that School District 15 had condoned the anti-Jewish/discriminatory conduct of teacher Malcolm Ross. Before the Board's first hearing, the School Board and the Teachers' Federation obtained a stay and applied for judicial review to prohibit the inquiry; Miller, J. quashed the Minister's order.
firac.rule: Prohibition may issue against a tribunal where there is a clear question of law, not dependent on particular facts, upon which the tribunal's jurisdiction depends (Bell v. Ontario Human Rights Commission, [1971] S.C.R. 756; Re CIP Paper Products (1978) 87 D.L.R. (3d) 609; R. v. Tottenham & District Rent Tribunal, [1957] 1 Q.B. 103). Courts must exercise curial deference and not usurp a tribunal's statutory functions (C.U.P.E. v. N.B. Liquor, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227), but have a duty to intervene where a tribunal acts without jurisdiction.
firac.application: The Court held the three substantive grounds (interpretation of s.5, Attis' status, and sufficiency of the complaint) were questions of law that could be decided on the uncontested affidavit facts without determining the merits. Miller, J. had not decided the merits but had identified genuine legal questions. The Teachers' Federation had not acquiesced in the Board's jurisdiction, having sought party status and immediately applied for review; unlike Re Colonial Coach Lines, there was no high-handed conduct.
firac.conclusion: Judicial review by prohibition was available; the first-instance judge properly exercised his jurisdiction to entertain the applications.

firac.issue: Does subsection 5(1) of the Human Rights Act cover education provided by the New Brunswick public school system?
firac.facts: Attis complained that the public school board's conduct deprived Jewish and other minority students of equal opportunity within the educational system provided as a service to the public. Miller, J. had held that school facilities and education programs are not 'accommodation, services and facilities' under s.5.
firac.rule: Human rights legislation is quasi-constitutional and must be given a fair, large and liberal, purposive interpretation (Insurance Corp. of B.C. v. Heerspink, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 145; Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Simpsons-Sears, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536; Robichaud v. Canada, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 84; s.17 Interpretation Act). A service offered to the public need not be offered to all members of the public, and eligibility criteria do not remove it from human rights scrutiny (Re Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission and Government of Saskatchewan (1988) 52 D.L.R. (4th) 253).
firac.application: The Court found the case law unsettled (Winnipeg School Division v. MacArthur declining coverage vs. Schmidt v. Calgary Board of Education and Rawala v. DeVry favouring it) but adopted the broad purposive approach. A narrow reading would allow a public school to refuse entry to Jewish, Indigenous or male children without contravening the Act — an absurd result. Public education under the Schools Act is a service provided to a client group meeting eligibility requirements and thus falls within s.5(1).
firac.conclusion: Public education in New Brunswick is within the purview of subsection 5(1); Miller, J. erred on this point.

firac.issue: Did David Attis have status as a 'person claiming to be aggrieved' and hence a valid complainant?
firac.facts: Attis is a Jewish parent with three children enrolled in District 15. Neither he nor his children had direct contact with Ross as their teacher. Miller, J. suggested Attis was not an aggrieved party and was purporting to speak for a group.
firac.rule: Section 17 of the Human Rights Act allows 'any person claiming to be aggrieved' to file a written complaint; the phrase is to be read broadly, especially at a preliminary stage. Whether someone is a 'victim' of a discriminatory practice is almost wholly a question of fact, looking to effects rather than intent, and may extend beyond the direct target (Re Singh (1988) 86 N.R. 69).
firac.application: The statute speaks of a 'person claiming to be aggrieved', not an established aggrieved party; it is for the Commission and Board to assess merit. Attis filed a written complaint on the prescribed form as a parent of enrolled children. The Court declined to treat this as a prohibited representative/group action, since the Minister conceded no group-action rules apply and Attis asserted his complaint concerned discrimination against him and his own children.
firac.conclusion: Attis met the s.17 standard and has status as a complainant.

firac.issue: Was Attis' written complaint sufficiently precise to be a valid complaint under the Act?
firac.facts: Attis' written statement identified himself, his children, the teacher (Ross), the School Board, the alleged conduct (racist/anti-Jewish statements, Holocaust denial, the Board's inaction and failure to condemn), the period (1977–1988) and cited s.5. Miller, J., relying on Mackin v. Judicial Council (N.B.), held it lacked the requisite specificity.
firac.rule: 'Complaint' in s.17 must be interpreted to advance the Act's broad purposes. A valid complaint should contain elements such as identification of complainant and victim, time, location, the nature of the discriminatory practice and the relevant section (Canadian Human Rights Commission v. Bell Canada (1981) 2 C.H.R.R. D/265). The stricter standard for complaints under the Provincial Court Act (Mackin) does not govern the Human Rights Act.
firac.application: The Attis complaint was in writing on the prescribed form and contained most of the essential Bell Canada elements. Any further detail could be obtained by demand for particulars, the Board of Inquiry having conciliation-board procedural powers (s.20(3) HRA; s.66(2) Industrial Relations Act). It is the Board's function, not the reviewing court's, to investigate the merits, and this was not a clear case of the tribunal lacking jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: The complaint met the statutory requirements of s.17 and was sufficient; Miller, J. erred.

keywords_rationale: K007 (Human rights) is the primary tier-1 area — the case turns on interpreting the New Brunswick Human Rights Act. K001 (Administrative law) and K011 (judicial review) capture the availability of prohibition against a Board of Inquiry and the deference/jurisdiction analysis. K069 (discrimination) reflects the alleged discriminatory practice under s.5, and K072 (human rights tribunal) covers the Human Rights Commission/Board of Inquiry machinery. K044 (school board) and K005 (Education law) reflect the central holding that public education is a 'service' under s.5 and that a school board is the respondent. K058 (antisemitism) and K062 (Holocaust denial) reflect the factual substratum — Malcolm Ross' anti-Jewish writings and denial that six million Jews died in the Holocaust — and K093 (Jewish) identifies the affected group and complainant. K062 and K058 are somewhat contextual (the Court expressly declined to rule on Ross' writings) but are engaged by the complaint's substance; they are slightly weaker picks. K005 is secondary since the dispositive vehicle is the Human Rights Act rather than education legislation itself.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF NEW BRUNSWICK', establishing the province. No sitting city or registry is stated in the text (appellate courts frequently omit this), so city and registry are left null.
registry_rationale: No registry or court office is named in the decision; only the Court of Appeal of New Brunswick and docket numbers (31/89/CA; 36/89/CA; 37/89/CA) appear, so registry is null.

case_name: Centre de santé et de services sociaux de la Montagne v. E.S.

name_verification.name_in_document: CENTRE DE SANTÉ ET DE SERVICES SOCIAUX DE LA MONTAGNE v. E. S.

defining_issues: Is E. a person of full age incapable of consenting to the care and lodging required by her state of health, such that court authorization is required under arts. 11–16 C.C.Q.?
Is a lodging order placing E. in a health-care facility against her expressed wishes in her best interest?
What restrictions on contact between E. and her mother are appropriate, and should the court grant a permanent three-year order or defer pending a progressive 'exit plan'?

firac.issue: Is E. incapable of consenting to the required care and lodging, so that court authorization is engaged under the Civil Code of Quebec?
firac.facts: E., aged 55, is intellectually handicapped, has chronic diabetes and paranoid schizophrenia. She is under full tutorship to the person and curatorship of property held by the Public Curator. Psychiatrist Dr. Lafontaine concluded she has no understanding of her medical condition or the need for treatment and no capacity to consent to care, lodging or her future; her refusal of placement is a direct consequence of her mother's psychotic domination ('folie à deux').
firac.rule: Arts. 11, 12, 15, 16 and 23 C.C.Q.: no one may be made to undergo care without consent; where a person of full age is incapable, consent is given by the mandatary, tutor or curator; court authorization is necessary where an incapable person of full age categorically refuses care required by their state of health. The notion of 'care' includes the choice and supervision of lodging (CSSS Rimouski-Neigettes c. T.C., 2010 QCCA 143; CHUQ c. L.R., J.E. 2000-1984 (C.A.)).
firac.application: The medical and psycho-social evidence established that E. does not understand her condition, cannot manage her medication or diet, and her health and safety are endangered living with her mother. She strongly opposes placement, so although the Public Curator could consent, the Court held it must intervene where the person manifests firm opposition, and authorization under art. 16 was engaged.
firac.conclusion: E. is incapable of giving a valid consent and, because she categorically refuses the care/lodging her health requires, the matter falls within the Court's authorization jurisdiction under arts. 11–16 C.C.Q.

firac.issue: Is placement of E. in a lodging facility, against her wishes and separated from her mother, in her best interest?
firac.facts: E. thrived medically after being removed to a Ressource Intermédiaire (controlled diet, stable glucose, medication), whereas in her mother's care she was hospitalized with pneumonia, poorly controlled diabetes and kidney problems, and suffered physical and verbal abuse. E. nonetheless wishes to return home, largely to prevent her elderly mother from moving to Israel and to avoid being alone; the mother wants E. back mainly for her own comfort.
firac.rule: Art. 12 C.C.Q.: a person consenting for another must act in the sole interest of that person, taking account of any wishes expressed; the court's paramount role is to decide in the person's best interest.
firac.application: The Court found it is in E.'s best interest to stop living with her mother, whose dominance operated for the mother's benefit rather than E.'s well-being; a break in cohabitation plus controls to reduce the mother's dominance were necessary. Yet total separation would annihilate a life-long relationship both need, so protective measures had to be balanced against maintaining contact.
firac.conclusion: Continued placement outside the mother's home is in E.'s best interest, but must be accompanied by preserved and progressively improved mother-daughter contact rather than near-total separation.

firac.issue: Should the Court grant a permanent three-year lodging order with the strict contact limits proposed, or defer pending a progressive 'exit plan'?
firac.facts: The CSSSM sought a three-year order effectively replacing the interim order of Peacock J., with limited, supervised telephone calls (three times weekly, 15 minutes) and supervised synagogue/community visits. The Court considered these restrictions too strict.
firac.rule: Art. 23 C.C.Q. requires the court to obtain expert and interested-party opinions and to consider the wishes of the person concerned; the court is not an expert and should act on the recommendations of treating professionals.
firac.application: The Court was not satisfied with simply making the interim regime permanent for three years without a progressive plan to relax supervision over six to nine months and eventually permit unsupervised calls and visits (while E. continues to reside in the facility). It declined to make a final order and instead directed the CSSSM to prepare such a plan and report back.
firac.conclusion: Final order postponed to March 2014; Peacock J.'s interim order renewed and continued for 90 days, the motion continued pro forma, and the CSSSM requested to examine an 'exit plan' improving contact between E. and her mother.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area: this is a civil application under the Civil Code for authorization of care/lodging of an incapable person of full age. K006 (Family law) is included because the matter turns on tutorship/curatorship of a vulnerable adult and the mother-daughter family dynamic, though it is a borderline fit since the controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated 'consent to care'/'protection of persons' term. The Jewish-community context is prominent: K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) reflect the Jewish Employment Montreal sheltered workshop, Miriam Home and Jewish General Hospital; K105 (synagogue) reflects the ordered synagogue visits; K027 (Jewish holidays) reflects the discussion of Yom Kippur fasting, Rosh Hashana and Sukkot. The vocabulary offers no keyword squarely covering consent to care or curatorship, so the legal-doctrine coverage is admittedly weak and the tier-3 entity terms are contextual rather than doctrinal.

registry_rationale: The decision is issued in the 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' of the Superior Court, so the registry is Montreal.

name_verification.name_in_document: 1110008 B.C. Ltd. v. Chang

defining_issues: Should portions of the defendant's response to civil claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules as disclosing no reasonable defence or as unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, vexatious, embarrassing or an abuse of process?
Was the defendant's pleaded defence of fraudulent misrepresentation (and his denial of the existence of the contract) adequately pleaded with the required material facts?
If portions are struck, should the defendant be granted leave to amend his response to civil claim?

firac.issue: Should the impugned portions of the defendant's response to civil claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules?
firac.facts: The plaintiff sued for breach of a residential tenancy agreement, seeking $180,000 in unpaid rent. Mr. Chang's response contained allegations about non-parties — that the plaintiff's principal Tariq Kassam was an unlicensed property manager who had been found by the Real Estate Council to have committed professional misconduct, that Canadian National Relocation Ltd. was his alter ego, and that Kassam's brother Khalil Kassam had been subject to regulatory orders over an earlier rental scam. The plaintiff sought to strike these as irrelevant to the contract dispute.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1)(a)–(d) permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim/defence, are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial, or are otherwise an abuse of process. A pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not establish the cause of action or advance a defence known in law (Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860). Scandalous matter is struck only if irrelevant as well as scandalous. Pleadings must state material facts concisely and must not contain evidence (Rules 3-7(1); PGT v. Johnston, 2016 BCSC 1388).
firac.application: The Court found the underlined portions largely concerned the conduct and regulatory history of non-parties (Tariq Kassam, CNR Ltd., Khalil Kassam) with no clear connection to whether the tenancy agreement between the plaintiff and defendants was formed or enforceable. Allegations of Kassam's professional misconduct and his brother's regulatory history amounted to smearing by association and 'misconduct by association', which is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous and vexatious. Some references to Mr. Wong/CNR Ltd. as the plaintiff's agent might be relevant but were ambiguous and required clarification.
firac.conclusion: Several impugned portions (para. 3 in part, para. 6 second/third sentences, para. 10 underlined portion, and Part 3 paras. 7 and 8) were struck; the agency references in paras. 5 and 6 (first sentence) required clarification on amendment.

firac.issue: Was the defendant's defence of fraudulent misrepresentation and his denial of the contract adequately pleaded?
firac.facts: Mr. Chang admitted executing the tenancy agreement and wiring or attempting to wire funds, but pleaded in Part 3 that the elements of a contract were not met and that he pleaded fraudulent misrepresentation, reciting the legal elements without tying them to specific facts.
firac.rule: The elements of a contract are offer and acceptance, meeting of the minds, certainty, consideration and intention to be bound (Vancouver Canucks LP v. Canon Canada Inc., 2013 BCSC 866). Fraudulent misrepresentation requires a false representation of fact known to be false, intended to be acted upon, inducing the victim to contract to their detriment (Wang v. Shao, 2019 BCCA 130; Derry v. Peek). Under Rule 9-5(1)(a) a defence is struck only if it is plain and obvious it cannot succeed; material facts for every essential element must be pleaded (PGT v. Johnston).
firac.application: Mr. Chang did not identify which elements of the contract were absent, and having admitted executing the agreement and attempting payment, did not clearly raise the absence of a valid contract. He also failed to plead the material facts needed for each element of fraudulent misrepresentation — who made the false representation, its content, reliance, and resulting loss. The pleaded misrepresentation defence was therefore deficient.
firac.conclusion: The Court found the denial of the contract and the fraudulent misrepresentation plea deficient, but did not finally dismiss them; instead it allowed amendment.

firac.issue: Should the defendant be granted leave to amend his response to civil claim?
firac.facts: Counsel for Mr. Chang requested leave to amend to cure any deficiencies if portions were struck.
firac.rule: A pleading should not be struck where, if amended, it could disclose a reasonable defence (Olumide v. British Columbia (HRT), 2019 BCCA 386; Carhoun & Sons Enterprises Ltd. v. Canada (AG), 2015 BCCA 163).
firac.application: Because the deficiencies could potentially be cured by proper pleading of material facts, and consistent with the principle favouring amendment, the Court held Mr. Chang should be allowed to reformulate his defences, including possibly incorporating the struck elements into a properly constituted amended plea.
firac.conclusion: Leave to amend was granted. The Court also noted the plaintiff's own amended notice of civil claim was deficient in failing to specify the basis on which it was entitled to rent the apartment. The plaintiff was awarded costs of the application, not payable forthwith.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the correct tier-1 area: this is a pleadings/civil-procedure motion to strike in a breach-of-tenancy action, the core subject of the decision. K013 (professional discipline) is engaged tangentially because the impugned pleadings rest on a Real Estate Council finding of professional misconduct against the plaintiff's principal under the Real Estate Services Act — moderate relevance, but it is not the operative issue. K086 (co-ownership) is a weak pick reflecting only that the apartment sits in a condominium residence; it is not analytically central. K015 (defamation) is weak and included only because the Court characterised the impugned allegations as an attempt to 'smear' the plaintiff by association — not a pleaded defamation claim. K011 (judicial review) is weak, noted only because the abuse-of-process discussion references collateral attacks on administrative decisions. The controlled vocabulary is oriented to a different subject matter and offers no keyword for pleadings, contract, tenancy or fraudulent misrepresentation, so apart from K002 these are the closest available and should be treated as weak.

case_name: Carhoun & Sons Enterprises Ltd. v. Canada (Attorney General)

name_verification.name_in_document: Carhoun & Sons Enterprises Ltd. v. Canada (Attorney General)

defining_issues: Should the corporate plaintiff be ordered to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act where it concedes it cannot pay a costs award if unsuccessful?
Would an order for security for costs unfairly stifle the plaintiff's claim, considering the plaintiff's and its principals' inability to raise funds?
Does the defendant's delay in bringing the application for security for costs weigh against granting it?

firac.issue: Should the corporate plaintiff be ordered to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act where it concedes it cannot pay a costs award if unsuccessful?
firac.facts: Carhoun, a corporate plaintiff, sued Canada in negligence and misfeasance over delay in granting a Fisheries Act s. 35(2) authorization. Carhoun conceded it could not pay costs if it lost; none of the Carhoun companies own real estate and the plaintiff had defaulted on numerous loans leading to foreclosures. Canada sought security for costs estimated at $306,191.45.
firac.rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 gives the Court discretion to order security for costs where a corporate plaintiff appears unable to pay the defendant's costs if the defendant succeeds. Once a defendant establishes a prima facie case of inability to pay, the onus shifts to the corporation. The discretion is guided by the seven Keary Developments Ltd. v. Tarmac Construction Ltd. factors, adopted via Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Courts Ltd. and Fat Mel's Restaurant Ltd.
firac.application: The Court accepted that the plaintiff conceded inability to pay and that Canada had a plausible defence, satisfying the threshold. However, the residual discretion required weighing all Keary factors, several of which favoured the plaintiff. The Court found the claim not obviously doomed (per Garson J.A. in 2015 BCCA 163), that any meaningful security would stifle the claim, and that the alleged connection between Canada's conduct and the plaintiff's impecuniosity was not without merit.
firac.conclusion: The Court declined to order security for costs; Canada's application was dismissed.

firac.issue: Would an order for security for costs unfairly stifle the plaintiff's claim, considering the plaintiff's and its principals' inability to raise funds?
firac.facts: Karel Carhoun deposed he was unemployed, owned no real estate or vehicle, lived rent-free, and could not borrow from friends or family; his parents would lend no more; his brother Philip (a labourer) and Philip's wife Susan (a realtor) were estranged and unwilling to assist. Canada sought an adverse inference from the absence of affidavits from Philip and Susan.
firac.rule: Under Kropp, to show that security would stifle the action the plaintiff must show more than a lack of assets — it must show the corporation lacks any means of raising money, including from directors, shareholders, and backers. The adequacy of evidence is assessed case by case; extensive financial documentation is not invariably required.
firac.application: The Court declined to draw the adverse inference urged by Canada, accepting that strained family relations explained the missing affidavits and that it was not left without information. It found the principals had exhausted their borrowing power and that neither the brothers nor Susan Carhoun could provide security in any amount, so any real security would stifle the claim.
firac.conclusion: The Court was satisfied the plaintiff could not post security in any amount and that an order would stifle a legitimate claim, favouring dismissal.

firac.issue: Does the defendant's delay in bringing the application for security for costs weigh against granting it?
firac.facts: The claim was filed May 24, 2013; Canada did not file its security-for-costs application until January 27, 2016. By then some 2,800 and 5,000+ documents had been assembled, examinations for discovery were substantially advanced, and a 342-page notice to admit had been served. Canada attributed the delay to seeking clarity of the case and to the trial estimate doubling in September 2015.
firac.rule: Under the seventh Keary factor (Honda Canada Inc. v. Tonka Motorcycle Sales Ltd.), the lateness of an application for security weighs against granting it, especially where the plaintiff has been lulled into a false sense of safety and prejudiced by the delay.
firac.application: The Court found neither explanation sufficient; the magnitude and nature of the claim had not changed, and even the original 25-day trial estimate implied significant costs. Canada's near three-year delay obliged the plaintiff to address issues that an earlier application could have avoided.
firac.conclusion: This factor weighed heavily in the plaintiff's favour and supported dismissal of the application.

keywords_rationale: This is a civil procedure interlocutory application within a civil action, so the tier-1 practice area K002 (Civil litigation) is the best fit; K001 (Administrative law) is a secondary tier-1 tag reflecting the underlying claim about the Crown's handling of a Fisheries Act authorization (negligence and misfeasance in public office by a public officer). The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward Charter, human rights, hate speech and religious-freedom themes and contains no specific keywords for security for costs, misfeasance in public office, negligence, or Crown liability. Accordingly only the two tier-1 practice-area keywords genuinely apply; I am flagging that fewer than five truly applicable keywords exist in the supplied vocabulary and no tier-2/tier-3 term fits this security-for-costs cost dispute.

registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Zaki v. University of Manitoba

defining_issues: Should the surreptitious recording of the disciplinary hearing, and the transcripts derived from it, be expunged from the application and affidavits as an abuse of process, and is it otherwise admissible as extrinsic evidence on judicial review?
Should the post-hearing Abner remediation report be expunged as inadmissible new evidence not before the administrative decision-maker?
Should other portions of Affidavit #1 be expunged as irrelevant, duplicative, or argumentative extrinsic evidence?
Should the applicant be granted leave to amend his application to particularize a reasonable-apprehension-of-bias allegation, and should the supporting evidence in Affidavit #2 be preserved?
Should third-party disciplinary decisions concerning another student be disclosed as relevant to the application?

firac.issue: Should the surreptitious recording of the UDC hearing be expunged as an abuse of process, and is it otherwise admissible extrinsic evidence on judicial review?
firac.facts: Contrary to the University's Student Discipline Appeal Procedure (s. 2.72 prohibiting recording), the UDC's express direction, and his own counsel's advice, Mr. Zaki secretly recorded his April 8, 2022 disciplinary hearing because he feared bias. He sought to rely on the recording and transcripts to show the Decision misstated the oral evidence and to support bias allegations.
firac.rule: Court of King's Bench Rule 25.11(1)(c) permits striking documents that are an abuse of process. Judicial review is normally confined to the record before the decision-maker, with narrow exceptions (procedural fairness, gaps in the record) requiring relevance and necessity (Manitoba Metis Federation Inc. v. Pallister, 2019 MBQB 118; Bernard v. Canada (Revenue Agency), 2015 FCA 263). Courts retain inherent discretion to prevent abuse of process focused on the integrity of the adjudicative process (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E.; Prouse v. Lands Appeal Board, 2015 SKQB 66; Spiring v. Gould, 2008 MBQB 282; Law Society of Saskatchewan v. Abrametz, 2022 SCC 29).
firac.application: The court found Mr. Zaki should have sought the UDC's permission to record before the hearing rather than unilaterally changing the terms on which the quasi-judicial proceeding proceeded. Allowing reliance on the recording would make a mockery of the tribunal's rules and directions and retroactively alter the hearing's parameters. The transcript's reliability was also doubtful (unidentified speakers, multiple versions). Balancing usefulness against the egregious manner of obtaining it, the abuse outweighed any benefit. Alternatively, the recording, though relevant, was not necessary: other participants including Mr. Zaki could depose to their recollections, and the reasonableness review could proceed on the existing record (Vavilov).
firac.conclusion: The recording, transcripts, and all references were expunged from the Application, Affidavit #1, and Affidavit #2 without leave to amend.

firac.issue: Should the post-hearing Abner report be expunged as inadmissible new evidence?
firac.facts: Dr. Abner's June 10, 2022 report on Mr. Zaki's completion of ethics/professionalism instruction post-dated the April 8, 2022 hearing. At the hearing only 6 of 9 sessions were complete and Mr. Zaki filed no interim report or called Dr. Abner as a witness.
firac.rule: Extrinsic evidence not before the decision-maker is generally inadmissible on judicial review, which is not a de novo hearing. The Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 fresh-evidence criteria do not apply to judicial review.
firac.application: The report is precisely the kind of new evidence the exclusionary rule targets; it post-dated the Decision and could have been adduced with due diligence had Mr. Zaki completed the sessions and called the author. Admitting it would improperly make the court a fact-finder. Even under Palmer, the first criterion (unavailability with diligence) was not met.
firac.conclusion: The Abner report and related paragraphs and exhibit were expunged from Affidavit #1 without leave to amend.

firac.issue: Should other paragraphs of Affidavit #1 be expunged as irrelevant, duplicative, or argumentative?
firac.facts: The University sought to expunge paragraphs 10–68, 74–75, 96–97 and 100 of Affidavit #1, describing Mr. Zaki's background, the postings, the investigation and remediation, the prior appeal, and editorial commentary.
firac.rule: Under Manitoba Metis Federation Inc., the context/background exception only assists the reviewing court in understanding the record; affidavits must not contain spin, advocacy, argument, conclusions of law, or irrelevant statements.
firac.application: Paragraphs 10–68 and 96–97 and 100 did not fall within any recognized exception, were duplicative of the record, and contained advocacy and editorial commentary. Paragraphs 74–75, however, recorded Mr. Zaki's observations at the hearing (including the admissible lay-opinion that the Dean appeared angry) and filled a gap in the record, so they were retained.
firac.conclusion: Paragraphs 10–68, 96, 97 and 100 were expunged without leave; paragraphs 74–75 remained.

firac.issue: Should leave to amend be granted to particularize a bias allegation, and should the supporting Affidavit #2 evidence be preserved?
firac.facts: Mr. Zaki sought to amend to allege reasonable apprehension of bias because the UDC Chair, a College of Pharmacy professor, reported through the Dean of the Faculty of Health Sciences, who was involved in his expulsion and testified. He raised bias generally at the hearing but not this specific reporting relationship, which he says he discovered only in 2024.
firac.rule: Rule 38.05.1(2) permits amendment unless uncompensable prejudice results; amendment factors include prejudice, delay/explanation, and whether the amendment raises an arguable point (Capitol Steel Corp., 2023 MBKB 76). Bias evidence may be admitted if not otherwise on the record (AOV Adults Only Video, 2003 MBCA 81), but objections available at first instance must be raised there (Bernard; Hennessey v. Canada, 2016 FCA 180).
firac.application: Although the underlying documents were largely publicly available before the hearing, Mr. Zaki did raise potential bias at the outset of the hearing and the UDC's in camera reasons for rejecting a conflict were unknown; he accepted that conclusion in good faith. If the alleged undisclosed reporting relationship is accurate it may affect the Application, so it was not plain and obvious Affidavit #2 should be expunged. On amendment, the application was still at an early stage (no cross-examinations or briefs), so no prejudice; delay was explained by late discovery; and the amendment raised an arguable point given the Dean's involvement and the working relationship between Chair and Dean.
firac.conclusion: The motion to expunge the balance of Affidavit #2 was dismissed and the motion to amend the Application was granted.

firac.issue: Should third-party disciplinary decisions concerning another student be disclosed?
firac.facts: Mr. Zaki sought two disciplinary decisions involving a College of Nursing student whose suspension for online posts (found antisemitic, discriminatory and unprofessional) was overturned despite no apology, arguing they showed differential treatment and the faculty's tolerance for expression. The student was personally served but neither responded.
firac.rule: The court has jurisdiction to order production of relevant documents on judicial review (Jewish Community Campus of Winnipeg Inc. v. Metaser, 2013 MBQB 303); a non-party cannot be compelled to respond and the matter may proceed in their absence. Extrinsic evidence post-dating the hearing is generally inadmissible and must be relevant.
firac.application: The decisions post-dated the hearing and were not relevant: that another student was reinstated after similar posts would not assist in determining whether the UDC was biased against Mr. Zaki. If factually similar cases decided differently by different tribunals within one institution automatically applied to one another, this would have no principled limit; the decisions had no probative value.
firac.conclusion: The disclosure motion was dismissed and Affidavit #3 expunged in its entirety.

keywords_rationale: The decision is a set of preliminary evidentiary and procedural motions in a judicial review of a university disciplinary expulsion, so K001 (Administrative law, the primary area) and K011 (judicial review) are core, as is K012 (procedural fairness) given the abuse-of-process analysis and the reasonable-apprehension-of-bias amendment. K005 (Education law), K041 (campus/university) and K045 (student discipline) capture the university disciplinary context (expulsion from the College of Medicine by the University Discipline Committee). K042 (code of conduct) reflects the professionalism/conduct standards at the heart of the discipline. Keywords such as antisemitism were considered but the antisemitic content related only to a third-party student's posts and was not the subject of the ruling, so it was omitted as too peripheral.
location_rationale: The heading identifies the Court of King's Bench of Manitoba and the docket bears the notation '(Winnipeg Centre)', placing the matter in Winnipeg, Manitoba.
registry_rationale: The docket line 'CI 22-01-36745 (Winnipeg Centre)' identifies the Winnipeg Centre registry of the Court of King's Bench of Manitoba.

case_name: Wood v Yukon (Highways and Public Works)

name_verification.name_in_document: Wood v Yukon (Highways and Public Works)

defining_issues: Does s. 18 of the Yukon Occupational Health and Safety Act give rise to a private civil cause of action?
Should the plaintiff's application to add seven new defendants under Rule 15(5)(a)(iii) be granted?
Should the defendant's application to strike the amended statement of claim as disclosing no reasonable cause of action, as vexatious, and/or as an abuse of process be granted?

firac.issue: Does s. 18 of the Yukon Occupational Health and Safety Act create a private civil cause of action for reprisal?
firac.facts: Wood was dismissed while on probation and framed her entire action on an alleged contravention of s. 18 of the OHSA, asserting she was terminated for raising safety concerns. She had already pursued the matter before the YWCHSB, which declined to prosecute.
firac.rule: Section 18 of the OHSA operates in a public summary conviction context, referring to an employer being 'convicted' and to 'the convicting court' (s. 18(2)); it creates the possibility of a summary conviction prosecution, not a private civil remedy.
firac.application: The court held that the language of s. 18 signals a public prosecution framework, not a civil one. Wood was 'simply mistaken' in asserting that s. 18 'creates a civil cause of action for a prohibited reprisal.' Her claim, based entirely on s. 18, therefore disclosed no reasonable cause of action.
firac.conclusion: Section 18 does not create a private civil cause of action; the claim founded on it cannot succeed.

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff be permitted to add seven new YG-employee defendants under Rule 15(5)(a)(iii)?
firac.facts: Wood sought to add seven YG employees and to raise numerous new causes of action (wrongful dismissal, breach of fiduciary/statutory duty, conspiracy, malfeasance in public office, negligent supervision, etc.), largely tied to the Ogilvie Conflict of Interest Mitigation Strategy.
firac.rule: Rule 15(5)(a)(iii) requires (1) a real, non-frivolous issue between the plaintiff and the proposed defendant relating to the subject matter (a low threshold), and (2) that it be just and convenient to add the party: Strata Plan No VIS3578 v Canan Investment Group Ltd, 2010 BCCA 329; Letvad v Fenwick. A pleading may be frivolous/vexatious or an abuse of process (collateral attack on a tribunal decision subject to appeal): Willow v Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083; Acumar, 2014 BCSC 814.
firac.application: None of the proposed individual defendants could grant the remedies sought (e.g., reinstatement); adding them would needlessly complicate proceedings; the Strategy was only an administrative policy creating no legal duty (Friends of the Oldman River; Arsenault); employer-employee relations are contractual, not fiduciary; government employees acting within scope cannot conspire together (Kuhn); malfeasance requires unlawful conduct (Odhavji); and the various framings did not rise above frivolousness. The action also collaterally attacked the YWCHSB and Human Rights proceedings.
firac.conclusion: The application to add defendants was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the amended statement of claim be struck under Rules 20(26)(a),(b),(d)?
firac.facts: The amended claim rested entirely on s. 18 of the OHSA and effectively sought to appeal Wood's probationary dismissal, a matter already addressed through the Public Service Act, Public Service Labour Relations Act, the Collective Agreement, and multiple tribunal proceedings.
firac.rule: A claim is struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action where it is plain and obvious it cannot succeed (Hunt v Carey; R v Imperial Tobacco); as vexatious where it advances no claim known in law; and as an abuse of process where it is a collateral attack on an appealable/reviewable administrative decision or relitigates decided issues (Willow; Cimaco; Toronto (City) v CUPE).
firac.application: Since s. 18 creates no civil cause of action, the claim disclosed no reasonable cause of action. It was vexatious as an attempt to appeal a probationary dismissal for which the statutory appeal was exhausted with no further right of appeal. It was an abuse of process as the fourth forum used to relitigate the dismissal, and a collateral attack on the YWCHSB Appeal Tribunal after Wood withdrew her further statutory appeal.
firac.conclusion: The application to strike the amended statement of claim was granted.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) and K085 (wrongful dismissal) capture the substantive core: a probationary dismissal and the failed attempt to litigate it as wrongful dismissal, displaced by the Public Service Act, PSLRA and the Collective Agreement. K002 (Civil litigation) reflects the procedural nature of the decision — applications to add parties and to strike pleadings for frivolousness/abuse of process. K001 (Administrative law) and K011 (judicial review) are engaged because the reasoning turns on collateral attack of the YWCHSB and Human Rights tribunal decisions that were subject to statutory appeal/review — these are somewhat weak fits as the case does not itself conduct judicial review, but they best capture the collateral-attack doctrine given the vocabulary lacks an 'abuse of process' term. K082 (employment discrimination) is a weak/borderline pick reflecting Wood's parallel sex-discrimination complaint to the Yukon Human Rights Commission, which forms part of the factual matrix but is not decided here. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward other subject matter, so several picks are approximations flagged as weak.
location_rationale: The header states 'SUPREME COURT OF YUKON' and 'Registry: Whitehorse', establishing the city as Whitehorse and the territory as Yukon.
registry_rationale: The decision expressly states 'Registry: Whitehorse'.

case_name: Canwest Mediaworks Publications Inc. v. Murray

name_verification.name_in_document: Canwest Mediaworks Publications Inc. v. Murray

defining_issues: Are the paragraphs asserting Canwest's pro-Israel editorial bias and centralized editorial policy relevant to a passing-off or copyright defence, such that they should not be struck under Rule 19(24)?
Do Charter values (freedom of expression under s. 2(b)) or the constitutional validity of the Trade-marks Act and Copyright Act make the truth of the mock paper's contents a relevant defence?
Should paragraph 11, which attacks the plaintiff's motives for bringing the suit as an abuse of process, be struck where no counterclaim for abuse of process is pleaded?
Should the document production motion be granted where the documents sought relate only to the struck paragraphs?

firac.issue: Are the pleadings asserting Canwest's editorial bias and policies relevant to a passing-off or copyright defence?
firac.facts: The defendants published a mock edition of the Vancouver Sun that duplicated the masthead and satirically criticized Israel's policy toward Palestinians and Canwest's Middle East reporting. Canwest sued in passing-off, breach of s. 7(b) of the Trade-marks Act and copyright. Paragraphs 2, 3 and 4 of Murray's defence alleged aggregate circulation of all Canwest papers and a centralized pro-Israel editorial bias, said to be relevant to confusion.
firac.rule: Under Rule 19(24)(a) a defence may be struck where it is plain and obvious it will fail assuming pleaded facts true (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959); under (b) and (c) the focus is on relevance to the cause of action (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress). Passing-off requires goodwill, deception by misrepresentation, and actual or potential damage (Ciba-Geigy v. Apotex, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 120); s. 7(b) is the statutory equivalent (Asbjorn Horgard). Copyright protects original works irrespective of their truth.
firac.application: Confusion is assessed by comparing the publications themselves, consumer/survey/expert evidence, not by the plaintiff's intentions or editorial policies. Canwest's actual policies were beside the point; at most the public's perception mattered, which is not what the paragraphs pleaded. The aggregate circulation of all Canwest papers was irrelevant since only the Vancouver Sun was in issue. Copyright likewise has nothing to do with the truth of the contents.
firac.conclusion: The paragraphs disclosed no defence and were unnecessary and apt to delay a fair trial; properly struck.

firac.issue: Do Charter values or the constitutional validity of the Acts make the truth of the mock paper relevant?
firac.facts: Murray argued that the common law and the Trade-marks Act must be interpreted consistently with Charter values, that truth should factor into balancing intellectual property against free expression (analogous to the defence of truth in defamation), and that if the Acts prohibited his parody they infringed s. 2(b).
firac.rule: Freedom of expression under s. 2(b) protects all communications conveying meaning regardless of content; courts refuse to consider the content of the expression (R. v. Zundel, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 731). Charter values are applied by balancing competing interests, as in BCAA v. OPEIU Local 378, 2001 BCSC 156.
firac.application: The defamation analogy was inapt: defamation turns on the falsity of statements, whereas passing-off concerns misrepresenting one's goods as another's and is indifferent to truth. In BCAA the court balanced competing interests without inquiring into truth. Since s. 2(b) analysis disregards content, the truth of the parody was irrelevant to the Charter-values or constitutional-validity arguments; the same reasoning applied to the copyright claim.
firac.conclusion: Truth of the parody's contents was not a relevant defence; the Charter and constitutional-validity pleadings failed.

firac.issue: Should paragraph 11 attacking the plaintiff's motives be struck absent a counterclaim for abuse of process?
firac.facts: Paragraph 11 (beyond its first sentence) alleged the lawsuit was intended to inflict harm and deter the defendants' pro-Palestinian expression, was an abuse of process, but no counterclaim for abuse of process was pleaded.
firac.rule: The tort of abuse of process requires the elements set out in Hemming v. Newton, 2006 BCSC 1748: subjection to legal process, predominant improper collateral purpose, a definite act/threat in furtherance, and actual damage. Absent a counterclaim, a plaintiff's motives are irrelevant; courts may even stay such counterclaims (Starbucks Corp. v. Second Cup Ltd.).
firac.application: Without a pleaded counterclaim, the plaintiff's motives were irrelevant, including to the question of special costs. Merely asserting abuse of process was an overly-polemical way of asserting the claim lacked merit and had no place in a pleading.
firac.conclusion: Paragraph 11 (except its first sentence) was struck.

firac.issue: Should the document production motion be granted?
firac.facts: Murray sought documents concerning Canwest's alleged pro-Israel bias, centralized editorial policy, and motives for bringing the lawsuit, as pleaded in the struck paragraphs.
firac.rule: Document production must relate to matters in issue in the pleadings.
firac.application: The documents sought related solely to the paragraphs that had been struck, so they were no longer connected to any live issue.
firac.conclusion: The production motion was denied; the appeal was dismissed with costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area: this is a pleadings-strike/appeal motion in a passing-off, trade-mark and copyright action. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) are central because Murray argued Charter values and constitutional invalidity, with the court applying Zundel and BCAA. K107 (Canadian Charter) captures the constitutional argument. K103 (Israel), K104 (Palestine), K106 (West Bank) and K102 (Gaza) reflect the subject-matter of the mock newspaper's satire of Canwest's Middle East coverage — these are topical/entity tags and are somewhat peripheral to the legal holding but accurately describe the content in issue. No intellectual-property or passing-off keyword exists in the vocabulary, which is the main doctrinal gap; the tags chosen are the closest available.
location_rationale: The header states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA', 'Registry: Vancouver', and the place of hearing is listed as 'Vancouver, B.C.'
registry_rationale: The decision header expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Bank of Montreal v. Tortora

defining_issues: Should the Bank's claims for breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, gross negligence, constructive fraud and unjust enrichment be struck under Rule 19(24) as disclosing no reasonable cause of action or as embarrassing/prejudicial?
Should the unjust enrichment claim against Mr. Punja be struck where no deprivation of the Bank corresponding to his enrichment is pleaded?
Can a conspiracy claim under the second (unlawful means) branch be maintained against Mr. Punja, who is not alleged to have committed any unlawful act?
Do the conspiracy claims against Ms. Tortora and Ms. Poonja survive, or do they merge into the pleaded claims for breach of contract and breach of fiduciary duty?
Did the amended statement of claim satisfy Rule 24(3) so as to defeat the application requiring a paragraph-by-paragraph marked-up amendment?

firac.issue: Should the Bank's claims for breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, gross negligence, constructive fraud and unjust enrichment be struck under Rule 19(24)?
firac.facts: The Bank sued two former employees, a Mortgage Specialist (Tortora) and a Financial Services Manager (Poonja), for secretly splitting commissions and for gross negligence in arranging ten 'Papas Mortgages' involving fraudulently altered appraisals, alleging breaches of the Bank's Code and Policies, breaches of employment contracts, fiduciary duty, constructive fraud and unjust enrichment.
firac.rule: Under Rule 19(24) of the B.C. Rules of Court, pleadings may be struck where it is 'plain and obvious' that no reasonable cause of action is disclosed, assuming all pleaded facts to be true (McNaughton v. Baker; Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959). Weakness or novelty is no ground to strike (Minnes v. Minnes). Embarrassing/scandalous/vexatious pleadings (subrules (b)–(c)) must be shown certain to fail (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform). An employee below senior management may in certain circumstances owe fiduciary duties (Barton Insurance Brokers Ltd. v. Irwin). Constructive fraud may arise absent actual deceit (Nocton v. Ashburton). Unjust enrichment may be pleaded as an alternative to contract (Isaac v. Guardian Capital).
firac.application: Accepting the pleaded facts as true, the amended statement of claim set out the elements of a fiduciary relationship (discretion/power, ability to affect the Bank's interests, and the Bank's vulnerability), so novelty of an employee fiduciary claim was no bar. The contract claims, though not drafted in the traditional way, made the gist clear (failure to follow Code/Policies plus breach of an implied duty of honesty and good faith) and were not embarrassing. The gross negligence claim adequately pleaded standard of care, breach and damages. Constructive fraud was viable since a fiduciary breach was disclosed and equity-falling conduct was alleged. The unjust enrichment claims against Tortora and Poonja pleaded enrichment, corresponding deprivation and absence of juristic reason as alternative claims.
firac.conclusion: The applications to strike these claims were dismissed; it was not plain and obvious that they disclosed no reasonable cause of action.

firac.issue: Should the unjust enrichment claim against Mr. Punja be struck?
firac.facts: The Bank alleged Mr. Punja, Ms. Poonja's husband, received over $245,000 'in turn' from Ms. Tortora, but pleaded no payments made by the Bank to him and no relationship between the Bank and him.
firac.rule: Unjust enrichment requires (a) enrichment of the defendant, (b) a corresponding deprivation of the plaintiff, and (c) absence of a juristic reason for the deprivation.
firac.application: There was no pleaded deprivation of the Bank corresponding to any enrichment of Mr. Punja; the only funds he received came from Ms. Tortora, not the Bank, and he had no relationship with the Bank that could cause the Bank to be deprived when he received those funds.
firac.conclusion: The unjust enrichment allegation against Mr. Punja was struck.

firac.issue: Can a conspiracy claim under the unlawful-means branch stand against Mr. Punja, who committed no unlawful act?
firac.facts: The Bank alleged the three defendants conspired to split commissions; only Tortora and Poonja were alleged to have breached the Bank's Code, Policies, contracts and fiduciary duties. Mr. Punja's role was receiving and transferring funds, with no unlawful act alleged against him.
firac.rule: The tort of conspiracy requires either a predominant purpose to injure the plaintiff or, under the second branch, unlawful conduct directed at the plaintiff with constructive intent (Canada Cement LaFarge Ltd. v. B.C. Lightweight Aggregate Ltd., [1983] 1 S.C.R. 452). The tort is an anomaly not to be extended (Frame v. Smith; Normart Management Ltd. v. West Hill Redevelopment). Under the second branch each conspirator sued must be alleged to have committed the unlawful act.
firac.application: There was no allegation of a predominant purpose to injure and none of Mr. Punja's acts were unlawful per se. To hold him liable where he neither intended injury nor committed a wrongful act would create an impermissible third category of conspirator drawn in only by his familial/business relationship. Clerk & Lindsell and Rookes v. Barnard did not assist, and Tracy (Instaloans) left the point undecided on distinguishable facts.
firac.conclusion: It was plain and obvious that no reasonable cause of action in conspiracy lay against Mr. Punja; the claim against him was struck.

firac.issue: Do the conspiracy claims against Tortora and Poonja survive or merge into the contract and fiduciary duty claims?
firac.facts: The unlawful acts pleaded against Tortora and Poonja in the conspiracy claim (breach of Code/Policies, contract and fiduciary duty) were the very same acts underpinning the separate contract and fiduciary claims; actual damage from the commission splitting was pleaded.
firac.rule: Where a tort has been committed by two or more persons, an allegation of prior conspiracy adds nothing and merges in the tort (Ward v. Lewis; Hovsepian v. Westfair Foods Ltd., 2001 ABQB 700; Napoleone v. Baraldi). A conspiracy claim survives only where the wrongful acts pleaded differ from those grounding the underlying torts (as in Hunt).
firac.application: Although actual damage was pleaded, the wrongful acts founding the conspiracy claim were identical to the breaches of contract and fiduciary duty already alleged, so the conspiracy added nothing. This was not a Hunt situation of distinct wrongful acts. Given the Bank had already amended once with very different allegations and still failed, leave to amend was refused.
firac.conclusion: The merger principle applied; the conspiracy claims against Tortora and Poonja were struck without leave to amend.

firac.issue: Did the amended statement of claim comply with Rule 24(3)?
firac.facts: Ms. Poonja and Mr. Punja sought an order requiring a paragraph-by-paragraph marked-up amended statement of claim; the Bank's amended pleading reproduced the entire original document crossed out and replaced with a 34-page version.
firac.rule: Rule 24(3) governs the form of amended pleadings.
firac.application: The amended statement of claim contained the entire original so changes could be discerned by comparison; the format proposed would be more difficult to read and serve no purpose, and the pleading as delivered complied with Rule 24(3).
firac.conclusion: The Rule 24(3) application was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the core tier-1 area: the decision turns on applications to strike pleadings under Rules 19(24) and 24 and on the tort of conspiracy, unjust enrichment and constructive fraud. K009 (Labour and employment law) is engaged because the claims arise from the fiduciary duties and employment contracts of two former bank employees. K022 (restitution) reasonably captures the unjust enrichment analysis (enrichment/deprivation/juristic reason). K085 (wrongful dismissal) is a weak/borderline pick — the employees were terminated but the suit is by the employer, so it is included only for the employment-termination context. K042 (code of conduct) is also borderline — the Bank's Code of business conduct and Policies feature centrally in the alleged breaches, though the canonical term sits in the Education area. The controlled vocabulary is oriented to human-rights/antisemitism matters and fits this commercial pleadings dispute poorly; K085 and K042 are flagged as the weakest choices.
