registry_rationale: The header expressly reads 'Registry: Vancouver'.

case_name: CAS of London and Middlesex v. T.S. and K.M.

name_verification.name_in_document: CAS of London and Middlesex v. T.S. and K.M.

defining_issues: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial on whether the child was in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b)(i) of the CYFSA?
If the child was in need of protection, what disposition order under s. 101 of the CYFSA was in the child's best interests, and was an extension of interim care under s. 122 warranted?
If extended society care was ordered, should any access to the child be granted under s. 105(5)-(6) of the CYFSA?

firac.issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial on whether the child, M-R, was in need of protection?
firac.facts: The society had extensive historical involvement with both parents over substance abuse, criminal activity and domestic violence; the mother used marijuana, methadone, Fentanyl and morphine during pregnancy, gave inconsistent accounts of her drug use, breached supervision conditions, was incarcerated four times after the application was commenced, and filed no material on the motion. The mother did not attend the hearing and her counsel made only legal submissions.
firac.rule: On a summary judgment motion under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules (as amended in 2015 to mirror Rule 20), the court may weigh evidence, assess credibility and draw inferences (Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7). The onus is on the society to show no genuine issue for trial; the responding party may not rest on bald denials but must set out specific facts showing a genuine issue (r. 16(4.1)). Protection under s. 74(2)(b)(i) CYFSA arises where there is a risk the child is likely to suffer physical harm from a person's failure to adequately care for, provide for, supervise or protect the child.
firac.application: The society's affidavits established a prima facie case of risk of harm; the mother filed nothing to rebut it and provided nothing for the court to weigh. Her counsel conceded a protection finding 'might be a foregone conclusion.' The mother's ongoing drug use, repeated incarcerations and unstable lifestyle raised no material dispute, and a mere heartfelt desire to parent does not create a triable issue.
firac.conclusion: No genuine issue for trial existed; the child was found in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b)(i) of the CYFSA.

firac.issue: What disposition order under s. 101 was in the child's best interests, and should interim care be extended under s. 122?
firac.facts: M-R, under six years old, had been in society care since February 2017 (14 months at the hearing, 17 at judgment). The mother had failed for a full year to complete any of the conditions of the May 2017 order (drug testing, ADSTV counselling, Heartspace, consents, punctual attendance). No parenting plan was filed; the father filed nothing and had one visit.
firac.rule: Under s. 101 CYFSA the court must make the order in the child's best interests (s. 74(3)); options are supervision, interim society care, extended society care, or a combination. Section 122 limits interim care to 12 months for a child under six, extendable by up to six months if in the child's best interests. Permanency planning for young children should not be delayed by 'litigation drift' (Children's Aid Society (Simcoe County) v. T.D., 2012 ONSC 6737).
firac.application: The maximum available interim-care extension was about one month, which could not realistically allow the mother to complete conditions she had failed to meet over a year. There was no evidence she was near completion or had a viable plan; the s. 74(3) factors—continuity of care with the foster family (her psychological parents), weak emotional ties, risk of harm on return, effect of delay—all favoured permanency. An extension would serve only a 'heartfelt desire to parent,' not the child's best interests.
firac.conclusion: No genuine issue for trial on disposition; the court ordered the child placed in extended society care under s. 101 until terminated under s. 116 or expired under s. 123.

firac.issue: Should any access to the child be granted following an order of extended society care?
firac.facts: The mother attended access when available and was affectionate, but was frequently late, missed visits due to incarceration, and put her access at risk through her own choices. The foster family wished to adopt.
firac.rule: Under s. 105(4) an existing access order terminates upon an extended-care order; under s. 105(5)-(6) the court may make a new access order only if satisfied it is in the child's best interests, considering whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful to the child (and, if relevant, impact on adoption prospects). 'Beneficial' means advantageous and 'meaningful' means significant; the applicant must prove the relationship brings a significant positive advantage to the child (Children's Aid Society of the Niagara Region v. J.C., 2007 CanLII 8919).
firac.application: While access visits were pleasant and affectionate, given the child's young age, the missed and suspended visits, and the mother's willingness to jeopardize access, the relationship was not shown to be beneficial and meaningful from the child's perspective. Love and pleasant visits alone are insufficient.
firac.conclusion: Access was not beneficial and meaningful to the child; no access order was made (making it unnecessary to consider s. 105(6)(b)).

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area — this is a child-protection proceeding under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is central to both the disposition and access analyses under ss. 74(3) and 105(6). K048 (custody/access) captures the placement (extended society care) and the denial of an access order. K002 (Civil litigation) is a borderline pick reflecting the summary-judgment procedure under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules, which framed the whole decision. K050 (parental support) is a weak/closest pick flagged as such — child support was not at issue; it is included only because the controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated child-protection/CYFSA or summary-judgment keyword, so genuinely on-point terms number fewer than five.
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE FAMILY COURT' and the applicant is the 'Children's Aid Society of London and Middlesex'; the reasons note 'There are very few places in London that would take a person more than two hours to get from,' confirming the court sits in London, Ontario.
registry_rationale: No formal registry line is given, but the court file number C240/12-03 and the London and Middlesex jurisdiction indicate the London (Middlesex) Family Court registry; inferred rather than expressly stated.

case_name: Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. A.M.Y.

name_verification.name_in_document: Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. A.M.Y.

defining_issues: On a motion for summary judgment under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules, was there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether the four children were in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
If the children were in need of protection, what disposition was in their best interests — return to the parents (with or without supervision), a community placement, or Crown wardship?
Should the parents be granted access to the children once made Crown wards under s. 59(2.1) of the CFSA?

firac.issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial on whether the four children were in need of protection under s. 37(2) CFSA?
firac.facts: C.C.A.S. became involved after Y.N.Y. disclosed his father hit him; later M.L.Y., Y.N.Y. and S.C.H.Y. disclosed repeated and severe physical and emotional abuse to multiple professionals. Three of the four children were diagnosed with PTSD, exhibited aggression, self-harm and suicidal ideation, and consistently said they feared and did not wish to return to their parents. The parents denied all abuse, claimed the children were manipulated by C.C.A.S., and alleged cultural bias and racism, offering mostly bald denials.
firac.rule: Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules permits summary judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; the responding party may not rest on mere allegations or denials but must set out specific facts showing a triable issue (r. 16(4.1)). The court must take a 'hard look' at the merits (Children's Aid Society of Hamilton v. M.N.). A child is in need of protection under s. 37(2)(a),(b),(f),(f.1),(g),(g.1) CFSA where physical/emotional harm or the risk thereof exists.
firac.application: The children's detailed, consistent disclosures to numerous professionals, the PTSD diagnoses, and their disturbed behaviours constituted overwhelming evidence. The court held that a protection finding did not even require proof of the alleged physical abuse — the risk of emotional harm alone sufficed. The parents' bald denials and blame of others did not raise specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial.
firac.conclusion: No triable issue existed; all four children were found in need of protection under the enumerated subsections of s. 37(2) (M.K.Y. under (b) and (g)).

firac.issue: What disposition was in the children's best interests?
firac.facts: C.C.A.S. sought Crown wardship for adoption. A prior supervision order (April–November 2011) had failed. The parents refused parenting-capacity assessments and most services, rejected the PTSD diagnoses, took no responsibility, and proposed only that the children be returned to them. No family or community alternative placements were offered.
firac.rule: Section 57(1) CFSA sets out available orders; s. 57(2)-(4) require the court to consider society efforts, less disruptive alternatives and community placements; s. 37(3) lists best-interests criteria. The test is not whether parents intend to change but whether they have in fact changed and can safely parent (CAS of Winnipeg v. R.; CCAS of Metro Toronto v. C.M.). Crown wardship is a remedy of last resort, 'the capital punishment of family law', reserved for the clearest cases.
firac.application: The same protection concerns present at apprehension persisted; the parents showed no insight, remorse or change and had engaged in no meaningful services. A supervision order depends on trust and cooperation, which were absent, so return even with supervision would not keep the children safe. No alternative plans existed. The parents' plan had no air of reality and no chance of success at trial.
firac.conclusion: Crown wardship for all four children was ordered as the only disposition serving their best interests and offering certainty and finality.

firac.issue: Should the parents have access to the children as Crown wards?
firac.facts: The parents had had no access for nearly two years; earlier access motions had been dismissed and not appealed. The three oldest children feared their parents and did not want visits, though S.C.H.Y. said she missed them and M.K.Y. asked about her father.
firac.rule: Section 59(2.1) CFSA bars an access order for a Crown ward unless the relationship is beneficial and meaningful to the child and access will not impair future adoption opportunities; s. 59(2) presumes access is revoked. The onus is on the party seeking access, focusing on the child's experience (NB (Minister) v. L.(M.); CCAS v. M.(C.)).
firac.application: With no access for two years and the children not wanting contact, no beneficial and meaningful relationship existed to support parental access. The parents failed to rebut the presumption or meet the s. 59(2.1) onus. Sibling relationships, however, were bonded and warranted access among the four children.
firac.conclusion: Parental access was denied; an order for access among the four siblings (at C.C.A.S.'s discretion and later as agreed) was made.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area — this is a child protection proceeding under the Child and Family Services Act. K047 (best interests of the child) is central, as s. 37(3) best-interests criteria drove the disposition. K048 (custody/access) captures both the Crown-wardship custody outcome and the access analysis under s. 59(2.1), including sibling access. K002 (civil litigation) is a weaker but defensible pick, reflecting the summary-judgment procedure under Rule 16 that framed the whole decision (there is no dedicated child-protection or summary-judgment keyword in the vocabulary). K065 (racism) is borderline — the parents alleged cultural bias and racism by the school and agency, which the court addressed and rejected as a 'smokescreen', but it was not an operative legal ground. No hate-speech, immigration or constitutional keywords apply despite the family's migration history.
location_rationale: The header states 'ONTARIO COURT OF JUSTICE' and the court file is 'Toronto C53764/11'; the children were 'apprehended on 16 November 2011 in Toronto, Ontario', confirming city and province.
registry_rationale: The court file number is recorded as 'Toronto C53764/11', indicating the Toronto registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

case_name: Axelrod v. Beth Jacob et al.

name_verification.name_in_document: Axelrod v. Beth Jacob et al.

defining_issues: Was the respondent dismissed on November 5th for cause, and was it an error to submit the question whether his conduct justified dismissal (a question of law) to the jury?
Did the individual defendants conspire to procure, or maliciously induce, the congregation's breach of the respondent's employment contract?
Were the three impugned publications defamatory, and did the trial judge err in excluding evidence of the truth of the facts stated in the third publication (the newspaper letter)?
Was the claim for conspiracy to libel properly left to and answered by the jury?

firac.issue: Was the respondent dismissed for cause on November 5th, and was it error to put the question of whether his conduct justified dismissal to the jury?
firac.facts: The respondent, engaged as rabbi, slaughterer, cantor and teacher for a three-year term, refused after October 22nd to continue teaching alongside Lederman and stopped performing his teaching duties. On November 5th Mausberg, the congregation's president, personally ejected him from the school and told him he was dismissed. The jury, answering Question 6, found he had not refused 'without lawful excuse' to discharge his teaching duties and found dismissal occurred December 20th.
firac.rule: Only questions of fact may be put to a jury under s. 60 of the Judicature Act, R.S.O. 1937, c. 100. Whether proved facts are sufficient in law to warrant dismissal is for the judge; whether the alleged facts are proved is for the jury (McIntyre v. Hockin (1889), 16 O.A.R. 498). An employee's refusal to perform duties justifies discharge (Boston Deep Sea Fishing & Ice Co. v. Ansell (1888), 39 Ch. D. 339).
firac.application: The evidence, including the respondent's own admission, was all one way that he refused to teach after October 22nd; the jury could not consistently have found otherwise. Question 6, however, asked whether the refusal was 'without lawful excuse' — a question of law improperly delegated to the jury. The respondent received no effective notice of dismissal until he was ejected on November 5th, and that dismissal was for cause (his refusal to teach). Because the jury was misdirected, it never addressed whether the parties' conduct after November 5th amounted to a resumption of contractual relations, which alone could support a December 20th dismissal. The conflicting evidence about the respondent acting as cantor and the parties' later dealings left the matter genuinely triable.
firac.conclusion: There was a dismissal for cause on November 5th; the real issue of whether contractual relations were resumed thereafter was untried. A new trial is ordered on the wrongful dismissal claim.

firac.issue: Did the individual defendants conspire to procure, or maliciously induce, the congregation's breach of the respondent's employment contract?
firac.facts: The jury found Mausberg and Lederman conspired to procure the wrongful dismissal and, apart from conspiracy, maliciously induced the breach. Lederman had quarrelled with the respondent over how he should be addressed; Mausberg acted as president in effecting the dismissal.
firac.rule: A plaintiff alleging conspiracy bears a heavy burden of proof (Sweeney v. Coote, [1907] A.C. 221); it is damage, not the agreement, that is the gist (Mogul S.S. Co. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. (1889), 23 Q.B.D. 598). A director or officer acting within the scope of authority in causing the company to breach a contract is not liable for inducing breach (Said v. Butt, [1920] 3 K.B. 497; Henderson v. Kane and Pioneer Club, [1924] N.Z.L.R. 1073).
firac.application: Since wrongful discharge had not been established, the conspiracy issue would in any event require retrial. But there was no admissible evidence of any combination or intention to injure. Lederman's quarrel did not establish a conspiracy and he had no shown connection with the discharge. Mausberg acted only within the scope of his duties as president, so the Said v. Butt principle shielded him from liability for inducing breach.
firac.conclusion: The claims for conspiracy to induce, and for inducing, the breach fail and are dismissed.

firac.issue: Were the impugned publications defamatory, and did the judge err in excluding evidence of the truth of the facts in the newspaper letter?
firac.facts: Three publications imputed that the respondent was unqualified as a slaughterer / that his Kashruth could not be relied on: (1) Mausberg's November 6th circular ('I am not responsible for his Kashruth'); (2) Zimmerman's newspaper advertisement annulling the respondent's Kabalah; and (3) Lederman's letter to a Hebrew newspaper. For the letter the defence pleaded qualified privilege and fair comment, and the judge excluded evidence of the truth of the stated facts, holding a separate plea of justification was needed.
firac.rule: Words must be reasonably capable of a defamatory meaning (Beswick v. Smith (1907), 24 T.L.R. 169). Where fair comment is pleaded, evidence of the truth of the facts commented on is admissible without a separate plea of justification (Boys v. Star Printing & Publishing Co., [1927] 3 D.L.R. 847, 60 O.L.R. 592; Gatley, 3rd ed., p. 675); Sutherland v. Stopes, [1925] A.C. 47 is not to the contrary. There can be no fair comment unless based on facts truly stated.
firac.application: The Beswick argument addressed only the innocuous words about ending employment, not the defamatory Kashruth phrase, so it failed as to the circular. Mausberg was fixed with the advertisement by the statement of defence admitting its publication, and with the letter by evidence connecting him to it. On the letter, however, the judge wrongly excluded evidence of the truth of the facts; that evidence was essential to the fair-comment defence, and its exclusion caused counsel to abandon fair comment.
firac.conclusion: The verdicts on the November 6th circular ($1,000) and the advertisement ($500) stand and those appeals are dismissed; the judgment on Lederman's letter cannot stand and a new trial is ordered on that libel because of the erroneous evidentiary ruling.

firac.issue: Was the claim for conspiracy to libel properly established by the jury's verdict?
firac.facts: The statement of claim alleged the defendants conspired to defame the respondent through the three publications; a general question on conspiracy to libel was answered affirmatively, but the jury assessed separate damages for each libel and awarded no damages for the conspiracy itself.
firac.rule: It is the damage done, not the conspiracy, that is the gist of the action (Mogul S.S. Co. v. McGregor, Gow & Co.). A jury finding unsupported by an assessment of damages tied to the pleaded cause is treated as an answer 'in the air' (Thomas v. Moore, [1918] 1 K.B. 555).
firac.application: The pleading disclosed only a joint cause of action for conspiracy to libel followed by the overt libels, not separate libel causes of action. Yet the case was tried and argued as though damages were claimed for each separate libel, and the jury assessed no damages for the conspiracy. The conspiracy finding therefore hung 'in the air.'
firac.conclusion: The conspiracy-to-libel claim is dismissed.

keywords_rationale: The case arises out of an employment relationship and its termination, so K009 (Labour and employment) and K085 (wrongful dismissal) are central. It equally sounds in tort — defamation and related claims — supporting K002 (Civil litigation) and K015 (defamation), with K016 (fair comment) and K018 (qualified privilege) engaged directly by the pleaded defences and the reversible evidentiary ruling on the newspaper letter. The parties and subject-matter are Jewish: the plaintiff is a rabbi (K098) employed by a Jewish congregation/community (K094, K093), and the defamatory sting concerned his 'Kashruth' and qualification as a religious slaughterer, engaging K028 (kosher/dietary law). Conspiracy and inducing breach of contract were also litigated but have no dedicated vocabulary entry, so they are captured under the civil litigation and employment headings. K093/K094 are somewhat contextual rather than doctrinal but reflect the identity of the parties and the religious character of the alleged libel.
location_rationale: The decision names the 'Ontario Court of Appeal' but does not state the city where it sits. The province is Ontario, confirmed by the court's identity and references to Ontario statutes (Judicature Act, R.S.O. 1937, c. 100). The congregation and Hebrew school were in Kitchener, but that is the situs of the events, not the seat of the appellate court, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: No court registry or office is identified in the decision text; appellate reports of this era do not state one, so registry is left null.

case_name: Watkins v Willow Park Golf Course Ltd

name_verification.name_in_document: Ralph Watkins v Willow Park Golf Course Ltd.

defining_issues: Did the plaintiff's verbal and sexual harassment of a subordinate constitute just cause for summary termination of his employment?
Was the employer required to give the plaintiff a warning before terminating him for cause?
Did the employer condone the plaintiff's misconduct?
Did the employer's inadequate investigation of the complaints defeat its claim of just cause?
Did the plaintiff's failure to demote or fire Ms. Li amount to insubordination justifying dismissal?

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff's verbal and sexual harassment of a subordinate constitute just cause for summary termination?
firac.facts: Watkins, the 61-year-old Golf Course Superintendent with almost 13 years' service, developed romantic feelings for Ms. Li, his direct subordinate 32 years his junior. After she repeatedly rejected him and asked that communications remain professional, he continued sending personal texts/emails, monitored her intrusively, argued with her within earshot of staff, asked about her pornography habits, and called her a 'cunt' or 'fucking cunt'; he also berated and fired seasonal employee Ms. Kent and poisoned the department atmosphere.
firac.rule: There is no fixed rule for summary termination; the analysis is contextual, assessing the degree of misconduct and surrounding circumstances (McKinley v BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38; Hodgins v St. John Council for Alberta, 2008 ABCA 173). Dismissal is justified where conduct violates an essential condition of the contract, is fundamentally inconsistent with the employee's obligations, or destroys the mutual faith of the relationship (McKinley at para 48). Sexual harassment is 'unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature that detrimentally affects the work environment' (Janzen v Platy Enterprises, [1989] 1 SCR 1252) and may justify summary dismissal (Geluch v Rosedale Golf Association).
firac.application: The court found the harassment sustained over several months, escalating from unwanted romantic pursuit to hostility, and aggravated by the fact that Watkins was Ms. Li's sole direct supervisor upon whom she was economically dependent. This distinguished the case from Brazeau and placed the conduct at the upper-middle of the severity spectrum. As a senior supervisor he had a duty to provide a safe, respectful workplace and to protect the employer from liability (Bannister; Poliquin), which he not only failed but personally breached, showing no recognition his conduct was wrong.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiff's conduct was incompatible with continued employment; summary termination was for just cause.

firac.issue: Was the employer required to warn the plaintiff before terminating him?
firac.facts: The employer had no respectful-workplace or harassment policy in 2011 and gave no warning before dismissal.
firac.rule: There is no hard-and-fast rule requiring a warning; the greater the wrong, the less likely a warning is required (Leach v Canadian Blood Services, 2001 ABQB 54; Bannister v General Motors of Canada). Management employees have a duty to protect other employees and the employer from civil claims.
firac.application: Given the severity of the harassment, the duty owed to Ms. Li and other staff, and the plaintiff's complete failure to recognize his conduct as unacceptable (indeed his immediate blanket denial), no warning was mandated before termination.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiff was not entitled to a warning before termination.

firac.issue: Did the employer condone the plaintiff's misconduct?
firac.facts: The plaintiff argued his behaviour was condoned, making a warning necessary.
firac.rule: Condonation requires more than mere delay and presupposes the employer's knowledge of the misconduct (Geluch v Rosedale Golf Association).
firac.application: There was no evidence the Board or senior employees knew the particulars of the plaintiff's treatment of Ms. Li or Ms. Kent until the fall of 2011, after which termination followed quickly.
firac.conclusion: No condonation was established.

firac.issue: Did the employer's inadequate investigation defeat its claim of just cause?
firac.facts: The employer met with the plaintiff and let him read and respond to Ms. Li's letter but never spoke directly with Ms. Li about her allegations and gave the plaintiff limited time to respond.
firac.rule: A proper investigation can enhance, and its absence can hurt, an employer's case for summary dismissal, but failure to investigate does not automatically obviate an otherwise justified termination (Foerderer v Nova Chemicals; Leach; Kinch v Amoco).
firac.application: The court found the investigation inadequate for failing to interview Ms. Li and rushing the plaintiff's response, but concluded that a proper investigation would only have confirmed Ms. Li's allegations and those of other employees; the admissions and evidence at trial independently justified dismissal.
firac.conclusion: The inadequate investigation did not defeat just cause; termination remained justified.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff's failure to demote or fire Ms. Li amount to insubordination?
firac.facts: Mr. Lyle told the plaintiff Ms. Li could not be 'Assistant Superintendent'; the plaintiff said he was told to terminate her, while Lyle said 'reclassify.' The plaintiff repeatedly asked to defer the decision, receiving silence, and the matter was still under discussion on October 24, 2011.
firac.rule: Refusal to follow an unlawful or unreasonable order may not be insubordinate (Karmel v Calgary Jewish Academy, 2015 ABQB 731). Insubordination requires a clear and unequivocal direction.
firac.application: The direction was equivocal and unresolved, and the plaintiff had general authority over hiring/firing in his department and had made deferral requests met with silence.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiff's conduct did not amount to insubordination, though this did not affect the finding of just cause on the harassment grounds.

defining_issues: Who should be granted custody of the child J.B., having regard to his best interests?
Should the nomination of D.F. as tutrix to the child be confirmed?

firac.issue: To whom should custody of the child J.B. be granted in accordance with his best interests?
firac.facts: J.B., 11½ years old, lost his mother at birth and his father when he was 8½. A custody-tutorship dispute arose among his paternal aunt (T.B.-C.) and her husband (M.C.), his maternal grandmother and step-grandfather (N.T.-B. and C.B.) with whom he had been living in British Columbia since January 1995, and the executrix/tutrix named in the father's will (D.F.). The paternal aunt claimed she had been cut off from the child and alienated by the grandparents; the grandparents said they had cared for the child continuously and met his needs.
firac.rule: Articles 32 and 33 of the Civil Code of Québec: every child has a right to protection, security and attention from parents or those acting in their stead, and every decision concerning a child must be taken in light of the child's interests and the respect of his rights, considering his moral, intellectual, emotional and material needs, age, health, personality and family environment. The applicant bears the burden of proving that the proposed custody serves the child's interests.
firac.application: Over five days of hearing, fourteen witnesses and extensive exhibits, the Court found the paternal aunt (T.B.-C.) not credible and lacking custodial capacity; her account of being prevented from returning the child to Montréal and of alienation by the grandparents was found to be false, and her failure to make any real effort to see the child between 1995 and 1997 undermined her claim. The Court rejected the expert report of Mr D'Abate as based uncritically on facts supplied solely by the aunt's family. By contrast, the maternal grandparents (N.T.-B. and C.B.) testified credibly and demonstrated through their day-to-day care that they loved the child and could meet his intellectual, religious, emotional and physical needs. D.F. withdrew her own custody request.
firac.conclusion: The aunt's motion for custody was dismissed and D.F.'s motion was dismissed on her withdrawal; custody of J.B. was granted to the maternal grandparents N.T.-B. and C.B., with access to D.F. and no access to the aunt, uncle or paternal grandmother, subject to psychological support for any future access.

firac.issue: Should the nomination of D.F. as tutrix to the child be confirmed?
firac.facts: The father's will appointed C.F./D.F. as executrix and tutrix to J.B. The Public Curator of Quebec was a mis en cause on the tutorship application.
firac.rule: Provisions of the Civil Code of Québec governing tutorship to a minor and confirmation of a testamentary tutor's nomination.
firac.application: Having disposed of the custody question in favour of the maternal grandparents and given the father's testamentary appointment of D.F. as tutrix, the Court confirmed her nomination, ordering provisional execution notwithstanding appeal.
firac.conclusion: The nomination of D.F. as tutrix to J.B. was confirmed, with provisional execution notwithstanding appeal, without costs.

defining_issues: Were the defendants entitled to their costs of the motion to dismiss/stay and the plaintiff's motion to vary, given divided success?
Should the plaintiff's solicitor be ordered to pay costs personally under rule 57.07 for causing costs to be incurred without reasonable cause or wasted by undue delay, negligence or other default?
To what extent should the plaintiff's impecuniosity relieve her of, or defer, liability for costs?
What quantum of costs is fair and reasonable and how should payment be allocated and timed?

firac.issue: Were the defendants entitled to their costs of the motion to dismiss/stay and of the plaintiff's motion to vary, notwithstanding divided success?
firac.facts: The defendants moved to dismiss or stay the action for non-payment of two costs orders; the court stayed the action until the first costs order was paid rather than dismissing. The plaintiff opposed both dismissal and a stay, brought three motions to vary (one withdrawn, two dismissed), and forced five attendances. The defendants argued 'clear divided success.'
firac.rule: Costs are discretionary under s. 133(1) of the Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, and rule 57.01; a fair and reasonable award is to be made having regard to success and conduct. Rule 57.03(1) presumes costs fixed and payable within 30 days unless a different order is more just.
firac.application: The Master rejected the 'divided success' characterization: a stay was the alternate relief the defendants sought and the plaintiff opposed both dismissal and stay. Staying only pending payment of one of two costs awards was a significant indulgence to the plaintiff, not a success for her. The plaintiff lost the motion to vary. The defendants acted reasonably while the plaintiff generated unnecessary costs.
firac.conclusion: The defendants were substantially successful on both motions and were entitled to their costs; the remaining questions were quantum, who pays, and timing.

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's solicitor be ordered to pay costs personally under rule 57.07?
firac.facts: Counsel withdrew a motion to vary before the Master to bring it before a judge (dismissed by Brown J.), then brought a third motion to vary before the Master on essentially the same grounds (also dismissed), causing repeated adjournments of the dismissal motion from January to September 2007. Counsel had been told repeatedly that the motions should be heard together by the Master who made the original order, that the proper route was an appeal, and that there were no grounds to vary under rule 59.06. The defendants gave the required rule 57.07(2) notice.
firac.rule: Rule 57.07(1)-(2): where a solicitor causes costs to be incurred without reasonable cause or wasted by undue delay, negligence or other default, the court may require the solicitor personally to pay another party's costs, provided the solicitor has a reasonable opportunity to make representations. Per Walsh v. 1124660 Ontario Limited (2007 CanLII 4789) and Young v. Young (1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)), abuse of process/bad faith need not be shown; it is enough that the acts described in the rule occurred, but courts must be extremely cautious to protect fearless advocacy, judging reasonableness at the time expense was incurred, not with hindsight.
firac.application: The Master found this was not hindsight second-guessing: counsel was warned in advance about the proper forum, the need to appeal, and the absence of grounds to vary, yet pursued repetitive motions to vary. This caused costs to be incurred without reasonable cause and through undue delay, negligence or other default, particularly the wasted March 8, June 7 and July 23 attendances and repeated preparation. Impecuniosity/access-to-justice arguments had already been considered and rejected. Counsel was found responsible for at least one third of the defendants' costs.
firac.conclusion: An order under rule 57.07 was warranted; the solicitor was ordered to pay $4,000 personally within 30 days.

firac.issue: To what extent should the impecunious plaintiff be relieved of, or allowed to defer, costs liability?
firac.facts: The plaintiff relied on disability pensions with a monthly surplus of about $102.70 (including a $25 charitable donation). She attended every appearance, was aware of the prior costs orders and of counsel's tactical steps, and sought to have any costs paid only after trial by set-off against any recovery.
firac.rule: Impecuniosity is a relevant but discretionary factor in awarding costs (as set out in the Master's November 2, 2007 reasons and Christian Jew Foundation v. Christian Jew Outreach, [2007] O.J. No. 2140). The court must balance access to justice against the defendants' right to compensation, and probe whether impecuniosity is invoked in good faith or as a means to avoid responsibility; modest means do not entitle a party to play by a different set of procedural rules.
firac.application: The Master had already found the plaintiff used impecuniosity as a means to avoid her litigant responsibilities, not in good faith. Allowing full deferral to after trial would let unreasonable procedures continue without consequence and risk no recovery if she lost. Balancing her finances, the Master found she could afford $50 per month (potentially foregoing the charitable donation), with the balance payable after trial.
firac.conclusion: Impecuniosity did not shield the plaintiff from costs but justified instalment payments; her share was payable at $50/month once the stay is lifted, with the balance on final disposition.

firac.issue: What quantum of costs is fair and reasonable, and how should payment be allocated and timed?
firac.facts: The defendants incurred actual costs of $28,897 and claimed $22,806 on a partial indemnity basis for the intertwined dismissal/stay and variation motions (excluding the motion before Brown J.). Counsel asserted the costs were unreasonable and sought to cross-examine on the Costs Outline but made no substantive quantum submissions.
firac.rule: Rule 57.01 factors govern; fixing costs is not merely multiplying hours by rates but must yield a fair and reasonable amount. There is no authority to cross-examine on a Costs Outline.
firac.application: The claimed hours and partial-indemnity rates were reasonable and at the lower end of the range, but the amount was reduced for similarity of issues across attendances, likely duplication between two counsel, the plaintiff's partial (indulgent) success and her financial circumstances. The Master fixed total costs at $12,000 inclusive of disbursements and GST, allocating $4,000 to the solicitor personally and $8,000 to the plaintiff by instalments.
firac.conclusion: Costs were fixed at $12,000: $4,000 payable personally by counsel within 30 days and $8,000 by the plaintiff at $50/month once the stay is lifted, balance on final disposition.

name_verification.name_in_document: B.M.G. v. S.J.S.

defining_issues: Is it in the best interests of the two children for the mother to relocate them from Vancouver to Portland, Oregon?
What income should be imputed to the mother and what amount of child support should be ordered?
Is the mother entitled to spousal support and, if so, in what amount and for what duration?
How should the family property be divided, in particular the mother's investment in Columbia Point Hospitality LLC?

firac.issue: Is it in the best interests of the children for the mother to relocate them from Vancouver to Portland, Oregon?
firac.facts: Both American-citizen parents work in academia and moved to Vancouver, where the two boys (born 2008 and 2011) have lived their whole lives; M has a learning disability supported by an IEP. Since separation the parties shared parenting roughly equally. The mother obtained contract teaching work at Portland State University and wished to move the children to Portland; the father opposed, wanting them to remain in Vancouver. Both parents testified they would move to whichever city the children lived in, so only the two shared-parenting scenarios (Vancouver vs Portland) were in issue.
firac.rule: Relocation is governed by s. 16 of the Divorce Act, under which the court considers only the best interests of the child (s. 16(8)). The governing factors are set out in Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27, as adapted to initial custody applications by Nunweiler v. Nunweiler, 2000 BCCA 300, Falvai v. Falvai, 2008 BCCA 503 and T.K. v. R.J.H.A., 2015 BCCA 8, and informed by the best-interests factors in s. 37(2) of the Family Law Act. S.S.L. v. J.W.W., 2010 BCCA 55 requires consideration of the four parenting scenarios.
firac.application: The court weighed the existing equal-parenting arrangement, the desirability of maximizing contact, the children's stated preference for Vancouver, the disruption a move would cause, and the parties' careers and finances. A move would remove the children from the only community they have known, disrupt M's established educational supports, and jeopardize the financial stability provided by the father's secure position at Capilano University; the mother's Portland employment was itself only guaranteed to June 2018, and both parents' post-move employment prospects were speculative. The Greek/Jewish cultural-heritage and extended-family factors were found insignificant against the disruption.
firac.conclusion: Relocation refused; it is in the children's best interests to remain in Vancouver, with joint custody and equal shared parenting on a 2-2-5-5 schedule once the mother returns.

firac.issue: What income should be imputed to the mother and what child support should be ordered?
firac.facts: The father's income for support was agreed at $88,250. The mother earned about $57,000 at PSU but would return to Vancouver with no immediate employment; she previously earned modest amounts as a UBC adjunct. The father sought imputation of $40,000; the mother argued for nil or, alternatively, $15,000.
firac.rule: Child support is set by reference to the Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175; with shared parenting the amount is determined by a straight set-off under s. 9. Income may be imputed based on earning capacity.
firac.application: Given the mother's narrow specialization and difficulty finding work, yet her high education and transferable skills, the court found $15,000 a reasonable imputed income while she re-establishes herself. Applying the set-off produced $1,362 payable by the father and $183 by the mother. The father's claim for repayment of alleged child-support overpayment (raised only at trial) was rejected given the agreement and the mother's likely hardship.
firac.conclusion: Income of $15,000 imputed; net child support of about $1,179/month payable by the father from July 1, 2018, with s. 7 expenses shared proportionately and reviews upon the mother obtaining Vancouver employment and annually.

firac.issue: Is the mother entitled to spousal support and, if so, in what amount and duration?
firac.facts: The father disputed compensatory entitlement but acknowledged possible needs-based entitlement once the mother returned to Vancouver. Using incomes of $88,250 and $15,000, the SSAG range was $988–$1,509/month over 4.5 to 12 years.
firac.rule: Spousal support is assessed under the Divorce Act with reference to the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines for quantum and duration.
firac.application: High-end support would give the mother roughly 54% of family income, which was unwarranted given similar household expenses; the mid-range figure was appropriate. Given the relationship history and the mother's education, intelligence and abilities, the minimum SSAG duration was appropriate.
firac.conclusion: The father pays spousal support of $1,242/month effective July 1, 2018 for 4.5 years, reviewable as to entitlement and quantum after two years and as to quantum within two months of the mother obtaining Vancouver employment.

firac.issue: How should family property be divided, particularly the mother's Columbia Point investment?
firac.facts: The father used $60,000 (USD) of family funds for pre-marriage student loans and an investment; the mother used $70,000 (USD) of family funds toward a $250,000 (USD) investment in Columbia Point, the $180,000 balance said to be a loan from her sister. The father claimed a 50% interest in the full investment ($125,000 USD plus $5,000 USD adjustment).
firac.rule: Family property is divided under the Family Law Act, with each retaining property/debt in their own name subject to equalization of family funds and jointly-held assets.
firac.application: Though the evidence of the sister's loan was weak, it was uncontradicted; the additional funds clearly came from the mother's family as loan or gift, so the father had no claim beyond his share of the $70,000 family money. The proper adjustment was payment by the mother to the father of $5,000 (USD), the difference between the parties' respective halves of the family money each had used.
firac.conclusion: Pensions and joint accounts divided equally; children's education accounts held in trust; the mother pays the father $5,000 (USD); otherwise each retains property and debt in their own name.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test for the central relocation/mobility issue. K048 (custody/access) captures the joint custody and shared parenting-time orders. case_name: Associations du Lac Paquet inc. c. Rodrigue

name_verification.name_in_document: Associations du Lac Paquet inc. c. Rodrigue

defining_issues: Do residents who revoked their membership in the Association still owe annual membership dues for the years before the revocation became effective?

How is the extent of the residents' obligation to contribute to the maintenance and repair of the access roads, lakes, dam and other installations to be determined where the servitude titles are ambiguous?
Must the residents' contribution include the Association's own operating expenses and be reduced by the municipal subsidy?
Should the special 2018 contribution of $500 be refunded, and are the Poulins entitled to $2,000 for trouble and inconvenience?

firac.issue: Do residents who revoked their Association membership owe membership dues for the years preceding the effective date of revocation?
firac.facts: After a conflict, the memberships of Rodrigue, Lapierre and the Poulins were revoked. Rodrigue clearly announced her withdrawal in 2018; Lapierre remained a director in 2019 and was present at the 2020 general meeting, and his spouse only wrote in May 2021 that they no longer wished to belong; the Poulins' revocation took effect in 2020.
firac.rule: Under art. 2276 C.c.Q. a member may withdraw from a legal person at any time but must pay dues owing at the time of withdrawal; the claimant bears the burden of proof by a preponderance of evidence (arts. 2803, 2804 C.c.Q.).
firac.application: Rodrigue's withdrawal in 2018 relieved her of the 2019 dues (with the $65 already paid to be credited). Lapierre failed to prove revocation was effective in 2019, so he owes dues of $350 for 2019 and 2020. The Poulins, whose revocation took effect in 2020, owe the $350 dues for 2019.
firac.conclusion: Rodrigue owes no 2019 dues; Lapierre must pay $700 in dues; the Poulins must pay $350 in dues.

firac.issue: How is the scope of the residents' obligation to contribute to maintenance and repair costs to be determined when the servitude titles are ambiguous?
firac.facts: Each resident's title contains real perpetual rights of way over the ring roads and access to the lake for swimming and fishing, with clauses making road repair/maintenance costs payable by those entitled to use them. The titles do not address cost-sharing for the lakes, dam, playground, lawn or fish stocking, and the evidence did not reveal the parties' original intention as to which roads were covered.
firac.rule: Servitude acts are interpreted using ordinary contract-interpretation principles (Hilborn c. De Koven, 2021 QCCA 58); where terms are clear they govern, but ambiguity requires resort to arts. 1425–1426 C.c.Q. (common intention, circumstances, prior conduct, usage) and art. 1434 C.c.Q., which allows the court to fill gaps and use equity to determine implied obligations (Churchill Falls c. Hydro-Québec, 2018 SCC 46; Baudouin/Jobin/Vézina; Lluelles/Moore).
firac.application: The clause requiring contribution to road maintenance was clear, but the titles were ambiguous on the extent of covered roads and silent on lakes/dam/installations. Absent proof of usage or original intent, the Court found the parties had consistently applied an equal per-resident annual contribution, and rejected the tri-annual average method used for 2019–2021. Under art. 1434 C.c.Q. and equity, the residents must contribute equally to actual prior-year expenses for roads and for installations they have a recognized right to use (dam, lakes, playground, lawn, fish stocking, and directly related insurance/taxes/permits), but not expenses purely tied to the Association's operations.
firac.conclusion: Contribution limited to actual prior-year maintenance/repair costs of the roads and shared installations for which residents hold usage rights; operating expenses excluded; the exact amounts for 2019–2021 left to the parties, with the Court reserving jurisdiction.

firac.issue: Must the contribution include the Association's operating expenses, and be reduced by the municipal subsidy?
firac.facts: The claimed sums included rentals, professional fees, insurance, taxes, permits and office supplies; the municipality paid the Association subsidies of $4,099.22 (2020) and $4,169.12 (2021) for road/lake maintenance, keyed to lots held by members.
firac.rule: Equity under art. 1434 C.c.Q.; the 10% administration fee was found just and reasonable; a subsidy conditioned on Association membership benefits only members (Municipal By-laws 322-2019 / 359-2021).
firac.application: Costs exclusively linked to the Association's functioning or activities (hall/arena rental, tax-return fees, office supplies) must be excluded, office items being covered by the 10% fee; but insurance, taxes, permits and licences directly tied to use of the shared installations are included. The subsidy reduction was refused because the subsidy depends on the Association's existence and is calculated on members' lots.
firac.conclusion: Operating expenses excluded; the residents' contribution is not reduced by the municipal subsidy.

firac.issue: Should the $500 special contribution be refunded and are the Poulins entitled to $2,000 for trouble and inconvenience?
firac.facts: Lapierre sought reimbursement of a $500 special 2018 contribution for acquisition of roads and lakes (a transaction that never occurred); the Poulins asked it be credited. The Association's minutes showed the special levy was for dam reconstruction, road/lake acquisition being funded from working capital. The Poulins claimed $2,000 for trouble caused by repeated demands but led no evidence.
firac.rule: Burden of proof by preponderance of evidence (arts. 2803, 2804 C.c.Q.).
firac.application: The 6 May 2018 minutes confirmed the special levy funded the dam, so no refund was due; Lapierre's counterclaim was dismissed and the Poulins ordered to pay the full 2019 dues. The Poulins offered no evidence supporting the $2,000 claim.
firac.conclusion: Both counterclaims dismissed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Bohbot c. Weinberger

defining_issues: Did the trial judge commit a palpable and overriding error in finding David was mentally capable until 'sometime in 2006' and that Thérèse did not exploit a vulnerable person contrary to art. 48 of the Quebec Charter?
Did the judge err in refusing to declare Thérèse unworthy of inheriting under art. 621 C.c.Q.?
Did the judge err in declining to hold the accountant Léonard Mintz personally liable?
Did the judge err in refusing to remove Thérèse and Léonard as liquidators (while removing Dan) and in ordering the estate to reimburse their legal fees?
Did the judge err in finding certain of the appellants' proceedings abusive and awarding moral damages to Thérèse?

firac.issue: Did the trial judge commit a reviewable error in finding David remained capable until around 2006 and that Thérèse did not exploit him as a vulnerable person under art. 48 of the Quebec Charter?
firac.facts: David Bohbot, a real-estate businessman diagnosed with a degenerative brain disease, sold numerous properties from 2003 onward, sometimes through his second wife Thérèse acting under a general mandate and an unhomologated protection mandate. His children argued he became incapable in June 2005 (after a fall) and was in any event a dependent, vulnerable person whom Thérèse exploited, seeking repayment of all spending above an arbitrary $185,000/year.
firac.rule: Capacity is a question of fact, provable by testimony and medical/psychosocial evidence. Appellate intervention requires a palpable and overriding error (Housen c. Nikolaisen, 2002 CSC 33). Art. 48 of the Quebec Charter grants aged or handicapped persons protection against exploitation, requiring a global, contextual analysis; absent exploitation, the provision does not apply (Vallée, 2005 QCCA 316). The burden of proving misappropriation lay on the plaintiffs.
firac.application: The judge relied not only on Thérèse's testimony but on numerous lay witnesses and the more nuanced expert evidence of the respondents, concluding David was competent until 2006-2007. The $185,000 ceiling was arbitrary; the plaintiffs' own forensic accountants identified no inappropriate expense, and the Deloitte report showed most spending benefited David and the family, decreasing after 2006. The appellants themselves benefited from David's generosity. The failure to homologate the protection mandate could be a fault but caused no proven prejudice. No exploitation was established, so art. 48 did not apply.
firac.conclusion: No palpable and overriding error; the ground was rejected.

firac.issue: Did the judge err in refusing to declare Thérèse unworthy of inheriting under art. 621 C.c.Q.?
firac.facts: The appellants alleged Thérèse dissipated assets and fabricated a document to conceal a $450,000 bonus David paid her in November 2005; they claimed to have discovered the bonus only in 2013.
firac.rule: Art. 621 C.c.Q. permits a declaration of unworthiness for seriously reprehensible conduct toward the deceased; the action must be brought within one year (art. 623 C.c.Q.) and requires grave, voluntary and intentional acts such as embezzlement or fraud, not mere faulty administration (Y.L. c. Yv.V., 2010 QCCA 808).
firac.application: David was capable when he paid the bonus. Even accepting that Thérèse tried to hide the payment (attributed by the judge to a clerical error), such conduct was not reprehensible conduct toward the deceased. The judge drew no negative inference; this factual finding disclosed no palpable and overriding error.
firac.conclusion: Ground rejected; unnecessary to decide prescription.

firac.issue: Did the judge err in declining to hold the accountant Léonard Mintz personally liable?
firac.facts: The appellants argued Léonard should have ceased serving David and Thérèse, warned the family of the spending, and that a conflict arose from preparing both spouses' tax returns.
firac.rule: Liability requires a fault; a professional cannot improvise as judge of a couple's spending absent knowledge and duty.
firac.application: Léonard's alleged faults were entirely derivative of the alleged faults of Thérèse. Since no misappropriation by Thérèse was established, the reproaches against Léonard failed. He had no precise knowledge of David's condition and no obligation to intervene; a related disciplinary complaint had been dismissed.
firac.conclusion: Ground rejected.

firac.issue: Did the judge err in refusing to remove Thérèse and Léonard as liquidators and in ordering reimbursement of their fees by the estate?
firac.facts: The three co-liquidators (Thérèse, Dan, Léonard) were in deep conflict; Dan systematically obstructed the liquidation. The judge removed Dan but maintained Thérèse and Léonard and ordered the estate to reimburse their liquidation-related legal fees.
firac.rule: Removal of a liquidator is an extreme and exceptional measure; the guiding question is whether the liquidator acted honestly and in the estate's best interest.
firac.application: Removal of Thérèse and Léonard was sought only conditionally on a finding of misappropriation, which failed. The judge found they acted honestly and in the estate's best interest, while Dan's quarrelsome, obstructive conduct justified his removal. No reviewable error was shown.
firac.conclusion: Ground rejected, including as to reimbursement of fees.

firac.issue: Did the judge err in finding certain proceedings abusive and awarding moral damages to Thérèse?
firac.facts: The judge held the original accounting action was not abusive but that Dan and Véronique's conduct during the litigation was, through improper safeguard motions, refusal to honour a transaction, and illegal subpoenas to third parties, awarding legal-fee reimbursement and $50,000 in moral damages.
firac.rule: Abuse of procedure is governed by arts. 51 ff. C.p.c.; awards of damages attract a particularly rigorous standard of appellate intervention (Laniel-Supérieur, 2019 QCCA 753).
firac.application: The proceedings the appellants called 'victorious' were not truly so; the safeguard order actually favoured the respondents, and the allegations supporting one motion were found false. The appellants did not challenge the illegal-subpoena finding. Given the humiliation Thérèse suffered and the needless impleading of third parties, the moral-damages award disclosed no error.
firac.conclusion: Ground rejected.

keywords_rationale: The core of the case is a succession dispute over estate administration, liquidation and a claim of unworthiness to inherit under art. 621 C.c.Q., squarely engaging K054 (wills/estates) and its tier-1 parent K006 (Family law). name_verification.name_in_document: Boardwalk Contracting Inc. v. Naples

defining_issues: What legal threshold governs an application for security for costs against an impecunious corporate plaintiff?
Do the applicants (defendants) have an arguable defence such that security should not be ordered?

Does the fact that the plaintiff's impecuniosity may be attributable to the defendants' conduct, or the existence of the defendant's counterclaim, displace the general rule favouring security for costs?
What is the appropriate quantum of security for costs?

firac.issue: What legal threshold governs an application for security for costs against an impecunious corporate plaintiff?
firac.facts: Boardwalk, a corporate plaintiff, conceded through the affidavit of Ms. Naples that it had no funds or assets to pay a costs award if it failed. It argued the jurisdiction should be exercised 'sparingly and in very special circumstances', relying on Tylon 1, while the defendant-applicants argued that once impecuniosity is shown security is 'generally ordered'.
firac.rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 empowers the court to order a plaintiff corporation to post security for a defendant's costs where it appears the corporation will be unable to pay them if the defence succeeds. Under Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd. (1997) and Fat Mel's Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co. (1993), corporate plaintiffs are not treated with the same generosity as natural persons; once a defendant shows a prima facie case that the corporate plaintiff cannot pay costs, security is 'generally ordered' unless there is no arguable defence, and the onus shifts to the plaintiff (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress (1999)).
firac.application: The court held the applicants' position correct. Tylon 1 concerned an application against an individual under the Builders Lien Act and involved a plaintiff seeking security for its own costs — fundamentally different circumstances. The authorities distinguish sharply between individuals (for whom poverty is no bar) and corporate plaintiffs, for whom security is generally ordered once impecuniosity is established. Boardwalk having conceded it lacked exigible assets, the onus shifted to it to displace the general rule.
firac.conclusion: An order for security for costs should generally issue against an impecunious corporate plaintiff lacking exigible assets, unless the plaintiff shows the defendant has no arguable defence or that the action would be stifled.

firac.issue: Do the defendant-applicants have an arguable defence such that security should not be ordered?
firac.facts: Boardwalk advanced a conspiracy claim (that Mr. Naples and Mr. Beiderwieden conspired to abandon Boardwalk and start Nixon) and a breach of fiduciary duty claim (that Mr. Beiderwieden, a senior employee, set up a competing business using former Boardwalk employees and clients).
firac.rule: Per Kropp, the court may have regard to the merits but should avoid detailed examination unless success or failure appears obvious. Once impecuniosity is shown, security is generally ordered unless the court is satisfied there is no arguable defence (Fat Mel's).
firac.application: On the conspiracy claim, the court found Mr. Beiderwieden and Nixon had an arguable defence and doubted Boardwalk even had an arguable claim, which counsel did not press. On the stronger fiduciary duty claim, the defendants argued Boardwalk had constructively dismissed Beiderwieden, could not perform the contracts, and that former clients approached Nixon; the court was satisfied arguable defences existed against this claim too.
firac.conclusion: The applicants have arguable defences to both central claims, so the general rule favouring security is not displaced on this ground.

firac.issue: Do the plaintiff's impecuniosity being attributable to the defendants' conduct, or the existence of the defendant's counterclaim, displace the general rule?
firac.facts: Boardwalk argued its financial collapse was caused by the defendants' conduct and that Mr. Beiderwieden's counterclaim for wrongful dismissal and breach of employment contract concerned the same events, making it unjust to order security.
firac.rule: Where a corporate plaintiff's impecuniosity is linked to the cause of action against the defendant, the court may exercise its discretion against ordering security or reduce the amount (Split Vision Eyewear Inc. v. The Economical Insurance Group, 2010 BCSC 396; Scotford Electrical). A plaintiff must also show it has no means of raising the funds, not merely that it lacks assets (Kropp; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform). Where a counterclaim is so intertwined that it constitutes the 'real dispute', security may be refused (Gray v. Powerassist Technologies Inc., 2001 BCSC 1208; Paul v. General Magnaplate Corp.).
firac.application: The court found it unclear that Boardwalk's failure was caused by the applicants — the defendants' thesis was that Ms. Naples and her father caused the collapse; and Nixon had only performed about $200,000 of work versus Boardwalk's ~$1.8M average annual revenues, making causation unlikely. Boardwalk also failed to show it could not raise funds — Ms. Naples, as director and principal shareholder, had assets (a Kelowna cabin, sale proceeds, a condominium) that were not addressed. On the counterclaim, unlike Gray, Beiderwieden's modest wrongful dismissal claim was dwarfed by Boardwalk's action in monetary terms and complexity; Boardwalk's claim was the 'real claim'.
firac.conclusion: Neither the alleged causal link nor the counterclaim displaced the general rule, though the counterclaim was relevant to quantum.

firac.issue: What is the appropriate quantum of security for costs?
firac.facts: The applicants sought $133,150, representing anticipated disbursements (including expert fees) and party-and-party costs for a 10-day trial, figures not challenged as unreasonable by Boardwalk.
firac.rule: The court can order any amount up to the full amount claimed, provided it is more than nominal, and should fix such security as is just in all the circumstances (Kropp; Fat Mel's adopting Procon (Great Britain) Ltd. v. Provincial Building Co.). An arbitrary discount of estimated future costs may be appropriate.
firac.application: The court accepted the applicants' figures as reasonable, possibly conservative, but weighed the relative complexity of Boardwalk's claim, its claims for general and punitive damages, Beiderwieden's counterclaim, the concern about stifling Boardwalk's claim, and Ms. Naples' failure to address alternate means of posting security. It declined to make a 'guillotine' order dismissing the claim, as such orders require exceptional circumstances (Global Banking Systems Inc. v. Datawest Solutions Inc., 2006 BCCA 577).
firac.conclusion: Boardwalk was ordered to post $60,000 as security within 30 days, failing which its claim would be stayed (not dismissed). Costs of the application in the cause.

keywords_rationale: This is a civil procedure/civil litigation matter, so K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area. The application concerns security for costs and the potential stay of proceedings — the closest available procedural remedy keyword in the controlled vocabulary is K021 (interlocutory injunction), used loosely for interim civil-procedure relief; this is a weak/borderline fit since the vocabulary has no dedicated 'security for costs' or 'stay of proceedings' term. K085 (wrongful dismissal) applies because the defendant Beiderwieden's counterclaim was for wrongful dismissal and breach of employment contract, a factor the court weighed. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward human rights, Charter, hate speech and immigration topics and offers no keywords for security for costs, impecunious corporate plaintiff, fiduciary duty, or conspiracy, so fewer than five genuinely applicable keywords exist; K021 and K085 are the closest procedural/substantive matches and are flagged as weak.

registry_rationale: The primary docket (S1610516) lists 'Registry: Vancouver', and the hearing and judgment both took place in Vancouver. (A related family docket E50347 is out of New Westminster registry, but the civil action giving rise to this application is in the Vancouver registry.)

name_verification.name_in_document: Gloria Augustus, personally and as legal heir of Anthony Griffin v. Allan Gosset and Montreal Urban Community; Orberth Griffin, Intervenant

defining_issues: Was Constable Gosset civilly liable under Art. 1053 C.C. for causing Anthony Griffin's death through an excessive and unjustified use of force?

Did Constable Gosset's conduct amount to an 'unlawful and intentional interference' with Griffin's right to personal security under s. 1 of the Quebec Charter, so as to warrant exemplary damages under s. 49?
Is the Montreal Urban Community vicariously liable for exemplary damages under Art. 1054 C.C. for the acts of its police officer?
Is the deceased victim's right to claim exemplary damages transmissible to his heirs?
What quantum of compensatory damages is recoverable by the parents under Arts. 1053 and 1056 C.C.?

firac.issue: Was Constable Gosset civilly liable under Art. 1053 C.C. for causing Anthony Griffin's death through excessive and unjustified use of force?
firac.facts: Gosset, a 14-year veteran, arrested the unarmed, cooperative Griffin on a bench warrant. In the Station 15 parking lot in broad daylight Griffin fled a few steps; Gosset ran after him alone with his revolver drawn, ordered him to stop, and Griffin stopped and turned to face him. Gosset raised the revolver one-handed with his finger on the trigger at close range and it discharged, killing Griffin.
firac.rule: Art. 1053 C.C. (delictual fault). Police have wide duties but limited powers and must act within the law; use of force in arrest/flight is governed by s. 25(1), (3) and (4) of the Criminal Code, which justify only 'as much force as necessary' and force likely to cause death only where reasonably necessary to prevent death/grievous harm; s. 25(4) is strictly construed (Roberge v. R.; Béliveau v. Lafond; Carrière v. Cité de Longueuil; Charrette v. Dorais). Firearms demand a duty of care bordering on strict liability.
firac.application: Griffin had been searched and had no weapon, made no threatening gesture, and stopped fleeing on the first order to stop, so no justification for lethal force existed. Gosset was negligent in running with a drawn revolver and in pointing it at close range with his finger on the trigger while it could be in single-action 'hair-trigger' mode. This negligence directly caused the death; the force was wholly unnecessary and unjustified.
firac.conclusion: Gosset is liable under Art. 1053 C.C. for the compensatory damages resulting from Griffin's death.

firac.issue: Did Gosset's conduct constitute an 'unlawful and intentional interference' with Charter rights, warranting exemplary damages under s. 49 of the Quebec Charter?
firac.facts: Gosset consciously and deliberately chased Griffin alone, drew his revolver, shouted 'Stop or I'll shoot', and raised the loaded revolver one-handed at near point-blank range; the gun then fired, though he did not intend to fire.
firac.rule: S. 49(2) Quebec Charter allows exemplary damages for 'unlawful and intentional interference' with a protected right (here s. 1 right to personal security and inviolability). Gross negligence ('faute lourde') alone is insufficient; the threshold is close to wanton/reckless misconduct ('faute lourde dolosive'), and the intention to cause the harmful result may be inferred from an act done with reckless disregard for known probable consequences (Baudouin; Rousseau-Houle; Chevalier in West Island Teachers' Assn v. Nantel; Perret).
firac.application: Pointing a loaded revolver one-handed with a finger on the trigger at near point-blank range demonstrated a wanton and reckless disregard for Griffin's life; the eminently foreseeable discharge could not be dismissed as accident. Subjective intent to breach the right need not be proven; the requisite intention is inferred from the act itself.
firac.conclusion: Gosset's conduct was an unlawful and intentional interference with Griffin's s. 1 rights; exemplary damages of $8,000 (split $4,000 to each parent) were awarded, reduced in view of his suspension and dismissal and lost salary.

firac.issue: Is the Montreal Urban Community vicariously liable for exemplary damages under Art. 1054 C.C.?
firac.facts: The MUC admitted compensatory liability, paid Gosset's defence costs under its collective agreement, but suspended, then dismissed him, and contested his reinstatement.
firac.rule: Vicarious punishment is contrary to fundamental principle; an employer (especially a public body) should not bear exemplary damages for a s. 1 Charter breach unless it expressly or implicitly authorized or ratified both the act and the manner of its commission (distinguishing Robichaud and Janzen, which rested on the statute itself, not vicarious liability).
firac.application: The MUC did not authorize the level of force used; payment of legal fees flowed from a contractual obligation, not ratification; and suspension, dismissal and opposition to reinstatement negated any inference of ratification. Imposing exemplary damages on a public body would only punish innocent taxpayers.
firac.conclusion: The MUC is not vicariously liable for exemplary damages (though it remains liable jointly and severally for compensatory damages).

firac.issue: Is the deceased victim's right to claim exemplary damages transmissible to his heirs?
firac.facts: Griffin died intestate with no siblings; his sole heirs are his mother (plaintiff) and father (intervenant). The Quebec Charter is silent on survival of the s. 49 claim.
firac.rule: Arts. 596, 607 and 626 C.C. transmit all transmissible rights and actions to heirs; only rights of action incapable by their nature of surviving the person are excluded (Green v. Elmhurst Dairy; Mayrand; Lévesque v. Malinosky). Art. 1085 C.C. (conditional obligations) applies by analogy. Ambiguous remedial legislation is read to fulfil the legislature's purpose.
firac.application: Barring transmission would perversely make it advantageous to kill rather than wound a victim and would defeat s. 49's deterrent purpose. The right to exemplary damages is patrimonial from its birth and, like the transmissible right to moral damages, passes to the heirs. Griffin's claim arose the instant Gosset unlawfully and intentionally pointed the revolver.
firac.conclusion: The right to claim exemplary damages is transmissible to Griffin's heirs, who recover it equally under Art. 626 C.C.

firac.issue: What quantum of compensatory damages is recoverable by the parents under Arts. 1053 and 1056 C.C.?
firac.facts: Griffin was 19, a school dropout with a criminal record, unemployed, estranged from both parents, and had never contributed financially to them; his estate was insolvent. The mother was financially secure; the father had abandoned the family and had other children.
firac.rule: Art. 1056 C.C. permits near relatives to recover funeral expenses (if the estate cannot pay), and loss of future support; Quebec law denies solatium doloris, loss of life expectancy (caused by death), and pain and suffering where the victim never regained consciousness (Pantel v. Air Canada; Driver v. Coca-Cola; Bergeron v. Gagnon-Ellefsen); awards for loss of a child must not be inflated by American precedents (Maheux v. Lavallée; Bulger).
firac.application: Funeral expenses of $3,591 were split equally as the estate was insolvent; no award for loss of life expectancy, pain and suffering (Griffin never regained consciousness), or solatium doloris. Given the improbability of any future material support, loss of support/moral support was fixed at $9,000 to the mother and $2,000 to the father.
firac.conclusion: Compensatory damages of $10,795 to the plaintiff and $3,795 to the intervenant, awarded jointly and severally against both defendants with interest and additional indemnity from service.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area: the action is a delictual/quasi-delictual damages claim under Arts. 1053, 1054 and 1056 C.C. K007 (Human rights) and K120 (Quebec Charter) capture the central s. 49 / s. 1 Quebec Charter claim for exemplary damages for interference with personal security. K069 (discrimination) and K065 (racism) reflect the plaintiff's substantial (though ultimately rejected) allegation that the shooting resulted from racial discrimination against a black youth by police — these are weaker picks since the court expressly found no racial discrimination, but the allegation was contested and argued at length. K071 (human dignity) is borderline, tied to the Charter preamble's protection of dignity relied on in the transmissibility analysis. No vocabulary term precisely captures 'exemplary damages,' 'police use of force,' or 'vicarious liability,' which are the true doctrinal core.
