registry_rationale: The court file line reads 'Toronto DFO-18-15996', indicating the Toronto registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

case_name: Attorney General of Canada (The Republic of France) v. Diab

name_verification.name_in_document: Attorney General of Canada (The Republic of France) v. Diab
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The style of cause and lead citation match the supplied metadata. The only irregularity is in the closing citation block, which reads 'Attorney General of Canada (Republic of France), 2010 ONSC 337' — an apparent typographical error in the year (2010) and an abbreviated party line — but the operative citation throughout is 2011 ONSC 337.

defining_issues: Did the Republic of France commit an abuse of process violating Hassan Diab's Charter rights such that a stay of proceedings should be granted?
Was the Bisotti handwriting-comparison report so manifestly unreliable that it should be excluded from the Record of the Case?
Was there sufficient evidence in the Record of the Case to justify committing Hassan Diab to stand trial in France?

firac.issue: Did the requesting state's conduct in preparing and presenting the Record of the Case constitute an abuse of process warranting a stay of the extradition proceedings?
firac.facts: Counsel for Diab identified nine alleged misrepresentations (omissions, inaccuracies, contradictions) between the ROC and material otherwise provided by France (MLAT affidavits, letters rogatory, exhibits, witness examinations), arguing France either deliberately manipulated the material to appear inculpatory or acted without due diligence. Examples included the Madrid-to-Paris false-passport theory, the Antwerp/Copernic comparison, the Sayeh reconnaissance timing, and the 'Zaki Helou' name.
firac.rule: A stay for abuse of process is reserved for the 'clearest of cases' (USA v. Cobb, 2001 SCC 19). In the extradition context a Charter/abuse claim requires an 'air of reality' (R. v. Larosa). A failure of due diligence amounts to abuse only where the certifying authority's conduct falls so far below a reasonable standard as to defeat the presumption of accuracy (UK v. Tarantino, 2003 BCSC 1134), and a remedy such as excision was granted for misrepresented evidence in USA v. Thomlison, 2007 ONCA 42. A requesting state has no duty of full disclosure (Germany v. Krapohl).
firac.application: The court found the air-of-reality threshold met but held that, examined individually, each alleged misrepresentation either arose from the unconventional, pleading-like nature of the ROC, was an inadvertent error (e.g. the Madrid passport theory, the 'illegible' Arabic stamps), concerned material with no bearing on committal, or amounted to non-disclosure of information the state was under no duty to disclose. All the impugned material had itself been provided by France, making deliberate malfeasance implausible. Unlike Tarantino and Thomlison, none of the irregularities touched the evidence actually relied on for committal (passport, PFLP membership, sketches/photos, handwriting).
firac.conclusion: No abuse of process and no Charter breach; even had one been found it would not meet the 'clearest of cases' threshold. Stay refused.

firac.issue: Should the Bisotti handwriting report be excised from the ROC as manifestly unreliable?
firac.facts: France's committal case rested substantially on Ms. Bisotti's report concluding a 'very strong presumption' that Diab authored the Celtic Hotel registration card. Three eminent document examiners (Lindblom, Osborne, Radley) testified the report was biased, that Bisotti was unqualified, and that her methodology was fatally flawed (counting similarities, treating dissimilarities as natural variation, comparing dissimilar signatures, using samples written 15 years later).
firac.rule: Under the Extradition Act, ROC evidence is presumptively reliable (s. 32; USA v. Michaelov, 2010 ONCA 819). The presumption is rebutted only by showing evidence is 'manifestly unreliable' or 'so defective' that it would be dangerous or unsafe to convict on it (USA v. Ferras, 2006 SCC 33; Thomlison). The extradition judge may not weigh competing inferences, assess credibility, or apply domestic admissibility standards such as R. v. Abbey (USA v. Anderson).
firac.application: The court found the report convoluted, confusing and highly susceptible to criticism, but held that to conclude the expert was biased, unqualified or used improper methodology required choosing between competing interpretations of the mandate wording and c.v., and preferring the Diab experts over the French expert — the very weighing of competing inferences reserved for the trier of fact. The critics had no experience with French practice, leaving open that France uses a different accepted methodology. Applying Canadian Abbey admissibility standards would offend the statute. This was strong criticism plus competing inferences, not manifest unreliability (contrasted with the earlier withdrawn reports that had used the wrong person's handwriting).
firac.conclusion: The report was not manifestly unreliable; the application to exclude it was denied.

firac.issue: Did the ROC contain sufficient evidence to justify committing Diab for trial in France?
firac.facts: With the 'intelligence', argument and speculation removed by agreement, the reduced circumstantial case had five components: Diab's 1980 passport (showing travel to Spain around the bombing), evidence of PFLP membership, divergent eyewitness descriptions of 'Panadriyu', composite sketches/photographs, and the Bisotti handwriting report. It was admitted a synagogue bombing occurred on 3 October 1980 killing four and injuring over 40, and that the fictitious Panadriyu was a perpetrator; the only live issue was identifying Diab as Panadriyu.
firac.rule: Under s. 29(1)(a) of the Extradition Act the test is whether there is evidence, available for trial and not manifestly unreliable, on which a properly instructed jury acting reasonably could convict (Ferras; USA v. Thomlison; Michaelov). The Ontario Court of Appeal's more restrictive reading — not the 'unreasonable verdict' test urged by Diab and reflected in the BC Graham line — governs; weakness or unlikelihood of conviction is irrelevant. Limited weighing of circumstantial evidence is permitted only to assess whether it can reasonably support the requested inference (R. v. Arcuri).
firac.application: The passport, PFLP membership, eyewitness descriptions and sketches/photographs, individually or together, created only suspicion and were insufficient. The handwriting evidence tipped the scale: if accepted, it provided a reasonably strong circumstantial link between Diab and Panadriyu. A jury considering the handwriting evidence with the other evidence could find Diab was Panadriyu. Although the judge considered the overall case weak and conviction unlikely, binding authority mandates committal where such evidence exists.
firac.conclusion: Sufficient evidence existed; Diab was ordered committed into custody under s. 29(1)(a) to await the Minister's surrender decision.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 anchor: extradition committal turns on whether the conduct discloses a prima facie criminal case (murder, attempted murder, mischief). K037 (terrorism) is central — the charges arise from a terrorist synagogue bombing attributed to the PFLP-SO. K058 (antisemitism) and K105 (synagogue) capture the antisemitic terrorist attack targeting a synagogue congregation, and K093/K027 reflect the Jewish victims and the fact the bombing coincided with Simchat Torah (a Jewish holiday). K107 (Charter) and K112 (Charter s. 7) are engaged by the abuse-of-process/liberty-and-security analysis grounded in s. 7 (Ferras). K012 (procedural fairness) is the closest vocabulary match for the abuse-of-process/due-diligence argument, since the controlled list has no dedicated 'abuse of process' or 'extradition' term — this and the absence of an extradition keyword are the main gaps in fit.

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff's action be dismissed or stayed under rules 57.03(2) and 60.12 for failure to pay two unpaid interlocutory costs orders?
What role does an impecunious litigant's inability to pay costs play in the court's discretion on a motion to dismiss or stay for non-payment of costs?

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's action be dismissed or stayed for failure to pay two interlocutory costs orders that were never appealed?
firac.facts: The plaintiff sued Peel police for assault, false arrest, false imprisonment and Charter breaches. Through years of default (unanswered undertakings, missed deadlines, two adjourned trial dates), Master Dash awarded costs of $5,000 (Oct. 19, 2006, the 'first unpaid costs order') and $1,250 on an amendment motion (Dec. 18, 2006, the 'second unpaid costs order'). Neither was paid or appealed; two motions to vary (before Brown J. and Master Dash) failed. The defendants moved to dismiss or stay under rules 57.03(2) and 60.12.
firac.rule: Rule 57.03(2): where a party fails to pay costs of a motion, the court may dismiss or stay the proceeding, strike the defence, or make 'such other order as is just.' Rule 60.12: where a party fails to comply with an interlocutory order, the court may stay or dismiss the proceeding or make such other order as is just. Costs are discretionary (Courts of Justice Act s. 133(1); rule 57.01). Authorities (Baksh, Stacey v. Barrie Yacht Club, Heu v. Forder Estate, Myers v. Toronto Police, Christian Jew Foundation, Larabie v. Montfils) hold orders must be enforced and impecuniosity is not an automatic shield, while dismissal is an extreme last-resort remedy.
firac.application: The Master found the costs had been imposed to sanction a 'total abandonment' of the plaintiff's litigant obligations rather than merely a lost motion; counsel Mr. Guiste had ignored undertakings and consent orders for ten months. A dismissal would be justified, but as an extreme remedy the court preferred to stay the action to give the plaintiff (or Mr. Guiste) a last chance to pay. The stay was tied only to the first unpaid costs order ($5,000), because the second order arose from a reasonable amendment motion rather than from flouting court orders.
firac.conclusion: The action was stayed; the stay may be lifted on payment of the balance of the October 19, 2006 costs order with interest. If not lifted within six months the defendants may move to dismiss. The December 18, 2006 costs need not be paid to lift the stay (payable after final disposition, in any event of the cause).

firac.issue: How should the court weigh a litigant's impecuniosity when deciding whether to enforce costs by dismissal or stay?
firac.facts: The plaintiff was disabled, on social assistance, with income of about $542.70/month against expenses of $440, and argued that dismissal for unpaid costs she could not afford would deny her access to the courts and a Charter s. 24 remedy. Her impecuniosity had already been considered when the costs were awarded.
firac.rule: Under rule 57.01(1)(i) ('any other matter relevant to the issue of costs') impecuniosity is a relevant but not determinative factor. Following Walsh, Christian Jew Foundation and Larabie v. Montfils, the court retains discretion to give impecuniosity whatever weight is just, probing the litigant's 'procedural good faith' — whether impecuniosity is a genuine explanation or merely a shield to avoid responsibilities. Access to justice must be balanced against the defendant's rights and the court's need to retain control over its process.
firac.application: The court accepted the plaintiff was impecunious but found no link between her poverty and the failures to answer undertakings or obey Master Clark's order; impecuniosity was raised solely to avoid the consequences of the defaults, not in good faith. This was not costs against a party who lost a motion brought in good faith, so impecuniosity carried little weight. Nonetheless the court tempered the sanction by staying rather than dismissing.
firac.conclusion: Impecuniosity did not shield the plaintiff from the costs sanction; a stay conditional on payment of the first costs order was the just result, recognizing both the need to enforce orders and the drastic nature of dismissal.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing practice area: the decision turns entirely on the Rules of Civil Procedure (rr. 57.03(2), 60.12, 57.01, 59.06) and the enforcement of interlocutory costs orders. The underlying claim was against police for assault, false arrest and Charter breaches, and counsel sought a remedy under s. 24 grounded in Charter s. 7, hence K107 (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms) and K112 (Charter s. 7). The plaintiff sought to add a plea of racial profiling in support of the Charter claim, engaging K065 (racism) and K069 (discrimination). name_verification.name_in_document: The Children's Aid Society of the Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. K.M. and J.R.

defining_issues: Did the procedural defects in service and timing under the Family Law Rules justify setting aside the summary judgment order granting Crown Wardship without access?
Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial such that summary judgment for Crown Wardship without access was improperly granted?

firac.issue: Did the procedural defects in service and timing justify setting aside the summary judgment order?
firac.facts: J.R. was served the summary judgment motion and affidavit on May 28, 2010, and the amended amended protection application seeking Crown Wardship without access on June 1, 2010. The motion was heard June 2, 2010. Under Rule 14(11) the motion could not be heard before June 3, and under Rule 11(2)1 J.R. had 14 days to file an answer.
firac.rule: Family Law Rules: r. 14(11) (motion with notice to be served not later than four days before motion date); r. 11(2)1 (14 days to amend/answer after amended application); r. 6(10) (courier service effective day after pickup); overarching primary objective of dealing with cases justly (r. 2), balanced against the best-interests imperative and time-line constraints in child protection cases.
firac.application: The court found that the order granted June 2, 2010 clearly violated the rules on time and service, and did not condone the CAS's 'rush to judgment,' noting a three-week adjournment would have been the better course. However, procedural fairness had to be weighed against the child's best interests and the danger of leaving children in 'litigation limbo,' and remitting the matter would only delay an inevitable outcome since J.R. had no viable plan.
firac.conclusion: Although the rules on service and timing were breached, the defect did not warrant setting aside the order because sending the matter back would merely delay the inevitable and would not serve the children's best interests.

firac.issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial precluding summary judgment for Crown Wardship without access?
firac.facts: The children (ages 8, 5, 2) had been apprehended amid long-standing family violence and substance abuse by both parents, drug trafficking charges, breaches of restraining orders, and no viable long-term plan of care. J.R.'s affidavit expressed love for his children and general intentions to improve but gave no particulars; there was no evidence he had ever cared for the children alone or could do so.
firac.rule: Family Law Rule 16(1),(4.1),(6): after an answer, a party may move for summary judgment; the responding party must set out specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial and cannot rest on mere allegations or denials; if there is no genuine issue the court shall make a final order. The court must take a 'good hard look' at the full evidentiary record (CAS of Waterloo v. V.L., 2006 CanLII 32610, aff'd 2007 ONCA 113; CAS of Toronto v. R.H.), guided by the best interests of the child (s. 1 CFSA; CAS of Toronto v. C.M., [1994] 2 SCR 165; CAS of Toronto v. D.P. and R.L., 2005 CanLII 34560). A genuine issue requires more than a heartfelt desire to resume care.
firac.application: J.R.'s affidavit contained only general boilerplate statements of future intention without particulars and no relevant fresh evidence. He offered no arguable evidence of new parenting ability or better prospects than at apprehension. Given the children's need for permanency and the record of unaddressed dysfunction, there was no genuine issue for trial.
firac.conclusion: Justice McSorley's summary judgment satisfied the test; the appeal was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area, this being a child protection/Crown Wardship appeal. K047 (best interests of the child) is central, as the court repeatedly grounded its analysis in the best-interests imperative and the danger of 'litigation limbo.' K012 (procedural fairness) captures the contested service/timing defects and the appellant's fairness argument. K048 (custody/access) is engaged because the order was Crown Wardship with no access — a weaker pick since access was not independently litigated. K014 (standard of review) applies to the court's discussion of the appellate standard for summary judgment, though it is a borderline tier-2 admin-law term used here in a family appeal context. There is no controlled-vocabulary term for child protection/Crown wardship or summary judgment specifically, so these are the closest fits.

The summary judgment motion was returnable in Kitchener and service documents were directed to a Kitchener address, indicating the matter proceeded at Kitchener; province is Ontario per 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE'.
registry_rationale: No registry is expressly named beyond court file FS-64/10, but the motions were returnable in Kitchener within the Waterloo region, so Kitchener is the most probable registry.

case_name: Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. A.M.

name_verification.name_in_document: Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. A.M.

defining_issues: Is the 11-month-old child in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b) of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017?
If the child is in need of protection, is intervention through a court order necessary to protect the child in the future?
What dispositional order is in the child's best interests?
What terms of access are in the child's best interests?

firac.issue: Is the child in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b) of the CYFSA?
firac.facts: The mother has a diagnosis of Bipolar 1 disorder, had recent suicidal ideation days before trial, is non-compliant with her medication (which she stopped unilaterally) and prescribed DBT therapy, lacks family or community supports, and has none of her four children in her care. She twice asked the society to take the newborn, brought the child to a kith caregiver (H.O.) in July 2023, and has left access visits early when triggered. The child is only 11 months old and requires full-time supervision.
firac.rule: Under s. 74(2)(b) CYFSA a child is in need of protection where there is a risk the child is likely to suffer physical harm from the caregiver's failure to adequately care for/supervise or a pattern of neglect. The society bears the onus on a balance of probabilities (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. RM, 2019 ONSC 2251). The risk must be real and likely, not speculative (CAS Rainy River v. B.(C.), 2006 ONCJ 458). Mental illness does not automatically place a child at risk; the court weighs the R.S. factors (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. R.S., 2019 ONCJ 866), and people with mental illness may be upset without their conduct being pathologized (Re Sim, 2020 ONCA 563). Past conduct is admissible under s. 93(1).
firac.application: Applying the R.S. factors, the court found the mother's mental illness severe, chronic and affecting her functioning and parenting; she lacked insight, was non-compliant with treatment, had no support system, and the child's young age made him more vulnerable. Her denial of her diagnosis in her affidavit (later admitted at trial) undermined her credibility. The real and likely risk of physical harm was established.
firac.conclusion: The child was found in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b)(i) and (ii).

firac.issue: Is a court order necessary to protect the child in the future?
firac.facts: The mother had not addressed the mental health concerns that led to society involvement, had unilaterally stopped medication, had no viable plan or supports, was hostile to her family services worker, and the father was in default and not involved.
firac.rule: Section 101(1) CYFSA requires the court to be satisfied that intervention through a court order is necessary to protect the child in the future; if not, s. 101(8) requires return to the prior caregiver. The court may consider concerns beyond those that brought the child into care (CAS Toronto v. S.P., 2019 ONSC 3482), and the best interests of the child are the determining element (CCAS Metro Toronto v. C.M., [1994] 2 SCR 165).
firac.application: The degree of risk remained high, the mother's mental health may be deteriorating, she had no viable plan or supports, and the court was not confident she would cooperate with a supervision order in her care. Less disruptive alternatives such as terms of supervision in her care would be inadequate.
firac.conclusion: A protection order was found necessary to protect the child in the future.

firac.issue: What disposition is in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The child had lived with H.O. (a kith caregiver) since July 16, 2023, was meeting developmental milestones, up to date on immunizations, and well-adjusted; the society had no concerns with H.O.'s care. The mother sought return, or alternatively a three-month supervision order.
firac.rule: Under s. 101(1) the court must make the order in the child's best interests, applying the s. 74(3) best-interests criteria, choosing the least disruptive alternative (s. 101(3)) and considering community/kith placement (s. 101(4)). A parent must not be judged by a middle-class yardstick (CAS Toronto v. B.-H.(R.), 2006 ONCJ 515) but must be able to provide a safe, stable and secure home (CAS Toronto v. S.B., 2014 ONCJ 518).
firac.application: Placement with H.O. preserved continuity and met the child's needs, and was the least disruptive alternative consistent with best interests. A three-month order was rejected because the mother had several steps to complete requiring a longer duration before status review.
firac.conclusion: The child was placed in the care and custody of H.O. for six months, subject to society supervision.

firac.issue: What terms of access are in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The mother had frequent lateness, cancellations, early departures, made inappropriate remarks in front of the children, and on April 18, 2024 asked to stop seeing the children. The society sought to reduce access from weekly to a minimum of once every two weeks with 24-hour confirmation; the mother sought unsupervised access three times per week.
firac.rule: Sections 104(1) and 105 CYFSA permit the court to make access orders on terms in the child's best interests, consistent with the paramount purpose of promoting the best interests, protection and well-being of children.
firac.application: The mother's inconsistency, cancellations and mental health struggles were causing the children distress. A minimum of one supervised visit every two weeks with 24-hour confirmation was reasonable and would prevent the child being brought when the mother cancels last minute, while allowing reassessment as the mother progresses. Unsupervised thrice-weekly access was not warranted.
firac.conclusion: Supervised access ordered at a minimum of once every two weeks, with 24-hour confirmation required; the mother's request dismissed.

K047 (best interests of the child) is central, being the determining element for both disposition and access. K048 (custody/access) captures the care-and-custody placement with the kith caregiver and the contested access terms. K045 (student discipline) does not fit and is a weak/incorrect option — flagged; the controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated 'child protection' or 'apprehension' keyword, so the family-law child-focused terms are the closest available. I am constrained to the vocabulary provided; only these family keywords genuinely apply, and I could not reach five strong picks without stretching, so K045 is included only as a placeholder and should be treated as weak.

The decision does not otherwise name the sitting city expressly, but the Toronto location is clear from the parties and society.

case_name: Woolworth Canada Inc. v. Human Rights Commission (Nfld.) and White

name_verification.name_in_document: Woolworth Canada Inc. v. Newfoundland (Human Rights Comm.)
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The style of cause is materially the same (Woolworth Canada Inc. as plaintiff/applicant against the Newfoundland Human Rights Commission and Thomas White). The supplied CanLII neutral citation (1994 CanLII 10410 (NL SC)) does not appear in the text, which gives the court file number 1993 St.J. No. 3651 and a decision date of December 2, 1993 (the metadata lists 1994-01-06); these are minor cataloguing differences, not a mismatched case.

defining_issues: Was an examination of the circumstances of White's termination within the jurisdiction of a board of inquiry under the Human Rights Code, i.e. was he terminated 'because of' disability so as to permit a discrimination complaint?
Is the Commission required by the Code to attempt to settle a complaint as a precondition to appointing a board of inquiry, and was an adequate attempt made?
Did the Commission act fairly and without creating a reasonable apprehension of bias in its dealings with the complainant before constituting a board of inquiry?

firac.issue: Was White's termination within the jurisdiction of a board of inquiry, given that he was terminated because of an admitted total inability to work?
firac.facts: White injured his back at work in April 1990, received total-disability Workers' Compensation, and was terminated by Woolco in February 1991. On the uncontradicted facts he supplied, he was incapable of doing his job (or any work) at termination, at the filing of his complaint (August 1991), and at the appointment of the board (March 1993).
firac.rule: Section 9(1)(a) of the Human Rights Code, R.S.N. 1990, c. H-14 prohibits refusing to employ or continue to employ 'because of' physical disability. A board of inquiry has no jurisdiction where the complaint could not, on the facts, involve a contravention of the Code (Bell v. Ontario (Human Rights Comm.), 1971 CanLII 195 (SCC); Re CIP Paper Products, 1978 CanLII 1847 (SK CA); Board of Education v. N.B. Human Rights Board of Inquiry, 1989 CanLII 208 (NB CA)). Direct and adverse-effect discrimination and the duty to accommodate short of undue hardship are governed by Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Comm.), 1990 CanLII 76 (SCC).
firac.application: The Court held termination because of a complete inability to do the job is not discrimination 'because of' disability. There was no direct discrimination (no facially discriminatory rule) and no adverse-effect discrimination: the only inferred rule—that employees must be able to attend and do the job—targets ability, not a prohibited ground, so no duty to accommodate arose. Because the facts were uncontradicted and were the complainant's own, this was the type of clear jurisdictional question a court may decide on a prohibition application. The Code addresses statutory standards of conduct, not contractual employment rights; White had already obtained a civil remedy for wrongful dismissal.
firac.conclusion: White was not terminated because of a prohibited ground; the board of inquiry had no jurisdiction to adjudicate the complaint.

firac.issue: Is a genuine attempt to settle a statutory precondition to appointing a board of inquiry, and was it satisfied here?
firac.facts: Commission representatives met only with White and his counsel, presented a settlement proposal, and, when White rejected it, stopped. Woolco was never informed of the proposal or asked its views before the board was appointed.
firac.rule: Section 21(1) of the Code provides the executive director 'shall investigate the complaint and try to settle the matter'; 'shall' is imperative (Interpretation Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. I-19, s. 11(2)). Read with ss. 21(3) and 23, the power to refer to a board arises only where settlement has not been effected. A bona fide settlement effort is a jurisdictional precondition (Alberta (Human Rights Comm.) v. Pro Western Plastics Ltd., 1983 ABCA 185).
firac.application: The Court found that presenting a proposal to one party and abandoning the effort on its rejection is not a bona fide attempt to settle. A meaningful process requires involving both parties and actively considering other options after a first proposal is rejected; keeping Woolco entirely in the dark fell short.
firac.conclusion: The statutory obligation to attempt settlement was not met, so the Commission lacked jurisdiction to appoint a board of inquiry.

firac.issue: Did the Commission breach procedural fairness or create a reasonable apprehension of bias by giving the complainant opportunities not afforded to the respondent?
firac.facts: The Commission let White and his counsel read the solicitor's memorandum, gave White the investigator's report, and invited (and received) written submissions urging appointment of a board. Woolco was given none of these opportunities and had no contact with the Commission after December 1, 1992.
firac.rule: A public body must observe procedural fairness and act without a reasonable apprehension of bias, particularly given the serious consequences of appointing a board of inquiry (which carries Public Inquiries Act powers and broad remedies under s. 28(1)(b) of the Code).
firac.application: Providing preferential access and input opportunities to one party while excluding the party most at risk offended basic fairness, regardless of whether Woolco would have participated or of Woolco's earlier delays (which had been resolved by December 1992). The close cooperation with White made the decision to appear as a joint effort, supporting a reasonable apprehension of bias.
firac.conclusion: The Commission breached procedural fairness and raised a reasonable apprehension of bias, further precluding it from proceeding.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the primary tier-1 area: the case is a prohibition/quashing application turning on jurisdiction, statutory preconditions, and fairness. K011 (judicial review) and K012 (procedural fairness) directly capture Issues 2–3 and the reasonable-apprehension-of-bias holding. K007 (Human rights) is the tier-1 parent for the substantive subject matter, with K072 (human rights tribunal) for the Commission/board of inquiry machinery and K069 (discrimination) for the disability-discrimination analysis (direct vs. adverse-effect). K068 (bona fide occupational requirement) and K031 (reasonable accommodation—synonyms 'duty to accommodate', 'undue hardship') reflect the court's Central Alberta Dairy Pool analysis, though K031's canonical label ('religious accommodation') is a slightly imperfect fit for a disability context. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is engaged because White's parallel civil dismissal action and remedy figured in the reasoning. K009 (Labour and employment) is included as the employment dimension of the dispute; it is a secondary/borderline pick relative to Administrative law and Human rights.
location_rationale: The court is identified as the 'Newfoundland and Labrador Supreme Court' / 'Newfoundland Supreme Court Trial Division, Orsborn J.'; White worked at Woolco's Village Mall store 'in St. John's', and the court file number '1993 St.J. No. 3651' indicates the St. John's registry, placing the proceeding in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador.
registry_rationale: The file number '1993 St.J. No. 3651' uses the 'St.J.' prefix denoting the St. John's registry of the Supreme Court, Trial Division.

name_verification.name_in_document: Karim AZIZ c. Ronald MASSIER

defining_issues: Was each party at fault in the physical altercation, and did that fault cause compensable prejudice under the ordinary rules of civil liability?
What quantum of damages should be awarded to Mr. Aziz, and how does his prior partial settlement affect recovery?
Was the defendant entitled to damages on his counterclaim for abusive proceedings?
Should the judge recuse himself for lack of impartiality?

firac.issue: Was each party at fault in the physical altercation, and did that fault cause compensable prejudice?
firac.facts: Following a long pattern of provocative and harassing visits by Mr. Aziz to the Tim Hortons where Mr. Massier worked as night manager, an altercation occurred on August 28, 2017. Mr. Aziz refused repeated instructions to leave, both men engaged verbally then physically, glasses were lost between the doors, and once outside Mr. Massier, who had lost his self-control and could not see well, punched Mr. Aziz on the ground, causing a 2 cm forehead laceration and rib bruising.
firac.rule: Civil liability requires proof of three elements: fault, prejudice and causality. Self-defence must be proportionate; excessive self-defence constitutes fault.
firac.application: The Court found both parties at fault: Mr. Aziz had no legitimate reason to be on the premises, repeatedly taunted Mr. Massier and refused to leave, engaging aggressively; Mr. Massier lacked the means and self-control to enforce his authority. The initial physical stage caused no harm and both acted in self-defence, but once Mr. Aziz was on the ground Mr. Massier's continued blows became disproportionate self-defence. That disproportionate conduct caused the pain, bruising and superficial facial wound.
firac.conclusion: Mr. Massier was liable for the prejudice caused by his disproportionate self-defence; Mr. Aziz was also at fault, including in grabbing and damaging Mr. Massier's glasses.

firac.issue: What quantum should be awarded, and how does the prior partial settlement affect recovery?
firac.facts: Mr. Aziz's claim, originally $100,000, was successively reduced to $14,000. His injuries were a superficial 2 cm laceration requiring no stitches and minor bruises. He had already received $1,000 in a homologated settlement with other former defendants. Mr. Massier claimed $500 for damaged glasses, proving he paid roughly $800 for two pairs.
firac.rule: Compensatory damages are arbitrated by the Court in the absence of expert proof; a plaintiff cannot recover more than the amount of his prejudice, so amounts already recovered are deducted.
firac.application: The Court arbitrated Mr. Aziz's compensatory damages at $2,000 globally, then deducted the $1,000 already received under the settlement, leaving $1,000. Mr. Massier's glasses were arbitrated at $400, the damage being caused by Mr. Aziz grabbing them.
firac.conclusion: Mr. Massier ordered to pay $1,000 to Mr. Aziz; Mr. Aziz ordered to pay $400 for the glasses.

firac.issue: Was the defendant entitled to damages for abusive proceedings?
firac.facts: Mr. Aziz brought multiple redundant and prolix proceedings arising from the same incident, using offensive, insulting and racially-tinged language, comparing Mr. Massier to a wild animal, and filing memes and photos. Mr. Massier counterclaimed $5,000 for the trouble and inconvenience of the abusive proceedings and kept his address confidential feeling threatened.
firac.rule: The Court may sanction abuse of procedure (and may raise it on its own motion); vexatious, excessive and quarrelsome proceedings that continue harassment and slur a person justify moral damages.
firac.application: The Court found the proceedings truly excessive, vexatious and quérulent, a continuation of the harassment of Mr. Massier with racist overtones designed to humiliate him. Moral damages of $5,000 claimed were not unreasonable, but $2,500 was sufficient.
firac.conclusion: Counterclaim granted in part; Mr. Aziz ordered to pay $2,500 in damages for abusive procedure.

firac.issue: Should the judge recuse himself for lack of impartiality?
firac.facts: Mr. Aziz sought recusal at the opening of trial, relying on his having filed an application for judicial review of the same judge's earlier September 22, 2021 judgment dismissing his related claims, and on harsh criticisms of the judge and repeated demands that the judge commit to a shortened judgment deadline.
firac.rule: Recusal under arts. 201-203 C.C.P. requires serious reasons to question impartiality; conflict, threats or insults (art. 202(6)) or a prior opinion on the subject matter (art. 203). The mere existence of a judicial review of a related decision is not a ground.
firac.application: The Court found no conflict, no threats or insults, and that it had not yet heard or opined on the present case; harsh criticism of the judge and the court system did not amount to serious grounds, and the pending judicial review of a related file was no basis for recusal.
firac.conclusion: Application for recusal dismissed, without costs; the judge continued to hear the matter neutrally.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area — a tort/civil-liability action for damages arising from an altercation, decided on fault, prejudice and causality. K083 (harassment) reflects the Court's central finding that Mr. Aziz engaged in a longstanding pattern of harassment of Mr. Massier, continued through the litigation; the canonical term is labour-oriented but the harassment concept is squarely engaged. K065 (racism) captures the Court's finding that the pleadings and name-calling had 'racist overtones' — borderline but expressly noted by the Court. K012 (procedural fairness) covers the contested recusal/impartiality challenge decided under arts. 201-203 C.C.P. K015 (defamation) is a borderline pick for the abuse claim's slurring/insulting character (comparing Mr. Massier to an animal), though no defamation cause of action was pleaded. K071 (human dignity) reflects the moral-damages award grounded in the affront to Mr. Massier's dignity. There is no controlled-vocabulary term for 'abuse of procedure' or 'self-defence/civil liability,' which are the true doctrinal cores, so several picks are proxies flagged as weak (K015, K065, K071).
location_rationale: The header states 'COURT OF QUÉBEC, Small Claims Division, PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC, DISTRICT OF MONTRÉAL, CITY OF MONTRÉAL'.
registry_rationale: The district and city of Montréal are stated in the header ('DISTRICT OF MONTRÉAL / CITY OF MONTRÉAL'); the file bears a 500- (Montréal) court number.

name_verification.name_in_document: A.E. v. A.B.

defining_issues: Should the mother and children be permitted to relocate from the Greater Toronto Area to Cleveland, Ohio, having regard to the children's best interests under the Divorce Act?
What parenting order and allocation of decision-making responsibility is in the children's best interests?
What child support and section 7 (special/extraordinary) expense order is appropriate, and is a departure from the Child Support Guidelines justified?
Is the mother entitled to spousal support and, if so, in what amount and for what duration?

firac.issue: Should the mother be permitted to relocate the three children to Cleveland, Ohio?
firac.facts: The mother, the primary residential parent since separation, remarried a Cleveland resident (Mr. Goldish) and wished to relocate the three children (JB 13, EB 11, SB 4½) to combine households in the Orthodox community there. The father opposed the move. The OCL clinical report did not support relocation, finding the mother had not consistently supported the children's relationship with the father; a Voice of the Child Report and both clinicians confirmed the two older children strongly and consistently wished to move. The children's relationship with their father was 'fragile' but recovering, and the mother had restricted the father's overnight and expanded parenting time for years.
firac.rule: Under s. 16 of the Divorce Act the court considers only the best interests of the child, giving primary consideration to safety, security and well-being, and weighing the enumerated factors (including each parent's willingness to support the child's relationship with the other, the child's views and preferences, and family violence under ss. 16(3)(j) and 16(4)). Section 16.92(1) adds relocation-specific factors, and s. 16.93(3) placed the burden on each party (no substantially-equal or vast-majority parenting order existing). Case law: Berry v. Berry (child-centred superordinate consideration); O'Brien v. Chuluunbaatar; Bourke v. Davis; Kazberov v. Kotlyachkova; Decaen v. Decaen (assessing children's views); on alienation, Bors v. Beleuta, Hazelton v. Forchuk, Moreton v. Inthavixay.
firac.application: The court found the mother a loving primary parent who had put forward a thoughtful, comprehensive plan and had complied with (and exceeded) parenting-time orders, but whose devaluation of the father approached alienating behaviour. It found no credible evidence of family violence and no evidence the father's addiction impaired his parenting. Weighing the children's clear, strong, age-appropriate and consistent wish to move, the changed family constellations, the impossibility of unwinding five and a half years, and the considerable risk to the children's best interests if the move were refused (as flagged by the OCL), the court concluded that risk outweighed the risk of further compromise to the father's relationship, provided both parents demonstrated flexibility and responsiveness.
firac.conclusion: Relocation to Ohio permitted; the mother may move with the children.

firac.issue: What parenting order and decision-making allocation serves the children's best interests?
firac.facts: Both parties filed parenting plans. The mother sought shared decision-making if relocation was allowed (sole if not); the father sought equal shared decision-making and generous parenting time. The father had a history of untimely responses and non-compliance with orders; the mother was the psychological anchor for the children.
firac.rule: Section 16 of the Divorce Act best-interests framework; sole decision-making 'would significantly disenfranchise the other parent' (OCL), and an order must not be misused to control the other parent (W.S. v. P.I.A.).
firac.application: The court adopted a plan combining elements of both parties' proposals, ordering primary residence with the mother, shared decision-making on major matters (health, education, religion, extracurriculars), a parenting coordinator for impasses, and a detailed schedule of the father's weekends, winter/summer breaks and equally shared Jewish holidays, with a mid-point exchange at Angola, New York. Both parents were required to honour their representations to promote the children's relationship with the other parent and extended family.
firac.conclusion: A combined Parenting Plan (Schedule A) ordered: primary residence with the mother in Ohio and shared decision-making.

firac.issue: What child support and section 7 expense order is appropriate, and is a departure from the Guidelines justified?
firac.facts: The father's income was set at $153,000 (table support $2,742/month for three children). Relocation would add travel costs for his parenting time. The mother claimed substantial s. 7 arrears (school tuition, camps, tutoring, counselling, caregiver costs), much of it incurred without the father's consent and partly subsidized by the community. Bennett J. had earlier ordered $79,993.29 in arrears without prejudice to recalculation at trial.
firac.rule: Sections 15.1 and 7 of the Divorce Act/Child Support Guidelines; s. 15.1(6) requires reasons for departing from the table amount; s. 7 requires necessity, reasonableness and consideration of subsidies (s. 7(3)); Romita v. Humphries (unfair to require retroactive contribution to expenses incurred without the other parent's knowledge/involvement).
firac.application: The court reduced table support to $2,000/month once the children relocate to account for the father's Ohio parenting-time costs, giving reasons as required. It disallowed the full-time caregiver claim (incurred without consent while the mother was largely not working) and adjusted the contested expenses (partial contributions to camps, tutoring and EB's assessment; extracurriculars denied as within table support), arriving at net s. 7 arrears of $65,560 after a $15,624 overpayment credit. Payment terms of the temporary order were varied to $1,250/month plus a portion of the father's annual bonus to preserve his ability to fund parenting time.
firac.conclusion: Table support reduced to $2,000/month post-relocation; s. 7 arrears fixed at $65,560 with varied payment terms.

firac.issue: Is the mother entitled to spousal support?
firac.facts: The parties, married about ten years with three children, were 32 at separation; both worked (except maternity leaves); the mother had remarried and intended to secure full-time, potentially higher-paying employment in Ohio. She abandoned the claim in closing provided the father paid child support.
firac.rule: Sections 15.2 and 15.3 of the Divorce Act; priority must be given to child support (s. 15.3(1)), with reasons where spousal support is thereby reduced or precluded (s. 15.3(2)), and subsequent reduction of child support is a change of circumstances (s. 15.3(3)).
firac.application: Given the impact of the child support order on the father's finances and the priority owed to child support, the court declined to order spousal support at this time, dismissing entitlement, amount and duration without prejudice to renewal.
firac.conclusion: No spousal support ordered; the mother may renew her claim before December 31, 2024, after which it is extinguished.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test for the central relocation and parenting determination. K048 (custody/access) captures the parenting-time and decision-making order. K050 (parental support / child support) and K053 (spousal support) reflect the support determinations, including the Guidelines departure and the s. 15.3 priority analysis. K052 (religious upbringing) is engaged by the Orthodox Jewish upbringing, Tefillin ceremony, holidays and schooling factors weighed under s. 16(3)(f). K095 (Jewish family) and K097 (Orthodox/Hasidic community) are entity keywords accurately describing the parties and their community context. Borderline: K095 and K097 are contextual descriptors rather than legal doctrines, but the family's Orthodox observance materially shaped the schooling costs and holiday-sharing analysis.
location_rationale: The header reads 'NEWMARKET / COURT FILE NO.: FC-19-58096-00' and identifies the court as the 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE', placing the matter in Newmarket, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The Newmarket court file number (FC-19-58096-00) and the 'NEWMARKET' notation in the style of cause indicate the Newmarket registry of the Superior Court of Justice.

case_name: CAS of S.D.G. v. S.F., B.F.-S. and A. B.-F..

name_verification.name_in_document: CAS of S.D.G. v. S.F., B.F.-S. and A. B.-F.., 2021 ONSC 3804

defining_issues: Did the Society establish reasonable grounds to believe the children are likely to suffer harm and that they cannot be adequately protected by returning them to the Mother, with or without a supervision order?

If the children cannot be returned to the Mother, is it in their best interests to be placed with the paternal grandmother under the Society's supervision, or must they remain in the Society's temporary care?
What interim access arrangement should be ordered for the Mother and the paternal grandmother?

firac.issue: Has the Society met its onus on a temporary care and custody hearing to justify keeping the children out of the Mother's care?
firac.facts: B, the Mother's partner and a father figure to the children, was charged with child pornography and sexual offences, and photographs of E performing fellatio on B were later discovered online despite an ongoing safety plan. The Mother had earlier photographed disturbing images on B's computer, was persuaded by B not to report them, threw out potentially evidentiary blanket, and continued to have virtual and physical contact with B despite a no-contact order. E disclosed abuse and said his Mother did not believe him or 'save him'.
firac.rule: Under ss. 94(2), 94(4) and 94(5) CYFSA the court applies a hierarchy of least-intrusive placements. The Society must show, on credible and trustworthy evidence (s. 94(10)), reasonable grounds to believe there is a real possibility the child will suffer harm if returned, and that the child cannot be adequately protected by a supervision order (Children's Aid Society of Ottawa-Carleton v. T.; L.D. v. Durham CAS). The burden is less than proof on a balance of probabilities (CCAS of Toronto v. M.L.R.). The court must choose the least disruptive placement consistent with adequate protection (s. 1(2)).
firac.application: The court found reasonable grounds to believe the children were likely to suffer harm: sexual abuse of E may have begun as early as 2017/2018, the Mother failed to act on E's disclosures, destroyed potential evidence, ignored red flags about B's history, and repeatedly breached the no-contact order. Although the Mother loved the children and had begun addressing issues, her demonstrated inability to follow court orders and lack of insight meant supervision terms would be inadequate to protect the children.
firac.conclusion: The Society met both parts of the test; the children could not be returned to the Mother even with a supervision order.

firac.issue: Should the children be placed in the paternal grandmother's kin care rather than remaining in the Society's care?
firac.facts: R, the paternal grandmother, was B's surety, had knowledge of B's earlier sexual-abuse allegation as a youth, permitted B to co-sleep with A in breach of Minnema J.'s October 27, 2020 order, and did not address in her affidavit key matters such as the disposal of the blanket. E told his counsel he did not want any contact with R, and the OCL opposed placement with her.
firac.rule: Section 94(5) CYFSA requires the court, before ordering Society care, to consider whether placement with a relative or extended family member under Society supervision is in the child's best interests. Terms and conditions must be reasonable and proportionate to the risks, and the court must be satisfied the caregiver will meaningfully adhere to supervision conditions (s. 74(3); CAS of Waterloo v. S.S.H.).
firac.application: Although R loved the children and proposed counselling and support, she had breached the existing supervision order by allowing B to co-sleep with A, failed to protect the children previously, and left significant allegations unaddressed. The court was not persuaded she would abide by court-imposed conditions, and returning E to the home where he was likely abused was not in his best interests; separating the siblings was also rejected.
firac.conclusion: Kin placement with R was refused; continued temporary Society care was the least disruptive placement consistent with the children's best interests.

firac.issue: What access should be ordered pending the protection proceeding?
firac.facts: The Society proposed access at its discretion: A to see the Mother two to three times weekly (supervised), E once weekly plus daily calls, with E able to attend A's visits. The Mother sought regular overnight access; R sought access on terms in the children's best interests. E wished to maintain the current schedule with his Mother and did not want contact with R.
firac.rule: Section 94(8) CYFSA permits access provisions on terms the court considers appropriate, guided by the paramount purpose of the Act (best interests, protection and well-being) and the s. 74(3) best-interests factors (Jewish Family and Child Services v. S.(H.B.); CAS of Oxford County v. C.O.).
firac.application: The Mother's central role in the children's lives and her engagement with services supported increasing, Society-discretion access along a graduated trajectory. Given E's trauma (some of it occurring at R's home) and his express opposition to contact with R, and the undesirability of separating the siblings, access to R was left to the Society's discretion pending counselling.
firac.conclusion: Access to both the Mother and R was ordered at the Society's discretion.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area — this is a child protection proceeding under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is squarely engaged, as the s. 74(3) best-interests test governs every placement and access determination. K048 (custody/access) covers both the temporary care/custody ruling and the access order under s. 94(8). K004 (Criminal law) is a contextual/weak pick: the outcome is driven by B's sexual offence charges (child pornography, sexual assault) and breaches of criminal no-contact conditions, though the court itself decides no criminal issue. K002 (Civil litigation) is a weak, generic pick reflecting the evidentiary/onus dispute; the controlled vocabulary has no dedicated child-protection keyword, so these are the closest available terms.
location_rationale: The decision is styled 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' with no city named in the heading, but the applicant is the Children's Aid Society of the United Counties of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry (Cornwall CAS), the family had moved to Cornwall, and the judgment (per Desormeau J.) proceeds in that jurisdiction, so the court sat in Cornwall, Ontario. Province is clearly Ontario given the CYFSA and the ONSC citation.
registry_rationale: No registry office is named in the decision; only court file no. 21-111 appears, so registry is left null.

case_name: Bankruptcy of the Jewish Foundation of Greater Toronto

name_verification.name_in_document: Bankruptcy of the Jewish Foundation of Greater Toronto

defining_issues: Was there a debtor/creditor relationship between the Foundation and the JLCF, or were the transferred funds irrevocable gifts?
Did any special circumstances exist that would permit a single creditor to obtain a bankruptcy order under the BIA?
Should the bankruptcy application be dismissed under s. 43(7) of the BIA, including as an abuse of process brought for a collateral purpose?
If not dismissed under the BIA, could and should the application be struck under Rule 21.01 of the Rules of Civil Procedure?

firac.issue: Were the funds transferred to the Foundation a debt owed to the JLCF or irrevocable gifts, such that no debtor/creditor relationship existed?
firac.facts: Between 2011 and 2016 the JLCF donated over $19M to a Donor Advised Fund managed by the Foundation, receiving acknowledgments confirming each as an irrevocable gift and claiming corresponding tax treatment with the CRA. After Joseph Lebovic's death, Wolf directed the Foundation to distribute the remaining ~$16M to named charities; when it did not, the JLCF alleged a $15,983,651.79 debt.
firac.rule: A donor cannot compel the return of a gift absent an express power of revocation (Bacic v. Millennium Educational & Research Charitable Foundation, 2014 ONSC 5875; Young v. Young; Berdette v. Berdette). A valid gift requires intention to give without consideration, acceptance, and sufficient transfer (Cassan v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 174; McNamee v. McNamee, 2011 ONCA 533).
firac.application: The acknowledgments signed on each donation confirmed irrevocable gifts and no benefit was received; the JLCF lost all interest in the funds once donated while the Foundation assumed control. No power of revocation existed and none could exist without jeopardizing the charitable-gift and tax-deduction status. Neither Wolf's affidavit nor the parallel DAF Action referred to a 'debt' — only to 'donations'. The relief sought was payment to third-party charities, not repayment to the JLCF.
firac.conclusion: The funds were legally valid, irrevocable gifts; no debtor/creditor relationship existed and there was no debt.

firac.issue: Did special circumstances exist to allow a single creditor to petition the Foundation into bankruptcy?
firac.facts: The JLCF brought the application as a single creditor, alleging the Foundation had ceased meeting liabilities generally and failed to meet obligations to the JLCF in the preceding six months. The Foundation's CFO deposed it was in 'excellent financial health' with $489.9M in assets under management as of June 30, 2020, and was not cross-examined.
firac.rule: Failure to pay a single creditor can constitute an act of bankruptcy only in three recognized special-circumstance categories: (a) repeated demands within six months; (b) a significantly large debt with fraud or suspicious handling of assets; or (c) a pre-petition admission of inability to pay creditors generally (Valente v. Fancsy Estate, 2004 CanLII 8018 (ON CA); Levesque (Re), 2016 ONCA 393). Bankruptcy is intended for creditors as a class, not individually.
firac.application: None of the three categories applied: there were no demands for payment (only demands that payments be made to charities), no fraud or suspicious circumstances, and the Foundation never admitted inability to pay. The unchallenged financial evidence showed the Foundation readily met its obligations. Unlike Levesque, there was not even an established, judgment-secured debt.
firac.conclusion: No special circumstances existed and no act of bankruptcy occurred; a single-creditor bankruptcy order was unavailable.

firac.issue: Should the bankruptcy application be dismissed under s. 43(7) of the BIA, including as an abuse of process for a collateral purpose?
firac.facts: The alleged facts were a $15M debt and general failure to meet liabilities, both unsupported by evidence. The JLCF had already commenced the DAF Action seeking to compel distributions and had sought a preservation order/injunction in that action.
firac.rule: Section 43(7) BIA requires the court to dismiss an application where it is not satisfied with proof of the alleged facts, is satisfied the debtor can pay its debts, or where for other sufficient cause no order should be made. The court may dismiss a bankruptcy application brought for a collateral purpose or as an abuse of process (Dallas/North Group Inc. (Re), 2001 CanLII 3636 (ON CA); La Scala Bakery Ltd., Re, 1984 CarswellOnt 191; Canam Enterprises Inc. v. Coles, 2000 CanLII 8514 (ON CA)).
firac.application: There was no debt and no proof of inability to pay. Even if the facts were proven, the application was brought to pressure the Foundation to pay amounts that were not debts and which the JLCF had no authority to direct, and the DAF Action was the more suitable forum. Concern for charitable payments had nothing to do with the purposes of the BIA. The court will not act as a collection or dispute-resolution device.
firac.conclusion: The application was dismissed under s. 43(7): the Foundation can pay its debts, the alleged facts were unproven, and the application was an abuse of process brought for a collateral purpose.

firac.issue: Could the application alternatively be struck under Rule 21.01 despite the BIA governing dismissals?
firac.facts: The Foundation sought, in the alternative, to strike the application under rr. 21.01 and 25.11. The JLCF argued the Rules were unavailable because the BIA already addresses dismissal of bankruptcy applications.
firac.rule: Rule 21.01 permits striking a claim that discloses no reasonable cause of action or is frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process; courts have inherent power to prevent misuse of process (Canam Enterprises Inc. v. Coles). Resort to the Rules is available where the BIA leaves a procedural gap.
firac.application: The application had no reasonable chance of success given the findings of no debt and no inability to pay. Public policy favouring integrity and efficiency supported striking it. The BIA sets out no specific procedure for dismissing such an application, so the court retained discretion to apply the Rules.
firac.conclusion: In the alternative, the application would be struck under Rule 21.01; the JLCF's argument that the Rules were precluded was rejected.

case_name: C.A.S. of Nipissing and Parry Sound v. S.B.

name_verification.name_in_document: C.A.S. of Nipissing and Parry Sound v. S.B. and M.B., 2019 ONSC 1352

defining_issues: Did the summary judgment motion judge apply the correct legal test under r. 16 of the Family Law Rules and the Hryniak framework in concluding there was no genuine issue requiring a trial?
Were the parents denied procedural fairness in the conduct of the summary judgment motion?
Did the motion judge err by failing to consider and weigh the parents' evidence, particularly where there was conflicting evidence?
Did the motion judge improperly rely on hearsay evidence and on the recommendations of the s. 54 parenting-capacity assessment?
Should fresh evidence be admitted on the appeal?

firac.issue: Did the summary judgment motion judge apply the correct legal test under r. 16 of the Family Law Rules in a child protection case?
firac.facts: The Society moved for summary judgment seeking to place the child in extended society care with no access. The motion judge decided the motion on the paper record, stating that summary judgment should be granted 'only in the clearest of cases' and that a trial with viva voce evidence could not lead to any other conclusion.
firac.rule: Under r. 16 of the Family Law Rules (aligned in 2015 with r. 20 of the Rules of Civil Procedure) and Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, the motion judge must first determine, on the record alone, whether there is a genuine issue requiring a trial, then whether the enhanced fact-finding powers (weighing evidence, assessing credibility, drawing inferences, ordering a mini-trial) can fairly resolve the matter without a trial. The 'clearest of cases' / 'no realistic possibility of another outcome' standard is no longer the test (Kawartha-Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2018 ONSC 2783).
firac.application: The motion judge did not follow the Hryniak roadmap. He never asked whether it was in the interest of justice to resolve the case summarily, and applied the outdated 'clearest of cases' standard, thereby failing to identify the factual and legal issues and determine whether they could be fairly adjudicated summarily. This was an error of law not entitled to deference.
firac.conclusion: The motion judge applied the wrong test, an error of law; his conclusion that there was no genuine issue requiring a trial cannot stand.

firac.issue: Were the parents denied procedural fairness?
firac.facts: The trial management conference converted into a motion process on very short timelines, with the Society serving affidavits as late as days before the parents' responses were due. Mr. M.B. sought in his responding affidavit to rely on affidavits filed earlier in the proceeding, but the motion judge considered only the material filed on the motion.
firac.rule: Fairness requires that responding parties in a high-stakes child protection summary judgment motion have adequate time to put their best foot forward; under s. 93(1)(b) of the CYFSA relevant statements and reports are admissible in 'any proceeding', and a party may incorporate earlier affidavits by reference (Kondovski v. Kondovski).
firac.application: The short timelines were unfair or unwise, but the parents insisted on proceeding, so that alone would not warrant allowing the appeal. The motion judge's refusal to consider Mr. M.B.'s earlier affidavits, incorporated by reference and unobjected to by the Society, had the potential to be unfair; however, the ground lacked specificity and the court declined to allow the appeal on this basis alone.
firac.conclusion: There were procedural fairness concerns, offered as guidance, but the appeal was not allowed on this ground alone.

firac.issue: Did the motion judge err by failing to consider and weigh the parents' conflicting evidence?
firac.facts: The motion judge relied on five reasons, including Ms. B.'s dependency on Mr. M.B. and the parents' failure to exercise access. Ms. B. deposed that she was not dominated by Mr. M.B. and explained missed access visits (weather, transportation from Sturgeon Falls to North Bay, a car accident, appointments); the motion judge did not mention this evidence.
firac.rule: A failure to mention relevant evidence justifies appellate intervention where the reasons lead to a reasonable belief the judge forgot, ignored or misconceived evidence in a way affecting the conclusion (Van de Perre v. Edwards, 2001 SCC 60).
firac.application: The motion judge did not consider the parents' evidence filed before the motion and ignored material conflicts on key factual issues such as Ms. B.'s alleged dependency and the reasons access visits were missed. These were central to both the disposition and the denial of access and could not be resolved on the paper record; the appellate court could not make the findings itself because of the conflicting evidence.
firac.conclusion: The motion judge erred by failing to identify and resolve genuine factual disputes, supporting the order remitting the matter.

firac.issue: Did the motion judge improperly rely on hearsay evidence and on the s. 54 assessment recommendations?
firac.facts: The motion judge relied on police arrest reports (double hearsay) regarding Mr. M.B.'s convictions and on the s. 54 parenting-capacity assessment's recommendations, while holding that the report need not be cross-examined because it was not fundamental to the Society's case.
firac.rule: Under r. 16(5) hearsay is admissible but should be approached with caution in child protection matters; the s. 54 report was admissible under s. 98(12) of the CYFSA, but reliance on its recommendations is inconsistent with treating it as unimportant and immune from cross-examination.
firac.application: The arrest reports were double hearsay that should have been treated with caution. By faulting the parents for not acting on 'even some' of the assessors' recommendations, the motion judge implicitly accepted those recommendations as valid, contradicting his ruling that cross-examination was unnecessary because the report was not fundamental to the Society's position.
firac.conclusion: The motion judge erred in his treatment of hearsay and in relying on the s. 54 recommendations, further supporting allowing the appeal.

firac.issue: Should the parents' fresh evidence be admitted on appeal?
firac.facts: The parents sought to introduce certificates of attendance at two 'selected' Triple P – Positive Parenting Program seminars held after the order, without a formal motion.
firac.rule: Section 121(6) CYFSA permits fresh evidence of post-order events; in child protection the test is relaxed (Re Genereux; Catholic Children's Aid Society v. C.M., [1994] 2 SCR 165) compared to R. v. Palmer, given the child-centred focus.
firac.application: The Society had notice and identified no prejudice, so the evidence was admitted, but little could be inferred from it given the absence of information about the program; it showed only that the parents still wished custody and were willing to improve.
firac.conclusion: Fresh evidence admitted but of minimal weight.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing practice area — this is a child protection appeal under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is the statutory touchstone for both the extended-care disposition and access. K048 (custody/access) captures the contested access order denying both parents contact. K012 (procedural fairness) reflects the extensively analysed fairness concerns about short timelines and ignored affidavits. K014 (standard of review) applies because the court applied Hryniak/Housen deference principles and found an extricable error of law. The controlled vocabulary lacks a specific 'child protection' or 'summary judgment' term, so these are the closest applicable picks; K014 is somewhat of an appellate-mechanics tag but is genuinely engaged by the analysis.
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE', establishing the province as Ontario. No city or hearing location is stated on the face of the decision (the Society is described as being of the District of Nipissing and Parry Sound, but the court's sitting city is not given), so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision states only the court file number (FS-18-0102) and 'Superior Court of Justice'; no registry office is named, so registry is left null.

case_name: Beaudoin v Agriculture Financial Services Corporation

name_verification.name_in_document: Sandra Beaudoin v Agriculture Financial Services Corporation

defining_issues: Did the employer establish just cause for summary dismissal based on the employee's alleged insubordination in providing appraisal information contrary to policy?
If just cause was not established, what was the reasonable notice period?
Did the employee fail to mitigate her damages by declining an alternative job offer?
Was this an appropriate case for punitive or aggravated damages?

firac.issue: Did AFSC establish just cause for summary dismissal based on alleged insubordination?
firac.facts: Ms. Beaudoin, a 15-year employee promoted to a Lender position, provided a customer with historical appraisal/asset-value information regarding the customer's own land, having earlier been told she could not share opinions of land values with outside parties. She documented her action in a file memo. She was dismissed for cause 20 days after being questioned, without being given a chance to respond, on the basis of wilful disobedience and insubordination breaching the Code of Conduct and Lending Policy Manual.
firac.rule: The employer bears the burden of proving just cause (Karmel v Calgary Jewish Academy, 2015 ABQB 731; Elgert v Home Hardware, 2010 ABQB 40, and others). Insubordination amounting to just cause requires ten elements set out in Karmel (citing Wilson v KP Manufacturers and Levitt), including that the disobedience be deliberate and intentional, involve a matter of importance, damage the relationship irreparably, and that the employee understood she risked termination. Wilful disobedience must be 'seriously incompatible with the employee's duties... conduct which goes to the root of the contract' (Panton v Everywoman's Health Centre, 2000 BCCA 621).
firac.application: The Court found the June email direction was understood by Ms. Beaudoin as concerning opinions of value on the daughter/son-in-law's land, whereas in August she gave dated information on the customer's own land — not in direct contradiction of the direction. Her unchallenged evidence was that she believed she was acting within the rules; she was transparent, made a file note, and had nothing to gain. AFSC failed to follow its own Code of Conduct investigation process and gave her no opportunity to respond before dismissal. The disobedience was not deliberate and intentional (element 4), the breach was of minor importance given the different property/owner/time (element 5), and nothing indicated she risked termination (element 8).
firac.conclusion: AFSC did not meet the burden of proving just cause. The dismissal was wrongful.

firac.issue: What was the reasonable notice period owed to the dismissed employee?
firac.facts: Ms. Beaudoin was 54, had 15 years' service, earned a base salary of $89,808, and held a lower 'management'-type Lender position with some autonomy in a remote small town (Hanna, population ~2,700). The dismissal for cause left her under a cloud with no favourable reference.
firac.rule: Reasonable notice is fact-specific, assessed on factors such as age, length of service, character of employment and availability of similar employment. The assertion of unproven just cause militates in favour of a higher assessment within the range.
firac.application: Considering her age, 15 years' service, seniority/autonomy, the geographic nature of AFSC's operations, the small community, and the damage from an unproven just-cause allegation, the Court fixed reasonable notice at 14 months.
firac.conclusion: Reasonable notice was 14 months; damages calculated as annual salary ÷ 12 × 14, with pre-judgment interest from the mid-point of the notice period.

firac.issue: Did the employee fail to mitigate her damages by declining a similar job offer shortly after dismissal?
firac.facts: About two weeks to a month after dismissal, a Chinook Credit Union agriculture lender orally asked if she would work with them in a similar Hanna position. She declined, saying she was not in a state of mind to work with the public. She searched local newspapers and webpages and pursued one administrative position.
firac.rule: The burden of proving failure to mitigate lies on the employer (see also Lee v 1554478 Ontario Inc, 2008 CanLII 55467, accepting delay in job search where termination was performance-related).
firac.application: The informal offer came too soon after a sudden dismissal for cause; her explanation for not immediately pursuing similar work was reasonable and consistent with Lee. AFSC provided no evidence of other available positions she failed to pursue, and the Court did not fault her for seeking a 'management' position given her prior role.
firac.conclusion: The employer did not establish a failure to mitigate.

firac.issue: Was this an appropriate case for punitive or aggravated damages?
firac.facts: AFSC dismissed Ms. Beaudoin without completing its own investigation process, but there was no evidence it knew it was seriously off-base, and no medical evidence of psychological harm; she did not use the EFAP coverage offered.
firac.rule: Punitive damages are reserved for exceptional 'malicious, oppressive and high-handed' misconduct representing a marked departure from decency (Whiten v Pilot Insurance, 2002 SCC 18; Hill v Church of Scientology). Aggravated damages arise from the manner of dismissal where conduct is unfair, bad faith, or 'untruthful, misleading or unduly insensitive' (Honda Canada v Keays, 2008 SCC 39; Wallace v United Grain Growers; Merrill Lynch Canada v Soost, 2010 ABCA 251).
firac.application: AFSC's error was the common one of acting too soon without seeking an explanation, not malicious or high-handed conduct, so punitive damages were unwarranted. There was no evidence of special psychological or physiological damage from unfair treatment, and EFAP access was continued, so aggravated damages were not justified. A failed just-cause defence simply results in an award at the higher end of the notice range.
firac.conclusion: Neither punitive nor aggravated damages were awarded.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a wrongful dismissal action. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the core issue, engaging just cause, reasonable notice, mitigation, and punitive/aggravated damages. K042 (code of conduct) is directly engaged because the alleged just cause rested on breaches of AFSC's Code of Conduct and Lending Policy Manual and the failure to follow its own investigation process. K002 (Civil litigation) applies as the claim was resolved via a civil summary judgment action. Only four keywords truly apply; the case does not engage the human rights, religious, or hate-speech vocabulary that dominates the controlled list, so no further specific keywords fit — the remaining terms would be weak or irrelevant picks.

registry_rationale: The header expressly lists 'Registry: Calgary'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Ayoub c. Canada (Attorney General)

defining_issues: Should Ahmed Ayoub be granted judicial interim release under s. 20 of the Extradition Act (incorporating s. 679(3) of the Criminal Code) pending his appeal from the committal order, and in particular has he shown that he would surrender himself into custody?

firac.issue: Has Ayoub established the criteria for judicial interim release pending appeal of his committal under the Extradition Act, especially that he would surrender himself into custody?
firac.facts: Ayoub, wanted by Florida for sexual assaults on a 14-year-old allegedly committed 22–26 March 2003, left Florida abruptly in early April 2003, entered Canada as a visitor, and filed a refugee claim on 16 April 2003 — the day after speaking with a Clearwater investigating officer. He works as an auxiliary nurse at the Jewish General Hospital, and had entered a relationship with Ms. Dalalian, with steps taken toward a civil union. A committal order issued 22 November 2005; he appealed, invoking the alleged unconstitutionality of ss. 32-33 of the Extradition Act under s. 7 of the Charter. He then applied afresh for release under s. 20.
firac.rule: Section 20 of the Extradition Act renders s. 679 of the Criminal Code applicable. Under s. 679(3), the applicant must establish on a balance of probabilities that (a) the appeal is not frivolous, (b) he will surrender himself into custody in accordance with the terms of the order, and (c) his detention is not necessary in the public interest. Section 11(e) of the Charter guarantees the right not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause.
firac.application: The Attorney General conceded the appeal was not frivolous, and the debate centred on whether Ayoub would surrender into custody. While Hilton J.A. accepted that the strengthened relationship with Ms. Dalalian removed one concern noted by Mongeau J., the circumstances of Ayoub's precipitous departure from the United States close in time to the alleged offences, and his delay in claiming refugee status until he learned Florida police were seeking him, supported a reasonable apprehension of flight. Being in Montreal would not prevent him from going elsewhere in Canada, and release would leave him at liberty for a lengthy period given the remaining extradition steps. His stated reasons for coming to Canada — harassment of Arabs in the U.S. and fear of persecution in Palestine for his conversion to Christianity — were unsupported by any illustration and thus unpersuasive.
firac.conclusion: Ayoub failed to satisfy all the criteria of s. 679(3), particularly the surrender-into-custody requirement; the application for judicial interim release was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary tier-1 area, as extradition bail is governed by the Criminal Code's release provisions. K112 (Charter s. 7) is engaged because the underlying committal appeal invokes the alleged unconstitutionality of ss. 32-33 of the Extradition Act under s. 7. K078 (refugee protection) and K079 (persecution) reflect the pending refugee claim and Ayoub's asserted fear of persecution in Palestine, central to his flight-risk and credibility arguments. K104 (Palestine) locates his claimed country of persecution. These are the closest fits; the controlled vocabulary lacks an extradition or bail/judicial-interim-release term, so K078/K079/K104 are context-based and comparatively weak, and the case has no genuine antisemitism/Jewish-law dimension despite the 'Jewish General Hospital' mention.
