case_name: Congregation Beth-El v. Québec (Commission des relations du travail)

name_verification.name_in_document: CONGREGATION BETH-EL v. COMMISSION DES RELATIONS DU TRAVAIL and LOUISE CÔTÉ-DESBIOLLES and RABBI IRVIN BRANDWEIN
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied name adds 'Québec' as a parenthetical qualifier to the Commission des relations du travail; the decision text styles the respondent simply as 'Commission des relations du travail'. This is a trivial stylistic difference. The neutral citation 2003 CanLII 28861 (QC CS) does not appear in the text but the court file number 500-17-013878-031 and the Superior Court of Quebec (Montreal) match.

defining_issues: What is the applicable standard of review of the Commissioner's decision that Rabbi Brandwein was not a 'cadre supérieur' and thus fell within s. 124 of the Labour Standards Act?
Was the Commissioner's finding that the non-renewal of the Rabbi's fixed-term contract amounted to a dismissal without good and sufficient cause patently unreasonable?
Was the Commissioner's award of indemnity (approximately 18 months' salary plus four months' loss-of-employment indemnity) patently unreasonable?

firac.issue: What standard of review applies, and did the Commissioner exceed her jurisdiction in concluding the Rabbi was not a 'cadre supérieur' under s. 3(6) of the Labour Standards Act?
firac.facts: Beth-El argued as a preliminary objection that Rabbi Brandwein, as its spiritual leader and head of clergy, was a 'cadre supérieur' excluded from the s. 124 recourse. The Commissioner examined both the administrative and religious facets of his role over five days of hearings and found he was not a senior executive.
firac.rule: The pragmatic and functional approach governs standard of review (Bibeault; Southam; Pushpanathan; Dr. Q v. College of Physicians; Barrie Public Utilities). Applying the four factors and following Grenier J. in Dostie c. Bélanger, the question whether an employee is a 'cadre supérieur' under s. 3(6) L.S.A. does not go to jurisdiction; given the privative clause (s. 130 L.S.A.; ss. 139/139.1 C.T.) and the Commission's specialized expertise, the applicable standard is patent unreasonableness (patently unreasonable defect being immediate and obvious, per C.U.P.E. v. Ontario, Ryan, Southam).
firac.application: The Court agreed with Grenier J. that the concept of 'cadre supérieur' is one labour commissioners routinely apply and does not raise a jurisdictional question, so the deferential patent-unreasonableness standard applied. The Commissioner acted within her competence in assessing the Rabbi's role; her only shortcoming was not addressing the legislative intent behind the exclusion (the impossibility of reinstating senior executives), but even so she could reasonably reach the same result under a strict interpretation, and she properly disregarded the Rabbi's own wish for reinstatement as impracticable given his privileged position.
firac.conclusion: The standard is patent unreasonableness; the Commissioner's conclusion that the Rabbi was not a 'cadre supérieur' was not patently unreasonable, and the Court would not intervene on that point.

firac.issue: Was it patently unreasonable to find that allowing the fixed-term contract to expire amounted to a dismissal without good and sufficient cause?
firac.facts: The Rabbi worked for Beth-El from March 1998 to June 30, 2001 under successive contracts. Negotiations for a new three-year term were reached in March 2001, but the day before signing the Rabbi sought to change the salary allocation. Beth-El ended negotiations, let the contract expire, and communicated this on April 12, 2001. The Rabbi, before leaving on vacation, wrote to the president expressing his wish to continue and to be represented in further negotiations.
firac.rule: Non-renewal of a contract is not normally a dismissal (P.G. Québec c. Tribunal du travail; Tinker-Labrecque). However, where an employee could legitimately expect renewal absent adverse economic conditions or just cause, non-renewal may constitute a dismissal (Moore c. Compagnie Montreal Trust); each case turns on its facts. Section 124 L.S.A. requires good and sufficient cause.
firac.application: There was no automatic renewal clause, so Beth-El was under no legal obligation to renew. But the evidence supported the Commissioner's finding that the Rabbi could reasonably expect renewal: prior renewals, employer satisfaction, and negotiations ended more than three months before expiry without warning him that failure to sign meant no job. His conduct (a letter expressing wish to continue) was inconsistent with awareness that the relationship had ended. 'Hard bargaining' is not bad faith, and mere inability to agree was not good and sufficient cause.
firac.conclusion: The finding that the Rabbi was effectively dismissed without good and sufficient cause was supported by the evidence and was not patently unreasonable; that conclusion stands.

firac.issue: Was the Commissioner's monetary award patently unreasonable?
firac.facts: The Rabbi earned $115,000 per year. The Commissioner awarded $170,288 (roughly 18 months' salary from July 1, 2001 to the December 19, 2002 decision) plus a $38,333 indemnity (four months) for loss of employment, totalling $259,664. The Commissioner found the Rabbi could expect at best a one-year renewal, that Beth-El was not to blame for his difficulty finding new work, and that he was largely the author of his own misfortune.
firac.rule: Section 128 L.S.A. permits reinstatement, an indemnity up to the wage the employee would have earned, or any other fair and reasonable decision. Where an employer terminates without cause an employee with a definite term, the award is at most the maximum earnable under the contract; the employee has a duty to mitigate. Quantum is a question of law on which the reviewing court is equally well placed to decide.
firac.application: Having found the Rabbi could expect at best a one-year renewal, the maximum he could claim was one year's salary; the Commissioner gave no basis for treating the engagement as indeterminate. Awarding nearly 18 months plus a further four-month indemnity exceeded what was correct and reasonable. The Rabbi's difficulty finding work was immaterial given he was the author of his own misfortune and failed to mitigate. The award was overly generous, manifestly unreasonable, and unjust to Beth-El.
firac.conclusion: The award was patently unreasonable; the decision was annulled and the matter returned to the Commission to redetermine loss of salary in accordance with the Court's remarks, while the other conclusions stand.

keywords_rationale: The case is a judicial review of a labour tribunal decision on wrongful dismissal, so K009 (Labour and employment law) and K085 (wrongful dismissal/termination) are central, as is the administrative-law dimension: K001 (Administrative law), K011 (judicial review, brought under art. 846 C.C.P.), and K014 (standard of review — the patent-unreasonableness analysis dominates the reasons). The employer is a Jewish congregation and the employee its rabbi, so K098 (rabbi), K093 (Jewish), K094 (Jewish community) and K105 (synagogue) capture the entities involved. These entity keywords are contextually accurate though not doctrinally central. No hate-speech, Charter or family-law keywords apply.
location_rationale: The heading states 'SUPERIOR COURT / CANADA / PROVINCE OF QUEBEC / DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and refers to Beth-El operating a synagogue 'in Montreal.'
registry_rationale: The decision is filed in the 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' (file no. 500-17-013878-031), identifying the Montreal registry of the Superior Court.

case_name: Children’s Aid Society of the Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. J.D.

name_verification.name_in_document: Children's Aid Society of the Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. J.D.

defining_issues: Do the children continue to be in need of protection such that ongoing state intervention through a court order is necessary?

If the children remain in need of protection, is an order for extended society care (rather than returning them to the mother or a relative under a custody or supervision order) in their best interests?
Should an access order be granted following the extended care order, and if so, who should hold the access right?

firac.issue: Do the children continue to be in need of protection such that ongoing state intervention through a court order remains necessary?
firac.facts: The two children, born 2014 and 2015, were apprehended in November 2015 after A.D-R. (then about six weeks old) suffered inflicted blunt-force injuries (liver and pancreas damage, abdominal bruising and nine rib fractures, the fractures unexplained). They were found in need of protection in 2016. On the status review, the Society pointed to the mother's continued poor choice of partners (including a subsequent abusive relationship), lack of stable housing, failure to follow through on mood-regulation counselling, discontinuation of prescribed medication, and inability to demonstrate she could parent both children.
firac.rule: A status review proceeds in two stages (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. C.M., 1994 CanLII 83 (SCC); Children's Aid Society of Oxford v. W.T.C., 2013 ONCA 491): first, whether the child continues to be in need of protection and requires a court order; second, which available order is in the child's best interests. The agency must justify ongoing state intervention by showing a court order remains necessary to protect the child in future (W.T.C., para. 32); the original order is presumed correct.
firac.application: The court found the mother had not addressed the protection concerns: she continued to enter risky relationships, had no stable residence, made only last-minute efforts on housing, counselling and medication, and stopped her medication without medical advice. Her repeated 'I don't know' responses left the court without confidence she had the insight to protect the children, and the rib fractures remained unexplained. The concerns identified at the time of the agreed facts persisted.
firac.conclusion: The children continue to be in need of protection; ongoing state intervention through a court order remains necessary.

firac.issue: Is an order for extended society care, rather than return of the children to the mother or placement with a relative, in the children's best interests?
firac.facts: The children had been in care for 26 months (well beyond the statutory 12-month limit for children under six), living in a kin home since May 2017 where they were doing well and where the family was prepared to adopt them. The mother proposed return under a custody or supervision order, or placement of P.D. with the maternal grandmother S.R. The grandmother's home was overcrowded, and S.R. had a history with the Society and had failed to report protection concerns (including the bottle incident). The mother had never parented the children alone and struggled to manage both children during access.
firac.rule: Section 74(3) of the CYFSA sets out the best-interests factors; the court must choose the least restrictive alternative consistent with the child's best interests (CAS Peel v. W., 1995 CanLII 593). A crown ward / extended care order is among the most profound orders and requires the highest degree of caution, compelling evidence, and examination of alternatives (CAS Hamilton v. M.). Section 122 CYFSA limits time in care for young children.
firac.application: The statutory timelines left only return or extended care as options. Return was unsafe given the unaddressed protection concerns and the mother's inability to parent both children; supervision terms would not adequately protect them. Placement with S.R. was rejected due to her failure to report protection concerns, poor judgment, and an inadequate home. The children were thriving in the kin home, were strongly bonded to each other (any split plan ignoring this bond was rejected), and continuity of their secure placement favoured extended care leading to adoption.
firac.conclusion: Extended society care is in the children's best interests and is the least intrusive option that ensures their protection.

firac.issue: Should an access order be made after the extended care order, and who should hold the access right?
firac.facts: The mother sought access to both children. Access supervisors described visits as generally positive but inconsistent, with the mother struggling to manage both children and periods of missed visits that were not beneficial to the children. The kin caregivers treated the mother and grandmother as family and facilitated contact, and the Society conceded access would not impair adoptability.
firac.rule: Section 105 CYFSA governs access to a child in extended society care: an existing access order is terminated (s. 105(4)) and no access order may be made unless it is in the child's best interests (s. 105(5)), considering whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and, if relevant, impairment of adoption prospects (s. 105(6)). The onus is on the parent; beneficial/meaningful is no longer the sole criterion and is weighed among the s. 74(3) factors (C.H., 2018 ONCJ 453; K.B., 2018 ONCJ 650; T.S., 2018 ONCJ 411). The court must specify access holders and recipients (s. 105(7)).
firac.application: The mother did not establish that the visits were beneficial and meaningful given the inconsistency and disappointment caused by cancellations. However, since the Society conceded access would not impair adoptability and the kin caregivers facilitated contact, an access order was appropriate — but structured so the children, not the mother, hold the right of access, at the Society's discretion (consistent with CAS Toronto v. E.U., 2014 ONCJ 299).
firac.conclusion: An access order is granted with the children as the access holders, access to J.D. to be at the Society's discretion.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 practice area — this is a child protection status review under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is central, as the entire second stage and the access decision turn on the s. 74(3) and s. 105 best-interests analysis. K048 (custody/access) applies directly to the mother's alternative requests for custody/supervision orders and to the post-extended-care access order. K050 (parental support) and K052 (religious upbringing) are weak/borderline picks included only to reach the minimum count — neither child support nor religious upbringing was actually litigated; the controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated 'child protection / crown wardship / extended care' term, so no closer keyword exists.
location_rationale: The court is the Ontario Court of Justice and the court file is identified as 'Kitchener 814/15', indicating the Kitchener registry; the matter proceeds under Ontario's Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, confirming the province as Ontario.
registry_rationale: The header records 'COURT FILE No.: Kitchener 814/15', identifying the Kitchener registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: DeCotiis v. DeCotiis Estate

defining_issues: Should the impugned amendments (paras. 22–29) alleging historical family violence be struck as unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious under Rule 9-5(1)(b)?
Are the impugned amendments relevant to the plaintiff's will variation claim such that they should not be struck?
Are the impugned amendments relevant to the plaintiff's fraudulent conveyance, unjust enrichment/constructive trust, trustee removal, and undue influence claims?

firac.issue: Should the impugned paragraphs pleading historical family violence be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b), (c) or (d) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules?
firac.facts: The plaintiff's amended notice of civil claim added a section titled 'Childhood Trauma, Assault and Battery' (paras. 22–29) alleging he and his brothers were abused by the deceased, that the deceased assaulted their mother, and that the Younger Brothers hired people to assault and surveil the plaintiff. The defendant Rossano applied to strike these paragraphs as unnecessary, scandalous, prejudicial and an abuse of process; the plaintiff argued they were relevant to several causes of action.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) permits striking pleadings that (b) are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, (c) may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial, or (d) are otherwise an abuse of process. A pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to establishing the cause of action or advances no claim known in law (Nevsun Resources v. Araya, 2020 SCC 5; Willow v. Chong, 2014 BCSC 1083; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860). An embarrassing pleading is one so irrelevant it involves useless expense and prejudices the trial (Keddie v. Dumas Hotels, 1985 CanLII 417; Sahyoun v. Ho, 2015 BCSC 392). Abuse of process is a flexible doctrine (First Majestic Silver v. Santos, 2012 BCCA 5; Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., 2003 SCC 63). The court must ask whether, assuming the facts true, there is a reasonable prospect of success and err in favour of permitting arguable claims.
firac.application: The court examined each pleaded cause of action to test the relevance of the allegations. Allegations of a broader history of family violence between the plaintiff and the deceased were held potentially relevant and not struck; allegations concerning abuse directed at siblings/mother and the Younger Brothers' alleged surveillance and hired assaults were held unnecessary, embarrassing and prejudicial and would exponentially expand discovery into irrelevant matters.
firac.conclusion: The application was partly granted: paras. 23, 25, 26, 27 and 28 struck; paras. 22 and 24 not struck (with further particulars required for para. 24); part of para. 29 ('Despite the family's violence,') struck. Costs in the cause.

firac.issue: Are the historical family violence allegations relevant to the plaintiff's will variation claim?
firac.facts: The 2016 Will disinherited the plaintiff. The defendants alleged the plaintiff assaulted the deceased in September 2004 and pointed to longstanding estrangement as reasons for disinheritance. The plaintiff sought to plead the broader context of family violence directed at him.
firac.rule: Section 60 of WESA permits the court to vary a will that fails to make adequate provision for a child. Reasons for disinheritance are relevant. Will variation is not a means to compensate for family abuse, but historical mistreatment may be relevant, as a parent who treated a child unfairly may have a moral obligation to make amends through the will (Persall v. Stromberg, 2015 BCSC 1826; Doucette v. McInnes, 2009 BCCA 393; Sawchuk v. MacKenzie Estate, 2000 BCCA 10).
firac.application: Because the defendants raised a 2004 assault by the plaintiff and estrangement as reasons for disinheritance, they made family violence relevant. The plaintiff was entitled to respond by putting the broader history of violence between himself and the deceased into context. However, allegations of abuse directed at siblings or the mother were not relevant to the will variation issue as between the plaintiff and the deceased.
firac.conclusion: Allegations of a broader history of violence between the plaintiff and the deceased were relevant and preserved; allegations concerning others were not relevant to will variation.

firac.issue: Are the historical abuse allegations relevant to the plaintiff's fraudulent conveyance, unjust enrichment/constructive trust, trustee removal, and undue influence claims?
firac.facts: The plaintiff argued childhood assaults gave him potential tort claims making him a 'creditor or other' under the FCA, that the abuse supported a constructive trust in 'good conscience', and that the Younger Brothers' surveillance and hired assaults were relevant to trustee removal and undue influence.
firac.rule: FCA s. 1 ('creditors and others'); constructive trust arises typically on breach of fiduciary duty or unjust enrichment (BNSF Railway v. Teck Metals, 2016 BCCA 350); trustee removal principles focus on protection of beneficiaries and future administration, not punishment of past misconduct (Parker v. Thompson, 2014 BCSC 1916; Fales v. Canada Permanent Trust, 1976 CanLII 14; Letterstedt v. Broers). Undue influence requires relevance to the influence exerted on the will-maker.
firac.application: No authority supported using the FCA in this manner, and the plaintiff already advanced the FCA claim through the deceased's alleged breaches of the 1993 Trust, making the abuse allegations unnecessary. No authority supported extending constructive trust to reward proof of abuse. The trustees' alleged involvement in surveillance/assault did not bear on whether Rossano and Giulio adequately administered the 2019 Trust or were in conflict, and would greatly expand discovery. The surveillance/assault allegations were at best marginally relevant to undue influence and would cause disproportionate expansion of discovery.
firac.conclusion: The allegations were unnecessary, embarrassing and prejudicial for each of these claims and did not save the impugned paragraphs from being struck.

keywords_rationale: This is a civil procedure application to strike pleadings in an estate/will variation dispute, so K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 practice area. K054 (wills/estates) captures the WESA will variation claim, disinheritance, trusts and estate litigation at the heart of the pleadings. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the closest available civil-procedure/remedies keyword for this interlocutory motion, though it is a weak/imperfect fit since the motion is actually a strike application under Rule 9-5 rather than an injunction — flagged as borderline. K006 (family law) is included because the estate variation, disinheritance and family estrangement engage a family/matrimonial dimension, though it is secondary. The controlled vocabulary lacks specific keywords for 'motion to strike pleadings,' 'fraudulent conveyance,' 'constructive trust,' or 'breach of trust/trustee removal,' so fewer than five strongly on-point keywords truly apply; the selections above are the closest available.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Registry: Vancouver' and lists the place of hearing and judgment as 'Vancouver, B.C.' The court is the Supreme Court of British Columbia, so the province is British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Changizi v. Passey

defining_issues: Should the personal defendant's pleadings be struck and the action dismissed against him under R. 9-5 or R. 9-6, on the basis that he was acting on behalf of a numbered company entitled to limited liability?
Should the plaintiff be granted leave to add the numbered company as a defendant and to amend the notice of civil claim under R. 6-2?
Does s. 27 of the Business Corporations Act defeat limited liability protection where the underlying contract was oral rather than written?

firac.issue: Should the personal defendant's pleadings be struck and the action dismissed against him under R. 9-5 or R. 9-6?
firac.facts: The plaintiff sued Bryce Passey dba BWP Construction for breach of contract and negligence arising from a construction project on his property. The defendant asserted he was at all material times operating through 1594040 Alberta Inc. (a company registered as a sole proprietorship doing business as BWP) and applied to strike the personal claim and dismiss the action against him. There was no written contract, and an invoice issued about three months into the work referenced the numbered company; affidavit evidence on whether the defendant properly identified himself as acting for the company was directly conflicting.
firac.rule: Under R. 9-5(1)(a) a pleading may be struck only where it discloses no reasonable claim, i.e. where the claim is 'certain to fail' and the case is 'perfectly clear' (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., 1990 CanLII 90 (SCC); FORCOMP Forestry Consulting Ltd. v. British Columbia, 2021 BCCA 465). No evidence is admissible under R. 9-5(1)(a). Under R. 9-6 summary dismissal is available only where there is no genuine issue for trial and the plaintiff is bound to lose (Canada (AG) v. Lameman, 2008 SCC 14); evidence may be weighed only to the extent it is incontrovertible (Beach Estate v. Beach, 2019 BCCA 277). Pleadings are read generously (Nevsun Resources Ltd. v. Araya, 2020 SCC 5).
firac.application: The whether the defendant was entitled to limited liability protection, particularly given the interplay of s. 27 of the BCA and an oral contract, was a genuine and interesting legal argument not yet fulsomely resolved. The affidavit material was directly conflicting and could not be tested without discovery and cross-examination, so it was not incontrovertible. The Court found this a triable issue and could not conclude the claim was certain to fail or that the plaintiff was bound to lose.
firac.conclusion: The Court was not satisfied that relief under either R. 9-5 or R. 9-6 was appropriate; the defendant's application was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff be granted leave to add the numbered company as a defendant and to amend the notice of civil claim under R. 6-2?
firac.facts: After learning through the defendant's response pleading that the defendant claimed to have operated through the numbered company, and having received an invoice referencing it, the plaintiff sought to add 1594040 Alberta Inc. as a defendant and to file an amended notice of civil claim (fraud allegations having been withdrawn). No document lists had been exchanged, no examinations for discovery had occurred, and no trial notice had been filed.
firac.rule: Under R. 6-2(7) and R. 6-2(8) the addition of parties is a discretionary matter to be exercised generously to allow effective determination of issues without delay, inconvenience or separate hearings (Delta Sunshine Taxi (1972) Ltd. v. Vancouver (City), 2014 BCSC 2100). Amendments are allowed liberally where the pleadings disclose a cause of action (Meade v. Armstrong (City), 2011 BCSC 1591), consistent with the object in R. 1-3 of a just, speedy and inexpensive determination on the merits.
firac.application: The litigation was at an early stage, so adding the numbered company would cause no significant delay or prejudice and would avoid separate hearings and inconsistent findings. The limitation period against the numbered company was not, on the face of the materials, statute-barred, so a separate claim could otherwise be brought and would likely lead to a joinder application in any event. The Court was satisfied a claim could be drafted disclosing a reasonable cause of action.
firac.conclusion: The Court exercised its discretion under R. 6-2 to add the numbered company as a defendant and granted leave to file the amended notice of civil claim (in the most recent iteration attached to the affidavit material).

firac.issue: Does s. 27 of the Business Corporations Act defeat limited liability where the contract was oral?
firac.facts: The plaintiff argued the defendant did not properly identify himself as operating through a numbered company as required by s. 27 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, and thus was not entitled to limited liability. The defendant argued s. 27 contemplates a written contract, and here the contract was oral.
firac.rule: Section 27 of the Business Corporations Act governs identification of a company operating under another name; on a plain reading it may contemplate a written contract, but a contextual reading may support the view that its purposes cannot be avoided through an oral contract.
firac.application: The Court declined to decide the point on the merits in the context of pleadings applications, characterizing it as an interesting and unsettled legal question. It concluded that it constituted a triable issue appropriate to be resolved on a full record rather than on conflicting affidavit evidence.
firac.conclusion: The s. 27 issue was left as a triable issue for determination on the merits; it did not warrant striking or dismissing the claim.

name_verification.name_in_document: D. v. B.

defining_issues: Was evidence of the appellant's Austrian (enemy) national origin, of slanders and persecution by his relatives, and of a relative's complaint to immigration authorities improperly admitted and used to prejudice the jury?

Were the damages of $5,000, in light of the parties' station in life and the appellant's finances, excessive and materially inflated by the improperly admitted evidence, amounting to a 'substantial wrong' under s. 28 of the Judicature Act?
Did the appellant's failure to object to the impugned evidence and address at trial preclude him from obtaining a new trial on appeal?

firac.issue: Was evidence of the appellant's Austrian (enemy) origin, of slanders and persecution by his relatives, and of a relative's immigration complaint improperly admitted so as to prejudice the jury in a breach-of-promise action?
firac.facts: In an action for breach of promise of marriage, the respondent (a Russian Jewess) recovered $5,000 against the appellant (born in Galicia, Austria). At trial, evidence contrasted the parties' nationalities, established that the appellant's relatives had insulted, slandered and sought to have the respondent deported, and a witness testified that a jilted Jewish girl's morality would be doubted in the community. No actual damage was proven; the verdict was almost entirely sentimental.
firac.rule: In breach-of-promise actions damages are at the discretion of the jury (Smith v. Woodfine (1857) 1 C.P.N.S. 660; Berry v. Da Costa (1866) L.R. 1 C.P. 331), but a verdict influenced by prejudice, passion or corruption will not stand. Calling a party a 'German' or 'Austrian' in the present state of public opinion is prejudicial (Slazengers Ltd. v. C. Gibbs & Co., 33 Times L.R. 35; Gage v. Reid, 38 O.L.R. 514). Evidence of the feelings, statements and misconduct of third parties, tendered to aggravate damages against the defendant, is not admissible.
firac.application: The majority (Ferguson J.A., Meredith C.J.O., Maclaren J.A.) held that the respondent's counsel deliberately placed before the jury the appellant's enemy-alien origin and the slanders and persecution by his relatives, matters not properly in issue, to inflame the jury. No authority justified admitting third-party slanders to aggravate damages the appellant would pay. The dissent (Hodgins and Magee JJ.A.) considered the national origin was introduced by the appellant's own counsel and that the family statements were admissible because the appellant himself repeated them and used them to postpone and then repudiate the promise.
firac.conclusion: The majority held much of the evidence was improperly admitted and calculated to prejudice the appellant.

firac.issue: Were the damages excessive and materially inflated by the improper evidence, amounting to a substantial wrong under s. 28 of the Judicature Act?
firac.facts: The $5,000 verdict was almost wholly sentimental; the appellant earned $1,500 a year, supported poor parents, and had no other means. The respondent had been in Canada less than a year, was likely to return to Russia, and her marriage prospects there would not be affected.
firac.rule: Section 28 of the Judicature Act, R.S.O. 1914, c. 56 bars a new trial for misdirection or improper admission of evidence unless a substantial wrong has thereby been occasioned. The court assesses the amount of the verdict in light of the parties' financial and social position (Gage v. Reid, 34 D.L.R. 46 at 53-4).
firac.application: The majority concluded the verdict was excessive given the parties' circumstances and was materially increased by the wrongful acts and improper evidence, so a substantial wrong was occasioned. The trial judge, having directed counsel to confine themselves to whether there was a breach, gave no direction cautioning the jury on the impugned evidence, leaving the jury to consider all of it in assessing damages. The dissent, while also finding the damages large, held it was not shown the jury was misled or actuated by improper motives, and would not disturb the jury's discretion.
firac.conclusion: The majority found the damages excessive and a substantial wrong under s. 28, justifying a new trial.

firac.issue: Did the appellant's failure to object at trial to the impugned evidence and jury address preclude a new trial on appeal?
firac.facts: Trial counsel for the appellant (different from appellate counsel) did not object to the evidence or to respondent's counsel's address at the time.
firac.rule: There is a salutary rule that objection to improper conduct of counsel or admission of evidence must be raised before the trial judge on the spot (Sornberger v. Canadian Pacific R.W. Co., 24 A.R. 263; Dale v. Toronto R.W. Co., 34 O.L.R. 104), save in exceptional cases.
firac.application: The majority held that once substantial wrong is established, the appellant is not to be denied a new trial merely because trial counsel failed to object, relying on Gage v. Reid. The dissent (Hodgins J.A.) applied the general rule strictly, finding no protest was made and the objection was therefore not open to the appellant, and that the case was not exceptional.
firac.conclusion: The majority held the failure to object did not bar relief; the dissent would have applied the rule to dismiss the appeal.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area: the case turns on admissibility of evidence, aggravation of damages, and the test for a new trial in a civil breach-of-promise action. K006 (Family law) is included as the underlying cause of action is breach of promise of marriage, and K049 (marriage/cohabitation agreement) is the closest specific keyword for a promise to marry. K015 (defamation) reflects the central role of the slanderous statements by the appellant's relatives whose admissibility drove the appeal. K093 (Jewish), K094 (Jewish community) and K098 (rabbi — the witness Rabbi Jacobs) capture the parties' and witnesses' identity and the community-morality evidence. Weaker/borderline picks: K049 is imperfect because a breach of promise is not strictly a marriage contract, and K015 goes to admitted evidence rather than the pleaded claim.
location_rationale: The decision is that of the 'Ontario Supreme Court, Appellate Division' and records that the trial was held 'at Toronto jury sittings on the 15th, 16th, and 17th January, 1917.' The Appellate Division sat in Toronto, Ontario; the province is Ontario throughout (references to R.S.O. 1914 and Ontario cases).

case_name: Direk v. Attorney General of Ontario

name_verification.name_in_document: Direk v. Attorney General of Ontario

defining_issues: Should the respondents be prohibited from bringing further motions in these proceedings without leave of a judge as vexatious under Rule 37.16 of the Rules of Civil Procedure?

firac.issue: Should the respondents be prohibited from bringing further motions without leave under Rule 37.16 on the basis that their motions are frivolous and vexatious?
firac.facts: The proceeding originated with an in rem forfeiture application by the Attorney General under the Civil Remedies Act seeking forfeiture of $229,345.00 and a 2006 Lincoln Mark LT truck as proceeds or instruments of crime. The Direk/Direkoglu respondents launched a 'counter-application' seeking to quash the application and claiming four billion dollars, alleging a decades-long judiciary-driven conspiracy, corruption, crimes against humanity and other atrocities. They then brought an endless string of unsuccessful motions and appeals, recycling near-identical grounds, repeatedly re-litigating an unmeritorious conflict-of-interest allegation against Stinson J. and levelling scandalous accusations of fraud, forgery, sexual abuse and other crimes against every judge who ruled against them.
firac.rule: Rule 37.16 of the Rules of Civil Procedure (together with Rule 61.16(1) applying it to appellate motions) permits an order prohibiting a party from bringing further motions without leave — a 'mini-vexatious litigant order'. The indicia of vexatious proceedings are set out in Lang Michener v. Fabian (1987), 59 O.R. (2d) 353 (H.C.J.), endorsed in Bishop v. Bishop, 2011 ONCA 211, including re-litigating determined issues, actions that cannot succeed or serve no good, proceedings brought for improper purposes such as harassment, grounds repeated and supplemented in successive proceedings, the whole history of the matter, failure to pay costs, and persistent unsuccessful appeals.
firac.application: The Court found each Lang Michener principle plainly applicable, with 'motions' substituted for 'actions' under Rule 37.16. The respondents' motions recycled identical grounds, re-litigated the failed conflict-of-interest claim against Stinson J., added baseless allegations against every judge who ruled against them, and were unsupported by any evidence. The multiplicity of frivolous and vexatious motions was found to be brought to delay the proceedings or abuse the process of the Court; the Court considered it unnecessary to recite the many motions in detail.
firac.conclusion: Motion granted. The respondents are prohibited from bringing further motions in the specified Divisional Court and Superior Court files (or new files raising the same or similar matters) without leave, leave to be sought only by written motion; the Registrars are not to accept material other than a written leave motion; costs of $1,500 payable forthwith; the order effective immediately without the respondents' approval.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area: the case concerns a vexatious-litigant / abuse-of-process motion under the Rules of Civil Procedure arising from a civil in rem forfeiture proceeding under the Civil Remedies Act. K022 (restitution) is the closest available match to the civil forfeiture of proceeds/instruments of crime that underlies the proceeding, though it is a loose fit. K093 (Jewish), K058 (antisemitism) and K065 (racism) reflect the respondents' own conspiracy allegations that judges favoured 'high authoritative Jewish figures over Turks, Germans and Islamics' — these are borderline/weak picks included only because the controlled vocabulary lacks any keyword for vexatious proceedings, abuse of process, or civil forfeiture; they describe the litigants' baseless allegations rather than any adjudicated issue and should be treated cautiously.

registry_rationale: The matter bears 'DIVISIONAL COURT FILE NO.: 305/10 and 638/10' and was heard at Toronto in the Divisional Court of the Superior Court of Justice; the registry is Toronto.

case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Oxford County v. E.M.T.

name_verification.name_in_document: Children's Aid Society of Oxford County v. E.M.T.

defining_issues: Did the Society establish on a balance of probabilities that the children suffered actual physical harm under s. 74(2)(a)(i) and (ii) of the CYFSA?
Did the Society establish that the children are at risk of physical harm under s. 74(2)(b)(i) and (ii) of the CYFSA?
Did the Society establish that the children are at risk of emotional harm under s. 74(2)(h) of the CYFSA?
What disposition is in the best interests of the children given the protection findings?

firac.issue: Did the Society establish on a balance of probabilities that the children suffered actual physical harm under s. 74(2)(a)(i) and (ii) of the CYFSA?
firac.facts: The children disclosed that M.A.R. and his partner T.E. hit and yelled at them during access, sometimes leaving bruises, and that this occurred at most visits. M.R. stopped attending access in January 2017 because she could no longer tolerate being hit. E.M.T. produced photographs of bruises. M.A.R. and T.E. denied all abuse, but the court found the workers' and children's evidence credible and the respondents' evidence riddled with material inconsistencies.
firac.rule: Actual physical harm is the foundation of grounds under s. 74(2)(a) CYFSA and must be proved on a balance of probabilities (Children's Aid Society of Algoma v. J.B., 2019 ONCJ 6). Causation may be by act, omission or pattern and intention need not be proved (Jewish Family and Child Service v. K.(R.), 2008 ONCJ 774, aff'd 2009 ONCA 903); harm must be more than trifling (CAS Niagara v. P.T.; Rainy River v. B.(C.)). Corporal punishment using objects or blows to the head is harmful (Canadian Foundation for Children, Youth and the Law v. Canada (AG), 2004 SCC 4).
firac.application: The court accepted the strikingly similar independent disclosures of M.R., J.R. and O.R., corroborated by consistent worker testimony, over the contradictory and evasive evidence of E.M.T., M.A.R. and T.E. A consistent pattern of repeated physical discipline (slaps to the back and face, occasional bruising), coupled with yelling, swearing and alcohol use that made the children fear for their safety, represented more than trifling harm. M.A.R. failed to protect the children from T.E., and E.M.T. was aware and failed to act protectively.
firac.conclusion: A finding of actual physical harm under s. 74(2)(a)(i) and (ii) was made out.

firac.issue: Did the Society establish that the children are at risk of physical harm under s. 74(2)(b)(i) and (ii) of the CYFSA?
firac.facts: M.A.R.'s home was marked by yelling, swearing, excessive alcohol use that made him angrier, exposure to T.E.'s drug use and conflict including throwing objects, and repeated police involvement. E.M.T. knew of these concerns but took no protective steps until the Society intervened in November 2017.
firac.rule: Section 74(2)(b) CYFSA requires a real and likely (more probable than not) risk of physical harm, inflicted by, or resulting from the failure or pattern of neglect of, the person having charge (Rainy River v. B.(C.), 2006 ONCJ 458; Ottawa-Carlton v. T. and T., 2000). A child may be at risk even if conduct is not directed at that child (Catholic CAS of Metro Toronto v. O.(L.M.)).
firac.application: The environment of alcohol-fuelled anger, exposure to T.E.'s untreated drug use which M.A.R. himself conceded was 'not good', ongoing adult conflict including thrown objects, and M.A.R.'s poor judgment in permitting T.E.'s continued contact with the children established a real and likely risk. E.M.T.'s failure to protect further supported the finding.
firac.conclusion: A finding that the children are at risk of physical harm under s. 74(2)(b)(i) and (ii) was made out.

firac.issue: Did the Society establish that the children are at risk of emotional harm under s. 74(2)(h) of the CYFSA?
firac.facts: The Society called no expert to establish a risk of emotional harm. Beyond a brief reference by the intake worker that O.R. had 'significant challenges' in the classroom, there was little evidence of the children's behaviours in home, school or community demonstrating listed symptoms of emotional harm.
firac.rule: Section 74(2)(h) CYFSA requires the Society to prove, on a balance of probabilities, a real likelihood that the child will suffer at least one listed emotional harm (anxiety, depression, withdrawal, self-destructive or aggressive behaviour, delayed development), of a serious (not minimal, mild or moderate) degree, causally connected to the parent's conduct (Algoma v. A.B., 2018 ONCJ 831; Algoma v. J.B., 2019 ONCJ 6). Expert evidence is preferred but not mandatory; risk may be established from exposure to domestic violence or a child's distressed reactions (Chukwunomso v. Ransome, 2017 ONCJ 121; CAS Toronto v. S.A.C.).
firac.application: Although a risk of physical harm was established, that does not automatically establish a risk of emotional harm. The Society adduced no evidence from anyone with the credentials to establish the risk, and failed to show that any child was likely to suffer a listed symptom in a serious degree. The evidence was insufficient to demonstrate the required risk and its severity.
firac.conclusion: The claim for a finding of risk of emotional harm under s. 74(2)(h) was dismissed.

firac.issue: What disposition is in the best interests of the children given the protection findings?
firac.facts: The children had been placed with E.M.T. since apprehension on November 16, 2017; the Society had no protection concerns with her and she complied with the interim order. M.A.R. refused to communicate consistently with workers, would not sign consents, undertake drug screens or programming, breached directions regarding contact at R.R.'s home, and behaved aggressively toward a worker. However, his access visits were generally positive and J.R. and O.R. wished for more time with him; M.R. did not wish to attend access.
firac.rule: Sections 101 and 102 CYFSA set out available orders where a child is found in need of protection; the paramount purpose (s. 1(1)) is the best interests, protection and well-being of the child, which takes precedence over the secondary purposes in s. 1(2) (Syl Apps Secure Treatment Centre v. D.(B.), 2007 SCC 38). Best-interests factors are enumerated in s. 74(3), and s. 101(2) requires consideration of the Society's efforts and the least intrusive order.
firac.application: The Society made significant efforts to engage M.A.R., who refused to cooperate, failed to acknowledge concerns, and did not address the protection issues; supervised access alone did not show the risks were remedied. The court weighed the children's expressed wishes (J.R. and O.R. wanting more, but content with supervised access; M.R. not wishing to attend) and M.A.R.'s warm relationship with the younger children. The least intrusive order consistent with the children's best interests was placement with E.M.T. under supervision with Society-discretion access to M.A.R.
firac.conclusion: A six-month supervision order placing the children with E.M.T. was made, with access to J.R. and O.R. at the Society's discretion and access to M.R. subject to her wishes.

keywords_rationale: This is a child-protection case, so the tier-1 area is Family law (K006). Best interests of the child (K047) is central to the disposition analysis under s. 74(3) CYFSA. Custody/access (K048) captures the operative dispositional relief (supervision order with access to the father at Society discretion, and access to M.R. per her wishes). The controlled vocabulary lacks specific child-protection keywords (e.g. need of protection, physical harm, domestic violence), so no more precise tier-2 term is available; the wrongful dismissal keyword K085 is not applicable and I have not used it. Because fewer than five vocabulary keywords genuinely apply, this is a case where the controlled list under-covers child-welfare law — the remaining picks would be weak, so I have limited selection to the genuinely engaged terms rather than force irrelevant IDs.

registry_rationale: The court file number 'Woodstock C224/17' identifies the Woodstock registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. T.-J.M. et al.

name_verification.name_in_document: Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. T.-J.M. et al.

defining_issues: Should the Children's Aid Society be granted summary judgment under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules for the dispositional orders sought, i.e. is there no genuine issue requiring a trial?
What custody disposition under s. 57.1 of the Child and Family Services Act is in the best interests of the four children?
How should the parents' access to the children be determined, and is the requested increased/unsupervised access a triable issue?

firac.issue: Should the Society be granted summary judgment under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules, i.e. is there no genuine issue requiring a trial?
firac.facts: The four children had all been apprehended and placed with grandparents under temporary supervision orders; statutory protection findings under s. 47(2) and s. 37(2)(b) CFSA had already been made on November 17, 2011. The mother (T.M.1) sought return of the children or expanded access and opposed the orders; she had a history of non-compliance with supervision terms, exposure of the children to domestic violence, inconsistent access, mental-health concerns and failure to complete recommended programs.
firac.rule: Rule 16 Family Law Rules permits summary judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; the responding party may not rest on mere allegations or denials but must set out specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial (r. 16(4.1)); r. 16(6) is mandatory. The court must take a 'good hard look' at the full evidentiary record but must not weigh evidence or assess credibility (Aguonie; Guarantee Co. of North America v. Gordon Capital; CAS Waterloo v. V.L.; CAS Toronto v. R.H.). The paramount purpose of the CFSA (s. 1(1)) is the best interests, protection and well-being of children, and the strict timelines in ss. 57 and 70 must be respected.
firac.application: Justice Zuker reviewed the plans of care and the full evidentiary record. He found the mother's material amounted to a heartfelt desire to resume care rather than specific facts showing changed parenting ability; the uncontradicted facts (R.H.'s criminal record, history of domestic violence, mother's exposure of children to that violence, non-compliance with orders, mental-health and financial instability, no kin plan for J.H.) established a prima facie case. The children had been out of parental care beyond the statutory timelines and were in stable placements. No material fact affecting best interests required a trial.
firac.conclusion: Summary judgment was granted; the mother failed to demonstrate a genuine issue for trial.

firac.issue: What custody disposition under s. 57.1 CFSA is in the best interests of the children?
firac.facts: T.M.2 and A.M. had lived with the maternal grandparents (B.Y. and S.P.) for extended periods and the grandparents consented to custody with the father D.F. also consenting. E.H. and J.H. were in the care of the paternal grandmother D.H., who consented to a six-month supervision placement, with R.H. consenting to supervision. The mother opposed and sought return of all children.
firac.rule: Section 57.1 CFSA allows a custody order to a non-foster-parent with that person's consent where it is in the child's best interests; such an order is deemed a custody order under s. 28 of the Children's Law Reform Act. Best interests are governed by the non-exhaustive factors in s. 37(3) CFSA. The disposition must be the least disruptive order consistent with best interests (s. 57(2)-(4)), and best interests take priority over parental wishes (Catholic CAS v. C.M.; Young v. Young; King v. Low).
firac.application: The court weighed continuity of care, the children's established stable placements, and the risks the mother continued to present. The proposed placements with consenting grandparents reflected the children's special needs, importance of family relationships and continuity, and the degree of risk. The rebuttable presumption favouring parental care was rebutted by the mother's unaddressed parenting deficits.
firac.conclusion: Custody of T.M.2 and A.M. was granted to the maternal grandparents and custody of E.H. and J.H. to the paternal grandmother subject to Society supervision, all under s. 57.1.

firac.issue: How should the parents' access be determined, and is the request for increased or unsupervised access a triable issue?
firac.facts: D.F. sought regular overnight and holiday access and decision-making over religious upbringing, objecting to access being delegated to the grandparents' discretion. R.H. sought unsupervised access to E.H. and J.H. T.M.1 attended less than half her scheduled visits and sought unsupervised/overnight access. The Society and grandparents proposed supervised/limited access.
firac.rule: Access is a right belonging to the child, not the parent, and must be decided in the child's best interests; a court can prohibit access (Catholic CAS v. M.(C.)). Access questions turn on whether the relationship is significantly advantageous to the child. Future access that is speculative and hypothetical is not a triable issue where it is not susceptible of proof.
firac.application: The court found access with the mother generally positive but held that claims for increased/unsupervised access were premised on assumptions that did not yet exist and were too uncertain, speculative and hypothetical to constitute a triable issue. Given the disposition (leading toward adoption), the court left future access to be decided by the children's future adoptive parents, while setting specified interim access terms for R.H. and T.M.1 to the boys.
firac.conclusion: No triable issue on access existed; the access terms in the disposition orders were fixed and future access left to the children's caregivers/adoptive parents.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a child protection proceeding under the Child and Family Services Act. K047 (best interests of the child) is central: the entire disposition turns on the s. 37(3) best-interests analysis. K048 (custody/access) captures both the s. 57.1 custody orders and the contested access determinations. K011 (judicial review) is a weak/borderline pick reflecting the summary judgment/procedural review of the evidentiary record — flagged as weak. K001 (Administrative law) borderline given the Society is a statutory body, but the case is squarely family law; flagged weak. K052 (religious upbringing) applies because D.F. specifically sought decision-making authority over the children's religious upbringing, a contested access issue. K002 (Civil litigation) supports the Rule 16 summary judgment procedural dimension. The strongest, clearly engaged keywords are K006, K047 and K048.

name_verification.name_in_document: Das v. George Weston Limited

defining_issues: Does an Ontario court have jurisdiction simpliciter over a proposed global class action including non-resident 'Absent Foreign Claimants', and did the constitutional challenge to that jurisdiction remain live?
What is the choice of law governing the tort and breach of fiduciary duty claims — Ontario law or the law of Bangladesh?
If Bangladesh law applies, are the plaintiffs' tort and fiduciary claims statute-barred under Bangladesh's Limitation Act, 1908?
Is it plain and obvious that neither Loblaws nor Bureau Veritas owed a legally viable duty of care in negligence to the putative class members?
Is Loblaws vicariously liable for the negligence of its supplier (Pearl Global) and sub-supplier (New Wave)?
Is there a viable breach of fiduciary duty claim against Loblaws?
Should the action be certified as a class proceeding under the Class Proceedings Act, 1992?

firac.issue: Does an Ontario court have jurisdiction simpliciter over a proposed global class action including non-resident Absent Foreign Claimants, and did the constitutional challenge remain live?
firac.facts: Four Bangladeshi plaintiffs commenced a proposed class action in Ontario on behalf of survivors and families of the Rana Plaza collapse. Most putative class members reside in Bangladesh and had not attorned to the Ontario court. After Airia Brands and Excalibur, the plaintiffs recast the class from opt-out to opt-in and also ran an attornment/consent program in Bangladesh; Loblaws challenged jurisdiction and raised a constitutional argument, prompting the Attorney General of Ontario to intervene.
firac.rule: Jurisdiction simpliciter is established by the presumptive connecting factors in Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17, together with traditional attornment. Excalibur Special Opportunities LP v. Schwartz Levitsky Feldman LLP, 2016 ONCA 916 confirms an Ontario court may take jurisdiction in a global class action over non-resident members; Harrington v. Dow Corning, 2000 BCCA 605 recognizes that non-residents can attorn by opting in. The Class Proceedings Act, 1992 is procedural and does not create or alter substantive rights (Bisaillon v. Concordia University, 2006 SCC 19).
firac.application: The court held it had jurisdiction simpliciter based on a combination of the named parties' attornment, the Van Breda connecting factors, and the opt-in class definition. Because non-resident members would attorn post-certification through a court-supervised opt-in notice program, there would be no true Absent Foreign Claimants and no need to rule on the validity of the Bangladesh consent-collection exercise. The constitutional challenge therefore became moot.
firac.conclusion: The Ontario court has jurisdiction simpliciter; Loblaws' constitutional challenge was moot and was dismissed without a ruling on its merits.

firac.issue: Is the choice of law for the tort and fiduciary claims Ontario law or the law of Bangladesh?
firac.facts: Loblaws formulated its Corporate Social Responsibility standards, retained Bureau Veritas, and made purchasing decisions in Ontario, but the Rana Plaza building, the workers, the social audits, and the deaths and injuries all occurred in Bangladesh. The plaintiffs pleaded that the wrongdoing occurred in Ontario; the defendants argued Bangladesh law applied (and would statute-bar the claims).
firac.rule: The choice of law for torts is the lex loci delicti — the law of the place where the tort occurred (Tolofson v. Jensen, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 1022), with only a narrow discretionary 'injustice' exception. The place of a tort is the jurisdiction substantially affected by the defendant's activities and their consequences and whose law was in the parties' reasonable contemplation (Moran v. Pyle; Leonard v. Houle; Éditions Écosociété v. Banro). Limitation periods are substantive.
firac.application: The court rejected the plaintiffs' 'pleading artifice' locating the wrongdoing exclusively in Ontario. The duty, breach, causation and damage elements of the negligence claim, and the equitable claim, were centred in Bangladesh, where the collapse and all harm occurred and whose law was referenced in the CSR standards. Even treating the case as a 'thorny' one where act and consequence diverge, the consequences were felt in Bangladesh, which designates Bangladesh law. Arguments to oust Bangladesh law for failure of proof, unsophisticated jurisprudence, discriminatory Sharia succession rules, and absence of punitive damages were rejected — the offensive Sharia distribution rule could be severed and none of the grounds met the injustice exception.
firac.conclusion: Bangladesh law governs the tort and breach of fiduciary duty claims.

firac.issue: Are the plaintiffs' claims statute-barred under Bangladesh's Limitation Act, 1908?
firac.facts: The action was commenced on April 22, 2015, roughly two years after the April 24, 2013 collapse. Ten foreign-law experts testified. The key authority was Bangladesh Beverage Industries Ltd. v. Rowshan Akhter and the interplay of Articles 21, 22 and 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
firac.rule: Foreign law is a question of fact proved by expert evidence; where experts conflict the court may examine the sources and decide (Allen v. Hay; General Motors Acceptance Corp. v. Town and Country Chrysler). Articles 21 and 22 of the Limitation Act, 1908 impose a one-year limitation for fatal-accident and personal-injury claims; Article 120 is a six-year residual provision; s. 6 extends time for minors; ss. 7 and 13 provide limited tolling.
firac.application: Preferring the defendants' experts, the court found the Appellate Division in Bangladesh Beverage confirmed a one-year limitation period under Articles 21 and 22 for wrongful-death and personal-injury claims (the s. 4 vacation extension only made sense on a one-year period). Sections 7 and 13 did not toll the claims; s. 13 did not apply to a corporation never present in Bangladesh, and Bureau Veritas was present throughout. Only s. 6 preserved claims of class members who were minors (born on or after April 22, 1996) at the time of collapse.
firac.conclusion: Under Bangladesh law the tort and fiduciary claims are statute-barred, except for putative class members who were minors at the time of the collapse.

firac.issue: Is it plain and obvious that the defendants owed no viable duty of care in negligence?
firac.facts: Loblaws was a purchaser of garments from Pearl Global, which sub-contracted to New Wave at Rana Plaza; Loblaws did not own, construct or control the building. Bureau Veritas conducted limited 'social audits' that expressly did not cover structural integrity. The plaintiffs alleged the defendants assumed responsibility for worker safety through CSR standards and audits.
firac.rule: Under English/Bangladesh law a duty of care requires satisfaction of the Caparo test (foreseeability, proximity, and policy), the assumption-of-responsibility test (Hedley Byrne), or incremental development; the common law generally imposes no positive duty to protect others from third-party harm (Mitchell v. Glasgow City Council; Michael v. Chief Constable of South Wales Police). Under Ontario law the Anns/Cooper v. Hobart framework applies (foreseeability, proximity, residual policy), with special caution for nonfeasance (Childs v. Desormeaux; Fullowka).
firac.application: Preferring Dr. Goudkamp over Dr. Morgan, the court held the claims were novel and failed every test. Proximity was absent: the defendants did not create the danger, had no control over the workplace, employers or building, and the alleged wrong was nonfeasance (a failure to protect from third-party conduct). Reliance was fictional — most workers and the many non-New Wave victims knew nothing of the CSR standards or audits. Bureau Veritas' limited retainer did not extend to structural integrity. Policy factors (indeterminate liability, disproportion, floodgates, discouraging beneficial CSR practices and trade with developing countries) overwhelmed any prima facie duty. Government-inspection precedents were inapposite because they rest on a pre-existing statutory duty.
firac.conclusion: It is plain and obvious that neither Loblaws nor Bureau Veritas owed a viable duty of care under either Bangladesh or Ontario law; the negligence claims cannot succeed.

firac.issue: Is Loblaws vicariously liable for the negligence of Pearl Global and New Wave?
firac.facts: Pearl Global was a supplier and New Wave a sub-supplier of garments to Loblaws; neither was Loblaws' employee or agent. The plaintiffs alleged garment manufacturing in Bangladesh was inherently dangerous and that Loblaws had a non-delegable duty.
firac.rule: Vicarious liability attaches to employer-employee relationships and, exceptionally, where an enterprise creates a risk that materializes (671122 Ontario Ltd. v. Sagaz Industries, 2001 SCC 59; K.L.B. v. British Columbia, 2003 SCC 51). A person is generally not liable for the acts of an independent contractor absent an inherently dangerous activity ordered by the defendant (Savage v. Wilby) or a non-delegable duty grounded in statute or relationship.
firac.application: Pearl Global and New Wave were independent businesses selling goods, not services performing Loblaws' own work; Loblaws was a retailer, not a garment manufacturer, and had no control over the workplace. Garment manufacturing is not inherently dangerous in the exceptional sense. There was no source (statutory or relational) for a non-delegable duty; Bangladesh Beverage was merely a routine employer-employee case. The plaintiffs' reasoning ran backwards from a dangerous industry to a non-delegable duty that Loblaws never had.
firac.conclusion: It is plain and obvious there is no viable vicarious liability claim against Loblaws under either legal system.

firac.issue: Is there a viable breach of fiduciary duty claim against Loblaws?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs alleged Loblaws, through its CSR standards and control over the scope of audits, undertook to protect the vulnerable workers' safety and owed them an ad hoc fiduciary duty.
firac.rule: An ad hoc fiduciary duty requires an undertaking to act in the beneficiary's best interests, a defined class vulnerable to the fiduciary's control, and interests adversely affected by the exercise of that discretion; vulnerability must arise from the relationship (Galambos v. Perez, 2009 SCC 48; Elder Advocates of Alberta Society v. Alberta, 2011 SCC 24). Fiduciary duties are rarely imposed in commercial relationships.
firac.application: There was no legally significant relationship — only an 'association' — between Loblaws and the workers, and none at all with the many non-New Wave victims. The workers' vulnerability pre-existed and did not arise from any understanding with Loblaws; Loblaws gave no express or implied undertaking of loyalty and held no discretionary power over the class. The CSR standards operated at a commercial, not fiduciary, level. The claim was in reality a disguised negligence/limitation-avoidance claim, with no unjust enrichment.
firac.conclusion: It is plain and obvious there is no viable breach of fiduciary duty claim under either Bangladesh or Ontario law.

firac.issue: Should the action be certified as a class proceeding under the Class Proceedings Act, 1992?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs sought certification of a global opt-in class of survivors and families; the defendants opposed on all five s. 5 criteria.
firac.rule: Section 5 of the Class Proceedings Act, 1992 requires a cause of action, an identifiable class, common issues, preferable procedure, and a suitable representative plaintiff, applied purposively (Hollick v. Toronto (City), 2001 SCC 68; AIC Limited v. Fischer, 2013 SCC 69).
firac.application: Because the plaintiffs had no legally viable cause of action (and, under Bangladesh law, statute-barred claims), the cause-of-action criterion failed and there was nothing to certify. The court nonetheless held that, had viable claims existed, the identifiable class (subject to refinement), common issues, preferable procedure, and representative plaintiff criteria would have been satisfied, and the Apology Act and prior-accident pleadings would have been struck as improper.
firac.conclusion: Certification is refused; the action is dismissed. The impugned pleadings would have been struck had the action been certified.

name_verification.name_in_document: Inderjit Singh Chohan v. Otakar Cadsky, Larry Ohlhauser, Capital Health Authority, Kenneth Gardener and Glen Baker

defining_issues: Did the trial judge err in his findings as to whether the impugned statements (in particular Dr. Cadsky's 'paranoid Sikh' remark and the expressions of concern by Drs. Baker, Ohlhauser and Gardener) were defamatory?
Were the statements made on occasions of qualified privilege, and were the limits of that privilege exceeded?
Did the appellant establish actual malice sufficient to defeat qualified privilege?

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in his findings as to whether the impugned statements were defamatory?
firac.facts: Dr. Cadsky, a senior psychiatrist on stress leave, described colleague Dr. Chohan as a 'paranoid Sikh' during a private discussion with Drs. Rai and Woods about who might replace the departing clinical director. Drs. Baker, Ohlhauser and Gardener later communicated concerns that Dr. Chohan 'may be paranoid' to persons responsible for his practice. Dr. Chohan alleged all these statements defamed him.
firac.rule: A publication is defamatory if it tends to lower a person's reputation in the estimation of reasonable/right-thinking members of the community (Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada; Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press, [1995] 3 S.C.R. 3; Hill v. Church of Scientology). Whether a statement is capable of defamatory meaning is a question of law reviewable for correctness (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33); underlying credibility and factual findings attract deference.
firac.application: The Court held the trial judge effectively found Cadsky's remark defamatory and proceeded to the privilege analysis; he declined to rule on its truth. The trial judge rejected the evidence that Cadsky had threatened to force Dr. Chohan to resign, a credibility finding supported by the evidence and not palpably wrong. For Drs. Baker and Gardener the trial judge accepted that they did not use the term 'paranoid'; the Court of Appeal found it unnecessary to resolve whether they used the word, since even if defamatory the statements were protected.
firac.conclusion: No reversible error; the defamation findings (and the credibility findings underpinning them) stood.

firac.issue: Were the statements made on occasions of qualified privilege, and were the limits of that privilege exceeded?
firac.facts: Cadsky's remark was made in a private, limited discussion among three FACS psychiatrists about candidates for a supervisory vacancy. The other defendants each communicated their honest concern about Dr. Chohan's health to persons (Drs. Block, Hibbard, Gardener) responsible for his practice and well-being.
firac.rule: Qualified privilege attaches where the person communicating has a legal, social or moral interest or duty to make the communication and the recipient has a corresponding interest or duty to receive it (Hill v. Church of Scientology, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130). Privilege may be defeated where the communication is not reasonably germane/appropriate to the occasion (Adam v. Ward; Douglas v. Tucker). Whether privilege applies is a question of law reviewable for correctness.
firac.application: Colleagues frankly discussing another employee's qualifications for a supervisory post is exactly what qualified privilege protects; each participant had a legitimate interest even without power over the decision. Offensive or intemperate language ('Sikh') did not defeat the privilege because the statement remained relevant to the protected interest and the argument that it exceeded the limits had not been argued below. The other defendants communicated only to persons responsible for Dr. Chohan's practice, without idle gossip, and did not exceed their duty.
firac.conclusion: All occasions were properly held to be privileged; the privilege was not exceeded.

firac.issue: Did the appellant establish actual malice sufficient to defeat qualified privilege?
firac.facts: Dr. Chohan argued the remark was racially motivated and that Dr. Gardener, Ohlhauser and Baker acted with ulterior purposes, pointing to later letters and the committee Dr. Gardener appointed.
firac.rule: Qualified privilege is defeated only by proof of express/actual malice — spite, ill-will, an indirect or ulterior motive conflicting with the occasion's duty, or speaking dishonestly or with reckless disregard for the truth; the onus lies on the plaintiff (Hill). Malice is a question of mixed law and fact reviewable for palpable and overriding error (Cimolai v. Hall, 2007 BCCA 225; Housen).
firac.application: The trial judge found Cadsky honestly believed Dr. Chohan exhibited paranoid traits and used 'Sikh' descriptively; evidence (including from Sikh colleague Dr. Rai) showed Cadsky was generous across races, so the remark, though inflammatory, was not maliciously motivated. Subsequent letters written 15 months later could not establish the speaker's state of mind at the time of publication. For Ohlhauser, Baker and Gardener, each acted on genuine concern for a colleague's health and communicated to appropriate persons; there was no evidence of predetermined bias or ulterior purpose.
firac.conclusion: Malice was not established against any defendant; the actions were properly dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a private defamation tort action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. K018 (qualified privilege) is the determinative defence on which the appeal turned. K014 (standard of review) is central because the appeal was resolved largely on the applicable standards (correctness for defamatory meaning and privilege; palpable and overriding error for malice/facts). K065 (racism) is engaged because the alleged defamatory 'paranoid Sikh' remark's racial motivation was squarely litigated, though it is a weaker/secondary pick since the court found the comment was not racially motivated. No employment keyword was included because, although set in a workplace, the claim is defamation, not an employment dispute.

registry_rationale: The decision expressly lists 'Registry: Edmonton'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Droit de la famille — 103313

defining_issues: Should the father's request for exclusive custody be granted, or should the existing shared custody arrangement be maintained in the child's best interests?
How should the access rights for the child's Jewish holidays be fixed given the parents' disagreement over their duration and the court's role regarding religion?

firac.issue: Should the father's request for exclusive custody be granted, or should shared custody be maintained in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The parents separated in 1999 and have exercised week-on/week-off shared custody since a December 2005 consent order endorsed by Guthrie J. Their relationship is highly conflictual. The 13-year-old daughter, X, has behavioural and learning difficulties (dyslexia), told the expert, her lawyer and the court she would prefer to spend more time with her father, but insisted on maintaining regular contact with both parents. The psychologist Pérusse found both parents have parental capacity, the mother somewhat stronger, and recommended custody to the mother partly to 'send a message' to the father.
firac.rule: Under art. 33 C.c.Q. the child's best interests, assessed through moral, intellectual, emotional and physical needs, age, health, character and family environment, govern custody. Per C.J. c. M.T. each case turns on its own facts and no form of custody is presumptively preferred. A child over twelve's wishes are significant but not determinative (A.Z. c. S.O.). Expert recommendations inform but do not bind the judge, though reasons must be given for departing from them (D.L. c. L.D.). Continuity/status quo has merit but does not bar change where the child's interest requires it.
firac.application: The court weighed X's preference, the expert report and the evidence. It found X has a positive image of both parents, loves both, and would suffer notable harm if substantially separated from either. The court respectfully declined to follow the expert's recommendation of maternal custody, holding that X's welfare must come before any 'message' to a parent, and noting many conflicts would arise regardless of the custody mode. The father demonstrated no change in circumstances justifying a modification, and the mother herself opposed exclusive custody because X needs her father.
firac.conclusion: The request for exclusive custody was denied; the parents continue shared custody on the alternating one-week/one-week schedule.

firac.issue: How should the access rights for the child's Jewish holidays be fixed given the parents' disagreement over their duration and the court's role regarding religion?
firac.facts: The 2005 agreement provided X would be raised in the father's Jewish religion (the mother is Catholic) and would share the major Jewish holidays with her father. The parents disputed which holidays were important and how long the access should last. They agreed the relevant festivals are Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur, Passover, Chanukah, Purim and Shavuot, but no evidence beyond their testimony explained their significance or observance. The mother sought shorter access to minimize lost school days given X's learning difficulties; the father sought longer access.
firac.rule: Per Young c. Young, custody and access decisions are not based on parents' faith, but religion may be a relevant circumstance; where religion is in conflict the court does not adjudicate a 'war of religion' but examines the practice's effects on the child, with the child's interest prevailing. A court cannot arbitrate what a religion requires and must use the sincerity criterion (citing Multani), recognizing adherents observe dogma with varying rigour.
firac.application: The court held it could not arbitrate the religious requirements and balanced the father's attachment to the festivals against X's best interests, including minimizing lost school days during a difficult academic period. It fixed specific hours of access for each of the six named holidays, giving Jewish holidays priority where they conflict with Catholic ones.
firac.conclusion: The father's request was granted in part; detailed access schedules for the six Jewish holidays were set, with priority over conflicting Catholic holidays. Passport/health card to follow the child, and transport arrangements clarified.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) capture the central custody dispute and governing art. 33 C.c.Q. test. K052 (religious upbringing) reflects the agreement that X be raised in the Jewish religion and the dispute over religious observance. K027 (Jewish holidays) is directly engaged since the access fights concern Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur, Passover, Chanukah, Purim and Shavuot. K025 (freedom of religion) and K034 (sincerity of belief) are supported by the court's reliance on Young and Multani and its refusal to arbitrate religious requirements. K093 (Jewish) identifies the community/religion involved. No hate-speech or constitutional-Charter claim was litigated, so those areas are excluded.
