registry_rationale: The header specifies 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' with court file no. 500-12-308000-110, identifying the Montreal registry of the Superior Court.

case_name: Gauvin (Solutions numériques Alexandre Gauvin) c. Gagné

name_verification.name_in_document: ALEXANDRE GAUVIN, f.a.s.n. SOLUTIONS NUMÉRIQUES ALEXANDRE GAUVIN c. MÉLANIE GAGNÉ

defining_issues: What was the agreement between the parties as to the services and price, and what balance remained owing to Mr. Gauvin?
Can Mr. Gauvin recover damages for the time and effort devoted to pursuing his lawsuit?
Was the service contract resiliated as a result of fault on Mr. Gauvin's part, engaging his contractual liability?
What damages are owed to Ms. Gagné as a result of the faulty resiliation, and how should the reciprocal debts be set off?

firac.issue: What was the agreement between the parties as to the services and price, and what balance remained owing to Mr. Gauvin?
firac.facts: Ms. Gagné retained Mr. Gauvin, initially at $50/hour, to transcribe her manuscript into LaTeX; he later took a broader role (layout, corrections, photos). She admitted the total value of his work was at least $5,000 and that $4,120.70 remained unpaid.
firac.rule: The contract is the law of the parties (art. 1434, 1385 C.c.Q.); the plaintiff bears the burden of proving the merits of the claim.
firac.application: Ms. Gagné did not contest that Mr. Gauvin performed the work or that $4,120.70 represented the unpaid balance of the agreed price. Mr. Gauvin therefore discharged his burden of proof.
firac.conclusion: Mr. Gauvin's claim was well founded; Ms. Gagné owes the balance, subject to set-off arising from the counterclaim.

firac.issue: Can Mr. Gauvin recover damages for the time and effort devoted to pursuing his lawsuit?
firac.facts: Mr. Gauvin claimed an additional $862.86 for the time and effort spent on his judicial recourse.
firac.rule: Such costs are recoverable only where the opposing party has abused, whether on the merits or in the conduct of the litigation (Viel c. Entreprises immobilières du terroir ltée, 2002 CanLII 41120; Dawcolectric inc. c. Hydro-Québec, 2014 QCCA 948).
firac.application: There was no abuse by Ms. Gagné, either on the merits or in the conduct of the case.
firac.conclusion: The claim for litigation-related damages was denied.

firac.issue: Was the service contract resiliated as a result of fault on Mr. Gauvin's part, engaging his contractual liability?
firac.facts: After the parties disagreed over the book's font size (Taille 10 vs 11) and format, Mr. Gauvin repeatedly threatened to withdraw, issued shifting ultimatums, and concealed his intention to keep control of the LaTeX-transcribed version while reassuring Ms. Gagné otherwise. The contract ended in late November 2020.
firac.rule: A service contract (art. 2098 C.c.Q.) may be unilaterally resiliated by the client at any time (art. 2125 C.c.Q.); a service provider may resiliate only for serious cause and not at an inopportune time (art. 2126 C.c.Q.). Every contract must be performed in good faith (art. 1375 C.c.Q.); source code has been held to belong to the client (Valade.net, 2007 QCCS 3213). Fault causing resiliation gives rise to damages.
firac.application: The court characterized the relationship as a service contract despite Mr. Gauvin's expanded role. Regardless of who formally ended it, the resiliation resulted from Mr. Gauvin's faulty conduct: he persisted against Ms. Gagné's clear instructions, made contradictory threats, and dissembled about retaining the LaTeX version, breaching his duty of good faith.
firac.conclusion: The resiliation resulted from Mr. Gauvin's fault, engaging his contractual civil liability.

firac.issue: What damages are owed to Ms. Gagné, and how should the reciprocal debts be set off?
firac.facts: Ms. Gagné had to hire a graphic designer, a photographer and an editor to complete the book, incurring $802.41, and suffered trouble and inconvenience (contacting 150 pre-sale buyers, delay, pressure) for which she claimed $3,000.
firac.rule: Damages compensate the loss suffered and profit deprived flowing immediately and directly from the co-contractor's fault (art. 1607, 1611 C.c.Q.); reciprocal debts are extinguished by compensation (art. 1673 C.c.Q.); interest and the additional indemnity run under art. 1619 C.c.Q.
firac.application: The $802.41 in replacement costs was justified by the invoices; the $3,000 for trouble and inconvenience was reasonable given the missed December publication and pressure caused. The counterclaim of $3,802.41 was granted in full and set off against the $4,197.47 owing to Mr. Gauvin as of notification.
firac.conclusion: Counterclaim allowed in full; after compensation a residual $395.06 remained payable to Mr. Gauvin, with interest and additional indemnity from 19 May 2021, and Mr. Gauvin bears the legal costs on both claims.

keywords_rationale: This is a Quebec small-claims civil dispute over a service contract (art. 2098 ff. C.c.Q.), its faulty unilateral resiliation, good faith (art. 1375) and damages, so the primary and only strongly-supported keyword is K002 (Civil litigation). K022 (restitution) is moderately engaged because art. 2129 C.c.Q. governs restitution of advances/value of work on resiliation, which framed the accounting between the parties. The controlled vocabulary contains no keyword for contracts of service, obligations, good faith, copyright or damages, so per instruction I list the closest remaining terms from the civil procedure/remedies and civil-liability families — K020 (class action), K021 (interlocutory injunction) and K015 (defamation) — as flagged weak/non-applicable placeholders; none of these doctrines actually arose in the case. The vocabulary is oriented toward human-rights/antisemitism themes that are absent here.
location_rationale: The header states 'COUR DU QUÉBEC, Division des petites créances', 'DISTRICT DE SAINT-FRANÇOIS', 'LOCALITÉ DE SHERBROOKE', so the city is Sherbrooke and the province is Quebec.
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the judicial district as 'DISTRICT DE SAINT-FRANÇOIS' with locality Sherbrooke; the file number is 450-32-701597-213, so the registry is the Saint-François district (Sherbrooke).

case_name: Girard c. Caisse populaire Desjardins de Saint-Raymond-Sainte-Catherine

name_verification.name_in_document: Girard c. Caisse populaire Desjardins de Saint-Raymond-Sainte-Catherine

defining_issues: Was the plaintiff's dismissal from her management position justified by a 'serious reason' (motif sérieux) under art. 2094 C.c.Q., relieving the employer of the obligation to give notice?
What was the effective date of the dismissal and what reasonable notice period (délai de congé) was owed, having regard to 35 years of continuous service across different Desjardins entities?
Must disability benefits received by the plaintiff be deducted from the severance indemnity under art. 1608 C.c.Q., and did she mitigate her damages?
Was the plaintiff entitled to additional moral (non-pecuniary) damages on the ground that the dismissal was carried out abusively (abus de droit)?

Was the plaintiff entitled to punitive damages under the Quebec Charter for an unlawful and intentional interference with her reputation/dignity and for discrimination based on a handicap (depression)?

firac.issue: Was the dismissal justified by a serious reason under art. 2094 C.c.Q.?
firac.facts: After 34 years of continuous service within the Desjardins Movement, the plaintiff was hired by the defendant in May 2013 as director of the personal-market and business-development division, supervising 23 employees. She was sent home on 17 April 2014 by the newly arrived general manager, Michel Truchon, who cited her authoritarian management style and the threatened departure of key employees. Before this she had received a superior performance rating and a certificate of recognition, and had never been reprimanded during her career; the only reproach was her handling of the Fabien Maltais file and the 2014 performance-management exercise, both conducted in accordance with objectives fixed by the Fédération.
firac.rule: Art. 2094 C.c.Q. allows unilateral resiliation of an employment contract without notice for a serious reason; the burden of proving serious cause rests on the employer (Sirois c. O'Neill; Lesage c. Lama Transport). For administrative/incompetence dismissals, the employer must ordinarily give the employee notice of deficiencies, a chance to correct, support and warning of dismissal (Costco Wholesale Canada Ltd c. Laplante).
firac.application: The Court found the defendant never advised the plaintiff of any deficiency before 11 April 2014, gave no clear reproach, imposed no corrective measures, and forced her onto vacation, undermining her authority after the board reversed course on the Maltais file. The employer met none of the five Costco prerequisites and did not prove incompetence, negligence or insubordination; at most she had a rigid, inflexible attitude consistent with her contractual mandate focused on financial objectives set by the Fédération.
firac.conclusion: The dismissal (the sending-home of 17 April 2014 followed by termination on 16 February 2015) did not rest on a serious reason.

firac.issue: What was the date of dismissal and the reasonable notice period, accounting for service across Desjardins entities?
firac.facts: Truchon told the plaintiff on 17 April 2014 to leave and propose terms for ending her employment; a written termination came only on 16 February 2015. She had worked continuously for three different Desjardins caisses from 1980 to 2015, about 35 years, but only about 22 months for the defendant. She was 52, in a senior position.
firac.rule: Under art. 2091 C.c.Q. an indeterminate contract may be ended with reasonable notice, assessed globally by factors such as age, nature and level of the position, length of service and difficulty of finding new work (Industries de Caoutchouc Mondo; Nurun c. Deschênes). The dismissal date is a factual question fixed at the moment the employee unequivocally knows she is dismissed.
firac.application: The 17 April 2014 statement invited negotiation and left open reassignment within the Movement, so it was not an unequivocal termination; no salary suspension or administrative measures followed. Termination occurred only on 16 February 2015. Continuous service across Movement entities counts (contrasting Boyer, where service was interrupted, and following Vallières). Given her age, senior rank, 35 years of service and greatly reduced re-employment prospects, notice of 24 months was warranted.
firac.conclusion: Dismissal took effect 16 February 2015; the plaintiff was entitled to a 24-month notice period.

firac.issue: Must disability benefits be deducted and did the plaintiff mitigate?
firac.facts: The plaintiff received disability benefits of $163,280.51 over 853 days (22 April 2014–22 August 2016) under a group plan funded 80% by the employer (65% before 2004) and 20% by the employee. She began new, lower-paid work in August 2016 and later started a business.
firac.rule: Art. 1608 C.c.Q. provides that benefits from a third party do not reduce damages except to the extent of subrogation; where the employer funds the disability plan, the employer-funded portion of benefits received during the notice period is deducted (Sylvester c. British Columbia). The employer bears the burden of showing failure to mitigate.
firac.application: The Court prorated benefits to the notice period ($105,854.77, being 70.58% of the total), then applied the employer's funding proportions (65% pre-2004, 80% post-2004), yielding $73,475.66 to be deducted. The plaintiff's job-search efforts were reasonable given her illness and age, so no failure to mitigate was shown; but income earned during the notice period ($31,317.61) was deducted.
firac.conclusion: Deductions reduced the severance indemnity to $129,709.14; no failure to mitigate.

firac.issue: Was the plaintiff entitled to additional moral damages for abusive dismissal?
firac.facts: Truchon sent her home abruptly and laconically, expressing loss of confidence without explaining reasons, offering no chance to respond or correct, and no Movement support; he then remained silent for weeks. The plaintiff fell into a serious depression and her reputation in the financial sector suffered.
firac.rule: Arts. 6, 7 and 2087 C.c.Q.; moral damages beyond the notice indemnity require a distinct fault—negligence, bad faith or an identifiable fault—causing harm beyond that normally flowing from termination (Standard Broadcasting c. Stewart; Bristol-Myers Squibb c. Legros; Structures Lamerain c. Meloche). A brutal or intempestive dismissal can constitute abuse of right even absent bad faith.
firac.application: The Court found the dismissal intempestive, cavalier and brutal, humiliating and lacking respect for the plaintiff's dignity, and that it seriously and durably injured her reputation in a small financial market. This negligent conduct was a distinct fault causing harm exceeding the notice indemnity, though the claimed $500,000 was grossly exaggerated.
firac.conclusion: Abuse of right established; $75,000 in non-pecuniary damages awarded.

firac.issue: Was the plaintiff entitled to punitive damages under the Quebec Charter?
firac.facts: The plaintiff claimed $500,000 for unlawful/intentional interference with reputation and dignity and a further $500,000 for being dismissed while suffering a handicap (major depression) on 16 February 2015.
firac.rule: Art. 1621 C.c.Q. and arts. 4, 49 and 10 of the Quebec Charter; punitive damages require the unlawful interference to be intentional, meaning the author wanted the consequences (St-Ferdinand). Art. 7 C.c.Q. requires an intent to harm.
firac.application: The Court found the conduct abusive but no intent to harm the plaintiff's reputation—it was driven by fear of losing employees. As the employer believed it had dismissed her on 17 April 2014 (before the depression arose), no unlawful intent to dismiss for handicap could be formed; and there was no evidence of the employer's knowledge of her medical condition on 16 February 2015.
firac.conclusion: Punitive damages refused; the $1,000,000 claim was excessive.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns termination of an indeterminate employment contract. K085 (wrongful dismissal/congédiement) is the central specific issue—dismissal without serious cause and reasonable notice. K002 (Civil litigation) captures the damages action (moral, punitive, pension) under the Civil Code. K069 (discrimination) and K082 (employment discrimination) are engaged by the plaintiff's Charter-based punitive claim alleging discrimination on the basis of a handicap (depression) in the employment context—borderline since the claim was rejected, but genuinely litigated. K120 (Quebec Charter) reflects the arts. 4, 10 and 49 Charter analysis for punitive damages. K082 is somewhat weak because the discrimination argument failed, but it was a distinct pleaded issue.
location_rationale: The header states 'COUR SUPÉRIEURE', 'PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC', 'DISTRICT DE QUÉBEC', identifying the Superior Court sitting in the district of Québec. City set to Québec and province to Quebec accordingly.
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the 'DISTRICT DE QUÉBEC' with file no. 200-17-023686-165, so the registry is the Québec district of the Superior Court.

name_verification.name_in_document: Halperin v. Halperin

defining_issues: Was legal cruelty proven of the kind required to entitle the petitioner to a decree of judicial separation?
Did the petitioner condone the cruelty by returning to and remaining in the marital home, and if so was that condonation revived by the husband's later conduct?
Did the parties' association after the petitioner's final departure (including inferred sexual intercourse) amount to a fresh condonation barring relief?

firac.issue: Was legal cruelty proven of the kind required to entitle the petitioner to a decree of judicial separation?
firac.facts: The petitioner, about 56 and already suffering from serious high blood pressure and albumen when she married the respondent in 1936, was subjected to frequent violent outbursts of temper, obscene language, vile epithets, orders to leave the house, a false accusation that she was poisoning him, opening of her trunk, and repeated demands that his difficult daughter Ida be brought into the home. Medical evidence showed her health progressively deteriorated during cohabitation.
firac.rule: Legal cruelty need not depend on physical violence but may arise from conduct operating on the mental condition of the aggrieved spouse where it creates mental distress sufficient to impair health or a well-founded apprehension of worse treatment (Lovell v. Lovell (1906) 13 O.L.R. 569). There must be 'danger to life, limb or health, bodily or mental, or a reasonable apprehension of it' (Russell v. Russell [1895] A.C. 315, aff'd [1897] A.C. 395).
firac.application: The court accepted the petitioner's account as substantially true and disbelieved the respondent where his evidence conflicted. The respondent's conduct created a reasonable apprehension that continuance would injure her health, and the medical evidence established her health was in fact seriously impaired. The court was convinced that a forced return would make his conduct worse and might materially hasten her death.
firac.conclusion: Legal cruelty was proven with respect to conduct occurring before 25 March 1940.

firac.issue: Did the petitioner condone the cruelty by returning to and remaining in the marital home, and was that condonation revived?
firac.facts: After first leaving on 25 March 1940 the petitioner returned on 13 April 1940 following a reconciliation meeting and lived as a wife in the home until 20 August 1940. The respondent soon breached the reconciliation agreement (dismissing the maid, renewing outbursts because Ida was not invited to a dinner, abusing a mutual friend, and accusing her of poisoning him).
firac.rule: Restoration of conjugal cohabitation, even apart from sexual intercourse, carries condonation with it, but condonation is always conditional and is wiped out if the respondent's subsequent conduct revives the original wrong (Cramp v. Cramp [1920] P. 158).
firac.application: By resuming cohabitation as a wife until 20 August 1940 the petitioner condoned the earlier cruelty. However, the respondent's renewed abusive conduct recreated conditions deleterious to her health similar to those before, thereby wiping out the condonation.
firac.conclusion: The plea of condonation based on the resumption of cohabitation from April to August failed; the condoned cruelty was revived.

firac.issue: Did the parties' association after the petitioner's final departure amount to a fresh condonation barring relief?
firac.facts: After leaving on 20 August 1940 the petitioner did not return to the marital home but dined and stayed overnight with the respondent at the 'Rio Vista' auto camp on seven or eight occasions, on the strength of his promise of a 'scheme' that would end their troubles. The scheme was never disclosed or fulfilled, and he ultimately used the association to argue she could no longer succeed in court.
firac.rule: For a husband, sexual intercourse is conclusive evidence of condonation, but the rule is less strict where the wife is petitioner; condonation is conditional and is established only if the condition on which cohabitation is resumed is fulfilled (Cramp v. Cramp).
firac.application: Although the court inferred sexual intercourse occurred, there was no restoration of conjugal cohabitation since the petitioner never returned to the home. The intercourse was allowed only on the strength of the respondent's promise of a resolving scheme; that condition was never fulfilled, so no condonation arose whether the promise was a genuine hope of reconciliation or a plot to defeat her claim.
firac.conclusion: No fresh condonation was established; the petitioner remained entitled to relief.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing practice area — a petition for judicial separation turning on cruelty and condonation. K053 (spousal support) is engaged because the petitioner's entitlement to maintenance and support and the money allowance disputes are woven through the facts, though it is a secondary/weak pick since the decree itself concerns separation not a support award. The Jewish identity and community context of the parties support tier-3 entity tags: K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) given the petitioner's reluctance 'for a Jewess' to litigate marital matters and her refugee-committee work, K098 (rabbi) from her introducing Ida to the Rabbi, K105 (synagogue) from the dress bought for synagogue attendance, and K027 (Jewish holidays) from references to Passover and the chief festival of the Jewish year. No controlled keyword captures 'cruelty' or 'condonation' directly, so the closest family-law and entity terms were selected.
location_rationale: The decision is a judgment of the British Columbia Supreme Court and repeatedly places events in Vancouver — the petitioner 'operated a travel bureau in the Hotel Georgia in this city' and other events (Hotel Georgia, the marital residence) occur in Vancouver — so the court sat in Vancouver, British Columbia.
registry_rationale: No registry office is expressly named in the text; the report simply identifies the British Columbia Supreme Court before Murphy J., so registry is left null.

case_name: Hôpital Fleury du CIUSSS du Nord-de-l'île-de-Montréal c. B.C.

name_verification.name_in_document: Hôpital Fleury du CIUSSS du Nord-de-l'Île-de-Montréal c. B... C...

defining_issues: Do the incapable adult's repeated absconding episodes (fugues) amount to a categorical refusal of care that would give the court jurisdiction over a care authorization?
Can the court, absent the substitute decision-maker's consent, issue orders directing peace officers to assist in returning the adult, by treating such assistance as 'care'?
Given the Curateur public's substituted consent and the absence of categorical refusal, does the court have jurisdiction to authorize the proposed care and ancillary orders?
Should the court grant the Curateur public interim custody (garde) of the incapable adult by way of a safeguard order?

firac.issue: Do the incapable adult's repeated fugues constitute a categorical refusal of care under art. 16 C.c.Q.?
firac.facts: The adult, declared incapable of consenting to or refusing care and under public curatorship since 2010, periodically leaves the hospital or residence. Her treating psychiatrist and occupational therapist attribute the absences to her mental illness and cognitive impairments, not a desire to avoid treatment; she generally returns on her own and accepts all treatment without resisting.
firac.rule: Under art. 16 C.c.Q., a 'categorical refusal' must result from an organized will to refuse to receive the proposed care (Kouri and Philips-Nootens); it need not be express and may be inferred from circumstances such as strategic feigned acceptance, but the objective of avoiding the care must be established.
firac.application: The court found the adult flees only to obtain gratifications unavailable in hospital, not to avoid treatment, and appears incapable of forming such a design. Her current conduct at the residence, where she returns on her own, confirmed the earlier finding. No organized will to refuse care was shown.
firac.conclusion: The fugues do not amount to a categorical refusal of care, so they cannot confer jurisdiction on the court in place of the substituted consent the legislator favours.

firac.issue: May the court order peace officers to assist in returning the adult, characterizing such assistance as 'care'?
firac.facts: The Hospital sought orders authorizing recourse to peace officers 'sans autre formalité' to transport the adult back for treatment. The Curateur public neither consented to nor opposed this conclusion. The Hospital argued police would refuse to act without such orders; no police representative testified, and police had in fact cooperated when the residence raised concerns.
firac.rule: 'Soins' under art. 11 C.c.Q. is generic, covering examinations, treatments and interventions of a medical, psychological or social nature, including preliminary lodging (M.B. c. Centre hospitalier Pierre-Le Gardeur, 2004 CanLII 29017). Police intervention is instead an accessory order meant to give effect to a care authorization (P. Deschamps). A court cannot make care orders without jurisdiction to do so.
firac.application: The court held that treating police intervention as a 'social intervention' required by the adult's health would be exorbitant; it is an accessory order to a care authorization. Since the court had no jurisdiction to authorize care (no categorical refusal and consent given), it could not grant the accessory order, and no Civil Code provision authorized it. The factual premise that police would refuse to act was unproven and contradicted by events.
firac.conclusion: The court declined to issue the peace-officer orders; the Hospital withdrew that part of its demand and the remainder was dismissed.

firac.issue: Does the court have jurisdiction to authorize the proposed care where the adult does not categorically refuse and the substitute decision-maker consents?
firac.facts: The Curateur public, curator to the person and property since 2010, accepted the treatment plan. Evidence showed the Hospital had been treating the incapable adult since 2008, apparently without substituted consent or judicial authorization, and had confirmed her incapacity to the Curateur public by 2012.
firac.rule: Under art. 16 C.c.Q., care may be given to an incapable adult with the consent of the person authorized to consent, or, where that person is prevented or unjustifiably refuses, with court authorization; outside emergencies (art. 13 C.c.Q.) no treatment may be given without such authorization. The court also emphasized the Curateur public's protective duties (art. 263 C.c.Q.) and notification duties toward it (art. 270 C.c.Q.; C.p.c. art. 395).
firac.application: Because valid substituted consent existed and there was no categorical refusal, the statutory conditions for judicial authorization were absent. The court noted the Hospital had improperly treated the adult without authorization for years and that the Curateur public should have intervened in the care plan from its appointment.
firac.conclusion: The court lacked jurisdiction to hear the care authorization demand and dismissed it (without costs given the consents).

firac.issue: Should the court grant the Curateur public interim custody of the incapable adult via a safeguard order?
firac.facts: At the November 28 hearing, counsel for the Curateur public confirmed a mandate to seek custody (garde) of the adult, fearing that police in other sectors might not cooperate if she left her current residence, but had not been authorized to file the demand owing to a lawyers' strike.
firac.rule: Article 272 C.c.Q. permits the court, even before the instance, to designate the Curateur public to protect the person of the adult; article 263 C.c.Q. excludes custody when the Curateur public is named tutor or curator, requiring a separate application. A safeguard order may issue for urgent protection.
firac.application: The court characterized the anticipated custody demand as part of the protection regime, akin to opening such a regime, and found urgency requiring rapid intervention to ensure the adult's health and safety pending a final ruling.
firac.conclusion: The court issued a time-limited safeguard order (valid until December 22) entrusting custody of the adult to the Curateur public, without costs.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area because the case concerns protection of an incapable adult, curatorship and the protection regime under the Civil Code, matters traditionally treated in Quebec droit des personnes/famille. K002 (Civil litigation) reflects that the matter proceeded as a civil authorization application in the Superior Court. K048 (custody/access) is the closest term for the 'garde' of the person ordered under art. 272 C.c.Q. K001 (Administrative law) is included because the case turns significantly on the statutory role and duties of the Curateur public, a public body. K071 (human dignity) loosely captures the protective, vulnerable-person dimension. name_verification.name_in_document: Feifer c. Feldman

defining_issues: Was Feldman in contempt of the interlocutory injunction prohibiting him from disseminating the defamatory allegations, given that he repeated them in pleadings and exhibits in a related file?
Was Feldman in contempt for failing to comply with the order to communicate all documents and remarks he had made concerning the Estate and the Plaintiffs?

firac.issue: Was Feldman in contempt of the non-dissemination injunction issued by Desfossés J. when he repeated the defamatory allegations in a plea, cross-demand and exhibits filed in the related Lande file?
firac.facts: Desfossés J. had ordered Feldman, a lawyer, not to disseminate defamatory allegations (that the Plaintiffs benefited from gold bars stolen from Holocaust victims) found in three paragraphs of his Long Form Affidavit, and had ordered certain exhibits sealed. Shortly after service of that judgment, Feldman's firm filed a plea, cross-demand, a revised long-form summary and similar exhibits repeating the allegations in the Lande defamation file without sealing them.
firac.rule: Contempt in civil proceedings is governed by arts. 57–62 C.c.p.; proof must be beyond a reasonable doubt (art. 61 C.c.p.). Per Carey v. Laiken, 2015 SCC 17, the plaintiff must prove three elements beyond a reasonable doubt: (1) the order states clearly and unequivocally what must and must not be done; (2) the alleged contemnor had actual knowledge of it; (3) the party intentionally did the prohibited act. Per Morasse v. Nadeau-Dubois, 2016 SCC 44 and Daigle c. St Gabriel de Brandon, ambiguity or multiple reasonable interpretations of the order must benefit the accused; contempt is an enforcement power of last resort.
firac.application: The court found the injunction covered only 3 of the 7 requested paragraphs, so allegations in other unprohibited paragraphs covered the same ground, making the order susceptible of at least two reasonable interpretations. Read as the Plaintiffs urged, the order would impermissibly deprive Feldman of his right to a full and complete defence and the audi alteram partem rule in two defamation actions where truth/fairness of his comments was in issue (art. 99 C.c.p.). The sealing order named only specific exhibits and did not extend to the Lande file. While Feldman had actual knowledge (served by bailiff by email on June 14, 2021) and intentionally directed the filings, the lack of clarity of the order defeated the contempt charge.
firac.conclusion: Feldman found not guilty; the order lacked sufficient clarity to sustain a contempt finding beyond a reasonable doubt.

firac.issue: Was Feldman in contempt for failing to communicate all documents and remarks made concerning the Estate and the Plaintiffs, as ordered?
firac.facts: Feldman provided nothing after the Desfossés J. order, but testified that all such information had already been provided following an earlier case-management order of Bélanger J.; no evidence of the earlier communications was filed.
firac.rule: The court has discretion to find contempt (arts. 57–62 C.c.p.). Per Morasse v. Nadeau-Dubois, 2016 SCC 44, contempt is an exceptional, last-resort power to be used only where genuinely necessary to safeguard the administration of justice. Sections 49 and 158 C.c.p. give courts broad powers, including alternative case-management remedies.
firac.application: A doubt subsisted because some documents had been provided under Bélanger J.'s order and Feldman swore they constituted all the information he was required to communicate. Because contempt is a last resort and the court has broad alternative powers likely more efficient, the issue should be addressed by other means.
firac.conclusion: Feldman found not guilty on this charge as well.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a contempt proceeding within a civil defamation action. K015 (defamation) is central — the underlying injunction restrained defamatory allegations. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the order Feldman allegedly breached. K088 (Holocaust) reflects the substance of the impugned allegations (gold stolen from Holocaust victims). K054 (wills/estates) applies because the dispute concerns the Estate of the late Sherry Lande Feifer and inheritances. K093 (Jewish) is engaged as the allegations concern property taken from Jewish Holocaust victims. The database vocabulary has no discrete 'contempt of court' keyword, so K002 carries the procedural dimension; K093 and K088 are somewhat contextual/borderline but reflect the factual matrix.

name_verification.name_in_document: G.G. and W.W. v. His Majesty the King in Right of the Province of Ontario et al.

defining_issues: Do the pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action (conspiracy, negligence, intrusion upon seclusion, misfeasance in public office) against the 49 independent CAS Defendants, given that each acted separately (the Ragoonanan problem)?
Do the plaintiffs have standing to advance Charter s. 7 and s. 15 damages claims against CAS Defendants that did not issue a Birth Alert affecting them?
Is the negligence claim against Ontario tenable, or is it barred by policy-decision immunity under s. 11(4) of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019?
Is it plain and obvious that the Charter s. 7 and s. 15 claims against Ontario, premised on the Ministry's acquiescence in and failure to stop Birth Alerts, must fail?
Are the s. 5(1) certification criteria of the Class Proceedings Act, 1992 met as against Ontario?

firac.issue: Do the pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action against the 49 independent CAS Defendants?
firac.facts: Each of the 49 CAS Defendants is a separately incorporated, independently governed entity that issued Birth Alerts on its own discretion, without top-down direction from the Ministry or coordination with other CASs. The plaintiffs relied on shared membership in the OACAS, the OACAS-authored Eligibility Spectrum, and the inter-governmental PT Protocol to allege concerted action.
firac.rule: Under s. 5(1)(a) CPA the test mirrors a motion to strike: a claim survives unless it is 'plain and obvious' it discloses no reasonable cause of action (Cloud v. Canada). Unlawful means conspiracy requires pleading, with particularity, each conspirator's overt acts and a meeting of the minds, not mere parallel conduct (Normart; Carcillo; Lilleyman/Bumblebee). In a class action there must be a representative plaintiff with a claim against each defendant — the Ragoonanan/Hughes v. Sunbeam problem.
firac.application: The plaintiffs pleaded no meeting or agreement among the CASs; membership in the OACAS and common use of the Eligibility Spectrum amounted only to conscious parallelism (analogous to lawyers following a CBA code), and the PT Protocol was a government-to-government agreement, not one among CASs. The independent, non-hierarchical structure meant there was no collective or concerted-action liability, so negligence, intrusion upon seclusion and misfeasance could not attach to the group. G.G. and W.W. each had a claim only against the one CAS that harmed them, not against the other 47-48.
firac.conclusion: It is plain and obvious that none of the common-law causes of action meets the s. 5(1)(a) threshold against the CAS Defendants; the conspiracy and other tort claims fail.

firac.issue: Do the plaintiffs have standing to bring Charter s. 7 and s. 15 damages claims against CAS Defendants that did not issue a Birth Alert affecting them?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs sought individual declarations and monetary damages under s. 24 of the Charter against all CAS Defendants; each named plaintiff was affected by only one CAS (Native Child and Family Services Toronto for G.G.; Chatham-Kent Children's Services for W.W.).
firac.rule: CASs are government actors under s. 32(1) of the Charter (H.(T.); Chatham-Kent). A personal Charter damages claim under s. 24, as opposed to a s. 52 declaration of invalidity, 'can only be made by the person whose Charter rights have been infringed' (R. v. Edwards); standing is tied to causation (Snell v. Farrell), and cannot be acquired 'through the back door of a class action' (Allee v. Medrano; Bailey v. Patterson).
firac.application: This was a private-interest, compensation-seeking claim, not a challenge to legislation (Birth Alerts had already been cancelled). Absent a causal link, G.G. had no standing against Chatham-Kent and W.W. had none against Native Child and Family Services Toronto; the other CASs were strangers to each plaintiff's claim. The same Ragoonanan defect infected the Charter claims.
firac.conclusion: It is plain and obvious the Charter claims against the CAS Defendants fail for lack of standing/causation and do not meet s. 5(1)(a).

firac.issue: Is the negligence claim against Ontario tenable or barred by policy-decision immunity?
firac.facts: The Ministry has extensive oversight, funding, directive and takeover powers over CASs (CYFSA ss. 4, 34, 42-44) but does not deliver services or direct individual cases. It was aware of Birth Alerts yet never assessed whether CASs stayed within jurisdiction; it terminated the practice by Policy Directive CW 005-20 on July 14, 2020 only after the MMIWG Report flagged them as discriminatory and ultra vires (fetuses are not legal persons: Tremblay; Winnipeg CFS).
firac.rule: Ontario is not vicariously liable for CASs (CYFSA s. 34(5)-(6)); liability must rest on the Crown's own wrongful conduct. A duty may arise from a statutory oversight mandate where no conflicting overarching duty exists (Syl Apps; Papassay; Dilico; Reilly). Section 11(4) CLPA immunizes good-faith 'policy matter' decisions (Bowman v. Ontario), but operational conduct is not immune (Francis v. Ontario).
firac.application: Ontario argued its non-action was a policy decision, yet it also insisted Birth Alerts were never a provincial policy but an operational/administrative practice at CAS level; the cessation directive was a policy decision (immune), but the failure to end a known, unauthorized and harmful practice was not. The alleged tort of omission — failing to keep regulated entities within their statutory bounds — did not attract immunity, and the commission/omission line was too fine to resolve on a pleadings motion.
firac.conclusion: It is not plain and obvious the negligence claim against Ontario fails; it passes s. 5(1)(a).

firac.issue: Must the Charter s. 7 and s. 15 claims against Ontario fail?
firac.facts: Birth Alerts intruded into pregnancy and the parent-child relationship, compelled disclosure of health information, and disproportionately impacted Indigenous, racialized and disabled parents, deterring prenatal care. The Ministry knew of the practice for years and acquiesced until 2020.
firac.rule: Section 7 protects liberty, security of the person and privacy in the pregnancy/child-protection context (Dobson; Cheskes; KLW; G.(J.)), and requires conformity with fundamental justice (arbitrariness, overbreadth, gross disproportionality: Bedford). Section 15 is engaged by pregnancy-based and adverse-impact discrimination (Fraser; Taypotat). Government actors are individually responsible under s. 32 (Eldridge), and Ontario is generally not liable for CAS conduct (C.R.; Selkirk).
firac.application: Because Ontario stood in the same relationship to all class members, the Ragoonanan problem did not apply. Although Ontario's role was passive acquiescence, its personnel knew or should have known Birth Alerts targeted fetuses beyond CAS jurisdiction and disproportionately harmed protected groups; the distinction between active discrimination and tolerated ongoing discrimination may be one without substantive difference. The alerts were arguably arbitrary, overbroad and disproportionate and not saved by s. 1.
firac.conclusion: It is not plain and obvious the s. 7 and s. 15 claims against Ontario fail; both pass s. 5(1)(a).

firac.issue: Are the s. 5(1) certification criteria met against Ontario?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs proposed a class of pregnant persons subject to Birth Alerts since May 10, 2007 (plus a Family Class and an Indigenous/racialized/disabled subclass), 20 common issues, and both named plaintiffs as representatives.
firac.rule: Section 5(1) CPA requires a cause of action, an identifiable class, common issues (some basis in fact: Pro-Sys; Hollick), preferable procedure viewed through judicial economy, behaviour modification and access to justice (AIC v. Fischer), and a suitable representative plaintiff with a workable litigation plan.
firac.application: Against Ontario a viable cause of action existed, the class and subclass were objectively defined, and common issues (reworded to remove the word 'scheme' and to target Ontario alone) had a basis in fact, including aggregate/aggravated/punitive damages questions. A class action was preferable to numerous individual actions given Ontario's resources and the behaviour-modification interest in its oversight failures. The representatives were suitable; the premature notice-mailing provision was struck from the litigation plan. Against the CASs, no cause of action meant no class, no common issues and no preferable procedure.
firac.conclusion: Certification is granted against Ontario on negligence and Charter ss. 7 and 15, with the modified common issues; the motion is dismissed against the CAS Defendants, with liberty to bring separate CAS-by-CAS actions.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 anchor: the case is a class-action/tort proceeding. K020 (class action) is central — the whole decision is a s. 5(1) CPA certification analysis. K003 (Constitutional law) and K107 (Canadian Charter) capture the Charter framework; K112 (Charter s. 7) and K109 (Charter s. 15) are the specific pleaded rights, with K023 (equality rights) reinforcing the s. 15 dimension. K069 (discrimination) reflects the adverse-impact/pregnancy and Indigenous discrimination allegations central to the s. 15 and MMIWG-based reasoning. K047 (best interests of the child) is a borderline pick — it captures the child-welfare/CAS statutory context (CYFSA) though the claim is really about parents; it is weaker than the others. No conspiracy-specific keyword exists in the vocabulary, so that doctrine is subsumed under civil litigation.

name_verification.name_in_document: E.T. v. L.D.

defining_issues: Was it in the children's best interests to continue the suspension of the respondent father's access?
Should the applicant mother be granted temporary sole custody to enable the children's participation in the Family Bridges Program?

firac.issue: Was it in the children's best interests to continue the suspension of the respondent father's access?
firac.facts: Following an interim support order, the father repeatedly disparaged the mother to the three boys, discussed the litigation with them, used them as 'pawns', and encouraged them to spend more time with him to reduce the mother's support entitlement. Professionals resigned as mediators, an intake for a reunification program failed because the children refused to attend, and the JFCS found the children were at risk of emotional harm. The father filed little proper evidence, failed to appear at later motions, and refused to cooperate with the JFCS.
firac.rule: Custody and access turn entirely on 'the best interests of the child', particularly the child's needs and circumstances: Children's Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12, s. 24.
firac.application: The court found the father continued to disregard orders not to disparage the mother or discuss the litigation, used even his one hour of weekly telephone access to disparage the mother, refused to meet the JFCS or affirm compliance with a parenting plan, and delayed reconsideration of the suspension. The evidence, including JFCS findings that the children were in need of protection and 'safe with intervention' only because of the suspension, reinforced that continued suspension served the children's best interests.
firac.conclusion: The suspension of the father's access was maintained, subject to structured, recorded telephone contact and the Family Bridges framework.

firac.issue: Should the applicant mother be granted temporary sole custody to enable participation in the Family Bridges Program?
firac.facts: The parties had joint custody and equal parenting under a 2015 Partial Separation Agreement, but the children resisted therapeutic intervention and the father would not compel their participation or cooperate. The Family Bridges Program typically requires temporary sole custody to the non-favoured parent and a no-contact period; the mother sought sole custody to enrol the children in the program and in schooling for 2018-2019.
firac.rule: Best interests of the child under s. 24 of the Children's Law Reform Act; standard provisions of reunification interventions requiring temporary sole custody to facilitate the program.
firac.application: Given the father's continuing conflict, non-compliance and refusal to cooperate, and the JFCS's protection concerns, the court concluded that granting the mother temporary sole custody was necessary to compel the children into appropriate therapy and to make educational decisions, and was in the children's best interests.
firac.conclusion: The mother was granted temporary sole custody until December 10, 2018, with the parties to comply with the Family Bridges Program terms and telephone calls to be recorded.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test under s. 24 CLRA and central to both issues. K048 (custody/access) captures the temporary sole custody grant and suspension of access. K050 (parental support) and K053 (spousal support) reflect the interim child and spousal support orders that triggered the father's conduct and remain part of the factual matrix. K049 (marriage/cohabitation agreement) reflects the 2015 Partial Separation Agreement establishing the original parenting terms. Support keywords are somewhat background rather than the operative dispute, so they are the weaker picks; the involvement of 'Jewish Family & Child Service' is only as the local child protection agency and does not engage the Jewish-community substantive keywords.

case_name: Iacovelli c. Union des routiers, brasseries, liqueurs douces et ouvriers de diverses

name_verification.name_in_document: Iacovelli c. Union des routiers, brasseries, liqueurs douces et ouvriers de diverses

defining_issues: Did the Labour Commissioner (confirmed by the Labour Court) commit an excess of jurisdiction by failing to disclose to the intervening employee the names/evidence of employees who withdrew their resignations, contrary to the rules of natural justice?
Does the secrecy provision of Art. 36 of the Labour Code apply to a revocation (cancellation) proceeding so as to justify withholding that information?

Did the failure to transmit a copy of the certification agent's second report to the interested parties, and the apparent acceptance of membership cards dated after the revocation petition, amount to an excess of jurisdiction?

firac.issue: Did the Commissioner and Labour Court exceed their jurisdiction by denying the intervening employee the right to know and refute the evidence relied on?
firac.facts: Iacovelli, an employee and member of the bargaining unit, was allowed to intervene in the employer's petition to revoke the Union's accreditation. She requested the names of employees who had withdrawn their resignations, but the Commissioner refused; the Commissioner instead ordered a survey with sworn declarations and based his dismissal of the revocation petition on that additional evidence, verified privately.
firac.rule: Under Art. 846 C.C.P. the Superior Court's superintending power survives the privative clause of the Labour Code where there is an excess of jurisdiction. Natural justice includes the right to be heard, which encompasses the right to be informed of the evidence used and to correct or refute it (Pépin & Ouellette; Harelkin v. University of Regina, 1979 CanLII 18 (SCC)).
firac.application: The Commissioner evidently relied on the renunciations of resignation and survey forms without disclosing them to the petitioner, depriving her of any opportunity to refute or correct that pertinent and fundamental information. The invitation merely to call witnesses did not cure this. Such a breach of natural justice constitutes an excess of jurisdiction under Art. 846(1) C.C.P.
firac.conclusion: The failure to disclose the evidence violated the petitioner's right to be heard and amounted to an excess of jurisdiction.

firac.issue: Does the Art. 36 secrecy rule extend to revocation proceedings?
firac.facts: The employer argued that Art. 36 of the Labour Code, which forbids revealing a person's union membership, authorized withholding the names.
firac.rule: Art. 36 imposes secrecy only 'au cours de la procédure d'accréditation'. Exceptions to the general right to know and refute proof must be narrowly construed. The Court of Appeal in Vassart v. Robert Simpson's affirmed the primacy of public debate even in certification.
firac.application: The Court held the secrecy condition applies only during certification proceedings, not to revocation/cancellation proceedings under Art. 41; extending it was not warranted by the express text. Being an exception, it must be read narrowly and could not justify the secret evidence.
firac.conclusion: Art. 36 did not authorize withholding the information in a revocation proceeding.

firac.issue: Did failure to send the second certification report and acceptance of late membership cards constitute an excess of jurisdiction?
firac.facts: After the May 11, 1981 hearing the Commissioner obtained a further report from the certification agent but did not send a copy to the interested parties, and appeared to accept membership cards dated after the February 20, 1981 filing of the revocation petition.
firac.rule: Art. 41(3) of the Labour Code requires the Commissioner to send a copy of the agent's report to the parties, who may contest it within ten days. Art. 36.1 fixes the representative-character assessment as of the date of filing of the petition. An erroneous interpretation contrary to common sense or giving the text an unsupportable meaning justifies intervention (Bradburn v. Wentworth Arms Hotel, 1978 CanLII 44 (SCC)).
firac.application: The Commissioner's failure to transmit the second report breached more than a simple preliminary rule, and acceptance of adherences posterior to February 20, 1981 misapplied Art. 36.1, denying the petitioner her right to refute the proof. Both errors reached the magnitude of an excess of jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: These procedural and interpretive errors amounted to an excess of jurisdiction warranting evocation.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally an administrative-law judicial review (K001) by way of evocation under Art. 846 C.C.P. (K011). The determinative doctrine is breach of natural justice / procedural fairness — the right to be heard and to know and refute the evidence (K012). The analysis turns on excess of jurisdiction and erroneous statutory interpretation, best captured by standard of review (K014). The underlying subject matter is labour relations — revocation of union accreditation under the Labour Code — so the Labour and employment tier-1 keyword (K009) applies, though the decision resolves on administrative-law grounds rather than substantive labour law.

registry_rationale: The heading names 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and file no. 500-05-001948-825, indicating the Montréal registry of the Superior Court.

name_verification.name_in_document: Droit de la famille — 19350

defining_issues: Is the mother entitled to child support arrears and, if so, in what amount and on what basis of calculation?
Is the claim for child support arrears prescribed in whole or in part under arts. 595 and 2904 C.C.Q.?
Is the mother entitled to a 20% increase in the parental contribution for the period the child was a minor because the father did not exercise access?
Is the father entitled to spousal support for himself?
Is either party entitled to a provision for costs under art. 588(2) C.C.Q.?
Should the family patrimony be partitioned unequally under art. 422 C.C.Q., and is the City A apartment an acquest?

firac.issue: Is the mother entitled to child support arrears and, if so, in what amount and on what basis?
firac.facts: The father paid the $575/month ordered in the 2004 Roy judgment only two or three times and contributed nothing to the child's needs from 2004 onward, despite working 2000-2004, 2006-2010 and 2012-2014. The mother raised the child, now 23, alone and paid all expenses. She offered two calculation scenarios: scenario A applying the $575 order indefinitely ($152,429.70), and scenario B using the father's actual income, federal guidelines and periods without income ($75,272.16).
firac.rule: A support order cannot be maintained as if a safeguard/interim order for 14 years (C.p.c. art. 158(8)); retroactivity of support requires a contextual approach in the best interests of the child (Droit de la famille — 17122, 2017 QCCA 107). Interest is permitted (Droit de la famille — 3235).
firac.application: The Court rejected the father's position that he owed nothing and refused to perpetuate the interim order indefinitely. It adopted the mother's scenario B as consistent with the evidence, reflecting the father's real income and unemployed periods, with interest.
firac.conclusion: Arrears fixed on the scenario B basis ($75,272.16 with interest); this obligation is compensated through the unequal partition of the family patrimony.

firac.issue: Is the claim for child support arrears prescribed under arts. 595 and 2904 C.C.Q.?
firac.facts: The father argued only arrears since 15 August 2015 (three years before the cross-application) were recoverable. He was abroad for years, gave no address, hid his return and full-time work in City B (2012-2014), behaved violently and unpredictably, and the mother had precarious health, no job security and periods without counsel.
firac.rule: Art. 595 C.C.Q. limits child support for past needs to three years unless the debtor parent behaved reprehensibly; art. 2904 C.C.Q. suspends prescription where a person is in fact unable to act. Blameworthy conduct is interpreted broadly (D.B.S. v. S.R.G., 2006 SCC 37, para. 106; Droit de la famille — 122743, 2012 QCCS 5164), including deliberately ignoring the obligation.
firac.application: The Court found the mother was in fact unable to act throughout: reconciliation attempts, the father's whereabouts unknown abroad, two foreign addresses, his concealed return and full-time employment, a default dismissal she did not consent to, and her exhaustion and lack of representation. His conduct was reprehensible.
firac.conclusion: The prescription argument was rejected; the arrears are not prescribed.

firac.issue: Is the mother entitled to a 20% increase in parental contribution for non-exercise of access?
firac.facts: The father did not exercise access for most of the child's life; the mother carried a heavy economic burden alone for 18 years.
firac.rule: A court may account for a parent's conduct and burden when fixing support, but has discretion on increases.
firac.application: Rather than granting the 20% increase, the Court chose to reflect the mother's heavy sole economic burden through the partition of the family patrimony.
firac.conclusion: No 20% increase awarded.

firac.issue: Is the father entitled to spousal support for himself?
firac.facts: The father, remarried and on welfare, amended his support claims three times (from $1,500/month, to $727/month, to $1,500/week). He worked until 2014, received EI, and his medical work restriction was only for six months (to 1 May 2019).
firac.rule: Bipolar disorder, when treated, is not in itself an impediment to work capacity (Y.A. c. M.B., 2004 CanLII 11044 (QC CA)).
firac.application: The Court found the escalating claims unfounded; the father had earning capacity and had never paid support while employed.
firac.conclusion: The father's application for spousal support is dismissed.

firac.issue: Is either party entitled to a provision for costs under art. 588(2) C.C.Q.?
firac.facts: The father sought a provision for costs but filed no counsel invoices or fee agreement and had never paid support while working; the mother sought $10,000 but there was no evidence of the father's ability to pay.
firac.rule: Art. 588(2) C.C.Q. governs provisions for costs, requiring consideration of the parties' means and conduct.
firac.application: The father could not seek a provision while having refused support and reactivated litigation; the mother's claim failed for lack of evidence of the father's ability to pay.
firac.conclusion: Both applications for a provision for costs are dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the family patrimony be partitioned unequally, and is the City A apartment an acquest?
firac.facts: The co-owned family residence was the only property to partition; the father lived there six years, made an $11,000 down payment and contributed nothing for over 15 years, while the mother paid over $400,000 in home expenses and $70,000 in tuition and incurred ~$160,000 in debt. The City A apartment was bought by the mother's mother in the mother's name to facilitate an inheritance; no money passed to the mother and the couple never lived there.
firac.rule: Art. 422 C.C.Q. permits unequal partition where equal partition would be unjust, tied to the failure of the economic partnership and a spouse's failure to contribute (M.T. c. J.-Y.T., 2008 SCC 50). Art. 450(2) C.C.Q. excludes property received by gift or succession from acquests.
firac.application: The father's total failure to contribute to the marriage's economic partnership justified departing from equal partition; the mother is declared sole owner of the residence, also compensating the unpaid child support arrears. The apartment, received gratuitously through inheritance, is not an acquest.
firac.conclusion: Unequal partition ordered; mother declared sole owner of the residence; the City A apartment is not an acquest.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K050 (parental/child support) is central to the arrears claim, prescription and calculation. K053 (spousal support) covers the father's dismissed claim for support for himself. K047 (best interests of the child) reflects the contextual retroactivity analysis grounded in the child's fundamental right to support. K086 (co-ownership) captures the partition of the co-owned family residence and the unequal partition under art. 422 C.C.Q. Prescription and provision for costs are engaged but have no dedicated vocabulary entry, so they are covered under the family law umbrella; K047 is somewhat supportive rather than doctrinally central.
