case_name: Impérial Tobacco Canada ltée c. Montréal (Ville de)

name_verification.name_in_document: Impérial Tobacco Canada ltée c. Montréal (Ville de)

defining_issues: Did the Tribunal administratif du Québec (TAQ) have jurisdiction to add to the assessment roll the contributory value of property (energy-producing systems, mechanical systems) that the municipal assessor had not taken into account when depositing the roll, absent a complaint on that point?

Are the palletization and materials-handling equipment 'machinery, apparatus and accessories used principally for industrial production' and therefore excluded from the roll under s. 65 of the Act respecting municipal taxation?
Could the TAQ set aside the parties' agreement (admissions) on the base cost of mechanical and electrical systems?

Are the electrical and mechanical systems (plumbing, heating, air-conditioning, humidification) integrated into the buildings principally used or destined for industrial production and therefore excluded from the roll under s. 65 LFM?
Did the TAQ err in applying the principle of institutional coherence, rather than deciding on the balance of the evidence, to fix the local adjustment factor (Factor F) for the 1995 roll?

Did the TAQ err in its treatment of depreciation (curable physical/functional obsolescence, precariousness of public-domain occupation, decline of the tobacco market, building configuration/layout obsolescence)?
Did the TAQ err on parameters for calculating rental value (inclusion of the non-residential immovables surtax and the property value to be used in the decapitalization method)?

firac.issue: Did the TAQ have jurisdiction to add to the roll the contributory value of immovables not accounted for by the assessor at deposit, absent a complaint?
firac.facts: Impérial had filed complaints contesting the value inscribed on the roll, including the mechanical systems. The TAQ added the contributory value of energy-producing systems (steam and chilled water) that the assessor had not initially computed, without a formal demand by a party.
firac.rule: Under the Loi sur la fiscalité municipale, for 'new generation' rolls the assessor and the TAQ must determine the value of the 'unité d'évaluation dans son entier' (art. 145 LFM), the value 'telle qu'elle aurait dû être portée au rôle' (art. 34 LFM), and may fix a value higher or lower than proposed (art. 147 LFM). Distinguished from 'old generation' rolls (Atlific, Shell Canada, Talisman) where the BREF could not add ultra petita. Jurisdiction is a question of law reviewed on correctness (Pushpanathan).
firac.application: Because Impérial had filed a complaint contesting the inscribed value, it conferred jurisdiction on the TAQ to review the entirety of the unit's value. As this is a new-generation roll governed by art. 34 LFM, the TAQ had to consider the whole evaluation unit under art. 145 LFM (Hewquip). The prior jurisprudence Impérial relied on concerned old-generation rolls and was inapplicable.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ had jurisdiction to take into account the contributory value of any property forming part of the evaluation unit within the meaning of art. 34 LFM, even where the assessor had not accounted for it. No error.

firac.issue: Are the palletization and materials-handling equipment excluded from the roll under s. 65 LFM as machinery used principally for industrial production?
firac.facts: Impérial's plant modernization ('Montréal 2001') automated central palletization. Cigarettes cannot be sold until fiscal control stamps (SAP) are affixed, which occurs at the end of the conveyor before removal by forklift. The equipment (palletizers, wrappers, conveyors) had a depreciated cost of $2,216,189.
firac.rule: s. 65(1) LFM excludes from the roll machinery, apparatus and accessories used or destined principally for industrial production. Industrial production is a continuous, integrated process ending when the marketable product is ready for storage; it is not complete until the product is saleable per applicable law (Irving Oil, Cie pétrolière Impériale, Société d'énergie Talisman, RJR MacDonald). This qualification question is a mixed question not within the TAQ's core specialization (Vigi Santé; Charny v. Alex Couture), reviewable for error of law/qualification.
firac.application: Since the product cannot be sold before the fiscal stamps are affixed, industrial production is not complete until that operation. The palletization equipment therefore forms the last integrated step of production, distinguishable from Procter & Gamble where no fiscal stamping was required. The TAQ erred in applying Procter & Gamble and in treating the equipment as post-production.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ erred; the equipment described at pp. 47-48 of report I-32F must not be entered on the roll (s. 65 LFM). Appeal allowed on this point.

firac.issue: Could the TAQ set aside the parties' agreement/admissions on the base cost of the mechanical and electrical systems?
firac.facts: The parties had agreed by written admissions on the base 1972 cost of the mechanical/electrical systems, expressly noting the sums represented only the portion corresponding to building services, excluding production services, and that nothing constituted an admission on whether these should be on the roll under s. 65.
firac.rule: An admission is a question of fact revocable only for error of fact (art. 1245 C.C.; Adricon; Gulf Canada). However, deciding whether an immovable is inscribed or excluded under s. 65 is a question of law which parties cannot derogate from by consent; a tribunal is not bound by such an agreement on a legal question. Jurisdiction question reviewed on correctness.
firac.application: The agreement was only on base cost, not an admission that the contributory value of the systems must (or must not) be on the roll. Whether to inscribe a mixed system is a legal question the TAQ had to decide; the agreement could not be a pretext to avoid inscribing the full related costs. The cited jurisprudence (Adricon, Gulf Canada) was inapplicable because there the party sought to revoke an admission on facts outside the res gestae.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ did not err; it could decide the s. 65 question notwithstanding the base-cost agreement. Appeal rejected on this point.

firac.issue: Are the integrated electrical and mechanical systems (electrical, plumbing, heating, air-conditioning/humidification) principally used or destined for industrial production, so as to be excluded from the roll under s. 65 LFM?
firac.facts: The complex had a single high-voltage electrical entry distributed throughout; ~77% of electricity served production. Plumbing had a 14-inch water entry, ~81% consumption for production. Heating/cooling/humidification maintained a constant 72°F and 62% humidity essential to tobacco production. Impérial argued single integrated systems principally serving production; Montréal argued multiple discrete systems (per panel); the TAQ invented a third theory (23 electrical systems by 'artère de moyenne tension') excluding only 13% (the electrical entry).
firac.rule: Since the 1993 amendment, s. 65(3)-(4) LFM: an integrated mechanical/electrical system is not part of the construction and, if used principally for industrial production, is entirely excluded (all-or-nothing rule; art. 2 proportionality excluded). Whether a system serves principally production or building is a mixed question outside the TAQ's core specialization (Charny v. Alex Couture; Vigi Santé), reviewed on correctness/error of law; the audi alteram partem rule requires notice where a tribunal adopts a theory not advanced by any party (Pétromont). Teleological interpretation of tax legislation (Notre-Dame de Bon-Secours; Ciment Québec).
firac.application: By adopting, without expert support or notice to the parties, the 'artère de moyenne tension' theory and rejecting both experts, the TAQ breached audi alteram partem. Limiting exclusion to 13% (the entry) contradicted the all-or-nothing rule of s. 65 and effectively re-applied art. 2 proportionality via the outdated 1972 Manuel. The proportion of consumption and connected loads is a relevant indicator for a mixed integrated system, and the 'destination' element was ignored. The installations form single integrated systems principally used/destined for production (electricity ~77%, plumbing ~81%, heating/gas ~99%/62%, chilled water ~74%, ventilation ~78%).
firac.conclusion: The TAQ erred; the electrical and mechanical systems (plumbing, heating, air-conditioning/humidification) are principally used or destined for industrial production and their contributory value must not be entered on the roll under s. 65 LFM. Appeal allowed on these points.

firac.issue: Did the TAQ err in relying on institutional coherence rather than the preponderant evidence to fix the local adjustment factor (Factor F) for the 1995 roll?
firac.facts: Impérial's expert (Caumartin) study yielded Factor F of 0.80; Montréal's expert (Lévesque) study yielded 1.05, and Montréal, for the first time, submitted a genuine Factor F study and critique (32 days of testimony, 86 exhibits). The TAQ acknowledged numerous deficiencies in Caumartin's study but retained 0.80 'par souci de cohérence institutionnelle.'
firac.rule: Institutional/decisional coherence is desirable but not absolute; decisional autonomy and appreciation of the specific evidence prevail (Domtar; Tremblay; Consolidated Bathurst; CSST v. Fontaine; ABI; Investissements Canpro). Each case must be decided on its own evidence on the balance of probabilities; whether to prefer coherence over new evidence is a question of law (correctness).
firac.application: Montréal's new, different evidence had never been before the TAQ in prior cases. The TAQ, having found Caumartin's study deficient, could not use coherence to grant it de facto res judicata. It had to weigh the two contradictory studies on the balance of probabilities or, if both deficient, neutralize the factor. Analyzing the evidence itself, the Court found Montréal's methodology preferable (indexation to reference date via Statistics Canada, homogeneous comparables), but both studies had deficiencies (dated/old-generation data). Accordingly the factor should be neutralized to 1.0, which enjoyed a presumption of accuracy at deposit.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ erred in law; Factor F is neutralized at 1.0 for the 1995 and 1995-modified rolls. Montréal's appeal allowed in part on this point.

firac.issue: Did the TAQ err in its treatment of the various heads of depreciation?
firac.facts: Impérial claimed curable physical/functional obsolescence on four elements, precariousness of public-domain occupation (tunnels/passageways revocable on 30 days' notice), decline of the tobacco market, supply/snow-removal difficulties, and building configuration/multi-level layout (prior BREF decision had allowed 20%; TAQ allowed 10%).
firac.rule: Depreciation lies at the core of the TAQ's specialized jurisdiction; review is limited to patently unreasonable error. Contributory value of refurbishment must be netted against its cost (General Motors; Camco; Schering; SIQ). One cannot depreciate for missing elements not in the reproduction cost (CAE; Camco). Institutional coherence does not bind where evidence differs.
firac.application: On curable obsolescence, the TAQ correctly followed doctrine (Desjardins) and jurisprudence by accounting for added value of refurbishment (de Grandpré method); no reviewable error. On public-domain precariousness, uncontradicted evidence showed Montréal never revoked such permissions and the past is guarantor of the future; the reasonable risk over 10 years' remaining life was too small to quantify. On tobacco-market decline, the TAQ erred factually in saying no evidence was led, but Impérial itself claimed no economic obsolescence and provided no quantum, so no operative error. Supply/snow-removal issues duplicated configuration and reflect age-related obsolescence captured by age-life tables; missing storage cannot depreciate. On configuration (10% vs prior 20%), the evidence had materially changed (Montréal 2001 project, primary processing moved to Aylmer, layout changes); the TAQ's finding was defensible and within its expertise; institutional coherence did not bind because the evidence differed.
firac.conclusion: Save for the factual misstatement on tobacco-market evidence (without operative effect), the TAQ did not commit patently unreasonable error on depreciation. Impérial's appeal on depreciation rejected.

firac.issue: Did the TAQ err on the rental-value parameters (inclusion of the non-residential immovables surtax and the property value used in decapitalization)?
firac.facts: For the 1995 rolls, the TAQ used 1993 reference-date tax rates (including a 1% water tax and 2.06% surtax that replaced water/business taxes for 1993 only) and applied them to the property value inscribed at the reference date. The assessor had not included the surtax when depositing the 1995 rental-value roll, so complainants like Impérial bore an added burden.
firac.rule: s. 69.5 LFM: rental value is the most probable gross annual rent including property taxes; s. 1 LFM defines the non-residential immovables surtax as a property tax (Germain v. Montréal, SCC). The tax amount included is that effectively expended in the reference year, requiring combination of reference-date rates with the value then inscribed (Hewquip; General Motors). These parameter questions are within the TAQ's core specialization; review for patently unreasonable error. The TAQ must render the decision the assessor should have made.
firac.application: The surtax is a property tax and must be included under s. 69.5; the TAQ correctly included it and rendered the decision the assessor should have made, despite the resulting unequal treatment of complainants. On the value to use, only combining reference-date tax rates with the value inscribed at the reference date respects the LFM requirement that the tax reflect the effective expenditure in the reference year.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ did not commit patently unreasonable error; inclusion of the surtax and use of the reference-date inscribed value are upheld. Impérial's appeal rejected on these points.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the tier-1 practice area: the case is a statutory appeal from a specialized administrative tribunal (TAQ) under the Loi sur la justice administrative, turning on jurisdiction, standard of review and procedural fairness. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) are central: the judgment applies the Pushpanathan/Dr Q pragmatic-and-functional analysis, distinguishing correctness (jurisdiction, s. 65 qualification) from patently unreasonable (valuation, depreciation) questions. K012 (procedural fairness) captures the audi alteram partem breach where the TAQ adopted an electrical-systems theory advanced by no party. K002 (Civil litigation) is included as the closest available tier-1 tag for the private-law dimensions (admissions/aveu judiciaire under art. 1245 C.C., balance of probabilities), though it is a weaker/borderline pick since the true subject is municipal property tax assessment, for which the controlled vocabulary offers no specific keyword. The vocabulary lacks specific terms for municipal assessment, valuation methods, industrial-production exemption (s. 65 LFM), or institutional coherence, so no more precise IDs exist; fewer than five strong administrative-law-specific keywords apply, and K002 is flagged as the weakest selection.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'COUR DU QUÉBEC ... PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC, DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL, Chambre civile' and lists the file number 500-80-003588-044, confirming the Court of Québec sitting in the district of Montréal.
registry_rationale: The 'DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL' designation and the parties' Montréal addresses identify the Montréal registry/district of the Court of Québec.

name_verification.name_in_document: E.L. v. Catholic Children's Aid (Toronto), 2010 ONSC 2426

defining_issues: What is the applicable standard of appellate review of a trial judge's findings in a child protection status review, and was it met?
Did the trial judge err in determining that the children's best interests required Crown Wardship with no access for the purpose of adoption?
Did the trial judge err in denying the grandparents access after making the children Crown Wards, given the statutory onus?
Did the participation and testimony of the foster/adoptive parents violate the appellant's right to a hearing free of bias and in the absence of the public?
Did the trial judge's findings and the CFSA disposition infringe the appellant's rights under ss. 7, 12 and 15 of the Charter?

firac.issue: What is the applicable standard of appellate review of a trial judge's factual and mixed fact-and-law findings, and was it met?
firac.facts: The grandmother appealed a Crown Wardship order made after a nine-day trial, alleging errors of fact and mixed fact and law, including undue weight on the foster-parent relationship.
firac.rule: Factual findings attract significant deference and may only be reversed for a 'palpable and overriding error' — one plainly seen on the face of the record (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33; Van de Perre v. Edwards, 2001 SCC 60). An appeal court cannot substitute its own view merely because it would weigh the evidence differently.
firac.application: The court found the trial judge's factual findings — including the assault, the credibility assessments, the acceptance of Dr. Kershner's parenting-capacity assessment, and the weighing of the children's relationships — were overwhelmingly supported by the evidence. The trial judge properly balanced the children's relationships with both foster parents and grandparents and correctly stated the legal framework, which the appellant did not dispute.
firac.conclusion: No palpable and overriding error was shown; deference to the trial judge's findings was warranted.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in finding that the children's best interests required Crown Wardship with no access for adoption?
firac.facts: The three children had lived with the grandparents since birth under supervision; the grandmother assaulted a child in 2007 (guilty plea) leading to apprehension; a consent parenting-capacity assessment found the grandparents unable to meet the children's psychological, social, medical and academic needs and unable to improve despite supports and parenting classes.
firac.rule: On a status review the sole issue is disposition, determined by the child's best interests under the criteria in s. 37(3) CFSA, from a child-centred perspective; good intentions are not enough — parents must have actually changed and be able to provide adequate care (Jewish Child and Family Services v. R.K.). The court must consider less disruptive alternatives (ss. 57(1), 57.1 CFSA).
firac.application: The trial judge considered the full evidence — expert assessments, support-worker observations, the children's low cognitive functioning and improvement in foster care, and the grandparents' inability to learn new parenting skills — and reasonably concluded the earlier voluntary placement reflected inadequate supervision rather than adequate parenting. Crown Wardship for adoption was in the children's best interests.
firac.conclusion: No error; the disposition was amply supported by the evidence.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in denying the grandparents access after making the children Crown Wards?
firac.facts: Once children are made Crown Wards, access is automatically terminated; the grandparents sought access. Evidence showed visits were difficult, the children had little attachment to the grandparents and strong attachment to their foster mother of three years; fresh evidence on appeal confirmed this.
firac.rule: Under s. 59 CFSA the person seeking access to a Crown Ward bears the onus of showing the relationship is beneficial and meaningful to the child and that access will not impair future adoption opportunities (s. 59(2.1); Children's Aid Society of the Niagara Region v. M.J.).
firac.application: The trial judge correctly placed the onus on the grandparents and found, on the totality of evidence and confirmed by fresh evidence, that access was not beneficial or meaningful and the children lacked strong attachment to them.
firac.conclusion: No error; the denial of access was properly grounded in the statutory test and the evidence.

firac.issue: Did the foster/adoptive parents' notice, attendance and testimony violate the appellant's right to an unbiased hearing held in the absence of the public?
firac.facts: The foster parents received notice, attended and testified at the protection hearing.
firac.rule: Section 39(3) CFSA entitles a foster parent who has continuously cared for a child for six months before the hearing to notice of and presence at the hearing; it is common practice for foster parents to testify.
firac.application: Because the statute expressly authorizes foster parents to receive notice and attend, they are statutorily mandated participants, not 'members of the public,' and their participation could not create bias or interference or breach the appellant's right to a hearing in the absence of the public.
firac.conclusion: This ground had no merit.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge's findings or the CFSA disposition infringe the appellant's Charter rights under ss. 7, 12 or 15?
firac.facts: The appellant argued the trial judge's characterization of her as intellectually and emotionally limited breached s. 15, that denial of custody/access breached s. 7, and that 'deprecatory' comments breached s. 12.
firac.rule: Section 7 guarantees life, liberty and security of the person; s. 12 prohibits cruel and unusual treatment or punishment; s. 15 addresses equality. A constitutional challenge to legislation requires joining the Attorney General under s. 109 of the Courts of Justice Act.
firac.application: The s. 15 argument failed because the characterization was a factual finding supported by evidence, not a breach of fundamental justice. Any challenge to the constitutionality of the CFSA access provisions could not be entertained as the Attorney General was not joined; treated as a challenge to the access ruling, the onus was correctly applied. The s. 12 argument was unsupported by authority and the court found no deprecatory comments were made.
firac.conclusion: The Charter grounds were rejected.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area — this is a child protection/Crown Wardship appeal. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test under s. 37(3) CFSA. K048 (custody/access) captures the contested access issue and the s. 59 onus. K014 (standard of review) is included for the appellate 'palpable and overriding error' standard central to the disposition, though its canonical synonyms lean toward administrative reasonableness/correctness (a slightly weak fit). K003 (Constitutional law) and K107 (Charter) reflect the Charter grounds raised; K112 (Charter s. 7) and K109 (Charter s. 15) are the specific provisions argued. Section 12 was raised but is not a listed keyword. The Charter picks are somewhat peripheral since the court dismissed them summarily, but they were genuinely argued grounds of appeal.
location_rationale: The heading states 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE' and the matter proceeds under the Ontario Child and Family Services Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.11, so the province is Ontario. No city is stated in the decision itself; although the respondent is the 'Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto,' that identifies the party, not the sitting location, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision gives a court file number (FS-09-16312-00) but does not name a registry or court office location, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: VADIM GINDIS v. RITCHIE SCOTT BRISBOURNE

defining_issues: Was the settlement and release signed by the plaintiff on June 3, 1991 an unconscionable bargain that should be set aside?
Did the negligence of the defendant in the motor vehicle accident cause the injuries (in particular the chronic pain syndrome) the plaintiff claims to suffer?
What is the appropriate quantum of damages, and to what extent should awards be reduced for failure to mitigate?

firac.issue: Should the release signed on June 3, 1991 be set aside as an unconscionable bargain?
firac.facts: After a July 1990 T-bone collision (liability admitted), Gindis, a Russian émigré with limited English and no meaningful assessment of his claim, negotiated directly with ICBC adjuster Larry Laws while financially destitute and effectively unrepresented. Laws instigated settlement talks knowing Gindis was desperate, relied selectively on Dr. Richards' October 17, 1990 report, refused to disclose that report, remained wilfully blind to other medical information showing ongoing problems under investigation, and secured a $25,000 global release (net cheque $16,054) for less than the claims committee's own reserves.
firac.rule: A bargain is presumptively unconscionable where (1) there was inequality of bargaining position due to ignorance, need or distress of the weaker party, and (2) there is proof of substantial unfairness; the onus then shifts to the stronger party to show the bargain was fair, just and reasonable: Morrison v. Coast Finance Ltd. (1965), Harry v. Kreutziger (1978), Smyth v. Szep (1992), Cougle v. Maricevic (1983). A Crown corporation exercising a monopoly (ICBC) is held to a high standard of commercial morality and must at least disclose to an unrepresented claimant all medical and other information underlying its settlement offer.
firac.application: Gindis was clearly the weaker party — naive, unsophisticated, without documented medical information, medically unassessed, and financially ruined after his wife left. Laws' refusal to disclose Dr. Richards' report and his deliberate failure to obtain available medical information (Dr. Ciszak's file, ongoing neurological assessment) left Gindis unable to make an informed decision. Laws' goal was to limit coverage and obtain a quick, cheap settlement, ignoring that a work-hardening program had been recommended. The settlement was premature and unfair; the court deferred final determination until it assessed proper compensation and, having found the injuries far exceeded the settlement, concluded the bargain was not fair, just and reasonable.
firac.conclusion: The release was set aside.

firac.issue: Did the accident cause the plaintiff's chronic pain syndrome and consequent losses?
firac.facts: Gindis suffered a mild concussion and soft-tissue injuries and, with pre-existing low back pain and paranoid/narcissistic personality traits, developed chronic pain syndrome (CPS) causing physical, cognitive and emotional impairment. Most specialists diagnosed CPS; none found malingering or exaggeration. He was not dysfunctional before the accident.
firac.rule: Causation in tort applies to psychological as well as physical injuries. The plaintiff must show the defendant's unlawful act was a cause-in-fact ('but for') and a proximate cause of the symptoms: Maslen v. Rubenstein (1993), Skelton v. Stewart (1994), Yoshikawa v. Yu (1996). A defendant takes the victim as found — the thin skull / 'eggshell personality' rule — and need only have materially contributed to the injury; the defendant is not excused because other causal factors also contributed: Athey v. Leonati, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 458.
firac.application: The court found Gindis' pre-existing personality traits and low back pain were aggravated and exacerbated by the accident's soft-tissue injury, and that the resulting interplay produced CPS which would not have occurred but for the defendant's negligence. The eggshell-personality principle applied; genuine, non-organic psychological symptoms are compensable. ICBC's failure to arrange an early work-hardening program contributed to his deconditioning, though Gindis' own refusal to exercise also contributed.
firac.conclusion: Causation was established; the CPS and related losses were compensable.

firac.issue: What quantum of damages is appropriate and how should it be reduced for failure to mitigate?
firac.facts: Gindis had a limited, intermittent work history (approx. $15,000/year combined employment and UI), was capable of light sedentary work from January 1991 but did not pursue it (later choosing to stay home to care for his son), and failed to follow medical advice to exercise.
firac.rule: Damages are assessed under distinct heads; awards may be reduced for a plaintiff's failure to mitigate: Janiak v. Ippolito, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 146; Watters v. Rose.
firac.application: Non-pecuniary damages assessed at $75,000, reduced 10% for failure to mitigate to $67,500. Past income loss (projected $90,802 based on ~$15,000/year) reduced 50% to $45,401 for his ability to do light work not pursued. Future income loss (projected $240,234) reduced 50% to $121,200 for residual earning capacity. Future care $15,000; special damages $88.
firac.conclusion: Total awards granted, less the $25,000 already received under the release, with court-ordered interest on past income loss and special damages and costs to the plaintiff.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the core practice-area keyword: this is a tort/personal-injury action turning on unconscionability of a settlement release, causation, and assessment of damages. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward human-rights, hate-speech and religious themes and contains no tier-2 terms for personal injury, unconscionable bargains, ICBC settlements, causation or chronic pain, so the remaining picks are admittedly weak/contextual. K008 (Immigration law), K078 (refugee protection) and K076 (deportation) reflect the extensive factual background of the plaintiff's refugee claim, deportation order and immigration appeals, but these were not the legal issues decided. K093 (Jewish) reflects the plaintiff's Jewish heritage and consequent discrimination in Russia and Israel, again purely background. All four secondary keywords are flagged as weak — no vocabulary term genuinely captures the tort/contract subject matter.
location_rationale: The decision names the Supreme Court of British Columbia and states the 'Place and Date of Hearing: Vancouver, B.C.'; the accident occurred at Georgia and Bute Streets in Vancouver, confirming the province as British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The header lists 'Registry: Vancouver' under docket B922611.

name_verification.name_in_document: Harun-ar-Rashid v. BC (Teacher Regulation Commissioner)

defining_issues: Does a person served with or put 'on notice' of a petition who files a response thereby automatically become a full party to the petition proceeding?
Should the pleadings and references to the 'on notice' entities (the Langley School District and Trish Kolotyluk) be struck and those entities removed from the proceeding under Rule 9-5?
Should the Petitioner be declared a vexatious litigant and barred from instituting further proceedings without leave under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act?

firac.issue: Does a person served with or put 'on notice' of a petition who files a response automatically become a full party to the petition proceeding?
firac.facts: Mr. Rashid designated the Langley School District and Trish Kolotyluk as 'on notice' without naming them as parties in the style of cause and sought no relief against them. When they applied to be removed, he argued their filing of responses made them 'parties' who were participating unlawfully.
firac.rule: Under Rule 1-1 a 'party' is a person named in the style of the proceeding. Kitimat (District) v. Alcan Inc., 2006 BCCA 562, holds that filing a response does not confer full party status; a person must apply to be added under Rule 6-2(7) or apply to intervene. Case law is unsettled (Kellogg, Delta Sunshine, Pierce, Louis), but Delta Sunshine implicitly applied Kitimat to petitions under Rule 16-1.
firac.application: The Court reviewed the conflicting authorities and followed the notation in Pierce (para. 39) that Delta Sunshine implicitly concluded Kitimat applies to Rule 16-1 petitions. Merely being served and filing a response makes a person a party of record but not a full party. The applicants had not been named in the style of cause and had not applied under Rule 6-2(7).
firac.conclusion: Ms. Kolotyluk and the Langley School District were not made full parties merely by filing responses; the Petitioner's assertion that they participated unlawfully was without merit.

firac.issue: Should the pleadings referring to the 'on notice' entities be struck and those entities removed from the proceeding?
firac.facts: The petition contained bald Charter allegations and factual assertions against the Langley School District, and referred to a letter by Ms. Kolotyluk, an Alberta employee who had provided no information about the Petitioner. No relief was sought against either and no facts supported any claim.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim (a), are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious (b), or are otherwise an abuse of process (d). A pleading is vexatious where it would serve no useful purpose and waste court resources (Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083; Nevsun Resources Ltd. v. Araya, 2020 SCC 5); abuse of process engages the court's inherent jurisdiction (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63).
firac.application: Charter relief was not available in a proceeding brought by petition; the allegations lacked any factual foundation; Edmonton Public Schools and Ms. Kolotyluk, being Alberta entities, could not be the subject of relief in British Columbia; and no order could be made against either applicant. The impugned paragraphs were scandalous, frivolous or vexatious and served no useful purpose.
firac.conclusion: The Court ordered the applicants have no role in the petition, struck the identified paragraphs without leave to amend, and removed all references to the applicants from the style of cause and elsewhere.

firac.issue: Should the Petitioner be declared a vexatious litigant and prohibited from bringing further proceedings without leave?
firac.facts: Mr. Rashid had pursued judicial reviews, a Human Rights Tribunal complaint (dismissed as premature), reconsiderations and appeals, an Alberta action against the RCMP (struck as disclosing no reasonable claim and abusive), and this petition, all repeating unsupported allegations of discrimination and conspiracy. He had been warned by the Alberta Court and by Edelmann J. (upheld by the Court of Appeal).
firac.rule: Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act permits an order barring further proceedings without leave where a person has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds instituted vexatious proceedings. Proceedings must be vexatious/without reasonable grounds and there must be a knowing, deliberate repetition, assessed objectively (British Columbia (Public Guardian and Trustee) v. Brown, 2002 BCSC 1152). Indicia of vexatiousness are set out in Holland v. Marshall, 2010 BCCA 243, and Pearlman v. ICBC, 2010 BCCA 362 (from Re Lang Michener and Fabian).
firac.application: Mr. Rashid repeatedly rolled forward the same unsupported claims across multiple forums despite clear warnings, and brought this 'on notice' proceeding against an Alberta employee over whom the Court had no jurisdiction, amounting to harassment. No reasonable litigant could expect relief by repeating such claims. The whole history showed habitual and persistent vexatious conduct without reasonable cause.
firac.conclusion: The Court declared the Petitioner a vexatious litigant, prohibited him under s. 18 from instituting further legal proceedings without leave of the Court, and awarded the applicants special costs payable forthwith after assessment.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally civil procedure and litigation management (K002 Civil litigation as primary practice-area tag), turning on petition-response party status, striking pleadings and vexatious-litigant orders. The underlying subject matter is judicial review of a teacher-certification decision (K011 judicial review; K001 Administrative law as the parent for review of the Commissioner's decision). The regulatory context is teacher regulation and professional certification (K013 professional discipline / professional regulation, engaged by the Commissioner for Teacher Regulation and Teachers Act). The recurring allegation animating all the litigation was discrimination based on ancestry, colour, place of origin and race (K069 discrimination), and the subject involves teaching certification and school districts (K005 Education law; K046 teacher misconduct/professional standards is borderline — the certification dispute touches teacher qualification standards; K042 code of conduct is a weaker pick reflecting the certification/professional-standards backdrop). K046 and K042 are the weakest picks and included only to capture the education-professional dimension.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Registry: New Westminster' and the place of hearing and judgment are given as 'New Westminster, B.C.'
registry_rationale: The docket header expressly states 'Registry: New Westminster'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Italy v. Seifert

defining_issues: What effect does the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Ferras have on the assessment of the sufficiency of evidence at an extradition committal hearing, and did the extradition judge apply the correct standard?
Where the committal predated Ferras, should the appellate court remit the matter for a new hearing or itself reassess the evidence, and does the evidence meet the Ferras sufficiency test?

Did the Minister of Justice's prior advocacy on behalf of Jewish organizations and against Nazi war criminals give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias in exercising the surrender discretion under s. 44(1)(a) of the Extradition Act?
Would surrender of Seifert to Italy be unjust or oppressive within the meaning of s. 44(1)(a) of the Extradition Act?

firac.issue: What effect does Ferras have on the assessment of sufficiency of evidence for extradition committal, and did the extradition judge apply the correct standard?
firac.facts: Italy sought Seifert's extradition on murder charges arising from alleged tortures and killings at the Bolzano Transit Camp in 1944-45, presenting its case by way of a Record of the Case. The committal judge decided the case in 2003, several years before Ferras, relying on the limited role of the judge described in Shephard, and committed on seven of nine counts.
firac.rule: Under United States of America v. Ferras; Latty, 2006 SCC 33, an extradition judge must be satisfied the requesting state's evidence is both reliable and available, and has discretion to engage in a limited weighing of the evidence to determine whether it is sufficient to enable a properly instructed jury, acting reasonably, to convict — thereby overruling a key element of United States of America v. Shephard (as the Court explained in United States of America v. Graham, 2007 BCCA 345).
firac.application: The judge took a careful look at all the evidence and even discharged on two counts, but framed his role in the narrower Shephard terms and could not be said to have anticipated the Ferras development, so his sufficiency assessment did not conform to the current standard and a reassessment was required.
firac.conclusion: A reassessment of the evidence under the Ferras standard was necessary.

firac.issue: Should the matter be remitted for a new committal hearing or should the Court of Appeal itself reassess the evidence, and does the evidence meet the Ferras test?
firac.facts: Seifert sought a new hearing, arguing credibility issues from his four days of oral testimony denying every allegation. The Record of the Case contained eyewitness statements from former prisoners, gathered through Italy's inquisitorial process and certified as available and admissible.
firac.rule: Following the approach in Ferras and Graham, an appellate court may review the evidence in light of the new rule to avoid delay; credibility is 'pre-eminently a jury question' (Hall J.A. in Graham), and evidence is examined 'through the lens of judicial experience' (R. v. Biniaris, 2000 SCC 15). Committal remains a prima facie determination.
firac.application: A new hearing would cause intolerable delay in an already protracted case; extradition partners are entitled to swift determinations. Seifert's testimony was a series of denials going to credibility, not to the reliability or availability of Italy's evidence. On a count-by-count review the eyewitness accounts (e.g., on counts 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9) were sufficient to put the case to a jury; the alleged defects (hearsay, age of allegations, deceased witnesses, possible collaboration, leading questions) went to credibility and did not render committal unjust.
firac.conclusion: The Court reassessed the evidence itself, found it sufficient on all committal counts under Ferras, and dismissed the appeal from committal.

firac.issue: Did the Minister of Justice's background give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias in exercising the surrender discretion?
firac.facts: The surrender decision was made by Minister Irwin Cotler, who as a law professor and advocate for the Canadian Jewish Congress and B'nai Brith had campaigned against impunity for Nazi war criminals. Seifert argued a reasonable person would doubt the Minister could bring an open mind to whether surrender of an elderly, long-blameless resident would be unjust or oppressive.
firac.rule: The test is the reasonable apprehension of bias held by a reasonable, right-minded, informed person viewing the matter realistically (Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board; Wewaykum Indian Band v. Canada, 2003 SCC 45). Impartiality does not require a decision-maker to have no opinions, only to keep an open mind (Arsenault-Cameron v. P.E.I.); the surrender decision is political, at the extreme legislative end of the administrative continuum (Idziak v. Canada).
firac.application: The Minister's record reflected the uncontroversial theme that there must be no impunity for war crimes — an international norm Canada embraced through the Rome Statute and the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act. Nothing showed he advocated punishment regardless of the merits or that he would negate the s. 44(1)(a) discretion, and he affirmed he brought an open mind. As a Minister he leaves behind the advocate's role but need not abandon his convictions.
firac.conclusion: No reasonable apprehension of bias was made out; the petition for judicial review was dismissed on this ground.

firac.issue: Would surrender be unjust or oppressive under s. 44(1)(a) of the Extradition Act?
firac.facts: Seifert was 83 during the appeal, had health problems, and had lived a peaceful, law-abiding life in Canada for over 50 years, working, raising a family and attaining citizenship. The offences were nine murders accompanied by extreme cruelty at the Bolzano camp.
firac.rule: Under s. 44(1)(a) the Minister must refuse surrender if it would be unjust or oppressive having regard to all relevant circumstances; the leading authority is United States of America v. Burns, 2001 SCC 7. The standard of review of this determination is correctness (Ganis v. Canada, 2006 BCCA 543).
firac.application: The Minister weighed Seifert's age, health, family and community ties, and Canada's interest in not being a safe haven for fugitives. The gravity of the crimes overwhelmed the personal circumstances; denying surrender would let Seifert escape justice and deny Italy's legitimate treaty request.
firac.conclusion: Surrender was not unjust or oppressive; the Minister was correct, and this ground of review was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary tier-1 area — this is an extradition case concerning murder charges. K001 (Administrative law) is the tier-1 parent for the judicial review of the Minister's surrender order. K039 (war crimes / crimes against humanity) captures the substance: SS crimes at the Bolzano camp. K011 (judicial review) and K012 (procedural fairness) cover the challenge to the surrender order, including the reasonable-apprehension-of-bias, disclosure and oral-hearing arguments. K014 (standard of review) reflects the correctness standard applied to the s. 44(1)(a) determination. K088 (Holocaust) and K093 (Jewish) reflect the camp context and Jewish victims. K066 (Nazi) is included because the accused was an SS guard in a Nazi-run camp; it is a borderline pick since the case is not about white-supremacist ideology today but about historical Nazi-era war crimes.
location_rationale: The header identifies the Court of Appeal for British Columbia and states 'Place and Date of Hearing: Vancouver, British Columbia' and 'Place and Date of Judgment: Vancouver, British Columbia'.
registry_rationale: The decision carries 'Docket: CA031164' and the Court of Appeal for British Columbia sitting in Vancouver; no separate registry office beyond Vancouver is named.

name_verification.name_in_document: Duguay c. Boutin

defining_issues: Is the plaintiff's action prescribed, and at what point did the limitation period begin to run?

Does the plaintiff disclose a sufficient legal interest and cause of action (lien de droit) against the mise en cause Autobus Laterrière inc. and against the dissolved company Les Transports Spécialisés du Saguenay inc.?
Is the plaintiff's proceeding abusive within the meaning of art. 54.1 C.p.c., warranting an award of extrajudicial costs?

firac.issue: Is the action prescribed, and when did the three-year limitation period begin to run?
firac.facts: The plaintiff claims ownership of 238.50 shares of Les Transports Spécialisés du Saguenay inc. evidenced by certificate no. 16 (1982). A 1984 sale contract (P-4) to Jean-Claude Roy was allegedly a simulation. Roy's heir, Danielle Boutin, allegedly sold all the company's shares to Autobus Laterrière inc. around 1998; the company was struck off in 2000. The plaintiff says he only learned of the sale in October 2009 by reading a local newspaper. The action was filed 9 June 2011. Defendants argued prescription running from 1984, 1998 or 2000.
firac.rule: Art. 165(4) C.p.c. (irrecevabilité) and art. 54.1 C.p.c. (rejet); on a motion to dismiss all alleged facts are taken as true and courts act with prudence, dismissing only where clearly the allegations cannot give rise to the relief sought (Entreprises Pro-Sag inc. c. Groupe Olson Construction inc.). Prescription runs from the day the right of action arises, or in cases of gradual/late damage from its first manifestation, when the plaintiff knew of fault, damage and causation (Gervais, La prescription); art. 2904 C.c.Q. suspends prescription where it is impossible to act.
firac.application: The court characterized the action as a personal recourse to recover the value of a good sold without right by a third party (Boutin), the transaction dating to 1998, more than three years before suit. However, the plaintiff alleged he learned of the sale only in 2009 and, on a motion to dismiss, these allegations must be taken as true. Whether his prior ignorance amounts to an impossibility to act under art. 2904 C.c.Q. is a question of fact or mixed fact and law to be resolved at trial after a full contradictory debate. Accordingly the action appears, on its face, to be within time.
firac.conclusion: The prescription argument cannot be upheld at this stage; the motion in irrecevabilité on that ground is dismissed.

firac.issue: Does the plaintiff have a sufficient legal interest and cause of action against Autobus Laterrière inc. and against the dissolved company?
firac.facts: The pleadings contain no allegation of fault against Autobus Laterrière and only paragraph 27 seeks to link it, asking to be declared a shareholder of Autobus Laterrière because Boutin struck off Les Transports Spécialisés and refused to revive it. Les Transports Spécialisés du Saguenay inc. was dissolved 7 December 1999 (certificate MC-1).
firac.rule: Sale of another's property gives the true owner only a restricted remedy: art. 1714 C.c.Q. allows annulment and revendication against the buyer, not a personal claim, and may require reimbursing the buyer. A simulation/contre-lettre cannot be set up against a third party without consent (arts. 1451, 1452 C.c.Q.). Under the Canada Business Corporations Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, s. 226(4)) a creditor's recourse lies against former shareholders; a company dissolved more than two years cannot be sued without first being reconstituted (Martel, La compagnie au Québec). Arts. 55, 216 C.p.c. require sufficient interest and necessity of a party; art. 152 C.p.c. requires an apparent right for injunctive relief.
firac.application: The plaintiff's claim against Boutin and 2786362 Canada inc. (declaration of simulation being an accessory that shares the principal action's apparent non-prescription, and opposable to Boutin as continuator of the co-contractant's juridical personality) is not manifestly unfounded. But against Autobus Laterrière the contre-lettre is not opposable, art. 1714 gives no personal money claim against the buyer, and the refusal to revive the dissolved company confers no right to shares in Autobus Laterrière. The company being dissolved, no action lies without reconstitution — a public-order issue the court may raise proprio motu. The injunction-type conclusion (production of the sale contract) rests on no apparent right (art. 152 C.p.c.) and is premature (art. 402 C.p.c.).
firac.conclusion: The plaintiff shows no sufficient legal interest against Autobus Laterrière inc. or the dissolved Les Transports Spécialisés du Saguenay inc.; the originating application is declared irrecevable and rejected as against both, with costs to Autobus Laterrière. The motion of Boutin and 2786362 Canada inc. is dismissed.

firac.issue: Is the plaintiff's proceeding abusive under art. 54.1 C.p.c.?
firac.facts: Autobus Laterrière sought a declaration of abuse and extrajudicial costs, characterizing the proceeding as improper.
firac.rule: Art. 54.1 C.p.c. permits sanctioning abusive proceedings.
firac.application: Although the pleading is poorly articulated and deficient in several respects, a plaintiff who believes he owns a right in a good he knows to be held by the mise en cause cannot be said to act in bad faith merely by attempting a flawed procedural route against it.
firac.conclusion: The proceeding is not abusive; the request for extrajudicial fees/costs on that basis is refused (the rejet motion is granted only in part).

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area: this is a private-law share-recovery dispute decided on motions to dismiss for prescription and want of legal interest. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is engaged because the originating application was styled in part as a demand for an injunction, and a conclusion seeking production of the sale contract was refused for want of an apparent right (art. 152 C.p.c.). K022 (restitution) reflects the true owner's remedy of nullity and revendication of shares sold without right under art. 1714 C.c.Q. K054 (wills/estates) is tangential — Danielle Boutin is sued as the heir (héritière) continuing the deceased co-contractant's juridical personality, relevant to opposability of the alleged simulation. K086 (co-ownership) is a weak/borderline pick used only as the closest available property-related term for the shareholding/ownership dispute. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward Charter/human-rights and antisemitism matters and fits this commercial corporate-law case poorly; there is no keyword for prescription, standing, simulation/contre-lettre, or dissolved corporations, so K054 and K086 are flagged as weak and included chiefly to reach the minimum count.
location_rationale: The header states 'COUR SUPÉRIEURE ... PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC, DISTRICT DE CHICOUTIMI', identifying the Superior Court sitting in the judicial district of Chicoutimi, Quebec.
registry_rationale: The decision is issued in the 'DISTRICT DE CHICOUTIMI' (file no. 150-17-002052-113), so the registry is Chicoutimi.

name_verification.name_in_document: Ingrid M. Eggertson v. Alberta Teachers' Association

defining_issues: What standard of review applies to the decision of the ATA's Professional Conduct Appeal Committee?
Was the finding that Ms. Eggertson's statements constituted unprofessional conduct reasonable, including where the statements were made off-duty and in a parental capacity?
Did the ATA's failure to produce the investigator's complete notes breach any statutory or common law disclosure obligation?
Does the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (freedom of expression, s. 2(b)) apply to the ATA Code of Ethics, and if so was it infringed?

firac.issue: What standard of review applies to the ATA Appeal Committee's decision?
firac.facts: The ATA's hearing and appeal committees, composed of teaching professionals, found Ms. Eggertson guilty of unprofessional conduct. The Teaching Profession Act contains no right of appeal but preserves judicial review (s. 56).
firac.rule: The pragmatic and functional approach in Pushpanathan v. Canada (1998) requires weighing the privative clause, tribunal expertise, purpose of the Act and provisions, and whether the question is one of fact or law; expertise is the most important factor.
firac.application: There was no full privative clause but a demonstrated legislative intent of limited court intervention. The committees possessed particular expertise to assess whether conduct was unprofessional and were acting within the Act's purpose. These factors weighed toward a patently unreasonable, or at least reasonableness, standard for the factual determinations, while disclosure (mixed fact and law) and the Charter question (pure law) attracted correctness.
firac.conclusion: Reasonableness applied to the committee's factual and unprofessional-conduct findings; correctness applied to the disclosure and Charter issues.

firac.issue: Was the finding of unprofessional conduct reasonable where the statements were made off-duty as a parent?
firac.facts: At school meetings Ms. Eggertson allegedly criticized two former teachers to Ms. Campbell-Davies, who was not a 'proper official', without informing the criticized teachers, contrary to the ATA Code. She denied making the comments; the committee found she did.
firac.rule: A teacher's conduct is evaluated on the basis of position rather than location (Ross v. New Brunswick School District No. 15, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 825); a teacher cannot choose which 'hat' to wear (Re Cromer v. B.C. Teachers' Federation (1986)). Unprofessional conduct may encompass off-duty conduct.
firac.application: The committee heard the witnesses, assessed credibility and had a reasonable basis for its finding; the court would not substitute its view. Ms. Eggertson could advocate as a parent but, as an experienced teacher whose criticism carries enhanced impact, she had to follow the Code's procedure. Deferring to the committee's expertise, the finding that the comments criticized other teachers and were unprofessional was reasonable.
firac.conclusion: The finding of unprofessional conduct was reasonable and would not be disturbed.

firac.issue: Did the failure to disclose the investigator's complete file breach any disclosure duty?
firac.facts: Ms. Eggertson requested all of the investigator's notes; she received formal witness statements, interview summaries, the complaint letter and the investigator's report, but not the complete file (including notes of the principal's interview).
firac.rule: Sections 30(3) and 37 of the Teaching Profession Act require reasonable particulars and provide for issuance of notices to witnesses, but do not impose full pre-hearing disclosure. The Stinchcombe level of disclosure does not apply to professional discipline (Kullman v. Borbridge (1995); Anderson v. Twin River School District (1994)); only fairness is required.
firac.application: The statutory provisions did not require production of all evidence, only sufficient particulars. The common law duty of fairness did not require full disclosure. Ms. Eggertson received adequate particulars, was not prejudiced, and was told the principal had no recollection of events.
firac.conclusion: There was sufficient disclosure; no breach of statutory or common law obligations occurred.

firac.issue: Does the Charter apply to the ATA Code of Ethics, and if so was freedom of expression infringed?
firac.facts: Ms. Eggertson argued the Code, made under the Act, was provincial legislation subject to the Charter and that her s. 2(b) freedom of expression was breached.
firac.rule: Section 32(1) Charter applies to government action. Authorities conflict: Re Cromer assumed application; Tomen v. Federation of Women Teachers of Ontario and Re Westerlund (relying on Stoffman v. Vancouver General Hospital (1990)) held such internal-management rules are outside government action. Reasonable and justified limits do not infringe s. 2(b).
firac.application: The court held the Code constitutes directives of internal management, not government action, so the Charter did not apply. Even if it applied, the Code's limits are reasonable and justified: it does not prohibit criticism but requires it be made to proper officials after notice, promoting professional standards and harmony, demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
firac.conclusion: The Charter did not apply to the Code, and in any event any limit on expression was reasonable and justified.

keywords_rationale: The case is a judicial review (K011) of a professional-discipline decision (K013) of the teachers' association, engaging teacher misconduct (K046) and requiring determination of the standard of review (K014) under Pushpanathan, all within Administrative law (K001, the primary tier-1 area). The disclosure issue turned on the duty of fairness (K012). The Charter argument concerned freedom of expression (K024) under s. 2(b) (K111) of the Canadian Charter (K107). Education law (K005) is included because the subject matter is teacher conduct and the ATA Code of Ethics; it is a secondary but genuine classification. No hate-speech or entity keywords apply.
location_rationale: The decision is styled 'IN THE COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH OF ALBERTA, JUDICIAL DISTRICT OF CALGARY' and is dated 'at Calgary, Alberta'.
registry_rationale: The heading identifies the 'JUDICIAL DISTRICT OF CALGARY', indicating the Calgary registry of the Court of Queen's Bench.

name_verification.name_in_document: Goldstein v. Walsh

defining_issues: Should custody (major decision-making) be sole or joint given the parents' inability to cooperate?
Where should the three-year-old child's primary residence be — with her mother in Buffalo or her father in Toronto — under the best interests analysis?
How should child support and section 7 special/extraordinary expenses be allocated?

firac.issue: Should the court order sole custody to the mother rather than joint custody, given the parents' conflict and history of one parent's exclusionary conduct?
firac.facts: The parents never married and share a week-about schedule for their daughter AB. The father obtained an ex parte custody order in June 2016 through significant misrepresentations to the court, imposed a racial bar on nanny selection, repeatedly made unilateral decisions about medical care, religion (enrolling AB at Temple Sinai over objection), schooling and activities without consulting the mother, and failed to facilitate the mother's relationship and the child's contact with her Irish family. The mother consistently consulted the father before making decisions.
firac.rule: Under s. 20 of the Children's Law Reform Act (CLRA) both parents are equally entitled to custody; sole custody requires justification (Rodriguez v. Guignard, 2013 ONSC 146). Joint custody principles are set out in Jackson v. Jackson, 2017 ONSC 1566: there is no default in favour of joint custody, effective communication and cooperation must be achievable, and where one parent is the major source of conflict or cannot put the child's needs first, joint custody is inappropriate. Past conduct is relevant only where it bears on the ability to parent (CLRA s. 24(3)).
firac.application: The court found the father deliberately misled the court on the ex parte motion, engaged in controlling and exclusionary behaviour, could not freely acknowledge the mother as a caring parent, refused to accept medical recommendations, and repeatedly resorted to counsel over minor disputes. An objective review showed the parties had never been able to cooperate or communicate effectively and that the father would not put AB's needs ahead of his desire for control. The mother, by contrast, consulted and facilitated the father's role. Joint decision-making would produce continued conflict contrary to AB's best interests.
firac.conclusion: Sole custody was granted to the mother, with an obligation to consult the father and give serious consideration to his views on major medical and educational decisions, but with final decision-making authority.

firac.issue: Is it in the child's best interests to have her primary residence with her mother in Buffalo, with generous access to the father in Toronto?
firac.facts: AB, age three, had lived week-about between Buffalo and Toronto since 11 months old. Both parents are physicians with uncertain future locations: the mother on a J1 visa in Buffalo (fellowship to ~2021), the father bound by an International Medical Graduate Return-of-Service Agreement requiring five years' work in a Ministry-approved underserviced community after 2020. AB thrived in both homes but faced continual cross-border commuting and duplicated medical providers.
firac.rule: CLRA s. 24(2) best interests factors (love and emotional ties, stable home, ability to provide guidance, plan of care, permanence and stability, ability to parent, familial relationships). The maximum contact principle is expressed through the best interests lens (Lemon v. Lemon, 2018 ONCA 684; Jackson v. Jackson, 2017 ONSC 1566). Proposed place of residence is a relevant factor (Terris v. Terris). Proceedings should be concluded with dispatch (Appiah v. Appiah).
firac.application: Both parents are loving, but the mother demonstrated the ability to parent independently and to foster the father's relationship, while the father lived with his parents with no certain future plan and drew an adverse inference for not calling the nanny. As AB ages, the two-country, two-school week-about arrangement is not sustainable; a single home base and school better serve stability. The father's proposals depended on speculative assumptions about remaining in Toronto and invited continued litigation, disadvantaging the mother given financial disparities. Primary residence with the mother in Buffalo, with generous weekend/holiday access to the father, best served AB's stability while maintaining her bond with her father and paternal grandparents.
firac.conclusion: AB's primary residence was ordered to be with the mother in Buffalo, with a detailed access, holiday and travel schedule for the father; the mother must obtain a further order to relocate outside the Buffalo-Niagara Falls area; Ontario retains jurisdiction for five years.

firac.issue: How should child support and section 7 special or extraordinary expenses be allocated?
firac.facts: The father's reported income was $76,134.12 and the mother's $66,726.11. The mother sought table support; the father sought set-off. Claimed expenses included JCC pre-school tuition, swimming lessons, toddler yoga, and uninsured medical/dental costs.
firac.rule: Federal Child Support Guidelines: s. 9 (shared custody threshold) and s. 7 (special or extraordinary expenses shared in proportion to incomes, with 'extraordinary' defined in s. 7(1.1)).
firac.application: Because the final order matched neither party's proposal, the parties had not calculated the residency percentages needed to determine whether the s. 9 shared-custody threshold was met; the court left this to be recalculated. On the claimed expenses, swimming lessons and toddler yoga were not 'extraordinary' within the Guidelines, whereas daycare/pre-school tuition and uninsured medical/dental costs qualified as special expenses.
firac.conclusion: The parties are to share eligible s. 7 expenses (JCC pre-school tuition and uninsured medical/dental) proportionate to income; table support and the shared-custody calculation were reserved for further submissions.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) are the core doctrinal keywords — the entire decision turns on the CLRA s. 24 best interests analysis and the sole-versus-joint custody and residence questions. K050 (parental/child support) covers Part III on child support and s. 7 expenses. K052 (religious upbringing) is genuinely engaged: the parties disputed AB's exposure to Judaism (Temple Sinai enrolment, Bat Mitzvah) and Catholicism (baptism, First Communion), and the order expressly addresses religious upbringing. K093 (Jewish) is a supporting entity keyword given the father's Judaism and the religious-upbringing terms of the order; it is a weaker/borderline pick tied to the religion provisions rather than a central legal issue.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE' with court file no. FS-16-20931, establishing the province as Ontario. No specific sitting city or registry office is stated in the text (the matter concerns parents in Toronto and Buffalo, but the court's location is not identified), so city and registry are left null.
registry_rationale: No registry or court office is named in the decision beyond 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice'; the court file number FS-16-20931 is given but no registry town is identified, so registry is null.

case_name: Institute of Edible Oil Foods v. Ontario (Ont. H.C.J.)

name_verification.name_in_document: Re Institute of Edible Oil Foods et al. and The Queen; Ontario Milk Marketing Board, Intervenor; Indexed as: Institute of Edible Oil Foods v. Ontario

defining_issues: Does s. 4 of the Oleomargarine Act, which regulates the colour of margarine, infringe the equality rights guaranteed by s. 15 of the Charter, and do corporate applicants enjoy the protection of s. 15?
Does s. 4 of the Oleomargarine Act infringe freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter, and if so, is it a reasonable limit justified under s. 1?
Does s. 4 of the Oleomargarine Act violate the right to liberty under s. 7 of the Charter by regulating economic/commercial rights?

firac.issue: Does s. 4 of the Oleomargarine Act infringe s. 15 equality rights, and can corporations claim s. 15 protection?
firac.facts: Three of the applicants were corporations (two margarine manufacturers and a trade association); the fourth was an individual consumer. Section 4 requires margarine to be coloured lighter or darker than butter, disadvantaging margarine producers relative to butter producers and limiting consumer colour choice.
firac.rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter guarantees equality to 'every individual.' Authorities (Re Aluminium Co. of Canada; Milk Board v. Clearview Dairy Farm; Surrey Credit Union v. Mendonca; Re Homemade Winecrafts) hold that s. 15 protects the dignity and worth of human beings and does not extend to corporations, distinguishing Big M Drug Mart (which concerned the unqualified freedoms in s. 2). Discriminatory inequality is assessed under the framework in R. v. Ertel and R. v. Century 21 Ramos Realty: identify the class, determine whether classes are similarly situated, and apply the 'pejorative' approach requiring the complainant to show the differential treatment is unfair or irrational.
firac.application: The word 'individual' in s. 15 does not include the corporate applicants; unlike the unqualified s. 2 freedoms, s. 15 inherently requires a differentiation in treatment tied to human dignity. Even assuming s. 15 applied, applying the Ertel steps, butter and margarine producers form part of a general class of edible-oil producers and are similarly situated, and the corporate applicants suffered an inherent disadvantage, but they failed to show the differential treatment was unfair or irrational given the legitimate objective of protecting the economic stability of the dairy industry. For the consumer applicant, any advancement of the consumer-protection objective was minor, and consumers' objections to colour were of minor importance next to the dairy-stability objective, since no one is barred from buying (or self-colouring) margarine.
firac.conclusion: Section 4 does not offend s. 15(1); corporations are not protected by s. 15, and in any event no unconstitutional discrimination was established.

firac.issue: Does s. 4 infringe s. 2(b) freedom of expression, and if so, is it saved by s. 1?
firac.facts: Section 4 prevents margarine producers from colouring their product a wholesome, appetizing (butter-like) colour, thereby restricting how the product is presented to the public.
firac.rule: Section 2(b) protects freedom of expression, construed broadly and not limited to particular kinds of expression; commercial advertising, including product presentation, is protected. A limit must be justified under s. 1 as a reasonable limit demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
firac.application: The colour and presentation of a product constitutes a form of advertising and expression, so s. 4 infringes the corporate applicants' s. 2(b) rights. However, protection of the dairy industry is of substantial economic and social importance, and although s. 4 detrimentally affects margarine production methods and market share, the restriction is not disproportionate to that important legislative objective.
firac.conclusion: Section 4 infringes s. 2(b) but is a reasonable limit justified under s. 1; the challenge fails.

firac.issue: Does s. 4 violate s. 7 by regulating economic or commercial rights?
firac.facts: Applicants argued the s. 7 right to liberty protects the commercial right to market and purchase products in a colour of one's choice.
firac.rule: Section 7 guarantees life, liberty and security of the person, subject to the principles of fundamental justice. Economic/commercial rights fall outside the ambit of s. 7 (Re Malartic Hygrade Gold Mines; Re Aluminium Co. of Canada; Re Gershman Produce; R. v. Video Flicks/Edwards Books).
firac.application: Economic rights such as the right to market or purchase a product in a chosen colour are not protected by s. 7. Moreover, s. 4 was enacted for rational social and economic purposes and no evidence showed any breach of the principles of fundamental justice.
firac.conclusion: Section 4 does not violate s. 7; the argument was rejected.

case_name: Goodhead v. Thomson Newspapers Co. Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: Barry Charles Goodhead v. Thomson Newspapers Company Limited, Globe and Mail Division and Mr. Robert Matas

defining_issues: Did the newspaper article defame the plaintiff by lowering his reputation in the eyes of right-thinking members of the community?
Was the article published with malice arising from an alleged grudge against the plaintiff's family?

firac.issue: Did the newspaper article defame the plaintiff by lowering his reputation in the eyes of right-thinking members of the community?
firac.facts: The Globe and Mail published an article about how any Canadian can create a charity and channel tax-subsidized dollars abroad, using the plaintiff's newly registered charity for Rwandan children as an illustration. The plaintiff complained of several statements: that he was described as inexperienced, that he alone could administer the charity, that no one would require him to account for the money, that the charity's name was inaccurate, that his floor of residence was wrong, and that he could give money to 'the most vicious murderers in Rwanda.'
firac.rule: To be defamatory, a statement must contain a misstatement of fact or comment that would lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of right-thinking members of the community.
firac.application: The court found the article described the plaintiff as 'good-hearted and well intentioned' and 'above reproach.' The identified errors (11th versus 15th floor, the charity's name) were trivial misstatements not capable of lowering his reputation. The description of him as the spearhead and spokesperson accurately reflected the situation, since his son was a minor and his mother-in-law's signature was affixed on her behalf. The statement about lack of accountability was a true comment directed at the government system, not the plaintiff, and the 'vicious murderers' passage was a true statement of legal possibility with no suggestion the plaintiff would act on it. Read as a whole, the article was thoughtful, well-researched investigative journalism about government charity policy.
firac.conclusion: The article did not lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of right-thinking people and was not libellous.

firac.issue: Was the article published with malice arising from an alleged grudge against the plaintiff's family?
firac.facts: The plaintiff alleged his father was a wealthy Ontario figure who owned a polluting disposal dump, that the Globe and Mail had written articles about the father in the 1980s, and that the article about him was motivated by mala fides against the Goodhead name. The author, Mr. Matas, testified he had never heard of the plaintiff's father, never seen any such articles, and knew nothing of the dump.
firac.rule: An allegation of malice must be supported by evidence establishing bad faith or improper motive on the part of the publisher.
firac.application: The court accepted Mr. Matas' evidence, finding no evidence from which it could conclude he was not telling the truth, and determined the article was written in good faith.
firac.conclusion: There was no malice; the article was written in good faith and without malice.

keywords_rationale: K015 (defamation/libel) is the central cause of action — the plaintiff sued for libel over a newspaper article. K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area governing this tort claim. K016 (fair comment) is engaged because the court treated the allegedly harmful statements as true comment on government charity policy rather than defamatory assertions about the plaintiff. Only three keywords genuinely apply given the narrow factual and legal scope; the case does not engage the antisemitism, constitutional, or other specialized vocabulary despite passing mentions of various charities. These three are the closest and strongest available picks.

registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

case_name: Fédération CJA c. Independant Jewish Voices Canada Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: Fédération CJA c. Independant Jewish Voices Canada Inc.

defining_issues: Do the facts alleged, taken as true, establish a prima facie case warranting the issuance of a special order to appear to answer a charge of civil contempt of court?

firac.issue: Do the facts alleged, taken as true at the filtering stage, justify issuing a special order requiring the mise en cause (an attorney of record) to appear to answer a charge of civil contempt for failing to redact an affiant's name from a transcript excerpt sent to the Barreau's syndic, contrary to Justice Masse's non-disclosure order of 15 March 2024?
firac.facts: Justice Masse's order of 15 March 2024 (subparagraph C.d)) prohibited disclosure, publication or dissemination of the names of various affiants. The mise en cause, counsel of record, filed a complaint with the syndic of the Barreau du Québec against opposing counsel concerning conduct during an out-of-court examination of an affiant, and attached an unredacted excerpt of the transcript in which the affiant's name appeared in the header. The plaintiffs applied ex parte for a special order to appear for contempt.
firac.rule: On an application for an order to appear for contempt the judge exercises a filtering role, taking the alleged facts as true (Droit de la famille — 122875, 2012 QCCA 1855, para. 26). A civil contempt finding is exceptional and should be pronounced only where genuinely necessary to protect the administration of justice, especially in litigation between private parties (Morasse c. Nadeau-Dubois, 2016 CSC 44; Centre commercial Les Rivières ltée c. Jean bleu inc., 2012 QCCA 1663). The role of a professional order's syndic requires a complete picture of the facts, and information given to the syndic enjoys various protections (Pharmascience inc. c. Binet, 2006 CSC 48; Code des professions, arts. 114, 122, 124; Loi sur le Barreau, art. 76).
firac.application: Although the facts, taken as true, showed the mise en cause was aware of Justice Masse's order, the mere failure to redact a name in the header of a stenographic transcript in a communication addressed solely to the syndic did not amount to any obstruction of the normal course of justice or any attack on the court's authority or dignity. Given the syndic's need for a complete factual picture and the confidentiality protections surrounding complaints, the conduct could not support a contempt conviction. The Court further found the application reflected misplaced rigorism and served merely to inflame already acrimonious litigation.
firac.conclusion: The facts, even taken as true, could not give rise to a contempt conviction; the application for a special order to appear was dismissed, without costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a civil contempt application within private litigation. K013 (professional discipline) is engaged because the underlying conduct was a complaint to the syndic of the Barreau du Québec and the Court relied on the Code des professions and Loi sur le Barreau. K104 (Palestine) reflects defendant pro-Palestinian organizations.
