name_verification.name_in_document: Dugal v. Manulife Financial Corporation

defining_issues: Did the original or amended statement of claim plead the constituent elements of a s. 130 Securities Act prospectus-misrepresentation claim, so as to interrupt the limitation period?
If the s. 130 claim was first raised only in the proposed fresh as amended statement of claim, was it time-barred under s. 138 of the Securities Act?
Does the court have jurisdiction to extend the s. 138 limitation period by applying the common-law 'special circumstances' doctrine in light of the Limitations Act, 2002?
If such jurisdiction exists, should the court exercise its discretion to permit the amendment?

firac.issue: Did the original or amended statement of claim plead the constituent elements of a s. 130 prospectus-misrepresentation claim so as to interrupt the limitation period?
firac.facts: The original claim (July 29, 2009) and the amended claim (November 17, 2009) alleged negligence and negligent misrepresentation in Manulife's 'disclosure documents' (annual reports, financial statements, MD&As) and foreshadowed a secondary-market claim under Part XXIII.1. Neither pleading mentioned a prospectus, s. 130, or deemed reliance; the plaintiffs purchased only in the secondary market. Specific prospectus allegations appeared for the first time in the proposed fresh as amended statement of claim served May 18, 2010.
firac.rule: A pleading must contain a concise statement of the material facts (rule 25.06); no particular formula is required (Almas v. Spenceley), but to assert a cause of action and give fair notice the pleading must state its constituent elements. A s. 130 claim requires pleading (a) the existence of a prospectus, (b) a misrepresentation in it, (c) purchase of a security offered by the prospectus during distribution, and (d) that the defendant was the issuer or a signer/director/expert. Section 130 is a complete statutory code dispensing with reliance (McKenna v. Gammon Gold). Compared with McCann v. CP Ships Ltd.
firac.application: Read fairly, generously and as a whole, the pleadings could only be understood as alleging negligence and misrepresentation in statutory 'disclosure documents' plus a foreshadowed secondary-market claim. None of the four constituent elements of a s. 130 claim was pleaded: no prospectus was mentioned, no purchase under a prospectus was alleged, and the incorporation of MD&As by reference into a prospectus was not pleaded. Given experienced securities counsel (who had run McCann), the certification notice and factum describing the s. 130 claim as an 'addition', it was inconceivable the existing pleading was understood to assert s. 130. McCann was distinguished because its pleading was broad enough to encompass a primary-market claim.
firac.conclusion: Neither the original nor the amended statement of claim contained a s. 130 claim; the limitation period was not interrupted.

firac.issue: Was the s. 130 claim time-barred when first raised on May 18, 2010?
firac.facts: The proposed fresh as amended statement of claim acknowledged the 'truth was revealed' on February 12, 2009, when Manulife announced its increased reserves and its share price fell. The s. 130 claim was first advanced when that pleading was delivered on May 18, 2010.
firac.rule: Section 138 of the Securities Act imposes a limitation of the earlier of 180 days after the plaintiff first had knowledge of the facts giving rise to the cause of action or three years after the transaction. A limitations issue may be decided on a pleadings-amendment motion where it is plain and obvious no additional facts could show the period had not expired (Beardsley v. Ontario).
firac.application: February 12, 2009 marked both the end of the class period and the date the plaintiffs had knowledge of the facts; the plaintiffs did not dispute this. May 18, 2010 was well more than 180 days later. Claims tied to 2005–2006 prospectuses were in any event outside the three-year cap and were withdrawn.
firac.conclusion: The s. 130 claim was time-barred as of May 18, 2010.

firac.issue: Does the court have jurisdiction to extend the s. 138 limitation period through the 'special circumstances' doctrine given the Limitations Act, 2002?
firac.facts: The Securities Act limitation period is listed in the Schedule to the Limitations Act, 2002 and thereby preserved. The plaintiffs invoked the special-circumstances doctrine (Basarsky v. Quinlan) to save an otherwise time-barred amendment.
firac.rule: Under Joseph v. Paramount Canada's Wonderland the Limitations Act, 2002 abolished the common-law special-circumstances doctrine for claims and rule 26.01 amendments governed by its general period. Under Guillemette v. Doucet, Giroux Estate and Bikur Cholim, s. 20 preserves extension/variation mechanisms where a scheduled statute contains its own discretionary provision or has a pre-existing common-law gloss (e.g., Solicitors Act, Trustee Act s. 38(3)).
firac.application: The court reasoned it made little sense for the legislature to preserve the relatively short s. 138 period, with its built-in discoverability regime, only to erode it through a doctrine it does not historically carry. The special-circumstances rule should be confined to existing statutory exceptions or pre-existing common-law exceptions engrafted on a scheduled limitation period, unlike s. 138.
firac.conclusion: The court doubted the doctrine applied to the Securities Act period, favouring confining it to statutes with existing exceptions; but it did not need to decide the point definitively because it would refuse relief in any event.

firac.issue: If the doctrine were available, should the court exercise its discretion to extend the limitation period?
firac.facts: The defendants were named in the original pleading; the s. 130 claim arose from the same events and documents; pleadings had not closed and no discoveries had occurred; refusal would affect putative class members. Experienced securities counsel possessed the material facts and consciously restricted the claim to the secondary market.
firac.rule: The expiry of a limitation period creates a presumption of prejudice that is determinative unless rebutted by special circumstances (Frohlick v. Pinkerton). Rule 26.01 does not contemplate adding unrelated statute-barred claims. Special circumstances are typically procedural or informational mistakes that did not mislead the opposing party.
firac.application: The s. 130 claim is an extraordinary, distinct cause of action (no reliance required), not incidental to or subsumed by the common-law and Part XXIII.1 claims. There was no procedural error; rather, informed counsel made a conscious tactical choice to plead only a secondary-market claim, as in Bikur Cholim and Meady. Allowing the amendment would defeat the purpose of the 180-day period and promote uncertainty in securities markets.
firac.conclusion: Even if available, the discretion would be declined; no special circumstances existed beyond the ordinary hardship of an expired limitation.

keywords_rationale: The case is a proposed securities class action, so K002 (Civil litigation) is the correct tier-1 practice area and K020 (class action) is squarely engaged as the proceeding is a proposed class action under s. 138.8 of the Securities Act. K054 (wills/estates) is a weak, proximity-based pick reflecting the court's extensive reliance on Trustee Act s. 38(3) authorities (Bikur Cholim, Giroux Estate) in analysing the special-circumstances doctrine. K021 (interlocutory injunction) and K022 (restitution) are flagged as weak padding: no injunction or restitution was sought — they are included only because the controlled vocabulary contains no keywords for securities regulation, prospectus/secondary-market misrepresentation, limitation periods, or pleadings amendments, which are the true subjects of the decision. name_verification.name_in_document: H... E... c. Peter Robert Lack

defining_issues: Does a Superior Court judge have jurisdiction to hear and decide a request by a person declared a vexatious litigant for authorization to bring proceedings before another court, notably the Court of Québec?
May a Superior Court judge assess the chances of success of such a request and refuse the authorization on that basis?

firac.issue: Does a Superior Court judge have jurisdiction to rule on a vexatious litigant's request for authorization to bring proceedings before another court (the Court of Québec)?
firac.facts: The appellant had been declared a vexatious and quarrelsome litigant on 10 June 2011, and was prohibited from taking any proceeding connected with the settlement of her parents' estates without prior authorization from the Chief Justice of the Superior Court or a designated judge. The underlying action she wished to attack by a motion in retraction (before the Court of Québec) stemmed from that estate litigation. She sought authorization from a Superior Court judge to present her retraction motion in the Court of Québec.
firac.rule: Articles 46 and 54.5 C.p.c. and the Superior Court's inherent power of control and supervision permit it to prohibit an abusive litigant from bringing proceedings before any tribunal subject to that supervisory power (Barreau du Québec c. Srougi; Dubé c. CRT; Joad c. Journal La Voix; Production Pixcom inc. c. Fabrikant, 2005 QCCA 703; Tremblay c. Charest, 2006 QCCA 204). The power to prohibit proceedings before another court carries with it the correlative power to authorize them.
firac.application: The Court of Québec file was directly covered by the 10 June 2011 prohibition order because it arose from the estate-settlement dispute. In ruling on an authorization request the Superior Court exercises its own jurisdiction, not that of the court where the right may be exercised. Since it can prohibit proceedings before another tribunal within its supervisory jurisdiction, it can equally authorize them—especially where the prohibition targets a well-defined dispute known to the Superior Court. The fact that the Court of Québec may itself issue quérulence orders under art. 54.5 C.p.c. does not oust the Superior Court's general supervisory jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: Yes; the Superior Court had jurisdiction to entertain and refuse the authorization request.

firac.issue: May a Superior Court judge evaluate the prospects of success of the proposed proceeding and refuse authorization accordingly?
firac.facts: The appellant failed to appear on the dates set to fix a timetable, transmitted an unauthorized and unserved defence and counterclaim, and had default judgment of $6,500 rendered against her. She then sought authorization to file a motion in retraction, which the designated judge (Déziel, j.c.s.) refused, finding it had no chance of success.
firac.rule: A vexatious litigant seeking authorization to file a proceeding bears the burden of demonstrating prima facie the seriousness of the request; there is a form of presumption that his proceedings are vexatious (Pixcom). The authorizing judge must conduct a preliminary analysis of the value of the asserted right (art. 88 R.P.C.).
firac.application: The Superior Court was not persuaded of the seriousness of the retraction motion. On the reported facts, the appellant did not demonstrate any error in that assessment—she had obtained leave to appear and set a timetable but failed to act diligently, allowing default judgment to be rendered.
firac.conclusion: Yes; the assessment was proper and the appeal was dismissed with costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area — the case concerns abuse of process and the management of a vexatious litigant within civil proceedings. K001 (Administrative law) and K011 (judicial review) are engaged because the ruling turns on the Superior Court's inherent power of control and supervision (pouvoir de contrôle et de surveillance) over inferior courts and tribunals; these are somewhat approximate given no keyword exists specifically for vexatious-litigant / quérulence powers. K021 (interlocutory injunction) reflects the courts' characterization of the quérulence remedy as 'de nature injonctive'. K012 (procedural fairness) is a weaker pick, tied to the discussion of a litigant's right to defend and access the courts. The controlled vocabulary lacks a precise term for vexatious litigants/abuse of procedure, so several picks are approximations and are flagged as such.
location_rationale: The header states « COUR D'APPEL … PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC … GREFFE DE MONTRÉAL », establishing Montréal, Quebec as the seat.
registry_rationale: The decision indicates « GREFFE DE MONTRÉAL », identifying the Montréal registry of the Court of Appeal.

name_verification.name_in_document: Hebrew National Association v. Kramer

defining_issues: On a motion to set aside an arbitral award under The Arbitration Act, is the court confined to errors appearing on the face of the award, and what may it consider?

Where the submission referred 'all matters in dispute' to arbitration and the arbitrators, having found a weekly hiring, awarded a sum said to be owed 'in good conscience', did the award disclose an error of law on its face?
Was the arbitrators' determination of what the dismissed employee was entitled to receive a question of law or a question of fact?

firac.issue: On a motion to set aside an arbitral award, is the court confined to errors on the face of the award?
firac.facts: The parties referred 'all matters in dispute between us' to the Canadian Jewish Congress Court of Arbitration under a submission that made the award final and not subject to appeal. The employer moved to set the award aside as defective on its face and wrong in law.
firac.rule: On a motion to set aside an award the court is limited to errors appearing on the face of the award, or corruption, fraud, excess of jurisdiction, or like matters; it may not go into the evidence (Re Grant v. Eastwood (1875), 22 Gr. 563). The submission and a letter of the arbitrators may be examined to ascertain the subject-matter dealt with (Attorney-General for Manitoba v. Kelly, [1922] 1 A.C. 268).
firac.application: Rose C.J.H.C. treated the matter strictly as a motion to set aside, not an appeal, since the submission excluded appeal. He accepted he was confined to what appeared on the face of the award but could look at the submission and the arbitrators' letter of 26 June 1942.
firac.conclusion: The court's review was confined to errors on the face of the award; the evidence could not be examined.

firac.issue: Did the award disclose an error of law on its face given the finding of a weekly hiring and an award made 'in good conscience'?
firac.facts: The submission did not expressly define the matters referred; it covered 'all matters in dispute'. The arbitrators found the hiring was weekly, not yearly, but concluded the employee was entitled 'in good conscience' to $200 covering his convalescence and re-establishment, more than legal damages on a weekly contract.
firac.rule: An award is not lightly set aside; it must be supported by the submission. Absent an express provision to the contrary, an arbitrator is to decide according to the legal rights of the parties, not according to what he considers fair and reasonable (Russell on Arbitration and Award, 13th ed., p. 332; Jager v. Tolme & Runge, [1916] 1 K.B. 939).
firac.application: Rose C.J.H.C. held that because the submission was undefined, it was possible the dispute submitted was what the employee should receive 'in good conscience' rather than his strict legal entitlement; the court could not determine the nature of the disputes without examining evidence it was not entitled to consider. The Court of Appeal, assuming arbitrators were confined to legal rights, nonetheless found no error of law on the face.
firac.conclusion: No error of law appeared on the face of the award; the award stood.

firac.issue: Was the arbitrators' assessment of the employee's entitlement a question of law or of fact?
firac.facts: Beyond the finding of a weekly hiring, the court knew nothing of the terms of the contract, the nature of the employment, the rate of pay, or the circumstances leading to the $200 conclusion.
firac.rule: Absent custom or an express or implied contractual provision, an employee is entitled to reasonable notice of termination, and what is reasonable notice is a question of fact (Payzu, Limited v. Hannaford, [1918] 2 K.B. 348; Carter v. Bell & Sons (Canada) Ltd., [1936] O.R. 290).
firac.application: Robertson C.J.O. held that even assuming the arbitrators were confined to legal rights, the matter on which error was alleged was reasonable notice on a weekly hiring, which is a question of fact. With no knowledge of the contract terms or surrounding circumstances, the arbitrators' conclusion was a finding of fact.
firac.conclusion: The conclusion was a finding of fact and, whether right or wrong, afforded no ground for setting aside the award; appeal dismissed with costs.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally about a dismissed employee's entitlement, so K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 area and K085 (wrongful dismissal) captures the 'improper dismissal' claim and the reasonable-notice analysis. K084 (labour arbitration) is central because the dispute was decided by an arbitration board and the review concerned setting aside an arbitral award. K002 (civil litigation) reflects the procedural setting of a motion to set aside and appeal. K090 (Canadian Jewish Congress) is apt because the tribunal was the 'Canadian Jewish Congress, Court of Arbitration', and K094 (Jewish community) reflects the court 'set up by the Jewish community for the amicable settlement of disputes'; both are somewhat contextual/borderline but genuinely engaged by the identity of the arbitral body.

registry_rationale: The first-instance motion was heard 'in Weekly Court at Toronto' and the solicitors of record are 'Toronto'; the appeal was heard by the Ontario Court of Appeal, which sits at Toronto.

case_name: Fondation B'Nai B'Rith Hillel de Montréal c. Québec (Commission municipale)

name_verification.name_in_document: LA FONDATION B'NAI B'RITH HILLEL DE MONTRÉAL c. COMMISSION MUNICIPALE DU QUÉBEC et MICHEL HAMELIN et VILLE DE MONTRÉAL
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied short form 'Québec (Commission municipale)' corresponds to the respondent 'Commission municipale du Québec' named in the style of cause. The neutral/CanLII citation 2005 CanLII 15641 does not appear in the text itself (only the court file number 500-17-021114-049), but the parties match.

defining_issues: What standard of review applies to the Commission municipale du Québec's decision on a property-tax exemption recognition under the Loi sur la fiscalité municipale?
Did B'Nai B'Rith use its building principally for admissible activities within art. 243.8 LFM so as to qualify the entire building for the property-tax exemption?

firac.issue: What standard of review applies to the CMQ's decision recognizing (or refusing) a property-tax exemption under the LFM?
firac.facts: B'Nai B'Rith sought judicial review of the CMQ's decision granting exemption for only part of its building. The City argued the CMQ was protected by a privative clause (relying on arts. 21 LCM and 94.2 C.p.c., and on Centre communautaire juridique de l'Estrie) and that the patent-unreasonableness standard applied; B'Nai B'Rith argued correctness.
firac.rule: The pragmatic and functional approach governs the choice among correctness, reasonableness simpliciter and patent unreasonableness (Southam; Pushpanathan; Dr Q; Ryan; Voice Construction Ltd), weighing four contextual factors: presence/absence of a privative clause or appeal right, relative expertise, the purpose of the statute and the provision, and the nature of the question.
firac.application: The Court found no privative clause in the LFM or LCM (arts. 21 LCM and 94.2 C.p.c. belong to civil procedure, not protection from judicial review; at most a 'timid' clause given the absence of an appeal), no special CMQ expertise in municipal taxation (its members need not be jurists), a fiscal statute whose exemption criteria involve little discretion, and a question that is mixed fact and law but turns essentially on interpreting art. 243.8 LFM applied to uncontested facts. The Estrie and Mont Baldy authorities declined to fix the standard because the decisions were patently unreasonable anyway.
firac.conclusion: The weighted analysis pointed to the correctness standard; the legislature required little or no deference to the CMQ on exemption recognition.

firac.issue: Did B'Nai B'Rith's building satisfy the conditions of art. 243.8 LFM for a full property-tax exemption?
firac.facts: B'Nai B'Rith, a non-profit society serving Jewish post-secondary students near McGill, used the 3460 Stanley building for courses, conferences, Holocaust education, cultural and social activities, community Shabbat meals, kosher food, transitional housing for young foreign students (17-18) with no family in Montréal, moral/psychological/legal/economic support, and a student newspaper. Commissioner Hamelin recognized only the first-floor library, applying a room-by-room (partitionist) analysis.
firac.rule: Under art. 243.8 LFM the user must, for a non-profit purpose, carry on one or more admissible activities such that this constitutes the principal use of the building; admissible activities include informative/educational activities (para. 2) and activities to promote/defend the interests of a group, combat discrimination, assist or prevent persons from falling into difficulty (para. 3, read with art. 243.11); exemption may be partial (arts. 2, 243.2), and accessory spaces cannot be dissociated from qualifying activities (Cinémathèque québécoise; YM-YWHA).
firac.application: The Court held the Commissioner erred by compartmentalizing the building instead of assessing its overall vocation and 'principal use.' His findings were also unreasonable on the merits: treating university students without family in Montréal as not socially vulnerable was arbitrary (they fall within art. 243.8(3)(a) and (d)); the caretaker's lodging, rabbi's office and accountant's office were accessory; refusing exemption for the kosher kitchen while proposing to tax its operator (not a party) was illogical; and characterizing a student newspaper as not informative was irrational. Prior CMQ decisions (Building a Jewish Tomorrow, Institut A. Reisen) granted full exemptions for materially similar buildings.
firac.conclusion: The building as a whole was used principally for admissible activities and qualified for exemption; the decision was quashed and, since the CMQ was to be abolished, the Court itself granted a full exemption effective 1 January 2001, with costs against the City.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally an administrative-law judicial review, so K001 (Administrative law, tier-1), K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) are central — the bulk of the reasons applies the pragmatic-and-functional analysis to choose correctness. K089 (B'Nai Brith) is the applicant; K093 (Jewish), K094 (Jewish community) and K096 (Jewish students) capture the group whose interests the qualifying activities served under art. 243.8. case_name: Impérial Tobacco Canada ltée c. Montréal (Ville de)

name_verification.name_in_document: Impérial Tobacco Canada ltée c. Montréal (Ville de)

defining_issues: Did the TAQ have jurisdiction to add to the assessment roll the contributory value of property (e.g., energy-producing systems) that the municipal assessor had not included at the time the roll was deposited, in the absence of a complaint on that point?

Are the palletizing and materials-handling equipment machines/appliances used principally for industrial production and therefore excluded from the roll under s. 65 of the Act respecting municipal taxation (LFM)?
Could the TAQ set aside the parties' agreement (admissions) on the base cost of the mechanical and electrical systems?

Are the electrical, plumbing, heating, air-conditioning, humidification and ventilation systems integrated into the buildings principally used or destined for industrial production so as to be excluded from the roll under s. 65 LFM, and did the TAQ err (including by breaching audi alteram partem) in its analysis?

Did the TAQ err in law by deciding the local adjustment factor (Factor F) for the 1995 roll on the basis of institutional coherence rather than by weighing the contradictory evidence on the balance of probabilities?

Did the TAQ err in its treatment of depreciation (curable physical/functional obsolescence, precarious public-domain occupation, decline of the tobacco market, supply/snow-removal, and functional obsolescence from building configuration)?
Did the TAQ err on the parameters for calculating rental value (inclusion of the non-residential immovables surtax and the property value to be used in the decapitalization method)?

firac.issue: Did the TAQ have jurisdiction to add to the roll the contributory value of components the municipal assessor had not taken into account when the roll was deposited, absent a complaint on that point?
firac.facts: Impérial contested the roll inscriptions for its industrial complex. The TAQ, at paras 219-237, took into account the contributory value of steam and chilled-water energy-producing systems that did not appear on the roll. Impérial argued a formal demand was indispensable to confer jurisdiction. The rolls in issue were 'new generation' rolls governed by the concept of unité d'évaluation.
firac.rule: For 'new generation' rolls under the Loi sur la fiscalité municipale (LFM), art. 34 defines the unité d'évaluation and arts. 144, 145 and 147 require the tribunal to consider the unit 'dans son entier' to assess real prejudice and permit fixing a value higher or lower than the parties propose. Jurisdictional questions attract the correctness standard (Pushpanathan v. Canada (MCI), 1998 CanLII 778 (SCC)). Leading authority: Pointe-Claire (Ville de) c. Hewquip Holdings, 1997 CanLII 6578 (QC CQ).
firac.application: The Court distinguished old-generation cases (Atlific, Shell Canada, Sedaz Parking, Talisman) which barred adding items absent a complaint, from new-generation rolls. Because Impérial filed a complaint contesting the roll value, it conferred jurisdiction on the TAQ to revise the entire value of the unit, including contributory value of components omitted by the assessor, since art. 145 requires considering the unit in its entirety.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ did not err; it had jurisdiction to consider the contributory value of any property forming part of the unité d'évaluation under art. 34 LFM even if the assessor had not taken it into account at deposit.

firac.issue: Are the palletizing and materials-handling equipment excluded from the roll under s. 65 LFM as machines used principally for industrial production?
firac.facts: Impérial's modernization ('Montréal 2001') centralized automated palletizing at AC-1. Cases of cigarettes are conveyed, robotically palletized, wrapped, and labelled with excise (SAP) labels before removal by forklift; the total value at issue was $2,462,432 (new) / $2,216,189 (depreciated). Products cannot be sold until required fiscal labels are affixed.
firac.rule: Section 65(1) LFM excludes from the roll machines, appliances and accessories used or destined principally for industrial production. Whether a good is used for industrial production is a mixed question of fact and law on which the TAQ has no privileged position (Vigi Santé c. Montréal, 1999 CanLII 13626 (QC CA); Charny c. Alex Couture). Industrial production is a continuous, integrated process ending when the marketable product is ready (Irving Oil, 1980 CanLII 176 (SCC); Cie pétrolière Impériale; Société d'énergie Talisman; R.J.R. MacDonald).
firac.application: The product cannot be marketed until the fiscally required labels are affixed at the end of the conveyor, so production is not complete before that step. The case is analogous to Irving Oil/Talisman (regulatory requirement completes production) and distinguishable from Procter & Gamble (no such fiscal requirement). Production is integrated and continuous, ending after affixing fiscal labels.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ erred; the palletizing/handling equipment is part of industrial production and is not to be entered on the roll under s. 65 LFM.

firac.issue: Could the TAQ set aside the parties' agreement/admissions on the base cost of the mechanical and electrical systems?
firac.facts: The parties filed written admissions (P-79, P-80) agreeing on the 1972 base costs of plumbing, heating, air-conditioning, ventilation, electricity and fire protection, expressly stating these represented only the portion corresponding to service to the building, and that nothing constituted an admission on whether the items were to be on the roll under s. 65.
firac.rule: Whether an immovable is entered or excluded under s. 65 LFM is a question of law; parties cannot derogate from it by agreement and the tribunal is not bound (correctness standard). Adricon Ltée c. East Angus, 1977 CanLII 197 (SCC) and Gulf Canada distinguished (those involved revoking admissions on facts within the res gestae).
firac.application: The admissions concerned only base cost, not whether contributory value must be on the roll. The determination of inscription/exclusion under s. 65 is legal; the TAQ was not bound and could decide whether to include the contributory value. The Adricon/Gulf jurisprudence was inapplicable since evidence and exhibits were led on the point.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ did not err; it could decide the s. 65 question notwithstanding the cost admissions, which did not admit inclusion or exclusion from the roll.

firac.issue: Are the integrated electrical and mechanical (plumbing, heating, air-conditioning, ventilation, humidification) systems used principally for industrial production and excluded under s. 65 LFM, and did the TAQ breach audi alteram partem?
firac.facts: About 77% of electricity and large proportions of steam (62%), chilled water (74%) and air (78%) served production; systems were hybrid/integrated. The TAQ rejected both parties' expert theories (one system vs 266 systems) and, on its own, held there were as many systems as 'medium-voltage arteries,' excluding only 13% (the main electrical entrance).
firac.rule: Section 65 LFM (as amended 1993) treats an integrated mechanical/electrical system as an immovable analyzed on the 'all or nothing' rule of the 4th paragraph: entirely excluded if used/destined principally for industrial production, otherwise entirely on the roll; art. 2 proportionality is excluded. Qualification is a mixed question (correctness/reasonableness simpliciter). Audi alteram partem requires notice where the tribunal adopts a theory not advanced by parties (Pétromont c. Varennes). Guiding cases: Aluminerie Alouette; Manac; Aluminerie Bécancour; PCI Chimie; Domco Tarkett.
firac.application: The TAQ breached audi alteram partem by adopting an 'arteries' definition no expert proposed, without inviting submissions, in a domain (electrical systems) outside its evaluation expertise. It also erred by limiting exclusion to 13% contrary to the all-or-nothing rule and by ignoring the 'destination' branch and the proportion of use. On the evidence, the complex has a single integrated hybrid electrical system principally used/destined for production; similarly the plumbing and the heating/air-conditioning/humidification/ventilation systems are principally used/destined for production.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ erred; the electrical and mechanical systems (plumbing, heating, air-conditioning, ventilation) are principally used or destined for industrial production and their contributory value is not to be entered on the roll under s. 65 LFM.

firac.issue: Did the TAQ err by resolving the local adjustment factor (Factor F) for the 1995 rolls on institutional coherence rather than on the balance of the evidence?
firac.facts: Impérial's expert (Caumartin) produced a Factor F study yielding 0.80; Montréal, for the first time, led a genuine competing study (Lévesque) yielding ~1.05, over 32 days and 86 exhibits. The TAQ found numerous deficiencies in Caumartin's study yet retained 0.80 'by institutional coherence,' while acknowledging Lévesque's study was more reliable.
firac.rule: Institutional coherence is desirable but not absolute; decisions must be based on the evidence adduced and the balance of probabilities (Tremblay c. Québec, 1992 CanLII 1135; SITBA c. Consolidated Bathurst, 1990 CanLII 132; Domtar c. CALP, 1993 CanLII 106; CSST c. Fontaine, 2005 QCCA 775; Aluminerie Bécancour). Whether to prefer coherence over prevailing evidence is a question of law (correctness).
firac.application: With two contradictory studies (one new), the TAQ was required to weigh the evidence, not defer to prior results. Montréal's method (indexing construction costs to the reference date via Statistics Canada and using the same conversion factor as the buildings assessed) was scientifically preferable, but its study also had deficiencies (BABN/Reban data, time lag), as did Caumartin's (non-contemporaneous, agrandissements, autoconstruction, non-homogeneous sample, indexation anomaly, asymmetry). Neither study was probative enough.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ erred in law; its 0.80 finding is null. On the record, no reliable Factor F was established, so a neutral factor of 1.00 is retained for the 1995 and 1995-modified rolls (Montréal's appeal allowed in part).

firac.issue: Did the TAQ err in its treatment of the various heads of depreciation/obsolescence?
firac.facts: Impérial claimed curable physical/functional obsolescence on four items, precarious occupation of the public domain (tunnels/passerelles revocable on 30 days' notice), decline of the tobacco market, supply/snow-removal difficulties, and functional obsolescence from multi-storey, multi-building configuration (prior BREF decision had granted 20%; TAQ granted 10%).
firac.rule: Depreciation lies at the core of the TAQ's specialized expertise; the reviewing court intervenes only for a patently unreasonable error. Contributory value of repairs must be netted against repair cost (Desjardins, Traité de l'évaluation foncière; General Motors; Camco; Schering; SIQ c. Montréal). A building cannot be depreciated for missing elements not in its cost (CAE; Camco). Each roll is decided on its own evidence.
firac.application: The TAQ correctly applied doctrine/jurisprudence on curable obsolescence (netting contributory value) and reasonably found the public-domain revocation risk too remote to quantify (uncontradicted evidence the City never revoked). On the tobacco-market decline, the TAQ wrongly stated there was 'no particular evidence,' but Impérial itself claimed no economic obsolescence and gave no quantum, so no error in result. Supply/snow-removal overlapped with configuration and reflected age-related obsolescence captured by the age-life table. On configuration/agencement, given significant factual changes since 1989 (Montréal 2001 project), the 10% finding was defensible and within the TAQ's expertise; institutional coherence did not compel following the 1989 20% because the evidence differed.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ's depreciation conclusions stand; no reviewable (patently unreasonable) error was established, so this branch of Impérial's appeal is dismissed.

firac.issue: Did the TAQ err on the rental-value parameters (inclusion of the non-residential immovables surtax and the property value used for decapitalization)?
firac.facts: For 1995, the assessor had not included the non-residential surtax in rental value; the TAQ included it. The TAQ also used the property value at the reference date (with reference-date tax rates) to compute the taxation component in the decapitalization method.
firac.rule: Rental value is the most probable gross annual rent including property taxes (s. 69.5 LFM). The non-residential immovables surtax is a property tax (Germain c. Montréal, 1997 CanLII 393 (SCC)). The tax amount included is that actually expended in the reference year, combining reference-date rates with the value then on the roll (Hewquip; General Motors). These parameters lie at the core of the TAQ's expertise (patently unreasonable standard).
firac.application: Because the surtax is a property tax, s. 69.5 requires its inclusion; the TAQ must render the decision the assessor should have. Although this disadvantages a complaining taxpayer relative to non-complainants, the TAQ and Court must apply the law. Using reference-date rates with the reference-date roll value is the only method respecting the LFM requirement that the tax reflect an actual reference-year expenditure.
firac.conclusion: The TAQ did not err (no patently unreasonable error); inclusion of the surtax and the use of reference-date value for the taxation component are upheld; Impérial's appeal on rental value is dismissed.

keywords_rationale: This is an administrative-law appeal from a specialized tribunal (TAQ) on municipal property assessment. K001 (Administrative law) is the tier-1 practice area. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) are central because the judgment turns on the pragmatic-and-functional analysis and selection among correctness/reasonableness simpliciter/patently unreasonable for each issue. K012 (procedural fairness/natural justice) applies squarely because the Court found the TAQ breached audi alteram partem by adopting an 'arteries' theory no party advanced. K002 (Civil litigation) is included as the closest available tier-1 tag for the private-party municipal tax/valuation dispute, since the controlled vocabulary lacks specific municipal-tax, property-assessment, or Factor F/section 65 LFM keywords. These four substantive picks (K011, K014, K012) plus the two practice-area anchors (K001, K002) capture the case; the vocabulary offers no keyword for property assessment, s. 65 exemptions, or industrial-production classification, so those defining themes cannot be tagged. K002 is a borderline/weak pick used to reach the minimum count and to reflect the civil, non-Charter, non-criminal nature of the underlying dispute.

registry_rationale: The header identifies 'DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL' with court file no. 500-80-003588-044, indicating the Montréal registry/district of the Court of Québec.

name_verification.name_in_document: Manya Greenberg v. Gary Greenberg

defining_issues: Was there a material change in circumstances since the July 22, 2005 final order sufficient to justify varying the joint custody arrangement?
If a material change was shown, does the best interests of the child require replacing joint custody with sole custody to the mother, and should the residential schedule be varied?
Should income be imputed to the father and child support and s. 7 expenses recalculated, and if so from what date?

firac.issue: Was there a material change in circumstances since the July 22, 2005 final order sufficient to justify varying the joint custody arrangement?
firac.facts: The parties held joint custody of Olivia under a detailed 2005 consent order. The mother sought sole decision-making, alleging chronic high conflict largely caused by the father; the father sought equal residential time, relying on his 2007 remarriage, his stepdaughter's presence, and Olivia's stated wishes. Extensive evidence and a psychological assessment by Dr. Weinberger showed persistent conflict over medical care, counselling, school, extracurricular activities, holidays and the weekend rotation, with Olivia drawn into the conflict.
firac.rule: Under s. 17(5) of the Divorce Act a custody order may be varied only if there has been a change in the condition, means, needs or circumstances of the child. Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27, requires a change that materially affects the child and that was not foreseen or reasonably contemplated when the original order was made. Montgomery v. Montgomery held that cumulative unrelenting stress on the child can itself constitute a material change.
firac.application: The court found the parents never established an effective co-parenting regime; the joint decision-making and conflict-resolution clauses had broken down, and the parents could not even agree on a process to resolve disputes. Olivia had been exposed to and negatively affected by ongoing conflict, aligned by her father against her mother. This breakdown was not reasonably foreseeable in 2005. By contrast, the father's remarriage, the stepdaughter's presence and Olivia's (influenced) views did not meet the threshold with respect to the residential arrangements.
firac.conclusion: A material change in circumstances was established warranting a change from joint to sole decision-making, but no material change justified altering Olivia's residential schedule.

firac.issue: Does the best interests of the child require sole custody to the mother rather than the joint custody with equal residential time recommended by the assessor?
firac.facts: Dr. Weinberger recommended continued joint custody with equal alternating-week residence, a mandatory arbitration clause, and counselling. He nonetheless found this a high-conflict case with the father largely responsible, harsh in his treatment of the mother, lacking self-insight, and improperly involving Olivia. The mother sought sole custody; she did not seek to reduce the father's time.
firac.rule: Once a material change is shown, the court considers the matter afresh with the child's welfare as the only issue (Gordon v. Goertz). Joint custody requires evidence of historical cooperation and an ability to communicate and agree on a dispute-resolution process (Kaplanis v. Kaplanis; Roy v. Roy; Lawson v. Lawson); it is inappropriate where conflict causes visible stress to the child (Montgomery; Wreggitt v. Belanger). A court cannot impose mandatory binding arbitration without consent.
firac.application: The court accepted Dr. Weinberger's factual findings but rejected his recommendations, finding them unsupported by his own observations and incapable of reducing conflict. A conflict-resolution clause had already failed, and the court could not order binding arbitration absent consent. The best approach was to remove areas of uncertainty by imposing a fixed, inflexible schedule and granting sole custody to the mother, who contributed less to the conflict and was less likely to marginalize the father. Increasing the father's time was found not to be in Olivia's best interests given his influence over her.
firac.conclusion: Sole custody was awarded to the mother (subject to limits on dentist, Jewish upbringing and residence in Ottawa), the existing residential schedule was maintained in a fixed inflexible form, and counselling was ordered for both parents and Olivia as a condition of custody and access.

firac.issue: Should income be imputed to the father and child support and s. 7 expenses recalculated, and from what date?
firac.facts: The father, a Bachelor of Commerce graduate, earned $30,000 working for his father's company since 2000, received a regular $1,061 monthly gift, had his $266 child support paid directly by the company, and enjoyed an employer health plan and annual family cruises. He had previously earned $50,000. The 2005 consent order fixed support at $266/month on a $30,000 income despite his 40%+ access. Both parties' incomes had since changed.
firac.rule: Section 14 of the Federal Child Support Guidelines defines a change of circumstances giving rise to variation. Income may be imputed where a parent is underemployed (Bak v. Dobell, 2007 ONCA 304). Where shared custody exists (40%+ access), s. 9 of the Guidelines requires consideration of the table amounts, the set-off, increased costs of shared custody, and the conditions, means and needs of each parent and child (Contino v. Leonelli-Contino, 2005 SCC 63).
firac.application: The court found the father underemployed and imputed $50,000 (grossing up his non-taxable $15,924 in gift and support payments plus health benefits). A material change under s. 14(a) was established as both incomes had changed. Variation was allowed only from April 1, 2007, midway between the parties' notices of motion. Applying s. 9 and Contino, and giving weight to the reliance factor and the father's failure to pay his share of activities, no change was warranted from April 2007 to September 2009. From October 1, 2009, given the mother's new cohabitant sharing expenses and the income shift, support was fixed at $150/month, with s. 7 expenses shared 54.55/45.45; the father owed $295 for the school uniforms.
firac.conclusion: Income of $50,000 was imputed to the father; child support remained $266/month to September 2009 and was reduced to $150/month from October 1, 2009, with proportionate sharing of specified s. 7 expenses.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) are the core doctrines, as the case turns on varying a joint custody order in the child's best interests. K050 (parental/child support) covers the imputation of income and s. 9 Guidelines analysis. K117 (Divorce Act) is the governing statute (ss. 16, 17). K052 (religious upbringing) applies because the order continues Olivia's upbringing in the Jewish faith. K093 (Jewish) reflects the family's Jewish identity and the Jewish-faith condition. K043 (denominational schools) is a weaker/borderline pick, engaged only through Olivia's attendance at Hillel Academy, a Jewish parochial school, and the high-school-boundary dispute; it is included for completeness but is peripheral to the ratio.
location_rationale: The decision does not state the city in a masthead, but the substance points clearly to Ottawa: the order forbids changing Olivia's residence 'to a point outside of the city of Ottawa,' and the events refer to local Ottawa institutions (the Ottawa Little Theatre, the Nepean Sportsplex, the Vanier neighbourhood). The court is the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, so the province is Ontario.
registry_rationale: No registry is expressly named, but the court file number 02-FL-2945 and the Ottawa-based facts (residence confined to the city of Ottawa, local venues) indicate the matter proceeded in the Ottawa registry of the Superior Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Halpern v. Wong, Clerk of the City of Toronto [Indexed as: Halpern v. Toronto (City) Clerk]

defining_issues: Does EGALE have a sufficient direct 'interest in the subject matter of the proceeding' to qualify for leave to intervene as an added party under rule 13.01(1)(a)?
Can EGALE make a useful contribution to the proceeding beyond repeating the applicants' perspectives so as to warrant added-party (rather than friend-of-the-court) status?
If intervention is warranted, what terms and conditions should be imposed to prevent undue delay or prejudice under rule 13.01(2)?

firac.issue: Does EGALE have a sufficient direct interest in the subject matter of the proceeding to qualify for intervention as an added party under rule 13.01(1)(a)?
firac.facts: EGALE, a national organization dedicated to legal equality for gays and lesbians with membership in every province and territory, moved for added-party status in an application by same-sex couples seeking marriage licences and a declaration that any law prohibiting same-sex marriage offends the Charter. It relied on its lobbying record, its Executive Director's witness experience, and its accumulated legal knowledge and research on equality rights.
firac.rule: Rule 13.01(1)(a) of the Rules of Civil Procedure requires a genuine and direct interest in the subject matter, over and above that of the general public (Gould Outdoor Advertising v. London (City); John Doe v. Ontario (Information & Privacy Commissioner)). Greater latitude is afforded in Charter challenges, but a direct interest and useful contribution must still be shown (Ontario Federation of Anglers & Hunters). A lobbyist's or witness's interest is insufficient (Ward v. Canada (A.G.)).
firac.application: The court held that EGALE's lobbying experience and its director's role as a witness could not ground intervention, since courts interpret rather than change law and expert evidence can be led through the applicants. However, EGALE's longstanding institutional legal knowledge, extensive legal research, and its representation of a broad spectrum of gays and lesbians who would be directly affected by the outcome gave it a genuine and direct interest beyond that of the general public.
firac.conclusion: EGALE satisfied the 'interest in the subject matter' requirement of rule 13.01(1)(a).

firac.issue: Can EGALE make a useful contribution beyond repeating the applicants' perspectives so as to warrant added-party status?
firac.facts: The applicants were 16 individuals in same-sex couples all seeking marriage licences, supported by up to 10 expert affidavits presenting a broad factual and expert record. EGALE proposed a series of legal arguments about the social reality of gays and lesbians and the dignity interest in choosing to marry.
firac.rule: An intervenor must offer something more than repetition of the parties' evidence and argument or a slightly different emphasis (Stadium Corp. v. Toronto (City); Schofield). The court weighs the likely useful contribution against injustice to the immediate parties (Peel (Regional Municipality) v. Great Atlantic & Pacific Co.; M. v. H.), and lack of a party's resources or the option of a separate proceeding are irrelevant.
firac.application: The court found much of EGALE's proposed argument duplicated the applicants' broadly-based record. However, EGALE could bring genuinely distinct perspectives: that of gays and lesbians who do not wish to marry but seek the freedom to choose whether to marry (the relationship-option/diminishment perspective), and a non-Toronto, national perspective reflecting diverse communities across Canada. These were perspectives the couple-applicants could not present.
firac.conclusion: EGALE could make a useful contribution on those limited, unique perspectives, justifying added-party status confined to those issues.

firac.issue: What terms should be imposed to prevent undue delay or prejudice under rule 13.01(2)?
firac.facts: EGALE sought unrestricted rights to file material, cross-examine and conduct the proceeding as a full party at a stage when the record was still being built; the Attorney General of Canada opposed, urging friend-of-the-court status limited to argument. EGALE undertook to work cooperatively and avoid duplication.
firac.rule: Under rule 13.01(2) the court must consider whether intervention will unduly delay or prejudice the parties' rights and 'may make such order as is just', typically specifying conditions; intervention at first instance where the record is being formed carries greater potential for delay than appellate intervention (M. v. H.; Little Sisters).
firac.application: To balance useful contribution against delay, the court restricted EGALE's role to its unique perspectives, requiring it not to repeat the applicants' arguments, to adhere to case-management timetables, to file no more than two affidavits, to cross-examine only on affidavits touching the designated issues, to file a factum limited to 20 pages, and to present oral argument only if later ordered, with liberty to vary the terms as circumstances changed.
firac.conclusion: Intervention was granted as an added party under rule 13.01(1) on specified, limiting terms, with no costs of the motion or proceeding for or against EGALE.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area because the decision turns on the civil-procedure test for intervention under rule 13.01. K011 (judicial review) is engaged because the underlying proceeding was a judicial review of the City Clerk's refusal to issue marriage licences. K003 (Constitutional law) and K107 (Canadian Charter) reflect that the intervention analysis was shaped by the fact that the main proceeding is a Charter challenge, and courts give greater latitude in Charter cases. K023 (equality rights) and K109 (Charter s.15) capture the substantive equality subject matter (same-sex marriage rights) that grounded EGALE's asserted interest. K030 (reasonable limits, s.1) is a weaker/borderline pick, included because EGALE's proposed arguments expressly addressed the government's s.1 justification onus; it is a passing merits reference rather than something decided here. The vocabulary contains no keyword for 'intervention' or 'same-sex marriage', so the tier-2 Charter picks are the closest fit.
location_rationale: The decision states it is a ruling of the 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Divisional Court' per Lang J., which establishes the province as Ontario. The city where the court sat is not expressly stated in the text, so it is left null; the underlying marriage-licence applications were made in Toronto but that goes to the merits, not the court's seat.
registry_rationale: No court registry or office is named in the decision (only the Court File No. 684/2000 and the Divisional Court designation), so registry is left null.

case_name: Durham Children's Aid Society v. R.B.

name_verification.name_in_document: The Durham Children's Aid Society v. R… B…

defining_issues: Was A.B. a child in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
What disposition was in A.B.'s best interests — Crown wardship with no access for adoption, or placement with her biological family under supervision?

firac.issue: Was A.B. a child in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
firac.facts: A.B. was apprehended by the Durham CAS at four months of age from a YWCA shelter amid concerns about her half-brother's behaviour, the presence of the violent M.C., a cigarette burn, and a kidney condition. The mother, R.B., had a history of poverty, substance abuse, poor decisions and repeated flight from child-protection authorities, largely tied to her destructive relationship with M.C.
firac.rule: Section 37(2)(b)(ii) CFSA: a child is in need of protection where the child has suffered physical harm resulting from the caregiver's pattern of neglect in caring for, providing for, supervising or protecting the child; s. 37(2)(e): where the child needs medical treatment the parent fails to provide. A protection finding is assessed on the facts from the time of apprehension forward.
firac.application: The s. 37(2)(e) allegations failed: the cigarette burn was an accident, the tissue damage minor, and no inadequate medication of the kidney condition was proven. However, under s. 37(2)(b)(ii), R.B. had repeatedly exhibited poor judgment — fleeing authorities, entangling herself in the criminal justice system, and prioritizing the violent M.C. over her children — a pattern that re-emerged in the unplanned move to Ontario.
firac.conclusion: The court found A.B. to be a child in need of protection under s. 37(2)(b)(ii), though based on a low level of risk.

firac.issue: What disposition was in A.B.'s best interests — Crown wardship for adoption or placement with the biological family?
firac.facts: A.B. had been in the same foster home since four months of age due to an inordinate three-year delay; the CAS sought Crown wardship with no access so she could be adopted. R.B. had turned her life around over the past year, moved in with her sister C.B., ended contact with M.C., and secured employment. C.B. committed to permanent care of A.B. whether or not R.B. succeeded. Dr. Berman assessed R.B. as capable of parenting and questioned anxiety in the foster attachment.
firac.rule: Sections 57 and 1(2) CFSA, with best-interests criteria in s. 37(3): the court must consider less disruptive alternatives (s. 57(3)), the biological family's plans (s. 57(4)), continuity of care, effects of delay, risk of harm, and the paramount purpose of protecting the child, supported by the autonomy and integrity of the family unit.
firac.application: The court could not place A.B. with R.B. alone because her lifestyle changes were too recent and unproven. However, C.B. had the skills, fortitude and commitment to permanent care to provide a stable placement, working with R.B. The finding rested on low risk, and the CAS had made little effort to assist R.B. or preserve access, funnelling energy into its Crown-wardship position. With best interests balanced between adoption and family placement, the additional purpose favouring the autonomy and integrity of the biological family tipped the scales.
firac.conclusion: The court ordered A.B. placed with C.B. and R.B. under CAS supervision with detailed conditions (including no contact with M.C.), with sole care reverting to C.B. if R.B. breached or the cohabitation broke down, and ordered therapeutic reintegration assistance funded by the CAS.

name_verification.name_in_document: G.B. v. Fortin

defining_issues: Should the court exercise its discretion under the Rules of Civil Procedure to appoint a litigation administrator for the estate of a defendant who died before the action was commenced?
For the purpose of deciding the appointment, is it plain and obvious that the two-year limitation period in s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act bars the action against the deceased defendant?
Is the person proposed by the plaintiff an appropriate individual to be appointed as litigation administrator?

firac.issue: Should the court appoint a litigation administrator for the estate of a defendant who died before the action was commenced?
firac.facts: G.B. sued Etienne Fortin and institutional defendants in April 2009 for historical sexual abuse alleged to have occurred in 1969–1970 at St. Joseph's Training School. Fortin had died on February 22, 2002, unknown to the plaintiff, and his estate was administered by the provincial executor. Les Frères opposed appointment, arguing there was no estate and the appointment was unreasonable.
firac.rule: Under rule 9.02 the appointment of a litigation administrator is discretionary, and rules 9.03(3) and (5) provide that a proceeding commenced against a person who died before its commencement is not a nullity but may be continued against a litigation administrator with the title amended accordingly.
firac.application: The court found the appointment reasonable because the plaintiff was motivated not by the existence of an estate to satisfy damages but by the possible existence of records, which is not an unreasonable litigation approach. Because live limitation arguments meant it was not clear the action was out of time, appointment was warranted.
firac.conclusion: The court ordered that a litigation administrator be appointed, with terms of appointment adjourned to be settled by the parties before June 30, 2011.

firac.issue: Is it plain and obvious, for the purpose of the appointment, that s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act bars the action against the deceased defendant?
firac.facts: The alleged assaults occurred in 1969–1970 while Fortin was in a position of trust/authority over the 15–16 year old plaintiff. Fortin died in 2002; the action began in 2009, more than two years after death. The plaintiff pleaded permanent incapacity and reliance on the sexual-assault provisions of the Limitations Act, 2002.
firac.rule: Section 38(3) of the Trustee Act imposes a two-year limitation for actions against estates, preserved by s. 19(1)(a) and the Schedule of the Limitations Act, 2002. However, s. 24(7)(2) transition provision provides there is no limitation period where s. 16(1)(h) (sexual assault by a person in a position of trust or authority) would apply, and s. 10(3) creates a presumption of incapacity. Doctrines of fraudulent concealment (Giroux Estate) and special circumstances (Bikur Cholim) may toll s. 38(3). Camarata v. Morgan and Swain Estate address the interplay of the periods; B.L. (P.T.) held it was not plain and obvious such a claim was statute-barred.
firac.application: The court held the motion required only a preliminary, non-final analysis akin to summary judgment. Distinguishing Bikur Cholim and Kramarz (which did not consider s. 24(7)(2)), the court found several live arguments could defeat the limitation: fraudulent concealment, special circumstances, application of s. 16(1)(h), the incapacity defence, and the transition provisions. Because these were all arguable, it was not clear the action was time-barred.
firac.conclusion: The court declined to make a final limitations determination and found that, given the live arguments, it was not clear the action was out of time, supporting appointment.

firac.issue: Is the plaintiff's proposed individual an appropriate litigation administrator?
firac.facts: The plaintiff proposed Mr. Jerome Gardner, a local lawyer. Les Frères objected, believing him to be a unilingual Anglophone whereas les Frères operated in French.
firac.rule: Rule 9.02 gives the court discretion over the appointment and its terms.
firac.application: The court did not resolve the objection but invited counsel to propose mutually acceptable terms and a name, failing which submissions could be made before the judge.
firac.conclusion: Terms of appointment, including the identity of the administrator, were adjourned to be settled by the parties before June 30, 2011.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the core practice area — a tort action for historical sexual abuse and a procedural motion under the Rules of Civil Procedure. K054 (wills/estates) is strongly engaged: the motion concerns appointment of a litigation administrator for a deceased defendant's estate and the Trustee Act limitation for actions against estates. K006 (Family law) is included as the vocabulary's tier-1 parent of the estates keyword, though the case is not a family dispute (weak/structural pick). K043 (denominational schools) and K005 (Education law) are contextual only — the abuse occurred at a Roman Catholic training school run by les Frères des écoles chrétiennes — but the legal issues are procedural/limitations, so both are flagged as weak. The controlled vocabulary has no keyword for limitation periods, litigation administrators, or civil sexual-abuse claims, which are the true substance of the case.
location_rationale: The decision is styled 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' but does not state the sitting city. The events took place at St. Joseph's Training School in Alfred, Ontario, and the institutional defendant operated in Ottawa, but no hearing city is given. Province is Ontario from the court identification.

They brought a motion bene esse for leave to appeal an interlocutory judgment (relating to security for costs). firac.application: The Court noted that the plaintiffs did not argue that posting security for costs would bar their access to the courts because of inability to pay, and concluded that the interests of justice did not require that leave be granted.

name_verification.name_in_document: Yafim Goikhberg v. Deborah Mankovitz

defining_issues: Was there a binding agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant lawyer for payment of $15,000, and could such an agreement be proven by testimony absent a writing?
Can the defendant lawyer be held liable in extracontractual damages for statements made on behalf of her client in immigration proceedings, given prescription and the immunity of counsel?
Is the plaintiff's action abusive, frivolous, vexatious or quarrelsome under arts. 51 ff. of the Code of Civil Procedure?

firac.issue: Was there a binding $15,000 agreement, and could it be proven by testimony absent a writing?
firac.facts: Goikhberg alleged that during a November 2014 telephone call Mankovitz admitted giving false information to authorities and agreed to pay him $15,000. Mankovitz admitted the call but denied any promise to pay, saying Goikhberg was distraught and she was merely empathetic. There was no writing evidencing the alleged deal.
firac.rule: Art. 2862 C.C.Q.: proof of a juridical act by testimony is not permitted between parties where the value in dispute exceeds $1,500, except where there is a commencement of proof in writing or the act was done in the ordinary course of an enterprise's business. The plaintiff bears the burden of proof (arts. 2803, 2804 C.C.Q.).
firac.application: Goikhberg had no writing, could not invoke the ordinary-course-of-business exception, and offered no commencement of proof in writing. In any event the Court accepted Mankovitz's version: it made no sense for a lawyer to promise such a sum over a single phone call, there was no prior contractual relationship, the call came years after the impugned statements, and any claim would have been handled by her liability insurer.
firac.conclusion: No agreement for payment of $15,000 existed; that part of the claim fails.

firac.issue: Can the lawyer be liable in extracontractual damages for statements made for her client in immigration proceedings?
firac.facts: The impugned statements were made in July 2009 and reiterated in a September 2010 Federal Court proceeding on behalf of Ms. Dakhova. Criminal charges against Goikhberg followed by September 26, 2011. He sued Mankovitz on December 14, 2015, claiming impossibility to act during his incarceration and late discovery of her involvement.
firac.rule: Art. 2925 C.C.Q.: a personal action is prescribed after three years. Incarceration does not, absent special circumstances, constitute impossibility in fact to act (Olivier v. Canada, 2013 QCCA 70). A lawyer is an officer of the court and enjoys immunity for allegations made within the scope of her mandate; immunity ends only where bad faith and absence of reasonable and probable cause begin (Juneau c. Taillefer; art. 1457 C.C.Q.).
firac.application: The action was instituted more than three years after both the statements and the resulting charges. Neither incarceration nor Goikhberg's failure to locate the Board decision earlier (obtained through disclosure over three years before) amounted to an impossibility to act. Alternatively, no fault was shown: Mankovitz acted in good faith and reasonably relied on her client's account, especially given Goikhberg's convictions.
firac.conclusion: The extracontractual claim is prescribed and, in any event, discloses no fault; it is dismissed.

firac.issue: Is the plaintiff's action abusive under arts. 51 ff. C.C.P.?
firac.facts: Mankovitz argued Goikhberg was a vexatious litigant and the suit abusive. The action arose out of Goikhberg's grievance over criminal convictions in which Mankovitz played no role.
firac.rule: Arts. 51-53 C.C.P.: the court may declare a judicial application abusive where it is clearly unfounded, frivolous, vexatious, quarrelsome, or defeats the ends of justice.
firac.application: Having dismissed the action for tardiness and absence of legal basis, the Court found it sufficient to note that the suit against Mankovitz defeated the ends of justice as retaliation for a criminal conviction in which she had no part.
firac.conclusion: The action is characterized as defeating the ends of justice; it is dismissed with court fees against Goikhberg.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a small-claims civil suit for contractual and extracontractual damages. defining_issues: Was Richard Jr. a child in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
Given that the children had been in care beyond the statutory time limits in s. 70 of the CFSA, should they be returned to their parents or made Crown wards for adoption?
Should the Crown wardship order be made with no access to the parents, and were there any safeguards to protect the parents' status-review rights?

firac.issue: Was Richard Jr. a child in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
firac.facts: Richard Jr., born November 2007, was apprehended in December 2007. His parents had a persistent history of domestic violence, unaddressed drug-testing concerns, and failure to complete counselling. His two older siblings had already been found in need of protection in November 2006. The CAS's amended application initially omitted the CFSA section relied on, which was corrected by amendment at trial under rule 26.01.
firac.rule: Section 37(2)(b) and (g) of the CFSA: a child is in need of protection where there is a risk of physical harm resulting from a parent's failure to adequately care for or protect the child, or a pattern of neglect, and where there is a risk of emotional harm from the parent's actions or neglect. Rule 26.01 of the Rules of Civil Procedure permits amendment of pleadings unless non-compensable prejudice results.
firac.application: The court permitted the pleadings amendment as no party was prejudiced. Although Richard Jr. had been little parented by the couple, their ongoing physical and verbal confrontations, frequent police intervention and criminal charges posed a risk that the child would be physically harmed during disputes or emotionally harmed by witnessing violence. The parents had shown minimal effort to address the issues that led to the original protection finding for the siblings.
firac.conclusion: Richard Jr. was found to be a child in need of protection under s. 37(2)(b) and (g) of the CFSA.

firac.issue: Should the children be returned to their parents or made Crown wards for adoption, considering the statutory time limits and best-interests factors?
firac.facts: Alizeah and Anthony had been in CAS care since July 2006, Richard Jr. since December 2007 — all well beyond the s. 70 statutory limits. The parents had ten to twenty separations marked by documented domestic violence, repeated breaches of no-contact court orders, unfulfilled promises regarding counselling and drug testing (R.B. never provided drug results after a positive cocaine test three years earlier), and no stable housing. Kinship placement with grandmothers was investigated and not recommended.
firac.rule: Section 70 of the CFSA caps society wardship duration (12 months for a child under six), leaving only return or Crown wardship where the limit is exceeded. Section 1 declares the paramount purpose to be the best interests, protection and well-being of children. Section 37(3) lists best-interests factors including the child's needs, cultural background, relationships, merits of the CAS plan, effects of delay, and degree of risk. Courts recognize that exposure to domestic violence harms children (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S.A.C., 2005 ONCJ 274; Jewish Family and Child Service v. R.K., [2008] O.J. No. 1940; CAS of Peel v. A.O., 2006 ONCJ 149).
firac.application: Only the factors of blood relationship and cultural background favoured the parents. Neither parent presented a viable plan: both lacked suitable housing after three years, and their unresolved domestic violence continued, with the same conditions persisting as justified the original 2006 protection finding. The children needed stability and could wait no longer; each was a good adoption candidate with no special needs. The court criticized both the CAS (for seeking adjournments contrary to time guidelines) and the parents for the inexcusable delays.
firac.conclusion: The children were made Crown wards for the purpose of adoption; return to the parents was not a viable option.

firac.issue: Should the Crown wardship be with no access, and what safeguard protects the parents' status-review rights?
firac.facts: The CAS sought Crown wardship with no access for adoption. The parents had attended most access visits and the hearing, showing some commitment. Under s. 65.1 a parent may seek status review, but s. 65.1(9) bars applications once a Crown ward is placed for adoption, and parents might not learn of placement.
firac.rule: Section 65.1 of the CFSA governs status-review applications by a parent, subject to timing and leave restrictions; s. 65.1(9) bars applications where the ward has been placed for adoption and still resides in that home.
firac.application: To preserve the parents' meaningful ability to exercise status-review rights before adoption placement forecloses them, the court ordered the Society to inform each parent in writing within seven days of the children being placed for adoption; this also served to discourage further delay by the Society.
firac.conclusion: Crown wardship with no access was ordered, coupled with a direction that the Society notify the parents in writing when the children are placed for adoption.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area — this is a child-protection/Crown-wardship proceeding under the CFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is central: the disposition turned on s. 37(3) best-interests factors and s. 1's paramount purpose. K048 (custody/access) applies because the outcome concerned custody through Crown wardship and the express 'no access' order. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward Jewish-law/antisemitism themes and lacks any dedicated child-protection, wardship, or domestic-violence keyword, so the remaining picks are weak fits offered to reach the minimum: K050 (parental support) touches the broader parental-responsibility dimension but is not squarely engaged, and K052 (religious upbringing) is invoked only loosely because the decision expressly notes the children have 'no religious affiliation' but weighs their cultural background under s. 37(3). Both K050 and K052 are flagged as weak; no antisemitism/Jewish-specific keyword genuinely applies despite the incidental citation of Jewish Family and Child Service v. R.K.

name_verification.name_in_document: ID v DB

defining_issues: What is the most appropriate parenting and decision-making arrangement for the two oldest children where one parent alleges parental alienation?
What consequences should flow from the father's contempt of court?

firac.issue: What parenting and decision-making arrangement is in the best interests of the two oldest children, given allegations of parental alienation?
firac.facts: Following the parents' 2018 divorce, the three children initially resided primarily with the mother (Ms. D). The two oldest children (16 and almost 14) ceased contact with her in 2019 and 2020 respectively and now live full-time with the father (Mr. B), while the youngest (11) has continued shared week-on/week-off parenting with both parents. Ms. D alleged Mr. B alienated her from the older children and sought a reversal of parenting; Mr. B claimed the children were merely exercising their own choices. Expert reports (Wilkinson, Torres) and Counsel for the Children documented alienating and estranging conduct.
firac.rule: Section 16 of the Divorce Act, RSC 1985, c 3 (2nd Supp), requires the court to consider only the best interests of the child, giving primary consideration to physical, emotional and psychological safety, weighing the enumerated s. 16(3) factors, family violence under s. 16(4), and the s. 16(6) maximum-contact principle subject to the child's welfare (Young v Young; SS v AS, 2020 ABQB 810). A court may find parental alienation on the facts alone without conclusive expert evidence (Malhotra v Henhoeffer, 2018 ONSC 6472; VMB v KRB, 2014 ABCA 334). Four post-alienation options exist (RMB v DTB, 2019 ABQB 826 at para 112; JLZ v CMZ, 2021 ABCA 200).
firac.application: The court found that although Ms. D engaged in some estranging behaviour, Mr. B engaged in a far more troubling campaign of alienation, encouraging the children to reject their mother, over-involving them in litigation, making unsubstantiated abuse allegations (an unfounded PN5), a public 'Go Fund Me' page vilifying the mother, and severing the children's Jewish faith and maternal family ties. The older children exhibited classic alienation behaviours. However, given the children are teenagers who 'vote with their feet' (unlike the younger children in RMB), the proposed transitional caregiver (Ms. X) was a stranger and unsuitable, and a full custody reversal would likely cause the children to run away, the court concluded neither 'doing nothing' nor an immediate reversal served their best interests. Reunification therapy while the children remained with the father, aimed at restoring shared parenting (as already worked for the youngest child), was appropriate.
firac.conclusion: The two older children are to remain with the father while reunification therapy continues for six months with the goal of returning to shared parenting; failure to attend therapy without reasonable excuse triggers a return to court to show cause why custody should not be reversed.

firac.issue: What consequences should follow from Mr. B's contempt of court?
firac.facts: Mr. B admitted knowing about and consenting to the March 19, 2021 Consent Order but largely refused to follow it — failing to arrange or pay for the children's counselling, breaching the prohibition on further applications by commencing PN5 abuse allegations and obtaining restraining orders, and failing to obtain counselling for AB. He had previously been warned and even held in contempt with unpaid costs by other judges.
firac.rule: Rule 10.52(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court permits a declaration of civil contempt where a person without reasonable excuse does not comply with an order of which they have knowledge; Rule 10.53 sets out sanctions including imprisonment. Civil contempt requires (1) a clear order, (2) knowledge of it, and (3) intentional act/omission breaching it (Carey v Laiken, 2015 SCC 17). Its dual goals are securing compliance and protecting the integrity of the administration of justice (United Nurses of Alberta, [1992] 1 SCR 901). Family-law contempt sentences have ranged from 2–90 days, often suspended for future compliance (Rea v Rea; Holt v Holt; Skalitzky v Skalitzky).
firac.application: Mr. B knew the order's terms and deliberately disobeyed them without reasonable excuse, so contempt was proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Monetary fines would only add pressure to a toxic family situation and were insufficient given the contumacy; prior threats, findings and costs awards had not curbed his behaviour. Some incarceration was necessary to protect respect for the administration of justice, but proceeding in civil rather than criminal contempt avoided a criminal record.
firac.conclusion: Mr. B was found in contempt and sentenced to six days' gaol, suspended for six months pending his cooperation with reunification therapy and capable of indefinite suspension based on future compliance; costs reserved for six months.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test under s. 16 of the Divorce Act and drives the parenting decision. K048 (custody/access) captures the parenting-time and decision-making dispute, including the requested custody reversal. K117 (Divorce Act) is the applicable statute expressly cited.
