name_verification.name_in_document: G.J. c. Auguste

defining_issues: Can the plaintiff relitigate the factual issue of whether the December 26, 2014 incident occurred as described by Ms. Auguste, given that Justice Morrison had already decided that question in the curatorship proceedings?
Did Ms. Auguste commit a fault giving rise to defamation liability by reporting and later testifying about the alleged incident?
Was the defamation action prescribed under article 2929 C.C.Q.?

firac.issue: Can the plaintiff relitigate the previously decided factual issue of whether the December 26, 2014 incident occurred, without committing an abuse of procedure?
firac.facts: In May 2015 Justice Morrison, in curatorship proceedings contested by Mr. J. (then represented by counsel), found Ms. Auguste credible and concluded that the incident of December 26, 2014 had occurred as she described. Mr. J. appealed but abandoned the appeal after his mother's death. In his later defamation action he again sought to prove the incident was fabricated.
firac.rule: Although res judicata under art. 2848 C.C.Q. did not apply, Quebec courts have a discretionary power to prevent relitigation of a previously decided issue where doing so would be an abuse of procedure (Construction S.Y.L. Tremblay inc. c. ARQ, 2018 QCCA 552; Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63). The party seeking to relitigate bears the burden of showing that an injustice would result otherwise; relitigation may be permitted where, e.g., stakes were minor, there was inadequate incentive to defend, new evidence emerged, or the original process was tainted.
firac.application: None of the exceptional circumstances existed. Mr. J. was represented by counsel before and during the May 2015 trial, had notice that the QPC would rely on Ms. Auguste's account and call her as a witness, and had ample incentive to defend. His claim of surprise was not credible. There was no newly discovered evidence and no unfairness in the earlier trial. All factors pointed to denying relitigation.
firac.conclusion: Mr. J.'s attempt to revisit the finding constituted an abuse of procedure; since the case turned on whether Ms. Auguste committed a fault and she could not have done wrong in reporting sexual misconduct against a patient, the action was dismissed.

firac.issue: Did Ms. Auguste commit a fault giving rise to defamation liability?
firac.facts: Ms. Auguste, a disinterested beneficiary attendant, filed a report within an hour of witnessing the incident and testified consistently. Mr. J. alleged her account was fabricated in retaliation for his complaints about his mother's care, and pointed to the absence of criminal charges.
firac.rule: To succeed in defamation the plaintiff must show a reasonable person would not have made the impugned remarks in the same context (Bou Malhab v. Diffusion Métromédia CMR inc., 2011 SCC 9; Prud'homme v. Prud'homme, 2002 SCC 85). The plaintiff bears the burden (art. 2803 C.C.Q.) on the balance of probabilities (F.H. v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53).
firac.application: The evidence was only circumstantial. Mr. J.'s claim of appalling care rested on his own uncorroborated testimony, contradicted by medical records and Ms. Mireault's testimony showing conflicts stemmed from his non-compliance with rules. His claim of no conflict at CHSLD Vigi Mont-Royal was contradicted by records. Ms. Auguste testified clearly and consistently and was found credible; the absence of charges was explained (her reluctance to testify criminally; the mother's cognitive impairment).
firac.conclusion: By way of obiter, Mr. J. failed to prove the account was false and fabricated; more likely Ms. Auguste acted in good faith, so no fault was established.

firac.issue: Was the defamation action prescribed under article 2929 C.C.Q.?
firac.facts: The originating application was filed May 4, 2016. Mr. J. knew of the allegations and their reputational impact by January 2015 and knew Ms. Auguste was their author before the May 2015 trial. However, he sued for injuries flowing from her May 5, 2015 testimony before Justice Morrison, not the December 2014 report.
firac.rule: Article 2929 C.C.Q.: a defamation action is prescribed one year from the day the defamed person learned of the defamation. Prescription runs from when the plaintiff could commence the action; mere reiteration of comments may not start a new period, but distinct injurious acts can.
firac.application: Mr. J. sued in relation to distinct injuries allegedly caused by the testimony given at the May 2015 trial, an act he could not have sued upon before that trial occurred. Therefore the one-year period ran from May 5, 2015, and the May 4, 2016 filing was timely.
firac.conclusion: By way of obiter, the prescription defence was not well founded; the action would not have been dismissed on that ground.

name_verification.name_in_document: Dwyer v. Bussey

defining_issues: Were the parties 'married' or capable of being deemed married under s. 44 of the Solemnization of Marriage Act despite the absence of an officiant, witnesses, or licence?

Did the parties go through a 'form of marriage ... in good faith, that is void' within the meaning of s. 2(1)(e)(iii) of the Family Law Act so as to be 'spouses' entitled to matrimonial property division — in particular, what does 'in good faith' require?

firac.issue: Were the parties married, or deemed validly married under s. 44 of the Solemnization of Marriage Act, notwithstanding the informal ceremony?
firac.facts: After living together for years, Bussey and Dwyer exchanged minister-blessed rings, read a biblical marriage verse, and echoed a Christian wedding, but there was no officiant, no witnesses, and no licence. Both had been married before and knew they were not complying with marriage law.
firac.rule: Section 44 of the Solemnization of Marriage Act, RSNL 1990, c. S-19 (successor s. 32(2) of the Marriage Act, 2009) validates a marriage 'solemnized in good faith and intended to be in compliance with this Act' despite an unauthorized officiant or an irregularity/insufficiency in the licence.
firac.application: The saving provision could not apply: there was no person who solemnized the marriage, no licence in which any irregularity could arise, and the parties did not intend to comply with the Act. The ceremony therefore fell outside the curative provision.
firac.conclusion: The parties were not married and could not be treated as validly married; they could only qualify as spouses under s. 2(1)(e)(iii) of the Family Law Act.

firac.issue: Did the couple go through a 'form of marriage ... in good faith, that is void' under s. 2(1)(e)(iii) of the Family Law Act, and does 'good faith' require an intention to be legally married?
firac.facts: The parties deliberately mimicked a wedding and held themselves out as husband and wife, but knowingly avoided the legal formalities of marriage, having each been previously married and understanding that they were not complying with marriage law.
firac.rule: Section 2(1)(e)(iii) of the Family Law Act, RSNL 1990, c. F-2 defines 'spouse' to include persons who 'have gone through a form of marriage with each other, in good faith, that is void' and have cohabited within the preceding year. Interpretation requires reading text in context (Placer Dome, 2006 SCC 20; Archean Resources, 2002 NFCA 43), and the Act draws a bright-line 'spouses'/'partners' distinction reflecting respect for autonomy (Nova Scotia (A.G.) v. Walsh, 2002 SCC 83).
firac.application: Per White J.A. (Harrington J.A. concurring): every word must be given meaning; since 'form of marriage' already implies intent to form a conjugal relationship and to be married, 'in good faith' is redundant unless it means an intention to be legally married. A long line of authority ties the good-faith exception to a belief in legal validity, the scheme of the Act requires a mutual positive step into the matrimonial-property regime, and the Act's unique automatic joint-tenancy provisions demand certainty. Couples who deliberately avoid legal marriage have not taken that step. Green C.J.N.L., dissenting, would have read 'good faith' as ordinary fair dealing and honest intention to create a permanent exclusive union, treating a ceremonial de facto marriage as within the provision given Newfoundland's history of informal marriage and s. 32(2)'s separate treatment of 'good faith' and 'intention to comply'.
firac.conclusion: The majority held the couple did not enter a form of marriage 'in good faith' because they deliberately chose not to be legally married; they were not spouses. Green C.J.N.L. dissented, finding they were spouses.

name_verification.name_in_document: Hughes (Estate of) v. Hughes

defining_issues: Does the pleading of 'undue influence' as a tort disclose a reasonable cause of action under Rule 129(1)(a)?
Are the claims of misrepresentation and deceit that challenge the religious doctrine of the Jehovah's Witness faith justiciable?
Is there a separate cause of action for breach of statutory duty under the Child Welfare Act?
Does the plea of conspiracy against the defendants disclose a valid, properly particularized cause of action?
Should the personal tort claims of Lawrence Hughes (deceit, misrepresentation, conspiracy) be struck under Frame v. Smith or as an abuse of process?
Should the claims on behalf of Bethany's estate against the Health Care Defendants (trespass and negligence) and against the Watch Tower Lawyers be struck?

firac.issue: Does the pleading of 'undue influence' as a tort disclose a reasonable cause of action under Rule 129(1)(a)?
firac.facts: The Statement of Claim alleged that the Watch Tower Defendants exerted undue influence over Bethany Hughes, a 17-year-old Jehovah's Witness, to dissuade her from accepting life-saving blood transfusions for her leukemia.
firac.rule: Under Rule 129(1)(a) a claim is struck only where, assuming the pleaded facts are true, it is 'plain and obvious' that it discloses no reasonable cause of action (Hunt v. T & N plc, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959; Tottrup v. Alberta, 2000 ABCA 121). Canadian law recognizes no separate tort of undue influence (Khaper v. Canada; Umstead v. Umstead) — it is a set of circumstances giving rise to an equitable remedy such as rescission, not damages.
firac.application: The Court accepted that undue influence is not an independent tort sounding in damages. Novelty alone would not defeat a pleading, but here the alleged wrong simply does not exist as a cause of action.
firac.conclusion: The undue influence allegations disclose no cause of action and were struck.

firac.issue: Are the claims of misrepresentation and deceit that challenge the religious doctrine of the Jehovah's Witness faith justiciable?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs alleged the defendants misrepresented that the chemotherapy/blood transfusion protocol was 'experimental' and, more broadly, that the faith's belief opposing blood transfusions was contrary to scientific truth and part of an indoctrination process.
firac.rule: Courts must not become arbiters of religious dogma or adjudicate the validity of religious doctrine (Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47; R. v. Big M Drug Mart); a court may only inquire into the sincerity of belief. Freedom of religion is not absolute and a tort committed in the course of a religious duty is not automatically shielded (Boer v. Watch Tower). The tort of deceit requires a knowingly false representation made to deceive and detrimental reliance (Klar, Tort Law).
firac.application: The claim did not challenge the sincerity of Bethany's belief or allege mistreatment (unlike Boer) or fraudulent recruitment practices (unlike Molko); it attacked the truth of the faith's teachings, which would require the court to interpret religious precepts. As to the hospital-conduct allegations, no particulars were pleaded and Bethany received the transfusions despite protest, so no detrimental reliance was shown.
firac.conclusion: The allegations were non-justiciable and/or disclosed no cause of action and were struck.

firac.issue: Is there a separate cause of action for breach of statutory duty under the Child Welfare Act?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs alleged ss. 4(1) and 4(6) of the Child Welfare Act required the defendants to report Bethany's medical situation to a director and that failure to do so was actionable.
firac.rule: There is no independent tort of breach of statutory duty unless the legislation creates a civil remedy (R. v. Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, [1983] 1 S.C.R. 205; Frame v. Smith; Tottrup).
firac.application: The Child Welfare Act created no separate civil remedy for a failure to report.
firac.conclusion: No cause of action for breach of statutory duty exists; the claim was struck.

firac.issue: Does the plea of conspiracy against the defendants disclose a valid, properly particularized cause of action?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs alleged all defendants combined to ensure Bethany received alternative (transfusion-free) treatment leading to her death, pleading joint and several liability.
firac.rule: An actionable conspiracy may exist where defendants combine to act unlawfully with known likelihood of injury (Hunt v. T & N plc), but the tort should not readily be extended beyond the commercial context (Canada Cement LaFarge; Frame v. Smith), and conspiracy must be pleaded with clarity and precision as to the overt acts of each conspirator (Normart Management v. West Hill; Hovsepian v. Westfair).
firac.application: The pleading did not set out with precision the overt acts of each conspirator; the only underlying 'unlawful acts' were the undue influence, misrepresentation and deceit already struck. Allowing the conspiracy plea against the Watch Tower Defendants would relitigate struck claims, and the lawyers and health care defendants were entitled to particulars.
firac.conclusion: The conspiracy allegations against all defendants were struck for lack of a valid, particularized cause of action.

firac.issue: Should the personal tort claims of Lawrence Hughes (deceit, misrepresentation, conspiracy) be struck under Frame v. Smith or as an abuse of process?
firac.facts: Lawrence Hughes claimed personally that the defendants conspired to move Bethany to a secret location and withheld information about her whereabouts and treatment, alienating her from him.
firac.rule: Tort claims arising from denial of access/information about a child are not to be extended to the family context (Frame v. Smith, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 99; Sturkenboom v. Davies). A claim may also be struck as an abuse of process under Rule 129(1)(d), where the whole history shows misuse of the court's process (Dykun v. Odishaw; J.A. Industries).
firac.application: In essence Mr. Hughes sought damages for denial of access to his daughter and information about her, a claim Frame precludes. Further, the court record showed he had pursued disclosure in the divorce proceedings, obtained Bethany's location and treatment protocol on August 11, 2002, and abandoned that application sine die; reviving the claims was vexatious and an abuse of process.
firac.conclusion: All of Lawrence Hughes's personal claims were struck.

firac.issue: Should the estate's claims against the Health Care Defendants (trespass, negligence) and against the Watch Tower Lawyers be struck?
firac.facts: The estate alleged the Health Care Defendants treated Bethany without valid consent (trespass) and were negligent in the treatment regimen; and that the Watch Tower Lawyers, being members/employees of the Society, were in a conflict of interest and could not properly advise Bethany.
firac.rule: Under Rule 129(1)(a) a pleading that on its face discloses a cause of action cannot be struck; consent by a mature minor or a guardian is a defence to trespass (C(J.S.) v. Wren); to strike as an abuse under Rule 129(1)(b)/(d) evidence may be considered but removal/challenge to counsel is a fact-sensitive matter (B.H. v. Alberta).
firac.application: On their face the trespass and negligence pleadings disclosed causes of action; the evidence on consent and standard of care was incomplete, making these matters for summary judgment rather than a strike. Regarding the lawyers, the merits of removing counsel had never been decided and it was unclear whether independent counsel advised Bethany during her transfer to the Cross Cancer Institute, so the claim was not an abuse of process — though any inquiry into the lawyers' religious beliefs remained non-justiciable.
firac.conclusion: These claims survived. The estate's trespass and negligence claims against the Health Care Defendants and its negligence/breach of fiduciary duty claims against the Watch Tower Lawyers (with the Society retained only for vicarious liability) were allowed to proceed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area: the decision is a motion to strike pleadings in a tort action (undue influence, deceit, misrepresentation, conspiracy, trespass, negligence). K025 (freedom of religion) and K034 (sincerity of belief) are engaged because the court applied Amselem to hold that challenging the doctrine of the Jehovah's Witness faith is non-justiciable and that only sincerity, not validity, of belief is reviewable. K006 (Family law), K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) apply because the court relied on Frame v. Smith and Sturkenboom to refuse to extend tort law to what was in substance a denial-of-access claim by the father. K054 (wills/estates) reflects that the action was brought by the Administrator ad litem of the deceased's estate under the Fatal Accidents Act and Survival of Actions Act. The family-law and estates picks are somewhat peripheral supports rather than the core holding; the controlled vocabulary lacks a precise 'striking pleadings/abuse of process/justiciability' term, so those doctrines are captured indirectly through Civil litigation and the freedom-of-religion tags.
location_rationale: The heading of the judgment states 'Registry: Calgary' and the decision is 'Dated at the City of Calgary, Alberta this 24th day of February, 2006.' The court is the Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly records 'Registry: Calgary' and the reasons were dated at Calgary.

name_verification.name_in_document: Family and Children's Services of Renfrew County v. A.R. et al.

defining_issues: Has the Society established, on credible and trustworthy evidence, reasonable grounds to believe there is a real possibility that it is more probable than not that the child will suffer harm if placed in the parents' care?
If so, has the Society established that the child cannot be adequately protected in the parents' care under terms of supervision?
What order for access between the child and his parents is in his best interests, and where should he be placed?

firac.issue: Did the Society establish reasonable grounds to believe there is a real possibility the child will suffer harm if placed in his parents' care?
firac.facts: The Society had been involved with B.T. for most of his life over concerns of parental substance misuse. Workers repeatedly observed A.R. and A.T. nodding off, slurring words, appearing intoxicated (including at a graduation and at the Society's offices), with sores on A.T.'s hands and face, a home overloaded with belongings and no space for B.T., and A.R. facing charges for forging fentanyl prescriptions. B.T. reported his parents fall asleep while caring for him.
firac.rule: Under s. 94(4) CYFSA the onus is on the Society to establish, on credible and trustworthy evidence (s. 94(10)), reasonable grounds to believe there is a real possibility that if the child is returned it is more probable than not he will suffer harm: Children's Aid Society of Ottawa-Carleton v. T., 2000 CanLII 21157 (ON SC); L.D. v. Durham CAS, 2005 CanLII 63827. The burden at this early stage does not require proof on a balance of probabilities of actual risk (CCAS Toronto v. M.L.R., 2011 ONCJ 652; CAS Ottawa v. S.G., 2021 ONSC 3177). Evidence must be viewed as a whole (Jewish Child and Family Services v. A.K., 2014 ONCJ 227).
firac.application: The court found the concerns ongoing and not shown to be isolated or resolved. The observed behaviours indicated substance abuse issues affecting the parents' ability to safely parent, and neither parent provided a viable alternative explanation; A.R.'s medical-issue and pay-as-you-go-phone explanations were unsupported and A.T. did not address the concerns at all. The court noted it is the behaviours, not their cause, that creates the risk of harm.
firac.conclusion: The Society met the s. 94(4) threshold; there are reasonable grounds to believe B.T. would likely suffer harm if placed with his parents.

firac.issue: Can the child be adequately protected in the parents' care under terms of supervision?
firac.facts: A.R. denied any substance abuse and proposed no plan to address the concerns; A.T. did not acknowledge or address them. The parents repeatedly failed to engage with the Society and did not respond to communications.
firac.rule: Section 94(4) CYFSA requires that a placement away from the parents (s. 94(2)(c) or (d)) not be ordered unless the child cannot be adequately protected by an order under s. 94(2)(a) or (b). The court must choose the least disruptive placement consistent with adequate protection, proportional to the degree of risk (CCAS Toronto v. J.O.1, 2012 ONCJ 269).
firac.application: Because the parents failed to acknowledge the concerning behaviours or the risk they create, the court concluded they could not adequately address those risks, so supervision terms would not suffice to protect B.T. in their care.
firac.conclusion: The Society established that B.T. cannot be adequately protected in his parents' care under supervision.

firac.issue: What placement and access order is in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: B.T. is 7, has ADHD and learning/speech needs, and has Metis heritage through his father with no identified community. He was already residing with his paternal aunt and uncle (the D.s) in Sudbury under a without-prejudice order and reported being content there while hoping eventually to return to his parents. The Office of the Children's Lawyer conveyed his views.
firac.rule: Best interests under s. 74(3) CYFSA, the access provisions of ss. 94(2)(c),(8) and 104, and the augmented best-interests test for Indigenous children under ss. 10 and 16 of An Act respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families, S.C. 2019, c. 24, which prioritizes placement with a parent then another family member and preserving cultural connections. The child's views must be considered (s. 94(11)).
firac.application: Placement with the paternal aunt and uncle (relatives) accorded with the Federal Act's placement priorities and the least-disruptive principle, maintaining family connection while protecting B.T. The court ordered supervised access to the parents at least monthly for two hours per day when they are in Sudbury, with additional visits as arranged.
firac.conclusion: B.T. was placed in the temporary care and custody of the D.s under Society supervision (s. 94(2)(c)) with supervised parental access; matter adjourned to July 14, 2025.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a child protection proceeding under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is central to the s. 74(3) and Federal Act analysis. K048 (custody/access) captures the temporary care and custody and supervised access orders that are the core relief. K001 (Administrative law) is a weak/borderline pick reflecting the statutory child-protection framework and society intervention, but is included cautiously; the case is fundamentally family/child-protection. No tier-2 keyword specifically covers child protection or Indigenous/Métis child placement, so the selection is limited to the closest available terms and falls short of five strongly-fitting keywords — the vocabulary lacks a dedicated child-protection term.
location_rationale: The court is the Superior Court of Justice - Ontario. The applicant is Family and Children's Services of Renfrew County, whose seat is Pembroke; the child now resides in Sudbury but the proceeding is a Renfrew County matter. The decision does not expressly state the sitting city, so Pembroke is inferred cautiously from the Renfrew County location; province is Ontario per 'SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE - ONTARIO'.
registry_rationale: No registry office is named in the decision beyond the court file number (FC-16-FO000468-0004); the specific registry town is not stated, so it is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Shirli Drori v. Marcio Martins

defining_issues: Should the father's proposed nesting arrangement for the four-year-old child be granted on an interim basis, and should the mother's cross-motion for primary care and limited paternal contact be granted?
Should the mother's breach of the prior court order prohibiting video-taping the child be addressed by referral of a contempt issue?

firac.issue: On an interim basis, is a nesting arrangement in the four-year-old child's best interests, or should the mother have primary care with limited contact between the child and his father?
firac.facts: The parties, married in 2010 and separated in 2016, continued to share a 'toxic' matrimonial home with their son EM, born in 2013. The mother is Jewish, the father Catholic; EM attended a Jewish daycare and was thriving. A s. 30 CLRA assessment was underway. The father sought a nesting arrangement whereby each parent would care for the child in the home while the other stayed with nearby relatives; the mother sought primary care and limited paternal contact, alleging (with disputed and uncorroborated evidence) that the father's family exposed EM to anti-Semitic influences.
firac.rule: Section 16(1),(2),(8),(10) of the Divorce Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.)) requires interim custody/access orders to be made considering only the best interests of the child and directs that the child should have as much contact with each spouse as is consistent with those interests, taking into account the willingness of the parent seeking custody to facilitate such contact. Reeves v. Reeves, 2001 CarswellOnt 277, holds that a parent who discourages the child's relationship with the other parent demonstrates an inability to act in the child's best interests.
firac.application: The court found the mother's evidence to be largely gratuitous, accusatory and demeaning of the father, with no indication she would support EM's relationship with his father — 'quite the opposite.' Objective communications (texts referring to 'my son', threats, non-compliance) contrasted with the father's measured, child-focused conduct. The anti-Semitism allegations, while troubling and requiring investigation, arose only after separation with no supporting evidence and appeared to be an 'ill-conceived strategy' not mindful of the child. The father's nesting proposal separated the parties, allowed each to parent, and respected each parent's religion; the mother's claim she had no alternative accommodation was unsupported.
firac.conclusion: The father's motion for a nesting arrangement (paragraphs 1 and 2 of his notice of motion) was granted effective March 21, 2017; the mother's cross-motion for primary care and limited contact was refused, and her additional relief was adjourned.

firac.issue: Should the mother's admitted breach of Kaufman J.'s order prohibiting video-taping of the child be addressed?
firac.facts: Less than three weeks after Kaufman J.'s January 30, 2017 order barring either parent from video-taping the child except for special occasions, the mother video-taped EM making anti-Semitic statements and sent three videos (taken while driving) to B'nai Brith in aid of her custody dispute. The father did not seek a contempt finding.
firac.rule: Court orders must be obeyed and non-compliance must carry consequences, particularly where a child's welfare is involved; the court retains authority to address breaches even absent a party's contempt request.
firac.application: The court found the mother's video-taping to be a clear breach of the order and held it could not ignore her conduct notwithstanding the father's silence on contempt.
firac.conclusion: The order includes a provision referring the question of whether the mother should be found in contempt of Kaufman J.'s order to him for directions at the July 6, 2017 combined settlement/trial scheduling conference.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test under s. 16(8) of the Divorce Act and central to the ruling. K048 (custody/access) captures the interim parenting/nesting dispute. K117 (Divorce Act) is the enabling statute expressly relied on. K052 (religious upbringing) applies given the interfaith context and orders requiring respect for each parent's religion and the Jewish daycare. K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) reflect the mother's allegations that the child was exposed to anti-Semitic statements and the family's Jewish faith, which figured heavily in the analysis. K089 (B'nai Brith) is engaged because the mother sent videos to that organization — a borderline but genuine entity reference. K058 is somewhat weak as the antisemitism was alleged rather than adjudicated, but it shaped the court's assessment.
location_rationale: The decision header reads 'CITATION: Drori v. Martins, 2017 ONSC 1713' followed by 'NEWMARKET' and 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE', establishing Newmarket, Ontario as the location.
registry_rationale: The header shows 'NEWMARKET' and 'COURT FILE NO.: FC-16-52318-00', indicating the Newmarket registry of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Droit de la famille — 17338

defining_issues: Was there a significant change in the child's circumstances justifying review of the 2012 custody order?
Is it in the child's best interests to grant shared custody on a weekly alternating basis rather than maintaining the status quo?
How should the custody modalities, in particular the Jewish and Christian holidays, be allocated between the parents?
How should the various claimed expenses (activities, camps, vaccinations, school fees, Hebrew program) be classified and apportioned as basic child support or special expenses?

firac.issue: Was there a significant change in the child's condition, means, needs or circumstances justifying a review of the 2012 custody order?
firac.facts: The 2012 agreement, homologated when the child was three, gave the mother custody with the father having visitation, at a time when the father worked full time and the mother was unemployed. Since then the child grew older and expressed a desire to see his father more; both parents relocated to the same town (Town B), with the father now living a five-minute walk from the child's school, and each parent's work and living situations changed.
firac.rule: Under art. 612 C.c.Q. a court may review decisions concerning a child at any time if warranted by circumstances; before varying a custody order the court must be satisfied there has been a change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances of the child since the order was rendered.
firac.application: The court found the child's needs, means and conditions had significantly changed since 2012 — the child was older and had expressed a wish to spend more time with his father, and the parents' residences and situations had changed materially.
firac.conclusion: A significant change was established and a review of the custody agreement was justified.

firac.issue: Is shared custody on a weekly alternating schedule in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The father sought shared custody on a weekly alternating basis; the mother, after reopening the hearing over safety concerns involving her partner's ex-wife, asked to maintain the status quo, citing the child's occasional anxiety. The father lived a short walk from the school; the child had a good relationship with both parents and the father's fiancée; the child already spent alternating weeks with each parent during winter and summer holidays without adjustment difficulties.
firac.rule: Shared custody is assessed against criteria including the child's age, needs and desires; each parent's ability, values, stability and availability; parental communication; proximity of residences; and absence of alienation (Droit de la famille – 131039, 2013 QCCS 1702; G.G. c. J.P., 2005 QCCA 210). Refusal by one parent or communication difficulties do not preclude shared custody.
firac.application: The new safety evidence did not affect the father's ability to provide a safe environment. The mother's contradictory testimony about the child's anxiety was rejected; the child's occasional anxiety was not an obstacle, given he already alternated weeks during holidays without difficulty and both parents were capable caregivers. The mother's refusal and communication difficulties did not bar shared custody.
firac.conclusion: Shared custody on a weekly alternating schedule was ordered as being in the child's best interests; progressive shared custody and play therapy were not warranted.

firac.issue: How should custody modalities regarding Jewish and Christian holidays be allocated?
firac.facts: The mother requested that the child spend important Jewish holidays with her (Passover, Shavuot, Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippour, Sukkot, Simchat Torah, Hanouka). The father sought to limit the days for multi-day Jewish holidays and to have priority when Jewish and Christian holidays conflict.
firac.rule: Custody modalities are set according to the child's best interests, maintaining workable arrangements agreed by the parties where appropriate.
firac.application: The court endorsed the modalities the parties agreed on and maintained the 2012 approach for holidays: the child would be with the mother for the listed Jewish holidays, with days exchanged when they fall on the father's time where possible, and with the father on Christmas Eve and Easter unless otherwise agreed.
firac.conclusion: Holiday modalities were fixed accordingly, integrating the Jewish holidays with the father's Christmas Eve and Easter time.

firac.issue: How should the claimed expenses be classified as basic child support or reimbursable special expenses, and apportioned?
firac.facts: The mother claimed inclusion of activities and camp fees in the basic contribution and reimbursement of vaccinations, school fees, camp fees, the Hebrew Studies P.E.L.O. program and activities, totalling over $8,500. The father contested many items, noting lack of consultation, refundable fees, tax credits already received, and his opposition to religious schooling.
firac.rule: Art. 587.2 C.c.Q. requires a parent to contribute to the basic parental contribution and specified expenses; special expenses must exceed basic needs (food, housing, clothing, leisure, etc.) and, under art. 587.1 al. 2 C.c.Q. and s. 9 of the Règlement, must be reasonable given the parents' means and tied to the child's particular needs (Droit de la famille – 3228, 1999 CanLII 13173). Leisure expenses up to about 5% of annual support fall within the basic contribution.
firac.application: The court treated activities and camp fees as special expenses (not proven recurrent or agreed). It dismissed the vaccination claim (no proof of dates or payment) and the [school A]/[school B] registration and supply fees (basic contribution). It granted 95% of the school uniform ($458.75), reimbursement for the Hebrew Studies program ($347) as a non-excessive language/cultural expense, $600 for camps (accounting for tax credits and the mother's unemployment), and $636.34 for 2016 activities after deducting the 5% leisure threshold. Child support was set at $382.02/month.
firac.conclusion: Child support fixed at $382.02/month; specified special-expense reimbursements ordered ($347 Hebrew program, $458.75 uniform, $600 camps, $636.34 activities); other claims dismissed; medical/dental to be paid directly by the father with the mother refunding her share of uncovered amounts.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) are the core custody issues. K050 (parental/child support) and the special-expenses analysis under art. 587.2 C.c.Q. support the support keyword. K052 (religious upbringing) and K027 (Jewish holidays) are directly engaged by the Hebrew Studies program dispute and the detailed allocation of Passover, Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippour, Sukkot, etc. K093 (Jewish) and K095 (Jewish family) reflect the family's Jewish identity and cultural context central to the holiday and Hebrew-program modalities; K095 is a slightly weaker/borderline entity tag but fits the family context.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'SUPERIOR COURT, CANADA, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC, DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and is dated February 23, 2017 at Montreal.
registry_rationale: The 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and file number 500-04-059037-128 indicate the Montreal registry of the Superior Court of Quebec.

name_verification.name_in_document: Droit de la famille — 241773

defining_issues: In a custody dispute between the surviving parent and a third party after the mother's death, should custody be awarded to the father or to Mrs. M.?
How should the attributes of parental authority (schooling, extracurricular activities, travel/passport, medical care) be allocated between the sole surviving parent and the third-party caregiver?
What financial (alimentary) contribution must the father provide for the child's needs and expenses?

firac.issue: Should custody of X be awarded to her father (the surviving parent) or to Mrs. M. (a third party) following the mother's death?
firac.facts: After a highly conflictual separation and the father's criminal charges relating to family violence, X lived exclusively with her mother for about 15 months and had no significant contact with the father. Before dying of cancer, the mother asked Mrs. M., who lives in Michigan, to become X's guardian. X, nearly 10, categorically refuses contact with her father and wishes to live with Mrs. M. A psychosocial expert found X to be in a conflict of loyalty instigated by the late mother and recommended the father have custody, though she never assessed Mrs. M.
firac.rule: The child's interest is the determining factor (art. 33 C.C.Q.). Under C.(G.) v. V.-F.(T.), [1987] 2 S.C.R. 244, to obtain custody a third party must rebut the presumption favouring the parent, show the child's development is likely compromised in the parent's care, and show she can provide care the parent cannot. Between ages 8 and 11 the child's wishes matter but are not determinative and carry less weight when tainted by a conflict of loyalty (Droit de la famille — 15754, 2015 QCCA 650; Droit de la famille — 201310, 2020 QCCA 1139).
firac.application: X's refusal to see her father, the allegations of family violence and the criminal conditions rebutted the parental presumption, so an inquiry into X's interest was warranted. However, the court found the past family violence less severe than the no-contact conditions suggested, that the father's parental capacity was adequate (demonstrated by his successful care of Z), and that X's rejection stemmed largely from a conflict of loyalty amplified by the mother. Mrs. M. gave excellent, loving day-to-day care and provided emotional security, but she treated the father as merely the 'biological father', perpetuated the parental conflict, instilled fear of the father in X, and unilaterally uprooted X to Michigan. The court concluded X needs both, that permanent placement with either alone would harm her, and that her long-term best interest lies with her father after therapeutic repair of the relationship.
firac.conclusion: Shared custody ordered: X to reside temporarily with Mrs. M. in Michigan from December 7, 2024 to June 27, 2025 subject to therapy and access conditions, then returned to Quebec to live permanently with her father as of June 28, 2025, with continuing access for Mrs. M.

firac.issue: How should the attributes of parental authority be allocated between the father and Mrs. M.?
firac.facts: Mrs. M. sought attributes of parental authority over schooling, extracurricular activities, travel/passport and medical care. The mother's will had designated Mrs. M. as tutor. Mrs. M. had enrolled X in a Michigan school and set up a new life there without the father's involvement.
firac.rule: On the mother's death the father alone exercises parental authority (art. 600 C.C.Q.) and retains the right to supervise the child's maintenance and education (art. 605 C.C.Q.); he is legal tutor by operation of law (art. 192 C.C.Q.), unaffected by custody (art. 195 C.C.Q.), and the will's designation of a tutor has no effect while the surviving parent is alive and not deprived of parental authority (arts. 197 and 201 C.C.Q.).
firac.application: There was no evidence justifying any partial deprivation of the father's parental authority. The father remained sole holder of parental authority and legal tutor. For minimal stability, X was authorized to finish the school year at the Michigan school, but that choice should have involved the father. The father alone controls passports and non-urgent medical decisions; extracurricular decisions are joint given day-to-day geography; medical emergencies allow Mrs. M. to consent if the father cannot be reached.
firac.conclusion: The father was declared sole holder of parental authority and legal tutor; Mrs. M. may make only the limited decisions authorized by the judgment, with the father retaining passport control, non-urgent medical decisions and access to all school and medical records.

firac.issue: What alimentary (financial) contribution must the father provide for X, and which of Mrs. M.'s expenses must he reimburse?
firac.facts: The father offered monthly child support of $649.17 based on a $103,000 income figure from the interim divorce order; no evidence of his actual income was led. Mrs. M. incurred relocation, tuition and medical expenses for X without the father's authorization.
firac.rule: Mrs. M., as a third party, has no alimentary obligation toward X; the parent bears the support obligation, quantified according to the child's needs and the payor's means, guided by the child's best interest.
firac.application: The court accepted the father's offer of $649.17 monthly support. It refused to order reimbursement of unauthorized relocation costs but required the father to pay tuition limited to $6,000 (since X was already in private school and completing the year without a change was in her interest) and to cover medical and dental costs from December 7, 2024 to June 27, 2025.
firac.conclusion: Father ordered to pay $649.17 monthly support from June 3, 2024 to June 27, 2025, to reimburse tuition up to $6,000 in two instalments, and to reimburse medical and dental costs (including insurance) for the temporary period.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) is the core dispute between a parent and third party. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing legal standard applied throughout under art. 33 C.C.Q. and C.(G.) v. V.-F.(T.). K050 (parental support) covers the father's child support and expense-reimbursement obligations. K054 (wills/estates) is engaged because the late mother's will designated Mrs. M. as tutor, and the court addressed its legal effect under arts. 197 and 201 C.C.Q. K052 (religious upbringing) and K093 (Jewish) are weaker picks — the family's Jewish identity (Bat Mitzvah, godparents, contrast with the Michigan school's Christian emphasis) is only a minor factual consideration, not a central issue, so both are flagged as borderline.
location_rationale: The header identifies the 'SUPERIOR COURT', 'PROVINCE OF QUEBEC', 'DISTRICT OF BEAUHARNOIS'. Province is expressly Quebec; the judicial district is Beauharnois, which is used as the city/registry designation.

case_name: Forged Construction Ltd. v Westurban Developments Ltd.

defining_issues: What is the applicable standard of review on an appeal from a Master's discretionary order for security for costs?
Did the Master err in law by ordering security for costs without finding that the respondent had established a prima facie case that the appellant had insufficient assets to pay costs?
Was the Master's conclusion that the appellant's assets were at risk of dissipation clearly wrong or based on mere speculation?

firac.issue: What is the applicable standard of review on an appeal from a Master's discretionary order for security for costs?
firac.facts: The appellant appealed a Master's order requiring $20,000 security for costs, a stay pending payment, and liberty to seek further security. The parties disagreed whether the first ground raised a question of law reviewable for correctness or a question of fact/discretion reviewable for clear error.
firac.rule: A purely interlocutory decision of a master is reviewed on a 'clearly wrong' standard; questions of law, final orders, or rulings vital to the final issue are reviewed by rehearing on the merits (Ralph's Auto Supply (B.C.) Ltd. v. Ken Ransford Holding Ltd., 2011 BCSC 999). An order for security for costs is an interlocutory, discretionary order, not a final order (Beta Properties Ltd. v. 4301 Hastings Development Ltd., 2018 BCSC 103).
firac.application: The court held that the appellant mischaracterized its first ground as a question of law. The Master had correctly stated the legal test; the true complaint was about how she assessed the evidence and exercised her discretion. That is a question of fact within a discretionary, interlocutory order. The parties agreed the second ground was governed by the 'clearly wrong' standard.
firac.conclusion: Both grounds are reviewed on the 'clearly wrong' standard; neither raised a reviewable question of law warranting a rehearing on the merits.

firac.issue: Did the Master err in law by ordering security for costs without finding that the respondent had established a prima facie case that the appellant lacked sufficient assets to pay costs?
firac.facts: The Alberta-based appellant owned no real property, its assets were subject to a general security agreement (GSA) in favour of Merchant Advance Capital giving priority over its cash, and it declined to provide particulars of the Merchant and Riviera loans. The Master ordered security, noting the lack of reliable evidence of the appellant's financial position.
firac.rule: On a security-for-costs application the court first determines whether the defendant has established a prima facie case that the corporate plaintiff has insufficient exigible assets to pay costs; once met, security is generally ordered unless there is no arguable defence (Ocean Pastures Corporation v. Old Masset Economic Development Corporation, 2016 BCCA 12; Fat Mel's Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Company). Where cash assets are encumbered by a GSA, a prima facie case of no exigible assets is established (Pixhug Media Inc. v. Steeves, 2016 BCSC 1714).
firac.application: The Master correctly set out the test, reviewed the evidence and authorities, and found at para. 22 that the Merchant GSA created a priority claim over the appellant's cash such that there was a real possibility no cash would remain to pay the respondent's costs if the action failed. Read as a whole, her reasons clearly found that a prima facie case had been made out; the appellant's argument ignored her reasons in their totality and recast a factual/discretionary assessment as legal error, as in Beta.
firac.conclusion: The Master applied the law correctly and made the necessary prima facie finding; the first ground of appeal fails.

firac.issue: Was the Master's finding that the appellant's assets were at risk of dissipation clearly wrong or based on mere speculation?
firac.facts: Uncontroverted evidence established a GSA over all the appellant's assets in favour of Merchant, whose particulars the appellant chose not to disclose; the appellant relied on cash holdings and ongoing income but produced no accountant-prepared financial statements.
firac.rule: Once a defendant establishes a prima facie case that a plaintiff lacks sufficient assets, the plaintiff must provide evidence of exigible assets (WestCorp Solutions Ltd. v. Collins, 2014 BCSC 1606; New Home Warranty of B.C. v. 462146 B.C. Ltd., 2000 BCSC 143). A discretionary risk assessment involving judgment is not 'mere speculation' (Beta Properties Ltd. v. 4301 Hastings Development Ltd., 2018 BCSC 103).
firac.application: The Master accepted that the appellant's assets were encumbered by the Merchant GSA and that the appellant failed to rebut the prima facie case with evidence of exigible unencumbered assets. WestCorp and New Home were distinguishable because there no GSA existed and the plaintiffs had sufficient unencumbered assets. The Master's risk assessment was a proper exercise of judgment on the evidence, not speculation.
firac.conclusion: The Master exercised her discretion judicially and was not clearly wrong; the second ground of appeal fails.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the correct tier-1 practice area: this is a commercial/construction dispute involving a builder's lien and a security-for-costs application. K014 (standard of review) is squarely engaged — the central contest was whether the Master's order was reviewable for correctness or 'clearly wrong.' defining_issues: Does a parent with day-to-day custody have the right to remove the children from the jurisdiction to reside elsewhere without the other parent's consent, in the absence of special circumstances?

Do the specific access terms in the consent decree, including detailed provisions for visitation and Jewish holidays, disclose an intention that the children remain in close proximity to both parents so as to bar relocation?

firac.issue: May a custodial parent relocate the children out of the province without the other parent's permission absent special circumstances?
firac.facts: Following a consent divorce decree granting joint legal custody but placing day-to-day care and the right to select the children's place of residence with the father (petitioner), the father proposed to move to California for about one year for business reasons. The mother (applicant) sought an order restraining removal of the children or varying the decree so the children would reside with her.
firac.rule: In the absence of special circumstances, a parent who has custody has the right to remove the children without the permission of the other parent, absent some specific agreement to the contrary or access terms clearly indicating the parties intended the children to remain in close proximity: Wright v. Wright (1973), 1 O.R. (2d) 337 (C.A.); Re Dube (1956), 3 D.L.R. (2d) 421; Beck v. Beck, [1949] 2 W.W.R. 1175. The welfare of the children is the paramount consideration.
firac.application: The decree expressly assigned to the father responsibility for the children's day-to-day care and decisions including their place of residence. Although the father's move was voluntary rather than employer-compelled, the governing authority permits a custodial parent to relocate. Considering the whole decree and, paramountly, the children's welfare, the court concluded the father should be permitted to have the children reside with him in California, and the relocation would not unreasonably deny the mother access.
firac.conclusion: The custodial father is permitted to take the children to California; the application to restrain removal or to vary custody is refused.

firac.issue: Did the detailed access provisions, including Jewish-holiday and Florida-visit terms, evidence an intention to keep the children in close proximity to both parents so as to prevent relocation?
firac.facts: The decree gave the mother alternate-weekend access, access on specified Jewish holidays (with an obligation to take the children to synagogue services), a portion of the summer, and a right to take the children to Florida annually. The mother had no permanent Ontario residence, spent considerable time in Florida and elsewhere, and was a woman of independent means.
firac.rule: Access terms bar relocation only where they clearly indicate the parties must have intended the children to remain in close proximity for the access right to be effective (Wright v. Wright); the children's welfare remains paramount.
firac.application: The court found the consent decree, read against the parties' way of life, disclosed no such intention. The mother's wealth and mobility meant she could readily visit the children in California; the Florida-visit clause lost its force as an indicator of an intention to keep the children nearby. Only the Jewish-holiday/synagogue clause gave slight difficulty, but such detailed provisions would need revision once relocation was permitted. Minor formal variations to visitation and birthday-party clauses were ordered.
firac.conclusion: The access terms did not indicate an intention to keep the children in close proximity; the application was dismissed subject to specified variations, without costs.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally a family law dispute (K006) about custody and access (K048) and the custodial parent's right to relocate children, decided with the children's welfare paramount (K047 best interests of the child). The decree's provisions on religious education and the obligation to attend synagogue on Jewish holidays engage religious upbringing (K052) and Jewish holidays (K027); the family is Jewish (K093). These last three are somewhat peripheral to the ratio (which is the mobility/access analysis) but are genuinely part of the decree provisions the court had to weigh, particularly the Jewish-holiday access clause the court flagged as giving 'a little difficulty.'
location_rationale: The decision is of the Ontario Supreme Court (High Court of Justice) and bears the notation '(Toronto)' before the judgment, indicating the matter was heard at Toronto in Ontario.
registry_rationale: The parenthetical '(Toronto)' following counsel's appearances indicates the Toronto registry/sittings.

defining_issues: Were the security and development of the children compromised within the meaning of the Youth Protection Act because of the parents' conflictual and violent behaviour and the child's serious behavioural problems?
What protective measures should be ordered in the children's best interests, including custody and the modality of contact with the father?

firac.issue: Were the security and development of the children compromised under the Youth Protection Act given the parental conflict, domestic violence, and the elder child's behavioural difficulties?
firac.facts: The Director of Youth Protection filed petitions alleging that the parents' behaviour and way of life created a risk of moral or physical danger. The father had a history of verbal and physical abuse toward the mother and children and faced an assault charge; both parents had pending assault/harassment charges. The elder child J... was aggressive toward his mother, had expressed suicidal ideations, threatened her with a knife and struck her with a broom, and admitted difficulty controlling his anger. Both parents admitted the majority of the allegations, and the children had witnessed violent outbursts.
firac.rule: Under the Youth Protection Act, security and development may be declared compromised where the parents' behaviour or way of life creates a risk of moral or physical danger (s. 38), and where a child has serious behavioural problems the parents cannot resolve (s. 38 h)). Section 90 requires the court to give reasons.
firac.application: The Court accepted the parents' admissions, the testimony of the Youth Protection Delegate Ms. Linda Murphy, and the Director's reports. The evidence showed an ongoing conflictual and violent relationship witnessed by the children, persisting tension, and an impact on the children's behaviour. This satisfied the statutory threshold.
firac.conclusion: The Court declared that the security and development of both children were compromised and granted the Director's petition.

firac.issue: What protective measures best served the children's interests, particularly regarding custody and contact with the father?
firac.facts: The mother had interim custody from the Superior Court and agreed with the Director's proposed measures. The Director recommended the children be entrusted to the mother with aid, counsel and assistance, and that the father's contacts be supervised. The father sought unsupervised visits, cited difficulty finding a supervisor, and said he saw no need for anger management or therapy.
firac.rule: Measures ordered under the Youth Protection Act must serve the children's protection and best interests; the court may entrust the child to a parent, order supervised contacts, order psychiatric assessment and treatment, and provide aid, counsel and assistance.
firac.application: Given the persisting tension, the Court found the parents must prioritize their children's needs and follow therapy at least to help the children cope. It maintained custody with the mother, ordered supervised paternal contacts until December 31, 2002, continued psychiatric follow-up and assessment at the Jewish General Hospital, and recommended therapy for both parents.
firac.conclusion: The Court ordered custody to the mother, supervised paternal contact, psychiatric assessment and follow-up, recommended parental therapy, and ordered one year of aid, counsel and assistance under the Director's supervision.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area, as this is a Quebec youth-protection proceeding. K047 (best interests of the child) captures the court's core reasoning that the parents must put their children's needs first. K048 (custody/access) reflects the orders entrusting the children to the mother and setting supervised paternal contacts. case_name: Family and Children’s Services of Guelph and Wellington County v. A.M.P. and K.D.S.

name_verification.name_in_document: FAMILY and CHILDREN'S SERVICES of GUELPH AND WELLINGTON COUNTY v. A.M.P. AND K.D.S.

defining_issues: Was this child protection matter appropriate for summary judgment, i.e. was there no genuine issue requiring a trial?
Were the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(k) of the CYFSA on the ground of the parent's unavailability to exercise custodial rights?
Were the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(h) of the CYFSA on the ground of a risk of serious emotional harm?
Were the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(d) of the CYFSA on the ground of a risk of sexual abuse or exploitation?
What disposition and access arrangements were in the children's best interests?

firac.issue: Was summary judgment appropriate in this child protection proceeding, or was there a genuine issue requiring a trial?
firac.facts: FACS moved for summary judgment under r. 16 of the Family Law Rules for protection findings and placement of the two children with their Mother. The Father opposed, alleging genuine credibility issues (coaching by the Mother and half-sister) requiring a trial. The record included multiple affidavits from FACS workers, the Mother, the Father and his family, and OCL submissions reflecting the children's consistent wishes.
firac.rule: Rule 16(4)-(6) of the Family Law Rules permits final judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; the moving party bears the burden. Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7 sets the fairness/proportionality test, and rr. 16(6.1)-(6.2) allow weighing evidence, assessing credibility and drawing inferences unless the interests of justice require a trial. Kawartha-Haliburton Children's Aid Society v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316 adapts Hryniak to child protection, requiring caution and application of the CYFSA objectives, including the child's best interests.
firac.application: The court screened the evidence, applied the state-of-mind hearsay exception to the children's statements (used to show their state of mind, not the truth of contents), and found the children's views consistent and non-suspicious despite the Father's coaching allegations. It concluded the record was sufficiently comprehensive to make the necessary findings of fact and apply the law proportionately, expeditiously and less expensively than a trial, while recognizing the Charter implications for vulnerable litigants.
firac.conclusion: There was no genuine issue requiring a trial for the s. 74(2)(h) and (k) grounds; summary judgment was the just, proportionate means of resolution.

firac.issue: Were the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(k) because the Father was unavailable to exercise custodial rights?
firac.facts: The Father was subject to bail conditions barring contact with the children arising from sexual offence charges involving their half-sister G.S. He had not sought to vary those conditions, offered no explanation, and had not seen the children in over two years. The care arrangements were made by FACS, and he proposed instead that the children live with his sister without explaining why that served their best interests.
firac.rule: Section 74(2)(k) CYFSA: a child is in need of protection where the parent is unavailable to exercise custodial rights and has not made adequate provision for the child's care. Unavailability is an objective determination independent of subjective intention (Children's Aid Society of Kingston (City) v. H.); incarceration or comparable constraints can trigger the analogous predecessor provision, s. 37(2)(i) CFSA (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. C.T.).
firac.application: Although not incarcerated, the Father's unremedied bail conditions rendered him unable to exercise custodial rights for over two years, and he had made no adequate provision for the children's care beyond arrangements FACS itself made. The court rejected his explanation blaming the Mother and G.S., noting he and his family had done little to promote a relationship with the children.
firac.conclusion: The children were found in need of protection under s. 74(2)(k).

firac.issue: Were the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(h) due to a risk of serious emotional harm caused by the Father?
firac.facts: The children reported the Father's degrading treatment of their half-sister G.S. (calling her a 'slut', 'ho', 'liar'), his stalking behaviour, involving them in that conduct (creating social media accounts, filming with a dashcam), erratic and frightening driving, appearing naked before S.R.S., and fear that he would 'turn on' them as he did with G.S. No expert report on emotional harm was filed.
firac.rule: Section 74(2)(h) CYFSA requires a risk of serious emotional harm (of the kinds in s. 74(2)(f)) causally connected to the parent's conduct (Children's Aid Society of Algoma v. A.B.). A clinical diagnosis or expert evidence is not mandatory; the court may draw inferences and take judicial notice from a panoply of evidence (Chukwunomso v. Ransome; Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S.A.P., 2020 ONCA 208). The children's statements are admissible under the state-of-mind hearsay exception (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. N.N.).
firac.application: The court relied on the children's consistent statements to show their state of mind — fear of the Father, experience of him as unstable and erratic — and found the risk of serious emotional harm, including anxiety, causally connected to his conduct. Having not seen him in over two years and being clearly frightened, the children would likely suffer emotional harm if returned.
firac.conclusion: The children were found in need of protection under s. 74(2)(h).

firac.issue: Were the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(d) due to a risk of sexual abuse or exploitation?
firac.facts: FACS relied on the Father's prior sexual assault conviction, the pending charges involving G.S., his statements about G.S., and his appearing naked before S.R.S. The children denied being touched. The only evidence of the details of the alleged offences against G.S. was worker D.W.'s account of witnessing G.S.'s police interview; G.S. swore an affidavit but declined to detail the assaults.
firac.rule: Section 74(2)(d) CYFSA: a child is in need of protection where there is a risk of sexual abuse or exploitation as described in s. 74(2)(c). Hearsay must satisfy the principled exception (necessity and reliability) of R. v. Khan, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 531.
firac.application: D.W.'s recounting of G.S.'s allegations, if offered for their truth, was hearsay; because G.S. had sworn an affidavit, the evidence was not 'necessary' and the Khan exception did not apply. There was thus no admissible direct evidence of the alleged offences. The Father and his supporting deponents raised sufficient disputed material facts that this ground could not be resolved summarily.
firac.conclusion: The court declined to find the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(d) on the summary judgment motion.

firac.issue: What disposition and access orders were in the children's best interests?
firac.facts: The children consistently expressed wishes to remain with their Mother, to have no forced contact with the Father, and to maintain a relationship with their half-sister G.S. The Mother was described as protective and supportive; FACS raised no protection concerns about G.S. The Father remained subject to no-contact bail conditions.
firac.rule: Sections 101-102 CYFSA govern disposition where a child is in need of protection, with best interests (s. 74(3)) as the governing principle; s. 105(2) requires an access order unless contact is not in the child's best interests, and s. 104(1) permits sibling access orders. The child's views and wishes must be given due weight per s. 74(3)(a) and Article 12 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (Ontario (Children's Lawyer) v. Ontario (IPC), 2018 ONCA 559).
firac.application: Weighing the s. 74(3) factors — the children's consistent mature wishes, the Mother as a protective factor, their need for stability and continuity, the risk of harm if returned to the Father, and the effects of delay — the court placed the children with the Mother under s. 102. Access to the Father was ordered in accordance with the children's wishes and at the Mother's discretion; sibling access to G.S. was likewise ordered.
firac.conclusion: Final order placing the children with the Mother under s. 102, with access to the Father and to G.S. governed by the children's wishes and the Mother's discretion.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 practice area for this child protection proceeding under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is central — the s. 74(3) best-interests analysis drove both the protection findings and the disposition. K048 (custody/access) reflects the s. 102 placement order and the access orders concerning the Father and sibling G.S. K012 (procedural fairness) is engaged through the Hryniak/Kawartha-Haliburton fairness analysis governing whether summary judgment could justly resolve the matter — a borderline pick, used here as the closest available tag for the summary-judgment fairness question. K107 (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms) reflects the court's express recognition of Charter implications for vulnerable litigants in child protection — a weak/peripheral mention. K050 (parental support) is weak, arising only from the passing reference to the Mother no longer paying support, and is included to reach the minimum count; it is flagged as marginal. The controlled vocabulary lacks specific tags for child protection/summary judgment/hearsay, so several closest-available terms were used.

defining_issues: Did the testator possess sufficient cognitive capacity to make a valid will on February 25, 2014?
Was the testator subject to undue influence when he made his will?

firac.issue: Did Aldo Occhionero have the mental capacity required to make a valid will on February 25, 2014?
firac.facts: Aldo, aged 76 and dying of terminal stomach cancer, signed a will three months before his death leaving everything to his sister Rina, with whom he had recently gone to live. Evidence from his wife, son, a domestic aide and a friend described marked cognitive and behavioural deterioration through 2013-2014 (disorientation, hiding, self-harm, incoherence). His hospital chart (CH Verdun, Feb. 5-14, 2014) recorded confusion and disorientation as to time, place and person on Feb. 5 and Feb. 11, needing full assistance to dress. The expert geriatric physician, Dr. Brock, opined Aldo probably suffered moderate-to-severe dementia and lacked capacity. The notary who prepared and took the will spent only 10-15 minutes with Aldo and did not verify capacity or know of his health history.
firac.rule: A testator must have sufficient memory, comprehension and judgment to understand the nature and consequences of the act — knowing the nature and extent of assets, the nature of the deed, the identity of and relationship with beneficiaries, and being able to relate and remember these factors (criteria drawn from Barette/Duguay). Capacity is presumed, but once that presumption is rebutted the party upholding the will bears the burden of proving capacity (Caron c. Forest (Succession de), 2010 QCCS 2604).
firac.application: The medical records and corroborated lay testimony rebutted the presumption of capacity. Dr. Brock's uncontradicted expert opinion, consistent with the CH Verdun chart, established probable dementia with an estimated MMSE score of 8-15 even on good days. Rina produced no contrary expertise, and her account of a normal, healthy Aldo conflicted with the medical file and was found not credible. The notary's brief, uninformed meeting could not establish capacity. Rina failed to prove that Aldo had regained sufficient capacity by February 25.
firac.conclusion: Aldo lacked the capacity to make a valid will; the will is null on this ground.

firac.issue: Was the will the product of undue influence exercised by the sister/sole beneficiary?
firac.facts: After Aldo moved in with Rina on February 3, 2014, Rina concealed his hospitalization and terminal diagnosis from his wife and children, refused Francesca's requests to see or speak with him, threatened Francesca ('my family will destroy yours'), and had a lawyer's letter sent demanding Francesca cease contact. Rina and her family were constantly at his bedside while his wife and children were kept away. She repeatedly denigrated Francesca, Lisa and Gianni to the social worker and medical staff in Aldo's presence. The will, made through Rina's son contacting the notary, named Rina sole heir and liquidator, despite Aldo never having excluded his family over the prior 30 years.
firac.rule: The party alleging undue influence bears the burden of proof. Undue influence is akin to fraud — reprehensible manoeuvres aimed at orienting a person toward a gift or legacy not otherwise granted; the court must be satisfied such conduct determined the testator's intentions. The situation is assessed globally, considering the testator's age, health, isolation, denigration of loved ones, and the circumstances of execution; it may be proven by presumption (Gatti c. Barbosa Rodrigues, 2011 QCCS 6734).
firac.application: The evidence showed Rina deliberately isolated a sick, frail and vulnerable Aldo, kept his family in ignorance, and fed him and third parties false, denigrating accounts of his wife and children. That Aldo never excluded his family across three decades but did so only once Rina took control of his affairs supported the inference that the will reflected her influence rather than his true intentions. The court was convinced Rina exercised undue influence to become sole beneficiary.
firac.conclusion: The will is also null on the ground of undue influence.

defining_issues: Did the June 1980 letter of commitment and subsequent discussions create a binding fixed-term contract of employment requiring no notice, or an indefinite hiring requiring reasonable notice of termination?
If reasonable notice was required, what was the appropriate length of notice and the resulting damages?

firac.issue: Did the June 1980 letter of commitment and subsequent discussions create a binding fixed-term contract requiring no notice, or an indefinite hiring requiring reasonable notice?
firac.facts: When the three Jewish schools were amalgamated under the defendant Board in 1980, Mr. Gilman, principal of the I.L. Peretz School, received a letter dated June 26, 1980 stating a 'Term of Contract' from September 1, 1980 to June 30, 1983 with set salaries, but expressly noting a formal contract would follow. Gilman accepted the letter subject to negotiation of a formal written contract covering benefits, notice of termination and renewal (like the contract later given to principal Cohen). No formal contract was ever negotiated or signed; Gilman continued as principal and drew the stated salaries until June 30, 1983.
firac.rule: Where documents relied on as a contract contemplate execution of a further contract, it is a question of construction whether that further contract is a condition of the bargain or merely a desire as to how an agreed transaction will proceed (Von Hatzfeldt-Wildenburg v. Alexander, [1912] 1 Ch. 284 (C.A.)). An agreement leaving critical terms to future negotiation is no contract or only an agreement to agree (May and Butcher v. R., [1929] All E.R. 679 (H.L.); National Bowling and Billiards v. Double Diamond Bowling Supply (1961), 27 D.L.R. (2d) 342 (B.C.S.C.)). Acceptance by conduct must be absolute and unequivocal, judged by what a reasonable person would believe (Welton Tool Rental Ltd. v. Douglas Aircraft Co.). A contract of service of indefinite duration contains an implied term of reasonable notice negatived only by clear words (Bagley v. Gustavson International Drilling Co.; Chadburn v. Sinclair Canada Oil Co.).
firac.application: The Court found Gilman's acceptance of the letter of commitment was conditional on negotiation of a formal contract containing additional substantive terms (pension, insurance, notice of termination and resignation). That condition was never fulfilled, so no binding fixed-term contract on the letter's terms arose. Continuing to work and accepting the salaries did not amount to an absolute and unequivocal acceptance, because Gilman had made clear his acceptance was conditional and never withdrew that condition, and Dr. Isler acknowledged the Board intended to draw up the formal contract but 'never got around to it'. What existed was a contract of service of indefinite duration carrying an implied term of reasonable notice.
firac.conclusion: There was no fixed-term contract; Gilman was employed under an indefinite hiring and was entitled to reasonable notice of termination.

firac.issue: What was the appropriate length of reasonable notice and the resulting damages?
firac.facts: Gilman, 41, held a B.A. and B.Ed., had been principal since 1977. The predecessor school board had a practice of giving about ten months' notice due to the difficulty of finding work in the Jewish school system. The comparable principal, Mr. Cohen, was given a contract terminable on six months' notice, and Gilman said he wanted a contract like Cohen's. Gilman ultimately sought and obtained work outside the Jewish system (Winnipeg School Division). Clear notice of dismissal came May 20, 1983, effective at the end of the school year (June 30, 1983); he received just over one month's notice. His 1982-83 salary was $43,200.
firac.rule: Reasonable notice is assessed by asking what the parties would have agreed to had they addressed the notice question at the time of hiring (Lazarowicz v. Orenda Engines, [1961] O.R. 141 (C.A.)).
firac.application: Applying the Lazarowicz test, the Court reasoned the Board, having given Cohen only six months, was unlikely to agree to more for Gilman, who himself wanted terms similar to Cohen's. The rationale for the predecessor board's ten-month practice (scarcity of parochial-school work) was diminished because Gilman was willing to and did look outside that system. Six months' notice was reasonable. Gilman received just over one month's notice, so he was short about five months. Five months of his $43,200 salary is $21,600, rounded to $21,000 given he received slightly more than one month.
firac.conclusion: Reasonable notice was six months; damages were assessed at $21,000 plus costs.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally a wrongful dismissal claim, so the tier-1 practice area K009 (Labour and employment law) and the specific tier-2 term K085 (wrongful dismissal) are central. The employer was a Jewish education board operating faith-based schools, engaging K043 (denominational schools) and the entity keywords K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community).
