case_name: Mercer Gold Corporation (Nevada) v. Mercer Gold Corp. (B.C.)

name_verification.name_in_document: Mercer Gold Corporation (Nevada) v. Mercer Gold Corp. (B.C.)

defining_issues: Should the portions of the amended counterclaim (ACC) claiming relief under Part 16.1 of the Securities Act (civil liability for secondary market disclosure) be struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action?
Should Mercer BC's claim for damages for the diminution in value of its shares be struck under the rule in Foss v. Harbottle?
Should the conspiracy claims against Powers and Jardine (and the diminution-based conspiracy claims generally) be struck?

Should the remaining tort claims (conspiracy to take control of the Property, passing off, slander of title, and fraudulent/negligent misrepresentation) be struck, or dealt with through the arbitration?
Are the pleadings so confusing as to be embarrassing or an abuse of process warranting that they be struck?

firac.issue: Should the ACC's Part 16.1 Securities Act (secondary market disclosure) claims be struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action?
firac.facts: Mercer BC pleaded a civil right of action under Part 16.1 of the Securities Act (s. 140.3) arising from alleged misrepresentations, but Mercer BC's shares were issued from Mercer Nevada's treasury upon execution of the Option Agreement, not acquired in the secondary market. Mercer BC had not obtained leave of the court to bring the claim.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) Supreme Court Civil Rules; the 'plain and obvious' test from Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959. Part 16.1 of the Securities Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418; s. 140.2(b), s. 140.3 and s. 140.8 (leave required). Round v. MacDonald, Dettweiler & Associates Ltd., 2011 BCSC 1416, holding that where an interest in shares was not acquired in the secondary market, no cause of action under Part 16.1 lies.
firac.application: The pleadings did not establish that Mercer BC received shares through a secondary market transaction; the shares came from Mercer Nevada's treasury, an exempt distribution outside the prescribed acquisitions, so Part 16.1 could not confer a cause of action (following Round). It was also fatal that Mercer BC had not obtained leave under s. 140.8 before advancing the claim.
firac.conclusion: The portions of the ACC claiming relief under Part 16.1 were struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action.

firac.issue: Should Mercer BC's claim for damages for the diminution in value of its shares be struck under the rule in Foss v. Harbottle?
firac.facts: Mercer BC (having taken assignments from Jivraj and his father) claimed damages for the diminution in value of the Restricted Shares in Mercer Nevada, alleging a 'pump and dump' scheme by the personal defendants that rendered the shares worthless. The pleaded loss was described as a loss common to the other shareholders of Mercer Nevada.
firac.rule: Foss v. Harbottle (1843), 67 E.R. 189 (Ch.): a company and its shareholders are distinct legal entities and only the company can sue for harm done to it; a shareholder may recover for lost share value only where there is both an 'independent relationship' with the wrongdoer and an 'independent loss' from that of the company (Robak Industries Ltd. v. Gardner, 2007 BCCA 61; Hercules Management Ltd. v. Ernst & Young, [1997] 1 S.C.R. 165).
firac.application: The Court found the claim analogous to Robak: Mercer BC's alleged loss was a consequential loss flowing from wrongs done to the company and common to all shareholders, not based on an independent relationship or independent loss. It therefore fell squarely within the rule in Foss v. Harbottle and could not be maintained by a shareholder personally.
firac.conclusion: The relief claiming damages for the diminution in value of the Restricted Shares was struck out.

firac.issue: Should the conspiracy claims against Powers and Jardine (and the diminution-based conspiracy claims) be struck?
firac.facts: Powers was alleged to have joined the conspiracy in January 2011 and Jardine in May 2011, both after the alleged conspiracy to take control of the Property through the Agreement. The conspiracy claims were founded on the alleged 'pump and dump' scheme causing diminution of Mercer BC's shares.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1); Hunt v. Carey 'plain and obvious' test; rule in Foss v. Harbottle.
firac.application: To the extent the conspiracy claims were founded on the 'pump and dump' scheme and resulting diminution of Mercer BC's shares, they were barred by the rule in Foss v. Harbottle for the same reasons as the diminution claim. The conspiracy to 'take control of the Property' by inducing Mercer BC to enter the Agreement was a matter within the arbitrators' jurisdiction (per Mercer #1).
firac.conclusion: The portions of the ACC advancing the diminution-based conspiracy claims were struck out.

firac.issue: Should the remaining tort claims (conspiracy re the Property, passing off, slander of title, and misrepresentation) be struck, or handled through arbitration?
firac.facts: Mercer BC alleged the named defendants conspired to take control of the Property, committed passing off and slander of title by asserting Mercer Nevada still held the Property rights, and made fraudulent/negligent misrepresentations (Pierce, Option Agreement and Newport Loans misrepresentations) inducing Mercer BC to enter the Agreement. These claims were closely tied to the Agreement, which was subject to arbitration.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1); Hunt v. Carey 'plain and obvious' test; s. 15 Commercial Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55 (stay of proceedings), as applied in Mercer #1.
firac.application: Mercer BC had amended its pleadings to plead the requisite elements of each tort and supporting facts; assuming those facts could be proven, it was not plain and obvious the claims were bound to fail, and the defendants had abandoned their general no-cause-of-action arguments. Because these claims were bound up with the Agreement and the roles of the personal defendants, and proceedings were already stayed pending arbitration, the Court considered it premature to strike; findings of the arbitration board might clarify or require amendment.
firac.conclusion: The applications to strike these claims were dismissed with leave to renew after the arbitration award is issued and Mercer BC has had an opportunity to consider amendments.

firac.issue: Are the pleadings so confusing as to be embarrassing or an abuse of process, warranting that they be struck?
firac.facts: Pierce argued the ACC was confusing because it cross-referenced paragraphs of the Response to Civil Claim and did not clearly identify the agreement or concerted action constituting the conspiracy, relying on cases such as Homalco Indian Band v. British Columbia.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1)(b),(d); the function of pleadings is to clearly define the issues of fact and law (Homalco Indian Band v. British Columbia, [1998] B.C.J. No. 2703; Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers Inc. (1988), 26 B.C.L.R. (2d) 349 (C.A.)).
firac.application: Although the ACC required considerable cross-referencing, given the complexity of the factual and legal issues the pleadings did not rise to the level of an embarrassing pleading that made it difficult or impossible to answer. Counsel and the court could determine the facts to be decided, and the cross-referencing did not create confusion.
firac.conclusion: The application to strike the pleadings as embarrassing/abuse of process was dismissed.

case_name: Jewish Family and Child Services of Greater Toronto v. H.R.G.

name_verification.name_in_document: Jewish Family and Child Services of Greater Toronto v. H.R.G.

defining_issues: Was summary judgment appropriate — i.e., was there no genuine issue requiring a trial on the disposition placing the child in the father's sole care under s. 57.1 of the Child and Family Services Act?

Was there a genuine triable issue on whether a joint/parallel parenting order allowing the mother to participate in decision-making, including the child's religious upbringing and Jewish education, was in the child's best interests?

firac.issue: On a motion under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules in a child protection case, was there a genuine issue requiring a trial such that summary judgment placing the child in the father's care should not issue?
firac.facts: The child had already been found in need of protection on consent (ss. 37(2)(b)(i) and (ii)) arising from both parents' history of drug and alcohol abuse. The child had lived with the father without incident since September 2013; reports from society workers, the pediatrician and school staff were uniformly positive. The society sought a s. 57.1 order for the father's care with access to the mother. The mother conceded the father parented appropriately but argued there was a triable issue on the form of the custody order.
firac.rule: Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules permits summary judgment in child protection cases; the moving party must show no genuine issue requiring a trial (r. 16(4)), and the responding party must set out specific facts showing a genuine issue (r. 16(4.1)). Under Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, the court first decides whether there is a genuine issue requiring a trial on the evidence before it, then whether enhanced fact-finding powers should be used. Only disputed facts that are material — that could affect the outcome — give rise to a triable issue (Kallaba v. Bylykbashi; CAS of Toronto v. K.T.).
firac.application: The court found the material facts largely undisputed: the child was in need of protection, the father provided a secure, stable and loving home and met the child's needs (the mother herself deposed the child showed no signs of neglect). The mother's concerns about the father's alcohol exposure, and the child's unclean hair and substandard clothing, were speculative or based on limited observations and were not material facts capable of changing the outcome. The court was confident it could fairly resolve the dispute on the record without invoking the expanded fact-finding powers.
firac.conclusion: There was no genuine issue requiring a trial on granting custody to the father; summary judgment was available and appropriate.

firac.issue: Was there a genuine triable issue on whether a joint or parallel parenting order — including shared decision-making over the child's education and Jewish religious upbringing — was in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The child was identified as Jewish on consent in the Statement of Agreed Facts. The mother, who was not enrolling in Jewish schooling herself, argued the father would not foster the child's Jewish identity and that she was better placed to make religious and educational decisions. The co-parenting proposal was raised only at the motion date and was absent from her Answer and Plan of Care. There was no history of effective communication or co-parenting; the parties had been barred from communicating by the father's probation order until December 2015 and had communicated little since. The father stated he could not communicate with the mother and was willing to accommodate the child's religious identity.
firac.rule: Custody disposition is governed by the child's best interests as defined in the Child and Family Services Act. A custodial parent has autonomy to make educational and religious decisions (Young v. Young, [1993] 4 SCR 3). Joint custody requires evidence that parents can communicate effectively; the mere hope that communication will improve after litigation is insufficient (Kaplanis).
firac.application: The court found the father had made appropriate decisions in all areas of the child's life since 2013 and sincerely intended to accommodate the child's Jewish identity. There was no evidence, beyond the mother's assertions, that Jewish schooling was in the child's best interests, and no history of effective communication or cooperation between the parents. Given the child's disrupted history and need for stability, the tensions inherent in a parallel parenting regime could destabilize a parent and put the child at risk. The disputed historical facts would not change the outcome; the animus shown by the mother reinforced that joint parenting was contrary to the child's interests.
firac.conclusion: There was no genuine triable issue: a co-parenting order was not in the child's best interests, and sole custody to the father was ordered, with access to the mother largely on the status quo.

name_verification.name_in_document: Jacobson v. Skurka

defining_issues: Should the defendant's statement of defence and counterclaim be struck (with leave to amend) for non-compliance with the rules of pleading because it pleaded evidence, argument, and conclusory character assassination rather than concise material facts?
Should the defendant's counterclaim for the tort of abuse of process be struck without leave under rule 21.01(1)(b) for failing to disclose a reasonable cause of action?

firac.issue: Should the defendant's statement of defence and counterclaim be struck with leave to amend for non-compliance with the rules of pleading?
firac.facts: Mr. Skurka's 132-paragraph statement of defence and counterclaim responded to Mr. Jacobson's provocative professional negligence claim with detailed recitations of diary entries, memos, lawyers' contemporaneous notes, transcript-like accounts of meetings, quotes from documents, and conclusory attacks on Mr. Jacobson's character (e.g., 'concoction of deliberate distortions and vicious fabrications'). Mr. Jacobson moved to strike 57 of the 132 paragraphs.
firac.rule: Rule 25.06(1) of the Rules of Civil Procedure requires a pleading to contain a concise statement of the material facts, not the evidence by which those facts are to be proved (Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. 401700 Ontario Ltd.; Grace v. Usalkas; Phillips v. Phillips). Rule 25.11 permits striking pleadings that may prejudice a fair trial, are scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, or abuse the court's process. Where probative value is outweighed by prejudicial effect, pleadings may be struck (Quizno's Canada Restaurant Corp. v. Kileel Developments Ltd.). Particulars serve to clarify and limit, not to import evidence (Cansulex Ltd. v. Perry; Copland v. Commodore Business Machines).
firac.application: Perell J. found that large portions of the statement of defence pleaded evidence and argument—quoting documents, reproducing diary and memo entries, recounting meetings as witness statements, and including useless padding and ad hominem character assassination. Provocation by Mr. Jacobson's improper claim did not justify Mr. Skurka's non-compliant response ('two wrongs do not make a right'). Mr. Skurka's attempt to justify the material as 'particulars' abused the concept of particulars, since the evidentiary detail was the means of proving his defence, not clarification of it.
firac.conclusion: The statement of defence and counterclaim was struck in its entirety, but with leave to deliver a fresh as amended pleading complying with the directions given, on the set timetable.

firac.issue: Should the counterclaim for the tort of abuse of process be struck without leave for failure to disclose a reasonable cause of action?
firac.facts: Mr. Skurka counterclaimed $1.8 million for abuse of process, pleading that Mr. Jacobson brought the negligence action for the predominant purposes of obtaining favourable media attention, restoring his own reputation and political connections (including aspirations to a Senate nomination, the Order of Canada, and the Israel Prize), and destroying Mr. Skurka's reputation. Mr. Jacobson's claim professed his innocence in 26 of 68 paragraphs under a heading 'Complete Vindication of Nathan Jacobson — An Innocent Man'.
firac.rule: Under rule 21.01(1)(b), a claim is struck only where it is plain and obvious that it cannot succeed (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.; R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.); novel or unsettled claims should not be struck (Nash v. Ontario; Folland v. Ontario; Johnson v. Adamson), and pleaded facts are taken as proven (Inuit Tapirisat). The tort of abuse of process (Grainger v. Hill) has four elements: the plaintiff was subject to a suit by the defendant; the defendant's predominant purpose was an improper collateral purpose outside the ambit of the process; a definite act in furtherance of that purpose; and special damages. The improper purpose must be dominant (Scintilore Explorations; Metropolitan Separate School Board v. Taylor; Westjet Airlines v. Air Canada).
firac.application: Perell J. held it was not plain and obvious that Mr. Skurka had conflated improper motive with an improper collateral purpose. It was arguable that Mr. Jacobson's dominant purpose in suing was to obtain a judicial determination of his own innocence and righteousness and favourable media attention—purposes beyond the proper ambit of a solicitor's negligence action, which is only to establish the lawyer's professional wrongdoing, not the client's innocence. A negligence claim does not require proving innocence; Mr. Jacobson unnecessarily made his innocence a material issue. The narrow scope of the tort (Westjet) did not clearly exclude these novel circumstances.
firac.conclusion: The motion to strike the counterclaim was dismissed; it was not plain and obvious the abuse of process claim could not succeed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Jacubovich v. Israel (State)

defining_issues: Does the Ontario Superior Court have jurisdiction simpliciter over the plaintiffs' claims against the State of Israel and CTCC, i.e. is there a real and substantial connection to Ontario?
If jurisdiction exists, should the court decline to exercise it under forum non conveniens on the basis that Israel is the clearly more appropriate forum?
Whether it is necessary to decide the State of Israel's sovereign immunity claim.

firac.issue: Does the Ontario Superior Court have jurisdiction simpliciter over the claims, based on a real and substantial connection to Ontario?
firac.facts: Two Argentine plaintiffs (heirs of an Argentine estate) sued the State of Israel and Computershare Trust Company of Canada (CTCC), Israel's Canadian fiscal agent, over Israeli bonds sold by Israel Bonds International (IBI) in Jerusalem, purchased from Panama, with proceeds paid to a Panama account allegedly controlled by the plaintiffs' grandfather. CTCC operated a bond register in Toronto and administered payments under the IFAA, a fiscal agency agreement between Israel and CTCC executed in New York. The plaintiffs relied on CTCC carrying on business in Ontario, commission of a tort in Ontario, and the IFAA contract connected to Ontario.
firac.rule: Van Breda (2012 SCC 17) establishes presumptive connecting factors for jurisdiction simpliciter in tort: defendant resident, defendant carries on business in the province, tort committed in the province, or a contract connected with the dispute made in the province. Presumptions are rebuttable by showing the factor points only to a weak or no relationship between the subject matter and the forum. The subject matter is assessed from the statement of claim (Sparkasse; Haaretz.com 2018 SCC 28). A transmission-of-false-information tort occurs where information is received and relied upon.
firac.application: The court found CTCC carries on business in Ontario and the IFAA is connected with the dispute, and that a minor administrative element of the alleged tort occurred in Ontario. However, the true subject matter was a multi-jurisdictional family dispute over bonds sold by IBI in Jerusalem, purchased from Panama, with alleged fraud by the grandfather. The IFAA governed only the Israel–CTCC relationship and expressly conferred no rights on third parties (s. 9.18); the bonds were Book-Entry bonds, so Schedule B's Ontario governing-law form was never issued. CTCC's role was purely administrative, occurring after the bond contracts were formed abroad. These Ontario connections were peripheral; the plaintiff's own witness admitted trying to 'get this action somehow located in Toronto.' Israel could not reasonably expect to answer proceedings in Ontario. The presumptive factors were thus rebutted as tenuous.
firac.conclusion: The court held it lacks jurisdiction simpliciter; Israel rebutted the presumptive connecting factors.

firac.issue: If jurisdiction existed, should the court decline it under forum non conveniens because Israel is clearly the more appropriate forum?
firac.facts: Sixteen potential witnesses, none resident in Ontario (seven in Israel, four in Argentina, one in UAE, four in New York); key documents and the 'nerve centre' of the bond transactions are in Israel, held by IBI's successor DCI International in Jerusalem. Israel has a seven-year limitation period versus Ontario's two years, and Israel undertook not to contest jurisdiction or assert immunity if the stay were granted. Related proceedings exist in Argentina, Panama and New York.
firac.rule: Under Van Breda (paras 103, 108), the party seeking a stay must show another forum is clearly more appropriate, weighing factors such as comparative convenience and expense, applicable law, avoiding multiplicity of proceedings, avoiding conflicting decisions, enforcement of judgment, and the fair and efficient working of the system. Contract formed where offeror receives acceptance (Eastern Power); tort governed by lex loci delicti (Tolofson; Das). Letters rogatory cannot compel Israeli witnesses in Ontario (Haaretz.com).
firac.application: Convenience strongly favoured Israel: critical witnesses and documents are there and cannot be compelled to Ontario. Applicable law: the bond contracts were formed in Israel and the lex loci delicti was likely Israel, so Israeli law would govern both contract and tort claims and the Securities Transfer Act argument was doubtful; proving Israeli law in Ontario adds cost. The plaintiffs would enjoy a juridical advantage (longer limitation period) in Israel and could have sued there since June 2017. Avoiding multiple proceedings and enforcement concerns (state property immunity, potential need to enforce in Israel) also favoured Israel. Avoiding conflicting decisions was neutral.
firac.conclusion: The court held that, had it possessed jurisdiction, Israel is clearly the more appropriate forum; the stay would be granted on forum non conveniens grounds as well.

firac.issue: Is it necessary to decide whether Israel enjoys sovereign immunity?
firac.facts: Israel argued sovereign immunity under the State Immunity Act; the plaintiffs argued the commercial-activity exception applied.
firac.rule: State Immunity Act; a court need not decide issues unnecessary to the disposition. Jurisdiction simpliciter is analytically distinct from state immunity (Bouzari v Islamic Republic of Iran, 2004 CanLII 871 (ON CA)).
firac.application: Because the court found no jurisdiction simpliciter and, alternatively, that Israel was the more appropriate forum, resolution of the sovereign immunity question was unnecessary.
firac.conclusion: The court declined to decide the sovereign immunity issue.

name_verification.name_in_document: Yelena Kuchumova et Yelena Kuchumova es qualités Yelizaveta Kuchumova c. Voyages Morrison-Viro Inc.

defining_issues: Did the travel agent breach her duty to inform and advise the client (obligation de renseignement) about visa requirements, thereby engaging the agency's liability?
Was the transcription of a telephone conversation secretly recorded by the plaintiff admissible in evidence?

firac.issue: Did the travel agent breach her duty to inform and advise the client about visa requirements, engaging the agency's liability for the plaintiff's losses?
firac.facts: The plaintiff, a Kazakhstan passport holder who habitually presented herself as 'Russian,' bought two Costa Rica vacation packages through the defendant. Agent Veena Sawhney phoned the Costa Rican tourism office in the plaintiff's presence and, believing the plaintiff to be a Russian national, was told no visa was required. In fact Costa Rica requires a visa for Kazakhstan nationals but not for Russian nationals. On arrival the plaintiff and her minor daughter were refused entry and sent back to Canada. The plaintiff claimed $12,562.80.
firac.rule: A travel agent's functions under s. 2 of the Loi sur les agents de voyages (L.R.Q., c. A-10) go beyond bookings; agents also owe a duty to assist and advise clients (obligation de renseignement). Liability requires a fault, assessed against the standard of a diligent agent given the information supplied by the client.
firac.application: The court found the agent inquired about visa requirements for a 'Russian national' who was a landed immigrant, based on how the plaintiff repeatedly and generally presented herself. The plaintiff, an educated person familiar with immigration procedures, bore the responsibility to be specific and to draw the appropriate distinction about her Kazakhstan nationality before the agent contacted the Costa Rican office. The agent acted diligently in light of the information she was given, and had also handed the plaintiff brochures advising her to verify visa questions. No fault was established.
firac.conclusion: The agent committed no fault; the agency's liability was not engaged and the action was dismissed with costs.

firac.issue: Was the transcription of a telephone conversation secretly recorded by the plaintiff admissible in evidence?
firac.facts: After returning from Costa Rica, the plaintiff recorded a phone conversation with the agent without her knowledge. Defence counsel objected to production of the transcription (P-12). Though the speakers' identity and authenticity were undisputed, the transcript contained some 120 inaudible gaps.
firac.rule: Admissibility of a surreptitiously recorded conversation is governed by the principles set out by the Court of Appeal in Denis Cadieux c. Le Service de Gaz naturel Laval Inc., 1991 CanLII 3149 (QC CA), [1991] R.J.Q. 2490.
firac.application: Applying those principles, and given the numerous inaudible gaps affecting reliability, the court upheld the objection.
firac.conclusion: The objection was maintained and the transcription declared inadmissible.

case_name: Jun et al v. Wantell Business Networks & Zang

name_verification.name_in_document: Jun et al v. Wantell Business Networks & Zang

defining_issues: Did the Provincial Court have jurisdiction under the Small Claims Act and Rules to determine the cross-applications (to add or to dismiss a party) at the pre-trial/case-management stage?

Should Andrew Zang, president and directing mind of Wantell, be added (or remain) as a personal defendant where claimants alleged he personally made negligent or fraudulent misrepresentations, notwithstanding the general immunity of corporate officers?
Were the claimants time-barred from adding Zang as a defendant given the passage of time?

firac.issue: Did the Provincial Court have jurisdiction under the Small Claims Act and Rules to hear the cross-applications at the pre-trial stage?
firac.facts: The applications to add Zang personally and Zang's cross-application to dismiss the personal claims came before the case-management judge overseeing all twenty-six related small claims. No party contested the Court's authority to rule at this stage.
firac.rule: Section 2 of the Small Claims Act, RSBC 1996, c. 430 directs that claims be resolved in a just, speedy, inexpensive and simple manner and empowers the Court to make any order or direction necessary to achieve that purpose; Small Claims Rule 16 governs applications to a judge, with Rule 16(6)(o) permitting 'any other order that a judge has the power to make'; Rule 17(13) permits orders where a party has not obeyed the rules; Belanger v. AT&T Canada Inc. 1994 B.C.J. No. 2792 supports discretion to hear a dismissal application under Rule 16.
firac.application: Given the voluminous nature of the twenty-six matters and the interests of justice, the Court found it appropriate to use its broad Rule 16(6)(o) jurisdiction, read with s. 2 of the Act, to determine the cross-applications now rather than leave the party-status question unresolved.
firac.conclusion: The Court held it had discretion and jurisdiction to determine the cross-applications at the pre-trial stage.

firac.issue: Should Zang be added or remain as a personal defendant where personal misrepresentation is alleged?
firac.facts: The claimants, Chinese students, alleged Zang, as president actively managing the College, personally gave them misleading information about student-loan eligibility and Mandarin instruction, on which they relied to their detriment; other claims contained no personal allegations against Zang or had been previously ruled on.
firac.rule: Small Claims Rule 8(1) allows amendment before a settlement conference without permission and afterward with a judge's leave; by analogy to Supreme Court Rule 15(5), a party may be added where just and convenient to effectually adjudicate all matters. An amendment is refused only where it is plain and obvious the pleading discloses no cause of action (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959; doubt resolved in favour of the pleading). Corporate officers ordinarily share the corporation's immunity, but personal liability may arise where their acts are themselves tortious or fraudulent or exhibit a separate interest (ScotiaMcLeod 'or test' as applied in Glenayre Manufacturing Ltd. v. Pilot Pacific Properties Inc., 2003 BCSC 303; Kepic v. Tecumseh Road Builders; Blacklaws v. Morrow, 2000 ABCA 175).
firac.application: The threshold for sustaining pleadings is low. Where claimants alleged Zang personally made misrepresentations, it was not plain and obvious that no reasonable cause of action existed, and no prejudice to Zang was shown beyond passage of time—delay to which Zang himself contributed by evading service and failing to provide a proper service address. Where claims contained no personal allegations against Zang, or where a judge had already dismissed or the claimant had failed to appeal an adverse ruling, the personal claim could not proceed.
firac.conclusion: Zang was added or retained as a personal defendant in twenty of the twenty-six cases; in six cases the actions proceed against Wantell only.

firac.issue: Were the claimants time-barred from adding Zang as a defendant?
firac.facts: Wantell and Zang argued the claimants were out of time to proceed against Zang, the impugned conduct dating to 2005.
firac.rule: A claim for damages for fraud falls under the residual limitation provision, not the shorter personal/property limitation (Chang v. Price Properties Ltd., 1978 CarswellBC 144); Limitation Act s. 4(1)(d) permits adding or substituting a new party with respect to claims relating to or connected with the subject matter of the original action notwithstanding lapse of time, and s. 4(4) permits amendment even where a fresh cause of action would otherwise be time-barred.
firac.application: The addition of Zang related to and was connected with the subject matter of the original claims (misrepresentation about student loans), so s. 4(1)(d) and s. 4(4) of the Limitation Act permitted the amendments notwithstanding the passage of time.
firac.conclusion: The limitation argument did not bar adding Zang; the amendments were allowed where personal misrepresentation was pleaded.

case_name: Jewish Family and Child Services of Greater Toronto v. Z.Y. and B.S.

name_verification.name_in_document: Jewish Family and Child Services of Greater Toronto v. Z.Y. and B.S.

defining_issues: Was it appropriate to decide the child protection status review summarily, i.e. was there no genuine issue requiring a trial under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules?
Was placing the child in the extended care of the society in the child's best interests under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act?
What access order was in the child's best interests and who should be named the access holder?

firac.issue: Was it appropriate to grant summary judgment in a child protection status review, i.e. was there no genuine issue requiring a trial?
firac.facts: The society moved for summary judgment on its status review application. The father was noted in default, having filed no Answer or affidavit and not attending. The mother, a 'special party' represented by the Public Guardian and Trustee, filed no responding evidence and did not attend; the PGT did not oppose the relief. The society relied on prior judicial findings of fact and updating affidavit evidence from a society worker.
firac.rule: Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules governs summary judgment; the moving party must show no genuine issue requiring a trial (subrules 16(4), (6)). Under Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, the court first determines if there is a genuine issue for trial, and may use enhanced fact-finding powers under subrule 16(6.1) where fair. Kawartha Haliburton Children's Aid Society v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316 requires exceptional caution in child protection cases given the Charter implications for vulnerable litigants, careful screening of admissible evidence, and application of the best interests objectives of the CYFSA.
firac.application: The court exercised exceptional caution but found it could make the necessary findings of fact and apply the law without resorting to enhanced powers of weighing evidence or assessing credibility; cross-examination would add little value. The society established a prima facie case on every aspect of relief, and no party met the onus of raising a genuine issue for trial. Summary disposition was proportionate, expeditious and just.
firac.conclusion: There was no genuine issue requiring a trial; the matter was properly decided summarily under Rule 16.

firac.issue: Was placing the child in the extended care of the society in his best interests?
firac.facts: The 11-year-old child had been in the society's care for 22 months, approaching the 24-month statutory limit, and was thriving in his foster home (sports, school, tutoring, therapy). The mother suffered from serious untreated delusional/paranoid mental illness, lacked insight, refused treatment, and her beliefs had previously caused the child harm through isolation and fear. Neither parent presented a plan of care; the father did not participate.
firac.rule: Sections 113–114 and 101(1) of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act permit, on a status review, an order for extended society care where in the child's best interests. Best interests are assessed under s. 74(3), including the child's needs, continuity of care, the merits of the society's plan, effects of delay, and the risk of harm and degree of risk that justified the protection finding.
firac.application: The high risk arising from the mother's untreated psychological fragility persisted and had not been mitigated; a return to her care was unsafe and she would likely not cooperate with a supervision order. The child required permanency, was thriving in care, and no alternative plan existed. The extended care order was unopposed and supported by the child's counsel.
firac.conclusion: An order placing the child in the extended care of the society was in his best interests; there was no genuine issue requiring a trial.

firac.issue: What access order was in the child's best interests and who should be the access holder?
firac.facts: The child wished to maintain access with his mother, finding it beneficial and meaningful (her expressions of love, gifts, and his concern for her health), though disappointed by her frequent no-shows. The mother's attendance had been inconsistent and her behaviour erratic. The society sought discretionary supervised access with a minimum frequency; the PGT sought the mother named as an additional access holder; the child's counsel supported the child as sole access holder.
firac.rule: Under s. 105(5)-(7) of the CYFSA, a court shall not make an access order for a child in extended society care unless satisfied it is in the child's best interests, considering whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and whether access impairs future adoption prospects; the court must specify access holders and recipients. Children's Aid Society v. Y.M., 2019 ONCJ 489 supports naming the child, not an unreliable parent, as access holder to avoid chilling adoption prospects.
firac.application: Access was found beneficial and meaningful, warranting an order preserving the society's broad discretion (location, duration, frequency, supervision) with a minimum of one weekly visit and power to suspend for the mother's instability — the order as formally sought, without the amendment. Given the mother's inconsistent attendance and erratic conduct, which could deter adoptive applicants, the child (who would be assigned counsel on any openness issue) was named sole access holder; no evidence supported naming the mother.
firac.conclusion: The discretionary supervised access order was granted with the child as sole access holder and the mother as access recipient; the society was also authorized to obtain government documents for the child. No genuine issue required a trial.

name_verification.name_in_document: Elizabeth Kraus Remer c. Ruth Remer, Esther Remer, Joseph Remer, Maunel Dalfen & Morris Birenbaum, ès qualités (et actions connexes)

defining_issues: Did Elo Remer have the mental capacity, given his Alzheimer-type dementia, to sign the codicil of 20 November 1992 and the Israeli bank form of 14 July 1993 making his wife a joint account holder?
What are the consequences of the nullity of the bank form for the wife's appropriation of the account funds, and is the estate entitled to restitution on its counterclaim?
Are the daughters Ruth and Esther Remer entitled to recover from the estate their share of their late mother's community of property?

firac.issue: Did Elo Remer have the requisite mental capacity to sign the codicil of 20 November 1992 and the bank form of 14 July 1993?
firac.facts: Elo Remer, in his eighties, was examined by neurologist Dr. Libman in 1991 and 1992 and by Dr. Deliakis in 1993 (Folstein score 13/30), all documenting a progressive Alzheimer-type dementia with severe recent-memory loss, disorientation and dependence on his wife who supplied his medical history. He signed the codicil two days after a neurological visit, and a bank form making his wife co-signatory of his Israeli account. His wife's expert Dr. Gauthier initially opined he was capable, but conceded on cross-examination that the transactions required 'complex instrumental abilities' the patient could not perform.
firac.rule: A testator must have the mental capacity to understand and appreciate the nature and consequences of a testamentary disposition; incapacity renders the act null (arts. 986 C.c.B.C. and 1398 C.c.Q.). The burden of proving incapacity lies on the party alleging it, on a balance of probabilities.
firac.application: The court preferred the unanimous evidence of Drs. Libman, Deliakis and Frank over Dr. Fried (rejected as evasive) and Dr. Gauthier (rejected for being poorly informed and self-contradictory). The medical evidence, corroborated by family members, established that Elo Remer suffered from progressive dementia and could not understand or appreciate the complex changes made by the codicil, nor the effect of adding his wife to the bank account. The wife's own testimony was found not credible.
firac.conclusion: The daughters established incapacity by a preponderance of evidence; Elo Remer lacked capacity to sign both the codicil (20 Nov 1992) and the bank form (14 July 1993), rendering both absolutely null.

firac.issue: What flows from the nullity of the bank form, and is the estate entitled to restitution of the funds appropriated by the wife?
firac.facts: After signing the July 1993 form, and even the day after the funeral, Mrs. Kraus Remer withdrew large sums (US$543,045.07 and CAD$330,173.09) from Elo Remer's Israeli Hapoalim account and transferred funds to a Swiss account. She claimed ownership based on the joint-account form.
firac.rule: An absolutely null juridical act confers no rights; funds obtained under it must be restored to the estate. Additional indemnity under art. 1619 C.c.Q. and interest run from the institution of the action. The court declined to rule on the Israeli-law ownership question (arts. 3148 ff. C.c.Q.) because the nullity of the bank form disposed of the wife's asserted title.
firac.application: Since Elo Remer lacked capacity to add his wife as signatory, the form was absolutely null and gave her no ownership; all sums and accumulated interest in the Hapoalim account (and the funds transferred to Switzerland) form part of the estate. The court granted the estate's counterclaim and suspended the wife's rights under the 1988 will until she complies with the restitution order.
firac.conclusion: The counterclaim was allowed; Mrs. Kraus Remer was ordered to reimburse the estate the withdrawn sums with interest and additional indemnity, and all funds remained part of the estate.

firac.issue: Are Ruth and Esther Remer entitled to recover their share of their mother's community of property from Elo Remer's estate?
firac.facts: Bertha Miller, Elo's first wife married in community of property, died in 1951 leaving a will benefiting her daughters after Elo's death or remarriage. Elo remarried in 1972 but never remitted the daughters' share, which was retained and administered; assets included shares in Remer Holdings omitted from the succession declaration. Experts valued the entitlement between roughly $5.6M and $9.9M actualised.
firac.rule: Beneficiaries under a will are entitled to their legacy; where a fiduciary retains and uses inheritance funds, the estate must account for the actualised value with interest and additional indemnity under art. 1619 C.c.Q.
firac.application: The court accepted the conservative valuation of $5,700,000 (accepted and recorded as a liability by the estate's own accountant), balancing fairness to the daughters against preservation of the grandchildren's eventual inheritance, and declared the daughters owners of the specified Remer Holdings shares.
firac.conclusion: The action was allowed; the estate was condemned to pay $5,700,000 in equal shares with interest and additional indemnity, and the daughters were declared owners of 250 class E and 1,250 class D shares.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally about testamentary capacity and the validity of a codicil and estate assets, so K054 (wills/estates) and its tier-1 parent K006 (Family law) are central. K002 (Civil litigation) captures the counterclaim and multiple civil actions; K022 (restitution) reflects the order requiring the wife to repay funds appropriated from the estate. The parties are a Jewish family and much lay evidence turned on synagogue attendance and religious observance, so K093 (Jewish), K098 (rabbi, several rabbis testified) and K105 (synagogue) are engaged as entity keywords. K028 (kosher/dietary law) is a weaker, borderline pick — it appears only as evidence of decline (eating non-kosher, 'il ne comprend plus') rather than as a legal issue, but it is a factual marker relied on in assessing capacity. A defamation keyword was considered for the rejected $250,000 reconventional claim but omitted as too marginal.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Cour supérieure (Chambre civile)', 'PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC', 'DISTRICT DE Montréal', identifying Montréal, Quebec as the seat of the court.
registry_rationale: The judgment is issued in the 'DISTRICT DE Montréal' of the Cour supérieure, with file numbers 500-05-... (the Montréal district numbering), so the registry is Montréal.

case_name: Jean-Yves Fortin Soudure inc. c. Québec (Procureure générale)

name_verification.name_in_document: Jean-Yves Fortin Soudure inc. c. Québec (Procureure générale)

defining_issues: Was the contractor's claim time-barred under the 120-day limitation period in art. 9.10 of the Cahier des charges et devis généraux, and when did the limitation period begin to run?

Did the contractor lose its legal interest (standing) to sue by reason of its May 1995 agreement with its subcontractor Structures de Beauce, and was that agreement a transaction or an assignment of debt?
Should the expert report of Marcel Bouchard be admitted at the opening of trial despite the Attorney General's failure to file a declaration de mise au rôle?

On the merits, what was the appropriate 'correction factor' and hourly rate, and what amounts were owed for the additional works (interior weld removal, cleaning and painting of interior edges, flat washers) and the second work trailer, and was the additional indemnity under art. 1619 C.c.Q. payable?

firac.issue: Was the claim prescribed under the 120-day period in art. 9.10 C.c.d.g., and what was the starting point of prescription?
firac.facts: Soudure received a 'recommandation de paiement' on 4 January 1994 that the Ministry treated as its 'estimation finale' (marked '8 FIN.'), then received a further payment and revised estimate on 24 January 1994 (marked '8 F.R.1'). Negotiations continued until 10 January 1994. Soudure filed its detailed claim (P-12) on 17 May 1994. No corrective or completion works had been required after the 30 September 1993 final inspection.
firac.rule: Art. 9.10, 3rd para. C.c.d.g. requires a detailed claim within 120 days of receipt of the final estimate; the 'estimation finale révisée' applies only to subsequent corrective/completion works (art. 8.14). Where a contract of adhesion (art. 1379 C.c.Q.) contains ambiguity, it is interpreted against the drafter and in favour of the adherent (art. 1432 C.c.Q.; also arts. 1425, 1426, 1429 C.c.Q.). Art. 9.10 creates only a rebuttable presumption of abandonment, not a strict/public-order forfeiture (P.G. Québec c. Armand Sicotte & Fils, [1987] R.R.A. 290 (C.A.); Entreprises P.E.B. Ltée c. P.G. Québec).
firac.application: The C.c.d.g. is an adhesion contract prepared solely by the Ministry. 'Final' ordinarily means the last estimate closing the file; the 24 January 1994 payment, though labelled 'révisée', concerned the same single contract and involved no corrective works, so the Ministry's terminology created a genuine legal ambiguity to be resolved in Soudure's favour. Continuing negotiations to 10 January and the later partial payment also postponed the starting point. The limitation therefore began on 24 January 1994, when Soudure knew the final amounts paid and refused.
firac.conclusion: The claim filed on 17 May 1994 was within 120 days of 24 January 1994 and was not prescribed.

firac.issue: Did Soudure lose its legal interest to sue because of the May 1995 agreement with Structures de Beauce?
firac.facts: Soudure was the general contractor; Structures was its subcontractor performing most of the work and owed the disputed sums. In April 1994 and May 1995 they agreed to allocate litigation costs and any recovery (90% Structures / 10% Soudure), and by the 1995 agreement Structures assumed all costs while Soudure undertook to remit any recovery to Structures.
firac.rule: Legal interest (art. 55 C.P.) must be direct and personal — the advantage a party derives from a well-founded action (Jeunes canadiens c. Fondation du théâtre du Nouveau-Monde, [1979] C.A. 491). A transaction (art. 2631 C.c.Q.) prevents a future dispute through reciprocal concessions. An assignment of debt is opposable to the debtor/third parties only on completion of the formalities in art. 1641 C.c.Q.; absent them the debtor need not recognize the assignment (Sherwin-Williams Co. of Canada c. Boiler Inspection, [1950] R.C.S. 187).
firac.application: The 1994 and 1995 agreements were transactions preventing a dispute between Soudure and its still-unpaid subcontractor; Soudure retained a real advantage (relief from litigation costs and discharge of its debt to Structures if successful). Fortin's testimony had to be read as a whole. Even if the 1995 agreement were an assignment, no proof showed the art. 1641 formalities were completed or that the Ministry acquiesced, so it was not opposable to the Ministry.
firac.conclusion: Soudure retained the legal interest to sue; the ground was rejected.

firac.issue: Should the expert report be admitted despite non-compliance with the rules on the declaration de mise au rôle?
firac.facts: The Attorney General had not filed a declaration de mise au rôle and was declared forclos; a certificat d'état de cause issued 19 December 1997. At the opening of trial in April 1999 the Crown sought to file Bouchard's report, a video and a model. Soudure had received the report more than two months earlier, did not claim surprise and did not seek an adjournment.
firac.rule: Rule 15 of the Superior Court Rules of Practice creates a form of judicial contract; forclusion crystallizes a party's procedural position but is not automatically fatal and remains subject to the court's discretion under Rule 17, exercised in the interests of justice and on just conditions (Harewood c. Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital, [1991] R.J.Q. 900; Raymond Chabot Fafard Gagnon inc. c. Latouche; Placements Grandterre inc. c. 147616 Canada inc.).
firac.application: The Crown's argument that non-compliance freed it from any judicial contract was rejected; a party cannot invoke its own lack of diligence to escape the Rules. However, the report was clearly relevant to the central 'correction factor' issue, and Soudure suffered no prejudice as it had known the report's content well in advance and neither claimed surprise nor sought a postponement. It was in the interests of justice to admit it.
firac.conclusion: The expert report was admitted; Soudure's objection was dismissed (subject to the noted criticism of the Crown's conduct).

firac.issue: What correction factor, hourly rate and amounts were owed for the additional works and the second trailer, and was the art. 1619 indemnity payable?
firac.facts: The bridge rehabilitation required unforeseen extra works: removal of interior welds, cleaning and painting of interior edges of the 'C' irons, and adding flat washers; total hours rose from an estimated 12,500 to about 16,760.5. Soudure claimed a correction factor of 5.35 (ratio of bid hours to 'laboratory' hours) at $72.75/hour; the Ministry proposed 1.88 at $43.57/hour and refused payment for the second trailer.
firac.rule: An adhesion contract is interpreted against the drafter (arts. 1379, 1432 C.c.Q.); the court considers how the parties themselves interpreted and behaved under the contract (art. 1426 C.c.Q.). Where the Ministry imposes changes making works more onerous (arts. 4.07, 4.09, 9.04 C.c.d.g.), it must pay the additional cost and cannot arbitrarily reject the claim (P.G. Québec c. Labrador Excavating; Entreprises P.E.B. Ltée). 'Régie' pricing (art. 9.04(c)) requires daily reconciliation of registers. The additional indemnity (art. 1619 C.c.Q.) is the rule and refused only for serious reasons such as the claimant's unreasonable delay (Houle c. B.C.N.; Cie d'assurance Missisquoi c. Bessette).
firac.application: The Ministry's 1.88 factor rested on Breton's non-contemporaneous, error-ridden compilation (D-1), which on correction of its premises yielded 5.05; Soudure's 5.35, based on verifiable laboratory measurements and unchallenged data, was preferred. The Ministry's own conduct in paying $72.99/$72.55/$72.94 equivalents showed an effective $72.75 rate. Interior edge works were genuinely different from the horizontal surfaces (not billable at unit price) and 'régie' conditions were unmet, so the correction factor applied. Amounts were computed for each item; the second trailer was required by art. 2.0 document 101 once two crews worked simultaneously, so it was not compensable. The art. 1619 indemnity was denied for the 1995–1997 period of delay attributable to Soudure and granted only from 6 October 1997.
firac.conclusion: Correction factor 5.35 and rate $72.75 accepted; the Ministry owed $34,650.21 (interior welds), $191,180.96 (interior edges), $20,608.75 (flat washers), nothing for the trailer; total $246,439.92 with interest and additional indemnity from 6 October 1997, plus costs and expert fees.

The controlled vocabulary is heavily oriented toward human-rights/religious/antisemitism subject matter and offers no keyword for construction, contract law, prescription or standing, so the remaining picks are the closest available and are flagged as weak: K001 (Administrative law) is borderline, engaged only because the defendant is the Crown (Ministry of Transport) and the court exercised discretion under the Rules of Practice; K022 (restitution) is a loose fit for the monetary recovery/payment claim; K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) are the nearest procedural entries but do not truly apply, as this was an ordinary civil trial, not judicial review. Fewer than five keywords genuinely apply; K001, K022, K011 and K014 are included only to meet the minimum and should be treated as tenuous.

case_name: Levitts Kosher Foods Inc. v. Levin

name_verification.name_in_document: Levitts Kosher Foods Inc. v. Levin et al.

defining_issues: Are the plaintiff's claims — libel, restraint of trade, and related civil causes of action — justiciable by a civil court where their essence is an attack on a rabbinical body's religiously grounded kashrut certification policies?
Should the court exercise its discretion to stay the action as oppressive, vexatious, or an abuse of process, and would a stay cause an injustice to the plaintiff?

firac.issue: Are the plaintiff's civil claims justiciable where their essence is an attack on a religious body's kashrut certification policies?
firac.facts: The Vaad Hakashruth, a Toronto council of orthodox rabbis, certifies foods (symbol 'COR') as meeting its interpretation of the laws of kashrut. It adopted a shomer Shabbat policy (requiring the vendor or corporate principals to be strictly observant) and a shechitas chutz policy (certifying only local slaughterers). Levitts Kosher Foods, a Montreal producer whose principals are not observant and whose products are certified kosher by other bodies (MK, Star-K), was refused certification/grandfathering of its fresh meat. It sued three rabbis alleging libel and restraint of trade.
firac.rule: Courts are reluctant to intervene in the internal affairs of a religious body and will not decide questions of religious doctrine (Kaddoura v. Hammoud; Lakeside Colony of Hutterian Brethren v. Hofer, 1992 CanLII 37 (SCC)). In church disputes courts look only to adherence to rules, procedural fairness and absence of mala fides (Brewer v. Anglican Church of Canada). Courts will intervene where the matter is one of property or civil rights resolvable by civil-law principles.
firac.application: Although pleaded as libel, restraint of trade, conspiracy and interference with economic relations, the essence of the claim was an attack on the shomer Shabbat and shechitas chutz policies. To succeed the plaintiff would have to challenge the rabbis' supervisory authority, their interpretation of kashrut, and their conscience-based standards of trustworthiness of non-observant Jews. The Vaad does not decide whether food is kosher but whether it meets its own religiously determined standards; the plaintiff's food is kosher but does not meet those standards. Certification is a religious function based on trust. Uditsky was distinguishable as concerning whether evidence went to the jury, and American cases (United Kosher Butchers; Korn) supported non-intervention in matters of religious practice and conscience. Cabinet v. Shapiro was distinguishable because there kashrut status itself was disputed, whereas here it was admitted.
firac.conclusion: The claims raised profoundly religious questions of belief and conscience and were not justiciable by the civil courts.

firac.issue: Should the action be stayed as an abuse of process, and would a stay unjustly prejudice the plaintiff?
firac.facts: The defendants moved to stay the action, arguing the issues were intrinsically religious and that the plaintiff had impliedly consented to rabbinical authority by operating a kosher business. The plaintiff argued it could not be forced to a Bet Din and would be prejudiced by loss of civil recourse.
firac.rule: A stay is granted rarely; the defendant must show that continuance would work an injustice by being oppressive, vexatious or an abuse of the court's process, and that a stay would not cause an injustice to the plaintiff.
firac.application: Because the claims were not justiciable, their continuance would be oppressive and an abuse of process. The plaintiff chose to operate within a religious environment and took the benefits of kosher certification (MK, Star-K) that give commercial advantage; it could not claim those benefits while rejecting the accompanying obligations and the authority of the rabbis (Cohen v. Silver). It remained free to sell in non-COR establishments and its own store. Following one of the basic rules of the religious business world it chose to profit from caused it no cognizable prejudice.
firac.conclusion: The defendants satisfied both branches of the test; the motion for a stay was granted.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns on a civil procedure motion for a stay of a libel/restraint-of-trade action. K015 (defamation) reflects the pleaded libel/slander claim. K025 (freedom of religion) and the justiciability of religious doctrine drive the outcome. K028 (kosher/dietary law) and K026 (halacha/Jewish law) capture the core subject matter — kashrut and its interpretation. K098 (rabbi), K097 (Orthodox community), K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) identify the parties and religious context (the Vaad Hakashruth of Toronto orthodox rabbis). No controlled keyword exists for 'justiciability' or 'stay of proceedings,' so those doctrines are captured through the practice area and religion keywords; K015 is somewhat secondary since the libel claim was not adjudicated on its merits.
location_rationale: The decision is of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice and concerns the Vaad Hakashruth, 'the Toronto council of 11 orthodox rabbis,' with the defendants being 'three Toronto rabbis.' The court file number 99-CV-163952-CM and the Toronto focus indicate the matter was heard in Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: No registry office is expressly named beyond the court file number (99-CV-163952-CM); Toronto is inferred as the registry given the Ontario Superior Court of Justice and the Toronto locus of the parties and dispute.

name_verification.name_in_document: M.D.L.C. v. D.S.C.

defining_issues: Was there a material change in circumstances since the final parenting order justifying a review of the week-to-week shared parenting arrangement, and if so what is in the child's best interests?
Was there a material change in circumstances justifying a change to the order granting the mother final decision-making responsibility, and what regime is in the child's best interests?
Was there a material change justifying a variation of the terms governing travel with the child and custody of the child's government-issued documents?
Was there a material change justifying a variation of the holiday parenting regime and of the police enforcement order?
How should the father's and mother's incomes be determined (including imputation of income), from what date should child support be varied, and in what amount?

firac.issue: Was there a material change in circumstances since the final parenting order justifying a review of the shared week-to-week parenting arrangement, and if so what is in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The father sought primary care, alleging the mother had abdicated large portions of her parenting time (claiming the child was in his care ~70% of the time), brought the child late to school and missed school days, and lacked parenting skills. He relied on tables and pie charts of care time. The mother acknowledged asking the father for childcare help, often at his own urging that she not use a babysitter, because she had no family supports in Canada and needed to work.
firac.rule: Section 29 of the Children's Law Reform Act bars variation of a custody/access order absent a material change in circumstances affecting the child's best interests. Per Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27 (and A.B. v. J.B., 2017 ONCJ 866), the change must be material (not trivial: Hickey v. Hickey), affecting the child in a fundamental way and not foreseen when the order was made; only if the threshold is met does the court reassess best interests afresh under s. 24 CLRA.
firac.application: The court found the father's care-time calculations misleading and unreliable — they contained mathematical errors, failed to exclude periods when a parent was on vacation or when he had agreed to provide childcare, and improperly treated exchange days as shared. The lateness/absence evidence fell short of a material change. The child was a thriving, happy five-year-old benefitting from both parents; the mother provided adequate day-to-day care. The parents' strengths and weaknesses balanced out.
firac.conclusion: No material change established; the father's motion to place the child in his primary care and reduce the mother's time was dismissed. The week-to-week shared regime continues.

firac.issue: Was there a material change justifying a change to the order giving the mother final decision-making responsibility?
firac.facts: The mother did not even realize the order gave her final decision-making authority. Since the order the father had consistently initiated and driven decisions (school enrollment, Portuguese classes, medical appointments) while the mother, facing language barriers and lack of familiarity with Canadian systems, deferred to him. The parties nevertheless agreed on some decisions.
firac.rule: Section 29 CLRA material-change threshold; if met, best interests reassessed under s. 24. Section 28(1)(b) CLRA allows the court to decide incidents of decision-making responsibility.
firac.application: The court found the father had in reality taken the lead on decisions and the mother deferred to him — a situation not contemplated when she was given final say. The father's evidence exaggerating the mother's 'refusal' to engage (e.g. emailing four days before school started then blaming her) was disingenuous, and both parents had breached the order, but the pattern of the mother deferring meant the existing decision-making order no longer reflected reality or the child's best interests.
firac.conclusion: Material change found; the order was varied to joint/shared decision-making, with the mother choosing the school in her catchment (after consultation) and the father having final say on doctor/dentist changes if the parties cannot agree.

firac.issue: Was there a material change justifying variation of the terms on travel with the child and safekeeping of her government documents?
firac.facts: The parties had agreed the father would take the child to Portugal in April 2023 and the mother to Spain in July 2023; the mother signed the father's travel consent but he reneged, refusing to let the child travel or to release her passport, alleging (without supporting messages) that the mother would abduct the child to Colombia. The mother had travelled abroad three times, each time on a round-trip ticket, always returning.
firac.rule: Section 29 CLRA material change and best interests under s. 24 CLRA.
firac.application: The court rejected the abduction claim as unsupported — the father's affidavit assertions were not backed by the text messages he cited, which did not mention removing the child. His refusal to honour the reciprocal travel agreement was manipulative and cruel, and denied the child the chance to meet her half-sister. The intense conflict over travel, unaddressed in the final order, amounted to a material change.
firac.conclusion: Material change found. Both parents may travel with the child on vacation without the other's consent on 14 days' notice with a detailed itinerary; the mother holds the passport (providing it to the father when he travels), and the father holds the health card (providing it to the mother on request).

firac.issue: Was there a material change justifying variation of the holiday parenting regime and termination of the police enforcement order?
firac.facts: The final order lacked specificity for many holidays, generating repeated conflict and three instances of police involvement (Father's Day and Christmas 2023, March 2024). The enforcement order authorized police enforcement and barred removal from the GTA. The mother admitted breaches but expressed remorse; no breach occurred after March 2024.
firac.rule: Section 29 CLRA material change and best interests under s. 24 CLRA; courts are reluctant to involve police in children's lives absent necessity.
firac.application: The lack of a detailed holiday schedule had produced conflict not anticipated at the time of the order, so the order no longer met the child's needs. A detailed Christmas, summer and March-break regime was set. On enforcement, both parents had breached the order, but the mother accepted responsibility and there had been no breach since March 2024; the court took her at her word, warning of consequences for future breaches.
firac.conclusion: Material change found. A specific holiday schedule was imposed and the November 23, 2022 enforcement order was terminated.

firac.issue: How should the parties' incomes be determined and from what date and in what amount should child support be varied?
firac.facts: The father, a criminal lawyer, was underemployed, having refused to abstain from alcohol as an LSO condition for reinstatement until March 2024, and failed to provide the mandatory financial disclosure. The mother had undeclared cash income and unexplained bank deposits inconsistent with her declared income. The mother sought retroactive variation to the date of the final order (June 3, 2021).
firac.rule: Section 34(1)(f) Family Law Act (retroactive support); Colucci v. Colucci, 2021 SCC 24, and the D.B.S./Michel v. Graydon factors; s. 19(1) Child Support Guidelines and Drygala v. Pauli (imputation for intentional underemployment/non-disclosure); s. 9 Guidelines (shared parenting).
firac.application: Because neither party's tax returns were reliable, income was imputed: $40,000/year to the mother (given her drive despite limited education/English), and to the father $70,000 (2023), $80,000 (2024) and $90,000 (2025), his refusal to abstain from alcohol being unreasonable underemployment at the child's expense. The presumptive start date was April 4, 2024 (the mother's amended request), but the father's blameworthy non-disclosure and the lack of hardship justified departing back to June 1, 2022 (the first disclosure-exchange date); however the mother could not reach back to the final order since she had not then argued underemployment. Given the lack of s. 9 evidence, a straight set-off was inappropriate; the father pays 67% of his table amount.
firac.conclusion: Income imputed to both parents; child support varied to $438/month (2023), $500/month (2024) and $559/month (from January 1, 2025), each 67% of the father's table amount, with credit for FRO payments.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 area — a Children's Law Reform Act motion to change parenting orders and child support. K048 (custody/access) captures the core parenting-time and decision-making disputes. K047 (best interests of the child) is the operative test applied at every stage after the material-change threshold. K050 (parental/child support) covers the imputation-of-income and retroactive support analysis under the Guidelines and Colucci. K052 (religious upbringing) is a borderline/weak pick, reflecting the disputes over Christmas, church attendance and the mother's refusal to 'impose religious things' — a minor sub-issue included to reach five keywords, as the controlled vocabulary offers no closer family-law terms (e.g. no 'material change' or 'motion to change' keyword exists).

No city of the court's sitting is stated in the text; while the parties and the father's law practice are associated with the Greater Toronto Area (the enforcement order barred removal of the child 'from the Greater Toronto Area'), the court does not expressly state the municipality where it sits, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision bears court file number D31344/19 but does not name a court registry or office, so registry is left null.

defining_issues: Has there been a material change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances of the child since the divorce judgment that would justify modifying the father's access rights?
Has there been a change of circumstances justifying a modification of the child support payable for the child?
Is the mother entitled to a provision for costs?

firac.issue: Was there a material change in the child's circumstances justifying modification of the father's access rights?
firac.facts: Under a 1994 agreement confirmed by the 1995 divorce judgment, the mother had custody of B. (age 7) and the father had access every second weekend, Wednesdays, one day on each of the high Jewish holidays (Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur, Passover), and shared vacation time. Both parents had remarried. The father sought expanded access (two of three weekends, longer holiday and vacation blocks, and specified division of Jewish holidays); the mother sought her own modifications. The father argued the child was two years older and needed more contact.
firac.rule: Section 17(5) of the Divorce Act requires a change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances of the child since the last order before a variation order may be made, with the child's best interests governing. Per Willick v. Willick, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 670, the change must be material — one that, if known at the time, would likely have resulted in different terms.
firac.application: The Court found the proof disclosed no material change: neither remarriage had changed B.'s situation in either household, and the child simply being older did not, on the evidence, warrant more generous access. Even if a material change existed, the evidence was insufficient to establish that spending two of three weekends with the father, or any particular new formula for dividing the Jewish holidays and summer vacations, would be in B.'s best interests. The disputes were minor and the parties treated the child as a pawn in their vendetta; such adjustments should be settled by agreement.
firac.conclusion: No material change was established; the father's amended motion to modify access was dismissed, as was the mother's motion to modify access.

firac.issue: Was there a change of circumstances justifying modification of the child support order?
firac.facts: The 1995 judgment set support at $150 per week. The mother sought an increase. The Quebec Child Support Guidelines had come into force, alimony was no longer taxable in the mother's hands, and B. had new orthodontic needs. The father earned roughly $51,400 gross in 1997; the mother earned about $32,000. Neither party contested the mother's right to claim under the new guidelines.
firac.rule: Section 17(4) of the Divorce Act requires a change of circumstances as provided in the applicable guidelines (here the Quebec Guidelines) before varying a child support order. Guided by s. 14 of the Federal Guidelines and cases such as Lavoie v. Paré, Vincent v. Lussier and Gabriel v. Osselyn, the coming into force of the new guidelines together with the de-taxation of support constitutes a sufficient change of circumstances.
firac.application: The coming into force of the guidelines and the fact that support was no longer taxable in the mother's hands constituted a material change even absent a large change in amount; B.'s orthodontic expenses were a new need. Using the child support determination form (D-1), the basic parental contribution plus child care and special expenses totalled $10,822; the father's 65.4% share was $7,075, or $590 per month, plus his 65.4% share of orthodontic expenses.
firac.conclusion: The mother's motion for support under the new guidelines was granted; the father was ordered to pay $590 per month plus 65.4% of orthodontic expenses.

firac.issue: Is the mother entitled to a provision for costs?
firac.facts: The mother claimed a $3,000 provision for costs under Rule of Practice no. 36, alleging severe financial hardship from the father's motion and his alleged harassment. No contempt motion had been filed and no proof of her legal expenses was made.
firac.rule: Rule of Practice no. 36 in family matters permits the Court to order a party to pay a provision for costs, applicable in divorce matters via art. 25(2) of the Divorce Act (D.F. no. 605, [1989] R.J.Q. 505 (C.A.)). A provision for costs is alimentary in nature and subject to the rules governing alimentary pensions.
firac.application: No contempt motion had been filed, no adequate proof of harassment was made, and no proof of legal expenses was adduced. Most of the parties' motions (except the guideline support claim) were unfounded, and the Court did not wish to encourage further litigation contrary to the child's interest.
firac.conclusion: The motion for a provision for costs was dismissed.

case_name: Joseph c. Concordia Student Union Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: Noah Joseph et Noah Sarna et al c. Concordia Student Union Inc.

defining_issues: Does a motion in irrecevabilité under art. 165 C.p.c. apply to an interlocutory injunction application?
Must the plaintiffs first exhaust the internal dispute-resolution mechanisms of Concordia University before pursuing their injunction, such that the court proceedings should be suspended?

firac.issue: Does a motion in irrecevabilité under art. 165 C.p.c. apply to an application for interlocutory injunction?
firac.facts: The CSU raised the inadmissibility of the injunction application; the plaintiffs objected that art. 165 C.p.c. applies only to an action, not to an injunction application, and the CSU then asked to amend its motion to also target the underlying action.
firac.rule: Article 165 C.p.c. governs motions for dismissal (irrecevabilité), traditionally directed at an action; the debate concerned whether a partial 'inscription en droit' could reach an injunction application.
firac.application: The court noted that the French text of art. 165 appeared to answer the plaintiffs' argument, and that the CSU asked to amend to reach the action itself, but the judge found it unnecessary to elaborate given the disposition he intended to reach on the substance.
firac.conclusion: The court declined to resolve this procedural point, treating it as unnecessary in light of its ruling on exhaustion of internal remedies.

firac.issue: Must the plaintiffs exhaust Concordia University's internal remedies before pursuing their injunction, warranting a stay of the proceedings?
firac.facts: Ten members, officers of Concordia Hillel (representing Jewish students), sought an interlocutory injunction to annul CSU resolutions of December 2002 that condemned Hillel, demanded a public apology and suspended its funding over materials said to recruit Jewish students for the Israeli Defense Forces. The dispute reflected a broader claim of discrimination against Jews at the university. A safeguard order had already been refused. The parties canvassed the university's Charter, Code of Rights and Responsibilities, various policies, and the powers of the Board of Governors.
firac.rule: Where internal or 'domestic tribunal' remedies exist, a party may be required to exhaust them before resorting to the courts; art. 30 of Concordia's Charter confers on the Board of Governors a broad 'superintending and reforming power' over all decisions affecting university activities, including power to revoke or modify decisions of internal structures and recognized organizations.
firac.application: The judge found the university's texts would at least permit the plaintiffs to seize the Board of Governors, whose broad powers under art. 30 could address the conflict; the rector's affidavit suggested the university could intervene and sanction. In the public interest it was preferable to let the university resolve a conflict concerning its own students, especially students of the same faith, given the very general nature of the injunction conclusions (ordering observance of all regulations under pain of contempt), the particular university milieu, and the students' limited means. The court would not require submission to the CSU's own Judicial Board because the CSU was itself a party and internally divided. Since only the claim for $100,000 in moral damages distinguished the action from the injunction, and quantum should reflect the outcome of any inquiry, suspending all proceedings was appropriate.
firac.conclusion: The court accepted the motion in the sense of imposing a preliminary obligation and suspended all proceedings until the plaintiffs exhaust their remedies under Concordia's Charter and relevant regulations, or are prevented from doing so as a Superior Court judge may assess; costs to follow.
