case_name: Lowen c. Procureure générale du Québec

name_verification.name_in_document: Yochonon Lowen et Clara Wasserstein c. Procureure générale du Québec et al.

defining_issues: Does a motion for declaratory judgment under art. 142 C.p.c. lie where the alleged real and current difficulty (secular-education deficiencies in Hasidic schools) has, according to the defendants, been resolved by later intervention and legislative change?
Can the court, on a motion for declaratory judgment, characterize the conduct of the government and school board as faulty, or does that trespass on non-justiciable political choices?

firac.issue: Does a motion for declaratory judgment under art. 142 C.p.c. lie where the alleged real and current difficulty has, according to the defendants, been resolved by later intervention and legislative change?
firac.facts: Lowen and Wasserstein, who left the Tash Hasidic community of Boisbriand in 2007, received an almost exclusively religious education in Yiddish, with little or no secular instruction (no French, history, geography, science). They sought declarations that the community's unlicensed schools breached the Loi sur l'instruction publique, the Loi sur l'enseignement privé, the Charte de la langue française and the Quebec Charter, and that the government and school board tolerated illegal schools. After the DPJ's 2014 intervention (finding presumed compromise for boys) and legislative changes—Bill 144 (2017), amendments to the Youth Protection Act, and the 2018 Règlement sur l'enseignement à la maison—hundreds of Tash children were enrolled in monitored homeschooling with satisfactory progress.
firac.rule: Article 142 C.p.c. permits a declaratory judgment only to resolve «une difficulté réelle»—a genuine, real and current controversy, not hypothetical or fictitious questions, and the judgment must be capable of ending the uncertainty (Ferland & Emery; jurisprudence cited).
firac.application: The court found the evidence showed the difficulty no longer exists: homeschooling now allows both boys and girls of the Hasidic communities to complete secular studies, and school attendance is now overseen by the MEQ, the school boards and the DPJ, whose intervention power is no longer limited to groups of fewer than five children. New inspection powers allow ministry agents to «pénétrer» unlicensed premises and demand student lists. To rule on the past would amount to rendering a mere opinion ending no live controversy.
firac.conclusion: There being no real and current difficulty, the motion for declaratory judgment fails.

firac.issue: Can the court, on a motion for declaratory judgment, characterize the conduct of the government and school board as faulty, or does that trespass on non-justiciable political choices?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs asked the court to declare that the Quebec government and the Commission scolaire de la Seigneurie-des-Mille-Îles had, through inaction, breached their statutory obligations by tolerating illegal schools. The historical legislative choice (from Bill 107/141 onward) had been to 'déjudiciariser' compulsory school attendance, relying on parents and leaving DPJ intervention as a backstop.
firac.rule: The declaratory power under the C.p.c. cannot be used to intervene in the political, as opposed to operational, sphere of government; the difficulty resolved must be litigious in nature, respecting separation of powers (Teja's Animal Refuge c. Quebec (A.G.), 2009 QCCA 2310; Cilinger; Just v. British Columbia).
firac.application: Several reproaches directed at the government and school board concerned political choices—notably the pre-2017 decision to de-judicialize school-attendance enforcement—which are matters of ministerial responsibility to the legislature, not justiciable questions for the courts.
firac.conclusion: Characterizing the government's and school board's conduct as faulty is not a permissible outcome on a declaratory-judgment motion; this further supports dismissal.

keywords_rationale: K005 (Education law) is the primary tier-1 area—the case concerns compulsory schooling and secular-education deficiencies. K043 (denominational schools) fits the yeshiva/faith-based religious schools at issue; K118 (Education Act) covers the Loi sur l'instruction publique and Loi sur l'enseignement privé central to the analysis. K097 (Orthodox/Hasidic community), K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) identify the Tash Hasidic community whose schooling was scrutinized. K052 (religious upbringing) reflects the almost exclusively religious instruction of the children. K025 (freedom of religion) is engaged through the Quebec Charter right of parents to give religious education. K120 (Quebec Charter) is one of the statutes the plaintiffs invoked. Borderline: K025 and K052 are peripheral since the ruling turned on procedure/justiciability rather than substantive religious-freedom analysis, but they capture the case's factual core.
location_rationale: The header states «COUR SUPÉRIEURE», «PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC», «DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL», and file no. 500-17-093778-168, establishing the court sits in Montréal, Quebec.
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the «DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL» of the Superior Court, so the registry/district is Montréal.

name_verification.name_in_document: Miroshnychenko v. Antufeay

defining_issues: Should the Notice of Civil Claim be struck in whole or in part under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules for disclosing no reasonable cause of action or being confusing?
Can the plaintiff maintain a claim under the Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act where the transaction was commercial rather than for personal, family or household purposes?
Does the pleading disclose a viable cause of action in fraudulent misrepresentation where the alleged misrepresentation was made after the contract was formed?
Should the individual defendants and the Class Proceedings Act reference be struck, and should the personal plaintiff be removed?
Should special costs be awarded against the self-represented plaintiff?

firac.issue: Should the Notice of Civil Claim be struck in whole or in part under Rule 9-5(1) for disclosing no reasonable cause of action or being confusing?
firac.facts: The plaintiff MCL, through its owner Mr. Miroshnychenko, filed a Notice of Civil Claim on December 8, 2020 concerning an incomplete electrical equipment installation by Houle Electric. The defendants sought to strike the entire claim as prolix, confusing and impossible to understand.
firac.rule: Rule 3-1 requires a concise statement of material facts, relief sought and legal basis; Rule 9-5(1) permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim, are unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, or are an abuse of process. Per Gateway Building Management Ltd. v. Randhawa, 2013 BCSC 350 and Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union, 2006 BCSC 750, a claim is struck where it is plain and obvious it cannot succeed or the pleadings are unintelligible.
firac.application: The Court found multiple defects, some conceded, but held the breach of contract allegations (paras. 8, 9, 11-27), while confusing and hard to understand, were not plainly bound to fail and were not frivolous or vexatious. The confusing portions were amendable rather than struck entirely.
firac.conclusion: The claim was not struck in its entirety; discrete defective portions were struck while the breach of contract claim was preserved with leave to amend within 60 days.

firac.issue: Can the plaintiff maintain a claim under the BPCPA where the transaction was commercial?
firac.facts: The plaintiff pleaded reliance on the BPCPA but acknowledged in its February 10, 2020 response that 'This was a commercial transaction between Mirochembiotech and Houle Electric Limited.'
firac.rule: Section 1 of the BPCPA defines a consumer transaction as a supply of goods or services for purposes primarily personal, family or household. Per A Speedy Solutions Oil Tank Removal Inc. v. Garraway, 2019 BCSC 1091 and Nanaimo Shipyards Ltd. v. Keith, 2008 BCSC 1150, the character turns on whether the purchaser acquired for primarily personal, family or household purposes.
firac.application: Because the plaintiff itself characterized the dealing as a commercial transaction and pleaded no personal, family or household purpose, the statutory precondition was absent.
firac.conclusion: It was plain and obvious the BPCPA claim could not succeed; paras. 31-33 and relief paras. 1 and 2 were struck without leave to amend, and the BPCPA claim dismissed.

firac.issue: Does the pleading disclose a viable claim in fraudulent misrepresentation where the alleged misrepresentation post-dated the contract?
firac.facts: The plaintiff alleged that an invoice supplied by Houle in December 2019, after the contract had been formed, was false and misleading.
firac.rule: Per Wang v. Shao, 2019 BCCA 130, fraudulent misrepresentation requires a false representation of fact known to be false, intended to be acted on, and inducing the victim to enter into the contract in reliance on it.
firac.application: Since the alleged misrepresentation was made after the contract was concluded, the plaintiff could not have been induced to enter the contract in reliance upon it, defeating an essential element.
firac.conclusion: It was plain and obvious no cause of action lay; paras. 10, 29 and 30 and relief para. 6 were struck without leave, and the punitive damages claim (which depended on the fraud allegation) was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the individual defendants, the personal plaintiff, and the Class Proceedings Act reference be struck?
firac.facts: Mr. Miroshnychenko was named as a plaintiff but conceded he sued only on behalf of MCL. The individual employees/director were named, but the plaintiff conceded the action was against Houle, not them personally. The claim purported to be brought under the Class Proceedings Act and in the Provincial Court.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1): pleadings disclosing no reasonable claim against a party may be struck; Rule 3-1 requires relief to be set out against each named defendant.
firac.application: No claims were pleaded personally by Mr. Miroshnychenko or against the individual defendants, and no basis existed for a class proceeding. The Provincial Court reference was an error.
firac.conclusion: Mr. Miroshnychenko's name, the individual defendants (and paras. 5-7), and the Class Proceedings Act reference were struck without leave; leave was granted to correct the court designation and describe MCL as plaintiff.

firac.issue: Should special costs be awarded against the self-represented plaintiff?
firac.facts: The defendants sought special costs, arguing the plaintiff persisted in spurious claims, alleged fraud without basis and refused to withdraw them.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) permits ordering costs of a strike application to be paid as special costs; special costs require reprehensible conduct worthy of rebuke.
firac.application: Although the pleadings were significantly flawed, the Court found the self-represented plaintiff did not intend to bring meritless claims for an improper purpose or to abuse the court's process.
firac.conclusion: Special costs were declined; the successful defendants were awarded ordinary costs under Appendix B, Scale B.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 practice area, as the case is an application to strike civil pleadings involving breach of contract, consumer protection and fraudulent misrepresentation. K020 (class action) applies because the Notice of Civil Claim purported to be brought under the Class Proceedings Act, an issue the court expressly struck. The remaining picks are weak: the controlled vocabulary is oriented toward human-rights/antisemitism matters and offers no term for striking pleadings, breach of contract, consumer protection or fraudulent misrepresentation. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is flagged as weak — the plaintiff only mentioned injunction/specific performance as a possible contract remedy. K022 (restitution) and K015 (defamation) are flagged as weak/marginal fillers to reach the minimum; restitution loosely relates to the damages/compensation sought, and defamation is only tangentially analogous to the fraudulent-misrepresentation/false-statement allegation. No genuinely fitting keyword exists for the core procedural subject matter.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Registry: Prince George' and gives the 'Place and Date of Hearing' and 'Place and Date of Judgment' as 'Prince George, B.C.' The court is the Supreme Court of British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: Prince George'.

case_name: Kiss et al. v. Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd. et al.

name_verification.name_in_document: Kiss et al. v. Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd. et al.

defining_issues: Was the defendant's legal non-conforming industrial use discontinued by reason of the 1967 fire and subsequent repairs?

Does the bona fide non-conforming use of part of the lands extend to the whole parcel, such that the proposed driveway over the rural-residential-zoned portion is a permitted continuation of the non-conforming use?
Does the zoning by-law prohibit erection of the proposed second building as a second main building on a residential lot?

firac.issue: Was the defendant's legal non-conforming industrial use discontinued because of the 1967 fire and the repairs that followed?
firac.facts: In 1959 the defendant's predecessors built a heat-treatment plant while the land was zoned rural agricultural. By-law 1760 (1962) rezoned the front 300 ft. to rural residential, so the plant's continued operation depended on the non-conforming use provision. In 1967 a fire seriously damaged but did not demolish the building; the work crew was not laid off, some work continued in the undamaged portion, and a building permit was issued to restore (repair and re-roof) the shop.
firac.rule: Section 35(7) of the Planning Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 349 (formerly s. 30(7), R.S.O. 1960, c. 296) protects a lawful use existing at the passing of a by-law 'so long as it continues to be used for that purpose.' A non-conforming use is not discontinued where there is a continuing intention to use the property for its purpose and actual use so far as possible: Re Hartley and City of Toronto (1925), 56 O.L.R. 433; City of Toronto v. Board of Trustees of R.C. Separate Schools, [1925] 3 D.L.R. 880 (JCPC).
firac.application: The court found the fire did not demolish the entire building, the crew was retained, and work continued in the undamaged portion during repairs. There was a continuing intention to use the building as a heat-treatment plant and actual use to the extent possible.
firac.conclusion: The non-conforming use was not discontinued; the legal non-conforming use survived the fire and repairs.

firac.issue: Does a bona fide non-conforming use of part of the lands extend to the whole parcel, making the proposed driveway over the RR1-zoned portion a permitted continuation rather than a new use?
firac.facts: The proposed second building on the rear (still rural agricultural) lands was to be served by a driveway running from East Main St. across the front portion zoned rural residential. That front area had not been actively used but was landscaped with trees and grass.
firac.rule: The meaning of 'use of land' under the Planning Act: use means holding or occupying/employment of property (Pickering Township v. Godfrey, 1958 CanLII 95 (ON CA), [1958] O.R. 429). A bona fide, good-faith use of part of lands or a building extends the exemption to the whole parcel or entire building (Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto, 1948 CanLII 3 (SCC), [1948] S.C.R. 101). Section 42 of the Planning Act allows the committee of adjustment to authorize minor variances, enlargements or changes in use, but contains no provision for extending a use to a different part of the land.
firac.application: Because a bona fide use of part of the lands extends to the whole parcel, the front portion over which the driveway was to run had been 'used' for industrial purposes. The construction of the driveway was therefore a change of degree, not of kind of use.
firac.conclusion: The driveway was part of the existing non-conforming use and not by itself an impermissible new use.

firac.issue: Does the zoning by-law prohibit erecting the proposed building as a second main building on a residential lot?
firac.facts: The whole parcel (200 ft. frontage by 635 ft. depth) was agreed to be a single 'lot,' and the court held it was a residential lot. The existing plant was a main building; the proposed heat-treatment plant (50' x 100') was conceded to be independent and 'an entity in itself.'
firac.rule: Under the by-law, 'Residential District' includes rural agricultural and rural residential districts (s. 5.24); s. 6.1 provides that no person shall erect more than one main building on any residential lot. Continuance of the existing non-conforming building depends entirely on s. 35(7) of the Planning Act except for variances/enlargements/changes authorized by the committee of adjustment. Accessory-building provisions were inapplicable because the front area's use was not a permitted use.
firac.application: The lot was a residential lot; the existing building was a main building and the proposed building, being 'an entity in itself,' was also a main building. Section 6.1 prohibits more than one main building on a residential lot, and the accessory-building exceptions did not apply.
firac.conclusion: The by-law prohibited the second main building; the building permit ought not to have been issued.

keywords_rationale: This is a municipal planning/zoning dispute, not one of the antisemitism/human-rights subject areas the controlled vocabulary is built around, so few tier-2 keywords fit. K002 (Civil litigation) is the best tier-1 practice area, since the action sought a declaration and injunction in the High Court. K021 (interlocutory injunction) applies because the plaintiffs sought and obtained an injunction restraining construction (though here it was final rather than interlocutory relief, it is the closest injunctive-relief term). K011 (judicial review) is a weak/borderline pick reflecting the challenge to the validity of a municipal building permit, but the case proceeded as a civil action for a declaration rather than a formal judicial review application. The controlled vocabulary lacks planning/zoning, non-conforming use, and declaratory relief keywords, so fewer than five strong matches exist; K011 and K021 are flagged as approximations. Note: Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto is cited only as a zoning authority and has no Jewish-community subject relevance here.
location_rationale: The court is the Ontario High Court of Justice. The lands and municipality at issue are in the City of Welland (former Township of Crowland, annexed to Welland), and the building permit was issued by the building inspector for the City of Welland, indicating the matter's situs; province is Ontario as stated in the heading 'ONTARIO / HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE'.
registry_rationale: The decision does not state a specific court registry office, so it is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: M.N. v. J.D.R.

defining_issues: What was the total length of time the parties cohabited for the purposes of s. 15.2(4)(a) of the Divorce Act and the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines?
What quantum and duration of spousal support (including retroactivity and review) should be ordered, and how should the wife's income and needs be determined?
How should the disputed net family property items (exclusions, handbag collection, family trust interest, vehicles) be treated in calculating the equalization payment?
Was the treating family doctor's opinion evidence about the wife's employability and the cause of her mental health admissible as a participant expert, and what weight should it receive?
Did the wife prove the intentional torts of assault, battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress on a balance of probabilities?

firac.issue: What was the total length of the parties' cohabitation for spousal support purposes under s. 15.2(4)(a) of the Divorce Act?
firac.facts: The parties married June 11, 2017 and separated October 13, 2022. The wife claimed cohabitation began December 7, 2001 (total ~20 years, 10 months); the husband ultimately conceded a November 7, 2011 start date with an eight-month separation in 2016-2017. The pre-2011 period was chaotic, marked by the husband's poverty, housing instability, drug addiction, criminal charges, and the parties' on-again/off-again relationship. Both parties had serious credibility problems and each tailored evidence knowing its effect on SSAG calculations.
firac.rule: Length of cohabitation is a statutory factor under s. 15.2(4)(a) of the Divorce Act and drives amount and duration under the SSAG Without Child Support Formula (Chapter 7, RUG). The cumulative cohabitation, including pre-marital cohabitation, is assessed using the Molodowich v. Penttinen (1980) seven clusters of factors, as confirmed in Kassabian v. Marcarian, 2025 ONCA 239; not every element need be present (M. v. H., 1999). The court may look to objective evidence to tip the scales (Macmillan-Dekker v. Dekker, 2000).
firac.application: Given conflicting and unreliable testimony, the court relied on objective evidence: parking tickets, leases, tenant insurance, utility bills, police occurrence reports, JF&CS records and the wife's contemporaneous 2011 health note showing she was 'presently staying with her b/f' after being removed from her parents' home. Before 2011 the wife only visited or stayed intermittently at the husband's various residences with no established shared-residence pattern; the husband's collateral witnesses supported his account. After 2011 the wife appeared on leases and insurance, the parties became engaged, financial support began, and others viewed them as a couple. An eight-month separation (June 2016–January 2017), following the wife's criminal charges and during the husband's relationship with another woman, was deducted per Chapter 7 of the RUG.
firac.conclusion: The court found cohabitation began November 7, 2011, deducted the eight-month separation, and fixed the total relationship at 10 years and 4 months (124 months).

firac.issue: What quantum, duration and structure of spousal support should be ordered?
firac.facts: A childless marriage; the wife (42) had long-standing mental health issues, minimal work history, savings from gifts/inheritance, and a bare-bones budget; the husband's income was agreed at $178,000 (2022-2024) and $165,000 going forward. Daurio J. had ordered temporary support of $2,800/month, which the husband was in arrears on. The wife sought high-range indefinite support; the husband sought a lower amount with imputed income of $40,000 to the wife and termination in about three years.
firac.rule: Spousal support is governed by s. 15.2 of the Divorce Act; the s. 15.2(4) factors are considered against the s. 15.2(6) objectives, with no single objective paramount (Bracklow v. Bracklow, 1999; Moge v. Moge, 1992; R.L. v. M.F., 2025 ONCA 595). The SSAG Without Child Support Formula, front-end loading (Chapter 10 RUG), the basic needs/hardship exception (Chapter 12.7 RUG), and review orders that must be tightly circumscribed (Leskun v. Leskun, 2006 SCC 25) apply. Retroactivity is governed by Kerr v. Baranow, 2011 SCC 10.
firac.application: Entitlement was predominantly non-compensatory and needs-based. The court declined to impute $40,000 or a nil income, instead imputing about $11,400/year (online sales plus investment income). It found the wife's claims that funds were 'locked in' were exaggerations. Applying front-end loading to allow the wife to budget, obtain treatment (including psychotherapy) and develop a self-sufficiency plan, the court ordered $4,000/month, exceeding the SSAG ranges on its face but falling within durational ranges when adjusted. It declined retroactive adjustment because Daurio J.'s figure fell within the SSAG ranges, ordered post-separation rent adjustments, and structured two reviews (a consent 2028 income review and a comprehensive 2030 review of the wife's circumstances). Indexing was refused.
firac.conclusion: Prospective support of $4,000/month from March 1, 2026, front-end loaded, subject to a 2028 income review and a 2030 comprehensive review; no additional retroactive support; indexing dismissed; life insurance of $60,000 and health benefits/$250 alternative ordered.

firac.issue: How should the disputed net family property items be treated in the equalization calculation?
firac.facts: The wife claimed she owed the husband $20,899.22; the husband claimed the wife owed him $251,224.56. Disputes concerned the wife's handbag collection, a Jean Paul Gaultier dress, jewelry, vehicles, gifted/inherited investments ($148,632.33), an alleged 1/3 interest in a family trust property (Oro Medonte), and the husband's business assets (resolved mid-trial).
firac.rule: Equalization under the Family Law Act requires proof of asset values on the valuation date and date of marriage; the party asserting a value bears the onus, and failure to lead adequate evidence may attract an adverse inference. Excluded property includes gifts and inheritances received during marriage.
firac.application: The court rejected the husband's fictitious figures, which omitted the wife's inheritance exclusion and improperly included ~$228,333 for the trust property that was and would remain inheritance. It valued the handbag collection at $14,840 (with a $5,840 date-of-marriage deduction for three purses), left the dress and jewelry off as offsetting inclusions/deductions, and used the most reliable available figures for vehicles and cryptocurrency ($9,266.96). Both parties' guessed and de minimis items were excluded.
firac.conclusion: The wife owes the husband a small equalization payment of $973.70 (Schedule 'A'), set off against post-separation rent adjustments of $14,364.63, leaving the husband owing the wife $13,390.93.

firac.issue: Was the treating family doctor's participant-expert opinion on employability and causation admissible, and what weight should it carry?
firac.facts: Dr. Swensen, the wife's family doctor since about 2013, provided diagnoses, and opined the wife was 'unable to work' and unlikely to change, attributing the wife's mental health significantly to the husband. The husband objected to the employability and causation opinions.
firac.rule: Expert evidence threshold and gatekeeping: Girao v. Cunningham, 2020 ONCA 260; White Burgess, 2015 SCC 23. Participant experts (Rule 20.2(1) Family Law Rules; Westerhof v. Gee Estate, 2015 ONCA 206) may give opinion arising from treatment, but there is a fine line with litigation experts (LaRoche v. Lynn, 2019 ONSC 6602; Davies v. Clarington, 2016 ONSC 1079); comparable opinions have been admitted (N.T. v. P.T.; Simcoe Muskoka CYFS v. A.H., 2021 ONSC 2789; Pike v. Wight, 2025 NLCA 33). Self-reporting is a normal part of mental-health diagnosis.
firac.application: Dr. Swensen qualified as a participant expert who had treated the wife for over a decade; no other professional could offer equivalent evidence and resources were limited. The court admitted the employability and causation opinions but treated the concerns as going to weight. In cross-examination the opinions were watered down (references to 'situational crisis' that could 'wax and wane', untried therapies, reliance on inaccurate self-reporting), and the wife's mental health troubles pre-dated the relationship and were not 'unifactorial'.
firac.conclusion: The evidence was admitted but given limited weight; the court found insufficient basis to hold the wife permanently unemployable and declined to impute income for intentional under-employment at this time.

firac.issue: Did the wife prove the torts of assault, battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress?
firac.facts: The wife originally pleaded the 'tort of family violence' (rejected in Ahluwalia v. Ahluwalia, 2023 ONCA 476) and reframed at trial as assault, battery and IIED, seeking $125,000. She alleged both patterns and specific incidents (2004 Hilton, 2007 assault/charge, 2014 property damage, 2015 assault linked to pregnancy loss, 2021/22 choking, a recorded 'murder' threat). The husband denied assaults, claimed he was often the victim, and alleged fabrication.
firac.rule: Onus on the plaintiff on a balance of probabilities. Assault: intentional creation of apprehension of imminent harmful/offensive contact (reasonable belief). Battery: non-consensual intentional physical contact of more than trivial nature, then onus shifts to defendant. IIED: flagrant and outrageous conduct calculated to harm causing a visible and provable illness (Ahluwalia v. Ahluwalia; Barreto v. Salema, 2024 ONSC 4972). Courts must guard against myths/stereotypes but the plaintiff is not relieved of proof and must be alive to fabrication/exaggeration.
firac.application: Both parties had serious credibility problems; the relationship was mutually toxic with corroborated evidence of the wife's harassment and abuse of the husband. Key evidence was incomplete: the KGB statement and peace bond materials were not introduced, the husband's father and nurse practitioner (Correa) were not called, the 2015 pregnancy-assault claim contained significant omissions and inconsistencies (contemporaneous notes recorded the fiancé 'away on business' and made no assault reference), the recorded threat was incomplete and the wife herself uttered 'murder', and the wife asked the husband very few questions in cross-examination. Prior statements were inconsistent (e.g., the March 25, 2021 message that the husband was not abusive before his stroke; a police statement that he was 'never physically abusive'). Several allegations (handgun, sexual abuse, sex workers, financial abuse) were unproven.
firac.conclusion: The wife failed to discharge her onus; the torts were not made out and the claim for damages was dismissed (contributory fault/apportionment would also have arisen had liability been found).

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area governing this Divorce Act/Family Law Act trial. K053 (spousal support) is the dominant issue — quantum, duration, front-end loading, reviews and indexing. K002 (Civil litigation) is included because the wife advanced intentional torts (assault, battery, IIED), which are civil claims lacking a more specific vocabulary term. K051 (religious divorce (get)) applies to the parties' consent to cooperate to obtain a Ghet (a genuine but minor issue). K049 (marriage/cohabitation agreement) is a borderline pick used to capture the heavily litigated cohabitation-length determination — flagged as weak because the term is really about contracts, not the fact of cohabitation. K083 (harassment) reflects the criminal harassment/extortion charges central to the credibility and tort-defence analysis; borderline. K054 (wills/estates) captures the family trust, the mother's Will and estate-trustee provisions argued in the equalization analysis. The controlled vocabulary is antisemitism/religion-focused and offers no close terms for equalization, spousal support quantification or intentional torts, so several picks are necessarily approximate.

Residences discussed are in the Toronto/North York/Vaughan area, but no sitting location is stated, so city is left null; province is Ontario per the court name and reliance on Ontario statutes (Family Law Act, Family Law Rules).

name_verification.name_in_document: Lofchick v. Belkin et al

defining_issues: Does a master of the Court of King's Bench have jurisdiction to set aside, as an abuse of process, notices of discontinuance filed in strict compliance with the Rules, or to amend them to add a 'with prejudice' provision?
If the master had jurisdiction, did the plaintiff's filing of the discontinuances after the delay motions were filed constitute an abuse of process warranting that they be set aside or modified?

firac.issue: Does a master have jurisdiction to strike or amend notices of discontinuance validly filed under the Rules as an abuse of process?
firac.facts: The plaintiff filed three actions for debt recovery in June 2018. After no steps were taken for three years, the defendants brought Rule 24.02 motions to dismiss for delay in November 2021. The day before the first appearance on those motions, the plaintiff filed notices of discontinuance under Rule 23.01(1)(b) without consent or leave, as no defences had been filed and pleadings remained open. The defendants moved before a master to strike the discontinuances as an abuse of process or to add a 'with prejudice' term, relying on the court's inherent jurisdiction, Rule 1.04 (proportionality) and s. 75 of The Court of King's Bench Act.
firac.rule: A master is 'a creature of statute, whose authority must be founded in specific legislative direction' (Jewish Community Campus of Winnipeg Inc. v. Metaser, 2013 MBQB 303; Zalizniak v. Zalizniak, 2007 MBCA 118; s. 11.15(1) of the Act). Masters have a limited supervisory jurisdiction to control their own process (Ryan v. Ryan, 2022 MBKB 198, applying R. v. Cunningham, 2010 SCC 10). Rule 23.01(1)(b) permits discontinuance by right before pleadings close. Section 75 of the Act preserves 'the authority of the court' to stay or dismiss a proceeding as an abuse of process; 'court' in the Act means the Court of King's Bench and does not include a master, whereas the Rules' broader definition of 'court' is confined to the Rules.
firac.application: Once the discontinuances were filed in strict compliance with Rule 23.01, they expunged the proceedings, leaving no action for the master to supervise, so the master was functus. Setting aside a validly filed discontinuance would require reviving a proceeding, which engages a superior court's inherent jurisdiction — a jurisdiction Rule 1.04 cannot extend to masters. Section 75's reference to 'the court' does not capture masters. Rule 25.11 (the only rule empowering masters to strike documents as an abuse of process) applies to documents in an active proceeding, not where the action has already been discontinued; every authority the defendants relied on involved a superior court judge exercising inherent jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: The master lacked jurisdiction to grant the relief sought; the abuse of process motions were dismissed on that basis.

firac.issue: Even if jurisdiction existed, did the timing of the discontinuances amount to an abuse of process?
firac.facts: The plaintiff discontinued only after the delay motions were filed, allegedly to avoid a hearing that could bar future actions. The defendants invoked the dominus litis principle (DLC Holdings Corp. v. Payne, 2021 BCCA 31; Kawaguchi v. Kawa Investments Inc., 2021 ONCA 770), arguing control of the litigation had shifted away from the plaintiff.
firac.rule: A court may, in appropriate circumstances, set aside a notice of discontinuance filed in compliance with the Rules as an abuse of process where it is filed for an improper purpose or after the plaintiff ceases to be dominus litis.
firac.application: Unlike the authorities relied on by the defendants, there were no facts showing the discontinuances were filed for an improper reason or that the dominus litis had shifted such that discontinuance was inappropriate. The plaintiff complied precisely with the process designed for discontinuance by right.
firac.conclusion: No abuse of process was established; the motions would have been dismissed on the merits in any event.

The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward a different subject area and contains no terms for discontinuance, abuse of process, or masters' jurisdiction, so the remaining picks are weak, domain-approximate selections flagged as such: K020 (class action), K021 (interlocutory injunction) and K022 (restitution) fall within the 'Civil procedure / remedies' cluster that is the closest conceptual home for the procedural motions here, and K011 (judicial review) is included only as the nearest analogue to the court's supervisory/inherent-jurisdiction analysis — none of these four squarely applies on the facts.

registry_rationale: The court file numbers are expressly designated '(Winnipeg Centre)', which is the registry/centre of the Court of King's Bench where the actions were filed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Levine c. Mohr

defining_issues: Did the defendant physicians commit professional faults (against the obligation-of-means standard) in the choice, timing, and management of Mark Levine's neurosurgical treatment?
Was valid and informed consent obtained for the tests, examinations, and surgeries, and if not, did any deficiency give rise to liability?
Did any proven fault cause Mark Levine's quadriplegic condition (causation)?
What damages, if any, were established?

firac.issue: Did the defendant physicians commit professional faults in treating Mark Levine?
firac.facts: Following a massive brain hemorrhage causing acute hydrocephalus, the neurosurgical team (Drs. Maleki and, in support, resident Atkinson, with Mohr as service director) managed Mark with external ventricular drains and VP shunts over an extended period. The plaintiffs' expert, Dr. Dimancescu, alleged 19 malpractice errors concerning the appropriateness and timing of drains, shunts, testing, and follow-up; none concerned the actual execution of any procedure.
firac.rule: Professional liability rests on art. 1457 C.c.Q. and the obligation of means: a physician's conduct is assessed against that of a prudent and diligent doctor placed in the same circumstances (Lapointe c. Hôpital Le Gardeur, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 351; St-Jean c. Mercier, 2002 SCC 15). A mere error of judgment, distinguishable from professional fault, does not attract liability where treatment corresponds to methods recognized by medical science, even amid competing theories.
firac.application: The Court preferred the defence experts (Séguin and Bojanowski) over Dimancescu, whose credibility was undermined by a prior professional suspension and reliance on an unfiled 'summary file' rather than the actual record. Examining each of the 19 allegations, the Court found each to be either a legitimate risk-benefit judgment call, a reasonable choice among valid options, or factually incorrect. Decisions such as changing the drain side and proceeding with a VP shunt on an infected patient were reasonable clinical choices, not faults. Atkinson, a resident without decisional power, committed no fault, and the suspicions about Mohr directing the case were unsupported.
firac.conclusion: No treatment-related professional fault was established against any defendant; some decisions were at most questionable judgment calls that do not amount to malpractice.

firac.issue: Was valid and informed consent obtained, and did any deficiency create liability?
firac.facts: No general admission consent form was completed (marked 'N/A' on Dec. 10, 1996). Routine tests, CT scans, and samplings were largely done without specific consent. Atkinson gave the parents inaccurate infection-risk figures (1-2%) for the Jan. 4, 1997 shunt when the real risk exceeded 10%. Maleki falsely wrote 'Emergency' on a Dec. 20, 1996 consent form when verbal consent had in fact been obtained.
firac.rule: Under arts. 10, 11, 14, 600 and 603 C.c.Q., consent to a minor's care is given by a person with parental authority, and a parent acting alone is presumed by third parties in good faith to act with the other parent's consent. Failure to obtain informed consent is a professional fault, but liability requires causation assessed by the subjective/objective (rational subjectivity) test (Parenteau c. Drolet, [1994] R.J.Q. 689; M.G. c. Pinsonneault, 2017 QCCA 607).
firac.application: Both parents exercised parental authority jointly and worked together; consent of both was not legally required and the presumption of art. 603 was not rebutted. However, the treating physician (Maleki) failed to obtain a general consent over 11 months, and Maleki's false 'Emergency' notation was improper. Applying the rational-subjectivity test, the Court found the parents would have consented to all procedures had they been properly informed, given their repeated insistence on aggressive treatment and later consent to a third shunt at higher risk.
firac.conclusion: The absence of a general consent and the false 'Emergency' notation were faults (one administrative), but they caused no damage and did not attract liability.

firac.issue: Did any proven fault cause Mark's condition?
firac.facts: Mark suffered a deep thalamic/intraventricular hemorrhage leaving him with decerebration and, ultimately, spastic quadriplegia. His neurological state remained essentially unchanged with or without drains and shunts throughout treatment.
firac.rule: A plaintiff must prove, on the balance of probabilities, a causal connection between fault and damage. Brain cells, once dead, do not regenerate; only 'shaken' neurons may recover through treatment of hydrocephalus.
firac.application: The preponderance of evidence showed the damage flowed from the initial hemorrhage and was irreversible. No neurosurgical procedure could repair that damage, and the fluctuating improvements were not correlated with the drains or shunts. Even the plaintiffs' expert admitted he could not determine how much Mark would have recovered with different treatment.
firac.conclusion: Causation was not established; the condition resulted from the irreversible initial hemorrhage, not from any fault.

firac.issue: What damages were established?
firac.facts: The parties admitted prospective loss of earnings of $1,326,140, conditional on causation. Non-pecuniary loss was not supported by expert reports; the Court observed Mark's quadriplegic, minimally responsive state.
firac.rule: Non-pecuniary damages are capped at the trilogy upper limit (Andrews; Thornton; Teno), $100,000 in 1978, equivalent to about $265,000 at the time of the action.
firac.application: Had liability and causation been proven, damages would have totalled $1,591,140 (loss of earnings plus $265,000 non-pecuniary). Since causation failed, no award was made.
firac.conclusion: No damages awarded; the action was dismissed with legal costs (excluding experts' fees).

If the vocabulary permitted, keywords for medical malpractice, obligation of means, and informed consent would be the accurate choices.

name_verification.name_in_document: Melissa (Lisa) Kolotinsky, Stephen Kolotinsky, Aviva Kolotinsky et Alison Lynn Kolotinsky c. Marilyn Kolotinsky et William Romoff
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The short style 'Kolotinsky c. Kolotinsky' reflects the lead plaintiff and lead defendant, both surnamed Kolotinsky, so it is consistent with the full style of cause. The neutral citation 2002 CanLII 3381 does not itself appear in the decision text, which shows only the court file number 500-05-003769-849 and the date 19 août 2002.

defining_issues: Can the defendant William Romoff, who managed the estate's rental properties, be held liable for the loss of estate assets despite his discharge from bankruptcy?
Is the executor Marilyn Kolotinsky personally liable to pay the particular legacies, and does her failure to render an account of her administration make her a personal debtor of those legacies?

firac.issue: Can William Romoff be held liable for the disappearance of the estate's assets notwithstanding his discharge in bankruptcy?
firac.facts: Romoff, husband of the executor Marilyn Kolotinsky and named substitute executor, managed the estate's income-producing buildings on his wife's behalf from the 1975 opening of the succession. He made an assignment of his property under the bankruptcy legislation in February 1986 and was discharged in January 1988. The plaintiffs, by amendment, sought to hold him solidarily liable for the vanished estate assets.
firac.rule: A discharge in bankruptcy releases the bankrupt from claims for acts predating the bankruptcy unless the claim arises from fraudulent dealing with property, per art. 178(1)(d) of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act. A mandatary who manages property is answerable only to his mandator, not to third parties, absent fraud.
firac.application: Romoff acted only as mandatary of the executor Marilyn, who continued to sign cheques and documents. The early-1980s economic depression harmed the estate's modest real-estate holdings. Although some transactions (e.g., the sale of the Bloomfield Avenue building) left the Court perplexed, the plaintiffs failed to prove fraudulent dilapidation or diversion of funds for Romoff's benefit needed to overcome his bankruptcy discharge.
firac.conclusion: The action against William Romoff is dismissed without costs; the evidence was insufficient to establish his solidary or fraudulent liability.

firac.issue: Is the executor personally liable for the unpaid legacies, and what is the consequence of her failure to render an account?
firac.facts: Marilyn Kolotinsky, residuary heir and testamentary executor, paid the small institutional legacies and one $10,000 legacy to her adult daughter, but could not pay the $20,000 legacies to the plaintiffs once the estate became deficitary. When plaintiff Melissa reached age 20 on 6 December 1983 and claimed her legacy, the executor did not render an account. Marilyn later went bankrupt in 1996 without ever accounting for her administration.
firac.rule: Under the last paragraph of art. 918 C.c.B.-C., where an executor's functions extend beyond a year and a day, the executor must, on request of an heir or legatee, render from time to time a summary account of the administration of estate assets.
firac.application: The executor was at fault for failing to render an account, leaving the legatees uncertain about the collapse of the estate's assets. However, on the evidence submitted, this breach of her duty as executor and fiduciary did not make her personally the debtor of the particular legacies claimed, since the estate had genuinely become deficitary. Her fault nonetheless justified imposing costs against her.
firac.conclusion: The action against Marilyn Kolotinsky is maintained for costs only; she is ordered to bear the entire costs of the proceeding but is not held personally liable for the legacies.

keywords_rationale: K054 (wills/estates) is the core subject — a dispute over unpaid testamentary legacies and the executor's administration and duty to account under art. 918 C.c.B.-C. K006 (Family law) is its tier-1 parent in this vocabulary. case_name: Katz et al. v. Little and Service Leasing Corporation of Canada Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: Katz et al. v. Little and Service Leasing Corporation of Canada Ltd.

defining_issues: What quantum of damages should be awarded under the Trustee Act for the death of a 62-year-old woman for the lost expectation of life/prospective happiness?

Which claimed expenses (funeral, moving, advertising, rent, clothing, probate fee) are recoverable under s. 49(1) of the Trustee Act, given the bar on damages calculated by reference to loss or gain consequent on death?
Can the sons recover under the Fatal Accidents Act for the loss of prospective financial assistance and services their mother would have contributed to a business the family proposed to purchase?
Can the son recover under the Fatal Accidents Act for the loss of free board, lodging and laundry his mother had provided?

firac.issue: What is the proper award under the Trustee Act for the deceased's lost expectation of life?
firac.facts: The deceased, aged 62 with an agreed life expectancy of 17 years, was in good health and had led a happy, purposeful life. She was killed instantly or died within minutes, so no allowance could be made for pain and suffering.
firac.rule: Damages for loss of expectation of life are assessed on an objective estimate of the future the deceased might have enjoyed, following Benham v. Gambling, [1941] A.C. 157, as applied in Bechthold v. Osbaldeston, [1953] 4 D.L.R. 783 (SCC) and Gayhart v. Registrar of Motor Vehicles (1956), 6 D.L.R. (2d) 474; other things being equal, damages must be reduced as life expectancy declines from the prime of life.
firac.application: The court reviewed comparable awards, distinguishing cases involving younger deceased persons (Canada Trust v. Pelletier, Jamieson v. Olsen) and noting that in Bryce the Supreme Court had restored the trial award. Given the deceased's age, health and quality of life, the court fixed a moderate award reflecting her declining life expectancy.
firac.conclusion: The main award under the Trustee Act was set at $4,000.

firac.issue: Which claimed expenses are recoverable under s. 49(1) of the Trustee Act?
firac.facts: Claims included funeral expenses of $812.60, moving furniture ($43.15), advertising the suite ($10), three months' rent ($360), damaged clothing ($275.55) and a probate fee ($112).
firac.rule: Section 49(1) of the Trustee Act, R.S.M. 1954, c. 273, provides that estate damages shall be calculated without reference to any loss or gain consequent on death, except that a sum for funeral expenses may be included at the court's discretion; funeral allowances should be kept within reasonable bounds (Crown Trust Co. (Cook Estate) v. Snowden (1960), 31 W.W.R. 238; Dowhy v. Lamontagne, [1945] 2 D.L.R. 515).
firac.application: The court exercised its discretion to allow $500 for funeral expenses. The moving, advertising and rent items (totalling $413.15) were disallowed as losses consequent on death barred by s. 49(1). The probate fee of $112 and $91 for clothing (as agreed by counsel) were allowed.
firac.conclusion: Total allowance under the Trustee Act was $4,703.

firac.issue: Can the sons recover under the Fatal Accidents Act for lost financial assistance and services connected to the proposed business purchase?
firac.facts: The sons planned to buy into the Chick-N-Rib night-club, with their mother to contribute financing and services (baking, cooking, supervising the kitchen, babysitting) in exchange for a 25% share. At her death no firm offer had been made; the mother had telephoned a third son to canvass his views and had not communicated with the bank.
firac.rule: There is no common-law claim; recovery depends entirely on the Fatal Accidents Act (Best v. Samuel Fox & Co., [1952] A.C. 716). The loss must flow from the family relationship, not merely from a contract (Burgess v. Florence Nightingale Hospital, [1955] 1 Q.B. 349; Sykes v. North Eastern R. Co. (1875)). Speculative and remote losses are not recoverable (Bingham v. Town of Trenton; Barnett v. Cohen; Baker v. Dalgleish Steam Shipping Co.).
firac.application: The court found the mother had not irrevocably decided to enter the financial arrangement, so the foundation for the claim was absent. Even assuming she had, the arrangement was in substance a partnership/contract, so any loss arose from contract rather than the mother-son relationship. The claim was also for prospective profits of a projected partnership, making it speculative and too remote.
firac.conclusion: No claim exists under the Fatal Accidents Act for the financial assistance and services; the claim was disallowed.

firac.issue: Can the son recover under the Fatal Accidents Act for the loss of free board, lodging and laundry provided by his mother?
firac.facts: Howard Katz, 28, unmarried, whose income exceeded his mother's, claimed the value of board ($2/day), lodging ($2/day) and laundry ($1.50/week), totalling about $1,534 per year, for gratuitous services she provided before her death. His interest in her estate was estimated at $8,000–$9,000.
firac.rule: Under the Fatal Accidents Act, contingencies and acceleration of benefits (including inheritance) must be weighed against any dependency claim.
firac.application: The court doubted the son genuinely received these benefits gratuitously without reciprocation, and weighed contingencies such as the mother remarrying or the son marrying, plus the acceleration of his substantial interest in the estate. Any allowance would have been less than what he already received under the Trustee Act.
firac.conclusion: No award was made under the Fatal Accidents Act.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary practice area: this is a tort/damages action for a fatal motor-vehicle accident, resolved under the Trustee Act and Fatal Accidents Act. K054 (wills/estates) applies because the principal recovery is an estate claim under the Trustee Act, and K006 (Family law) is included as its tier-1 parent and because the dependency claims arise from the mother-son family relationship. K093 (Jewish) and K095 (Jewish family) are supported by the deceased's Jewish family and the reference to the son 'sitting Shiva', a Jewish mourning ritual — these are weak, contextual picks flagged as such, as religion was not a legal issue; they are included to reach the minimum and reflect the only identity markers in an otherwise doctrinally narrow tort/estates case. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated fatal-accidents/wrongful-death or damages term, so no closer keyword exists.

case_name: J.S.R. v. Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa

name_verification.name_in_document: J.S.R. v. Children's Aid Society of Ottawa

defining_issues: Should the fresh evidence tendered by H. and by the mother be admitted on appeal?
Can a party raise ineffective assistance of counsel on appeal without giving notice to former counsel, and was there an evidentiary basis for the claim?
Did the trial judge err in ordering that the two children be placed in extended society care?
Did the trial judge err in law by delegating all terms and conditions of access to the discretion of the Children's Aid Society?

firac.issue: Should the fresh evidence tendered by H. and by the mother be admitted on appeal?
firac.facts: H. sought to file a sworn affidavit describing the limited visits she had had with her siblings since the trial and her fear of being cut off; the mother filed no motion and only after argument attempted to file an affidavit about her community treatment, ultimately filing one two days after the hearing without leave.
firac.rule: Section 121(6) CYFSA permits the court to receive further evidence relating to events after the appealed decision; the L.M. v. Peel Children's Aid Society, 2019 ONCA 841 test requires that fresh evidence: (a) could not have been adduced before; (b) is highly relevant; (c) is potentially decisive to the child's best interests; (d) is credible; (e) is uncontroverted; and (f) updates the record, applied flexibly given the need for accurate, up-to-date information on the child's best interests.
firac.application: H.'s affidavit concerned post-trial events, was sworn, the affiant was available for cross-examination, was uncontradicted, and bore on the children's discretionary access as access holders, so it met the test and was in the children's best interests. The mother's material was not the subject of any proper motion, was unclear in content, lacked the requisite notice to the CAS, and the December affidavit was filed after argument without leave and in any event failed the criteria.
firac.conclusion: H.'s fresh evidence was admitted; the mother's purported fresh evidence was not admitted.

firac.issue: Can ineffective assistance of counsel be raised on appeal without notice to former counsel, and was it established?
firac.facts: The mother, self-represented until shortly before the hearing, argued in oral submissions that former counsel had made two questionable litigation decisions, but never served former counsel with notice, provided no waiver, and filed no affidavit evidence or the lawyer's file.
firac.rule: Per Windsor-Essex Children's Aid Society v. R.H.C., 2016 ONCA 595, and K.R. v. CAS, 2015 ONSC 3769 (drawing on R. v. Archer), the Superior Court of Justice Protocol–Allegations of Incompetence applies in child protection proceedings; notice to former counsel is a basic requirement of natural justice, binding even on self-represented litigants.
firac.application: The mother gave former counsel no notice, no opportunity to respond, and provided no evidentiary foundation—relying only on inferences—so the court could not properly consider the allegations, and even with notice there was no evidence to support a finding.
firac.conclusion: The ineffective assistance of counsel ground was dismissed.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in ordering the children placed in extended society care?
firac.facts: After a summary judgment finding that the children needed protection and a three-day disposition trial, the judge found the mother had a paranoid personality disorder impairing her parenting, that R. suffered physical and emotional harm, that frequent moves caused educational delays, and that the mother had failed over 21 months to address the Society's concerns; the mother did not contest that the children needed protection but sought a supervision order or specified access.
firac.rule: The best interests of the children are paramount (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. V.L., 2012 ONCA 890); the Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33 appellate standards apply—correctness for law, palpable and overriding error for fact, with the mixed standard varying.
firac.application: The trial judge's factual findings were fully supported by the evidence, including the uncontradicted parenting-capacity evidence of Dr. Woods; the mother established no error of law, no error of principle, and no palpable and overriding factual error, and the discretion was exercised consistently with the children's best interests.
firac.conclusion: The extended society care order was upheld and this ground of appeal dismissed.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in law by delegating all terms and conditions of access to the discretion of the Society?
firac.facts: Having found access to the mother, sister H. and grandmother to be in the children's best interests, the trial judge ordered that access be entirely at the Society's discretion and in accordance with the children's best interests, leaving type, frequency and duration to the Society; since trial H. had had only limited visits.
firac.rule: Sections 104 and 105 CYFSA require the court to make access orders and to impose the terms and conditions it considers appropriate; the best-interests factors in s. 74(3) apply; the principle against sub-delegation (A.G. of Canada v. Brent, [1956] SCR 318) bars delegating adjudicative discretion reserved to a judicial decision-maker; H.C. v. Durham CAS (temporary orders) is distinguishable, and Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. J.G., 2020 ONCA 415 (and Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. D.P., 2005 CanLII 34560) permit a Society to control day-to-day visits only once the court has fixed minimum access rights.
firac.application: Nothing in ss. 104 or 105 authorizes sub-delegating the discretion over type, frequency and duration to a non-judicial party; s. 105(9) confirms Society discretion exists only where no access order is in effect. J.G. was distinguishable because there the court set minimum access; here the judge delegated all discretionary elements, including whether access would occur at all, which offends the anti-sub-delegation principle. A Society may supplement court-fixed minimum access with discretionary visits, but the minimum must be set by the court.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge erred in law; the appeal was allowed on terms and conditions of access only and the matter remitted to the trial judge to fix minimum access, with a request to expedite.
