case_name: Kramarz v. KMH Cardiology & Diagnostic Centres

name_verification.name_in_document: Kramarz et al. v. KMH Cardiology & Diagnostic Centres et al. [Indexed as: Kramarz v. KMH Cardiology & Diagnostic Centres]

defining_issues: Does the two-year limitation period in s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act apply to a derivative claim brought under s. 61(1) of the Family Law Act arising from the death of a family member?

Do the transition provisions of the Limitations Act, 2002 (ss. 24(4) and 24(5)) apply so as to render the s. 38(3) limitation a 'former limitation period' and leave the action subject to 'no limitation period'?
Does s. 6 (as applied through s. 19(5)) of the Limitations Act, 2002 extend the limitation period for the minor grandchild plaintiff?

firac.issue: Does the two-year limitation in s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act govern a derivative action brought under s. 61(1) of the Family Law Act following a death?
firac.facts: Maria Kramarz died in hospital on June 10, 2003. Her spouse, children and minor grandchild sued the cardiologist and clinic for negligence causing her death, invoking s. 61(1) of the Family Law Act. The action was commenced December 5, 2005, roughly two-and-a-half years after death.
firac.rule: A claim under s. 61(1) of the Family Law Act is derivative of an estate's right to sue under the Trustee Act; s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act bars any such action brought more than two years after death (Smith Estate v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario; Swain Estate v. Lake of the Woods District Hospital; Waschkowski v. Hopkinson Estate).
firac.application: Because the Family Law Act right to recover is derivative of the estate's Trustee Act action, the two-year limit in s. 38(3) applied. The claim was commenced more than two years after the death, so absent the new Limitations Act it was plainly out of time.
firac.conclusion: The s. 38(3) two-year limitation applied and, on its face, barred the action.

firac.issue: Do the transition provisions of the Limitations Act, 2002 convert the Trustee Act limitation into a 'former limitation period' so that s. 24(4) leaves 'no limitation period'?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs argued the s. 38(3) limitation was a 'former limitation period' that had not expired by the effective date, and that since no limitation period 'under' the new Act would apply, s. 24(4) meant there was no limitation period at all, allowing the action to proceed.
firac.rule: Limitations Act, 2002, s. 19(1) continues limitation periods in other Acts listed in the Schedule (s. 38(3) is so listed); s. 24(1) defines 'former limitation period' as one that applied 'before the coming into force of this Act'; s. 24(4)/24(5) are transitional (York Condominium Corp. No. 382 v. Jay-M Holdings Ltd.). A provision merely listed in the Schedule is not incorporated as a limitation 'under' the new Act (Bikur Cholim Jewish Volunteer Services v. Langston; British Columbia (A.G.) v. Canada (A.G.); Sullivan and Driedger on the Construction of Statutes).
firac.application: Reading the Act purposively (to balance access to justice against certainty and finality), the court held s. 38(3) is not a 'former limitation period' because, by operation of s. 19(1), it continues in force unchanged — it is not 'of the past.' There is no transition from one regime to another. The scheduling of s. 38(3) validates but does not incorporate it into the new Act, so it is not a limitation 'under' the new Act. Even if s. 24(4) applied, s. 19(4) resolves any conflict between 'no limitation period' and the Trustee Act limit in favour of the Trustee Act; and s. 24(5) could not apply because there is no limitation period under the new Act.
firac.conclusion: The transition provisions did not apply; the s. 38(3) two-year limitation continued to govern and barred the action.

firac.issue: Does s. 6 (via s. 19(5)) of the Limitations Act, 2002 extend the limitation period for the minor grandchild plaintiff?
firac.facts: The minor grandchild of Maria Kramarz sued through a litigation guardian.
firac.rule: Limitations Act, 2002, s. 19(5) applies ss. 6, 7 and 11 to limitation periods continued under s. 19(1); s. 6 suspends the running of a limitation period for a claimant who is a minor and is not represented by a litigation guardian.
firac.application: Because the minor grandchild was represented by a litigation guardian, the s. 6 suspension did not apply and the limitation period continued to run against him.
firac.conclusion: The minor's claim was also out of time.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area: this is a negligence/wrongful-death civil action turning on limitations and statutory interpretation. K006 (Family law) is engaged because the plaintiffs' right to sue arises under s. 61(1) of the Family Law Act. K054 (wills/estates) is the closest available term for the Trustee Act s. 38(3) estate/derivative limitation that governs the outcome. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated 'limitations' or 'statutory interpretation' keyword, so no perfectly on-point tier-2 term exists. The remaining picks are weak and flagged: K047 (best interests / child) is only tangentially relevant via the minor grandchild litigation-guardian point, and K093 (Jewish) is engaged only because a cited authority, Bikur Cholim Jewish Volunteer Services v. Langston, involved a Jewish organization — it does not reflect the substance of this case. Both are included only to meet the minimum count.
location_rationale: The decision identifies the court as the 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' per Lederer J., establishing the province as Ontario. No city or sitting location is stated in the text.
registry_rationale: No registry or court office is named in the decision; it is reported only as an Ontario Superior Court of Justice judgment, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Lotin v. Gregor

defining_issues: Was it appropriate to determine these defamation actions by summary judgment rather than trial?
Were the statements attributed to Tomas Gregor made and defamatory of Henry Lotin?
Were the statements attributed to Andrea Gregor made and defamatory of Henry Lotin, including whether they satisfied a slander per se exception?
What quantum of general damages should be awarded for the proven defamatory statements?
Should a permanent injunction be granted to restrain future defamatory statements?

firac.issue: Was it appropriate to resolve these defamation actions by summary judgment under Rule 20?
firac.facts: The record contained 13 affidavits and 10 cross-examination transcripts; both parties asked the court to decide on that record, and the judge additionally heard viva voce evidence from two non-party witnesses (Peter and Gabor) under Rule 20.04(2.2).
firac.rule: Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7 sets a two-stage test: whether there is a genuine issue requiring a trial and, if so, whether the fact-finding powers in Rules 20.04(2.1) and (2.2) can be used in the interest of justice to reach a fair and just determination consistent with timeliness, affordability and proportionality; Mason v. Perras Mongenais, 2018 ONCA 978.
firac.application: Although the written record prima facie raised factual disputes about what was said, the court used its fact-finding powers, weighed evidence, assessed credibility and heard limited oral testimony, concluding no better evidence would emerge at trial and that proceeding summarily would dispose of both actions fairly.
firac.conclusion: Summary judgment was appropriate; a trial was not required to justly adjudicate the disputes.

firac.issue: Were the statements by Tomas Gregor defamatory of Henry?
firac.facts: Tomas allegedly told Gabor and Sandy that Henry and Judy had taken items (including silver trays) from Agnes without authorization. Tomas denied accusing them of theft; the recipients did not testify that he alleged unauthorized taking or that they understood the words as accusing theft.
firac.rule: Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61 requires the words to be defamatory (tending to lower reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person), to refer to the plaintiff, and to be published; the words must be reasonably capable of, and in fact bear, a defamatory meaning (Botiuk; Color Your World; Bernstein v. Poon).
firac.application: On Gabor's and Sandy's accounts, Tomas was circumspect, sought help mediating return of items and emphasized only that Agnes was upset; no words reasonably capable of a defamatory meaning were identified, nor did the recipients understand them defamatorily, and nothing imputed a crime or disparaged Henry's profession.
firac.conclusion: Henry failed to prove defamation by Tomas; summary judgment was granted dismissing the action against Tomas.

firac.issue: Were the statements by Andrea Gregor defamatory of Henry?
firac.facts: Andrea allegedly (1) told Sandy Henry took photographs and a carpet, (2) loudly called Henry a thief at a birthday party, (3) told Gabor by phone that Henry stole items from Agnes, and (4) texted Peter that Henry and Judy 'ransacked' Agnes's place and 'took things'.
firac.rule: Same Torstar defamation test; libel (written) is actionable per se with presumed damages (Campbell v. Cartmell); slander per se requires an exception such as imputing a criminal offence or, under s. 16 of the Libel and Slander Act, words calculated to disparage the plaintiff in his profession.
firac.application: Statement #1 (Sandy) and the birthday-party accusation were not established on the evidence. However, the court accepted Gabor's credible reaffirmed account that Andrea twice said Henry had stolen from Agnes, imputing the crime of theft (s. 322 Criminal Code), which was conceded to be defamatory; and the text to Peter, being libel, was reasonably capable of and in fact bore a defamatory meaning through 'ransacked' and 'took things'. The professional-disparagement exception failed since the accusations were personal and Andrea was unaware of Henry's profession.
firac.conclusion: Two of Andrea's four statements (to Gabor and the text to Peter) were defamatory; summary judgment was granted for Henry against Andrea on those statements.

firac.issue: What quantum of general damages was warranted?
firac.facts: Henry proved no special damages and intended to donate any award to charity. Dissemination was limited to family friends familiar with the family dispute; no actual reputational harm or impact on security clearance was shown, and Andrea conceded Henry is not a thief.
firac.rule: On proof of defamation, falsity and damage are presumed and damages may be awarded at large (Hill v. Church of Scientology); quantum factors include the plaintiff's standing, seriousness, extent of publication, absence of apology, and the defendant's conduct and motive (Barrick Gold v. Lopehandia).
firac.application: Given the limited scope of publication, the personal (not professional) motive, absence of proven harm, and Andrea's concessions, but declining to award merely contemptuous damages, the court fixed a modest amount and refused aggravated damages.
firac.conclusion: Henry was awarded $2,000 in general damages against Andrea, with pre- and post-judgment interest; no aggravated damages.

firac.issue: Should a permanent injunction be granted?
firac.facts: Henry sought a permanent injunction to prevent continued defamation, fearing the defendants would keep making accusations within the family; the statements at issue were more than two years old and no evidence of an ongoing campaign was led.
firac.rule: Astley v. Verdun, 2011 ONSC 3651 permits a permanent injunction where there is a likelihood the defendant will continue defaming the plaintiff, or a real possibility that any damage award is unenforceable.
firac.application: Only the first branch was argued; there was no evidence of recent or ongoing defamatory conduct, and the court expected Andrea, now informed of the imputation of her comments, would be circumspect. An injunction against speech is a serious restriction on freedom of expression not justified here.
firac.conclusion: The request for a permanent injunction was refused.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as these are civil defamation actions. K015 (defamation) is the central doctrine, covering both slander (statements to Gabor) and libel (text to Peter), including the per se exceptions and damages analysis. K021 (injunction) applies because the plaintiff sought a permanent injunction and the court applied the Astley test, refusing it as an unjustified restriction on freedom of expression. K093 (Jewish), K094 (Jewish community) and K095 (Jewish family) are engaged because the dispute arises within a close-knit community of Hungarian Jews who emigrated to Toronto and the matriarch Agnes's family; these tier-3 entity tags are contextual rather than legally determinative, so they are flagged as peripheral to the legal holdings.
location_rationale: The decision is from the Ontario Superior Court of Justice; Kimmel J. directs costs submissions to be delivered to 'Judges' Administration, Superior Court of Justice at 361 University Avenue (Room 170), Toronto, Ontario', confirming the court sits in Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The court file numbers (CV-17-574700 and CV-17-569860) and the Toronto address for filing costs submissions indicate the Toronto registry of the Superior Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Irwin Lande and Claude-Andrée Pion v. Joseph Feldman and Khadija El Hachmi El Alaoui

defining_issues: Are the conditions for issuing a Mareva order met in respect of the Paulian Action against Feldman and his wife?
Can a Mareva order be issued in the file relating to execution of an already final and executable judgment, and does article 657 C.C.P. authorize such a post-judgment order?
Should a sealing order be granted over Exhibits R-6, R-22 and R-27?

firac.issue: Are the conditions for issuing a Mareva order met in respect of the Paulian Action against Feldman and his wife?
firac.facts: After the $1.2M Davis Judgment for defamation was rendered and confirmed on appeal, Feldman fled to Florida, avoided examination on his assets, transferred nearly $3M from a Canadian account to his wife Alaoui's account in Morocco, and assigned a $1.6M hypothecary claim to her. Alaoui refused to attend her scheduled examination. The Paulian Action alleges fraudulent, undervalued transfers designed to render Feldman judgment proof.
firac.rule: Under Quebec law the Mareva injunction is inspired by the interlocutory injunction (Giroux c. Entreprises Bertrand Roberge ltée, 2024 QCCA 928): the applicant must show (i) a prima facie/appearance of right, (ii) serious and irreparable harm, (iii) that the balance of convenience favours the applicant, and, for a provisional-type order, (iv) urgency. It is an exceptional in personam order granted only where there is convincing evidence of a real risk assets may disappear through deceptive acts (Desjardins Assurances générales inc. c. 9330-8898 Québec inc., 2019 QCCA 523).
firac.application: The Court found urgency in the mounting series of asset-shielding measures coupled with tepid cooperation on examinations; a strong appearance of right flowing from the fully executable Davis Judgment and the post-judgment transfers to the wife; irreparable harm because moving assets beyond creditors' reach could defeat realization; and a balance of convenience favouring the plaintiffs, mitigated by allowances of $5,000/month for living expenses and $40,000 for legal fees to avoid financial asphyxiation.
firac.conclusion: The conditions were met; the Court granted the Mareva order, but limited to the Paulian Action file, for a 30-day period subject to renewal.

firac.issue: Can a Mareva order be issued in the execution file of an already final and executable judgment, and does article 657 C.C.P. authorize such a post-judgment order?
firac.facts: Plaintiffs also sought the same Mareva order in the file executing the Davis Judgment, arguing article 657 C.C.P. empowered a post-judgment freezing order; they conceded they could find no motivated Quebec precedent granting such an order after a final executable judgment.
firac.rule: A Mareva injunction is injunctive in nature and serves to preserve the status quo en route to a final and executable judgment. Article 657 C.C.P. lets the Court interpret or clarify a judgment to facilitate execution but cannot modify the judgment; any order must be the 'natural extension' of the original decision and not a disguised appeal, review or revocation (Air Canada c. P.A., 2025 QCCA 518).
firac.application: The Court declined the argument. A Mareva order preserves the status quo before final judgment, so it does not fit an already-adjudicated defamation judgment. Issuing, ex parte, an entire set of conclusions grounded in post-judgment conduct never before the Court cannot be a 'natural extension' of the original order under art. 657 C.C.P. In any event, granting the order solely in the Paulian file achieved the plaintiffs' objective of freezing the defendants' assets.
firac.conclusion: No; the Mareva order was refused in the execution file and article 657 C.C.P. did not authorize it. The order issued only in the Paulian Action.

firac.issue: Should a sealing order be granted over Exhibits R-6, R-22 and R-27?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs requested a sealing order over three exhibits but offered nothing in their application to support it.
firac.rule: Under Sherman (Estate) v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25, the open court principle yields only exceptionally; a court may depart from it where disclosure of highly sensitive information seriously threatens a person's dignity, but mere embarrassment is insufficient, and the burden on the party seeking to depart from the strong presumption of openness is high.
firac.application: There was nothing in the plaintiffs' application supporting the request, so the high threshold to displace the open court presumption was not met.
firac.conclusion: The sealing request was denied.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns execution of a civil judgment and a Paulian action. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the core doctrine — the Mareva/freezing order is treated as a species of interlocutory injunction with the prima facie case/irreparable harm/balance of convenience/urgency test. K015 (defamation) is engaged because the underlying Davis Judgment awarding $1.2M arose from Feldman's defamatory statements and supplies the appearance of right. K058 (antisemitism), K088 (Holocaust) and K093 (Jewish) reflect the defamatory content — the false accusation that the plaintiffs possessed gold stolen by the Nazis from Jewish victims during the Holocaust; these are background/context to this procedural ruling and are flagged as weaker picks since the present judgment turns on injunctive relief, not the merits of the defamation.
location_rationale: The header states 'SUPERIOR COURT ... PROVINCE OF QUEBEC ... DISTRICT OF MONTRÉal' and para. 44 refers to examination 'in person in Montréal, Québec, Canada.'
registry_rationale: The decision is filed in the District of Montréal (court file No. 500-17-136338-251), so the registry is Montréal.

name_verification.name_in_document: Malak v. Hanna

defining_issues: Which defendants were responsible for authoring and publishing the impugned internet articles, poem, emails and ethics-line complaint, in particular whether Mr. Hanna was the person behind the 'Jim Arthur' pseudonym?
Did the plaintiffs establish the three elements of defamation (defamatory meaning, reference to the plaintiffs, and publication to a third party)?
Did the defences of justification, qualified privilege and fair comment, and the plea of malice, succeed or fail?
Were the defendants jointly liable on the basis of a common design to vilify the plaintiffs?
Was Valley Traffic Systems Inc. vicariously liable for Mr. Hanna's conduct?

firac.issue: Which defendants authored and published the defamatory material, and in particular was Mr. Hanna the pseudonymous 'Jim Arthur'?
firac.facts: The 'Uncovered Article', a poem, YouTube videos, a September 27, 2012 email to the Premier and Minister Coleman, and a Telus ethics-line complaint were disseminated, mostly under the pseudonyms 'Jim Arthur' and 'Mike Flagger'. Mr. Hanna had worked for and fallen out with the Ansan Group, disliked Mr. Malak, and stood to gain financially only if VTS won the BC Hydro contract. He forwarded the ethics-line 'Follow-Up Notes' to Mr. Jackman with the subject line 'FYI', and gave implausible explanations for deleting emails and for the 'Guess need new ones! lol' message about the WIPO decision. Documents were disclosed only days before trial.
firac.rule: Credibility is assessed under Faryna v. Chorny (1951 CanLII 252 (BC CA)) by testing testimony against the preponderance of probabilities; the civil standard is proof on a balance of probabilities requiring clear, convincing and cogent evidence (F.H. v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53).
firac.application: The Court found Mr. Hanna not credible: his stated wish to have 'nothing to do with' the Jim Arthur email was contradicted by his copying and pasting the Follow-Up Notes to Mr. Jackman, and his time-zone and 'joke' explanations were rejected. The Court found Mr. Hanna had the background and motive to write the material and was 'Jim Arthur' who wrote the Telus complaint and established the defamatory websites, blogs and videos. Mr. Jackman and Mr. Paine were also found not credible and to have known Hanna was Jim Arthur. The computer forensic evidence, though given reduced weight for want of ISP server data, was consistent with these findings.
firac.conclusion: Mr. Hanna authored and published the defamatory materials as 'Jim Arthur'; Mr. Jackman and Mr. Paine knew this and participated in circulating the material.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiffs prove the three elements of defamation?
firac.facts: The publications accused Mr. Malak and his companies of money laundering, kickbacks, bribery, prostitution, tax evasion and other criminal conduct. The materials named Mr. Malak and the Ansan Group and were posted on numerous 'sister-ship' domain names, shared by email and links, and viewed by third parties including Mr. Marr, Mr. Young and lawyer Ms. Rossos, and municipal recipients.
firac.rule: Under Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61 at para. 28, a plaintiff must prove (1) defamatory words that lower reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person, (2) reference to the plaintiff, and (3) publication to at least one other person; falsity and damage are then presumed. Defamatory meaning may be literal, by legal innuendo, or by inferential/popular innuendo (Lawson v. Baines, 2012 BCCA 117; Weaver v. Corcoran, 2017 BCCA 160). Publication is not deemed for non-broadcasts (Crookes v. Newton, 2011 SCC 47).
firac.application: The Court found the literal and inferential meanings of the Uncovered Article, poem, September 27 email and Telus complaint were defamatory of Mr. Malak and each corporate plaintiff (and Island Traffic after its September 21, 2012 acquisition). Each publication named or clearly referred to the plaintiffs. Although the Court declined to infer publication merely from the existence of the websites, it found actual publication to third parties who read the material, none of whom were the plaintiffs' 'alter ego' (applying Motoretta Inc. v. Twist & Go Power Sports Inc., 2014 ONSC 2469).
firac.conclusion: All three elements were established on a balance of probabilities for each publication.

firac.issue: Did the defences of justification, qualified privilege and fair comment succeed, or were they defeated by malice?
firac.facts: Mr. Hanna pleaded justification and fair comment; Mr. Jackman, Mr. Paine and VTS pleaded qualified privilege. Hanna's justification particulars concerned the Granville Island Hotel, dealings with Martin Chambers, employment of Brian Slobogian, Ms. Chun's origins, acquisitions, and alleged statements including the 'rubber gloves' warning. The defendants intended to damage the plaintiffs' reputation to gain a competitive advantage on the BC Hydro and Telus work.
firac.rule: The defendant bears the onus of proving substantial truth of the sting (Brown on Defamation; Taseko Mines Ltd. v. Western Canada Wilderness Committee, 2016 BCSC 109). Malice — spite, an indirect or ulterior motive, or speaking dishonestly or with reckless disregard for truth — defeats qualified privilege and fair comment (Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto, 1995 CanLII 59 (SCC); WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40).
firac.application: The Court accepted Mr. Malak's evidence and found none of Hanna's particulars justified the stings; a general charge of bad conduct cannot be proven by isolated instances, and Hanna himself testified he did not believe the Follow-Up Notes to be true, deflating his truth plea. The 'rubber gloves' and 'dirty Jew' allegations were rejected. All defendants were found to have acted with malice, intending to destroy the plaintiffs' reputation for competitive advantage, which defeated the qualified privilege and fair comment defences.
firac.conclusion: Justification failed; qualified privilege and fair comment were defeated by malice. The defences failed.

firac.issue: Were the defendants jointly liable on the basis of a common design?
firac.facts: Following the Ansan Group's termination of acquisition negotiations, on May 1, 2012 Mr. Hanna sent Mr. Jackman a list of 'Raoul's lawsuits', shared with Mr. Paine. Hanna's remuneration from VTS was purely contingent on winning the BC Hydro (and possibly Telus) work, and its terms were never documented or disclosed.
firac.rule: Concurrent tortfeasors acting in furtherance of a common design are jointly liable, without needing to realise they are committing a tort (Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press Publications Ltd., 1995 CanLII 60 (SCC), citing Fleming, The Law of Torts).
firac.application: Because Hanna was 'Jim Arthur', and Jackman and Paine knew this yet took no steps to disassociate, and given shared financial motive and non-disclosure of documents, the Court found a common design to destroy, diminish or undermine the plaintiffs' reputations existed by May 1, 2012. The 'Mike Flagger' September 19, 2012 email was also part of that common design.
firac.conclusion: Mr. Hanna, Mr. Jackman, Mr. Paine and VTS acted in furtherance of a common design and are jointly liable.

firac.issue: Was Valley Traffic Systems Inc. vicariously liable for Mr. Hanna's conduct?
firac.facts: VTS engaged Mr. Hanna (through Advanced Traffic, which had no assets, operations or other employees) to help prepare and front the BC Hydro tender under VTS's name, on a contingency basis. Hanna took a high-profile role communicating with BC Hydro on behalf of 'the team', with Jackman's approval, and represented that the parties were 'in partnership'.
firac.rule: Vicarious liability turns on whether the wrongful act is sufficiently related to authorized conduct and whether there is a significant connection between the creation/enhancement of risk and the wrong (Bazley v. Curry, 1999 CanLII 692 (SCC)), with control being key (Sagaz Industries, 2001 SCC 59). A principal may be liable for slanders uttered by an agent engaged to solicit legal relations on its behalf (Colonial Mutual Life Assurance Society Ltd. v. Producers and Citizens Co-Operative, applied through Bazley/Sagaz).
firac.application: The Court found Hanna was VTS's agent with considerable authority to represent VTS to BC Hydro, and that VTS controlled whether he made representations on the team's behalf. Applying the Bazley factors, VTS afforded Hanna the opportunity to abuse his power, his wrongful acts furthered VTS's aims and were incentivized by the contingency arrangement, and the plaintiffs were vulnerable to such internet 'hit pieces'.
firac.conclusion: VTS is vicariously liable for Mr. Hanna's defamatory conduct, including where Jackman or Paine shared or sent the material.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a private defamation tort action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action, with the Court applying the Grant v. Torstar three-part test. K018 (qualified privilege) and K016 (fair comment) were the pleaded defences, both defeated by malice, so both are directly engaged. K017 (group defamation) is a weak/borderline pick — the action involved multiple corporate plaintiffs alongside the individual Mr. Malak, but the reasoning turned on defamation of named parties rather than a diffuse collectivity, so it is flagged as marginal. The controlled vocabulary lacks dedicated terms for the case's other live doctrines (justification/truth, common design/joint tortfeasors, vicarious liability, malice, internet publication), which limited the available specific matches.
location_rationale: The header states 'Registry: Vancouver' and lists the 'Place and Dates of Trial' and 'Place and Date of Judgment' as 'Vancouver, B.C.', confirming the Supreme Court of British Columbia sitting in Vancouver.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly records 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Martin Lauzon c. Guy Noel, Marco Folini, Les Vallons inc. et Les Entreprises Béram inc.

defining_issues: Is there a lien de droit between the plaintiff and each defendant, and can they be held solidarily liable for the 2011 transaction?
Did the defendants commit a fault by failing to disclose the parallel $50,000 agreement, and does the conduct amount to civil fraud (dol)?
Were the clandestine audio recordings and their transcriptions admissible and probative once the whole of the evidence was heard?
Should the $50,000 damages award be reduced by the $25,000 the plaintiff later received, under the duty to mitigate?
Did the plaintiff and Les Vallons agree to share the cost of draining their co-owned land, and is Les Vallons liable for its share?

firac.issue: Is there a lien de droit between the plaintiff and each defendant, and can they be held solidarily liable for the 2011 sale transaction?
firac.facts: Only Béram was named as vendor/co-contractant in Lauzon's offer to purchase the undivided half of the farmland. Marco Folini signed for Béram, while Guy Noël (through Les Vallons and J.-G. Noël et fils) drafted and signed the fictitious $500,000 offer that induced Lauzon to raise his bid. Lauzon sued all defendants solidarily.
firac.rule: Arts. 1457 and 1458 C.c.Q. distinguish contractual from extracontractual liability; art. 1521 C.c.Q. governs solidarity where several persons' faults cause a single injury. Corporate veil-piercing rules apply where individuals participate personally in the wrongful conduct.
firac.application: Béram, as Lauzon's lessor and vendor, was in a contractual relationship and bound by a duty of good faith. Noël, Folini and Les Vallons had no contract with Lauzon but participated personally and knowingly in preparing and presenting the sham offer, engaging their extracontractual liability. Noël signed both the $500,000 offer and the documents directing the $50,000 to J.-G. Noël et fils, so his own liability, not merely his company's, was engaged.
firac.conclusion: All defendants are liable — Béram contractually, the others extracontractually — and the criteria of art. 1521 C.c.Q. are met, permitting a solidary condemnation for the first claim.

firac.issue: Did the defendants commit a fault by failing to disclose the parallel $50,000 agreement, and does the conduct amount to civil fraud?
firac.facts: The $500,000 offer presented to Lauzon secretly included a $50,000 payment to Noël's holding company to settle Rudy Folini's alleged old debt; Béram in fact kept only $450,000 for the land. Lauzon, unaware, matched the offer to keep land he had farmed for years, then learned the truth weeks later when Noël refused an exchange, saying the land was worth only $450,000.
firac.rule: Art. 1375 C.c.Q. imposes good faith in negotiation and performance; art. 1399 C.c.Q. requires free and enlightened consent. Good faith is presumed (art. 2805) and bad faith/fraud must be proved on a balance of probabilities by the party alleging it (arts. 2803-2804). Civil fraud (dol) requires proof at a higher threshold than mere fault, per the case law on dol.
firac.application: A reasonable co-contractant would have been influenced by disclosure of the side agreement; the parallel deal was a relevant fact that Béram, as lessor and prospective vendor, was obliged to disclose. By concealing it, all defendants induced Lauzon to overpay by $50,000. However, the object of the scheme was to offload Rudy's supposed debt onto Lauzon, not to defraud him as such; the evidence did not meet the higher bar for civil fraud, especially since it was not clear Lauzon would have declined at $500,000 given his own plan to swap the land.
firac.conclusion: The defendants committed a fault (breach of good faith / failure to secure enlightened consent) but not civil fraud; the $50,000 claim is well founded.

firac.issue: Were the clandestine audio recordings and their transcriptions admissible and probative once the whole of the evidence was heard?
firac.facts: After being advised by the SQ to record the suspects, the Lauzons secretly recorded hours of conversations with the defendants in 2012. The recordings were admitted 'sous réserve' at the start of trial; the defendants challenged their integrity, authenticity and probative value, noting gaps and missing 'bips'.
firac.rule: Admissibility of clandestine recordings is governed by the criteria set out in Cadieux c. Service de gaz naturel Laval Inc. (1991) and the court's own interlocutory judgment (2018 QCCS 3903); the outstanding criterion was probative value, to be assessed against the whole record.
firac.application: The recordings and transcriptions contained sufficient reliable content to be contextualized against the balance of the evidence; the defendants were sophisticated businessmen not obliged to speak as they did, had received disclosure well in advance, and had a full opportunity to explain discrepancies. No party was deprived of a full defence. The gaps were not on sensitive points and did not suggest tampering; the disputed laugh was found to be Roger Lauzon's, not Noël's.
firac.conclusion: The reservation is lifted; the recordings and transcriptions (P-13 and P-13a to P-13n) are admissible and probative, though they were not strictly necessary for the first claim, which was established independently.

firac.issue: Should the $50,000 award be reduced by the $25,000 the plaintiff received in 2012, under the duty to mitigate?
firac.facts: In 2012, Béram paid Lauzon $25,000 to suspend his right of first refusal so Les Vallons could buy the second undivided half. The defendants argued this offset the 2011 loss under the mitigation principle (art. 1479 C.c.Q.).
firac.rule: Art. 1479 C.c.Q. requires a victim to minimize damages; recoverable contractual damages are limited to foreseeable loss (arts. 1611, 1613 C.c.Q.).
firac.application: The $25,000 arose from a separate contract with different consideration (suspension of the right of first refusal) and a different context; Marco Folini himself testified the two payments were unrelated. It caused no negative consequence to Béram or Noël, unlike the 2011 payment, and was Lauzon's legitimate gain.
firac.conclusion: No reduction; the $25,000 is not connected to the 2011 loss. The separate $15,000 damages claim was dismissed for lack of a direct, foreseeable link and insufficient proof.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff and Les Vallons agree to share the drainage costs of their co-owned land, and is Les Vallons liable?
firac.facts: After Les Vallons became co-owner in May 2012, Noël stated he would pay his share of drainage if he became owner and the lease was respected. Noël participated in choosing the contractor, negotiated drain and fitting prices, received explanations, and told the contractor to begin 'when you can'. Lauzon paid the entire $107,443.55 bill; Les Vallons denied any agreement.
firac.rule: Art. 2862 C.c.Q. bars testimonial proof of a contract over $1,500 absent a commencement of proof (art. 2865); admitted recordings can supply that commencement. Arts. 1018-1019 C.c.Q. impose common expenses on co-owners; unjust enrichment provides an alternative basis.
firac.application: The admitted recordings and Noël's own testimony supplied both a commencement of proof and direct evidence that Noël's two conditions (becoming co-owner and the lease continuing) had materialized and that he had actively participated in implementing the drainage. Alternatively, as co-owner Les Vallons would owe its share under the co-ownership rules, and unjust enrichment applied since Noël admitted the works increased the land's value. Additional works were refused for lack of preponderant proof.
firac.conclusion: Les Vallons is condemned to pay its just share, fixed at $52,759.28, with interest and additional indemnity.

defining_issues: On a temporary motion, should the father be granted equal (2/2/3) decision-making and parenting time, with the children parenting at his separate residence, in the children's best interests?
Should the mother be granted temporary exclusive possession of the matrimonial home?

firac.issue: On a temporary motion, should the father be granted equal decision-making and an equal (2/2/3) parenting schedule with the children spending time at his separate residence?
firac.facts: The parties married in 2016, separated in January 2020, and continued to live in the matrimonial home. They have two young children (born 2017 and 2019). Since a February 2020 consent order of Akbarali J., the parents shared decision-making and equal parenting under one roof, but the arrangement became tense and unworkable. The father rented a separate home nearby and sought a 2/2/3 equal schedule; the mother opposed, claiming to be the primary parent and alleging poor and dangerous parenting, seeking sole decision-making and roughly 4 of 14 days for the father.
firac.rule: The sole test for custody and access is the best interests of the child: Divorce Act, s. 16(8); courts often consider the factors in s. 24(2) of the Children's Law Reform Act. Section 16(9) directs the court not to consider past conduct unless relevant to parenting ability, and s. 16(10) requires effect be given to the maximum contact principle. Best interests are assessed from the child's perspective (Young v. Young, [1993] 4 S.C.R. 3). On interim motions, stability and maintenance of the status quo are paramount unless there is a compelling reason to disturb it (Kimpton v. Kimpton, 2002 CanLII 2793).
firac.application: The court found the status quo was the February 2020 consent order providing equal parenting and joint decision-making, entered into with counsel. What had changed was that co-parenting under one roof had become unworkable, not the shared nature of parenting. The court declined to resolve conflicting credibility, noting the mother's numerous allegations (car seat, chin laceration, hygiene, food) largely reflected ordinary daily parenting disagreements and were exaggerated, detracting from her credibility (Alsawwah v. Afifi). Breastfeeding was not a trump card (Holomey v. Hillis) and the medical evidence was dated. The nannies' evidence was of limited value. The young age of the children did not preclude equal parenting (Schmidt v. Haley). Separating the parties physically would reduce conflict; the s. 24(2) CLRA factors favoured the father's plan as the only one giving equal time, though a graduated schedule (Schedule B) was preferred to ease adjustment.
firac.conclusion: The father's motion for equal decision-making and a revised, graduated equal-time parenting schedule (Schedule B, commencing February 1) was allowed.

firac.issue: Should the mother be granted temporary exclusive possession of the matrimonial home?
firac.facts: The mother sought exclusive possession citing need for privacy, non-interference during her parenting, and protection from her allegedly abusive (psychologically violent) husband. The father undertook not to return to the matrimonial home but opposed exclusive possession as prejudicial to a potential future sale, given his significant equity was tied up in the home. No motion to sell was pending.
firac.rule: Section 24(1) of the Family Law Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3 sets out the criteria for ordering exclusive possession, including the best interests of the children and any violence (Mohajeri v. Stroedel; Pinto v. Pinto).
firac.application: The s. 24(1) factors did not favour the mother. Given the order for equal decision-making and parenting, the best interests of the children were not advanced by granting exclusive possession, which could be seen as tilting the field toward the mother. The relief was unnecessary in light of the father's undertaking not to return, and inadvisable at the outset of a new parenting arrangement. Exclusive possession should not be used pre-emptively to block a possible future sale motion. The father categorically rejected the allegations of violence, and the court was not satisfied the alleged psychological violence warranted an order; the case was distinguishable from Pinto v. Pinto.
firac.conclusion: The mother's cross-motion for temporary exclusive possession of the matrimonial home was dismissed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Janice Miller v. Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and Margo Harper

defining_issues: Was the matter suitable for summary disposition under Rule 18A?
What was the true defamatory meaning ('sting') of the impugned statement?
Did the defendants establish justification (truth or substantial truth) of that meaning on the evidence?

firac.issue: Was the matter suitable for summary disposition under Rule 18A of the Supreme Court Rules?
firac.facts: The CBC broadcast about Canada's hate movement referred to the plaintiff, wife of Aryan Nations leader Terry Long, including a statement that the Longs dressed their children in 'pint sized Klan uniforms' for a cross burning. The plaintiff sued in defamation and opposed proceeding by Rule 18A, arguing viva voce and expert evidence were needed. She adduced no evidence of her own, relying essentially on an insufficiency-of-evidence position.
firac.rule: On a Rule 18A application the court must decide whether it can find the facts necessary to decide the issues and whether it would be unjust to do so, weighing sufficiency of evidence, amount involved, complexity, urgency, prejudice from delay, cost of a conventional trial and the course of proceedings (Inspiration Management Ltd. v. McDermid St. Lawrence Ltd. (1989), 36 B.C.L.R. (2d) 202 (C.A.)).
firac.application: There were no issues of credibility or conflicting evidence. Examinations for discovery were complete and the plaintiff's own admissions supplied ample evidence. The likely damages were modest since the plaintiff's alleged losses predated the broadcast, and a ten-day trial would impose unnecessary expense for little gain given the six-year lapse since the statement.
firac.conclusion: The issues were appropriate for disposition under Rule 18A and the court could and should give judgment.

firac.issue: What was the natural and ordinary defamatory meaning (the sting) of the impugned statement?
firac.facts: The plaintiff variously characterized the sting as association with her husband's public racist activities, insinuation that her children were KKK members, and forcible indoctrination of her children in racist ideology. The defendants pleaded a lesser meaning—that with her husband she exposed her children to a racist ideology to which she was sympathetic—or substantial justification.
firac.rule: A defendant may plead any defamatory meaning the words are capable of bearing and prove it true or fair comment, so long as it does not act oppressively (Pizza Pizza Ltd. v. Toronto Star Newspapers Ltd. (1998), 167 D.L.R. (4th) 748; Polly Peck Holdings v. Trelford, [1986] 2 All E.R. 84). The trier of fact determines the natural and ordinary meaning, including reasonable innuendo, as what the words convey to the ordinary reasonable viewer reading between the lines (Rubber Improvement Ltd. v. Daily Telegraph Ltd., [1964] A.C. 234; Lucas-Box v. News Group Newspapers Ltd., [1986] 1 All E.R. 177), and is not bound by either party's interpretation.
firac.application: Viewing the statement in the context of the whole broadcast and the other references to the plaintiff and the Long children, the court found the sting was neither as mild as mere exposure to racist beliefs nor as strong as forcible indoctrination, but that notorious racist Terry Long had involved his wife and children in his expression of racist ideology as 'a family affair.' The literally untrue detail about the Klan uniforms was simply another insinuation to that effect.
firac.conclusion: The sting of the libel was that the plaintiff was involved with, and involved her children in, her husband's expression of racist ideology.

firac.issue: Did the defendants establish justification (truth or substantial truth) of the defamatory meaning?
firac.facts: On discovery the plaintiff admitted she never publicly opposed her husband, was proud of his positions in the movement, attended some five or six annual Aryan Nations congresses at Hayden Lake with her children where cross lightings occurred with people in Klan and Nazi-style dress, helped with children's activities, took no steps to disassociate from the beliefs expressed, and recorded a telephone message for the Canadian Liberty Net referring critically to Jewish people as controlling society.
firac.rule: Truth (justification) is a complete defence to defamation; the defendant need only prove the impugned meaning is true or substantially true on a balance of probabilities, and minor inaccuracies of detail that do not alter the substance are immaterial.
firac.application: The plaintiff's uncontradicted admissions proved she and her children were involved with Terry Long's racist beliefs and activities. Sub-paragraphs (a) through (e) of the defence were made out, and the immaterial and literally untrue detail about how the children were dressed did not defeat the defence because what the viewer took away—that the Longs supported Long's proclamation as a racist leader as a family—was true and would shock the ordinary reasonable person.
firac.conclusion: The defamatory statement was justified in fact and at law; the substantial truth defence succeeded.

name_verification.name_in_document: Medvedovsky c. Solidarity for Palestinian Human Rights McGill (SPHR McGill)

defining_issues: Should a provisional injunction be granted to ban all demonstrations within 100 metres of 154 McGill buildings and to enjoin nuisance, intimidation and obstruction, given the encampment and protests on campus?
Should the plaintiffs' affidavits be placed under seal?

firac.issue: Should a provisional injunction be granted to ban demonstrations within 100 metres of McGill's 154 buildings and to enjoin nuisance, intimidation, harassment and obstruction of access?
firac.facts: Two McGill students sought a quia timet provisional injunction after a pro-Palestinian encampment was set up on campus on 27 April 2024. They alleged fear for their safety, discomfort, perceived antisemitic and violence-inciting slogans, and McGill's failure to enforce its student code of conduct. Their affidavits and those of nine others contained much hearsay and largely subjective fears; no one established blocked access to buildings or missed exams arising from the current encampment. McGill considered the encampment illegal, had tried to negotiate, issued warnings, and called police, but took no position on the injunction.
firac.rule: Provisional injunction under the Code de procédure civile requires urgency, plus a colour of right (apparence de droit), irreparable harm, and the balance of convenience. The remedy is discretionary. Universities are special places where freedom of expression and peaceful assembly carry significant weight (R. v. Whatcott, 2012 ABQB 231; UAlberta Pro-Life v. Governors of the University of Alberta, 2020 ABCA 1).
firac.application: The Court found no urgency: no affidavit showed access to exam venues was blocked or exams missed; fears of blockage stemmed from earlier, distinct protests, and past conduct does not guarantee future conduct; McGill had acted proactively within only five days. On colour of right, a content-neutral ban on all demonstrations within 100 metres of 154 buildings was far broader and more restrictive of freedom of expression and peaceful assembly than dismantling the encampment, and contrary to McGill's own policies. The nuisance/harassment order raised serious but discretionary concerns and would be difficult to enforce. On irreparable harm and balance of convenience, the plaintiffs' evidence was fragile and largely subjective; they had not personally suffered harassment, violence or threats; the balance favoured protecting the protesters' fundamental freedoms.
firac.conclusion: The provisional injunction was dismissed for failure to demonstrate urgency, though McGill and the plaintiffs may return to court if circumstances deteriorate; the Court invited protesters to reconsider words perceived as calls to violence or antisemitic.

firac.issue: Should the plaintiffs' affidavits be placed under seal?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs asked that the affidavits they filed be sealed.
firac.rule: Sealing orders are governed by the criteria in A.B. c. Robillard, 2022 QCCA 959, and Sherman (Succession) c. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25.
firac.application: The allegations in the record were insufficient to meet those criteria.
firac.conclusion: The sealing request was dismissed.

case_name: Jewish Family and Child Service of Toronto v. J.Z.

name_verification.name_in_document: Jewish Family and Child Service of Greater Toronto v. J.Z. (mother) and H.S. (father)

defining_issues: Did the society (or the mother) engage in non-disclosure or delayed disclosure of documents/information that prejudiced the father in presenting his case?
If the father was prejudiced by non-disclosure or late disclosure, does the appropriate remedy require declaring a mistrial, or can lesser measures cure the prejudice?
Does the familial connection between the presiding judge and a proposed witness (the mother's Woman Abuse counsellor) create a reasonable apprehension of bias requiring recusal?

firac.issue: Was there non-disclosure or delayed disclosure by the society or the mother that prejudiced the father?
firac.facts: The father sought a mistrial partly on the ground that Jennifer Shneer's therapeutic notes (mother's Woman Abuse counsellor, employed by JFCS) were disclosed only in February 2014, after 20 trial days. The society maintained a 'wall' between its child-protection and Woman Abuse therapeutic functions and had no access to those records absent mother's consent or a court order; it saw the notes at the same time as the father. The mother disclosed the notes once she decided to call Shneer as a witness. The father argued Shneer had actively participated in child-protection decisions, but the notes/emails he produced concerned only mother's safety during access transfers.
firac.rule: A children's aid society, as a quasi-state actor, has a continuing obligation to make reasonable disclosure of documents in its possession so respondents know the case to meet (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S. (A.), 2007 ONCJ 596). The onus is on the moving party to prove on a balance of probabilities that disclosure was withheld and that the party was misled/prejudiced.
firac.application: The society could not access the Woman Abuse records without consent or court order, and the father never brought a production motion despite being invited to by Justice Sherr. The notes the father tendered did not show Shneer making or influencing child-protection decisions; they showed her addressing mother's safety concerns, consistent with her counselling role. The father failed to establish he was misled. The court also declined to fault the mother, noting the father himself was in continuing breach of a production order (his Utah psychiatric/criminal records) and thus came with unclean hands.
firac.conclusion: No breach of disclosure obligations by the society, and the mother's February 2014 disclosure did not prejudice the father's ability to meet his case.

firac.issue: If the father was prejudiced, must a mistrial be declared or can lesser measures cure any prejudice?
firac.facts: The father argued the prejudice was irreparable and that recalling three society witnesses would create confusion. The trial had run 20+ days, was to resume April 28, 2014, and was scheduled to continue intermittently for 43 more days; the society's case was still ongoing and the father's case had not begun.
firac.rule: A mistrial is a last resort; a decision to proceed must be 'consistent with the interests of justice and the maintenance of public confidence in the fairness of the trial' (R. v. M.Q., 2012 ONCA 224). Courts must canvass any conceivable way to save the trial before ordering a mistrial (Tupper v. Van Rooy; Carey v. Ontario). The inquiry is fact-driven (Onuselogu v. Okeke; Carbone v. De La Rocha).
firac.application: The evidence in this trial had not been confusing or disjointed (distinguishing Onuselogu, where a mistrial was ordered on already-confused evidence). Substantial time remained before the father's case in chief, and if genuine prejudice appeared, the court could recall witnesses or grant a brief adjournment. Declaring a mistrial would add roughly a year of delay, contrary to the remedial, timely-resolution objectives of the Child and Family Services Act and harmful to the children's interests — and ironic given the father's own delay-based Constitutional Motion.
firac.conclusion: Even assuming prejudice, any prejudice could be remedied by orders short of a mistrial; no basis to declare a mistrial at this stage.

firac.issue: Does the judge's distant familial connection to a proposed witness create a reasonable apprehension of bias requiring recusal?
firac.facts: The judge disclosed before trial that Shneer 'may be a distant relative' and invited any concerns by 14B form; none were raised until after 20+ trial days. The judge explained Shneer would, if related, be his step-second cousin — not a blood relative, friend, social contact, or someone he had seen in decades. Father argued any familial relationship, however remote, creates apprehension of bias.
firac.rule: The test is whether a reasonable, informed person would think it more likely than not the judge would not decide fairly (Committee for Justice and Liberty v. Canada (NEB); R. v. S. (R.D.) — high threshold, strong presumption of impartiality; Bailey v. Barbour). Consent of parties cannot cure a genuine apprehension of bias, and the recusal decision rests with the judge alone (Lacey-House v. Lambert). Mechanical 'connection rules' are rejected in favour of a realistic, fact-based assessment (Boardwalk Reit LLP v. Edmonton; CAS of Waterloo Region v. B.(L.-A.); recusal on trifling grounds wastes resources and risks injustice).
firac.application: The father's position rested on a 'mechanical rule' that any relationship disqualifies, which the case law rejects. The connection was highly tenuous — a 'step-second cousin' label with no real relationship. Weighed against the strong presumption of judicial impartiality and the enormous waste of resources and year-long delay recusal would cause, a fully informed reasonable person would not perceive a real likelihood of bias.
firac.conclusion: No reasonable apprehension of bias would arise from Shneer testifying; recusal not warranted.

defining_issues: Does the Superior Court have jurisdiction under art. 16 C.C.Q. to authorize medical treatment, i.e. is the defendant incapable of consenting to care?
Has the plaintiff established that the defendant categorically refuses the proposed care?

firac.issue: Does the Superior Court have jurisdiction under art. 16 C.C.Q. to authorize medical treatment where the defendant is alleged to be incapable of consenting?
firac.facts: A 30-year-old man was admitted to the Jewish General Hospital in a psychotic, paranoid state and was refusing psychiatric medication. The hospital's experts recommended a court-ordered 36-month regime of long-acting injectable antipsychotic medication. The expert report answered only one of the five incapacity sub-questions; the treating physician (Dr Geagea) did not testify, and the psychologist who testified could not address the nature, purpose, risks or benefits of the treatment.
firac.rule: Article 16 C.C.Q. requires court authorization where a person of full age incapable of giving consent categorically refuses care. Per Centre universitaire de santé McGill (Hôpital Royal-Victoria), 2015 QCCA 1139, the court must first verify two essential jurisdictional conditions: (1) incapacity to consent, assessed through five sub-questions (understanding of the illness, nature and purpose of treatment, risks/benefits of undergoing it, risks of refusing it, and whether capacity to understand is affected by the illness); and (2) a categorical refusal.
firac.application: The Court found the defendant did not understand his illness (he believed his only problem was high blood pressure) and that his capacity to understand was impaired by his illness. However, the evidence failed to answer the remaining incapacity sub-questions: the report was silent on whether he understood the nature and purpose of the treatment, the risks and benefits of undergoing it, and the risks of not undergoing it, and no witness could fill these gaps.
firac.conclusion: The evidentiary gaps prevented the Court from being satisfied of full incapacity, and combined with the failure to prove categorical refusal, the jurisdictional threshold was not met.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiffs establish a categorical refusal of the proposed care?
firac.facts: Following the earlier confinement order of Justice Lewis (June 9, 2016), the defendant accepted to take oral medication, though he stated it was 'because he was blackmailed.'
firac.rule: Under art. 16 C.C.Q. and the McGill (Hôpital Royal-Victoria), 2015 QCCA 1139 analytical grid, the court may only intervene where there is proof of a categorical refusal; the treatment must have been offered, considered and discussed and then refused.
firac.application: Because the defendant had accepted oral medication after the Lewis judgment, the Court could not conclude that a categorical refusal existed, notwithstanding his stated reluctance.
firac.conclusion: No categorical refusal was proven; a further essential condition for jurisdiction was absent.

firac.issue: Did neither parent in fact assume the care, maintenance or education of the children for at least six months under art. 559(2) C.c.Q.?
firac.facts: Both children, M... (born 2001) and R... (born 2002), were placed in foster care from birth by court order. The father never appeared, ceased attending a violence-intervention program, and stopped contacting the agency after July 2002. The mother attended some parenting-support programs but participated poorly, denied her difficulties, disappeared for long periods, and the children's severe distress at contact forced the director to suspend visits.
firac.rule: Art. 559(2) C.c.Q. allows a child to be declared eligible for adoption where 'ni les père et mère ni le tuteur n'ont assumé de fait le soin, l'entretien ou l'éducation depuis au moins six mois.' Case law (Droit de la famille — 1544, 1992 CanLII 3971 (QC CA)) requires the court to assess, in light of the particular circumstances of a placed child, whether the parent nonetheless assumed the essential parental burden through concrete, materially identifiable acts, including efforts to eliminate the causes of the placement.
firac.application: Although both parents were kept from the children's daily life by judicial placement orders, the court examined whether they nevertheless assumed their parental role through concrete acts. The father did nothing and abandoned intervention. The mother's efforts were superficial and 'apparents' only; she failed to acknowledge her difficulties, did not correct the situation that led to placement, ended her relationship with the father only belatedly, and went long periods without inquiring about the children. Neither made the tangible efforts the jurisprudence demands.
firac.conclusion: The court found that neither the father nor the mother had in fact assumed the care, maintenance or education of M... and R... during the last six months.

firac.issue: Did the parents rebut the presumption under art. 561 C.c.Q. of improbability of resuming care?
firac.facts: Psychological assessments found the father had an antisocial personality disorder with marked aggression and the mother had significant cognitive limits, affective dependency, denial of her problems and a poor prognosis. The children reacted with acute distress to the mother; M... showed anguish and R... entered crisis on seeing her.
firac.rule: Art. 561 C.c.Q. presumes it improbable a parent will resume care once art. 559 is met; the probability of resumption is assessed from the standpoint of both the parent and the child, including whether a significant attachment bond can be created (Droit de la famille — 1741, 1993 CanLII 3555 (QC CA)).
firac.application: The parents' conduct since the children's birth, their failure to correct the situation, and the children's negative reactions to the mother demonstrated no realistic prospect of a significant bond. The mother's more insistent requests to see the children were not matched by genuine interest or change. The presumption was reinforced rather than rebutted.
firac.conclusion: The parents did not rebut the presumption; it was improbable either would resume care of the children.

firac.issue: Is a declaration of eligibility for adoption in the best interests of the children?
firac.facts: M... and R... had lived in their foster families essentially since birth, were developing normally, had formed secure attachment bonds and a sense of belonging in those homes, while showing distress toward their biological mother.
firac.rule: The best interests of the child is a relevant criterion throughout the adoption-eligibility process and adoption cannot be pronounced if contrary to the child's interest (Droit de la famille — 1544; Droit de la famille — 1914).
firac.application: The children had taken root in stable foster families that met their needs, and the attachment bonds served their development. Breaking these consolidating bonds would be harmful. An adoption project was manifestly in their interest.
