name_verification.name_in_document: The Estate of Helen Martindale, by her Litigation Administrator, Daryl Borneman v. Dr. Bharat Bahl et al

defining_issues: Did Dr. Lee fall below the standard of care of a community-based emergency physician in his assessment, diagnosis, and discharge planning of the plaintiff on November 21, 2014?
Did Dr. Chiu fall below the standard of care of a community-based general surgeon in his assessment and follow-up planning for the plaintiff on December 31, 2014?
If a breach were established, did the plaintiff prove on a balance of probabilities that but for the breach the need for an ileostomy would have been avoided (causation)?
If liability were found, to what extent should the plaintiff be held contributorily negligent for failing to follow medical advice?

firac.issue: Did Dr. Lee breach the standard of care in his emergency-room treatment of the plaintiff on November 21, 2014?
firac.facts: The plaintiff attended the Scarborough Hospital E.R. with a seven-day history of perianal pain described as a hemorrhoid flareup, a mild fever and slightly elevated pulse. Dr. Lee, an emergency physician of over 40 years' experience, took a history, conducted visual and physical examinations, diagnosed a likely perianal abscess in the early stages of infection, performed an incision and drainage, arranged home nursing wound care and (per his usual practice) advised follow-up with a primary care practitioner within two weeks. He did not order an ultrasound, perform a digital rectal exam (DRE), or chart the follow-up instruction. The plaintiff, whose evidence the court found unreliable, denied being told to follow up.
firac.rule: A physician must exercise the degree of skill and care of a normal prudent practitioner of the same experience and standing (ter Neuzen v. Korn, [1995] 3 S.C.R. 674; Crits v. Sylvester; Gent v. Wilson). The standard is measured against a reasonable practitioner in similar communities, assessed through the eyes of a physician of the same background (Wilson v. Swanson), and expert evidence from the same care setting carries greater weight (Stepita v. Dibble; Bogdan v. Folman). A physician need not order every test, only usual tests (Watson v. Soon; Wade v. Nayernouri), and honest, properly-founded clinical judgment satisfies the standard (Tacknyk; Williams v. Bowler). Usual practice is good evidence of what occurred where records are incomplete (Turkington v. Lai; Power v. Carroll). A differential diagnosis is required only where a patient presents with non-specific complaints.
firac.application: The court preferred the defence expert Dr. McMillan, whose community-hospital and CPSO assessment experience more closely matched Dr. Lee's setting than the plaintiff's expert Dr. Kingsley, who practised only in a tertiary academic centre. The court found Dr. Lee's assessment, working diagnosis of perianal abscess, and incision and drainage reasonable and consistent with the plaintiff's specific presentation (low-grade fever, elevated pulse). Because the complaints were specific, no differential diagnosis of serious conditions was required; nothing suggested cancer, and there was no life-threatening emergency requiring imaging. Declining an ultrasound and DRE were reasonable clinical judgments (Kingsley conceded the DRE call belonged to the treating physician). The discharge plan, including home nursing and a two-week follow-up instruction, met the standard; the absence of a chart entry did not mean the advice was not given (Turkington; Power v. Carroll).
firac.conclusion: Dr. Lee met the standard of care of an emergency physician practising in Ontario in 2014; no breach.

firac.issue: Did Dr. Chiu breach the standard of care in his general-surgery consultation of the plaintiff on December 31, 2014?
firac.facts: Called to consult in the E.R., Dr. Chiu, a general surgeon of 30 years' experience, took a history, performed a full physical examination including a DRE, diagnosed a prolapsed mucosa and hardened incision area, recommended sitz baths, stool softeners and laxatives, and directed follow-up at his office in two weeks (or a return to E.R. if symptoms worsened), recording this in a note dictated about 2½ hours later. He did not provide a community CT requisition or refer to a colorectal surgeon/oncologist. Neither Scarborough nor comparable community hospitals had a colorectal surgeon on staff. The plaintiff's pain was rated 3/10 and there was no palpable rectal mass.
firac.rule: Same standard-of-care framework (ter Neuzen; Crits v. Sylvester). Expert evidence from the same specialty and care setting is preferred; a specialist opining critically about a physician outside the expert's own setting is given less weight (Williams v. Bowler; Stepita; Bogdan).
firac.application: The court preferred defence expert Dr. Hagan, a community-hospital general surgeon, over the plaintiff's expert Dr. Vasilevsky, a tertiary-centre colorectal surgeon who conceded Dr. Hagan was better placed to assess a community general surgeon's scope and who was unfamiliar with Ontario inter-hospital referral and imaging procedures. Vasilevsky conceded a community CT requisition would have met the standard and that admission/transfer was not required; her contrary opinions rested on incorrect assumptions (e.g. that the plaintiff was in severe pain preventing a DRE). Given the absence of a rectal mass, low pain score and no life-threatening emergency, there was no requirement to requisition hospital imaging or refer out, and the two-week office follow-up was reasonable. The court preferred Dr. Chiu's account, supported by his contemporaneous note, over the plaintiff's unreliable memory.
firac.conclusion: Dr. Chiu met the standard of care of a community general surgeon in Ontario in 2014; no breach.

firac.issue: Would the need for an ileostomy have been avoided but for any breach (causation)?
firac.facts: The plaintiff developed a recto-vaginal fistula and underwent an ileostomy in April 2015, with anal cancer (squamous cell carcinoma) confirmed weeks later. The plaintiff argued the defendants' failure to requisition imaging created an evidentiary gap warranting an adverse inference.
firac.rule: Causation is determined by the 'but for' test: the plaintiff must show on a balance of probabilities that the injury would not have occurred but for the defendant's negligence (Clements v. Clements, 2012 SCC 32). Causation must be linked to the specific act said to breach the standard (Chasczewski). Speculation or mere possibility is insufficient (Rothwell v. Raes; Salter v. Hirst). A defendant may rebut by showing the injury would have occurred regardless (Clements).
firac.application: Because no breach was found, causation did not arise and the court's comments were obiter. Even so, no expert evidence connected any alleged breach by Dr. Lee to an earlier diagnostic pathway. As to Dr. Chiu, even a community CT requisition would have yielded a diagnosis no earlier than mid-March 2015, and by January 2015 the plaintiff already had indications for an ileostomy (incontinence, obstruction, pain). No imaging was clinically warranted in November/December 2014, so no adverse inference was drawn.
firac.conclusion: Causation not established; the ileostomy could not have been avoided even had the diagnosis occurred earlier. Issue moot given no breach.

firac.issue: Would the plaintiff have been contributorily negligent had liability been established?
firac.facts: The plaintiff did not follow Dr. Lee's two-week follow-up instruction, did not attend Dr. Chiu's office follow-up, delayed three days after Dr. Feldman advised her to go to the E.R., declined a nursing re-assessment (ending wound care), and did not seek further medical attention until April 8, 2015, a week after stool began passing through her vagina.
firac.rule: A plaintiff who fails to take reasonable care for her own health may have damages apportioned for contributory negligence.
firac.application: The court found the plaintiff repeatedly failed to follow medical advice and follow-up instructions. Had negligence and causation been established, this conduct would have justified an apportionment.
firac.conclusion: Obiter: the court would have found the plaintiff 40% contributorily negligent, had liability otherwise been established.

keywords_rationale: This is a medical malpractice / negligence action turning on standard of care and 'but for' causation, so the only genuinely applicable controlled-vocabulary term is K002 (Civil litigation), the tier-1 practice area covering tort/civil claims. The supplied controlled vocabulary is heavily oriented toward human-rights, Charter and antisemitism subject matter and contains no tier-2 keyword for medical negligence, standard of care, causation, or contributory negligence. I deliberately did not force in tangential or misleading picks (e.g. K054 wills/estates would be wrong — the estate appears only because the plaintiff died and sues through a litigation administrator; K014 standard of review is an administrative-law concept distinct from the medical 'standard of care' at issue here). Accordingly fewer than five keywords truly apply; K002 is the sole accurate selection.
location_rationale: The decision's heading identifies only the court — 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE' — and does not state the sitting city. The events occurred at Scarborough and Rouge Hospital (Toronto area) and later St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto, but these are hospital locations, not the court's registry. Province is Ontario from the court name; city left null as unstated.
registry_rationale: No registry office is named in the decision. Only the court file number (CV-17-572998) appears, which is not an explicit registry designation, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Levin v. Levin

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff father be granted interim access to the child despite unsubstantiated allegations of physical and sexual abuse and an ongoing police investigation?
Should the plaintiff be required to pay for the child's continued play therapy?
Should the interim spousal support order be reviewed and reduced given the defendant's failure to seek employment?

firac.issue: Should the father be granted interim access to the child where allegations of abuse and a police investigation exist but remain unsubstantiated?
firac.facts: The parties are in an ongoing matrimonial dispute; the mother has custody and the father has access. A court-ordered s. 15 psychological assessment by Robert Colby found the father posed no risk to the child and recommended gradually increased overnight visitation. After the report, the mother refused unsupervised access, relying on letters from a police detective and a social worker recommending suspension of visits pending a criminal investigation into an abuse disclosure. The nature, date, time, place and source of the allegation were not identified, and prior similar complaints had been investigated to no effect.
firac.rule: On interim access applications the governing principle is the best interests of the child; parents ought to have as much contact with their children as is good for them. The court weighs the risk of harm against the benefit of parental contact, and evidence advanced (here hearsay letters) must rise to a threshold creating a realistic concern of actual danger to the child.
firac.application: The court found the complaint 'inchoate, so amorphous, so poorly documented' that, given the context of prior unsubstantiated complaints and the timing after a favourable psychological report, it did not create a realistic concern of actual danger. The hearsay letters could have been presented in a more reliable form. Balancing the principle of maximum beneficial contact against the unsubstantiated concern, the material failed to reach the threshold justifying denial of access, though the court noted access could be revisited if better evidence emerged.
firac.conclusion: Access reinstated on a defined schedule (Tuesday/Wednesday and Saturday periods, with monthly overnight), pick-up and drop-off arranged, and unrestricted telephone contact with the mother facilitated.

firac.issue: Should the father be ordered to pay for the child's continued play therapy?
firac.facts: An earlier judge (Kirkpatrick J.) had noted the need for play therapy was nearly at an end; Mr. Colby recommended it continue as valuable. The parents disagreed on its value and the mother sought an order that the father pay for it.
firac.rule: An expense will not be imposed on a parent where, on the evidence, the activity does not amount to a necessity and the parents disagree as to its value.
firac.application: The court found play therapy was not, on the evidence, the sort of activity amounting to a necessity, and given the parents' disagreement about its value, the father should not be required to pay, though he was encouraged to support and participate in the therapy.
firac.conclusion: No order made requiring the plaintiff to pay for the play therapy.

firac.issue: Should the interim spousal support order be reviewed and reduced given the defendant's failure to seek employment?
firac.facts: Spousal support was fixed at $2,200. Kirkpatrick J. had directed a review and firmly recommended the defendant seek part-time work, recognizing a disability preventing full-time work. Little or nothing had been done to seek employment, and the defendant said her involvement with the child left no time, a burden aggravated by her cutting off the father's access.
firac.rule: Interim spousal support may be adjusted on review; a recipient spouse is expected to make efforts toward self-sufficiency where able, and the court may set a graduated reduction to allow adjustment to a lesser income stream.
firac.application: The court signalled, in stronger terms than Kirkpatrick J., that efforts to obtain employment were required. To avoid a sudden income drop, it ordered a graduated reduction from $2,200 (through 2001) down stepwise to $1,500 by May-June 2002, with liberty to seek a review thereafter, expecting the defendant to produce evidence of her employment efforts.
firac.conclusion: Spousal support ordered reduced on a graduated schedule to $1,500, with a review mechanism and mutual income-disclosure directions.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) is central — the main issue was interim access to the child. K047 (best interests of the child) is the controlling legal test applied to the access decision. K053 (spousal support) covers the graduated reduction of the $2,200 interim spousal support order. K050 (parental support/child expenses) is the closest fit for the play-therapy payment dispute, though slightly weak as it concerns a therapy expense rather than base child support. No hate-speech, Jewish-community, or constitutional keywords apply; the passing reference to the Jewish New Year is immaterial to the decision.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA' and 'Registry: Vancouver', and the reasons were delivered at 'Vancouver, B.C.'
registry_rationale: The document expressly lists 'Registry: Vancouver' and the judgment was given in Vancouver.

name_verification.name_in_document: Jeffrey Kent v. Humphrey Waldock carrying on business as the firm of Oliver Waldock

defining_issues: Did the defendant solicitor breach the retainer agreement — an entire contract to conduct the action to its end — by refusing to proceed with the personal injury trial unless a guardian ad litem was appointed for the client?
Was the proposed appointment of a guardian ad litem in the interests of the client under Rule 6(10) of the Supreme Court Rules?
Given the breach, is the solicitor entitled to his contingency fee, a solicitor's lien, and/or his disbursements?
Is the client entitled to punitive damages for the solicitor's conduct that resulted in the mistrial?

firac.issue: Did the solicitor breach the retainer agreement by refusing to continue unless a guardian ad litem was appointed?
firac.facts: Waldock was retained under a written contingency agreement to 'obtain an offer ... or, if necessary, proceed to a trial'. Midway through the personal injury jury trial he insisted a guardian ad litem be appointed for Kent and declared he would not proceed without it; both Kent and his father were adamantly opposed, and Kent then discharged him, leading to a mistrial.
firac.rule: A contingency retainer to prosecute a claim to settlement or judgment is 'an entire contract to conduct the action to the end' (Underwood, Son & Piper v. Lewis, [1894] 2 Q.B. 306; Gray v. Firm of Solicitors (1979), 17 B.C.L.R. 392; Trainor v. Deverell, Harrop (1980), 22 B.C.L.R. 322). Counsel may only withdraw in a civil case with leave of the court, and cannot refuse to proceed on his own terms.
firac.application: The court found that Waldock's true position throughout was that he 'refused to proceed further without the appointment of a guardian' — a condition he was not entitled to impose, since under Rule 6 the appointment is for the court. This refusal was a repudiation of the entire contract, or at least an anticipatory breach, entitling Kent to discharge him.
firac.conclusion: Waldock unilaterally breached (or anticipatorily breached) the retainer agreement; Kent was entitled to discharge him.

firac.issue: Was the proposed guardian ad litem appointment in the client's interests under Rule 6(10)?
firac.facts: Waldock told the trial judge his client was not mentally incompetent but 'under a disability as to this case'. He had advised the Kents in writing to appoint a committee, adjourn, obtain a mistrial and appeal the rulings, and admitted he was suggesting they 'orchestrate a mistrial'. He discussed 'tactical' benefits of keeping Kent out of the jury's view.
firac.rule: Rule 6 of the Supreme Court Rules governs guardians ad litem; Rule 6(9) requires appointment where a party becomes mentally incompetent, and Rule 6(10) permits appointment 'if it is in the interest of a party who is under disability'.
firac.application: Assuming an appointment could have been made under Rule 6(10) on grounds short of incompetency, the evidence compelled the conclusion it was not in Kent's interest: it was tied to Waldock's plan to orchestrate a mistrial and re-open the excluded evidence, to purported tactical advantages unrelated to the client's need, and to Waldock's inability to obtain the single instruction the client refused — consent to a guardian. The trial had gone 'off the rails' because of the judge's evidentiary rulings, not Kent's conduct.
firac.conclusion: The proposed guardian ad litem appointment was not in the client's interests and was not intended for that purpose.

firac.issue: Is the solicitor entitled to fees, a solicitor's lien, and disbursements?
firac.facts: Waldock counterclaimed for 25% of the $325,000 settlement plus taxable costs and a solicitor's lien, and alternatively quantum meruit. Kent had settled his ICBC costs claim for $95,000, and roughly $31,700 in Waldock disbursements were outstanding; earlier disbursements of $32,261.10 had been paid.
firac.rule: Having undertaken an entire contract on a contingency basis, a solicitor who breaches by withdrawing/refusing to continue receives no remuneration (Trainor v. Deverell, Harrop). Disbursements may nonetheless be recoverable from sums received.
firac.application: Because Waldock breached the entire contract, he was not entitled to any fee or solicitor's lien. Disbursements were allowed subject to taxation, but the court disallowed disbursements connected to the mistrial-related conduct — witness fees, trial-filing and per diem fees, and expenses for the mislabelled x-rays and erroneous special-damages list.
firac.conclusion: Declaration that Waldock has no claim for fees or a solicitor's lien; disbursements allowed subject to taxation, with specified deductions.

firac.issue: Is the client entitled to punitive damages for the solicitor's misconduct?
firac.facts: Kent claimed punitive damages for misconduct causing the mistrial, including Waldock failing to correct the court after Dr. Hendler repeatedly denied having his clinical records, and wrongly telling the court Dr. Stevens had never examined Kent.
firac.rule: Punitive damages in contract are rare, require an actionable wrong, and are reserved for harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious conduct (Vorvis v. Insurance Corporation of British Columbia, [1989] 4 W.W.R. 218).
firac.application: Although Waldock should have corrected the record about Dr. Hendler, wrongly represented Dr. Stevens' examination, and orchestrated the mistrial, the court held these did not amount to an actionable wrong toward Kent of the character warranting punitive damages. Kent's remedy lay in the declaration denying fees.
firac.conclusion: No punitive damages awarded.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the anchor and correct tier-1 area: the case is a contract/negligence dispute over a solicitor's retainer, fees, lien and disbursements. K013 (professional discipline / barristers and solicitors regulation) is engaged moderately — the case turns on a solicitor's professional obligations, withdrawal rules, and conduct in misleading the court (references to a Law Society citation). K012 (procedural fairness) is a weak/borderline pick tied to the guardian ad litem and mistrial fairness concerns and the court being misled; it is flagged as tangential. K027 (Jewish holidays) and K093 (Jewish) are weak entity tags reflecting only the passing reference that Dr. Hendler wished to return to New York for the Jewish holidays; flagged as tangential. Overall the controlled vocabulary (oriented to antisemitism/Charter/Jewish-law matters) is a poor fit for this solicitor-client fee dispute, so several picks are the closest available rather than strong matches.
location_rationale: The heading states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA', 'Vancouver Registry', and 'Heard at Vancouver, B.C.'; the reasons are signed 'K.C. Murphy, J.' at 'Victoria, B.C.' Province is British Columbia; the proceeding was heard and registered in Vancouver, though the judgment itself was released from Victoria.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly names the 'Vancouver Registry' with file No. C886158.

name_verification.name_in_document: Kavanagh v. Barbeau

defining_issues: Is it plain and obvious that the impugned portions of the response to civil claim are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious under Rule 9-5(1)(b), or prejudicial or embarrassing under Rule 9-5(1)(c), such that they should be struck?

Do the pleadings concerning the deceased's alleged tax evasion, the uncollected cash rents (paras. 70, 73, 74) and the Petra Capital dealings (paras. 109-119) remain relevant and material to the respondents' defence?
Should sweeping allegations that the deceased was engaged in 'illegality' and 'lifelong'/'decades' of tax avoidance be struck, and on what terms?

firac.issue: Is it plain and obvious that the impugned portions of the response to civil claim should be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b) or 9-5(1)(c)?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs, an estate executor/trustee and an amalgamated company, sue Isachsen (former sole director of the deceased's companies) and Wolf Consulting for breach of fiduciary, contractual, statutory and common-law duties. The RTCC pleads that the deceased, Mr. Johansson, retained ultimate control, was engaged in tax evasion and 'deception', and caused the losses. The plaintiffs applied to strike numerous passages as inflammatory attacks on the deceased's reputation.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) SCCR permits striking pleadings that are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious (b) or that may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial (c). Per Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083 and Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860, a scandalous allegation is struck only if irrelevant as well as scandalous; the 'plain and obvious' standard applies to all branches (Huang v. Silvercorp; B.C. (Director of Civil Forfeiture) v. Lam). Pleadings are read generously and as a whole (Lee v. G.Y. Lee & Associates).
firac.application: The court found the RTCC generally responsive to the claim: a key plank of the defence was that Johansson retained ultimate control and his own mismanagement and tax evasion caused the losses. Allegations of his mismanagement, tax-evasion practices and deception were relevant and material to a bona fide defence. Though the pleadings could have been more carefully drafted, they were not, in general, a gratuitous attack on reputation, and the presumptive-language argument (Bari Cheese) was rejected where the words related to a genuine defence.
firac.conclusion: But for a narrow exception, it was not plain and obvious that the pleadings were unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, vexatious, prejudicial or embarrassing; the application was largely dismissed.

firac.issue: Do the pleadings about uncollected cash rents (paras. 70, 73, 74) and the Petra Capital dealings (paras. 109-119) remain relevant and material to the defence?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs had removed from the Amended Claim the allegations that Isachsen failed to collect, deposit and account for rents. They argued the corresponding response paragraphs were now irrelevant, and that the Petra gold-investment paragraphs were an irrelevant strawman requiring extra disclosure.
firac.rule: A pleading is not struck merely for being superfluous; it must be irrelevant and materially prejudicial (Huang; Carr v. Cheng). Relevance is assessed against the bona fide defence advanced.
firac.application: The court held the rent allegations remained relevant because they supported the respondents' theory that Johansson personally collected cash rents and used improper accounting to avoid tax. The Petra paragraphs (his signing a $1.5M gold purchase, ordering Carlton funds to repay his RBC loan, investing $2.6M) were relevant because they demonstrated Johansson's continuing control over the Companies and assets after Isachsen became director and offered a defence to the capital-gains claim regarding Carlton's property sale.
firac.conclusion: Paras. 70, 73, 74 and 109-119 were relevant and material and were not struck.

firac.issue: Should the sweeping allegations of 'illegality', 'bad acts for decades' and 'lifelong efforts to avoid paying taxes' be struck?
firac.facts: Paragraphs 7, 10 and 17 of the RTCC alleged the deceased was 'engaged in illegality' and 'bad acts…for decades', 'long been…intent on avoiding taxes', and made 'lifelong efforts to avoid paying taxes'.
firac.rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(b)/(c), pleadings so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is pleaded, or so disconnected in time as to be irrelevant and to involve the parties in a dispute apart from the issues, may be struck (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform; Willow v. Chong).
firac.application: The court found the sweeping words suggested other unspecified 'illegal' activities and 'bad acts' whose nature, scope and relevance were unclear, and that terms like 'decades' and 'lifelong' obscured the relevant time period. The pleadings were confusing and appeared to encompass allegations too disconnected in time to be relevant, creating prejudice.
firac.conclusion: The identified portions of paras. 7, 10 and 17 were struck, with leave to amend by April 15, 2026 to clarify the nature and scope of the allegations.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area: the decision is an interlocutory application to strike pleadings under the Supreme Court Civil Rules. K054 (wills/estates) is engaged because the lead plaintiff sues as executor/trustee of a deceased's estate and the suit is estate-related litigation over the deceased's companies. K022 (restitution) reflects the unjust-enrichment claim advanced over the alleged wrongful bonus payment. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is included only as the closest procedural-remedies keyword to a chambers striking application and is a weak pick — no injunction was sought. The controlled vocabulary is heavily oriented to human-rights/hate-speech/religious subject matter and offers no term for striking pleadings, fiduciary duty, corporate directors or tax; the last two picks are flagged as weak on that basis.

case_name: Montréal (Ville de) c. Cie d'administration de stationnement populaire inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: Montréal (Ville de) c. Cie d'administration de stationnement populaire inc.

defining_issues: Did the defendants prove, on a balance of probabilities, that they held acquired rights (droits acquis) to operate an outdoor commercial parking lot on the lots in question?
Does the demolition of a building housing an indoor parking garage extinguish acquired rights, such that they cannot extend to a subsequently established outdoor parking use?
Is the City of Montréal barred (préclusion/forclusion under Chapdelaine) from prosecuting given long delay, the collection of taxes and the issuance of permits?
Where the offence describes the location by reference to several former lots grouped into one new lot, must the defendants be acquitted if only a portion of the location enjoys acquired rights?

firac.issue: Did the defendants prove, on a balance of probabilities, that they held acquired rights to operate an outdoor commercial parking lot on the lots?
firac.facts: The defendants operated an outdoor parking lot facing the Centre Bell, admitting the essential elements of the offences but pleading acquired rights. The zoning history showed no prohibition before 1 December 1960, then progressive prohibitions on outdoor parking (by-laws 2583, 5415, 5591) subject to narrow exceptions. Evidence (aerial photographs, land-use plans, occupancy permits, resolutions) was led about the actual use of lots P-594, P-595, 1925, 604, 605 and 596-2 over time.
firac.rule: The party invoking acquired rights bears the burden of proving them on a balance of probabilities; the conditions are set out in Huot c. L'Ange-Gardien (1992) — the prior derogatory use must have been legal, actually exercised (not merely intended), continued without significant interruption, and attaching to the immovable. Acquired-rights regimes are interpreted restrictively (Frelishburg c. Sibeca). Existence of a permit or payment of taxes does not create acquired rights; only the legality of the actual use matters.
firac.application: The court found that P-595 held acquired rights only to an indoor 'garage public' (lost on demolition — see issue 2); P-594 was a gas station never used for parking before 1995-96; lot 1925 had parking before 1960 but the use was abandoned for over ten years during a prolonged excavation, extinguishing the rights; lots 604 and 605 were within the 150-foot/45 m prohibited strip and were never legally used for outdoor parking; only the southern strip of lot 596-2 (4.25 m wide, outside the 45 m band) was proven to have acquired rights. The permits and personal, non-transferable authorizations were not sources of rights.
firac.conclusion: Stationnement Populaire and 9090-6421 Québec inc. failed to prove acquired rights on any of the former lots; Masdev proved acquired rights only on the southern portion of lot 1851392.

firac.issue: Does demolition of a building housing an indoor parking garage extinguish acquired rights so they cannot extend to a later outdoor parking use?
firac.facts: The two-storey garage on lot P-595 was demolished in 1995-96 and immediately replaced by an outdoor parking lot under a personal, non-transferable authorization granted under s. 649a of the Charter of the City of Montréal, since the zoning by-law (94-077) did not permit that use.
firac.rule: The municipal legislator has always distinguished indoor parking (requiring a building) from outdoor parking as distinct uses; acquired rights attached to a building are lost upon its demolition (St-Denis-de-Brompton c. Courtois; Hoppenheim c. Ville de Montréal), and by-law 94-077 art. 704 expressly provided that a destroyed derogatory construction must be rebuilt in conformity with current norms. A personal, non-transferable authorization does not create rights (2630-2042 Québec inc. c. Ville de Montréal).
firac.application: The commercial activity remained 'public parking,' but the regulatory scheme treated indoor and outdoor parking as different uses. The acquired right protected an indoor 'garage public'; its demolition extinguished that right and the protection could not be transferred to outdoor parking, which was then prohibited in the sector.
firac.conclusion: Demolition of the garage in 1995-96 extinguished the acquired right to indoor parking, and that protection could not extend to the newly established, prohibited outdoor parking use.

firac.issue: Is the City precluded (préclusion/forclusion) from prosecuting given delay, taxes and permits?
firac.facts: Over many years the City tolerated the parking activity, collected various taxes, and issued occupancy permits (one containing a gross error later corrected); several applications by the defendants had, however, been refused since 1972.
firac.rule: The préclusion theory (per Rochon J.A. in Montréal (Ville de) c. Chapdelaine) allows courts, in exceptional and rare circumstances, to refuse a municipality's remedy where all listed factors are present (exceptional circumstances, interests of justice, diligent good-faith contravenor unaware of the breach, no serious consequences, unreasonable and inexcusable delay usually over 20 years, positive municipal act, no danger to health/safety). Public-law estoppel cannot prevail against a clear statutory provision (Mont-Sinaï). In statutory penal matters the court has no discretion once the essential elements are proven beyond reasonable doubt and the defence rejected.
firac.application: Although the City tolerated the situation, collected taxes and issued permits, these do not confer rights. The defendants were not without fault, having known since 1972 that the use was prohibited and having had numerous requests refused. In a statutory penal proceeding the court has no discretion to refuse to convict where the offence is made out and the defence fails.
firac.conclusion: The préclusion/forclusion theory does not apply to bar the prosecution.

firac.issue: Must the defendants be acquitted if only a portion of the described location enjoys acquired rights?
firac.facts: The offences described the location as new lot 1851391 (with the former lots enumerated) and lot 1851392; defendants argued the location was an indivisible whole so acquired rights on any former lot required acquittal.
firac.rule: The prosecution must describe the offence location as precisely as possible to allow full answer and defence; where a single new lot regroups former lots, mention of the former lots is for precision only and does not add to the prosecution's burden. Once illegal occupation of the lot is established, the offence is proven regardless of the proportion occupied illegally.
firac.application: The court held that once it was satisfied there was illegal occupation of lot 1851391 (or 1851392), whether on 10%, 50% or 100% of the lot, the offence was proven; the defendants had admitted all essential elements on the offence dates.
firac.conclusion: The indivisibility argument was rejected; partial acquired rights do not require acquittal.

name_verification.name_in_document: M.J. R. et P.B. c. Dre Isabelle Girard, Dre Mélinda Hall, Dr Samir Khalifé, Dre Stéphanie Leah Klam, Dr David S. Rosenblatt

defining_issues: Did the defendant physicians breach the applicable standard of practice by failing to use advanced cytogenetic techniques (array comparative genomic hybridization or a targeted FISH 4p- probe) that could have detected Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome prenatally?

Did the defendants breach their duty to inform the parents of the risk of a genetic/chromosomal anomaly and of the possible outcomes of the fetus's significant early growth restriction, so as to allow the mother to make an informed choice about terminating the pregnancy?
Can the defendants be held collectively and solidarily liable for a 'collective fault' under art. 1480 C.c.Q. on the theory that the care team practised in silos?

firac.issue: Did the defendants breach the standard of practice by not resorting to aCGH or a targeted FISH 4p- probe that might have identified Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome before birth?
firac.facts: The fetus showed significant, early and unexplained intrauterine growth restriction that worsened over the last 13 weeks, but was otherwise vigorous, symmetrical, without structural malformation, facial dysmorphism or the usual markers of Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome. Standard screening (trisomy screen, TORCH, general FISH, cystic-fibrosis testing) and the amniocentesis karyotype of 7 October 2011 were all negative. The syndrome (a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4, prevalence 1:50,000) was masked because a similarly sized duplication of chromosome 2 translocated onto the deleted portion of chromosome 4, rendering the karyotype normal. It was diagnosed only about 11 months after birth.
firac.rule: A physician's obligation is one of means, not of result: liability requires proof that the physician did not act as a reasonably prudent and diligent specialist placed in the same circumstances, assessed in abstracto and according to the standards of practice in force at the relevant time (St-Jean c. Mercier, 2002 SCC 15; Ter Neuzen c. Korn, [1995] 3 SCR 674; Lapointe c. Hôpital Le Gardeur, [1992] 1 SCR 351). The plaintiff bears the burden of proving fault (art. 2803 C.c.Q.); the court must rely on expert evidence and must avoid reasoning backward from the known outcome (second-guessing).
firac.application: The Court preferred the geneticist expert Dr Maranda and fetal-medicine expert Dr Morin over the plaintiffs' experts (Dr Gekas and Dr Gouin), who reasoned a posteriori from the result and offered their own practice as the standard. The evidence, including CCGM/SOGC guidelines (2005–2013), showed that in 2011 aCGH was standard postnatally but only exploratory prenatally, appropriate only where ultrasound revealed fetal structural anomalies — none of which were present here. A targeted FISH 4p- probe would only be ordered given a high index of suspicion for Wolf-Hirschhorn, but the fetus displayed none of its markers (the dolichocephaly, cardiac axis, amniotic fluid level and echogenic bowel relied on by Dr Gekas were not structural anomalies or markers of the syndrome). Earlier amniocentesis would have changed nothing since the karyotype was normal.
firac.conclusion: No fault: it was consistent with 2011 standards of practice to rely on standard cytogenetic testing; the plaintiffs failed to prove a breach on this ground.

firac.issue: Did the defendants breach their duty to inform the parents of the genetic risk and possible outcomes so the mother could choose whether to continue the pregnancy?
firac.facts: From the first detection of growth restriction (29 August 2011), Dr Girard explained the possible etiologies (placental, infectious, genetic/chromosomal, or constitutionally small baby), gave an example of a genetic anomaly (cri-du-chat), and told the parents an abortion remained available at any time. The same message was repeated by Drs Hall, Khalifé, Klam and by genetic counsellor Maria Lalous; Dr Klam's detailed contemporaneous notes recorded discussion of 'abnormal baby', increased morbidity/mortality and the limits of the karyotype. The educated parents researched the issues and repeatedly questioned the physicians. The mother said she would seek an abortion if a serious handicap were revealed but set no risk threshold.
firac.rule: The duty to inform is assessed first on a subjective standard (the patient's testimony and all circumstances) tempered by a test of rational subjectivity (Chouinard c. Landry; Pelletier c. Roberge; Ferland c. Ghosn). A physician cannot guarantee results (Code de déontologie des médecins, art. 83); where the pregnancy is not itself a medical condition, the duty is to inform the parents of the possible outcomes and that termination remains an option and to leave the decision to the patient (art. 29 C.déont.; Hopp c. Lepp).
firac.application: The Court found, on the balance of probabilities and relying on the physicians' credible testimony and contemporaneous records (presumed truthful), that the parents were repeatedly warned that a genetic/chromosomal cause could not be excluded despite the normal karyotype and that outcomes ranged from a healthy small baby to a severely handicapped child. Because no percentage could honestly be attached to any outcome and the fetus retained the potential to be born normal, physicians were not required in 2011 to recommend abortion. Applying rational subjectivity, the birth resulted from the informed decision of the parents; there was no basis for the 'more dramatic warning' Dr Gekas said was owed.
firac.conclusion: No fault: the defendants adequately informed the parents; the claim fails on this ground as well.

firac.issue: Can the defendants be held collectively and solidarily liable for a 'collective fault' under art. 1480 C.c.Q. for compartmentalized (silo) practice?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs argued each physician committed at least a minor fault that others should have caught, and that as members of a care team they engaged in a collective wrongful act and operated an organized economic activity (art. 1525 C.c.Q.), justifying solidary liability.
firac.rule: Article 1480 C.c.Q. addresses the apportionment, not the conditions, of liability; civil liability requires proof of a fault by each person (act or omission). Hébert (Hôpital de l'Enfant-Jésus), 2011 QCCA 1521, applied a traditional obligation-of-means analysis and did not impose collective liability. Solidarity under art. 1525 requires an integrated economic chain and regularity of services (Ceracaise c. Catalfamo).
firac.application: The Court rejected 'liability by association': merely being part of a care team does not make each member liable, and the conditions of art. 1525(3) were not met (no economic integration or regularity). Each defendant had to be, and was, assessed individually; none committed a fault, and the physicians in fact communicated diligently among themselves and with consultants.
firac.conclusion: No collective or solidary liability; since no individual fault was established, the collective-fault theory cannot succeed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Helen Marie Joe v. Insurance Corporation of British Columbia, Per and Renay Turner Claims Representative for ICBC, Shook, Wickham, Bishop & Field Per and Vishal K. Bajpai

defining_issues: Does the statement of claim disclose a reasonable cause of action for breach of Charter rights, intimidation, professional misconduct, breach of trust, abuse of power, or conspiracy to suborn perjury under Rule 19(24)?
Can the Charter be invoked against private-party defendants (a law firm and its lawyer) and against ICBC absent any pleaded reliance on a statute or regulation?
Should the action be summarily dismissed under Rule 18(6) on the ground that the plaintiff is bound to lose because her evidence cannot establish the alleged torts?
Does the good-faith immunity in s. 30(3) of the Insurance Corporation Act bar the claim against the ICBC claims representative?

firac.issue: Does the statement of claim disclose a reasonable cause of action under Rule 19(24)(a)?
firac.facts: The self-represented plaintiff's one-page statement of claim alleged that ICBC, its claims representative and defence counsel infringed her Charter rights (ss. 2, 7 and 12), and committed intimidation, defamation, professional misconduct, breach of trust, abuse of power and conspiracy to suborn perjury, arising from a dispute over her account of a motor vehicle accident and a warning about breach of insurance coverage.
firac.rule: On a Rule 19(24)(a) application the applicant must show the action has no chance of success and is certain to fail; the court assumes the pleaded material facts are true (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959). Rule 19(1) requires a statement in summary form of the material facts relied upon.
firac.application: The court found no material facts pleaded to support the ss. 7 and 12 Charter claims, and that mere disbelief of the plaintiff's account could not infringe freedom of thought or expression under s. 2(b). No material facts supported defamation, professional misconduct, breach of trust or abuse of power, which were subsumed by the intimidation and conspiracy allegations. However, the court found it arguable that the claim could be amended to allege conspiracy to suborn perjury, as the outline of the alleged wrongdoing and its purpose was present.
firac.conclusion: The statement of claim failed to disclose reasonable causes of action for the Charter and most tort claims; only the conspiracy/intimidation allegations were potentially amendable.

firac.issue: Can the Charter apply to private-party defendants and to ICBC absent any pleaded reliance on a statute or regulation?
firac.facts: The law firm and Mr. Bajpai were private parties; ICBC was assumed for argument to be a governmental entity. No pleading alleged reliance on any statute, regulation or common-law rule to justify infringing the plaintiff's rights.
firac.rule: The Charter does not generally apply to private litigation (R.W.D.S.U. v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 573); Charter application requires government action, such as reliance on a statute or regulation.
firac.application: As against the firm and Mr. Bajpai, the Charter had no application as they were private parties and no statutory reliance was pleaded. Even assuming ICBC were governmental, no material fact alleged that it invoked any statute or regulation to justify an infringement, and disbelief of an insured's account could not itself infringe freedom of expression.
firac.conclusion: No viable Charter claim lay against any defendant.

firac.issue: Should the action be summarily dismissed under Rule 18(6)?
firac.facts: The plaintiff's affidavit evidence never asserted that Bajpai or Turner asked her to change her story, nor that she was told coverage would be cancelled if she did not do so; she maintained she consistently gave one account. She did not allege she was induced to make a false statement or that she suffered damage.
firac.rule: On a Rule 18(6) summary judgment application the defendants must establish the plaintiff is 'bound to lose' — that there is no bona fide triable issue (Serup v. School District No. 57 (1989), 54 B.C.L.R. (2d) 258 (C.A.); Skybridge Investments Ltd. v. Metro Motors Ltd., 2006 BCCA 500).
firac.application: The plaintiff's evidence disclosed only her subjective belief that the defendants wanted her to change her story; beliefs are not evidence. Defence counsel and ICBC acted properly under ss. 73 and 74.1 of the Insurance (Vehicle) Regulation in reviewing her account and controlling the defence. The evidence could not support intimidation or conspiracy to suborn perjury, and no loss was shown, so the plaintiff was bound to lose even if the claim were amended.
firac.conclusion: Summary judgment was warranted; the claims were bound to fail.

firac.issue: Does s. 30(3) of the Insurance Corporation Act bar the claim against the ICBC claims representative?
firac.facts: Ms. Turner sent a defective 'breach of coverage' warning letter after settling Mr. Knight's claim, which she should not have sent, but the plaintiff alleged Turner acted in bad faith.
firac.rule: Section 30(3) of the Insurance Corporation Act bars any action against a person for acts or omissions done in good faith in the administration or carrying out of the Act, regulations or an insurance plan.
firac.application: The facts deposed by the plaintiff could not support a finding that Ms. Turner acted in bad faith; her evidence supported good faith despite the erroneous letter sent after settlement.
firac.conclusion: The statutory immunity provided a further ground for dismissing the claim against Ms. Turner.

case_name: Kootenay Sleds & Wheels Inc. v. Peace Hills General Insurance Company

name_verification.name_in_document: Kootenay Sleds & Wheels Inc. v. Peace Hills General Insurance Company

defining_issues: Should the corporate plaintiff be ordered to give security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act, and if so in what amount?
Has the plaintiff established that an order for security for costs would improperly stifle its claim?

firac.issue: Should the insolvent corporate plaintiff be ordered to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act, and in what amount?
firac.facts: KSW, an insolvent recreational-vehicle dealer, sued its insurers over a December 31, 2008 fire loss. The insurers, more than two years into the litigation, sought security for costs of over $200,000 (later argued at $100,000) plus a stay until security was posted. KSW conceded its insolvency, which was at least partly linked to the fire and the insurers' refusal to pay.
firac.rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 permits the court to require a corporate plaintiff to give security where it appears it will be unable to pay a successful defendant's costs, and to stay proceedings until security is given. The court applies the discretionary factors endorsed in Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd. (1997) and affirmed in Galaxy Sports Inc. v. Umbro Holdings Ltd., 2004 BCCA 208: complete discretion on all circumstances, balancing oppression against unfair pressure, avoiding the merits unless obvious, timing/lateness of the application, and the amount lying in the judge's discretion. The staged test in Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform / Scotford asks whether the plaintiff can pay costs, whether it has exigible assets, whether the defence is arguable, and whether an order would visit undue hardship stifling the claim.
firac.application: The court found the plaintiff insolvent, the defendants having at least an arguable (not obviously winning or losing) defence, and that the defendants could not recover costs if successful. It weighed against ordering security the fact that the application came late, after the plaintiff was heavily invested in a two-year-old action, and the link between the fire loss and the insolvency. Balancing these, the court declined the full amount sought and fixed a reduced sum of $40,000.
firac.conclusion: Security for costs of $40,000 was ordered; the claim and counterclaim were stayed pending its posting.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff establish that an order for security for costs would stifle a genuine claim?
firac.facts: Mr. Streichert's affidavit stated KSW had exhausted its resources, had borrowed from family, sold property, faced foreclosure and debt litigation, and that any more-than-nominal security order would bar KSW from advancing its fire claim.
firac.rule: Under Kropp and Galaxy, to show an order would stifle the action the plaintiff must do more than assert impecuniosity; it must lead evidence that it has no means of raising money for security, including from third parties. The court must be satisfied it is probable the claim would be stifled before refusing security on that ground.
firac.application: The court accepted the plaintiff's evidence of insolvency and the connection between the fire loss and its impecuniosity, and treated the stifling concern as a genuine consideration weighing toward a reduced order rather than a refusal or full award. It concluded that a reduced amount appropriately balanced the risk of stifling a legitimate claim against the defendants' inability to recover costs.
firac.conclusion: The stifling concern justified reducing the security to $40,000 rather than declining an order or awarding the full amount sought.

case_name: Lalonde v Sena Solid Waste Holdings Inc

name_verification.name_in_document: Kerry Lalonde v Sena Solid Waste Holdings Inc.

defining_issues: Do the employment letters signed by the plaintiff limit his entitlement to reasonable notice, and what is the appropriate reasonable notice period (including bonus/retention entitlements)?
Is the plaintiff entitled to aggravated (moral) damages for the manner of his dismissal?
Is the plaintiff entitled to punitive damages?

firac.issue: Do the signed employment letters limit the plaintiff's reasonable notice, and what notice period (with retention bonuses) is appropriate?
firac.facts: Lalonde, a 62-year-old (56 at dismissal) journeyman millwright, worked for the defendant continuously from April 2008 until his dismissal in July 2012. He signed an April 2008 employment letter and a February 2011 letter after ownership changed. The April 2008 letter's termination clause limited entitlement to statutory minimums except where termination was for 'willful or professional misconduct, conflict of interest, disobedience or willful neglect of duty.' The defendant purported to dismiss him for disobedience/professional misconduct (later withdrawn). His compensation included short- and long-term retention initiative payments.
firac.rule: Reasonable notice is assessed on the Bardal factors — character of employment, length of service, age, and availability of similar employment (Bardal v Globe & Mail; Wallace v United Grain Growers, 1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)); the factors are non-exhaustive and assessed prospectively (Nelson v Champion Feed Services, 2010 ABQB 409). Damages must place the employee in the position he would have occupied had proper notice been given, including bonuses that are an integral part of compensation (Paquette v TeraGo Networks, 2016 ONCA 618).
firac.application: The court found the April 2008 letter applicable but held that because the plaintiff was dismissed for alleged disobedience and professional misconduct, the clause's carve-out meant his entitlement was not limited to statutory minimums (and the 2011 letter would not have limited notice either). Applying Bardal — length of service (just over 4 years), age (56), technical tradesman role with occasional minor supervisory duties, and difficulty finding comparable millwright work — the court set reasonable notice at 6 months, within a 4–8 month range drawn from comparable cases. The retention initiative, expressly payable pro rata on release without cause, was an integral part of compensation, so 6 months of the retention bonus was added to 6 months' salary, less mitigation earnings.
firac.conclusion: The employment letters did not limit notice. Reasonable notice fixed at 6 months' salary plus 6 months of short- and long-term retention bonuses, less amounts earned in mitigation.

firac.issue: Is the plaintiff entitled to aggravated (moral) damages for the manner of his dismissal?
firac.facts: The plaintiff was summarily accused of serious safety violations and insubordination, given little chance to respond, suspended, and escorted off the site in front of co-workers. The defendant made up its mind to terminate within days, ignored a supporting letter from co-worker Larry Dakin, maintained cause allegations (framed in the Statement of Defence as dishonesty, serious misconduct, insubordination) for nearly five years until withdrawing them on the eve of trial. His EI was delayed, rumours of theft circulated in his small community, and his wife's uncontradicted letter described depression, humiliation and family strain.
firac.rule: Damages for the manner of dismissal are available where the employer's conduct during dismissal is 'unfair or in bad faith by being untruthful, misleading or unduly insensitive,' and the mental distress was within the reasonable contemplation of the parties (Wallace; Honda Canada v Keays, 2008 SCC 39; Fidler). Such moral/aggravated damages reflect actual damages, not an arbitrary extension of notice (Elgert v Home Hardware, 2011 ABCA 112). Attacking the employee's reputation and misrepresenting reasons for dismissal are compensable examples.
firac.application: The court found the defendant 'shot first and asked questions later': the investigation ignored the plaintiff's side and Dakin's supporting account and was 'at best incompetent and unfair and at worst a sham.' Maintaining unsubstantiated cause allegations implying dishonesty for almost five years, the public humiliation, the delayed EI, and reputational harm in a small community breached the duty of good faith and caused proven mental distress. The court distinguished Boucher and Karmel as involving more prolonged, vindictive conduct warranting higher awards, and canvassed comparators ($50,000–$100,000).
firac.conclusion: Aggravated damages awarded in the amount of $75,000.

firac.issue: Is the plaintiff entitled to punitive damages?
firac.facts: The plaintiff relied on the manager's internal email showing a termination decision made without hearing from him, and characterized the one-sided investigation as high-handed and oppressive.
firac.rule: Punitive damages serve retribution, deterrence and denunciation, not compensation, and are restricted to cases where the employer's conduct is so malicious and outrageous as to deserve punishment (Ram v Michael Lacombe Group, 2017 BCSC 212).
firac.application: Although the defendant's conduct was insensitive, inappropriate and caused mental distress, the court found it was not malicious. The threshold of malicious, outrageous conduct deserving of punishment was not met.
firac.conclusion: The claim for punitive damages was dismissed.

case_name: Jewish Eldercare Centre v. J.H.H. Foundation-Fondation J.H.H.

name_verification.name_in_document: The Jewish Eldercare Centre and The Jewish Eldercare Foundation v. J.H.H. Foundation-Fondation J.H.H., Morris Freedman, Gerry Weinstein, Martin Labow, Ted Salonin, Sheldon Weinstein and Rhoda Lazarus

defining_issues: Did a tacit or implicit contract of mandate exist between the Hospital/Eldercare Centre and the Foundation such that its revocation would preclude the Foundation from fundraising and oblige it to account for and remit funds?
Did the Eldercare Centre retain an exclusive right to the name 'Jewish Hospital of Hope' enforceable against the Foundation, or had it lost that right through tolerance and abandonment?
Could the Foundation obtain a declaratory judgment holding the Eldercare Centre's September 6, 2000 letter ultra vires and null under art. 453 C.C.P.?
Could the Foundation obtain a permanent injunction preventing the Eldercare Centre from replacing it as fundraiser with a new foundation?

firac.issue: Did a tacit or implicit contract of mandate exist between the Hospital/Eldercare Centre and the Foundation whose revocation would bar the Foundation from fundraising and require it to account and remit funds?
firac.facts: The Foundation was incorporated federally in 1972 to shield the Hospital's reserves from anticipated government appropriation; the Hospital transferred nearly $1.8 million to it in perpetuity with no conditions. No resolution, contract or agreement ever documented the relationship, and no instructions were shown to have been given by the Hospital to the Foundation.
firac.rule: A mandate under art. 2130 C.c.Q. requires a power of representation to accomplish a juridical act with a third party and an obligation of the mandatary to execute the mandator's instructions (arts. 2138, 2139, 2141 C.c.Q.; Popovici, La couleur du mandat). A charitable foundation must devote all its resources to charitable purposes and remain independent to preserve its power to issue tax-deductible receipts (Vancouver Society v. M.N.R., [1999] 1 S.C.R. 10; Income Tax Act ss. 149.1, 168, 248).
firac.application: The evidence disclosed no instructions the Foundation obliged itself to execute and no power in the Foundation to bind the Hospital. Fundraising 'for the benefit of' the Hospital did not create a mandator-mandatary relationship; any obligation to remit funds arose from the contract between third-party donors and the Foundation, not from a mandate with the Hospital. As a charitable body the Foundation was legally required to remain independent and retain final decision-making over the use of funds it collected.
firac.conclusion: No tacit or implicit mandate existed; its purported revocation could not bar the Foundation's activities or compel accounting/remittance. This branch of the action failed.

firac.issue: Did the Eldercare Centre retain an exclusive right to the name 'Jewish Hospital of Hope' enforceable against the Foundation?
firac.facts: The name originally belonged to the 1942 Hospital charter. For nearly thirty years the Foundation operated and was known as the 'Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation', a use tolerated and even encouraged by the Hospital, which itself later abandoned the name in favour of 'Jewish Eldercare Centre'.
firac.rule: Rights in a commercial name are acquired and lost by use; exclusivity can be lost through prolonged tolerance of another's use, amounting to abandonment or estoppel — a question of fact (Simon, Le nom commercial; Fox, The Canadian Law of Trade Marks and Unfair Competition).
firac.application: The Hospital's long tolerance and encouragement of the Foundation's use of the full name, combined with the Hospital's own abandonment of that name for 'Jewish Eldercare Centre', meant the Hospital had lost the exclusive right to the words. After thirty years it was too late to assert an exclusivity never enforced, and continued use by the Foundation would not create confusion given the parties now bore different names.
firac.conclusion: The Eldercare Centre lost its exclusive right to the name; no injunction restraining the Foundation's use, and no exemplary damages against the Directors, could be granted. The action was dismissed.

firac.issue: Could the Foundation obtain a declaratory judgment declaring the September 6, 2000 letter ultra vires and null under art. 453 C.C.P.?
firac.facts: The Foundation sought a declaration that a letter from the Eldercare Centre summarizing a negotiating position was ultra vires and contrary to the LSSSS and the Canadian and Quebec Charters. Negotiations continued after the letter.
firac.rule: Article 453 C.C.P. permits a declaratory judgment only in respect of a contract, will or other 'written instrument' (écrit instrumentaire), statute, order or by-law; the instrument must be a formal document creating or confirming rights, and courts do not render advisory opinions (art. 462 C.C.P.; Ferland & Émery).
firac.application: The letter was merely a written summary of a negotiating position, not a formal instrument creating rights or obligations, and did not fall within the meaning of 'written instrument'/'écrit instrumentaire'. Treating such correspondence as declaratory-judgment material would turn the courts into a testing ground for negotiating positions.
firac.conclusion: Article 453 C.C.P. did not apply; the declaratory conclusion was dismissed (and the court declined to formally opine on ultra vires/Charter arguments).

firac.issue: Could the Foundation enjoin the Eldercare Centre from replacing it with a new foundation as fundraiser?
firac.facts: The Eldercare Centre, after unifying the Hospital and Nursing Home, invited the Foundation to reconstitute as the Jewish Eldercare Foundation; when it refused, the former Nursing Home Foundation was renamed to serve that role.
firac.rule: The Loi sur les services de santé et les services sociaux (L.R.Q. c. S-4.2), ss. 129-132.2, contemplates that an establishment may have one or more foundations; to be the 'fondation d'un établissement' a foundation must name the establishment in its constituting act.
firac.application: Neither the Foundation's charter nor the Nursing Home Foundation's charter named the Hospital or Eldercare Centre, so the Foundation was never the exclusive statutory foundation of the establishment. The Act permits multiple foundations, and the Foundation is not 'replaced' — a new foundation simply enters the field; both may pursue their goals.
firac.conclusion: No legal basis supported an injunction against creation of the new foundation; the cross-demand's injunctive relief (and the disappearance concern, which was neither alleged nor proven) was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area: the dispute turns on contract (mandate), commercial-name/trade-mark rights, declaratory judgment and injunctions among charitable institutions. K021 (injunction/injunctive relief) is squarely engaged — both the principal action and the cross-demand sought permanent injunctions, though the canonical label is 'interlocutory'. K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) reflect that all parties are Jewish-community institutions serving the aging Jewish population, the context in which the naming and fundraising dispute arose. K054 (wills/estates) is a weak, borderline pick tied only to the recurring references to donors, testators, legacies and bequests handled by the Foundation; it is included to reach the minimum count. The controlled vocabulary lacks dedicated terms for charitable-foundation law, mandate, trade-name/abandonment and declaratory judgment, which are the true doctrinal core, so several central concepts could not be tagged.
