name_verification.name_in_document: SA MAJESTÉ LA REINE c. JEAN-CLAUDE ROCHEFORT

defining_issues: Did the accused's online publications 'foment hatred' within the meaning of s. 319(2) of the Criminal Code, or were they merely satire, exaggeration and derision?
Did the publications target an 'identifiable group' — women — under s. 318(4), as opposed to feminists only?
Did the accused act 'wilfully' — with the intent or conscious purpose of promoting hatred — as required for the s. 319(2) offence?

firac.issue: Did the accused's online publications foment hatred against a group, or were they protected satire and exaggeration?
firac.facts: Jean-Claude Rochefort authored public blogs (notably 'Antimasculiniste') accessible without a password and followed by roughly 60,000 readers. Between September 1 and December 5, 2019, in the lead-up to the 30th anniversary commemorations of the Polytechnique massacre, he posted texts and photomontages glorifying Marc Lépine (who murdered 14 women), depicting decapitated and dismembered women, promoting a 'St-Marc Lépine Day', calling for 'feminist slayers', and portraying women/feminists as an evil, conspiratorial menace. He testified these were satire, exaggeration and derision involving imaginary characters (e.g., 'Ulrich').
firac.rule: Section 319(2) Cr.C. criminalizes wilful promotion of hatred against an identifiable group. In R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 SCR 697, 'promotes/fomente' means active support or instigation and 'hatred' denotes only the most intense and extreme forms of detestation and vilification. In Mugesera, 2005 SCC 40, and Whatcott, 2013 SCC 11, the court asks how a reasonable person, aware of the historical and social context and the audience, would understand the communication; the judge must avoid finding hatred merely because the speech is offensive.
firac.application: The court found Rochefort's explanations — that imaginary characters could not be serious, and that words like 'slayer/trucideur' or 'burn down' were harmless — to be facile, simplistic and non-credible after-the-fact justifications. The content, not the fictional form, controlled. A reasonable person aware of the Polytechnique commemorations context and the incel audience would conclude the publications instigated intense, extreme emotions of calumny and detestation: they glorified Lépine, associated women with savages and the devil, presented them as a violent conspiratorial threat and the source of society's ills, and displayed weapons alongside calls for a 'feminist slayer' profession.
firac.conclusion: The court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the publications fomented hatred within the Keegstra/Mugesera/Whatcott framework; the satire/derision defence was rejected.

firac.issue: Did the publications target women as an identifiable group under s. 318(4), rather than only feminists?
firac.facts: Rochefort maintained his posts targeted feminists, not women in general, and filed dictionary definitions distinguishing 'femme/woman' from 'féministe/feminism/feminazi'. However, many publications used the words 'femmes'/'women', sometimes side-by-side with 'féministes'/'feminists', and he wrote that all women are feminists-in-waiting.
firac.rule: Section 318(4) Cr.C. defines 'identifiable group' as any section of the public distinguished by, among other things, sex. The communication must target such a group.
firac.application: The court disbelieved Rochefort's claim that references to 'femmes'/'women' were mere errors, finding the recurrence too frequent and the side-by-side use of both terms inconsistent with error. Context and content showed that even where only 'féministe' was used it carried a broader sense encompassing women generally, and Rochefort himself conflated the two by asserting all women would become feminists.
firac.conclusion: The court found beyond a reasonable doubt that the publications targeted women, an identifiable group under s. 318(4); hatred of women was their common denominator.

firac.issue: Did the accused wilfully promote hatred — with the required intent — under s. 319(2)?
firac.facts: Rochefort published deliberately over multiple blogs, translated texts into English, prepared image montages to maximize readership, timed the posts to the Polytechnique commemorations, and stopped around December 6. He knew part of his audience were 'incels' (frustrated young men), communicated with incel groups, authorized use of his material, and promised and produced 65 texts in 65 days to satisfy them and not lose readers.
firac.rule: Under Mugesera (para. 104-106), citing R. v. Buzzanga and Durocher (1979) and Keegstra, the s. 319(2) mens rea requires a conscious purpose of promoting hatred or certainty that the communication would have that effect; intent may be inferred from the nature of the statements viewed objectively in light of the circumstances, manner, tone and audience. R. v. Harding (2001, ONCA) holds wilful blindness suffices, though recklessness does not.
firac.application: Considering the statements objectively with their violent tone (words like 'tuer/kill', images of firearms and decapitated women), the repetition and cross-posting showing deliberateness and insistence, the timing, and the incel audience Rochefort knowingly courted, the court inferred a conscious purpose to promote hatred against women. Rochefort could not have been unaware that his statements fomented hatred; the satire claim was again rejected.
firac.conclusion: The court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Rochefort acted wilfully and had the conscious purpose of promoting hatred against women.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area. K067 (wilful promotion of hatred) is the precise offence charged under s. 319(2). K061 (hate speech) captures the subject matter — hateful expression against a group. K115 (Criminal Code s. 319(2)) is the exact charging provision. K063 (online hate / social media) fits because the impugned statements were public blog/Internet publications. K024 (freedom of expression) is engaged because the Keegstra/Whatcott framework the court applies balances the offence against expression; it is somewhat background here rather than a contested Charter issue, so it is the weakest pick. The case does not involve antisemitism-specific keywords despite the corpus's focus, so those were excluded.
location_rationale: The header states 'COUR SUPÉRIEURE ... PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC ... DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL' and the offence is alleged to have occurred 'à Montréal, district de Montréal'.
registry_rationale: The proceeding bears the district and file number '500-01-198566-199' for the District de Montréal, indicating the Montréal registry of the Superior Court.

case_name: Parmar v. Blenz The Canadian Coffee Company Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: Parmar v. Blenz The Canadian Coffee Company Ltd.

defining_issues: Should portions of the amended statement of claim be struck under Rules 19(7) and 19(24) as inconsistent pleadings or as disclosing no reasonable claim, particularly where the corporate plaintiff Mya did not exist when the alleged representations were made?
Should the corporate plaintiff Mya Enterprises be ordered to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act?

firac.issue: Should portions of the amended statement of claim be struck under Rules 19(7) and 19(24), especially claims premised on representations made to or reliance by Mya before it was incorporated?
firac.facts: Parmar acquired a Blenz franchise, executing the franchise agreement on September 17, 2001, and later assigned it to Mya Enterprises, which was not incorporated until October 11, 2001. The pleadings alleged that Blenz made negligent misrepresentations and breached a duty of good faith and a collateral agreement, and that both Parmar and Mya relied on them. The defendants argued these pleadings were inconsistent with Parmar's sworn affidavits (said to be admissions under R. 31(6)) and contrary to R. 19(7) and R. 19(24)(a)-(d), and further that entire-agreement clauses barred the claim.
firac.rule: Rule 19(7) prevents a party pleading facts inconsistent with a previous pleading, but primarily bars contradiction between a subsequent pleading (e.g. reply) and an earlier one (Gabbs v. Bouwhuis, 2005 BCSC 1782). Under R. 19(24), pleadings may be struck only where it is 'plain and obvious' they disclose no reasonable claim, are scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, embarrassing, or an abuse of process; the court assumes pleaded facts true, does not weigh evidence, and resolves doubt in the plaintiff's favour (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 SCR 959; Isaac v. Guardian Capital Group, 2004 BCSC 254; McNutt v. Canada, 2004 BCSC 1113).
firac.application: R. 19(7) applies to inconsistency between successive pleadings, not between a statement of claim and affidavit admissions, so it was not a basis to strike. On R. 19(24), the alleged dual capacity of Parmar and the estoppel argument were triable matters not plain and obvious to fail; the exclusion/entire-agreement clause argument was likewise for trial given Zippy Print Enterprises Ltd. v. Pawliuk. However, allegations that Mya relied on or received representations before its October 11, 2001 incorporation could not be true, since a non-existent company cannot rely on representations. Those specific portions were obviously unsustainable.
firac.conclusion: Motion granted in part: the paragraphs and subparagraphs referring to reliance by or misrepresentation to Mya before its incorporation (paras. 16.3, and portions of 22, 24(f), 25, 26.1, 26.2, 27, 28, 29, 29(b), 30) were struck, with para. 24(f) amended to refer only to Parmar. The balance of the striking application was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the corporate plaintiff Mya be ordered to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act?
firac.facts: Mya had no assets, its only former assets (the franchise and leasehold) having been assigned away and lost—loss the pleadings attributed to the defendants' conduct. Parmar, Mya's sole principal, had no assets or means to fund security beyond possibly borrowing from family. The defendants sought $53,595.15 in security based on Scale B and an assumed ten-day trial.
firac.rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 permits ordering security where a corporate plaintiff appears unable to pay a successful defendant's costs. The discretion is governed by the principles in Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course (1997), 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 252 (C.A.): the court balances the injustice of stifling a legitimate claim against the misuse of impecuniosity to pressure a defendant, may consider the merits only where success or failure is obvious, must be satisfied a claim would probably be stifled before refusing on that ground, and may consider whether the impecuniosity was caused by the defendant (Grey v. Power Assist Technologies Inc., 2001 BCSC 1208).
firac.application: The claim was at least arguable given conflicting Court of Appeal authority on exclusion clauses in franchise agreements, so success was not guaranteed and Parmar likely could not borrow to fund security. Ordering security would probably halt the action. Mya's impecuniosity arose from the loss of the very assets the defendants were alleged to have caused. There was no indication of unfair pressure on the defendants from the plaintiffs' impecuniosity.
firac.conclusion: The application for security for costs was dismissed; it would be unjust and inequitable to stifle the corporate plaintiff's claim.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the strong, controlling practice-area keyword: this is a commercial/franchise dispute involving an interlocutory chambers application to strike pleadings and for security for costs. K022 (restitution) is moderately apt because the plaintiffs sought rescission and repayment of the 'Parmar Payment' on the basis that consideration wholly failed. The remaining picks are weak and flagged: the controlled vocabulary contains no term for striking pleadings, franchise agreements, or security for costs, so K020 (class action) and K021 (interlocutory injunction) are used only as the nearest civil-procedure/remedies proxies, and K015 (defamation) is included only because the pleadings reference 'damage to their business and reputation' — there is no actual defamation cause of action. Fewer than five vocabulary terms genuinely fit this commercial civil-procedure matter.
location_rationale: The header states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA', 'Registry: Vancouver', and the hearing was held 'Vancouver, B.C.' on March 15, 2007.
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly lists 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Protection de la jeunesse — 138295

defining_issues: Were the late motions filed on August 20, 2013 receivable given the stage of the protection enquiry?
Was the security and development of the children in danger by reason of physical abuse under the Youth Protection Act?
Was the security and development of the children in danger by reason of psychological ill-treatment under s. 38(c) of the Youth Protection Act?
What protective measures should be ordered if endangerment is established?

firac.issue: Were the mother's late-filed motions receivable when they were filed on August 20, 2013 for presentation on September 16, 2013, after the evidence on the protection motions had closed?
firac.facts: After eight days of hearing on the Motions for Protection and closing arguments scheduled for September 16, the mother filed motions in the files of Y and X alleging facts from August 11 and facts already raised at the hearing.
firac.rule: Motions of this kind are governed by criteria of urgency and necessity; Article 77 of the Youth Protection Act confers broad powers on the Court over the administration of proof and imposes a duty to hear all the evidence before deciding.
firac.application: The Court found the motions did not meet urgency and necessity: they were filed August 20 for September 16 presentation, several alleged facts had already been testified to, and the August 11 facts lacked sufficient probative weight to justify further delay. Admitting new evidence at that stage would contravene the spirit of the Act.
firac.conclusion: The motions were dismissed as not receivable.

firac.issue: Was the children's security and development in danger due to physical abuse under the Youth Protection Act?
firac.facts: The older daughters alleged past incidents of being tied with ropes by the father and paternal grandmother and being hit; more recently the father twisted Z's arm during a television dispute. The father and grandmother denied the historical events and the mother said she never witnessed them.
firac.rule: Section 38.2 YPA requires consideration of the nature, gravity, persistence and frequency of the reported facts, and the child's age and characteristics; proof is on the balance of probabilities (art. 2804 C.C.Q.; F.H. v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53).
firac.application: The historical rope allegations were contradictory, general and imprecise, lacking probative weight. While the arm-twisting of Z was not a reasonable method of upbringing and hurt and scared the children, it was a single incident causing no physical injury and could not, given the s. 38.2 factors of gravity, persistence and frequency, ground a finding of physical abuse.
firac.conclusion: No declaration of endangerment on the basis of physical abuse.

firac.issue: Was the children's security and development in danger due to psychological ill-treatment under s. 38(c) of the Youth Protection Act?
firac.facts: After a ten-year separation marked by acrimony over the father's refusal to grant the get, the parents reconciled in summer 2012. The father imposed sudden strict religious rules, denigrated the mother, sought to control the children (removing TV, Internet, phones, imposing curfews, converting a room to storage), and the mother became submissive and abandoned her get quest. The children, drawn into the parents' conflict for years, reacted with anger and refused contact; the parents accused the children of lying and repeatedly disrupted the placement.
firac.rule: Section 38(c) YPA defines psychological ill-treatment as behaviour by parents that could seriously or repeatedly harm the child, including denigration, isolation, threats and exposure to conjugal or domestic violence, where the parents fail to end the situation. Parental authority (arts. 597–612 C.C.Q.) is not absolute and is subordinate to the child's interest and rights (art. 33 C.C.Q.; art. 3 YPA). Freedom of religion (art. 3 Quebec Charter) belongs to both parents and children but cannot justify transgressing s. 38. Criteria from prior youth-protection jurisprudence (Boudreau J., 1997) include the duration of the conflict, its intensity, the parents' conduct before the children, and use of the children as bargaining tools.
firac.application: The Court, drawing on the Superior Court's 2008 findings (Trahan J.) about the father using the get as leverage and control, found the father prioritized imposing his strict religious values over the children's interests and the mother failed to protect them, putting the father ahead of the children. The chronology showed the children were used in the parents' decade-long conflict; the parents' ongoing acrimony, disruptive conduct and refusal to acknowledge responsibility created a poisoned environment. Individually credible and consistent testimony of the older, articulate daughters established repeated harmful behaviour. Respecting the family's religious beliefs, the Court held religion could not excuse conduct endangering the children.
firac.conclusion: The Court declared the security and development of A, Z, Y and X in danger by reason of psychological ill-treatment under s. 38(c) YPA.

firac.issue: What protective measures were appropriate?
firac.facts: The children had been entrusted since 2012 to their eldest sister D, were doing well in school, had a strong bond, and wished to stay together; the parents proposed foster care and disputed D and the agency.
firac.rule: Sections 91 (measures) and 3 YPA (child's interest) govern the choice of measures.
firac.application: Splitting the siblings into foster homes would be against their interest given their exceptional bond and stability with D. Withdrawing certain attributes of parental authority (health, school, activities, passports, travel) to D was warranted given the parents' acrimony and the stream of interim motions. The Court ordered counselling for the children and mother (and father when appropriate), respite care, supervised contacts determined by the Director, and reassignment of a new social worker, with review in August 2014.
firac.conclusion: Motions granted; children entrusted to D with the enumerated measures under s. 91 YPA.

keywords_rationale: K006 Family law is the tier-1 practice area (youth protection / child protection). K047 best interests of the child is the governing standard for the endangerment finding and the choice of measures (art. 3 YPA, art. 33 C.C.Q.). K051 religious divorce (get) is central: the father's decade-long refusal of the get and its use as leverage drives the family conflict that grounded the psychological ill-treatment finding. K052 religious upbringing captures the father's imposition of strict religious values and rules on the children. K025 freedom of religion is engaged because the Court expressly addressed that religious freedom belongs to parents and children alike but cannot justify endangering the children. K048 custody/access reflects the entrustment of the children to their eldest sister and the contact regime ordered. K093 Jewish identifies the Orthodox Jewish family context (Shabbat, kosher, beth din). K117 Divorce Act is cited for the s. 21.1(2) affidavit concerning removal of barriers to religious remarriage. Borderline: K025 and K093 are contextual rather than dispositive, but the get/religious-rules dimension makes them genuinely engaged.
location_rationale: The decision is rendered by the Court of Québec, Youth Division, in the Province of Québec ('PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC'). The judicial district is redacted ('DISTRICT OF [...]') and no city is stated, so city is left null while province is Quebec.
registry_rationale: The district/registry name is anonymized in the text ('DISTRICT OF [...]') to protect the children's identity under the Youth Protection Act; only file numbers (525-41-...) appear, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: His Majesty the King v. Maxime Bernier, Peter Christoph Boettcher, Bartel Boot [et al.]

defining_issues: Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt, for each defendant, identity and presence at the prohibited gathering, particularly where identity rested on comparing rally video with SGI driver's-licence photographs?
What constitutes 'attending' a gathering in excess of 10 persons for the purposes of the actus reus, and could a defence of due diligence succeed?
Was the court bound by prior Saskatchewan decisions under horizontal and vertical stare decisis, and could the Alberta decision in Ingram displace R v Wong?
Was the Public Health Order ultra vires The Public Health Act, 1994?
Was the police use of the SGI database rendered inoperative by federal paramountcy (the Identification of Criminals Act), and was this a criminal proceeding rather than an administrative one?
Were the defendants entitled to a stay of proceedings for abuse of process based on alleged selective/discriminatory enforcement?

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove identity and attendance beyond a reasonable doubt for each defendant, including where identity rested on comparing rally video with SGI photographs?
firac.facts: Forty-four defendants were prosecuted for attending a May 9, 2021 gathering at the Vimy Memorial that exceeded the 10-person limit set by a Public Health Order. Some defendants self-identified to police or were identified in court; most were identified by police searching names in the SGI AutoFund databank and comparing driver's-licence photos with rally video (Vimy 1, Vimy 2, WUC).
firac.rule: A trier of fact may identify an accused solely from video/photographic evidence if the material is of sufficient clarity and quality, exercising care (R v Nikolovski, 1996 CanLII 158 (SCC); R v Delorme, 2017 SKCA 3; R v John, 2021 SKCA 83; R v Field, 2018 BCCA 253). Recognition evidence from officers with no prior acquaintance is inadmissible, as they are in no better position than the judge.
firac.application: The court disregarded the officers' comparison opinions where they lacked personal knowledge, and instead personally compared the videos with SGI photographs. It convicted where identity and non-trivial attendance were established beyond a reasonable doubt, but acquitted where video resolution or matching left doubt (Bourassa, Bubnick, Cooper), where the charged name did not match the identified person (Keesyn Larocque vs 'Laroque'), or where no SGI photo was in evidence (S. Wintringham). The Crown conceded insufficient evidence for Wayne Peters.
firac.conclusion: Identity/attendance was proven for most defendants; acquittals entered for Peters, Bourassa, Bubnick, Cooper, Keesyn Larocque, E. Schmidt, T. Schmidt and S. Wintringham.

firac.issue: What constitutes 'attending' a gathering over 10 persons, and could due diligence excuse the offence?
firac.facts: Kosowska claimed she only dropped off cupcakes; Machiskinic came to hear Bernier speak and limited her contacts and health risk; the Schmidts stood on the fringe with a young child observing.
firac.rule: The actus reus under s. 61 of The Public Health Act, 1994 has two parts: attending an event, and the event being in excess of 10 persons; there is no distance or minimum-contact requirement. Due diligence (R v Sault Ste. Marie, 1978 CanLII 11 (SCC)) requires all reasonable steps to avoid the specific offence charged.
firac.application: Kosowska deliberately entered the centre of a crowd she knew exceeded 10 persons, so she 'attended'; Machiskinic came expressly to attend a gathering she knew was large, and her precautions (distancing, feeling well, timing) addressed transmission, not the elements of attending an over-10 gathering, so due diligence failed. The Schmidts, merely on the fringe observing with family, did not 'attend'.
firac.conclusion: Kosowska and Machiskinic attended and had no due-diligence defence (guilty); the Schmidts did not attend (not guilty).

firac.issue: Was the court bound by prior Saskatchewan COVID-19/PHO decisions, and could Ingram (Alberta) displace R v Wong?
firac.facts: Many issues had already been decided in Saskatchewan Provincial Court and King's Bench cases. Defendants relied on Ingram v Alberta, 2023 ABKB 453, to argue Wong's ultra vires reasoning had been undermined.
firac.rule: R v Sullivan, 2022 SCC 19: vertical stare decisis binds courts to higher courts in their own chain of authority; horizontal stare decisis/comity permits departure from coordinate courts only in three narrow situations (undermined by subsequent appellate decisions; per incuriam; not fully considered).
firac.application: The binding higher courts for the Saskatchewan Provincial Court are only the Saskatchewan King's Bench, Saskatchewan Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Canada. An Alberta King's Bench decision, though a 'higher court', is not in the chain of authority and is merely persuasive; it does not trigger Sullivan's first exception. However, the arguments in Ingram could still be advanced anew.
firac.conclusion: The court remained bound by the listed Saskatchewan decisions (including Wong); it was not bound by Ingram, but considered the substance of the argument.

firac.issue: Was the Public Health Order ultra vires the enabling legislation?
firac.facts: Defendants argued, relying on Ingram, that the PHO was made by the Minister of Health rather than a medical health officer, exceeding statutory authority.
firac.rule: An order must be made by the body authorized by the enabling legislation; s. 25.2 of The Disease Control Regulations empowers the minister to order the listed measures.
firac.application: The legislative landscape had changed since Wong: the PHO was enacted under s. 25.2, which expressly authorizes the minister. Moreover, the defendants misquoted the PHO — it was in fact made by Dr. Saqib Shahab, Chief Medical Health Officer, under authority delegated by the Minister, so the 'authorized by the Minister of Health' language described the source of Dr. Shahab's power, not the maker of the order.
firac.conclusion: The ultra vires argument failed.

firac.issue: Was police use of the SGI database ousted by federal paramountcy, and was this an administrative rather than a criminal proceeding?
firac.facts: Defendants argued the federal Identification of Criminals Act occupied the field of identification photographs, making the SGI database or its police use unconstitutional, and that the court was sitting as an administrative tribunal conducting judicial review.
firac.rule: Paramountcy requires actual conflict — either operational conflict (dual compliance impossible) or frustration of federal purpose; the 'occupied field' theory is not the test (Saskatchewan (AG) v Lemare Lake Logging, 2015 SCC 53); paramountcy is narrowly construed. Courts are constitutionally distinct from administrative tribunals, which implement government policy (Ocean Port Hotel, 2001 SCC 52). Constitutional challenges require notice under The Constitutional Questions Act, 2012.
firac.application: No notice was given, which was fatal, and in any event compliance with both the ICA and SGI is possible and SGI complements rather than frustrates the ICA. The Provincial Court of Saskatchewan is a court of record with guarantees of independence (Provincial Court Act, 1998), not an administrative tribunal, and has no power of judicial review; the arguments premised on an administrative-law characterization necessarily failed.
firac.conclusion: The paramountcy and administrative-proceeding arguments failed.

firac.issue: Were the defendants entitled to a stay for abuse of process due to selective/discriminatory enforcement?
firac.facts: Defendants argued police ticketed the Vimy Memorial rally but not a 'Free Palestine' rally and counter-protesters, alleging targeting based on viewpoint. No Charter notice alleging abuse of process was filed.
firac.rule: Since R v O'Connor and R v Nixon, 2011 SCC 34, abuse of process must be pursued under s. 7 of the Charter, and a stay requires notice under The Constitutional Questions Act, 2012, s. 13. The residual-category test (R v Babos, 2014 SCC 16) asks whether state conduct offends societal notions of fair play and decency such that a trial would harm the integrity of the justice system. Police enjoy investigative and charging discretion (R v Beare; R v Beaudry, 2007 SCC 5), limited by subjective good faith and objective reasonableness.
firac.application: No Charter notice was filed, which was fatal, and the request for exclusion of evidence also breached the notice requirements. On the merits, the defendants' witnesses could speak only to what they personally observed; there was no evidence of a policy to target the defendants' viewpoint, no evidence whether tickets issued at the Free Palestine rally, and no proof discretion was exercised improperly. Finite police resources being directed at one event does not itself establish abuse of process.
firac.conclusion: The abuse-of-process claim failed; no stay or exclusion granted.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary practice area: this is a quasi-criminal prosecution requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt, engaging identification law (Nikolovski), due diligence (Sault Ste. Marie) and abuse of process (Babos/Nixon). K003 (Constitutional law) covers the ultra vires and paramountcy analyses (Lemare Lake) and the 31 Charter motions. K107 (Canadian Charter) reflects the Charter framework underpinning the abuse-of-process and other motions. K001 (Administrative law) is engaged because defendants argued the court was sitting as an administrative tribunal and the ultra vires/paramountcy of the PHO was litigated (Ocean Port). K011 (judicial review) is squarely addressed — the court held it has no power of judicial review — so it is genuinely engaged though only to be rejected. K087 (protest/demonstration) fits the underlying rally/gathering. K024 (freedom of expression) is a weaker/borderline pick: free-speech and 'censorship' arguments were raised by defendants but not developed and not decided, so it is flagged as marginal. The antisemitism-oriented tier-3 entity keywords (e.g., the 'Free Palestine' rally reference) are not substantively engaged and were not selected.
location_rationale: The header states 'IN THE PROVINCIAL COURT OF SASKATCHEWAN' and 'Location: Saskatoon', and the event underlying the charges was 'held in the park surrounding the Vimy Memorial in Saskatoon.'
registry_rationale: The decision lists 'Location: Saskatoon' and the matter was heard in the Provincial Court of Saskatchewan sitting at Saskatoon.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Johnson

defining_issues: Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Johnson had the intent required for assault with a weapon — either to strike Mr. Babili or to threaten/intimidate him — such that his car was a 'weapon' under s. 267(a) of the Criminal Code?

Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Johnson's driving constituted a marked departure from the standard of care of a reasonable driver, so as to establish dangerous operation of a conveyance under s. 320.13(1)?

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove the intent required for assault with a weapon — intent to strike or to threaten/intimidate — so that the car was a 'weapon' under s. 267(a)?
firac.facts: During a pro-Palestinian rally at the B.C. Legislature, Mr. Johnson, sympathetic to Israel, argued with protesters. After making eye contact with marshal Omar Babili, who waved a Palestinian flag and shouted 'Free Palestine', Johnson executed a sharp, sudden left turn ('the Sudden Left Turn') into the driveway where Babili stood, forcing Babili to run out of the way; the car came to rest partly on the crosswalk. Johnson then confronted another protester and stated words equating what he had 'just did' to what 'is being done to Jews all the time.' Video evidence documented the event.
firac.rule: Assault under s. 265(1)(b) is committed where a person attempts or threatens, by act or gesture, to apply force, having or appearing to have present ability. 'Weapon' (s. 2) means anything used, designed or intended for use in causing injury or for threatening/intimidating a person. For a threatening act the actus reus requires that a reasonable person perceive a risk of force, and the mens rea requires an intention to intimidate or to have the person believe force would be applied (by analogy to R. v. McRae, 2013 SCC 68). Intent to hit is not required; a threat to apply force suffices (R. v. Dawydiuk, 2010 BCCA 162). Where the accused testifies, the W.(D.) framework (R. v. W.(D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742) applies. Circumstantial proof of intent must be the only reasonable inference.
firac.application: Applying W.(D.), the court could not reject Johnson's denial that he intended to actually hit Babili — supported by video showing he braked — so a reasonable doubt remained on the 'attempt to apply force' branch. However, on the threat/intimidate branch, Johnson's exculpatory evidence was evasive and internally inconsistent and was rejected. His admissions (equating the turn to terrorising Jews, believing Babili was a 'soccer player' who could dodge, wanting protesters to feel fear) plus the natural inference that adults intend the natural consequences of their acts, the last-instant turn toward Babili, and Babili being directly in front in a safety vest, made the only reasonable inference that Johnson intended to intimidate Babili and to make him believe force would be applied. The car was thus used for the purpose of threatening/intimidating and was a 'weapon'.
firac.conclusion: Intent to threaten/intimidate proven beyond a reasonable doubt; the car was a weapon; guilty of assault with a weapon under s. 267(a).

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove that the driving was a marked departure from the standard of care establishing dangerous operation under s. 320.13(1)?
firac.facts: Johnson made eye contact with Babili immediately before turning sharply into a sidewalk/driveway area occupied by Babili, forcing him to flee; video showed Babili directly in the line of the windshield and Johnson turning even further left at the last instant, coming to rest on the crosswalk.
firac.rule: Section 320.13(1) requires operating a conveyance dangerously to the public. The mens rea is assessed by a modified objective test: objectively dangerous conduct amounting to a marked (not mere) departure from the standard of care of a reasonable person in the accused's situation (R. v. Hundal, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 867; R. v. Beatty, 2008 SCC 5; R. v. Roy, 2012 SCC 26; R. v. Chung, 2020 SCC 8). Deliberately creating a danger supports a marked departure; overemphasis on 'momentariness' is an error of law.
firac.application: No reasonable driver would suddenly turn into a sidewalk area occupied by a pedestrian, requiring that pedestrian to run to avoid being struck. Because Johnson made eye contact with Babili beforehand and Babili was directly in front, this was not a momentary lapse but the intentional creation of a dangerous situation. The court rejected as fabricated Johnson's claim that Babili waved him in. Intentionally creating the danger satisfied the mental element.
firac.conclusion: The driving was a marked departure and dangerous; no reasonable doubt as to any element; guilty under s. 320.13(1).

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Akbari

defining_issues: Did the accused in fact utter the threat to bomb Toronto synagogues and kill Jews attributed to him by the complainant?
If the threat was uttered, are the elements of the threatening offences made out?

firac.issue: Did the accused in fact make the threatening statement attributed to him, assessed under the credibility framework in R. v. W.D.?
firac.facts: Akbari attended a BMW dealership and, during a conversation with sales manager Cameron Ahmad, made antisemitic remarks about Israel and Jews. Ahmad testified that Akbari concluded by stating he would plant bombs in every synagogue in Toronto to kill as many Jews as possible and would film and post the attacks. Akbari denied making any such statement, claiming he did not even know what a synagogue or Judaism was, and said he only mentioned a joke about blowing up a casino because of his gambling losses. The only trial witnesses were the two men; surveillance video had no audio.
firac.rule: Under the analytical framework in R. v. W.D., if the trier believes the accused, or if his evidence raises a reasonable doubt, or if the accepted evidence does not prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the accused must be acquitted. A trial is not a mere credibility contest; the presumption of innocence and the Crown's burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt govern. The trier may accept some, none, or all of any witness's evidence.
firac.application: The court found Akbari's testimony brief, disjointed, vague, evasive and internally inconsistent — particularly his shifting claims about knowledge of Judaism and synagogues and his implausible assertion that he raised the Israel conspiracy merely to deter a salesman he had just sought out. Ahmad, by contrast, was direct, detailed and unshaken in cross-examination, acknowledged his own sympathy for Palestinians (undermining any motive to fabricate), and clearly distinguished the specific synagogue-bombing threat from any casino joke or accent-based misunderstanding. The court neither believed Akbari nor was left in reasonable doubt by his evidence, and accepted Ahmad's evidence beyond a reasonable doubt.
firac.conclusion: The court found that Akbari did make the threatening statement as described by Ahmad.

firac.issue: If the threatening words were spoken, are the legal elements of the threatening offences established?
firac.facts: The threat targeted Toronto synagogues and the Jewish people generally, was delivered in a calm, serious tone, and Akbari confirmed he was 'serious.'
firac.rule: Per R. v. McRae, 2013 SCC 68, the Crown need not prove the target was aware of the threat, nor that it was directed at a specific person or property; a threat against an ascertained group suffices. The mens rea is met where the accused intended the words to intimidate or to be taken seriously; intent to carry out the threat is unnecessary.
firac.application: The parties agreed that if the statement was made the offences were made out. The threats targeted an ascertained group (Toronto synagogues and Jews inside them) and were delivered in a serious tone, satisfying both the actus reus and mens rea regardless of any intention to act.
firac.conclusion: The elements of both threatening offences were satisfied.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case concerns charges of threatening to damage property and threatening death. K058 (antisemitism) and K057 (antisemitic slurs) capture the substance of Akbari's remarks, including equating Jews to 'roaches' and 'insects.' K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) reflect the ascertained group targeted by the threats. K105 (synagogue) is central, as the threat was to bomb every synagogue in Toronto. K103 (Israel) and K104 (Palestine) reflect the Israeli/Palestinian conflict backdrop that framed the conversation. There is no controlled keyword specific to 'uttering threats' or credibility assessment, so the case is captured through subject-matter and criminal-law keywords; K103/K104 are somewhat contextual rather than legally operative.

registry_rationale: The Ontario Court of Justice sitting is identified as Newmarket, both in the heading and the transcript certificate.

name_verification.name_in_document: Alina Polak v. Stanislav Polak

defining_issues: Should custody of the two children be changed from the mother to the father, and what access should be ordered, given the best interests of the children?
How should the access schedule accommodate the mother's Jewish religious observance while maximizing the children's contact with their father?
What income should be imputed to the mother for child support, and what amount of spousal support (and duration) should the father pay?

firac.issue: Should custody be awarded to the father rather than the mother, and what access regime serves the children's best interests?
firac.facts: After separation the mother, who converted to Orthodox Judaism, had primary residence of two young boys. She had them circumcised and given Hebrew names without the father's consent, repeatedly breached access orders (including keeping the children in Florida six weeks past a falsified travel-consent return date and defying Gilmore J.'s return order), marginalized the father, and neglected the children's schooling once they were enrolled in public school (chronic lateness, poor hygiene, inadequate lunches). The OCL investigator's final report recommended the father have sole custody.
firac.rule: Under s. 16(8), (9) and (10) of the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), custody is decided by reference only to the best interests of the child, past conduct is relevant only where it bears on parenting ability, and the court must give effect to maximizing the child's contact with each spouse, considering the custodial parent's willingness to facilitate that contact. Joint custody is generally inappropriate where parties cannot communicate other than in a toxic manner (Kaplanis v. Kaplanis, 2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)).
firac.application: The court found the father more credible; the mother took no responsibility, deceived the court and the father, and was an ungovernable litigant who would obey orders only when convenient. Her educational neglect flowed from her refusal to accept public schooling, and her conduct showed she would not maximize the children's contact with their father. The father, by contrast, had complied with orders, sought the court's assistance, and would respect the children's religion. Joint custody was ruled out because the parties could not communicate.
firac.conclusion: The father was granted sole custody; the mother received generous access, including three weekends out of four and choice of four Jewish holidays per year, with holidays such as Christmas, Easter and Thanksgiving shared or spent with the father.

firac.issue: How should the access schedule reconcile the mother's religious observance with the children's best interests?
firac.facts: The mother observed Shabbat on Saturdays and celebrated numerous Jewish holidays, repeatedly cancelling the father's access for religious holidays (including refusing Thanksgiving access). Religion had become a source of conflict, with the children caught in the middle.
firac.rule: The best interests of children must always prevail over the rights to freedom of religion and freedom of expression under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (Young v. Young, 1993 CanLII 34 (SCC); R.A. v. H.D.A., [2004] O.J. No. 1341 (S.C.J.)).
firac.application: To support the children's religious upbringing and synagogue attendance on Saturdays, the court gave the mother the majority of weekends and the right to choose four Jewish holidays annually (with notice by January 1), while reserving Christmas, Easter and Thanksgiving for or shared with the father, and ordering both parents to respect and not deprecate the other's religion in front of the children.
firac.conclusion: A structured access order was crafted to accommodate the mother's religious practices without subordinating the children's best interests to either parent's religion.

firac.issue: What income should be imputed to the mother for child support, and what spousal support should the father pay and for how long?
firac.facts: The mother worked part-time earning just over $12,000; her best year was $17,728. The father's 2012 income was $83,140. The parties cohabited about eight years; the father had paid interim support since separation and had suffered depression and reduced income in 2009-2010.
firac.rule: Child support under the Federal Child Support Guidelines (SOR/97-175), with ongoing disclosure under s. 21; spousal support assessed on means, needs and compensatory grounds with reference to the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines, time-limited by length of cohabitation.
firac.application: The court imputed $20,000 per annum to the mother, giving her time to upgrade and obtain full-time work, yielding child support of $306 per month from January 1, 2014. Using the father's 2012 income and the SSAG mid-range, spousal support of $550 per month was set, time-limited to seven years from separation given eight years' cohabitation. No retroactive adjustment was made for the father's depression-era reduced income, and no s. 7 contribution for Hebrew school or soccer was ordered.
firac.conclusion: Mother to pay $306/month child support from January 1, 2014; father to pay $550/month spousal support from August 1, 2013 until February 28, 2016, when it ceases permanently.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) are central, as the case turns on a change of custody decided under the Divorce Act best-interests test. K052 (religious upbringing) captures the dominant conflict over the children's Jewish upbringing, circumcision, Hebrew names and schooling. K050 (parental/child support) and K053 (spousal support) cover the support determinations. K117 (Divorce Act) is the governing statute expressly applied (s. 16(8)-(10)). K025 (freedom of religion) applies because the court invoked Young v. Young for the principle that best interests prevail over Charter freedom of religion. K093 (Jewish) reflects the mother's conversion and the religious dimension throughout; it is a contextual tier-3 tag and thus a weaker, descriptive pick.
location_rationale: The decision is of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, and the reasons state the trial 'took six days during the May, 2013 sittings in Newmarket,' establishing Newmarket, Ontario as the hearing location.
registry_rationale: The trial was heard at the Newmarket sittings of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice (court file FC-09-032864-00); Newmarket is therefore the registry/court office.

defining_issues: What is a fit and proportionate global sentence for the accused given the seriousness of the offences and the totality principle?
Should the sentences for the multiple offences be imposed consecutively or concurrently?
Do the anti-Semitic threats uttered during the extortion constitute an aggravating factor on sentencing?
What emotional harm and property loss from the victim impact statements may properly be considered as aggravating?
Do the accused's post-offence rehabilitation efforts constitute a significant mitigating factor warranting a reduced sentence?

firac.issue: What is a fit and proportionate global sentence given the seriousness of the offences and the totality principle?
firac.facts: The accused was convicted on 13 counts, the most serious being break and enter with intent (s. 348(1)), extortion (s. 346(1)(b)) and intimidation (s. 423(1)(a)), arising from an October 24, 2021 break-in at the Grossman residence during which artwork was stolen and threatening extortion calls demanding $1 million were made. He is 37 with 94 prior convictions. The Crown sought 13 years reduced to 10 by totality; the defence sought 3.5 years.
firac.rule: Sentencing is governed by s. 718 et seq. of the Criminal Code. The primary principle is proportionality to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender (R v Ipeelee, 2012 SCC 13 at paras 37–39). Where multiple/consecutive sentences are imposed, the totality principle requires that the combined sentence not be unduly long or harsh (s. 718.2; R v M(CA), 1996 CanLII 230 (SCC)).
firac.application: The court found the accused's blameworthiness at the high end given planning, an extensive record, offending while bound by court orders, and serious continuing psychological harm to the victims. However, it held that a 13-year sentence clearly violated the totality principle and would be harsh and excessive. An unusual and significant mitigating factor—extensive genuine rehabilitation—led the court to accept the defence position.
firac.conclusion: The court imposed a global sentence of 3.5 years' incarceration.

firac.issue: Should the sentences for the multiple offences be imposed consecutively or concurrently?
firac.facts: The convictions spanned breaches of orders, break and enter, theft, extortion and intimidation, occurring in a connected sequence within a short time frame.
firac.rule: Whether sentences are consecutive or concurrent is analyzed by reference to the time frame, similarity of offences, whether a different mens rea accompanied each offence, and whether the total sentence remains fit after applying the totality principle (R v Maroti, 2010 NBCA 54; R v M(CA), 1996 CanLII 230 (SCC)); s. 718.2 requires that a combined consecutive sentence not be unduly long or harsh.
firac.application: The court accepted the analytical framework proposed by the Crown and the Maroti factors, but ensured the overall result respected proportionality and totality so that the total sentence did not exceed the offender's overall culpability.
firac.conclusion: The court arrived at a global sentence of 3.5 years, structured to respect the totality principle rather than the aggregate figures sought by the Crown.

firac.issue: Do the anti-Semitic threats uttered during the extortion constitute an aggravating factor?
firac.facts: During the extortion calls the accused uttered multiple anti-Semitic words to Dr. Grossman, who is Jewish. The victims described the impact of the anti-Semitic threats on their sense of safety and on the Jewish community, reviving childhood fear for Mr. Grossman.
firac.rule: Sentencing courts must identify aggravating and mitigating circumstances (s. 718 et seq.); evidence that an offence was motivated by hatred based on religion or ethnic origin is an aggravating factor.
firac.application: The court found the explicit anti-Semitic threats impacted not only the victims but the Jewish community as a whole and caused significant continuing psychological harm, treating this as a relevant aggravating factor within the sequence of planned offending.
firac.conclusion: The anti-Semitic threats were treated as an aggravating factor increasing the accused's blameworthiness.

firac.issue: What emotional harm and property loss from the victim impact statements may properly be considered as aggravating?
firac.facts: The Grossmans and their daughter filed detailed victim impact statements, updated two years later, describing ongoing psychological harm and listing stolen items including jewelry and documents. The defence argued only the two stolen artworks could be linked to the October 24, 2021 break-in and that harm from an earlier October 21 break-in (not charged) could not be counted.
firac.rule: Victim impact and loss considered on sentencing must be connected to the offences of which the accused was convicted; the court may only consider emotional harm, property damage or economic loss flowing from the commission of the proven offence.
firac.application: The court accepted that the accused was not charged with the October 21 break-in and considered the continuing psychological harm from the October 24 offences as aggravating, while the defence's submissions on limiting property loss to the recovered/linked artwork informed the analysis. The psychological harm to the victims two years later was expressly recognized.
firac.conclusion: The court relied on the continuing psychological harm from the proven offences as aggravating, consistent with the constraint that only harm connected to the October 24 offences be counted.

firac.issue: Do the accused's post-offence rehabilitation efforts constitute a significant mitigating factor warranting a reduced sentence?
firac.facts: After submissions, the accused made a lengthy statement showing he appeared a changed man: he had completed university-level courses, addressed severe addiction issues through programming and reflection while in pre-trial custody, apologized to the victims and expressed insight into the harm caused.
firac.rule: Sentencing must give weight to rehabilitation and the overarching principles of restorative justice; genuine rehabilitative efforts and insight are mitigating factors (s. 718 et seq.).
firac.application: The court found the specificity and extent of the accused's rehabilitation went much further than the standard often seen, and combined with his relatively young age, constituted an unusual and significant mitigating factor not captured in the pre-sentence report or submissions, leading the court to accept the defence's proposed sentence.
firac.conclusion: The rehabilitation was found to be a significant mitigating factor justifying the 3.5-year global sentence.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a sentencing decision for break and enter, extortion and intimidation. K060 (hate motivation) is central because the court treated the anti-Semitic threats as an aggravating factor engaging hatred based on religion/ethnicity. K058 (antisemitism) and K057 (antisemitic slurs) capture the anti-Semitic words uttered during the extortion. K093 (Jewish) and K094 (Jewish community) reflect that Dr. Grossman is Jewish and the court found the threats impugned the Jewish community at large. K071 (human dignity) is a weaker, borderline pick reflecting the dignitary harm to the victims. name_verification.name_in_document: R v. H.M.T.

defining_issues: Was the sentencing judge correct that R v. McFarlane precluded a conditional discharge for a violent/weapons offence in these circumstances?
Was the suspended sentence with a resulting criminal record a fit sentence for an offender who committed the offence while in a full psychotic state, or should a conditional discharge be substituted?

firac.issue: Did R v. McFarlane bar the imposition of a conditional discharge for this weapons-related offence of violence?
firac.facts: Ms. T., a first offender with no record, drew a knife and threatened its use while in a psychotic episode caused by paranoid schizophrenia. The sentencing judge considered himself bound by R v. McFarlane to refuse a discharge and imposed a suspended sentence with two years' probation instead.
firac.rule: R v. McFarlane (1976), 55 A.R. 222 (Alta. S.C.A.D.) generally speaks against a conditional discharge for offences of violence or those committed with a weapon, save in exceptional circumstances.
firac.application: Justice Martin agreed McFarlane counsels against discharges for violent or weapons offences, but held that its reasoning was not intended to apply to a first offender so mentally ill as to be completely out of touch with reality at the time of the offence. Such a situation fell within the exceptional circumstances contemplated by McFarlane.
firac.conclusion: McFarlane did not preclude a conditional discharge in these exceptional circumstances.

firac.issue: Was the suspended sentence with a criminal record a fit sentence, or should a conditional discharge be substituted?
firac.facts: Ms. T. committed the offence during a psychotic state; she had no prior record, was responsive to anti-psychotic medication, and posed minimal continuing risk if medicated. The Crown opposed a discharge, characterizing the offence as a racist act involving threats with a weapon; defence showed she held no anti-Semitic views when well. A discharge was in her best interests and not contrary to the public interest.
firac.rule: A conditional discharge is available where it is in the best interests of the accused and not contrary to the public interest; sentencing must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender. Serious mental illness attracts more lenient dispositions reflecting diminished responsibility (R. v. Taylor (1975), 24 C.C.C. (2d) 551 (Ont. C.A.); R. v. Moreau (1992), 76 C.C.C. (3d) 181 (Que. C.A.)); see also the s. 16 and Part XX.1 regime and Winko v. British Columbia (1999).
firac.application: The offender's blameworthiness was nominal because she was in a full psychotic state; no one was injured. A conditional discharge coupled with a probation order requiring her to attend her physician and take her prescribed medication achieved the same protective safeguard as the suspended sentence while sparing her a criminal record. Nothing was to be gained by fixing her with a record.
firac.conclusion: The suspended sentence and resulting record were unfit; appeal allowed and a conditional discharge with a two-year probation order substituted.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a sentence appeal turning on the availability of a conditional discharge and the principles of proportionality and diminished responsibility. K057 (antisemitic slurs) and K058 (antisemitism) reflect that the offence involved the appellant shouting 'terribly offensive anti-Semitic comments,' and K093 (Jewish) identifies the targeted group. K060 (hate motivation) is included because the Crown characterized the conduct as 'a racist act,' though it is a weaker pick since the court accepted the conduct flowed from psychosis rather than genuine hateful belief. The vocabulary lacks a specific sentencing/mental-disorder keyword, so these are the closest applicable terms.

registry_rationale: The header expressly lists 'Registry: Calgary'.

case_name: Newfoundland and Labrador (Human Rights Commission) v. Newfoundland and Labrador (Health and Community Services)

name_verification.name_in_document: Newfoundland and Labrador (Health and Community Services) v. McEvoy
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied style of cause names the Human Rights Commission as the leading party against Health and Community Services, whereas the decision is captioned 'Newfoundland and Labrador (Health and Community Services) v. McEvoy'. In the body the appellants are the Human Rights Commission and Sharon McEvoy, and the respondents include Her Majesty the Queen (Minister of Health and Community Services), Best of Care Ltd. and the Estate of Vincent Dalton. Same case and citation (2009 NLCA 9), but party naming/order differs.

defining_issues: Did the refusal to continue employing a home care worker after her maternity leave constitute discrimination on the basis of sex contrary to s. 9(1) of the Human Rights Code?
Where a client expresses a personal preference for a replacement worker, does that preference support or negate a finding of a prima facie case of pregnancy/sex discrimination?

firac.issue: Did the refusal to continue employing Sharon McEvoy after her maternity leave amount to discrimination based on sex under s. 9(1) of the Human Rights Code?
firac.facts: McEvoy was a home care worker for 80-year-old Vincent Dalton from April 2000 until she began maternity leave in August 2001. Patricia Power was hired as a temporary replacement. During the leave Dalton had gallbladder surgery, requiring bathing and washroom assistance, and became more comfortable with Power (whom he had long known) and preferred her cooking. When McEvoy was ready to return in March 2002, Dalton decided to keep Power permanently, citing a higher level of care. There were no complaints about McEvoy's prior performance.
firac.rule: Section 9(1) of the Human Rights Code, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. H-14 prohibits refusing to continue to employ a person because of sex. Discrimination on the basis of pregnancy is a form of sex discrimination (Brooks v. Canada Safeway Ltd., [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1219), and the test is one of effect, not intention (O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd., [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536; Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143). A tribunal must consider all circumstances and ask whether it is reasonable to infer that maternity leave was a causative factor in the refusal to continue employment.
firac.application: Unlike Hazelwood, Dorvault, Parry and Vestad, Dalton did not decide to retain Power permanently while McEvoy was on leave; his decision was made on March 1, 2002 when McEvoy was ready to return and could compete for the position. The uncontradicted evidence showed the reason was Dalton's greater familiarity and comfort with Power providing new personal-care duties arising from his surgery, plus his preference for her cooking — reasons unrelated to a prohibited ground and rebutting any inference of discrimination. There was no evidence of any unintended discriminatory effect within the Andrews definition.
firac.conclusion: The refusal to continue McEvoy's employment was not based on her pregnancy or maternity leave; the Board's finding of sex discrimination was unreasonable. The Trial Division was correct and the appeal was dismissed.

firac.issue: Can a client's personal preference for a particular caregiver support the refusal to employ following maternity leave without constituting discrimination?
firac.facts: Dalton, the client whose home care was funded, expressed a preference for Power over McEvoy. The Board treated this as mere customer preference incapable of defending discrimination.
firac.rule: Customer or client preference cannot justify a discriminatory act where the preference relates to a prohibited ground (Middleton v. 491465 Ontario Ltd. (1991), 15 C.H.R.R. D/317; Berry v. Manor Inn (1980), 1 C.H.R.R. D/152). However, a client's preference may still be considered in determining the actual reason for a refusal to employ.
firac.application: Dalton never said he declined to employ McEvoy because she had been pregnant; he gave valid reasons unconnected to any prohibited ground (familiarity, comfort with intimate personal care post-surgery, meal preferences). Because the preference was not tied to a prohibited ground, the employer's acting on his instructions did not discriminate. The timing at the end of the leave, though a factor to weigh, did not make an inference of discrimination reasonable given Dalton's legitimate stated preferences.
firac.conclusion: The client's preference here was grounded in legitimate, non-prohibited reasons; it did not establish discrimination, and no prima facie case was made out on the effect analysis either.

K069 (discrimination) and K082 (employment discrimination) capture the core substantive claim of pregnancy/sex discrimination in employment. case_name: New Generation Woodworking Corp. V. Arviv

name_verification.name_in_document: New Generation Woodworking Corp. V. Arviv

defining_issues: Did either party repudiate the millwork contract, and what were its consequences?
Was NGW entitled to payment of its contract and extras invoices despite the work not being fully complete?
Did NGW preserve and perfect its construction lien within the statutory time limits?
Should the defendant's set-off and counterclaim be struck and a trial adjournment be denied for non-compliance with directions and failure to appear?
Should the presiding master recuse himself on the basis of a reasonable apprehension of bias?

firac.issue: Did either party repudiate the millwork contract, and with what consequences?
firac.facts: NGW almost completed the millwork by mid-December 2016; only minor touch-ups (kitchen handles to be supplied by the owner, filler pieces) remained. Arviv complained about design features not in the contract, stopped paying after paying about 59%, denied NGW access, ceased all communication, and stated he would not pay 'a penny' until satisfied. NGW repeatedly sought access to complete the work and later registered and perfected its lien.
firac.rule: Contractor 'abandonment' requires cessation of work plus a lack of intention to complete (Baeumler Quality Construction Inc. v. Pirraglia, 2018 ONSC 7610; Nigeco Contracting Ltd. v. Aizenstros, 2019 ONSC 3364; Heyday Homes Ltd. v. Gunroj, 2004 CanLII 34324). Repudiation occurs where 'the very thing bargained for has not been provided' (Guarantee Co. of North America v. Gordon Capital Corp., 1999 CanLII 664 (SCC)), assessed on the five factors in 968703 Ontario Ltd. v. Vernon, 2002 CanLII 35158 (ONCA). The innocent party may elect to end or continue the contract.
firac.application: NGW did not abandon the contract, having shown a continuing intention to complete through nine unanswered requests for access and handles. Arviv, by ceasing payment, refusing access, complaining only about design (which was not NGW's responsibility) and cutting off communication, repudiated the contract in December 2016/January 2017. NGW elected to accept the repudiation by perfecting its lien and commencing the action on February 21, 2017, which excused NGW from performing deficiency correction work.
firac.conclusion: Arviv repudiated the contract; NGW did not abandon it and was excused from further deficiency correction obligations.

firac.issue: Was NGW entitled to payment of its contract and extras invoices despite incomplete work?
firac.facts: Only about $1,500-$2,000 of work (roughly 1% of the $183,767.28 price) remained, undone because Arviv failed to deliver handles and refused access. NGW invoiced $56,250 for the contract balance and $17,517.28 for authorized extras (girls' closets, laundry cabinetry, wall frame). The expert Walker independently valued the extras at $17,993.93, close to the invoice.
firac.rule: A contractor is entitled to payment upon 'substantial completion'; minor defects do not prevent fulfilment of the condition precedent (Heyday Homes Ltd. v. Gunroj, quoting Goldsmith on Construction Contracts). 'Completion' is deemed under Construction Act s. 2(3) when the cost to complete is the lesser of 1% of the contract price or $1,000. An owner alleging quality deficiencies must notify the contractor and allow correction (Turano's Home Improvement Inc. v. Stern, 2018 ONSC 201).
firac.application: The value of outstanding work was about 1% of the price, so NGW substantially completed the contract and was entitled to the full $56,250. The extras were outside the contract scope but authorized by Arviv ('just make it the same...I trust you') at a reasonable fixed price confirmed by the expert. The Scott Schedule 'deficiencies' were largely design changes, owner-caused issues, or wear and tear; at most a few items totalling roughly $675 might have succeeded had the counterclaim not been struck, and Arviv had not spent money correcting them.
firac.conclusion: NGW was entitled to be paid the full $73,767.28 for the contract and extras invoices.

firac.issue: Did NGW preserve and perfect its lien within the statutory time?
firac.facts: NGW registered its claim for lien on January 27, 2017, commenced the action on February 21, 2017, and registered a certificate of action on February 28, 2017. The value of work remaining when it ceased was $1,500-$2,000.
firac.rule: Under the pre-July 2018 Construction Act, a contractor's lien must be preserved within 45 days and perfected within 90 days of 'completion' or 'abandonment' (ss. 31(1)(b), 36). 'Completion' is deemed under s. 2(3) when the remaining cost is the lesser of 1% of the price or $1,000.
firac.application: Since the value of remaining work ($1,500-$2,000) exceeded the $1,000 threshold, the contract had not been 'completed' by December 12, 2016, and NGW did not abandon it. As NGW did no further work, the 45-day and 90-day periods had not begun to run, so registration and perfection were timely.
firac.conclusion: NGW properly preserved and perfected its lien; the lien is $73,767.28, with priority over the CIBC mortgage to the extent of the unpaid $18,376.72 holdback and full priority over the NHE second mortgage.

firac.issue: Should the defendant's set-off and counterclaim be struck and adjournment denied for non-compliance?
firac.facts: Arviv failed to deliver any of his seven fact-witness affidavits despite directions, cycled through five lawyers, walked out of a settlement conference, barred NGW's principal from a consented site visit, and admitted being 'too busy' and that the case was 'a waste of his time.' On the eve of the summary trial he sought an adjournment to retain counsel.
firac.rule: Rule 60.12(b) allows striking a defence for non-compliance with an interlocutory order; striking is not a first resort and requires consideration of the merits of the defence, the context of the misconduct, and whether the lawyer rather than the party was at fault (Koohestani v. Mahmood, 2015 ONCA 56; Rock Precast Erectors Ltd. v. Canadian Precast Ltd., 2012 ONSC 5924). Rule 50.01(2)(b) permits dismissing a counterclaim where a defendant fails to appear at trial.
firac.application: Arviv's defence appeared blatantly unmeritorious, his non-compliance was entirely his own doing and part of a delay strategy, and an eight-month adjournment would prejudice NGW whose trial evidence was already filed. The master struck the set-off and counterclaim but preserved the defence so Arviv could cross-examine, and denied the adjournment.
firac.conclusion: The set-off and counterclaim were struck and the adjournment denied; the defence was preserved.

firac.issue: Should the master recuse himself for a reasonable apprehension of bias?
firac.facts: Arviv, an Israeli Jew, alleged the master said 'you're one of those people,' creating an apprehension of anti-Semitic or anti-elitist bias. The audio recording showed the master actually said 'so you were one of those people who were travelling abroad,' referring to the COVID-19 controversy about foreign travel.
firac.rule: The test for reasonable apprehension of bias is whether an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically and having thought it through, would conclude the judge would not decide fairly (R. v. S. (R.D.), 1997 CanLII 324 (SCC); R. v. Richards, 2017 ONCA 424). There is a presumption of judicial integrity and a high onus on the moving party; stereotyping may raise an apprehension. Recusal on trifling or invalid grounds wastes resources and risks injustice (Jewish Family and Child Service of Toronto v. J.Z., 2014 ONCJ 165).
firac.application: The statement actually made concerned travelling abroad contrary to public-health advice during the pandemic, not Arviv's ethnicity or name, and would not lead a reasonable person to perceive anti-Semitic or anti-elitist bias. The complaint was invalid, and recusing on such grounds would waste resources and cause delay.
firac.conclusion: The recusal motion was denied.

case_name: Nayyar v. Manufacturers Life Insurance Company

name_verification.name_in_document: Annu Radha Nayyar and Sanjay Nayyar et al v. Manufacturers Life Insurance Company/La Compagnie D'Assurance Vie Manufacturers Carrying on Business as Manulife Financial and Costco Wholesale Canada Ltd.

defining_issues: Should the plaintiffs' New Claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules as disclosing no reasonable claim, as frivolous/vexatious, or as an abuse of process?
Should Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar be declared vexatious litigants under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act?

firac.issue: Should the New Claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1) as disclosing no reasonable claim, as vexatious, or as an abuse of process?
firac.facts: Mrs. Nayyar's original 2004 disability benefits claim against Costco and Manulife was ultimately dismissed by the Court of Appeal, and costs and execution proceedings (including sale of her home) were concluded. The Nayyars repeatedly attempted to re-litigate, including a Judicial Review Petition dismissed by consent on their undertaking not to re-advance the same issues. They then filed the New Claim (February 22, 2016), an almost incomprehensible pleading citing unrelated rules, statutes and cases, claiming 43 heads of loss, and apparently asserting Mr. Nayyar's unregistered one-half interest in the sold property and re-asserting the benefits claim.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1)(a),(b),(d) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules permits striking a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim (plain and obvious test: Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959), that is frivolous or vexatious, or that is otherwise an abuse of process. Abuse of process is a flexible doctrine, an adjunct of res judicata, protecting judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of justice (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63). Under the Family Law Act ss. 81, 82, 103(2) and Land Title Act s. 29, an unregistered spousal interest in land is unenforceable against a third-party judgment creditor.
firac.application: The New Claim was incoherent and could not be saved by redrafting because its deficiencies were fundamental. Any claim by Mr. Nayyar to a one-half interest failed: Registrar Cameron's unappealed report confirmed Mrs. Nayyar was sole registered owner, and under the FLA/Land Title Act an unregistered interest is unenforceable against creditors like Costco and Manulife. To the extent the claim revisited the Benefits Claim and the Execution Proceedings, those matters had been fully litigated and were res judicata, making relitigation an abuse of process.
firac.conclusion: The whole of the New Claim was struck under Rule 9-5(1).

firac.issue: Should Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar be declared vexatious litigants under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act?
firac.facts: The New Claim was the fourth proceeding in which the Nayyars sought to challenge the outcomes of the Benefits Claim and/or Execution Proceedings. They had been told by both the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal that their claims had no merit, had repeatedly failed to pay costs orders (one still outstanding), continued to demand $99 million, and sent rude and threatening communications to opposing counsel. Mr. Nayyar was found throughout to be the directing mind driving the litigation.
firac.rule: Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act permits an order that a person who has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds instituted vexatious proceedings may not institute proceedings without leave. The non-exhaustive Fabian factors (Re Lang Michener v. Fabian (1987), 59 O.R. (2d) 353), affirmed in Harrison, 2016 BCCA 210 and Pearlman, 2010 BCCA 362, guide the analysis, including relitigating decided issues, hopeless actions, improper purpose, rolling forward grounds, the whole history, failure to pay costs, and persistent unsuccessful appeals.
firac.application: Virtually all hallmarks of vexatious conduct were present: repeated relitigation of conclusively determined matters despite express warnings, hopeless claims, improper demands, rolling forward of grounds, failure to pay costs orders, and threatening/abusive communications. Simply striking the claim would not deter the Nayyars given their relentless, unceasing pattern. Because Mr. Nayyar was the directing mind even where earlier proceedings named only Mrs. Nayyar, courts may declare an assisting spouse a vexatious litigant (Daniel v. I.C.B.C., 2003 BCSC 475; Griffith, 2004 BCSC 1443).
firac.conclusion: Both Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar were declared vexatious litigants, precluded from instituting any proceeding against Costco or Manulife and related persons without leave of the court.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 practice area — this is a civil pleadings/abuse-of-process matter. K086 (co-ownership) applies because the court analysed Mr. Nayyar's asserted unregistered one-half/tenant-in-common interest in the family property under the Family Law Act and Land Title Act. K011 (judicial review) reflects the earlier Judicial Review Petition that formed part of the abuse-of-process/res judicata history, with K001 (Administrative law) as its tier-1 parent. K020 (class action) is a weak pick, included only because the pleadings invoked the Class Proceedings Act — it is not a substantive issue and should be treated as marginal. The controlled vocabulary lacks dedicated terms for the core concepts here (striking pleadings, vexatious litigants, abuse of process, res judicata), so several genuinely central doctrines are unrepresented; the selected keywords are the closest available and K020 in particular is flagged as tenuous.
