name_verification.name_in_document: R v Smith-Lowe

defining_issues: Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt, on circumstantial evidence, that the accused was the perpetrator of the break and enter, extortion, intimidation, impersonation and related offences?
Must the Crown prove actual authorship of the threatening calls and text messages in order to establish the identity of the perpetrator?

firac.issue: Was identity proven beyond a reasonable doubt on the circumstantial evidence?
firac.facts: The Grossman residence was broken into on October 21 and 24, 2021; a neighbour saw a masked man leave in a black Porsche sportscar with plate ending '895'; the accused was arrested driving a stolen Porsche (NZY 895) with an open satchel containing a crowbar, gloves and a cellphone; the calls and texts extorting and threatening the Grossmans came from 403-679-1568, the authentic number of the seized cellphone, which stopped once the phone was in police custody. The defence conceded all elements except identity.
firac.rule: Where identity rests on circumstantial evidence the Court must apply R v Villaroman, 2016 SCC 33: guilt must be the only reasonable inference; the Crown must negative any other reasonable inference consistent with innocence. The Court also relied on R v Banovic, 2012 BCCA 471 (evidence assessed as a whole, not piecemeal) and R v Wheyee, 2019 ABQB 548 (two-step inference process; facts underlying an inference must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt and inferences must be reasonable, rational and logical, avoiding speculation).
firac.application: The Court found the civilian and police witnesses credible and reliable, much of their evidence corroborated by body-worn and HAWCS helicopter video. The matching licence-plate digits, the seized cellphone bearing the authentic number 403-679-1568 that made all the extortion calls, the expert forensic analysis (the 'My Number' display of 403-690-8794 was a ruse leaving the true ICCID-linked number 403-679-1568), the break-in tools in the accused's satchel, and the cessation of calls after seizure together left no reasonable inference other than guilt. Defence suggestions of other inferences were speculative.
firac.conclusion: Identity was proven beyond a reasonable doubt; the accused was found guilty on the remaining counts (9, 10, 11, 12 and 17), in addition to the conceded breach counts 2 through 8.

firac.issue: Did the Crown need to prove actual authorship of the calls and texts to establish identity?
firac.facts: The threatening/extorting calls and texts were sent from the cellphone found on the accused at arrest; the defence argued the Crown had to prove he personally authored the messages.
firac.rule: The Crown must prove identity of the perpetrator beyond a reasonable doubt; proof of identity may be by direct and/or circumstantial evidence (Villaroman).
firac.application: The Court rejected the defence position, holding that proof of actual authorship is not a separate requirement; the totality of circumstantial evidence linking the accused to the seized phone and offences established identity.
firac.conclusion: The Crown was not required to prove authorship separately; identity was established, and the accused was found to be the author and instigator of the offences.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area — the case concerns Criminal Code offences (break and enter, extortion, intimidation, impersonation, breach of release conditions) turning on identity proven through circumstantial evidence. K058 (antisemitism) and K057 (antisemitic slurs) apply because the extortion calls used anti-Semitic language ('All you Jews know each other, you can get money') targeting the complainants' ethnicity. K093 (Jewish) and K095 (Jewish family) reflect that the complainants identified as Jewish and were targeted as a Jewish family. K060 (hate motivation) is a borderline pick — the anti-Semitic character coloured the offences, though the charges were not laid or sentenced as hate-motivated at this liability stage. K107 (Canadian Charter) is a weak/minor pick, engaged only through the reading of the accused's Charter rights on arrest. No controlled-vocabulary term captures 'circumstantial evidence/identity' directly, so keywords focus on the criminal and antisemitism dimensions.

registry_rationale: The decision expressly lists 'Registry: Calgary'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Noble v. York University Foundation

defining_issues: Which relevance test governs a motion to compel answers on discovery heard after the January 1, 2010 Rules amendments?
Are the refused questions asking whether the Foundation's listed directors are 'pro-Israel' relevant and therefore required to be answered given the pleadings?
Should the court order the witnesses to re-attend to provide the answers?

firac.issue: Which relevance standard applies to a motion to compel answers when the examinations occurred before, but the motion was heard after, the January 1, 2010 Rules amendments?
firac.facts: Marsden and Marcus were examined in May 2008 under the former 'semblance of relevance' regime; the motion, though scheduled in December 2009, was not heard until January 15, 2010, after the amended Rules came into force. The amendments contain no transition provisions on the change from 'semblance of relevance' to 'relevance'.
firac.rule: Rule 31.06(1) of the Rules of Civil Procedure, as amended effective January 1, 2010, replacing the 'semblance of relevance' test with a stricter 'relevance' test; the reform derives from the Civil Justice Reform Project (Osborne). The Master relied on the approach in Onex Corp. v. American Home Assurance, 2009 CanLII 72052 (ON SC), applying amended rules to motions heard after the effective date.
firac.application: Because there were no transition provisions and the motion was heard after January 1, 2010, the Master held the amended 'relevance' test applied, consistent with Justice Belobaba's treatment of the summary judgment amendments in Onex. He applied the stricter standard mindful of the Osborne report's aim of restraint and proportionality in discovery.
firac.conclusion: The 'relevance' test in Rule 31.06(1) applied to the motion.

firac.issue: Are the questions asking whether the Foundation's listed directors are 'pro-Israel' relevant and required to be answered?
firac.facts: The plaintiff's flyer alleged the Foundation was 'biased by the presence and influence of staunch pro-Israel lobbyists.' In their statement of defence the defendants pleaded (paras 7-9) that this allegation was false and that they were concerned the flyer suggested listed directors were pro-Israel lobbyists controlling the University. On discovery, both witnesses refused to say whether the listed board members were pro-Israel.
firac.rule: It is well settled that the pleadings determine whether a question is relevant and must be answered; a party is entitled on discovery to test the statements made by the opposing party in its pleading. Relevance is measured under Rule 31.06(1).
firac.application: Having pleaded that the plaintiff's allegations about the Foundation's directors were false, the defendants must answer questions about what they know of those directors' relevant beliefs and activities. The witnesses had already agreed to answer whether they personally were pro-Israel, implicitly conceding relevance. The refused questions were directly relevant to issues the defendants themselves raised and more than met the Rule 31.06(1) standard.
firac.conclusion: The questions were relevant and must be answered within 30 days.

firac.issue: Should the court order the witnesses to re-attend to provide the answers?
firac.facts: The plaintiff sought an order compelling Marsden and Marcus to re-attend at examinations to give the answers. Only two related questions per witness were at issue, and their answers were not yet known.
firac.rule: There is no automatic right to require re-attendance to obtain answers where it serves no useful purpose: Senechal v. Muskoka (Municipality), 2005 CanLII 11575 (ON SC), at para 7.
firac.application: Given the limited number of questions and that the answers were unknown, ordering re-attendance was premature and served no useful purpose at this stage. The Master declined to exercise his discretion to order re-attendance.
firac.conclusion: Re-attendance request denied as premature; answers to be provided within 30 days.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a discovery motion within a civil defamation action. K015 (defamation) is the substantive cause of action framing what is relevant. K056 (anti-Zionism/pro-Israel) captures the core subject-matter of the flyer and the refused questions about directors being 'pro-Israel.' K103 (Israel) and K104 (Palestine) reflect the Israel-Palestine framing of the disputed discovery questions. K093 (Jewish) reflects that the flyer listed Jewish board members and the press release condemned singling out members on the basis of ethnicity. K104 and K093 are somewhat peripheral to the procedural holding but tie to the case's factual matrix.
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the Superior Court of Justice - Ontario and records that the plaintiff 'is a professor who teaches history ... at York University in Toronto.' The events (lectures, film event) all took place on the York University campus in Toronto, and the court file number (07-CV-329851CM3) is a Toronto commercial/case-managed file, supporting Toronto as the registry.
registry_rationale: No registry office is expressly named, but the court file number 07-CV-329851CM3 and the Toronto location of the parties and events indicate the Toronto registry of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Pryers Construction Ltd. v. MVMB Holdings Inc., et al

defining_issues: Does the former Construction Lien Act or the new Construction Act govern where the contract for the improvement was entered into before July 1, 2018?
Could Riverside Ford be added as a defendant after the two-year period in the Limitations Act, 2002 had elapsed?
Was MVMB Holdings Inc. an 'owner' within the meaning of s. 1(1) of the Construction Lien Act?
Should the corporate veil be pierced to hold Scott Birnie personally liable?
Did the plaintiff establish its entitlement to the amount claimed on the merits?

firac.issue: Does the former Construction Lien Act or the new Construction Act govern where the contract for the improvement was entered into before July 1, 2018?
firac.facts: The last significant work was done April 27, 2016 and the lien was registered May 19, 2016. The new Construction Act came into force July 1, 2018. The parties disputed which statute governed.
firac.rule: Legislation is strongly presumed not to be retroactive; retroactive application requires clear language (St. Jean (Litigation Guardian of) v. Cheung, 2008 ONCA 815, citing Sullivan on the Construction of Statutes).
firac.application: Nothing in the new Construction Act expressly makes it retroactive, and the contract and improvements predated July 1, 2018.
firac.conclusion: The former Construction Lien Act (R.S.O. 1990, c. C.30) governs the parties' rights.

firac.issue: Could Riverside Ford be added as a defendant after the two-year Limitations Act period had elapsed?
firac.facts: Riverside was added on a motion at the opening of trial on November 19, 2018, more than two years after the last supply of services. Birnie was sole director/officer of both corporate defendants and had full knowledge of all dealings; the co-defendants had pleaded that Riverside was the proper 'owner'.
firac.rule: Section 57(2) of the Construction Lien Act permits the court to add parties at any time; s. 19(1) of the Limitations Act, 2002 renders limitation periods in other Acts (including ss. 31 and 36 of the Construction Act, listed in the Schedule) governing; the common-law doctrine of special circumstances survives the Limitations Act, 2002 and allows adding parties despite expiry (Bikur Cholim Jewish Volunteer Services v. Langston, 2009 ONCA 196; Gracey v. Thomson Newspapers Corp., (1991) 4 O.R. (3d) 180; Basarsky v. Quinlan, [1972] S.C.R. 380).
firac.application: Because ss. 31 and 36 of the Construction Lien Act are listed in the Schedule to s. 19(1), the Act's restrictive 90-day commencement regime, not the two-year Limitations Act period, applies to preserving/perfecting a lien. The special-circumstances doctrine survived and applied: Birnie was fully aware of all matters, no new claim was advanced (only a new party), and there was no prejudice to Riverside, whose co-defendants had themselves said Riverside was the proper owner. Becerra v. Ronchin was distinguished because it involved new claims, not merely a new party.
firac.conclusion: Riverside was properly added as a party defendant; the two-year Limitations Act bar did not apply.

firac.issue: Was MVMB Holdings Inc. an 'owner' under s. 1(1) of the Construction Lien Act?
firac.facts: MVMB held title to the property; Riverside was its tenant. Pryer dealt only with Birnie and believed Riverside owned the land until a title search revealed MVMB's ownership. Birnie controlled both companies.
firac.rule: 'Owner' under s. 1(1) means a person with an interest in the premises at whose request and upon whose credit, on whose behalf, with whose privity or consent, or for whose direct benefit an improvement is made.
firac.application: Riverside was clearly an owner as Birnie was its representative. Birnie, controlling MVMB, unknowingly to the plaintiff created a situation in which MVMB (registered title-holder) requested the improvements, extended its credit, and consented to and benefited from them.
firac.conclusion: MVMB also qualified as an 'owner' within the definition, so the lien properly attached to its interest.

firac.issue: Should the corporate veil be pierced to hold Scott Birnie personally liable?
firac.facts: Birnie was the sole owner, director and officer of both corporate defendants. The plaintiff sought to hold him personally liable for the unpaid amount.
firac.rule: Canadian courts reject an independent just-and-equitable ground for piercing the veil; the corporate form may be disregarded only where it is used to facilitate fraudulent or improper conduct (Yaiguaje v. Chevron Corporation, 2018 ONCA 472, applying Transamerica; Sun Indalex Finance v. United Steelworkers, 2013 SCC 6).
firac.application: There was no significant evidence of bad faith and no evidence of fraudulent activity. There are legitimate reasons to incorporate, and the equitable ground for piercing has been rejected.
firac.conclusion: Birnie is not personally liable; judgment lies only against the two corporate defendants.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff establish its entitlement to the amount claimed on the merits?
firac.facts: The work was a time-and-material renovation. Disputed invoices covered subcontractor payments and materials as well as labour. Birnie complained of overcharging and a cost cap; the defendants' project manager Richard Gummer reviewed the time sheets and receipts but did not testify, and a document attributed to him was objected to.
firac.rule: The plaintiff bears the burden of proving its claim; contested untested hearsay documents not served as business records are entitled to no weight. The action is to be, as far as possible, of a summary character (s. 67(1)).
firac.application: Pryer's evidence on the invoices was reasonable and largely uncontradicted; Birnie could not contradict that subcontractors and materials had been supplied and paid. It was uncontested that Gummer was satisfied with the work and hours and had recommended the defendants pay the claim. The Exhibit #4 notes attributed to Gummer, who did not testify, could not be relied on and were given no weight.
firac.conclusion: Judgment granted for the plaintiff in the amount of $34,101.66 against the two corporate defendants.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the clear tier-1 practice area — this is a construction-lien/contract action. The controlled vocabulary has no dedicated construction-lien, limitations, or piercing-the-veil term, so the remaining picks are the closest available and are flagged as weak: K054 (wills/estates) reflects the court's reliance on Trustee Act s. 38(3) and Estates Act authorities (Bikur Cholim) for the surviving special-circumstances/limitations analysis; K022 (restitution) reflects the tangential unjust-enrichment authority (Becerra); K086 (co-ownership) is a weak property-interest proxy given the 'owner' analysis over the MVMB/Riverside title-tenant relationship; K021 (interlocutory injunction) is a weak proxy for the lien's property-tying remedial character. Only K002 is a strong fit; the others are borderline placeholders given vocabulary gaps.

The property and lien are located in Brockville, Ontario, and the Claim for Lien was registered in the Land Registry Office of the Registry Division of Leeds.
registry_rationale: The hearing took place 'at Brockville' and the file bears Court File No. CV16-0378; the lien was registered in the Registry Division of Leeds. Brockville is therefore the sitting registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: His Majesty the King v. Dennis Rowsell
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The style of cause matches (R. v. Rowsell). The decision text carries the neutral citation 2025 NLPC 1324, whereas the metadata supplies the parallel CanLII citation 2025 CanLII 52176 (NL PC); these are parallel citations for the same decision, not a mismatch.

defining_issues: What is a fit and proportionate sentence for the multiple offences committed by Mr. Rowsell?
How does the intimate-partner-violence sentencing regime (ss. 718.2(a)(ii) and 718.201) affect the weight given to denunciation and deterrence?
Is the racial/ethnic motivation of the threats uttered against the police officer an aggravating factor under s. 718.2(a)(i)?
How should the individual sentences be structured (concurrent vs. consecutive) and adjusted for totality?

firac.issue: What is a fit and proportionate global sentence for the numerous offences committed by the offender?
firac.facts: Rowsell was convicted after trial of aggravated assault, two assaults, uttering a threat, unlawful confinement and two breaches against his intimate partner Ms. X, whom he struck on the head with a golf club and confined until she escaped through a window; he also pleaded guilty to further threats (including racially charged threats against a police officer), interference with property and an indecent act. He is 51, has an alcohol addiction, and has 63 prior convictions including aggravated assault and many breaches.
firac.rule: Sentencing must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender (s. 718.1; R. v. Nasogaluak, 2010 SCC 6; R. v. Parranto, 2021 SCC 46), individualized (R. v. Suter; R. v. Boudreault, 2018 SCC 58), and informed by parity (s. 718.2(b)) and the purposes in s. 718 (R. v. Hills, 2023 SCC 2).
firac.application: The court weighed the gravity of the offences (an extended attack on an intimate partner with a golf club causing a scalp laceration, unlawful confinement, and repeated threats) and the offender's high moral culpability and extensive record. His alcohol addiction did not lessen moral culpability given his awareness of alcohol's effect on his violence. Deterrence and denunciation were paramount; rehabilitation prospects were dim. Individual sentences were fixed offence-by-offence (five years for the aggravated assault, nine months for each assault, six months confinement, etc.).
firac.conclusion: A global sentence of six years' incarceration is appropriate and proportionate, less 327 days' credit for 218 days of pre-sentence custody.

firac.issue: How does the statutory intimate-partner-violence regime affect the sentencing analysis?
firac.facts: The offences against Ms. X were committed within an intimate relationship, and Rowsell had prior convictions for violence against former intimate partners.
firac.rule: Sections 718.2(a)(ii) and 718.201 make abuse of an intimate partner an aggravating factor and require consideration of the increased vulnerability of female victims; denunciation and deterrence must be prioritized (R. v. Bear, 2022 SKCA 7; R. v. Cunningham, 2023 ONCA 36; Bill C-75 reforms). Section 718.3(8)(d) even permits a sentence above the statutory maximum where the offender has a prior intimate-partner violence conviction.
firac.application: The court held these provisions mandated prioritizing denunciation and deterrence, cautioned that pre-2019 precedents must be applied carefully because the law changed after R. v. Squires, 2012 NLCA 20, and treated the intimate-partner context as significantly aggravating in fixing the aggravated-assault sentence.
firac.conclusion: The intimate-partner regime elevated denunciation and deterrence and supported a higher, more condign sentence for the offences against Ms. X.

firac.issue: Do the racial slurs accompanying the threats against the police officer aggravate the sentence?
firac.facts: During his arrest, Rowsell repeatedly directed vile racial and ethnic slurs at Constable Anjum (including the N-word, 'Paki', 'terrorist', and 'Jew') while threatening to stab and shoot him.
firac.rule: Section 718.2(a)(i) deems evidence that an offence was motivated by hate based on race to be an aggravating circumstance (R. v. Woodward, 2011 BCCA 251; R. v. J.R.B., 2004; Prejudice and Discrimination as Aggravating Factors in Sentencing).
firac.application: The court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the threats were racially motivated, going well beyond threatening an officer for his position, and found such hate-motivated conduct antithetical to Canada's pluralistic values, warranting enhanced denunciation.
firac.conclusion: The racial motivation was a significant aggravating factor increasing the sentences for the threats against the officer (six months each).

firac.issue: Should the individual sentences run concurrently or consecutively, and how does totality apply?
firac.facts: Rowsell committed multiple distinct offences against Ms. X in one time frame and separate offences on April 6 and September 17, 2024.
firac.rule: Multiple sentences are presumptively consecutive unless there is a valid reason for concurrency (R. v. Hutchings; R. v. B.H., 2022 NLCA 54); breach offences should generally be consecutive (R. v. Tuglavina, 2020 NLCA 30); and s. 718.2(c) totality requires that the combined sentence not be unduly long or harsh (R. v. O'Keefe, 2018 NLCA 11).
firac.application: Applying the three-step Hutchings/Roberts framework, the court set individual sentences, noted that a fully consecutive structure would total eight years, six months and fifteen days, and found that unduly long. It achieved a proportionate result by making most sentences concurrent while keeping the aggravated assault, one assault on Ms. X, and the threat against her consecutive.
firac.conclusion: A proportionate overall sentence of six years was reached by adjusting concurrency to satisfy totality.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area, this being a sentencing decision. K060 (hate motivation) is central because the court applied s. 718.2(a)(i) to treat the racially motivated threats as aggravating. K065 (racism) captures the racially charged slurs directed at Constable Anjum. K057 (antisemitic slurs) is included because the offender used 'Jew' as a slur among his epithets, though it is a weaker/borderline pick since the slurs were predominantly anti-Black and anti-South Asian racist rather than specifically antisemitic. K116 (Criminal Code s. 430) reflects the conviction for interfering with the lawful use of property under s. 430(1)(c). K085 (wrongful dismissal) is not applicable — instead the intimate-partner violence dimension is significant; however no controlled keyword squarely covers domestic/intimate-partner violence, so this is flagged as a gap; K085 should be disregarded. The strongest, clearly-engaged keywords are K004, K060, K065 and K116.
location_rationale: The header states 'IN THE PROVINCIAL COURT OF NEWFOUNDLAND AND LABRADOR, JUDICIAL CENTRE OF CORNER BROOK' and 'Place of Hearing: Corner Brook, NL.'
registry_rationale: The decision identifies the 'JUDICIAL CENTRE OF CORNER BROOK' as the court office where the matter was heard.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. c. Sohier-Chaput

defining_issues: May the court take judicial notice, as an incontestable historical fact, of the role of Nazism in the persecution and extermination of Jews during the Second World War, without formal proof?
Did the first part of the article (admitted authorship) promote hatred against an identifiable group and, if so, did the accused do so wilfully within the meaning of s. 319(2)?
Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused authored the second part of the article?
Does the accused's defence that his writings were mere satire, irony or parody negate the intent required to wilfully promote hatred?

firac.issue: May the court take judicial notice of the historical role of Nazism in the persecution and extermination of Jews during the Second World War?
firac.facts: The impugned article referred to 'Nazis' and 'Nazism', but the Crown led no expert evidence on their meaning and only raised judicial notice at closing argument. Defence counsel resisted, advancing statements minimizing the Nazi regime's responsibility. The court gave the defence an opportunity to reply and the Crown filed a statement of the historical facts to be noticed.
firac.rule: Under R. c. Find, 2001 SCC 32, a court may take judicial notice of facts that are (1) so notorious as not to be the subject of debate among reasonable persons, or (2) capable of immediate and accurate demonstration by resort to readily accessible sources of indisputable accuracy (the strict Morgan approach adopted in Find; see also Spence and Krymowski). R. v. Zundel (No. 1 and No. 2) held that a court may take judicial notice of historical fact, and that the mass murder and extermination of the Jews of Europe by the Nazi regime during the Second World War is so notorious as not to be disputed among reasonable persons; procedural fairness requires notice to the parties before noticing a fact.
firac.application: The court found the Nazi regime's responsibility for the massacre and extermination of European Jews to be patently indisputable and squarely governed by Zundel (No. 2). It respected procedural fairness by alerting the defence and permitting reply, yet the defence offered no expert or documentary counter-evidence and instead sought to rewrite history. The exact number of Holocaust victims was immaterial to noticing the Nazi role. Unlike Zundel, the accused did not deny the Holocaust occurred, so noticing this fact did not impair his right to a full and fair defence.
firac.conclusion: The court took judicial notice, per Zundel (No. 2), that the Nazi regime was responsible for the massacre and extermination of Jews during the Second World War, without requiring the Crown to prove it.

firac.issue: Did the first part of the article promote hatred against Jewish people and, if so, was it done wilfully?
firac.facts: The accused admitted writing three sentences published on The Daily Stormer commenting on a Global News report about neo-Nazi posters, including 'Non-Stop Nazism, everywhere, until the very streets are flooded with the tears of our enemies' and 'We need to make sure that no SJW or Jew can remain safely untriggered.' The site featured images of Hitler and Nazi symbols and rubrics such as 'Jewish Problem' and 'Race War'.
firac.rule: Section 319(2) Cr.C. criminalizes wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group (defined in s. 318(4)). Per R. v. Keegstra, 'promotes' means active support or instigation, and 'hatred' denotes an emotion of an intense and extreme nature clearly associated with vilification and detestation—only the most intense forms of aversion. Per Mugesera and Whatcott, the analysis is objective, from the standpoint of a reasonable informed person considering the context, audience, tone and historical/social setting. Intent (Keegstra/Buzzanga) exists where the accused consciously desires to promote hatred or foresees it as certain or substantially certain; intent may be inferred from the nature of the statements.
firac.application: A reasonable, contextually informed reader would view the passages as a call to renewed persecution of Jews, promoting Nazi ideology, provoking violence and forming a collective hostile identity—satisfying the Keegstra definition of hatred. Given the historical context of Nazism and the Holocaust, the words exposed Jewish people to detestation. The structured, repetitive, aggressive tone and the chosen forum showed the accused intended to promote hatred; his after-the-fact rationalizations were rejected as not credible, and at minimum he was wilfully blind (R. v. Harding).
firac.conclusion: The first part promoted hatred and the accused did so wilfully; the court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt.

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused wrote the second part of the article?
firac.facts: The accused admitted writing only three sentences and attributed the balance—including antisemitic content, the 'Christ-killers'/'stinky Jews' remarks and the gassing-soldier caricature with 'oven-dodger' text—to the site editor Andrew Anglin. The article bore only his pseudonym 'Zeiger'; he raised the denial for the first time at trial, five years later.
firac.rule: Credibility is assessed under R. v. W.(D.), [1991] 1 SCR 742. Intent and authorship may be inferred from the whole of the evidence, including the consistency of ideology across an author's body of writings.
firac.application: The court found the accused's denial invraisemblable and not credible: he made no effort over five years to disavow authorship; he was the site's most prolific contributor with power to comment; only his pseudonym appeared; Anglin never claimed authorship; and the second part's antisemitic, pro-Nazi message was consistent with the admitted first part and with his other articles (P-6, P-10). The court inferred the same person wrote both parts.
firac.conclusion: The court concluded beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused authored the second part; it too promoted hatred wilfully.

firac.issue: Does the defence that the writings were satire, irony or parody negate the intent to promote hatred?
firac.facts: The accused testified his writings were ironic humour aimed at 'triggering' the left and undermining political correctness, meant to be understood as absurd jokes by insiders while shocking others. His writings repeatedly linked Nazism and the Holocaust to Jews (e.g., 'Nothing less than 6 million is acceptable').
firac.rule: Per Whatcott, expression that ridicules or is offensive does not by itself justify limiting free expression; ridicule only becomes actionable where taken to an extreme exposing a group to hatred. Buzzanga illustrates satire negating intent (there the accused mocked prejudice against their own community). As Professor Rainville notes, irony is not immune from criminal law where the author foresees his text will certainly or almost certainly generate hatred.
firac.application: The court rejected the satire defence as a disguise for hateful ideology. The repeated antisemitic theme, the public forum, the trivialization of genocide, and the aggressive tone showed a deliberate intent to actively promote detestation of Jewish people rather than mere humour. Unlike Buzzanga, the accused targeted the very group with an intent to attack them. The nature of the writings permitted the inference of the required intent.
firac.conclusion: The satire/irony/parody defence was rejected; it did not raise a reasonable doubt about the intent to promote hatred.

case_name: Pollock and Pollock v. Winnipeg Free Press and Reynolds

name_verification.name_in_document: Pollock and Pollock v. Winnipeg Free Press and Reynolds

defining_issues: Were the words complained of in the newspaper column reasonably capable of bearing the alleged defamatory meaning (that the brother and sister were in an incestuous relationship)?
Did the plaintiffs have a viable innuendo claim based on extrinsic facts?
Was summary judgment appropriate because there was no genuine issue for trial, and did the defence of consent/absolute immunity apply?

firac.issue: Were the words in the column reasonably capable of bearing the alleged defamatory meaning of incest?
firac.facts: Lindor Reynolds' Winnipeg Free Press column of October 17, 1995 described mayoral candidate Natalie Pollock and her brother Ron, identified as roommates and campaign manager, in terms the plaintiffs claimed implied an incestuous relationship. The column's underlined passages did not expressly assert any sexual relationship between the siblings.
firac.rule: Whether words are defamatory is judged by their natural and ordinary meaning as understood by the average or reasonable reader, taking account of reasonable implications (Grubb v. Bristol United Press Ltd., [1963] 1 Q.B. 309). The reasonable reader is not one 'avid for scandal' (Steele v. Mirror Newspapers Ltd., [1974] 2 N.S.W.L.R. 348) nor one overly sensitive. What the plaintiffs themselves understood the words to mean is not evidence of the words' ordinary meaning (Fairfax v. Hook (1982), 47 A.L.R. 477).
firac.application: Krindle J. read the column when published and repeatedly for the motion, and no suggestion of incest crossed her mind. Only a reader avid for scandal could read the words as implying an incestuous relationship. The plaintiffs' own understanding was relevant only to hurt feelings, not to the words' capacity to bear the alleged meaning.
firac.conclusion: The words were not reasonably capable of suggesting that the relationship between the brother and sister was sexual.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiffs have a viable true innuendo claim based on extrinsic facts?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs pleaded that they had told Reynolds of gossip circulating that their relationship was incestuous, and of Ms. Pollock's 'legitimate' sexual relationships, and argued this constituted an innuendo.
firac.rule: A true innuendo arises only where extrinsic facts known to readers would reasonably induce them to understand the words in a secondary, defamatory sense beyond their ordinary meaning; a meaning implied from the words themselves without support from extrinsic facts is not a true innuendo (Eagleson v. Dowbiggan, Ont. Ct. J., Feb. 1, 1996).
firac.application: The plaintiffs were not arguing that the words carried a special meaning known to particular readers; they argued the words themselves conveyed incest. There was no extrinsic evidence that would give the words a meaning they did not otherwise convey. Though the court would have allowed the self-represented plaintiffs to amend to plead extrinsic facts had innuendo been arguable, none existed.
firac.conclusion: There was no true innuendo; the claim rested only on the ordinary meaning of the words, which was not defamatory.

firac.issue: Was summary judgment dismissing the claim appropriate, and did consent bar the claim?
firac.facts: The defendants moved for summary judgment. Natalie Pollock had consented to be interviewed knowing a column would be published; she never told Reynolds her relationship with her brother was sexual, though she referred vaguely to hurtful gossip.
firac.rule: Summary judgment may be granted where there is no genuine issue for trial, including in defamation actions (Lloyds Bank Canada v. Sherwood (1990), 64 Man.R.(2d) 288; Carey v. Phillips (1995), 101 Man.R.(2d) 236). Absolute immunity attaches to statements invited by or published with the plaintiff's consent, provided the account is fair and accurate.
firac.application: Because the words were not reasonably capable of the defamatory meaning alleged, there was no genuine issue for trial. Had the words suggested a sexual relationship the account would not have been fair and accurate and consent could not be relied upon, but the words did not carry that meaning, so nothing warranted a trial.
firac.conclusion: There being no genuine issue for trial, the motion for summary judgment dismissing the claim was allowed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 practice area for this civil defamation suit. K015 (defamation) is the central cause of action and directly engaged, as the court analysed whether the words were capable of a defamatory meaning and the true-innuendo doctrine. K018 (qualified privilege) is a weak/borderline pick — the defendants raised a consent/absolute-immunity defence that is privilege-adjacent, though the case turned on capacity to defame rather than privilege. K016 (fair comment) is weak — invoked only loosely via the court's reference to a 'fair and accurate account' of the interview, not a fair-comment ruling. K093 (Jewish) is a weak entity match, arising only from the column's passing reference to a 'nice Jewish girl'; it has no bearing on the legal analysis. The controlled vocabulary is skewed toward antisemitism/Charter matters and offers little for a general defamation case, so the last three picks are flagged as thin.

name_verification.name_in_document: Perreault v. Goudreau

defining_issues: Was the respondent a 'successful party' entitled to costs under r. 24(1) of the Family Law Rules where the motion was rendered moot by the applicant's compliance before argument?
Did the applicant act in bad faith within the meaning of r. 24(8), requiring full recovery costs payable immediately?
What amount of costs is appropriate, and should ancillary terms restraining further motions be imposed?

firac.issue: Was the respondent a 'successful party' entitled to costs under r. 24(1) of the Family Law Rules where the motion was rendered moot by the applicant's compliance before argument?
firac.facts: The respondent mother brought a motion under r. 1(8) to strike the applicant father's pleadings for failing to comply with a December 20, 2022 costs order. The applicant paid the outstanding $250 on January 16, 2024, before the February 13, 2024 motion could be argued, so the striking issue was not decided. The applicant argued there was no successful party because the motion did not proceed.
firac.rule: Rule 24(1) of the Family Law Rules creates a presumption that a successful party is entitled to costs. Rule 1(8) provides broad remedial discretion to enforce compliance; striking pleadings is a means to enforcement of the underlying substantive right (Bouchard v. Sgovio, 2021 ONCA 709, paras. 49-51).
firac.application: The court found the respondent's aim in bringing the motion was to enforce the costs award and move the matter forward, and she achieved that aim: the applicant conceded he complied only after being served with the motion. Rendering an issue moot after a motion has been prepared and filed does not allow a party to escape r. 24(1); a party who persuades another to their position by filing a motion is no less successful than one who persuades the court.
firac.conclusion: The respondent was a successful party within the meaning of r. 24(1) and presumptively entitled to costs.

firac.issue: Did the applicant act in bad faith within the meaning of r. 24(8), requiring full recovery costs payable immediately?
firac.facts: The applicant told the court on June 13, 2023 he would pay the costs, then two days later told opposing counsel he would not; he threatened in writing to destroy the child's belongings (toys, iPhone, trading cards, lunch bag); and he repeatedly threatened and attacked the respondent's counsel with suits for misconduct, misrepresentation and defamation, warnings, and a Law Society complaint, without evidentiary foundation.
firac.rule: Rule 24(8) requires costs on a full recovery basis payable immediately where a party has acted in bad faith. Bad faith requires a high threshold of egregious behaviour — conduct done knowingly for a concealed purpose, involving dishonest purpose, moral obliquity, intentional duplicity, obstruction or obfuscation (Kumar v. Nash, 2024 ONCJ 16, paras. 13-15; Scipione v. Del Sordo). Bad faith on one step does not necessarily justify full recovery across all steps (Kumar, para. 19). Malicious attacks on justice participants without evidentiary foundation warrant serious costs consequences (Kumar, paras. 24-27).
firac.application: The court identified three instances of bad faith: (1) the applicant's duplicity in professing on June 13, 2023 an intention to pay while truly aiming to delay enforcement and hold the award hostage; (2) his intentionally cruel and provocative threat to destroy the child's belongings during settlement discussions; and (3) his baseless attacks on opposing counsel that permeated the motion to strike. General rudeness, unwillingness to negotiate, and disruptive courtroom conduct were unreasonable but did not meet the bad faith threshold. The court refused to go behind the earlier costs order to excuse his willful non-compliance.
firac.conclusion: The applicant acted in bad faith in three respects, so costs for the corresponding periods and steps of the litigation are assessed on a full recovery basis, payable immediately.

firac.issue: What amount of costs is appropriate, and should ancillary terms restraining further motions be imposed?
firac.facts: The respondent sought full recovery of $3,091.12. Of the claimed fees, $141.25 (incl. HST) related to the period before the bad faith conduct; the remainder totalled $2,949.87. The applicant had paid the original order over a year late and only after being served with enforcement materials.
firac.rule: Full recovery does not follow automatically; the court must screen against unreasonable or disproportionate claims (Kumar v. Nash, para. 29; Jackson v. Mayerle, 2016 ONSC 1556). Rule 24(12) governs setting amounts. Rule 1(8) broadly empowers the court to respond to a party's failure to obey an order, with tools (other than contempt) available even absent a motion.
firac.application: The court found the rate, fees, disbursements and time reasonable and proportionate. It fixed costs at $3,000 inclusive of HST, payable immediately. To prevent further delay and expense while costs remained owing, the court invoked r. 1(8) to preclude the applicant from bringing motions or obtaining relief without leave until he files proof the costs order is satisfied.
firac.conclusion: Costs fixed at $3,000 inclusive, payable immediately, and the applicant is barred from bringing further motions or obtaining relief without leave until the costs are paid and proof filed.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a family law costs endorsement in a motion to change a final order. K002 (Civil litigation) is added because the decision turns on costs and litigation-conduct principles (Family Law Rules r. 24, presumption of costs to the successful party, bad faith, full recovery) that are core civil-procedure/litigation doctrines. K047 (best interests of the child) is engaged because the applicant's conduct — threatening to destroy the child's belongings and his professed fear of being barred from advancing his child's best interests — figured in the bad faith analysis. K048 (custody/access) applies as the underlying dispute concerned parenting time. These last two are somewhat peripheral to the costs ruling itself but reflect the family context. No hate-speech, human-rights, or constitutional keywords apply. Only four strong picks exist given this is a narrow costs endorsement; the vocabulary lacks a dedicated 'costs' keyword, so K002 is the closest procedural anchor.

case_name: Nogdawindamin Family and Community Services v. J.N.

name_verification.name_in_document: Nogdawindamin Family and Community Services v. J.N.

defining_issues: Did the court have jurisdiction over the proceeding despite the mother's pseudo-legal / Indigenous 'natural law' challenge?
Was the child in need of protection under s. 74 of the CYFSA on the grounds of risk of physical harm or emotional harm?
Was a court order necessary to protect the child in the future?
What disposition order under ss. 101 or 102 of the CYFSA, considering the child's Indigenous heritage, was in the child's best interests?
What access provisions for the mother were in the child's best interests?

firac.issue: Did the court have jurisdiction over the child protection proceeding despite the mother's pseudo-legal / 'natural law' jurisdictional challenge?
firac.facts: The self-represented mother filed an 'Official Notice of Law' and argued she had 'no contract with the society', invoking Magna Carta, natural law and an Indigenous foundation to deny the court's jurisdiction. Justice Peterson had already dismissed the identical argument two months before trial.
firac.rule: Pseudo-legal arguments are frivolous and unfounded in law (Meads v. Meads, 2012 ABQB 571); 'no one in this country is entitled to their own law' (R. v. Barton, 2019 SCC 33). Issue estoppel and its residual discretion apply (Danyluk v. Ainsworth Technologies Inc., [2001] 2 SCR 460). The CYFSA, the federal Act respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, UNDRIP legislation and s. 25 of the Charter govern Indigenous rights within these statutory channels.
firac.application: The trial judge declined to revisit the challenge, treating it as governed by issue estoppel: the mother filed no new material, and the same parties had litigated the same point two months earlier. Exercising discretion to re-open would waste finite judicial resources contrary to the Family Law Rules. In any event, the judge would have reached the same conclusion on the merits, as Indigenous-law arguments must be advanced through the governing statutes or the Charter, not pseudo-law.
firac.conclusion: The jurisdictional challenge was rejected; the court had and retained jurisdiction over the proceeding.

firac.issue: Was the child in need of protection under s. 74 of the CYFSA?
firac.facts: The society alleged (i) risk of physical harm from the mother's March 18, 2022 intoxication while caregiving, and (ii) risk of emotional harm from the mother's sustained campaign alleging the father sexually abused the child, including coaching, social media posts, invasive medical exams, defamatory attacks, and repeated withholding of the child in breach of court orders.
firac.rule: 'Child in need of protection' is defined in s. 74 CYFSA; the pathways pursued were s. 74(2)(b)(i)-(ii) (physical harm) and s. 74(2)(f),(h) (emotional harm). 'Likely' means 'more probable than not' (CAS of Algoma v. J.B., 2019 ONCJ 6). Risk must be real and likely, not speculative (CAS Rainy River v. B.(C.), 2006 ONCJ 458); a flexible approach considers whether the risk persists or may return (K.R. v. CAS London and Middlesex, 2023 ONSC 3798). Parental alienation can ground a risk of emotional harm without expert psychiatric evidence (Catholic CAS of Hamilton v. V.A., 2022 ONSC 4684; CAS of Toronto v. L.R., 2020 ONCJ 22, aff'd 2020 ONSC 4341; A.M. v. C.H.).
firac.application: On physical harm, the March 2022 event was a singular incident; the mother had since remediated her substance-abuse concerns (conceded by the society), so more than two years later the risk fell below threshold. On emotional harm, the accepted evidence showed the mother posted defamatory sexual-abuse content, coached the child, discussed allegations in front of the child despite repeated warnings, subjected her to invasive exams, made threats to the father's family, breached multiple access orders, and absconded with the child leading to her arrest — a continuing pattern of alienation. The finding did not depend on the truth of the allegations; the mother was entitled to disagree with investigations but not to 'practice vigilantism'.
firac.conclusion: No protection finding on physical harm; the child was found in need of protection for risk of emotional harm under s. 74(2)(h).

firac.issue: Was a court order necessary to protect the child in the future?
firac.facts: The mother's alienating conduct continued up to and during trial; multiple prior court orders and a contempt-style declaration had failed to curb it, and police intervention had been required after she absconded with the child.
firac.rule: Section 101(1) CYFSA requires the court to consider whether a court order is necessary to protect the child in future; s. 101(8) requires the child be returned to the pre-intervention caregiver if no order is necessary.
firac.application: The persistence and recency of the mother's behaviour showed a complete lack of insight; earlier orders had proven ineffective. Protection in future plainly required a court order.
firac.conclusion: A court order was necessary to protect the child in the future.

firac.issue: What disposition order under ss. 101 or 102, given the child's Indigenous heritage, was in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The child is Indigenous (mother MFN, father BFN). The society, father and BFN sought a s. 102 custody order to the father. Evidence showed the child thriving in the father's care — safe, stable home, school enrolment, met medical needs, extended family relationships, and cultural connection through BFN.
firac.rule: The court must select the disposition in the child's best interests applying s. 74(3) and the purposes in s. 1 CYFSA, and, for an Indigenous child, ss. 9, 10, 16 and 17 of the Act respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis Children, Youth and Families (S.C. 2019, c. 24) — the 'augmented best interests test' emphasizing cultural continuity and substantive equality. Sections 101(4) and 97(1)(d)(ii) require consideration of less disruptive alternatives; s. 16(1) of the Federal Act sets a placement hierarchy.
firac.application: Placement with the mother, even on strict conditions, would not protect the child, as she would not obey conditions and it would sever the father-child relationship. The father posed no risk of sexual abuse (medical/psychological evidence and the finding that disclosures were coached). Applying the augmented best-interests factors, cultural continuity and substantive equality, custody to the father served the child's best interests; a s. 102 order (ending society involvement) was preferable to a supervision order that would trigger a status review, given the protracted history.
firac.conclusion: A s. 102 custody order granting sole custody/decision-making to the father, in accordance with his plan of care, was made.

firac.issue: What access provisions for the mother were in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The mother had been the primary caregiver for most of the child's life and cares for her, but had absconded and repeatedly breached orders. Current supervised virtual weekly access (with a culture worker) was going well and respectfully.
firac.rule: Sections 104 and 105(2) CYFSA govern access after a s. 102 custody order; access exists for the child's benefit; restrictions must be proportionate, child- and harm-specific and evidence-based (CAS of Brant v. A.C., 2020 ONCJ 505; CAS of Algoma v. S.P., 2011 ONCJ 93).
firac.application: Some access served the child's benefit and maintained connection to the mother and MFN. But given the mother's lack of insight, disregard of orders and recent abduction, in-person access carried too great a risk of abduction and renewed alienating discussions; supervised virtual access remained the least restrictive option consistent with the child's best interests. Ancillary terms barred discussing abuse allegations, disparaging the father, and contacting the child's service providers.
firac.conclusion: The mother's access was limited to supervised virtual access at least weekly, subject to conditions, with ancillary restrictive orders.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing practice area — a child protection proceeding under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is central to both disposition and access, engaging s. 74(3) and the augmented best-interests test for an Indigenous child. K048 (custody/access) captures the s. 102 custody order and s. 104/105 access determination. K012 (procedural fairness) is genuinely engaged: the self-represented mother's contested adjournment, disclosure, service, amicus and recusal requests all turned on the court's duty to ensure a fair trial. K015 (defamation) is a weaker/borderline pick — defamation was not the issue tried, but Justice Gareau's $75,000 defamation judgment against the mother was admitted under s. 93 CYFSA and formed part of the alienation pattern. case_name: Pryers Construction Ltd. v. MVMB Holdings Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: Pryers Construction Ltd. v. MVMB Holdings Inc.

defining_issues: Does the 'special circumstances' doctrine apply to extend the mandatory time limits for preserving and perfecting a construction lien under the Construction Lien Act, so as to permit adding Riverside as a defendant after those periods expired?
Was MVMB an 'owner' within the meaning of s. 1 of the Construction Lien Act such that Pryers was entitled to a lien on MVMB's interest, and could the corporate veil be pierced to reach that result?

firac.issue: Does the 'special circumstances' doctrine operate to extend the mandatory preservation and perfection time limits under the Construction Lien Act, allowing Riverside to be added as a defendant after expiry?
firac.facts: Pryers performed renovation work for Riverside (MVMB's tenant) under an oral agreement, but a number of invoices went unpaid. Pryers registered a lien against MVMB's freehold title but never preserved a lien against Riverside's leasehold interest, which expired in July 2016. Riverside was only added as a defendant at the commencement of trial in 2018, and it pleaded the two-year limitation under the Limitations Act, 2002. The trial judge invoked the 'special circumstances' doctrine to extend time.
firac.rule: Under ss. 31 and 36 of the CLA, a lien expires if not preserved (by registration) and perfected (by commencing an action and registering a certificate) within the prescribed periods; these deadlines are mandatory and leave no room for judicial discretion (Delview Construction Ltd. v. Meringolo; K.H. Custom Homes Ltd. v. Smiley). The 'special circumstances' doctrine (from the Basarsky v. Quinlan line) was abolished for actions governed by the Limitations Act, 2002 (s. 21; Joseph v. Paramount Canada's Wonderland), though it may survive for actions where the limitation period is prescribed by another statute such as the Trustee Act (Bikur Cholim Jewish Volunteer Services v. Langston; Swain Estate). Where a contractual claim is joined with a lien claim, the two-year limitation of the LA2002 applies (LA2002, s. 19).
firac.application: The court held the trial judge erred in law. The doctrine has never been held to apply to actions to enforce a construction lien; the CLA's time limits are statutory and mandatory, preserving reliance on the state of title. Pryers had failed to preserve its lien against Riverside's leasehold interest, so it expired. Insofar as the claim against Riverside was contractual, the CLA contains no applicable limitation period and there is no conflict with the LA2002, so the two-year LA2002 limitation applied and had expired in March 2018, about eight months before the motion to add Riverside.
firac.conclusion: The 'special circumstances' doctrine did not apply; the claim against Riverside (whether as lien or in contract) was time-barred, and the appeal on this point was allowed.

firac.issue: Was MVMB an 'owner' under s. 1 of the CLA, and could the corporate veil be pierced to hold its interest liable?
firac.facts: The land was owned by MVMB and leased to Riverside; Scott Birnie was the sole officer, director and shareholder of both corporations. Pryers contracted with, invoiced, and was paid by Riverside, and only learned of MVMB through a title search. The trial judge found MVMB to be an 'owner' by reasoning that because Birnie controlled both corporations, in requesting the improvements on Riverside's behalf he was also acting on MVMB's behalf.
firac.rule: Under s. 1(1) of the CLA an 'owner' must (i) have an interest in the premises, (ii) have requested the improvement, and (iii) have had the improvement made upon its credit, on its behalf, with its privity/consent, or for its direct benefit. A corporation is a distinct legal entity; the corporate veil may be lifted only where the company is completely dominated and controlled and used as a shield for fraudulent or improper conduct (Parkland Plumbing and Heating Ltd. v. Minaki Lodge Resort; Transamerica Life Insurance; Kosmopoulos v. Constitution Ins. Co. of Canada).
firac.application: The trial judge's finding effectively pierced MVMB's corporate veil, treating Riverside's acts as MVMB's solely because Birnie controlled both. But he made no finding of conduct akin to fraud; indeed he expressly found no bad faith or fraudulent activity and refused to hold Birnie personally liable. Absent improper or fraudulent conduct, common ownership and control alone did not justify disregarding MVMB's separate legal personality, so it was an error of law to treat Riverside's request for improvements as MVMB's.
firac.conclusion: MVMB was not an 'owner' under the CLA; the trial judge erred in piercing the corporate veil, and the appeal on this point was allowed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Regina v. Surjit Singh Dosanjh

defining_issues: Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the fire was an incendiary (deliberately set) fire rather than accidental, so as to establish the unlawful act?
Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt that it was the accused who set the fire (identity), and not the deceased E.L. or some other person?
Did the Crown prove the specific intent required for second degree murder under s. 229 of the Criminal Code, or only the elements of manslaughter?

firac.issue: Was the fire an incendiary fire (unlawful act) proven beyond a reasonable doubt?
firac.facts: E.L. and K. died in a fire that broke out in the master bedroom of the family's suite in the early hours of April 13, 2015, minutes after the accused and his son G. left the unit. Fire investigators and the retained expert Mr. Reed determined the fire originated on or near the master bedroom bed. No ignition source (matches, lighter, gas canister) and no burned remains of any electrical device were found; forensic testing detected no accelerant residue on carpet samples; the gas system functioned properly. The defence hypothesized an electrical device left charging on the bed short-circuited.
firac.rule: Under s. 222(5)(a) of the Criminal Code culpable homicide includes death caused by an unlawful act. The Crown must prove each element beyond a reasonable doubt (R. v. Lifchus; R. v. Starr). For circumstantial evidence, guilt must be the only reasonable inference; reasonable doubt cannot arise from speculation, and the Crown need not negate every fanciful conjecture (R. v. Villaroman). Evidence must be weighed cumulatively, not item-by-item (R. v. Morin; R. v. Smith).
firac.application: The court accepted Mr. Reed's NFPA 921-based opinion that the most probable cause was an incendiary act igniting light combustibles on the bed. No ignition source or burned electrical remains were found despite two thorough investigations; any short-circuiting device would ordinarily have tripped the circuit breakers, and the failure would have had to occur within a roughly ten-to-twelve minute window after the accused and G. left. The defence's electrical hypothesis was found speculative and contrary to human experience.
firac.conclusion: The court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the fire was an incendiary fire, establishing the unlawful act.

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove the accused set the fire?
firac.facts: In the weeks before the fire the accused was angry and distraught after L.L. ended the relationship, was obsessed that she had a boyfriend, feared losing access to his sons, and made threatening statements to Mr. Dobson and others. In the 24 hours before the fire he vandalized E.L.'s SUV, shouted at police, struck G., and threw L.L.'s clothes in the master-bathroom toilet minutes before the fire. He re-entered the residence alone for 30-60 seconds while G. waited outside, and was found with two lighters when arrested. The defence suggested E.L., who suffered depression and had elevated medication levels, may have set the fire.
firac.rule: Identity must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt; the inference of guilt must be the only reasonable inference from the circumstantial evidence (R. v. Villaroman). A trier may accept some, all or none of a witness's evidence (R. v. Mathieu).
firac.application: The court found the accused had motive, opportunity and means: the 30-60 seconds he re-entered alone was sufficient to reach the bed and ignite it. It rejected the theory that E.L. set the fire: she was asleep, had a deep long-standing fear of fire, would not have harmed herself in the very manner she feared with her beloved grandson present, was heavily sedated, and the flashover timeline left no realistic window; her medication side-effect and serotonin-syndrome scenarios were inconsistent with her sedated state and unsupported. G. and any third party were excluded on the timelines.
firac.conclusion: The court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused set the fire that killed E.L. and K.

firac.issue: Did the accused have the specific intent for second degree murder, or only for manslaughter?
firac.facts: The accused's anger and preoccupations centred on L.L. and his children, not E.L.; the fire was set on the matrimonial bed, not at E.L.'s bedroom door. The accused was impulsive, reactive and volatile; he did not run or appear stressed as he left. He had been told K. was not at the residence and mistakenly believed only E.L. was present.
firac.rule: Second degree murder under s. 229(a)(ii) requires intention to cause bodily harm, subjective knowledge that the harm is likely to cause death, and recklessness (R. v. Moo; R. v. Simon; R. v. Nygaard). Transferred intent under s. 229(b) applies only where the requisite murderous intent exists. Unlawful act manslaughter requires a dangerous predicate offence plus objective reasonable foreseeability of non-trivial bodily harm, without foreseeability of death (R. v. McRae; R. v. Creighton; R. v. DeSousa; R. v. Jackson). Arson is defined in s. 434; its mens rea is intentional or reckless damage to property (R. v. Tatton).
firac.application: The court found the accused's conduct reflected impulsive, spiteful behaviour focused on L.L., and that murderous intent was not the only reasonable inference; it was left in reasonable doubt on subjective foresight of death, so murder was not made out. However arson was established as a dangerous predicate offence, and starting a fire in a small enclosed space with E.L. sleeping nearby made non-trivial bodily harm reasonably foreseeable. For K., because there was no murderous intent, s. 229(b) transferred intent did not apply; but the accused's mistaken belief that K. was absent and lack of subjective intent were irrelevant to manslaughter, which requires only objective foreseeability of non-trivial harm from the unlawful act.
firac.conclusion: The Crown failed to prove the intent for second degree murder; the accused was found guilty of the manslaughter of both E.L. and K.

name_verification.name_in_document: La Reine c. Anthony Polyzos

defining_issues: Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused's ability to drive was impaired by alcohol or a drug, so as to establish impaired driving causing bodily harm?

Did the police infringe the accused's right to counsel of his choice under s. 10(b) (and ss. 7, 9, 10(a)) of the Charter such that a stay of proceedings or exclusion of evidence was warranted on the charge of refusing to provide a breath sample?
Was the accused nonetheless guilty of refusing to comply with a breath demand, absent any reasonable excuse under s. 254(5) of the Criminal Code?

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused's ability to drive was impaired by alcohol or a drug?
firac.facts: On October 8, 2011, the accused, a 23-year-old on a probationary licence, ran a red light at high speed at the intersection of Côte-Sainte-Catherine and Côte-des-Neiges and collided with a taxi whose driver suffered a fractured nose. Police observed a strong odour of alcohol, bloodshot eyes, shuffling gait, unsteady balance, confusion, repeated questions, and fleeing the scene. The accused admitted drinking one bottle of beer finished about 70–75 minutes before the collision and pleaded inattention linked to emotional distress.
firac.rule: The Criminal Code sets no fixed test for impairment; it is a question of fact requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an impairment of the ability to drive, even slight, caused by alcohol or a drug (R. c. Guibord 1998 CanLII 13287; Aubé c. R.; R. c. Stellato [1994] 2 R.C.S. 478; R. c. Andrews 1996 ABCA 23). Poor judgment, inattention or an accident alone do not establish alcohol-related impairment (R. c. Caux 2006 QCCA 642; R. c. Dumont 2007 QCCA 1414). Post-offence conduct must be weighed cautiously (R. c. White 2011 CSC 13).
firac.application: The Court found the quantity consumed inconclusive without expert evidence, and speeding and inattention as consistent with reckless conduct unrelated to alcohol. Although the accused's incoherent remarks, flight and equivocal post-collision behaviour were troubling and the Court disbelieved parts of his account, the totality of circumstances—including a long stressful day, the shock of the collision, injury and the panic of arrest—could not be clearly dissociated from any alcohol effect. Even drawing an adverse inference under s. 258(3) from the refusal, the evidence left a reasonable doubt whether one beer impaired his ability to drive.
firac.conclusion: The Crown failed to prove impairment beyond a reasonable doubt; the accused was acquitted on count 1, rendering causation of the injuries moot.

firac.issue: Did the police infringe the accused's s. 10(b) right to counsel of his choice, justifying a stay or exclusion of evidence?
firac.facts: After being read his rights and given the chance to call counsel of choice, the accused repeatedly asked to call his notary uncle/father (not permitted). He spoke to duty counsel for several minutes, then in the breathalyzer room demanded to speak to a specific lawyer, Me Giannis, whose coordinates he did not know. Officer Meilleur looked up and dialled the only Giannis in the lawyers' directory (an outdated number), left no confirmed message, and got no reply. The accused refused the breath sample at 2:37 a.m.
firac.rule: Section 10(b) imposes two duties: to inform of the right to counsel and to give a reasonable opportunity to exercise it, with abstention from eliciting evidence meanwhile (R. c. Manninen [1987] 1 R.C.S. 1233; R. c. Sinclair). The detainee may choose counsel (R. c. Ross [1989] 1 R.C.S. 3), but if chosen counsel is unavailable within a reasonable time, must act promptly to consult another (R. c. Dozois). The accused bears the burden of proving a breach on a balance of probabilities.
firac.application: The Court found the accused's evidence inconsistent and unreliable (confusion about uncle vs. father; contradictory allegations about timing and number of call attempts). It accepted that Meilleur genuinely attempted to reach Giannis after the accused had already exercised his right by speaking with duty counsel. Police cannot guarantee the content or usefulness of counsel's advice; the accused never told police he had received no satisfactory advice, only expressed discomfort speaking to a stranger. The police went beyond their obligations. Failure to formally re-arrest after the refusal was an overly formalistic reading of the Charter, since the accused was repeatedly warned of the consequences.
firac.conclusion: No breach of s. 10(b) or other Charter rights was established; the requête en arrêt des procédures and for exclusion of evidence was dismissed.

firac.issue: Was the accused guilty of refusing the breath demand, having no reasonable excuse under s. 254(5) of the Criminal Code?
firac.facts: The accused, already under arrest, was twice warned of the criminal consequences of refusing, understood the qualified technician's explanations, yet refused to provide a breath sample at 2:37 a.m.
firac.rule: Under s. 254(5) of the Criminal Code a reasonable excuse may defeat the refusal offence; s. 255(2.2) sets out the offence elements. The burden question re a reasonable excuse (R. c. Aubut; cf. R. c. Tremblay 2004 QCCQ 369) need not be resolved where facts disclose no excuse.
firac.application: The Court held that whatever the applicable burden, the facts did not support any reasonable excuse; it would be incoherent for the same facts that failed to establish a Charter breach to establish even a prima facie excuse. The refusal, the accused's own testimony and the surrounding facts proved all elements beyond a reasonable doubt.
firac.conclusion: The accused was found guilty on count 2 (refusing to comply with a breath demand causing bodily harm).

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the core practice area: two Criminal Code driving offences (impaired driving causing bodily harm and refusing a breath demand). K003 (Constitutional law) and K107 (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms) apply because the defence squarely raised Charter arguments (ss. 7, 9, 10(a) and 10(b)) seeking a stay and exclusion of evidence; K112 (Charter s. 7) is one of the sections expressly invoked. K011 (judicial review) is a weak/borderline pick included only because the controlled vocabulary lacks any term for the right to counsel, breathalyzer/impaired-driving offences, stay of proceedings, or exclusion of evidence; it is flagged as tenuous, as this was a criminal trial applying the Charter to police conduct, not a judicial review proper. The vocabulary is oriented toward antisemitism cases and offers no closer match, so fewer than five keywords truly fit.

registry_rationale: The decision indicates the 'DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL', which serves as the judicial district/registry for this Cour du Québec matter.

case_name: Oberg v Saskatchewan (Board of Education of the South East Cornerstone School Division No. 209)

name_verification.name_in_document: Wade Oberg v Board of Education of the South East Cornerstone School Division No. 209 of Saskatchewan

defining_issues: Should the application for judicial review be dismissed for undue delay under Rule 3-56(3) of The Queen's Bench Rules?
Did the Board breach the duty of procedural fairness it owed to Mr. Oberg in the process of demoting him?
Were the Board's decisions to remove Mr. Oberg's principal duties substantively reasonable?
What is the appropriate remedy, and should the matter be remitted to the Board?

firac.issue: Should the application for judicial review be dismissed for undue delay?
firac.facts: The Board made its Second Decision on December 5, 2017; Mr. Oberg filed his judicial review application on January 24, 2019, more than 13 months later. He had spent about nine months obtaining records under LAFOIPP, receiving the final ones September 7, 2018, and filed 4.5 months thereafter. The Board had permanently filled his position by March 2018.
firac.rule: There is no prescribed limitation period for judicial review, but Rule 3-56(3) of The Queen's Bench Rules permits the court to refuse relief where the applicant has delayed unduly and the delay is likely to cause substantial hardship, prejudice, or detriment to good administration. The court first assesses whether delay is undue (Henry v Saskatchewan (WCB), 1999 CanLII 12241 (SK CA)), then considers hardship/prejudice; the ultimate decision is discretionary.
firac.application: Given the complexity of the multi-faceted issues, the rarely-used statutory regime under The Education Act, 1995, and the time needed to obtain LAFOIPP records, the delay was not undue. Even if it were, the Board could not manufacture prejudice from its own decision to permanently fill the position, and there was no evidence it relied on Mr. Oberg's inaction as a representation that he would not apply.
firac.conclusion: There was no undue delay; the application would not be dismissed on that basis.

firac.issue: Did the Board breach the duty of procedural fairness owed to Mr. Oberg?
firac.facts: Following an October 20, 2017 incident, the Board's staff investigated and produced an Investigation Report finding conflict of interest, misuse of authority, failure to supervise students and damage to reputation. The Board removed his principal duties (First Decision), held a show cause hearing, and confirmed the demotion (Second Decision) communicated only by telephone with no written reasons.
firac.rule: Whether procedural fairness was met is a legal question requiring no standard-of-review analysis (Moreau-Bérubé; Saskatoon Cooperative Association). The content of the duty is assessed using the Baker factors, and a high standard applies where employment/profession is at stake (Kane). The Education Act, 1995 does not oust the common law duty (Collins; Knight v Indian Head). The central tenets are knowing the case to meet and a fair opportunity to respond (audi alteram partem), plus adequate reasons where a decision is critical (Baker; Vavilov).
firac.application: The Board owed a high degree of fairness given the impact on employment, its own investigation-manual policies creating legitimate expectations, and the finality of the process. The investigators failed to put specific factual allegations (quoted statements, bullying/harassment findings) directly to Mr. Oberg, denying a fair opportunity to respond. The Board provided no reasons for the Second Decision, so it could not demonstrate it had listened to and considered his show cause submissions. Any participation by report author Ms. Little in rebutting his submissions would also have been unfair given the onus under s. 215(3).
firac.conclusion: The Board breached its duty of procedural fairness in at least three fundamental ways; the cumulative effect rendered the Decisions void ab initio.

firac.issue: Were the Board's decisions substantively reasonable?
firac.facts: Accepting the Investigation Report's findings, Mr. Oberg committed misconduct in a single incident. Mitigating factors were uncontroverted: 25 years' service (20 as an administrator), no prior discipline, a single incident, and expressed remorse. The Board demoted him from principal, its only options under s. 215(3) being to confirm or reverse the amendment.
firac.rule: Reasonableness is the standard for the penalty (Vavilov; Dunsmuir). A decision must fall within a range of reasonable outcomes defensible on the facts and law, and be untenable if it ignores relevant factual/legal constraints. Proportionality between misconduct and sanction is required of all employers (McKinley v BC Tel). Demotion amounting to a fundamental change is akin to dismissal (Farber; Potter).
firac.application: Even accepting the findings, the penalty was disproportionate given the significant mitigating factors and the principle of progressive discipline. A survey of educational-administrator authorities showed demotion is reserved for misconduct going to the heart of the employment relationship, far more serious than a single embarrassing incident. The absence of reasons made it impossible to know what weight was given to mitigation, and the professional regulatory board had imposed a far lighter penalty for the same conduct.
firac.conclusion: The penalty did not fall within the range of reasonable alternative outcomes; the Decisions were quashed as unreasonable.

firac.issue: What is the appropriate remedy — should the matter be remitted to the Board?
firac.facts: The Court found both procedural unfairness and substantive unreasonableness. Under s. 215(3) the Board's only options after a show cause hearing were to confirm or reverse the demotion; it had no power to impose an alternative penalty.
firac.rule: Generally a quashed decision is remitted for reconsideration, but a court may decline to remit where a particular outcome is inevitable and remission would serve no useful purpose (Vavilov, para 142; Retail, Wholesale Department Store Union v Yorkton Cooperative, 2017 SKCA 107 — where only one reasonable solution is possible).
firac.application: Because demotion was the only disciplinary option the statute afforded and that option was unreasonable, the sole possible outcome was reinstatement. Remitting would serve no useful purpose since reinstatement was inevitable.
firac.conclusion: The Court declined to remit; it reinstated Mr. Oberg's duties as principal and awarded costs on Column 3.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the tier-1 practice area — the case is a judicial review of a school board's decision. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review, expressly reasonableness per Vavilov/Dunsmuir) capture the review framework, and K012 (procedural fairness/natural justice) is the central doctrine engaged via the Baker factors. K118 (Education Act) is the governing statute and the matter arises in an education-law setting; K045 covers school discipline/demotion of a principal (student-discipline is the closest school-discipline keyword though the discipline here is of the principal, so it is a borderline pick), and K046 (teacher/administrator misconduct) directly fits the professional-misconduct finding. K085 (wrongful/constructive dismissal) reflects the Court's analysis that demotion was akin to dismissal (Farber/Potter). K045 is the weakest pick as it targets pupil discipline rather than employee discipline.
