registry_rationale: The judicial district is stated as "DISTRICT DE Montréal" with file no. 500-05-060659-008, indicating the Montréal registry of the Superior Court.

name_verification.name_in_document: R.S. c. D.S.

defining_issues: Did Ms. A. have the legal capacity to sign the protection mandate of April 26, 2016?
Did R. exercise undue influence (captation) over Ms. A. in the appointment of R. as mandatary?
Is homologation of the protection mandate in Ms. A.'s interest and does it respect her rights, wishes and autonomy?

Must D. reimburse the $48,000 he received from Ms. A. — i.e., were the transfers gifts, were they annullable for the donor's incapacity known to D., and is D. entitled to restitution for work performed?

firac.issue: Did Ms. A. have the legal capacity to sign the protection mandate of April 26, 2016?
firac.facts: Ms. A. signed her protection mandate before Notary Lamarre on April 26, 2016. The first observed cognitive problems appeared in September 2017; a dementia diagnosis followed in 2018. D. contested the mandate, alleging his mother lacked capacity to sign it, but led no evidence on the point and made no submissions on it at trial.
firac.rule: Capacity is presumed (art. 4 C.C.Q.). The party alleging incapacity bears the burden of establishing an habitual state of insanity or mental weakness, on a balance of probabilities; a simple doubt is insufficient (Bertrand c. Opération Enfant Soleil; S.P. c. V.P., 2022 QCCS 495; Brusenbauch c. Young).
firac.application: D. adduced no evidence — not even a doubt — as to his mother's cognition in April 2016. There was no sign of cognitive impairment before September 2017. Notary Lamarre testified she had no doubt as to Ms. A.'s capacity to understand the mandate.
firac.conclusion: Ms. A. had the capacity to sign the protection mandate.

firac.issue: Did R. exercise undue influence (captation) over Ms. A. in her appointment as mandatary?
firac.facts: R. was already assisting her mother and was present for most of the notary meetings. D. was under a restraining order following a supermarket altercation and was not appointed. D. alleged undue influence and 'elder abuse' but gave only vague testimony about events occurring in 2019, after the mandate was signed.
firac.rule: The party alleging undue influence bears the burden (Savoie c. Savoie). Captation is akin to fraud vitiating consent, characterized by alienation of the person from relatives and abuse of the influencer's position; the manoeuvres must be determinative of consent (Stoneham and Tewkesbury v. Ouellet, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 172). It may be proved by serious, precise and concordant presumptions (arts. 2846, 2849 C.C.Q.).
firac.application: D. produced no probative evidence of undue influence. Ms. A. initiated the change to add a living-arrangement clause, was not shown to be vulnerable in 2016, chose R. because R. already helped her, and reasonably declined to name D. given the restraining order. The notary noted no concern about R.'s presence. Ms. A. expressed no fear of R.
firac.conclusion: R. did not exercise undue influence; the mandate reflected Ms. A.'s free choice.

firac.issue: Is homologation of the protection mandate in Ms. A.'s interest and does it safeguard her autonomy, wishes and preferences?
firac.facts: Ms. A.'s total and permanent incapacity was established and uncontested. The psychosocial report recommended homologation and R.'s appointment. R. had long managed her mother's affairs and acted promptly when cognition declined.
firac.rule: The mandatary must ensure the moral and material well-being of the person, taking account of her condition, needs, faculties and circumstances (art. 2167.3 C.C.Q.), respecting her wishes and preferences as expressed before incapacity.
firac.application: Ms. A. had set out her wishes (remaining at home) in the mandate. The social worker, after consulting the family and physician, concluded homologation and R.'s appointment were in Ms. A.'s best interest. R. demonstrated attentive, appropriate care and a commitment to her mother's well-being.
firac.conclusion: The protection mandate is homologated and R. is confirmed as mandatary to Ms. A.'s person and property.

firac.issue: Must D. reimburse the $48,000, and is he entitled to restitution for work he performed?
firac.facts: Between September and November 2018, D. received $48,000 from his mother's accounts after she offered him money. By June 21, 2018, medical evidence showed Ms. A. was incapable of administering her property. D. claimed the money was a gift and that he did equivalent work on her properties, producing dubious backdated receipts totalling $45,000 for 2018-2020.
firac.rule: A gift is a contract by gratuitous title (arts. 1806, 1381(2) C.C.Q.). A contracting party must have capacity (art. 1398). Acts before homologation may be annulled on proof the incapacity was notorious or known to the other party (art. 2170 C.C.Q.); this may be shown by serious, precise and concordant presumptions (arts. 2846, 2849). On annulment each party restores prestations received (art. 1422(2)); protected persons restore only to the extent of enrichment retained, with the claimant bearing that proof (art. 1706); restitution presupposes property received (art. 1699(1)).
firac.application: The transfers were gifts. Ms. A. was incapable by June 2018. Though incapacity was not notorious, serious and concordant facts (D.'s contradictory positions on his mother's capacity, her visible decline, the bank's $6,000 limit that D. circumvented at another bank) permitted the inference that D. knew of her incapacity. The gifts were therefore annullable under art. 2170. Art. 1706 did not apply because Ms. A. received no prestation to restore; the work D. claimed was neither requested nor a contractual obligation, and he failed to prove any enrichment retained by his mother.
firac.conclusion: The five gifts totalling $48,000 are annulled; D. is condemned to repay $48,000 with interest and indemnity from February 13, 2019, and no restitution is owed to him.

keywords_rationale: The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward Charter/hate-speech matters and offers little that maps precisely to this Quebec protection-mandate and gift-annulment case, so several picks are close approximations flagged as weak. K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 area for the contract characterization, annulment and reimbursement claim. K006 (Family law) is included because protection-mandate homologation and capacity of a vulnerable adult are matters of the law of persons commonly grouped with family. K022 (restitution) is directly engaged — the court analysed arts. 1422(2), 1699 and 1706 C.C.Q. on restitution of prestations. K054 (wills/estates) is the closest specific term for the testamentary/estate-planning and elderly-capacity dimension (protection mandate), though it is an imperfect fit — weak. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is a weak pick, offered for the conservatory court order protecting Ms. A.'s property pending proceedings; there is no dedicated keyword for protection mandates, capacity, undue influence or annulment of gifts.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'SUPERIOR COURT ... PROVINCE OF QUEBEC ... DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and dates it January 24, 2023, establishing the city as Montreal and the province as Quebec.
registry_rationale: The court file is in the 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' (No. 500-14-055402-192), so the registry is Montreal.

name_verification.name_in_document: R.C. v. L.C.

defining_issues: What temporary parenting time (custody/access) arrangement is in the best interests of the four children, and should the father's access be supervised?
Should the two children be returned to their former school or remain in the new school to which the mother unilaterally transferred them?
What weight should be given to allegations of family violence and controlling/coercive behaviour, and to the coerced video and letter, in assessing parenting arrangements?

firac.issue: What temporary parenting arrangement is in the best interests of the children, and is supervised access of the father justified?
firac.facts: The mother left the matrimonial home with all four children on December 2, 2020, alleging years of physical and emotional abuse. Two children have special needs (autism, ADHD, blindness). JCFS investigated and found no safety concerns for the children in either parent's care, but verified concerns of cruel/inappropriate treatment (the father telling S. he might 'jump off his balcony') and exposure to post-separation conflict. The father sought week-on/week-off; the mother sought supervised access.
firac.rule: Under ss. 21(1) and 24(2) of the Children's Law Reform Act, custody/access is determined by the best interests of the child, considering all needs and circumstances (Wilson v. Wilson, 2015 ONSC 479). There is no presumption of equal parenting time (Bembenek v. Bembenek, 2019 ONSC 4050) but a presumption that regular access by a non-custodial parent serves the child's best interests (V.S.J. v. L.J.G.; C.A.S. v. C.F.). A parent seeking supervision bears the burden of justifying that intrusion (Young v. Hanson, 2019 ONSC 1245).
firac.application: The court declined week-on/week-off given the level of conflict, the father's controlling behaviour, and concerns about his inappropriate treatment of the children. However, since JCFS found no genuine safety concerns, supervised access was not justified, and the mother failed to discharge her burden. The court crafted a middle arrangement: alternate weekends with all four children plus one weekday evening with two children at a time.
firac.conclusion: No week-on/week-off and no supervision. The father was granted alternate weekends with all four children and rotating weekday overnights with pairs of children, plus a Passover Seder arrangement.

firac.issue: Should the two children be returned to their former school or remain in the school to which the mother unilaterally transferred them?
firac.facts: The mother transferred T. and A. to a new school without notifying the father when she left the home. A school letter confirmed both children had adjusted well and were thriving. Both schools are within the York Region District School Board. The father sought their return, arguing the mother should not benefit from unilateral self-help conduct.
firac.rule: Best interests governs (CLRA s. 24(2)). A status quo cannot be established or altered by unilateral 'self-help' conduct that gains a litigation advantage (Rifai v. Green, 2014 ONSC 1377), but the decision must serve the children's best interests, not punish a parent.
firac.application: Although the court agreed the mother should not be rewarded for unilateral conduct, removing the children from a school where they were thriving late in the term would not serve their best interests. The court emphasized this did not establish a new status quo and could be revisited at the June 15 Case Conference, with OCL input on the children's views.
firac.conclusion: The children remain in their current school on a temporary basis; the mother must disclose the school's name; no further school changes without consent or court order.

firac.issue: What weight should be given to the family violence allegations and the coerced video and letter?
firac.facts: The mother alleged physical, verbal and emotional abuse and controlling behaviour. The father relied on a February 2019 video and April 2019 signed letter in which the mother 'confessed' to leaving without reason. The letter was addressed 'To Whom It May Concern' and included statements about future divorce at a Rabbinical Court.
firac.rule: The expanded definition of 'family violence' in ss. 18(1) and (2) of the CLRA includes coercive and controlling behaviour and psychological abuse, and need not constitute a criminal offence. Findings on interim motions are limited where affidavits conflict and there is no cross-examination.
firac.application: The court found the video and letter bore 'all the earmarks of a coerced document,' likening it to something a hostage might write. Far from exculpating the father, they supported the mother's allegations of controlling and emotionally abusive behaviour. The court approached both parties' evidence with scepticism given their shared history of fraud and dishonesty.
firac.conclusion: The court accepted evidence of the father's controlling and emotionally abusive behaviour, which informed its refusal to order equal parenting time.

defining_issues: Does the Migratory Birds Convention Act, 1917 and its Regulations remain valid (intra vires) federal legislation implementing a treaty made under s. 132 of the B.N.A. Act, notwithstanding the Statute of Westminster, 1931 and later federal Acts extending its operation?

Do the hunting rights guaranteed to Indians under Treaty 11 shield an Indian who shot a migratory bird for food out of season from conviction under the Migratory Birds Convention Act, where the Act derogates from those treaty promises?

firac.issue: Does the Migratory Birds Convention Act and its Regulations remain valid federal legislation under s. 132 of the B.N.A. Act despite the Statute of Westminster and subsequent extending statutes?
firac.facts: The Migratory Birds Convention was entered into by Great Britain on behalf of Canada with the United States in 1916 and implemented by the Migratory Birds Convention Act, 1917. The respondent argued the Act was now ultra vires because the Statute of Westminster, 1931, the Extra-territorial Act, 1933, and the 1949 Act admitting Newfoundland had the effect of "reaffirming" the Act, allowing its validity to be re-examined; since game preservation is a matter of provincial jurisdiction, the Act should fall.
firac.rule: Section 132 of the B.N.A. Act empowered Parliament to legislate to implement Empire treaties. Statutes validly enacted before the Statute of Westminster to implement a treaty properly made under s. 132 remain valid, and may be amended as necessary to carry out the treaty, so long as the treaty has not been denounced, even if the subject matter falls within provincial competence (contrasting A.-G. Can. v. A.-G. Ont., [1937] A.C. 326 and Johannesson v. West St. Paul, which concerned post-Westminster treaties). Per A.-G. Ont. v. Canada Temperance Federation, [1946] A.C. 193, a matter that by its inherent nature is the concern of the Dominion as a whole falls within federal competence though it may touch provincial matters.
firac.application: The Court held the treaty had not been denounced, so the implementing legislation remained valid. Neither the Extra-territorial Act, 1933 (extending Canadian statutes extra-territorially) nor the 1949 Newfoundland Act (extending federal statutes to the new province) amounted to a re-ratification or re-implementation of the Convention; they were general extensions of all federal Acts to Canada's enlarged territorial jurisdiction, not fresh implementation. Statutes implementing s. 132 treaties may still be amended to carry out the treaty. In any event, preservation of migratory birds—a source of food and destroyer of injurious insects—may well fall within federal competence as a matter of national concern apart from s. 132, leaving room for both federal and provincial legislation.
firac.conclusion: The Migratory Birds Convention Act and Regulations remain valid federal legislation; the ultra vires argument failed.

firac.issue: Do Treaty 11 hunting rights protect an Indian from conviction under the Migratory Birds Convention Act for shooting a migratory bird for food out of season?
firac.facts: The respondent, an Indian and member of Band 84 under Treaty 11, shot a female mallard duck for food near Yellowknife on 7 May 1962, out of season (the open season being 1 September to 15 October). He was unable to work due to tuberculosis and was heading to the bush to trap, taking no food and expecting to shoot game. Treaty 11 (1921) covenanted that the Indians "shall have the right to pursue their usual vocations of hunting, trapping and fishing... subject to such regulations as may from time to time be made by the Government".
firac.rule: Indian hunting and fishing rights originate in the Royal Proclamation of 1763 and the treaties surrendering land (R. v. Wesley, [1932] 4 D.L.R. 774). Treaty covenants amount to a "promise and agreement", a personal obligation of the Crown (A.-G. Can. v. A.-G. Ont., [1897] A.C. 199), which can be breached; nothing prevents Parliament, legislating competently within s. 91 of the B.N.A. Act, from doing so. The treaty right to hunt cannot stand against derogating legislation that goes beyond the regulations contemplated (regulations meant only to ensure a maintained game supply for the Indians' needs).
firac.application: The Court found the language of s. 5(1) of the Regulations ("no person shall... kill... a migratory bird" except in open season) admits no exception, and the express provisions permitting Indians and Eskimos to take only certain birds (scoters, auks, etc.) confirmed that the treaty hunting right as to other migratory birds had been abrogated, abridged or infringed. Although this was an apparent "breach of faith"—likely an oversight, the left hand forgetting the right hand—Parliament had competently legislated to implement the Convention, so the breach did not invalidate the Act. The mallard was a wild bird ferae naturae even if once domesticated (Blackstone), and "scoter" did not encompass it; the trial judge's doubts on these points were rejected.
firac.conclusion: The treaty rights did not provide a defence; the prohibition binds the Indian who shot the duck for food. Appeal allowed and the conviction affirmed.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally about constitutional division of powers and the treaty-implementation power under s. 132 of the B.N.A. Act, so K003 (Constitutional law) is the core tier-1 keyword. The proceeding arose from a quasi-criminal conviction for unlawfully killing a migratory bird, prosecuted, appealed by way of trial de novo, and finally by Crown appeal, engaging K004 (Criminal law). The underlying magistrate's conviction and the trial de novo before Sissons J.T.C. occurred at Yellowknife, and the offence occurred "not far from Yellowknife airport in the Northwest Territories"; Yellowknife is the associated locale, though the decision does not expressly state where the Court of Appeal sat.
registry_rationale: No court registry or office is named in the decision, as is common for an appellate court report of this era; left null.

defining_issues: Did the defendant's cartoons and accompanying commentary constitute a prima facie defamation of the plaintiff?
Did the defence of fair comment protect the depiction of the plaintiff as an anti-Semite, a racist and a Nazi?
What damages, if any, should be awarded for the defamation established?
Was the New Brunswick Teachers' Association vicariously liable for the defamation?

firac.issue: Did the defendant's cartoons and accompanying commentary constitute a prima facie defamation of the plaintiff?
firac.facts: At an NBTA Social Studies Council workshop on the Holocaust and anti-Semitism held in Saint John on May 6, 1993, cartoonist Josh Beutel gave a presentation with cartoons and dialogue that a reasonable person would find depicted Malcolm Ross as an anti-Semite, a racist and a Nazi.
firac.rule: Defamation consists of a false statement about a person to his or her discredit, made without lawful excuse, causing damage (Scott v. Sampson (1882), 8 Q.B.D. 491). A cartoon is subject to the ordinary rules of defamation, the difficulty being to ascertain the meaning conveyed to an ordinary fair-minded person (Vander Zalm v. Times Publishers (1980), 109 D.L.R. (3d) 531). A bad existing reputation is no answer to a defamation action (Hobbs v. Tinling and Co., [1929] 2 K.B. 1).
firac.application: The cartoons and dialogue were published to third persons, referred to the plaintiff, and would be found by a fair-minded person to discredit him by lowering him in the estimation of right-thinking members of society. The argument that Ross had no credible reputation to lose was rejected as a bar; it goes only to damages.
firac.conclusion: A prima facie case of defamation was established, shifting the onus to the defendants to justify it.

firac.issue: Did the defence of fair comment protect the depiction of the plaintiff as an anti-Semite, a racist and a Nazi?
firac.facts: Beutel honestly believed Ross was an anti-Semite, racist and Nazi. Ross was a public figure who had published controversial views and had been ordered removed from the classroom by a Human Rights Act board of inquiry. His publications showed vehement opposition to Judaism and racialist views, but the evidence did not establish him as a Nazi.
firac.rule: Fair comment protects honest expression of opinion on matters of public interest based on true facts (Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada). Its three elements are: the matter must be comment on true facts (or a true statement of fact); it must concern a matter of public interest; and it must be a fair, honest expression of the real view of the commentator (Cherneskey v. Armadale Publishers Ltd., [1979] 1 S.C.R. 1067). Comment need not be temperate and may be severe, but statements of fact that are untrue are not protected, and the words must appear with reasonable clarity to be comment and not statement of fact (Baxter v. CBC (1980), 28 N.B.R. (2d) 114).
firac.application: The court found the presentation honest and made on a matter of public interest. The characterizations of Ross as anti-Semitic and racist were fair comment on facts shown to be true from his publications and testimony. However, the depiction of Ross as a Nazi was a statement of fact not established as true; his views were founded in his religious beliefs, not substantively in Nazism, and equating him with Hitler and Goebbels went too far.
firac.conclusion: Fair comment succeeded as to the anti-Semite and racist characterizations but failed as to the Nazi characterization, which was actionable defamation.

firac.issue: What damages should be awarded for the defamation established?
firac.facts: Ross's reputation as an anti-Semite and racist was already well known; he was no longer permitted to teach because of his views. Much of Beutel's presentation was fair comment, and no malice was found as it was based on honest belief. The defamation occurred while Ross's removal from teaching was still under judicial review.
firac.rule: Damages assessment considers all circumstances: the plaintiff's conduct, position and standing, the nature of the libel, the mode and context of publication, any retraction or apology, and the defendant's whole conduct (Baxter v. CBC).
firac.application: The court weighed mitigating factors (Ross's pre-existing reputation, the fair-comment portions, absence of malice) against aggravating factors (the seriousness of being labelled a Nazi and the ill-considered timing during pending litigation). Ross's reputation was hurt though his loss of employment was largely self-authored.
firac.conclusion: General damages, including mitigation and aggravation, were assessed at $7,500.

firac.issue: Was the New Brunswick Teachers' Association vicariously liable for the defamation?
firac.facts: The Social Studies Council, operating under the NBTA's auspices, organized the workshop. Beutel was first contacted and paid an honorarium by the Saint John Jewish Museum, then invited by the Council. Neither the Council nor the NBTA knew the content of his presentation or supervised speakers, and Beutel had no employment or contractual relationship with the NBTA.
firac.rule: Vicarious liability requires a relationship of employment, agency or control; ratification requires acceptance of responsibility for the tortious conduct.
firac.application: The NBTA exercised no control or direction over the content of Beutel's presentation and had no employment/agency relationship with him. A post-workshop refusal to apologize did not amount to ratification, and ratification was not pleaded. Autonomy of the Council did not automatically insulate the NBTA, but no basis for liability existed.
firac.conclusion: The NBTA was not vicariously liable; the claim against it was dismissed. However, given that the NBTA knew a confrontation was likely and that the timing was ill-advised, it was ordered to pay the plaintiff's costs of $2,170 and denied its own costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a private defamation tort action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. K016 (fair comment) is the central defence analysed and the determinative issue. K018 (qualified privilege) is engaged because the judgment frames fair comment as protection by qualified privilege per Brown. K058 (antisemitism) and K065 (racism) are directly engaged because the court examined whether Ross was truly anti-Semitic and racist as findings of fact. K062 (Holocaust denial) reflects Ross's characterized view that the Holocaust was exaggerated by Jews. K088 (Holocaust) and K093 (Jewish) are the entity/context keywords central to the workshop and the defamatory depictions. Vicarious liability is significant but has no vocabulary entry; the borderline picks are K018 and K062 (weaker, contextual).

registry_rationale: The court is identified as the 'Judicial District of Moncton' of the New Brunswick Court of Queen's Bench, Trial Division.

defining_issues: What is the source of authority and the test for granting a common-law (rather than statutory) restraining order in a family law situation?
Did the applicant establish a reasonably held and objectively legitimate fear for the safety of her child sufficient to justify a permanent restraining order against the father?
Should the shared-parenting provision of the existing order be stayed in light of the findings?

firac.issue: What is the source of authority and the test for granting a common-law restraining order in a family law situation?
firac.facts: Ms. P. sought a permanent common-law restraining order on behalf of her son against the father, rather than a Queen's Bench protection order under the Protection Against Family Violence Act.
firac.rule: A family-law restraining order is a form of injunction rooted in the superior court's inherent jurisdiction and its equitable power to grant injunctive relief, codified in the Alberta Judicature Act, ss. 8 and 13(2) (Caron, 2011 SCC 5; Canadian Pacific v. BMWE, [1996] 2 SCR 495). Guided by permanent-injunction factors (Qureshi v. Gooch, 2005 BCSC 1584; Cadbury Schweppes, [1999] 1 SCR 142) and statutory analogues such as the PAFVA and Fuda v. Fuda, 2011 ONSC 154, the test is whether the applicant has demonstrated a reasonably held and legitimate fear for the safety of herself, a person under her care, or her property as a result of the respondent's harassing, intimidating, molesting, threatening or violent behaviour.
firac.application: The Court confirmed its inherent jurisdiction and equitable authority, distinguished the broader common-law reach from the familial scope of the PAFVA, and articulated that the applicant's fear, while subjectively held, must also be objectively reasonable to prevent abuse of the Court's equitable powers.
firac.conclusion: The Court adopted a standard requiring a reasonably held and legitimate fear of harm arising from the respondent's conduct, subject to overarching equitable discretion.

firac.issue: Did the applicant establish a reasonably held and legitimate fear for the child's safety justifying a permanent restraining order?
firac.facts: The 13-year-old son reported to his mother and her husband that the father caned him and threatened to cane him 'to the bone' during study sessions, hit him in the face, forced him to shower with him, and accused him of being racially impure; the father owned a Taser-like instrument. The father denied caning and characterized his discipline as yelling and withholding privileges.
firac.rule: The applicant must demonstrate a reasonably held and legitimate fear for the safety of a person under her care resulting from the respondent's harassing, intimidating, threatening or violent behaviour.
firac.application: Justice Hughes found the mother's June 30, 2010 email corroborated the caning allegations long before the application, rejecting the father's claim the application was a 'back door' to vary shared parenting. The child's insistence on having nothing to do with his father, despite encouragement to maintain a safe relationship, was treated as confirmatory. The father's evidence was rejected where it conflicted, given his 'I can't recall' answer on threats, his demonstrated intolerance (including derogatory remarks about the son's teacher), his superior attitude, and the implausible explanation for the joint showering. The Court found the father's discipline included caning and threats of caning.
firac.conclusion: The applicant established the necessity of a restraining order; a permanent restraining order was granted on the same terms as the interim order, to end July 31, 2012.

firac.issue: Should the shared-parenting provision be stayed?
firac.facts: The May 2004 consent order provided for shared parenting; the Court had found the father caned and threatened to cane the child.
firac.rule: The Court exercises jurisdiction guided by the best interests of the child.
firac.application: While a healthy relationship with both parents was in M.'s best interests, residing in the father's home was not presently a safe environment; rebuilding the relationship required M. to feel safe.
firac.conclusion: The shared-parenting provision of the May 2004 Order was stayed until further order of the Court.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area, as the case concerns a restraining order and parenting arrangements involving a child. K047 (best interests of the child) and K048 (custody/access) are engaged because the Court stayed the shared-parenting provision based on the child's best interests and safety. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is the closest vocabulary match for the restraining order, which the Court expressly characterized as a form of injunction grounded in inherent equitable jurisdiction. K002 (Civil litigation) captures the equitable-remedy/injunction framework and inherent jurisdiction analysis. K058 (antisemitism) is a weak, borderline pick, included only because the father's derogatory remarks about the child's teacher being Jewish featured in the credibility assessment; it is not a legal issue in the case and could reasonably be omitted.
location_rationale: The header identifies the 'Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta', 'Registry: Calgary', and the judgment is 'Dated at the City of Calgary, Alberta this 25th day of May, 2012.'
registry_rationale: The docket header expressly states 'Registry: Calgary'.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Banon

defining_issues: What is the fit sentence for an offender who pleaded guilty to manslaughter arising from a fatal assault on his intimate partner in a domestic context?

firac.issue: What is the appropriate length of custodial sentence for manslaughter committed in a domestic context, taking into account the aggravating and mitigating circumstances?
firac.facts: Raphael Banon, 20 at the time, fatally assaulted his 19-year-old girlfriend Asha Morar in his Vaughan apartment on the night of May 5–6, 2021. He inflicted multiple blunt force injuries, including a nearly split liver, rib and spinal fractures, and neck compression; the cause of death was hemorrhagic shock from blunt force trauma. Ms. Morar was small, intoxicated on alcohol and street Xanax, and vulnerable. Banon knew she was badly injured, did not call 911, cleaned up the scene, and called his mother rather than seeking medical aid. He pleaded guilty to manslaughter, was a 22-year-old first offender at sentencing, had endured harsh pre-sentence custody (numerous lockdowns, segregation after inmate assaults), and had taken rehabilitative steps including completing school credits and reconnecting with his Jewish heritage through study with a rabbi.
firac.rule: Under s. 236 of the Criminal Code the maximum penalty for manslaughter is life imprisonment (R. v. Head). Sentencing is governed by ss. 718–718.2: the fundamental purpose (s. 718), proportionality as the fundamental principle (s. 718.1; R. v. Friesen, 2020 SCC 9; R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64), and aggravating/mitigating factors including intimate-partner and abuse-of-trust aggravation under s. 718.2(a)(ii)-(iii). Sentencing for manslaughter is fact-specific and context-driven (R. v. Simcoe; R. v. Devaney), with the usual domestic-context range being seven to twelve years (R. v. Kimpe, 2010 ONCA 812).
firac.application: The court found high gravity and high moral blameworthiness: a brutal, prolonged assault on a vulnerable, intoxicated intimate partner in her own home, anger fuelled by her involvement with other men, knowledge of her injuries, and a callous failure to summon help. Aggravating factors under s. 718.2(a)(ii)/(iii) applied. Against these, the court weighed a significant constellation of mitigating factors: a guilty plea, sincere remorse and acceptance of responsibility, youth and first-offender status, particularly harsh pre-sentence custody conditions (lockdowns described as inhumane, plus assaults and segregation), rehabilitative efforts, and a supportive pro-social family. Denunciation and deterrence were paramount, but rehabilitation had to be considered given his youth. Absent the mitigating circumstances the court would have imposed the nine years sought by the Crown.
firac.conclusion: A global sentence of eight years' imprisonment was imposed, less pre-sentence custody of 2 years and 109 days credited at 1.5:1 (42 months), leaving 54 months (4 years 6 months) to serve, together with a DNA order, s. 109 weapons prohibitions, and a s. 743.21 non-communication order.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary practice area — this is a manslaughter sentencing under ss. 236 and 718–718.2 of the Criminal Code. The remaining picks are weak because the controlled vocabulary lacks any manslaughter/sentencing/domestic-violence term. K093 (Jewish) and K098 (rabbi) are engaged only by the mitigation finding that Banon reconnected with his Jewish heritage and studied with a rabbi in custody — genuine but peripheral. K094 (Jewish community) and K052 (religious upbringing) are flagged as weak/borderline, included only to reach the minimum count; they touch the same religious-rehabilitation detail rather than any core issue. No hate, human-rights, or Charter keyword applies.
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, so the province is Ontario. No sitting city is stated in the reasons; the offence occurred in Vaughan and custody was in the Greater Toronto Area, but the court's own location/registry is not identified in the text, so city is left null.

defining_issues: Who bears the burden of proving a testator's mental incapacity, and did the estate discharge it so as to render the codicil void?

Do Quebec courts have jurisdiction to rule on the validity of a bank authorization signed in Israel, and under the applicable Israeli law was the appellant entitled to the funds she withdrew from the deceased's account?
Did the appellant's conduct render her 'unworthy to inherit' (indigne) under art. 621 C.c.Q.?

firac.issue: Who bears the burden of proving testamentary incapacity, and did the estate meet it so that the codicil is void?
firac.facts: Elo Remer was diagnosed with progressive Alzheimer's-type dementia in 1991; by November 18, 1992 he could not recall his address, phone number, the day, month, or year. Two days later, on November 20, 1992, he signed a codicil (drafted on instructions from his nephew) benefiting his second wife, the appellant.
firac.rule: Per Touchette c. Touchette, [1974] C.A. 575, a testator is presumed sane and the party alleging nullity bears the burden of proving incapacity; however, where a prima facie showing seriously casts doubt on capacity, the burden shifts to the party asserting the act's validity to prove the disposer had capacity when signing.
firac.application: The evidence adduced by the estate raised a very serious doubt about Elo Remer's capacity to consent to the codicil, shifting the burden to the appellant to establish a lucid interval at signing. The Court found she failed to do so.
firac.conclusion: The trial judge was correct to declare the codicil of November 20, 1992 void for incapacity; the appeal in file 500-05-008880-955 was dismissed with costs.

firac.issue: Do Quebec courts have jurisdiction over a bank authorization signed in Israel, and under Israeli law was the appellant entitled to the withdrawn funds?
firac.facts: On July 14, 1993 in Israel, Elo Remer signed a form at Bank Hapoalim authorizing his wife to transact on his account; she subsequently withdrew over a million dollars, transferred to a Swiss account held with her daughter. The estate sought a declaration of nullity and reimbursement.
firac.rule: Arts. 172 C.p.c. and 3139 C.c.Q. permit Quebec courts to hear a defence and cross-demand connected to the principal action; a declinatory exception must be raised in a timely way. Israeli law governed the substance, under which a person claiming ownership of funds in an account bears a very high burden to prove the original owner's donative intent, preferably by documentary evidence.
firac.application: Jurisdiction existed because the issue arose within the estate's defence and cross-demand against the appellant's action, and she never timely raised a declinatory exception. Applying Israeli law, the appellant relied essentially on her own testimony, to which the trial judge gave little credibility, and other witnesses' statements were too vague to establish donative intent. Moreover, the presumption of incapacity led by necessary inference to nullity even under Israeli law.
firac.conclusion: The Quebec courts had jurisdiction and the withdrawals were not opposable to the estate; the appellant was ordered to reimburse the estate USD 543,045.07 and CAD 330,173.09 (total CAD 1,139,581.67) with interest and the additional indemnity.

firac.issue: Was the appellant 'unworthy to inherit' under art. 621 C.c.Q.?
firac.facts: The estate, by incidental appeal and a motion to amend (its first-instance pleadings lacking the conclusion), sought a declaration that the appellant was unworthy to inherit because of undue influence she allegedly exercised over Elo Remer.
firac.rule: Art. 621 C.c.Q. requires 'highly reprehensible conduct' (comportement hautement répréhensible) before a person may be declared unworthy of inheriting.
firac.application: While the appellant may have exerted undue influence to obtain a modification of the will, the Court found this did not reach the threshold of highly reprehensible conduct; generally the evidence showed she had been an attentive spouse toward the deceased, so the drastic measure sought was unjustified.
firac.conclusion: The appellant was not declared unworthy; the motion to amend was granted but the incidental appeal seeking indignity was dismissed with costs.

keywords_rationale: The case is fundamentally a succession/estate dispute, so K054 (wills/estates) and its tier-1 parent K006 (Family law) are the core selections. K002 (Civil litigation) captures the private-law action/cross-demand structure and reimbursement litigation. K022 (restitution) reflects the order requiring the appellant to repay the estate the funds withdrawn from the bank account. K103 (Israel) applies because the impugned bank authorization was signed at Bank Hapoalim in Israel, Israeli law governed the account, and a condominium in Israel is involved. K095 (Jewish family) is a weaker, contextual pick — the parties, Hebrew given names, and Israeli property strongly suggest a Jewish family, but the decision does not expressly discuss Jewish identity or Jewish law, so it is flagged as inferential.

defining_issues: Should the second (Charter-based) action be struck as res judicata, frivolous, vexatious, an abuse of process, or improper claim-splitting given the earlier dismissal of the wrongful-dismissal action for lack of jurisdiction?
Does the statement of claim fail to disclose a violation of s. 7 or s. 15 of the Charter such that it should be struck?
Should the plaintiff's jury notice be struck out?

firac.issue: Should the second, Charter-based action be struck as res judicata, an abuse of process, or improper claim-splitting given the 1990 dismissal of the wrongful-dismissal action for lack of jurisdiction?
firac.facts: The plaintiff, a probationary teacher dismissed in 1988, sued for wrongful dismissal in 1990; that action was dismissed by Speyer J. for lack of jurisdiction because the collective agreement's grievance and arbitration procedures were the exclusive recourse. In 1994 the plaintiff issued a fresh statement of claim alleging infringements of ss. 7 and 15 of the Charter, seeking reinstatement and $1.5 million, and adding new allegations of coercion, denial of recourse, and discrimination based on his Jewish Spanish-Moroccan ethnicity and religion.
firac.rule: A court lacks jurisdiction over disputes arising from a collective agreement (St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. C.P.U., Local 219, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 704), but Charter claims are individual constitutional rights that civil courts may entertain notwithstanding the availability of arbitration (Weber v. Ontario Hydro (1992), 11 O.R. (3d) 609 (C.A.)). Claim-splitting/res judicata principles from Henderson v. Henderson (1843) and Doering v. Grandview (Town), [1975] were also raised.
firac.application: The first action was dismissed for want of jurisdiction before pleading or trial; what was adjudicated was only that the wrongful-dismissal claim fell within the collective agreement's exclusive recourse. The Charter allegations were absent from the first action, and under Weber their inclusion could not have been dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. The second action is not merely a recycling of the earlier facts but pleads new allegations and, for the first time, Charter infringements, so it is entitled to be treated as a separate action.
firac.conclusion: The action is not res judicata, frivolous, or an abuse of process; this branch of the defendant's motion is refused.

firac.issue: Does the statement of claim fail to disclose a violation of s. 7 or s. 15 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The defendant argued that s. 7 does not protect economic interests, so a dismissal cannot infringe it, and that s. 15 applies only to inequality created by 'law,' raising complex questions about whether the board is governed by the Charter.
firac.rule: Section 7 does not protect purely economic interests (O.P.S.E.U. v. Northern College). Section 15's application, and whether a public body is bound by the Charter, can be a question 'of some complexity' requiring a factual record (Weber v. Ontario Hydro; McKinney v. University of Guelph; Douglas College).
firac.application: The plaintiff did not frame his claim as one for economic loss even though his dismissal is central. The applicability of s. 15 and whether the board is governed by the Charter are issues of some complexity that cannot responsibly be resolved on a record consisting essentially of only the statement of claim; a hard look at the facts must await trial.
firac.conclusion: The claim should not be struck for failing to disclose a Charter violation; the issues should proceed to trial.

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's jury notice be struck out?
firac.facts: The plaintiff sought declaratory relief (paras. 1(a) and 1(b)) as well as damages, and delivered a jury notice.
firac.rule: Section 108(2)10 of the Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, disqualifies an action seeking declaratory relief from trial by jury; cogent reasons may also justify dispensing with a jury where the case raises difficult mixed questions of fact and law (Fulton v. Fort Erie (Town) (1982), 40 O.R. (2d) 235).
firac.application: The claim for declaratory relief itself disqualifies the action from jury trial; the court rejected the suggested distinction between a declaration and relief pursuant to a declaratory order. Moreover, the difficult questions of law and mixed fact and law make the case unsuitable for a jury.
firac.conclusion: The jury notice is struck out; this branch of the motion is granted.

The underlying dispute is a teacher's wrongful dismissal (K085) governed by a collective agreement's grievance/arbitration regime (K084), engaging Labour and employment (K009). The plaintiff's fresh claim rests on the Charter (K003, with K112 for s. 7 and K109 for s. 15, and K107 for the Charter itself) and alleges discrimination based on ethnic origin and religion (K069). K093 Jewish reflects the plaintiff's pleaded identity as 'a Jewish person of Spanish-Moroccan ancestry' underlying the discrimination allegation. name_verification.name_in_document: REX v. CURRY

defining_issues: Was there sufficient corroborative evidence to warrant a conviction for perjury?

Where a witness was sworn with uplifted hand, without the use of the Scriptures and without being asked whether he objected to the regular form, was a valid and binding oath administered such that he could be convicted of perjury?

firac.issue: Was there sufficient corroborative evidence to warrant a conviction for perjury?
firac.facts: Before a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act (ch. 104, R.S.C.), Curry swore that customs officer John J. McDonald had solicited his vote and sent him to Joseph McPherson, who gave him liquor and money, and that McDonald later told him not to vote if he would not support McKenzie. Both McDonald and McPherson denied the whole story. No single Crown witness could contradict every constituent fact.
firac.rule: In perjury the corroboration is required for the perjured fact as a whole, not for every detail or constituent part: Wigmore on Evidence, s. 2042(3); Regina v. Roberts, 2 C. & K. 607 at 614 (Patteson J.); The King v. Houle, 12 Can. Crim. Cas. 56.
firac.application: The accused himself connected McDonald and McPherson in one continuous transaction — the alleged attempt to bribe him. The Crown's two witnesses each denied any dealing with the accused, and because the transaction as sworn necessarily connected both men, their denials together established the falsity of the perjured fact as a whole; each corroborated the other. The trial judge was entitled to look at the whole of the accused's evidence.
firac.conclusion: All four judges agreed there was sufficient corroboration; the first reserved question was answered in favour of the Crown.

firac.issue: Was a valid and binding oath administered where the witness was sworn with uplifted hand, without the Scriptures and without inquiry as to any objection to the regular form?
firac.facts: The commissioner, having no Bible readily available, directed Curry to raise his right hand and recited the usual formula ending 'so help you God.' Curry was not asked whether he objected to being sworn in the regular way, no Scripture was used, and he raised no objection. He was, presumably, an ordinary Christian.
firac.rule: At common law an ordinary Christian must be sworn touching or kissing the Gospels; exceptional forms (uplifted hand, other books, etc.) are permitted only where the witness objects or declares that another form is binding on his conscience: Omichund v. Barker, Willes 538 / 1 Atk. 21; the declaratory statute 1 & 2 Vict. ch. 105 and Oaths Act 1888 confirm ceremony is part of the oath; R. v. Moore, R. v. Deakin, The King v. Lee Tuck. Perjury under s. 170 of the Criminal Code requires an assertion made 'upon oath,' and s. 16 imports common-law defences; there is no estoppel by silence where the irregular form is imposed by the tribunal.
firac.application: Graham E.J. (Townshend C.J. concurring) held that Curry did not fall within any recognized exception: he made no objection and the commissioner conducted no inquiry, so he was not qualified to be sworn other than on the Gospels; a Christian's oath so administered was not binding, and mere silence created no estoppel because the irregular form was the tribunal's own act — 'no oath, no perjury.' Russell J. and Drysdale J. dissented, holding that under Omichund v. Barker the substance of the oath is calling God to witness, the kissing of the book being a mere ceremony; the uplifted-hand form with the invocation of the Deity satisfied the essential requirement, and a witness who so swore and then testified falsely could not escape a perjury conviction.
firac.conclusion: The Court was equally divided (2–2) on the second question; by operation of the equal division the conviction stood.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary tier-1 area — the case is a reserved case on a perjury conviction under s. 170 of the Criminal Code. K025 (freedom of religion) is engaged loosely because the entire second-question analysis turns on the common-law principle that an oath must be administered in the form binding on the witness's religion/conscience (Omichund v. Barker), discussing Christian, Jewish, Mohammedan, Hindu and other forms. K093 (Jewish) and K026 (halacha) are weak/borderline picks reflecting the judgments' extended treatment of how Hebrew witnesses were sworn on the Old Testament / 'law of Moses' as an exception to the Christian form. K012 (procedural fairness) is a weak pick capturing the duty of the tribunal to inquire whether the witness objected before departing from the regular oath. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward Charter/antisemitism matters and offers no direct 'perjury,' 'oath' or 'evidence/corroboration' term, so beyond K004 the matches are approximate and are flagged as such.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'Nova Scotia Supreme Court' with the judges Townshend C.J., Graham E.J., Russell and Drysdale JJ., establishing Nova Scotia as the province. No city or hearing location is stated in the text.
registry_rationale: No registry or court office is named anywhere in the decision, so registry is left null.

case_name: Re Child & Family Services and McKee

name_verification.name_in_document: Re Child & Family Services and McKee

defining_issues: Does a Manitoba court retain jurisdiction over the guardianship and care of a child who is ordinarily resident in Manitoba but has been clandestinely removed from the province?

If jurisdiction exists, should the court exercise it by refusing temporary guardianship to the child care agency and instead ordering the child to reside with an out-of-province relative, or should it appoint the agency temporary guardian?
Who should bear the costs of the guardianship application and the appeal?

firac.issue: Does a Manitoba court retain jurisdiction over the guardianship and care of a child ordinarily resident in Manitoba who has been wrongfully removed from the province?
firac.facts: Bridget, age 13, had lived in Manitoba with her grandparents since 1979 and was apprehended by the statutory child care agency as a child in need of protection. While the protection petition was pending and she remained under apprehension, she was clandestinely removed from the agency's custody and taken to Indiana, where her mother and a proposed relative caregiver lived. The grandparents and mother argued the court lost jurisdiction because the child was no longer physically present and no order could be directly enforced.
firac.rule: The courts of Manitoba possess the jurisdiction exercised by the English courts of common law and equity in 1870. Ordinary residence within the jurisdiction is a sufficient basis for the exercise of jurisdiction over an infant, even where the child is physically absent (Hope v. Hope; Johnstone v. Beattie; Re P. (G.E.) (an infant), [1965] Ch. 568; Elash v. Elash; Re Walker and Walker; Nielsen v. Nielsen; Harnish v. Harnish). Absence of physical presence goes to the power of enforcement, not to the existence of jurisdiction, and residence is not displaced by wrongful removal.
firac.application: The court found Bridget was ordinarily resident in Manitoba and that this residence could not be displaced by her wrongful removal. It distinguished Hannon v. Eisler as not turning on ordinary residence and as not involving wrongful removal. The grounds for retaining jurisdiction were even stronger here because the issue of the child's future care was already before the Court of Queen's Bench when she was taken, and both grandmother and aunt had submitted to that court's jurisdiction; her removal was an affront to the court. While enforcement would depend on the willingness of the Indiana court to respect a Manitoba order, jurisdiction nonetheless existed.
firac.conclusion: The court held it retained jurisdiction over Bridget notwithstanding her removal to Indiana, because she was ordinarily resident in Manitoba and that residence was not lost by wrongful removal.

firac.issue: Should the court appoint the child care agency temporary guardian rather than leaving the child to reside with an out-of-province aunt?
firac.facts: After the abduction the agency applied for temporary guardianship. The motions judge refused guardianship but ordered that the apprehension remain in place and that Bridget reside with her aunt in Indiana pending a home study. The agency lacked certain status to seek a custody order in Indiana without a guardianship appointment; the aunt's home had not yet been assessed.
firac.rule: Where a child has been wrongfully removed, a court should fashion its order to respect the discretion of the foreign court while ensuring the child's need-of-protection issue can be raised there and that no conflicting order undermines the agency's care of the child if she returns. The court must give effect to reciprocity of respect between jurisdictions and act in the child's best interests without prejudging the merits.
firac.application: The court held the agency should be appointed temporary guardian so that it would have clear status to apply for custody in Indiana and to protect the child if she returned to Manitoba. Approving the aunt's home was premature, was based on insufficient evidence, was tantamount to acquiescing in the wrongful taking, and was inconsistent with the order that the apprehension remain in place. The guardianship was to be temporary, pending final disposition of the petition, and subject to displacement by a competent Indiana court.
firac.conclusion: The motions judge erred; the appeal was allowed and a temporary order of guardianship in favour of the agency was substituted, subject to displacement by an Indiana court.

firac.issue: Who should bear the costs of the guardianship application and the appeal?
firac.facts: The Manitoba-resident grandparents (the McKees) opposed the agency's application after the child was abducted and did not deny their complicity in her removal.
firac.rule: Costs follow the event and may be ordered against parties whose conduct necessitated the proceedings.
firac.application: Because the McKees opposed the agency and had not denied complicity in the abduction, they were ordered to pay the agency's costs of both the application and the appeal, fixed globally at $400 inclusive of a $100 factum fee and disbursements.
firac.conclusion: The McKees were ordered to pay costs fixed at $400 for both courts.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area — this is a child protection/guardianship proceeding under Manitoba's Child and Family Services Act. K047 (best interests of the child) is central: the court framed its order around the child's need of protection and best interests, and reciprocity between jurisdictions in serving those interests. K048 (custody/access) fits the guardianship and residence disputes over the child. K002 (Civil litigation) is a borderline tier-1 pick reflecting the jurisdictional/procedural dimension (whether the court could adjudicate at all). K021 (interlocutory injunction) is a weak pick — there was no injunction, but a temporary/interim guardianship order was the interim relief granted; flagged as weak. The controlled vocabulary is heavily oriented to Charter/hate-speech/Jewish-community themes and offers no dedicated 'child protection' or 'jurisdiction' term, so the family-law keywords are the closest genuine matches.

name_verification.name_in_document: Samuels c. Ville de Gatineau

defining_issues: Did the plaintiff establish a reasonable apprehension of bias sufficient to displace the presumption of judicial impartiality and warrant the presiding judge's recusation?
Should the court adjudicate the Defendants' motion to dismiss the recusation application (Demande en rejet) on its merits?

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff establish a reasonable apprehension of bias sufficient to warrant the judge's recusation?
firac.facts: Following a routine 12 December 2024 hearing on three interlocutory applications in a proceeding rooted in an alleged discriminatory-profiling claim at the Human Rights Tribunal, the self-represented plaintiff launched a stream of emails and filed a Motion to Recuse alleging, among other things, 'collusion' and a 'Deep State operation' between the judge and opposing counsel, bigotry/antisemitism/'Muslim-related religious extremist ideology', a conspiracy to deny counsel and ultra vires conduct, obstruction of his access to files, and obstruction of his interpreter. The plaintiff had a history of seeking recusation of other judges in related matters.
firac.rule: Article 201 para. 2 and art. 205 CCP govern recusation. The law establishes a strong presumption of judicial impartiality not easily displaced (Yukon Francophone School Board v Yukon (AG), 2015 SCC 25; Giroux c Entreprises Bertrand Roberge ltée, 2024 QCCA 1527). The applicant bears a heavy burden of showing a 'real likelihood or probability of bias'; the test is what an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically and having thought it through, would conclude about whether the decision-maker would not decide fairly (Committee for Justice and Liberty v National Energy Board, 1976 CanLII 2 (SCC)).
firac.application: The judge examined each ground and found them without foundation: the courtroom mix-up was an ordinary misunderstanding; litigants cannot choose their judge absent a special case-management order under art. 157 CCP, and art. 48 CCP concerns only inter-district transfers, not the movement of judges; the accusations of bigotry and antisemitism were contrived, conclusory and unsupported (the judge had granted the plaintiff's Hanukkah-based deadline request without hesitation); no decision on the Motion for a Lawyer had even been made, and the request for a chronology of proceedings was a legitimate case-management tool, not a 'legal ambush'; keeping the active physical file is standard practice and the plaintiff had misunderstood directions to review his own files; and the judge had actually assisted with translation to safeguard the parties' rights. The plaintiff's pattern of seeking recusal of judges who ruled against him (before Justices Pilon, Mandeville, and the Ontario findings of vexatious conduct) further undermined the motion's credibility. A reasonable, informed person would find no basis for questioning impartiality.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiff failed to displace the strong presumption of impartiality; the Motion to Recuse was dismissed with costs.

firac.issue: Should the Defendants' Demande en rejet of the recusation application be adjudicated on its merits?
firac.facts: The Defendants filed a motion under art. 51 CCP to dismiss the recusation application as frivolous, calumnious and dilatory.
firac.rule: The court retains discretion over whether it is necessary to adjudicate an application under art. 51 CCP.
firac.application: Although many observations in the Demande en rejet were accurate and were cited by the court, adjudicating it on the merits became unnecessary once the Motion to Recuse itself was dismissed.
firac.conclusion: The Demande en rejet was dismissed without adjudication on the merits and without costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area for this interlocutory recusation ruling. K012 (procedural fairness/natural justice) is the closest doctrinal keyword for judicial impartiality and the reasonable-apprehension-of-bias test that drives the decision. K072 (human rights tribunal) reflects that the underlying claim sits before the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal and shaped the procedural context. K093 (Jewish) and K058 (antisemitism) are engaged because the plaintiff identifies as Jewish and levelled (baseless) accusations of antisemitism against the judge — borderline, since antisemitism is not a substantive issue decided but a characterization of the accusations. K065 (racism) reflects the underlying discriminatory-profiling claim based on race and colour; also somewhat peripheral to the recusation ruling itself. No dedicated 'recusal' keyword exists in the vocabulary, so procedural fairness is the best available fit.
location_rationale: The decision is issued by the Superior Court, 'DISTRICT OF GATINEAU', file no. 550-17-012903-231, and dated 15 January 2025 in the Province of Quebec.
registry_rationale: The heading identifies the 'DISTRICT OF GATINEAU' and the judge notes he will return the physical file 'to the courthouse in Gatineau', confirming the Gatineau registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Robinson

defining_issues: Can a mandatory minimum sentence for robbery with a prohibited weapon be reduced below the minimum on account of the offender's Gladue/Indigenous background?
Does horizontal stare decisis bind the court to follow the most recent Superior Court decision (Hilaire) holding that Duncan credit cannot reduce a sentence below a mandatory minimum?

Do the particularly harsh and demeaning pre-trial custody conditions endured by the offender warrant enhanced Duncan credit that effectively results in a time-served sentence despite the mandatory minimum?

firac.issue: Can the offender's Indigenous background and reduced moral culpability justify a sentence below the five-year mandatory minimum for robbery with a prohibited weapon?
firac.facts: Jaiden Robinson, a 31-year-old Black and Status First Nations man with a textbook Gladue profile of intergenerational trauma, abuse, addiction and systemic disadvantage, pleaded guilty to robbery with a prohibited weapon carrying a five-year mandatory minimum. The parties jointly recommended the five-year minimum.
firac.rule: Section 718.2(e) of the Criminal Code requires courts to consider the unique circumstances of Indigenous offenders, but R. v. Hilbach, 2023 SCC 3, holds that Gladue factors cannot justify a sentence below a mandatory minimum unless the minimum is grossly disproportionate under s. 12 of the Charter. Section 718.1 requires proportionality to the gravity of the offence and the offender's responsibility.
firac.application: The Court accepted that Mr. Robinson's Indigeneity and background significantly mitigated his moral culpability, but applied Hilbach and Hilaire: Parliament may prioritize denunciation and deterrence for armed robbery, and although the minimum departs from parity and proportionality in his case, it is not grossly disproportionate. His heritage and the effects of intergenerational trauma therefore could not reduce the sentence below the minimum or, on their own, ground Duncan credit.
firac.conclusion: The five-year mandatory minimum stood; Indigenous background alone could not lower the sentence below the minimum.

firac.issue: Was the sentencing judge bound by the most recent Superior Court authority (Hilaire) that Duncan credit cannot reduce a sentence below a mandatory minimum?
firac.facts: Superior Court authorities conflicted: Vassel and Fogah-Pierre allowed Duncan credit to reduce a mandatory minimum, while the more recent Hilaire distinguished Vassel on the basis that it predated Hilbach and held Duncan credit could not reduce a sentence below the minimum.
firac.rule: R. v. Sullivan, 2022 SCC 19, provides that a judge faced with conflicting coordinate authority must follow the most recent decision unless the Spruce Mills criteria are met: (1) the earlier decision's rationale was undermined by later appellate authority; (2) it was reached per incuriam; or (3) it was not fully considered.
firac.application: The Court accepted Justice Denison's analysis in Hilaire and its refusal to follow Vassel. However, it distinguished Hilaire on its facts: Justice Denison had not confronted a situation where the correctional institution acted with such deliberate disrespect and flagrant disregard for the cultural and traditional beliefs of Indigenous inmates, conditions that increased the harshness of detention well beyond what Gladue mitigation contemplates.
firac.conclusion: The judge accepted Hilaire's legal analysis but found it did not govern the exceptional conditions here, leaving room to grant Duncan credit for the institution's conduct rather than for Indigeneity as mitigation.

firac.issue: Did the particularly harsh and demeaning pre-trial custody conditions warrant enhanced Duncan credit resulting in a time-served sentence?
firac.facts: Over 809 days at the Toronto South Detention Centre, Mr. Robinson endured at least 128 days of 24-hour lockdown, triple bunking, denial of medical and dental care for injuries sustained on arrest despite judicial recommendations, elimination of the Indigenous range and vacant NILO position, refusal to rebuild a ceremonial teepee, and the September 2025 disposal of Indigenous artwork, teachings, prayers and medicine pouches in garbage bins, which inmates had to retrieve themselves. His affidavit was unchallenged.
firac.rule: R. v. Duncan, 2016 ONCA 754, and R. v. Marshall, 2021 ONCA 344, hold that particularly punitive pre-trial conditions are a mitigating factor in arriving at a fit sentence (over and above the s. 719(3.1)/Summers 1.5 credit) but must not skew the sentence or take on unwarranted significance; quantification is permissible though not preferred (also R. v. Brown, 2025 ONCA 164; R. v. Reid, 2026 ONSC 136).
firac.application: The Court found the conditions constituted state conduct falling below acceptable standards of humane detention, reflecting deliberate institutional neglect and contempt for Indigenous culture rather than isolated deficiencies. These conditions, not attributable to Mr. Robinson's conduct, made his remand significantly more punitive than tolerable and demanded a message be sent to the institution. Given a Summers entitlement of 1,213 days for 809 actual days, the Court granted a further Duncan credit of 611 days for the particularly harmful conditions.
firac.conclusion: Enhanced Duncan credit of 611 days was granted, leaving one further day to be served on the five-year (1,825-day) sentence.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the core practice area — this is a sentencing decision for robbery with a prohibited weapon involving mandatory minimums, Gladue principles and Duncan/Summers credit. K074 (systemic discrimination) captures the court's extensive treatment of Indigenous overrepresentation, colonialism and systemic institutional neglect. K071 (human dignity) reflects the reasoning that conditions of detention undermined human dignity (drawing on Hilbach). K031 (religious accommodation) is used broadly for the failure to accommodate the offender's Indigenous spiritual/cultural practices (ceremonies, smudging, medicine pouches, NILO access) — a central factual driver of the enhanced credit. K007 (Human rights) and K069 (discrimination) are added as the conditions engage humane-detention and discrimination concerns. These picks are somewhat constrained: the controlled vocabulary lacks dedicated terms for sentencing, mandatory minimums, Gladue/Indigenous offenders or Duncan credit, so K074, K071, K031, K007 and K069 are best-available proxies and should be treated as borderline rather than exact matches.
location_rationale: The decision is of the Ontario Court of Justice and the court file is designated 'Toronto'; the offence and detention (Toronto South Detention Centre) occurred in Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The header states 'COURT FILE No.: Toronto', identifying the Toronto registry of the Ontario Court of Justice.

name_verification.name_in_document: Sealy c. R.

defining_issues: Did the trial judge err in refusing to adjourn the trial to permit a complete psychiatric assessment of the accused's criminal responsibility (mental disorder under s. 16 C.cr.), thereby compromising trial fairness?
Was the first degree murder verdict unreasonable?

firac.issue: Did the trial judge's refusal to adjourn the trial to allow a full psychiatric assessment of the accused's criminal responsibility compromise the fairness of the trial?
firac.facts: Sealy, who had a documented psychiatric history including a prior diagnosis of schizophrenia and a previous NCR verdict, was tried for the murders of his aunt and uncle committed shortly after being unconditionally discharged. Judge Mascia had ordered an assessment of his criminal responsibility on reasonable grounds, but it was never completed because the accused denied involvement. At the opening of trial, defence counsel relayed the Philippe-Pinel Institute's position that a proper evaluation of the accused's deteriorating and fluctuating mental state required 30 days of continuous, full-time, 24-hour observation, which was impossible if the trial continued with daily court attendance. The trial judge refused the adjournment and ordered the assessment be done within five days during the ongoing trial; no meaningful evaluation of his criminal responsibility was completed and no such evidence went to the jury.
firac.rule: A stay or adjournment of a trial should not be ordered without compelling reason, and appellate deference is owed to a refusal to adjourn; however, the court must intervene to protect trial fairness. The framework in R. c. Swain, [1991] 1 R.C.S. 933 permits deferring the mental-disorder issue and its determination until after a guilty verdict but before it is entered.
firac.application: The Court found the Philippe-Pinel Institute's request, relayed by counsel at the outset, was reasonable given the deterioration of the accused's mental state and the complexity of the case. Although accommodating the request would have delayed the trial by at least 30 days, the arrest had occurred three and a half years earlier, so the adjournment would not have significantly affected the overall delay. The issue of criminal responsibility was crucial, and the procedure followed caused the accused significant prejudice, so despite the deference owed, intervention was required to ensure a fair trial.
firac.conclusion: The refusal to adjourn undermined trial fairness; the appeal was allowed on this ground.

firac.issue: Was the first degree murder verdict unreasonable?
firac.facts: The aunt was attacked while in bed, dying from blunt cranial trauma and sharp-force cervical injury; all circumstances supported planning and deliberation. The appellant relied on R. c. Denison, 2001 BCCA 703.
firac.rule: A verdict may be set aside if it is unreasonable; the reviewing court assesses whether the evidence supports the verdict.
firac.application: The Court held the appellant had not shown the verdict to be unreasonable: the evidence established the victim was in bed at the time of the attack and all circumstances supported the verdict. Denison was distinguishable because there the evidence did not establish the victim was in bed ('perhaps as she lay in bed').
firac.conclusion: The first degree murder verdict was not unreasonable; this ground failed, but the appeal succeeded on the fairness ground.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the clear primary classification, as the case concerns murder convictions and the mental-disorder defence under s. 16 C.cr. K112 (Charter s. 7) is a moderate fit because the decisive ground is trial fairness/fundamental justice, though the Court frames it as 'équité du procès' rather than expressly invoking s. 7. K107 (Canadian Charter) is included as the parent for that fairness reasoning but is a weak/inferential pick. K002 (Civil litigation) and K011 (judicial review) are weak fillers reflecting the appellate review of a discretionary refusal to adjourn — flagged as weak because the controlled vocabulary is oriented toward antisemitism/Jewish-related matters and contains no keyword for mental disorder/NCR, fitness, adjournment, or unreasonable verdict, which are the true subjects here.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'COUR D'APPEL', 'PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC', 'GREFFE DE MONTRÉAL', and the appeal is from a Superior Court jury trial in the 'district de Montréal'.
registry_rationale: The heading expressly states 'GREFFE DE MONTRÉAL', indicating the Montréal registry of the Quebec Court of Appeal.

case_name: Ross v. New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15 (No. 1)

name_verification.name_in_document: Malcolm Ross v. The Board of School Trustees, District No.15, Human Rights Board of Inquiry, David Attis, Human Rights Commission, The Minister of Labour, Department of Education, New Brunswick Teachers' Federation, The Canadian Jewish Congress
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The short style of cause 'Ross v. New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15 (No. 1)' is a conventional abbreviation of the full style of cause printed in the decision. The decision text carries the reporter reference 'CHRR Doc. 90-056' rather than the neutral citation '1990 CanLII 12491 (NB QB)', but there is no substantive inconsistency.

defining_issues: Does an applicant in a proceeding commenced by Notice of Application (as opposed to an action) have a right to examine the respondents on discovery?

Should the Court exercise its discretion to permit examination of the sole board-of-inquiry member, the Minister of Labour, and the Human Rights Commissioner to investigate an alleged reasonable apprehension of bias in the board of inquiry?

firac.issue: Does an applicant proceeding by Notice of Application have an automatic right to examine the respondents for discovery under the Rules of Court?
firac.facts: Malcolm Ross, a teacher facing a human-rights complaint that he and his School District discriminated against David Attis and his children, commenced a Notice of Application and sought to examine for discovery the board-of-inquiry member Brian Bruce, the Minister of Labour, and the Chief Commissioner of the Human Rights Commission, all of whom had refused to appear.
firac.rule: Rule 32.02(1) of the New Brunswick Rules of Court (N.B. Reg. 82-73) permits a party to 'an action' to examine an adverse party for discovery, and Rule 1.04 defines 'action' as a proceeding commenced by issuing a Notice of Action. Rule 38.09(b) allows conversion of an application to a trial only where there is a substantial dispute of fact; Rule 39.02(1) allows examination of a non-party before hearing.
firac.application: The proceeding was commenced by Notice of Application, not by Notice of Action, so it did not fall within the definition of 'action.' Only parties to an action have an automatic right of examination for discovery; applicants and respondents in an application do not. There was no substantial dispute of fact warranting conversion of the application to an action under Rule 38.09(b).
firac.conclusion: The applicant had no automatic right to examine the respondents for discovery, and no basis existed to convert the application into an action.

firac.issue: Should the Court exercise its discretion to allow examination of the board-of-inquiry member, the Minister of Labour, and the Human Rights Commissioner to gather evidence of a reasonable apprehension of bias?
firac.facts: Ross alleged a reasonable apprehension of bias in the one-person board of inquiry (Brian Bruce) and wanted to examine Bruce, the Minister of Labour and the Commissioner to gather further information, relying on an affidavit and materials referring to utterances of the Minister and Commissioner but containing very scant evidence directly implicating Bruce.
firac.rule: An applicant alleging reasonable apprehension of bias must ordinarily support the allegation by affidavit evidence; the court retains discretion over pre-hearing examinations and must ensure the process is fair to all parties, that all relevant facts are before it, and that matters are disposed of expeditiously.
firac.application: The affidavit offered virtually no evidence relating directly to Brian Bruce, so permitting his examination would amount to an impermissible 'fishing expedition.' As Bruce was the person who would hear and decide the complaint, the only potentially relevant bias was his own; examining the Minister of Labour and the Commissioner was neither warranted nor proper, and the interests of justice would not be served by allowing it.
firac.conclusion: The Court declined to order any of the requested examinations.

K072 (human rights tribunal) applies because the adjudicator was a board of inquiry appointed to hear a Human Rights Commission complaint, and K069 (discrimination) reflects the underlying complaint of religious discrimination. K093 (Jewish) and K090 (Canadian Jewish Congress) are entity keywords tied to the complainant's family and a named respondent. No judicial-review keyword was used because this was a discovery/procedural motion, not a review on the merits.
