registry_rationale: The decision identifies the district and locality as Laval («DISTRICT DE LAVAL / LOCALITÉ DE LAVAL»), so the registry is Laval.

name_verification.name_in_document: Her Majesty the Queen v. Harding [Indexed as: R. v. Harding]

defining_issues: Is wilful blindness a constitutionally sufficient mens rea for the offence of wilfully promoting hatred under s. 319(2) of the Criminal Code, consistent with the freedom of expression guarantee in s. 2(b) of the Charter?

Did the trial judge err in interpreting and applying the s. 319(3)(b) defence (good-faith expression of an opinion on a religious subject) narrowly, so as to deny it where hate-promoting statements were intermingled with protected religious comment?

firac.issue: Is wilful blindness a constitutionally adequate mens rea for wilfully promoting hatred under s. 319(2), given s. 2(b) of the Charter?
firac.facts: Harding wrote and distributed pamphlets and a telephone message portraying Muslims in Canada as violent, dangerous and part of a conspiracy to take over Canada. The trial judge found he intended to promote hatred, or at least was wilfully blind to that being a substantially certain consequence. On appeal Harding argued wilful blindness falls short of the stringent mens rea required to justify s. 319(2)'s limit on free expression.
firac.rule: Under Keegstra (1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)), s. 319(2) infringes s. 2(b) but is justified under s. 1 in part because it carries a stringent mens rea—an intent to promote hatred or knowledge of the substantial certainty of that result; Buzzanga (1979) excludes recklessness. Sansregret (1985 CanLII 79 (SCC)), Hawkins and Davis establish that wilful blindness is a purely subjective form of mens rea equivalent to knowledge: the accused suspects a fact, realizes its probability, and deliberately refrains from confirming it to be able to deny knowledge.
firac.application: The court examined the nature of wilful blindness and held it is distinct from recklessness (which has an objective dimension) and is the legal equivalent of actual knowledge. Because it requires subjective suspicion, realization of probability, and deliberate avoidance of confirmation, it meets the stringent, subjective standard Keegstra demanded for s. 2(b) purposes. Neither s. 2(b) nor any principle of statutory construction (the word 'wilfully' does not exclude wilful blindness, which equals knowledge) bars it. The court also found the trial judge had actually made a clear finding of intent, merely acknowledging he could not eliminate the remote possibility of wilful blindness.
firac.conclusion: Wilful blindness is a constitutionally sufficient mens rea for s. 319(2); the trial judge committed no error even if he convicted on that basis. Ground of appeal rejected.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err by construing the s. 319(3)(b) religious-opinion defence too narrowly and denying it where hateful statements were mixed with religious comment?
firac.facts: Harding's communications contained sincerely held religious opinions about the falseness of Islam, but also intermixed false allegations that all Muslims in Canada are dangerous terrorists calculated to arouse fear and hatred. He argued the trial judge isolated statements from their context rather than conducting a contextual analysis under Charter values.
firac.rule: Section 319(3)(b) of the Criminal Code provides a defence where the accused, in good faith, expressed or attempted to establish by argument an opinion on a religious subject. The defence must be construed contextually but consistently with the purpose of s. 319.
firac.application: The court found the trial judge did analyze the statements in context, accepting the religious opinions were sincerely held but finding the hate-promoting allegations were separate, false statements calculated to arouse fear and hatred. The defence cannot protect statements promoting hatred merely because they are embedded within a larger statement containing religious opinion; otherwise religious opinion could be used with impunity as a 'Trojan Horse' to carry a forbidden message of hate. The defence rationally protects only the rare case where the very statements promoting hatred are themselves a good-faith expression of a religious opinion.
firac.conclusion: No error; the defence was properly held unavailable. Ground of appeal rejected.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary tier-1 area—this is a Criminal Code hate-propaganda prosecution and appeal. K067 (wilful promotion of hatred) is the core offence under s. 319(2); K115 (Criminal Code s. 319(2)) pins the specific provision. K061 (hate speech) captures the hate-propaganda subject matter. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) reflect the constitutional argument that the mens rea/defence interpretation must respect free expression. K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 parent for those Charter issues. K058 (antisemitism) is a borderline/weak pick—the material was anti-Muslim, but the vocabulary lacks an Islamophobia term; included cautiously only because it is the closest hate-target descriptor, though it is arguably inapt since the target was Muslims, not Jews. Better justified is K032 (religious symbols/dress) — also weak; on reflection the target group is Muslims and religion-based hatred, so I retain it loosely as religion-related. The strongest, cleanly applicable keywords are K004, K067, K061, K024, K111, K115, K003.

The underlying conviction was entered by Chief Judge Linden of the Ontario Court (Provincial Division) 'in Toronto', and the offending conduct concerned Western Collegiate and Toronto; the appeal court sits in Toronto. name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Gabriale Rene St. Constantine, aka David Paul Holder, aka Daniel Thomas MacCabee

defining_issues: What is a fit sentence for returning to Canada without authorization after having been deported, contrary to s. 52(1) and s. 124(1)(a) of the IRPA?
Do the offender's claimed fears (US political unrest and COVID-19) constitute mitigating factors reducing the sentence?
Does the COVID-19 pandemic, as a collateral consequence, warrant a reduction in the period of incarceration?

firac.issue: What is a fit sentence for an offender who returns to Canada without authorization after deportation, contrary to s. 52(1) and s. 124(1)(a) of the IRPA?
firac.facts: Mr. St. Constantine, a US citizen with a prior criminal record and three deportation orders, re-entered Canada near Surrey some 20 minutes after being escorted to the US border on September 14, 2020, having told CBSA he would keep trying to enter. He pleaded guilty. Crown sought 12 months; defence sought time served (32 days, 47 days enhanced credit).
firac.rule: Section 52(1) IRPA bars a foreign national from returning after a removal order is enforced; s. 124(1)(a) makes contravention an offence, punishable on indictment under s. 125 by up to a $50,000 fine and/or up to 2 years' imprisonment. Sentencing is governed by the purposes and principles in s. 718 of the Criminal Code, with deterrence and denunciation emphasized for such immigration offences (R. v. Polnac, 2017 BCSC 2408; R. v. Williams; R. v. Luckstein, [1995] B.C.J. No. 2206; R. v. Dosson, [2018] B.C.J. No. 3298; R. v. Suarez, 2019 QCCA 649).
firac.application: The court found the four elements of the offence proven by the guilty plea. It weighed mitigating factors (early guilty plea, dated record, expressed remorse, no contraband, no assault on officers) against strong aggravating factors (familiarity with deportation orders, flagrant re-entry 20 minutes after removal, prior removal orders, stated intention to keep returning). Emphasizing that the key sentencing considerations for this offence are general and specific deterrence rather than rehabilitation, and reviewing the case law range, the court found a step-up from his previous 4-month conviction warranted.
firac.conclusion: A sentence of 9 months' incarceration was imposed, less credit for 47 days (32 days at enhanced credit).

firac.issue: Do the offender's asserted fears of US political unrest and COVID-19 constitute mitigating factors?
firac.facts: Defence submitted that Mr. St. Constantine, having read online media at an Oregon shelter, feared political turmoil, open carrying of firearms, the Confederate flag, and COVID-19, and briefly made (then withdrew) a refugee claim seeking safety in Canada and ultimately Israel because he is Jewish.
firac.rule: Mitigating factors must have a genuine nexus to the offender's personal circumstances; general or broad-sweeping fears unsupported by evidence of personal threat do not mitigate (drawing on R. v. Polnac, 2017 BCSC 2408, paras. 27, 31).
firac.application: The court found no evidence that Mr. St. Constantine, a Caucasian US citizen of Jewish faith, had been personally intimidated, threatened, or subjected to violence. His COVID-related fear was undercut by his admitted awareness that COVID is a global pandemic and that the border had been closed since March 20, 2020, and that the vast US afforded him safer options within his own country.
firac.conclusion: The court was 'not convinced'; the asserted fears were rejected as mitigating factors.

firac.issue: Does the COVID-19 pandemic warrant a reduction in the period of incarceration as a collateral consequence?
firac.facts: Defence urged a reduced sentence given custodial infection risk during the pandemic; the offender is 59, diabetic, with two prior heart issues, but otherwise healthy.
firac.rule: COVID-19 is a collateral consequence relevant to proportionality but does not itself justify a disproportionately lenient sentence or one drastically outside the range (R. v. Hearns, 2020 ONSC 2365; R. v. Stevens, 2020 BCPC 104, para. 47; R. v. Morgan, 2020 ONCA 279; R. v. Lemmen, 2020 BCPC 67; R. v. Parasmothy, 2020 ONSC 2314).
firac.application: The court balanced custodial infection risk against the offender's own flagrant conduct in exposing himself, CBSA officers, and the public to COVID by crossing the closed border. It found no personalized circumstances making incarceration disproportionate and noted the irony of his invoking COVID after choosing to put others at risk.
firac.conclusion: COVID-19 was treated as a collateral consequence considered in the analysis but did not justify a reduced sentence.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary practice area: this is a criminal sentencing proceeding by indictment applying Criminal Code s. 718 principles. K008 (Immigration law) and K076 (deportation) are central because the offence is unauthorized return after enforced removal under IRPA ss. 52(1) and 124(1)(a) and turns on prior deportation orders. K078 (refugee protection) is engaged because the offender made and quickly withdrew a refugee claim, though weak as it was abandoned. K093 (Jewish) and K103 (Israel) are drawn from his stated desire to seek refuge as a Jewish person and reach Israel; both are borderline/contextual mentions and are flagged as weak, included to reach the minimum and capture the offender's asserted motivation.

case_name: Rhodes v. All Pro Building Maintenance Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: Rhodes v. All Pro Building Maintenance Ltd.

defining_issues: Should the claimants' Reply be struck in whole or in part under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules on the grounds that it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, vexatious, embarrassing or an abuse of process?

Do particular impugned passages of the Reply improperly plead evidence, argument, or new causes of action, or create confusion inconsistent with the Amended Notice of Civil Claim, so as to warrant striking?

firac.issue: Should the claimants' Reply be struck in whole or in part under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs alleged breach of a contract concerning cleaning of B.C. Ferry Authority vessels. The defendants applied to strike the Reply filed February 16, 2011 in its entirety, or alternatively portions of it, as unnecessary, frivolous, vexatious, embarrassing, an abuse of process or likely to cause delay. No evidence was advanced by the claimant in support of the pleading.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) and 9-5(2) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules permit striking a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim/defence, is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial, or is otherwise an abuse of process. The moving party must show it is "plain and obvious" that the pleading offends the subrule (347202 B.C. Ltd. v. CIBC). Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union, 2006 BCSC 750 and Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860 set out when pleadings are unintelligible, without substance, scandalous, embarrassing, unnecessary or frivolous. Rule 3-7(1) forbids pleading the evidence, Rule 3-7(6) forbids inconsistent allegations, and Rule 3-7(15) requires answering the point of substance.
firac.application: The Master declined to strike the Reply in its entirety but reviewed each impugned passage individually, applying the principle that poor drafting alone is insufficient and that it must be plain and obvious the pleading offends the Rule. Most impugned italicized portions were found to plead evidence, advance argument, be scandalous, or attempt to raise new causes of action.
firac.conclusion: The application succeeded in substantial part: numerous portions of the Reply were struck, though a few (paragraphs 15 and 16) were left standing. The respondents were awarded costs in any event of the cause.

firac.issue: Do the particular impugned passages improperly plead evidence, argument, or new causes of action, or create confusion inconsistent with the pleadings?
firac.facts: The Reply contained passages such as "There is ample evidence that...", references to admissions made by Ko at his examination for discovery, allegations that Allpro was "created by Ko" (inconsistent with the Amended Notice of Civil Claim's assertion that Ko "assumed ownership" and paragraph 7's "set up"), and allegations about diversion of funds and contract extensions "into the future".
firac.rule: Rule 3-7(1): a pleading must not contain the evidence by which facts are proved. Rule 3-7(6): a party must not plead facts inconsistent with a previous pleading. A pleading is embarrassing/irrelevant when so confusing it is difficult to understand what is pleaded (Gittings; Keddie); scandalous allegations are struck only if also irrelevant; new causes of action improperly raised in a Reply are objectionable.
firac.application: The Master struck: para 1 (confusing/inconsistent as to who created Allpro), para 2 (pleading of evidence – reference to union agent confirmation), paras 3-4 (argumentative and irrelevant), para 5 ("ample evidence" phrasing and duplication of ANCC), para 6 (pleading discovery evidence), para 7 (same confusion as para 1), para 8 (pleading of evidence), para 9 (evidence and scandalous), para 11 (evidence/new cause of action re future extensions), para 12 (evidence), para 13 (argument/submissions), para 14 (submissions and evidence), para 17 (argument), para 18 (confusion re ownership, scandalous diversion allegations, discovery evidence, irrelevant proper-party assertion), para 19 (unnecessary/argument). Paragraph 15 did not offend the Rules and paragraph 16 was treated as effectively a traverse.
firac.conclusion: The bulk of the impugned italicized portions were struck as pleadings of evidence, argument, scandalous material or improper new claims; paragraphs 15 and 16 survived.

The controlled vocabulary contains no term for striking pleadings, pleadings practice, or limitation defences, so the remaining picks are weak/borderline and included only to reach the minimum: K020 (class action), K021 (interlocutory injunction), K011 (judicial review) and K022 (restitution) are all civil-procedure/remedies tier-2 items but none is actually engaged by this decision — they are the closest available terms and should be treated as non-substantive. name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied style of cause is 'R. v. F.(J.E.)' using initials, whereas the decision is styled and indexed 'R. v. defining_issues: Was the Crown's evidence of the complainant's prior consistent statements (recent-complaint evidence) admissible, and did the absence of a limiting instruction constitute reversible non-direction?
Was lay evidence of the complainant's episodes of emotional upset admissible as direct evidence of sexual assault in the absence of expert evidence linking the emotional state to the assaults?

Did the trial judge err in failing to give a limiting instruction on evidence of the accused's bad character, and in his treatment of Crown counsel's unsubstantiated suggestion that the accused was anti-Jewish?

firac.issue: Was the Crown's evidence of the complainant's prior consistent statements admissible, and did the lack of a limiting instruction amount to reversible error?
firac.facts: The Crown, in examination-in-chief, elicited from the complainant that she had told her aunt, her father, her Grade 5 teacher, a school friend (Marla), and a social worker (Rose Szaba) that the appellant was abusing her, and that her father then told her mother she had been sexually abused. Defence objected and sought a mistrial before any allegation of recent fabrication had been made. The trial judge admitted the evidence as 'historical background' and gave no limiting instruction.
firac.rule: Prior consistent statements are generally inadmissible (R. v. Jones (1988); R. v. Campbell (1977); Wigmore). Following abrogation of the recent-complaint rules by s. 275 of the Criminal Code, such statements are admissible only (1) to rebut an allegation of recent fabrication once that issue is a live one, (2) as res gestae (a narrow exception, per R. v. Khan (SCC)), or (3) as part of the narrative — relevant, essential facts explaining the victim's experience and how the matter came to authorities (R. v. Owens; R. v. Cassibo; R. v. George). In every case the trial judge must instruct the jury that the statements are admitted only for the fact they were made, not for the truth of their contents (R. v. Lajoie).
firac.application: The statements could not be admitted to rebut recent fabrication because no such allegation had yet been raised when the Crown led the evidence in chief. Most of the evidence, however, met the narrative criteria, explaining the child's silence and how the offence came to light — except the double hearsay about what the father told the mother and the statements to the Grade 5 teacher and the school friend, which neither advanced nor enlarged the narrative and should have been excluded. Crucially, the trial judge gave no limiting instruction, so the jury was never told not to use the content of the statements as proof; the content could be perceived as self-corroboration of the complainant's story.
firac.conclusion: The narrative portion was admissible with a proper limiting direction, but the total absence of any limiting instruction was serious non-direction amounting to misdirection.

firac.issue: Was lay evidence of the complainant's emotional upset admissible as direct evidence that she was sexually assaulted, without expert evidence connecting it to the assaults?
firac.facts: The aunt, mother and father described four episodes of emotional disturbance (nervousness, clinging, hysterical crying in a mall, despondency, sleep disruption) occurring at various times, some years after the alleged assaults. The trial judge admitted this as showing the effect of the sexual assaults; no expert evidence linked the emotional state to the assaults, and in one episode the complainant's actual words were never disclosed.
firac.rule: Contemporaneous physical injury or hysteria may be admissible as corroborative of a sexual assault where there is a nexus to the assault. Expert evidence of psychological/physical conditions typically arising from sexual abuse is admissible to assist the trier of fact (R. v. B.(G.), SCC). Where the Crown relies on lay descriptions of emotional condition as direct evidence of assault, expert evidence relating that condition to sexual abuse is required; absent a nexus such evidence has no probative value and is prejudicial.
firac.application: Nothing connected the four episodes to the sexual assaults. The mood changes could equally reflect ordinary childhood difficulties or unhappiness in the household. The Crown was obliged to call an expert to relate the emotional trauma to the alleged assaults. Left uncontextualized, the evidence had no probative value and was highly prejudicial, and again no limiting instruction was given despite the Crown's forceful closing reliance on the complainant's emotional condition.
firac.conclusion: The emotional-state evidence was of no probative value and highly prejudicial, and its admission without expert linkage or any limiting instruction was error.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err by failing to give a limiting instruction on bad-character evidence and by his handling of Crown counsel's unsubstantiated 'anti-Jewish' suggestion?
firac.facts: Evidence of the appellant's physical abuse of the complainant's mother was admitted. In cross-examining defence character witness Dr. Spinner, Crown counsel stated (not as a question) that he was 'led to believe' the appellant would not let the complainant play with the witness's daughter because she was a Jewish girl; there was no follow-up or supporting evidence. The trial judge told the jury there was 'not a shred of evidence' for it but added 'in my view discrimination is violence'.
firac.rule: Evidence of an accused's discreditable conduct, though admissible for a permissible purpose, requires a limiting instruction that the jury not reason from bad character to guilt (R. v. B.(F.F.), SCC). Crown counsel must not put unsubstantiated allegations to witnesses on collateral issues.
firac.application: The physical-abuse evidence was properly admitted because the complainant witnessed it and it explained her fear and silence, but the jury should have been told not to treat it as showing the appellant was the type to commit the offence. The 'anti-Jewish' remark was a gratuitous, unsupported smear raising a poisonous, irrelevant side issue; rather than condemning it, the trial judge lent it respectability by equating discrimination with violence in a trial about violence against a child.
firac.conclusion: The failure to give a proper limiting instruction on the bad-character evidence, together with the mishandling of the improper cross-examination, added to the accumulation of non-direction/misdirection.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Lee

defining_issues: Did the accused have the requisite intent to threaten (to intimidate or cause fear) when he posted the message on his Facebook page, so as to be guilty of uttering a threat to cause death?

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused intended his November 10, 2009 Facebook posting as a threat to cause death?
firac.facts: Harold Lee was charged with one count of threatening death after posting on his own Facebook page (accessible to 273 'friends') a message stating he was 'bringing death with me this time around' and referencing priests, judges, cops, lawyers and teachers. His Facebook history contained swastikas, a reference to the Virginia Tech massacre, and anti-Semitic comments, and he had been cautioned earlier by police. Lee testified the posting referred to his work transporting dead bodies for the Coroner during the H1N1 outbreak and reflected his habitual practice of documenting his experiences and religious thoughts.
firac.rule: To convict of uttering a threat (Criminal Code s. 264.1), the court must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused intended to intimidate and/or cause fear. The test is objective, requiring assessment of the words used, the context, the person(s) to whom they were directed, and the accused's explanation.
firac.application: The court noted the message was posted on Lee's own page rather than sent to any target, and that Facebook's passive format diminished the seriousness attachable to the words. Reviewing Lee's habitual, often religious and mundane postings, the court found his explanation credible: the colour black referred to his uniform and his vehicle, the biblical reference was one he could pinpoint precisely, and his Coroner work transporting bodies during H1N1 was an undisputed fact. Although the postings were offensive and disturbing, they were not the subject of the charge and showed no connection to the impugned message. The explanation, combined with the context, left the court in reasonable doubt as to intent.
firac.conclusion: The Crown failed to prove the requisite intent beyond a reasonable doubt; Lee was found not guilty.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Kazman

defining_issues: Did the Crown prove the actus reus and mens rea of fraud over $5,000 (s. 380(1)(a)) against each defendant, i.e. a dishonest act (false documents, inflated/false invoices, fabricated leases) causing deprivation or risk of deprivation to the banks?
Did the Crown prove that the banks relied to their detriment on the misrepresentations, given that the underwriters who approved the loans were not called as witnesses?
Who owned and controlled the 'Disputed Construction Companies,' and were they sham corporations used to divert fraudulently obtained SBL proceeds?
Were Kazman and Levy guilty of laundering the proceeds of crime under s. 462.31(1)?
Did Kazman, Levy and others commit fraud for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with a criminal organization under s. 467.12, and did such an organization exist?
Where knowledge was in issue, were the defendants (particularly Kazman) actually knowing participants or at least wilfully blind?

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove fraud over $5,000 against each defendant?
firac.facts: Sixteen SBLs (~$2.8M) were obtained from BNS, TD, BOM, RBC and CIBC between June 2007 and March 2010 through newly incorporated companies owned by Ms. Cohen and the defendants. Loan files contained altered GICs, forged Notices of Assessment/T1 Generals, fraudulent leases, and construction/supply invoices for leasehold improvements and equipment that were largely never done or supplied, inducing the banks to advance funds.
firac.rule: Under R. v. Théroux, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 5 and R. v. Olan, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 1175, the actus reus of fraud (s. 380(1)(a)) requires a dishonest act (deceit, falsehood or other fraudulent means, including non-disclosure) plus deprivation (actual loss or risk of prejudice to economic interests). The mens rea requires subjective knowledge of the prohibited act and that it could cause deprivation. Circumstantial evidence is assessed cumulatively (R. v. Villaroman, 2016 SCC 33), the only reasonable inference from which must be guilt.
firac.application: For the four 'Cohen SBLs' (ELFI, ELI, LHC, LSC), Contempo, CDI, Alta, Modernito, Kube, Homelife, Uzeem and Bluerock, the court found leasehold improvements were not done and/or equipment not supplied, and invoices were fraudulently inflated or the loans were complete shams. Levy prepared the fraudulent documents and invoices; Kazman (with Levy and Cohen) controlled the Disputed Construction Companies that received the proceeds. For Qua, Roxy and World/Exclusive the court retained a reasonable doubt (no evidence of pre-renovation condition; possible legitimate operation; no kickbacks), acquitting on those.
firac.conclusion: Fraud was proven beyond a reasonable doubt on numerous counts against Kazman and Levy, on Alta against Ali Vaez Tehrani, and on Uzeem and Kube against Madjid Vaez Tehrani; not proven against Chapkina, Ghatan and Armand Levy.

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove detrimental reliance by the banks without calling the underwriters?
firac.facts: The Crown called bank representatives (account managers) who dealt with the borrowers, not the underwriters who approved the loans. The defence argued the Crown failed to prove the banks relied on the misrepresentations.
firac.rule: Causation/reliance is a question of fact provable by direct evidence or reasonable inference (R. v. Park, 2010 ABCA 248; R. v. Steinhubl, 2010 ABQB 602; R. v. Winning, [1973] O.J. No. 461). The dishonest conduct need only be one contributing cause outside the de minimis range; reliance may be inferred from loan documents and lender policies, and the underwriters need not testify. Where a misrepresentation is not material or not relied upon (Winning), fraud is not made out.
firac.application: Where invoices misrepresented that work had been done or equipment supplied, the court readily inferred reliance because the banks advanced funds to pay those invoices. However, for misrepresentations of income, GICs and 'arm's length' status alone (e.g. World/Exclusive), the court held the general evidence that misrepresentation was a 'deal breaker' did not establish what the bank actually relied on, particularly where Ms. Hsu was subpoenaed but not called; reliance was not proven for those items.
firac.conclusion: Reliance was proven for the fraudulent invoice-based frauds but not for certain document misrepresentations standing alone, contributing to acquittals on some counts.

firac.issue: Were the Disputed Construction Companies shams controlled by Kazman, Levy and Cohen?
firac.facts: Six companies (Northwood, Eastern, Oakwood, Icon, Whitehorse, A&P), plus Levy's companies (Mosaic, MDC, Trust Inc.), issued near-identical 'Total Gut Job/Total Rebuild' invoices; Kazman incorporated them through nominees and was signing officer; Levy faxed several invoices and admitted subcontracting; the Coort forensic analysis showed proceeds circulated among companies of Kazman, Levy and Cohen with little spent on suppliers or payroll.
firac.rule: Circumstantial evidence assessed cumulatively; the ultimate standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt applies to central findings of fact. A finding of who controls corporations that received fraudulently obtained SBL proceeds is determinative of party liability.
firac.application: Ms. Chapkina's evidence that Kazman used his companies and Levy his own, the nominee incorporators' evidence, Kazman's admissions ('happy to get the job'), the Whitehorse Declaration of Trust, Levy's control-freak character and the flow of funds led the court to reject both men's attempts to blame the other. The court found the companies were sham corporations created to receive and divert SBL proceeds.
firac.conclusion: Kazman, Levy and Cohen were all directing minds of the Disputed Construction Companies; had control not been established, Kazman would at least have been wilfully blind.

firac.issue: Did Kazman and Levy launder proceeds of crime (s. 462.31(1))?
firac.facts: SBL proceeds were circulated among dozens of accounts, used to buy and mortgage properties, pay personal expenses, luxury items and repay loans, in circuitous patterns.
firac.rule: Section 462.31(1) is proven where the accused dealt with monies with intent to conceal or convert, knowing they were derived from an offence (here fraud over $5,000).
firac.application: Mr. Coort's tracing demonstrated overwhelming back-and-forth circulation of SBL funds among companies of Kazman, Levy and Cohen, with the intent to conceal the fraudulent source; the court rejected the explanations that all payments were legitimate loans or debts.
firac.conclusion: Kazman and Levy were each found guilty of Count 6 (laundering).

firac.issue: Did a criminal organization exist and did any defendant commit fraud in association with it (s. 467.12)?
firac.facts: The Crown alleged an organization of three or more persons whose main purpose was to fraudulently obtain SBLs. Kazman incorporated companies and prepared documents, Levy fronted the applications and renovations, and Cohen borrowed and recruited; borrowers were recruited over 32 months.
firac.rule: Section 467.1(1)/467.12 and R. v. Venneri, 2012 SCC 33 require a group of three or more with structure and continuity (not a mere ad hoc conspiracy) having as a main purpose the commission of serious offences for material benefit, and proof the accused knew of that character.
firac.application: The court found Kazman, Levy and Cohen formed a structured, continuing organization with divided roles and a sophisticated repeated scheme. However, the Tehranis were recruited borrowers with no proven knowledge of the organization; there was no evidence they knew Cohen or of the group's structure.
firac.conclusion: Kazman and Levy guilty of Count 7; Ali and Madjid Vaez Tehrani not guilty of Count 7; Chapkina and Ghatan acquitted on all counts including Count 7.

K021 (interlocutory injunction) is genuinely engaged though minor: RBC obtained an ex parte injunction freezing Northwood's account in the Contempo litigation, and Kazman and Levy swore affidavits to release the funds. The remaining picks are weak/contextual and reflect the limits of the supplied controlled vocabulary, which is oriented toward antisemitism and Jewish-community themes not central to this financing-fraud case: K093 (Jewish), K105 (synagogue) and K097 (Orthodox/Hasidic community) appear only incidentally (e.g., witnesses met 'in the synagogue during Kiddush,' donations to the Kehila Centre, meetings during 'the Jewish holidays'). I flag K093, K105 and K097 as borderline; no vocabulary term captures fraud, money laundering, wilful blindness or criminal organization, which are the true doctrinal core.

The city is not expressly stated, but is inferred to be Toronto: the indictment was preferred by the Attorney General of Ontario, the investigating RCMP officer worked in the Financial Crimes Division, and virtually every property, bank branch and business referenced (Eglinton Ave., Queen St., Champagne Dr., Barton Plaza in Hamilton excepted, etc.) is in Toronto. Province is Ontario (ONSC).

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. B. B.

defining_issues: Are the accused's communications to a rabbi protected by a case-by-case religious-communications privilege under the Wigmore/Gruenke framework?
Are the accused's communications to a Jewish Family and Child Services supervisor protected by privilege under the Wigmore framework?
Is the after-the-fact conduct evidence arising from these interactions admissible, or excluded under the Arcangioli principle?

firac.issue: Are the accused's statements to Rabbi Berman protected by a case-by-case religious-communications privilege?
firac.facts: Mr. B. attended Shaar Shalom Synagogue, spoke privately with Rabbi Berman behind a closed door, said he had marital problems and had hit his wife, and asked about faith and prayer. The rabbi, told that Mr. B. was wanted and considered armed and dangerous, urged him to turn himself in and voluntarily reported the conversation to police. Mr. B. did not testify or file an affidavit about his expectation of confidentiality.
firac.rule: Religious communications are not subject to a prima facie or class privilege but may be excluded case-by-case where the four Wigmore criteria are met (R. v. Gruenke, 1991 CanLII 40 (SCC)): (1) the communication originated in a confidence it would not be disclosed; (2) confidentiality is essential to the relationship; (3) the relationship is one the community should sedulously foster; (4) the injury from disclosure exceeds the litigation benefit. Section 2(a) Charter freedom of religion informs the analysis. The onus is on the defence to satisfy all four on a balance of probabilities.
firac.application: With no evidence from Mr. B. of an expectation of confidentiality and no discussion of confidentiality, the first criterion failed. Rabbi Berman regarded confidentiality as non-essential (saving a life precedes all else in Jewish law) and disclosed voluntarily, defeating the second criterion. Given disclosure of a crime and a genuine safety concern, there was no universal expectation of confidentiality, defeating the third. The rabbi voluntarily disclosed and the evidence had probative value, defeating the fourth.
firac.conclusion: None of the Wigmore criteria were met; the communications are not privileged and their admission does not infringe Mr. B.'s freedom of religion.

firac.issue: Are the accused's statements to Simon Kalkstein of Jewish Family and Child Services protected by privilege?
firac.facts: Mr. B. dropped in at the JFCS office asking for money, food and a lawyer's name, and stated words along the lines that he had threatened his wife. Kalkstein was a supervisor, not Mr. B.'s counsellor, gave him lawyers' names, cash and a food voucher, and later voluntarily reported the conversation to police. Again Mr. B. gave no evidence of any expectation of confidentiality.
firac.rule: Same four Wigmore criteria per Gruenke apply to claimed counselling/confidential communications; defence bears the onus.
firac.application: The absence of evidence from Mr. B. was fatal: there was no proof he believed the conversation confidential, nor even that confidentiality was desired. It was a drop-in visit for emergency help and a lawyer referral, not a counselling relationship, and Kalkstein disclosed voluntarily and without concern. No Wigmore criterion was satisfied.
firac.conclusion: The communications with Kalkstein are not privileged and are not excluded.

firac.issue: Is the after-the-fact conduct evidence admissible or excluded under the Arcangioli principle?
firac.facts: The Crown sought to lead Mr. B.'s admissions that he hit and threatened his wife, his flight when told police were called, and his search for a lawyer. Mr. B. is charged with sexual assault, assault with a weapon (knife) and uttering threats, arising from an alleged prolonged forcible confinement on August 11, 2007.
firac.rule: Post-offence conduct must be relevant to a live issue and has no probative value if equally explained by consciousness of guilt of two or more offences where the accused admits one (R. v. Arcangioli, 1994 CanLII 107 (SCC); R. v. White, 1998 CanLII 789 (SCC)). Probative value must not be outweighed by prejudice.
firac.application: If the jury finds the admissions related to the day of the alleged assault, the statement that he hit his wife is relevant to the assault-with-a-weapon charge and may corroborate the complainant; the threat statement could establish an element of the uttering-threats charge. Flight is relevant to guilt though largely explained by the assault admission. The probative value was not outweighed by prejudice, which could be addressed by jury instructions. Final instructions will depend on all the evidence.
firac.conclusion: The Crown's application to introduce the after-the-fact conduct is granted; a pre-charge conference will determine the jury instructions.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is an evidentiary ruling in a criminal prosecution for sexual assault, assault with a weapon and uttering threats. K025 (freedom of religion) and K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) are engaged because the religious-communications privilege from Gruenke is grounded in s. 2(a); the court expressly considered whether admitting the evidence would infringe freedom of religion. K098 (rabbi) and K105 (synagogue) reflect the central factual setting of the confidential communications claim. K093 (Jewish) and K026 (halacha) apply because the rabbi explained Jewish law (saving a life precedes all else) as the basis for disclosure. K026 is borderline but supported by the explicit reference to Jewish law governing the confidentiality exception.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE - ONTARIO', establishing the province as Ontario. No city is stated in the text. Although the synagogue and the Bloor and Spadina offices of Jewish Family and Child Services suggest Toronto, the court's sitting city is not expressly stated, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: No registry or court office is named in the decision, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: SJB v RDBB

defining_issues: Should the existing parenting schedule remain, and should the mother be granted sole decision-making authority given the parties' high conflict and the father's conduct toward the children?

How should the father's interests in closely held corporations be valued and distributed as matrimonial property, and what remedy secures the equalization payment where a third-party shareholder resists transfer and the father defies court orders?
Did each party establish that money advanced by their respective mothers constituted a joint matrimonial debt rather than a gift?
What is the father's Guideline income (including whether income should be imputed), and should retroactive and prospective child support be ordered as a lump sum?
Is the wife entitled to spousal support and, if so, in what amount and for what duration?

firac.issue: Should the current parenting schedule remain and should the mother be granted sole decision-making power?
firac.facts: The two children (ages 14 and 11) live primarily with the mother, who has been their primary caregiver. The father exercised alternate weekends plus Thursday evenings, but the children reported feeling neglected during his time, and he made hurtful comments including anti-Semitic remarks to the Jewish children and disparaging statements about their mother. The parties were in substantial, protracted conflict and repeatedly failed at cooperative dispute resolution.
firac.rule: The best interests of the child governs parenting; Divorce Act s. 16(10) directs maximizing contact only insofar as consistent with the child's best interests (Young v Young, 1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)); joint/shared decision-making should not be imposed where parents are in substantial conflict (Richter v Richter, 2005 ABCA 165; Rensonnet v Uttl, 2016 ABCA 196).
firac.application: The Court found the parties incapable of cooperating, that the father repeatedly leveraged his consent (e.g. travel) against his own interests, and that he sometimes acted contrary to the children's mental health. The status quo schedule was maintained but not compelled if the children, given their age, chose otherwise, and the mother — who fostered the paternal relationship — was granted final decision-making authority.
firac.conclusion: Parenting schedule maintained (subject to the children's wishes and the father refraining from harmful comments); mother granted sole/final decision-making power with shared guardianship, and may travel without the father's consent.

firac.issue: How should the father's closely held corporate interests be valued and distributed, and how should the equalization payment be secured?
firac.facts: The father held 50% of corporate entities owning Calgary real estate. The wife's expert (Mr. Siebert) valued the interests on an asset basis; the father led no contrary expert evidence but disputed the input value, alleged double-counting of shareholder loans, and sought a discount for personal tax. The father repeatedly ignored court orders, drew down corporate funds, and the co-shareholder resisted an unconditional transfer.
firac.rule: Matrimonial property is valued and distributed at trial (Hodgson v Hodgson, 2005 ABCA 13). Matrimonial Property Act ss. 9(2), 9(3)(j) and 35(3), Judicature Act s. 8, and the equitable-interest/oppression remedy in Peregrym v Peregrym, 2015 ABQB 176 (with Business Corporations Act s. 242 and preservation order under American Cyanamid).
firac.application: The Court accepted Mr. Siebert's mid-point valuation, deducted 2018 shareholder loans and the father's personal capital-gains tax liability (distinct from business valuation), and rejected the father's conditional in specie share transfer (distinguishing DBF v BF). Given the father's disregard for orders, the Court declared the wife holds an equitable/trust interest in his shares, ordered her to bring a s. 242 oppression action, and granted a preservation order over corporate assets.
firac.conclusion: Net corporate value found at $2,075,515; equalization payment of $917,816 secured by declaring the wife's equitable trust interest in the shares, an oppression action, and a preservation order over BI Corp. and 905 Ltd.

firac.issue: Did the advances from each party's mother constitute a joint matrimonial debt?
firac.facts: The maternal grandmother's $330,000 loan was documented by a contemporaneous promissory note, an irrevocable assignment, a caveat and joint tenancy security; the father conceded it was owing. The paternal grandmother's alleged $400,000 loan rested on inconsistent, unsigned/altered documents, a late caveat, and inconsistent stated amounts; the wife knew nothing of it.
firac.rule: Whether family advances are loans or gifts is decided case by case on factors including contemporaneous documentation, repayment terms, security, demand, partial repayment and expectation of repayment (Dhariwal v Dhariwal, 2015 ABQB 50).
firac.application: The $330,000 maternal loan met the factors and was a joint matrimonial debt. The wife's post-separation borrowings were loans but her sole responsibility, not joint debt. The paternal loan documents were unreliable and the father evasive, so he failed to prove the advance was intended as a loan.
firac.conclusion: The maternal $330,000 loan is a joint matrimonial debt; the wife's post-separation loans are her own; the alleged $400,000 paternal loan is not a matrimonial debt.

firac.issue: What is the father's Guideline income, should income be imputed, and should support be ordered as a lump sum?
firac.facts: The father, a shareholder-employee, gave incomplete, unreliable disclosure and drew large shareholder loans; his Guideline incomes were $325,582 (2015), $488,210 (2016) and $221,403 (2017). He claimed to be unemployed with zero income going forward but had transferable construction skills and high spending habits.
firac.rule: Federal Child Support Guidelines ss. 15-19; self-employed/shareholder payors bear the disclosure onus (Cunningham v Seveny, 2017 ABCA 4); income may be imputed for inadequate disclosure under s. 19(1)(f) (Graham v Graham, 2018 ABCA 66); s. 17 averaging (Metcalfe); lump sum available where a payor defies obligations or fails to disclose (Hunt v Smolis-Hunt, 2001 ABCA 229; TA v ST, 2017 ABQB 414).
firac.application: The Court accepted Mr. Siebert's figures, averaged 2018 income at $345,065, rejected both the mother's high average and the father's zero claim, and imputed $135,000 prospectively based on skills and s. 19(1)(f) poor disclosure. Given the father's defiance and non-payment, retroactive and prospective child support were ordered as lump sums, secured by trust over his shares. No DBS analysis was needed since prior orders were interim.
firac.conclusion: Retroactive s. 3 support of $78,656 and s. 7 of $31,132; prospective lump sums of $89,148 (s. 3) and $22,680 (s. 7); imputed go-forward income of $135,000; private-school contribution refused.

firac.issue: Is the wife entitled to spousal support, and in what amount and duration?
firac.facts: After 19 years of cohabitation (14 married), the wife was the primary caregiver whose real-estate career was secondary to family needs, while the father developed lucrative corporate ventures. Her post-separation income fell to $22,000-$35,000. The father continued lavish spending while underpaying support.
firac.rule: Divorce Act ss. 15.2(1), (4) and (6): compensatory and non-compensatory support considering conditions, means, needs and functions during marriage (Chutter v Chutter, 2008 BCCA 507); the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines inform quantum and duration; lump sums must be discounted for tax (Samoilova v Mahnic, 2014 ABCA 65).
firac.application: The Court found strong compensatory and non-compensatory entitlement, rejected the parties' inflated budgets, recalculated the SSAG ranges properly reflecting income types and tax, selected mid-to-high amounts, discounted them to lump sums, and ordered prospective support given the father's pattern of avoidance.
firac.conclusion: Retroactive spousal support of $198,000 and prospective lump sum of $42,000 (support ordered to a total of 10.5 years), all secured by trust over the father's shares.

case_name: S.P. c. Conseil de la communauté juive de Montréal

name_verification.name_in_document: S... P... c. Conseil de la communauté juive de Montréal

defining_issues: Did the defendants (the wife and the Conseil de la communauté juive de Montréal) commit a civil fault by knowing that a get could be obtained in Quebec under art. 21.1 of the Divorce Act and by pursuing proceedings before Israeli rabbinical courts allegedly lacking jurisdiction?
Did the plaintiff establish recoverable damages flowing from his prolonged stay and detention in Israel?
Could the court render enforceable the $15,000 undertaking forming part of the get agreement ratified by the Israeli rabbinical courts, absent any request for recognition of those foreign decisions?
Was the plaintiff's action abusive?

firac.issue: Did the defendants commit a civil fault (bad faith, intent to harm) by knowing of art. 21.1 of the Divorce Act and pursuing get proceedings in Israel despite alleged lack of jurisdiction?
firac.facts: After a three-month marriage the husband left the wife in September 2009; he began civil divorce proceedings in December 2009. The wife sought a get through the Montréal Beth Din, which sent three summonses in 2010 that the husband ignored. When the husband travelled to Israel in July 2011, the wife, advised by a rabbinical lawyer, launched proceedings before Israeli rabbinical courts to compel the get, resulting in exit-suspension orders and a brief detention. The husband claimed the defendants acted in bad faith, knowing art. 21.1 offered a Quebec remedy and that the Israeli courts lacked jurisdiction because he was not resident there and a Quebec divorce was pending.
firac.rule: Civil liability under art. 1457 C.c.Q. requires proof of fault, injury and causal connection. Article 21.1 of the Divorce Act (adopted 1990, discussed in Bruker c. Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54) gives courts a procedural tool to prevent a get being used as leverage, but imposes no obligation on a party to use it and offers no guarantee of obtaining the get.
firac.application: The court found that although the wife and the Council knew of art. 21.1, that mechanism is merely optional and its non-use was not opposable to them, especially since the husband had already ignored three Beth Din summonses. On jurisdiction, in the absence of any expert report on Jewish and Israeli law the court could not rule on the rabbinical courts' jurisdiction; the decisions showed the residency-based jurisdiction question was genuinely controversial at the time, and both defendants believed, rightly or wrongly and on the rabbinical lawyer's advice, that jurisdiction existed. The evidence did not establish that they knew the Israeli courts lacked jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: No fault, bad faith or intent to harm was proven against the wife or the Council; the liability claim failed.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff establish recoverable damages flowing from his stay and detention in Israel?
firac.facts: The husband claimed $80,000 for stress and inconvenience, $90,000 for infringement of fundamental rights (liberty, loss of enjoyment of life, including a brief detention), $30,000 for lost income and expenses, and $100,000 in punitive damages.
firac.rule: A plaintiff must prove the injury claimed and its causal link to the alleged fault; damages resulting from one's own conduct are not recoverable, and punitive damages require proven bad faith.
firac.application: Shared custody had gone well until his departure, undercutting the claim he was deprived of his son. His detention of a few hours resulted from his own lie about a lost passport and his failure to surrender it as ordered, and none of the exit-suspension orders were appealed. He offered no proof of prior good reputation (indeed he had an extensive criminal record), no proof of lost income, and inadequately documented expenses. Absent proven bad faith, punitive damages could not be awarded.
firac.conclusion: Even had a fault been shown, the claimed damages were largely unproven or self-caused; the analysis was moot given dismissal.

firac.issue: Could the court render enforceable the $15,000 undertaking from the get agreement ratified in Israel, absent a request for recognition of the foreign decisions?
firac.facts: As part of the agreement ratified by the Israeli rabbinical courts leading to the get, the wife (through a support organization) was to pay the husband $15,000. Neither party sought recognition of the Israeli judgments before the Quebec court. On his return the husband immediately repudiated the agreement, claiming the get was extorted and not 'kosher,' and announced his intention to sue.
firac.rule: A court cannot render a foreign decision enforceable absent a demand for its recognition; a party attacking the validity of a judicial settlement must do so before the competent forum or its appellate courts; the clean-hands doctrine bars injunctive relief to a party who has not respected his own obligations or acted fraudulently or in bad faith.
firac.application: No recognition of the rabbinical judgments was requested, so the court could not declare the undertaking enforceable. Even if requested, relief would be refused because the husband repudiated the very agreement and its validity upon returning, did not claim the $15,000 in his demand letter, and breached his undertaking not to sue the wife — coming to court with unclean hands.
firac.conclusion: The subsidiary claim for $15,000 was rejected.

firac.issue: Was the plaintiff's action abusive?
firac.facts: The husband repeatedly lied before the rabbinical courts (about custody interference, flight risk, being expelled from the home, theft), was found to be a liar and manipulator, obtained a fraudulent replacement passport, and pursued the litigation driven by rancour over supervised access imposed in 2010. The Council sought a declaration of abuse and $20,000; the wife ultimately amended her defence to seek a reservation of rights.
firac.rule: The court's power to sanction abuse of procedure under arts. 51–56 C.p.c.
firac.application: The evidence showed the action rested essentially on the husband's quest for vengeance against the wife and the Council, his determination to have the last word, and repeated bad-faith conduct. There was no valid reason for delaying the get, precisely the mischief art. 21.1 targets. The court was not persuaded he ever intended to grant a valid get.
firac.conclusion: The action was declared abusive; the defendants' rights to claim damages were reserved.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area, since the dispute centres on a Jewish religious divorce and the Divorce Act. K051 (religious divorce (get)) is the most specific engaged keyword, as the entire case turns on the granting of the get. K117 (Divorce Act) is directly engaged through the analysis of art. 21.1. K026 (halacha) applies because the court explained Jewish divorce law, the Beth Din's role, aguna and kosher-get concepts. K098 (rabbi) and K094 (Jewish community) reflect the central role of the rabbinical courts and the defendant Conseil de la communauté juive de Montréal; K093 (Jewish) situates the parties and the religious framework. K002 (Civil litigation) is included because the action was a damages claim in civil liability that was ultimately declared abusive under arts. 51–56 C.p.c. There is no controlled keyword for abuse of process or foreign-judgment recognition, so those doctrines are captured indirectly through K002.

registry_rationale: The 'DISTRICT DE MONTRÉAL' designation in the header identifies the Montréal registry of the Superior Court.

name_verification.name_in_document: Regina v. Lelas; Indexed as: R. v. Lelas

defining_issues: Should the Crown be granted leave to appeal and was the six-month concurrent sentence for racially/religiously motivated mischief to property demonstrably unfit?
To what extent may an offender's repugnant political and racist beliefs be taken into account when sentencing for mischief?

firac.issue: Was the six-month concurrent sentence for anti-semitic mischief to property demonstrably unfit, warranting appellate intervention to increase it?
firac.facts: Lelas, a Ku Klux Klan member who described himself as a racist, spray-painted swastikas (encircled in red, as worn by SS guards), 'Smash the Zog', 'WP' (White Power), 'Nazism' and similar slogans on the Shaarei Shomayim Synagogue, on the Yeshiva Yesodei Hatorah Hebrew school, and on an automobile. He admitted wishing 'to enrage the Jewish community'. Roughly 65-70% of the synagogue's 1,400 members were Holocaust survivors; the desecration caused extreme distress, including to a wedding party scheduled the next day. He pleaded guilty to three counts of mischief to property over $1,000, expressed remorse and apologized, and was ordered to pay $1,435 restitution. The trial judge imposed six months' imprisonment concurrent plus two years' probation.
firac.rule: On a Crown sentence appeal, the court may intervene where the sentence is unfit or reflects an error in principle. Under the Criminal Code the maximum penalty for mischief to property exceeding $1,000, tried by indictment, is ten years. Per R. v. Ingram and Grimsdale (1977), 1977 CanLII 2018 (ON CA), 35 C.C.C. (2d) 376, an offence directed against a particular racial or religious group is more heinous because it attacks the fabric of society, invites imitation and incites retaliation. Mischief that is racially or religiously motivated and done to cause emotional injury calls for a far more severe penalty than mischief done merely to damage property; general deterrence is paramount.
firac.application: The majority held the mitigating factors advanced (guilty plea, apology, cooperation, intoxication, spontaneity, minor record, youth and good work history) were relevant but did not justify a six-month sentence when weighed against the aggravating features. The desecration of a place of worship of any faith is serious, and is aggravated where done not merely to damage property but to strike fear and cause emotional injury to a segment of society. Lelas intended to enrage and terrorize the Jewish community, the incident was widely publicized and followed by copycat swastika daubings across Canada. The trial judge's concern about creating a 'martyr' was unfounded. Six months was insufficient for general deterrence and to mark society's abhorrence.
firac.conclusion: Leave to appeal granted and appeal allowed; sentence increased to one year concurrent on each count, with the probation order affirmed. Galligan J.A., dissenting, would have dismissed the appeal, finding the trial judge properly balanced the aggravating and mitigating factors and the sentence was not shown to be unfit.

firac.issue: To what extent may an offender's repugnant racist and political beliefs be taken into account in sentencing for mischief?
firac.facts: Lelas held white-supremacist and Holocaust-denial beliefs, was an 'Exalted Cyclops' in the Ku Klux Klan, and possessed Nazi paraphernalia. His beliefs explained his motivation to enrage the Jewish community, but the charge was mischief, not promotion of hatred.
firac.rule: An offender is not to be sentenced or punished for his political or social beliefs, however repugnant. Such beliefs may be considered only insofar as they explain the offender's actions, and a sentence must not appear to impose punishment for beliefs or opinions.
firac.application: The majority made clear Lelas was not being sentenced for his beliefs; those beliefs were relevant only because they explained that his conduct was designed to cause emotional injury to the Jewish community, elevating the gravity of the mischief. Galligan J.A., dissenting, emphasized the need to ensure a sentence could not be seen as punishing beliefs, and considered the trial judge had struck a fair balance between expressing society's abhorrence and avoiding punishment for opinion.
firac.conclusion: Both the majority and dissent agreed the beliefs themselves could not be punished; they diverged only on whether the resulting sentence properly reflected the aggravating motivation without over-punishing, the majority finding it did not and the dissent finding the balance fair.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area, this being a sentence appeal. K036 (mischief) and K116 (Criminal Code s. 430) are the precise offence and provision. K038 (vandalism/desecration) captures the spray-painting of religious property. K058 (antisemitism) and K060 (hate motivation) are central, the mischief being anti-semitic and done to enrage the Jewish community, the decisive aggravating factor. K066 (white supremacism) reflects the offender's KKK/neo-Nazi affiliation. K105 (synagogue), K122 (swastika) and K088 (Holocaust) are concrete entities engaged (target, symbol, and the survivor congregation). K093 (Jewish) identifies the targeted group. Weaker/borderline: K093 and K088 are entity tags rather than legal doctrine, but they are directly material given that the victims' Holocaust survivor status drove the sentencing analysis.
location_rationale: The decision header identifies the court as the 'ONTARIO Court of Appeal', establishing the province as Ontario. No city or registry is stated in the text, as is common for appellate decisions; the underlying offences occurred in Toronto but the court's sitting location is not specified.
registry_rationale: No registry or court office is named in the decision; the action number (347/90) appears but no registry office is identified.

case_name: Scott & Associates Engineering Ltd. v. Ghost Pine Windfarm, LP

name_verification.name_in_document: Scott & Associates Engineering Ltd. v. Ghost Pine Windfarm, LP

defining_issues: Are the redacted portions of the Asset Purchase Agreement and the email protected by solicitor-client, litigation, and/or common interest privilege?
Does the crime-fraud exception operate to defeat any privilege over the redactions?
Have the respondents waived privilege by putting their state of mind in issue, or does fairness require waiver?

firac.issue: Are the redacted portions of the APA and the email protected by solicitor-client, litigation, and common interest privilege?
firac.facts: In an action alleging knowing receipt of assets subject to a constructive trust, the respondents (Ghost Pine and Fortuna) redacted four portions of the Asset Purchase Agreement and part of an email between Ghost Pine's counsel and its representative. The redactions concerned communications and legal advice relating to the Finavera Litigation and the purchase of the Ghost Pine Assets. The court reviewed the unredacted documents and affidavit evidence.
firac.rule: Solicitor-client privilege protects confidential communications between lawyer and client made in the course of seeking or providing legal advice, and extends over a continuum of related communications (McClure 2001 SCC 14; Blank 2006 SCC 39; Balabel v. Air India). Litigation privilege protects documents whose dominant purpose was preparation for litigation, actual or reasonably apprehended (Blank; Moseley 1996 ABCA 141; Keefer Laundry). Common interest privilege allows parties sharing a common interest — in litigation against a common adversary or in completing a commercial transaction — to share privileged material without waiver (Buttes Gas; Griffiths McBurney; Pitney Bowes 2003 FCT 214). The party asserting privilege bears the onus.
firac.application: Having read the unredacted documents and the Contave affidavit, the court found the APA Redactions were prepared by counsel for the dominant purpose of preparing for and aiding the ongoing Finavera Litigation, attracting litigation privilege, and that common interest privilege applied because Ghost Pine, Fortuna and Finavera faced a common adversary on the same constructive-trust issue. The First and Fourth APA Redactions and the Email Redaction expressly referred to confidential legal advice sought and given in connection with the Ghost Pine purchase, and sharing them between the parties did not waive privilege because of common interest in completing the transaction.
firac.conclusion: All redactions are privileged: the APA Redactions under litigation and common interest privilege, and the First and Fourth APA Redactions and the Email Redaction additionally under solicitor-client privilege.

firac.issue: Does the crime-fraud exception defeat the privilege claimed over the redactions?
firac.facts: The applicant alleged equitable fraud and fraud under s. 203 of the Land Titles Act, arguing the respondents knowingly received trust property (including confidential information) and used a $1 million holdback to neutralize their knowledge, and that counsel advised on how to perpetrate this in drafting the APA.
firac.rule: There is a well-established exception to solicitor-client privilege where advice is sought to facilitate a crime or fraud; the client must know or ought to know the facilitated activity is unlawful when the advice is sought (R. v. Campbell). A mere allegation is insufficient — the applicant must adduce prima facie evidence giving colour to the charge (O'Rourke v. Darbishire; Yawrenko; Refco). Where facts are equally consistent with a legitimate transaction, no prima facie case of fraud is made out (Canbrook). Under s. 203(3) Land Titles Act, knowledge of an unregistered trust is not itself fraud; an additional element of dishonesty is required (1198952 Alberta Ltd. 2010 ABCA 42).
firac.application: The evidence went no further than showing the respondents purchased the Ghost Pine Assets while aware of the Finavera Litigation and sought to indemnify themselves against it; a holdback/indemnity is a standard commercial term. The applicant did not show the respondents knew or ought to have known the facilitated activity was unlawful, so nothing gave colour to the fraud or knowing-receipt charge, even assuming the exception could extend beyond fraud.
firac.conclusion: The crime-fraud exception does not apply; privilege stands.

firac.issue: Have the respondents waived privilege by putting their state of mind in issue, or does fairness require waiver?
firac.facts: The applicant argued the respondents' state of mind was central to the knowing-receipt claim and that, because counsel drafted the APA and gave advice to complete the purchase, the respondents had relied on legal advice and put their state of mind in issue; alternatively, fairness required disclosure. The applicant conceded it was itself who raised the respondents' state of mind.
firac.rule: Evidence justifying waiver must be clear and unambiguous (Maximum Ventures). A party waives privilege only by an affirmative allegation voluntarily injecting its own state of mind and relying on the legal advice received (Fraser v. Houston), and must have simply adopted counsel's advice without independent reflection (Freyberg 2007 ABQB 80). Fairness may compel waiver where a party did not voluntarily place its state of mind in issue only in rare, compelling cases (Ed Miller); privilege's importance otherwise prohibits broader release (Refco).
firac.application: The applicant led no evidence that the respondents put their legal knowledge in issue, and admitted it was the applicant who raised the respondents' state of mind — a party does not waive privilege when the opposing party makes such an allegation. There was no evidence the respondents adopted counsel's advice without independent reflection; merely obtaining legal advice is insufficient. The fairness grounds were neither compelling nor exceptional.
firac.conclusion: There was no waiver; fairness did not require disclosure. The application was dismissed with costs to the respondents.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the correct tier-1 practice area: this is an interlocutory dispute over documentary privilege in a commercial action. K022 (restitution) is engaged because the underlying claim is a constructive trust / knowing receipt of trust property, which is restitutionary in nature. The controlled vocabulary contains no keyword for legal professional privilege, solicitor-client/litigation/common interest privilege, or the law of evidence, which is the true subject of the decision; accordingly K021 (interlocutory injunction), K020 (class action) and K011 (judicial review) are included only as the closest available procedural/administrative terms and are weak, imperfect fits flagged as such — none of these remedies or proceedings actually featured in the case. The decision is poorly served by this vocabulary, which is oriented toward human-rights and Charter subject matter absent here.
location_rationale: The header lists 'Registry: Calgary' and the decision is signed 'Dated at the City of Calgary, Alberta this 20th day of May, 2011,' establishing Calgary, Alberta as the location.
registry_rationale: The decision header expressly states 'Registry: Calgary'.

defining_issues: What custody arrangement for the child JB is in his best interests where the court has found he was deliberately and irrationally alienated from his mother by his father, and can the court order a change of custody coupled with participation in a therapeutic 'Workshop' and a period of no contact with the alienating parent and others?

How should the mother's income be determined under the Federal Child Support Guidelines — in particular, should one-time taxable and non-taxable dividends received in 2006 be included as income — and had she overpaid or underpaid her child support obligations?

firac.issue: What custody order is in the child's best interests given a finding of deliberate irrational parental alienation, and may the court order a change of custody, therapeutic intervention and a no-contact period?
firac.facts: The father SGB deliberately alienated the two sons from their mother SJL over several years; the arbitrator and appeal judge both found irrational alienation. The younger son JB (16, with Klinefelter's Syndrome and a learning disability) refused all meaningful relationship with his mother. Expert psychiatrists (Dr. Goldstein, Dr. Fidler, Dr. Warshak, and even the father's expert Dr. Korenblum) agreed that in severe irrational alienation the child must be removed from the favoured parent. The mother sought sole custody, authority to enrol JB in the 'Family Bridges' Workshop, and cessation of contact with the father, older brother LB, the father's friend and JB's therapist.
firac.rule: Under s. 16(8)-(10) of the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), custody is determined solely by the best interests of the child, past conduct is considered only if relevant to parenting ability, and the maximum-contact principle applies subject to best interests. Courts have ordered changes of custody coupled with the Workshop in comparable alienation cases (e.g., A. (A.) v. A. (S.N.); L. (J.K.) v. S. (N.C.)).
firac.application: The court found that doing nothing would not repair the relationship, that all experts agreed JB must be separated from the alienating parent, and that intensive therapy alone required the father's participation, which he refused. The Workshop coupled with a change of custody was the only remedy with a chance of success. JB's special needs and separation from his brother did not outweigh the benefits (LB was leaving home anyway). The father's past conduct showed he would not foster contact and could not meet JB's needs, while the mother could parent appropriately and put JB's interests first. JB, though 16, was not mature enough to decide to sever ties with a parent.
firac.conclusion: The mother was awarded sole custody of JB with authority in her sole discretion to obtain treatment/intervention including the Workshop; for three months the father, LB, the father's friend Nila and Dr. Harman were prohibited from contacting JB and vice versa, with enforcement and travel/passport provisions.

firac.issue: How is the mother's income determined under the Federal Child Support Guidelines, and had she overpaid or underpaid support?
firac.facts: The mother was beneficiary of a family trust owning an investment corporation (SJIL). On the 2005 sale of the Hopedale Mall she received a one-time taxable dividend of about $2 million in 2006 and SJIL received a one-time non-taxable capital dividend; those funds became SJIL's only asset and generated her ongoing income. The father argued her income should be imputed based on lifestyle (~$375,000) or a five-year average (~$854,405). The mother had paid $119,469 in support since LB moved to the father in 2004.
firac.rule: Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175: income is determined from line 150 (s. 16), adjusted by Schedule III (dividends replaced by actual amount), with power under s. 17(1) to depart where line 150 is not the fairest determination given non-recurring amounts, and s. 19(1) imputation only in enumerated circumstances. Capital is not income.
firac.application: None of the s. 19(1) imputation grounds applied; the mother was not underemployed, exempt or diverting income, and lawfully encroached on capital. Averaging or depleting capital has no basis in law. The 2006 one-time taxable and non-taxable dividends were non-recurring capital forming her ongoing income source, so they were excluded and her 2006 income fixed at $74,499. Computing table amounts for each year (2004-June 2010) yielded a total obligation of about $99,968 against $119,469 paid.
firac.conclusion: The one-time dividends were excluded from 2006 income; the mother had overpaid by roughly $19,500 but did not seek reimbursement. Her obligation to pay the father ended July 1, 2010; the father's undue-hardship circumstances meant no order against him, and support for adult child LB would be arranged directly between LB and his mother under s. 3(2).

K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) are the core of the custody analysis under s. 16 of the Divorce Act, including the parental-alienation remedy. K050 (parental support / child support) covers the extensive Guidelines income and over/underpayment analysis, and K117 (Divorce Act) is the governing statute for both custody and support. K052 (religious upbringing) is a weaker, borderline pick — the judgment notes the father and his friend negated the children's Jewish upbringing and the boys abandoned their faith, but this is peripheral to the outcome; it is included only because the religious estrangement forms part of the alienation findings.

defining_issues: Must a sentencing court disclose to a convicted person the prejudicial contents of a probation officer's pre-sentence report so that the offender may agree with, explain, or deny them?
Where such a report was considered without disclosure, does the failure warrant appellate intervention with the sentence, or was there no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice?

firac.issue: Must a sentencing court disclose to the convicted person the prejudicial contents of a probation officer's pre-sentence report so that the offender may respond to them?
firac.facts: The appellants pleaded guilty to attempted armed robbery and were sentenced to five years. The magistrate had before him a pre-sentence report prepared by a Provincial Probation Branch officer and appears to have considered it, but its contents were never disclosed to the accused, who were unrepresented at sentencing.
firac.rule: Following R. v. Campbell (1911), 6 Cr. App. R. 131, R. v. Van Pelz (1942), 29 Cr. App. R. 10, R. v. Butterwasser, [1948] 1 K.B. 4, and the Canadian authorities R. v. Piluk (1933), R. v. Markoff, [1937] 1 D.L.R. 77, R. v. Lim Gim, and the Court's own unreported decisions (Tolmie & Rambo, Nahanee), prejudicial factual material placed before a sentencing court must be disclosed to the accused; if denied, proof should be given in open court subject to cross-examination, or the material must be ignored. Justice must be seen to be done (R. v. Sussex Justices, Ex p. McCarthy). A probation officer's pre-sentence report stands on no higher footing than a police officer's pre-sentence statement.
firac.application: The Court held that a pre-sentence probation report, insofar as it contains factual allegations prejudicial to the prisoner, cannot be placed in a different category from a police officer's pre-sentence statement; the same principles apply. The convicted person must be informed of the substance of the detrimental portions so he may agree, explain, or deny; if denied and considered material, the allegation must be proved in open court or ignored. The Court distinguished Williams v. New York (1949), 337 U.S. 241, reading it narrowly and refusing to adopt any principle permitting secret prejudicial information to found a sentence, while accepting Goddard L.C.J.'s caution in R. v. Dickson that undisclosed psychiatric/mental-condition material may sometimes properly be withheld.
firac.conclusion: A convicted person must be informed of the substance of a probation officer's report insofar as it is detrimental to him, with an opportunity to concur, explain, deny, and test it by cross-examination.

firac.issue: Does the non-disclosure of the report in this case warrant appellate interference with the sentences?
firac.facts: The magistrate considered the undisclosed pre-sentence reports, which the Court reviewed on appeal.
firac.rule: An appeal against sentence will succeed only where the appellant has suffered a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.
firac.application: Although the Court found a violation of the disclosure principle, it concluded that the reports contained so little prejudice to the appellants that the magistrate could have placed little if any reliance on them as factors influencing him against the accused. No other ground justifying interference was advanced.
firac.conclusion: No substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice resulted; leave to appeal was granted but the appeals were dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary tier-1 area: this is an appeal from sentence in a criminal matter. K012 (procedural fairness / natural justice) is the core doctrine — the offender's right to be told of, and to answer, prejudicial material relied on at sentencing, grounded in the 'justice must be seen to be done' principle. The remaining three are weak/contextual picks flagged as such: K058 (antisemitism), K060 (hate motivation) and K093 (Jewish) arise not from the appellants' own facts but from the Court's extended reliance on its earlier R. v. Tolmie & Rambo decision, where a magistrate's undisclosed report attributing anti-Semitic motivation to window-breaking against Jewish businesses illustrated the disclosure rule; they are contextual to the reasoning rather than to the ratio. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated 'sentencing' or 'pre-sentence report' term, so these are the closest available choices to reach the minimum.

The text does not state where the Court of Appeal itself sat; 'City of Victoria' appears only as the place where the Police Magistrate imposed sentence below, not as the appellate court's location, so city is left null.
