registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: New Westminster'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Re Faber and The Queen [Indexed as: R. v. Faber]

defining_issues: Is mandamus available to compel the Attorney-General to exercise his discretion to prosecute in a particular way?

Can the exercise of the Attorney-General's discretion to stay criminal proceedings by way of nolle prosequi be judicially reviewed, and does the entry of a stay against Simard infringe the applicant's rights under ss. 7 and 15 of the Charter, entitling him to a remedy under s. 24(1)?

firac.issue: Is mandamus available to compel the Attorney-General to exercise his prosecutorial discretion in a particular way?
firac.facts: After the applicant Faber, committed for trial on the second degree murder of Ménard, swore out an information against Simard and obtained a warrant under s. 455.3, the head Crown counsel filed a nolle prosequi staying the proceedings against Simard. Faber sought to compel continuation of the prosecution against Simard.
firac.rule: Mandamus lies only against an inferior tribunal, functionary or public body that refuses to exercise its jurisdiction; it cannot force the exercise of a discretion in a particular way (Pépin and Ouellette, Principes de contentieux administratif). The nolle prosequi power under Criminal Code s. 508 is a discretionary prosecutorial power.
firac.application: The Attorney-General did exercise his discretion — he decided to stay the proceedings. Because the discretion was exercised (whether to the applicant's satisfaction or not), mandamus was unavailable; this was not a case of refusal to act but of a decision the applicant disliked.
firac.conclusion: Mandamus is not available; the applicant cannot compel the Attorney-General to continue the prosecution against Simard.

firac.issue: Can the Attorney-General's exercise of the nolle prosequi/stay power be judicially reviewed, and did staying the proceedings against Simard violate the applicant's ss. 7 or 15 Charter rights so as to ground a s. 24(1) remedy?
firac.facts: Faber alleged the stay of proceedings against Simard was arbitrary, partial and discriminatory, invoking his rights to equality (s. 15) and to life, liberty and security (s. 7). Faber remained in custody awaiting his own trial for second degree murder; Simard had already pleaded guilty to being an accessory after the fact.
firac.rule: Courts traditionally do not review the appropriateness of the Attorney-General's prosecutorial discretion (separation of powers; the flood-gate principle) — R. v. Chabot, Re Arviv, R. v. Moore, Campbell v. A.-G. Ont. Since the Charter, executive/ministerial acts are reviewable only where they affect a citizen's constitutional rights (Operation Dismantle Inc. v. The Queen; Reference re s. 94(2) Motor Vehicle Act; Schmidt v. The Queen). A s. 24(1) remedy is available only to a person whose own Charter right has been infringed (Rahey v. The Queen). Courts retain control over abuse of process (R. v. Jewitt).
firac.application: The stay did not deprive Faber of life, liberty or security — he was in custody by reason of his own committal, not from any breach of fundamental justice. While a citizen has a right to lay an information (Re Dowson), neither the Charter, Code nor common law gives a right to compel the Attorney-General to follow up on it. No differential treatment under s. 15 was shown: Faber laid his information and it was received, and he was treated like other accused. The public interest, not the mere existence of a crime, governs prosecutorial decisions (Shawcross; R. v. Catagas). The court declined to follow Chartrand v. Minister of Justice (which had rescinded a stay) and preferred Campbell and Harvey, holding that even flagrant impropriety is answerable only to Parliament and public opinion, subject to the abuse-of-process power. Rescinding the stay would risk futile confrontation since the Attorney-General could enter a nolle prosequi toties quoties (R. v. Allen).
firac.conclusion: The stay did not affect Faber's rights as denunciator or as accused; no Charter breach was established and no s. 24(1) remedy was available. The application was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary practice area — the case concerns prosecutorial discretion under the Criminal Code (s. 508 nolle prosequi). K003 (Constitutional law) and K011 (judicial review) capture the core question of reviewability of executive/ministerial acts. K023 (equality rights) and K109 (Charter s. 15) reflect the applicant's discrimination argument; K112 (Charter s. 7) reflects the life, liberty and security argument. K107 (Canadian Charter) anchors the Charter analysis, including the s. 24(1) remedy discussion. No keyword specifically covers 'prosecutorial discretion' or 'stay of proceedings,' so the selection relies on the closest available constitutional/administrative terms; K011 is somewhat borderline since the court frames the matter in criminal rather than administrative-law terms.
location_rationale: The decision is from the Quebec Superior Court, Criminal Jurisdiction. The underlying committal and informations were dealt with by the Court of Sessions of the Peace in St-Jérôme, and the proceedings arise from events at Ste-Adèle; the Superior Court proceeding is tied to the St-Jérôme district, so Saint-Jérôme, Quebec is the seat.
registry_rationale: No specific court registry or file office is stated in the decision; only the court (Quebec Superior Court, Criminal Jurisdiction) and the locale of the underlying proceedings are given.

case_name: R.N. c. Procureure générale du Québec

name_verification.name_in_document: R. N. v. PROCUREURE GÉNÉRALE DU QUÉBEC

defining_issues: Are the plaintiff's damages claims against the social workers, CIUSS, Public Curator and CDP investigator prescribed under arts. 2925-2926 C.C.Q.?
Do the CDP, its investigator and its attorneys enjoy immunity from civil liability under s. 68 of the Quebec Charter such that the claims must be dismissed?
Are the plaintiff's abuse-of-proceedings and related claims manifestly unfounded/frivolous within the meaning of arts. 51 and 168 C.C.P.?

firac.issue: Are the plaintiff's damages claims against the social workers, CIUSS, Public Curator and CDP investigator prescribed?
firac.facts: The plaintiff's mother was removed from the plaintiff's home on March 20, 2012 following social-work evaluations begun in October 2010. The plaintiff filed complaints about the reports in November 2012 and commented on the investigator's report by April 2013, yet only instituted her damages action on June 5, 2018.
firac.rule: Arts. 2925 and 2926 C.C.Q.: an action to enforce a personal right prescribes by three years, running from the day the injury first appears (Monopro Ltd. v. Montreal Trust, 2000 CanLII 7400 (QCCA)). On a motion to dismiss the alleged facts are taken as true but not their legal characterization (Bohémier v. Barreau du Québec, 2012 QCCA 308; Canada (A.G.) v. CSN, 2014 SCC 49).
firac.application: The plaintiff had sufficient knowledge of the alleged faults at the latest by November 16, 2012 (social workers) and April 10, 2013 (investigator Royer). Even accepting that medical records arrived in January 2014, the three-year period had run before suit was filed in June 2018. The claim against the Public Curator, appointed curator on September 24, 2014 after seeking a protective regime from August 2012, was likewise out of time and amounted to an indirect appeal of a final, appeal-affirmed judgment.
firac.conclusion: The claims against CIUSS, Lamontagne, Gouin, the Public Curator and Royer are prescribed and dismissed.

firac.issue: Do the CDP, its investigator and attorneys enjoy immunity from civil liability?
firac.facts: The CDP investigated a complaint of exploitation of the vulnerable mother under s. 48 of the Quebec Charter and pursued a claim before the Human Rights Tribunal, which dismissed it for insufficient evidence while noting irregularities but denying costs due to the plaintiff's own abusive conduct.
firac.rule: Section 68 of the Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms grants the CDP and its investigators absolute immunity for investigative powers (s. 16 of the Act Respecting Public Inquiry Commissions) and relative immunity to employees in the exercise of their functions; the immunity is overcome only by a prima facie showing that the body knowingly and in bad faith acted outside its jurisdiction (Morier and Boily v. Rivard, [1985] 2 SCR 716). Attorneys benefit from relative immunity (Lallier v. Boulanger, 2017 QCCS 2164).
firac.application: The plaintiff pleaded only legal characterizations of bad faith, not supporting facts, which are not deemed true. The Tribunal made no finding of abuse of proceedings. Normal litigation decisions by counsel do not evidence bad faith, and Me Régimbal (Public Curator's counsel) had no duty to advance the plaintiff's interests.
firac.conclusion: The immunity applies and is not displaced; the claims against the CDP, Royer, Me Turenne and Me Régimbal are dismissed.

firac.issue: Are the abuse-of-proceedings and related claims manifestly unfounded within arts. 51/168 C.C.P.?
firac.facts: The plaintiff based her action solely on the CDP's allegedly abusive Tribunal proceedings and each defendant's participation, though many defendants (CIUSS, social workers, Public Curator, Me Régimbal) were not parties bringing that claim.
firac.rule: Arts. 51, 53 and 168 C.C.P.: a claim may be dismissed where manifestly unfounded, frivolous or an abuse; in doubt the court should let the action proceed (Bohémier).
firac.application: Defendants who did not bring the CDP claim cannot be liable for it. Any defamation theory was expressly abandoned and would have been prescribed under art. 2926 C.C.Q. The plaintiff's suit was in substance an attempt to relitigate matters already decided and lacked any factual foundation for abuse.
firac.conclusion: The claims are manifestly unfounded and dismissed with legal costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary practice area — a damages action decided on motions to dismiss for prescription and manifest unfoundedness. K007 (Human rights) and K072 (human rights tribunal) apply because the underlying dispute arose from a CDP exploitation complaint prosecuted before the Human Rights Tribunal. K120 (Quebec Charter) is squarely engaged: the CDP was created under s. 57, prosecuted under s. 48, and its immunity flows from s. 68 of the Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. K054 (wills/estates) is a weak/borderline pick offered for the curatorship and protective-regime dimension (incapacity, Public Curator administration of person and property); the controlled vocabulary has no term for prescription, immunity of public officials, or abuse of process, which are the doctrinal core, so this selection is imperfect.
location_rationale: The header states 'SUPERIOR COURT, CANADA, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC, DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and the court sat in Montreal (hearing June 3-5, 2019).
registry_rationale: The 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and file number 500-17-102510-180 indicate the Montreal registry of the Superior Court.

name_verification.name_in_document: Rogerson v. Havergal

defining_issues: Whether an allegation made by opposing counsel that a party was effectively seeking to avoid a Jewish judge, combined with the presiding judge being Jewish, gives rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias or actual bias requiring recusal?

Whether the judge's conduct of the proceedings — including tone at case conferences, endorsements said to exceed jurisdiction, and consulting the public court file — demonstrated actual or perceived bias warranting recusal?

firac.issue: Does an opposing party's factum characterizing the plaintiffs as wishing to avoid a Jewish judge, together with the presiding judge in fact being Jewish, create a reasonable apprehension of bias or actual bias requiring recusal?
firac.facts: The defendants' March 10, 2020 factum stated that a December 5, 2019 letter from plaintiffs' counsel requesting that the mediating judge have no 'professional, social or religious' connection to defence counsel meant the plaintiffs wished to avoid appearing before a Jewish judge. Mr. Rogerson, a barrister, felt this wrongly accused him of antisemitism and argued that because the presiding judge (Kimmel J.) is Jewish, she must be assumed to have taken offence and could not be impartial.
firac.rule: The recusal test asks whether an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically and having thought the matter through, would think it more likely than not that the decision-maker, consciously or unconsciously, would not decide fairly (Yukon Francophone School Board v. Yukon (A.G.), 2015 SCC 25, paras. 20-21). The informed person must be objectively reasonable, knowing all relevant circumstances including the nature of judging (Duca Financial Services Credit Union Ltd. v. Smith, 2016 ONSC 6289, para. 18). There is a strong presumption of judicial impartiality; apprehension of bias must rest on strong grounds and cogent evidence (Wewaykum Indian Band v. Canada, 2003 SCC 45; R. v. S.(R.D.), 1997 CanLII 324).
firac.application: The question was not whose interpretation of the December 5 letter was correct, nor whether Mr. Rogerson is antisemitic, but whether the airing of both interpretations before the judge gave rise to bias. A reasonably informed person understands that litigants routinely accuse each other of unpleasant things and that it is the judge's role to sort out what is overstated. The strong presumption of impartiality cannot be overcome by a speculative assumption that a judge will be tainted by a lawyer's submission about a party. Mr. Rogerson's fears were subjective and speculative, allowing no possibility that the judge would interpret the comment in the non-racist manner he intended. There was no evidence of actual bias or any change in the judge's conduct after the factum.
firac.conclusion: No reasonable apprehension of bias and no actual bias arose from the factum's characterization; this ground for recusal failed.

firac.issue: Did the judge's conduct of the proceedings — tone at case conferences, endorsements alleged to exceed jurisdiction, conduct of the settlement conference, and consulting the public court file — establish actual or perceived bias justifying recusal?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs complained of a stern look and admonishment at the March 12, 2020 case conference (following Mr. Rogerson's unexplained absence contrary to a direction), the February 28, 2020 endorsements said to exceed jurisdiction, the conduct of the December 19, 2019 settlement conference, and the judge consulting the public court docket to check whether affidavits potentially breaching a confidentiality order for a minor (Student Q) had been filed after plaintiffs' counsel failed to respond.
firac.rule: Displeasure with a case management judge's ruling is not grounds for recusal, and judge-shopping is not permitted (Beard Winter LLP v. Shekhdar, 2016 ONCA 493, para. 10). A tone of voice or appearance of a judge cannot overcome the strong presumption of impartiality (Beard Winter, para. 12). The moving party bears a high burden to show a real likelihood of bias (Stephenson v. Gravenhurst, 2012 ONSC 5368, para. 11; Duca, para. 18). Recusal motions are properly made to the judge asked to recuse (Arsenault-Cameron v. P.E.I., 1999 CanLII 641).
firac.application: Evidence of the settlement conference was inadmissible as subject to settlement privilege, and plaintiffs had consented to the judge's continued involvement and Rule 77 appointment, belying any perception of bias. Challenges to the February 28 endorsements were properly the subject of a pending motion for leave to appeal, not recusal. Any displeasure at the March 12 conference had an objectively good reason — a party's unexcused absence contrary to direction — and did not rise to bias. Consulting the public court file to verify whether affidavits breaching a minor's confidentiality order had been filed, after plaintiffs' counsel failed to answer, was objectively reasonable judicial control over the court's process, especially amid COVID-19 restrictions. The plaintiffs' case rested on subjective perceptions, which are not the yardstick. This was also the second recusal request against a case management judge in the proceeding, a relevant consideration.
firac.conclusion: No right-minded, reasonably informed person would conclude the judge's conduct raised a real or perceived apprehension of bias; the conduct grounds failed and the recusal motion was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a procedural motion within a civil action. K011 (judicial review) is a borderline pick used loosely for the impartiality/review dimension — it is weak here since this is a recusal motion rather than statutory judicial review, but no dedicated 'recusal/bias' keyword exists in the vocabulary. K012 (procedural fairness / natural justice) is the closest doctrinal fit, as recusal and reasonable apprehension of bias fall within natural justice principles. K093 (Jewish) and K058 (antisemitism) are engaged because the core allegation concerned the presiding judge being Jewish and the perceived accusation that the plaintiff wished to avoid a Jewish judge / was antisemitic. K011 and K058 are flagged as somewhat weak/contextual but reflect the substance the vocabulary allows.
location_rationale: The decision is from the Superior Court of Justice - Ontario, and refers to the 'Acting Regional Senior Justice for Toronto (ARSJ)' and matters managed under the Toronto court, indicating the matter proceeded in Toronto. Court File No. CV-19-629398 is a Toronto commercial/civil list number.
registry_rationale: The proceeding was case managed under Rule 77 in the Toronto Superior Court of Justice, and references to the Acting Regional Senior Justice for Toronto confirm the Toronto registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Boujikian

defining_issues: Was the credibility of the Crown witnesses to be preferred over that of the accused, such that the Crown proved the offences beyond a reasonable doubt?
Did the accused's removal of the 'Flat Rate' sign from the TPM lot constitute mischief under s. 430(1) of the Criminal Code even though the lot was an automated pay-and-display lot?
Did the accused commit theft under $5000 by taking parking fees from motorists parking in the TPM lot?

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt where the case turned on the credibility of the competing witnesses?
firac.facts: Private investigator Snowdy and by-law officer Clermont, hired by lot-owner TPM after a revenue drop following automation, conducted video surveillance and observed Boujikian, an attendant from a lot across the street, remove a rate sign, direct traffic into the TPM lot, and collect $5 from motorists. Boujikian denied wrongdoing, claimed an understanding permitting him to collect fees, said he removed the sign as a courtesy, and alleged harsh treatment and denial of a phone call. Officer Janes testified independently. Boujikian called a character witness and evidence of partly Jewish ancestry to rebut alleged anti-Semitic remarks.
firac.rule: W.(D.) v. The Queen, 1991 CanLII 93 (SCC), sets the three-step credibility analysis: acquit if the accused's evidence is believed; acquit if it raises a reasonable doubt; and even if not believed, acquit unless the accepted evidence proves guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The Crown bears the onus throughout.
firac.application: The court found Boujikian's explanations contrived, confusing and internally inconsistent — regarding his authority to collect money, his reasons for removing only one rate sign, and his account of the length of custody and requests to phone. His attempt to bribe Snowdy was cogent evidence of guilt. By contrast, Snowdy and Clermont were trained investigators with careful contemporaneous notes and were not successfully impugned; Officer Janes was independent. The character evidence did not repair the accused's undermined credibility. The court neither believed the accused nor was left in reasonable doubt by his evidence, and was convinced of guilt on the accepted evidence.
firac.conclusion: The Crown proved the offences beyond a reasonable doubt; the accused's evidence was rejected and did not raise a reasonable doubt.

firac.issue: Can removing a 'Flat Rate' advertising sign from an automated pay-and-display parking lot constitute mischief?
firac.facts: Boujikian removed the $5.00 'Flat Rate' card facing westbound traffic and placed it inside the A-frame, making it invisible to passing motorists. The defence argued a flat-rate sign is inconsistent with, and its removal cannot be mischief on, an automated pay-and-display lot.
firac.rule: Criminal Code s. 430(1): everyone commits mischief who wilfully (b) renders property useless, inoperative or ineffective, or (c) obstructs, interrupts or interferes with the lawful use, enjoyment or operation of property.
firac.application: The court held an automated lot can still charge a flat rate and that the sign served an advertising function informing passing motorists of the cost to park. Concealing the sign rendered it useless and interfered with the owner's use of its property, satisfying s. 430(1)(b) and (c), notwithstanding the automated system.
firac.conclusion: Removal of the sign constituted mischief under s. 430(1) of the Criminal Code.

firac.issue: Did the accused commit theft under $5000 by collecting parking fees for the TPM lot?
firac.facts: Boujikian directed motorists into the TPM lot and took $5.00 from four persons, keeping it for himself. He claimed an arrangement authorized him to collect fees, but could not confirm any authorization and gave shifting accounts of who the money was for.
firac.rule: Theft under $5000 (Criminal Code); the Crown must prove the taking/conversion of property without authority with intent to deprive the owner.
firac.application: The court found as fact that Boujikian had no authority to take money from persons parking in the TPM lot and that he took the fees intending to keep and did keep them for his own use. His explanations of purported authority were disbelieved as inconsistent and unbelievable.
firac.conclusion: Theft under $5000 was proven beyond a reasonable doubt; the accused was found guilty.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the accused was tried for mischief and theft. K036 (mischief) and K116 (Criminal Code s. 430) go to the central mischief conviction and the statutory provision the court applied. K057 (antisemitic slurs) and K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) reflect the evidence that the accused allegedly made anti-Semitic remarks about the Jewish lot owners and the defence's rebuttal evidence about his partly Jewish ancestry; these are flagged as weak/peripheral because the trial judge expressly found the remarks did not affect the issues to be resolved and they were relevant only to a collateral credibility argument. There is no controlled keyword for 'theft' or 'witness credibility', so those core aspects are not separately tagged.
location_rationale: The heading states 'COURT FILE No.: Toronto, Old City Hall, Information No. 04-120127970' and the offences occurred 'in Toronto'; the court is the Ontario Court of Justice, so the province is Ontario.
registry_rationale: The court file line identifies the registry/office as 'Toronto, Old City Hall'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Saleh v. Reichert

defining_issues: Upon whom does the common-law duty to dispose of a deceased's remains fall where the surviving spouse (administrator of the estate) and a parent disagree?
What is the nature of that duty — specifically, does the law require burial rather than cremation where the deceased was raised in the Muslim faith?
Can the deceased's religious tenets, the administrator's earlier religious conversion pledge, or the Charter override the administrator's right to choose the method of disposal?

firac.issue: On whom does the duty and right to dispose of a deceased person's remains fall when a surviving husband/administrator and the father disagree?
firac.facts: Layla Reichert died intestate on May 7, 1993. Her husband Andreas Reichert was appointed administrator of her estate by letters of administration dated May 21, 1993. Her father sought to prevent cremation and compel burial in accordance with Muslim faith.
firac.rule: Upon death a duty arises to dispose of remains in a decent and dignified fashion; that duty and the corresponding right of possession fall on the executor or administrator (Hunter v. Hunter, [1930] 4 D.L.R. 255; Williams v. Williams (1882), 20 Ch. D. 659; Abeziz v. Harris Estate, [1992] O.J. No. 1271, treating executors and administrators interchangeably).
firac.application: As administrator of Layla Reichert's estate, Andreas Reichert bore the legal obligation to dispose of the remains and therefore had the right to possess them for that purpose. The father's challenge to the validity of the marriage (and thus to the grant of administration) failed: at most the marriage was voidable, and a voidable marriage can only be attacked in a nullity proceeding by a party during their lifetime, not after death. No nullity application had ever been made.
firac.conclusion: The duty and right to dispose of the remains fell on Andreas Reichert as administrator, and the grant of letters of administration could not be impugned.

firac.issue: Does the duty to dispose of remains require burial rather than cremation?
firac.facts: The father argued that Muslim faith requires burial and that cremation would not be dignified in the circumstances; the husband wished to cremate consistent with Layla's expressed wishes.
firac.rule: The old common-law duty of a 'decent Christian burial' has been modernized (R. v. Price (1884), 12 Q.B.D. 247); the fundamental obligation is that the body be disposed of in a dignified fashion, and both burial and cremation are specifically sanctioned in Ontario under the Cemeteries Act (Revised), R.S.O. 1990, c. C.4 (Abeziz v. Harris Estate).
firac.application: Both burial and cremation are recognized as dignified methods of disposal in Ontario. Either would satisfy the administrator's obligation. Although Layla had expressed a wish to be cremated, such expressed wishes are not legally enforceable (Williams v. Williams), but an administrator may lawfully choose to honour them.
firac.conclusion: The duty is only to dispose of the remains decently and with dignity; the administrator could choose either burial or cremation.

firac.issue: Do the deceased's religious tenets, the administrator's conversion pledge, or the Charter constrain the administrator's choice?
firac.facts: The husband had converted to Islam and signed a pledge to obey the faith's orders and prohibitions (which prohibit cremation); the father invoked this pledge, Criminal Code s. 182, and the spirit of the Charter (preamble supremacy of God; s. 27 multiculturalism).
firac.rule: The Charter does not apply to private litigation absent state or governmental action (RWDSU, Local 580 v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 573; Tremblay v. Daigle, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 530). Religious law has no bearing on the legal obligation to dispose of remains (Abeziz).
firac.application: The conversion document was a statement of conscience and a pledge to God, not a civil undertaking enforceable by the father. The Charter could not apply between private parties. Criminal Code s. 182 provided no basis in this civil case, and no estoppel arose. In the legal sense none of the father's rights as a parent were affected; he was simply relieved of an obligation that would otherwise fall to the administrator.
firac.conclusion: Religious obligations, the conversion pledge, and the Charter did not constrain the administrator; the plaintiff's action was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the primary tier-1 area, as the case turns on estate administration and the duties of an administrator of an intestate estate (K054 wills/estates — administrator, letters of administration, disposition of remains). K021 (interlocutory injunction) applies because the litigation arose from an ex parte injunction restraining cremation, later set aside. K025 (freedom of religion) and K107 (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms) with K121 (s. 27 multiculturalism) reflect the plaintiff's arguments based on Muslim religious tenets and the Charter's spirit, which the court considered and rejected (holding the Charter inapplicable to private parties). K002 (Civil litigation) is a supporting tier-1 classification given the civil action, estoppel, and injunction dimensions; it is a weaker/secondary pick since the substance is estate law. There is no controlled-vocabulary keyword for Islam/Muslim faith, so the religious dimension is captured via K025.

case_name: Rose v. Canada (Royal Canadian Mounted Police)

name_verification.name_in_document: Rose v. Canada (Royal Canadian Mounted Police)

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff's statement of claim be struck out and the action dismissed under Rule 19(24) as disclosing no reasonable claim, being frivolous or vexatious, or being an abuse of process?
Should the plaintiff be restrained under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act from instituting further legal proceedings without leave of the court?

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's statement of claim be struck out and the action dismissed under Rule 19(24)?
firac.facts: The self-represented plaintiff alleged that the RCMP implanted a microchip in his brain and a radio-frequency chip in his neck to monitor, record and control his thoughts and to communicate with him. This was the fourth similar action; three earlier Supreme Court statements of claim had been struck by A.F. Wilson J. (2008 BCSC 1661) and Halfyard J. (2009 BCSC 1116). He sought a broad range of damages and an order that the defendants pay to remove the implant, and relied on three articles said to prove the technology exists.
firac.rule: Rule 19(24) permits striking a pleading that (a) discloses no reasonable claim, (b) is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, (c) may prejudice/embarrass/delay, or (d) is an abuse of process. Under Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, the test for (a) is whether it is plain and obvious the claim discloses no reasonable cause of action; assumptions and speculation need not be taken as true (Operation Dismantle Inc. v. The Queen, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 441). A pleading is frivolous if without substance, groundless or fanciful (Borsato v. Basra, 2000 BCSC 28), and vexatious where the action obviously cannot succeed or re-litigates decided matters (Skender v. Farley, 2007 BCCA 629; Re Lang Michener and Fabian). Estoppel and re-litigation render pleadings abusive (Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union, 2006 BCSC 750).
firac.application: Although the pleadings, read with the affidavit, might arguably disclose a cause of action in assault, the essential allegations were clearly fictional and incapable of proof. The scientific articles submitted did not support the existence of technology able to read or control thoughts remotely; the one supportive article came from non-reputable websites and failed the R. v. Mohan standard for novel scientific evidence. There was no rational possibility a court could find the technology existed, so the claims were groundless, fanciful and doomed, and no amendment could cure the defect. The action also repeated claims already dismissed by two judges, making it barred by estoppel and an abuse of process.
firac.conclusion: The pleadings were struck in their entirety and the action dismissed against all defendants as frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of process under R. 19(24)(b) and (d).

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff be restrained under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act from bringing further proceedings without leave?
firac.facts: The plaintiff filed four actions over 15 months raising essentially the same allegations, did not appeal the earlier dismissals, and commenced this action after assuring Halfyard J. he would not file another action on the same issues pending a s. 18 application. He had not paid the costs ordered in the prior judgments.
firac.rule: Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act allows the court to bar a person who has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds instituted vexatious proceedings from starting further proceedings without leave. Per British Columbia (Public Guardian and Trustee) v. Brown, 2002 BCSC 1152, the applicant must show the proceedings are vexatious (annoying/harassing and without reasonable grounds) and, objectively, a knowing and deliberate repetition of the vexatious conduct; the whole history, including unpaid costs, is considered (Lang Michener). A s. 18 order should not extend to unrelated pre-existing proceedings absent express terms (Kaiser (Re), 2008 BCSC 451).
firac.application: Three judges had found the plaintiff's actions vexatious and he had paid none of the costs orders. Although he sincerely believed his allegations, knowledge of vexatiousness is not required; after Halfyard J.'s judgment he ought to have known this action would also be vexatious, yet knowingly repeated the conduct. Without an order he would likely continue filing derivative claims, burdening defendants. The order was declined only as to the pending Small Claims action, whose personal-injury claims were largely unrelated and could be sorted by a Provincial Court judge.
firac.conclusion: The s. 18 order was granted: the plaintiff may not institute proceedings in any B.C. court without leave, except the already-commenced Provincial Court (Small Claims) action; costs awarded to the defendants on Scale B.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the strong, primary classification: the decision concerns striking pleadings and vexatious-litigant control in a civil tort action. The remaining picks are weak/borderline, flagged accordingly because the controlled vocabulary (heavily oriented to Charter/human-rights/antisemitism matters) has no dedicated terms for 'striking pleadings,' 'abuse of process' or 'vexatious litigant.' K011 (judicial review) is the weakest and included only to reach the minimum; it does not truly apply. No genuinely fitting keyword exists for the core civil-procedure subject matter.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Katsnelson

defining_issues: What is the fit sentence for an offender who pleaded guilty to sexual assault causing bodily harm against a 17-year-old and to sexual assault of a second victim committed in a serial predatory episode?
How should the paramount objectives of denunciation and deterrence, including the statutory direction under s. 718.01 for offences involving abuse of a person under 18, shape the sentence?
How much mitigating credit should be given for a guilty plea entered on the eve of trial after a full preliminary inquiry?
Does the principle of parity require a sentence comparable to the three-year term imposed on the co-offender?

firac.issue: What is the fit sentence for an offender who pleaded guilty to sexual assault causing bodily harm and to sexual assault committed as part of a serial predatory episode in a university residence?
firac.facts: Katsnelson, 25, with no record and a good background, entered a York University residence with a friend by deception during Frosh Week, roamed the floors trying doors, vaginally raped 17-year-old C.C. (causing week-long bleeding) while photographing his friend assaulting her, and later raped 18-year-old B.M. on another floor, using no condom in either case. He pleaded guilty to sexual assault causing bodily harm (C.C.) and sexual assault (B.M.). The Crown sought at least ten years; defence three to five.
firac.rule: Sentence must be proportionate to gravity and responsibility (s. 718.1) and reflect the totality principle (s. 718.2(c)); sentences for rape vary widely with circumstances (R. v. L.M., 2008 SCC 31; R. v. C.A.M., [1996] 1 S.C.R. 500).
firac.application: The court considered the whole of the conduct, finding the serial, premeditated targeting of vulnerable young women leading to two separate rapes of two victims distinguished the case from the precedents. The three-to-five-year range was inadequate, but a ten-year term over-emphasised the offence and undervalued his positive history and rehabilitative prospects; 'there is no need to crush.'
firac.conclusion: A global sentence of eight years was fit: five years for sexual assault causing bodily harm and a consecutive three years for the sexual assault, less 30 days' credit, with s. 109 (life), DNA and 20-year SOIRA orders.

firac.issue: How should denunciation and deterrence, including the s. 718.01 direction for offences abusing a person under 18, govern the sentence?
firac.facts: C.C. was under 18 at the time; the offences were premeditated invasions of sleeping students' bedrooms, involving two strangers, cell-phone photography, no condom (exposing victims to pregnancy and disease risk), and profound lasting psychological harm.
firac.rule: Section 718.01 requires primary consideration of denunciation and deterrence where the offence involves abuse of a person under 18; s. 718.2(a)(ii.1) deems abuse of a person under 18 an aggravating factor; denunciation communicates society's condemnation (R. v. C.A.M.).
firac.application: Because C.C. was under 18, and independently given the intensely intrusive nature of rape, denunciation and deterrence were the paramount objectives. Numerous aggravating features—serial predation, stranger assaults, targeting vulnerable first-year students, campus-safety concerns (R. v. Mai; R. v. Mizra)—demanded a clear and unequivocal response.
firac.conclusion: Denunciation and deterrence were paramount and justified a substantial custodial term, though tempered by rehabilitative considerations.

firac.issue: How much mitigating credit is warranted for a guilty plea entered on the eve of trial after a full preliminary inquiry?
firac.facts: Forensic evidence (semen and DNA) tied Katsnelson to both rapes, and the co-offender was ready to testify. He did not indicate a guilty plea until days before the Superior Court trial, after both victims had testified and been cross-examined at the preliminary inquiry.
firac.rule: A guilty plea is generally mitigating but its weight varies; a plea where conviction was inevitable and the accused was 'caught red-handed' attracts less credit (R. v. Daya, 2007 ONCA 693; R. v. R.W.E., 2007 ONCA 461).
firac.application: Conviction was all but inevitable given the forensic case and the co-offender's availability. Although the plea spared the victims a further public recounting, its late timing—after a full preliminary inquiry and forcing the victims to prepare to testify again—attenuated the credit.
firac.conclusion: The guilty plea was mitigating but its effect was significantly reduced by its late timing and the inevitability of conviction.

firac.issue: Does the parity principle require a sentence comparable to the three-year term imposed on the co-offender Connort?
firac.facts: Connort, of similar age, background and lack of record, pleaded guilty at the end of the preliminary inquiry to a single sexual assault (digital penetration of C.C.) and received three years. Katsnelson was sentenced for two offences and had vaginally raped both C.C. and B.M.
firac.rule: Section 718.2(b) requires similar sentences for similar offenders in similar circumstances, but this permits justified disparity based on individual roles; sentences need only be 'understandable... when examined together' (R. v. Issa (1992), 57 O.A.C. 253).
firac.application: Though the two men shared a joint enterprise and similar backgrounds, Katsnelson faced two convictions, committed the actual rapes without a condom, and pleaded guilty far later. His role was readily distinguishable from Connort's.
firac.conclusion: Parity was not offended by a markedly higher sentence; indeed failing to impose one would have offended the principle.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the core practice area—this is a sentencing decision under the Criminal Code for sexual assault offences. K041 (campus/university) is genuinely engaged: the offences occurred inside a York University residence during Frosh Week and campus safety was an explicit sentencing consideration (R. v. Mai; R. v. Mizra). The remaining picks are weak and reflect a mismatch between this sexual-assault sentencing case and a vocabulary oriented toward antisemitism/hate-related matters: K093 (Jewish) rests only on the offender's passing remark ('a couple of Jewish guys') and his background; K096 (Jewish students) and K045 (student discipline) are included only as the closest remaining terms because the victims were first-year students and the setting was a university—neither doctrine is actually litigated. No sexual-offence, sentencing, or parity keyword exists in the vocabulary, so these last three should be treated as low-confidence.
location_rationale: The indictment alleges the offences occurred 'in the City of Toronto, in the Toronto Region,' and the court is the Ontario Superior Court of Justice; the file caption and offence particulars establish Toronto, Ontario as the location.
registry_rationale: The charges are laid 'in the Toronto Region' and the matter proceeded in the Superior Court of Justice sitting for that region, so the registry is taken to be Toronto (Toronto Region).

case_name: R. v. Big M. Drug Mart Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: Her Majesty the Queen v. Big M. Drug Mart Ltd.

defining_issues: Is the Lord's Day Act ultra vires the Parliament of Canada, or is it valid federal legislation under the criminal law power?
Can a corporation, and can the Provincial Court of Alberta, invoke and apply the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms?
Does the Lord's Day Act infringe the fundamental freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed by s. 2(a) of the Charter?
If it infringes s. 2(a), is the Lord's Day Act a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter?

firac.issue: Is the Lord's Day Act within the criminal law power of the Parliament of Canada, or is it ultra vires?
firac.facts: The trial judge acquitted Big M Drug Mart on the ground, among others, that the Lord's Day Act was no longer valid criminal law because changed social conditions and the Charter had removed its constitutional underpinning, since it rested on the discredited premise that Christianity was part of the common law.
firac.rule: Sunday observance legislation has been consistently characterized as criminal law within s. 91(27) of the British North America Act: Attorney General for Ontario v. Hamilton Street Railway Co. (1903); Ouimet v. Bazin (1912); Henry Birks & Sons v. Montreal (1955); Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen (1963); Corporation of the City of Hamilton v. Canadian Transport Commission (1978). Charter s. 31 provides the Charter does not extend legislative powers.
firac.application: The majority held the vires of legislation is fixed and that a long line of binding authority classified the Act as criminal law because of its religious/morality purpose. The Charter did not redistribute legislative powers (s. 31), and nothing demonstrated the profound change in public attitudes needed to displace nearly a century of authority. Belzil J.A. agreed, noting vires is determined at the date of enactment and does not fluctuate with social change, and stare decisis bound the trial judge.
firac.conclusion: The Lord's Day Act is valid federal legislation under the criminal law power (s. 91(27)); the trial judge erred in holding it ultra vires.

firac.issue: Can a corporation rely on the Charter in its defence, and is the Provincial Court a court of competent jurisdiction to apply it?
firac.facts: The Crown argued a corporation has no conscience or religion and cannot claim s. 2 freedoms or apply under s. 24, and that the Provincial Court was not a 'court of competent jurisdiction'.
firac.rule: The Charter must be interpreted generously, avoiding 'the austerity of tabulated legalism' (Minister of Home Affairs v. Fisher; Edwards 'living tree'). 'Everyone' and 'anyone' include corporations (Union Colliery Co. v. The Queen). Standing tests: Thorson, McNeil, Borowski. A 'court of competent jurisdiction' means any court with independent jurisdiction over the matter (per Gibson; R. v. Garrett).
firac.application: The majority held the task is to assess the nature of the impugned law, not the attributes of the accused; a law infringing one Canadian's rights infringes all. A corporation directly charged with a criminal offence has standing regardless of its corporate character. Restricting the Provincial Court would leave an accused with a valid Charter defence unable to raise it, which would be absurd.
firac.conclusion: The corporation may rely on the Charter in its defence, and the Provincial Court of Alberta is a court of competent jurisdiction.

firac.issue: Does the Lord's Day Act infringe the freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed by s. 2(a) of the Charter?
firac.facts: Police observed clerks selling groceries, cups and a bicycle lock on Sunday. The Act's purpose and history are religious — enforcing the Christian Sunday — as confirmed by its title and internal references.
firac.rule: Charter s. 2(a) freedom of conscience and religion. The declaratory Bill of Rights and Robertson and Rosetanni (1963) are distinguishable because the Charter is entrenched supreme law (s. 52) not limited to rights as they existed in 1960; Cartwright J.'s dissent in Robertson (a law compelling conduct for a purely religious purpose infringes religious freedom) is persuasive; compare Sherbert v. Verner (1963).
firac.application: The majority held the Act has a religious purpose — to enforce the Christian Sunday — imposing a coercive burden both economic (denying a competitive day of business) and moral (the state throwing its weight behind one side of a sectarian dispute). Government must not choose sides in sectarian controversy. Robertson does not bind because the Charter's language and status differ. Belzil J.A. dissented, reading 'freedom of religion' as protection only against oppression/compulsion to a doctrine, not against establishment; the Act compels neither Christian nor non-Christian to observe Sunday as a holy day, so no infringement.
firac.conclusion: Per the majority, the Lord's Day Act infringes the freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a). Belzil J.A. would have held it does not.

firac.issue: If the Act infringes s. 2(a), is it saved as a reasonable limit under s. 1 of the Charter?
firac.facts: The Crown argued that a weekly day of rest is a universally recognized societal value and that Sunday is chosen merely by habit, so the religious genesis is immaterial.
firac.rule: Charter s. 1: limits must be 'demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society'; the burden rests on the party invoking the limitation (Re Southam Inc. and the Queen; Quebec Association of Protestant School Boards). Courts cannot rewrite a statute to make it a more reasonable limit (R. v. Oakes (Ont. C.A.); R. v. Southam).
firac.application: The majority found the Act's undoubted religious purpose and effect fatal: it enforces the Christian Sunday, not merely a day of rest, with few exemptions (unlike U.S. statutes with religious-observance exemptions). The Crown, bearing the burden, could not justify the limit; the Court would not rewrite the Act to save it.
firac.conclusion: The Act is not saved by s. 1; the appeal is dismissed and the acquittal upheld (Belzil J.A., having found no infringement, did not reach s. 1).

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the primary practice area — the case turns on division of powers and Charter analysis. K004 (Criminal law) is engaged because the Act's validity depends on the s. 91(27) criminal law power and the accused was criminally charged. K025 (freedom of religion) and K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) are the core of the majority's holding and the dissent. K030 (reasonable limits s. 1) covers the final Oakes-style justification analysis. K107 (Canadian Charter) anchors the constitutional instrument at issue. K033 (shabbat) is a borderline pick reflecting the discussion of Sabbatarians and Jewish believers who observe Saturday as their holy day and the coercive effect on them; it is weaker than the others but genuinely engaged by the reasoning on the burden imposed on non-Sunday observers.
location_rationale: The header states 'In the Court of Appeal of Alberta', 'Registry: Calgary', and the reasons are 'DATED AT CALGARY, ALBERTA'. The offence occurred 'in the City of Calgary in the Province of Alberta.'
registry_rationale: The decision header expressly lists 'Registry: Calgary'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Rosenberg v. Minster

defining_issues: Should a court order an access/non-custodial parent to comply with a specific religious practice (Jewish dietary/kosher laws) during parenting time?
Should the father's access be suspended during the Jewish holidays?

firac.issue: On an interim basis, should the court order the father to comply with Jewish dietary (kosher) laws during his access visits with the child?
firac.facts: The parents, married 14 months, separated ten weeks after their daughter Chayala was born. The mother and her Orthodox family demanded the father observe strict Orthodox practices, including feeding the child only kosher food during his parenting time; the father described his own practice as moderate to traditional. The mother alleged emotional and spiritual harm to the child from non-kosher food; her counsel conceded non-kosher food would not physically harm the child.
firac.rule: Under s. 16(8) of the Divorce Act the court considers only the best interests of the child. Courts do not choose between the religious practices of parents (H.(B.) v. Z.(S.), 2000 CanLII 26912 (ON CJ)). Per Young v. Young (1993), religious expression by an access parent may be overridden only where its application leads to consequences more significant than inconvenience or upset — a risk of substantial harm to the child must be shown, and the burden lies on the party asserting harm (Fruitman v. Fruitman, 1998 CarswellOnt 1941).
firac.application: The court declined to determine whether the parents had agreed to raise Chayala in a strictly Orthodox manner, finding it would answer the wrong question and require resolving diametrically opposed credibility. The mother's counsel conceded non-kosher food would not harm the child; the asserted emotional/spiritual harm was undercut by the child's young age and by the mother's own distress being distinct from the child-focused best-interests test. There was no evidence the father's manner of feeding placed the child at any risk.
firac.conclusion: The motion to require the father to comply with Jewish dietary laws during access was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should the father's access be suspended during the Jewish holidays, with makeup visits before and after?
firac.facts: The mother sought suspension of the father's access during Jewish holidays. Access had only begun once the father retained counsel and had been refused for lengthy periods; the kosher issue arose only after other access obstacles were resolved. The parties had already consented on June 15 to an expanded parenting schedule including alternating statutory holidays. Excluding the father from Jewish holidays had not been raised before this motion.
firac.rule: Best interests of the child under s. 16(8) of the Divorce Act; risk of substantial harm must be shown to restrict a parent's religious involvement and time with the child (Young v. Young; Fruitman v. Fruitman).
firac.application: The court found religious holidays are central markers of faith and family bonding, and no evidentiary basis beyond the mother's finding the father's practices offensive supported suspension. The pattern of events suggested alienation. The father's proposed schedule continued the June 15 consent, placing the child with him on specified dates; as a consent order was already in place, no further order was needed.
firac.conclusion: The motion to suspend the father's access during the Jewish holidays was dismissed; the father's schedule was preferred.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) are the core doctrines — the s. 16(8) best-interests test governed both issues. K025 (freedom of religion) and K052 (religious upbringing) reflect the central dispute over religious practice in child-rearing. K028 (kosher/dietary law) is directly engaged by the kosher-food demand. K117 (Divorce Act) is the governing statute cited (s. 16(8)). K097 (Orthodox/Hasidic community) reflects the mother's demand for strict Orthodox practices, and K093 (Jewish) situates the parties' faith. K028 and K052 are somewhat overlapping but each captures a distinct facet (diet vs. general upbringing).

registry_rationale: The decision bears court file number FC-10-36576 but does not name a registry office or city, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Robinson v. Pickering (City)

defining_issues: Does the municipal Integrity Commissioner perform an investigative or an adjudicative function under the Municipal Act, 2001?
Was Council's First Decision (30-day pay suspension) based on the First Report unreasonable?
Was Council's Second Decision (60-day pay suspension) unreasonable, tainted by bias, or an unjustified limit on freedom of expression?
Should the applicant be granted leave to amend to raise new allegations of bias against the mayor?

firac.issue: Under the Municipal Act, 2001, does the Integrity Commissioner exercise an investigative function while municipal council performs the adjudicative role, and who holds the statutory power of decision?
firac.facts: Principles Integrity, appointed under s. 223.3(1), investigated complaints against Councillor Robinson and reported its opinions and recommended sanctions to Council. Council then voted to impose salary suspensions. The applicant argued the Commissioner was the de facto adjudicator, relying on Assaly and Jubenville; the respondents argued the Commissioner was merely an investigator.
firac.rule: Sections 223.2–223.6 of the Municipal Act, 2001; the definition of 'statutory power of decision' in s. 1 of the Judicial Review Procedure Act; and Divisional Court authority in Chiarelli v. Ottawa (City), Villeneuve v. North Stormont and Fallis v. City of Orillia, which hold the Commissioner's role is 'investigative, not adjudicative' and that council performs the adjudicative function.
firac.application: The court preferred the full-panel reasoning in Chiarelli, Villeneuve and Fallis over the obiter single-judge comments in Assaly and Jubenville. Section 223.4(5) states the municipality 'may' impose a penalty where the Commissioner reports that, 'in his or her opinion,' a member contravened the code — signalling that the Commissioner offers an opinion, not a binding decision, and that council may decline to impose any sanction. Council therefore holds the de facto adjudicative decision-making power; the Commissioner investigates and reports.
firac.conclusion: The Integrity Commissioner performs an investigative function and municipal council is the effective adjudicative decision-maker. This determination raised the bar for any bias allegation against the Commissioner to proof of a 'closed mind.'

firac.issue: Was Council's acceptance of the First Report, finding a breach of s. 05.01 of the Code of Conduct and imposing a 30-day pay suspension, reasonable?
firac.facts: After the committee of adjustment denied her minor variance for a shipping container, Robinson posted on Facebook naming the three residents who opposed her, 'thanking' them for cancelling her charity Halloween event. The post circulated widely and generated complaints that it was an intimidating attack that could deter public participation.
firac.rule: Reasonableness review under Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 — justification, transparency and intelligibility; the burden is on the party challenging the decision; s. 05.01 of the Code requiring members to treat the public with respect and dignity, without abuse, bullying or intimidation.
firac.application: The Commissioner reasonably rejected the applicant's claim of sincere gratitude and characterized the post as a sarcastic 'bully tactic' capable of inviting attacks on the residents; the finding that the post reached a wide audience was supported by evidence of the screenshot circulating. The Commissioner's plain-language definition of bullying was acceptable, and the belated bias allegation against the Commissioner could not be raised for the first time on judicial review (Chiarelli).
firac.conclusion: The First Decision was reasonable; the application to set it aside was dismissed.

firac.issue: Was Council's acceptance of the Second Report and imposition of a 60-day suspension unreasonable, biased, or a disproportionate limit on the applicant's freedom of expression?
firac.facts: Days later Robinson addressed a crowd by megaphone outside a Durham school board meeting, promoting three motions (on 'adult live performances,' flag-raising, and change-rooms) targeting Pride events and drag queen story time. The Commissioner found the conduct promoted homophobic and transphobic attitudes and that she had filed reprisal counter-complaints against two councillors, breaching ss. 05.01 and 17.01.
firac.rule: Vavilov reasonableness review; the Doré/Loyola/Trinity Western framework requiring administrative decisions limiting Charter rights (here freedom of expression under s. 2(b)) to reflect a proportionate balance with the statutory objective; the 'closed mind' test for bias by an investigator (Chiarelli).
firac.application: The Commissioner's interpretation of s. 05.01 was transparent and defensible; failing to treat individuals with respect and dignity contravened the Code. The applicant did raise bias with the Commissioner, who addressed it and maintained an open mind (agreeing with her on some points, e.g., that her conduct was not hate speech), so no closed mind was shown — and, having found the Commissioner to be an investigator, the applicant conceded bias was no longer in play. On expression, the Commissioner expressly balanced the councillor's important free-speech role against the rights of marginalized LGBTQ+ persons and imposed a sanction below the 90-day maximum, a proportionate response.
firac.conclusion: The Second Decision was reasonable, unbiased, and a proportionate limit on freedom of expression; the application was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should leave be granted to further amend the notice of application to allege bias against the mayor arising from the October 2023 Council meeting?
firac.facts: After the respondents had already consented not to oppose extending time to commence the applications, the applicant sought to add the mayor as a respondent and allege bias for conduct at the meeting she personally attended, a video of which was posted online the next day.
firac.rule: A claim of bias must be raised before the original decision-maker and cannot be advanced for the first time on judicial review (Chiarelli); leave to amend may be refused where it would cause non-compensable prejudice or procedural unfairness.
firac.application: The applicant never raised the mayor's alleged bias before Council, depriving the mayor of the opportunity to consider recusal or give reasons — fatal to the claim. The delay was unexplained given her attendance and the promptly available recording, and permitting the amendment after the respondents had foregone opposition to the extension motions would cause procedural unfairness and prejudice.
firac.conclusion: Leave to amend was denied.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a judicial review of municipal integrity-commissioner and council decisions. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) are central given the Vavilov reasonableness analysis. K012 (procedural fairness) captures the bias allegations against the Commissioner and mayor and the 'closed mind' test. K042 (code of conduct) is the governing instrument (Municipal Act code of conduct). K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) reflect the contested limit on the councillor's expression, analyzed through K010 (Doré/Loyola framework) proportionate balancing. K069 (discrimination) is a weaker but genuine pick — the Commissioner's homophobia/transphobia findings and the court's remark that the essence of discrimination is failing to treat individuals with respect engage it, though there is no dedicated municipal-law keyword in the vocabulary.

registry_rationale: The file numbers are labelled 'OSHAWA DIVISIONAL COURT FILE NOs.', indicating the matter was filed in the Oshawa registry of the Divisional Court.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. B.M.

defining_issues: Was the similar fact evidence of the accused's admitted indecent assaults on two sisters admissible, and was it tainted by collusion, in proving the disputed indecent assaults on the third sister?
Did the Crown prove beyond a reasonable doubt on the Gardiner hearing that the accused had sexual intercourse with M.L.C. and committed multiple indecent assaults on her?
What is the fit and proportionate sentence for a first offender of advanced age and poor health convicted of historical sexual offences against three child victims?

firac.issue: Was the similar fact evidence admissible, and untainted by collusion, in proving the disputed conduct against M.L.C.?
firac.facts: The accused admitted indecently assaulting his three nieces and one act with M.L.C., but disputed the number of assaults on M.L.C. and denied intercourse. The three sisters had opportunity over 30 years to discuss the abuse, though discussions were vague and detailed disclosure came only after M.L.C. told her sisters in 2006.
firac.rule: Similar act / other discreditable conduct evidence is presumptively inadmissible; the Crown must establish threshold relevance, probative value exceeding prejudicial effect, and, on a balance of probabilities, that the evidence is not tainted by collusion where there is an air of reality to collusion (R. v. Handy, 2002 SCC 56; R. v. Shearing, 2002 SCC 58; R. v. G.(M.A.)). Propensity reasoning is forbidden.
firac.application: The Court found only opportunity, not actual collusion; the sisters' conversations were vague ('he did something'), and detailed disclosure post-dated M.L.C.'s own 2006 disclosure. It was satisfied on a balance of probabilities the evidence was not tainted. The evidence could not be used to prove intercourse (forbidden propensity reasoning), but was probative of whether the multiple indecent assaults on M.L.C. actually occurred, its prejudicial effect being minimized in a judge-alone trial with limiting self-instruction.
firac.conclusion: The similar fact evidence was admitted to support the occurrence of the multiple indecent assaults on M.L.C. but not to prove the intercourse charge.

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove the disputed intercourse and multiple indecent assaults on M.L.C. beyond a reasonable doubt?
firac.facts: M.L.C., aged roughly 8-10, described masturbation incidents in the car and home progressing to one act of painful intercourse. The accused admitted only a single dining-room masturbation incident and denied intercourse, giving inconsistent testimony that conflicted with his police statement and the Agreed Statement of Facts.
firac.rule: On a Gardiner hearing the Crown must prove disputed aggravating facts beyond a reasonable doubt (R. v. Gardiner). Credibility is assessed applying R. v. W.(D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742.
firac.application: The Court found M.L.C. credible, detailed and consistent, corroborated by her sisters on family circumstances and transportation. It rejected the accused's self-absorbed, minimizing and internally inconsistent testimony, including his implausible dining-room account, and was not left in reasonable doubt.
firac.conclusion: The accused was found guilty of sexual intercourse with a female under 14 (s. 146(1)) and found to have committed multiple indecent assaults on M.L.C., though the exact number was not proven.

firac.issue: What is the fit and proportionate sentence for these historical sexual offences against three child victims?
firac.facts: The accused, 69, in poor health, was a first offender who pleaded guilty to three counts of indecent assault and was convicted after trial of intercourse with a child. The offences occurred 1972-1974 against nieces in his care; he showed limited insight and partial remorse.
firac.rule: Sentencing objectives of denunciation and deterrence (s. 718), proportionality (s. 718.1; R. v. McArthur), totality (R. v. Gramlick), the range for historical sexual offences (R. v. D.(D.)), treatment of delay (R. v. Stanzel; R. v. R.(A.)) and mitigation for advanced age/infirmity (R. v. R.(A.); R. v. Oziel), plus credit for guilty pleas (R. v. R.W.E.).
firac.application: A penitentiary sentence was required, foreclosing a conditional sentence under s. 742.1. Weighing aggravating factors (multiple vulnerable victims, frequency, quasi-breach of trust, violence, lasting harm) against mitigation (guilty pleas, first offender, age, health, rehabilitation steps), the Court imposed three years for the intercourse count, one year consecutive on one indecent assault, and one year concurrent on the other two, applying the totality principle. Ancillary orders (s. 109, DNA, SOIRA, s. 161) were imposed.
firac.conclusion: Total sentence of four years' imprisonment, plus mandatory and discretionary ancillary orders.

The similar fact / collusion analysis is an evidentiary issue best captured by class action?—no. name_verification.name_in_document: Rapoport v. Rapoport

defining_issues: Was there a material change in circumstances since the April 16, 2009 Divorce Order sufficient to justify a fresh inquiry into custody and access?
What custody and access arrangement is in the best interests of the two children?
Were the wife's surreptitiously obtained tape recordings admissible in the family law proceeding?
How should the payor husband's annual income be determined for child support purposes, including retained earnings, corporate losses and RRSP/capital-gain income?
Should the amount and duration of spousal support be varied?
Was the wife in contempt for failing to deliver household contents said to be owed to the husband?

firac.issue: Was there a material change in circumstances warranting a fresh inquiry into custody and access?
firac.facts: The 2009 consent Divorce Order granted joint custody with week-about shared residence, settled on the shared understanding that the older child Jacob was not developmentally disabled after paediatrician Dr Montgomery ruled out autism. After the Order, Jacob was diagnosed with Asperger's Syndrome (a form of autism), and the parents' conflict and inability to communicate continued unabated.
firac.rule: Section 17(5) of the Divorce Act permits variation only where there has been a change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances of the child since the making of the order; a 'material change' is one that, if known at the time, would likely have resulted in different terms (Willick v. Willick; Gordon v. Goertz). Identification of a child's special needs can constitute good reason for a fresh custody inquiry (Rail v. Rail).
firac.application: The husband's agreement to shared custody was predicated on the false negative autism diagnosis; the confirmed diagnosis of Asperger's Syndrome fundamentally changed the care and routine the child required. In addition, the assumption underlying joint/shared custody—that the parents could communicate and co-operate—had proven false, as their high conflict, mistrust and non-communication had continued.
firac.conclusion: The court found a material change in circumstances on two bases (Jacob's autism diagnosis and the breakdown of the co-operation assumed by shared custody) and undertook a fresh best-interests inquiry.

firac.issue: What custody and access arrangement is in the best interests of the children?
firac.facts: Both parents love the children, but the husband had consistently led on education, health and recreation, understood and pursued Jacob's autism needs, and maintained a structured, routine household with a nanny; the wife was found less consistent, prone to distraction, denial and lapses, and had conceded that the husband should direct education and health care. Joint/shared custody had not brought peace.
firac.rule: On variation the court considers only the best interests of the child (s. 17(5)–(6) Divorce Act) and gives effect to maximum contact consistent with best interests (s. 17(9)); the s. 24(2) Children's Law Reform Act factors are a helpful guide. Joint custody requires a high level of co-operation and communication (Kaplanis v. Kaplanis; Giri v. Wentges); parallel parenting is an option where parents cannot co-operate (Ursic v. Ursic).
firac.application: Given the persistent conflict, joint and parallel parenting were unworkable. The husband was better equipped to provide the consistency, routine and academic/health leadership the autistic child (and possibly Levi) required. The husband's earlier verbal abuse of the wife was situational, pre-February 2007, and there was no credible evidence he was abusive toward the children, so past conduct did not bar custody. The boys should not be separated.
firac.conclusion: Sole custody was awarded to the husband, with generous specified access to the wife (alternate weekends, a mid-week evening, shared holidays and religious festivals, and a summer month).

firac.issue: Were the wife's surreptitious tape recordings admissible?
firac.facts: The wife had secretly recorded conversations with the husband, mostly October 2006–February 2007, to demonstrate his controlling, profane and verbally abusive behaviour toward her in front of the children. The husband initially opposed admission, then agreed to admit certain tapes.
firac.rule: There is no statute governing admissibility of evidence illegally obtained by private parties; the common law leans toward inclusion of relevant evidence (The Law of Evidence in Canada). Family law authorities are split: Reddick v. Reddick admits reliable, relevant, probative recordings; Hameed v. Hameed excludes them on policy grounds as heightening conflict and being unreliable.
firac.application: Adopting the Reddick line, the court held it could not rule on admissibility without hearing the tapes to assess reliability, accuracy, context and probative value. After the parties agreed which tapes/transcripts would be entered, recordings of very poor quality (where transcript could not be verified against the recording) were excluded; admitted recordings were weighed cautiously, the court noting the 'staged' quality and the wife's role in provoking and capturing the exchanges.
firac.conclusion: The tapes were admissible in principle (following Reddick); poor-quality recordings were excluded and the admitted ones given limited, carefully weighed weight, confirming the husband engaged in situational verbal abuse.

firac.issue: How should the husband's annual income be determined for child support?
firac.facts: The husband was the sole shareholder of his professional corporation (RPC), his 'alter ego'. His income fluctuated sharply: 2008 substantial, declining steeply in 2009–2010 due to the recession, with collapsed RRSPs, capital gains, retained earnings and, latterly, corporate operating losses.
firac.rule: Under ss. 15–20 of the Federal Child Support Guidelines annual income is 'Total income' (Line 150) adjusted per Schedule III; s. 18 permits attribution of a corporation's pre-tax income (retained earnings) where Line 150 does not fairly reflect available income (Brophy v. Brophy). RRSP withdrawals are included with no Schedule III adjustment (Mylrea v. Benoit; Stevens v. Boulerice), and 'double dipping' concerns do not apply to child support because it benefits the children.
firac.application: The court accepted the expert's approach: retained earnings were attributed to the husband, and by parity of reasoning corporate operating losses were also attributed (Cunningham v. Montgomery); the 2010 income-tax refund was excluded. RRSP and capital-gain income equalized with the wife were nonetheless included for child support since 'double dipping' does not affect child support. Resulting annual incomes: 2008 $387,991; 2009 $300,149; 2010 $49,705.
firac.conclusion: Child support was fixed on those Guideline incomes ($4,753, then $3,734, then $794/month), with arrears payable, and only nominal child support ordered going forward given the wife's nil income.

firac.issue: Should spousal support be varied?
firac.facts: The 2009 Order required $7,250/month spousal support to March 31, 2015, apparently based on the SSAG. The husband's income later fell substantially and he obtained sole custody; the wife had no income, faced possible bankruptcy and loss of her home.
firac.rule: Moge v. Moge governs entitlement/quantum; the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines are a 'useful tool' and significant authority (Fisher v. Fisher). A material change permits variation. For spousal support, RRSP and capital-gain amounts already equalized may be excluded to avoid double dipping (s. 17 discretion; Cunningham v. Montgomery).
firac.application: A material change (declining income, depleted property, and now sole custody) was established. For spousal support the court excluded the equalized RRSP/capital-gain amounts, producing $351,989 (2008), nil (2009), $49,705 (2010). Given the fluctuation, the court used the three-year average income ($133,898) to set fair prospective support at the SSAG midpoint with the children in the husband's sole custody.
firac.conclusion: Spousal support was varied: $8,248 (from Feb 2009), $0 (2010), $963 (2011), then $682/month from January 2012, with arrears at $1,500/month; duration to 2015 was not disturbed.

firac.issue: Was the wife in contempt for failing to deliver certain household contents?
firac.facts: The husband alleged the wife failed to deliver furniture and artwork he said had been agreed to be his; the items had not been listed or initialled, the wife said furniture was left in the sold home for him to collect, and she had sold the 'Chicago' picture when support went unpaid.
firac.rule: Para. 49/50 of the Divorce Order provided for equal division of contents (excluding items brought into the marriage), with disputes to be arbitrated or decided by the court. Contempt requires reliable proof of a clear obligation and its breach.
firac.application: There was no reliable proof of an agreement that the disputed items were to go to the husband, and the furniture may have been left at the home for him to retrieve. The evidence was uncertain, vague and conflicting.
firac.conclusion: The motion for contempt was denied.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) and K047 (best interests of the child) capture the central custody variation and the best-interests analysis, including the autistic child's special needs. K050 (parental/child support) and K053 (spousal support) reflect the extensive Guideline income and SSAG analysis and the variation of both support obligations. K117 (Divorce Act) is the governing statute for the s. 17 variation. K052 (religious upbringing) applies because the Order required the children be raised in the Jewish faith and religious-school attendance and Rosh Hashanah/Chanukah access were addressed. K093 (Jewish) reflects the family's Jewish identity and the wife's conversion to Judaism. K088 (Holocaust) is a borderline but genuine pick: the husband's parents were Holocaust survivors and the wife's whispered 'It's too bad Hitler didn't kill your parents' remark was a material credibility finding. Antisemitism (K058) was considered but rejected, as the court found the remark was not made out of bigotry. Evidentiary admissibility of the tapes is significant but no vocabulary keyword fits it well.
