case_name: Sandor c. Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital

name_verification.name_in_document: Sandor c. Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital

defining_issues: Did the plaintiffs prove that it was in fact impossible for them to act within the strict time limit under article 173 C.C.P. to set the case down for trial?
Should the court exercise its discretion under article 177 para. 2 C.C.P. to relieve the plaintiffs of the consequences of their failure to set the case down for trial, applying the Zodiac criteria?

firac.issue: Did the plaintiffs prove it was in fact impossible for them to act within the strict time limit of article 173 C.C.P.?
firac.facts: The self-represented plaintiffs had to file a request to set their $25M malpractice action down for trial by December 15, 2022 (a second extension). On December 1, 2022 the Hospital filed an application to dismiss (art. 51 C.C.P.) presentable December 15, and the plaintiffs believed the setting-down deadline would be addressed at that hearing. No hearing occurred; the application was dismissed on the record December 20, 2022, and the plaintiffs only learned of this from the Hospital's lawyers on December 28, 2022.
firac.rule: Article 173 C.C.P. imposes a strict six-month limit and article 177 para. 1 deems the action discontinued for non-compliance; article 177 para. 2 permits relief where it was 'impossible in fact' to act. Impossibility is a relative, factual matter with a low but clear-and-convincing burden on the plaintiff, and diligence is a sine qua non (Zodiac 2015 QCCA 175; Heaslip 2017 QCCA 1273; Air Canada 2016 QCCA 710; Marineau 2023 QCCA 832). Where the deadline is a second extension, 'compelling reasons' are required. Self-represented status is a factor and judges owe a duty to assist and promote access to justice.
firac.application: The court found the plaintiffs' confusion during December 1–28, 2022 understandable and not the product of negligence; the December 20 judgment was never entered in the plumitif nor served by a notice of judgment under art. 335 C.C.P. Had the announced December 15 hearing occurred, the setting-down issue would likely have been raised. Unlike Gauthier (2023 QCCA 502), where a year of non-follow-up showed lack of diligence, these plaintiffs acted diligently and had compelling reasons.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiffs proved factual impossibility to act within the December 15, 2022 deadline and demonstrated compelling reasons for missing it.

firac.issue: Should the court exercise its discretion under article 177 para. 2 C.C.P. to relieve the plaintiffs of the deemed discontinuance?
firac.facts: Refusing relief would deem the action discontinued, requiring payment of the Hospital's costs (art. 213 C.C.P.) and, more significantly, ending the interruption of prescription (art. 2894 C.C.Q.) — with alleged faults occurring 2011–2016 and proper treatment obtained 2017–2018, risking prescription of the claim. The Hospital had twice failed to obtain preliminary dismissal (Oct. 5, 2021 and Dec. 20, 2022). Thirteen days elapsed before discovery of the missed deadline and 65 days before notifying the application over the Christmas holidays.
firac.rule: The discretion under art. 177 para. 2 must be exercised judicially, weighing the four Zodiac criteria (2015 QCCA 175, para. 24): harm from refusing relief; apparent seriousness of the claim (caution required before finding a claim insufficiently serious — Heaslip); time elapsed since expiry (two periods examined, second must be short but assessed against the litigant's legal knowledge — Vidal 2019 QCCA 1621; Villeneuve 2020 QCCA 1287); and conduct of the parties, distinguishing gross negligence/disorganization from good-faith errors (9243-9579 Québec inc. 2021 QCCA 1564).
firac.application: Harm favoured relief given the real prescription risk. The claim was not manifestly ill-founded, having survived two dismissal attempts, so the plaintiffs were entitled to their day in court. The 13-day and 65-day delays were reasonable given the holiday period and the plaintiffs' minimal familiarity with the legal system. Their conduct reflected a good-faith error about the effect of the dismissal application on the art. 173 delay — an error even a lawyer might make — not gross negligence. All four criteria favoured relief.
firac.conclusion: The court exercised its discretion in the interest of justice to relieve the plaintiffs of the consequences of their default, extended the setting-down deadline to October 1, 2023, and ordered a case protocol.

K012 (procedural fairness) is engaged because the reasoning turns heavily on the judicial duty to assist self-represented litigants and to promote access to justice, and K001 (Administrative law) is included as the tier-1 parent of that keyword. Davis Jewish General Hospital; the substantive dispute has no Jewish-law or community content, so these are flagged as tenuous. The controlled vocabulary offers no specific civil-procedure keyword (e.g., limitation/setting-down deadlines), so no closer specific term exists.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Veltman

defining_issues: What findings of fact are necessarily inherent in the jury's verdicts, and what independent findings must the sentencing judge make where the verdicts are ambiguous?
Should the offender's claimed mental disorders and intoxication be treated as mitigating factors on sentence?
Did the murders and attempted murder constitute 'terrorist activity' within the meaning of ss. 231(6.01) and 83.01 of the Criminal Code?
What is the appropriate sentence for the attempted murder of Fayez Afzaal?

firac.issue: What findings of fact are necessarily inherent in the jury's verdicts, and what independent findings must the sentencing judge make where the verdicts are ambiguous?
firac.facts: A jury convicted the offender of four counts of first degree murder and one count of attempted murder after he drove his truck into the Afzaal family. The jury gave no reasons. The defence argued the jury may have accepted parts of the defence evidence (offender's testimony and Dr. Gojer's psychiatric opinion) that his acts were driven by an uncontrollable compulsion rather than a genuine intent to kill.
firac.rule: Section 724(2) of the Criminal Code requires the sentencing judge to accept as proven all facts essential to the jury's verdict and permits finding other relevant facts disclosed at trial. Per R. v. Ferguson, 2008 SCC 6, the judge is bound by the express and implied factual implications of the verdict, must not accept evidence consistent only with a rejected verdict, and where the verdict is ambiguous must make independent findings (beyond a reasonable doubt for aggravating facts, balance of probabilities for other facts). The W.(D.) framework governs assessment of the exculpatory defence evidence.
firac.application: The attempted-murder verdict, which requires an intention to kill, showed the jury found an intention to kill all five victims and rejected the compulsion/recklessness theory. Resolving remaining ambiguity, the court independently assessed the offender's police statements and 'A White Awakening' manifesto, finding them genuine expressions of his belief system rather than concocted justifications, and found the offender was in full control of his faculties, having planned a murderous attack on Muslims for months.
firac.conclusion: The court found the offender had the intention to kill, that the murders were planned and deliberate, and that the offender was a deliberate, conscious actor — findings anchored in the verdicts and the judge's independent assessment of the evidence.

firac.issue: Should the offender's claimed mental disorders and intoxication be treated as mitigating factors on sentence?
firac.facts: The offender claimed OCD and Autism Spectrum Disorder and asserted that isolation and repeated consumption of extremist content, together with psilocybin ingested about 40 hours earlier, drove his conduct. Dr. Gojer's opinion rested solely on the offender's uncorroborated account; the offender barred contact with family and refused counselling records. Dr. Gojer's trial opinion differed from his report, was selective, and relied on novel, unsupported science.
firac.rule: An offender must prove disputed mitigating factors on a balance of probabilities. Mental illness may reduce moral blameworthiness in some cases but there is no inevitable correlation between illness and mitigation; the illness must be relevant to the offence.
firac.application: The court gave no weight to Dr. Gojer's testimony given its unreliability and the withholding of collateral sources. The jury had rejected the notion that compulsion blinded the offender to consequences. The court found the offender's immersion in extremist content reflected his subjective preferences, not illness, and that any disorders did not interfere with his ability to plan and carry out the murders.
firac.conclusion: The defence failed to establish the disorders on a balance of probabilities or their relevance; they were not treated as mitigating and did not reduce moral blameworthiness.

firac.issue: Did the murders and attempted murder constitute 'terrorist activity' within the meaning of ss. 231(6.01) and 83.01 of the Criminal Code?
firac.facts: The offender, a self-described white nationalist, targeted and killed the Afzaal family because he believed them to be Muslim, intending to send a 'brutal message' to 'Muslim grooming gangs' and to inspire others to carry out similar vehicular attacks, hoping to make Muslims leave the country.
firac.rule: Section 231(6.01) makes murder first degree where the act also constitutes terrorist activity. Section 83.01 defines terrorist activity through three elements: (1) a motive clause (act committed in whole or part for a political, religious or ideological purpose), (2) an intention clause (intention to intimidate the public or a segment with regard to its security), and (3) a consequence clause (intentionally causing death or serious bodily harm by violence). Per R. v. Khawaja, 2012 SCC 69, the definition does not capture non-violent expression and sets a high, stringent threshold (see also R. v. O.S., 2023 ONSC 4142).
firac.application: The consequence clause was clearly met by the killings. The motive clause was satisfied: the offender's views cohered into a white-nationalist ideology, a lens through which he saw the world, not mere disconnected opinions. The intention clause was satisfied: the offender intended to intimidate the broader Muslim community, evidenced by his statements and his manifesto, which he intended to be published; his 'lone wolf' secrecy was tactical and did not negate the ulterior intention.
firac.conclusion: All three elements were proved beyond a reasonable doubt; the murders satisfied s. 231(6.01) and the attempted murder met the s. 83.01 definition — 'a textbook example of terrorist motive and intent.'

firac.issue: What is the appropriate sentence for the attempted murder of Fayez Afzaal?
firac.facts: Nine-year-old Fayez Afzaal survived the attack that killed four members of his family but suffered serious physical and psychological injuries. The Crown sought a concurrent life sentence; the defence sought 10 years, arguing the orphaning should not aggravate the attempted-murder sentence (double punishment) and that vengeance had no place.
firac.rule: Proportionality is the overarching sentencing objective. Terrorist activity is a statutory aggravating factor under s. 718.2(a)(v). For terrorism, denunciation, deterrence and protection of society are paramount (Khawaja SCC), tempered by rehabilitation, which reflects human dignity (R. v. Bissonnette, 2022 SCC 23). Retribution and denunciation, distinct from vengeance, apply (R. v. M.(C.A.), 1996 CanLII 230 (SCC)).
firac.application: The court found high moral blameworthiness given the sophisticated planning, use of a truck fitted with a grill guard, targeting of children as 'collateral damage', random ethnic selection of victims, and racist motivation. These factors alone could justify life; the terrorism designation made a life sentence inevitable. The attempted murder was part of a single terrorist act; while Fayez was not to be punished twice for the murders, the offence could not be hived off from its terrorist context. Rehabilitation remained relevant but subordinate.
firac.conclusion: The offender was sentenced to life imprisonment for the attempted murder of Fayez Afzaal, concurrent to four life sentences with 25-year parole ineligibility for the first degree murders, plus ancillary weapons, DNA, forfeiture and non-communication orders.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a sentencing decision following murder and attempted-murder convictions. K037 (terrorism) is central: the court's principal legal finding was that the attack was terrorist activity under ss. 231(6.01) and 83.01. K060 (hate motivation) and K065 (racism) capture the racist, hate-fuelled motive driving the crime and its treatment as aggravating. K066 (white supremacism) reflects the offender's self-described white-nationalist ideology, the ideological purpose element of the terrorism definition. K061 (hate speech) and K063 (online hate / social media) reflect the offender's immersion in and radicalization through extremist internet/dark-web content, which the court discussed at length. K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) is engaged by the open-court/publicity discussion and the court's decision not to name the offender while upholding public access. The victims were Muslim, but no Muslim-community keyword exists in the vocabulary; the antisemitism keywords do not fit as the target group was Muslim, so they were excluded.

name_verification.name_in_document: HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN — and — MARY WAGNER

defining_issues: Did the Crown prove the actus reus of mischief interfering with private property and of breach of the two probation orders?
Could Ms. Wagner rely on self-defence / defence of others (former s. 37 or the new s. 34 of the Criminal Code) to justify her conduct, and does a foetus fall within 'anyone' / 'another person'?
Was the common-law defence of necessity available to excuse her conduct?

Was the trial judge entitled to decline a viva voce evidentiary hearing on the constitutional status of the foetus, and is a foetus a 'human being'/'everyone' such that s. 223 of the Criminal Code is inconsistent with s. 7 of the Charter?
Does the rule against collateral attack bar Ms. Wagner from defending the breach-of-probation charges by attacking the validity of the probation orders?

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove the actus reus of mischief interfering with private property and breach of the probation orders?
firac.facts: While bound by two probation orders requiring her to keep the peace and, in one case, prohibiting her from being on the premises of, or communicating with anyone at, an Ontario abortion provider, Ms. Wagner entered a locked Toronto abortion clinic on 15 August 2012, approached patients with roses and pamphlets urging them to reconsider, refused repeated demands to leave, disrupted procedures, and had to be physically removed. She admitted attending and intending to disrupt the clinic.
firac.rule: Mischief interfering with private property under the Criminal Code requires wilful interference with the lawful use or enjoyment of property in a more than trivial manner; probation conditions require keeping the peace and being of good behaviour and, here, staying away from and not communicating with abortion providers.
firac.application: The court found Ms. Wagner's own testimony and the Crown witnesses largely consistent; she clearly and wilfully entered and communicated in breach of the orders and disrupted the clinic's operations and patient treatment in a non-trivial way. The only factual conflict (whether Dr. Markovic swore at her) was irrelevant.
firac.conclusion: The actus reus of mischief and the resulting breaches of both probation orders were proved beyond a reasonable doubt, subject to consideration of the asserted defences.

firac.issue: Could self-defence / defence of others under former s. 37 or new s. 34 justify her conduct, given the status of the foetus?
firac.facts: Ms. Wagner believed the foetuses of clinic patients were about to be killed and that she was duty-bound to protect them; her intervention was non-violent verbal persuasion and passive resistance.
firac.rule: Former s. 37 justified 'force' used to defend anyone 'under his protection'; new s. 34 (S.C. 2012, c. 9) exempts an 'act' committed to protect oneself or 'another person' from force where the act is 'reasonable in the circumstances' (s. 34(2) factors, including availability of other means (b) and whether the force resisted was known to be lawful (h)). Statutory interpretation per R. v. Conception, 2014 SCC 60; common-law defences preserved by s. 8(3) 'except in so far as altered by' the Act.
firac.application: 'Force' throughout the Criminal Code connotes violence/constraint, not verbal persuasion, so s. 37 did not fit; the foetuses were not 'under her protection' as that phrase requires a special relationship. Under new s. 34, even accepting a genuine belief of imminent lethal force, she failed s. 34(2)(b) and (h): reasonable legal alternatives existed (a Superior Court application) and she knew the abortions were lawful. Critically, a foetus is not 'another person' in Canadian law.
firac.conclusion: Neither the former nor the new self-defence/defence-of-others provisions justified her conduct.

firac.issue: Was the defence of necessity available?
firac.facts: Ms. Wagner argued she was compelled to act to save human lives she believed were in imminent danger.
firac.rule: Perka v. The Queen, [1984] 2 SCR 232: necessity is an excuse of last resort; it is unavailable where a reasonable legal alternative exists (the act must be inevitable, unavoidable, with no reasonable lawful alternative); the law will not validate illegality merely because the actor believes it conflicts with a higher value.
firac.application: A reasonable legal alternative existed — pursuing advocacy, lawful demonstration, or a Superior Court application challenging the abortion law. Her personal penury was irrelevant. Her situation was one of principled disagreement with the law, precisely the 'greater good' formulation rejected in Perka.
firac.conclusion: Necessity was not available; her defence foundered on the existence of reasonable legal alternatives.

firac.issue: Could the judge decline a viva voce hearing on foetal personhood, and is a foetus 'everyone' under s. 7 such that s. 223 is unconstitutional?
firac.facts: Ms. Wagner sought to call expert evidence (Drs. Condic and Thorp) to establish that human life begins at conception and that s. 223's definition of 'human being' violates the Charter. She was asked to file an outline of the anticipated evidence, taken as true for the threshold assessment.
firac.rule: R. v. Kutynec, R. v. Durette, R. v. Felderhof, R. v. Pires and Lising: a trial judge may decline an evidentiary hearing where, even taking the proffered facts as true, it cannot affect the outcome. Bedford, 2013 SCC 72 and Carter, 2015 SCC 5: precedent may only be revisited on a new legal issue or evidence that 'fundamentally shifts the parameters of the debate.' Borowski, Tremblay v. Daigle, Winnipeg CFS, R. v. Morgentaler (1988): a foetus is not a legal person or 'everyone'; personhood is a normative legal, not scientific, question.
firac.application: The proffered scientific material was conclusory and failed to show any material change from the science before the Supreme Court in the 1980s; it did not fundamentally shift the parameters of the debate. Given the weight of binding authority holding a foetus is not a legal person, the hearing could not conceivably change the result. Section 223 does not offend the Charter.
firac.conclusion: The judge was entitled to decline the viva voce hearing; the constitutional argument could not succeed and s. 223 was upheld.

firac.issue: Does the rule against collateral attack bar the challenge to the probation orders?
firac.facts: Ms. Wagner defended the breach-of-probation charges by arguing the orders were constitutionally invalid because they impaired foetal s. 7 rights.
firac.rule: R. v. Wilson, [1983] 2 SCR 594 and R. v. Domm (1996): a court order made by a court with jurisdiction is binding unless set aside on appeal and cannot be attacked collaterally in proceedings not aimed at reversing it; Canada (C.H.R.C.) v. Taylor: an order stands until set aside even if its statutory foundation is unconstitutional.
firac.application: Ms. Wagner could have appealed the probation terms but instead chose to 'breach first, challenge later.' The rule against collateral attack barred her from resisting the breach charges by attacking the orders' validity, so even a meritorious foetal-rights argument would not save her on those counts.
firac.conclusion: The collateral attack rule independently defeated her defence to the breach-of-probation charges.

keywords_rationale: K004 (Criminal law) is the primary practice area — the charges were mischief and breach of probation. K036 (mischief) is the specific offence charged (mischief interfering with private property). K003 (Constitutional law) and K112 (Charter s. 7) capture the central constitutional argument that a foetus is 'everyone' with a right to life and that s. 223 is unconstitutional. K087 (protest/demonstration) reflects the anti-abortion clinic intervention that gave rise to the charges. K025 (freedom of religion) is a borderline/weak pick — the 'supremacy of God' and religious-conviction arguments were discussed but decided against her and were not outcome-determinative; included only because her motivation and the preamble analysis figure in the reasons.

registry_rationale: The court file line names 'Toronto', which is the registry/office of the Ontario Court of Justice hearing the matter.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. Behrens et al.

defining_issues: Does the Legislative Precinct of the Ontario Legislature, over which the Speaker enjoys parliamentary privilege, include the grounds surrounding the Legislative building?
Was the Speaker acting within the recognized parliamentary privilege of 'ejection of strangers from the House and its precincts' when he issued the trespass bans against the defendants?
Does the court have jurisdiction to review the Speaker's exercise of parliamentary privilege for conformity with the Charter, and was Vaid correctly decided on that point?
Did the Speaker lose the protection of parliamentary privilege by relying on the Trespass to Property Act, the police and the courts to enforce the bans?
Did the Crown prove the trespass charges against the defendants beyond a reasonable doubt?

firac.issue: Does the Legislative Precinct of the Ontario Legislature include the grounds surrounding the Legislative building?
firac.facts: The defendants demonstrated on the driveway/front steps of the Legislative building at Queen's Park, within the area described in Order-in-Council 957/90. They admitted being within the geographical description but denied in law that it constituted the Legislative Precinct. The Clerk, Mr. Desrosiers, testified that control over the grounds was necessary to ensure Members' access, and cited several past disruptive demonstrations.
firac.rule: Parliamentary privilege is founded on necessity: courts may determine whether a category of privilege is necessary to the legislature's capacity to function (New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia (Speaker), [1993] 1 S.C.R. 319). The 'ejection of strangers from the House and its precincts' is a recognized privilege (Maingot, Parliamentary Privilege in Canada, 2d).
firac.application: Order-in-Council 957/90 and the Memoranda of Understanding define the Precinct to include 'the entire Legislative building, the grounds bounded on the east by Queen's Park Crescent East, on the north by Wellesley Street West and on the west by Queen's Park Crescent West.' The House adopted the Report on Security in the Legislative Precincts confirming this definition. The evidence, unchallenged, established that control over the grounds was necessary to ensure access and the dignified functioning of the Legislature, consistent with other Canadian and Commonwealth jurisdictions.
firac.conclusion: The Legislative Precinct includes the grounds surrounding the Legislative building; the defendants were within it when banned.

firac.issue: Was the Speaker acting within parliamentary privilege when he issued the trespass bans?
firac.facts: After the defendants poured stage blood on the wall on October 1, 1998, refused to leave when asked, and demonstrated in an inaccessible area, the Sergeant-at-Arms, on the Speaker's authority, issued notices banning them from the Legislative Precinct.
firac.rule: Once a court determines a category of privilege is necessary, it does not scrutinize each individual exercise; it asks only whether the particular exercise falls within the recognized category (New Brunswick Broadcasting; Ontario (Speaker) v. Ontario (Human Rights Commission) (2001), 54 O.R. (3d) 595).
firac.application: Banning strangers from the Precinct falls squarely within the recognized privilege of 'ejection of strangers from the House and its precincts.' Since the grounds were within the Precinct and the reasons for the ban related to ensuring the proper functioning of the Legislature, the act fell within the category and could not be reviewed for its correctness.
firac.conclusion: The Speaker was acting within a recognized category of parliamentary privilege when issuing the bans.

firac.issue: Does the court have jurisdiction to review the exercise of privilege under the Charter, and was Vaid correctly decided?
firac.facts: The defendants argued that even if privilege applied, the court could review the bans for Charter compliance (ss. 2(b) and (c)), relying on Canada (House of Commons) v. Vaid, 2002 FCA 473.
firac.rule: Parliamentary privilege enjoys constitutional status; one part of the Constitution cannot override another. 'The Charter recognizes Parliamentary Privilege, it does not override it' (Harvey v. New Brunswick; The Legislative Prayer Case). Courts may test necessity of a category but not the rightness of a particular exercise.
firac.application: The court held that Vaid was wrongly decided because it effectively reviewed a particular exercise of a recognized privilege (staff management), contrary to New Brunswick Broadcasting, The Legislative Prayer Case, and Telezone. Because the privilege here was necessary and the bans fell within it, the court lacked jurisdiction to review the Speaker's actions, including under the Charter.
firac.conclusion: The court had no jurisdiction to review the Speaker's exercise of privilege under the Charter; it declined to follow Vaid.

firac.issue: Did the Speaker lose privilege by relying on the Trespass to Property Act, police and courts to enforce the bans?
firac.facts: The bans warned that contravention would result in charges under the Trespass to Property Act; the police, not the Speaker, decided to charge and prosecute. In Casselman the Speaker had obtained an injunction against picketers without losing privilege.
firac.rule: Courts may be used to enforce parliamentary privilege (R. v. Casselman, [1996] O.J. No. 5343). Under the Trespass to Property Act the 'occupier' (s. 1) issues bans; delegating enforcement does not defeat privilege.
firac.application: The bans were issued under the Speaker's privilege, not the Act; the Speaker did not initiate or control the prosecution, which was the domain of police and Crown. Even if the Speaker were viewed as 'occupier' invoking the Act, that itself would be an act of privilege. Invoking court processes cannot confer jurisdiction to review an act immune from the Charter.
firac.conclusion: The Speaker did not lose the protection of parliamentary privilege.

firac.issue: Did the Crown prove the trespass charges beyond a reasonable doubt?
firac.facts: On January 18, 1999 the defendants entered the front grounds of the Legislative building while subject to valid trespass bans and demonstrated peacefully before dispersing.
firac.rule: Section 2(1)(a)(i) of the Trespass to Property Act prohibits entering premises when entry is prohibited.
firac.application: The evidence was uncontested that the defendants entered the Legislative Precinct from which they were banned. With the bans valid and within privilege, the elements were established beyond a reasonable doubt.
firac.conclusion: All defendants were found guilty; their application for costs was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the primary tier-1 area because the case turns on parliamentary privilege, a doctrine of constitutional status. K024 (freedom of expression) and K111 (Charter s. 2(b)) capture the defendants' asserted Charter rights to protest and freedom of peaceful assembly. K107 (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms) reflects the central role of the Charter and the holding that it recognizes but does not override privilege. K087 (protest/demonstration) matches the factual core — a demonstration at Queen's Park. K011 (judicial review) is a borderline pick, included because the case is fundamentally about whether courts have jurisdiction to review an exercise of parliamentary privilege. No controlled keyword exists specifically for parliamentary privilege or for provincial trespass offences, so these were the closest available terms.
location_rationale: The heading states 'COURT FILE No. Old City Hall, Toronto' and the court is the Ontario Court of Justice; the events concern Queen's Park in Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The court file line reads 'Old City Hall, Toronto', identifying the Old City Hall registry of the Ontario Court of Justice in Toronto.

name_verification.name_in_document: R.J.R. v. P.M.R.

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff's Notice of Civil Claim against MCFD be struck under Rule 9-5(1) for disclosing no reasonable cause of action, given that social workers owe their duty of care to children rather than parents?
Should the plaintiff's Notice of Civil Claim against the RCMP be struck for disclosing no reasonable cause of action in negligent investigation, wrongful detention, or misfeasance in public office?
Should the plaintiff's Notice of Civil Claim against his former spouse be struck as disclosing no reasonable claim and as an abuse of process?

firac.issue: Should the claim against MCFD be struck for disclosing no reasonable cause of action given that child protection social workers owe their duty of care to children, not parents?
firac.facts: R.J.R. alleged MCFD negligently investigated child protection concerns, ignored a retracted accusation, overruled court-ordered access, denied him 'due process,' and caused his alienation from his children. The Director removed the children under s. 30(1) of the CFCSA and obtained interim custody orders; R.J.R. did not contest the protection finding.
firac.rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(a) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules a pleading may be struck where it is 'plain and obvious,' assuming the pleaded facts to be true, that it discloses no reasonable cause of action (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42). Social workers and the Director owe a 'transcendent statutory duty' to promote the best interests of children, and there is insufficient proximity between parents and the Director to ground a duty of care for negligent investigation (Syl Apps Secure Treatment Centre v. B.D., 2007 SCC 38; Quinn v. British Columbia, 2018 BCCA 320).
firac.application: The court found the NOCC failed to match material facts to causes of action and was confusing. Read generously as a negligence action, it could not succeed because social workers owed no duty of care to R.J.R. as a parent; their duty ran to the children under the CFCSA. Claims relating to witness testimony would also be barred by witness immunity, and sweeping speculative allegations need not be taken as true.
firac.conclusion: It was plain and obvious the claim disclosed no reasonable cause of action against MCFD; struck out in its entirety without leave to amend, primarily under Rule 9-5(1)(a) but also (b)-(d).

firac.issue: Should the claim against the RCMP be struck where the plaintiff was neither a recognized victim owed a duty nor pleads facts supporting negligent investigation, false imprisonment, or misfeasance in public office?
firac.facts: R.J.R. alleged the RCMP failed to investigate his complaint that P.M.R. kidnapped their children, 'emotionally detained' him by telling him not to leave Squamish, investigated and cleared him of sexual abuse allegations, and 'interfered' with files. His children, not he, were the alleged kidnapping victims, and he was never charged.
firac.rule: Police owe a private-law duty of care to suspects being investigated (Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police, 2007 SCC 41) and, exceptionally, to a specific class of potential victims (Jane Doe), but not generally to victims or potential victims (Callan v. Cooke, 2012 BCSC 1589). False imprisonment requires a total deprivation of liberty (Linden, Canadian Tort Law). Misfeasance in public office requires more than bald allegations.
firac.application: R.J.R. was not a suspect owed a duty for the kidnapping complaint (his children were the alleged victims) and was cleared, never charged, on the abuse allegations, with no facts pleaded showing a breach of any standard. His 'emotional detention' claim pleaded only a conditional restriction, not total deprivation of liberty. His misfeasance-flavoured allegations were bald and contextless. No novel duty warranted proceeding to trial.
firac.conclusion: The claims against the RCMP disclosed no reasonable cause of action and were struck out in their entirety without leave to amend.

firac.issue: Should the claim against the former spouse be struck as disclosing no reasonable claim and as an abuse of process?
firac.facts: R.J.R. alleged P.M.R. kidnapped the children, had her boyfriend file a false sexual assault accusation, and abused the children. He sought withdrawal of accusations, an apology, and reinstatement of the original shared custody arrangement, but no financial redress. P.M.R. was not properly served and did not appear.
firac.rule: A pleading may be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a) where it is plain and obvious it discloses no reasonable claim, and under (d) where it is an abuse of process; relitigating or indirectly attacking an existing court order is an abuse of process (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63).
firac.application: R.J.R.'s allegations were not tied to recognized civil causes of action. His attempt to obtain shared custody through the NOCC was an indirect attack on the 2016 consent order of Josephson J. under the Family Law Act, properly pursued only by a variation application, and thus an abuse of process. The remaining allegations of kidnapping and lying sought vague remedies and disclosed no reasonable claim.
firac.conclusion: The NOCC against P.M.R. was struck out under Rule 9-5(1)(a) and (d).

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area — this is a civil tort action struck under Rule 9-5(1). K011 (judicial review) is a weak/borderline pick; the motion to strike engages procedural/administrative dimensions but is not truly a judicial review — flagged as weak. K047 (best interests of the child) is central because the court held social workers' 'transcendent statutory duty' to promote children's best interests defeats any duty of care to the parent. K048 (custody/access) and K006 (Family law) apply because the litigation arises from child protection and custody proceedings and the abuse-of-process finding turns on an attempt to relitigate a Family Law Act custody consent order. The vocabulary lacks specific keywords for 'motion to strike,' 'negligent investigation,' 'duty of care,' or 'child protection,' so the closest available terms were chosen; K011 is the weakest fit and is flagged.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'Registry: Victoria' and 'Place and Date of Hearing: Victoria, B.C.' and 'Place and Date of Judgment: Victoria, B.C.' The court is the Supreme Court of British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The header expressly states 'Registry: Victoria'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Reisher v. Westdale Properties

defining_issues: Did the Landlord and Tenant Board apply the wrong test in determining that the landlord met its duty to accommodate the tenant's disability under the Human Rights Code?
Did the Board fail to comply with its statutory duty under s. 83 of the Residential Tenancies Act to consider all the circumstances relating to relief from eviction?
Was the tenant denied procedural fairness by the Board's reliance on hearsay evidence from the property manager?

firac.issue: Did the Landlord and Tenant Board apply the wrong test in assessing whether the landlord discharged its duty to accommodate the tenant's disability-related needs under the Human Rights Code?
firac.facts: Jeanette Reisher, a long-term tenant with recognized mental-health disabilities, engaged in disruptive and threatening conduct toward other tenants. A prior Consent Order (August 16, 2021) required her to cease the conduct and to retain support services; her psychiatrist increased medication and her support team increased visits. She breached the order, and the landlord applied under s. 78 RTA to terminate the tenancy.
firac.rule: Under s. 47(2) of the Human Rights Code and s. 3(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, the Code prevails and the Board cannot give effect to an eviction that breaches it. Section 2(1) guarantees equal treatment in occupancy of accommodation without discrimination based on disability, and s. 17 provides that a person is not to be found incapable unless their needs cannot be accommodated 'without undue hardship,' considering cost, funding and health and safety. The duty to accommodate has both procedural and substantive components; undue hardship must rest on cogent, not speculative, evidence (Adga Group Consultants v. Lane; Meiorin; Grismer). Standard of review on this statutory appeal (RTA s. 210) is correctness.
firac.application: The Court held the accommodation analysis had to be viewed from the start of the proceeding, including the Consent Order, which itself represented an accommodation the parties agreed was practical and without undue hardship, satisfying the procedural component. The tenant also bore a duty to cooperate. On the substantive component, the record of repeated threats, forced entries, screaming, banging and profanity toward multiple tenants, and the tenant's continued conduct despite medication and initiated (but still waitlisted) support services, amply supported the Board's finding of undue hardship. Undue hardship could exist without violence and extended to the impact on other tenants' quiet enjoyment.
firac.conclusion: The Board applied the correct test; its finding of undue hardship was correct and disclosed no error of law.

firac.issue: Did the Board fail to comply with s. 83 of the Residential Tenancies Act by not considering all the circumstances relating to relief from eviction?
firac.facts: The 2022 Order arose under s. 78(11)(b) following breach of the Consent Order. The Board terminated the tenancy but postponed the move-out date, exercising discretion under s. 83.
firac.rule: Section 83(1) permits the Board to refuse eviction unless satisfied, having regard to all the circumstances, that refusal would be unfair, or to postpone enforcement; s. 83(2) requires review of the circumstances. There is a difference between 'having regard to' the circumstances and cataloguing each one in reasons; discretionary relief-from-eviction decisions attract deference absent an error in principle (Lerose v. Princess Apartments).
firac.application: The Board was aware of the tenant's mental-health issues, the ongoing interference with other tenants, the prior consent-based relief that failed, and the absence of any reasonable expectation of change. It exercised its discretion to postpone rather than refuse eviction. Tribunals like the Board need not be held to the same standard as courts in articulating every circumstance.
firac.conclusion: The Board considered all the circumstances and did not err in law; its discretionary decision was entitled to deference.

firac.issue: Was the tenant denied procedural fairness through the Board's reliance on hearsay evidence from the property manager?
firac.facts: The Board's reasons noted that, beyond the two tenants who testified, three additional tenants had complained but were 'too afraid to testify.' The tenant argued this reflected reliance on untested hearsay and mischaracterized the property manager's actual testimony (that other tenants 'felt threatened' but 'don't want to report').
firac.rule: Section 15(1) of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act allows a tribunal to admit and act on evidence whether or not admissible in a court; hearsay is freely admissible before administrative tribunals, its weight being for the tribunal, unless receipt amounts to a denial of natural justice (audi alteram partem).
firac.application: Characterizing the tenants as 'too afraid' was a conclusion reasonably open to the member who heard the evidence, and undue hardship turned on whether it was reasonable for tenants to feel threatened, not solely on objective safety risk. The finding rested on all the evidence before the Board, not solely the property manager's hearsay; the Review Order confirmed sufficient evidence supported the findings.
firac.conclusion: There was no denial of procedural fairness; the Board did not err in weighing the evidence.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the primary tier-1 area: the case is a statutory appeal reviewing a tribunal on correctness. K007 (Human rights) is engaged because the core issue is the duty to accommodate a disability under the Human Rights Code. K014 (standard of review) is central given the extended correctness/deference discussion. K012 (procedural fairness) directly captures Issue 3. K031 (religious accommodation) is used for its synonyms 'duty to accommodate/reasonable accommodation/undue hardship'—a weak, borderline pick because the canonical label is religious, but it is the closest vocabulary term for the disability-accommodation analysis. K069 (discrimination) reflects the s. 2(1) HRC equal-treatment-in-accommodation analysis. K119 (Human Rights Code) is the governing statute. K011 (judicial review) is borderline since this was a statutory appeal rather than judicial review, but it captures the administrative-oversight nature; flagged as weak.
location_rationale: The header states 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE DIVISIONAL COURT' and 'HEARD at Toronto by video conference: February 8, 2023', establishing Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The decision is a 'DIVISIONAL COURT' matter with 'DIVISIONAL COURT FILE NO.: 456/22', identifying the Divisional Court as the relevant registry/office.

name_verification.name_in_document: Seaton v. Zheng

defining_issues: Should the court exercise its discretion under Rule 18(13) of the Family Law Rules to grant summary judgment enforcing the accepted (severable) child-related terms of the mother's 2016 Offer to Settle?
How should the children's views and preferences be placed before the court for trial — by way of a s. 30 assessment or by appointment of private counsel for the children?
Should the paragraphs and exhibits in the mother's affidavit referring to the confidential child protection proceeding be struck?

firac.issue: Should the court grant summary judgment enforcing the accepted child-related terms of the mother's 2016 Offer to Settle?
firac.facts: The mother made a severable Offer to Settle dated April 19, 2016 proposing shared custody, week-about parenting, a parenting coordinator and a $400,000 payment. Three years later, on March 21, 2019, the father accepted only the child-related parenting portions and moved for summary judgment to incorporate them into a final order. In the intervening period the children (then 14 and 16) had ceased seeing their father and access had become highly conflictual.
firac.rule: Rule 18(13) of the Family Law Rules permits the court to turn accepted parts of an offer into a court order. Courts are wary of enforcing settlements where the children's circumstances have changed or unfairness would result: Bailey v. Plaxton, 2001 CanLII 28180 (ON SC) (enforced, but dealt only with financial issues); Hand v. Hand, [2018] O.J. No. 5422 (declined to follow Bailey where children's circumstances had materially changed and enforcement without trial was contrary to their interests). The best interests of the children and the maximum-contact principle under the Divorce Act govern parenting outcomes.
firac.application: The court found joint parenting by these parties patently unreasonable given their inability to communicate and their diametrically opposed accounts of events. The children's circumstances had materially changed since 2016 — they had stopped seeing their father and resumption of access created chaos. Imposing a new shared-parenting regime on a 14- and 16-year-old without their input was untenable, and a trial was necessary to set a long-term arrangement.
firac.conclusion: The father's motion for summary judgment to enforce the Offer to Settle was dismissed; the court refused to exercise its discretion under Rule 18(13).

firac.issue: How should the children's views be ascertained for trial — a s. 30 assessment or private counsel?
firac.facts: The children were 14 and 16, had been in litigation for seven years, each had a therapist, and had been contacting Jewish Family & Child Services asking about their rights and to have their views on access heard. A prior request for a Voice of the Child Report had been refused by Shore, J. as too cursory and open to manipulation.
firac.rule: Section 29 of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act requires children to be engaged in decisions about them and their views given due weight according to age and maturity; the Children's Law Reform Act mandates the court to consider children's views and preferences where they can reasonably be ascertained. A s. 30 assessment is one mechanism; appointment of private counsel for the children is another.
firac.application: The court held the children's views must be before the trial judge. A s. 30 assessment was rejected as likely beyond the parties' means, causing up to six months' delay, and subjecting the children to yet more process. Private counsel could be ready within a month for an early fall trial, would filter and professionally present the boys' views without requiring them to testify, and responded to the children's own requests to be heard.
firac.conclusion: The s. 30 assessment motion was dismissed; the motion to appoint private counsel for the children was allowed, cost shared by the parties, counsel to be appointed within 30 days.

firac.issue: Should the references to the confidential child protection proceeding in the mother's affidavit be struck?
firac.facts: The parties had been respondents in a JF&CS protection proceeding (2012–2015). The mother's affidavit contained references to that proceeding and documents obtained in it. The father moved to strike them, relying on confidentiality provisions of the former Child and Family Services Act and the Child, Youth and Family Services Act and the order of Sherr, J. dated December 7, 2012, which required a court order before such documents could be used outside the protection proceeding.
firac.rule: Confidentiality provisions under the CFSA/CYFSA and the prior order of Sherr, J. require an order of the court to use protection-proceeding documents for other purposes; irrelevant or prejudicial material may be struck.
firac.application: The court found the protection material unnecessary at the motion stage — there was ample other evidence of conflict to decide the motions — and that the impugned material served largely to denigrate the father. It struck the material but preserved access to the protection file for trial counsel, the children's counsel and the trial judge if found relevant, the issue to be revisited at a Trial Management Conference.
firac.conclusion: The father's motion to strike was allowed; the mother must redact the offending paragraphs and remove the exhibits, without prejudice to use of the protection file at trial.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) drives the refusal to enforce the settlement and the decision to ascertain the children's views. K048 (custody/access) is the core parenting subject matter — shared parenting, week-about access, resumption of visits. K117 (Divorce Act) is expressly invoked via the maximum-contact principle. K049 (marriage/cohabitation agreement) is used loosely for the enforceability of the severable Offer to Settle — it is the closest available term for the settlement-enforcement issue, though the vocabulary lacks a precise 'offer to settle/summary judgment' keyword, so this is a weaker pick. The controlled vocabulary offers no keyword for the child-protection confidentiality / motion-to-strike issue or for appointment of children's counsel/s.30 assessment.

registry_rationale: No registry office/city is named in the decision. The header states only 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' with a file number, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: R. v. MacDonald

defining_issues: Does the Kienapple principle bar concurrent convictions for participating in a terrorist group's activity (s. 83.18) and facilitating terrorist activity (s. 83.19) where the same acts underlie both?
What is the fit and proportionate sentence for the three terrorism-related offences given the applicable sentencing objectives?
Has the offender met his onus under s. 743.6(1.2) to be exempt from serving one half of his sentence before parole eligibility?

firac.issue: Does the Kienapple principle bar entering convictions on both the s. 83.18 participation count and the s. 83.19 facilitation count where they arise from the same conduct?
firac.facts: MacDonald's participation in producing three AWD propaganda/recruitment videos and posting hateful imagery grounded convictions under both s. 83.18 (participating in/contributing to a terrorist group's activity) and s. 83.19 (facilitating a terrorist activity). The defence argued the same acts underlay both, so Kienapple should preclude one conviction.
firac.rule: Kienapple v. R., [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729 precludes multiple convictions only where there is both a factual and legal nexus between offences. Per R. v. Prince (1986) and R. v. Kinnear (2005 ONCA), the rule does not apply where offences protect different societal interests, allege violence against different victims, or proscribe different consequences; the court asks whether there are 'no additional and distinguishing elements'. R. v. Ahmed, 2017 ONCA 76 held Kienapple did not bar convictions under both s. 83.18 and s. 83.19 on the same factual foundation.
firac.application: Although MacDonald's acts of producing and posting the videos underlay both counts, s. 83.18 protects society from participation in a terrorist group's activities while s. 83.19 protects against knowingly facilitating a terrorist activity — different legal nexuses. His facilitation acts (recruiting members, sharing videos with Terror Wave Refined for online publication) had additional and distinguishing elements. Following Ahmed, the same factual foundation can support both convictions.
firac.conclusion: The Kienapple principle does not apply; convictions on both s. 83.18 and s. 83.19 stand.

firac.issue: What is the fit and proportionate total sentence for the three terrorism-related offences?
firac.facts: MacDonald, aged 20-21 at the time, used his graphic-design skills to create AWD propaganda and recruitment videos and hateful imagery glorifying Nazi leaders under the alias 'Dark Foreigner', including cover art for James Mason's 'Siege'. AWD is a neo-Nazi accelerationist terrorist group promoting lone-wolf attacks to spark a race war. He had no criminal record, expressed remorse, renounced his views, completed two years of Project Reset counselling, and volunteered with minority groups. The Crown sought 14 years; the defence sought 6-8 years.
firac.rule: Sentencing principles under s. 718 of the Criminal Code, with denunciation and individual and general deterrence paramount for terrorism offences (R. v. Khawaja; R. v. Khalid, 2010 ONCA 861; R. v. Ahmed, 2017 ONCA 76; R. v. Hersi, 2019 ONCA 94). Terrorism is a statutory aggravating factor under s. 718.2(a)(v), and hate motivation under s. 718.2(a)(i). Consecutive sentences required under s. 83.25; proportionality and totality apply. Time on stringent bail is mitigating (R. v. Downes, 2006 CanLII 3957).
firac.application: Aggravating factors included the seriousness of terrorism offences, planning over a lengthy period, creation of ideologically motivated violent extremist content, hate motivation, and material encouraging murder of identifiable groups. Mitigating factors included his youth, lack of record, remorse, renunciation, two years of counselling, volunteer work, and two years on house-arrest-like bail. Unlike Khawaja (bomb detonator, life sentence) and given rehabilitation prospects distinguishing this from more serious cases, the court fixed four years each on counts 1 and 2, and two years on count 3, for a ten-year total, reduced by three months for pre-sentence custody.
firac.conclusion: A total of ten years imprisonment was imposed, reduced by three months for pre-sentence custody to nine years and nine months.

firac.issue: Has the offender met his onus under s. 743.6(1.2) to avoid serving one half of his sentence before parole eligibility?
firac.facts: The defence submitted MacDonald had renounced his extremist beliefs, expressed remorse, completed roughly two years of Project Reset counselling, volunteered assisting minority immigrant groups, and complied with stringent house-arrest-style bail for about two years.
firac.rule: Section 743.6(1.2) of the Criminal Code creates a presumption for terrorism offences that the offender serve one half of the sentence before parole eligibility, unless the offender meets the onus (balance of probabilities) to displace it; supported by Ahmed, where the offender was found to have met this burden.
firac.application: Given the offender's renunciation of his beliefs, apology, two years of Project Reset counselling, volunteer work with minority immigrant groups, and roughly two years on stringent house arrest, the court found rehabilitation prospects sufficient to displace the presumption.
firac.conclusion: The offender met his burden; he need not serve one half of his sentence and is eligible for parole in the usual course under the Corrections and Conditional Release Act.

name_verification.name_in_document: Her Majesty the Queen v. Leon Epp

defining_issues: Does a registration order under s. 490.012(1) of the Criminal Code have retrospective application where the offence pre-dated the Sex Offender Information Registration Act but the offender had not yet been sentenced?

Should the court decline to order sex-offender registration under the exception in s. 490.012(4) of the Criminal Code because the impact on the offender's privacy or liberty would be grossly disproportionate to the public interest in the effective investigation of sexual crimes?

firac.issue: Does a registration order under s. 490.012(1) of the Criminal Code apply retrospectively to an offence committed before SOIRA came into force where sentence had not yet been imposed?
firac.facts: Mr. Epp committed the sexual assault before SOIRA took effect but had not yet been sentenced when the Crown applied for a registration order. The defence argued the order could not have retrospective application in these circumstances.
firac.rule: Section 490.012(1) requires a registration order on the prosecutor's application as soon as possible after sentencing for a designated offence; the retrospectivity question was raised as a threshold argument.
firac.application: Having decided to grant the offender's application on the merits under s. 490.012(4), the court found it unnecessary to resolve the retrospectivity argument.
firac.conclusion: The court declined to address the issue, leaving it undecided because it was moot in light of the disposition on the exception.

firac.issue: Should the court exercise the s. 490.012(4) exception and decline to order registration because its impact on the offender would be grossly disproportionate to the public interest?
firac.facts: Epp, age 54, was convicted of one count of sexual assault (s. 271) against a 15-year-old neighbour, arising from an incident in which he plied her with alcohol and undid her bra in his vehicle. He had no related record (only dated impaired-driving convictions), was assessed as a low risk to re-offend sexually with no deviant sexual interest, and had significant health and communication limitations, including severe hearing impairment requiring lip-reading and possible cognitive limitations. Sentence was a suspended sentence with one year probation.
firac.rule: Section 490.012(4) allows a court not to make a registration order if the offender establishes that the impact on him, including on privacy or liberty, would be grossly disproportionate to the public interest in protecting society through effective investigation of sexual crimes (SOIRA s. 2). The court adopted the three-part analysis from R. v. R.E.M. (2005 BCSC 698) — impact on the offender, public interest served, and gross disproportionality — and the comparative/balancing approach of Cromwell J.A. in R. v. Jordan (2002 NSCA 11) (drawing on Baron v. Canada) developed for the analogous DNA-databank exception, considering the nature of the offence, the nature of the intrusion, and the offender's circumstances.
firac.application: The court found the offence at the low end of the range of sexual offences and likely less serious than any reported comparator. The reporting and information obligations under SOIRA were substantial and, given Epp's hearing impairment and limited literacy, more onerous for him, exposing him to prosecution for non-compliance over ten years and to potential intrusive police contact during investigations. The principal purpose of SOIRA is to identify offenders who may pose a future risk; Epp had no related record and was a low risk to re-offend sexually, so the public interest in registering him was minimal. Weighing these factors together against the balance Parliament struck for the general run of cases, his circumstances varied markedly from those Parliament had in mind.
firac.conclusion: The offender established that the impact of registration would be grossly disproportionate to the public interest; the Crown's application was declined and no registration order was made.

name_verification.name_in_document: Scory v. Krannitz

defining_issues: Is it plain and obvious that the plaintiff's pleadings against the defendant DeWitte disclose no reasonable cause of action, such that the claim should be struck under Rule 9-5(1)?
Should the defendant DeWitte be awarded special costs on the basis that the action was a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP)?

firac.issue: Is it plain and obvious that the plaintiff's pleadings against DeWitte disclose no reasonable cause of action, warranting striking under Rule 9-5(1)?
firac.facts: Scory, an owner of agricultural-reserve land in the Township of Langley, sought a permit to deposit fill for farming. DeWitte, who lives about 250 metres north of the plaintiff's land, publicly stated at an April 26, 2010 Township Council meeting that his well had been covered with rocks and debris allegedly from an upstream farm soil-deposit site years earlier. Scory sued DeWitte and others for economic losses, invoking defamation, injurious falsehood, the Farm Practices Protection Act, ss. 7 and 8 of the Charter, negligence, negligent misrepresentation, conspiracy, and unlawful interference with economic interests. DeWitte applied to strike.
firac.rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(a) and (b) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules, a pleading may be struck where it discloses no reasonable claim or is unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious; the applicant must show it is 'plain and obvious' the pleading cannot succeed (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959; Xu v. Foo, 2006 BCCA 525). Defamation requires defamatory words referring to the plaintiff that are published (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). Injurious falsehood requires a false statement concerning the plaintiff or his property (Captain Developments; Fleming, The Law of Torts). Negligent misrepresentation requires a special relationship and reasonable detrimental reliance (Queen v. Cognos Inc., [1993] 1 S.C.R. 87). Duty of care for pure economic loss is assessed under Cooper v. Hobart, 2001 SCC 79, requiring proximity and absence of negating policy concerns. The Charter does not apply between private citizens (Dolphin Delivery, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 573).
firac.application: The court found DeWitte's statement referred to the upstream farmer, not the plaintiff, and the plaintiff pleaded no reputational harm, so defamation could not succeed. Injurious falsehood failed because the statement did not concern the plaintiff or his property. The Farm Practices Protection Act creates defences for farmers, not a cause of action. The Charter claim failed because the alleged conduct was that of other defendants and the Charter does not govern private litigation. Negligent misrepresentation failed for want of any representation to, or reliance by, the plaintiff and any special relationship. For negligence, the plaintiff's pure economic loss fit no recognized category, no proximity existed between adversarial parties lobbying against each other, and no close causal connection linked DeWitte's statement to the Council's decision; even if a prima facie duty existed, indeterminate liability and the chilling of democratic participation negated it. Conspiracy failed for lack of any pleaded combination, and unlawful interference failed because no underlying unlawful act survived.
firac.conclusion: It was plain and obvious the claim against DeWitte could not succeed; the claim was dismissed.

firac.issue: Should DeWitte be awarded special costs because the action was a SLAPP?
firac.facts: DeWitte argued the meritless claim was intended to intimidate him and others with similar interests from participating in public debate about the plaintiff's soil-deposit application, harming the public interest in free and open democratic discussion.
firac.rule: Special costs may be awarded where a meritless action is a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation used to stifle citizens' democratic activities and is deserving of censure (Fraser v. Saanich (District), [1999] B.C.J. No. 3100 (S.C.)).
firac.application: The court found the claim without merit and, like the neighbourhood residents in Fraser v. Saanich who had opposed a redevelopment, DeWitte had merely exercised his right to advocate before Council on a matter of public interest; the action operated to stifle that democratic participation.
firac.conclusion: DeWitte was entitled to his costs as special costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area — the case concerns striking a tort/economic-loss pleading under the Civil Rules. K015 (defamation) is directly engaged, as the court applied the Grant v. Torstar test and the related tort of injurious falsehood. K107 (Canadian Charter) and K112 (Charter s. 7) reflect the plaintiff's ss. 7 and 8 Charter claims, which were dismissed because the Charter does not apply between private parties — these are somewhat weak since the Charter argument was quickly rejected. K087 (protest/demonstration) is a borderline pick used to capture the public-participation/SLAPP dimension of the special-costs ruling, as the vocabulary has no dedicated SLAPP or civil-procedure-striking term; it is a weak fit. The controlled vocabulary is oriented toward antisemitism/religious-freedom themes not present here, so several selections are approximations flagged accordingly.

name_verification.name_in_document: Dans l'affaire de : X, Y, Z, A

defining_issues: Was the security and development of the four children compromised within the meaning of the Youth Protection Act (art. 38 LPJ)?
Did the father commit sexual abuse against the child X, given the balance-of-probabilities standard applicable in youth protection?
Were the child's out-of-court statements admissible and sufficiently corroborated to ground a finding of sexual abuse?
Could the half-sister's testimony of her own abuse be received as similar-fact / relevant evidence in a youth protection case?

firac.issue: Was the security and development of the four children compromised under art. 38 of the Youth Protection Act?
firac.facts: The father admitted at the outset that his methods of physical correction compromised the four children; a 1999 signalement, voluntary measures (Feb. 2000) and therapy had followed. The mother, children's counsel and father were prepared to accept a finding of compromission, but the DPJ insisted the court also rule on sexual abuse allegations concerning X.
firac.rule: Under art. 38 LPJ a child's security or development may be found compromised; the child's interest is the paramount consideration (Protection de la jeunesse — 795) and the applicable standard is proof on the balance of probabilities, not proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
firac.application: The father conceded physical maltreatment, and the evidence showed a closed, controlling household. The court accepted the compromission based on the parents' conduct and lifestyle and, for X, on inadequate sexual conduct by the father.
firac.conclusion: The security and development of all four children were declared compromised; they were entrusted to their mother with supervised, DPJ-organized paternal contact and a one-year order of aid, counsel and assistance.

firac.issue: Did the father sexually abuse the child X on a balance of probabilities?
firac.facts: After bathing his sister X, aged five, was seen by the mother attempting anal penetration of his younger sister ('the butterfly'); he later told his mother, a social worker, a police officer and Dr. Worenklein that his father inserted a finger or 'pee-pee' in his anus. Experts (Greenberg, Worenklein) could neither confirm nor rule out abuse; the psychiatrist Morissette found the father's account contrived and the mother's more probable.
firac.rule: Sexual abuse in youth protection requires an act of a sexual nature, assessed on the civil balance-of-probabilities standard (para. 63; more probable than not). The court, not experts or tests, weighs credibility and probative value.
firac.application: The court could not rely on the mother's questioning of X (leading questions) or the suggestive police interview, but accepted the spontaneous statements to social worker [intervenante 3]. These required corroboration, which was supplied by X's markedly sexualized behaviour toward his sister and the cleaning lady and by the credible testimony of the half-sister. The court rejected the father's account of unknowing anal sex imposed by his wife and his repeated 'no choice' explanations as not believable.
firac.conclusion: The court found on a balance of probabilities that the father engaged in inadequate sexual conduct toward X, contributing to the finding of compromission.

firac.issue: Were the child's out-of-court statements admissible and sufficiently corroborated?
firac.facts: The parties agreed X would not testify; the court relied on his verbalizations to the mother, social workers, police officer and Dr. Worenklein. The half-sister B was heard in court with recording, counsel then suggesting further questions for a second examination.
firac.rule: Per R. c. Khan, [1990] 2 R.C.S. 531, a child's spontaneous hearsay statements may be admitted under the necessity and reliability exception, and sworn testimony is not a prerequisite (s. 16 Canada Evidence Act). A child's statement cannot corroborate itself; extrinsic corroboration is required, more strictly than in criminal matters (Sirois).
firac.application: The court applied Khan to admit X's statements but held it could not decide on the social-worker statement alone; corroboration came from X's sexualized conduct and the half-sister's credible in-court account, obtained in child-sensitive conditions inspired by ss. 486 and 715.1 of the Criminal Code (R.C.L.).
firac.conclusion: The statements were admissible and, once corroborated, capable of supporting the finding of sexual abuse.

firac.issue: Could the half-sister's evidence of her own abuse be received as relevant evidence?
firac.facts: B, aged ten, testified she had been touched anally with a vaseline-coated finger by the same man (her stepfather), the mother's ex-husband being the father of the children under review.
firac.rule: In youth protection, the strict criminal similar-fact rules do not apply; the governing lens is relevance under art. 2857 C.c.Q. (Protection de la jeunesse — 1125).
firac.application: The court found it could not conclude the father abused the half-sister herself, but treated her credible testimony as corroborative evidence of the probability that X was abused, given the closed household with no exposure to sexual imagery.
firac.conclusion: The half-sister's evidence was received as relevant and corroborative, though not as a separate finding of abuse against her.

case_name: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital c. B.Z.

name_verification.name_in_document: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital c. B.Z.

defining_issues: Did the Superior Court have jurisdiction under art. 16 C.C.Q. to authorize the proposed treatment where the patient was not categorically refusing care?
Could the court order forced transportation to hospital and placement in a supervised living setting where the hospital did not seek authorization to treat the patient against his will?
Could the court grant an authorization for treatment based on anticipated future non-compliance rather than a present refusal of care?

firac.issue: Did the Superior Court have jurisdiction under art. 16 C.C.Q. to authorize the proposed treatment where the patient was not categorically refusing care?
firac.facts: Mr Z., a 50-year-old man diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, was hospitalized after threatening his brother-in-law with a knife. Although he initially refused treatment, he became compliant, his condition improved, and the day before the hearing he told his psychiatrist, the resident, his brother-in-law and the Hospital's lawyer that he agreed with the motion and did not wish to attend court or be represented.
firac.rule: Under art. 10 and 11 C.C.Q. every person is inviolable and no one may be made to undergo care without consent. Art. 16(1) C.C.Q. requires court authorization only where a person of full age incapable of consenting 'categorically refuses to receive care'. Per Institut Philippe-Pinel de Montréal v. G. (A.), [1994] R.J.Q. 2523 (C.A.), it is the patient's refusal that triggers the need for judicial authorization.
firac.application: The Court found that Mr Z. was compliant with treatment and had expressly agreed to the motion; the motion and medical report alleged only past non-compliance and generalized concerns rather than a present, categorical refusal. Since the triggering condition of art. 16(1) C.C.Q. — a categorical refusal of care — was absent, the statutory basis for the Court's intervention did not exist.
firac.conclusion: The conditions of art. 16 C.C.Q. were not met; the Court lacked jurisdiction to grant the authorization sought.

firac.issue: Could the court order forced transportation to hospital and placement in a supervised living setting where the hospital did not seek authorization to treat the patient against his will?
firac.facts: The motion asked that Mr Z. be forcibly brought to the Hospital by police if he failed to attend out-patient appointments and be placed in a supervised living setting, but contained no conclusion authorizing forced administration of medication. The Court twice questioned the physician and raised the point during argument, confirming this was not a drafting oversight.
firac.rule: Authorization to control a patient's movements or residence and to compel attendance flows from a valid authorization to treat against the patient's will under art. 16 C.C.Q.; such conclusions (e.g. intramuscular injection, use of reasonable force) must be sought and are only available where the Court has jurisdiction over refused care.
firac.application: Because the Hospital did not seek — and could not obtain, given the absence of refusal — authorization to treat Mr Z. against his will, it could not obtain ancillary orders permitting police to seize him or dictate his residence. The forced-transportation and supervised-living conclusions rested on a treatment authorization that did not exist.
firac.conclusion: The Court could not grant the forced-transportation or supervised-living orders; these could only issue if the Court had jurisdiction, which it did not.

firac.issue: Could the court grant an authorization for treatment based on anticipated future non-compliance rather than a present refusal of care?
firac.facts: The Hospital argued it wanted the order 'in case we need it in the future', to be placed in the file and used if Mr Z. later stopped complying.
firac.rule: Following M.B. v. Centre hospitalier Pierre-Le Gardeur, [2004] R.J.Q. 792 (C.A.), the conditions of art. 16 C.C.Q. must be satisfied at the time of the application; the law does not permit adjudicating in advance a hypothetical future refusal, as respect for autonomy, inviolability and integrity of the person is a fundamental value of Quebec law.
firac.application: The Court adopted Chamberland J.C.A.'s reasoning that it is imprudent and contrary to law to decide today on the basis of a situation that may arise tomorrow. Mr Z.'s situation could evolve, and the anticipated non-compliance did not confer present jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: An authorization could not be granted on the basis of anticipated future non-compliance; the motion was dismissed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Shore-Kalo v. Kalo

defining_issues: Is a prevention order under The Domestic Violence and Stalking Act tied to, and does it lapse with, the custody and access provisions of a final order once the children reach the age of majority?
Is it 'fit and just' under s. 19(1) of the DSVA to delete or vary the terms of the prevention order restricting the respondent's contact with his now-adult children?

firac.issue: Does a prevention order under the DSVA lapse when the children reach adulthood or when the custody/access terms of the final order cease to apply?
firac.facts: The respondent argued that because his children were now adults and no longer under the petitioner's care and control, the prevention order was 'outdated and anachronistic' and should be seen as having 'aged out' or lapsed alongside the custody and access provisions.
firac.rule: Custody and access terms were made under the federal Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), while the prevention order was made under The Domestic Violence and Stalking Act, C.C.S.M. c. D93, s. 14(1), whose 'pith and substance ... is in the nature of crime prevention' (Baril v. Obelnicki, 2007 MBCA 40). A prevention order 'admits of no specified time period of application, and remains in place indefinitely, pending further court order' (R. v. Dilk, 2016 MBCA 98, para. 14).
firac.application: The court held the prevention order's fate is not entwined with or dependent on the custody order. The two orders arise under separate legislative schemes (federal Divorce Act vs. provincial DSVA), and the prevention order remains in effect indefinitely until a judge, on application, is satisfied it is fit and just to vary or revoke it. The children attaining majority does not automatically terminate the prevention order.
firac.conclusion: The prevention order does not lapse automatically; it remains in force notwithstanding that the children are now adults and the custody/access provisions may no longer apply.

firac.issue: Is it 'fit and just' under s. 19(1) of the DSVA to delete or vary the prevention order restricting the respondent's contact with his adult children?
firac.facts: The respondent sought removal of all restrictions on contact with his two children. Both daughters, now adults, filed affidavits and appeared before the court expressing fear of the respondent's emotionally abusive and erratic conduct. The younger daughter had terminated contact and described his disruptive behaviour at her convocation; the older maintained limited contact but described him as unable to manage his temper. Neither wanted the order removed. The respondent's own affidavits disclosed continued problematic conduct and denials the court found unpersuasive.
firac.rule: Section 19(1) of the DSVA permits the court, if satisfied it is 'fit and just to do so,' to delete or vary terms of a prevention order or revoke it. The matter is treated as a s. 19(1) application requiring no material change in circumstances (T.L.L. v. J.J.L., 2015 MBCA 68, para. 17). The DSVA's purpose is crime prevention and protection of stalking victims through early intervention (Baril v. Obelnicki).
firac.application: Assessing the legislative purpose, the trial judge's original findings on the respondent's outrageous conduct, and the recent evidence, the court found any improvement in the respondent's self-control was modest. Although the literal terms had not been breached since variation, the respondent had, contrary to its spirit and the daughters' express wishes, repeatedly contacted at least the younger daughter in circumstances causing her to feel harassed and fear for her safety, while both daughters continued to express fear. The court found the daughters' evidence far more persuasive than the respondent's.
firac.conclusion: It is not fit and just to delete or vary the prevention order; it is fit and just that it remain in place. The motion was dismissed as to the children (with agreed variations concerning the Jewish Community Centre and synagogue already conceded).
