name_verification.name_in_document: Warman v. Kay

defining_issues: Did the trial judge apply the correct legal test for determining whether allegedly defamatory words that do not name the plaintiff nonetheless refer to him?
Did the trial judge commit a palpable and overriding error in applying that test to the evidence about whether the tweets referred to Mr. Warman?

firac.issue: Did the trial judge apply the correct legal test for determining whether words that do not name the plaintiff refer to him?
firac.facts: The respondents posted two tweets referring to @antihateca, the Twitter handle of the Canadian Anti-Hate Network (CAHN), a not-for-profit corporation. The tweets did not name Mr. Warman, a CAHN board member. He sued for defamation, relying on his board membership, claimed co-founder status, and the group-defamation principle in Bou Malhab.
firac.rule: A plaintiff in defamation must prove the words were defamatory, referred to the plaintiff, and were published (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). Where the plaintiff is not named, a two-fold test applies: (1) are the words capable of referring to the plaintiff (question of law); and (2) if yes, would the words reasonably lead persons who know the plaintiff to believe he was referred to (question of fact) (Arnott v. College of Physicians, [1954] SCR 538; Knupffer v. London Express, [1944] A.C. 116; Sykes v. Fraser; Walker v. CFTO; Foulidis v. Ford, 2014 ONCA 530). Group defamation principles from Bou Malhab v. Diffusion Métromédia CMR inc., 2011 SCC 9 apply to comments about groups of individuals. Standard of review on questions of law is correctness (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33).
firac.application: Though the trial judge did not quote the test verbatim, he paraphrased both branches: he found the words 'could refer to Warman' (satisfying the first branch) and that Warman had not proven the tweets 'would lead a reasonable person to believe they referred to' him. The formulation 'reasonable people to conclude they did in fact refer' is well established in Canada (Sykes, Walker, Foulidis, Cormier-Grant) and is not an error. Reliance on the Foulidis trial decision, including consideration of whether Warman was the 'face' or 'alter ego' of CAHN, was proper as those were merely circumstances among several. Bou Malhab was of little assistance because the tweets concerned a corporation, not a group of individuals. Small Claims Court reasons are read in light of that court's informal, efficient mandate (Maple Ridge).
firac.conclusion: The trial judge applied the correct legal test; no error of law was established.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge make a palpable and overriding error in applying the test to the evidence?
firac.facts: CAHN had more than 15 board members. Media articles and Wikipedia entries named Bernie Farber and Evan Balgord as founders/co-founders but never mentioned Warman. Warman admitted on cross-examination that a reader might not associate the tweets with him and led no evidence that anyone reading the tweets believed they were about him. The tweets and hyperlinked headline criticized CAHN policy but named no individual; the underlying Federalist article named Warman, but he did not plead the article's contents as defamatory.
firac.rule: Findings of fact and mixed fact and law are reviewed for palpable and overriding error; appellate courts will not interfere unless a clearly identifiable error affected the result (Housen; H.L. v. Canada (A.G.), 2005 SCC 25). The trier of fact considers all circumstances, including relevant extrinsic evidence connecting the words to the plaintiff (Morgan v. Odhams Press; Sykes).
firac.application: The trial judge scrutinized Warman's involvement with CAHN and reasonably found he was not its public face or alter ego. His finding that the tweets' ordinary meaning was that CAHN—not Warman—assisted Antifa was well supported. Warman could not rely on the article's contents as 'context' having declined to plead them as defamatory, as that would import the article's meaning into the tweets. Considering the respondents' knowledge of Warman's association with CAHN was permissible as part of the circumstances, given Warman called no witnesses on reference; it was not determinative, and any error would not have affected the result.
firac.conclusion: No palpable and overriding error was shown; the application of the test was well supported by the record.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as this is a private defamation action. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. K017 (group defamation) is directly engaged because Warman invoked Bou Malhab's collectivity principle, which the court analysed and rejected. K014 (standard of review) is central given the appeal turned on correctness for law and palpable and overriding error for facts (Housen, H.L.). K063 (online hate/social media) applies because the impugned publications were tweets on Twitter/social media—a slightly borderline pick used to capture the online context. K020 (class action) is weaker/borderline: it is included only because the court discussed Bou Malhab, itself a class action; the present case is not a class action, so this is flagged as a weak pick.

Kay (10 November 2022), Ottawa, SC-20-156136 (Small Cl. Ct.)' and costs submissions are directed to the Ontario Superior Court. Ottawa is the underlying registry location; province is Ontario.
registry_rationale: The Divisional Court file is 'DC-22-2753' and the Small Claims Court matter was in Ottawa; the appeal proceeds through the Ottawa registry of the Superior Court of Justice (Divisional Court).

case_name: Vu c. Société de transport de Montréal (STM)

name_verification.name_in_document: Vu c. Société de transport de Montréal (STM)

defining_issues: In what order should the court decide the several preliminary motions filed across the three class-action authorization files?
Should the Autorité régionale de transport métropolitain (ARTM)'s uncontested voluntary aggressive interventions in files 1386 and 1387 be granted?
Should file 1387 be stayed in favour of file 1386 under the lis pendens / 'first to file' rule?
Should the plaintiff Vu be permitted to amend her authorization application in file 1419 to extend the class period?
Should files 1386 and 1419 be joined into a single instance under art. 210 C.p.c.?

firac.issue: In what order must the court decide the competing preliminary motions across the three files?
firac.facts: Three proposed class actions (files 1386, 1387, 1419) arose from STM transit strikes in June, September, October and November 2025. Vu and Saint-Onge each proposed a distinct sequence for deciding the intervention, stay, amendment and joinder motions, Saint-Onge insisting the stay be decided last and Vu insisting the amendment and joinder be decided first.
firac.rule: The court has inherent power to control the conduct of its proceedings; logical dependency between motions dictates the order in which they must be resolved.
firac.application: The court rejected both parties' proposed sequences. The ARTM interventions had to be decided first to know which parties were in file 1386 before ruling on the stay. The stay of 1387 in favour of 1386 had to be decided next, assessing file 1386 alone, because the requested stay was measured only against 1386 and any amendment to 1419 had no bearing; allowing the joinder or amendment to be decided first would indirectly modify file 1386, which had not been sought directly. The amendment to 1419 then had to be decided before joinder, since the court needed the final content of 1419 before deciding whether it could be joined to 1386.
firac.conclusion: The court set the order: (1) ARTM interventions; (2) stay of 1387; (3) amendment of 1419; (4) joinder of 1386 and 1419.

firac.issue: Should ARTM's uncontested voluntary aggressive interventions in files 1386 and 1387 be granted?
firac.facts: ARTM, already a defendant in file 1419, filed voluntary aggressive intervention acts to become a defendant in files 1386 and 1387, invoking its statutory role of collecting all transit revenue and remunerating the STM under RLRQ, c. A-33.3, such that any judgment against the STM would affect it. No party opposed.
firac.rule: Arts. 184–187 C.p.c. govern intervention; under art. 186 C.p.c., where no opposition is filed within 10 days, the third party's interest is presumed sufficient and the terms of intervention accepted. J.J. c. Province canadienne de la Congrégation de Sainte-Croix, 2023 QCCS 1073, summarizes that interventions at the authorization stage are rare but permitted in exceptional circumstances where the third party has a real, direct, juridical interest.
firac.application: This was an aggressive (not amicable) intervention, unopposed and not subject to any motion to dismiss, so art. 186 C.p.c. applied and the court had to take note of the presumed interest and accept the terms. Even though not technically required, ARTM's stated grounds (its financing relationship with the STM) sufficed to justify its interest and participation, constituting exceptional circumstances; it would be odd for ARTM to be a party in 1419 but not in 1386 and 1387.
firac.conclusion: The interventions were declared valid; ARTM was granted full defendant status in files 1386 and 1387, without costs given the absence of contestation.

firac.issue: Should file 1387 be stayed in favour of file 1386 under lis pendens and the 'first to file' rule?
firac.facts: File 1386 (filed 11 June 2025 by Vu against the STM) and file 1387 (filed 12 June 2025 by Saint-Onge against the STM and the Syndicat) both sought compensation for holders of STM weekly/monthly passes deprived of service by the June 2025 strike. Saint-Onge opposed, arguing no identity of parties or cause because the Syndicat was absent from 1386 and that file 1386 was flawed for ignoring post-2010 case law (Montréal (Ville de) c. Biondi, 2013 QCCA 404).
firac.rule: Where competing authorization applications create lis pendens (identity of parties, object and cause), only the first validly filed may proceed and the others are stayed under the 'first to file' rule, applied through the Superior Court's inherent power (art. 49 C.p.c.): Schmidt c. Johnson & Johnson, 2012 QCCA 2132; Hotte c. Servier Canada; Grondin c. Volkswagen. Only an apparent/quasi-lis pendens is required; identity of parties is assessed by juridical identity (membership in a group), a single common defendant suffices, and the priority principle may be displaced only if the prior application is not in members' interest or suffers serious deficiencies, the burden lying on the party challenging priority.
firac.application: Object was identical (obtaining authorization) and uncontested. The two proposed groups covered exactly the same persons, so parties were juridically identical; the Syndicat's absence from 1386 did not matter because a single common defendant (STM, and ARTM) suffices. Cause was identical: the same June 2025 strike, the same alleged breach of the STM's contractual obligation, the same single compensation sought regardless of who pays. All three lis pendens criteria met. File 1386 was precise, complete and rested on a clear legal syllogism, with no serious deficiency; the omission of the Syndicat reflected a legitimate legal-interpretation divergence, not a flaw, and no one sought double or triple recovery, so a stay would not force members into a later separate action.
firac.conclusion: The stay was granted; file 1387 stayed until the first of a final judgment, approved settlement or discontinuance in file 1386, with costs against Saint-Onge only.

firac.issue: Should Vu be permitted to amend her authorization application in file 1419 to extend the class period?
firac.facts: File 1419 (filed 11 September 2025 against the STM and ARTM) initially covered September 2025 pass holders. Following announcement of further strikes, Vu sought leave to add October and November 2025, without adding parties or causes of action. Only Saint-Onge, not a party to 1419, opposed.
firac.rule: Amendments to an authorization application require leave under art. 585 C.p.c. and must respect arts. 206–207 C.p.c.; the right to amend is the rule, but must not create an entirely new claim unrelated to the original, be contrary to the interests of justice, or delay the proceeding, all assessed with the proportionality principle (art. 18 C.p.c.): Lacerte c. Bruneau, 2025 QCCS 1853. Persons whose rights may be affected have standing to make representations.
firac.application: Saint-Onge had standing as his rights could be affected. The amendment merely broadened the temporal scope while preserving the underlying facts, allegations, nature of the remedy, questions of fact and law and conclusions; it did not delay the file (still at preliminary stage, no authorization hearing set), served judicial economy and proportionality (avoiding a third separate application), and caused no prejudice to putative members or to the STM and ARTM, who did not contest. Saint-Onge's objections were in substance a re-argument of the stay.
firac.conclusion: The amendment was authorized, without costs; no costs ordered against Saint-Onge since his objection was really a stay objection.

firac.issue: Should files 1386 and 1419 be joined into a single instance under art. 210 C.p.c.?
firac.facts: Vu sought joinder of files 1386 and 1419 (same defendants, STM and ARTM) so they would be tried together on the same evidence; alternatively she sought common case management. No party contested.
firac.rule: Art. 210 al. 2 C.p.c. permits joinder of instances between the same parties before the same court absent undue delay or serious prejudice to a third party. The former Code (art. 1051) expressly prohibited joinder of class actions; that prohibition was not carried into the current Code.
firac.application: The court held that authorization applications are not 'instances' within art. 210 C.p.c. and involve a burden of demonstration, not trial-quality evidence, so formal joinder is not available at the authorization stage. However, common management, including a simultaneous hearing of both authorization applications, would avoid the risk of contradictory judgments while respecting proportionality; joinder of authorized class actions remains available since those proceed on the merits.
firac.conclusion: The joinder request was dismissed, but common case management before Justice Bisson, including a simultaneous hearing of both authorization applications, was ordered, without costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area, as the decision turns entirely on civil-procedure questions in the context of class actions. K020 (class action) is the central and strongest keyword, since all three files are demandes d'autorisation d'exercer une action collective and the reasoning applies class-action-specific doctrine (first to file, art. 585 amendments, joinder under art. 210). K021 (interlocutory injunction/stay) is a weak but usable match for the suspension/stay of file 1387 (sursis/suspension d'instance), though technically it is a stay rather than an injunction. K009 (Labour and employment) and K084 (labour arbitration/grève) are contextual only — the underlying cause is the STM employees' strike — and are flagged as weak, since no labour-law issue is decided. The controlled vocabulary lacks specific terms for lis pendens, intervention, joinder or amendment, so these five are the closest available; K009 and K084 are the weakest picks, included to reach the minimum.

case_name: Souveraine, cie d'assurance générale c. Protech 4D Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: La Souveraine, Compagnie d'assurance générale c. Protech 4D Inc. (et Omega Recycling Technologies Inc., défenderesse en garantie)

defining_issues: Should the court, after issuance of the certificat d'état de cause, grant special permission under art. 17 of the Règlement de procédure de la Cour supérieure to allow a party to produce, mid-trial, a document (a competitor's operation manual) that was never disclosed before trial?
Is the proposed document relevant to the litigation such that its production should be admitted?

firac.issue: Should the court grant special permission under art. 17 of the Règlement de procédure to allow the mid-trial production of a document never disclosed before trial?
firac.facts: After the parties had filed their declarations of readiness and the clerk had issued the certificat d'état de cause, and after the trial had already run five days, Protech (defendant/plaintiff in warranty) sought to introduce SRS Environnement inc.'s solvent-recovery operation and maintenance manual to show that Omega's manual was inadequate. The manual had never been disclosed or referenced in the record. Counsel's only explanation for the lateness was that he had not thought of it earlier or did not know Omega had a Quebec competitor, though Omega's representative had been examined about that competitor as early as 7 February 2001.
firac.rule: Art. 15 of the Règlement de procédure de la Cour supérieure requires a declaration confirming the file is complete; once the certificat d'état de cause is issued, art. 17 provides that no further document may be produced 'sans la permission du tribunal, laquelle ne sera accordée que s'il le considère nécessaire dans l'intérêt de la justice.' Art. 17 is an exceptional provision (Air Saguenay). The certificate and readiness declaration form a kind of judicial contract, and delay must be justified by serious reasons (Raymond, Chabot; Parizeau). Factors (Modes Striva, per Rochon J.A.): reasons preventing timely disclosure; prejudice to the moving party if refused; prejudice to the adverse party; responsibility of counsel/client for the delay; conduct of the file; sound administration of justice. Art. 17 is applied strictly once trial has begun to avoid adjournments and surprise.
firac.application: The manual was never communicated or announced before trial and supported an argument never pleaded, creating a new debate. The only explanation — that counsel had not thought of it or was unaware of the competitor — was not sufficiently serious, since counsel had known of SRS since at least February 2001 and no elaborate search was shown to be required. The delay was entirely imputable to Protech and its counsel. Admitting it would take Omega by surprise, as it had never possessed or prepared argument on the document; conversely, refusing it caused Protech little prejudice given Protech itself had never treated the document as important.
firac.conclusion: Permission to produce the document late was refused; this alone justified maintaining Omega's objection.

firac.issue: Is the SRS Environnement manual relevant to the dispute such that its production should be admitted?
firac.facts: The underlying action is one in civil liability arising from the 6 April 1998 explosion and fire, Protech alleging a manufacturing/design defect in Omega's solvent distiller. The SRS manual (with its certificate of compliance and CSA authorization) was dated 19 May 1999, and Quebec norms (standard UL2208) had only come into force on 10 March 1998, one month before the fire. Protech admitted the Omega machine had a known defective lid seal (a missing ring) for about a month before the explosion, unrepaired at the time.
firac.rule: Relevance limits the freedom of proof; it is assessed against the applicable rules of law, the pleadings and conclusions, and the overall circumstances (Domaine de la Rivière; Royer). Evidence must tend to establish the facts generative of the claimed right and help the court, and the court may exclude evidence that will not advance the file or establish the constituent elements of the claim or defence.
firac.application: The francophone SRS manual was created in 1999, after both the fire and the entry into force of the March 1998 norms, so it could not validly serve to establish, by comparison, the inadequacy of Omega's 1998 English manual, which did not yet exist under the new norms. Even if comparison were possible, differences between the manuals would not automatically establish a manufacturing or design defect in the Omega distiller. Given the recent regulation and Protech's own admission of an unrepaired lid defect, a post-incident, post-regulation manual could not prove a defect in a device conceived before the norms.
firac.conclusion: The document was found irrelevant — non-contemporaneous with the events and apt to generate a new, unhelpful debate — providing a second and independent ground to refuse its production.

keywords_rationale: The case is squarely one of civil procedure and the law of evidence within a tort/insurance subrogation and product-liability dispute, so K002 (Civil litigation) is the genuine tier-1 classification and the only firmly applicable keyword. The controlled vocabulary contains no tier-2 term for admissibility of evidence, late document production, or civil-procedure rules; its evidence/procedure family (K020 class action, K021 interlocutory injunction, K022 restitution) is the closest domain but none of these doctrines is actually engaged — they are included only as the nearest available domain markers and should be treated as weak/non-applicable. K015 (defamation) is likewise a Civil liability domain term included to reach the minimum count and does not genuinely apply. In short, only K002 truly fits; the vocabulary lacks appropriate procedural/evidentiary keywords for this decision.

case_name: UBS Holding Canada Ltd. v. Harrison et al.

name_verification.name_in_document: UBS Holding Canada Ltd. v. Harrison et al.

defining_issues: What standard of proof must a court apply, on a stay motion in a dispute governed by the UNCITRAL Model Law, to decide whether an arbitration clause exists and whether the dispute falls within its scope?

Did the respondents' oppression claim under the New Brunswick Business Corporations Act fall, at least in part, within the scope of the arbitration clause in the Arrangement Agreement so as to require a stay and referral to arbitration?

Where some issues fall within an arbitration clause and some do not, must the court stay all proceedings and leave the arbitrator to determine the scope of jurisdiction, or may it retain all issues to avoid a multiplicity of proceedings?

firac.issue: What standard of proof must a court apply, on a stay motion in a dispute governed by the UNCITRAL Model Law, to decide whether an arbitration clause applies?
firac.facts: The Arrangement Agreement contained an arbitration clause referring disputes 'arising out of or relating to' the agreement to arbitration under Ontario's International Commercial Arbitration Act, engaging the UNCITRAL Model Law. On the appellant's stay motion the motion judge asked whether, on a balance of probabilities, the claim arose out of or in relation to the arrangement.
firac.rule: Under articles 8(1) and 16(1) of the UNCITRAL Model Law and the competence-competence principle affirmed in Dell Computer Corp. v. Union des consommateurs, 2007 SCC 34, jurisdictional challenges are presumptively for the arbitrator to decide first; a court departs only where the challenge is a pure question of law or a question of mixed law and fact requiring only superficial review of the record. On a Model Law stay motion the court applies a prima facie / 'arguable' standard (Gulf Canada Resources; Dalimpex; Secure Solutions), not a balance of probabilities standard.
firac.application: The Court held the motion judge erred by applying a balance-of-probabilities test to an UNCITRAL-related dispute. Following Dell, the court treated 'prima facie' and 'arguable' as synonymous, preferring 'prima facie' as connoting the minimal 'reasonable likelihood' threshold. The correct question was whether the appellant established a prima facie case that an arbitration clause existed and applied, not whether the claim more probably than not arose out of the agreement.
firac.conclusion: The motion judge applied the wrong standard; the prima facie threshold governs Model Law stay motions.

firac.issue: Did the oppression claim fall, at least prima facie, within the scope of the arbitration clause?
firac.facts: The respondents sued only under the oppression remedy in s. 166(3) of the NBBCA, relying in their pleadings on the appellant's alleged misrepresentations (US tax-evasion scheme, subprime overexposure, rogue-trading losses, and the LIBOR scandal). They argued the Arrangement Agreement was silent on these matters and that fraud could not have been contemplated. Articles 3 and 4 of the Agreement contained representations, warranties and general obligations.
firac.rule: An arbitration clause covering disputes 'arising out of or relating to' an agreement can capture allegations of fraud and misrepresentation (Strata Plan BCS 3165 v. 1100 Georgia Partnership, 2013 BCSC 1708). The court need only find a prima facie case that the clause applies.
firac.application: Because the parties' relationship existed only by virtue of the Arrangement Agreement, and the Agreement's Articles 3 and 4 (representations and obligations) prima facie contemplated recourse for the very conduct complained of, and the statement of claim repeatedly alleged misrepresentation, the Court found the dispute arose, at least in part, out of or in relation to the Agreement. Applying the correct standard on the affidavit and documentary record (no oral testimony or credibility findings), the appellate court could itself decide the matter under Rule 62.21(1).
firac.conclusion: The appellant made out a prima facie case that the dispute fell within the arbitration clause.

firac.issue: Where some issues fall within the arbitration clause and some do not, must all proceedings be stayed?
firac.facts: The motion judge found some issues arbitrable and some not, and chose to retain all issues to avoid a multiplicity of proceedings.
firac.rule: Consistent with the Model Law and the competence-competence principle (Opron Inc. v. Canaport Ltd.; SNC-SNAM v. Opron Maritimes), once some issues are found appropriate for arbitration the court must stay all proceedings and let the arbitrator determine the scope of its jurisdiction; the plaintiff may later return to court for judicial review or to litigate matters over which the arbitrator declines jurisdiction.
firac.application: The desire to avoid a multiplicity of proceedings did not justify retaining arbitrable matters. Having found some issues arbitrable, the motion judge was required to stay the whole action and leave the arbitrator to delineate jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: A stay of all proceedings should have been ordered, with the arbitrator to determine scope.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area — this is a commercial dispute over an arbitration clause and stay of proceedings. K001 (Administrative law) and K011 (judicial review) are engaged because the competence-competence framework expressly contemplates later judicial review of an arbitrator's jurisdictional ruling. K014 (standard of review) is used as the closest available label for the central controversy over the correct standard/threshold (prima facie versus balance of probabilities), though it is a borderline fit since the case concerns the standard for a stay/referral rather than review of an administrative decision. K021 (interlocutory injunction) is a weak/closest-available pick standing in for the stay-of-proceedings remedy, as the controlled vocabulary contains no dedicated arbitration or stay-of-proceedings keyword. The vocabulary is poorly suited to a commercial arbitration matter, so several picks are flagged as weak; no Jewish/antisemitism keywords were selected despite the passing reference to a 'Beis Din' in the cited Finkelstein case, as that was only an authority discussed, not an issue here.

name_verification.name_in_document: Volzhenin v. Haile

defining_issues: Was the plaintiff a credible witness whose self-reported symptoms could be relied upon?
Did the plaintiff prove on a balance of probabilities that he sustained brain damage and a resulting loss of income-earning capacity caused by the motor vehicle accident?
What non-pecuniary damages, loss of income and special damages were established given the plaintiff's credibility problems?

firac.issue: Was the plaintiff a credible witness whose self-reported symptoms could be relied upon?
firac.facts: Liability for the March 18, 1997 accident was admitted; only the extent of injuries was in dispute. The treating and retained physicians all relied on what Mr. Volzhenin told them. The evidence disclosed numerous inconsistencies: he claimed to be unable to work while in fact working, claimed natural-healing income to ICBC yet never declared it for tax, gave conflicting accounts of employment and earnings to lenders, immigration and tax authorities, and denied pre-accident headaches, neck problems and forgetfulness that were documented in earlier medical records from the 1993 border incident.
firac.rule: A plaintiff bears the onus of proving his claim on a balance of probabilities. Where there is little or no objective evidence and complaints persist beyond the usual recovery period, the court must be exceedingly careful (Butler v. Blaylock Estate, [1981] B.C.J. No. 31). Where a litigant practises to deceive by falsehood or gross exaggeration, doubts arising from the resulting web of deceit fall on the litigant (Le v. Milburn, [1987] B.C.J. No. 2690).
firac.application: The court catalogued numerous contradictions between the plaintiff's testimony, his statements to doctors, and objective records; lay witnesses uniformly described a physically healthy, energetic, high-performing individual before the accident, contradicting the disabling picture he presented to physicians. Plaintiff's own counsel conceded that lack of credibility had been established. The court found the plaintiff was on a 'financial mission' and had deceived his doctors and others.
firac.conclusion: The court found Mr. Volzhenin wholly lacking in credibility, so his self-reporting could not be relied upon.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiff prove brain damage and loss of income-earning capacity caused by the accident?
firac.facts: Plaintiff alleged a significant traumatic brain injury with cognitive, language and executive-function deficits. MRI and CT scans, EEG, and neurological examinations disclosed no objective abnormality (no hemosiderin, no atrophy, normal intracranial contents). Expert opinions supporting brain damage (Drs. Stewart, Allan, Anderson) rested heavily on self-reporting and on each other's untested reports; Dr. Jones and neuropsychologist Dr. Wilkinson found only a mild head injury with no objective evidence of brain damage. Pre-accident writing samples were as messy as post-accident samples.
firac.rule: The test is whether, on a balance of probabilities, the plaintiff has established his case; it is not for the court to render a medical opinion (Cloutier v. Wong, [1991] B.C.J. No. 3843). Diagnoses grounded on unreliable self-reporting cannot be given weight.
firac.application: Because the supporting expert opinions depended on the plaintiff's discredited self-reporting and on reports not in evidence, and the objective imaging was normal, the court preferred Dr. Jones's evidence that the plaintiff had a head injury, not brain damage. The plaintiff's extensive travel and active social life were inconsistent with the alleged deficits.
firac.conclusion: Brain damage of any more than a transitory nature was not established; the claim for loss of income-earning capacity was dismissed.

firac.issue: What damages were established despite the credibility findings?
firac.facts: The plaintiff sustained a blow to the head, bruising, jaw injury, a concussion, and soft-tissue injuries to neck and shoulder. Defence accepted soft-tissue, teeth and jaw injuries and a concussion resolving by October 1997. Employment evidence suggested he was capable of a paid ITV position at about $40,000/year. Numerous therapy accounts (massage, physiotherapy, chiropractic) lacked proof of causal connection to the accident.
firac.rule: Recoverable damages must be proven on a balance of probabilities and causally connected to the accident; special damages require substantiation of the causal link.
firac.application: The court accepted the concussion and soft-tissue injuries and assessed non-pecuniary damages at $30,000. Giving the plaintiff the benefit of the doubt on employment, it allowed six months' loss of income at $40,000/year, i.e. $20,000. Only travel ($360), the July/August 1997 massage ($40) and dental/orthodontic accounts were allowed; the Tai massage, physiotherapy and chiropractic accounts were disallowed for want of proven causation.
firac.conclusion: Non-pecuniary damages of $30,000, loss of income of $20,000, and limited special damages were awarded; the balance of the claims failed.

case_name: Sterritt v Canada (Her Majesty the Queen)

name_verification.name_in_document: God, Prince Kitsilano, Skidegate ‑ Sterritt Family, in James Sterritt & Marya Watson, on behalf of all Indians & Muslims v. Her Majesty The Queen in Right of Canada, & The Province of British Columbia (AG Fernando De Lima), the City of Prince Rupert, P. Lindquist, Bylaw Officer, Nicholas Najdae, M'Akola Group of Societies
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied short-form style 'Sterritt v Canada (Her Majesty the Queen)' is a reasonable abbreviation of the full, unusual style of cause printed in the decision, and the citation 2017 BCSC 1064 matches exactly.

defining_issues: Should the plaintiff's Notice of Civil Claim be struck out under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules as disclosing no reasonable claim and as frivolous, scandalous and an abuse of process?
Should James Sterritt be declared a vexatious litigant under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act and be enjoined from instituting proceedings without leave?

firac.issue: Should the plaintiff's Notice of Civil Claim be struck out under Rule 9-5(1) as disclosing no reasonable claim and as frivolous, scandalous and an abuse of process?
firac.facts: James Sterritt, self-represented and purporting to act on behalf of 'all Indians & Muslims' and as 'God/Prince Kitsilano', filed a Notice of Civil Claim mixing assertions of divine and aboriginal title to all land in British Columbia, a demand that defendants enter tenancy under him as 'paramount world landlord', a residential tenancy dispute concerning 438-8th Avenue West, and a challenge to a dog bylaw ticket. He had a long history of substantially identical claims that had been struck or dismissed.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules permits striking a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim, is unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, may prejudice or embarrass a fair trial, or is otherwise an abuse of process. A claim is struck for no reasonable claim only where it is plain and obvious it discloses no cause of action (Imperial Tobacco, 2011 SCC 42; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress). Aboriginal title is communal and cannot be asserted by an individual (Louison v. Ochapowace Indian Band #71, 2011 SKQB 87). Abuse of process is a flexible doctrine protecting judicial economy, finality and integrity of justice (Krist v. British Columbia, 2017 BCCA 78).
firac.application: The court found the claim an incoherent mixture of unintelligible assertions that failed to establish any cause of action known to law; an individual cannot assert communal aboriginal title. The pleadings were groundless, fanciful, embarrassing and scandalous, would involve useless expense, and the claims against the City and its bylaw officer amounted to a collateral attack. The pleadings were fundamentally flawed, disconnected from reality and incapable of amendment.
firac.conclusion: The Notice of Civil Claim was struck in its entirety.

firac.issue: Should James Sterritt be declared a vexatious litigant under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act and enjoined from instituting proceedings without leave?
firac.facts: Counsel documented an extensive litigation history dating to 1995 in which Sterritt repeatedly styled himself as God, Christ, Prince and Indian, claimed paramount title to all B.C. land, purported to act for all Indians, and re-litigated the same issues across the Federal Court, Supreme Court of Canada, BC Supreme Court and Provincial Court, several of which had already imposed leave requirements and a contempt sentence.
firac.rule: Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 443, permits an order barring proceedings without leave where a person has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds instituted vexatious legal proceedings. Hallmarks of vexatious conduct include re-litigating decided issues, actions that cannot succeed or serve no good, actions for improper purpose, rolling issues forward into successive actions (R.D. Backhoe Services v. Graham Construction, 2017 BCCA 91, citing Lang Michener). Court resources are finite and must not be squandered (Canada v. Olumide, 2017 FCA 42).
firac.application: Sterritt's numerous actions were strikingly similar, reiterated claims on behalf of God, styled him as a 'Prince', purported to act for all First Nations, lacked merit, were in some cases brought for improper purposes and lacked any rational connection to reality. He persisted despite repeated rulings that he could not advance such claims, and the Provincial Court had already required leave. His conduct fell within multiple R.D. Backhoe hallmarks.
firac.conclusion: Sterritt was declared a vexatious litigant; he was enjoined under s. 18 from instituting proceedings or filing documents in the Supreme or Provincial Courts of B.C. without leave (with limited leave-application exceptions), registry staff were directed to discard contravening filings, and the defendants were awarded costs.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area, as the decision turns on civil-procedure powers to strike pleadings (Rule 9-5) and to control vexatious litigants (s. 18 Supreme Court Act). K021 (interlocutory injunction) is included because the operative relief was an injunctive order restraining the plaintiff from filing without leave — a moderate fit for injunction/injunctive relief. The remaining picks are weak and flagged: K022 (restitution) appears only in the plaintiff's list of relief sought and formed no part of the reasoning; K011 (judicial review) is a stretch reflecting the collateral attack on the bylaw ticket; K054 (wills/estates) reflects only Sterritt's historical self-description as 'Executor of the Estate of Jesus Christ' and is not a live issue. The controlled vocabulary, oriented toward Charter/antisemitism/human-rights matters, fits this procedural striking-and-vexatious-litigant decision poorly, so fewer than five keywords genuinely apply.
location_rationale: The header states 'Registry: Prince Rupert' and the 'Place and Date of Hearing' and 'Place and Date of Judgment' are both given as 'Prince Rupert, B.C.' The court is the Supreme Court of British Columbia.
registry_rationale: The decision expressly records 'Registry: Prince Rupert' in its heading.

name_verification.name_in_document: Spence et al. v. BMO Trust Company et al. [Indexed as: Spence v. BMO Trust Co.]

defining_issues: Can a will be declared void as contrary to public policy where the will's stated reason for disinheritance is neutral on its face, but extrinsic evidence establishes that the true motive was racist?
Is extrinsic evidence of the testator's oral statements admissible and material to determining whether the will offends public policy?

firac.issue: Can a will be void as contrary to public policy where its face is neutral but extrinsic evidence shows a racist motive for disinheritance?
firac.facts: Rector Emanuel Spence's 2010 will disinherited his daughter Verolin, stating only that she had 'had no communication with me for several years and has shown no interest in me as a father,' and left the estate to his other daughter Donna and her children. Extrinsic evidence (affidavits of Verolin and of the deceased's friend Imogene Parchment) established that the deceased ceased contact with Verolin in 2002 solely because she had a child with a Caucasian man, and that he chose Donna's children because their father was black. The deceased had had no relationship with Donna for years.
firac.rule: Courts may intervene to strike testamentary provisions that offend public policy, notwithstanding the general freedom to dispose of one's property (Canada Trust Co. v. Ontario Human Rights Commission (Leonard (Re)) (1990), 74 O.R. (2d) 481 (C.A.); Egerton v. The Earl of Brownlow (1853)). Following McCorkill v. McCorkill Estate, 2014 NBQB 148, a will may be scrutinized and set aside even where its terms are not offensive on their face, where the underlying purpose contravenes public policy. If a will is set aside, an intestacy results under the Succession Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.26.
firac.application: The court accepted the uncontradicted evidence of Ms. Parchment, who had no stake in the outcome, that the deceased disinherited Verolin because the father of her son was not black. There was no other explanation for the sudden and complete cessation of an otherwise close relationship in which the father had financed years of Verolin's education. Donna, though properly served, did not appear, leaving the evidence uncontradicted. The court held that although the will's stated reason was neutral, the true motive was a clearly stated racist principle, and it offended public policy that Donna should receive the entire estate simply because her children were fathered by a black man.
firac.conclusion: The will was set aside as contrary to public policy, producing an intestacy in which the estate is divided equally between Verolin and Donna.

firac.issue: Is extrinsic evidence of the testator's oral statements admissible and material to assessing whether the will offends public policy?
firac.facts: BMO argued that the public policy doctrine cannot apply absent a testamentary document manifestly contrary to the public interest, and that the applicants' extrinsic evidence of the deceased's utterances was immaterial and did not comply with the Ontario Evidence Act. The applicants relied on the unchallenged Parchment affidavit, which was not cross-examined.
firac.rule: Courts ordinarily confine themselves to the wording of a will, but McCorkill supports going behind the face of a document where the purpose is contrary to public policy; extrinsic evidence of a testator's motive may be received where it establishes such a purpose.
firac.application: The court found no reason not to accept Ms. Parchment's uncontradicted evidence, given she was a disinterested witness who was neither beneficiary nor executor. Combined with Verolin's affidavit, the evidence clearly established the racist motive. Were it not for this unchallenged evidence, the court would have gone no further than the will's wording, but here the extrinsic evidence was decisive.
firac.conclusion: The extrinsic evidence was admitted and treated as material and reliable, and it grounded the finding that the disinheritance offended public policy.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area under which wills/estates are classified in the vocabulary, and K054 (wills/estates) is the directly engaged doctrine — the case is about setting aside a will and the resulting intestacy under the Succession Law Reform Act. K065 (racism) captures the core public policy ground: the disinheritance was motivated by the grandchild's father not being black. K069 (discrimination) reflects the discriminatory basis of the testamentary decision. K002 (civil litigation) covers the estate litigation/application procedure. K119 (Human Rights Code) is engaged because the leading authority, Canada Trust Co. v. Ontario Human Rights Commission, applied public policy as informed by the Human Rights Code, 1981. K071 (human dignity) is a borderline pick tied to the court's observation that the racist motive offended human sensibilities and public policy; it is the weakest selection. There is no dedicated 'public policy' or 'testamentary freedom' keyword in the vocabulary, so these are the closest applicable terms.
location_rationale: The decision identifies the court as the 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' before Gilmore J., establishing the province as Ontario. No sitting city is stated in the text (the deceased's property was in Maple, Ontario, but that is a fact about the estate, not the court's location), so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The decision does not name a court registry or office; it identifies only the Ontario Superior Court of Justice and the neutral citation, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Snyder v. Montreal Gazette Ltd.

defining_issues: Was the jury's award of $135,000 in moral (non-pecuniary) damages for defamation 'unreasonable' within the meaning of art. 380 C.C.P., such that judgment should not have been rendered in conformity with the verdict?

What is the proper quantum of non-pecuniary damages payable by a single defendant newspaper for defamation where the plaintiff has launched eight separate actions against different media over the same underlying statement?
Having found the verdict unreasonable, what remedy (new trial, reduction of the award, or publication of the judgment) should the Court of Appeal grant under art. 381 C.C.P.?

firac.issue: Was the jury's $135,000 moral-damages award unreasonable under art. 380 C.C.P.?
firac.facts: A jury found that Gerald Snyder had been defamed by a Montreal Gazette article headlined that a former civic official was described as a 'representative of the Jewish Mafia in Montreal', that he suffered no actual/pecuniary damages, but that he suffered $135,000 in moral damages (pain, suffering, anguish and humiliation) attributable to the Gazette alone, independently of similar statements in other media. Snyder had brought eight separate actions over the same underlying testimony, claiming $2,680,535 in non-pecuniary damages in total. The trial judge confirmed the verdict as not unreasonable.
firac.rule: Art. 380 C.C.P. required the judge to render judgment in conformity with a civil jury verdict 'unless it appears to him to be unreasonable.' Jury verdicts must be treated with considerable respect and great weight but are not untouchable (Vancouver-Fraser Park District v. Olmstead; Vineberg v. Larocque); a verdict may be set aside where there is a clear denial of justice or where no reasonable person could reach it. Guidance on the moderation of non-pecuniary awards is drawn by analogy from the Supreme Court 'trilogy' (Andrews, Thornton, Teno), which fixed roughly $100,000 as the upper limit of non-pecuniary loss for a young quadriplegic.
firac.application: The majority (Owen and Monet JJ.A.) held that to reach $135,000 as the Gazette's share alone, the jury must have valued Snyder's total non-pecuniary damages at nearly $1,000,000 — far above the trilogy's upper limit of less than $100,000 for the worst personal injuries, and far above comparable Quebec defamation awards (e.g., $15,000 in Larouche; $10,000 in Melasco; $2,000 in Drapeau). The pain and humiliation of a middle-aged man whose reputation was attacked but vindicated could not approach that of a quadriplegic, and Quebec law recognizes no private/punitive penalty. The 'in addition to, and distinct from' framing and the excessive multiplied claims confirmed the award was patently disproportionate. L'Heureux-Dubé J.A., dissenting, would have deferred to the properly instructed jury, whose directions were 'above criticism', holding the award not so offensive as to warrant substitution of the court's view.
firac.conclusion: By majority, the verdict of $135,000 was unreasonable within art. 380 C.C.P. and should not have been confirmed.

firac.issue: What is the proper quantum of non-pecuniary damages against the single defendant newspaper?
firac.facts: Snyder claimed $367,680 in non-pecuniary damages against the Gazette and a total of $2,680,535 across all eight actions. No pecuniary damages were proven. A prompt reply and a retraction had been published, and the article closely tracked the police-inquiry testimony.
firac.rule: Non-pecuniary/moral damages in defamation cannot be calculated with mathematical precision and are, of necessity, a 'well-reasoned guess' (Langlois v. Drapeau, per Casey and Owen JJ.). General damages from defamation are largely effaced by the judgment condemning the defendant, so courts have resisted generosity and kept awards moderate; substantial sums risk importing an impermissible element of punishment. The trilogy's upper-limit reasoning applies by analogy.
firac.application: Taking the upper limit for total non-pecuniary damages in all eight actions as less than $100,000, and noting Snyder's claims were at least 27 times that ceiling, Monet J.A. divided the claim against the Gazette ($367,680) by 27 to obtain $13,618, corroborating a reasonable figure of about $13,500. Owen J.A. adopted the same figure. Factors such as the accuracy of the report, the published reply and retraction, the Gazette's mid-sequence role among many media, the absence of aggravated or punitive damages, and comparable Quebec awards all supported a modest sum.
firac.conclusion: The reasons fixed the reasonable award at $13,500 (with the formal disposition recording $18,500), plus agreed interest at 10% from May 27, 1975.

firac.issue: What remedy should the Court of Appeal grant under art. 381 C.C.P.?
firac.facts: The appellant sought reduction of damages to $13,500 or, alternatively, a new trial on moral damages. The jury had also recommended publication of the judgment in the Gazette. Nearly eight years had elapsed since publication.
firac.rule: Art. 381 C.C.P. empowers the Court of Appeal to confirm or reverse the judgment or order a new trial, 'applying the remedy by which it considers that the ends of justice will best be attained.' Ordering a new trial is a specific, exceptional aspect of the appellate power of review; publication may serve as partial redress for non-pecuniary loss in defamation.
firac.application: A new trial was inappropriate given the passage of time, cost, and possible unavailability of witnesses, and the good administration of justice did not require it. Publication of the appellate judgment would have limited compensatory value and was not ordered. The just remedy was to amend the trial judgment by substituting a reasonable award and striking the publication order.
firac.conclusion: Appeal allowed with costs; no new trial and no publication ordered; the award was reduced (to $13,500 in the reasons; $18,500 per the recorded disposition) with interest, and the publication order struck.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area: this is a civil defamation action and appellate review of a jury award. K015 (defamation) is the core cause of action. K018 (qualified privilege) captures the Press Act s. 10(d) privilege for accurate, good-faith reports of court sittings, argued as a defence though not ultimately dispositive on quantum. K057 (antisemitic slurs), K058 (antisemitism) and K093 (Jewish) are engaged because the defamatory statement labelled Snyder 'representative of the Jewish Mafia in Montreal' — an antisemitic characterization central to the gravity of the libel. K057 and K058 are somewhat borderline since the case turns on damages assessment rather than antisemitism as a legal doctrine, but the antisemitic content of the libel is material to the harm. No controlled keyword squarely captures 'non-pecuniary damages' or 'jury verdict review', which are the true doctrinal focus.
location_rationale: The decision is headed 'Quebec Court of Appeal' and reviews a Superior Court judgment 'handed down in Montreal on March 8, 1978'; the libel action arose from an article in the Montreal Gazette and proceedings before the Quebec Police Commission in Montreal, placing the appeal in the Montreal district of Quebec.
registry_rationale: No registry is expressly stated, but the appeal is from the Montreal Superior Court and the Court of Appeal sitting is in Montreal, so the registry is taken to be Montreal.

case_name: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital c. N.G.

name_verification.name_in_document: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital c. N.G.

defining_issues: Did the patient have the capacity to consent to the proposed psychiatric treatment plan?
Should the court authorize treatment (a treatment order) over the patient's refusal, and for what duration?

firac.issue: Did the patient have the capacity to consent to the proposed psychiatric treatment plan?
firac.facts: Mr. N. G., 79, has a 40-year psychiatric history and a recent expert report (Dr. Propst and Dr. Frank, May 31, 2021) concluding he suffers from a delusional disorder requiring anti-psychotic medication. He denies having any mental illness, attributing his conduct to life circumstances, and has no insight into his condition, though he understands some side effects.
firac.rule: Authorization of care over a patient's refusal requires that the patient be incapable of consenting, applying the criteria established in F.D. v. Centre universitaire de santé McGill (Hôpital Royal-Victoria), 2015 QCCA 1139.
firac.application: The Court accepted the expert conclusion that Mr. N. G. suffers from a delusional disorder and lacks insight into his own mental condition due to his illness. He denies being ill, does not recognize the benefits of the treatment or the risks of stopping medication, demonstrating incapacity to appreciate his situation and to consent.
firac.conclusion: The Court found Mr. N. G. did not have the capacity to consent to the proposed treatment plan.

firac.issue: Should the court authorize the treatment order over the patient's refusal, and for what duration?
firac.facts: Mr. N. G. categorically refuses the treatment, claiming the medication is redundant and that he would not take it absent a safeguard order. Under an interim safeguard order since September 2019 he has received the treatment, shown improvement, and avoided hospitalization. Side effects included fatigue. He is active in his HLM building committee and attends synagogue.
firac.rule: Where a patient is incapable of consenting and categorically refuses, the court may authorize treatment where the benefits outweigh the disadvantages, applying the F.D. v. Centre universitaire de santé McGill criteria; the duration must be reasonable.
firac.application: The Court found a categoric refusal and that the benefits of the plan far outweighed the manageable side effects, since ceasing medication would lead to more hospitalizations, isolation and distress. Given the long history of mental illness, the need to ensure compliance, and the success of the injectable medication since September 2019, a three-year order was reasonable.
firac.conclusion: The Court granted the treatment order for a duration of three years.

keywords_rationale: This is a Civil litigation matter (K002) — an application for authorization of psychiatric care over a patient's refusal, decided under the F.D. v. McGill capacity criteria. The controlled vocabulary is heavily oriented toward Charter, hate-speech, and Jewish-community themes and offers no keyword for medical consent, capacity, or authorization of care, so few genuine matches exist. K105 (synagogue) reflects the noted fact that the patient regularly attends synagogue, and K093 (Jewish) is tangentially engaged via the Jewish General Hospital; both are weak, incidental picks flagged as such. No stronger tier-2 keywords in the vocabulary fit a mental-health treatment-authorization case.
location_rationale: The decision header states 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' and identifies the Superior Court, Province of Quebec; the district of Montreal indicates the city.
registry_rationale: The court file is in the 'DISTRICT OF MONTREAL' (No: 500-17-109374-192), so the registry is Montreal.

name_verification.name_in_document: Sitchon v. Shia

defining_issues: Should the father's parenting time with the child be increased beyond the existing schedule, applying the best-interests-of-the-child test under the Children's Law Reform Act?
If parenting time were increased, would the father be entitled to a reduction in child support under section 9 of the Child Support Guidelines?
How much retroactive (table) child support does the father owe the mother?
Which of the child's activities and health costs qualify as section 7 special or extraordinary expenses, who decides on them, and how are retroactive and future amounts to be shared?

firac.issue: Should the father's parenting time be increased beyond the current 5-of-14 overnight schedule, in the child's best interests?
firac.facts: The eight-year-old child, M., lives primarily with his mother in North York and spends 5 of every 14 overnights with his father in Stouffville. The parents separated in 2022 after the father was charged (later withdrawn) with assaulting the mother, an incident M. witnessed. M. shows distress, breakdowns and inconsistent statements about both parents; CAS verified concerns that M. is exposed to post-separation conflict. The father sought one additional overnight per week; the mother sought to maintain the status quo.
firac.rule: Section 24 of the Children's Law Reform Act requires the court to decide parenting solely on the best interests of the child, giving primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, with enumerated factors in s. 24(2)-(4), including family violence (s. 18). Subsection 24(6) directs as much time with each parent as is consistent with best interests. There is no presumption of equal parenting time (J.P. v. W.W., 2023 ONSC 1931).
firac.application: The court found both parents capable and loving and that the father sincerely wanted more time. It found an incident of family violence occurred on May 22, 2022 with the father as primary aggressor, but was not persuaded the father choked the mother or posed an ongoing risk. M. was traumatized by the parents' arguments and expressed no strong preference. The child's paramount current need was stability, aided by a 'home base' with his primary caregiver mother; the existing schedule was already slightly more generous than the AFCC Parenting Plan Guide recommends for his age, and the father still had work to do managing his emotions and communication.
firac.conclusion: Parenting time was not increased; the existing schedule was maintained (with a one-time flip of alternating weekends to align with the mother's partner's schedule, and a restriction barring the mother from scheduling new activities on the father's mid-week day without consent).

firac.issue: Had parenting time been increased, would the father be entitled to a reduction of child support under section 9 of the Child Support Guidelines?
firac.facts: The father's imputed 2023 income was $160,766 and the mother's $75,000; table support was $1,377/month. He sought a $400 (roughly 29%) monthly reduction, providing a hours-based calculation showing time would reach about 41% and a childcare budget of $2,745.56/month.
firac.rule: Section 9 of the Child Support Guidelines applies where a parent exercises at least 40% of parenting time; it is discretionary and changes only the method of determination (not an automatic reduction), requiring consideration of the table amount, increased costs of shared parenting, and the condition, means and needs of each parent and child (Contino v. Leonelli-Contino, 2005 SCC 63; M.A. v. N.M., 2021 ONSC 5468). The applicant bears the burden.
firac.application: The court accepted the father would have crossed the 40% threshold (about 41%), satisfying the first question, but found his cost calculations unpersuasive and unsupported by receipts. Given the income disparity and the need to maintain M.'s standard of living while the mother continued to bear most expenses and majority parenting, a fine-grained reduction would not serve M.'s best interests.
firac.conclusion: The court held that, even had parenting time been increased, it would not have reduced the father's child support; the reduction request was dismissed.

firac.issue: How much retroactive table child support does the father owe?
firac.facts: The parties agreed on arrears of $1,754 (2022), $2,756 (2023) and $1,290 (Jan-June 2024). Table support from July 1, 2024 was $1,377/month; the parties disputed whether it had been paid, the mother relying on an FRO statement and the father asserting full payment.
firac.rule: Table child support is payable per the Child Support Guidelines; arrears are enforceable, and a payor asserting payment must establish it.
firac.application: The court accepted the agreed arrears totalling $5,800 and required the father to prove payment for July-September 2024, failing which additional arrears would accrue.
firac.conclusion: The father was ordered to pay $5,800 in arrears within 30 days, plus $645 more if he fails to prove payment of $1,377/month for July-September 2024.

firac.issue: Which activities and health costs are section 7 expenses, who decides on them, and how are they shared?
firac.facts: The mother sought proportionate sharing of hockey, baseball, muay thai, go-karting, swimming, camps, tutoring, a private Sun Life health premium, uninsured health/dental (including play therapy) and a cell phone. The father agreed to some items but objected to the mother unilaterally enrolling M. in numerous and increasingly expensive programs, and to duplicate health premiums.
firac.rule: Section 7 of the Child Support Guidelines covers necessary and reasonable expenses beyond the table amount; for education and extracurricular activities the expense must be 'extraordinary' assessed under s. 7(1.1) (amount relative to income, nature/number of activities, the child's special needs or talents, overall cost). Expenses must be necessary in the child's best interests and reasonable in relation to means and pre-separation spending (Ostapchuk v. Ostapchuk; Titova v. Titov, 2012 ONCA 864).
firac.application: The court analysed each expense by category, need/talent, cost, family spending pattern and family dynamic. It found additional health coverage, play therapy, and the mother's tutoring met M.'s needs, but the father's duplicate Sun Life premium and separate nanny-tutoring were not necessary. Baseball and hockey (long-standing, costly, meeting M.'s physical and emotional needs) qualified as extraordinary; the newer, cheaper, ad hoc muay thai and go-karting did not and fell within table support. It criticised the mother's peremptory approach of informing rather than consulting the father.
firac.conclusion: The father was ordered to pay retroactive section 7 amounts per the mother's charts except Sun Life, muay thai and go-karting; future proportionate sharing (68/32) was ordered for baseball, hockey (with 10% caps and defined inclusions), swimming, camps, tutoring, uninsured health/dental including play therapy, and cell phone, with new future expenses requiring advance written consent not to be unreasonably withheld.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing test for the central parenting-time issue under CLRA s. 24. K048 (custody/access) captures the parenting-time/schedule dispute. K050 (parental/child support) covers the section 9 reduction analysis, retroactive arrears and the section 7 expenses determinations. K049 (marriage/cohabitation agreement) is a weaker pick, included because the parties executed a partial consent agreement addressing decision-making and holidays, but it is peripheral to the contested issues. The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated family-violence or evidence/credibility term that would otherwise apply to the CLRA s. 18 family-violence findings and the surreptitious-recording admissibility ruling.
location_rationale: The decision header identifies only 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE' and court file no. FS 22-30431, without naming a hearing city. Province is Ontario, evident from the court and the application of Ontario statutes (CLRA, Ontario Child Support Guidelines). The parties reside in Stouffville and North York and the York Region CAS was involved, but no registry city is stated in the text.
registry_rationale: No registry/office is expressly named in the decision; only the court file number (FS 22-30431) appears, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: WEISS v. KOPEL

defining_issues: Did the arbitration clause requiring disputes to be submitted to a Beth Din bar the parties from seeking relief under the Family Law Reform Act, 1978?
Could the mother's waiver of spousal support in the domestic contract be set aside under s. 18(4)(a) (unconscionability) or s. 18(4)(b) (public-money allowance) of the Family Law Reform Act?
Was the mother entitled to reimbursement of obstetrical/hospital expenses and the cost of the child's ritual circumcision despite the release in the domestic contract?
What access to the child should the father be granted, applying the best-interests-of-the-child standard?

firac.issue: Did the agreement's clause requiring disputes to be arbitrated before a Beth Din prevent the parties from seeking relief under the Family Law Reform Act, 1978?
firac.facts: The parties, Orthodox Jews, signed an agreement dissolving their religious marriage that contained (para. 7) a clause requiring any dispute over the meaning of the agreement to be submitted to binding arbitration before three Orthodox rabbis (a Beth Din). The father sought a court order for access and the mother sought various new relief.
firac.rule: An arbitration clause binds parties only to the matters it covers; a stipulation to submit disputes over the 'meaning' of an agreement to a Beth Din governs interpretation, not applications for new statutory relief.
firac.application: The court found the parties were seeking not an interpretation of the agreement but new relief under the Family Law Reform Act, and that neither party could invoke the clause against the other while asking to be exempt from it themselves.
firac.conclusion: The parties were not bound by the Beth Din arbitration stipulation and could proceed under the Family Law Reform Act.

firac.issue: Could the mother's waiver of spousal support in the domestic contract be set aside under s. 18(4)(a) or (b) of the Family Law Reform Act?
firac.facts: The August 1979 agreement was a 'separation agreement' and thus a 'domestic contract'; in para. 6 the mother released the father from all claims arising from the marriage and birth of the child. She was receiving municipal welfare assistance, alleged she signed under duress and while unwell, and chose not to work in order to care for the child. The marriage's cohabitation lasted only about ten months.
firac.rule: Family Law Reform Act, 1978, s. 18(4): a court may set aside a support provision where (a) the provision for support or the waiver of the right to support results in unconscionable circumstances, (b) the provision for support is to a spouse who qualifies for a public-money allowance, or (c) default in payment. Courts should not lightly interfere with contracts freely entered into (Re Stevenson; Dal Santo v. Dal Santo; MacNeill v. MacNeill). Interpretation Act, s. 10; expressio unius est exclusio alterius.
firac.application: Section 18(4)(b) conspicuously omits the words 'waiver of the right to support' found in (a); the court held it could not read those words in, since the omission was deliberate, and it was not for a judge to correct a legislative deficiency. Under (a), it is the results flowing from the agreement, not circumstances at signing, that must be unconscionable; the mother's position was essentially unchanged from before the short marriage except that she chose not to work to care for the child (for whom she received support), and the father was not wealthy. There was no fraud, duress, undue influence or public-policy invalidity.
firac.conclusion: The waiver could not be set aside under either s. 18(4)(a) or (b); the mother remained bound by her waiver of support for herself.

firac.issue: Was the mother entitled to reimbursement of obstetrical/hospital expenses and the cost of the child's ritual circumcision despite the release?
firac.facts: The mother sought her semi-private hospital room cost, an uncovered obstetrical bill, and a $200 fee for the child's ritual circumcision, which the father had unilaterally arranged by bringing a mohel from Montreal without consulting her or explaining why a local person could not be used.
firac.rule: Family Law Reform Act, s. 55(1): in determining matters respecting a child, the court may disregard any provision of a domestic contract where doing so is in the best interests of the child; s. 19(1)(h) (birth-related expenses).
firac.application: Having upheld the mother's waiver, the court could not consider the obstetrical and semi-private room expenses, as these were incurred for her own sake. The circumcision, however, related to the child; under s. 55(1) the court disregarded the waiver of claims concerning the child's birth and, given the father's unexplained arrangement of a costly out-of-town mohel, held him responsible for the full expense.
firac.conclusion: Reimbursement of obstetrical and hospital room expenses refused; the mother awarded $200 for the circumcision cost.

firac.issue: What access should the father be granted, applying the best-interests-of-the-child standard?
firac.facts: The father lived in Brooklyn with a net income under $10,000, could afford to come to Toronto only about once every two months by bus, and stayed in inexpensive hotels unsuitable for meeting the child. He sought four hours' access per day away from the mother; she offered supervised visits of 1–1½ hours in her presence. Relations between the parties had deteriorated.
firac.rule: Family Law Reform Act, s. 35(1): access is determined in accordance with the best interests of the child; access is a right of the child, not the parent (M. v. M.; Knudslien v. Rivard). Custodial parents must facilitate access (Jones v. Jones; Tassou v. Tassou; Woodburn v. Woodburn; Re Petryczka).
firac.application: To develop a genuine father-son relationship, access each day the father is in Toronto (up to three days at a time) for four hours was found reasonable and desirable; shorter visits would not achieve this. Weekday visits were to occur at Jewish Family and Child Services with a worker supervising until the child was comfortable; when that agency was closed, the mother was to arrange use of a friend's or relative's property, on a week's written notice. The court emphasized both parents' duty to protect the child's right to know his father.
firac.conclusion: The father was granted access of four hours on each day (up to three days) he is in Toronto, with supervision and notice arrangements; both parents were reminded of their obligation to facilitate the child's contact with his father.

name_verification.name_in_document: Jack Singer c. 1867054 Alberta Inc. et Gregory Martin et Douglas Martin et Dan Lett et Bunzl PLC et Bunzl Distribution USA Inc. et Bunzl Canada Inc.

defining_issues: Should Singer's re-amended claim against Lett and the Bunzl entities be dismissed under art. 168(2) C.p.c. for want of any legal basis (no juridical link, commission payable only by the seller, no personal liability of the corporate officer, and unfounded punitive damages)?
Is Singer's proceeding against Lett and the Bunzl entities abusive within the meaning of art. 51 C.p.c., justifying an order to reimburse their extrajudicial fees under art. 54 C.p.c.?

Which of Singer's claims against 1867054 Alberta Inc., Greg Martin and Doug Martin are inadmissible (punitive damages, personal liability of the officers, the claim for antisemitic remarks), and is that proceeding abusive?

firac.issue: Should Singer's re-amended claim against Lett and the Bunzl entities be dismissed under art. 168(2) C.p.c. for want of legal basis?
firac.facts: Singer, a business broker, contacted GF Inc.'s principals in 2012 offering to find a buyer for a 3% finder's fee payable by the seller, and separately contacted Bunzl (through Lett) as a potential buyer. He never obtained a signed mandate and never had any agreement with Lett or the Bunzl entities. When GF was later acquired by a Bunzl entity, Singer sued all defendants solidarily for the fee and punitive damages, alleging Lett acted in bad faith and circumvented him.
firac.rule: Art. 168(2) C.p.c. allows summary dismissal, in whole or part, of a claim that is unfounded in law even if the alleged facts are taken as true. Under Boucher c. Pitre (2001 QCCA) and Constructions Serafini inc. c. Gold Coin Development Corp. (2000 QCCA), a corporate fault in performing a contract does not by itself engage the personal liability of an administrator; lifting the corporate veil requires specific alleged facts of fraud or abuse.
firac.application: Even taking the facts as true, no juridical link existed between Singer and Lett or the Bunzl entities; they never engaged Singer or promised any commission. Any commission owed would be payable by the seller, never the buyer, as Singer himself acknowledged. The extracontractual allegation that Lett 'circumvented' Singer disclosed no breach of any obligation, since the buyer never undertook to deal exclusively through Singer. Lett acted only as an officer of Bunzl USA and no facts justified lifting the corporate veil. The punitive-damages claim under arts. 6 and 49 of the Quebec Charter failed because a mere refusal to pay an (unowed) debt is not an unlawful and intentional interference with peaceful enjoyment of property.
firac.conclusion: The claim against Lett and the Bunzl entities was wholly unfounded in law and dismissed.

firac.issue: Is Singer's proceeding against Lett and the Bunzl entities abusive under art. 51 C.p.c., warranting reimbursement of extrajudicial fees under art. 54 C.p.c.?
firac.facts: Singer's out-of-court examinations confirmed he had no written or verbal agreement with Lett or Bunzl, never participated in the negotiation, and always understood his commission was payable by the seller. On the eve of the hearing he re-amended his pleading to add an extracontractual bad-faith theory against those defendants.
firac.rule: Art. 51 C.p.c. defines abuse of process, which may result, regardless of intent, from a claim that is manifestly unfounded, frivolous or dilatory (art. 51(2)); Royal Lepage commercial inc. c. 109650 Canada Ltd. sets the standard of what a reasonable and prudent person would do. Art. 54 C.p.c. permits ordering reimbursement of extrajudicial fees.
firac.application: Given the total absence of any juridical link and the admissions in Singer's examinations, suing Lett and Bunzl reflected a reckless disregard a reasonable person would not have shown, and the last-minute re-amendment revealed an attempt to keep these defendants in the case solely to pressure Alberta/the Martins. The claimed fees ($56,070.83 taxes included) were reviewed and found reasonable, and Singer's counsel had agreed to proceed on the filed exhibits without contesting the amounts.
firac.conclusion: The proceeding against Lett and the Bunzl entities was declared abusive, dismissed, and Singer was ordered to reimburse $56,070.83 with interest and the additional indemnity from 25 November 2016.

firac.issue: Which claims against Alberta, Greg and Doug Martin are inadmissible, and is that proceeding abusive?
firac.facts: Singer alleged a verbal mandate from Greg Martin, sought punitive damages of $2,200,000 and personal condemnation of the officers, and claimed $100,000 for an alleged antisemitic remark by Greg Martin ('when a Jew buys a company, he makes sure that every pen and pencil remains in the desk'). Singer had lost family in the Holocaust.
firac.rule: Art. 168(2) C.p.c. (partial inadmissibility); Quebec Charter arts. 6 and 49 and the intentionality standard from Québec (Curateur public) c. Syndicat national des employés de l'hôpital St-Ferdinand (1996 SCC) for punitive damages; Boucher c. Pitre and Serafini for officer/corporate-veil liability; art. 51 C.p.c. for abuse.
firac.application: The punitive-damages claim and the personal claims against Greg and Doug Martin failed for the same reasons as against the Bunzl group — a refusal to pay a commission is no unlawful, intentional Charter breach, and no characterized fault was alleged to pierce the corporate veil. However, the antisemitic-remark claim, taken as true, could support damages including punitive damages and could not be dismissed at this stage. The abuse claim regarding the commission failed because credibility of the alleged verbal mandate required a trial, so the proceeding against Alberta was not abusive.
firac.conclusion: The punitive-damages claim and the personal claims against Greg and Doug Martin were declared inadmissible; the antisemitic-remark claim against Greg Martin and the commission claim against Alberta were held admissible; no abuse declaration or fee reimbursement was ordered against these defendants.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing practice area — the case turns on dismissal for want of legal basis (art. 168(2) C.p.c.) and abuse of process (arts. 51/54 C.p.c.). K120 (Quebec Charter) applies because the punitive-damages analysis rests on arts. 6 and 49 of the Charter (peaceful enjoyment of property, unlawful and intentional interference), and K071 (human dignity) captures the surviving claim founded on the affront to Singer's dignity. K057 (antisemitic slurs) and K058 (antisemitism) are engaged by the specific antisemitic remark that grounds the one admissible personal claim; K093 (Jewish) and K088 (Holocaust) reflect the factual context (a Jewish claimant who lost family in the Holocaust). The antisemitism-related keywords are somewhat secondary to the core commercial/abuse-of-process dispute but are genuinely engaged by the sole surviving personal claim.
