case_name: Tim Keith Contracting Ltd. v. Richform Construction Supply Company Limited

name_verification.name_in_document: Tim Keith Contracting Ltd. v. Richform Construction Supply Company Limited

defining_issues: Has the defendant made out a prima facie case that the plaintiff corporation would be unable to pay the defendant's costs if the action fails, so as to engage s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act?

Should the court decline to order security because doing so would stifle a valid claim, because the claim is intertwined with a related builders-lien action/counterclaim, or because the plaintiff's inability to pay was caused by the defendant's own conduct?
Does the stay of proceedings that accompanies a security-for-costs order extend to an outstanding document-disclosure request and to a scheduled mediation?

firac.issue: Did the defendant establish a prima facie case of the plaintiff corporation's inability to satisfy a costs award, triggering the security-for-costs power under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act?
firac.facts: The plaintiff, a concrete-pouring company, sued over the Surrey conference-centre project. The defendant filed evidence of numerous unpaid liens ($350,000–$460,000), unpaid WorkSafe BC premiums, six Provincial Court and one Supreme Court actions (over $150,000), charges under the Income Tax Act and Excise Act, an Equifax 'very high risk of delinquency' rating, and an affidavit recounting the principal Mr. Keith's remarks that the company had no assets and might declare bankruptcy. Mr. Keith denied dire circumstances and said he could pay any costs order.
firac.rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 permits the court to order a corporate plaintiff to give security where it appears it will be unable to pay the defendant's costs; the court also has inherent jurisdiction. The first stage requires the applicant to make out a prima facie case of inability to pay: Integrated Contractors Ltd. v. Leduc Development Ltd., 2009 BCSC 965; Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golfcourse Ltd.; Fat Mel's Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co.
firac.application: The court found the confluence of the number and quantum of actions, the federal charges on the plaintiff's property, its poor credit rating and Mr. Keith's admissions to Mr. Denevers 'defies innocent coincidence' and led to an overwhelming inference of significant financial pressure. It preferred Mr. Denevers' evidence over Mr. Keith's, and found no exigible assets disclosed. The defendant also had at least an arguable defence based on written no-warranty rental agreements.
firac.conclusion: A prima facie case of inability to pay was established; the first stage of the test was met.

firac.issue: Did discretionary factors — stifling a valid claim, an intertwined lien claim/counterclaim, or defendant-caused hardship — weigh against ordering security?
firac.facts: The plaintiff argued the litigation was involuntary, a 'race to the registry' arising from the defendant's separate Vancouver builders-lien action (over $230,000), to which the plaintiff had filed a near-identical counterclaim. It alleged the defendant orchestrated the other liens and damaged its credit. Nothing in the plaintiff's material asserted that posting security was impossible.
firac.rule: Security may be refused where it would unfairly stifle a valid claim (Kropp), where a defendant's intertwined counterclaim merely defends the main action (Gray v. Powerassist Technologies Inc., 2001 BCSC 1208; Integrated Contractors), or where the inability to pay stems from the applicant's own impugned conduct (Tour-Mate; Middlekamp).
firac.application: The court found no evidence security would stifle the claim, so no unfairness from unequal treatment. The plaintiff was a plaintiff pursuing its own action, not a defendant forced to counterclaim; the timing did not support a 'race to the registry'; and the plaintiff's near-identical Vancouver counterclaim undercut the notion the present action was merely reactive. Several actions (e.g. Luso Concrete, a law firm) were unrelated to the Surrey project, and no defence pleadings attributed the inability to pay to the defendant; the orchestration allegation was a bare, unsupported assertion.
firac.conclusion: None of the discretionary factors displaced an order; security for costs was warranted and the action stayed until posted.

firac.issue: Does the stay accompanying the security-for-costs order extend to an outstanding document-disclosure request and to a scheduled mediation?
firac.facts: Before the application, there was an outstanding document-disclosure request, and defendant's counsel had already obtained responsive documents. A notice to mediate had been given, with mediation scheduled for January 2011.
firac.rule: Section 236 permits staying 'all legal proceedings until the security is given'; the court also retains inherent jurisdiction and a discretion to do what is just in the circumstances.
firac.application: For disclosure, the court held that requests exchanged between counsel are communications within the Rules; it would be unjust to bar the defendant from disclosing material already gathered at the plaintiff's request and intended for disclosure, so the stay did not affect it. For mediation, although a parallel process, it is a legal proceeding intimately related to the main proceeding; the purpose of a security order is that the defendant need not take further legal steps until its costs are secured, so the stay applied.
firac.conclusion: The disclosed documents were to be produced in the usual way and were not caught by the stay; the mediation was caught by the stay.

keywords_rationale: The controlled vocabulary is heavily oriented to Charter, human-rights and hate-speech subject matter and contains no term for 'security for costs' or general commercial/construction litigation, so the fit is imperfect. K002 (Civil litigation) is the genuine anchor: this is a procedural application within a commercial civil action. K015 (defamation) reflects a claim actually pleaded (defamatory statements about the plaintiff's competence), though the merits were not decided here; K016 (fair comment) is included only as a related defamation concept and is a weak pick. K021 (interlocutory injunction) and K022 (restitution) are drawn from the 'Civil procedure / remedies' bucket as the closest available procedural-remedy terms to a stay/security-for-costs order, but both are weak placeholders selected to reach the minimum count rather than doctrines the court applied.
location_rationale: The header states 'IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA', 'Registry: Chilliwack', and lists the place of hearing and judgment as 'Chilliwack, B.C.'
registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly records 'Registry: Chilliwack', and the action was commenced 'in the Chilliwack registry' (para. 5).

name_verification.name_in_document: Susan Beverley Snider v. Stewart Laszlo

defining_issues: Should the court immediately enforce the access/parenting provisions of the Divorce Judgment pending completion of the s. 30 Children's Law Reform Act assessment, or defer enforcement pending the assessment?
Should the father's informational (joint custody consultation) rights be enforced?
Should an order be made requiring the children to be referred to by the surname 'Laszlo,' including a 'multi-directional' order binding third parties?
Should the court order the children into reunification (reconciliation) therapy at this stage, and with the therapist proposed?

firac.issue: Should the court immediately compel compliance with the access schedule in the Divorce Judgment pending the s. 30 CLRA assessment, or defer to a therapeutic approach?
firac.facts: The 2004 Divorce Judgment (incorporating the parties' Separation Agreement) provided joint custody and liberal access. The father has been estranged from his sons (now 12 and 14) for over three years and two years respectively. The court found the mother largely responsible for the estrangement, but the father also contributed and the estrangement is deeply entrenched. A s. 30 CLRA assessment by Linda Chodos is just underway; a motion to vary and OCL counsel involvement are outstanding. The father sought a 'compliance' (not contempt) order.
firac.rule: The best interests of the children are the sole governing consideration on a motion concerning children's relationship with a parent. Court orders must be complied with, but enforcement in alienation/estrangement cases is fact-specific. The father relied on Sickinger v. Sickinger, 2009 CanLII 28203 (ON SC) and V.(S) v. I.(T.), 2009 CanLII 9396 (ON SC), holding a parent must 'require' (not force) a child to attend court-ordered access, failing which contempt may follow.
firac.application: The court distinguished Sickinger: that was a contempt motion with a finding of contempt, involved a shorter estrangement and only one of three children, and no assessment was underway. Here the estrangement is longer and more entrenched, both children are estranged, there is a fresh assessment and a pending variation, and causes/cures are complex. The father conceded reconciliation counselling is needed and there is no easy fix. Although his expert Dr. Goldstein urged immediate resumption of access, Dr. Goldstein had been rejected as assessor and the actual assessor (Chodos) gave no evidence on required interventions; adopting Goldstein's views would let him usurp the assessment. The court held the access issues should await the assessor's report.
firac.conclusion: The court declined to make any access order; enforcement or variation is deferred until the assessor reports, with the father at liberty to re-apply upon receipt of the report.

firac.issue: Should the father's informational and consultation rights as a joint custodial parent be enforced?
firac.facts: The parties retained joint custody. The Divorce Judgment (para. 8(e)) required consultation on substantial questions including religious upbringing, education and health. The mother unilaterally changed the children's place of worship, enrolled them in Hebrew School, and arranged Evan's Bar Mitzvah without consulting the father.
firac.rule: Joint custody carries enforceable rights to be consulted and informed about substantial questions affecting the children, per the terms of the Divorce Judgment; estrangement does not extinguish those rights.
firac.application: The court found the mother had blatantly disregarded the consultation provisions and that the reasons for estrangement should not deprive the father of information about the children's lives. The court ordered immediate compliance and continuing provision of all material information regarding the children's health, education and welfare.
firac.conclusion: Informational/consultation rights enforced; the mother must comply immediately and provide ongoing material information.

firac.issue: Should the court order that the children be referred to as 'Laszlo,' including a multi-directional order binding third parties?
firac.facts: The children's surnames were never legally changed (which would require the father's consent). Brett had de facto adopted 'Snider' (e.g., on sports jerseys) and the mother acquiesced. The father sought an order binding the parties and specified third parties to use 'Laszlo.'
firac.rule: A change of a child's surname (formal or de facto) must be justified by the child's best interests; orders binding non-parties require notice to those to be bound.
firac.application: The court found no sufficient basis that a change to 'Snider' served Brett's best interests, and the mother should not have acquiesced. It ordered the mother to refer to Brett as 'Laszlo' and to require him to use that name. It refused the multi-directional order because the third parties had no notice of the motion.
firac.conclusion: Name order granted against the mother (must use and require 'Laszlo'); the multi-directional order binding third parties refused for want of notice.

firac.issue: Should the court order reunification therapy at this stage, and with Dr. Berman?
firac.facts: The father sought an order that the children undergo reunification therapy with Dr. Graham Berman; Dr. Goldstein urged immediate therapy. Three of four proposed participants (the mother and both boys) opposed it. The father himself had earlier impugned Dr. Berman's credentials and cited a court decision criticizing Berman's work.
firac.rule: The court has inherent jurisdiction to order reconciliation counselling, but such orders are made sparingly and require compelling evidence of likely benefit: Kramer v. Kramer, 2003 CanLII 64318 (S.C.J.).
firac.application: Given the resistance of three participants and, more importantly, the assessment just underway, the court found it best to have the assessor's views before imposing counselling. Even if inclined to order counselling, it would not appoint Dr. Berman, whose credentials the father had himself attacked.
firac.conclusion: Reunification therapy order refused as premature, subject to re-application after the assessor's report; Dr. Berman would not be appointed in any event.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. K048 (custody/access) is the core dispute — enforcement of joint custody and access under the Divorce Judgment. K047 (best interests of the child) is the governing legal test the court applied throughout. K049 (marriage/cohabitation agreement) captures the 2004 Separation Agreement whose parenting terms were in issue. K052 (religious upbringing) is directly engaged — the unilateral change of synagogue, Hebrew School enrolment and Evan's Bar Mitzvah are central examples of breached consultation duties. K117 (Divorce Act) is the source of the Divorce Judgment being enforced. K093 (Jewish) and K095 (Jewish family) reflect that both parties are Jewish and the children were raised in the Jewish faith, relevant to the religious-upbringing consultation issue; these are borderline/contextual picks but supported by the Bar Mitzvah and synagogue facts. Parental alienation, the substantive theme, has no controlled-vocabulary keyword, so it is captured through custody/access and best-interests terms.
location_rationale: The decision identifies the court as the 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' and is signed by Boswell J., establishing the province as Ontario. No hearing city is stated in the text (only court file no. FC04-018975-00), so city is left null; references such as the Thornhill baseball league are incidental facts, not a stated sitting location.
registry_rationale: The decision states only 'Ontario Superior Court of Justice' and a court file number (FC04-018975-00); it does not name a specific registry or court office, so registry is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Sidhu v Canada (The Attorney General)

defining_issues: Is it plain and obvious that the pleadings alleging past and ongoing police conduct should be struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action, being unnecessary/vexatious, or being embarrassing/scandalous under Rule 20(26)?
Should the defamation-related pleading in paragraph 22 be struck for failure to plead the material facts necessary to establish defamation?

firac.issue: Is it plain and obvious that the pleadings alleging historical (2006–2012) and ongoing police conduct should be struck under Rule 20(26)?
firac.facts: Sidhu, a Whitehorse resident of East Indian descent, sued the RCMP and the Attorney General over interactions on December 2 and 5, 2012, alleging torts and Charter breaches including racial profiling/discrimination under s. 15. His amended statement of claim included numerous paragraphs (8–19, 58, and portions of 22, 48, 61) describing prior stops, detentions, arrests and 'unwarranted police attention' between 2006 and 2012 and continuing thereafter. The defendants applied to strike these as unnecessary, vexatious, embarrassing and disclosing no reasonable claim.
firac.rule: Under Rule 20(26), pleadings may be struck if they disclose no reasonable claim, are unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, or may prejudice/embarrass/delay a fair trial. The test is whether it is 'plain and obvious' the pleading offends a ground (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress). Material facts must be pleaded; a bald allegation of racial profiling without particularity must be struck (Hamalengwa v. Bentley, 2011 ONSC 4145). Racial profiling requires facts from which discrimination can be inferred (Peart v. Peel Regional Police Services Board), and a s. 15 claim requires a distinction based on race.
firac.application: The court found the historical pleadings vague and imprecise, often not identifying officers, giving no particulars of conduct, and pleading no material facts showing the plaintiff was treated differently from persons not of East Indian descent. Unlike Anoquot v. Toronto Police, there was no allegation of a systemic police practice targeting East Indian persons, and no connection between the plaintiff's individual experience and any collective. The claim was merely a myriad of individual interactions; 'nothing plus nothing equals nothing.' Paragraph 26's assertion of being 'singled out on the basis of his race' was a bald allegation without particularity. Allowing the pleadings would require relitigation of prior matters, causing disproportionate expense and delay.
firac.conclusion: It was plain and obvious the pleadings should be struck; the court struck paras. 8–19 and 58, and the impugned portions of paras. 48 and 61.

firac.issue: Should the words in paragraph 22 alleging the officer 'defamed his recent campaign to run as mayor of Whitehorse' be struck?
firac.facts: Paragraph 22 alleged the December 2, 2012 detention 'defamed his recent campaign to run as mayor of Whitehorse.' Defendants said no material facts supporting defamation were pleaded; plaintiff argued the word went to malice, or alternatively should be replaced with 'degraded.'
firac.rule: To plead defamation a plaintiff must establish (1) the defendant made defamatory statements; (2) the words referred to the plaintiff; and (3) the words were published to at least one other person. Material facts must be pleaded to support the cause of action.
firac.application: The court held that pleading the officer 'defamed' the plaintiff meant what it said and required the material facts of defamation, which were absent. If counsel intended to plead malicious intent she should have done so and could have sought to amend, but did not.
firac.conclusion: The court rejected both of the plaintiff's arguments and struck the words 'and defamed his recent campaign to run as mayor of Whitehorse' from para. 22.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the tier-1 practice area — this is a civil action and an interlocutory motion to strike pleadings. K069 (discrimination) and K065 (racism) capture the core allegation of racial profiling of a person of East Indian descent. K023 (equality rights) and K109 (Charter s. 15) reflect the constitutional tort of racial discrimination that the impugned pleadings were meant to support. K107 (Canadian Charter) is engaged given the Charter claims (ss. 7, 9, 10, 15). K015 (defamation) reflects the second discrete issue on the para. 22 wording. Charter s. 7 was mentioned as a pleaded cause of action but was not analytically central to the striking application, so it was omitted as a weaker pick.
location_rationale: The header states 'SUPREME COURT OF YUKON', 'Registry: Whitehorse', and the plaintiff is described as 'a Whitehorse resident'; the incidents occurred in Whitehorse.
registry_rationale: The decision header expressly states 'Registry: Whitehorse'.

case_name: Valoris v. J.W., C.R. Muskeg Lake Cree Nation

name_verification.name_in_document: Valoris v. J.W., C.R. Muskeg Lake Cree Nation

defining_issues: Are N and A 'First Nations children' within the meaning of s. 90(2) of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017 and O. Reg. 155/18?
Are the children in need of protection under s. 74(2) CYFSA, and on which grounds (sexual abuse, failure to provide treatment, emotional harm/risk of emotional harm)?

What disposition is in the children's best interests — extended society care, return to the mother, or placement with the maternal grandmother — given the applicable federal and provincial Indigenous child-welfare framework?
Should access be ordered to the parents, the maternal grandmother, and the Muskeg Lake Cree Nation, and on what terms?

firac.issue: Are the two children First Nations children under the CYFSA and O. Reg. 155/18?
firac.facts: The mother and maternal grandmother are members of the Muskeg Lake Cree Nation in Saskatchewan and identify as First Nations, though neither the mother nor the children hold registered 'status'. Both parents identified the children as First Nations, and the band was added as a party.
firac.rule: Under s. 90(2) CYFSA the court must make statutory findings including whether a child is First Nations, Inuit or Métis. Per Children's Aid Society of the Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. N.H., 2021 ONSC 2384, and O. Reg. 155/18 s. 1, identification does not depend on 'status' under the Indian Act; identification by a child or parent, membership/identification with a band, or a connection to a First Nations community suffices.
firac.application: Both parents identified N and A as First Nations, and the maternal line connects the children to the Muskeg Lake Cree Nation. Lack of registered status is not determinative under the CYFSA.
firac.conclusion: The court found both children are First Nations children whose band is the Muskeg Lake Cree Nation, engaging both the CYFSA and the federal An Act respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis Children, Youth and Families.

firac.issue: Are the children in need of protection under s. 74(2) CYFSA, and on what grounds?
firac.facts: The children, removed December 13, 2019 following disclosures of inappropriate sexual touching, had significant speech, language and developmental delays. They had been over-interviewed by the child protection worker, statements were elicited through leading questions and an interpreting foster mother, and a key video was lost. The parents moved roughly ten times, the children attended about five Ontario schools with frequent absences, and there was an ongoing pattern of domestic violence and the mother's alcohol abuse.
firac.rule: Section 74(2) CYFSA sets out grounds including (c)/(d) sexual abuse or risk thereof, (e) failure to provide/access treatment, (f) emotional harm, and (h) risk of emotional harm. The Society bears the onus on a balance of probabilities; s. 93(2) bars disposition-only evidence at the finding stage. Risk of emotional harm requires prescribed symptoms, serious degree, and a causal connection to parenting (Children's Aid Society of Algoma v. A.B., 2018 ONCJ 831; Children's Aid Society of Algoma v. J.B., 2019 ONCJ 6). Exposure to domestic violence can ground a finding (Windsor-Essex CAS v. E.W., 2020 ONCA 682), as can neglect of medical/educational needs and parental substance abuse (Children's Aid Society of Simcoe County v. W.(T.), 2012 ONSC 3635).
firac.application: Because of the children's communication difficulties, over-interviewing, leading questions and missing recordings, the court could not identify the perpetrator on a balance of probabilities and declined findings under s. 74(2)(c) and (d), despite accepting the children had been inappropriately touched. However, residential instability impaired access to needed treatment and caused developmental delay (s. 74(2)(e),(f)); the ongoing cycle of domestic violence and the mother's unaddressed alcohol addiction created a real likelihood of serious emotional harm causally connected to the parents (s. 74(2)(h)). The mother's mental illness alone was not enough for a finding.
firac.conclusion: The children were found in need of protection under s. 74(2)(e), (f) and (h) CYFSA; the sexual-abuse and other grounds were not established.

firac.issue: What disposition is in the children's best interests?
firac.facts: The children had been in interim care ~806 days. The father withdrew his plan; the mother sought their return with support from partner R.T.; the maternal grandmother (N.A.) sought placement. The mother had chronic residential instability, ongoing alcohol abuse, and continuing contact with abusive partners; N.A. also had housing instability and an unassessed home. The band had no available placement but supported reunification.
firac.rule: Under s. 101 CYFSA the court makes the least restrictive order in the child's best interests only if intervention is necessary to protect the child in future, after considering Society efforts, less restrictive alternatives, and kin placement (s. 101(4)-(5)). For Indigenous children the court must apply ss. 9, 10, 16 and 17 of the federal Act (best interests, cultural continuity, substantive equality, placement priority) and s. 74(3) CYFSA — the 'augmented best interests test' (C.A.S. v. E.B.). Courts take judicial notice of over-representation of Indigenous children in care (Native Child and Family Services of Toronto v. A.B., 2022 ONCJ 75). Extended society care is the most profound order and requires compelling evidence; a supervision order requires confidence in compliance.
firac.application: The court found the Society, despite early failures in facilitating access and belated notice to the band, ultimately met its service obligations. The risk of returning the children to the mother or N.A. was too high given unremedied addiction, domestic conflict, instability and lack of insight; both understated the mother's drinking and were not forthcoming, so a supervision order could not be trusted. No Cree or extended-family placement was available, and further extension of time limits would not remedy the concerns.
firac.conclusion: The court ordered both children placed in extended society care, consistent with their views, while continuing existing services and the goal of a First Nations placement.

firac.issue: Should access be ordered and on what terms?
firac.facts: A loved both parents and enjoyed positive visits; N had refused contact with her father since mid-2020 and her mother since August 2020. The band sought contact to maintain cultural connection; the grandmother's benefit could not be assessed.
firac.rule: Section 105(5)-(7) CYFSA applies a best-interests test to access for children in extended society care (no presumption against access post-2017): whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and whether access impairs adoption are factors among many (Kawartha-Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316; CAS of Toronto v. J.G., 2020 ONCA 415). Section 17 of the federal Act directs promotion of emotional ties, and ss. 10/74(3) require weighing cultural continuity and the children's wishes.
firac.application: The court found the parent-child relationships meaningful and beneficial, particularly given A's strong bond and the plan to keep the siblings together, while respecting N's wish not to attend by making her participation discretionary. Insufficient evidence prevented a specific N.A. access order, and cultural connection warranted band access.
firac.conclusion: The court granted the mother and father specified supervised and virtual access (with the children's participation according to their wishes), ordered access between the children and the Muskeg Lake Cree Nation (an elder, possibly N.A.), and sibling access at least monthly if separated; parents, children and band designated as access holders/recipients.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the governing tier-1 practice area — this is a child protection proceeding under the CYFSA. K047 (best interests of the child) is central to both the finding and disposition, applying the augmented best-interests test under the federal Act and s. 74(3) CYFSA. K048 (custody/access) captures the substantial access analysis and final access order. K074 (systemic discrimination) is engaged because the court took judicial notice of the over-representation of Indigenous children in care and systemic discrimination as part of the Indigenous best-interests framework — a somewhat borderline but genuinely discussed point. K069 (discrimination) is included as the tier-2 parent concept tied to that same Indigenous-equality analysis; it is a weaker pick. The controlled vocabulary lacks dedicated 'child protection' or 'Indigenous/First Nations child welfare' terms, so no more precise keyword was available for the core subject matter.
location_rationale: The decision is styled 'Superior Court of Justice / Ontario' and the applicant is 'Valoris for Children & Adults of Prescott-Russell'; the children were removed 'in the Prescott-Russell jurisdiction' (para 455). Province is therefore Ontario. No specific sitting city is stated in the reasons, so city is left null.
registry_rationale: The document shows only 'COURT FILE NO.: 284/19' and 'Superior Court of Justice / Ontario' without naming a registry office (e.g. L'Orignal). No registry is expressly stated, so it is left null.

name_verification.name_in_document: Wise v. Broadway Properties Ltd.

defining_issues: Did the trial judge err in dismissing Wise's claim for quantum meruit / unjust enrichment for property-management duties he performed beyond his caretaker role?
Did the trial judge err in finding that Broadway had just cause to summarily dismiss Wise?

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in dismissing the claim in quantum meruit / unjust enrichment?
firac.facts: Wise, resident caretaker for about 10 years, claimed he also performed property-management tasks (setting rents, hiring and supervising contractors) after Broadway dropped its outside property manager, and valued those services at 3.5% of gross rentals ($179,676.54). He received caretaker raises and separate $15/hour payments for extra work, and continued working despite his dissatisfaction over pay.
firac.rule: Unjust enrichment requires proof of a benefit, a corresponding deprivation, and the absence of a juristic reason for the enrichment. On appeal, where the argument concerns the application of law to facts rather than an error of legal principle, the matter is one of mixed fact and law attracting deference to the trial judge's findings.
firac.application: Wise framed the challenge as an error of law but was really disputing the application of the law to the facts, so the deferential standard applied. Even assuming a benefit and corresponding deprivation, Wise failed to establish the third element—the absence of a juristic reason—because he maintained and renewed his contractual relationship, accepted raises and extra payments, and could have walked away if underpaid. He could not build an equitable claim merely by carrying on.
firac.conclusion: The Court of Appeal would not interfere with the dismissal of the quantum meruit claim.

firac.issue: Did the trial judge err in finding just cause for summary dismissal?
firac.facts: Frustrated over unpaid property-management work, Wise wrote a 1999 letter (later enclosed with a January 2001 letter) comparing his treatment by Broadway's principal, Roadburg—an elderly Jewish man—to the treatment of Jews forced into unpaid labour during the Second World War. He also threatened a civil action. Roadburg was deeply offended and said he could never work with Wise again; Wise testified he 'couldn't have cared less.' Broadway fired him.
firac.rule: Whether misconduct justifies dismissal requires a contextual analysis of the nature and circumstances of the conduct (McKinley v. BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38). An appellate court will not interfere with the trial judge's assessment absent palpable and overriding error.
firac.application: The trial judge conducted the contextual analysis McKinley requires, considering that Wise knew Roadburg was Jewish and elderly, had held the letter for 18 months aware of its likely effect, and showed no remorse. He found Roadburg's reaction was not disproportionate and that the insult irretrievably destroyed the working relationship. The Court of Appeal held the decision could be upheld solely on the finding about the insult, without deciding whether the threat to sue was independently sufficient. That conclusion was bound up in the trial judge's appreciation of the evidence and was not palpably wrong.
firac.conclusion: The finding of just cause was upheld; the wrongful dismissal claim was properly dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K009 (Labour and employment law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns on wrongful dismissal and just cause. K085 (wrongful dismissal) is the central employment doctrine, including the McKinley contextual just-cause analysis. K022 (restitution) is the closest vocabulary term for the quantum meruit / unjust enrichment claim, which was the second live issue. K014 (standard of review) reflects the appellate deference analysis (mixed fact and law; palpable error) that governed both grounds. K088 (Holocaust) and K093 (Jewish) capture the offensive comparison to Jews used as forced labour and the fact that the offended principal was Jewish—central to the finding of cause. K088 and K093 are contextual/entity picks rather than the legal core, but they are genuinely engaged by the misconduct that grounded dismissal.
location_rationale: The decision header states the Court of Appeal for British Columbia sat at Vancouver: 'Place and Date of Hearing: Vancouver, British Columbia' and 'Place and Date of Judgment: Vancouver, British Columbia'.
registry_rationale: Docket 'CA032723' with Vancouver as the place of hearing and judgment; the underlying trial was 'Vancouver S012489 (B.C.S.C.)', confirming the Vancouver registry.

case_name: The Public Guardian and Trustee of British Columbia v. Johnston

name_verification.name_in_document: The Public Guardian and Trustee of British Columbia v. Johnston

defining_issues: Should David's Response and Counterclaim be struck or amended under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules for failing to comply with the rules of pleading?
Should the Proof of Will Action be severed from David's other claims and those other claims stayed until it is decided?
Should the claims against the solicitor, Mr. Miller, be severed from the balance of the litigation and stayed?

firac.issue: Should David's Response and Counterclaim be struck or amended under Rule 9-5(1) SCCR for failing to comply with the rules of pleading?
firac.facts: David's 32-page amended Response and 11-page Counterclaim mixed material facts with evidence and argument, contained vague, repetitive and cross-referenced allegations of undue influence, misrepresentation, breach of fiduciary duty, mutual wills, and fraudulent conveyance, and pleaded legal conclusions (duty of care/fiduciary duty against Mr. Miller) without supporting material facts or the mandatory particulars for fraud/undue influence.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) SCCR permits striking or amending pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim/defence, are unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial, or are an abuse of process (Doyle; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. CJC; Sahyoun). Pleadings must state material facts concisely, not evidence (Rule 3-7(1)); legal conclusions require supporting material facts (Rule 3-7(9)); fraud, undue influence and misrepresentation require full particulars (Rule 3-7(18)); reliance is essential to actionable misrepresentation (Proprietary Industries); whether a pleading can be cured by amendment is a crucial factor (International Taoist Church).
firac.application: The Court found the Response plainly embarrassing because it was laden with evidence and argument and the allegations of undue influence, pressure and misrepresentation were confused and did not always identify the actionable wrong or the responsible party. The misrepresentation claims omitted reliance and lacked particulars. Paragraph 16.1's duty-of-care plea was convoluted and disclosed no reasonable claim. The claim that Mr. Miller owed David a beneficiary's duty not to follow the testator's inconsistent instructions was bound to fail (Korpiel; Graham v. Bonnycastle) and was struck. The negligent infliction of mental suffering plea lacked foreseeability facts and questionable severity (Mustapha). However, the fraudulent conveyance claim under the FCA was not plainly bound to fail. The deficiencies were curable by amendment.
firac.conclusion: Save for the beneficiary-duty claim against Mr. Miller, which was struck as hopeless, David was granted leave to amend the Response and Counterclaim by August 31, 2016 to remedy the deficiencies rather than having the pleadings struck outright.

firac.issue: Should the Proof of Will Action be severed from David's remaining claims and those claims stayed pending its determination?
firac.facts: The PGT, executor named in the Impugned Wills, brought a proof-in-solemn-form action. David counterclaimed asserting mutual wills, breach of contract/trust, unjust enrichment, fraudulent conveyance, wills variation, and negligence/breach of fiduciary duty against the PGT, Mr. Miller and others, and argued these should be heard first or together because of overlapping parties and witnesses.
firac.rule: Rules 22-5(6) and (7) SCCR permit ordering separate trials where joinder would unduly complicate/delay or be inconvenient. Severance factors: Schaper (2000 BCSC 1575) and O'Mara (2007 BCSC 871); discretion exercised sparingly (Morrison-Knudsen; Lawrence); severance appropriate where determination of one issue may render another moot. Mutual-wills doctrine: an agreement not to revoke does not prevent a will's admission to probate (University of Manitoba; Hall; Re Heys), though breach may sound in damages or constructive trust. A court of probate is confined to validity issues (Ali; Clark v. Nash), and a wills variation claim is premature before validity is decided.
firac.application: The Court held the mutual-wills and FCA points did not need to be decided before or with validity, since a breach of a not-to-revoke agreement does not stop a will being probated. Re: Langford raised doubt about the PGT's authority as committee to defend the broader claims, and David's allegations against the PGT in its corporate capacity created a potential conflict of interest, favouring severance. Validity of the Impugned Wills was the centrepiece: if invalid, David inherits everything and most other claims fall away. The Proof of Will issues (testamentary capacity/suspicious circumstances, freedom from delusion and undue influence, and due execution) were sufficiently distinct that separate trials would not cause undue expense or prejudice.
firac.conclusion: Severance granted: the Proof of Will Action is to be tried first and separately, and all of David's other claims are stayed pending its determination.

firac.issue: Should the claims against the solicitor, Mr. Miller, be severed from all other claims and stayed?
firac.facts: Mr. Miller, the solicitor who prepared all the wills, sought to have the claims against him (largely solicitor's negligence and breach of fiduciary duty) severed and stayed, arguing they might not arise depending on the outcome of the other claims.
firac.rule: The Court may stay proceedings under Rule 9-5(1), its inherent jurisdiction, or s. 8(2) of the Law and Equity Act (Zurich), weighing benefits and prejudice; sequential trials with a temporary stay of dependent claims are a common approach where the first action will narrow the others (Zurich; Peh; Ainsworth), and the temporary nature of a stay supports granting it.
firac.application: The Court found the allegations against Mr. Miller deeply intertwined with allegations against other parties and potentially extending beyond ordinary solicitor's negligence. As pleaded, separating them from the remainder carried too great a risk of prejudice to David for too little benefit to Mr. Miller and the trial process.
firac.conclusion: The Court declined to sever the claims against Mr. Miller; they are stayed with all other claims pending the Proof of Will Action, and Mr. Miller may re-apply for severance and revive his special-costs request once that action is determined.

case_name: Super Sam Red Deer Ltd. v. Lethbridge (City)

name_verification.name_in_document: Super Sam Red Deer Ltd. v. Lethbridge (City)

defining_issues: Does a municipal Sunday-closing by-law that requires large retail stores to close on Sundays, without any exemption or option for Saturday-observing retailers, infringe freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
If freedom of religion is infringed, can the by-law be saved as a reasonable limit under s. 1 of the Charter where the municipality made no serious attempt to accommodate Saturday observers?
What is the appropriate remedy where the by-law fails the s. 1 justification analysis?

firac.issue: Does a Sunday-closing by-law requiring large retail stores to close on Sundays, with no exemption for Saturday observers, infringe s. 2(a) of the Charter?
firac.facts: The City of Lethbridge enacted by-law 4341 under s. 241 of the Municipal Government Act requiring retail food stores exceeding 10,000 square feet to close on Sundays and holidays. Unlike the Red Deer by-law, it fixed Sunday as the pause day and gave retailers no choice of closing day. Lethbridge had 35 Jewish families and 150 listed Seventh-Day Adventists, both Saturday Sabbath observers. The plaintiffs' food store and pharmacy exceeded the size threshold and would have to close on Sundays.
firac.rule: Section 2(a) of the Charter guarantees freedom of conscience and religion. Under R. v. Edwards Books & Art Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713, impugned legislation is tested first for purpose, then for effect; Sunday-closing legislation with a secular common-pause-day purpose may nonetheless infringe s. 2(a) by its effect on Saturday observers. Can. Safeway Ltd. v. R. (BC CA) held that the option to choose one's closing day is the entitlement, and legislation impairing that option infringes religious freedom.
firac.application: The court accepted the by-law had a valid secular common-pause-day purpose. Following Can. Safeway and Edwards Books, however, the effect of fixing Sunday as the mandatory closing day impaired the religious freedom of Saturday observers, who are denied the option to close Saturday and open Sunday. The court rejected the argument that Lethbridge's small population or small number of Saturday observers rendered the burden trivial or insubstantial. Unlike the Red Deer by-law upheld in London Drugs Ltd. v. Red Deer (City), the Lethbridge by-law offered no free choice of closing day.
firac.conclusion: The by-law infringes freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter.

firac.issue: Can the by-law be justified as a reasonable limit under s. 1 where no serious attempt was made to accommodate Saturday observers?
firac.facts: The Lethbridge by-law contained no Sabbatarian exemption or option to close on a day other than Sunday. The City argued the smaller geographic/population area reduced the impact and that the higher 10,000 square-foot exemption threshold (versus 225 m²/2,500 sq ft in BC) constituted accommodation.
firac.rule: Under the Oakes proportionality test as applied in Edwards Books, a limit must be rationally connected to the objective, impair the right as little as possible, and be proportionate in effect. Dickson C.J.C. held that a legislature enacting Sunday-closing laws must 'attempt very seriously to alleviate the effects of those laws on Saturday observers'; a satisfactory Sabbatarian exemption is central to minimal impairment. La Forest J.'s view that no exemption was required was a solitary view not to be followed (per Can. Safeway).
firac.application: The court accepted the objective was sufficiently important (first branch satisfied). However, the City made no attempt, let alone a serious attempt, to accommodate Saturday observers. Merely increasing the size threshold for exempt stores was not the kind of accommodation contemplated by the Supreme Court and did not truly alleviate the effect on those whose religious freedom was affected. The reduced population base did not diminish the affected persons' rights. The by-law failed to draw any accommodating line, which was fatal.
firac.conclusion: The by-law is not a reasonable limit under s. 1 and cannot be saved.

firac.issue: What remedy follows from the by-law failing s. 1 justification?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs sought a declaration that the by-law was void; interim injunctions had already restrained enforcement pending trial. The court declined to consider the plaintiffs' secondary vagueness and ultra vires arguments as academic.
firac.rule: Following Can. Safeway, where legislation cannot be saved and it is not feasible to fashion a partial invalidation or constitutional exemption, the legislation must be declared inoperative.
firac.application: Having found no accommodation could distinguish the case from Can. Safeway, the court held the by-law must be struck down. It found the secondary arguments (vagueness of 'greenhouse' definition, ultra vires) unmeritorious and academic, and awarded the plaintiffs $4,000 special costs for written argument.
firac.conclusion: The by-law is declared inoperative; declaration granted accordingly with $4,000 costs to the plaintiffs.

keywords_rationale: K003 (Constitutional law) is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turns on Charter analysis. K025 (freedom of religion) and K110 (Charter s. 2(a)) capture the core right at issue. K030 (reasonable limits s. 1) reflects the Oakes/Edwards Books justification analysis that decided the case. K031 (religious accommodation) is central because the by-law's fatal defect was the absence of any Sabbatarian accommodation. K033 (shabbat) applies because the affected Jewish and Seventh-Day Adventist retailers are Saturday Sabbath observers. K107 (Canadian Charter) is the governing instrument. K093 (Jewish) is engaged because Jewish families are expressly identified among the Saturday observers; it is a somewhat peripheral entity tag but grounded in the agreed facts.

case_name: Whitehall Entertainment Incorporated v. Kafka Pictures Inc.

name_verification.name_in_document: Whitehall Entertainment Incorporated and Brenda Whitehall v. Kafka Pictures Inc. (and Alicia Kaffka)

defining_issues: Who owns the copyright in the Film, and can the s. 53 registration presumption, an oral agreement, joint authorship, or a joint venture establish Kaffka's co-ownership?
Did Kaffka infringe copyright in the Film through the enumerated post-shoot activities (editing, screening/posting, submission to festivals, marketing)?
Were Whitehall's moral rights in the Script/Film infringed?
Was there an enforceable contract with implied terms that Kaffka breached?
Did Kaffka breach a duty of good faith?
Did Kaffka commit the tort of conversion by withholding property?
Did the defendants commit passing off?
What damages, if any, are payable, and are the claims against Kafka Pictures Inc. maintainable?

firac.issue: Who owns copyright in the Film, and does the s. 53 registration presumption, an oral agreement, joint authorship, or a joint venture give Kaffka co-ownership?
firac.facts: Whitehall and her sister wrote and registered copyright in the Script (CIPO certificate dated Jan. 3, 2017, owner Whitehall Entertainment). Kaffka conceded she did not own the Script. Kaffka claimed Whitehall orally promised her co-ownership of the Film, profits, and co-executive producer credit during telephone calls; her husband corroborated, but the only contemporaneous email (May 25, 2017) referred only to co-executive producer credit, to which Whitehall replied 'Agreed'. No written ownership agreement existed.
firac.rule: Copyright is a creature of statute (Compo Co. v. Blue Crest Music). The s. 53(2) certificate creates only a rebuttable presumption of ownership (Andrews v. McHale; Close Up International). The plaintiff bears the legal burden of proving infringement including lack of consent (Harmony Consulting; Pinto). Joint authorship requires substantial, non-distinct contributions, collaboration in a common design, more than ideas, and a common intention to create a joint work (Seggie v. Roofdog Games; Neudorf); originality requires exercise of skill and judgment (CCH Canadian). Joint venture requires the Canlan Investment Corp. v. Gettling factors, including a joint property interest.
firac.application: The court held the registration presumption was rebutted by the Kaffkas' evidence, so it could not decide ownership on the certificate alone. On the totality of evidence, the defendants failed to prove any agreement granting co-ownership or profits (no documentation; independent witness Bazuta only confirmed 'co-executive producer'). Kaffka's contributions, though substantial, did not amount to the exercise of skill and judgment making her a joint author/maker of an original work distinct from the Script, and there was no common intention to create a joint work. No joint property interest, and no shared right of mutual control, so no joint venture. However, Whitehall did agree to give Kaffka a co-executive producer credit.
firac.conclusion: Whitehall Entertainment owns the Script and the Film; Kaffka is not a co-owner by agreement, joint authorship, or joint venture, but is entitled to co-executive producer (and director/producer) credit.

firac.issue: Did Kaffka infringe copyright through the specific post-shoot activities alleged?
firac.facts: The claimants alleged infringement by editing raw footage after May 28, 2017, screening the director's cut, posting the Film/clips online, submitting to festivals, and marketing the Film. Kaffka edited a rough cut before her June 16, 2017 termination; a cease-and-desist followed July 10, 2017; the Film was 'completed' by Aug. 1, 2017; she later uploaded the full Film to password-protected Vimeo and Facebook (June 4, 2018) for cast/crew only. Google screenshots, alleged Netflix posting, and Kafka Pictures postings were unproven or hearsay.
firac.rule: Copyright includes the sole right to reproduce, adapt and publicly present a dramatic/cinematographic work (ss. 2, 3, Copyright Act); s. 27 makes doing such acts without consent an infringement. 'Publication' means making copies available to the public (s. 2.2). The claimants bear the burden on a balance of probabilities (F.H. v. McDougall).
firac.application: Editing carried on under an implied licence until termination; but Kaffka remained involved in editing after the June 16 termination and July 10 cease-and-desist through completion (Aug. 1, 2017) and minor 2018 work, which was infringing. The password-protected screening/posting to a group in June 2018, after ownership was in dispute and a CRT decision favoured the claimants, constituted infringement. The Google/Netflix/Kafka Pictures postings and the 30-second clip were unproven, de minimis, hearsay, or not attributable to Kaffka; festival submissions were not shown to have been publicly displayed; marketing was done with Whitehall's knowledge/creative licence.
firac.conclusion: Infringement established only for editing continuing after termination and for the June 2018 screening/posting; the remaining alleged infringements were not proven.

firac.issue: Were Whitehall's moral rights in the Script/Film infringed?
firac.facts: Whitehall claimed unauthorized editing and distribution prejudiced her honour and reputation, though she admitted she had not seen the Film. She led no expert or public-opinion evidence.
firac.rule: Section 14.1 grants the author the right to integrity; s. 28.2 provides integrity is infringed only where the work is distorted, mutilated or modified to the prejudice of the author's honour or reputation, requiring both a subjective and an objective evaluation based on public or expert opinion (Collett v. Northland Art; Wiseau Studio; Maltz v. Witterick; Prise des Paroles).
firac.application: Whitehall offered only her subjective view; there was no expert or public-opinion evidence to satisfy the required objective evaluation of prejudice.
firac.conclusion: Moral rights claim dismissed.

firac.issue: Was there an enforceable contract with implied terms that Kaffka breached?
firac.facts: There was no written contract. Whitehall, a self-described 'newbie' with little filmmaking experience, offered Kaffka the volunteer roles of director/producer for credits. The claimants argued implied terms required Kaffka to follow Whitehall's instructions, ensure Whitehall's ownership, and obtain signed rights assignments from cast/crew.
firac.rule: Contract formation requires offer, acceptance, consideration, intention, certainty and completeness, judged by manifested (not subjective) intentions (Le Soleil Hotel; Reon Management; Pacific Vending). Terms are implied only by custom/usage, as legal incidents, or to give business efficacy/officious bystander (M.J.B. Enterprises; Canadian Pacific Hotels), used sparingly and never inconsistently with express terms (Kaban Resources); subjective intention is inadmissible.
firac.application: No conditions were discussed when the roles were offered; the parties worked collaboratively without a chain of command. Whitehall's after-acquired ('ex post facto') experience and subjective intentions could not ground implied terms, and Mr. Kim's expert evidence was equivocal (arrangements vary case-to-case; no single model). It was not established that ensuring signed releases fell to Kaffka or was uncompleted (Matzov testified releases were signed and binder given to Kaffka). Any editing after termination could not breach a contract that had already ended.
firac.conclusion: No breach of contract established; the alleged implied terms were not proven and would not be read in.

firac.issue: Did Kaffka breach a duty of good faith?
firac.facts: The claimants alleged Kaffka breached good faith by threatening to shut down production on May 25, 2017 and by the post-production activities. The May 25 emails show Whitehall first wrote 'WE ARE NOT FILMING THIS WEEKEND'.
firac.rule: Good faith is an organizing principle requiring honest, non-capricious performance; it is not a free-standing remedy and imposes only a duty not to lie or mislead about contractual performance (Bhasin v. Hrynew; Pareto Capital; Kaban Resources).
firac.application: It was Whitehall who first threatened to call off filming; Kaffka responded in kind. Kaffka's conduct was not capricious or dishonest, and Bhasin provides no free-standing remedy.
firac.conclusion: No breach of the duty of good faith; punitive damages refused.

firac.issue: Did Kaffka commit conversion by withholding property?
firac.facts: Kaffka withheld two Toshiba hard drives (paid for by Whitehall) containing the Film footage, and the claimants also sought return of a red dress, blouse, canvases, walkie-talkies, a yoga mat and supplies. Kaffka said she withheld the hard drives to protect her asserted IP rights and had tried to return the dress.
firac.rule: Conversion is a strict-liability tort: a wrongful act involving another's chattel, consisting of handling/disposing/destroying it, with the effect or intention of denying the owner's title (Boma Manufacturing; Ast v. Mikolas; Pang v. Zhang).
firac.application: Kaffka's retention of the hard drives paid for by Whitehall and holding the Film was inconsistent with the owner's title and amounted to conversion. Possession of the miscellaneous items was unproven; the dress/blouse Kaffka had tried to return.
firac.conclusion: Conversion established for the two Toshiba hard drives (ordered returned, with credits preserved and one personal copy allowed to Kaffka); no conversion finding for the other items; the $28,000 re-shoot claim refused.

firac.issue: Did the defendants commit passing off, and what damages and party issues follow?
firac.facts: The claimants alleged the defendants passed off the unauthorized cut as associated with Whitehall Entertainment via festival submissions and online posting. Whitehall Entertainment was a nascent company; The Curtain had not yet completed the festival circuit. Kafka Pictures Inc. was incorporated only January 17, 2019, after the impugned conduct.
firac.rule: Passing off requires (1) goodwill/reputation at the relevant time, (2) a misrepresentation likely to deceive the relevant public, and (3) actual or potential damage (Greystone Capital; s. 7(b) Trademark Act). Statutory damages under s. 38.1 range $100–$5,000 for non-commercial infringement, aimed at compensation and deterrence with proportionality (Trader Corp. v. CarGurus).
firac.application: Whitehall Entertainment had no established reputation/goodwill at the relevant time and there was no misrepresentation causing confusion, especially as the Film was never publicly displayed. The Film was non-commercial, so statutory damages fell in the non-commercial range. Kafka Pictures Inc. did not exist when the causes of action arose.
firac.conclusion: Passing off dismissed; $3,000 statutory damages and $500 special damages awarded to Whitehall Entertainment; all claims against Kafka Pictures Inc. dismissed; Kaffka's counterclaim dismissed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Succession de Moore / In the Matter of the Estate of the Late Richard W. Moore: Lianne J. Moore v. John R. Moore et al.

defining_issues: Did Richard Moore lack the testamentary capacity to understand and appreciate the effects of the impugned provisions of the Will when he signed it on February 12, 2014?
Was the Will the product of undue influence (captation) within the meaning of the jurisprudence?
Is Lianne foreclosed from, or did she renounce, claiming the nullity of the Will?
What is the appropriate remedy — full nullity of the Will or partial nullity preserving certain bequests?

firac.issue: Did the testator lack the capacity to understand and appreciate the effects of the impugned testamentary provisions?
firac.facts: Mr. Moore, aged 83, suffered from mild cognitive impairment with impaired short-term memory and moments of confusion. The Will, signed in haste on February 12, 2014 under a sense of urgency triggered by his daughter's apprehended marriage to a man with a criminal record, drastically departed from his long-standing intent to divide his estate equally: it placed Lianne's share in a discretionary trust paying a limited monthly allowance with capital ultimately going to John's children, named John sole manager of the businesses, and excluded Lianne as liquidator/trustee. John initiated the meeting with the lawyer, and third parties suggested key conditions. No one probed Mr. Moore's understanding of the effects on Lianne.
firac.rule: Arts. 703 and 707 C.C.Q.; capacity is presumed (art. 4 C.C.Q.) and the party seeking nullity bears the burden on a balance of probabilities (Brusenbauch c. Young, 2019 QCCA 914). It suffices to show the testator did not sufficiently enjoy his intellectual faculties to understand and reasonably appreciate the scope of his dispositions (Pagé c. Henley, 2016 QCCA 964). Surrounding circumstances — undue haste, absence of usual advisors, unexplained changes — may establish incapacity (Guérin v. Guérin, [1962] SCR 550; Phillips c. Douek, 2018 QCCS 3794). Consent must be free and enlightened (art. 1399 C.C.Q.).
firac.application: The Court weighed the medical evidence (finding the experts' conclusions on capacity unreliable because based on incomplete facts, and preferring Dr. Shulman's task- and situation-specific analysis), the testimony of employees and family observing decline, John's contemporaneous texts showing surveillance and confusion, the drastic and unexplained departure from the equal-division intent, the haste, the induced and unwarranted fear of Bowen, the participation of others in shaping the terms, and the total absence of probing of Mr. Moore's understanding. It concluded he could not reasonably have consented to provisions producing an inequitable division and was probably led to believe his estate was still shared equally.
firac.conclusion: Mr. Moore lacked the capacity to form valid consent to the impugned provisions; those dispositions are invalid.

firac.issue: Was the Will the product of undue influence (captation)?
firac.facts: John initiated the process, wanted to run the business without Lianne and her boyfriend, and had third parties remind his father of conditions favourable to him. However, everything was done openly with the apparent support of Vincent, Mtre Liber and Mtre Raich, who considered a paternalistic, protective approach reasonable.
firac.rule: Undue influence is assimilated to fraud and requires lies, calumny, deception, stratagem or deliberate false statements inducing decisions the testator would not otherwise have made (Thivierge c. Thivierge, 2024 QCCA 54). The burden is on the plaintiff, dischargeable by direct or circumstantial evidence forming serious, precise and concordant presumptions on a balance of probabilities (Brusenbauch c. Young, 2019 QCCA 914).
firac.application: The Court found that a person without capacity cannot have vitiated consent, and that although John influenced his father and benefited from the timing, his conduct was open and did not amount to the fraud-like deceit required for captation.
firac.conclusion: Undue influence is not established; the nullity flows from incapacity, not undue influence.

firac.issue: Is Lianne foreclosed from or has she renounced claiming nullity of the Will?
firac.facts: Lianne negotiated $5,000 cheques and corresponded with the Estate, but always under express reserve of her rights, and pleaded Mr. Moore's impaired condition and reserved her right to seek annulment in her 2017 originating demand.
firac.rule: Art. 773 C.C.Q. (acknowledgement of a will) — of uncertain application to a notarized will; arts. 1420 and 1423 C.C.Q. on confirmation of a relatively null contract. Renunciation/confirmation requires prior knowledge of the cause of nullity and a clear, certain and unequivocal will to renounce; mere passage of time does not suffice (Industrielle Alliance c. Gouveia, 2012 QCCA 793).
firac.application: Lianne consistently reserved her rights in correspondence and pleadings and never clearly renounced her right to invoke nullity.
firac.conclusion: Lianne is not foreclosed from invoking the nullity of the Will.

firac.issue: Should the Will be declared wholly null or only partially null?
firac.facts: The specific bequests to family members and employees (arts. 5 and 6) had been settled since 2011, were uncontested, straightforward, and remote from the impugned, complex provisions concerning John and Lianne. Lianne confirmed she would not seek their reimbursement.
firac.rule: Doctrine (Beaulne & Morin) suggests complete nullity is the normal consequence of incapacity while partial nullity may attend a defect of consent; art. 1438 C.C.Q. (severability, transposable to wills per Khan c. Katiya, 2021 QCCA 1065); art. 1422 C.C.Q. (a null act is deemed never to have existed). Capacity is task- and situation-specific.
firac.application: The Court found Mr. Moore probably had capacity for the simple, long-settled specific bequests, which were distinct and severable from the complex impugned provisions forming an indivisible whole; the interest of justice favoured preserving them.
firac.conclusion: The Will is annulled except for the specific bequests under arts. 5 and 6.

case_name: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital (CIUSSS du Centre-Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal) c. D.P.

name_verification.name_in_document: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital (CIUSSS du Centre-Ouest-de-l'Île-de-Montréal) c. D.P.

defining_issues: Did the hospital establish that D. is incapable of giving or withholding consent to the proposed treatment, so as to give the Court jurisdiction to impose care against his wishes?
Does the criterion of 'categorical refusal' under article 16 C.C.Q. apply where the incapable person has no one able to give substitute consent?

firac.issue: Did the hospital establish that D. is incapable of consenting to or refusing the proposed treatment?
firac.facts: D., a young man who has just reached majority, has autism spectrum disorder, mild intellectual disability, and has experienced psychotic episodes with auditory hallucinations. He was voluntarily hospitalized for about three months and undergoing antipsychotic treatment. The hospital sought a three-year treatment order; D. objected mainly to the duration, and its two expert witnesses opined he was incapable of refusing treatment, largely because past side effects (akathisia) had led him to stop treatment.
firac.rule: To impose treatment against a person's will, the court must be satisfied the person is himself incapable of engaging in the rational process of weighing the pros and cons of consent according to the established criteria (Institut Philippe Pinel de Montréal c. A.G., 1994 CanLII 6105 (QC CA); F.D. v. Centre universitaire de santé McGill, 2015 QCCA 1139). The utility or necessity of an order to secure compliance is not the test.
firac.application: The experts' opinion that D.'s three diagnoses prevented meaningful participation in the decision was a bald, unsupported assertion. Having heard D. as required by law, the Court found he clearly acknowledged his illness and hallucinations, wanted them to stop, understood the antipsychotic medication and its benefits, had taken it before, researched the disease, and was prepared to consent to treatment in pill form. He could not be held to a standard requiring mastery of the scientific intricacies of his disease. The likelihood that he would cease treatment without an order does not equate to incapacity to consent.
firac.conclusion: The legal test for inability to consent was not met; the burden was not discharged, so the Court lacked jurisdiction to impose treatment.

firac.issue: Does the 'categorical refusal' criterion in article 16 C.C.Q. apply where an incapable person has no one able to give substitute consent?
firac.facts: D. had no tutor, mandatary or other person able to give substitute consent. The parties debated the categorical-refusal criterion drawn from F.D. c. CUSM, 2015 QCCA 1139.
firac.rule: Article 16, para. 1 C.C.Q. sets out two distinct scenarios separated by a semicolon: (I) authorization is needed where the person is incapable and substitute consent cannot be secured (no authorized person, or unjustified refusal); (II) authorization is 'also' needed where an incapable person of full age categorically refuses care despite substitute consent having been given, except for hygienic care or emergencies. The categorical-refusal requirement, introduced by 'it is also necessary,' attaches only to the second scenario.
firac.application: Because D. had no one to give substitute consent, the matter would have fallen under scenario I had he been found incapable. In that scenario no additional categorical-refusal criterion applies; otherwise an incapable person with no substitute decision-maker whose refusal was merely lukewarm would fall into a legal vacuum, which could not have been the legislature's intent. In any event, had the criterion applied, D.'s agreement (limited to subtherapeutic doses) could properly be characterized as a categorical refusal.
firac.conclusion: The categorical-refusal criterion does not apply in scenario I; but this did not change the outcome, as the application failed on the incapacity criterion.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary practice-area classification: this is a civil application for authorization of care under the Civil Code of Québec. K112 (Charter s. 7) is engaged conceptually — the Court frames imposing treatment as 'violating the physical integrity of a human being,' the right to refuse medical treatment and bodily integrity being the core value at stake, though the Charter is not formally cited (flagged as inferential). K071 (human dignity) reflects the protection of personal integrity and autonomy underlying the consent analysis (borderline). K093 (Jewish) is a tier-3 entity match for the Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital, though the Jewish character is incidental to the legal issues (weak). K007 (Human rights) is included as the fundamental right to physical integrity and autonomy of the person is central, though the case is decided on civil-law consent principles rather than human-rights statute (flagged as weak). The controlled vocabulary lacks a dedicated 'consent to care / capacity / mental health' keyword, so these are the closest available matches.
