case_name: Steele v. Riverside Forest Products et al. and Raboch v. Riverside Forest Products et al.

name_verification.name_in_document: Steele v. Riverside Forest Products et al. and Raboch v. Riverside Forest Products et al.

defining_issues: Should the claims against the individual defendant Thorlakson be struck out and should he cease to be a proper party under Rules 15(5) and 19(24) of the Supreme Court Rules?
Do the pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action against Thorlakson personally for inducing breach of contract, given that he acted as a director and officer of the corporate defendants?

firac.issue: Should the claims against the individual defendant Thorlakson be struck and should he cease to be a proper party under Rules 15(5) and 19(24)?
firac.facts: Two former senior executives of Riverside (its former CEO and CFO) sued Riverside, its majority-shareholder Tolko, and Thorlakson, who was president and CEO of both companies, alleging wrongful dismissal and non-payment of retirement benefits following Tolko's 2004 hostile takeover of Riverside. Thorlakson applied to be removed as a party or to have the references to him struck.
firac.rule: Rule 19(24) permits striking a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim or is otherwise an abuse; the test (per Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, adopting Hunt v. Carey Canada) is whether it is 'plain and obvious' that no reasonable cause of action is disclosed, assuming pleaded facts to be true, with doubts resolved in favour of the pleading. Rule 15(5) allows removal of a party who is not or has ceased to be a proper or necessary party; by analogy the same criteria apply. Applications may be brought 'at any stage of a proceeding,' so filing a defence is no bar.
firac.application: Master Patterson assumed the pleaded facts to be true and examined each paragraph referring to Thorlakson. Since the actual doctrinal question turned on whether any independent cause of action was pleaded against him, the striking analysis merged with the inducing-breach analysis.
firac.conclusion: Because no independent cause of action survived, the claims against Thorlakson were struck, the actions against him dismissed, and he was declared no longer a proper party to either action.

firac.issue: Do the pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action against Thorlakson personally for inducing breach of contract despite his acting as an officer/director of the corporate defendants?
firac.facts: Paragraphs 17–20 alleged Riverside 'acting on the instructions of Tolko and/or Thorlakson' refused to pay vacation pay, notice, a lump-sum payment and pension benefits; para. 21 alleged bad faith; para. 22 alleged Thorlakson and Tolko induced Riverside to breach its contracts. The defence asserted Thorlakson acted bona fide within the scope of his duties, not from personal interest, fraud or malice.
firac.rule: Under Said v. Butt, [1920] 3 K.B. 497, a servant or officer of a company acting bona fide within the scope of his authority who causes or procures a breach of contract does not thereby become personally liable for the tort of inducing breach of contract. Canadian authority (Dorus v. Tech Corp.; Normart Management; Lasik Vision; Digital Document Service v. Future Shop; Glenayre Manufacturing v. Pilot Pacific, 2003 BCSC 303) confirms that to establish personal liability a plaintiff must plead that the officer/director committed a tortious act demonstrating an identity or interest separate from that of the company, or acted maliciously, without authority, or through fraud/deceit.
firac.application: The pleadings framed the conduct as that of Riverside acting on instructions, disclosing no act by Thorlakson outside his authority and no identity or interest separate from the company. No particulars of bad faith, malice, fraud or dishonesty were alleged. Paragraph 21 added nothing, and paragraph 22 fell squarely within the Said v. Butt principle.
firac.conclusion: No independent cause of action was pleaded; the claims against Thorlakson were bound to fail and no amendment could save them, so they were struck out and dismissed with costs to Thorlakson on Scale 3.

case_name: Val-Morin (Municipalité) c. Congregation of the Followers of the Rabbis of Belz to Strengthen Torah

name_verification.name_in_document: Municipalité de Val-Morin c. Congregation of the followers of the rabbis of belz to strengthen torah

defining_issues: Were the two buildings used as a synagogue and religious school a derogatory (non-conforming) use of the buildings under Val-Morin's zoning by-law, which permits only residential use in zone R3-3?
Did the zoning by-law, by prohibiting places of worship and schools in the residential zone, infringe the congregation members' freedom of religion under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms?
Did the municipality's long delay or apparent tolerance over some twenty years bar it from seeking cessation of the derogatory use under article 227 of the Loi sur l'aménagement et l'urbanisme?

firac.issue: Were the two buildings used as a synagogue and religious school a derogatory use under the zoning by-law that permits only residential use in zone R3-3?
firac.facts: The congregation acquired cottages near Lac Dream in a residential summer-cottage zone (R3-3) and used one (781, 15e Avenue) as a synagogue and another (rue du Rêve) as a religious school. Interior partitions, kitchens, bathrooms, bedrooms and all household furnishings had been removed and replaced by benches, desks, lockers, urinals, books and religious objects (including the Torah). The congregation admitted in its written defence and at trial that the buildings had always been used as synagogue and school, while arguing they could still qualify as 'residences'.
firac.rule: Article 227 of the Loi sur l'aménagement et l'urbanisme allows a municipality to seek cessation of a use that contravenes the zoning by-law. Words in a by-law take their ordinary meaning (P.-A. Côté, Interprétation des lois); a 'residence/domicile/habitation' is essentially the place where a person lives. A complementary/accessory use requires a relationship of dependence on a principal use (L. Giroux) and cannot itself be a second principal use.
firac.application: The court found no one lived, even occasionally, in either building, which lacked every characteristic of a dwelling. A synagogue and a school do not fall within the ordinary meaning of 'residence', and could not be complementary uses since there was no residential principal use to which they were subordinate, and there cannot be two principal uses. The buildings were dedicated by their layout to worship and religious teaching.
firac.conclusion: The buildings were being used in a manner not permitted in zone R3-3, constituting a derogatory use of zoning by-law No. 360.

firac.issue: Did the zoning by-law infringe the congregation members' freedom of religion under the Charter?
firac.facts: The by-law prohibits places of worship and schools in zone R3-3 but permits them in at least three other zones, including P3-1, where the congregation already owned a 4.3-acre property (17,313 m²) on rue des Vacanciers, a seven-minute walk away, which it used as a religious summer camp and where a synagogue already existed. The congregation argued relocation would be an undue hardship (cost, lack of space, Sabbath travel restrictions).
firac.rule: Freedom of religion (s. 2(a) Charter). A zoning by-law that permits a place of worship somewhere on municipal territory is not prohibitive and does not restrict freedom of religion (Congrégation des témoins de Jéhovah de St-Jérôme-Lafontaine v. Lafontaine, 2004 SCC 48, per LeBel J.; R. v. Big M Drug Mart; Edwards Books). A negligible or insignificant burden does not engage s. 2(a); the municipality owes religious neutrality but need not actively assist a religious group.
firac.application: The by-law does not prohibit any religion; it applies equally to churches, mosques, temples and synagogues, so there is no direct infringement. As several zones (including the congregation's own P3-1 land) permit worship and schools, there was no direct or indirect infringement. The claimed cost/space and hardship arguments were unsupported by evidence; the congregation owned ample land and had knowingly established itself in a residential zone.
firac.conclusion: Neither the by-law nor its application had the purpose or effect of infringing the members' freedom of religion; the Charter argument and the reconventional demand failed.

firac.issue: Did the municipality's delay or tolerance bar its action to end the derogatory use?
firac.facts: The municipality had issued infraction notices, letters and even obtained a provisional injunction from 1982 onward, but the situation persisted for roughly twenty years, during which the congregation repeatedly misrepresented the buildings as residences.
firac.rule: In Quebec law a derogatory use never becomes lawful with the passage of time, even absent municipal intervention; no acquired right arises from an unlawful use (MRC d'Abitibi v. Ibitiba ltée; Ville de Montréal v. Chapdelaine). The municipality is subject to no limitation period for an art. 227 application.
firac.application: The court found there had in fact been no tolerance—only patience—as the municipality had consistently opposed the use since 1982. In any event, tolerance could not create rights, and no time bar applied. The municipality need not prove inconvenience to neighbours once a derogatory use is established.
firac.conclusion: The delay/tolerance defence was rejected; the municipality was entitled to obtain cessation of the use.

keywords_rationale: K003 Constitutional law is the tier-1 practice area, as the case turned on a Charter freedom-of-religion challenge to a zoning by-law. K025 freedom of religion and K110 Charter s. 2(a) capture the central constitutional issue, with K107 (the Charter) as the invoked statute. name_verification.name_in_document: Sofaer (Estate of) c. Mashaal

defining_issues: Should the defendant Wiener's motion to immediately remove and replace liquidators and trustees Rhonda Sofaer and Norton Paish be granted?
Should the Estate's motion to remove Wiener as liquidator and trustee and appoint an ad hoc replacement be granted?
Is Wiener entitled to reimbursement of the extrajudicial fees and disbursements incurred to prepare and present his removal motion?

firac.issue: Should Wiener's motion to remove liquidators and trustees Rhonda Sofaer and Norton Paish be granted?
firac.facts: Under article 9 of Jack Sofaer's will, Rhonda (the testator's daughter and a beneficiary) was the testator's designated first-choice replacement liquidator, and the will required at least three liquidators acting by majority. Wiener, a consultant named as an initial liquidator, alleged Rhonda and Paish were excluding him from the administration. No complaints existed between Rhonda and Paish as to each other's performance.
firac.rule: Under arts. 783, 789, 791, 805, 1277 and 1310 C.C.Q. and art. 49 C.C.P., replacement of a liquidator/trustee is an exceptional measure, especially where the person was chosen by the testator, and the testator's wishes cannot be set aside absent malversation, conflict of interest, or a lack of loyalty and diligence opposing the liquidator's interest to that of the heirs (Perreault (Succession de) c. Perreault). A provisional removal order requires the Vachon c. Riopelle (2003 CanLII 75014) criteria: a prima facie right, irreparable harm, and balance of convenience.
firac.application: None of the disqualifying factors (malversation, conflict, disloyalty) applied to Rhonda or Paish. Any apparent conflict from Rhonda being both beneficiary and Dan's guardian was best reserved for the Ontario courts. Wiener failed to establish a prima facie right, showed no irreparable harm, and the balance of convenience favoured maintaining the status quo of Rhonda's and Paish's appointments.
firac.conclusion: The motion for removal was dismissed; it was not in the best interests of the Estate to replace Rhonda or Paish.

firac.issue: Should Wiener be removed as liquidator and trustee and replaced by an ad hoc liquidator?
firac.facts: Wiener had commenced a libel and defamation action against Rhonda personally, creating a serious ongoing personal conflict. Rhonda had serious concerns about how Wiener was carrying out his duties, and there was an apparent conflict with Wiener's lawyer also acting for other defendants.
firac.rule: The Vachon c. Riopelle criteria (prima facie right, irreparable harm, balance of convenience) govern the appointment of a provisional/ad hoc liquidator; best interests of the estate justify replacement of a liquidator where a conflict impairs administration.
firac.application: Rhonda demonstrated prima facie a conflict of interest arising from Wiener's personal lawsuit against her, established irreparable harm to herself and the Estate if he remained, and the balance of convenience favoured his removal since she was the testator's daughter and a beneficiary while Wiener was merely a consultant. The ongoing conflict interfered with the liquidators' duties.
firac.conclusion: The motion to appoint was granted; Wiener was immediately removed and replaced by Me Richard McConomy as ad hoc liquidator and trustee during the suit.

firac.issue: Is Wiener entitled to reimbursement of his extrajudicial fees for preparing his removal motion?
firac.facts: Wiener claimed $36,493.32 in extrajudicial fees and disbursements incurred to prepare and present his motion. The statements of account showed the fees appeared incurred for business relating to the Estate.
firac.rule: Fees and disbursements incurred by a liquidator for legitimate estate business may be reimbursed by the estate where reasonable.
firac.application: The claimed fees appeared to have been incurred for Estate business, and given the history and complexity of the matter the amount was not unreasonable.
firac.conclusion: The Estate was ordered to reimburse Wiener the $36,493.32 claimed.

K021 (interlocutory injunction) applies because the court expressly used the Vachon c. Riopelle provisional-order test (prima facie right, irreparable harm, balance of convenience). K015 (defamation) is engaged because Wiener's libel/defamation action against Rhonda was the conflict driving his removal. K093 (Jewish) is a weaker, contextual pick reflecting that this is a Jewish testator's estate benefiting several Jewish charitable institutions; it is peripheral to the ratio.

case_name: Transform Compost Systems Ltd. v. Jayendee Farms Ltd.

name_verification.name_in_document: Transform Compost Systems Ltd. v. Jayendee Farms Ltd.

defining_issues: Have the defendants satisfied the preconditions for an order requiring the corporate plaintiffs to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act?
Should the defendants be awarded special costs on the basis that Dr. Paul gave false or misleading affidavit evidence about the plaintiffs' exigible assets?

firac.issue: Have the defendants satisfied the preconditions for an order requiring the corporate plaintiffs to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act?
firac.facts: Transform, corporate plaintiffs in a complex contract/tort dispute over an oral lease and composting operation on the defendants' Abbotsford farm, was in diminished financial circumstances following its eviction, was indebted to its major creditor VEI for $556,000 and to a supplier for $60,000, and one plaintiff (Transform Plant Products Inc.) had been wound down and might cease to operate. However, Transform owned 16 appraised pieces of equipment worth $395,477, leaving roughly $197,830 in equity after secured charges.
firac.rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 permits the court to order a corporate plaintiff to give security for costs where it appears the corporation will be unable to pay the defendant's costs if the defence succeeds. The four-part test in Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC) requires: (1) apparent inability to pay costs; (2) whether the plaintiff has shown exigible assets sufficient to satisfy costs; (3) an arguable defence; and (4) whether an order would cause undue hardship stifling the claim. The first three are preconditions to discretion, which is then exercised on the Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd. (1997) factors.
firac.application: The court found on a prima facie basis that the plaintiffs would be unable to pay a costs award (estimated at $75,000 on Scale B, not the $110,000 claimed), given their diminished finances and the risk one plaintiff would be wound down. The court also found the defendants had an arguable defence to the claims, including conversion and detinue, on their pleadings of termination for cause, reasonable notice, and lawful bolting of equipment. However, the plaintiffs demonstrated exigible assets of almost $198,000 in equipment equity—substantially exceeding potential costs—after VEI discharged its security and agreed to subordinate its loan. One of the three preconditions was therefore not met.
firac.conclusion: The application for security for costs was dismissed because the plaintiffs established sufficient exigible assets.

firac.issue: Should the defendants be awarded special costs on the basis that Dr. Paul gave false or misleading affidavit evidence about the plaintiffs' exigible assets?
firac.facts: In his fifth affidavit Dr. Paul, president of Transform, deposed there were no security agreements over the valued equipment, but a Personal Property Registry search revealed nine registered security agreements. Once confronted, he promptly swore a corrective sixth affidavit providing full disclosure and explaining he had not understood the scope of the charges and believed VEI had written off its loans.
firac.rule: Where a party deliberately attempts to mislead the court by giving false evidence, that conduct may found an award of special costs: Laface v. McWilliams, 2005 BCSC 1766; Webber v. Canadian Aviation Insurance Managers Ltd., 2003 BCSC 274.
firac.application: The court found Dr. Paul's errors reflected an initial lack of attention, a flawed memory and a lack of sophistication in commercial matters rather than a deliberate attempt to mislead or reckless disregard for the truth. He promptly corrected the record. However, both parties incurred additional unnecessary expense because of the misinformation.
firac.conclusion: Special costs were refused, but the court departed from the usual rule that costs follow the event and ordered each party to bear its own costs of the application.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the solid tier-1 fit: this is an interlocutory application for security for costs within a commercial contract/tort action. No entity keyword was used for the merely cited Canadian Jewish Congress precedent.

name_verification.name_in_document: Seggie c. Roofdog Games Inc.

defining_issues: Was the video game Extreme Road Trip a 'work of joint authorship' under the Copyright Act, entitling Seggie to 50% of the profits from ERT (and ERT2)?
Did Seggie hold copyright in his drawings, and did he assign that copyright or licence its use, so as to determine whether Roofdog infringed and what compensation is owed?
Did Seggie defame Germain, entitling Germain to damages on the counterclaim?
Did Seggie's conduct of the litigation amount to an abuse of process warranting reimbursement of extrajudicial professional fees?

firac.issue: Was Extreme Road Trip a work of joint authorship under the Copyright Act, giving Seggie a right to 50% of the profits?
firac.facts: Germain, a programmer, conceived and coded the car-racing/acrobatics game and made all final decisions on content. Seggie, an illustrator working full-time elsewhere, voluntarily supplied six vehicle drawings, a background and some accessories (about 100 hours' work) and offered occasional suggestions, while Germain invested $20,000 and over 1,200 unpaid hours designing, programming, monetizing, marketing and launching the game. Seggie admitted there was never any profit-sharing agreement and initially worked 'probono'. He did not participate in ERT2 at all.
firac.rule: Section 2 of the Copyright Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42) defines a work of joint authorship as 'a work produced by the collaboration of two or more authors in which the contribution of one author is not distinct from the contribution of the other.' Case law (Neugebauer, Drapeau v. Girard, Pinto) requires a substantial (not necessarily equal) contribution by each, collaboration in pursuit of a common design, proof of more than mere ideas or suggestions, and, on one line of authority, a common intention to create a joint work. Copyright protects the expression of ideas, not ideas themselves (CCH Canadian Ltd. v. Law Society of Upper Canada, 2004 SCC 13).
firac.application: The Court found Germain put the idea into practice, programmed the game and controlled all decisions; Seggie's isolated artistic contribution stopped after mid-April and was distinct and identifiable (he received separate credit for the drawings). There was never any common intention to create a joint work — Seggie congratulated Germain in admirer's terms ('your new venture'), did not react to another illustrator being hired, and conceded he would not have absorbed any loss. His contribution was clearly not indistinct from Germain's. ERT2 was significantly different and involved no work by Seggie.
firac.conclusion: ERT is not a work of joint authorship. Seggie cannot claim 50% of ERT profits, has no claim to ERT2 profits, and no compensation for the alleged value of the user base (which was in any event unproven).

firac.issue: Did Seggie hold and assign or licence copyright in his drawings, and what compensation is owed for their use?
firac.facts: Seggie drew six vehicles, a background and accessories that were online in ERT from 3 August to 11 October 2011, when a modified version by another illustrator (Denes) replaced them. Seggie was kept informed, congratulated Germain, and never asked that the drawings be removed until his demand letter of 28 March 2012. Germain offered $10,000 before litigation. Denes was paid about $2,500 and the ERT2 illustrator $5,500.
firac.rule: Sections 3, 13(4) and 27(1) of the Copyright Act: copyright is the sole right to reproduce/communicate a work; an assignment must be in writing and signed by the owner; infringement occurs when someone does a reserved act without the owner's consent. Mere transfer of possession is not assignment (Massie & Renwick). Consent/licence may be inferred from conduct, the burden lying on the party asserting it (Tajdin v. Aga Khan), and a gratuitous consent is revocable (Katz v. Cytrynbaum).
firac.application: Seggie's emails/texts, though electronic, were treated as signed writings, but none referred even implicitly to an assignment of copyright, so there was no assignment. However, the written exchanges showed Seggie voluntarily authorized use of his drawings (he offered to draw the cars, knew of the launch and did not object). Denes's modified cars were similar but not identical, based only on the online game, and formed a small part of the evolved game with no intent to create disguised imitations. Given amounts paid to comparable illustrators, Germain's pre-litigation $10,000 offer represented fair compensation for the licensed use, payable only by Roofdog as publisher.
firac.conclusion: Seggie held copyright in the drawings but licensed their use; Roofdog is ordered to pay $10,000 for that use, without pre-judgment interest or costs given the earlier adequate offer.

firac.issue: Did Seggie defame Germain, entitling Germain to damages?
firac.facts: Seggie accused Germain of bad faith, abuse and fraud in his demand letter, to mutual acquaintances, and in his pleadings (alleging blatant/abusive infringement, fraud, that Germain removed his name as illustrator and that Seggie devised the monetization concept). Several allegations were false and were withdrawn only at trial at the Court's suggestion.
firac.rule: Under Quebec civil liability, defamatory statements made maliciously or with recklessness equivalent to malice engage liability; punitive damages are available where the injury is intentional (Vary v. Vary; Genex Communications, 2009 QCCA 2201 on interest).
firac.application: The Court found the accusations of bad faith, abuse and fraud unsupported and made maliciously or recklessly, causing injury to Germain's reputation and friendships. Germain, not Roofdog (which showed no specific pecuniary prejudice), suffered the harm.
firac.conclusion: Counterclaim allowed in part: Germain awarded $15,000 for reputational injury, $2,000 in moral damages (interest from the demand letter) and $5,000 in punitive damages (interest from judgment). Roofdog's defamation claim dismissed.

firac.issue: Did Seggie's conduct of the litigation constitute an abuse of process warranting reimbursement of extrajudicial professional fees?
firac.facts: Roofdog and Germain claimed $59,237 in extrajudicial fees, arguing Seggie pursued unfounded claims (joint authorship, ERT2 profits, $100,000 database value) despite offers of compensation.
firac.rule: Abuse of the right to litigate is a fault committed on the occasion of a legal action (Viel v. Entreprises immobilières du terroir ltée, 2002 QCCA); a court should not find abuse merely because a party's theory is weak without being abusive (Industries Lassonde).
firac.application: While Seggie's claims were weak, the Court declined to treat the mere pursuit of a weak theory as abusive conduct sufficient to award extrajudicial fees, distinguishing this from the malicious defamatory allegations already sanctioned.
firac.conclusion: The claim for reimbursement of extrajudicial professional fees was not granted as an abuse-of-process remedy.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the correct tier-1 practice area, as this is a private copyright/civil-liability dispute. K015 (defamation) squarely applies to the successful counterclaim for injury to Germain's reputation with moral and punitive damages. The remaining picks are weak because the controlled vocabulary contains no intellectual-property/copyright or abuse-of-process terms: K021 (injunction) is a partial fit since Seggie sought an order to cease infringing his copyright; K022 (restitution) loosely captures the $10,000 monetary compensation ordered for the licensed use of the drawings; K016 (fair comment) is a defamation-adjacent term included only to reach the minimum count and is a marginal fit. The core copyright/joint-authorship issues have no matching keyword ID in the vocabulary.

registry_rationale: The decision is issued in the 'DISTRICT OF MONTRÉAL' of the Quebec Superior Court, so the registry is Montréal.

name_verification.name_in_document: UNIVERSITÉ DE MONTRÉAL c. CLAUDE CÔTÉ

defining_issues: Should a permanent injunction be issued restraining the defendant from sending harassing, insulting and defamatory emails, faxes and communications to the university and its members?
Was the defendant's cross-demand (demande reconventionnelle) prescribed, or was it saved by its connexity with the principal demand?
Is the defendant entitled to unpaid remuneration under the August 2002 research mandate?

firac.issue: Should a permanent injunction be issued restraining the defendant from sending harassing, insulting and defamatory communications to the university?
firac.facts: Following a dispute over a research mandate and unpaid sums, Côté sent nearly a hundred emails and faxes over 2004–2005 to the university's rector, deans, administrators, professors and employees, accusing the administration of corruption, banditry and criminal conduct, some labelled 'Communication de Presse – pour distribution immédiate'. A safeguard order in December 2005 had stopped the communications.
firac.rule: Under art. 7 C.c.Q. no right may be exercised with intent to injure another or in an excessive and unreasonable manner contrary to good faith. Freedom of expression is not absolute. For a permanent injunction the criteria of irreparable harm and balance of convenience do not apply; the court decides on the merits whether the right to the injunction is established (Ferron, Piché-Messier, Poitras). Defamation is judged objectively by whether an ordinary citizen would find the words discredited the reputation of another (Prud'homme c. Prud'homme; Radio Sept-Îles); good faith of the defendant is irrelevant (Baudoin; Fondation Le Corbusier).
firac.application: The evidence clearly established that Côté sent massive, threatening and injurious communications that paralyzed the university's communications and impugned the dignity and reputation of its members. Although Côté genuinely felt wronged and was in great personal distress, his writings were objectively defamatory and exceeded the limits of legitimate expression. The right to an injunction was established, following authorities such as Doré c. Turmel and CSSS de la Vallée de l'Or c. A.
firac.conclusion: The demand for a permanent injunction was granted in part; the defendant was ordered to abstain from sending communications relating to the 2002–2005 conflict similar to the offending exhibits, the order to remain in force notwithstanding appeal.

firac.issue: Was the defendant's cross-demand prescribed, or was it saved by connexity with the principal demand?
firac.facts: The injunction proceeding was instituted in October 2005; Côté filed his cross-demand in September 2007 seeking unpaid salary, damages for sabotage of his mandate and damages for defamation of his reputation. The university argued prescription under arts. 2925 (3 years) and 2929 (1 year, defamation) C.c.Q.
firac.rule: Article 2896 C.c.Q. provides that interruption of prescription by a judicial demand has effect for all rights flowing from the same source. Under art. 172(2) C.p.c. a cross-demand must arise from the same source as, or a source connected to, the principal demand, requiring a close link or relationship of dependence or similarity (Ferland & Emery; F.N.G. Gibraltar c. Aziz; Cabba c. American Express).
firac.application: The court found a close and visible connection between the university's demand (based on Côté's harassing communications) and Côté's claims (the unpaid sums and alleged attack on his reputation), which all stemmed from the same 2002–2003 dispute. It was therefore a single problem, and prescription of the contractual claim was interrupted. Since no evidence supported the delictual (defamation) claims, whether their prescription was interrupted need not be decided.
firac.conclusion: The cross-demand was found connected and not barred as to the contractual claim; the delictual claims failed for lack of proof.

firac.issue: Is the defendant entitled to unpaid remuneration under the August 2002 research mandate?
firac.facts: Dean Vinay offered Côté a three-month mandate at $5,000/month to study researchers' careers. Côté worked from August 2002, delivered a synopsis in October, and a cheque of $5,000 (24 October 2002) was withheld/never received. The mandate was not renewed after the faculty committee found the synopsis unsatisfactory; Côté's 31 October 2002 email was misread as ending the mandate.
firac.rule: Contractual obligations must be honoured; damages bear interest and the additional indemnity under art. 1619 C.c.Q. from the date of the reconventional demand.
firac.application: The court found the mandate ended around 15–22 November 2002 and that one amount had not been fully paid on the 8 August 2002 contract. In equity the university had to pay the outstanding sum, but the other claims (large damages, mea culpa, defamation damages) were unproven and rejected.
firac.conclusion: The university was ordered to pay $5,000 with interest and the additional indemnity under art. 1619 C.c.Q. from the service of the cross-demand (25 September 2007, per the corrected judgment); each party to bear its own costs.

K021 (injunction) is the central remedy sought and granted, although the vocabulary term is worded 'interlocutory'; here it is a permanent injunction, so it is a slightly imperfect but closest available match. case_name: Vancouver Area Network of Drug Users v. British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal

name_verification.name_in_document: Vancouver Area Network of Drug Users v. British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal

defining_issues: What evidence is required to establish the third step of the prima facie test for discrimination under s. 8 of the Human Rights Code, and did the Tribunal apply too strict a standard by requiring a 'causal connection' rather than the protected characteristic being 'a factor'?
Did the Tribunal err in framing the comparative analysis by comparing protected and non-protected members within the affected Class rather than comparing the Class to the general public?
Did the Tribunal err by importing an intention or 'targeting' requirement into the discrimination analysis?
Is a finding of discrimination available against the City of Vancouver given its argument that the matter is moot?

firac.issue: What evidence is required to satisfy the third step of the prima facie test for discrimination under s. 8 of the Code, and did the Tribunal apply too onerous a standard?
firac.facts: The Tribunal accepted that a disproportionate number of the street-homeless Class were Aboriginal or had disabilities and that Class members suffered adverse treatment under the Ambassadors Program, but dismissed the complaint because there was no direct evidence of a 'nexus' between the adverse treatment and protected grounds; there was statistical/demographic evidence and expert evidence from Dr. Miller but no testimony from an affected homeless individual of Aboriginal descent or with a disability.
firac.rule: Under Moore v. British Columbia (Education), 2012 SCC 61 at para. 33, a claimant must show (1) a protected characteristic, (2) an adverse impact regarding the service, and (3) that the protected characteristic was 'a factor' in the adverse impact. The Code is quasi-constitutional and must be interpreted broadly and purposively (Tranchemontagne, 2006 SCC 14); evidentiary requirements must be sensitive to the evidence likely available and statistical evidence is helpful but not essential (Radek v. Henderson Development, 2005 BCHRT 302). Standard of review is correctness under s. 59(1) ATA.
firac.application: The court held the Tribunal misstated the test by requiring a 'causal connection' (drawn from Coast Mountain, 2010 BCCA 447) and evidence that the group was 'treated or affected differently,' which is stricter than the 'a factor' standard in Moore. Requiring a causative connection elevates the burden and risks importing intention. The court found the Tribunal misread Chapdelaine and Meiorin, where statistical evidence alone established the nexus, and that Radek confirms inference, judicial notice and common sense may prove systemic discrimination. On the whole of the evidence—the demographics, the ambassador data, and Dr. Miller's unrejected expert evidence—the protected characteristics were a factor; no 'something more' was needed.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal erred in law by applying too strict an evidentiary standard; applying the correct 'a factor' test, all three steps of the prima facie test were established.

firac.issue: Did the Tribunal err in its characterization of the comparative analysis?
firac.facts: The Tribunal reasoned that there was no evidence Ambassadors were more likely to remove Aboriginal than non-Aboriginal individuals 'in similar circumstances,' comparing protected and non-protected members within the Class.
firac.rule: Per Moore (paras. 29-30) and Withler, 2011 SCC 12, the comparator should not be defined so as to descend into a 'separate but equal' formalism; the comparison is with the general public who enjoy the service, not with a sub-group defined by the impugned treatment.
firac.application: The court found the Tribunal made the same error the Court of Appeal made in Moore—comparing dyslexic special-education students to other special-education students. The correct comparison is between Class members subjected to adverse treatment and the general population who have unrestricted access to downtown public space. Framing the comparison within the Class was a legal error.
firac.conclusion: The Tribunal erred in law in its comparative analysis, vitiating its conclusion that prima facie discrimination was not proven.

firac.issue: Did the Tribunal err by importing an intention requirement into the analysis?
firac.facts: The Tribunal used the language of 'systemically targeted' and 'selectively targeted,' and the respondents argued the Program aimed only at illegal behaviours, not at people with protected characteristics.
firac.rule: Section 2 of the Code states intention to discriminate is not required; discrimination is defined by effect/impact (Andrews, 1989; Action Travail, 1987). Adverse effect, not intent or design, is the focus.
firac.application: The court accepted the Program was not intentionally discriminatory but held that lack of intent does not eliminate discrimination. The 'targeting' language reflected a focus on the Program's intent/design rather than its impact, which flowed from the same error of applying too strict a nexus test. The proper focus is disproportionate impact.
firac.conclusion: By focusing on targeting and requiring stricter proof of disproportionate impact, the Tribunal effectively imported an intention element, an error of law.

firac.issue: Is a remedy available against the City of Vancouver despite its mootness argument?
firac.facts: The City funded overnight operation of the Program for one year under a contract that was not renewed; it also promoted the Program, provided some training, and owned the data collected. It argued no live dispute remained.
firac.rule: Mootness (Borowski v. Canada, 1989) bars adjudication where a decision would have no practical effect on the parties' rights.
firac.application: The court found the issues were not abstract: the City funded, promoted and was involved in the Program, and its funding directly enabled overnight ambassador interactions with more rough-sleeping homeless people. A finding of discrimination could stand against the City, but only for the one-year period it funded the Program.
firac.conclusion: Relief is available against the City for the one year it funded the Program; the matter is not moot.

keywords_rationale: The case is a statutory human rights matter, so K007 (Human rights) is the tier-1 practice area. It arises on judicial review of a Human Rights Tribunal decision, engaging K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review — correctness under s. 59 ATA). The core dispute is the test for K069 (discrimination) and specifically K073 (prima facie discrimination) and K074 (systemic discrimination), which are the doctrinal heart of the reasons. K119 (Human Rights Code) is the governing statute (s. 8 BC Code). registry_rationale: The style of cause expressly states 'Registry: Vancouver'.

name_verification.name_in_document: Albert Stieber v. Joseph Élie Ltée

defining_issues: Can the Court rectify the previously approved class action settlement to correct miscalculations of the Total and Net Indemnity caused by inadvertent computer/human error under art. 475 C.C.P.?
Is a private agreement fixing the Fonds d'aide aux recours collectifs' contribution at a lesser amount enforceable, or must the Fonds receive its statutorily prescribed percentage?
How should the Court distribute the remaining balance ('reliquat') of the settlement funds under art. 1036 C.C.P., and does the 'interest of the members' permit distribution to Measurement Canada?

firac.issue: Can the Court rectify the approved class action settlement to correct indemnity miscalculations caused by inadvertent error?
firac.facts: After the settlement was approved, Joseph Élie Ltée discovered its computer software ('Minifuel') had been mis-encoded, creating duplicate transactions that inflated the diverted volume by about 20% (60 million vs. 49 million litres) and the customer count by 400. Independent forensic accountants (Navigant Consulting) confirmed the error was inadvertent human error and validated the corrected figures. Class counsel verified the correction caused no prejudice to members and did not oppose.
firac.rule: Art. 475 C.C.P. permits the Court to correct a judgment containing a miscalculation (Potvin v. Gagnon, [1967] B.R. 300). Under arts. 1036, 1037 and 1040 C.C.P. the judge has broad discretion and acts as administrator of the settlement's execution (St. Lawrence Cement Inc. v. Barrette, 2008 SCC 64).
firac.application: The Court engaged forensic accountants who confirmed the error resulted from inadvertence, not bad faith, and that customers had in fact been properly indemnified for the actual volume diverted. The Court accepted the corrected Net Indemnity of $3,268,195.08 and Total Indemnity of $3,570,488.03. Because the miscalculation relied on by both the parties and the Court was inadvertent and its correction prejudiced no class member, it fell squarely within art. 475 C.C.P.
firac.conclusion: The Court rectified the May 28, 2009 judgment to establish the corrected Total and Net Indemnity amounts.

firac.issue: Is a private agreement reducing the Fonds d'aide aux recours collectifs' contribution enforceable, or must the statutory percentage apply?
firac.facts: The parties and the Fonds had agreed (letter of March 30, 2009) that the Fonds would receive 20% up to a maximum of $20,000. The Fonds later moved to rectify, asserting its statutory entitlement of 60% of a reliquat between $100,000 and $200,000, i.e. $89,790.60 on a reliquat of $149,651.
firac.rule: Arts. 38 and 42 of the Loi sur le recours collectif, R.S.Q. c. R-2.1, and the Règlement sur le pourcentage prélevé par le Fonds d'aide fix the Fonds' entitlement on a reliquat or liquidated claim; regulations once adopted have the force of law (Ruel v. Québec (Éducation), 2001 CanLII 27967; Le Fonds d'aide v. Syndicat des employés d'entretien, [1995] R.J.Q. 2002).
firac.application: The Court held the Fonds' entitlement is statutorily determined and is a matter of public order; the parties and the Fonds could not agree to a lesser amount than that prescribed by regulation. Sixty percent of the corrected reliquat of $149,651 equalled $89,790.60.
firac.conclusion: The March 30, 2009 letter was declared unenforceable as contrary to law; the Fonds was awarded its statutory entitlement of $89,790.60, without costs on its motion since it had contributed to the error.

firac.issue: How should the remaining reliquat be distributed under art. 1036 C.C.P., and can it go to Measurement Canada?
firac.facts: After indemnifying members and paying the Fonds, a reliquat of $59,860.40 remained representing funds intended for members who could not be located. The parties proposed distribution to hospitals and their respiratory departments and to local community charities/United Way. Measurement Canada's inspections had originally uncovered the fraudulent flow-meter tampering.
firac.rule: Art. 1036 C.C.P. gives the Court broad discretion to dispose of the balance 'taking particular account of the interest of the members,' after hearing the parties and any designated persons. Execution must be 'practical and rational' (Comité de citoyens de St-Césaire, [1986] R.J.Q. 1061); the compensatory function and correspondence between victim and beneficiary must be respected (Lafond); cy-près-type distributions must reasonably benefit class members (cf. Ontario Class Proceedings Act, s. 26(4)).
firac.application: The Court found the hospitals, respiratory departments and general charities lacked a sufficiently direct 'interest' connection to the class, there being no evidence heating oil posed a respiratory health risk. It corrected its own omission of the word 'Government' from the recipient categories and heard the Attorney General. Because Measurement Canada's inspections uncovered and deter the very tampering that caused the loss, funding it serves the interest of all heating-oil consumers, including the overcharged members. The Court recommended the funds be added to (not replace) Measurement Canada's budget, respecting that only Parliament allocates federal funds.
firac.conclusion: The Court ordered the reliquat of $59,860.40 be paid to the Receiver General of Canada with a strong recommendation that it be allocated to the fuel-oil inspection section of Measurement Canada in Greater Montreal.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area, as this is a private-law class action settlement dispute. K020 (class action) is the central procedural vehicle — the entire decision concerns approval, rectification and distribution in a recours collectif under arts. 1003, 1036 and 475 C.C.P. name_verification.name_in_document: Shapiro v. Shapiro

defining_issues: Did Michael and Nikki Shapiro procure the October 2018 Wills by undue influence through testamentary fraud, such that Carol-Sue's elimination of Tracy's financial inheritance should be set aside?
Was the reduction of Jack Shapiro's inheritance in the October 2018 Wills the product of undue influence through fraud perpetrated or encouraged by Michael and Nikki?

firac.issue: Did Michael and Nikki procure the October 2018 Wills by undue influence through testamentary fraud with respect to Tracy's inheritance?
firac.facts: Carol-Sue Shapiro, whose estate of roughly $7 million derived from the 'Swedlove Legacy' left by her father, progressively reduced her daughter Tracy's inheritance over successive wills from 2013 to 2018, culminating in the October 2018 Wills that left Tracy only specific jewelry and made her son Michael the sole residuary beneficiary. Carol-Sue was preoccupied by fear that Tracy's husband, Jo Corcos, would gain access to the family wealth. Tracy alleged Michael and his wife Nikki fraudulently fed Carol-Sue false beliefs (Jo's mafia/criminal ties, that Tracy and Jo were back together) to disinherit her.
firac.rule: The party attacking a will bears the onus of proving undue influence, whether by coercion or fraudulent means, on a balance of probabilities (Vout v. Hay, 1995 CanLII 105 (SCC)). Testamentary fraud is a species of undue influence: inducing a testator, by a program of falsehood and manipulation, to make a gift she otherwise would not make (Poyser, Capacity and Undue Influence; Patterson Estate (Re), 2017 NSSC 221; Mayrand v. Dussault, 1907 CanLII 94 (SCC); Anderson v. Walkey, 1961 CanLII 112 (ON CA)). Evidence is usually circumstantial; indicators include dependence, social isolation, recent family conflict, bereavement, wills inconsistent with prior wills, and substantial pre-death transfers of wealth (Gironda v. Gironda, 2013 ONSC 4133; Tate v. Gueguegirre, 2015 ONSC 844).
firac.application: The court reconstructed the family history from Carol-Sue's perspective, principally through her emails. Most alleged 'falsehoods' were not manifest lies: Jo's romantic involvement with another woman, his interest in the money, and that Tracy remained with Jo were substantiated or reasonably believed, and Tracy admitted the Fall 2018 sighting was true. Only the belief that Jo was a mafia member/criminal was false, but there was no evidence Michael and Nikki manufactured it. Applying the Gironda/Tate indicators, Carol-Sue was not dependent on Michael and Nikki (she used her financial power to try to force them to reconcile with Tracy), was not socially isolated (she had many advisors and friends who reported on Tracy and Jo), and the family conflict was not exploited (Michael and Nikki urged Tracy to leave Jo, which would have preserved her inheritance). The October 2018 changes were consistent with Carol-Sue's stated intentions dating to 2013-2016, and pre-death gifts to Michael's family were explained by tax planning, income disparity, travel assistance and keeping money from Jo. Jo's own threatening conduct was the strongest catalyst.
firac.conclusion: Undue influence through fraud was not established; Carol-Sue made up her own mind gradually to protect the Swedlove Legacy. Tracy's objection was dismissed.

firac.issue: Was the reduction of Jack's inheritance the product of undue influence through fraud?
firac.facts: Jack, Carol-Sue's husband, had his bequest reduced across successive wills to $250,000 plus a life interest in the condominium. He alleged Michael and Nikki convinced Carol-Sue falsely that he had ample savings and would pass any inheritance to Tracy (and thus to Jo).
firac.rule: Same rule: the objector must prove undue influence by fraudulent means on a balance of probabilities, supported by direct or circumstantial evidence (Vout v. Hay; Gironda; Tate).
firac.application: While it was untrue that Jack had a million dollars in savings, the court found this was Carol-Sue's own erroneous assumption (the spouses kept separate finances) rather than a lie planted by Michael and Nikki. Carol-Sue's belief that Jack would share money with Tracy reflected his genuinely more trusting attitude toward Jo, not a fabrication. There was no evidence, direct or circumstantial, that Michael or Nikki induced these beliefs.
firac.conclusion: Jack's claim of undue influence through fraud was dismissed.

keywords_rationale: K054 (wills/estates) is the core substantive keyword: the case is a contested application for a certificate of appointment of estate trustee turning on will validity, undue influence and testamentary fraud; K006 (Family law) is its tier-1 parent and the practice area. name_verification.name_in_document: Wang v. Epoch Press Ltd.

defining_issues: Should the derivative claims advanced on behalf of the company be struck where the plaintiff has not obtained leave of the court under s. 232 of the Business Corporations Act?

Should the Notice of Civil Claim be struck under Rule 9-5 for failing to disclose a reasonable cause of action and/or for being so prolix and confusing that the defendants cannot understand the case to meet?
Should the action be dismissed outright, or should the plaintiff be granted leave to amend, and should discovery precede repleading?

firac.issue: Should the derivative claims be struck where the plaintiff never obtained leave under s. 232 of the Business Corporations Act?
firac.facts: The plaintiff, a founder, shareholder, director, officer and creditor of Epoch, pleaded numerous claims, some of which sought recovery for losses to the company itself (e.g. failure to collect receivables, misappropriation, transfer of assets to Vanstar rendering Epoch insolvent). She intended these to form a derivative action on behalf of Epoch but had not applied for or obtained leave of the court.
firac.rule: Section 232 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 requires leave of the court to bring a derivative action on behalf of a company. Claims that are fundamentally derivative — for loss to the company rather than a personal loss — must be struck unless leave is granted (Hoet v. Vogel; Robak Industries Ltd. v. Gardner, 2007 BCCA 61). A shareholder has no personal cause of action for loss of investment or share value arising from a wrong to the corporation (Foss v. Harbottle; Hercules Management Ltd. v. Ernst & Young).
firac.application: The plaintiff wished to pursue both personal and derivative claims but had not distinguished them and had not sought the required leave. The pleadings blended losses personal to her with losses to Epoch (e.g. under the defined 'Harmful Acts'). To the extent the claims were derivative, they could not proceed without leave; and the plaintiff was simultaneously suing Epoch while proposing to sue on its behalf.
firac.conclusion: The derivative claims must be struck; if the plaintiff wishes to pursue a derivative action she must first bring an application for leave under s. 232.

firac.issue: Should the Notice of Civil Claim be struck under Rule 9-5 for failing to disclose a reasonable claim and for being confusing?
firac.facts: The NOCC and proposed amended NOCC asserted a plethora of causes of action (conspiracy, intentional interference, deceit, fraud, negligence, misrepresentation, breach of fiduciary duty to the plaintiff and to Epoch, breaches of contract, oppression, and derivative claims) against multiple defendants occupying overlapping capacities, based on events spanning several years. It was often unclear which claims were made against which defendant, in which capacity, and on what facts.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1)(a),(b),(d) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim, are unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, or are an abuse of process. The 'plain and obvious' test governs (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42; Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.). Pleadings must clearly define the issues of fact and law and plead the material facts for each cause of action (Rule 3-1(2); Stoneman v. Denman Island Trust Committee). Prolix, confusing pleadings that prevent the opposing party from knowing the case to meet may be struck (Gateway Building Management Ltd. v. Randhawa; Canfor Pulp Limited Partnership v. Siemens).
firac.application: The pleadings failed the basic purpose of defining issues: they lumped defendants together, did not identify the capacity in which each party was liable, and did not tie material facts to particular causes of action. Complexity did not relieve the plaintiff of the duty to plead properly; she could not rely on discovery to supply facts she was obliged to plead. However, the NOCC did set out facts that could potentially support viable causes of action.
firac.conclusion: The NOCC is struck out in its entirety under Rule 9-5, but outright dismissal is not warranted because viable claims may exist.

firac.issue: Should the action be dismissed, or should leave to amend be granted, and should discovery precede repleading?
firac.facts: The plaintiff asked that the application be adjourned to permit discovery, arguing she lacked information because she had been ousted and blocked from the company's records.
firac.rule: A claimant must plead the material facts on which the claim relies whether or not able to prove them at the pleadings stage (Imperial Tobacco). Pleadings define the issues and therefore the scope of discovery; discovery cannot precede adequate pleadings (SunOil Ltd. v. Big Snowy Resources L.P.). Where a defect can be cured by amendment the court may grant leave to amend rather than dismiss (Henry v. British Columbia (AG)).
firac.application: Because the NOCC contained facts capable of supporting viable non-derivative claims, dismissal was inappropriate; the appropriate remedy mirrored Stoneman. The plaintiff could not obtain discovery before filing intelligible pleadings.
firac.conclusion: The NOCC is struck with leave to amend to plead non-derivative causes of action within 90 days; the action is stayed meanwhile; if no amended NOCC is filed the defendants may apply to dismiss, and may later apply to strike any amended pleading. The defendants, being substantially successful, were awarded costs payable in any event of the cause.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the primary tier-1 area — this is a civil/commercial pleadings dispute concerning striking a Notice of Civil Claim, derivative actions and oppression under the Business Corporations Act. The controlled vocabulary contains no corporate-law, pleadings, or derivative-action keyword, so the remaining picks are the closest available and are flagged as weak: K085 (wrongful dismissal) and its parent K009 (Labour and employment law) reflect the plaintiff's claim that she was fraudulently terminated as President/employee, though this is only one strand of a corporate dispute; K021 (interlocutory injunction) reflects the injunctive relief sought against Vanstar but was not itself decided; K015 (defamation) is included only because the NOCC originally pleaded defamation, but those claims were being abandoned and so are weak. K011 (judicial review) is arguably inapposite and is a stretch reflecting the court's supervisory function over pleadings — flagged as weak. Overall the vocabulary is a poor fit for this corporate-procedure decision; K002 is the only firmly applicable term.

case_name: Wang v. British Columbia Medical Association

name_verification.name_in_document: Wang v. British Columbia Medical Association

defining_issues: Should the individual defendants be ordered to produce further documents (their own agendas, minutes, notes, calendars and electronic communications) as material to proving or disproving malice under Rule 7-1?
Should the BCMA be ordered to produce further meeting minutes, agendas and post-litigation audio recordings, or are those recordings protected by solicitor-client privilege?
Are the BCMA's communications with counsel regarding governance and the special committee, and the drafts of the president's letters, protected by privilege and thus not producible?
Should each defendant be required to swear an affidavit verifying their list of documents under Rule 7-1(8)?

firac.issue: Should the individual defendants be ordered to produce further documents said to be material to proving malice under Rule 7-1?
firac.facts: The plaintiff, a physician suing BCMA directors and officers for defamation arising after her 2008 electoral defeat, sought the individual defendants' own agendas, minutes, handwritten and electronic notes, arguing defamation cases can turn on candid but damaging notes and that malice could be inferred from them. Affidavit evidence showed several defendants had deleted emails, suffered hard-drive failures, or had no relevant documents; others had disclosed all documents.
firac.rule: Rule 7-1(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules limits initial production to documents that could be used to prove or disprove a material fact, consistent with the proportionality principle in Rule 1-3(2) (Biehl v. Strang, 2010 BCSC 1391). Materiality focuses on the material issues in dispute; the material fact here is malice, which may be proved by extrinsic evidence of the defendant's conduct and state of mind (Brown on Defamation; Simpson v. Mair, 2004 BCSC 754; Turner v. MGM Pictures).
firac.application: The court found the individual defendants had produced their documents and that the only potential source of further disclosure was deleted or lost emails of Appleton, Cavers, Fritz and Vance. Whether recoverable emails exist could be explored at the upcoming examinations for discovery. Rather than order production now, the court would permit the plaintiff to renew the application before the case-managing judge if discovery revealed that relevant documents exist or could be recovered.
firac.conclusion: The application to compel the individual defendants to produce additional documents was dismissed, with liberty to renew after examinations for discovery.

firac.issue: Should the BCMA be ordered to produce further meeting minutes, agendas and post-litigation audio recordings, or are they privileged?
firac.facts: The plaintiff demanded all BCMA board and executive audio recordings from June 2008 to October 2011. The BCMA had already produced digitized recordings from June 2007 to February 2009 (which the plaintiff refused to pay for). In-house counsel Cathy Cordell swore that the plaintiff was referred to only on a small number of occasions, always in the context of legal advice, litigation strategy or costs.
firac.rule: Documents whose dominant purpose is seeking or giving legal advice, or relating to litigation strategy and instructions to counsel, are protected by privilege. Production still requires materiality to a material fact under Rule 7-1.
firac.application: The court accepted Ms. Cordell's evidence that the vast majority of meeting content concerned the ordinary business of the BCMA and that references to the plaintiff arose only in privileged contexts. It saw no meaningful distinction between the parties' claimed purposes for recording meetings (accuracy) and concluded the plaintiff's name arose only in privileged discussions.
firac.conclusion: The application for further minutes, agendas and audio recordings was dismissed; the court would not order production of the recordings.

firac.issue: Are the BCMA's communications with counsel on governance and the special committee, and drafts of the president's letters, privileged?
firac.facts: The plaintiff sought pre-February 2008 communications with internal/external counsel on governance, process and procedure, communications about the ad hoc special committee struck to investigate her alleged breach of the code of conduct, and drafts of the president's letters/bulletins. Cordell's affidavit stated the letters were prepared or edited by the BCMA's external counsel and reflected confidential legal advice. The plaintiff was in acknowledged conflict with the board, had retained counsel, and had earlier litigated the special committee (2008 BCSC 1559; 2010 BCCA 43).
firac.rule: Solicitor-client privilege belongs to the corporation (BCMA), not its individual members, and a director-litigant in conflict with the corporation cannot negate that privilege (Dublin v. Montessori Jewish Day School of Toronto, 2007 CanLII 8923 (ON SC)). Legal advice must also be material to a fact in issue to be producible.
firac.application: The court held the plaintiff was in conflict with the board and not entitled to its solicitor-client communications. The advice on process, procedure and governance of the special committee, and the counsel-prepared drafts of the president's letters, did not tend to prove whether the impugned communications were defamatory or whether the BCMA breached its contract with her — questions for the court, not counsel.
firac.conclusion: The communications with counsel and drafts of the president's letters were held privileged and need not be disclosed; those parts of the application were dismissed.

firac.issue: Should each defendant be required to swear an affidavit verifying their list of documents under Rule 7-1(8)?
firac.facts: The plaintiff sought verifying affidavits from each of the 15 defendants. The broadened disclosure demand was only served on October 17, 2011; the action had been stayed pending payment of outstanding costs paid on the last day (September 6, 2011); and no examinations for discovery had yet occurred, the trial being set for January 2012.
firac.rule: Rule 7-1(8) permits an order that a party verify its list of documents by affidavit; the court exercises discretion having regard to fairness and the proportionality principle.
firac.application: The court found it would be unfair to order verifying affidavits given the late broadening of the demand and the plaintiff's own delay in conducting discoveries, which she bore responsibility for. Whether such affidavits were warranted would be better assessed after the examinations for discovery.
firac.conclusion: The application for verifying affidavits was adjourned, with liberty to bring it before the trial management judge if the plaintiff determined it was required after discovery.

keywords_rationale: K002 (Civil litigation) is the governing tier-1 area — this is an interlocutory document-disclosure application in a civil defamation suit under the Supreme Court Civil Rules. K015 (defamation) is central: the underlying action pleads defamation and the disclosure test turns on materiality to that claim. K016 (fair comment) and K018 (qualified privilege) are directly engaged because the defendants pleaded these defences and the entire relevance analysis focused on whether documents could prove malice needed to defeat them. K013 (professional discipline) is a borderline pick — the BCMA is a professional body and the dispute arose from a code-of-conduct investigation via an ad hoc committee, though the action itself is defamation/contract, not discipline. K042 (code of conduct) is likewise borderline, tied to the code of conduct the plaintiff agreed to and its alleged breach, but it is catalogued under Education and is only contextual here. The vocabulary lacks specific terms for document production, discovery, or solicitor-client privilege, which are the true operative doctrines, so these are the closest available matches.
