case_name: Vellacott v Saskatoon Starphoenix Group Inc

name_verification.name_in_document: MAURICE VELLACOTT v. SASKATOON STARPHOENIX GROUP INC., DARREN BERNHARDT and JAMES PARKER

defining_issues: Were the words complained of in the two newspaper articles defamatory of the plaintiff?
Did the defence of responsible communication on matters of public interest protect the defendants?
Did the defence of qualified privilege protect the defendants?
Did the defence of fair comment protect the defendants?

firac.issue: Were the words complained of in the two newspaper articles defamatory of the plaintiff?
firac.facts: The plaintiff, a Member of Parliament, used his franking and 'ten percenter' mailing privileges to distribute materials supporting a party leadership candidate. The StarPhoenix published two articles (March 4 and 5, 2002) quoting party members and MPs criticizing this use, including statements that it was 'crooked' to send such mail by franking and that MPs were 'put in office ... not to steal from us', plus references to the Bakkers and to 'abusing' privileges and not passing 'the smell test'.
firac.rule: A plaintiff must prove the words were defamatory (would tend to lower reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person), referred to the plaintiff, and were published: Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61. Words are judged objectively by the standard of an ordinary, right-thinking, reasonably informed person, avoiding the worst possible meaning: Color Your World Corp. v. CBC (1998); Lund v. Black Press Group Ltd., 2009 BCSC 937. Criticism of public officials is not automatically defamatory, but words imputing moral fault or criminality cross the line: Wells v. Puddister, 2007 NLCA 25.
firac.application: Reference and publication were conceded. The court found most passages, though harsh, were legitimate criticism of a politician. However, the Ballantyne quote calling the conduct 'crooked' and the Fyfe quote suggesting the plaintiff was 'stealing' from the public imputed moral fault/criminality and would lower reputation in the eyes of a reasonably informed reader; these two passages in the Bernhardt article were defamatory. The Bakker comparison was mere hyperbole, and none of the four impugned passages in the Parker article were defamatory.
firac.conclusion: Two passages in the first article were defamatory; the second (Parker) article was not, so the action against Parker was dismissed outright.

firac.issue: Did the defence of responsible communication on matters of public interest protect the defendants?
firac.facts: Both articles concerned a federal party leadership race and an MP's use of publicly funded communication allowances. Reporters interviewed multiple named sources, obtained copies of the mailouts, sought the plaintiff's response (obtained by Bernhardt, unsuccessfully attempted by Parker who reiterated prior comments), and an expert testified the articles met best journalistic practices.
firac.rule: Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61 and Quan v. Cusson, 2009 SCC 62 establish the defence of responsible communication: the publication must be on a matter of public interest, and the publisher must have acted responsibly, assessed against the eight factors in Grant (seriousness, public importance, urgency, source reliability, whether the plaintiff's side was sought, justifiability of inclusion, reportage, and other circumstances).
firac.application: The leadership race, internal party strife, and use of taxpayer-funded privileges were matters of genuine public interest. Applying the Grant factors, the allegations did not seriously impute criminality, the matter was publicly important, sources were named and reliable, the plaintiff's side was sought and prominently reported, inclusion of the impugned statements was justifiable, and the repetition qualified as reportage. The defendants met and exceeded the standard, and there was no malice.
firac.conclusion: The defence of responsible communication succeeded and the claim was dismissed on this basis.

firac.issue: Did the defence of qualified privilege protect the defendants?
firac.facts: The articles reported on infighting during a national leadership race and the propriety of an elected official's use of communication allowances, disseminated to the public through the newspaper.
firac.rule: Qualified privilege attaches to an occasion where the maker has a duty or interest to communicate and the recipient a corresponding interest to receive; it presumes bona fides and is defeated only by proof of malice: Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309; Hill v. Church of Scientology, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130; Brown, The Law of Defamation. Courts have recognized the media's legitimate interest in reporting on the conduct of governments and elected officials (Loos v. Robbins; Stopforth v. Goyer; Parlett v. Robinson).
firac.application: The public had a real interest in the leadership race and in whether elected representatives spent their allowances properly, and the media had a corresponding interest in publishing it. There was a sufficient nexus between the defendants' publication and the public interest to establish a privileged occasion, and no malice was proven.
firac.conclusion: Qualified privilege availed all defendants and provided an alternative basis for dismissal.

firac.issue: Did the defence of fair comment protect the defendants?
firac.facts: The impugned 'crooked' and 'steal' statements were opinions expressed by third parties about the plaintiff's admitted use of his franking privilege to support a leadership candidate, reported in the context of a leadership race.
firac.rule: Fair comment protects prima facie defamatory words that are recognizable as comment, based on true facts, on a matter of public interest, that any person could honestly express on the proven facts, absent proof of express malice: WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Myers v. CBC (1999); Cherneskey. The objective test is not a high threshold and protects obstinate, prejudiced or offensive opinion.
firac.application: The 'crooked' and 'steal' statements were recognizable as opinion/characterizations rather than fact, rested on the true and admitted underlying facts (the franked mailouts supporting a candidate, ultimately at public expense), concerned a matter of public interest, and were comments an honest person could make on those facts. No malice was established.
firac.conclusion: The defence of fair comment also availed the defendants, and the action was dismissed on this basis as well, with costs to the defendants on Column 4.

keywords_rationale: The case is a defamation action, so K002 (Civil litigation, the tier-1 practice area) and K015 (defamation) are core. K019 (responsible communication) was the primary defence and outcome-determinative under Grant/Quan. K018 (qualified privilege) and K016 (fair comment) were the two alternative defences the court analyzed and upheld. K024 (freedom of expression) is engaged as the underlying policy animating the responsible-communication and fair-comment analyses and the protection of criticism of public officials; it is a slightly weaker, contextual pick but justified given the court's repeated reliance on free political debate.
location_rationale: The header states 'QUEEN'S BENCH FOR SASKATCHEWAN' and 'Judicial Centre: Saskatoon', and the body refers to 'IN THE COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH FOR SASKATCHEWAN, JUDICIAL CENTRE OF SASKATOON'.
registry_rationale: The decision expressly designates the 'Judicial Centre: Saskatoon' (Docket Q.B.G. No. 1725/2002), which is the registry.

name_verification.name_in_document: Marilyn Anne Solomon v. Gerald David Solomon

defining_issues: Was the wife's Workers' Compensation Appeal Board award an exempted (non-matrimonial) asset, and how should the matrimonial assets be divided?
What level and duration of spousal and child maintenance should be ordered given the parties' means and needs?
Does the Court have jurisdiction to, and should it, order as a condition of custody/access that the two boys become bar mitzvah at age 13?

firac.issue: Was the wife's Workers' Compensation award excluded from matrimonial assets, and should the matrimonial assets be divided equally?
firac.facts: The parties, married in 1983, separated in 1989 with two young children. The husband, a veterinarian with a 1/4 partnership interest, and the wife, a former nurse now working in day care, disputed the treatment of a $15,000 Workers' Compensation Appeal Board award received by the wife, and whether assets should be split equally. A $10,000 sum from the husband's parents was found to be a repayable loan.
firac.rule: Section 4(1)(b) of the Matrimonial Property Act, 1980 excepts 'an award or settlement of damages in court in favour of one spouse' from matrimonial assets; s. 4(2) qualifies this for awards paid in respect of a matrimonial asset. Section 13 authorizes an unequal division of matrimonial assets where an equal division would be unfair, having regard to factors including s. 13(b) and (h).
firac.application: The Court held a Workers' Compensation Board award is not the equivalent of an award or settlement of damages 'in court', so it is not exempt; and in any event it was paid in respect of lost income which, if accumulated, would be a matrimonial asset. The partnership interest was found to be a business asset, not a matrimonial asset. Because the wife would have custody of the children with attendant needs, and given the difficulty of dividing the partnership interest, an equal division would be unfair.
firac.conclusion: The compensation award was a matrimonial asset. The Court ordered a 70%/30% division of matrimonial assets in favour of the wife, allocating the specific assets accordingly and directing sale of the matrimonial home to give effect to the split.

firac.issue: What maintenance should be ordered given the parties' means and needs?
firac.facts: The husband earned about $5,750/month with a projected deficit driven partly by business debts of some $47,000; he had voluntarily paid $1,800/month without prejudice. The wife earned about $305/month in day care plus family allowance, and could not resume nursing because of a lumbar disc protrusion for which she reasonably declined surgery.
firac.rule: Sections 15(5), (7) and (8) of the Divorce Act, 1985 require consideration of the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of each spouse and child, promotion of economic self-sufficiency so far as practicable, and apportionment of the joint obligation to maintain children according to relative abilities to contribute.
firac.application: The Court accepted the wife was doing her best and could not resume nursing, but found the husband could not sustain $1,800/month while repaying business debts essential to preserving his income; requiring the present level short-term would harm his long-term ability to pay. The long-term interests of the children and wife should prevail.
firac.conclusion: Maintenance was reduced to $1,400/month for two years to allow debt reduction, after which the husband is to resume the current level or such level as a court then orders.

firac.issue: Should the Court order that the two boys become bar mitzvah at age 13 as an incident of custody/access?
firac.facts: The husband is Jewish (though non-observant) and wanted the boys, who were circumcised according to Jewish rites, to become bar mitzvah to know Jewish tradition and understand anti-Semitism. The wife, a convert to Judaism who returned to Catholicism, intended to raise them Catholic but agreed to expose them to Judaism; she opposed compelled bar mitzvahs. The parties had agreed the wife would have custody with liberal access to the husband.
firac.rule: Under the Court's inherent parens patriae jurisdiction and s. 16 of the Divorce Act, 1985, custody/access orders are governed solely by the best interests of the child. Courts do not choose between faiths (In re J.M. Carroll; Re Custody of Pamela A.) and a custodial parent generally directs religious upbringing (Henderson; Gunn; Brown; Fougere), while a non-custodial parent's religion may be exposed to the children (Pfeifer).
firac.application: The Court held it had jurisdiction to make the order. Assessing the children's condition, means, needs and circumstances, it found exposure to both faiths would not be damaging and would foster understanding and tolerance; it doubted the wife's commitment to expose them to Judaism given the secret baptism. Delaying the decision would in effect favour the mother's position, so an immediate decision was preferable. The decision was framed not as choosing a religion but as giving the children the opportunity to know both faiths and eventually choose.
firac.conclusion: The Court directed both parents to encourage and give the two children the opportunity to study and celebrate their bar mitzvahs, with liberty to apply to Family Court for directions if the parents cannot agree.

keywords_rationale: K006 (Family law) is the tier-1 practice area. The case turns on best interests of the child (K047), which governed both the maintenance apportionment and the religious-upbringing order. K052 (religious upbringing — its synonyms include bar mitzvah) captures the distinctive third issue. K053 (spousal support) and K050 (parental/child support) cover the maintenance analysis, and K048 (custody/access) reflects the s. 16 framework the bar-mitzvah order was decided under. K117 (Divorce Act) is the governing statute for maintenance and custody/access. K093 (Jewish) and K095 (Jewish family) capture the religious-community context of the bar mitzvah dispute. Matrimonial property division has no dedicated vocabulary entry, so it is covered under the family-law tier-1 term. K093/K095 are somewhat contextual/entity picks rather than legal-doctrine ones.
location_rationale: The decision states it was 'HEARD at Halifax, Nova Scotia, before the Honourable Mr. Justice Nathanson, Trial Division' and is signed 'Halifax, Nova Scotia December 28, 1990', in the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, Trial Division.
registry_rationale: The matter was heard and the judgment issued at Halifax in the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia (Trial Division), so the registry is Halifax.

case_name: The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs v. Minister of Public Affairs and Business Delivery and Procurement

name_verification.name_in_document: The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs/Le Centre consultatif des relations juives et israéliennes v. Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement and University of Windsor
name_verification.discrepancy_note: The supplied name matches the document's 'CITATION' line verbatim (Minister of Public Affairs and Business Delivery and Procurement). However, the style of cause in the BETWEEN block names the respondent as 'Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement' and adds the University of Windsor as a co-respondent. This is a minor internal wording variation in the ministry's title; the citation (2025 ONSC 5477) is consistent.

defining_issues: Was the Director's determination that the Discriminatory Business Practices Act did not apply because the University was not a business nor 'engaging in business' in relation to the impugned Provision reasonable?
Was the Director's alternative finding that the agreements did not meet the requirements of s. 4(1)3(ii) of the Act reasonable?

firac.issue: Was the Director's determination that the Discriminatory Business Practices Act did not apply because the University was not 'engaging in business' in relation to the impugned Provision reasonable?
firac.facts: The University of Windsor entered into two agreements with student groups to resolve protest encampments, including a Provision that the University would not pursue institutional academic agreements with Israeli universities until Palestinian self-determination was realized, unless supported by the Senate. CIJA complained to the Director under the Act, who concluded in a December 23, 2024 letter that the Act was not engaged because the University is a public academic institution whose primary purpose is education and research, not profit.
firac.rule: The standard of review is reasonableness (Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65); the court assesses whether the Director's statutory interpretation is reasonable, not conducting a de novo interpretation. The Act (Discriminatory Business Practices Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. D.12) aims at business relationships; s. 2 targets discrimination against 'persons employed in or engaging in business', and s. 4 deems certain 'discriminatory business practices'. Whether an entity carries on business turns on the 'preponderant purpose' test: if profit-making is the preponderant purpose it is a business (Ontario (Regional Assessment Commissioner) v. Caisse Populaire de Hearst, [1983] 1 S.C.R. 57). Beauchamp v. North Central Predators AAA Hockey Assn. (2004 CanLII 48698) is the leading interpretation of the Act.
firac.application: The Court held that the analysis could be resolved on the specific facts of the Provision. The Provision concerned the University's institutional academic partnerships with Israeli universities — a core non-business, academic purpose. Reading s. 4(1)3(ii) in the context of the Act's title, purpose and wording (all directed at 'business' relationships), it was reasonable for the Director to conclude the University was not engaging in business in relation to this Provision. Reliance on Beauchamp (hockey associations not businesses due to non-profit preponderant purpose) was not unreasonable, and the 1991 Ontario Science Centre 'assurance of voluntary compliance' — a profit-generating contract with Oman — was distinguishable and had little precedential value.
firac.conclusion: The Director's conclusion that the Act did not apply to the Provision in the student agreements was reasonable.

firac.issue: Was the Director's alternative finding that the agreements did not meet the requirements of s. 4(1)3(ii) of the Act reasonable?
firac.facts: CIJA argued the Provision meant Israeli academics could not teach or research at the University and that University faculty would be precluded from opportunities at Israeli universities affecting their advancement. The Provision was subject to Senate approval and expressly stated it did not prevent individual academics at the University from working or collaborating with academics in Israel.
firac.rule: Section 4(1)3(ii) requires a contract that includes a provision that a party 'will refuse or fail to employ or promote or will dismiss or suspend from employment' a second person on account of an attribute. The modern principle of statutory interpretation requires reading the plain language in light of purpose and context (Vavilov, para. 118).
firac.application: The Court found the Provision was not mandatory — it was subject to the Senate's statutory role under the University of Windsor Act and by-laws, not a device to evade the Act. Any uncertainty about impact on professors was addressed by the Provision's express carve-out allowing individual academics to collaborate with Israeli academics. As for Israeli professors, the applicant did not demonstrate any employment relationship between the University and those professors that would engage the 'refuse to employ/promote/dismiss/suspend' language of the Act.
firac.conclusion: The Director's conclusion that the requirements of s. 4(1)3(ii) were not met was reasonable.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the tier-1 practice area — the case is a judicial review of a statutory decision-maker's interpretation. K011 (judicial review) and K014 (standard of review) are central, the entire decision turning on reasonableness review under Vavilov of the Director's interpretation of the Discriminatory Business Practices Act. K059 (boycott) captures the impugned 'academic boycott provision' and the Act's origins in the Arab boycott of Israel. K041 (campus/university) and K040 (academic freedom) reflect the university encampment agreements and institutional academic partnerships at issue (academic freedom is somewhat peripheral but was raised in supporting letters). K091 (CIJA) identifies the applicant. K087 (protest/demonstration) reflects the encampment context giving rise to the agreements. K103 (Israel) and K104 (Palestine) are the geopolitical subjects of the Provision. Weaker/borderline picks: K040 (academic freedom) and K104 (Palestine) are contextual rather than legally determinative.
location_rationale: The decision states 'ONTARIO SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE DIVISIONAL COURT' and 'HEARD at Toronto: September 29, 2025', establishing Toronto, Ontario.
registry_rationale: The header identifies the 'DIVISIONAL COURT' with 'COURT FILE NO.: 066/25', indicating the Divisional Court of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice as the registry/office.

case_name: Spence et al. v. Manitoba et al.

name_verification.name_in_document: Spence et al. v. Manitoba et al.

defining_issues: On judicial review of the Minister's Final Licence decision, must Manitoba produce an unredacted Final Licence Record where the redactions concern the confidential consultation and funding information of non-party Indigenous communities?

Should the Court order Manitoba to add six documents (correspondence, an op-ed and third-party letters) to the Consultation Record when Manitoba does not consider them part of the Final Licence consultation process?
Should the Court order Manitoba to produce internal government deliberative documents that informed the recommendation to the Minister but were never before her?

firac.issue: Must Manitoba produce an unredacted Final Licence Record where the redactions withhold confidential consultation and funding information relating to non-party Indigenous communities?
firac.facts: Tataskweyak Cree Nation (TCN) seeks judicial review of the Minister's decision to issue a Final Licence to Manitoba Hydro for the Churchill River Diversion, alleging breach of the Crown's duty to consult. Manitoba redacted portions of the Final Licence Record containing budget/funding tables, a consultation participation table, information provided in confidence by other Indigenous communities, and financial figures relating to the Augmented Flow Program.
firac.rule: The Crown has a common law duty to provide the record of proceedings on judicial review (Kalo v. Winnipeg, 2019 MBCA 46). Redactions may be justified where the redacted portion is clearly irrelevant and the redaction is necessary to protect an important interest or prevent significant harm; the onus rests on the party seeking to maintain the redaction (WSIB Investments v. Plenary Group, 2022 MBQB 145; Duhamel, 2018 BCSC 601; McGee, 2010 ONSC 1408). Adequacy of consultation is a group-specific factual inquiry, not a comparative exercise (Haida Nation, 2004 SCC 73; Bigstone Cree Nation, 2018 FCA 89; Tsleil-Waututh, 2018 FCA 153). Confidential commercial and third-party interests can constitute an important interest (Sierra Club, 2002 SCC 41; Sherman Estate, 2021 SCC 25).
firac.application: The Court found the redacted funding, consultation-table and community information clearly irrelevant because the adequacy of consultation with TCN must be judged only on TCN's own consultation record, not by comparison to other communities; TCN's premise that Manitoba rejected its work plans over funding amounts was unsupported. The AFP financial figures were only one reason for incorporating the AFP and were irrelevant. Disclosure would harm Manitoba Hydro's confidential commercial interests and, more significantly, undermine the confidentiality that Indigenous communities reasonably expect, threatening the free, open, reconciliatory dialogue essential to Crown-Indigenous consultation (relying on the uncontested Silva affidavit and Métis Nation of Alberta, 2021 ABQB 282). The proposed sealed-filing alternative would not avoid the harm because confidential community information would still be disclosed to a third party.
firac.conclusion: Order #1 refused; Manitoba need not produce an unredacted Final Licence Record.

firac.issue: Should the Court order Manitoba to include six additional documents in the Consultation Record?
firac.facts: TCN sought to add to the Consultation Record letters between TCN and the Deputy Minister about the AFP, an open letter and Winnipeg Free Press op-ed by TCN and OPCN, and correspondence to the Minister from religious organizations (the Interchurch Council and the Mennonite Church Manitoba).
firac.rule: The Administrative Record consists of the material that was before the original decision-maker, and evidence not before the decision-maker is generally inadmissible on judicial review (Kalo, 2019 MBCA 46). Extrinsic material may be introduced only through the applicant's own affidavit evidence establishing a proper foundation, within recognized exceptions (Pimicikamak, 2018 MBCA 49 and 2014 MBQB 143; Manitoba Métis Federation Inc. v. Pallister, 2019 MBQB 118).
firac.application: The Court found TCN conflated the Administrative Record with the Consultation Record and cited no authority requiring the Crown's affiant to swear a new affidavit attaching documents the Crown does not regard as part of the consultation process. The proposed documents were not related to the Final Licence consultation process, and the proper route for TCN was to adduce its own extra-record affidavit evidence.
firac.conclusion: Order #2 refused.

firac.issue: Should the Court order production of internal government deliberative documents that informed the recommendation to the Minister but were never before her?
firac.facts: TCN sought production of internal input from technical experts, the Wildlife and Fisheries Branch, and correspondence between Manitoba Conservation and Climate and Manitoba Hydro concerning the proposed licence terms — documents acknowledged not to be part of the Final Licence Record or Consultation Record.
firac.rule: Discovery is generally unavailable in applications (Jewish Community Campus of Winnipeg v. Metaser, 2013 MBQB 303); a court may order production only of documents actually or potentially admissible as extrinsic evidence, judicial review not being a hearing de novo (Pimicikamak (QB), 2014 MBQB 143). A decision-maker's internal files do not form part of the Administrative Record if they were not before the decision-maker (Waverley v. Nova Scotia, 1993 NSCA; Manitoba Métis Federation Inc., 2018 MBQB 131). The Gitxaala Nation (2016 FCA 187) participatory right arose from a specific statutory step under the National Energy Board Act with no equivalent under The Water Power Act.
firac.application: The documents were prepared internally to give ministerial advice and consider options, were never before the Minister, and were irrelevant to the adequacy-of-consultation issue. Ordering their production would transform the application into a de novo hearing of public servants' deliberations. Gitxaala's participatory-rights holding was distinguishable because it depended on a statutory recommendation step absent here, and Manitoba Métis Federation Inc. supported treating such deliberative advisory documents as irrelevant and normally not subject to access; disclosure would also harm free and open internal deliberation.
firac.conclusion: Order #3 refused; the motion is dismissed in its entirety.

keywords_rationale: K001 (Administrative law) is the primary tier-1 area — the case is a motion within a judicial review of a statutory licensing decision. K011 (judicial review) is central: the dispute concerns the proper scope of the record of proceedings on judicial review and the rule that review is not a hearing de novo. K012 (procedural fairness) is genuinely engaged because TCN argued that procedural fairness required an opportunity to comment on the recommendations to the Minister. K014 (standard of review) is a weaker pick, included because the underlying application alleges the Minister's decision was unreasonable, though the motion itself did not turn on it. K002 (Civil litigation) is a borderline pick reflecting the civil-procedure/document-production character of the motion; the controlled vocabulary lacks a specific keyword for the duty to consult, Aboriginal/Crown consultation, or administrative-record disclosure, so no closer term was available.
location_rationale: The header identifies the 'COURT OF KING'S BENCH OF MANITOBA' with docket 'CI 22-01-34789 (Winnipeg Centre)', establishing Winnipeg, Manitoba as the location.
registry_rationale: The docket line reads '(Winnipeg Centre)', identifying the Winnipeg Centre registry of the Court of King's Bench of Manitoba.

name_verification.name_in_document: Volpe v. Wong-Tam

defining_issues: Did the moving-party defendants establish that the defamation action arises from an expression relating to a matter of public interest under s. 137.1(3) of the Courts of Justice Act?

Did the plaintiffs establish grounds to believe that their causes of action (defamation, misfeasance in public office, inducing breach of contract, and interference with economic relations) have substantial merit under s. 137.1(4)(a)(i)?

Did the plaintiffs establish grounds to believe that the defendants had no valid defence (fair comment, qualified privilege, justification, statutory immunity, responsible communication) under s. 137.1(4)(a)(ii)?

Did the plaintiffs establish that the harm suffered was sufficiently serious that the public interest in permitting the action to continue outweighed the public interest in protecting the expression under s. 137.1(4)(b)?

firac.issue: Did the moving-party defendants establish that the action arises from an expression relating to a matter of public interest under s. 137.1(3)?
firac.facts: Volpe, publisher of the Italian-Canadian newspaper Corriere Canadese, wrote articles attacking TCDSB trustees and the LGBTQ2S+ community, including calling an LGBT YouthLine link a 'recruitment site' and 'smut site.' City councillors (Wong-Tam, Ainslie) and TCDSB trustees responded with tweets, a City Council motion, a joint letter and press-conference statements describing the plaintiffs as homophobic, transphobic and anti-LGBTQ2S+; Yahoo published an article stating Volpe had 'well documented anti-LGBTQ+ views.'
firac.rule: Under s. 137.1(3) the moving party must show on a balance of probabilities that the proceeding arises from its expression and that the expression relates to a matter of public interest, defined broadly and without qualitative assessment (1704604 Ontario Ltd. v. Pointes Protection Association, 2020 SCC 22; Grant v. Torstar, 2009 SCC 61; Grist v. TrueGrp Inc., 2021 ONCA 309).
firac.application: All impugned statements were communications ('expressions') from which the action arose. The expressions related to the TCDSB's removal and reinstatement of the LGBT YouthLine link, the use of public taxpayer funds for City advertising, and the councillors' and trustees' statutory duties (CTA s. 131, HRAP; Education Act s. 169.1) to represent constituents and ensure a safe, inclusive school environment. These are quintessential matters of public interest, not private disputes or attempts to 'censor' the newspaper.
firac.conclusion: The defendants met the s. 137.1(3) threshold; the burden shifted to the plaintiffs under s. 137.1(4).

firac.issue: Did the plaintiffs establish substantial merit of their causes of action under s. 137.1(4)(a)(i)?
firac.facts: The plaintiffs advanced defamation, misfeasance in public office (and abuse of authority), inducing breach of contract, and wrongful interference with economic relations, seeking over $30 million; the impugned statements characterized the plaintiffs as homophobic, transphobic and anti-LGBTQ2S+.
firac.rule: The plaintiff must show a 'real prospect of success' that tends to weigh more in its favour (Pointes, paras. 49-50). Defamation requires publication, reference to the plaintiff, and words tending to lower reputation (Bent v. Platnick, 2020 SCC 23). Misfeasance requires a deliberate unlawful act in bad faith intended to harm (Odhavji Estate; Catalyst v. Dundee Kilmer). Inducing breach of contract requires a breached contract known to the defendant (Drouillard). Interference with economic relations requires unlawful means against a third party (A.I. Enterprises v. Bram).
firac.application: Calling the plaintiffs homophobic/transphobic/anti-LGBTQ2S+ would tend to lower reputation, so defamation had substantial merit; the court declined to take a 'deep dive' into existing reputation. However, there was no evidence of bad faith, unlawful acts, an existing City advertising contract (advertising was 'buy-as-we-need'), knowledge of any contract, or intent to injure economic interests; councillors and trustees acted within their statutory duties. The other torts therefore lacked a real prospect of success.
firac.conclusion: Only the defamation claim had substantial merit; the remaining claims failed s. 137.1(4)(a)(i).

firac.issue: Did the plaintiffs establish that the defendants had no valid defence under s. 137.1(4)(a)(ii)?
firac.facts: Defendants relied on fair comment (all), qualified privilege (councillors and trustees), justification (councillors, Li Preti, Yahoo), statutory immunity under CTA s. 391 (councillors), and responsible communication (Yahoo Defendants). The impugned characterizations were grounded in Volpe's own published articles.
firac.rule: The plaintiff must show a real prospect of success that none of the defences would succeed. Fair comment requires public-interest comment, a factual basis, recognizability as comment, an opinion any person could honestly hold, and absence of express malice (WIC Radio v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Awan v. Levant; Mondal v. Evans-Bitten). Qualified privilege attaches to reciprocal duty/interest communications, including elected officials and their electorate (Hill; Prud'homme; Stopforth; Parlett). Justification requires truth of the sting (Bent). Responsible communication requires public interest and diligence (Grant v. Torstar). CTA s. 391 immunizes good-faith acts of councillors.
firac.application: Calling someone homophobic is recognizable as comment, was based on Volpe's own inflammatory articles (a 'sufficient launching pad'), could be honestly held (others including Pizza Nova and LGBT YouthLine reached the same view), and showed no malice, being made in good faith in a public debate the plaintiffs initiated. Qualified privilege applied to the councillors' and trustees' communications made under their duties to constituents on the HRAP and public spending, within appropriate scope and without malice. Justification could succeed if the statements were facts. The Yahoo Defendants reported diligently on a public-interest matter. The plaintiffs failed to show any defence lacked a real prospect of success.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to establish no valid defence; the fair-comment finding alone was sufficient to dismiss the action.

firac.issue: Did the plaintiffs establish that harm was sufficiently serious to outweigh the public interest in protecting the expression under s. 137.1(4)(b)?
firac.facts: Volpe asserted lost advertising and reputational harm but produced no contracts, no revenue figures and no financial records; Pizza Nova had withdrawn advertising on November 17, 2020, before any impugned statement.
firac.rule: The plaintiff must show on a balance of probabilities that harm is causally connected to the expression and sufficiently serious that the public interest in continuing the proceeding outweighs the public interest in protecting the expression (Pointes, paras. 61-82; Levant v. DeMelle, 2022 ONCA 79; Armstrong v. Corus, 2018 ONCA 689). Bald assertions are insufficient.
firac.application: There was little or no evidence of monetary harm and no causal link, since Pizza Nova's earlier withdrawal preceded the statements. Against negligible harm stood strong public-interest expression: political speech by elected officials protecting the LGBTQ2S+ community, oversight of public spending, and free-press reporting, all lying at the core of s. 2(b). The plaintiffs had injected themselves into a heated public debate and should expect forceful rebuttal; permitting the claim would chill public debate.
firac.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed the weighing test; the balance strongly favoured protecting the expression.

case_name: United Association of Journeyman and Apprentices of Plumbing v. Hawco

name_verification.name_in_document: United Association of Journeyman and Apprentices of Plumbing v. Hawco

defining_issues: Did the arbitration board err in law by failing to interpret the collective agreement as amended by s. 6 of the Individual's Rights Protection Act?

Does the failure to schedule work on Jewish religious holidays (per the owner's contract) constitute discrimination in employment under s. 6(1) of the Individual's Rights Protection Act, and can the owner (Olympia) fall within 'any other person'?
Could the court, on certiorari/mandamus, amend the collective agreement in light of the statute, and was the grievance the proper remedy?

firac.issue: Did the arbitration board err in law by not treating the collective agreement as amended by the Individual's Rights Protection Act?
firac.facts: The company agreed with Olympia (cl. 46) not to work from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset or on Jewish holidays. Union members were consequently limited to fewer than the normal 35–36 weekly hours. The union grieved a breach of art. 5.05 of the collective agreement, arguing the agreement should be read as amended by s. 6 IRPA.
firac.rule: Under the Alberta Labour Act, 1973, s. 138(4) model clause para (f), an arbitration board 'shall not alter, amend or change the terms of the collective agreement.' Article 5.05 guarantees no less than 35 hours pay for an employee 'working' the complete normal hours in the pay period.
firac.application: Moore J. held the key word in art. 5.05 is 'working': the guarantee applies only to days actually worked. A day on which no work is scheduled because the company could not work under its Olympia contract is not a 'working day'. Nothing in the collective agreement precluded the company from scheduling fewer than five days, and the union had not challenged the board's finding that the agreement guaranteed no weekly or daily hours. The agreement did not conflict with the IRPA.
firac.conclusion: The board did not err in law; its interpretation of the collective agreement was correct.

firac.issue: Did the closure of the site on Jewish holidays amount to employment discrimination under s. 6 IRPA, and can the owner fall within 'any other person'?
firac.facts: The company argued the arrangement flowed from the owner's contract; no one worked on the specified days. The union argued the company was an employer under s. 6(1) and that Olympia fell within 'any other person' in s. 6(1)(b).
firac.rule: Section 6(1) IRPA prohibits an employer from refusing to employ or discriminating in terms of employment because of religious belief of that person 'or of any other person.'
firac.application: The board found no differentiation against these employees over and above others, since no one worked on the specified days. Moore J. agreed and further held that Olympia, the owner, could not properly fall within the words 'or any other person', as the section addresses discrimination by an employer against someone working for him, not the religious observance driving the site closure.
firac.conclusion: No discrimination under s. 6 was established; the owner did not fall within 'any other person'.

firac.issue: Could the court amend the collective agreement in light of the statute, and was the grievance the appropriate remedy?
firac.facts: The union sought certiorari and mandamus asking the court to read the agreement as entitling members to pay for work not done on Jewish holidays.
firac.rule: The Alberta Labour Act prohibits altering the terms of a collective agreement; a complaint of statutory discrimination must be pursued under the IRPA's own procedure.
firac.application: The court held it could not amend the agreement, as doing so would contravene the Alberta Labour Act. If the union had a genuine discrimination complaint, the proper course was to file proceedings under the IRPA rather than to seek amendment of the agreement through arbitration/judicial review.
firac.conclusion: The court would not amend the agreement; the IRPA route was the proper remedy. Application for certiorari and mandamus dismissed with costs to the company.

keywords_rationale: The case is primarily a labour matter (K009) turning on the interpretation of a collective agreement through grievance/labour arbitration (K084), reviewed by the court on certiorari and mandamus, i.e. judicial review (K011) engaging administrative law (K001). case_name: Zylberberg v. Sudbury Board of Education

name_verification.name_in_document: Re Zylberberg et al. and Director of Education of Sudbury Board of Education; League for Human Rights of B'Nai Brith Canada et al., Intervenors — Indexed as: Zylberberg v. Sudbury Board of Education (Director)

defining_issues: Does s. 28(1) of R.R.O. 1980, Reg. 262 (mandatory Scripture readings and the Lord's Prayer in public schools) infringe freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
Does the statutory right to claim exemption (s. 28(10)-(12); s. 50(2) Education Act) cure or mitigate any such infringement?
If s. 28(1) infringes s. 2(a), is it incapable of justification under s. 1 because its purpose is religious — and would it fail minimal impairment even if s. 1 applied?
Do s. 28 and s. 50 also violate equality rights under s. 15(1) of the Charter?

firac.issue: Do mandatory Christian opening exercises in public schools infringe s. 2(a)?
firac.facts: Sudbury Board schools opened daily with O Canada and the Lord's Prayer, with Scripture readings in some; the Board had not exercised its s. 28(1) option to use non-Christian prayers/readings. The three appellants were parents (one Jewish, one Muslim, one non-religious) of public-school pupils.
firac.rule: s. 2(a) Charter. Per R. v. Big M Drug Mart (1985), freedom of religion means freedom from coercion (direct and indirect), protects minorities from the 'tyranny of the majority', and protects non-believers' right to abstain. First step of Charter analysis is prima facie interference (Oakes).
firac.application: Reciting the Lord's Prayer (a Christian prayer) and reading Christian Scriptures imposes Christian observances on non-Christian pupils and religious observance on non-believers. Judged from the standpoint of religious minorities in the sensitive public-school setting, s. 28(1) compels conformity to majority practice; peer pressure on children is real and pervasive. The infringement is not trivial or insubstantial (Jones; Edwards Books).
firac.conclusion: On its face s. 28(1) infringes s. 2(a) (conceded by the respondents).

firac.issue: Does the exemption provision cure the infringement?
firac.facts: s. 28(10)-(12) and s. 50(2) allow a pupil/parent to seek exemption; the appellants declined, to avoid singling out their children.
firac.rule: Coercion includes indirect control (Big M); Abington School District v. Schempp (Brennan J.) — an excusal procedure can itself coerce by stigmatizing dissenters.
firac.application: Requiring pupils to seek exemption penalizes them by stigmatizing them as non-conformists, compels a religious statement, and discriminates against minorities (adopting the Mackay Committee). Its chilling effect discourages use of the exemption.
firac.conclusion: The exemption does not mitigate but aggravates the infringement.

firac.issue: Can the s. 2(a) breach be justified under s. 1?
firac.facts: The AG/Board asserted secular educational and moral objectives; appellants argued the purpose was religious.
firac.rule: s. 1 / Oakes proportionality. Where a law's purpose is to compel religious observance it is incapable of s. 1 justification (Big M; A.-G. Que. v. Quebec Ass'n of Protestant School Boards). Purpose, not effect, fixes constitutional character.
firac.application: After reviewing the Act, Regulations and history (Ryerson; Hope Commission; Mackay Report), the Court found the purpose of s. 28(1) religious, its moral/educational effects merely derivative — so s. 1 is unavailable. In any event it fails minimal impairment: the Toronto Board's multi-faith book of readings shows less intrusive means exist.
firac.conclusion: Incapable of s. 1 justification, and would fail s. 1 (minimal impairment) even if available.

firac.issue: Do s. 28 / s. 50 violate s. 15(1) equality rights?
firac.facts: Appellants also sought declarations under s. 15(1), the Religious Freedom Act, and the Ontario Human Rights Code.
firac.rule: s. 15(1) Charter; a court need not decide issues unnecessary to disposition.
firac.application: Having found s. 28(1) of no force or effect under s. 2(a) + s. 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982, the majority held it unnecessary to address the s. 15/statutory claims. Lacourciere J.A., dissenting, would have held s. 28 does not violate s. 15, but the Board's exclusively Christian practice did.
firac.conclusion: Not decided by the majority; addressed only in dissent.

K005 (Education law) is the second tier-1 area: the impugned provision is a public-school regulation under the Education Act. K025 (freedom of religion) is the core doctrine (s. 2(a)). defining_issues: Did the 1981 census questions concerning housing (Qq. 13–22) and employment/income (Qq. 39–46) fall within a “census of population” authorized by ss. 18 and 20(1) of the Statistics Act, or was the Order in Council prescribing them ultra vires?
Can an unreasonable intrusion upon an individual’s right to privacy constitute a “lawful excuse” under s. 29(b) of the Statistics Act for refusing to complete the census form?

Was the respondent “the occupant” liable to fill in and return the form under s. 31 of the Statistics Act, given that the form was not addressed to a named person and the dwelling had more than one occupant?

firac.issue: Were the housing and employment questions within a “census of population” under ss. 18 and 20(1) of the Statistics Act, or ultra vires the Order in Council?
firac.facts: The 1981 census, ordered by Order in Council P.C. 1980-477 (Feb. 8, 1980) under ss. 18 and 20(1) of the Statistics Act, used a long form (Qq. 1–46) delivered to one-fifth of households and a short form (Qq. 1–13) for the rest. Qq. 13–22 concerned housing (age and type of dwelling, rooms, heating equipment and fuel, state of repair, payments) and Qq. 39–46 concerned employment and income. The trial judge held these were not part of a “census of population” and were ultra vires.
firac.rule: Sections 18 and 20(1) authorize a “census of population,” which is undefined in the Act; in its ordinary meaning it is an official enumeration of the population (14 C.J.S. 101; Webster’s Third). Section 20(1) requires the Governor in Council to prescribe the census questions; s. 7.1 lets the Minister authorize the obtaining of non-census information on a voluntary basis; s. 8(2) empowers the Minister (not the Governor in Council) to authorize sampling; s. 21 lets the Governor in Council request statistics on a particular subject from the Minister. A discretionary delegated power must be exercised only by the delegate to whom it is committed: delegatus non potest delegare (de Smith, Judicial Review of Administrative Action, 4th ed.).
firac.application: The court doubted that questions such as the state of repair of a house (Q. 19) or its fuel bill (Q. 20) fell within any reasonable meaning of a “census of population.” More significantly, it disagreed with Meyer J. in R. v. Churchill (1978), 45 C.C.C. (2d) 312: the Order in Council purported to act solely under ss. 18 and 20(1), yet by confining Qq. 13–46 to one-fifth of households the Governor in Council had used the sampling power (s. 8(2)) and the voluntary/compulsory-designation power (s. 7.1) that the Act delegates only to the Minister. Such statistics ought to have been sought by a s. 21 request directing the Minister, who alone could authorize sampling and designate voluntary questions.
firac.conclusion: The Order in Council, insofar as it folded sampling and extraneous housing/employment questions into the exercise of the census power, was ultra vires; the court concurred in the trial judge’s result, though on this different (delegatus non potest delegare) footing.

firac.issue: Can an unreasonable intrusion upon the respondent’s right to privacy constitute a “lawful excuse” under s. 29(b)?
firac.facts: Otto refused to complete the form as a matter of principle, considering it an invasion of privacy. The long form sought, among other things, information on common-law relationships, the number of children ever born to a married woman (Q. 37), ethnic or cultural origin, religion, language, education and income.
firac.rule: A “lawful excuse” must rest on a legal principle usable as a shield against the statutory power. No Canadian enactment or judgment had yet formulated a general right to privacy, but privacy — “the right to be let alone” (Warren & Brandeis; Prosser; Katz v. United States; Hunter v. Southam Inc.; Motherwell v. Motherwell) — falls within the residuum of human rights and fundamental freedoms preserved by s. 5 of the Canadian Bill of Rights and s. 26 of the Charter, and the Statistics Act is not excepted from the Bill of Rights. The protected interest is a “reasonable expectation of privacy” (Hunter v. Southam), so only an unreasonable intrusion engages it. Charter s. 8 was held not to apply retrospectively, so the Canadian Bill of Rights governed events in 1981.
firac.application: Most census questions, though intrusive, were reasonable and required no justification beyond the form’s “Message to All Canadians.” But questions touching religion, ethnic origin, common-law relationships and children born to a married woman concern deeply private matters — especially for members of minorities who have experienced repressive state action — and the Census Guide offered no explanation of their necessity. Reasonableness is the handmaiden of necessity; absent a factual basis demonstrating that such sensitive inquiries were necessary, they were unreasonable intrusions.
firac.conclusion: To the extent the form contained questions of that sensitive genre, it was an unreasonable intrusion on Otto’s reasonable expectation of privacy, which furnished a “lawful excuse” for not responding.

firac.issue: Was the respondent “the occupant” liable under s. 31 to fill in and return the form?
firac.facts: The census taker left one long form at the Otto dwelling (4931 Cedar Crescent, Delta) without addressing it to any named person, relying on s. 31 rather than a s. 22 form addressed to a named person. The household had at least two adult occupants — Mrs. Otto and Mr. Otto — and each refused to complete it; Mr. Otto was never charged. The charge alleged refusal “between” June 2, 1981 and Feb. 27, 1982 rather than on census day, June 3, 1981.
firac.rule: Section 31 provides that leaving a form at a house bearing a notice to fill it in and sign it is, “as against the occupant, a sufficient requirement” for the occupant, or in his absence some other member of the family, to do so, even though the occupant is not named. Read with s. 26(7) of the Interpretation Act (singular includes plural), “the occupant” is properly construed in the singular; where only one construction is feasible, it prevails (R. v. Noble, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 632). Refusing to fill in a form under s. 31 is a distinct offence from refusing to furnish information.
firac.application: Because only one form was left and it named no one, only a single person could be “the occupant” made liable by s. 31; the alternative reading (“the occupants”) would render the section’s “or in his absence … some other member of the family” meaningless. With at least two adult occupants each refusing, the Crown could not prove that Otto rather than her husband was “the occupant.” The charge’s timing was also defective, since liability arose on census day (June 3, 1981), not over the alleged range.
firac.conclusion: Otto was entitled to the benefit of the doubt as to whether she was “the occupant” required to complete the form under s. 31, providing a further reason to dismiss the appeal.

name_verification.name_in_document: Y.L.M. v. J.B.M.

defining_issues: On an application under s. 44(4) of the Family Law Act to set aside or vary a term of a separation agreement respecting parenting arrangements, may the court extend any deference to the agreement, or is the best interests of the child under s. 37 the only consideration?

Is it in the children’s best interests to enforce the separation agreement’s School Provision (the children attending school on the North Shore) or to vary it so that the children attend school in Gibsons?

firac.issue: May the court extend any deference to the parties’ separation agreement in the s. 44(4) best-interests analysis?
firac.facts: The parties’ 2018 separation agreement contained a “School Provision” requiring the children to attend school on the North Shore as of September 2022. The mother sought to enforce it; the father cross-applied under s. 44(4) of the FLA to vary it. The parties disputed whether the Agreement itself could be a factor in the s. 44(4) analysis; the mother relied on Dosch v. Wimmer, 2021 BCSC 2167 (citing Leiding v. Leiding, 2016 BCSC 2567), for extending deference to the agreement on Miglin contractual principles.
firac.rule: FLA s. 44(4) requires the court to set aside or replace all or part of a parenting-arrangements agreement if satisfied the agreement is not in the best interests of the child. FLA s. 37(1) makes the best interests of the child the only consideration on a Part 4 application, and s. 37(3) reinforces that focus. In the case law, Leiding para. 29 (deference / material-change reluctance, drawing on Miglin v. Miglin, 2003 SCC 24) is obiter dictum; B.A.C. v. K.C., 2018 BCSC 2111 (Gomery J.), adopting Niijar v. Gill, 2017 BCSC 1362, and S.C.B. v. K.M.B., 2018 BCSC 1148, rejects any reluctance to change an agreement absent a material change and treats the existence of an agreement as a background fact, not a factor.
firac.application: The court held Leiding para. 29 to be obiter, and Dosch’s citation of it (even if read as approval) likewise obiter. Section 37’s word “only” precludes giving weight to the parties’ contractual expectations in the guise of “deference”; the agreement is a background fact, not a factor. It remains relevant only insofar as it assists the court in identifying and assessing the children’s needs and circumstances. Where, after a fresh and full best-interests assessment, the options are a “dead heat,” the tie goes to the agreement — not because of any deference, but because the s. 44(4) applicant has then failed to discharge the onus to satisfy the court that the agreement is not in the best interests of the child.
firac.conclusion: Section 37 does not permit extending any deference to the Agreement in the s. 44(4) analysis; best interests governs, with the onus on the party seeking to set the agreement aside and any true tie resolved in the agreement’s favour.

firac.issue: Is enforcing the School Provision (schooling on the North Shore) rather than varying it (schooling in Gibsons) in the children’s best interests?
firac.facts: The status quo — split school-week parenting enabled by the mother home-schooling on Fridays — could not continue once O. entered high school, as the children must attend school five days a week in one place. The competing options were North Shore schools (mother) and Gibsons (father). There were no family-violence issues; the parents were capable and able to co-operate. Evidence included Dr. Bolgar’s s. 211 Views of the Child report, the children’s relationships with step-siblings A., B. and M. and partners K. and T., the children’s Jewish cultural/community involvement, their academic ability and O.’s interest in film-making, and O.’s Crohn’s disease.
firac.rule: FLA s. 37(1) makes best interests the only consideration; s. 37(2) requires all of the child’s needs and circumstances to be considered, including the child’s health and emotional well-being (a), the child’s views unless inappropriate (b), the nature and strength of relationships with significant persons (c), and the need for stability given age and stage (e). Section 37(3) requires an arrangement to protect the child’s physical, psychological and emotional safety, security and well-being to the greatest extent possible. A child’s expressed views may be given little weight where the conditions of their elicitation undermine reliability.
firac.application: The children’s expressed preference for Gibsons was given little weight: they were asked to compare a vague hypothetical (unknown schools, residence and route) to the familiar, the report did not address whether their views had been influenced, and the father had disregarded a witness-exclusion order; their views were fairly neutral. The children were resilient and adapted well to change (separation, moves, blended families). The father overstated the impact of a North Shore schedule on the children’s relationships with A., B., M. and K.; overlap would continue, and O. and A. could gain weekend time. Fuller participation in the Vancouver Jewish community, education and culture — and connection to extended family in Israel — was beneficial. O. (bright, studious, keen on film-making) would be better served by an academically focused school offering advanced courses and specialized extracurriculars, and N. would benefit similarly and from a schedule matching O.’s. O.’s Crohn’s disease was well managed by the physician-father, and health-care continuity in Gibsons could be maintained if needed.
firac.conclusion: Enforcing the School Provision — the children attending school on the North Shore — is in the children’s best interests.

name_verification.name_in_document: Y.T. v. J.K.1

defining_issues: Who should have custody of A.J.K., the parties’ six-year-old daughter, determined on the best interests of the child under s. 24 of the Children’s Law Reform Act?
If the mother has custody, should she be permitted to relocate with A.J.K. to Japan, applying the mobility factors in Gordon v. Goertz?

firac.issue: Who should have custody of the six-year-old child on the best interests of the child?
firac.facts: A.J.K. (born 2000) is the daughter of Y.T. (from Japan) and J.K.1 (from Poland), who married in New York and immigrated to Toronto in 2002. The mother was the full-time primary caregiver from birth; the father worked and studied and (as the court found) overstated his early involvement, and the child’s first language is Japanese with limited English. The mother alleged controlling, obsessive and intimidating conduct; the father kept 120–180 pages of intensely emotional access journals and sought a shared residency / joint decision-making arrangement, while the mother sought sole custody.
firac.rule: Children’s Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12, s. 24: custody is determined by the best interests of the child, with s. 24(2) factors including (a) love, affection and emotional ties, (b) the child’s views, (c) stability of the home environment, (d) each applicant’s ability to provide guidance, education and the necessaries of life, (e) the proposed parenting plans, (f) the permanence and stability of the family unit, and (g) the blood relationship. A joint-custody order requires evidence that the parents can communicate effectively (Kaplanis v. Kaplanis, 2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)); the maximum-contact principle (Divorce Act s. 16(10)) applies by analogy (Woodhouse v. Woodhouse).
firac.application: The mother had most consistently cared for A.J.K. and had the more substantial connection; at six the child was too young for meaningful views; the mother provided stability despite the post-separation move, which was prompted by her fear of the father. Both parents could provide the necessaries, but the father’s practices (always carrying the child, never refusing her, aspiring to be her “friend,” and sobbing publicly at an exchange) offered poorer guidance. Joint custody / shared residency was unworkable because the parties could communicate only through a written book and the mother feared the father. A.J.K. had stronger ties to her extended maternal family (Japan) than to her paternal relatives; the blood-relationship factor was neutral.
firac.conclusion: It is in A.J.K.’s best interests to be in the sole custody of her mother, with access to her father.

firac.issue: Should the custodial mother be permitted to relocate with A.J.K. to Japan?
firac.facts: The mother, as custodial parent, sought to move to Japan for family support, employment and emotional stability, and would not move without the child; the father opposed, citing reduced contact, loss of exposure to the child’s Polish heritage, an alleged risk of discrimination in Japan, and that Japan is not a signatory to the Hague Convention.
firac.rule: Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27: there is no legal presumption in favour of the custodial parent, though that parent’s views merit great respect; the only issue is the child’s best interests, not the parents’ rights. The court considers, inter alia, the existing custody and access relationships, the desirability of maximizing contact, the child’s views, the custodial parent’s reasons for moving (only in the exceptional case where relevant to that parent’s ability to meet the child’s needs), and the disruption of a change in custody or removal from family, school and community. Maximum contact is important but not absolute (Young v. Young).
firac.application: The mother’s views as custodial parent merited great respect, whereas the father improperly focused on his own rights. This was an exceptional case in which the custodial parent’s reasons for moving were relevant to her ability to meet A.J.K.’s needs: she had no family or close friends in Canada, feared the controlling father, and would obtain employment, financial independence and family support in Japan, where A.J.K. speaks Japanese, holds citizenship and has close maternal relatives. The maximum-contact principle was tempered by the father’s obsessive fixation (though there was no evidence of sexual misconduct). Disruption was limited: A.J.K. was six, had lived in Toronto only about 3½ years across two neighbourhoods, and her young friendships were not yet significant (distinguishing Bartlett v. Bartlett); the discrimination concern was unsubstantiated for the relevant area.
firac.conclusion: It is in A.J.K.’s best interests to relocate to Japan with her mother; the father was granted defined summer and in-Japan access with telephone, internet and web-camera contact, and the mother was ordered to post a $20,000 security bond (Japan not being a Hague Convention signatory).

name_verification.name_in_document: Yeoh v. Rawat

defining_issues: Whether Ms. Yeoh’s notice of civil claim should have been struck under Supreme Court Civil Rule 9-5(1) — under any of subrules (a) discloses no reasonable claim, (b) scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, (c) may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial, or (d) otherwise an abuse of process.
Whether Ms. Yeoh’s application to adduce fresh evidence on appeal should be granted.

firac.issue: Whether the notice of civil claim should have been struck under R. 9-5(1).
firac.facts: Ms. Yeoh bought an $800 puppy from the Rawats, was dissatisfied, and sued them in the Supreme Court of British Columbia for breach of an alleged one-month guarantee and misrepresentation of the dog’s health, training and temperament, invoking the Sale of Goods Act and the Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act. The Rawats applied under R. 9-5(1) to strike the claim as frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of process, seeking special costs. A chambers judge, on conclusory one-paragraph reasons, struck the claim, dismissed the action and ordered $3,000 in costs.
firac.rule: Rule 9-5(1) permits the court to strike a pleading that (a) discloses no reasonable claim or defence, (b) is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, (c) may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial or hearing, or (d) is otherwise an abuse of process; no evidence is admissible under subrule (a) (R. 9-5(2)). A pleading is struck only where, assuming the pleaded facts true and reading the pleading generously as a whole, it is plain and obvious that the attack is well founded (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42; Nevsun Resources Ltd. v. Araya, 2020 SCC 5; Lee v. G.Y Lee & Associates Ltd., 2014 BCCA 400). A pleading is frivolous/vexatious only if it is obvious it cannot succeed (Skender v. Farley, 2007 BCCA 629). Susceptibility to striking under subrule (a) is a question of law reviewed for correctness (Situmorang v. Google, LLC, 2024 BCCA 9); striking under (b)-(d) is discretionary and reviewed deferentially, but only limited deference is owed to wholly conclusory reasons.
firac.application: (a) Though not a model pleading, the notice of civil claim presents an understandable claim for breach of contract and breach of the BPCPA, and read generously it is not obvious that it fails to state a reasonable cause of action. (b) It is not frivolous or vexatious — not repeatedly advanced and not brought in the teeth of a settlement — and claiming excessive or disproportionate damages does not qualify; any scandalous elements were not the argument advanced and could not justify striking the whole claim. (c) Nothing in the pleading would prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial. (d) It is not an abuse of process to bring in the Supreme Court a claim that could be advanced in the Provincial Court or before the Civil Resolution Tribunal; there is no lower bound to the Supreme Court’s monetary jurisdiction (R. 14-1(10) addresses costs for such claims). The judge’s wholly conclusory reasons showed he had misdirected himself as to the legal test.
firac.conclusion: The notice of civil claim could not be struck under any subrule of R. 9-5(1); the appeal is allowed and the orders striking the claim, dismissing the action and requiring the appellant to pay costs are set aside.

firac.issue: Whether the appellant’s fresh-evidence application should be granted.
firac.facts: Ms. Yeoh applied to adduce fresh evidence on appeal, all of which went to the merits of her underlying claim against the Rawats.
firac.rule: Fresh evidence is governed by the Palmer test affirmed in Barendregt v. Grebliunas, 2022 SCC 22, which requires the court to consider, among other things, whether the evidence could reasonably have affected the result below.
firac.application: The issue before the chambers judge and on appeal was not whether Ms. Yeoh’s claim should succeed at trial, but only whether the pleading should be struck. The proffered fresh evidence, going to the merits, did not bear on that question.
firac.conclusion: The fresh-evidence application is dismissed.

case_name: York University, et. al. v. M.P.A.C., et al.

name_verification.name_in_document: York University, FCS Holdco Inc., and FCS Holdco P2 Inc. v. Municipal Property Assessment Corporation and the City of Toronto (cited as “York University, et. al. v. M.P.A.C., et al.”)

defining_issues: Does the use-and-occupation-for-purposes condition in s. 18 of the York University Act, 1965 permit multiple simultaneous users and occupiers, or does the private, for-profit head lessee’s (FCS’s) occupation of the residences defeat the exemption?
Are the Quad student residences “actually used and occupied for the purposes of the University” under s. 18, so as to be exempt from City of Toronto property tax?

firac.issue: Whether s. 18 confines the exemption to a single (university) occupier or permits multiple simultaneous users and occupiers.
firac.facts: A private developer, FCS, holds 70-year triple-net head leases of the four Quad residences, bears all construction/operation/maintenance costs and collects student rents for profit (over $13M rental income, ~$9M gross profit in 2024), while the buildings remain part of York’s freehold; the leases restrict FCS’s use to housing York/Seneca students “for the Purposes of the University.” MPAC reclassified the residences as taxable, arguing FCS’s for-profit occupation displaced university use, analogizing to the retailers in Donaldo and to the “solely occupied” cases under s. 3 of the Assessment Act (e.g. Loyalist College v. MPAC).
firac.rule: Section 18 is a single, conjunctive exemption (Donaldo Pianezza Beauty Salon v. Borough of North York (1978), 1978 CanLII 1284 (ON CA)) exempting York property “so long as the same are actually used and occupied for the purposes of the University.” The modern principle of interpretation applies (Bell ExpressVu v. Rex, 2002 SCC 42; Driedger), with no special rules for tax exemptions (Diocese of Toronto Camps v. MPAC). The passive phrase “are used and occupied” does not restrict the user/occupier to any one person; this contrasts with the Assessment Act s. 3 (“occupied solely by a university”) and with the Occupiers’ Liability Act, which recognizes more than one occupier of the same premises (Moody v. Toronto). The absence of “solely” implies possible multiple simultaneous occupancies (Sullivan, Construction of Statutes).
firac.application: The triple-net leases make FCS a possessory user/occupier for profit, as the retailers were in Donaldo. But s. 18’s passive wording does not require the head lessee to be the sole occupier: the lease confines FCS to housing York/Seneca students, creating a defined class of student sub-occupiers, and York is itself an occupier because it controls student eligibility, allocates residence availability, can expel students, and supervises the complex. Donaldo is distinguishable — the retailers served outside customers and occupied for their own profit, whereas the residents have rights of occupancy tied to York — and the “solely occupied” Assessment Act cases turn on statutory language absent from s. 18.
firac.conclusion: Section 18 permits multiple simultaneous users and occupiers; FCS’s for-profit head-lease occupation does not, by itself, defeat the exemption.

firac.issue: Whether the residences are used and occupied “for the purposes of the University” under s. 18.
firac.facts: York built the Quad to revitalize an isolated commuter campus and support its academic mission (the Scion report and 2012 Housing Strategy); it guarantees first-year residence, controls eligibility and allocation, and (under a 2025 MOU) staffs the residences with trained live-in student dons, while FCS finances, builds and operates. York’s statutory objects (s. 4) are the advancement of learning and dissemination of knowledge, and the intellectual, spiritual, social, moral and physical development of its members.
firac.rule: Purpose — not the buildings’ utility or the occupier’s commercial motive — governs the second clause; operative wording prevails over policy (Ross Southward Tire v. Pyrotech). Commercial documents are read objectively but through a purposive lens (London Jewish Community Village v. MPAC, 2020 ONSC 6794). The court scrutinizes York’s decision path but does not adjudicate in the abstract whether residences are integral to a university (Re University of Ottawa/Carleton: a residence’s primary purpose is collaborative academic space, not mere housing).
firac.application: The relevant question is why York had the buildings built, not merely what they are. Located on campus, the residences fulfil York’s s. 4(b) mission (experiential learning, mentorship, crisis management, secure off-hours access to resources) and its s. 4(a) purpose (dissemination of knowledge through student proximity), which cannot be reduced to MPAC’s “profit centre / dormitory” view. FCS’s tenant tax liability under the triple-net lease does not create a liability for York or defeat the exemption, and the microeconomic and ratepayer policy consequences are not for the court to weigh in construing s. 18.
firac.conclusion: The Quad residences are used and occupied for York’s statutory purposes and are exempt from City of Toronto property tax; the City must cancel or refund taxes paid on the student-housing portion.

name_verification.name_in_document: Yosyk v. Westfair Foods Ltd.

defining_issues: Whether the plaintiffs were dismissed for just cause justifying summary dismissal without notice.
What are the proper criteria for determining the reasonable notice period, and did the trial judge err in fixing the notice periods by over-weighting length of service?

firac.issue: Whether the plaintiffs’ conduct constituted just cause for summary dismissal without notice.
firac.facts: Each plaintiff, a non-union cosmetic-department supervisor, was dismissed without notice for conduct the employer characterized as insubordination toward the divisional manager. The trial judge found the conduct inappropriate but not of a magnitude that justified summary dismissal.
firac.rule: Under an individual employment contract the employer has an absolute right to end the relationship, and the only question on a dismissal without notice is whether the conduct justified summary dismissal — distinct from “just cause” under a collective agreement, which asks whether the employer may bring the relationship to an end at all. An appellate court will not interfere with a trial judge’s finding on this factual question without basis.
firac.application: The Court of Appeal found no basis to interfere with the trial judge’s conclusion that the plaintiffs’ conduct, while inappropriate, did not justify dismissal without notice.
firac.conclusion: The appeal against liability is dismissed; there was no just cause for summary dismissal.

firac.issue: The proper criteria for determining the reasonable notice period and whether the trial judge erred.
firac.facts: The plaintiffs were junior-management supervisors promoted from unionized clerk positions, with relatively short total service (about 39–49 months); equivalent positions elsewhere were scarce and the employer led no evidence they were available, while the employer could readily find replacements. The trial judge awarded notice of roughly one month per six months of service (seven, six and eight months), emphasizing length of service.
firac.rule: The employment relationship is contractual; absent a statutory minimum or an express agreement, trade custom or established employer practice, reasonable notice is an implied term measured by the intention of the parties — the Lazarowicz v. Orenda Engines Ltd. (1960 ON CA) test of what the parties would have answered about notice at the time of hiring — refined so that the relevant intent is that held when the contract was last changed before the events leading to termination. Relevant, non-exhaustive factors include the nature and duration of prior employment, job security, the character of the work, length of service, and the availability of alternative employment (for the employee) and of a replacement (for the employer). Case-to-case fact comparison is of limited value (M’Cartan v. Belfast Harbour Com’rs). An appellate court intervenes only if the period is considerably outside the standard established by principle.
firac.application: The trial judge over-weighted the plaintiffs’ short length of service and ignored the factors the parties themselves would have considered. Each plaintiff occupied an upwardly mobile junior-management position in which a lengthy notice period would have disadvantaged the employee (who would want to be free to take a better job) more than the employer; length of service was not yet a significant factor; replacement was not a concern. But because equivalent positions were scarce, and the employer offered no evidence they were available, the parties would have agreed on notice longer than the common one-month standard.
firac.conclusion: The reasonable notice the parties would have agreed on was three months for each plaintiff; the appeal on the notice period is allowed and the awards reduced accordingly, with the employer to pay the costs of the appeal.
