case_name: Youlden v. London Guarantee and Accident Co.

name_verification.name_in_document: Youlden v. London Guarantee and Accident Co.

defining_issues: Whether the insurance contract on which the beneficiary sues is the renewal receipt alone or the renewal receipt together with policy No. 65996 (incorporated by the words “according to tenor of policy No. 65996”), so that the policy’s conditions — including the fourteen-day notice-of-injury condition — form part of the contract.
Whether s. 144 of the Ontario Insurance Act (requiring the terms and conditions to be set out in full) was satisfied, or whether it barred reliance on the policy’s conditions.
Whether the beneficiary, suing under her statutory right and not herself a contracting party, is bound by the policy’s condition subsequent (the notice requirement) that would defeat her claim.

firac.issue: Whether “according to tenor of policy No. 65996” incorporates the policy and its conditions into the renewal contract.
firac.facts: The 1909 renewal receipt insured Youlden’s life for $2,500 plus weekly indemnity “according to tenor of policy No. 65996.” The receipt set out no conditions, but the original policy contained an endorsed condition requiring written notice of injury within fourteen days as a condition precedent to any claim. The beneficiary argued the renewal receipt alone was the contract and carried no conditions.
firac.rule: On long-settled criminal and civil authority (e.g. The King v. May; Rex v. Bear; Miller v. Salomons) and in the dictionaries, “tenor” denotes the entire instrument — an exact copy or the whole of it — not merely its form; a reference “according to tenor” imports the whole of the instrument referred to.
firac.application: The words “according to tenor of policy No. 65996” therefore import the policy and everything contained in or endorsed on it, including the fourteen-day notice condition. The beneficiary’s contention that only the bare receipt (carrying no conditions) is the contract cannot be sustained.
firac.conclusion: The policy and its conditions, including the notice condition, form part of the renewal contract.

firac.issue: Whether s. 144 of the Ontario Insurance Act was satisfied.
firac.facts: Section 144(1) (R.S.O. 1897, ch. 203) requires that, where an insurance contract is evidenced by a sealed or written instrument, all the terms and conditions be set out in full on the instrument; conditions not so set out that impair or modify the contract are invalid and inadmissible against the insured or the beneficiary. The policy was under seal and the renewal was effected by a receipt referring to it.
firac.rule: Conditions impairing or modifying the contract must be set out in full; but under the Interpretation Act “instrument” may be read as “instruments,” so two documents together may form or evidence the contract (per Maclennan J.A. in Wintemute v. Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen).
firac.application: The renewal receipt and the original policy together form and evidence the contract, and the conditions are set out in or endorsed on the policy; the statute is thus literally complied with, and the conditions are valid and admissible.
firac.conclusion: Section 144 was satisfied and the policy’s conditions may be relied on.

firac.issue: Whether the statutory beneficiary is bound by the policy’s condition subsequent.
firac.facts: Nina Youlden sued as a preferred beneficiary under the statutory trust created by the Insurance Act; she was not herself a party to the contract; the fourteen-day notice requirement is a condition subsequent that, if valid, defeats the claim.
firac.rule: A beneficiary’s right to sue is statutory, but the statutory trust arises subject to the terms of the contract out of which the trust fund arises; on the authorities (Home Life Association of Canada v. Randall; Accident Insurance Co. of North America v. Young; Employers’ Liability Assurance Corporation v. Taylor; Atlas Assurance Co. v. Brownell) a beneficiary is bound by the policy’s conditions, including conditions precedent and subsequent such as notice requirements, and non-compliance is a good defence against the beneficiary.
firac.application: Although it may seem unjust that a condition often unknown to the beneficiary, and arising after the insured’s injury, should defeat the statutory trust, the same rule has been applied in all the cases; the beneficiary takes her right subject to the contract’s conditions and is bound by the notice condition.
firac.conclusion: The beneficiary is bound by the notice condition and cannot recover; the appeal is dismissed with costs.

case_name: Young and Young v. McLellan et al

name_verification.name_in_document: Young and Young v. McLellan et al (Eric Young and Marlene Young v. Anne McLellan and Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada)

defining_issues: On a motion to strike under Rule 19(24), which of the plaintiffs’ pleaded causes of action — breach of fiduciary duty, defamation, invasion of privacy, abuse of public office, and infliction of nervous shock — disclose no reasonable cause of action and should be struck?
Whether the action should be stayed or struck as an abuse of process because it duplicates the damages relief sought in the plaintiffs’ parallel constitutional petition.
Whether Anne McLellan (sued for conduct in a representative capacity) and Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada are properly named parties, or should be struck/substituted.

firac.issue: Which of the pleaded causes of action should be struck under Rule 19(24)?
firac.facts: The self-represented plaintiffs pleaded breach of fiduciary duty (paras 14, 49, 50), defamation (paras 29, 32, 45, 53), invasion of privacy (para 46), abuse of public office (paras 42–44, 47), and infliction of nervous shock (para 48), arising from Health Canada’s handling of their s. 56 medical-cannabis exemptions and an internal email alleging a bomb threat that was reported to the RCMP and Saanich Police.
firac.rule: Under Rule 19(24) a pleading is struck only where it is plain and obvious the action is bound to fail (Hunt v. Carey), with doubts resolved in favour of the pleading (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress); pleadings must be framed with certainty and clarity. Fiduciary duties do not arise from public-law discretionary functions (Guerin v. Canada; Rogers v. Faught). Abuse of public office is an intentional tort requiring bad faith — targeted malice, or knowing unlawfulness plus probable injury (Powder Mountain Resorts Ltd. v. British Columbia; Three Rivers). Invasion of privacy under the BC Privacy Act s. 1 requires a wilful violation “without a claim of right” (with defences under s. 2(2) and s. 74 of the federal Privacy Act). Nervous shock is founded in negligence and requires foreseeable psychiatric injury (Rhodes Estate v. C.N.R.).
firac.application: Fiduciary duty was struck: s. 56 of the CDSA confers an administrative discretion exercised in the public interest and creates no fiduciary obligation to exemption-holders. Abuse of public office was struck: a refusal to extend an exemption is not an illegal act but falls within the s. 56 discretion, no material facts of bad faith were pleaded, and the plaintiffs in fact held exemptions throughout. Nervous shock was struck: no tortious conduct was disclosed that made psychiatric injury foreseeable. Defamation was not struck — the plaintiff conceded the whole email was not false — but particulars were ordered. Invasion of privacy was not struck but had to be amended to plead the statutory elements and material facts.
firac.conclusion: The fiduciary-duty, abuse-of-public-office and nervous-shock pleas were struck; the defamation plea stands subject to particulars; and the invasion-of-privacy plea stands subject to amendment.

firac.issue: Whether the action should be stayed or struck as duplicative of the parallel petition.
firac.facts: Eric Young (later joined by Marlene Young) had a pending petition (Victoria Registry 02 3057) challenging the CDSA/MMAR and seeking damages; much of the statement of claim overlapped, and the plaintiffs intended to move the constitutional issues into this action while keeping the petition alive.
firac.rule: Seeking the same relief already claimed in an extant proceeding is vexatious and an abuse of the court’s process, and the later of two proceedings claiming the same relief may be struck (Great Pacific Contracting Ltd. v. Harwyn Properties Ltd.).
firac.application: The two proceedings sought the same damages relief, which would ordinarily warrant striking the later action; but in light of the self-represented plaintiffs the court declined to strike and instead stayed this action while the damages claim in the petition remained alive, to continue once that claim is withdrawn or the petition discontinued.
firac.conclusion: The action was stayed (not struck) pending resolution of the duplicative damages claim in the petition.

firac.issue: Whether Anne McLellan and Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada are properly named parties.
firac.facts: McLellan was sued for conduct as Minister, with no personal-capacity allegations; the Crown was named as “Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada.”
firac.rule: An official sued only for representative-capacity conduct is not a proper party (Cairns v. Farm Credit Corp.); proceedings against the Crown are taken in the name of the Attorney General of Canada (Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, s. 23).
firac.application: All of McLellan’s alleged actions were in a representative capacity, so she is not properly a party; and the Crown should be named as the Attorney General of Canada.
firac.conclusion: Anne McLellan was struck as a defendant, and the Attorney General of Canada was substituted for Her Majesty the Queen, amending the style of cause.

name_verification.name_in_document: Yu c. Tse (Yu, Yuk Lin Catherine c. Tse, Mei-Wah; mis en cause: CLSC St-Laurent, Hôpital chinois de Montréal et Curateur public)

defining_issues: Whether the court should order the hébergement (institutionalization) and treatment of Mme Tse despite her refusal — that is, whether she is incapable of consenting to the care required by her condition, such that her refusal must be set aside and forced hébergement authorized.

firac.issue: Whether to authorize the hébergement and treatment of Mme Tse despite her refusal, given her alleged incapacity to consent to care.
firac.facts: Mme Tse (aged 74, Cantonese-speaking, widowed) lived in Montréal with her daughter and the daughter’s family. She had become a heavy-care case — nighttime agitation and shouting, memory and orientation problems endangering her safety (leaving a pot to melt, repeatedly getting lost, an incident at a bank requiring police) — and could not be left alone. With the CLSC’s help a place was found at the Hôpital chinois de Montréal (a long-term-care centre), but after about a day she insistently refused to remain, and the facility said it could not keep her without judicial authorization. The daughter applied for authorization of care despite the refusal, with the Curateur public, CLSC and hospital impleaded; Mme Tse did not attend court.
firac.rule: Under the Civil Code of Québec a court may authorize care that has been refused by a person who is incapable of consenting to it; incapacity to consent to care is assessed on the criteria in Institut Philippe-Pinel de Montréal, [1994] R.J.Q. 2523 (C.A.); and forced hébergement can constitute care required by the person’s state (Curateur public du Québec c. R. (E.)).
firac.application: The uncontradicted medical and social evidence established Mme Tse’s incapacity to consent: her family physician of 25 years diagnosed chronic brain syndrome and concluded she could not stay alone safely; a geriatric-psychiatry social worker found her “unable to judge due to dementia”; and a further physician opined she was wholly unable to care for herself and required urgent placement. She was therefore incapable of consenting to the care her condition required, her refusal had to be set aside, and hébergement at the Hôpital chinois (constant supervision day and night, medication for her diabetes and other conditions, and adapted activities) was care required by her state.
firac.conclusion: Authorization was granted: the hospital may receive and treat Mme Tse despite her refusal, police may escort her if needed, and the hospital must report on her adaptation to the daughter and the Curateur public at three months and annually; the whole without costs.

name_verification.name_in_document: Z.(A.) v. W.(J.) (A.Z., Applicant v. J.W., Respondent)

defining_issues: Whether custody of the child should be sole (to the mother) or joint, applying the best-interests test under the Children’s Law Reform Act, given the mother’s conduct toward the father’s access and the Office of the Children’s Lawyer investigation.
Whether the father’s access to the child should be supervised.
Whether the child’s access to his paternal grandfather, a former child abuser, should remain restricted or supervised.
Whether the ex parte restraining order against the father should be continued.

firac.issue: Whether custody should be sole (to the mother) or joint, on the best interests of the child.
firac.facts: The mother obtained interim sole custody by an ex parte motion (2001) on evidence later shown at trial to have no basis in truth; she repeatedly ignored, stalled or sabotaged a string of access orders, failed access-centre intake, chose a distant centre forcing the father onto long public-transit trips, and undermined the Office of the Children’s Lawyer investigation (withholding the child from an observational visit and attacking the worker). The father sought joint custody with the child’s primary residence remaining with the mother, had never sought to impair the child’s relationship with the mother, and had been cooperative and flexible.
firac.rule: Custody is determined by the best interests of the child under the Children’s Law Reform Act (ss. 18, 24). Joint custody generally presupposes a high degree of parental cooperation (Kruger v. Kruger; Baker v. Baker), but that requirement should not preclude joint custody where one parent deliberately provokes and engineers discord expecting to be rewarded with sole custody; a joint-custody/parallel-parenting plan may serve the child’s best interests where it would not serve the child to entrust the primary caregiver with sole decision-making. An ex parte interim order, resting on untested evidence, is a weak foundation for a status-quo/continuity argument.
firac.application: The evidence showed the mother’s enthusiasm for the father-child relationship was lukewarm to mean-spirited, and the court could not trust her as sole custodian; the child’s bond with the father was strong despite her efforts to frustrate it, and the father’s incremental parenting plan respected the child’s ties to the mother. Removing sole decision-making from the mother would centre disruptive decisions (health, education) on the child’s needs rather than the mother’s whims.
firac.conclusion: Sole custody to the mother is contrary to the child’s best interests; joint custody within a parallel-parenting plan is ordered (primary residence with the mother, secondary with the father), with final decision-making split — religious upbringing to the mother, education and non-emergency health/dental care to the father.

firac.issue: Whether the father’s access to the child should be supervised.
firac.facts: Supervised access had ended about two years earlier; the mother sought its return but offered no trial evidence to justify doing so, and the evidence did not support any conclusion that the father posed a risk to the child.
firac.rule: Supervised access is an interim measure reserved for resolving an impasse over access that should evolve toward a more normal regime; it carries distinct disadvantages — it conveys the message that the child’s safety cannot otherwise be entrusted to the access parent, reduces access time to fit the centre’s hours, and costs money — so a step to (or back to) supervision requires justification.
firac.application: The mother offered no evidence justifying a step backwards to renewed supervised access, and the evidence showed the father presented no risk to the child, so the pernicious message of supervision was unwarranted.
firac.conclusion: The claim for supervised access (and supervised exchange) between the child and the father is dismissed.

firac.issue: Whether the child’s access to his paternal grandfather should remain restricted or supervised.
firac.facts: About ten years earlier the grandfather had pleaded guilty to sexually touching his then-11-year-old daughter, received a suspended sentence and probation, completed the probation, and had no criminal record before or since. The Office of the Children’s Lawyer worker recommended continued restriction but could identify no risk specific to this boy and this grandfather, relying on an “once labelled, forever labelled” assumption.
firac.rule: A restriction on contact (supervised access) to protect a child requires evidence of a likelihood of risk of harm to the child, not speculation or conjecture.
firac.application: The worker’s reliance on a vague, unaccredited “once labelled, forever labelled” dogma was speculation and conjecture, not evidence of a likely risk to this child, and the court could find no likelihood of risk to the boy in his grandfather’s unsupervised presence.
firac.conclusion: The claim to continue the restriction on the child’s access to his paternal grandfather is dismissed.

firac.issue: Whether the ex parte restraining order against the father should continue.
firac.facts: The mother obtained an ex parte interim restraining order (2001) alleging spousal abuse and a fear of its recurrence; at trial her evidence was exposed as untruthful, and she adduced no evidence of any abuse or threatening behaviour by the father.
firac.rule: A restraining order for harassment, molestation or annoyance requires evidence; an allegation of abuse is not proof of abuse, and a claim of fear is not by itself proof of a good reason for that fear.
firac.application: The mother’s “fear” was at best a figment of her imagination and at worst a deliberate fabrication, marketed as a reason to avoid complying with access orders and sharing information about the child; there had never been a need for a restraining order against the father.
firac.conclusion: The restraining-order claim is dismissed.

name_verification.name_in_document: Zando v. Ali (Iram Kareemi Zando v. Dr. Syed N. Ali a.k.a Dr. Sayed N. Ali)

defining_issues: Whether, on a balance of probabilities, Dr. Ali sexually assaulted Dr. Zando on June 22, 1999.
If the assault occurred, the quantum of damages (non-pecuniary, aggravated and punitive), including whether the assault materially caused or contributed to Dr. Zando’s psychological injury.

firac.issue: Whether Dr. Ali sexually assaulted Dr. Zando (civil sexual battery) on June 22, 1999.
firac.facts: Dr. Zando alleged that Dr. Ali, attending her Sarnia home ostensibly to have an insurance form completed, undressed and sexually assaulted her, masturbating and ejaculating on her rug; Dr. Ali denied any assault, said Dr. Zando made an advance on him, and — on the eve of trial after 15 years — alleged a consensual 1992–93 affair (never pleaded, contradicting his discovery evidence). Her related claims against the hospital had settled, leaving only the assault claim. DNA testing matched semen on the rug to DNA from a mug Dr. Ali used; he refused to provide a DNA sample. Three witnesses corroborated her contemporaneous reports.
firac.rule: Civil sexual battery is proved on a balance of probabilities; a court may draw an adverse inference from a party’s refusal to provide relevant evidence (here, a DNA sample); consistency of account and corroboration bear on credibility.
firac.application: Dr. Zando’s account was consistent across the 15-year proceeding and corroborated by Kathy Tjoelker, Dr. Kaloni and Catherine Patterson; the DNA on her rug matched Dr. Ali’s, and his refusal to provide a sample (with no tenable innocent explanation, the rug having been acquired in 1994) supported an adverse inference. His shifting, late-disclosed and unpleaded affair allegation undermined only his own credibility, and the timing of Dr. Zando’s complaint amid a hospital privileges dispute did not show fabrication (Tjoelker’s report predated those problems).
firac.conclusion: Dr. Zando proved on a balance of probabilities that Dr. Ali sexually assaulted her.

firac.issue: The quantum of damages, including causation of Dr. Zando’s psychological injury.
firac.facts: Dr. Zando was diagnosed with major depressive disorder with features of PTSD; she had settled with the hospital defendants. Dr. Ali argued that the hospital harassment, not the assault, caused her condition, and that she had already been compensated.
firac.rule: Causation requires only that the defendant caused or materially contributed to the injury (Athey v. Leonati; Snell v. Farrell). Damages for sexual assault are assessed on the Blackwater v. Plint factors — the victim’s circumstances and vulnerability; the assault’s number, frequency, violence, invasiveness and degradation; the defendant’s circumstances and any position of trust; and the consequences — within a range of about $144,000–$290,000 (inflation-adjusted). Punitive damages require high-handed, malicious or reprehensible conduct (K.T. v. Vranich); aggravated damages reflect aggravating features rather than forming a separate head.
firac.application: The assault was a materially contributing factor to Dr. Zando’s major depressive disorder, even if not its only cause. A single sexual assault between adults falls toward the lower end of the range; given her shame, humiliation and loss of dignity, $175,000 in non-pecuniary damages was appropriate (aggravating features reflected therein). Because the morally reprehensible conduct had gone unpunished — no criminal charge and no atonement — $25,000 in punitive damages was warranted.
firac.conclusion: Damages of $175,000 non-pecuniary and $25,000 punitive were awarded, with aggravated features reflected in the non-pecuniary award.

name_verification.name_in_document: Jalal Naoman Zangana v. John Doe and Margaret Doe, Hope Pregnancy & Adoption Services Society (No. A940134, heard with Ingrid Benz v. Zangana, Doe et al., No. F940207)

defining_issues: Who should have custody of the child — the biological father (Zangana), the biological mother (Benz), or the adoptive parents (the Does) — on the paramount consideration of the child’s best interests, and what weight the biological parents’ blood ties carry against the child’s bond with the adoptive family.
Whether the biological father should be granted access to the child if custody is denied.

firac.issue: Who should have custody of the child, on the paramount consideration of her best interests.
firac.facts: The unmarried birth parents had a brief, violent relationship in Winnipeg. Eleven days after the birth, the mother (the child’s sole guardian) placed the baby for private adoption in British Columbia with John and Margaret Doe, who had raised her for about nine months and with whom she had bonded. The biological father, not a “parent” under the Adoption Act (his consent was not required), petitioned for custody; the mother supported the Does but sought custody herself in the alternative.
firac.rule: Under s. 24 of the Family Relations Act (BC) the best interests of the child are the paramount consideration (health and emotional well-being; ties of love and affection; education and training; each claimant’s capacity to exercise custody; conduct only insofar as it affects those factors); by s. 27 the unmarried, non-cohabiting mother was sole guardian, entitled to place the child for adoption without the father’s consent. A biological parent’s blood tie is relevant but a child is not a chattel or proprietary interest (K.K. v. G.L.; A.N.R. v. L.J.W.), and parental claims yield where the child’s welfare requires; the natural-parent preference applies only where the competing claims are otherwise equally balanced (M.(C.G.) v. W.(C.)), with the child’s bond to the adoptive family and the known-versus-unknown environment weighed (Tearoe v. Sawan).
firac.application: This was not a case of equally balanced claims, so the natural-parent presumption did not apply. The Does offered more for the child’s health, emotional well-being and education; strong bonds had formed; and she was safe, secure and happy in the only home she had known. Awarding custody to the father would move her to an uncertain situation; his superficial understanding of parenting, unsettled living and financial plans, and abusive conduct toward the mother counted against him. The birth parents’ divergent religious and cultural heritage could not be accommodated, and the mother (sole guardian) had chosen the Does.
firac.conclusion: Custody is awarded to the Does; the custody petitions of both the biological father and the biological mother are dismissed.

firac.issue: Whether the biological father should be granted access if custody is denied.
firac.facts: The father sought access, having had a single supervised two-hour visit with the child; the Does live outside the lower mainland, and their adoption of the child is an “open adoption.”
firac.rule: Access to a natural parent is granted only where it is in the child’s best interests — it must add something positive to the child’s life — and there is no proprietary right to access (H. and H. v. Y. and L.).
firac.application: There was no existing relationship between the father and the child (a single visit she would have enjoyed with any congenial adult), access would be infrequent and difficult, and no evidence showed that contact was in her best interests; the open adoption meant she could choose contact when older.
firac.conclusion: The application for access is denied.

name_verification.name_in_document: Zesta Engineering Ltd. v. Cloutier et al
name_verification.discrepancy_note: Minor internal inconsistency in the decision (not a mismatch with the supplied metadata): the style of cause / heading reads “Zesta Engineering Ltd.” (matching the supplied case name), but the body of the reasons refers to the plaintiff as “Zesta Engineering Inc.” A reviewer may wish to confirm the correct corporate designation. No neutral citation is printed in the text (only court file 00-CV-188172CM); “2008 CanLII 2618” is a CanLII identifier.

defining_issues: Whether solicitor-client privilege attached to Christie’s notes of meetings 1–3 — i.e., whether Cloutier and Christie were in a solicitor-client relationship (seeking or providing legal advice) at those meetings.
Whether the presence of third parties at meetings 2, 3 and 4 impeded the formation of privilege by defeating the required confidentiality.
Whether Cloutier waived any privilege by putting his state of mind in issue and relying on Christie’s legal advice to justify concealing the transactions.
Whether the “future crime and fraud” exception applies to communications made with the intention of committing an unlawful (including civil-tortious) act.
Whether the notes contain non-privileged facts and should be produced, and the proper approach to redaction.

firac.issue: Whether Cloutier and Christie were in a solicitor-client relationship (seeking or providing legal advice) at meetings 1–3, so the notes are privileged.
firac.facts: There were four meetings (Oct 21, Nov 5, Nov 9 and Nov 28, 1999); Cloutier was terminated Nov 27 and the action began Nov 26, both between meetings 3 and 4. Meeting 4 was conceded to be after the retainer. For meetings 1–3, Cloutier’s sworn affidavit and discovery evidence were unequivocal that the meetings were social and not for legal advice (“Absolutely,” the first legal advice was the night he was fired); Christie’s evidence was equivocal, describing meeting 1 as a “beauty contest.”
firac.rule: For solicitor-client privilege, communications must be made in seeking or providing legal advice, within “the continuum” of the relationship (Descoteaux v. Mierzwinski; Solosky v. The Queen; TD Bank v. Leigh Instruments); the client’s intention governs, and privilege does not apply where advice is neither sought nor offered. A party is bound by its discovery evidence unless it corrects the record (Rule 31.09).
firac.application: As the client, Cloutier’s intention governs; his clear, uncorrected evidence that the meetings were social — and that Christie attended for his own business interests — meant no advice-seeking continuum arose. The court declined to use the notes’ contents to contradict his sworn evidence; even on Christie’s account, meeting 1 was a “beauty contest” (an audition), not a retainer.
firac.conclusion: No solicitor-client relationship or privilege arose at meetings 1–3; the notes are relevant and not privileged.

firac.issue: Whether third-party presence at meetings 2, 3 and 4 defeated the confidentiality essential to privilege.
firac.facts: Peatling (never a client) was present at meetings 2 and 3; an unexplained group (including Jeffries, separately represented) attended meeting 4 at a restaurant, where Cloutier spoke about “the heaters” loudly enough to be overheard. No evidence explained why the third parties were present or that they were to keep the discussions confidential.
firac.rule: Confidentiality is essential to solicitor-client privilege (Wigmore; Slavutych v. Baker); the presence of a third party generally negates confidentiality unless reasonably necessary to advance the client’s interest and understood to be confidential (Manes & Silver; Sopinka), and the party invoking privilege must establish this.
firac.application: There was no evidence explaining Peatling’s presence or role at meetings 2–3, or that the group of strangers to the action at meeting 4 was necessary or bound to confidence; Cloutier speaking openly enough to be overheard was inconsistent with an intention to keep the discussions confidential at the time.
firac.conclusion: Confidentiality was not established, so no privilege arose as to the notes of meetings 2, 3 and 4.

firac.issue: Whether Cloutier waived any privilege by relying on legal advice to account for his conduct.
firac.facts: In his affidavit, Cloutier stated that he gave Christie full details of the funds received from Codlin and of the transactions, that Christie advised him not to report the sales, and that he followed that advice — thereby putting his state of mind and the advice in issue.
firac.rule: Privilege is impliedly waived where a party places its state of mind in issue and relies on legal advice that helped form it (Bank of Leu AG v. Gaming Lottery Corp.); the waiver extends to all communications on that subject matter, not merely the specific advice, to prevent selective, self-serving disclosure (Land v. Kaufman; Leadbetter v. HMQ; Bentley v. Stone).
firac.application: Cloutier’s reliance on Christie’s advice to explain concealing the transactions waived privilege over those communications; the waiver extended to the “full details of the transactions” — the background and the roles of Watlow and Husky and how and why Codlin became involved — not merely the flow of money.
firac.conclusion: Any privilege in the notes of meetings 1–3 was waived by Cloutier’s reliance on legal advice to form his state of mind.

firac.issue: Whether the future-crime-and-fraud exception defeats any privilege.
firac.facts: Zesta alleged fraud and related torts (breach of fiduciary duty, interference with economic relations, conversion, breach of contract, conspiracy) in the Codlin scheme; Cloutier acknowledged undisclosed involvement in the heater sales and maintained his “Jones sting” defence; the notes of meetings 2–4 reflected Cloutier laying out future plans.
firac.rule: Communications to facilitate a crime or fraud are not privileged (Solosky v. The Queen), and the exception extends to civil unlawful acts and torts (Goldman Sachs & Co. v. Sessions; Dublin v. Montessori Jewish Day School of Toronto); it applies to future or contemplated (not past) acts, requires some prima facie evidence, and the onus lies on the party invoking it.
firac.application: The exception was available for the alleged torts; Zesta met its onus because Cloutier’s acknowledged undisclosed involvement and maintained sting defence gave “colour to the charge.” The notes of meetings 2–4 dealt with future plans furthering the alleged fraud and torts, whereas meeting 1 contained only facts and opinions.
firac.conclusion: The future-crime-and-fraud exception applies to the notes of meetings 2, 3 and 4, so any privilege cannot protect them.

firac.issue: Whether the notes contain non-privileged facts and should be produced, and the proper approach to redaction.
firac.facts: Christie produced only the cover page of each set (date and participants), redacting the remainder; the notes are a mix of fact, opinion and (for the later meetings) future plans.
firac.rule: Facts are not privileged communications; privileged and non-privileged content may be severed by redaction, but where they are inextricably intertwined and the document is privileged it should be listed in schedule “B” of the affidavit of documents (not produced in redacted form).
firac.application: The meeting-1 notes are purely factual and opinion, containing no privileged communication. For meetings 2–4, factual and future-plan content are intertwined; had they been privileged, none should have been produced (they should have been listed in schedule “B”), but for the reasons above they are not privileged.
firac.conclusion: The notes contain producible facts and, on each independent ground, are not protected; all four sets are to be produced in full within 30 days.

name_verification.name_in_document: Zorchinsky c. SPHR Concordia (Anastasia Zorchinsky, Michael Eshayek, Hillel Concordia, The Start Up Nation v. SPHR Concordia, Independent Jewish Voices Canada Inc., Mahmoud Khalil, Montréal4Palestine, Alliance4Palestine.QC, Direct Action Montréal Now / Direct Action Concordia, Reema Aboudraz; Concordia University, mise en cause)

defining_issues: Whether the plaintiffs met the four criteria for a provisional injunction under art. 509 C.C.P. — urgency, appearance of right, irreparable prejudice, and balance of convenience — to protect access to Concordia and prohibit intimidating, threatening and harassing conduct by the defendants.
Whether a protection order should issue against Mahmoud Khalil and Reema Aboudraz to protect the two Jewish student plaintiffs whose safety was threatened.

firac.issue: Whether the four criteria for a provisional injunction under art. 509 C.C.P. were met.
firac.facts: Two Jewish Concordia students, the Jewish club Hillel Concordia and the group SUN sought a ten-day provisional injunction against pro-Palestinian student/activist entities and individuals (SPHR Concordia, Independent Jewish Voices Canada, Khalil, Montréal4Palestine, Alliance4Palestine.QC, Direct Action Concordia, Aboudraz) following campus class blockades (the five largest classes), a September occupation, and a planned “Week of Rage Oct 7-11” / “October 7th Celebration,” together with threatening and antisemitic social-media posts (including a slur- and threat-laden post by Khalil and dehumanizing “zionist supremacist state” content by Alliance4Palestine.QC). The defendants were notified (by bailiff, social media and public notice) but did not appear; most of the evidence came from the defendants’ own social media.
firac.rule: A provisional injunction under art. 509 C.C.P. (maximum ten days, art. 510) requires four interrelated criteria, assessed globally — urgency, appearance of right, irreparable prejudice, and balance of convenience (FLS Transportation Services v. Fuze Logistics; Tremblay v. Cast Steel Products); the clearer the right, the less weight is given to inconvenience; caution applies at this early stage on the plaintiffs’ evidence alone, and relief may be granted quia timet. The appearance of right may rest on the Québec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, art. 1457 and arts. 6–7 C.C.Q., and an institution’s code of conduct.
firac.application: Urgency was met on a quia timet basis: the defendants’ own social-media evidence showed past disruptions and planned escalation the following week. The plaintiffs had a clear appearance of right to pursue their education free of violence, harassment, obstruction and intimidation under the Québec Charter (security, freedom from discrimination and harassment), arts. 6–7 and 1457 C.C.Q., and Concordia’s Code of Rights and Responsibilities. The prejudice — fear for personal safety and disruption of time-sensitive studies — was irreparable and not compensable in money. The balance of convenience favoured the plaintiffs, since the defendants suffered no inconvenience from abiding by basic rules of civility and good faith, the order being content-neutral and directed only at intimidation, threats, harassment and obstruction.
firac.conclusion: All four criteria were met; a ten-day provisional injunction issued barring the defendants from blocking access to Concordia’s pavilions, facilities and buildings, from intimidating/threatening/harassing people there, and from obstructing or disturbing the delivery of courses.

firac.issue: Whether a protection order should issue against Khalil and Aboudraz.
firac.facts: The safety of Zorchinsky and Eshayek was threatened, including by a post in which Khalil expressed a desire to punch Eshayek and by conduct in the record that would cause any reasonable person immediate, imminent fear for physical security.
firac.rule: Article 509 C.C.P. permits a protection order to protect a natural person whose life, health or safety is threatened (including violence based on a concept of honour), for a period not exceeding three years and on the conditions the court determines.
firac.application: The threats to Zorchinsky and Eshayek justified a protection order; the court, cautious not to unduly restrict the defendants’ movement, imposed a five-metre distance within or at Concordia’s buildings and within a 300-metre radius, together with a no-contact term.
firac.conclusion: A ten-day protection order issued prohibiting Khalil and Aboudraz from coming within five metres of the two students (within 300 metres of campus) and from contacting them, with police enforcement authorized and execution notwithstanding appeal.

name_verification.name_in_document: Zuckerman c. MGM Resorts International (Evan Zuckerman c. MGM Resorts International, No. 500-06-001078-209; consolidated with Marc Dahan c. MGM Resorts International, No. 500-06-001280-235)

defining_issues: Whether the proposed class-action settlement (the “Transaction”) resolving the MGM data-breach class actions is fair, equitable and in the fundamental interest of the class members, such that it should be approved under art. 590 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

firac.issue: Whether the proposed class-action settlement should be approved as fair, equitable and in the fundamental interest of the class members.
firac.facts: Two class actions against MGM Resorts International arose from data breaches in July 2019 (Zuckerman) and September 2023 (Dahan), affecting millions of members Canada-wide (with parallel BC/Ontario proceedings). The proposed $4-million settlement provided undocumented claims capped at $150 (one incident) / $300 (both), documented claims up to $20,000 (paid first), and one year of credit-monitoring reimbursement, against class-counsel fees of $1.2 million (plus tax), administrator fees over $134,000, $15,000 representative payments, a broad release, a cy-près/residual to organizations including Chai Lifeline Canada, and a written claims process with a 90-day deadline.
firac.rule: Under art. 590 C.p.c. a class-action settlement is subject to court approval after notice to members; the court must be satisfied it is fair, equitable and in the members’ fundamental interest (Option Consommateurs c. Banque Amex; Sable Offshore Energy c. Ameron) and cannot rewrite it. The factors (A.B. c. Clercs de Saint-Viateur) are the benefits to members (the most important), the claims process and administration costs, the litigation risks, the scope of the release (which must correlate to the compensation), the members’ opinion, and the integrity of the process / absence of collusion (disproportionate fees being a red flag). Representative payments are not legitimate in Québec (art. 593 C.p.c.); cy-près payments should relate to the nature of the action; and, absent proven injury, a mere risk of future harm is not compensable (art. 1611 C.C.Q.; Sofio c. OCRCVM — data theft alone is not a compensable injury).
firac.application: The benefits to the millions of members were feeble relative to the fees and administration costs: at most about $2.4 million of the $4-million fund would reach members, so only a tiny fraction could realistically be compensated (illustratively ~15,635 members at $150, or 500,000 at roughly $0.85 each) — far below comparable settlements (Desjardins: over $200 million plus free five-year monitoring; Condon c. Canada: $17.5 million with an uncapped real-loss fund). The release was disproportionately broad (unknown and future claims, regulatory complaints) for minimal compensation, dangerous given that data-breach harm may surface only years later. The Chai Lifeline cy-près had no connection to the action (counsel’s personal preference); the $15,000 representative payments were illegitimate under art. 593; the claims process was onerous (a written claim even for undocumented claims, a 90-day deadline, and no direct communication to the ~1.5 million members without an email address); and the $1.2-million fee was grossly disproportionate to the members’ benefit (Walid c. Royal Air Maroc). The litigation risks (proving compromise and causation of privacy injury) did not justify so poor a settlement.
firac.conclusion: The Transaction is not in the members’ fundamental interest and risks bringing the administration of justice into disrepute; approval — and the fees and notice — is refused, and the parties are ordered to propose, within 30 days, a notice to members of the refusal, a dissemination program and a case protocol; without costs.

case_name: Zundel v. Liberal Party of Canada

name_verification.name_in_document: Zundel v. Liberal Party of Canada (and the Reform Party of Canada, the New Democratic Party, the Progressive Conservative Party, the Bloc Québécois, the Canadian Jewish Congress, Ronen, and various Members of Parliament)

defining_issues: Whether the defendant federal political parties have the legal capacity to be sued.

Whether the claim against the defendant Members of Parliament should be struck as barred by parliamentary privilege — including whether the House of Commons’ resolution banning Zundel from its precincts met the constitutional test of necessity, and whether the conspiracy claim arising from statements made in the House is barred.

firac.issue: Whether the defendant federal political parties have the legal capacity to be sued.
firac.facts: Zundel sued the five federal political parties (among many defendants); the parties moved under rule 21.01(3)(b) to dismiss for want of capacity, being unincorporated with no assets, real estate or employees. The plaintiff argued that the Canada Elections Act’s registration and chief-agent scheme conferred capacity on the parties.
firac.rule: An unincorporated association lacks the capacity to sue or be sued unless conferred by statute, expressly or by necessary implication (Taff Vale Railway Co. v. Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants; McKinney v. Liberal Party of Canada; Monroe v. Canada); registration under a regulatory statute does not, without more, confer such capacity.
firac.application: The Canada Elections Act’s registration and chief-agent provisions are essentially regulatory and do not confer the capacity to sue or be sued; the parties have no assets, property or employees and are not legal entities. Warkentin (athletic associations named as parties in their own name) was distinguishable because Zundel was not a member of any of the parties.
firac.conclusion: The federal political parties lack the capacity to be sued; the claim against them is dismissed.

firac.issue: Whether the claim against the Members of Parliament is barred by parliamentary privilege.
firac.facts: The House of Commons unanimously resolved to deny Zundel — a “stranger” to the House — admittance to its precincts for the remainder of the session; Zundel sued the MPs for violating his Charter s. 2(b) rights, conspiracy to injure and misfeasance of public office.
firac.rule: Parliamentary privilege has constitutional status and is not subject to the Charter; a court may inquire whether a claimed privilege exists and, for privileges asserted by resolution, whether the action is necessary to the proper functioning of the House (a jurisdictional test of necessity — preserving the dignity, integrity and efficiency of the House), examining more closely privileges affecting persons outside the Assembly (Harvey v. New Brunswick; New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia). No civil judgment can arise from statements made in the House, and the court cannot inquire into what was said or the members’ motives (Roman Corp. v. Hudson’s Bay). A pleading is struck only where it is plain and obvious there is no cause of action (Hunt v. Carey).
firac.application: The House was exercising parliamentary privilege in restricting the use of its precincts by Zundel, and that exercise met the test of necessity — preserving the dignity and integrity of Parliament — so the court would not interfere, especially as the ban restricted only the use of the precincts, not Zundel’s ability to speak elsewhere. The conspiracy claim against the MPs, arising from their statements and the motion in the House, was equally barred by privilege.
firac.conclusion: The statement of claim against the named Members of Parliament is struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action.

keywords_rationale: This decision disposes of two motions in an action by Holocaust denier Ernst Zundel after the House of Commons banned him from its precincts: the political parties’ motion to dismiss (no capacity to be sued) and the MPs’ motion to strike (parliamentary privilege). defining_issues: Is the arbitrator's second award vitiated because it rests on the premise that the 6 January 1993 transaction was subcontracting rather than a sale?
Do the individual agreements (options A/B, resignations and releases) relate to 'conditions de travail' within art. 2.02 of the collective agreement?
Did the arbitrator exceed his jurisdiction by ruling on the civil-law validity of the employees' consent (contract of adhesion, art. 1437 C.c.Q., vitiated consent)?
What standard of review governs the award?

firac.issue: Is the award vitiated by resting on the premise that the transaction was subcontracting rather than a sale?
firac.facts: EUMR sold the goodwill and equipment of its transport sector to Transport Guilbault, Transport Papineau and Transport L.F.L. for a total of $2,191,303, effective 4 February 1993, and notified the union on 5 January 1993 under the collective agreement's letter of understanding on sale. The arbitrator's first award had characterized the operation as a contract for services and subcontracting; in the second award he stated the grievance 'doit donc s'analyser en fonction d'une sous-traitance'.
firac.rule: The characterization of the underlying juridical operation governs; an award expressly founded on a premise the reviewing court has annulled cannot stand.
firac.application: By judgment of the same date in file 500-05-009797-943 the Court annulled the first award, holding the operation was a sale and not subcontracting, for error of law in interpreting the contracts and patently unreasonable error in the exercise of the arbitrator's specialized jurisdiction. The arbitrator himself acknowledged his second decision rested on that premise. Moreover, if it had been subcontracting there would have been no closure of the sector, no layoff and no grievance at all — an internal contradiction.
firac.conclusion: The second award rests on a false premise and is internally contradictory; this alone would justify quashing it.

firac.issue: Do the individual agreements relate to 'conditions de travail' under art. 2.02?
firac.facts: Art. 2.02 invalidates any individual agreement on working conditions differing from, or not provided in, the collective agreement absent the union's written approval. Options A and B offered statutory notice, accrued vacation and unused sick days (already conferred by cl. 14.10 and 21.02(d)) plus two extras: a four-week lump sum and $1,000 (option A) or $500 (option B) per year of service, in exchange for a resignation and release. As of 4 February 1993 the drivers were dismissed and the employment contract was ruptured.
firac.rule: Four cumulative conditions must be met for art. 2.02 to ground jurisdiction: an individual agreement, relating to working conditions, not provided in the agreement, and not approved by the union. A 'condition de travail' is the employer's counter-prestation to the employee's work and is inseparable from a subsisting contract of employment (Syndicat catholique des employés de magasins de Québec c. Cie Paquet Ltée; Building Service Employees' International Union v. Hôpital St-Luc et Jewish General Hospital, [1960] B.R. 875).
firac.application: Benefits already conferred by law or the collective agreement fall outside art. 2.02, so only the two extras could ground a grievance. Those were offered after the employment contract had been ruptured by a collective dismissal for economic reasons, which the arbitrator himself characterized as a 'licenciement collectif pour cause économique'. Converting the dismissal into a resignation and waiving the hiring priority in exchange for enhanced benefits creates a new obligation substituted for the old — a novation under arts. 1660 and 1661 C.c.Q. With no subsisting contract of employment, what a former employee agrees with the former employer cannot be a working condition.
firac.conclusion: The individual agreements do not relate to working conditions; art. 2.02 is inapplicable and the arbitrator had no jurisdiction over the grievance.

firac.issue: Did the arbitrator exceed his jurisdiction by adjudicating the civil-law validity of the employees' consent?
firac.facts: The arbitrator found the resignations and releases were imposed, characterized them as contracts of adhesion, invoked art. 1437 C.c.Q. on abusive clauses, and concluded the employees 'n'ont pas voulu démissionner' — without summoning or hearing the employees concerned. The grievance of 13 January 1993 pleaded only a breach of art. 2.02.
firac.rule: An arbitrator has exclusive jurisdiction over the interpretation and application of the collective agreement, reviewable only for patently unreasonable error; but when exercising general jurisdiction over laws of general application (Charters, Civil Code, Criminal Code) he is reviewable for simple error of law, and he cannot by an error of law confer on himself a jurisdiction he would not otherwise have (U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault).
firac.application: A contract of adhesion carries no presumption of abuse, fraud or bad faith; annulment requires demonstrating an abusive clause, and here the employer offered conditions superior to those in the collective agreement. The grievance did not ask the arbitrator to rule on vitiated consent, and he decided that question without the principal interested parties assigned before him.
firac.conclusion: The arbitrator committed simple errors of law and exceeded his jurisdiction.

firac.issue: What standard of review governs the award?
firac.facts: The award turned on whether the individual agreements engaged art. 2.02, which determined whether the arbitrator had jurisdiction at all.
firac.rule: Where an arbitrator's error has the consequence of conferring a jurisdiction he would not otherwise have, his decision is reviewable without the court assessing whether the error is patently unreasonable; the supervisory role of the superior courts enjoys constitutional protection (Bibeault; Crevier v. A.G. Quebec).
firac.application: The determination that the agreements concerned working conditions was the gateway to jurisdiction, so the error was jurisdictional rather than an error within jurisdiction.
firac.conclusion: The award is reviewable on that jurisdictional footing and must be quashed.
